Report_1_Narrative: Began initial descent into ZZZZ. The controller called to change the STAR. I had to ask 3 times to repeat the prescribed STAR to be flown. His English was very broken. Traffic on the frequency was light. We determined a change of STARs. I input into the FMS and confirmed and executed with the Captain. By this time we were either over [the IAF] to or just past the point. The aircraft overflew [the fix]. The Captain went into heading select and turned to course. Two to three miles past [the fix]; the aircraft was back on an intercept outbound [from the fix]. Then the controller said turn to a heading to intercept inbound course; which we had already initiated. Continuing descent the controller instructed us to fly the circuit which was part of the STAR and we did as planned. During the descent the controller gave us 5 altitude step downs to comply with; 4 of the 5 were then subsequently modified back to a higher altitude. After the compliance with circuit instructions; controller changed the runway. I then reprogrammed the FMS; and confirmed execute with the Captain. After so many changes by the controller and workload was lowered in the cockpit; I queried the controller one final time to ensure we were all on same page. I stated to controller confirm ILS XXR; controller said negative ILS XXL; are you ready to commence approach. I quickly for 3rd time reprogrammed the FMS for ILS XXL confirmed with the Captain and executed. I then told controller ready to commence; and then briefed the Captain on differences of approaches; and new Baro; and landing distances. We landed uneventfully.Poor English by controller almost inaudible. Very late approach instructions modifications. Could be solved if controller gave us changes to STAR and approach a few minutes prior to descent instead of at last moment; and past Anchor points on STAR.
Report_2_Narrative: We were filed to [the IAF] and we set up for the ILS Approach. As we approached [the fix] the controller issued a new arrival but we had difficulty understanding the new clearance [due to] language problems. Finally it was determined after 3 difficult queries what we were to fly. After installing the new clearance into the FMS the Aircraft did not make the turn towards [the] next point. As pilot flying I recognized the overshoot and made a correction back to course just prior to ATC issuing vectors. During the arrival numerous runway changes were issued and at least 5 or more altitude instructions given. Just prior to base turn the First Officer queried the controller one final time to confirm ILS XXR. The controller said negative ILS XXL. We quickly for 3rd time reprogrammed the FMS for the ILS XXL; briefed and executed an uneventful landing on XXL.Language problems which caused confusion and delayed FMS programming on our part. Late arrival insertion caused overshoot. Overshoot caused workload to increase. Do a better job anticipating what other options may be available to your crew and get an early confirmation on what arrival to expect. Better to reprogram the FMS after sequencing to the next point then forcing a FMS change close to a turn point.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight crew reported numerous late clearances due to language barrier from a foreign controller.

Report_1_Narrative: In VMC conditions; we were cleared by Center for the RNAV Approach. Reaching [the IAF] I noticed that the FMS was programmed to make a turn outbound. We had briefed a Visual Approach backed up by the RNAV Approach and had the runway in sight. I thought that there was an error in the programming of the FMS. Most RNAV approaches with a 90 degree T-shaped base to final turn do not include a procedure turn. This approach is an exception. I overlooked that detail. I disconnected the autopilot and turned inbound to the runway. I called for the flight director to be cleared and hand flew the rest of the approach visually with no flight director. The First Officer sequenced the FMS so I had lateral and vertical guidance in addition to the PAPI and runway; which I could see visually. The approach; landing; and taxi in was uneventful. The cause of the event was the expectation of doing a Visual Approach and not noticing that No PT was not depicted. With clear weather and the runway in sight; I was in the mindset of doing a visual approach even though we were cleared for the RNAV. Additionally; there were 2 other aircraft in the pattern. A light single engine aircraft and a military C-130. After crossing a fix I was thinking about the spacing between us and the other aircraft in the pattern based on making a turn inbound. We were warned that this airport was an unstable high energy approach airport; so I was focused on slowing and configuring for landing early. We are also experiencing light to moderate turbulence; so more attention than normal was required to maintain the desired airspeed. I selected continuous ignition during the approach due to moderate turbulence.We should have noticed that this approach was unusual in that it did not have No PT. We could have requested the visual approach from center; so we would not be required to fly the 7NM holding pattern in lieu of a procedure turn.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier pilot reported flying a Visual Approach instead of the RNAV they were cleared for at a non-towered airport.

Report_1_Narrative: We were cleared for takeoff on Runway XR in ZZZ.  Both myself and the other pilot heard the phrase from the Controller 'Runway XR cleared for takeoff.'  We did not hear any other instructions.  We were on the ZZZZZ 2 departure.  It states to fly heading 011 until reaching 820 feet then heading 340 or assigned by ATC.  We started our turn at 820 feet and a few seconds later the Controller told us to immediately turn and fly runway heading.  No other problems came about from this situation.  It seems like there was some miscommunication between the pilots and ATC.  We were flying the appropriate procedures and did not hear ATC tell us to fly runway heading you're cleared for takeoff Runway XR.  Both pilots only heard 'Runway XR cleared for takeoff.'
Report_2_Narrative: Departing Runway XR we were cleared for takeoff. We followed the SID heading of 340 when ATC told us runway heading. After correcting to runway heading we discussed the departure and both of us were sure that we were just cleared for takeoff with no other instructions. We were both mistaken - he did issue runway heading on the takeoff clearance. Having been unfamiliar with this airports procedures I may have had some expectation bias towards just flying the SID and clearly missed the runway clearance; not to mention having not flown since April [and] a bit of tunnel vision during the before takeoff.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported a track heading deviation.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Confusion; Communication Breakdown; Distraction; Situational Awareness; Time Pressure; Workload
Report_1_Narrative: I am not in this department but I would like to know what is a 'Typical' time frame to clean an aircraft with one person doing the job. We came in from ZZZ1 with XX people and 1 jump seat. The personnel came on after everyone except the X throughs. I was busy helping a customer and about 5 minutes later the 'Cleaner' came off. I told ops which in turned called for a Supervisor. The Supervisor came and I asked how long does it take to clean seats and trays. He said there is no time frame. I told him this employee wasn't on the plane 5 minutes. He asked if I wanted another cleaning crew to come. I said no; I just want to know he did ALL trays. I have through customers on board and they watch us. I was just making sure we are KEEPING OUR PROMISE to the customers. I thought they are supposed to do ALL tables? The cleaners don't know where people sat.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Attendant reported concerns with cleaners sanitizing the aircraft too quickly.

Report_1_Narrative: Passenger X was sitting in XXC.  His relative; Passenger Y; was sitting across the aisle at XXD.  They decided to upgrade themselves to better seats.  We told them that they were welcomed to upgrade; but they would have to pay the extra fee.  After much ado; they decided to move further back in the cabin.  Then Passenger X decides that he doesn't need to wear his mask.  We asked countless times for him to wear his mask.  Many announcements were made.  Every time; after we walked away; he took his mask off.  Once I awakened him; asking him to put his mask back on.  He said that he was eating.  I said; 'Sir; you were sleeping.'  He was putting all other passengers on board at risk.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Attendant reported a passenger did not comply with face mask policy during flight.

Report_1_Narrative: Flight ABCD from ZZZZ to ZZZ I was the position C. After we landed in ZZZ; and taxiing of the aircraft was complete Flight Attendant A announced to the flight attendants to prepare the cabins for departure. I went to my forward service door and pulled the girt bar from the bracket and inserted back into the mount where it was disarmed then put the red flag back up. I turned around to cross check with FA A who I saw bend down to disarm the door. I then started talking to a first class passenger seated in X5. I heard FA A call the aft cabin via inter phone to verify their doors were disarmed. Then we waited till the agent came to knock on the forward entry door. I saw FA A give the thumbs up after the agent knocked and the agent starting opening the door. All of a sudden FA A said; 'stop' and I saw the slide peeping from the compartment after she moved to the side. FA A notified the flight deck of the situation and they called for a mechanic. Two mechanics came quickly and moved the slide out of the housing. We then began to deplane from the front entry door. Managers X and Y came to talk to me and FA A on the aircraft after all the passengers deplaned and was told by her to fill out a report as a partial inadvertent slide deployment.
Report_2_Narrative: It was a routine flight; upon arrival at gate in ZZZ I did a P.A. for Flight Attendants to verify and disarm. I bent down to disarm the 1L door left side girt bar bracket and I was thinking what I had to do next: (turn on lights for passengers; all-call the back). For some reason I stood up to turn on the lights. That's not like me; I always focus and follow through on my doors when arming and disarming. The C [FA] had just beat me to the lights; then I did all-call to the back; then C mentions passengers are actually sitting down after health PA to stay seated; because they never listen and crowd the aisle. Then there were 2 knocks on the door from the agent; I gave them thumbs up and looked down and saw the girt bar attached; at same time the agent was gently cracking the door I said stop; the door had opened maybe 1 foot? and the agent and I were face to face; I said stop. The slide partially fell out of housing intact. The mechanics were called; they came fast; they held the bottom portion of the intact slide and they opened the door; and we started deplaning. When I got home my heart was pounding and body shaking from lack of sleep; low blood sugar; and wearing mask. Was a bad combination.Suggestions:*SLEEP- Circadian rhythm. Lack of sleep 4 nights in a row; early morning sign-ins. *FOOD- PLEASE on flights where you can't bring your food into other countries; or you can't bring your own food from the USA back into USA customs does not allow it; if it's too early or too late to get any food; places are closed or nothing is open; or lines are too long to make boarding. PLEASE have a little something for us to eat so our blood sugar does not drop so safety related accidents don't happen. *MASK- Sometimes feel headaches; feel suffocation; can't breathe; lack of oxygen.All of the above create fatigue which decreases the body's ability to focus; and decreased attention.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight attendants reported a partial slide deployment while opening the cabin door due to the door inadvertently not being disarmed.

Report_1_Narrative: Guest was noted with a short face shield only during the compliance walk prior to departure. Apologized to guest. Inquired due to policy change if she had a face mask as a shield alone was no longer sufficient. She said she did and was able to don it.Please make everyone happier by catching this prior to boarding. Flight attendants already have tons on [their] plate.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Attendant reported that a passenger was wearing only a face shield and was asked to wear a face mask to be in compliance.

Report_1_Narrative: Aircraft Fleet X task cards for the X; XX and XY day checks have a non-existent AMM (Aircraft Maintenance Manual) reference listed for servicing the APU while the aircraft is in storage (49-XX-XX-XXX-XXXA) for the APS XXXX is incorrect. The correct AMM is 49-XX-XX-XXX-YXXA. We have brought this issue up several time here locally and sent several feedback requests in hopes of getting them corrected; with no joy. Please find someone to fix the paperwork.
Report_1_Synopsis: Technician reported that task cards for servicing the APU of aircraft in storage do not have the correct reference number.

Report_1_Narrative: An aircraft had an air return for the loss of number 1 engine; green; hydraulic pressure; no loss of fluid. The aircraft was moved to the hangar on day shift for repair. We motored the engine and observed the pressure coming from the pump: it increased to 3000 psi then fell off. The aircraft was moved inside and the cowlings were opened up for inspection of the EDP (Engine Driven Pump). There were no external leaks or external damage to the EDP. We continued to inspect the fluid lines from the pump to the pylon disconnect. It was found that the fluid supply line had become disconnected at the pylon connection; it was further noticed that the locking section of the pylon side of the fluid supply line quick disconnect was not locking to the line side. We suspect the line vibrated off; starving the pump and the loss of pressure. The disconnect; pump; and case drain were replaced.
Report_1_Synopsis: Maintenance Technician reported loss of hydraulic pressure due to disconnected fluid supply line.

Report_1_Narrative: I briefed my flight with Garmin Pilot on my iPhone and noted the fire TFR. While enroute I was using my iPad to follow my route. Because the TFR was not yet displayed I thought I was still outside of the Southern boundary. I realized there was an error somewhere. I had recently had issues with Garmin Pilot on my iPad so I had unloaded and reloaded the program to fix the problem. Unfortunately; I had neglected to turn the TFR display back on. When I discovered this I immediately enabled the TFR display and to my dismay realized I was already approximately four miles into the TFR. I immediately turned ninety degrees east to exit the TFR as quickly as possible. Fortunately a recent snowstorm had greatly dampened the fire and there was no air traffic fighting the fire at that time. This was very educational experience for me. I learned I must be more in tune with my navigational equipment at all times. Pilot error!
Report_1_Synopsis: GA pilot reported penetrating a TFR.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Confusion; Distraction; Situational Awareness; Training / Qualification
Report_1_Narrative: I was flying a J3 Cub to ZZZ. I'm a new sport pilot having only gotten my license about two weeks ago. I got caught up with finding the airport; making frequency changes; getting the winds from the automatic weather reporting station; and trying to figure out how I should enter the pattern. I was not scanning outside the aircraft because I was too focused on everything inside the aircraft. I did not see an aircraft; or hear it on CTAF because I was listening to the weather; departing a runway that I was crossing the extended centerline of. I was around 2 miles away. I finally saw the aircraft as it was coming up on my right side. We both turned left and it was fine; but it scared me quite a bit. After that scare; I just turned away from the airport and left while scanning for other aircraft. Things that I think contributed to this near miss are:-I did not plan the cross country because it was short and I figured I could figure it out on the fly by getting frequencies from my sectionals. -I did not make a radio call when I was close to the airport because I had not yet planned out how I would enter the pattern. -I was too focused on planning my pattern entry that I was not aware of my surroundings. -I did not expect traffic at the airport; because I had flown there the day before and had not seen or heard anyone at the airport. Thinking about what I will do differently; I will:1. Plan out every flight I do that is not just around my home airport. Route; frequencies; predicted weather; airport runways; traffic pattern direction; all available for quick reference on a knee board. 2. Make radio calls as soon as I am within 10 miles of an airport; even if I cannot say where I plan to enter the pattern in an initial call. 3. Keep an eye on airports for traffic below me and above me; and watch out for traffic on extended centerline. Next time I am at ZZZ I will try to avoid crossing centerline unless midfield. 4. Keep in mind that airport traffic can vary day to day.
Report_1_Synopsis: J3 Cub pilot reported a near miss approaching the airport.

Report_1_Narrative: [In] my preflight noticed that both engines needed a quart of oil. Filled both back to the proper indication. Closed both engines then continued with my preflight. Found nothing else that needed attention. I took my first load. I noticed a slightly low oil pressure on that flight and called another King Air pilot that trained me to ask about it. As I got out of the plane the owner and I noticed that oil was all over the left wing. Opened it up and I did not properly secure the oil stick/cap. A small amount of oil was still visible on the stick. I called the A and P and we were advised to put oil back in the engine; clean it up out of the bay and try a run up. The start went normally; oil pressure was back. I taxied down to the end of XX did another run up. Everything was in the normal range. Did a normal takeoff left hand pattern while watching the left engine. Proceeded to a normal approach rounded out; pulled power back then heard the gear unsafe warning. A split second later heard tick of a prop hitting the ground. My initial reaction was to push the power forward and take off but reason took over and I pulled power all the way back and bellied the plane in. Then I secured the plane and got out.I did several things wrong that day most importantly I did not follow the checklist and I did not do a GUMPS (Gas; Undercarriage; Mixture; Prop; Switches) check. I also had been driving 4 hours prior to the event. I am devastated. I should have followed the checklist.
Report_1_Synopsis: Pilot reported a gear up landing.

Report_1_Narrative: I was on an IFR Flight Plan from ZZZ to ZZZ1.  I had poor speed control on the approach.  I was legally IFR current; but; as it turned out; I was clearly not proficient.  The COVID-19 prevented me from flying with a (COVID safe) safety pilot and getting recent practice.  I was scheduled for simulator training for the following week.I flew VFR out to ZZZ for two days.  The weather was predicted VMC for the next several days.  The day after we arrived; the wind shifted and blew in severe smoke from forest fires.  We considered staying for a few more days; but there was no available lodging and the smoke was getting worse.  I reviewed an IFR plan to go back to ZZZ1 and when the destination weather improved enough; I filed IFR; got my clearance; and departed.  The departure; on route; and vectors to final were smooth and uneventful. There was an aircraft ahead that was going slower and ATC requested that I slow to 90 knots; which is what I should have already been slowing to.  I agreed and reduced power.  The autopilot was holding the altitude coming up to the IAF and I inadvertently pulled off too much power.  I was coming up on the IAF and descent and I was verifying that everything (else) was ready to go; when I noticed that the speed was rapidly reducing.  The autopilot (AP) was trimming nose up to maintain altitude.  I hit control wheel steering; nosed down; and added power.  I had to do a lot of trimming to get the nose back down and I over shot the altitude and rapidly picked up speed.  I got the nose back up; on altitude; and thought that the AP would acquire the glide slope.  Nope; in the excitement; I missed arming the approach and flew right through it.  Now I dove for the GS and picked up more speed again.  Now I'm on the GS and check to see if the AP would acquire it and no it started another excursion and so I shut it off and hand flew the rest of the way.  It was stabilized at this point; so I continued the approach and landed.Mistake 1.  I should have already been planning and reducing speed approaching IAF.Mistake 2.  I should have paid more attention to my speed reduction technique.Mistake 3.  I should have requested ATC to bring me around again to have time to set up properly.Mistake 4.  I should have done what I normally do and that is to turn off the AP and hand fly anytime things get weird.My takeaway is that my IFR currency should be done more often; even if it is done in a simulator.
Report_1_Synopsis: Pilot reported conducting an unstable instrument approach and cited lack of proficiency due to difficulty finding a safety pilot for practice during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Report_1_Narrative: Required maintenance/inspection interval was inadvertently overflown. Upon investigation of the cause of the overflight the following root causes were identified. Bell 505 maintenance was developed in accordance with the MSG-3 methodology (Maintenance Steering Group-3). Different than other helicopters/airplanes that we have operated this method does not permit any tolerance for hourly inspection intervals and requires calendar based maintenance actions be conducted to the day rather than the calendar month. For example; a 1 year inspection conducted on May 3; 2019 is required on May 3; 2020 - not May 30 like many other aircraft. A review of the Bell 505 Maintenance Manual found that this information is present in the manual but is in the definitions section not in Chapter 5 where other manufacturer's include the data. The previous operator of the aircraft was not properly utilizing the block provided on each page of the aircraft log to record next maintenance due date and time information. This block is used on other aircraft to convey this information to the flight crew. It is unknown why flight crews and maintenance personnel did not utilize this block in the same manner that is done for the other helicopters. Maintenance planned to operate the aircraft up to 110 hours flight time since the last 100 hour inspection (10% overage as is allowed for other helicopters) or through 7/31/2020 (12 calendar months since last 1 year inspection) whichever came first. [Before the end of July] we made aware by the Bell Tech representative of the date and hour tolerances (none) for the 505 and operations were stopped until maintenance was completed.
Report_1_Synopsis: During an aircraft records check by Quality Assurance Inspectors; it was found that an aircraft maintained under MSG-3 methodology was instead maintained under MSG-2; causing overflights of many required checks.

Report_1_Narrative: I was working two sectors during smoke and haze conditions requiring all aircraft to pick up IFR flight plans. A large TFR for firefighting was on the east side of my airspace and encroached on the finals for HWD and OAK departures which normally depart on 170 heading across the OAK [Runway] 30 final and towards SFO final which then have to be vectored back across the [Runway] 30 final to the northeast and across the HWD final and then the OAK [Runway] 28 final. Because of the TFR and traffic complexity; I issued a right turn of 040 and maintain 4000 ft. to HWD to issue to Aircraft Y. Per the NorCal TRACON and HWD LOA; released aircraft are to be airborne within 2 minutes. Aircraft X was approximately 11 miles from HWD and cleared for the ILS 30 approach to OAK when I released Aircraft Y. Aircraft Y took 3 mins and 7 seconds to tag up on radar; well outside the LOA requirements. I observed Aircraft Y going upwind and not turning which prompted me to call HWD Tower to confirm the heading to 040 which they affirmed. Aircraft Y was first observed in a turn at 1200 ft. and 1.5 miles upwind. This is well beyond expected pilot performance. Our Quality Control Department is stating that even if Aircraft Y had turned; it would not have been separated because divergence is not permitted with this aircraft. I have looked through JO 7110.65 and found nothing that should prevent me from applying the provisions of that paragraph. I contest that I had applicable divergence separation as Aircraft Y was assigned 040 (and not complying) and Aircraft X was assigned the ILS 30 which is a 296 heading.I am requesting the development of new departure headings and procedures to eliminate the congestion under the OAK final and eliminate the current procedures which are unsafe and nearly unusable given the noise abatement restrictions; which are in effect at all times; and wake re-categorization separation. I also propose new training for how management expects us to get HWD departure aircraft safely out of our airspace given such significant constraints. Also; I'm requesting a follow up to occur with the pilot since he failed to comply with his ATC assigned heading in a timely matter as this was clearly a pilot deviation. Furthermore; had HWD Tower complied with our LOA; I do not believe a conflict would have even been triggered through automation.
Report_1_Synopsis: TRACON Controller reported an aircraft departed after the release time and became a conflict with an arrival aircraft into another airport.

Report_1_Narrative: We were given a taxi clearance of Runway 20C via T5 S7; cross 31/13.  While entering 31/13; the FO called out Stop Stop Stop!  We used maximum braking and came to an abrupt stop narrowly avoiding a single engine small aircraft taxiing at high speed from right to left.  Ground apologized saying they weren't talking to the small aircraft.  Flight then progressed without incident to destination.
Report_2_Narrative: We were given a taxi clearance to Runway 20C via T5; S7 cross 13/31. While attempting to cross 13/31; I looked to my right and saw a single engine small aircraft taxiing down Runway 13/31 with a converging path to our aircraft. I called out; 'Stop; Stop; Stop!!' to the Captain; who then brought our aircraft to an abrupt stop in order to avoid collision with the small aircraft. The small aircraft continued to taxi in front of us; right to left without slowing. We stayed put until Ground then again gave us clearance to cross 13/31 S5; T7 to 20C. Ground also apologized to us and said they were not talking to the small aircraft.There was an obvious miscommunication between the small aircraft and Ground; as Ground said; they were not talking to the small aircraft; and the small aircraft stated they had clearance to turn left onto Runway 13/31.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported a ground conflict with a small aircraft during taxiout at BNA airport.  Reportedly; ATC was not communicating with the small aircraft.

Report_1_Narrative: Good rest; day VFR with clear skies throughout the flight. This was the second leg of the day; the first leg being a ferry flight. Uneventful flight. On arrival to the airport we both noticed and mentioned it to each other that ATC left us up a little high. Passing through 15;000 ft. or so and very close to what we thought was the airport. I mentioned 'rather than getting a lot of vectors let's just cancel and make a 360 to the left and go to ZZZZZ; which is the IAF on the RNAV GPS RWY XX); which we did. In no rush; I extended the outbound leg of the 360 turn. Coming out of the turn a little disoriented I asked; 'can you extend the centerline of the runway.' The SIC (Second In Command) which has little time in the plane and not very experienced with the FMS was having trouble putting in the centerline. I asked for a centerline from the RUNWAY; the SIC drew the path from ZZZZZ1; a fix on the approach. The approach is a 45 degree angle from the runway; so when he put the extended line it was from ZZZZZ1 not the runway. I asked again 'I don't think that's right; it doesn't line up.' It was still showing the 45-degree angle to the runway. I again queried him and said; 'What is the runway heading? Make the centerline off that; not any of the fixes.' By then; at around 1000 ft. AGL; we both saw RWY XX painted on the runway in front of us and thought; no worries; I see the numbers.On the landing roll out the chart did not pop up. I asked 'why are we not on the chart? The 350 shows the plane on all the charts'.Reaching the end of the runway the passenger came up and said 'guys; you are at the wrong field; ZZZ is 8 miles south of here; this is ZZZ1' He is a pilot also and was very sympathetic and said 'this happens so often; the operations people don't come out anymore.'I apologized and started planning the trip to ZZZ. I called dispatch and advised them of what happened and what we needed. We taxied back to the approach end of RWY XX and found a place to park and called the FODM (Flight Operations Duty Manager) while the SIC was getting the clearance from ATC. I was told 'he's not answering his phone'. I asked them to 'please find him; I need to talk to him'. A minute or so later [he] answered. I explained what happened. He was very calming and eager to work with me. We talked about the weather; the runway length and width; parachute activity in the area; VFR daytime only airport; he even gave me the frequencies to both airports. Our phones started to beep; at that time [he] said; 'I think they are trying to shut you down; I'll take care of it'. I mentioned that we both had plenty of duty time and felt fine to do the 8-mile flight. It is hard to recall every word but he mentioned something to the effect; 'ok; it looks good; let me check on something; I'll call you back'.After waiting a few minutes and thinking that we had covered everything we needed to for the flight; I decided to depart.The flight to ZZZ was uneventful. The passenger had no problem with the event and being a pilot himself in that area; he kept telling me 'don't worry it really does happen here a lot; ZZZ3 had a RWY XX also. They finally had to change the numbers to XY even though its heading is [different]'. We helped them load their car and they drove off.   Things we should/could have done...-Stayed with ATC and gotten better vectors to the airport.-Made sure the centerline was indeed off the runway NOT the FAF.
Report_1_Synopsis: CL-350 flight crew reported landing at the wrong airport.

Report_1_Narrative: Afternoon launch - sort late 90 minutes.  My freight recovery specialist; informed me Aircraft X blocked even though the ramp notified the crew to wait for new DG (dangerous goods) paperwork.  ACARS was sent to the crew to hold; new DG paperwork on the way.  I asked the Captain to call me on the phone to explain that the current DG paper work indicated no DG however; there was IDG (international dangerous goods) onboard and new paperwork is required.  We both agreed a block turn back was the best way to handle this situation.  Aircraft returned to the blocks for correction of DG paperwork; new release was sent and weight and balance (per Captain's request). Ramp agent made a mistake most likely due to high workload/task saturation and work distractions/interruptions.  The sort was over 2 hours late and the load teams were overwhelmed.  I had at least 4 adhocs with double legs (out and back) and some with 3 legs. This flight was on hold during most of the sort along with other flights; then decisions were made to reroute the adhocs and add legs.  There was a lot of confusion and decisions were being made last minute. We are in unprecedented times.  Everyone is doing their best.  Some of us are better equipped to handle the constant changes and challenges.  Errors will be made; I am glad we were able to correct it and move on.
Report_1_Synopsis: Airline Dispatcher reported a ground gate return request of flight to correct Hazmat documents.

Report_1_Narrative: On takeoff from PDX; in IMC conditions from takeoff up to about 15;000 ft. MSL. Everything seemed normal until 400 ft. AGL. The captain called 'verify NAV' and I did and then I noticed the EICAS displayed in cyan advisory messages 'Autoland 1 not available' and a second message which I believe was 'RNP (Required Navigation Performance) 0.1 not available.' I am certain about the first message but not about the second. I also noticed that the yellow square with 'RA' was displayed on the PFD in the bottom right corner. This seemed indicative of a radio altimeter malfunction or miscompare. The EICAS messages extinguished quickly and immediately we received an aural warning 'too low; terrain' GPWS message. I did not see a message on the PFD and there was no guidance provided; only the aural warning. I believe the aural warning was only announced once and then went away.This Aural warning is usually only for being low to terrain and not in a correct Landing configuration. We were taking off in takeoff configuration. The gear was up right after takeoff and the flaps were set to 2 for takeoff and had not been retracted since we had not achieved acceleration height. So the aural warning did not make any sense.We both quickly began scanning the instruments and found that the aircraft was already pitched to take off pitch of around 18 degrees nose up. Wings were mostly level. The aircraft was on the flight director. The altitude and vertical speed indicated a climb. Both PFDS displayed the same information. The backup instrument panel displayed the same. The MFD was on terrain display on the map page and showed black terrain in the immediate area and distant green terrain around the aircraft. And thrust was in the TOGA (Takeoff Go Around) position.So everything cross referenced to show a normal; terrain free; take off and climb. Also; we were already in full take off climb thrust; pitch; and configuration. So we continued flight.We got to acceleration height and retracted flaps and continued the remainder of the flight without issue. The issue did not repeat itself again.Another thought is that the IMC conditions were caused by smoke from wild fires. Perhaps the smoke particulates caused a radio altimeter malfunction and the RA briefly read the altitude as too low for only a split second.We were already in GPWS response pitch and configuration. So there was not much else to do. Especially when all indications seemed normal for climb out and the GPWS message was brief and seemed associated with RA malfunction. The only possible extra effort that could be made would be thrust to MAX but that didn't seem necessary in this case as the aural warning had already stopped.
Report_2_Narrative: The flight departed PDX into immediate IMC because of fog and smoke in the area. Everything was functioning normal and it was standard takeoff and climb. At about 500-600 ft. MSL the FO's (First Officer) PFD indicated an issue with the radar altimeter: amber rectangle with RA. Two EICAS messages appeared. One of them was AUTOLAND 1 NOT AVAIL and I think the second message was something with the RNP (Required Navigation Performance). At which point the EGPWS warning 'TOO LOW; TERRAIN' was heard once. I immediately verified again that the aircraft is pitching up; climbing at takeoff power; on speed; and following the RNAV departure; according to standard profile. Terrain map did not indicate any colors but green and black on the MFD. After a few seconds all messages extinguished and the flight proceeded without any other malfunctions or anomalies.Upon discussing the event with my FO later in cruise; we both thought that it was a radar altimeter anomaly and that the aircraft was at all times operated following normal operating procedures and never outside the normal flight profile/envelope. We also discussed the possibility of an oversized vehicle on the I-205 bridge as that would have been about the point in the air this event occurred.Please monitor if this was a onetime occurrence or there is a trend.
Report_1_Synopsis: EMB175 flight crew reported GPWS message during climbout.

Report_1_Narrative: During an ILS approach to Runway XXR; the PF failed to slow early enough on final approach. PF configured later than desired considering the situation (fast due to earlier ATC request) resulting in the aircraft becoming high on glide path while slowing to configure for landing. PF needed to use a sink rate higher than desired to return to glide slope. We met the published parameters at all of our approach gates; but the first portion of the approach was unstable. We landed safely on XXR and proceeded routinely to the gate.The main lesson learned was to slow earlier on final approach to allow a more stable approach. We accomplished all checklists and procedures and landed safely; but the crew would have been more able to look for potential threats if the PF had flown a more stable approach during the first portion of the approach. PNF was just back from several months off - take away for PNF was to address a rapidly evolving situation sooner and prompt the PF to configure sooner.
Report_2_Narrative: [Narrative contained no additional information.]
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported that the first portion of the approach was unstable due to not slowing early enough on final approach.

Person_2_Human_Factors: Distraction; Workload; Training / Qualification; Human-Machine Interface; Situational Awareness
Report_1_Narrative: While on RNAV RWY 4 approach into UIN; between the initial fix (JISNA) and the FAF (WUSIS); we descended below the minimum altitude prescribed for that segment of the approach; which was 2100 ft. MSL . I did not recognize that we were below until about 1600 ft. MSL and by the time I had corrected our pitch and added power we between 1500 ft. and 1600 ft. MSL. We immediately climbed back up to 2100'; and at about 2 miles prior to the FAF; we re-evaluated our position; flight guidance panel and configuration and felt that we could resume the approach as normal; which was an autopilot coupled LPV approach. Part of the cause of this issue was my set up of the flight guidance panel. We had been descending from about 7000 ft. and navigating direct to the initial fix of JISNA. At some point in the descent; ATC cleared us for the approach and told us to maintain 2700 ft. until JISNA. We were given the frequency change from Center to CTAF at this point as well. At that point; I thought I was in VNAV mode and descending. I hit APPR (Approach); since we were cleared for the approach; and dialed my altitude selector to the bottom of the approach; which was 960 ft. MSL for the minimums. My assumption was that we would then VNAV to 2700 ft. at JISNA; or essentially just VNAV to 2100 ft. by WUSIS; grab the glideslope and continue the descent. I felt I had set it up so that all stepdown altitudes would be met. At that point; I may have become distracted with other radio calls and prepping for landing. During this time; the SIC (Second In Command) was running checklists; trying to reach the FBO  on unicom; and also conferring with ATC to ensure we had a good way to cancel IFR  once we were on the ground. Neither of us were totally focused on the task at hand; which was to monitor the plane as we were beginning this approach. I estimate we were doing about an 800 fpm descent rate. We may have been in VNAV mode; but I was not coupled to the glide path; so we were descending in such a way that would not allow the autopilot to level us off at each fix. 1. PIC/SIC should have been totally focused on the primary task at hand: entering; establishing; and flying the approach as published. This would have caught any errors in my programming of the descent and flight guidance panel before we descended below published altitude. 2. Both pilots should be looking at the flight guidance panel in these critical times to verify proper mode; and calling out altitudes around these fixes. 3. Once the altitude deviation was realized; I should have climbed up; executed a missed approach; and called ATC to vector us back around for the approach. 4. My decision not to go missed was influenced by my desire to keep my passenger's schedule. That is a hazardous attitude that I want others to be aware of and learn from.
Report_2_Narrative: As our passengers were boarding the plane; they decided to change the destination to UIN due to the fact we were unlikely to be able to get into ZZZ due to low ceilings. The altitude deviation occurred on the RNAV (Area Navigation) approach to RW 4 at UIN. We had been cleared for the approach and we were to instructed to maintain 2700 ft. until established on the approach and had been approved to change to advisory frequency. I was the nonflying pilot and was busy verifying everything on the checklist had been completed and communicating with KC center and UNICOM at UIN to make position reports. I also verified with KC center that we would be able to contact them on the ground using that frequency or did we need to cancel our IFR through flight service. This took a little extra time to complete due to my lack of experience with the Proline Fusion avionics so I was not monitoring the PFD as closely as I should have. We were inside JISNA (IAF)and I was trying to determine our position from the airport in order to give an accurate position report when the pilot flying said something to the effect of wait why are we low. He immediately added power selected vertical speed up and set our altitude selector to 2100 ft. I was focused on other tasks in the cockpit so I cannot say with 100% certainty what autopilot modes were selected previously. We were somewhere between 1600 ft. and 1500 ft. MSL when he started the recovery. We reached 2100 ft. two miles prior to the WUSIS (FAF) intercepted the glide path and landed without further issue. During the debrief with my captain after the flight we discussed the need to treat such a critical phase of flight with the utmost respect and after getting established on the approach to keep all attention on the task at hand which is flying/monitoring the approach. We also discussed the need to make a verbal call out of all autopilot/ flight director mode changes to make sure both pilots are on the same page and are totally aware of what the automation is doing if it is engaged.
Report_1_Synopsis: BE-300 flight crew descended below minimum altitude on approach.

Report_1_Narrative: We had just fully configured for landing; crossed the FAF and began our final descent on the RNAV RWY 17R approach into DWH. I was the pilot flying and had a customer pilot in the right seat for a demo flight. Tower called out traffic at our 1 o'clock and 2 miles unknown altitude that was apparently on final then began to turn north 'possibly NORDO'. We called visual and were instructed to continue the approach. Both of us in the cockpit saw Aircraft Y turning what looked to be base to final converging on our path. I broke off the final approach course to the left keeping Aircraft Y in sight and let tower know. Aircraft Y appeared to notice us as it made an abrupt climbing right turn away from us. Once I felt we had enough separation I elected to resume the approach; notified tower; received landing clearance and landed uneventfully. If I had to guess; we came within about 200-300 ft. of Aircraft Y. There is a lot of student traffic and flight schools at DWH. Aircraft Y was most likely a student training flight. Tower was transmitting in the blind to Aircraft Y repeatedly and told them not to circle on final and to look for light gun signals.Exercise heightened awareness when flying to/from airports where there is a lot of student training.
Report_1_Synopsis: Pilot reported NMAC with another aircraft on approach.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Time Pressure; Troubleshooting; Workload; Communication Breakdown
Report_1_Narrative: At 10;000 ft.; sterile FD; descent into DFW; we began preparation procedures [in the] galley and cabin. Once finished; FA3 (Flight Attendant) asked who was in the forward lavatory and we determined the wheelchair passenger at 1F must have gone to the bathroom. FA3 knocked and told her we were landing now and to return to her seat now. She said; 'Ok; I'm coming.' FA1 & FA3 continued asking her to return to her seat and when the wheels dropped. She was still in the bathroom saying she was coming. FA3 and FA1 continued communicating with her and at less than 1 minute to landing the decision was made that she would not be able to safely make it to a seat and she was informed to 'stay in the lavatory.' The flight landed and taxied to toward Gate A19 at which time FA1 informed the Captain we had a passenger land in the lavatory. The Captain asked for basic information at this time. FA1 informed him that the passenger was still in the lavatory and if we were going to be stopped so she could return to her seat. The Captain stated; 'We're going to keep moving.' The passenger was told to remain in the lavatory until the seatbelt sign was turned off. Once we parked at the gate; the passenger came out on her own and apologized saying she was getting sick. FA1 confirmed her name as Passenger A. The Captain then brought FA1 into the cockpit and stated that he should have known we didn't have a passenger in their seat for landing and that he had to do reports now.
Report_2_Narrative: After [the] Captain made [the] 'prepare for landing announcement' I; FA3 (Flight Attendant); walked up to [the] front and started clearing the cabin from there to [the] back. I finished preparing the cabin and headed up to my seat. When I was getting ready to sit; I saw that there was someone in front lavatory and asked FA1 if he saw anyone go in there. He explained that passenger 1F who came on [a] wheelchair had to use [the] lavatory last minute. I noticed how close we were getting to the ground so I started knocking on [the] door and told her; 'We are approaching landing and you need to come out;' to which she responded; 'I'm coming;' so I kept knocking on door and telling her she needed to come out already. Then; I noticed the landing gear is coming out. I then tell her; 'You need to come out NOW; landing gear is down we are about to land.' She said; 'Okay;' and seemed like she was going to come out but then didn't. That's when FA1 got up and told tell her to stay in the lavatory; which at that point; [was] so close to [the] ground and [since there was] such little time; [it] seemed like the best decision.We landed safely and checked on [the] passenger; she said she was okay. FA1 called [the] flight deck and explained to the Captain that we had someone in the lavatory [and] to let us know if we were going to make any stops so that we could have her go back to [her] seat safely since it takes her time to walk to her seat. The Captain told FA1; 'We are going to keep moving;' so [the] passenger remained in [the] lavatory until we came to a safe stop. The passenger came out and apologized for what she had done and said she understood she had done wrong but she really needed to go. Captain asked us why we didn't call him in the air we explained everything happened just so suddenly and we were so close to [the] ground with sterile flight deck and basically not much time.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier flight attendants reported an ill passenger remained in the lavatory during landing.

Report_1_Narrative: I was told to go to the gate at ZZZ airport to inspect a write up on an ERJ175. The write up stated that the pilots were not able to get cool air in the cockpit during cruise; but the packs worked and blew cool air on ground. It was written up previously and was a repeat write up. Because this was a repeat and there were no EICAS (Engine Indication and Crew Alerting System) messages reported; I decided to interrogate the CMC (Central Maintenance Computer) for active faults and faults stored on the previous flight. I found two fault codes on the current leg as active with no inactive time stamp showing it was resolved. I then went to active faults and both codes were stored as active there as well. The two fault codes were 21000020AM2 and 21000030AM2. Following the FIM (Fault Isolation Manual); the problem was a fault with SPDA (Secondary Power Distribution Assembly) 2 Module 26. I inspected the MEL (Minimum Equipment List) list and there was no deferral for this item. I informed my lead and ordered parts needed for repair. The parts would not arrive until the next morning so I was told it would be days. Shortly after arriving at work; I was informed that it was signed off as left pack deferred and flew out. Looking at the fault codes; the fault was for more than just the pack system which made it non-deferrable.Days did not follow the turn over stating that the faults were active and that the problem was with the SPDA 2 Module 26. They also did not look up fault in FIM and followed the procedures. This allowed for a broken plane to have a different part to be deferred while the actual problem was not addressed. Mechanics need to follow manuals and carefully read shift turnover.
Report_1_Synopsis: Aircraft Technician reports that an incorrect aircraft part was deferred per Minimum Equipment List.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Situational Awareness; Training / Qualification; Communication Breakdown; Distraction
Report_1_Narrative: Aircraft X was operating on an IFR flight plan; and was transitioning through the practice area. During the transition; we received no less than 3 altitude alerts from ATC about company traffic. However; we were in and out of the clouds; IMC. Aircraft Y and Aircraft Z were both observed passing 500 ft. above our aircraft. While observing these two aircraft; they came within 500 ft. both horizontally and vertically of clouds while they were operating VFR. This included Aircraft Y endangering our aircraft by flying within 1;000 ft. of us while we were IMC; presumably bringing them well within the VFR cloud clearance requirements. Aircraft Y later called Approach and was absconded for interfering with multiple aircraft; including coming 'close to' aircraft operating under IMC. The instructor onboard exhibited defiance and no acknowledgement of wrongdoing; exhibiting Macho; Invulnerability; and Anti-Authority. Approach additionally informed the instructor on Aircraft Y that 'multiple VFR [company] Aircraft were interfering with IFR aircraft.'
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Instructor reported VFR aircraft violating cloud clearance requirements.

Person_2_Human_Factors: Situational Awareness; Communication Breakdown; Time Pressure
Report_1_Narrative: [Report narrative contained no additional information.]
Report_2_Narrative: The crew and plane had arrived 4 hours earlier (XA:46) on an empty reposition leg. The passengers were originally scheduled to arrive at XC:00. The flight plan was delayed through handler 4 times due to uncertainty of passenger arrival time; with the most recent scheduled target takeoff time of XE:30.After engine start; the crew was instructed to taxi to Runway 05 holding point 'Hotel'. The aircraft initially stopped at H1 as a smaller business jet was taking Runway 05. We reported 'holding point H1' and the Controller responded 'holding point Hotel hold short Runway 05'. We moved forward the short distance from holding point Hotel 1 to Hotel. The Controller stated; 'Aircraft X; be prepared for an immediate takeoff. Do you have traffic 4 mile final in sight?' I responded 'affirmative; traffic in sight.' The Tower issued another instruction and I read back 'Line up and wait Runway 5; be ready for immediate takeoff.' We taxied ahead briefly then the Tower instructed us to 'hold position.' The Tower Controller stated that we were instructed 'Behind landing traffic; line up and wait Runway 5; be ready for immediate takeoff.' I replied that I heard 'Line up and wait Runway 5; be ready for immediate takeoff.'The Tower Controller was speaking with 2 inbound aircraft on the ILS (Instrument landing System) for Runway 5. There was another aircraft intercepting the ILS approximately 12 miles out. The inbound aircraft had been on a 4 mile final when we crossed the hold short point by approx. 100 ft. It was instructed to go around at approximately 2 miles out. After the inbound aircraft started its go-around; we were instructed to 'line up and wait; Runway 5.' We were cleared for takeoff and the Tower Controller stated that he would be submitting a report.A rough estimate indicates that the distance between holding point H and the actual runway is approximately 650 ft. We taxied about one 100 ft. across the hold short line but stopped approximately 500 ft. short of entering the runway. The term 'selective attention bias' seems appropriate here. I heard part of a message that included the phrase 'be ready for immediate takeoff' and was ready to act quickly. This situation was complicated by a language barrier and I missed or didn't understand the first part of the Controller's message of 'after landing traffic'. Operating frequently at busy Class B airports in the US where it's not unusual to be expected to expedite takeoff with closely spaced traffic; this situation was not out of the ordinary. In hindsight; it was the intention of the Controller to put us between the landing traffic and the next aircraft that was 12 miles out; not in front of the first aircraft that was landing.What both crew members could agree on is that we heard a transmission with an instruction to 'Line up and wait Runway 05. Be prepared for an immediate takeoff'.Contributing factors included language as LIEO is a popular international destination. There are many non-native English speakers on frequency. Phraseology can be different than what is used in the US and when accents and cultures are mixed; message transmission and reception aren't always in alignment.Time pressure [was a factor]. There had been numerous delays in the schedule. There was a sense of wanting to 'get things moving' since we were running 3 hours late. The weather at subsequent airports were forecast to have low ceilings and possible fog; so we didn't want to endure any unnecessary delays. The scheduled takeoff time of XE:30 was close to expiring.Also we were expecting to be sequenced into landing traffic and the pace was rapid. The instruction 'Be prepared for an immediate takeoff' had us ready to respond quickly. Recent landing experience [corroborated this]. Upon arrival 4 hours earlier; we were given landing clearance a few miles out. Instructions had a bit of a 'at the last minute' feel.PNF (Pilot Not Flying) had a Bose noise cancelling headset and PF(Pilot Flying) had a Telex over-the-ear headset. Neither pilot understood the first part of the ATC transmission. PF thought PNF might have understood the message better since he had a higher performance headset. What we did correctly [includes the following]. We read back what we thought we heard; assuming we would be corrected if wrong. We proceeded slowly across the hold short line. We stopped immediately when instructed and did not enter runway. We kept the incoming aircraft in sight and watched it go-around.What we did incorrectly [includes the following]. PNF missed or didn't understand the first part of an ATC transmission and didn't ask for clarification from the Controller or confirmation from the other pilot. With the 'Be prepared for immediate takeoff' instruction; we were spring-loaded to react versus stopping to ask for the message to be repeated or have a discussion between 2 pilots. [Also] since there was ambiguity in what we heard; we should have asked for clarification. After operating at busy class B airports in the US; there's a bit of hesitation in stopping to ask for an instruction to be repeated. Doing this at such an airport can result in getting lectured by ground and tower controllers.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Crew reported a runway incursion due to human factors.

Report_1_Narrative: I was doing some pattern work at my home field to work on my landings and maintain currency. After receiving permission to taxi to XXL behind a business jet; I confirmed with Tower that I was cleared for XXL. In hindsight; I may have missed a radio call from Tower; and similarly during Run Up I had to repeat my initial call to Ground.Once in the air I completed one circuit of the pattern without issue.On a subsequent circuit I was to land behind another aircraft ahead of me. I made my base turn; at which point Tower notified me that I was cutting off an aircraft behind me. I thought I was number 2 for XXR; but it turns out I was number 3. During this time; if I recall correctly; there was a change of staff in process at the Tower and I had to change frequency. I know I missed a call at this point.On the next circuit the controller called my crosswind turn after takeoff. Traffic appeared to be busy plus there was another aircraft in the vicinity that the controller mentioned was not responding to radio calls. I continued flying west; as I had silence on the radios; then received a call from Tower telling me that my next landing would be full stop. I complied with that.After landing on XXR I exited [the runway]. I was then directed to taxi and hold short of XXL. Upon stopping short of XXL the communications in my aircraft died. Surprising as the alt has been showing a positive charge. My medical has a restriction where I can't accept light gun signals during the daytime. As I was already on the ground there was no way I could divert; squawk 7600. Fortunately as a comms backup I have the tower's phone no. in my cell phone so I called the tower; explained where I was and that I had lost comms. I was directed to cross XXL and taxi straight into the ramp.I advised the front desk at the flight school/club about the radio issues and they said they would let the mechanic know.In future; if I think I am missing radio calls; I will try and confirm such with ATC ideally during the run up. Also; despite the METAR noting 10 SM visibility; the haze in the air from forest fires may have contributed to spotting other aircraft.
Report_1_Synopsis: C-172 pilot reported intermittent radio communication with ATC.

Report_1_Narrative: Flight was from ZZZ-ZZZ1 IFR clearance in VMC albeit some smoke.Flight was cleared to 14;000 feet then changed to 13;000 after passing 12;000. Looking directly into the sun through smoky haze I did not get it level at 13;000 and busted. ATC made no comment; perhaps due late change. No traffic in the area and no conflicts. This was the second flight in the airplane in 6 months due to COVID shutdown. I attribute this to my fault with a little help from late altitude change and general overall COVID-19 rust.
Report_1_Synopsis: Corporate pilot reported an altitude deviation and cited lack of recent flying as a contributing factor.

Report_1_Narrative: Apparently one of the flight school aircraft; a Cessna 172-L model; has been technically un-airworthy. The local mechanic shop did perform a pre-buy inspection when the flight school purchased the aircraft. The aircraft has undergone routine 100 hour inspections since the plane started working in the flight school. However; it wasn't until the most recent 100 hour inspection which was early September of this year that the local mechanic shop found that the aircraft was overdue on an Airworthiness Directive on a component on the propeller. It was overdue for about 500 hours on that particular AD. The mechanic shop was not certified to do the inspection on the propeller for that given AD for the propeller to be complied with. The flight school requested a ferry permit to fly the aircraft to the nearest propeller mechanic shop but was denied by the local FSDO. The next option was to remove the propeller and drive it to a propeller shop so that AD could be complied with. Such action was taken and the propeller shop found no defects with the propeller. The propeller was later driven back to the home airport to be placed back on the aircraft. Alas; the aircraft was complied with all known Airworthiness directives. The local mechanic shop staff admitted that they overlooked the AD. However; at the end of the day it is the owner/operator of the aircraft that is ultimately responsible for determining the airworthiness of the aircraft; which includes me; the flight instructor when using the aircraft to train student pilots. The flight school staff; meaning all the instructors and chief pilot were essentially responsible for this oversight of the airworthiness of the aircraft. I believe that the flight school staff trusted the mechanic shop to ensure the aircraft complies with all known AD's for every 100 hour inspection. The flight school has every intention to ensure the aircraft meets all inspections including ADs; and that by paying the mechanic shop for their services would suffice for ensuring the aircraft is airworthy. Over-relying on the mechanic shop in my opinion has been the root cause of this issue. I've personally shown the logbooks of the aircraft and ADs to my students prior to every checkride to show the aircraft is airworthy. I've even presented the ADs to my examiner for my CFI initial checkride. I honestly just never knew how to look up ADs or even know how to make sure that all ADs are complied with. The resolution that the chief pilot and I want to take to prevent this mishap from happening again is to learn how to look up ADs ourselves as a secondary check on top of the routine inspections done by the mechanics. Had I known that the AD wasn't complied with no one would've flown that aircraft until it is absolutely airworthy. A more thorough overview on the flight school's ADs is needed to make sure we are complying with them; and to make sure none have been overlooked. Again; the Chief pilot and I want to be able to double check AD compliance after routine inspections; and enhance communication between the instructors and mechanics.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Instructor reported that an Airworthiness Directive had been overlooked on a flight school aircraft.

Report_1_Narrative: While practicing landings in the pattern at ZZZ. Myself and my student were downwind at 1400 feet MSL when we noticed a drone flying at the same altitude but heading north directly in our path. We took an evasive maneuver by banking to the right to fly around the drone. The drone did not alter course; heading; or altitude. Had we not maneuvered a head on mid-air collision was inevitable.  After I reported this over the CTAF; Unicom attempted to contact the drone operator via the radio frequency but with no luck. This drone seemed to resemble that of an amateur photography style not a professional.
Report_1_Synopsis: Instructor Pilot reported a NMAC with a UAV while in the traffic pattern.

Report_1_Narrative: I was flying the RNAV (GPS) 34 straight in approach into FHR. The airport wall veiled in smoke/haze. The approach went well and I had visual contact with the airport 2 miles out. As I approached the runway; I was a little high and floated; so I decided to go-around. It was a mental slip. As I was flying downwind; I realized that I messed up; but I had visual contact with the airport and at that point thought it was safer to continue the pattern. I turned to base and then as I turned to final; I turned late. I decided then that I would just over fly the airport and fly the published missed. I contacted Whitney Approach for instructions to get back on the approach. Approach rightfully rebuked me for the go-around and then gave me instructions to return me to the approach. I flew the approach and landed without incident. Key learning from this event:1. If you cannot land for any reason; you must fly the published missed; regardless of prevailing conditions; unless you have cancelled IFR with ATC or until ATC has given other instructions.2. As time permits; scan the missed procedure on final to aid in preparation.3. Increase the time spent briefing the missed procedure when briefing the approach.
Report_1_Synopsis: GA pilot reported having to go-around after being high on the final approach to FHR airport. Reporter stated a missed approach should have been executed rather than a go-around.

Report_1_Narrative: Aircraft X was in my Tower pattern; making right traffic for Runway 17R. Aircraft Y was given left downwind for Runway 17R. I told Aircraft Y change to Runway 17L; Runway 17L clear to land; and he read it back. Aircraft X was on a 2-mile final when Aircraft Y turned base. I gave Aircraft Y; traffic 2-mile final; Aircraft X; for the parallel runway. Aircraft Y said; I thought I was cleared to Runway 17R. I said negative; Runway 17L cleared to land. At the time Aircraft X took evasive maneuvers. Aircraft Y landed on the right and Aircraft X said we are on the go with that near miss. Aircraft Y was given possible pilot deviation. I'm not sure anything could have been done different from a Controller stand point. Aircraft Y was cleared to land Runway 17L and he read it back. It was a pilot deviation.
Report_1_Synopsis: A Tower Controller reported an aircraft turned base and lined up with the wrong runway; causing a NMAC with traffic on short final.
