Report_1_Narrative: A family boarded with the 2 year old child not wearing a mask. After boarding was almost done; Flight Attendant (FA) D advised me that the child in row X is not wearing a mask.  I walked to their row and asked the parents if the child had a mask or would they like one of ours.  Both parents quickly stated; 'He's 2 and he won't wear a mask.  Good luck if you want to try.'  'We were told 2 is okay for no mask.'  'He won't wear a mask.'I decided to disengage and have the Customer Service Agent (CSA) contacted. I advised them that a CSA would be down to have a conversation with them. The Captain was advised and I asked for a CSA to come down to the aircraft. The boarding agent talked to the party and advised me that the parents were attempting to put a mask on the child.A second CSA came down and asked me about the age and our mask policy. She advised me they had a conversation with the party prior to boarding and wrongly advised the parents of the age requirement for wearing a mask. I advised the CSA it clearly states on policy that age 2 and up must wear a mask; no exceptions. The ZZZ Station needs to retrain or re-examine the Mask Policy because it is very clear on all guest facing touch points that our policy is stated age 2 and up. Our ZZZ Station CSA's are advising guests incorrect age requirements for our mask policy. I advised both CSA's that due to the statements made by the parents that their child would not wear a mask that the FA crew wanted them removed from the flight.As the family deplaned they yelled and blamed me for getting them kicked off this flight. I apologized but I reiterated our mask policy as they were deplaning.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Attendant reported a family with child were removed from the flight because of non-compliance regarding face mask policy. The family was incorrectly told by station agents; a mask was not required for the 2 year old.

Report_1_Narrative: In traffic pattern with 2 other aircraft. RWY XX in use. A 3rd high wing joined pattern from either the 45 to downwind in front of me or straight in. Didn't see where they came from. I was downwind; #3 to land; with 2 on final. Strobes and ADSB on. I extended downwind for spacing and in doing so entered Class C for ZZZ1 briefly before turning base. On final; a C172 turned in front of me but was slightly above. I inquired on the freq 'Do you see me below you?' His response was 'you flew into ZZZ1 2 miles'. (It was actually about half a mile.) I told him I extended my downwind for spacing. His response was that 'you had options'. I am not sure what he meant by that. But evidently he insisted on flying a tight standard pattern regardless of other traffic.
Report_1_Synopsis: Pilot flying RV7 aircraft reported near miss with C172 aircraft on final approach.

Report_1_Narrative: The event occurred on a flight between ZZZ and ZZZ1. We had been delayed multiple times at our base of operations due to mechanical issues and eventually were switched to a different aircraft that became available late in the day. Throughout the rescheduling and refiling/updating flight plans we had taken consideration of our duty time and had set a latest takeoff time from base that would allow us to complete our flights and return to base before the end of our duty time. However in all that I failed to consider night landing currency for carrying passengers. It was not until after we had picked up our passenger and were enroute to ZZZ1 and the sun had set that the FO (pilot flying) looked at me and said that he couldn't make the landing as he was not night current. Then I realized I was not night current either. At this point we realized it was too late and continued to our destination. I had the FO do the landing which in retrospect as PIC I should have shown more initiative in taking full responsibility by taking the landing instead of putting the FO in the position of making a landing out of currency.A contributing factor is that in the past I have seldom carried passengers for my employer. Most often I am doing other type of flying with only required crew on board due to the aircraft being in the restricted category. But I have more recently been doing an occasional passenger carrying flight where I have to think about passenger carrying currency more. Also due to economic slow down there has been less opportunity to keep up currency especially night currency with our normal operations. For corrective actions I have made a checklist for myself that goes in my knee board specifically for passenger carrying flights; because they are so infrequent; that lists the pertinent things that should be considered during pre-flight and more specifically the more pertinent things like passenger carrying currency. This will be a checklist that I see when I open my knee board prior to flight and work through at the latest; just before engine start.
Report_1_Synopsis: Corporate Captain reported neither crew member was current to make a landing on a night flight and realized it after they had departed.

Report_1_Narrative: Our helicopter's annual expired the last day of Month. The closest maintenance facility was closed for flights due to the COVID pandemic. On [date] we requested a special flight permit (SFP) to the FAA for a ferry flight to be conducted 5 days later. This was the first time I have done this type of application. The FAA takes time to process these applications and I became anxious; thinking the owner would not like [it] if we continued to delay the helicopter's maintenance. So; I made the decision to continue the flight 5 days later; although the SFP was pending. I let a non-existent external pressure influence my decision to conduct the ferry flight. The helicopter was in perfect condition; but I realized that it was a mistake and should have waited for the FAA SFP response to conduct the flight. I believe more training on CRM and aeronautical decision making and FAR knowledge will help me deter these types of situations in the future.
Report_1_Synopsis: Pilot reported being under pressure and flew a ferry flight without proper documentation.

Report_1_Narrative: On practice ZZZ LOC XX; approximately 4 miles from the end of the runway; flight in VFR conditions above an undercast we received a low altitude alert from ZZZ Tower. We advised Tower were VFR and leveling at the MDA (900 MSL) and; at the same time; while cross checking our position on the LOC both pilots noted that the GPS had not updated from the Final Approach Fix (ZZZZZ) to the end of the runway. After cross checking position on the EFB display we elected to execute a missed approach at the end of the runway.The reason for this report is both systems and human factors related. Both pilots were concentrating on the descent and level off from FAF altitude to MDA using a 'dive and drive procedure' which is no longer commonly used in heavy jet aircraft. Concentrating on the altitude an equipment error to update the next waypoint automatically was missed and the low altitude alert from Tower compounded the 'startle factor'. The startle factor was amplified by the fact we were VFR above an overcast with no terrain in sight.  Based on training; we executed a missed approach to create time and regain situational awareness; from a personal perspective when an unexpected event occurs; even in seasoned pilots; it takes a few minutes to understand what happened; not second guess yourself and reset situational awareness.As a follow-up to the event; I contacted ZZZ Tower who related that they have issued numerous low altitude alerts on this approach; for aircraft at the correct altitude; usually involving a high descent rate approach to MDA. I reviewed the approach with the PF (Pilot Flying)and confirmed that he had set an excessive rate (1500 feet/min) when our company procedure calls for less than 1;000 feet/min within 1;000 feet of the terrain.A better briefing on use of automation during the crew brief may have mitigated the high descent rate; and as Pilot Not Flying validating the waypoint switch over at FAF should have been accomplished. Although we were given missed approach instructions ahead of time from approach control (practice approach); if we were relying on GPS for the published missed; it would have been difficult to reprogram the GPS (during the missed approach) to fly the published missed approach (our aircraft does not have TACAN (Tactical Air Navigation system) (raw data) capability and in this situation would require GPS to fly the published missed). As a final observation; we did not receive any onboard GPWS (Ground Proximity Warning System) or TAWS (Terrain Avoidance and Warning System) warning with respect to terrain and have asked company maintenance to verify proper operation of both systems.
Report_1_Synopsis: Corporate flight crew report aircraft navigation equipment anomalies on approach.

Report_1_Narrative: My student on his second solo landed and veered off the runway about 5 feet during the attempt to do a touch and go. His approach was stable and landing was on centerline. There are a couple factors that I believe led to this runway excursion. First; I believe he rushed into taking off after landing; without taking the time to ensure the flaps were up and that the aircraft was still under control. Second; I believe he accidentally applied more left rudder than he had intended causing him to veer off to the left of the runway. After applying full power he began to veer to the left of the runway. He corrected for this by pulling back power and applying right rudder; but not fast enough to prevent momentarily veering off the runway.
Report_2_Narrative: Too much rudder control causing veer off the left of the runway. No damage or injuries.
Report_1_Synopsis: C172 Student Pilot reported veering off runway during touch and go landing.

Report_1_Narrative: After lifting off Runway XX; I retracted the gear; allowed the aircraft to accelerate to 120 knots and was about to retract the takeoff flaps setting. The Tower cleared me to a right turn for my westerly heading; when suddenly there was a loud noise and a strong rush of air as the canopy departed. I looked at my ground position and airspeed. I added power called the Tower and informed them of the situation and asked to return. I continued climbing to pattern altitude. Tower cleared me to land. I waited until my base turn to lower the gear. On short final I added full flaps. I kept the airspeed about 10 knots higher than normal (100 knots). Landed and taxied to hanger. Ground Control informed me that someone saw the canopy land not far from the end of the runway. I retrieved the canopy which landed in the dirt. No objects or persons were hit. I debriefed with Tower personnel and Airport Manager. Because of aircraft behind me [which were ready] to go; I rushed my final prep for takeoff and did not lock the canopy. I cannot tell you that after XX years and thousands of hours of flying many aircraft how I could have made such a mistake. I am ashamed of myself. I plan on making a checklist that you have to check off each box before moving on; and continue going to safety seminars as I had for years.
Report_1_Synopsis: Pilot flying jet trainer reports canopy departed after takeoff.

Person_2_Human_Factors: Training / Qualification; Confusion; Distraction; Communication Breakdown; Situational Awareness
Report_1_Narrative: I was watching a trainee in the Local Control position when ground/flight data/clearance delivery passed inbound information from ZZZ ARTCC of Aircraft X two miles south east of the airport for a visual approach to Runway XX. This was an extremely late inbound as our LOA reads center will inbound aircraft at least 10 miles out. We had several VFR aircraft in the rectangular pattern to Runway XX with aircraft on final to Runway XX with almost no time to build a hole. We coordinated with center to not descend Aircraft X below 4;000 and requested control which he was at 5;000. Center descended Aircraft X to 4;000 and cleared the aircraft for the visual approach to Runway XX and switched the aircraft to us. We had to move at least two aircraft out of Aircraft X way with little to no notice to accommodate the IFR arrival. Because we were advertising Runway XX/XY in use and Aircraft X was so high (5;000); I thought since we didn't get an inbound that center was vectoring the aircraft around potentially for spacing. Never did I think Aircraft X was going to be cleared a visual approach to Runway XX at the altitude the aircraft was at. Common practice is center inbound aircraft outside of 10 miles for the IFR approach and descends them to 3;000 feet before switching them to us. This created a dangerous situation with very little time to react or plan; especially with a trainee who was on day 4 of re-entering training after six months plus of not working local due to COVID and me not training anyone for just as long if not longer due to COVID.Follow the LOA between  ZZZ ARTCC and ZZZ Tower.
Report_2_Narrative: I was training on local; which I had not worked local in about 6 months due to the COVID pandemic; it was my fourth day back into training. I had numerous aircraft in the local pattern and on final for Runway XX. ZZZ Center called flight data (FD) / Ground Control (GC) and in bounded Aircraft X; who was two miles south east of the field at five thousand feet. I coordinated with FD/GC and ZZZ Center to stop Aircraft X's descent at four thousand because I had several VFR aircraft in the pattern and lining up on final. Shortly thereafter Aircraft X calls me about one to two miles northeast of the field saying he is on a visual approach to Runway XX. I asked Aircraft X how long he would need to continue north before he would turn base in which he told me about another mile and then he would turn his base. I acknowledged him and told him to report turning base. I then started moving aircraft out of the way and sequencing aircraft behind him in order to make it work. I had very little time to plan and build a gap for Aircraft X to fit into. Per our LOA with ZZZ Center; ZZZ Center is supposed to inbound aircraft at least 10 miles out. This aircraft was not inbounded until two miles southeast of the field. Being that I had not got a position on Aircraft X when I noticed him so close to the airport on the STARS; I was under the impression that center was vectoring the aircraft for an RNAV XX approach only to find out last minute that the aircraft was going to be doing a visual approach to XX and then I was not given any time to build a gap to fit the aircraft into.In accordance with the LOA between ZZZ Tower and ZZZ Center; the Center is supposed to call with a position on inbound aircraft with a type of approach to expect. My recommendation is for center to follow the LOA and inbound the aircraft sooner; allowing tower time to build gaps for IFR aircraft.
Report_1_Synopsis: Tower Instructor and Developmental reported overlying Center not complying with the two facilities' LOA.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Situational Awareness; Workload; Troubleshooting; Time Pressure; Communication Breakdown; Confusion; Distraction
Report_1_Narrative: I plugged in to work Position 1 and Position 2 Low by myself. Staffing was a major issue. The Controller-in-Charge had tried to call in overtime; but no one was available until later in the afternoon. (Our only overtime was Controller Z. He had worked the mid the previous night.We had multiple controllers go over 2 hours on position; many without D-sides or any help.The Controller in Charge; Controller Y; worked over almost 11 hours. This is of course well over the prescribed 10-hour shift. He was forced to work Controller A's handoff and D-side while he also worked the Controller-in-Charge position.I was aware of the staffing situation; but at the time I was not aware that they would mandate Controller Y work more than 10 hours in a row. Thus; I was anticipating the loss of another Controller. Position 1 and Position 2 would be going red (or above the facility delineated 'safe' number) in the next 45 minutes. And I knew that I would still be on position.I called the surrounding ZZZ1 Center Sectors XX; YZ; YA; YB and advised them that we were short staffed; and I was going to be on a 'red' sector. As a result; I needed 25 nm in trail to ZZZ Center International. ZZZ1 Center was extremely accommodative. The operations manager at ZZZ Center then came down to the area and began to pressure the CIC Controller Y to relieve the mile in trail restriction. With XX years' experience working arrival aircraft into ZZZ; I did not think that was a prudent decision. The Operations Manager countermanded my request and told ZZZ1 [Center] to disregard my control instructions. I was made aware of this development; and I reiterated to ZZZ1 Center that for safety; staffing and volume I would have to enforce the restriction. Keep in mind that I gave ZZZ1 at least 45 minutes lead time on this development. I was not springing anything on them. All the controllers were extremely accommodative; and I thanked them for their help. Operations Manager came up to me in an intimidating manner while I was working; and told me that I was not allowed to put in-trail restrictions on ZZZ1. I told him to call me on the line if he was going to order me to do something. I wanted any interaction recorded for self-preservation purposes. He did leave but refused to call me on a recorded line. He appeared later and told me that I was not allowed to make in-trail restrictions for my sector. I told him that if he wanted to take responsibility for the aircraft he could; but I did not think that it was safe. I refused to be intimidated. He then threatened me with an investigation and told me that I would 'need a rep.' I told him that I no longer felt safe working a busy sector by myself with the threat of an investigation hanging over my head. [Thankfully]; CIC Controller Y assigned newly-arrived overtime Controller Z to relieve me.Operations Manager called the X area and ordered CIC Controller Y page me back to work. I advised him that I would return shortly after using the bathroom. Controllers should be allowed what restrictions they put in place for their sector. There is a culture of fear; intimidation and completely disregard for law; rule and regulation.
Report_1_Synopsis: Center Controller reported disagreement with Operations Manager when Controller put in aircraft flow coming into the sector reporter was working.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Distraction; Workload; Situational Awareness; Human-Machine Interface
Report_1_Narrative: I was working all RADAR positions combined in the Tower cab due to the COVID schedule.  We had a priority handling aircraft land at ZZZ1 which caused multiple aircraft to be placed in holding/kept in the RADAR pattern. While this was going on I had a heavy increase in traffic volume.  I based Aircraft X to a 240 heading after an extended downwind; about 15 miles out at 020 MSL. Shortly after basing the aircraft I received multiple calls from aircraft and became saturated with traffic and transmissions. I realized Aircraft X had gone through final and was headed towards a man-made obstruction with the obstruction height of 2;XXX feet. I issued a right turn to heading 050 to get them away from the obstruction. I started issuing a climb to Aircraft X when I realized I had a VFR aircraft receiving radar serve at 030 directly about him. This caused me to cancel the climb and stick with just the turn. I then tried to turn the VFR aircraft so I could climb Aircraft X but between my voice quality and the other aircraft on frequency he didn't understand my transmission. I believe Aircraft X came within 3 miles of the obstruction.I believe working on the TDW (Tower Display Workstation) display which is smaller than our normal stars displayed caused a higher complexity of traffic. I'm not really sure what could have prevented this event other than going back to normal staffing levels and working back in the RAPCON.
Report_1_Synopsis: Tower Controller reported an aircraft missed a turn and came within less than the required separation from a tall obstruction.

Report_1_Narrative: I forgot to coordinate ODO (Opposite Direction Operation) with ZZZ Tower. Their active runway in use was Runway XX and I ran Aircraft X in for a practice RNAV YY approach without ODO coordination. I had cleared the aircraft for the approach and then the satellite sectors were split and forgot to tell the other Controller about the ODO operation. ZZZ Tower right now is on reduced operating times due to the COVID-19 pandemic. Their Tower operation opening and closing times are out of the norm and may have been a contributing factor in forgetting that they were open and coordination was needed for the ODO operation.ZZZ1 Tower was on a XY's operation while ZZZ Tower was on a Runway XX operation which added to the confusion of what runway was in use at ZZZ.I just need to do a better job of remembering everything.
Report_1_Synopsis: TRACON Controller reported failing to coordinate an Opposite Direction Operation with Tower.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Training / Qualification; Confusion; Communication Breakdown; Workload
Report_1_Narrative: I was plugged in with a trainee in local control when we received inbound information from Flight Data that they had just received it from Center on Aircraft X on a Visual Approach. The trainee and I looked at the RADAR display and saw him turning onto a 5 mile final moving pretty quick with several VFR aircraft in the rectangular pattern on the intersecting runway. We had no time to build a hole for Aircraft X and the spacing was going to be too tight so we sent Aircraft X around. This was an issue since our LOA (Letter of Agreement) with the Center says they shall pass inbound information 10 miles or more which they did not do after they had just had a similar situation minutes before with Aircraft Y they had inbounded 2 miles south east of the airport on the Visual Approach with a busy pattern.I plugged a handset in the CIC (Controller in Charge) position and called Center and told them they need to inbound these IFR arrivals a little sooner. I did this at the CIC position as Local Control was busy and I was trying to not distract the trainee as he was working the traffic. The response I got from Center was he was waiting for a down time for Aircraft Y. I told him that he should review our LOA. I found this unacceptable as there is a reason why we have a LOA and it allows us time to make plans to adjust traffic to accommodate IFR arrivals and lets us know what Center is going to do with the inbounds. Its difficult to separate aircraft that we don't know about that may be descending or on an approach. After we sent Aircraft X around we coordinated for the missed approach with Flight Data. Flight Data informed us that Center wanted runway heading to 3;000 feet. We issued the missed approach instructions to Aircraft X and switched the aircraft to Center.A minute or so later Flight data passes us the next inbound information on Aircraft Z south east of the field then follows it up that Center is going to turn Aircraft X north bound and he is doing the Visual Approach. Very shortly after Aircraft X checks on roughly 3 miles northwest of the field. This is a problem because again we thought Aircraft Z was going to be number 1 who was well over 10 miles from the airport; followed by Aircraft X. We had let the VFR traffic on the rectangular pattern on resume and started to plan for Aircraft Z arrival. As soon as Aircraft X checked on; we were shocked and began moving aircraft out of his way that were roughly a mile in front of Aircraft X. I asked another controller to relieve us as this now was 3 situations back to back that the trainee had handled very well but was very dangerous. I wanted to call over to Center and try to figure out what was going on. Follow the LOA between ZMP and TVC.
Report_2_Narrative: After Aircraft X was sent around Center inbounded Aircraft Z about 20 miles southwest for a Visual Approach. A minute or two later Center called back and asked what we wanted to do with Aircraft X and if it was ok if they turned him north. I said affirmative but we have a lot of small aircraft using Runway 18 and Center said that they saw that. Center then said ok I will turn Aircraft X to the north and clear him for the Visual Approach. A minute or two later Aircraft X calls local inbound on the Visual Approach about 3 miles northwest and about 1 mile in trail of a Cessna doing more than double their speed. The Cessna on approach to the intersecting runway was broken off to bring Aircraft X in. Local Control and I were surprised that Aircraft X turned in like that and was switched over. We thought that the aircarrier was number 1 to the field since we never got an official inbound on Aircraft X. We thought that Aircraft X was being sent north to get setup on the visual approach after the air carrier.Follow the LOA.
Report_1_Synopsis: Four Tower Controllers reported the Center was coordinating IFR arrivals too late and not in compliance with the Letter of Agreement; causing airborne conflicts and arrivals being issued go around instructions.

Report_1_Narrative: I was working both South and West sectors combined.  I was moderately busy working many VFR's; one or two IFRs; and two practice approaches.  The traffic was not overly complex; but I had to keep a good scan for traffic advisories due to many VFRs in the area.  Earlier I was even busier with more traffic resulting in a split of the airspace while losing our main frequency and dealing with several automated handoff problems.  We have fusion radar with 7 radars acquiring aircraft and I had at least a half dozen non ARTS (Automated Radar Terminal System) tracks resulting in adjacent airspace calling about 'handoff.'  There were also numerous wrong automated handoffs from adjacent airspace; i.e. aircraft should be handing off to S scope; but is in hand off status to D scope.  I had to slew and correct over a dozen bad handoffs.  I can only type and slew so fast (MF handoff OK S slew enter) while working a busier session.   That's how great the technology was working that day and may have led to the airspace violation.  Over on W airspace I saw Aircraft X with white coloration and a C tag indicating it would be handing off to me from CMH.  I grabbed the strip and noticed it was landing just outside W airspace in Toledo airspace.  I kept my scan going.  Numerous aircraft needed instructions on the S airspace.  By the time I got back to the Aircraft X it was 2 miles in my airspace flashing.  I accepted the handoff and descended the Aircraft X per the LOA.  A simple airspace violation by an IFR aircraft that I could have prevented.  I do not know if automated handoff was an issue on this; but it's pretty easy for a flashing white data block to catch your eye.  CMH may have had an issue on their end trying to get the aircraft to handoff to us.   Our facility has sent hundreds of reports about our automation issues. HUNDREDS.  We still get numerous wrong handoff status aircraft (flashing to D scope when it needs to flash to S scope).  We reconfigured the scopes twice on this day just to see if it was a configuration problem.  This was not an issue.  If we are to have this problem fixed then whoever we send these reports to; they and their team need [to] fix the computers and how they process our inbound aircraft to determine which scopes they go to.  We combined Akron Canton radar and Cleveland radar over a year ago and are still having problems.  Its a distraction that increases your workload.  Automation should make my job easier; right now; at CLE...it isn't.
Report_1_Synopsis: CLE TRACON Controller reported automation issues resulting in airspace violations and increased workload.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Distraction; Workload; Situational Awareness; Human-Machine Interface
Report_1_Narrative: I accepted the hand-off on Aircraft X from ZZZ approach and put a PVD (Plan View Display) on what I thought was ZZZ Approach LO's scope. I was very busy working three sectors combined and simply climbed Aircraft X on check on. A few minutes later in my hurried scan I noticed that he was in ZZZ Approach lows airspace climbing through 110 but the P [position symbol] was still a P not an A [position symbol]. I looked at the P and noticed why. I had put it on sector XY's scope not sector XX's. Just a mistake of being busy and being in an expect things to go as planned and hope for the best mode instead of a calm verify everything and plan for the worst mode. There really isn't a recommendation. While we're in this skeleton crew phase there's nothing that can be done and this is just the way things are day in and day out.
Report_1_Synopsis: Center Controller reported a mistake involving handing off an aircraft to the wrong sector and cited staffing levels as a contributing factor.

Report_1_Narrative: I had just taken position a few minutes prior to the event. The controller who I relieved informed me about traffic that departed east bound and was unsure if they were still on frequency. Aircraft X checked in on the approach. I issued traffic 12 o'clock and 2 miles opposite direction intentions unknown. I reached out to the VFR opposite direction traffic Aircraft Y with a traffic alert and the pilot happened to be on frequency and reported traffic in sight. Aircraft X turned north of course to avoid traffic and stated that 'that was close'. Educate pilots to not fly close to final when departing eastbound. Controllers should remind aircraft to remain north of final eastbound.
Report_1_Synopsis: Local Controller reported during receiving communications transfer an airborne conflict resulted in a NMAC.

Report_1_Narrative: This could be called a systemic problem; as it happens all the time. I filed it as an event since you can specifically look at this event. Aircraft X departed and did not tag up. The Tower controller called to coordinate the 'no tag'; but failed to recognize from Clearance Delivery; Ground Control and Local Control that the flight plan had timed out completely. They launched an aircraft with no flight plan in the system. I called the tower to ask them if they could re-enter the flight plan as they had all the information in front of them via the flight plan; they told me 'we don't do that'. So in one of the most critical phases of flight; we have to ask the IFR commercial jet; where he is going; off one of the busiest airports in the country. This is not only embarrassing; but unprofessional that a tower is unwilling or worse incapable of entering a basic flight plan into the FDIO. This happens daily and is unacceptable and unsafe.Force Tower controllers to DO THEIR JOB. Entering clearances is basic air traffic and should be mastered before they work any actual air traffic.
Report_1_Synopsis: TRACON Supervisor reported that Tower allowed an aircraft to depart IFR without a flight plan on file.

Report_1_Narrative: I was notified by the Company [10 days after flight] that a dry ice shipment of 1042 kg was not included in the weight and balance on Aircraft X. To the best of my recollection; that dry ice was included.  I operate Aircraft X quite frequently and it almost always requires a Dry Ice Exception.  I reviewed the Flight Plan Release for that flight and confirmed that Dry Ice Supplementary Procedures was listed.  Also; to the best of recollection; I was notified of Dry Ice Supp. Proc. when I initialized ACARS as well as on the ACARS Weight and Balance. [Caused by] oversight on final paperwork. [Suggest to] have a separate acknowledgement line on the ACARS Weight and Balance for dry ice only.
Report_1_Synopsis: B767-300 Captain reported company notification of Hazmat documentation error ten days after flight operated.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Workload; Situational Awareness; Time Pressure; Distraction; Confusion
Report_1_Narrative: 3rd day of flying. 3rd flight of day. We had set up for the ILS Approach in accordance with ATIS. No mention was made of Visual Approaches being in use. Despite that fact; we briefed the restrictions over a satellite airport as a precaution.We were taken off the RNAV Arrival and were given a series of step down clearances as we approached the field. Simultaneously; we were told to expect the RNAV Visual Approach. The Pilot Monitoring loaded the new approach as we were below 10;000 ft. which I as the Pilot Flying rapidly briefed. Shortly thereafter; we were cleared to a point not on the arrival nor the RNAV Visual. As the Pilot Monitoring began searching for the fix; I maintained a 3:1 descent rate via VSpeed/Open Des. I was also approaching the point where I was going to need to configure if I wished to have a stabilized approach. The Pilot Monitoring found the fix on the RNAV (GPS) Approach and raced to reconfigure the FMS. Then; having given no prior warning; the Approach Controller cleared us for the ILS Approach which would have been impossible at this point. Having the runway in sight and fearing that any further 'assistance' from the controller would do little to aid my rapidly deteriorating situational awareness; I elected to disconnect the autopilot; and fly the approach visually. I pulled my Pilot Monitoring back into the loop by asking for him to clear my flight directors; configure the aircraft; and ask approach for the Visual Approach. The controller cleared us for the Visual Approach; 'as long as we fly the glideslope down'; which I'd submit is not a legal clearance; but was in any case irrelevant as following the glideslope had always been our intention. After doing some fishing to configure the aircraft and get down onto glideslope; the Pilot Monitoring reselected the approach and flight directors and we flew a stabilized approach to landing. In debriefing this event; we discovered that the fix was also present on the ILS Approach; which was the approach that ATIS had specified; the approach that we had initially briefed; and presumably the approach that the controller wished us to fly all along. I can't say what the Approach controller was thinking during this event. However; on an approach as infamous as any to I can only suggest that last minute changes are inappropriate and unsafe. I also think that the controller has an inaccurate impression of what is required of aircrews when changing approaches. I would suggest that the reality of flying this approach be made clear to her as controlling that is this cavalier will only lead to further unstabilized approaches in the future; or worse. The last minute change to the RNAV Visual followed by clearing us to a point not on the approach; followed by a second clearance for the ILS risked completely overwhelming the aircrew. That this was on a runway that is notorious for unstabilized approaches only exacerbated matters. Frankly; any acceptance of other than ILS approaches to this runway should be disallowed. Flying Visual Approaches to this runway; with it's unique peculiarities is a procedure designed by ATC; for the benefit of ATC. By definition and data; flying this Visual Approach is a compromise of safety for the sake of expediency; and sets aircrew up to be 'the last line of defense'; with generally predictable results.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier pilot reported last minute route clearances and unnecessary Approach changes by ATC caused an unsafe workload and unstable approach.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Workload; Time Pressure; Situational Awareness; Confusion; Distraction
Report_1_Narrative: A flight called me when they were in Country X airspace saying Country Y would not let them enter because they did not have a flight plan on file. I resent a filing and requested assistance. After about 5 minutes the crew called back saying they were still being told to hold and that they would need to head to divert soon due to fuel constraints. I had also called Flight Plan Scheduling (FPS) requesting assistance. They called back and said that route should have not been used due to no overflight. The overflight had been requested yesterday; but we did not have approval yet. Other personnel also said that we did not have overflight approval. When we looked at the approved routeing document in the computer; it said that Aircraft X did have approval for Country Y so we were all confused. A few minutes later the document was taken down and then modified to say overflight approval pending. Also; that route was the route the FPS was the preferred route. The flight diverted for a planned gas and go.
Report_1_Synopsis: Dispatcher reported a flight was dispatched over foreign airspace without the proper approval and had to divert.

Person_2_Human_Factors: Training / Qualification; Situational Awareness; Distraction; Communication Breakdown
Report_1_Narrative: While executing a visual approach to Runway XX ZZZ airport; I was on a proper visual glide path until approximately 1/2 - 1/4 mile final.  A breakdown in my scan resulted in descending below a normal glide path; as a result we were unstable below 500 feet AGL.  Neither pilot called for a go-around; though; after debrief it was agreed that a go-around would have been appropriate. I was able to correct back on profile; approximately at 1/4 mile short final. The landing was safe; on speed and uneventful.Contributing factors included light turbulence requiring constant power adjustments. Also; lack of recent flight time due to taking leave--this was my first approach/landing in a number of weeks on top of very limited flight time in the past 6 months. Additionally; as experienced from the previous ILS approach to the same runway conducted earlier the same day; it was noticed that while on or above glide path; the PAPI's indicated well below; despite glide slope and VGSI not being coincident per the procedure.  The note on the procedure indicated that the VGSI would bring the aircraft across the threshold at approximately 50 feet; however; coming across the threshold at 80 feet; the PAPI's still indicated low (one white over three red).  This issue was briefed to be mitigated by referencing altitude/distance check points on descent; however; it still became an issue.  The lack of proper visual guidance may have contributed to a departure from a stable glide path; however; did not contribute to the failure to call a go-around.  The PAPI guidance issue was brought to the attention of the airport manager.The potential lack of flight time/currency due to COVID is a potential universal issue.  I have a luxury of flying with the X Group to maintain a scan but for those that don't; a severely reduced schedule will likely result in some loss of proficiency.  A solution may be to promote those with reduced flying to take more legs/landings than normal within a given pairing.  Additionally; aside from notifying the airport or ATC of malfunctioning equipment; e.g.; PAPI's; there should be a means by which to relay this information to the company for immediate communication to air crew; as there is no guarantee of a swift response or fix.  (aside from NOTAMs).
Report_2_Narrative: Was pilot monitoring. We were coming in to land on the visual to Runway XX in ZZZ. During the last 1/4 to 1/2 mile on the approach. The pilot flying misjudged the distance and descent rate during the approach and started to get low on the approach. Pilot flying corrected but we were unstabilized on the approach and did not execute a go-around. We landed from the approach without incident within the touchdown zone area on the runway. The pilot flying had not been flying very much recently so lack of recent experience was a factor. A failure of the pilot monitoring to call for a go-around from an unstable approach. A failure of the pilot flying to call for a go-around from an unstabilized approach. Complacency on approach and not wanting to inconvenience passengers. Poor decision making by pilots.As pilots we have to always remember safety is top priority. Even if it's an inconvenience to both [of] you and everyone on board. If an approach becomes unstabalized a go-around or missed approach must be executed. Even if the landing happens safely and the landing is 'salvaged' it's important to remember that one day it might not be.  As a pilot monitoring if you see an unstabilized approach you should speak up. Don't worry about hurt feelings. Missed connections. We can't get complacent and think that we can just continue from an unstabilized approach.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported an unstablized approach and landing and cited lack of flying as a contributing factor.

Report_1_Narrative: At 11;000 feet Flight Attendant called; notified of passenger face mask non-compliance; causing a distraction with announcement location and announcement briefing. Once on course with Runway XX; approximately 2-3 miles before ZZZZZ; during flap extension to flaps 45; autopilot disconnected. We believe the autopilot disconnected because during flap extension speed dropped off. As the First Officer was adding power and correcting; autopilot disconnected. First Officer then hand flew and we tried autopilot again. It engaged normally.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported being distracted by a Flight Attendant call and the autopilot disconnected during flap extension.

Report_1_Narrative: Shortly after reaching cruise; Flight Attendant let me know that a passenger's children (10 - 12 years old) were not complying with the face mask policy. That after being asked to ensure they wear their face masks the passenger (mother) threw trash at the Flight Attendant. I said I would contact Dispatch and they should contact their ops if possible. Flight Attendant said they would proceed with the necessary paperwork. I made a PA again reminding people of the airline face mask policy. The FA let me know the passenger and children then fully complied. We continued and landed without further incident.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported Flight Attendant advised them of passengers not complying with face mask policy.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Workload; Troubleshooting; Human-Machine Interface; Distraction; Situational Awareness
Report_1_Narrative: We were operating a flight to get some maintenance after having sat for awhile. After takeoff; at around 4;000 ft. we received a RT Windshield Heat Caution message. While running the QRH for that at approximately 7;500 ft.; the windshield cracked. We immediately stopped climbing and slowed to 200 kts. and requested a turn back to the airport while running the QRH for that. The windshield really wasn't a problem. The issue was when after I turned off the autopilot for the Visual Approach; I noticed right away that the flight controls felt strange. They seemed to be much less effective mostly in pitch. I was having a hard time staying in the flight director because it felt like I was having to make large inputs with delayed response from the plane. We were able to land safely. I wrote up that the controls were spongy less responsive. We went to the hotel. In the morning; I called maintenance to ask what they had found. I was told that they checked the cables and pulleys and that nothing was found. I told the maintenance controller that I wasn't going to fly it until something was found. We went to the hangar in the morning a bit early so I could talk to the maintenance team. I saw that the logbook was signed off and that it indicated 'flight control check satisfactory'; and it was signed off. I told my concerns to a few mechanics. Some didn't seem real concerned. A couple were curious. I took one to another aircraft in the hangar and had him do a flight control check. Then went back to my plane and did one. He immediately said 'wow; this one is much harder; and I feel a catch in the elevator'. He said that is definitely the pitch feel system and the plane was then put back on maintenance to get fixed. My concern is that if another crew had been assigned to this plane; they might've not noticed the odd feeling flight control check and tried to go flying with potentially bad results. Flight control concerns from pilots need to be taken seriously! The First Officer who was in the right seat and did the flight control check; said they felt fine when he did the check before takeoff.I suggest Maintenance take major issues such as flight control concerns from pilots more seriously. I also suggest the mechanic that signed the plane off get more training. Their procedures for flight control checks might need to change. Another aircraft should've been used as an example to see if the problem aircraft felt the same.
Report_1_Synopsis: CRJ flight crew reported a cracked windshield and flight control malfunction resulted in a return to the departure airport; where an elevator control problem was found.

Report_1_Narrative: I am working C position on this flight. I briefed the OWWE (Over Wing Window Exit) and all were in compliance. My A FA; upon doing her final walk through for takeoff had to tell passenger seated XX2 to stow her bag back under the seat in front of her. Passenger in doing so FA A noticed she was wearing a small boot on her left foot. FA A informed the pilots we had to re-seat passenger. Pilots pulled over; passenger was reseated and we went on our way.I do not know the exact time of day this happened; but was told we arrived 5 minutes late. But it says differently on our payroll sheet which says we arrived early. With that being said; we had a few mask situations during descent; one passenger complaining another wasn't wearing her mask; both passenger were through passenger. Announcements were made; 2 of the 4 FAs spoke to the unmasked passenger. During cleaning of aircraft a passenger informed me of the passenger not wearing her mask. I spoke to the unmasked passenger explaining why she had to wear a mask; but we ended up requesting either Operations or a Supervisor to speak to unmasked passenger because she told me the old lady needs to mind her own business. Operations agent took unmasked passenger to jetway to talk and situation was resolved. Unmasked passenger sat YY4 the complaining passenger moved fwd about row XD. Now we're boarding. One passenger tried to sit in OWWE using a seatbelt extension; passengers were letting their masks fall below their nose; a passenger received a call and took her mask off while walking through cabin; I got her attention by stepping into the aisle and put my hand in front of my face. She understood what I was getting at; she stopped; put her mask back on and was apologetic. Both the D & I had heavy mask patrol that flight. While briefing my OWWE I never noticed the boot wearing lady's foot with boot. All items were stowed.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Attendant reported multiple passengers did not comply with face masks policy.

Report_1_Narrative: Passenger would not wear appropriate face cover and became confrontational. The event escalated to the point I had a stress related ocular migraine and was forced to call out sick from the aircraft and seek medical attention. In the event I possibly broke a minimum crew regulation by not waiting for a crew member replacement before attaining medical attention.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Attendant reported a confrontational passenger who did not want to comply with face mask policy.

Report_1_Narrative: Passengers blatantly refused to wear masks. Masks must be worn at all times; even while sleeping in flight. The only time the masks can be removed is while actively eating or drinking. This was the most non-compliant flight to date. There were passengers only covering their mouth and not their nose. There were many passengers who didn't have a mask on at all. When we would ask them to put a mask on they would roll their eyes; pretend to put it on and take it off as soon as we walked away. We all have families to go home to. This is not acceptable. Every other airline firmly enforces the mask policy.Enforce the mask wearing policy strictly for all passengers and all airline crew; including mechanics; flight attendants; grounds ops personnel and pilots.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Attendant reported several passengers did not complying with face mask policy during flight.

Report_1_Narrative: The passenger in seat X1 kept pulling his mask down; he did comply but kept doing it. He was also agitated when we told him we needed his mask to cover his nose and mouth. We were kind about it too. At one point he claimed to have a health condition. It did not say anything in the paper work of mask/face covering exemptions. I informed the other Flight Attendant and she agreed to let the flight deck know. The flight deck asked if he had been verbally aggressive towards us. He had not. The flight deck had a [CSR] meet the plane. We talked to [CSR] because the passenger told them we were rude and we were not. [CSR] told us we handled it perfectly.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Attendant reported a passenger did not comply with face mask policy.

Report_1_Narrative: Passenger X was wearing a face shield without a mask. I noticed during boarding process. I informed him policy is to wear a face mask over his nose and mouth as well. He said for me to stop talking to him and go away.  He said he had a condition. He repeated; that he wanted me to go away and stop talking to [him]. I asked him if he had talked to an agent? He said there was no one to talk to at the gate. I offered for him to talk to a gate agent. He again said for me to go away and did not want to talk to me. He appeared to be pulling a mask out of his bag; as I was offering to go get one for him. The FA C came and [offered] some masks. He told her to go away. Next time I was in the aisle about 10 minutes later; he had the mask on but below his nose and mouth. I asked him to make sure he had his mask pulled up; he was hostile and said he was not going to speak to me. Told me to 'Go away; I'm not talking to you.' I informed the A FA; she informed the CA. They decided to remove the passenger. An employee flying in Row XX witnessed the exchange. He was not in compliance and a safety hazard to other passengers and crew for COVID-19.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Attendant reported a passenger was removed from the flight due to non-compliance with face mask policy.

Report_1_Narrative: I am suggesting that an investigation is launched into the possibility of contract aircraft cleaners unknowingly scratching aircraft windshields while performing their duties. After thinking more about the Tech Ops Update and a recent CBT (Computer Based Training) on 737 Windshield scratching I wonder if the uptick in B737 windshield replacements is from non-certificated individuals inadvertently imposing damage to the windshields. I am not sure what method the cleaners use; what cleaning agents; what type of cloth; etc. Do the materials conform to the Boeing Maintenance Manual? Not pointing a finger here; but just thinking that we may have an opportunity to reduce inadvertent damage to the windshields here if we initiate a change management process. Again; the cleaners are just doing what they believe is their job; but it may have been an oversight that we (company) requested them to clean the windshields; or didn't realize that they were cleaning the aircraft windshields; potentially using a damaging process; chemical or consumable item (rags; paper towels; etc.).
Report_1_Synopsis: Aircraft Technician suggests a link between aircraft cleaning and windshield damage.

Report_1_Narrative: Sorry to have come to you for issues pertaining to night shift but we as Aircraft Maintenance Technicians feel the need to write to you all as our requests to night shift supervisors have gone into one ear and come out the other without any interest to these issues. As you all probably know we at nights perform different checks and routine maintenance on the airplanes sitting out there on the remote pads. We have expressed our concerns to night shift supervisors about the need to add more entry door Stairs/Stands...for Aircraft X/Y types as well as Lighting Fixtures since it's completely dark at night.Now that more airplanes are being parked; what do we have to do so that our requests/concerns are answered?  Answers Supervisors like to say like 'We just gotta work around these issues' are not of people with sound judgment...hence as working group we felt the need to write to you all to explore better possibilities to these specific issues.  Again these are safety concerns we feel need to be address as more planes are being parked in these remote areas we need more lighting fixtures and as well as entry door stairs to better accomplish all the required work assigned.Need management to provide us with entry door stands.
Report_1_Synopsis: Technician reported work environment concerns that aren't being taken care of by management.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Situational Awareness; Distraction; Confusion; Time Pressure; Workload
Report_1_Narrative: While dispatching two aircraft at the same time last night we had an APU door fault on one of the aircraft. While filling out the MEL log item and placard for the APU door message I filled out the log page and started to sign off item and got involved adding a statement to the yellow placard requested by maintenance control. I forgot to come back to that log page and put my signature; I had the date filled out but missed the signature. It was an error on my part trying to get a flight crew out before they timed out. I was trying to comply with too many tasks at one time. Had two departures at the same time and a deadline. Take more time and attention to task at hand.
Report_2_Narrative: A Fuel door recycling Airworthiness Directive (AD) was complied with but the misc. 91 was not sent correctly. We were unaware that there was required text that was supposed to be sent along with the misc 91. This was a relatively new AD and the specifics of compliance were confusing. Since neither the First Officer or I had flown since this AD came out; the fact that wording was supposed to accompany the misc 91 was missed. It would be nice if the exact steps required were readily available in the logbook or somewhere handy during the preflight.
Report_1_Synopsis: Maintenance Technician and a Flight Crew reported the log book was not signed off by maintenance and did not comply with an Airworthiness Directive.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Human-Machine Interface; Situational Awareness; Training / Qualification
Person_2_Human_Factors: Human-Machine Interface; Situational Awareness; Training / Qualification
Report_1_Narrative: We were flying to ZZZ; assigned the XX LDA starting at ZZZ1 VOR. We were instructed to cross ZZZ1 VOR at or above 15;000 and cleared for the approach. We had programmed the avionics to fly the approach and descend on the approach to the glide slope intercept altitude. During the setup we neglected to arm the VNAV. After passing ZZZ1; descending; the aircraft did not level off at 14;000. We noticed the missed level off just before the controller alerted us to a probable altitude deviation. The Captain immediately disconnected the autopilot and returned to the appropriate altitude. The flight concluded uneventfully.I believe there were several factors that contributed to the event. Primarily; the flight crew was legally current but a little out of practice.  A full procedure instrument approach in real-time in mountainous terrain is different than currency and maintenance flights in non mountainous terrain. We have a very strong safety culture; attend recurrent training more frequently than required; and have extensive backgrounds including airline and corporate jet experience but are still susceptible to being 'rusty'.
Report_2_Narrative: [Report narrative contained no additional information]
Report_1_Synopsis: First Officer reported flight missed an altitude level off because they were a little rusty.

Report_1_Narrative: I was riding along with an owner in his experimental aircraft. The weather conditions were VFR; however; visibility was somewhat reduced due to likely smoke/haze and light scatter in the area. Departed normally from ZZZ and headed northwest bound. Listened to ATIS and contacted Approach control and indicated our intentions for continued northwest bound flight for their awareness. We were not planning to fly near ZZZ1 airport; but the airspace is very busy within approximately 30 nm of the field; so participating in traffic advisories is good practice. Typically; TRACON would provide a squawk code and RADAR identification; however; this evening approach control responded to our request and stated 'aircraft calling in; maintain VFR'. As the airspace was very busy with multiple VFR and IFR aircraft during this time; we took this response from ATC as 'we're not interested in another VFR aircraft' particularly since we were not directly arriving into or departing from ZZZ1 airport itself. Despite this response from ATC; we continued to monitor ZZZ1 approach frequency on 132.3.  We leveled-off at 4;500 ft. MSL continued flying northwest bound. Approximately 10-15 mins later; about 5-8 nm south of ZZZ2 airport when we noticed potential conflict traffic on the aircraft's MFD and through the Foreflight App with ADS-B in. Using technology; we noticed the aircraft was flying directly towards us and climbing into our altitude; with altitude difference noted as 500; 400; 300; etc. below and difference decreasing. We attempted to establish visual contact with the aircraft; cross-referencing the iPad display and MFD. The aircraft was noted crossing under our right wing; approximately 300-400 ft. before we noticed the aircraft. Although we were monitoring Approach; it was unclear what instructions the other aircraft was provided regarding our position. In either case; the other aircraft was closer than I typically prefer; without prior coordination. Later on that same flight; we contacted Center to request flight following for the return leg through the ZZZ1 airspace. Center provided us a squawk code; then a few minutes later stated 'Aircraft X; I seem to have lost your altitude squawk; state your altitude.' As we were now returning and southeast bound; I responded with 'Aircraft X; level; five-thousand five hundred.' After receiving this call from ATC; I queried the aircraft owner to see if the transponder 'ALT' reporting was selected on through his MFD. Upon checking; it appeared the transponder was 'ON' but had inadvertently been selected out of the 'ALT' squawk mode. It is possible this inadvertent selection could have contributed to the earlier potential traffic hazard witnessed earlier in the flight. I discussed the setting with the owner and indicated that the transponder should be left in the 'ALT' setting continuously (unless otherwise requested by ATC). We continued uneventfully for the remainder of the flight; despite very active ATC communications; active vectoring and traffic avoidance while returning in and through the airspace into ZZZ. The vectoring; traffic avoidance and unexpected headwinds upon the return slightly delayed our arrival into ZZZ; however; we landed uneventfully.
Report_2_Narrative: On way to Walhalla area from ZZZ to look at fall colors noticed an aircraft from UND Aerospace on a general track towards us at about 1000 ft below our altitude. I believe they were also changing course somewhat also. We monitored as the distance closed. We were on autopilot at 4500 ft MSL and on course of 320. As the other plane closed to 1-2 mi. they began to climb. They seemed to level off about 500 ft. below us but just before our paths crossed they climbed to an estimated 300 ft. below us. My plane is equipped with ADS-B in and out. I was accompanied by my son-in-law who is a CFI. Later in the flight he noticed that the transponder was set to ON not ALT. Because of this I am not sure if the other aircraft was receiving information on our altitude. In hind sight we should have altered our course to avoid crossing like this. I believe this was an instance where having two pilots was a factor in not taking action. In the past when flying with my wife; I have taken action to maneuver around another aircraft in a similar situation. On The other hand; based on the maneuvering the other aircraft was doing it was not clear which direction we would need to go to avoid crossing paths. A lesson learned for me is to check that my transponder is set to ALT on future flights.
Report_1_Synopsis: Sport/Recreation Pilots reported their transponder was not in the ALT position during the flight and this probably contributed to the NMAC.

Report_1_Narrative: I was on Visual Approach backed up with the RNAV Approach. On Visual Approach had a couple big down drafts around 1500 ft. with some precipitation when I went near a big dark cloud. The rest of approach was normal. Fully configured by 1;000 ft and on speed and glide path stable approach. The winds reported were variable at 4 kts. Over the threshold began to flare and pull engine to idle; at about 15-20 ft; at 115 kts; all lift went away; felt bottom drop out of us; and aircraft dropped approximately 15 ft to runway. Control inputs did very little to correct situation to arrest the increased rate of descent. I got a big tail wind gust or got caught in a microburst of some sort. The aircraft slammed onto the runway right main first; breaking and collapsing the right main gear. I slid down runway 2;000 ft. or so before leaving the pavement to the right. No injuries. Pilot and passenger unhurt.
Report_1_Synopsis: Pilot reported a possible microburst or other weather event resulted in a hard landing that caused a runway excursion and damage to the aircraft.

Report_1_Narrative: As I finish my descent checklist and approached to ZZZ from the East 20 NM out I got my ATIS; called ZZZ tower and reported my position. I was instructed to enter the left downwind for runway XX. As I entered the left downwind and completed my before landing checklist I called the tower to let them know my position and I was clear to land. Abeam the numbers I began configuring my flaps after I slow down to my white arc. On base I selected my second notch of flaps and slow to 80 kts; on final I configured to flaps landing and I maintained my final approach speed. On final I stay on my center line; followed the PAPI and crossing the threshold I kept my airspeed about 70 kts began my flare and landed. It wasn't until my mains touched down and the nosewheel was on the ground and on the centerline that I felt a pulled to the left. I corrected to the right to no avail. The nosewheel did not steer to the right. As the airplane slowed down it continue to pull me to the left while I attempted to correct but there was no response on the airplane's nosewheel. The aircraft's left main gear and nosewheel went off the runway. I proceeded to do my shutdown checklist followed by a call to ZZZ Tower to informed them of the event. The tower sent a vehicle to pick us up. I called the tower on the telephone number as requested to provide my information.
Report_1_Synopsis: Pilot reported the nose gear steering became inoperative on landing; resulting in a runway excursion.

Report_1_Narrative: Attempted to load approach into Garmin 3000 touchscreen controller. Slight turbulence caused pilot to touch load/activate button. This single action changes navigation mode; auto pilot guidance; and flight plan screen. Several pilot actions are required to undo the situation; allowing aircraft to leave the designed STAR until either reverting to manual control or completing to navigation system corrections. Perhaps a function that undoes the last command would be valuable.
Report_1_Synopsis: Pilot reported turbulence caused them to activate the wrong button on their Garmin 3000 navigation screen which caused them to lose their current navigation modes and flight plan screen.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Troubleshooting; Training / Qualification; Time Pressure; Situational Awareness; Confusion
Report_1_Narrative: Shortly after takeoff at around 2;000 ft. the right wing tip tank ran out of fuel. The engine then quit. I tried the fuel pump magnetos mixture and throttle. I then squawked 7700 and advised ATC on 121.5. TRACON then contacted me on 121.5 with vectors back to my departure airport and I told them I was unable and landing on the beach. Shortly after that it occurred to me to switch the fuel tanks so I did and what felt like about 30 seconds later the engine roared back to life. I then climbed and proceeded direct to my destination and informed the controller of what I was doing. I landed safely and talked to the police and fire department that was already waiting for us on the ground.I think the contributing factors are earlier in the day was my first time flying this aircraft type in over a year. Another contributing factor is most of my recent time is in an aircraft which does not require fuel tank switching. And the last contributing factor in my opinion is that the fuel gauges were not lit. I believe if they were lit I would have seen them in my scan and noticed the low fuel in the right tip tank before it ran out.
Report_1_Synopsis: Pilot reported that forgetting to switch fuel tanks resulted in a momentary loss of engine power; which was restored shortly after switching tanks.

Report_1_Narrative: We were on a VFR descent into the airport. Approach gave us a handoff to tower. As I was making contact with Tower a white Cessna passed underneath us by 200 to 300 feet. The traffic did not show up on the Garmin 430 and no warning was given by ATC. I suspect that the traffic did not have an operable transponder. They did not seem to notice our aircraft.
Report_1_Synopsis: C182 pilot reported a NMAC with an aircraft that did not appear on their TCAS.

Report_1_Narrative: While being vectored and cleared for an on RNAV Approach as soon as frequency change was advised it was noted a plane was on runway opposite direction that cleared within 15 seconds and another that had taken runway took off at the same time. Evasive maneuver taken by me and no accident happened. As I turned eastbound another aircraft was noted to be on left base for runway 19. Three aircraft had been flying runway that winds did not favor and an accident could have occurred. I am interested in understanding what should have been done differently.
Report_1_Synopsis: Pilot on approach to a non towered airport reported a NMAC with an opposite direction departure.

Report_1_Narrative: Descending to assigned altitude of 13;000 ft traffic with below at 12;000 ft. The aircraft leveled off with autopilot in alt hold at 13;000 ft. I looked down at the FMS; selected direct to assigned intersection; looked up and aircraft was in a descending right hand turn. The Co-pilot indicated autopilot had disconnected and applied back pressure to regain altitude but because of bank co-pilots back pressure increased bank from standard rate angle of bank to 45 degrees of bank. The Pilot applied unusual attitude recovery procedures. Leveled wings then increased back pressure to climb back to assigned altitude of 13;000 ft. There was a loss of 500 ft with altitude deviation.
Report_1_Synopsis: Pilot reported the auto pilot disconnected causing a temporary loss of control and altitude loss.

Report_1_Narrative: Circling for 34 At Chicago Executive. Following a Citation Jet & Challenger Jet. Was circling for 34. Got a lot of wake turbulence behind the jets on the circling approach. Reported it to the Tower [who] suggested [I] do a 360 but because of the altitude of Class B decided not to do a 360 but wanted to stay out of the wake turbulence so could not descend below the Class Bravo. Due to the long base to final to maintain separation and avoid the jet wake [I] encroached the Class B airspace. Was aware of the fact [and] exited as soon as safely possible and landed at PWK.
Report_1_Synopsis: Single Engine Turboprop pilot reported an airspace incursion resulted from his efforts to avoid wake turbulence on approach to PWK in trail of two corporate jet aircraft.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Communication Breakdown; Confusion; Distraction; Situational Awareness; Workload
Report_1_Narrative: Was being vectored for the GPS XX approach at ZZZ.  Was a plane ahead with a similar call sign.  Controller gave me a approach clearance for the ILS XX; I was expecting the GPS XX and the position sounded off.  I turned to join the approach course as I was positioned for this; but then questioned the Controller telling him I thought he meant to give the clearance to the plane ahead.  He said he had but the plane ahead also stated they were given no clearance.The Controller had given me; Aircraft X; the clearance in error.  I then turned back to my assigned heading and the Controller then cleared the other plane.  I never left my assigned altitude.  The Controller seemed over loaded throughout the flight.  The current staffing at ATC seems to be straining their capacity with controllers covering many more frequencies which means pilots tend to step on each other as we can't hear the other frequencies.
Report_1_Synopsis: GA pilot reported ATC clearance issues involving similar call signs and cited Controller workload as a contributing factor.

Report_1_Narrative: During the ZZZZZ X Arrival; a late clearance was issued and believed to have been to 'Expect ZZZZZ1 at 250 knots.' That 'Expect' clearance was read back by the Pilot Flying (First Officer) due to the fact that the Pilot Monitoring (Captain) was speaking to the flight attendants on the interphone. After passing ZZZZZ1; ATC asked to verify that we were at 250 knots; the First Officer/PM responded that we were awaiting the expect 250 knots clearance. The ATC Controller made reference to the fact that he was wearing a face mask and the clearance may have been miss-understood. The Captain returned from speaking with the flight attendants and the First Officer briefed him on the miss-understanding of the 'expect 250 knot' clearance. The aircraft was slowed to 250 knots and the flight continued on the ZZZZZ X Arrival uneventfully.Communication with ATC can be difficult enough. Controllers wearing face masks doesn't seem like a good idea.
Report_2_Narrative: We were descending on the ZZZZZ X. I notified my First Officer that I would be off for a moment; so as to notify the flight attendants to take their seats due to the turbulence. When I notified my First Officer I was back; he informed me that ATC had told us to expect ZZZZZ1 intersection at 250 knots. Shortly after passing ZZZZZ1; ATC queried our speed. We notified ATC that we were at 280 knots but were never assigned the 250 knots at ZZZZZ1 that he told us to expect. ATC commented that he was wearing a face mask and that it was probably hard for us to understand him. We slowed to 250 knots and the remainder of flight was uneventful.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported missing a speed restriction clearance possibly due to the Controller wearing a face mask.

Report_1_Narrative: After an uneventful approach; landing; and taxi to the gate; we approached the J-line for our gate. While verifying that the safety zone was clear; we noticed that a provisioning truck was servicing the forward galley of the aircraft at the adjacent gate. The lower tailgate of the truck was very close to the edge of the safety zone but we determined that it was outside the line and continued. I taxied very slowly because the box of the truck looked close from my angle of sight. We did not receive any signal to stop and parked without incident. However; the wing walker came up to the cockpit to talk to us afterwards and mentioned that he noticed me looking at the wingtip; and he had the same concerns I did. He stated that the wingtip and the truck box seemed very close; approximately one foot in his estimation. He also was wondering if I could see his wand because; at that point; he and the Marshaler had no line of sight with each other due to the jetbridge. My concern is that if I am looking at the Marshaler and he cannot see the left Wing Walker in this situation; then we are essentially blind. Even though nothing happened; I feel like I should have stopped and waited for the truck to move. The Wing Walker and the rest of the Ground Crew did an excellent job getting us parked without incident but that seems like a situation with a high potential for a negative outcome. Although a negative outcome was avoided; it may be beneficial to have a note in the SIP to let Crews know that the Marshaler and Wing Walker cannot see each other at a certain point in the parking process. I don't know if this is a common issue at every gate; but I always thought they could see each other the entire time.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier pilot reported the wing walker told them they missed contacting a parked truck at an adjacent gate by one foot while taxiing in.

Report_1_Narrative: The Pilot Flying (PF) was flying the LINKK1 arrival to ILS 27 at IAH. The PF initiated a VNAV descent on the LINKK1 and was below path during the arrival. Inside of RDFSH while in VNAV we were cleared for the ILS 27. 1500' was called for and set in MCP. Since we were in VNAV and the step downs were in the legs page; I agreed with this altitude in the MCP. Just inside TRANN the PF asked for approach mode; this disengaged VNAV and since we were below the VNAV path we continued to 1500 no longer protected to 2000' at DENTO or FESTA. We were VMC the entire time and had the airport ad runway insight. ATC issued a low altitude warning. We climbed to 2000' and completed the approach normally.
Report_1_Synopsis: Pilot reported receiving a low altitude warning from ATC while on the ILS 27 into IAH; which they attributed to the change from VNAV to approach mode.
