Person_2_Human_Factors: Distraction; Situational Awareness; Workload; Time Pressure
Report_1_Narrative: While descending on the RNAV ARRIVAL within a mile or two of waypoint ZZZZZ the autopilot; for unknown reasons; went into a degraded mode. While in the degraded mode the aircraft continued straight ahead at ZZZZZ not staying on the LNAV course. By the time we recognized the situation and got the autopilot out of the degraded mode the controller informed us we had missed the turn and he gave us a heading. Flight continued normally from there.
Report_2_Narrative: I was the flying pilot. We were arriving on the RNAV STAR into ZZZ. At the time of the incident we were between the ZZZZZ and ZZZZZ1 waypoints; very close to the ZZZZZ waypoint. ATC instructed us to descend. The autopilot was engaged. I pushed the MCP FLCH button to start the decent. Immediately afterward I expected the aircraft to pull the power back and start a descent via the FLCH mode. Immediately the aircraft showed an 'autopilot mode' caution message on the ECAIS. Both the captain and I then realized that the aircraft was not descending as per the selected mode. We did not get a horn or a red autopilot warning message. Also the PFD showed that the autopilot was still engaged via the A/P FMA but the aircraft was not descending. We weren't sure if the aircraft was connected to the autopilot or not as per the conflicting information the aircraft was indicating. We then noticed that the aircraft airspeed was slowing and wasn't descending. I disconnected the autopilot and pushed the throttles forward to correct the low airspeed and pushed the yoke forward to start the aircraft descent. We also disconnected and reengaged the flight directors. We then noticed that the yellow 'autopilot mode' caution message had disappeared. Since we believed that the problem had been resolved I reengaged the autopilot. At that time the aircraft continued to descend and fly at the correct assigned airspeed. We didn't however notice that LNAV had not reengaged since we had just reengaged the autopilot and believed that all the modes had been reengaged correctly via the autopilot. At this time; only about 10 seconds later; we noticed that the aircraft was not tracking the arrival course correctly and immediately turned to the left towards the FMC arrival course to intercept. About 5 seconds later ATC said 'it appears that you missed your turn'; and the gave us a 090 heading. The captain told ATC that we were having autopilot issues and were already correcting back to the STAR arrival course. We were then given two more heading changes. We followed ATC directions for the remainder of the approach and landing to a safe landing with no further incident. I'm not certain; but I may have accidentally pushed the autopilot disengage bar while I was reaching for the FLCH button to start the descent.
Report_1_Synopsis: B787 flight crew reported an autopilot malfunction that caused a track deviation.

Report_1_Narrative: Got too low flaps warning on short final. Flap indicator showed Flaps 25. Flap handle was in landing flaps position. Recycled to no effect. Airspeed was below max flap speed. Aircraft was on safe path and speed for landing. Considered go-around with First Officer but concluded the safest action since all other parameters we stable; was to continue. We continued the approach and landed normally in touchdown zone with normal rollout without event. Flaps operated properly on ground.
Report_1_Synopsis: B737 flight crew reported receiving a Too Low Flaps warning on short final and an incorrect flap setting indication but landed safely with no issues.

Report_1_Narrative: In the logbook and on our flight plan we had MEL 27-88-02 which was suppose to deactivate the Kruger flap system. The logbook was reviewed and the MEL was discussed between the First Officer and myself. All the placards were in place and signed off by maintenance that the DMP was accomplished. We started the aircraft and taxied out to the runway. I did notice a Kruger light on the SFPI; which was in the MEL that it might be displayed. We took off and climbed out. As we retracted the slats we received an ECAM warning and a single chime. The First Office was flying so I handled the ECAM. The ECAM message showed a Kruger not retracted and a notation of MAX SPD 300KIAS/.65. We did our after takeoff flows and checklist and I told the First Officer to fly the airplane and to not exceed the speed shown in the notation on ECAM. I did remember that besides getting the Kruger light that you could also get an ECAM message saying Kruger Fault. This was not the message we received after bringing up the flaps. I decided to get Maintenance Control on the line with Dispatch. I queried the maintenance people about our situation. I explained what we were showing and that it did not correspond with the MEL we had in the log book. We both concluded that if we could we would continue .65/300 knots. Maintenance was sure that the MEL was complied with and that it was probably an erroneous message; but to be safe we would comply with the speeds on the ECAM. After a discussion with dispatch about extra fuel burn and a longer duration flight we decided we were safe even if the Kruger Flap was extended. The dispatcher did run the numbers for fuel burn with Kruger Flap extended. The flight was uneventful and we landed with no further problems. I did make a comment in the logbook about what had transpired during the flight so if this was an anomaly maintenance could add this message to the MEL. We exited the aircraft where I noticed the Kruger Flap on the left side of the aircraft was partially extended. I immediately got the mechanics involved and told them of the situation. We headed to hotel for a 3 hour layover where we were to return to fly later. After returning to the gateway; and heading to the same aircraft we noticed the gear doors down and a panel on the wing root open. I met up with the maintenance people and asked if there was a problem. He told me that the aircraft was out of service. I asked him what was going on and we were told that the DMP for the KRUGER Flap MEL had not been complied with even though it had been stated so in the log book. Our flight was eventually cancelled as they were having some issues with the log book and could not do the DMP for this MEL.
Report_2_Narrative: The aircraft had MEL 27-88-02. During initial climb we received an ECAM for kruger flap not retracted. The MEL did not mention this warning so we complied with the restrictions and called dispatch and maintenance to see if they had any additional information for us and if they preferred us to come back or continue to our destination. Maintenance and the crew felt safe continuing to destination using the restrictions for the ECAM message and dispatch agreed.
Report_1_Synopsis: A300 Flight Crew reported they had a flap problem but continued to their destination then later discovered they were not in compliance with the MEL.

Report_1_Narrative: Received communication from Operations that flight ZZZ to ZZZ1 was coming back to [the] gate because a customer had O2 oxygen tanks not approved for flying.  Went onboard to investigate customer who was traveling with her infant.  The oxygen bottles were for the infant.  I asked if the baby could fly without oxygen.  Customer assured me that yes; the baby could fly; the oxygen was for tonight at bed time when she arrived in ZZZ1.  I advised customer of our policy and that these canisters could not fly.  Customer advised me that both she and the baby and the oxygen all flew in from ZZZ2.  I relayed our policy and advised her that I would take the oxygen down to baggage claim area. Passenger had two full canisters in a black roller board bag; and the 3rd O2 container was in a small pouch with a shoulder strap that easily looked like a shoulder strap purse.  The CSR boarding the aircraft was senior and did not notice any discrepancies that may have alerted her to the fact that there was oxygen canisters being transported.  Once the plane pushed off the jet bridge the flight attendant onboard witnessed the customer with the O2 bottle and inquired about it. Baggage Service is advised and has customer's phone contact; but bottles cannot be flown; customer will need to make arrangements in ZZZ1 for the babies oxygen tonight.  Will also follow up with a report on how the oxygen canisters made it through TSA in ZZZ2 undetected.
Report_1_Synopsis: Ground Agent reported notification of aircraft ground gate return to remove unauthorized oxygen canister.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Time Pressure; Workload; Communication Breakdown; Distraction
Report_1_Narrative: Small airport with a horrible FBO. No line help or marshaling. Got distracted on the walk around by pulling chocks and passengers trying to find his ID. No GPU; so we were rushing to get the engines running to cool down the cabin with pax. Got everything running and programmed. Went to taxi out and realized that the nose gear pin was still disconnected. Shut down the left so FO can jump out and put it back in. We get the pin in; he sits down; start to taxi out again. 7 small aircraft in the traffic pattern and 4 on the taxiway around us; so both of our heads were outside watching for traffic. None of the checklists or flows; after start; have you look at the engines until you set takeoff power. So we accomplished the 'Before Takeoff' checklist; received a 'Takeoff OK'. Took the runway; held the breaks; go to set takeoff power and the left engine is still off. We quickly asked ATC for a short delay on the runway; started the left engine; and made sure everything was ready and all checklist were complete. We were able to depart without any issues. We noticed that the steering was not responsive. Got distracted on the walk around and when being rushed; the nose pin was missed. That led to shutting the left engine down. Shut down the left engine and sent the FO out to put the pin back in. Just need to slow down and pay attention better. And not having any line service made the situation more difficult and rushed. If we had a marshaler; they may have been able to bring our attention to the nose wheel not connected when they removed the chocks. But at the end of the day; it still was my responsibility to make sure it was in.
Report_1_Synopsis: EMB505 First Officer reported lack of ground support; heat; and traffic; resulted in failed compliance with aircraft configuration and procedures.

Person_2_Human_Factors: Workload; Time Pressure; Communication Breakdown; Distraction
Report_1_Narrative: Throughout the arrival ATC requested best forward speed; comply at ZZZZZ: 230kts; 10;000 ft. After ZZZZZ; we were vectored for the approach to XXL. We called the airport in sight and ATC cleared us for the approach. We were also requested to slow to 160kts for spacing with an aircraft in front of us for the same runway. At this point I had flaps 8; and requested flaps 20. [Another] flight was also being vectored for XXL; coming from the west. ATC then asked us to slow to final approach speed and if we had the aircraft ahead insight. We did not have it insight; so were quickly told to turn left to a heading of 270. I believe the [other] flight was then cleared for the approach ahead of us; behind the first aircraft we were following. They then gave us a right turn back to the East and told us to intercept the localizer for XXL; but we were 90 degrees to the course and wouldn't have been able to make it and we weren't configured. I think I remember the controller stating that 'this isn't going to work' and asked if we could accept runway XXR. We said yes; and ATC began vectoring us for XXR. At this point I was very task saturated and should've done a go around. I was very concerned that the aircraft was set up for XXR and verbalized this. He said it was. In hindsight; I should have just disconnected the autopilot. We were configured by the FAF and a stable approach was completed. A go around should have been executed before this situation got so far. We did not have time to find the original aircraft in front of us; and then the [other] flight was thrown into the situation. When ATC switched us to XXR; a localizer frequency should have been offered. The Captain called the tower after we landed to discuss what happened with the supervisor. He said they were happy he called; and the supervisor was watching the whole situation. He also agreed a report should be completed.
Report_2_Narrative: After being vectored on to final for runway XXL from the west at on approach control frequency; I called the airport in sight after we descended below the clouds; approximately 3;000 ft. AGL; ATC cleared us for the visual approach and instructed a speed reduction to 160 KIAS. There was another aircraft on final about 4 miles ahead of us. I offered to slow to approach speed and the controller immediately requested for us to do so while asking if we could also see the aircraft ahead of us. I indicated that I was unable to see an aircraft ahead. First Officer already had flaps 8 and called for flaps 20 to start slowing when I replied that I was unable to see the other aircraft. Suddenly ATC issued instructions for us to turn left to a heading of 270. At the same time; [another] flight was cleared to join the localizer ahead from the opposite direction; from the east; and midway between us and the previous aircraft. As we rolled out on the 270 heading; we were instructed to turn back to the right to a heading of 090 to intercept the localizer. As we rolled through 360 I could clearly see the [other] aircraft; rolling onto final about 2 miles ahead of us. By then it appeared as if the controller was going to want us to join the LOC on almost a 90 degree angle; not fully configured on a 3 mile final. I was about to ask for re-sequence when the controller asked if I could take runway XXR. I responded that we could; without taking the time to consult the flying pilot. As we crossed the approach path for XXL I was quickly pulling up the LOC frequency for XXR and trying to get the frequencies retuned. [Pilot Flying] asked if I was sure it was XXR and not XXC. I followed procedure and got verification from ATC prior to tuning it on the RTU (Radio Tuning Unit). This seemed to take longer than [Pilot Flying] had expected and I was not yet fully aware of his level of stress over the sudden unnecessary changes. We were then vectored through the XXR LOC and given right turns back towards the airport and cleared for a visual to XXR. The approach and landing was stabilized and without further incident. In retrospect; I think not giving [Pilot Flying] time to give his input about accepting a different runway; understandably added to his stress. While I may not have been uncomfortable with what I saw outside the window; I could have made my fellow pilot less comfortable by not asking him what he was thinking. Other contributory factors were compounded when the controller did not offer a LOC frequency whilst changing runways after getting us to less than optimal airspeed and giving us an impromptu tour of his airspace. Our company procedures require us to use an ILS as a backup whenever available; even in visual conditions. This meant that our crew had to simultaneously deal with clarification of communications; following ATC instructions; practice slow flight; and setting up navigation for a late runway change. To add to the equation; there were 80 souls in the main cabin who were certainly wondering why we were zig-zagging around the airport. I think most pilots don't like being loaded up that much in the simulator. Even less do we enjoy such practice in a real airplane at low altitude; and in the most critical phase of flight. Once at the gate; I asked the tower for a phone number to Approach and was given the number that connected me immediately to the supervisor who had been standing behind the controller during the entire ordeal. ATC stated first that he was glad I called. He then explained to me that he had told the controller to re-sequence us and not try to save the situation after his first mistake had put us in a position for an unstable approach. He apologized for the inconvenience and indicated that the [other] aircraft should not have been squeezed into the line. He should have sent the [other] aircraft to runway XXR to begin with. But by the time the situation had developed; it was better for us to break off of the approach than toattempt to turn the other aircraft around. [The supervisor] was professional and wanted to reassure me that such traffic management is not acceptable and that the controller at the helm during the situation was made well aware of that fact. He and I agreed that a report should be filed if it has the potential prevent at least some similar situations from occurring. I can't speak for the ATC practices and procedures; but from my perspective; there are a few variables at play here that should receive a little more focus in the near future. This applies several large class B airports facilities as well warrants adequate and candid discussion. I can't speak for the ATC practices and procedures; but from my perspective; there are a few variables at play here that should receive a little more focus in the near future. This applies several large class B airports facilities as well warrants adequate and candid discussion. RNAV arrivals have been created to help reduce controller and pilot work load as well as simplify clearance delivery. Issue them; let us all fly them as published; line us up; and watch us keep the line moving as you switch us to the next sector. Trust us to do our part as pilots. TCAS tells us how far behind the next aircraft we are. You want separation; ask us to keep 4 to 5 miles and we will do it. We will be far less confused and take up less time on frequency getting clarification of what you actually need us to do. Keeping the frequency more clear will also allow for us confused pilots to actually ask for the help we need when we don't understand something rather than have to wait for a lengthy exchange while a potentially adverse situation gets worse. It would also be nice if there were some regularly scheduled meetings between professional pilot groups and ATC groups. Before 9/11; it was as easy as asking on the radio if we could come visit the tower in between flights. But after all the bureaucrats got involved; common sense seemed to get tossed right out the window and now we have a generation of pilots who have never been to an ATC facility; seen a radar screen; or had the chance to ask questions directly to a controller and vice versa! I would love to see that decision get more attention.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight crew reported ATC sequencing error on approach.

Report_1_Narrative: While in climb to FL410 we were given a turn 20 degrees left for traffic.  Passing through 36;600 feet Controller said a mistake had been made and descend to FL360.  As we were descending Controller gave us a right turn to 110. At that time we received an RA which we followed to 35;500 before we were clear of conflict. We then climbed back to FL360 and reported our altitude and RA event to ATC.  ATC stated there was confusion between two controller's plans. The controllers [should be] on the same page. What happened today isn't a surprise to me. Since the reduction in staffing of the controllers from the COVID-19 pandemic flying has been miserable and less safe. Most controllers are controlling several frequencies and are overloaded. We have had more TA's in the last 2 months than the last 3 years.
Report_1_Synopsis: Corporate jet Captain reported a communication issue between ATC facilities resulted in an airborne conflict.

Report_1_Narrative: During boarding a passenger came on not wearing his mandatory face mask. I asked him to put it on. Before closing the door for pushback; same passenger came to the front to use the lav. In front of the C D [flight attendants] and Ops agent I asked him to put his mask on again. He stated he was eating. I informed the Captain and Ops I told him twice now to wear his mask. The Captain made an announcement about masks and Ops talked to him. He stated he was eating and didn't have to wear the mask. During the flight he continued to eat and never wore his mask. Even to use the lav a second time or when he got into the overhead bin. I called the Captain and asked for a Supervisor to meet the plane. The passenger walked off with no mask on.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Attendant reported a passenger did not comply with face mask policy.

Report_1_Narrative: During taxi out; passenger wouldn't put his seatbelt on.  His Mom told me to 'Force him to put it on.' I declined.  The Dad and Mom both attempted to put seatbelt on their son; but no success.  He screamed and refused all of the way out to runway.  I asked the Mom 'How old is your son'?  She told me that he was 4 years old.  I then told her that he also has to wear a face mask.  Her response was; 'Good luck with that.' Another Flight Attendant also tried to get compliance from them; no luck as well.  I called the CA to inform him.  The other FA informed the Mom that we were going to have to return to gate; and remove them.  We returned to gate; and [they] deplaned.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Attendant reported a child would not wear a seatbelt; nor a face mask and was eventually deplaned.

Person_1_Function: Flight Attendant (On Duty); Flight Attendant In Charge
Report_1_Narrative: During boarding Flight Attendant B let me know there was a passenger who was speaking on her cell phone while not wearing a mask. Flight Attendant B asked her to put the mask on and the passenger said she can't talk on the phone through a mask. Flight Attendant B insisted and the woman begrudgingly put the mask on. As I passed by the passenger she was again not wearing the mask and speaking on her phone. I stood by the seat in front of her waiting for a good break in the conversation for a time to talk with her and she wrapped up the conversation and said sorry and put the phone away. I told her it wasn't an issue with the phone; but the health and safety of those around her. She put her mask on. Shortly thereafter as we were preparing the cabin for departure I noticed her mask was below her nose. She was wearing her headphones and did not hear me; but when she saw me she pulled the mask up over her nose. Based on the attitude she gave Flight Attendant B and the fact that the mask was off again when I came by; and then not properly worn a third time Flight Attendant B and I concurred that if we had to speak with her again it would merit a disciplinary action. We also told the flight deck this; so that they would be aware. Throughout the flight we did have close eyes on her; as one does when a passenger has already exhibited behavior that is against the rules; but I tried not to hound on her. During service I saw her and some others wearing their mask below their nose or off in the long times between sips and I made a PA asking everyone to be compliant (in no way singling her out).Once it came time for final compliance for landing I came back through and again her mask was fully below her nose. I stopped and kneeled down and told her that we had already spoken with her about the mask and that wearing it under the nose does not comply. During the conversation that followed she did not pull her mask over her nose until after I had walked away.She told me that she has a medical condition that makes her light headed and that she has been doing her best with the mask. I told her that while for several months we had mask exemptions for medical cases for the last month it has been mandatory regardless of individual. She asked me for my full name and asked if she could take a picture of my name tag. I told her I was not comfortable giving my last name but if she reached out to the company they would know who I was. She said that I was rude for hounding her and briefly said the word 'Nazi' in reference to my strict adherence to the mask policy and 'targeting' of her.The specifics of timing between what was said during this conversation and what was said in the conversation after I brought disciplinary action and later during final compliance all kind of meld; but these things were said.She said that it was wrong to single out people who have medical conditions and that they don't have to share what the condition is. I reminded her that at no point did I ask her what her condition is and that she only shared that she had a condition at the end of the flight after things came to a head. I also explained again that regardless of condition the mask policy is for anyone who wants to fly.Some guests in the nearby rows thanked me for sticking to the policy as they had had concerns with the passenger in question not wearing her mask throughout the flight. I did my best to thank them for their support; but also to not rile up the non-compliant passenger nor the woman across the aisle who seemed to have befriended and come to the passenger's side (however this woman never spoke up to me or in my earshot). I did not want to put passengers against each other or cause more disruption.Passenger also said that she was not planning on flying [Airline] ever again. We let the Captain know [of the situation] and he called ahead to have a Supervisor meet passenger. During deplaning several of the other passengers that were in surrounding seats and had spoken up again thanked me for the way I handled the situation and said they'd be writing in to the company.
Report_2_Narrative: Passenger was sitting in seat XX1. When securing the cabin before door closure she was on phone and had mask looped on one ear and hanging down and I asked her to put it on she said 'but I can't talk on the phone with it' and I said 'I apologize but it has to be worn over your nose and mouth at all times it is our policy' then she just looked at me with an attitude and then I asked her again if she could please put it on to which she said 'sssuurrreeee' and put it on. Then I informed another FA and told him to keep an eye on her and then he immediately walked through the cabin and she had it off again; not even one minute later. So he also asked her to put it on. After safety demo passenger had mask on but not covering her nose FA A asked her to pull it up and make sure it is covering both her nose and mouth.Inflight there were times she took exaggerated time to eat and drink. As were others in the cabin so we made a PA; (overall I bet we made 20 mask policy PAs during the entire flight).Then during descent FA A observed her with it off again. I seen him having a conversation with her so I approached and he mentioned to her the policy and the reasons and the procedure and then told her he would be back.He said she said she knows the policy. And around that time she mentioned to him that she was trying her best but she has a medical condition. She continued to argue with him and ask for his name to file a complaint. Passengers in front of and behind her gave thanks to FA A for enforcing the policy and said he handled it well. I do believe she overheard them praising him. We notified Captain and he informed [the] arrival station.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight attendants reported a passenger did not comply with face mask policy during flight.

Report_1_Narrative: Passenger in seat X1 had an unusual device that he was wearing.  FA 'A' and I approached the passenger; and asked about his device. He said that it's a Powered Air Purifying Respirator. Powered Air Purifying Respirator had a hose that was attached to the face hood. We talked to gate agent and asked about the device; gate agent did not know anything that pertained to such device. FA 'A' and I looked through our manual and couldn't find anything about this specific device. It's not an Air Purifier which is a prohibited on all flights; it's a respirator which is similar to MPEDs (Medical Portable Electronic Device). The passenger was very compliant; he had a face mask on and a hood shield on. Since we were not sure about this device; we talked to our pilot. Our pilot called operations; and operations said that it's OK with them if we allow passenger to have this device on flight. We allowed passenger to have the device on board.More information needed for situations like these.
Report_2_Narrative: [Report narrative contained no additional information.]
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight attendants reported a passenger boarded wearing a powered air purifier respirator during the flight and they were not sure if it was allowed.

Report_1_Narrative: Aircraft X had a tail pipe fire on Number 2 engine. [Maintenance] troubleshot the issue and found the oil over serviced. The aircraft did an RON (Remain Overnight) in ZZZ. The engines were oil serviced twice. Suggest [safety reports] from both techs on the log pages attached.
Report_1_Synopsis: Maintenance reported aircraft engines were over serviced with oil.

Report_1_Narrative: VFR departure normal. Right turn at shoreline. I departed with flight following but was informed ATC would be too busy along my route and was told to squawk VFR. Limited to the Class Bravo shelf; I set my altitude select to 4500 ft. and engaged the autopilot in the climb. Monitoring the climb; I saw the plane continue the climb past 4500 ft. and where I expected it to settle back to 4500 ft.; instead go through 4600 ft. upon which I disengaged the auto pilot and pushed on the yoke. However; the trim up elevator wouldn't relax; I couldn't turn the trim wheel and all I could do was push hard against the yoke as I busted Bravo and the plane climbed at least another 400 ft. with the trim stuck. I pulled the circuit breaker but it still wouldn't release and I manually pushed the yoke hard to get the plane below the bravo. I cycled the breaker and the switch and finally got the trim under control. I hand flew at 4500 ft. until passing the shelf and continued on my flight climbing to 8500 ft. with no difficulties. Later; I determined that I have a faulty autopilot altitude switch. Getting it fixed tomorrow. In retrospect; I feel I handled the problem calmly but expeditiously.
Report_1_Synopsis: BE58 pilot reported overshooting altitude during climb due to autopilot runaway.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Training / Qualification; Distraction; Communication Breakdown; Confusion
Report_1_Narrative: There are way too many airfields in Central/South Florida that are in somewhat close proximity on the same CTAF (Common Traffic Advisory Frequency) frequency 123.05.   These airfields include GIF Winter Haven; 2IS Airglades; X04 Apopka; PCM Plant City; X26 Sebastian; and X39 Tampa North. On busy days usually towards the end of the week including Thur; Fri; Sat and Sun when the weather is good and many people are out flying; this frequency is completely jammed up much of the day with radio calls from all of the different airfields all at once. It is difficult sometimes to even get a quick call in. Some of these airfields to include GIF; PCM; X04 and X26 are very busy with flight school traffic; local GA (General Aviation) traffic and skydiving (at X26). This creates an unsafe situation when pilots cannot even hardly get a word in on CTAF to give a standard traffic call. Often times pilots will step on each other making calls which creates a jamming type sound which further makes comm more difficult. There shouldn't be this many airfields this close on the same frequency.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Instructor reported that the close proximity of several airports using the same CTAF causes frequency jamming.

Report_1_Narrative: Went out for practice approaches. Wind was calm on departure and enroute; cold front came in on the way back and encountered severe turbulence; severe downdrafts and heavy precipitation in IMC after I was cleared for the GPS RNAV 1L approach. Lost about 2300 ft. causing me to go below IFR minimum altitude in the approach. Could not control the aircraft because of downdrafts and turbulence. Ended up breaking the clouds at about 1200 ft.; no downdrafts at this point but still encountered severe turbulence because of the gusty winds at low level. I was cleared for the visual. Landed safely and no injuries for both pilots on board. Aircraft got inspected by maintenance and there is no damage.
Report_1_Synopsis: PA28 Instructor reported loss of control in IMC in approach due to downdrafts and turbulence.

Report_1_Narrative: During a routine IFR training flight and upon departure from 0S9 (Port Townsend; WA - Jefferson County Intl); we were following the published Obstacle Procedure like we have many numerous times in training and filing IFR. On this day; it was Intermittent IMC above 1500 and VFR under and notable that day was 20 knots plus winds aloft from the Northwest. Upon departure from Runway 09; take off and turning right to heading 090 and in the climb; Turbulence and Tailwind were increasing; and IMC Conditions now present in and out of Cloud Banks. When I went to intercept the 166 radial off the Penn Cove VOR turning North; what was now strong tail winds and light to moderate chop; quickly became a pronounced quartering tail wind with well defined moderate turbulence present. I became disoriented with the leans as the plane was not easily coming level. This created the beginning of an unusual attitude that was best corrected by recovering out of the right turn and remaining in said turn to get back on what was now the controllers vectors of 320 vs As Filed; I was able to recover from this and then began working to comply with ATC as they were inquiring why we were deviating course. I explained to the controller after the plane was stable and back on course that I had entered IMC in Turbulence and experienced spatial disorientation and had to recover. Once the plane neared 4;000 MSL; turbulence lightened; and I was able to proceed on course and as filed to Friday Harbor with no further issue. The rest of the day we experienced strong winds into Bellingham and then back into Port Angeles but nothing else of note. I am writing this to call out what I learned and what I also believe is a risk to myself and other pilots. I believe this Obstacle Departure Procedure places aircraft and pilots while under a potentially heavy workload in IMC in an area that is well known and proven for strong weather convergence with little to no information to fully assess conditions in such a micro climate. I believe there is a safety issue here that could be mediated by reducing the greater than 45 degrees requirements that exists today from 090 degrees bearing to intercepting the 166 Radial and a 346 Bearing. This ODP creates risk and added another link in the chain against me that day; with the strong quartering wind; and turbulence created an unusual attitude and deviation to course. The Instructor and I briefed on what went right and wrong there. We concluded that unusual attitude training cannot be emphasized enough as part of initial and continued training. We also agreed that the use of the Autopilot in heading mode would have helped avoid this situation as I was hand flying through the strong quartering and side wind/turbulence. I also called out that the aircraft has a leaning tendency to the right which I believe was not a key item; but could have added another link in the chain as it may have magnified the strong action the plane took to shift/turn to the right. I am having a Mechanic from a certified service center further evaluate to ensure the plane is in proper rigging beyond what was observed in the last annual inspection.
Report_1_Synopsis: GA pilot reported compliance with unsafe ODP with turbulence and wind required a turn greater than 45 degrees resulted in spatial disorientation.

Report_1_Narrative: [Aircraft X] checked on and I advised him to expect vectors around an active Fire Fighting TFR for a Visual Approach. After a couple vectors and descents; he was crossing the 6700 ft. and 6000 ft. MVA (Minimum Vectoring Altitude) line. I realized he was already level at 6000 ft. I called the airport and cleared him for Visual Approach once he called the field in sight. I called the supervisor over and told him that I may have issued 6000 ft. to the pilot. When the supervisor listened to the tapes and I did clear him to 6000 ft. and he read back 6000 ft.
Report_1_Synopsis: A TRACON Controller reported vectoring an aircraft below the Minimum Vectoring Altitude.

Report_1_Narrative: ZZZ1 started a side-stream handoff on Aircraft X at 60;000 ft. to ZZZ ARTCC. Center flight plan showed the route of flight ZZZ5 […] ZZZ5. The flight plan showed a delay of 4+55 at ZZZ4 and never coming close to ZZZ. The pilot ended up on an incorrect ZZZ UHF frequency and they in turn shipped the aircraft to the correct sector frequency which was the sector that the aircraft was in. The CIC (Controller in Charge) called the ZZZ1 supervisor to try and figure out the route of flight. The CIC was unsuccessful in finding out what the exact route of flight was. I was told about the situation and I directed our TMU (Traffic Management Unit) to contact ZZZ1 TMU to try and determine what the aircraft's intentions were. ZZZ MOS (Military Operation Specialist) was able to contact ZZZ1 MOS and they faxed a depiction of the route of flight which had no flight plan information. The depiction showed the aircraft flying southeast after ZZZ2 but the map did not have the range to display ZZZ's portion of the flight. I called the ZZZ1 Operation manager who was not aware of the situation. The ZZZ1 MOS provided a point of contact (Person A) for the mission. I called Person A and he was unwilling to provide the route of flight. I explained that this aircraft was in controlled airspace and the controllers had no idea where the aircraft was going. By this time the aircraft was 190 miles inside of our airspace. He said that he was unable to provide the route of flight on an unsecured line. He said that the aircraft was going to go a little bit further east and then make a loop back to ZZZ2. Then he said that the aircraft was going to go to ZZZ3 and make a loop. I said that he obviously knew what the points along the flight plan was and that is what I was looking for. He again was unwilling to provide the route of flight. I inquired about this 'loop'. I asked if the aircraft was making a left turn direct ZZZ2 after ZZZ3. We were concerned about the aircraft turning right into Mexico. Person A stated that a loop meant that the aircraft would do one turn in holding with a 30 mile leg at ZZZ3. Then he stated that the pilot may make another loop 100 miles east of ZZZ2 before heading to ZZZ2. Person A stated that this was all coordinated with ZZZ1. I explained that the aircraft is now over 200 miles inside of ZZZ's airspace and that we have no coordination of what is happening. The aircraft flew from ZZZ2 to ZZZ3 where the pilot made a left hand turn in holding and then proceeded to the ZZZZZ area and made a right hand turn in holding and then back into ZZZ1 airspace.ZZZ put in a route that would get the datablock to process back to ZZZ1 but was still not the exact routing that the pilot was cleared. We never did figure out what the route of flight was. ZZZ1 needs to properly update an aircraft's route of flight before making a handoff. These types of missions need to be coordinated with ZZZ's airspace and procedures office before the mission begins.
Report_1_Synopsis: A Center Traffic Management Specialist reported a military aircraft entered their airspace without proper coordination from the adjacent Center.

Report_1_Narrative: During vectors to ICN we got a delay due to unauthorized drone activity. Approach Control was unable to predict the length of the delay. We were at least the 6th aircraft in line being delay vectored. We evaluated our fuel and the number of aircraft ahead of us being delayed and transmitted Pan Pan to Approach Control for vectors to land at ICN. Approach Control would not vector us to ICN. They asked for our alternate airport which was ZZZZ1. We reported to Dispatch of our diversion and followed another flight diverting to ZZZZ1. We landed; parked and later departed again to complete the flight to ICN. This diversion was due to the unauthorized drone activity. No one had the ability to predict the length of the delay. The only known and the safest course of action was to divert to our alternate airport.
Report_2_Narrative: Upon switching approach control we could here holding instructions being given to aircraft.  We immediately began evaluating options for fuel and landing.  After being vectored for around 10-15 minutes Captain made the decision to declare minimum fuel.  The approach controller  responded that we were number 7 for landing at Incheon and requested our alternate airport.  We informed him that Gimpo (RKSS) was the alternate given a vector for approach.  Landing was uneventful.  Apparently there was drone activity near RKSI which prevented aircraft from landing.  Without any clear time frame as to when we would be landing and being number 7 for landing we made the decision to divert.  Don't really have any.  Can't control rogue drone activity.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Captain reported diverting to the alternate airport due to a UAV blocking traffic at the primary airport and holding fuel becoming an issue.

Report_1_Narrative: During the walk around; my First Officer discovered oil leaking from multiple points inside the number one engine exhaust area. I notified maintenance and approximately 30 minutes later it appeared that their corrective action was to add more oil. No attempt was made to investigate where the oil was coming from or to stop the oil from dripping. The line mechanic at this point in time informed me that the number one engine was on a high oil consumption watch. I didn't see anything about the number one engine being on a high oil consumption watch in the maintenance history. The aircraft was refused and I received a new aircraft about 15 minutes later. Lack of investigation into my maintenance concern. Investigate why oil is actively dripping from areas it doesn't normally drip from when an engine is on a high oil consumption watch.
Report_1_Synopsis: B737 Captain reported oil leaking from engine exhaust.

Report_1_Narrative: I was conducting a visual approach to [Runway] XXR backed up by the RNAV Y XXR. I was the Pilot Flying and the Captain was the Pilot Monitoring. We had briefed all the threats and the approach per the AOM prior to the TOD and were planning flaps full for the landing configuration. We were being vectored onto a base leg to join the final visually. I was faster than I should have been on the base for the distance we were out (180 selected speed I think) and so I had to delay calling for the flaps. I think the last altitude we were given was 8;000 feet on the base before we reported the field in sight and were cleared for the visual. The approach had been activated and I went to managed speed. We then set a lower altitude just above the altitude for the next fix after the one just ahead of us on the approach so I could use vertical speed to start down and stay on the path since the approach was not quite captured. I had armed the approach and it annunciated FINAL APP as we were joining the final and the aircraft continued descending on the path. I was using the auto pilot for lateral and vertical NAV until established on final. We extended the gear prior to joining the final to help with slowing the aircraft to flap deployment speeds. The vector had put us in closer than I had anticipated and I had also started slowing later than I should have. The speed did not come back very quickly; possibly because of a tailwind shifting to a headwind as were turning final; so I had to disconnect the autopilot and arrest the descent to get the aircraft slowed for flap deployment and also to prevent an overspeed. Both the Captain and I noticed the RA was close to 1;000 [feet] as we deployed final flaps; and our speed was still well above approach speed; but we were VMC and our assessment was that we had been in final configuration prior to 1;000 AGL. We continued the approach and were stable at 500 [feet] so we landed out of the approach within the required criteria. We were at the gate when the ACARS printed a Self-Assessment Flight Report. We weren't surprised to see Y for speed and descent; but we were surprised to see a Y for flap change. We discussed it; and although we were unstable at 1;000 [feet]; we felt that we had been configured and thought the report generated a flap change Y at 0974 RA because the terrain rises to the north and the spot elevations are around 300-600 feet higher than the airport elevation near where we selected final configuration. Regardless; the final configuration selection was closer to 1;000 AGL than it should have been and we decided we would file an report just in case. Normally; I call for gear down and managed speed at 2;000 AGL so as to have plenty of time to reach final configuration prior to 1;000 AGL; but I missed that cue because I was in the yellow due to being tighter and faster than I had anticipated; and I didn't realize it because I was busy trying to get back in the green slowing and turning final and descending to stay on the path. This is also a case where my experience exceeded my performance due to being new to being back in the right seat and not flying much in September. I also didn't say anything about being in the yellow; and so I didn't get as much help as I could have used. I also failed to brief that we may need to be configured on base depending on where the base leg is and to say something if I don't ask for the gear down by 2;000 AGL. The other factor was conducting a visual approach to a high-altitude airport where AGL altitudes happen at much higher MSL altitudes than were are used to and neither I nor the Captain had been into ZZZ in a long time. I will more thoroughly brief visual approaches regarding the gates I want for configuration and speed changes that provide plenty of margin for a stabilized approach.
Report_2_Narrative: As we turned to intercept final and configure for landing with a near 0 VSI; a hill on final gave us an unexpected 1;000 ft. radio alt call. We where visual and comfortable with continuing the approach due to distance. I recall being fully configuration when the second 1;000 foot reading on final and on speed at 500 ft. We failed to slow down in time on base leg not taking into effect high alt difference and ground speed. We did not brief the ground speed difference and the delayed slow down or terrain around the base turn. Haven't been to ZZZ in years.
Report_1_Synopsis: A319 flight crew reported radio altimeter 1000 foot indication due to irregular terrain resulted in a late configuration for landing warning.

Report_1_Narrative: During cruise flight; approximately one hour and 30 minutes from landing; a call was received from the cabin regarding a passenger; who was not complying with the face covering policy and disturbing nearby passengers. I asked the A Flight Attendant if any assistance or a diversion will be required; the reply was that more information was needed. A short time later; I received a call from the cabin informing me that the situation had been diffused and that passenger was now compliant.While on approach to landing in ZZZ; I received a call from the cabin stating that passenger was out of his seat creating a disturbance. The A Flight Attendant requested personnel meet the aircraft at the gate. Personnel met the aircraft and escorted passenger to the terminal without further incident.Due to the first flight attendants calm demeanor; I allowed myself to believe the incident was not an issue. From this point further; I will involve my Dispatcher as well as other available resources.Monitoring of passengers behavior during the boarding process can sometimes identify potential problems. Whenever possible; it is better to deal with these potential problems on the ground before the flight.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier pilot reported an in-flight passenger misconduct event.

Person_1_Function: Pilot Not Flying; Check Pilot; Captain
Report_1_Narrative: The FA (Flight Attendant) came up about 30 minutes prior to departure and said there was a smell; similar to when a gas stove is turned on but not lit; around the exit row. I was eating and asked the FO (First Officer) to go check it out. He came back and said the report was accurate; so I called Maintenance. I was busy eating and asked MX (Maintenance) if he wanted me to write it up; and he said no. He came on and said he had smelled something outside approaching the plane. Once I was done eating; I went back and smelled for myself. It was just as described. The confusing thing was that I had never smelled anything like it before; nor could myself; any passengers; Maintenance or the flight attendants determine what it could be. We continued trying to solve the problem; going up and down the cabin seeing if it was stronger one place versus the other; and seeing if it was dissipating. We did have a family of four leave the flight; English was not their first language so I am unsure if they understood my briefings. As we were dealing with that; we called OPS to notify them of the delay. Shortly after; our mechanic came up and said they noticed a ramp sweeping machine that runs on propane nearby. Then Operations called and said it was a tug nearby that was leaking fuel. With this information; we decided we would pushback and see if it goes away after we left the gate area. We did and checked with the flight attendant twice during taxi to get an update. The first time she said it was dissipating; and on the before takeoff check to the line; she said it was gone. During descent; in the mid-teens; we got a call saying the smell was back. It wasn't busy so we asked for a quicker route to the airport; which was granted and we landed uneventfully. I have no good answer as to why I didn't write this up. I have thought about it since I got off the phone with Maintenance in ZZZ1; and I cannot think of a reason why I decided to not write this up. Referring to [the] manual. Mechanical Irregularities; D. Reporting Mechanical Irregularities; it does not specifically state to write anything in the MX Log. It simply states if the item is notice prior to block out; to contact Maintenance and they will determine the action required to correct or defer the irregularity. I will re-write to read that any time Maintenance is contacted; a write muse ensue.
Report_2_Narrative: As we were doing preflight duties a FA (Flight Attendant) reported an odd smell in the cabin while passengers were boarding around the exit row. The Captain (CA) asked me to go back and see what I smelled and I did. It was like a natural gas smell mixed with garbage. Nothing I could place a finger on. I reported it to the CA and he went back to check it out. I continued preflight work and he called Mx (Maintenance) out. I didn't hear his and Mx conversation as I continued preflight activities But at the end he told me that the Mx guy could smell it outside and that there was a fuel spill reported from a ground truck in the gate next to us that was the most likely cause of the smell. I continued preflight activities as the Captain finished working with Mx. and he said we were good to depart as long as the smell disappeared when we taxied out. We called the FA on taxi and she said it had dissipated and we departed. On arrival the smell returned and after we reached the gate and shutdown the Captain determined that he had not written up the issue properly in the origin airport before we departed. I believe the Captain was distracted with many tasks and worrying about departing on time which caused him to forget to write up the issue. It's difficult to find a single reason on how to avoid this event. Perhaps more training on specific events that require Mx write ups.
Report_1_Synopsis: CRJ-700 flight crew reported a fumes event during pre-flight; which was described as a natural gas" smell. Maintenance told the crew there was a fuel spill outside the aircraft which was most likely the cause of the smell.  The crew decided to depart and the smell dissipated on taxi-out."

Report_1_Narrative: ZZZ to WRG with 6000 overcast weather 10 miles visibility. Flew a visual pattern to runway 10 WRG at intersection JAXIS with flaps and gear down in the landing configuration. I got a hard terrain warning with all terrain and runway in sight on a visual approach following the track of the RNP 10 WRG. I must have been lower and a 1/2 dot or so west of the RNP approach course. And this is the first time I've flown this approach since the approaches have been updated in WRG; so that warning I got surprised me.
Report_1_Synopsis: Pilot reported terrain warning on approach.

Report_1_Narrative: On touchdown at ZZZ; spoilers came out and caused the nose to rise. As a result; we had a tail strike. Reported this to MX (Maintenance) Control. Green band on tail strike cartridge was still showing but paint was scraped off. FAs (Flight Attendants) in rear of aircraft also heard the strike. Also spoke with [Company Safety] and [Flight Operations].I realize this is mentioned in the FH (Flight Handbook). I will add this to the brief for now on. I have personally only experienced it once. We may also want to add this to the initial or recurrent sim training.
Report_1_Synopsis: B737-900 Captain reported tail strike during landing.

Report_1_Narrative: I was sitting standby and had a mask on for at least 4 hours.  It has been a long time since I walked into in-flight.  I feel very uncomfortable and unsafe not knowing who people are because we are all covered up.  There is no way to look at your ID and know that it is the same person behind a mask.  Again; as I traveled home; once released from stand by; I had a headache.  This is a reoccurring event due to wearing a mask; and this time I was not even on a plane. As I return to work full time; I am very concerned about not feeling comfortable being able to see my pilots' and crews' faces.  I have many studies showing that healthy people should not be wearing masks.  This is not a new subject; it has been studied years ago.And I believe OSHA says that it is not safe as well.  I am also very concerned about the spraying of the aircraft and would like to know the chemicals used.  I take my health seriously and would never put it in the trust of anyone other than myself.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Attendant reported several concerns with individuals having to wear face masks.

Report_1_Narrative: I have flown into MYF several times on an Instrument Approach; ILS 28R. Every time; I am given headings and vectors to final. I have asked for the full approach sometimes; but usually given vectors. The issue is that the altitudes and heading make it very difficult to fly a controlled and standard approach. This last approach I was given a heading to the final approach course at a higher altitude; then turned right and left and then back to final and then a steep descent to be able to get back on the right altitudes for the approach. This has happened about 5 times and usually the same sequence. I am kept high; then a step descent; various headings and then cleared for the approach at the last few minutes. It makes it very difficult to manage speed and altitude. Also; when in instrument conditions it provides an opportunity to become spatially disoriented with the turns and the assigned descent profile. I believe it would be MUCH safer to be given the full approach and follow the listed altitudes. I can tell there is a lot of traffic and a lot of training going on in the area; 2 parallel runways at MYF also present a challenge for controllers; but we should find a way to make the instrument approach be according to the plate. I believe this will make it safer for us all. I respect the Approach controllers and they are dealing with all the traffic the best they can. It just makes the Approach more difficult to fly correctly. If the approach is not workable; perhaps it should be revised.
Report_1_Synopsis: Private Pilot reports on non-standard Air Traffic Control procedure at MYF.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Distraction; Confusion; Situational Awareness; Workload; Time Pressure
Report_1_Narrative: I was working Local Control which manages the class D during north flow operations. Aircraft X had been doing air work at an adjacent airport which is about 8 to 9 miles west of this airport. Aircraft Y was inbound on the ILS. Aircraft Z and Aircraft A were inbound from the southwest. Approach called for a point out to Flight Data/Clearance delivery on Aircraft X and when asked what he was going to do we were told he was going back towards the adjacent airport. Aircraft X entered from the southwest and made maneuvers about 2 to 3 southwest at 2;300 feet and then turned southeast directly overflying Aircraft Y on the ILS by 400 feet. Aircraft Y was issued traffic alerts and broken off the approach to a 090 heading. This put them in conflict with Aircraft B; inbound from the southeast. Another traffic alert was given to Aircraft Y for Aircraft B. Just before Aircraft Y was broken off the ILS approach; Aircraft Z a VFR inbound from the southwest was issued a traffic alert since Aircraft X initially turned opposite direction to them. Aircraft A VFR from the southwest also had to be diverted to the east prior to Aircraft Y being broken off the approach because Aircraft X's intentions were unpredictable and not as described. When asked why flight check was turning east (right instead of left) toward our traffic we were told by approach that 'it is what it is.'Flight Check operations are a high risk to anyone else operating in the area. When they arrive their intentions are incredibly vague other than what they are checking. They often seem to just do whatever they want and let you know as they are doing it. From a local standpoint I think that flight check needs to be a lot more clear of their exact intentions) while operating in the vicinity. VFR arrivals need to be rerouted or placed in holding by approach to a different quadrant other than the one that Flight Check is operating in. This is not the first close call Flight Check has caused over the past few years.
Report_1_Synopsis: A Tower Local Controller accepted a point out of a Flight Check aircraft which did not maneuver as expected causing conflicts with traffic on the final approach course.

Report_1_Narrative: Was kept fast by ATC; and while configuring for landing; inadvertently had a 5 knot flap overspeed when selecting flaps 3.A little tired.  Accepted an ATC clearance to keep our speed up too long. Recent return to flying after 6 month absence.I will feel free to tell ATC 'unable' in such scenarios in the future.
Report_2_Narrative: Was kept fast and high by ATC. While configuring for landing; had an inadvertent 5 knot overspeed while selecting flaps 3.Saw speed reducing below the threshold speed; and lowered flaps; but should have waited for speed to be 10 knots below.Will tell ATC unable if presented with a similar scenario.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported a flap overspeed issue on initial approach.

Report_1_Narrative: We were on a 6 mile final when tower cleared a Cirrus to land in front of us. When this happened separation from the traffic began to decrease; tower then cleared the Cirrus for a low approach. This seemed to cause confusion in the Cirrus cockpit. We continued until the spacing was unsafe; the Cirrus appeared to be on the runway. At around 400 ft. we executed a go around. As we began to climb at go around thrust flaps 8 the Cirrus began to climb as well giving us a TA and tower asked us to side step to the right. I began a turn to the right as the pilot monitoring watched the traffic below us carefully. While our focus was on avoiding the traffic we neglected to call 'positive rate' and raise the gear. This led to a delay is raising the flaps form 8 to 0 to clean up the airplane. Since we were already at pattern altitude we made the decision to leave the gear down since we were moments away from needing to lower it again. Towers poor spacing was the initial cause of the event. However our focus on keeping visual separation from the traffic led us to neglect some of our duties. Although traffic avoidance was and should be our top priority in that situation. We could have called a go around earlier when we saw that there could be a potential conflict. This would have given us more time and led to less task saturation.
Report_2_Narrative: While on about a six mile final tower cleared a Cirrus to perform a short approach to a touch and go in front of us. As we continued the rate of closure was greater than tower anticipated and tower changed the Cirrus clearance to a low approach only. We continued our approach until about 400 ft. AGL. At this time it appeared the Cirrus did a touch and go and was on the runway for a long time. I felt that the separation margin was too small and called for a go around. We completed the first portion of the go around but then the Cirrus had started his upwind and was directly in our path. We prioritized maintaining visual separation with the Cirrus and complying with ATC separation instructions and failed to bring gear up and do a climb sequence until we were on a downwind and ran the after takeoff and then another decent check. After this we completed all check lists and had a safe landing. Poor aircraft separation by ATC. It sounded like there were two controllers in the tower; one being trained and the other a supervisor. Waiting too long to call for the go around. We waited until a go around caused too much going on and made us miss checklists and call outs due to high work load. Misinterpreted instructions by the Cirrus. When ATC changed the landing clearance for the Cirrus it was unclear if they understood what ATC actually wanted. I think the biggest thing that could be done to avoid similar situations is to call for a go around earlier when we saw there might be a conflict with spacing. There were cues earlier in the approach indicating a potential for loss of separation; but it was also possible for us to land had the Cirrus followed instructions in a timely manner. We should have erred on the conservative side to not put us in an overloaded task situation.
Report_1_Synopsis: CRJ-200 flight crew reported failing to retract landing gear during a go around due to ATC vectored traffic.

Report_1_Narrative: [Captain and I] operated from ZZZ to ZZZ1. On this flight we had MEL 29-11-XX; which was for an inoperative hydraulic pump 1B. This MEL required our minimum flight weight to be above 38;500lbs. Our flight load for this particular flight was extremely light with 3 Pax; 1 [standard] bag; 0 Heavy bags; 1 plane side bag and 300 lbs of ballast. Along with excess fuel to help our weight we landed roughly at 38;900 pounds; giving us only 400 pounds of useable fuel on the plane; not enough for the 45 minute reserve buffer; planned at 2099lbs; legally required under IFR.This was my first time experiencing this MEL and I saw the extra fuel for the MEL on the release and after considering the light passenger load both myself and the Captain concluded that we were going to be close to our minimum flight weight upon landing so he asked the fueler to add 300lbs of fuel and 300lbs of ballast to help pad our landing weight; but at the time we both failed to consider the reserve fuel and it was not until I mentioned at a later date that we would have been below our flight weight if we had to go around. At this point he realized we did not have our proper reserve fuel. We had plenty of fuel in the tank but we would have not been in compliance with the new limitation in place set by the MEL.Possibly more awareness on the flight plan of low passenger flights in conjunction for this MEL or a separate fuel column on the release when the fuel is to be used as weight so the crew can consider the fuel as unusable.
Report_1_Synopsis: CRJ200 First Officer reported landing below minimum fuel requirements.

Report_1_Narrative: After leveling off for cruise. I pulled the power levers to set cruise power. As I did I noticed the torque continued to decrease even as I pushed the power levers further and further forward. Eventually the N1 reached below 30% and torque was bouncing between 300 and 500. The plane was losing airspeed rapidly so I request a descent. The propeller was wobbling in the air stream and the plane was shaking. I tried everything I could think of; then came to the conclusion I would need to shut the engine down and feather the propeller. After [advising] ATC I diverted to a nearby airport. Loss of power [occurred] right away. At the time I had no idea [why]. Maintenance came to where I was and determined a failure in the FCU (Fuel Control Unit) caused the engine to lose almost all powerFollowing training procedures securing the engine and landing as soon as practical.Maintenance [is] checking the state of the FCU; but it seemed like a rare event that might be difficult to predict and train for.
Report_1_Synopsis: Beechcraft 1900 Captain reported loss of engine power during flight due to FCU failure.

Report_1_Narrative: While being vectored by Approach Control on approach to Runway XXC at ZZZ; we were held at 4;000 ft. on the base leg with instructions to maintain 210 KIAS. We were subsequently given clearance for a Visual Approach to Runway XXC. The pilot flying from the left seat was the PIC (Pilot in Command). I was the SIC (Second in Command)/pilot monitoring from the right seat and acknowledged the visual approach clearance. The pilot flying made appropriate use of power levers; speed breaks; flaps; and landing gear to set up for a stabilized approach as he attempted to descend and intercept a normal glide path on final approach to the runway; while maintaining the requested 210 knot speed restriction. Once established on final; but still above a normal glide path; the PIC asked me to query ATC as to whether we could resume normal approach speed. The controller replied; 'When I clear you for a visual approach; the speed restriction is removed.' Noting that we were still above the PAPI and glidepath on final approach as a result of being kept at high altitude on the base leg and while descending through approximately 2;000 ft.; both crewmembers agreed that the aircraft could likely be configured to salvage a stabilized approach. However; as we descended through approximately 1;000 ft.; we realized that we had not been handed off to the control tower. As the approach control frequency was busy; I attempted to switch to the control tower frequency automatically; and was trying to reference the approach chart on the pilot's side display for the appropriate frequency; as there were three listed for the various runways. As a break in communications presented itself; I quickly queried approach control; 'Aircraft X to tower?' The controller responded that we should already be on the tower frequency; which he had not yet instructed us to do; and which was not the published frequency for Runway XXC. As the aircraft was now on short final; slightly above glide path; notwithstanding the long length of the runway; and the fact that we had not received landing clearance from the tower; the crew immediately agreed to go around; and smoothly initiated a go around procedure. I checked in with ZZZ Tower to advise we were going around. We were vectored by tower in a left hand traffic pattern at an appropriate altitude; without speed restriction; and were able to properly configure; execute a visual approach and land without incident.The crew could have solicited a lower altitude from Approach on the base leg and/or stated that we were unable to maintain the 210 KIAS speed restriction in order to establish ourselves on the final approach course at an appropriate altitude and speed for a stabilized approach. We could also have solicited a handoff from approach to tower frequency sooner. The decision to go around was prudently made and smoothly executed. However; we should have made the decision to do so at 1;000 feet AGL due to our position above the normal glide path (unstable approach) and not having been handed off to tower.
Report_2_Narrative: While being vectored for a visual approach to XXC at ZZZ; approach had us turning a close in base at 4;000 ft. and 210 knots as assigned. Once we were on the final approach course; we were cleared for the visual approach. I knew that we were both too high and too fast; however I thought with the use of drag devices we could become stable prior to 1000 ft. per our FOM. I noticed that we were on a 2-3 mile final and had not been switched to the tower controller yet and asked the PNF (Pilot Not Flying) to query the approach controller. The approach controller stated that he had handed us over to the tower controller; neither of us in the cockpit heard that or acknowledged that instruction. The PNF was searching on the approach chart for a tower frequency and there was some confusion as he was trying the read the chart and which frequency he should be on. By the time I could have the PNF query the controller again; I realized that we were not going to be stable within the parameters of the FOM. I made the decision to go-around and informed the PNF to tell the approach controller we were executing a missed approach. The approach controller gave us instructions to fly runway heading to 3000 ft. and vectored us around for another visual approach which ended up in a stable; uneventful landing.I should have realized earlier on in the approach that we were vectored onto the final approach course too fast and too high. The PNF should have preloaded the tower frequency into the Radio Tune page. The decision to execute a go-around was correct but could have possibly been made sooner.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight crew reported a go around due to unstable approach and late handoff from approach controller.

Report_1_Narrative: On taxi out the flight attendants contacted us to advise of a passenger disturbance regarding the use of face coverings.  Two passengers were asked up to four times regarding the proper use of the mask and were advised that both the nose and mouth must be covered at all times unless actively eating or drinking.  They initially complied; however; they continued to pull the mask below the nose which was the cause for the several attempts by the flight attendants.  Upon first contact; I made an additional announcement regarding the policy of face coverings and stated to the flight attendants that returning to the gate may be an option to remove those individuals that were non-compliant.  Shortly after I was advised that the passengers were finally cooperating and we continued on to our destination and advised to keep us advised to any further issues. I contacted Dispatch in-flight and advised of the situation; I asked that an airline representative and security meet the plane to discuss further policies regarding face coverings which concluded the incident.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier pilot reported being advised by flight attendants during taxi out that passengers were not complying with face mask policy.

Report_1_Narrative: At ZZZ; my student and I were taxing to runway XX when we observed a man standing past the runway threshold marker off of [the] taxiway. He was standing in the grass just off of the runway and another [aircraft] was doing touch and goes. I alerted the landing Aircraft Y that the man was there and that it would be a runway incursion if he chose to land. He did not respond and continued to come down to land. He got off on the taxiway next to the man and taxied behind us. Aircraft Z started taxing and we asked if the man was still on runway XX as it was out of our visual range. Aircraft Z confirmed that he was still standing on the runway so we continued to wait. After a few minutes passed we got a call over the radio from the FBO at the airport that the man had entered Aircraft Z and he was no longer on the runway. Much to our surprised after we got going on runway XX the man was still present on the runway but he was crouching next the runway by the taxiway sign which is still past the runway threshold. We continued on our flight.
Report_2_Narrative: On taxiing for takeoff; my instructor and I noticed several people seemingly wandering out toward the runway environment. We waved them to go back toward the hanger area. As we continued taxiing; we saw another male standing alone at the edge of runway XX/XY. He was beyond the taxiway hold markings and physically standing on the runway where it meets the taxiway. We notified the FBO that there were people on the active runway; and warned the incoming landing aircraft of the imminent probability of an incursion. The pilot did not acknowledge our transmission and continued to land; pass by the person standing in the runway edge and taxied up behind us. We had completed run-up; while my instructor was on the radio notifying the FBO again of this additional person on the runway. We held our position in the run-up area for runway XX; and another taxiing plane confirmed that the individual was still on [the] taxiway; and still on the runway side of the hold markings. A few moments later; the plane that had landed with the person on the runway finally came over the radio and stated the individual was his instructor; and he was just soloing. We informed him to please reach out to him and have him move off the runway. No response. During this time; the individual was beyond visual range; so we waited to take the runway until the FBO resolved the issue. After a couple more minutes; the FBO radioed that he was now gone; and had gotten into Aircraft Z probably; but was gone from the area. We took the runway; and made our takeoff run. Just after takeoff; we observed the man crouched behind the taxiway identification sign; still in the active runway area. We radioed back to the FBO to notify them that he was in fact; still on the runway environment. We were not in close enough proximity or on a path to collide with him; so we took no evasive action; and processed with our climb out and continued our flight as scheduled.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight instructor and student reported a man standing near the active runway environment.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Distraction; Situational Awareness; Training / Qualification; Confusion
Report_1_Narrative: Pilot and a singe passenger were returning for a landing in VMC (winds light and variable); and cleared For landing by Tower. After what appeared to be a normal landing; on-centerline and during roll-out;(the plane was rolling below 30 kts); the aircraft unexpectedly began to pull to the right. The pilot attempted to correct using left rudder pressure and toe brake. The combination of left rudder pressure and left toe brake did not appear to exert sufficient braking authority or correct the turn. The aircraft seemed very slow to correct direction. The pilot continued with left rudder pressure and applied the handbrake. The plane immediately slowed; but rolled off the right side of the marked runway (and onto the apron) as the pilot was able to regain directional control. This was just past the first taxiway; where the underside of the right wing scraped the top edge of the taxiway sign. There did not appear to be any damage to the sign; but the bottom skin of the right wing was later found to be torn; in a line perpendicular to the leading edge; on the outboard side of the wing; about half-way to the from the front of the wing; and the skin tear exposed the bottom edge of the wing spar; which appeared to be nicked. Using the handbrake only from that point on; the pilot was able to return to the runway centerline and taxi the plane on the runway to the next taxiway and then navigate to parking with no further directional control problems. The incident was promptly reported and the plane was grounded for inspection and repair at visual inspection by a qualified A&P.It had been noted that on one prior flight that the plane had unexpectedly pulled to the right; but that the problem had been evaluated and resolved. On pre-flight taxi and takeoff during the flight on which the incident occurred; the plane did not appear to be pulling excessively to the right; so the pilot believed that the earlier squawk had been resolved; and the pilot decided to conduct the flight as planned. The pilot was well-rested; in good health; and alert during the flight. A potential distractor was that the oil access door on the cowling popped open on climb-out after takeoff (this resulted in the decision to return to land and correct the issue before continuing the flight). It is possible that this issue may have distracted the pilot. Also; the pilot may not have reacted quickly enough when the plane began pulling to the right on roll-out; and may not have transitioned quickly enough from applying the toe brake (which did not appear to be effective)to using the handbrake (which applied effective braking on both mains). Finally; as a final possible preventive action; the pilot might have elected to touch-down on the left side of the wide runway; anticipating the possibility of the plane pulling to the right.
Report_1_Synopsis: PA28R pilot reported runway excursion on landing.

Report_1_Narrative: 4;500 ft MSL ZZZ to ZZZ1; about 22 mile straight in for RWY XX at ZZZ1 over near the town. While flying my student asked me what the object was to our 10 o'clock headed our direction. As I looked over I thought it originally was a bird; then as it got closer I realized it was bigger and red. I first thought it might be a red ballon floating; but then I saw a red flashing light on the top and thought we might be getting close to hitting a tower; but saw nothing below the object. No tower; no string or ribbon; nothing attached below it. Upon closer inspection quickly as it passed by my left wing; approximately 2 wingspan away and just a couple feet high; it looked like a spinning top or dreidel; larger up top and smaller on the bottom; reddish orange in color with a flashing light on the top. I immediately notified Approach and they said they had nothing on radar in the area. I gave a description to the best of my ability in my surprised state. I also requested a phone number from them to speak with them when finished. Nothing else noted or resulted from the event.
Report_1_Synopsis: C-172 Flight Instructor reported an uneventful NMAC event with an unreported drone during training flight.

Report_1_Narrative: [Aircraft X] checked in at 6000 ft. It appeared to be deconflicted. I hadn't noticed it was at an incorrect altitude for said airway. I noticed the aircraft at 6000 feet on the airway. I presumed Approach put him at the correct altitude. At this area on the airway there are no depicted intersections or compulsory reporting points. At 6000 feet he was the right altitude for direction of flight. I moved on to other D Side (Radar Assist) duties. Minutes later the Radar Controller was checking the airway altitudes; MSAW (Minimum Safe Altitude Warning) alert went off and the aircraft was given a climb. At check on 6000 feet was appropriate per the MIA (Minimum IFR Altitude) though not the MEA.Recommend a better vigilance. I would normally check routes and altitudes prior to taking a hand off.
