Report_1_Narrative: During a flight to maintain currency an upset event occurred.  Aircraft X took off from ZZZ on a VFR flight with flight following.  After takeoff and communication hand off from ZZZ Tower to Departure; Aircraft X was instructed by ATC to maintain runway heading due to traffic.  After watching the traffic pass on the moving map display and no other traffic in the immediate area; asked ATC for permission to proceed on course.  ATC apologized for the delay and cleared Aircraft X to proceed on course.  Leveling off at 5;500 feet MSL and after visually and electronically checking for traffic; setup for slow flight and approach to stall practice.  Retarded throttle; airspeed was already below 165 knots so landing gear was extended; verified all gear was down and locked.  Held altitude while speed bleed off; applying flaps incrementally until fully extended.  Began stabilized slow flight; adjusting throttle and pitch as necessary to maintain 5;500 feet.  Winds at 5;500 MSL were 18 knots and there was some light turbulence.  After 1-2 minutes of steady slow flight the airspeed indicator dropped quickly even though there were no rapid throttle or control surface adjustments.  The stall horn began sounding continuously and the aircraft experienced very slight buffeting at which point full throttle and downward pitch were applied simultaneously and in the same instant the right wing dropped extremely rapidly as if the aircraft had been commanded into a snap roll.  The roll continued even as left aileron and left rudder were applied with no effect and in less than 2 seconds the aircraft was inverted.  At this point the nose dropped and the aircraft entered a right-hand spiral dive.  The throttle was immediately retarded and standard recovery efforts begun.  Attempts to level the wings were complicated by the g-forces as the pilot struggle to remain upright.  At least 5-7 right hand turns occurred in spite of left aileron input.  At approximately 500-700 feet AGL; control was reestablished and the aircraft returned to zero roll.  A climb was initiated and as the airspeed dropped the pilot remembered the aircraft was still in full landing configuration with the throttle at idle.  Power was added; flaps retracted one notch and the landing gear was retracted.  Continued retracting flaps one notch at a time as speed and altitude increased.After returning to a safer altitude; all aircraft controls were checked and seemed to be normal with no apparent explanation for the un-commanded roll.  Only after landing and examining the aircraft was the extreme damage noted.  Apparently during the spiral dive; the aircraft exceeded speed and g-force limitations even though the pilot does not recall an overspeed warning.
Report_1_Synopsis: PA46 pilot reported loss of aircraft control and aircraft damage.

Report_1_Narrative: I had flown several days prior to ZZZ2 past Yakima and passed West of Boardman (R-5701) making sure to avoid that restricted airspace.  Then a few days later; October XX again passed East of Boardman making sure to avoid it on my way to ZZZ. Living [in area] and interacting with many military pilots; I am fully aware of the MOA and Restricted airspace as they are heavy users of it.  That morning when landing at ZZZ we planned to make a brief visit to stretch our legs and make a bathroom pit stop.I had created a VFR flight plan at ZZZ2 and felt the stop at ZZZ was a good layover. Around XA00 I determined from my cell phone that conditions had improved to VFR but with smoke fairly heavy.  We had already flown through a layer of it coming to ZZZ.  My concern was that we were not sure if the smoke would create a problem through the mountains.  The afternoon was heating up and on departure I was focused on keeping my #2 cylinder temp within reasonable limits so was paying a lot of attention to it as we continued the climb out headed straight towards ZZZ3 and the mountain pass.  I never even realized I was in restricted airspace or I would have turned around.  I was climbing throughout the time in the R-6714A area and did not reach my altitude of 6;500 feet until I was pretty much out of it as near as I can recall.  We were also busy watching for other airplanes in the haze recognizing that some still do not have ADS-B.  By the time we reached ZZZ3 it was clear to me that the smoke was not that bad and we still had adequate visibility.  We did not encounter any aircraft in the [area].We flew home without incident and landed at ZZZ shortly after XB00.  One aircraft was in front of us upon landing.  We landed and put the plane in the hanger and went home.  The pilot that landed prior to us texted me that NAS ZZZ Approach had called for me; at least that is what he thought.  Since neither I nor my wife had heard anything I did not know what to think.  Later I was wondering if they had but couldn't understand why they would have had reason.  I decided to return to my hanger and get my tablet out to review my flight.  At that time I realized that I had unknowingly flown directly through R-6714A; a huge no- no.  That is when I called ZZZ Ops and they passed me onto Approach who passed me to Center.  I spoke with a staff member and made sure he had all the information needed.  He assured me he had what he needed to finish his part and the case would then move to FSDO.Having realized what a blunder I had made I began to reconstruct all my actions and thinking that got me into flying into R-6714A without realizing I was in restricted airspace.  I would never have know had Seattle Center and ZZZ1 not followed me home to ZZZ1.  Of course; I fully realize there are no secrets as I have ADS-B.  I know the whole things falls onto me for not having paid more attention to the map.  Lesson learned is that I need to pay more attention.  I think I got complacent in thinking I knew the area because I had flown by ZZZ3 many times through the years; but not by this airspace.  I use FlyQ EFB and keep on top of being current so that system provides the correct data for me to note; I just need to pay more attention to it.  I will explore if it can be more helpful by informing me when I am about to fly into airspace that is controlled.   I also think as pilots we pay more attention now to the ADS-B Traffic we get on our tablets than to what the map is sharing below that traffic.  I wonder if we shouldn't be having more training on tablets and their use in the cockpit.  In summary; I regret that my incursion interfered with a military exercise and hope that the distraction was minimal.  I am not fond of these kinds of hard lessons and will work to make sure that does not happen again.  I also apologize for the extra work everyone is doing as a result of this incursion.  I hope my story can be useful in improving safety.
Report_1_Synopsis: RV6 single pilot reported a Restricted Airspace Violation.

Report_1_Narrative: At approximately XA00 local time; at ZZZ at an uncontrolled field; I taxied out to the threshold of RWY XXL in biplane single place open cockpit with no Radio. Seeing [no] aircraft in the pattern or on final; I proceeded to take off. Unknown and unseen by myself; a Beech aircraft lowing four-place mono airplane was approaching to land on Rwy XXL. The Beech pilot initiated a go-around to an uneventful landing; announcing that a runway incursion had occurred. Aircraft separation was estimated as several hundred yards; and no damage was incurred by either Aircraft. Difficulty in seeing a blue and white aircraft with blue sky background; and the Aircraft was not flying the designated traffic Encourage all traffic to fly a designated flight pattern and maintain visual awareness and alert to all traffic.
Report_1_Synopsis: An Experimental Biplane pilot; no radio; reported runway incursion when pilot failed to observe traffic on final; resulted in aircraft go around.

Report_1_Narrative: I was in communication with ZZZ Center; I checked in and the check in was acknowledged.  With COVID I have become accustomed to long periods of silence on the radio.  After a while; I think about 30 minutes; I realized it had been too long since I heard a radio communication.  So I tried to raise ZZZ Center; but received no reply.  I asked any aircraft on my last assigned frequency if they would ask Center what frequency I should be using.  A helpful pilot relayed that frequency; and at the new frequency I was able to contact ZZZ1 Center.  There were no further issues after that.
Report_1_Synopsis: GA pilot reported having communication issues with Center.

Report_1_Narrative: Aircraft Y landed prior to student pilot landing. Student experienced wake turbulence while touching down. ATC had not advised student pilot of wake turbulence separation.
Report_1_Synopsis: Student pilot reported encountering wake turbulence at touchdown from the preceding small turbojet aircraft.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Time Pressure; Troubleshooting; Situational Awareness; Distraction; Confusion; Communication Breakdown
Report_1_Narrative: Lead FA brought to attention of flight deck crew that she had requested PPE and it was not delivered. We requested through operations that we needed PPE for FAs. Cockpit crew gave our bag of gloves to FAs while we waited. Gloves delivered to FAs; but were extra small and did not fit. Called Operations said they were all out of proper sized gloves and they were on back order. I advised Lead FA (she was upset) wanted to know name of station manager. I advised her to write [a] report and I would write report. No conflict with FA and cockpit crew.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported flight attendants did not have correct sizes of Personal Protection Equipment to work safely.

Report_1_Narrative: Coming into Scottsdale from ZZZ; we were cleared direct to DSERT for the DSERT2 RNAV (Area Navigation) arrival; then given instructions to cross YOLOW at 7;600 ft. and 250 kts. I put the altitude and speed in the FMS (Flight Management System) and the PF (Pilot Flying) set the AAD to 7;600 ft. and initiated the descent. Prior to reaching YOLOW; we acquired the runway at SDL and informed Approach; who simply acknowledged our transmission. We crossed YOLOW at 7;600 ft. and 250 kts; and shortly after were cleared for the visual approach to Runway 21 and instructed to contact Tower. The PF (Pilot Flying) began slowing the aircraft by reducing throttle and extending speed brakes while I activated the secondary flight plan containing the DSERT visual Runway 21 approach and activated the leg from YOLOW to EEDGR. The PF put 3;400 ft. into the AAD and activated VS (Vertical Speed) and dialed in a descent rate to reach 3;400 ft. at EEDGR. The PF directed me to extend the gear to assist with the descent and speed. Just prior to EEDGR we received a SINK RATE alert; and the PF shallowed the descent slightly; so we crossed EEDGR at approximately 200 kts and 3;600 ft. At the appropriate speeds; I extended the flaps; and shortly above 1;000 ft. AGL (Above Ground Level) we received a TERRAIN PULL UP alert; at which point I called for a go-around; which the PF executed. We climbed to 3;000 ft; ran the appropriate checklists; and then made a normal visual approach and landing.As we crossed EEDGR; the PF dialed the AAD to TDZE (Touch Down Zone); allowing the aircraft to continue descending while we attempted to get on profile.The PF and I were both distracted attempting to configure the aircraft and meet the profile of the approach. We both felt that the altitude and airspeed assignment at YOLOW made the switch to the REQUIRED visual approach with RNAV waypoints very difficult; and if we had simply flown a normal visual approach (which we've been doing for 15 years); we would have been fine. We were unable to configure early due to the ATC (Air Traffic Control) clearance; and the extra altitude carried past YOLOW forced a potentially unsafe descent rate. In the future; I will refuse a clearance to cross YOLOW at 7;600 ft and 250 kts if I expect to fly the visual to Runway 21. I feel the [Company] procedure as published actually reduces safety by drawing one or both pilots' attention into the cockpit during a critical phase of flight.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Crew reported terrain alert on approach.

Report_1_Narrative: At AVL; there are two (parallel) runways. One is a temporary runway with an ILS and GPS approach. The other runway is new (under construction) with fresh asphalt pavement and markings. On a five mile visual approach; it can be confusing as to which runway is the active runway and which runway is under construction. During the daytime; the flashing 'X' at the approach end of the runway under construction is difficult to see until approximately a 2 mile final. Unless you are tracking the localizer or the GPS course to the 'west' runway; it is entirely possible to line up and land on that new runway. Also; there are no NOTAMs associated with the new runway except for some taxiway NOTAMs. Add to [the company's] release a note describing the two runways and to not mistake the east runway as an active/open runway. Also; there should/could be a NOTAM filed regarding the current runway situation.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Captain reported there is not a NOTAM or company flight plan note regarding runway construction.

Report_1_Narrative: As we were taxing out in SMF to RWY 35L; the taxiway narrows and becomes a GA taxiway with a weight limitation. I was the First Officer and I was running the Before Take Off checklist when the Captain stopped the aircraft and informed me that he had missed the turn to the runway. He said that he had been distracted by his PFD that had gone blank for a moment. We informed ATC and they said that they were going to send out a tug. The aircraft didn't go past the intersection more than 5 feet; but it was to tight to make the turn; so we waited for the tug and were pushed back a few feet. After completing the push back we continued with the normal operation of the flight.
Report_2_Narrative: As we were taxing out in SMF to RWY 35L; the taxiway narrows and becomes a GA taxiway (250;000 lbs limit). As the First Officer was running the before take off checklist; my PFD went blank and distracted me enough to miss the taxiway. I quickly reacted and applied the brakes. Once the aircraft stopped I reassessed the situation. the aircraft nose wheel was still on the taxiway but the nose was just far enough as to not be able to make the turn. I informed ground of the situation and they sent out a tug. We were then pushed back approximately 5 feet. Once the tug and bypass pin were removed my First Officer re-ran the before taxi and before takeoff checklist. There is little to no indication that the taxiway narrows and become a weight restricted taxiway. Had there been visual cues of this; the incident more than likely would not have happened.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Pilot Crew reported inadequate warnings available for weight limitation change for a taxiway at SMF Airport.

Report_1_Narrative: Climbing to 7;000 feet with Aircraft Y traffic at 8;000 feet MSL.  Turning from departure heading of 035 to assigned heading of 320.  Received a TCAS TA and a TCAS RA at about 6;700 feet MSL to 'Level Off.'  Complied with the RA and notified ATC.  Traffic passed above and behind us.Climbing turn near traffic with light aircraft climbing faster than normal (235;800 lbs).Shallow climb rate near traffic.  We were very light with a takeoff gross weight of 235;800 lbs.
Report_2_Narrative: We were climbing to our initial level off altitude of 7;000 feet on a 035 heading. Departure alerted us to traffic at our 12:00 O'clock at 8;000 feet and had us turn to 320. At approximately 6;700 feet; the TCAS alerted us to traffic and then in the turn leveling at 7;000 feet the TCAS alerted us with an RA to level off. We complied and traffic passed behind us. We alerted ATC of the RA and are filing this report.Light aircraft (235.8 lbs) out of ZZZ maybe confused departure and we climbed to altitude faster than other airline aircraft usually do. Also busy terminal area with lots of GA traffic all could be potential causes. No one felt threatened likely in either aircraft but RA did go off.Earlier vector from departure away from oncoming traffic despite altitude separation.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier flight crew reported over shooting an assigned altitude with a light aircraft; resulting in an airborne conflict.

Report_1_Narrative: Earlier today; I received a phone call from my Chief Pilot asking about a plane that I flew over the weekend that had a fuel leak. I explained to him that while we were on a turn; we requested a lavatory service. When the lav tech came out to service the plane; he indicated to me that he was unable to service the lav; nothing would come out. I ended up calling line Maintenance to come out and trouble shoot. Once they arrived and tried to fix the issue I was made aware that they would be unable to fix the issue in a timely manner and said that we would be swapped into a another aircraft. Shortly thereafter; I received a text (which I did not hear) and then a phone call asking me to close out of Software from the company. I then proceeded to log out and started to pack up my stuff to head to the new aircraft when the fueler; who was just outside with the original aircraft; said 'I have something you need to see'. When I followed him outside; he showed me that when he added pressurized fuel to the plane; fuel slowly started coming out of the bottom of the right wing root; about 3 feet down from the fuel panel. I then called line Maintenance back (as they had already left the aircraft) to let them know about the fuel leak and that I was no longer logged into Software and was unable to write up the this new issue. I confirmed with them my gate and that I was the plane with previous lav issue. I said that I would leave a hand written note describing the new fuel issue on the captain's yoke and line Maintenance said that would be fine.This event was caused by the discovery of a new mechanical issue after I was logged out of Software. Contributing factors include: my inability to sign back into Software with an old aircraft after I have been assigned a new one; trying to maintain a timely schedule for the passengers who were moved to another aircraft/gate and trusting that line Maintenance would note the new mechanical issue from my phone call and the hand written note that I left on the yoke and write it up themselves when I am unable. Allowing a pilot to log back into an aircraft after they have already signed out and discover a mechanical issue. Or maybe having Maintenance write up the issue while the pilot is still on the phone when they are notified that the pilot is logged out and unable to write up an issue.
Report_1_Synopsis: Captain reported being unable to report a Fuel Leak on an aircraft using the electronic log book; causing a cancelled flight and a long delay for the passengers.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Time Pressure; Workload; Confusion; Distraction; Situational Awareness
Report_1_Narrative: ZZZ Arrival ATIS C was current; advertising visual approaches to Runways XYL; XXL; and XXR. Prior to descent the Captain and I had thoroughly briefed visual approaches to both Runway XYL and Runway XXL. We requested Runway XXL on initial contact with ZZZ TRACON and were granted the request before ZZZZZ on the ZZZZZ2 STAR. We were vectored after ZZZZZ1 onto a left base to Runway XXL; then a turn to join final; which accompanied the visual approach clearance and change to Tower on [frequency]. I called Tower advising we were on a visual approach to Runway XXL and would be parking at gate. Tower responded with 'Runway XXL; cleared to land.' About a minute later; I noted that Tower instructed traffic to cross Runway XXL downfield at either Taxiway V or Taxiway R without referencing us; which I noted as strange. While on final; I noticed that a different aircraft had pulled up to the hold short line for Runway XXL at Taxiway Y10; and that I had not yet heard that crew interact with Tower. When we were on approximately a 1-mile final; the crew of the aircraft holding short called Tower advising they were ready for departure. Without referencing us; Tower stated 'RNAV to ZZZZZ3; Runway XXL; cleared for takeoff.' As soon as we heard this; the Captain stated to me that we would be going around; and we recited the first 3 calls we would make when that happened. I keyed up on the radio and stated 'Traffic on short final; Runway XXL.' By then the departing aircraft had entered the runway. Tower responded with go around instructions including a right turn to a 270 heading and a climb to 4;000. I read them back; and the Captain and I properly executed a go-around. I cleared the right side of the aircraft for any traffic landing XXR; noted there was none; and stated 'Clear on the right.' As we began the turn; TCAS sounded a traffic advisory. I noted the yellow target on TCAS was indicating 800 feet; and stated aloud that the traffic had just lifted off and that we could disregard the advisory; as we were turning away. Tower apologized for the mistake and sent us to approach for re-sequencing and an uneventful visual approach and landing on Runway XXR.The crew of the departing aircraft appears to have failed to visually check the final for traffic before calling Tower for a takeoff clearance; and again prior to taxiing onto the runway for departure. The Air Traffic Controller appears to have forgotten about having cleared us to land; or appears to have been situationally unaware of our position prior to issuing the takeoff clearance. The Runway Status Lights (RWSL) on Runway XXL appear not to have worked; either because my aircraft's position on short final failed to trigger the red stop bars; because the departing aircraft ignored the RWSL red stop bars; the RWSL malfunctioned; or because the system was improperly overridden by the Controller. Another system that appears to have failed is the Controller's ASDE-X safety logic; because it appears my radio transmission was the primary reason he initiated the go-around instructions. Typically; when departing traffic crosses the hold short line with an arriving aircraft on short final; ASDE-X safety logic sounds an alarm. An additional contributing factor is the resurgence of traffic levels after a significant prolonged drop stemming from the outbreak of COVID-19; which may have led to complacency on the part of the departing crew and the Controller.Departing crews need to diligently check the final for traffic before taxiing onto the runway for takeoff; and ideally before even calling ready for departure. Failing to do so before calling ready violates basic airmanship and sets the Controller up for failure. That said; the Controller should have had use of a memory aid or reliable automation to indicate and help him remember that Runway XXL was being used as an active arrival runway; that we had been issued a clearance to land; and that we were on short final to that runway at the time heissued the departing aircraft's takeoff clearance. Interviewing the crew of the departing aircraft would also shed light on whether the RWSL had illuminated and; if so; whether they proceeded onto the runway with the RWSL stop bars illuminated. If this is the case; retraining would mitigate this event from happening again. Interviewing the Controller would provide insight as to whether he overrode the RWSL; whether the ASDE-X safety logic worked properly; and other details about the work conditions that shift including staffing and fatigue; which; if undesirable; could be corrected to help mitigate the recurrence of this event.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported a go-around due to ATC clearing another aircraft for takeoff while reporter's flight was on short final.

Report_1_Narrative: Captain; in his briefing; stated he would not wear a mask in the cockpit (whether a Flight Attendant was present or not) and would probably forget to wear one when he came into the cabin. When I (#2 Flight Attendant) questioned this and stated we did not have to enter the cockpit if the pilots refused to wear a mask----he said he would issue a directive and we would comply.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Attendant reported the Captain advised the crew that he would not be wearing a mask in the cockpit.

Report_1_Narrative: Long Beach Harbor has a long history of sea plane operations that reach back to the dawn of Aviation.  One of the first commercial aviation operations was passenger service to Catalina Island from Long Beach and the iconic Spruce goose flew it's only Flight there.Late on a hazy but otherwise benign weather weekend afternoon; I departed the Long Beach Airport for a short flight to the Harbor. From a vantage point at the foot of the LA River; I could see conditions were conducive to seaplane operations. I contacted the tower to inform them of my intentions to conduct multiple seaplane operations within the southern boundary of their Class D airspace and received the usual acknowledgment with the catchphrase 'At your own risk.'The area chosen for those operations lay parallel to the shoreline and 150 feet south of the swimming buoys.  (I have conducted many seaplane operations in this same area over the last XX years; as have other seaplane pilots.)My first pass remained airborne at 50 feet above the surface to insure there were no hazards in the water.  The next three passes involved multiple touch and goes from the surface.  I saw no swimmers south of the buoys.I departed the area southbound; climbing to pattern altitude plus 500 feet before turning 180deg back to the airport.While taxing to parking; the tower informed me there had been a complaint that my operations were too close to swimmers.
Report_1_Synopsis: Seaplane pilot reported Long Beach Tower advising pilot that their operation was too close to swimmers in the area.

Report_1_Narrative: Arrived in area at CCC under IFR. Cancelled IFR and proceeded to HWV under VFR from the northeast. Upon switching to CTAF (Common Traffic Advisory Frequency) learned aircraft were landing Runway 33. Announced position and intent for midfield transition to enter downwind Runway 33 several times starting at 4 miles. Noted significant traffic entering downwind from the southwest and parachute activity on southwest corner of airport. While tracking several aircraft entering the pattern and landing/taking off noted tow plane and sailplane being released at pattern altitude turning right crosswind Runway 33 at 0.25 miles from airport. They were approximately 300 ft. away at same altitude as me. Took evasive action and banked right towards 270 heading and pitched down resulting in descent to 800 ft. Other aircraft continued on approximate crosswind course where I lost sight of them. Continued to enter downwind Runway 33 and uneventful landing Runway 33. Looking back; I did not expect right hand traffic when all other aircraft were left traffic for Runway 33. I didn't hear announcement of that traffic on CTAF although frequency was very busy and I was focused on left hand traffic entering from southwest.
Report_1_Synopsis: Pilot reported Near Mid Air Collision in traffic pattern.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Communication Breakdown; Situational Awareness; Training / Qualification; Distraction
Report_1_Narrative: After completing an IFR flight with student to the ZZZ1 airport; we canceled IFR on short final and requested a Tower to Tower departure to ZZZ2 with intent to request the published hold at ZZZ VOR. The airspace was very congested with VFR training airplanes.We were given a frequency change to ZZZ2 Tower by the ZZZ1 Tower Controller; and the student; under the hood continued his climb while I attempted to contact ZZZ2 Tower; which was extremely congested.After several attempts; I instructed the student to turn to a heading of 150 and level off prior to 2;700 MSL to exit the local airspace and was focused outside. Due to the heavy training activity; I could not contact ZZZ2 Tower.I looked inside and noted that the student had climbed to above 2;900 MSL which was inside the Class C shelf of ZZZ; but nearly clear to the south.I instructed the student to level off and depart the airspace; and we returned to our home base without further incident. In retrospect; due to the congestion; I would have landed at ZZZ1; taxied to the ramp; and amended my plan with the student. Traffic congestion since COVID has been significant; and has made training IFR training a challenge. I have begun to mitigate this by filing direct to airports as previously described with a plan to return home under VFR. In the future; I will no longer request Tower to Tower and plan to leave and attempt holds at airports in northern ZZZ3 County.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Instructor reported a Class C airspace incursion.

Report_1_Narrative: I was enroute to ZZZ1 from ZZZ; the flight was clear with no clouds and had flight following with Seattle Center. I was beginning to notice that the mountains were being obscure and heard Seattle Center talking to a Medavac flight with a PIREP that a wall of smoke from the ground to 12;000 ft with chop was reported and the pilot confirmed the conditions. I called Seattle Center to ask about ZZZ1 weather and it was report VFR 5+ miles. I climbed up to 10;500 ft to see if the visibility might improve but then I hit this wall of smoke that I just heard about. I was then about 5;000 ft AGL and I could not see the ground. I knew exactly where I was above the ground with the aircraft GPS and my EFB (FlyQ). I quickly notified Seattle Center of my situation and started a slow descent to see if I can see Highway 97. At about 3;000 ft AGL I see Highway 97. I told Seattle Center I know where I was and that I believe the visibility is no more than a mile but I have my bearings and request to divert to ZZZ2 as I know that area quite well. I kept Highway 97 off my left wing and made a bearing to the center line of Klamath Lake. Seattle Center kept in contact and ensure I had my bearings; which I had. Once mid section of Klamath Lake; I believe I had 2 - 3 mile visibility. Seattle Center hand me off to ZZZ2 Tower. I reported I was over [Landmark] and they told me to report 3 miles for Runway XX. I reported 3 miles north of Runway XX with approach lights in sight; ZZZ2 Tower reported that they could not see me but again cleared my to land. Landing was uneventful and on the numbers. NOTE: ZZZ2 was reporting VFR with 5+ miles but I don't think the Klamath Basin area had that kind of visibility. The smoke came in quick; a wall that was from the ground to at least 12;000 ft.
Report_1_Synopsis: Pilot reported low visibility due to smoke enroute.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Communication Breakdown; Confusion; Distraction; Fatigue; Situational Awareness
Report_1_Narrative: I took sector X/Y/Z shortly after Aircraft X checked in from ZZZ Approach headed to ZZZ airport. I switched Aircraft X from frequency to different frequency. Usually when I switch an aircraft or they check in I would normally ask them to advise when they have the weather and issue any NOTAMs. I do not know why I did not ask this VFR aircraft if he had the weather or advise him of the PPR (Prior Permission Required). This is something very uncharacteristic of me. I did call traffic to Aircraft X twice before sending him to advisories and terminating his flight following. I generally treat VFR the same as IFR with regards to weather and NOTAMs. The aircraft apparently landed without calling into the airport and missed the trucks on the runway. My only conclusion is that the memory jogger for the airport 10 minute PPR was not next to the airport on the scope; it was quite a bit north of the airport. We also have a lot of other things written on the scope at this time with all the TFRs in the area. I did have several other things that required coordination and switching of frequency transmitter sites at the time but traffic was not that busy. Aircraft Y was orbiting in the TFR just outside of approach and was going to be a factor with another aircraft descending into ZZZ.I do remember being mentally exhausted from the day. We are continually forced to work combined sectors with a lot of frequency congestion; a lot of moving aircraft from frequency to frequency. Missing numerous TFRs and traffic orbiting the TFRs and listening to pilot readbacks on complex clearances. Lots of VFR aircraft with many traffic calls and aircraft not listening. We are busy in our area and keeping sectors split is not a priority. We just end up making things work and pushing through it. While this is not an excuse for why I did not do my job and issue the NOTAM I do believe it is contributing to the event in the long run.We need to return to normal staffing. We need to have sectors split out more. Ultimately we are straining our people and causing unnecessary stress in how we are currently running the area.
Report_2_Narrative: I assumed the CIC desk at XA:47. At XA:55 a runway incursion took place with a VFR Aircraft X who was not notified of the ten minute prior permission required for landing at ZZZ. I was unaware the incident took place until the next day. I was confident that the airspace wasn't too busy or complex for the configuration.Prior permissions for landing at ZZZ are very commonplace. The written note on the radar scope to remind us of the closure may be causing oversight because we see it so often. Perhaps we can change our way of indicating the closure using the draw function so it stands out more in our scan.
Report_1_Synopsis: Center Controllers reported an aircraft landing at an airport where the runway was closed.

Report_1_Narrative: We started our takeoff roll at ZZZ. It was the FO's (First Officer's) leg. Shortly after the 'set takeoff thrust call' my window on the Captain's side started to slide open. I'd estimate our speed at 40 kts. It was barely open so I said 'continue' and reached up to close it. However; the window would not close and actually felt like it was coming out of the track. I assumed the window would easily close and that we still had plenty of time to safely reject at low speed if it wouldn't. At that point I became distracted and was worried that the window was falling in. At that point the FO asked if I wanted to reject and I said 'yes'. He initiated the reject as he saw that I was handling the window. As I brought my scan away from the window the reject was started and I noticed the airspeed was about 100 kts. The aircraft quickly decelerated as it was very light. I expected the airspeed to be less than 80 kts based on the short amount of time we had been rolling. The FO continued to stop the aircraft. At that point I took controls. He called the Tower and I made a PA to the passengers to remain seated. We then taxied off the runway at Taxiway X and coordinated with Maintenance to have the brakes checked. They gave us a thumbs up and we taxied to the gate. At that point the window was stuck in a half open position. We shutdown at the gate and switched to another aircraft. Rejecting immediately when the window started to slide open would have prevented the distraction and the rejection would have started at a slower speed. I assumed two things: that the window would easily close and that we were still below 80 kts when the decision was made. It may have been; but at the light weight the aircraft accelerated quickly and I think by the time the actions began we were over 80 kts.
Report_2_Narrative: At approximately 40 kts during takeoff roll; Captain side window slid open. Captain called continue and attempted to close the window. A few seconds later I looked over and saw the Captain was struggling to get it closed. I stated that I recommend we reject and he agreed. His hands were still on the window to prevent it from slamming back so I initiated the reject procedure. I did not notice the top airspeed; but I would estimate visually about 100 kts; autobraking did engage. Aircraft came to a stop abeam Taxiway X. Notified the Tower. We were instructed to exit on Taxiway. We stopped on Taxiway and called Company. Maintenance met us on ramp and checked the brakes. We taxied in. Window was unable to be shut. When Maintenance came to the flight deck and were able to move the window forward the handle seemed loose and the squeeze grip seemed loose so we all conferred and removed the aircraft from service.I specifically remember observing the Captain check his window just prior to calling for the before takeoff checklist so I think it was secure. We should have rejected as soon as the window slid open to prevent from getting to the higher speed. The aircraft was light so acceleration was very rapid.
Report_1_Synopsis: B737 Flight Crew reported cockpit window opening during takeoff roll.

Report_1_Narrative: There is an important FDC NOTAM (#5631) that adds climb gradients to all runways in Chicago for the MDW 5 Departure. It is currently on page 7 of a 14 page packet under 'Station Information FDC NOTAMs.' Being 'buried in the NOTAMs' is no excuse to miss this; but the chances of it being missed are high. This might deserve explanation as well.  Crews seem to have a limited understanding of climb gradients and this one applies to 2900 feet in Chicago. All directions; not just toward downtown. It is in the weather packet but deserves more attention perhaps the front cover of the weather packet or in a safety publication.
Report_1_Synopsis: A Pilot reported an important change to the MDW5 SID climb gradient is easy to miss in the NOTAMs and should be highlighted in a more prominent area of their pre flight.

Report_1_Narrative: BZN ATIS can be received late due to terrain; no Digital ATIS; and early descent to land RWY 30.  When we initially tried to get ATIS; it was actually Johnson City; WY.  When we did actually get it; it was a little late and required re-briefing to change the plans.In addition; the company pages need more information.1 - Runway 12 is preferred; even up to a 10 knot tailwind (per AirNAV.com); although that information is not specific or clear on the chart; which simply says Runway 12 is preferred.  The additional information of up to a 10 knot tailwind would be helpful to ensure we are planning; for the most likely scenario.  In our case; the wind was 6 knots from the NW; so we were not sure which runway to plan without ATIS.  Knowing they operate with up to a 10 knot tailwind on Runway 12 would have helped. 2 - Company pages note a safety alert that states; 'terrain east of the airport does not allow for a normal descent to a straight-in-landing to Runway 30.'  Note it does not state what 'normal' is; prohibit a landing west; or prohibit 'trying' with early configuration and being prepared to go around or joining a left downwind visual to 30.  To me the Company page sounds a little like a prohibition; or at least; that it is not recommended.  But it needs to be clearer.  If it is prohibited; it should say that.  If it isn't; provide additional information.  Maybe it should state something like:'Terrain to the East of the airport does not allow for a normal descent to a straight-in landing on Runway 30.  If attempted; configure and slow early to maintain the VNAV path; and if unable; prepare for a go-around and fly the RNAV 30 via the FIDEP transition or if in day visual conditions with terrain in sight; enter a left visual downwind and visual approach to Runway 30.'
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported more arrival information is needed for BZN Airport.

Report_1_Narrative: Arrival into IAH was changed from LINKK to NNCEE. We were told to expect Runway 8R; but it would be decided by next controller. We left Runway 9 in the box with appropriate transition. Approaching KONZZ at 12;000 ft.; we were given 8R. We both discussed quickly putting in the Runway 8R with the assumption that we would go north to GOVVV after PRAYY. Flight director went to LVL CHG with the confusion and briefly we descended below 10;000 slightly above 250 kts. At PRAYY; within seconds of beginning a turn for GOVVV; the controller corrected us and vectored us for the south downwind.
Report_1_Synopsis: Captain reported flying over 250 knots while descending below 10;000 feet due to confusion around a runway clearance change.

Report_1_Narrative: Just after entering Mexico airspace flying level at FL 350. The autopilot kicked off and the flight director disappeared. We lost all functionality of the MCP panel. I decided to return. We requested radar vectors back to US airspace. When in US airspace we advised ATC and got radar vectors. I contacted the company via AIRINC and informed them of our situation; and requested latest weather. Cause unknown. Performed air return.
Report_1_Synopsis: B737 Captain reported loss of MCP; autopilot and flight director; which resulted in diversion.

Report_1_Narrative: I neglected to notice that the Airworthiness Certificate was missing from the plane in the morning. It should be in a little pocket on the front of the pilot's door side pocket that's difficult to get the certificates out of it. And without pulling all the certificates out of the pocket; it's not possible to make sure that the 3 certificates are in there (registration; airworthiness; and radio license). Only the front one can be seen. And if we are constantly pulling all the certificates out that's a lot of extra wear and tear on the certificates. I happened to pull the certificates out of the pocket while waiting for the evening freight and discovered that the Airworthiness Certificate was missing. Dispatch figured out how to make it legal for me to get home. Perhaps have 3 pockets (or one wide pocket) on the door instead of just one small pocket so all 3 certificates can be seen without pulling them out of the pocket. That way they're easy to check without any wear and tear. Or make the pocket larger so that they are easier to pull out.
Report_2_Narrative: It was brought to my attention that the Airworthiness Certificate for Aircraft X was missing. At this time; it is not known when it was removed from the aircraft. I have recently flown the aircraft in question. To the best of my knowledge; the certificate was on board the aircraft. It was not my intention to operate the aircraft without the required documents on board.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Taxi Pilot reports aircraft airworthiness certificate missing.

Report_1_Narrative: Takeoff on Runway XXR full length. At around rotation got a push to the right.  Rotated safely and the airplane was climbing normally and no abnormal indications on the ECAM. There was however a heavy aircraft sitting perpendicular waiting to cross Runway XXL. Captain asked if they were cleared to cross that runway because our push to the right seemed to happen around the same time we passed them. Can't really remember what the response was from the Controller.They need to staff the ATC facilities properly. One person handling more than one frequency; or both Ground and Tower. This is not just ZZZ. ZZZ1 is also bad when you add construction to the mix.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported possible jet blast from a heavy aircraft crossing a parallel runway; while departing.

Report_1_Narrative: After takeoff and during normal cleanup procedures; the caution light came on with an associated ECAM.  The Captain pulled speed to ensure we did not over speed; a quick glance at ECAM said max speed 230; I believe.  As PM; I confirmed it was not a Quick Action or ECAM exception.  I assumed control of aircraft and radios; and stated ECAM Action.  The Captain reviewed the ECAM and began to troubleshoot [the] problem.  The ECAM had very little information; and then he referenced the QRH.  I was coordinating with ATC to stop climb at 10;000 feet (safe alt in sector) and advised them of our speed and desire to hold. Captain confirmed max speed of 230 knots from QRH; so we slowed to 220 to provide a margin.  The slat/flap indicator showed slats were almost up; significantly less than 1.  We lowered gear to burn down gas to below max landing weight.  While still in holding; we selected flaps 1 and obtained normal indications on the slats.   Once all briefings; checklists and QRH procedures were complete; the Captain resumed flying duties and I requested to exit holding and obtain vectors for approach to Runway XX.  Flaps and slats moved normally and the landing was uneventful and normal. Captain taxied to gate and passengers deplaned. Flaps and slats retracted normal on the ground.  We discussed the need to declare an emergency; but did not initially since we were not sure of the actual problem; once flaps/slats moved normally; it seems all systems were normal.Aircraft may have sat on the ground during the COVID flying reduction; and therefore it seemed; to me; there might have been an indication problem or squat switch problem.  We did not declare an emergency because the aircraft seems to have a computer or indication problem and slats lowered normally once we started to configure.  In retrospect; any flight control problem is reason to declare emergency; but not sure if we then should undeclared once all was normal.  I have not flown much in the past 7 months; so I may have reverted to previously learned procedures.Any flight control issue is an emergency; even when corrected.  Better maintenance on aircraft.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported a slat/flap indication problem on departure resulting in a return to departure airport.

Report_1_Narrative: We went around at 900 AGL due to improper configuration on an autoland.  We were doing an Autoland approach and the system did not arm at GS intercept on the practice CAT III.  PM was watching outside for traffic on a parallel approach. As the flying pilot I got totally sucked into my display and did [not] configure in time for a stabilized approach and decided at 900 AGL to initiate [a] go-around. Go-around was uneventful.Having not flown a lot in the last couple months I allowed myself to get distracted with the display and lost overall situational awareness in regards to proper aircraft configuration.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported conducting a go-around due to improper aircraft configuration and cited loss of situational awareness as a contributing factor.

Report_1_Narrative: On Sunday; (date) I was called off reserve to fly Aircraft X under Ops Spec XXXX; with a ferry permit; from ZZZ1 to ZZZ. As far as I knew the flight went smoothly and according to plan; but I got a call on Tuesday; (date); informing me that the R1 slide had deployed when maintenance personnel opened the door later that day. I am not positive what happened; but here is what I recall: being that no flight attendants were on board; it was up to the flight crew to disarm the doors. During our approach briefing; the Captain had briefed me about disarming the doors prior to maintenance personnel opening the L1 door. I understood the Captain to be saying 'it is critical that we disarm the L1 door quickly upon arrival; before personnel open it from outside.' Upon shutdown I reiterated to the Captain that I would disarm the L1 door right away; which I did. I can not remember exactly the captain's response when I read the 'cabin doors' item on the parking checklist; but I was under the impression that we were only worried about the L1 door; and that we were turning it over to Maintenance; so they would handle the rest. If I remember correctly; I only disarmed the L1 door. My recommendation would be to not perform the parking checklist until all doors were disarmed. As a brand new First Officer with 3 trips under my belt since consolidation; I should not have assumed anything; instead of assuming there must have been an exception to the '6 disarmed' response on the parking checklist; or assuming that the Captain had done this before and knew a procedure that I did not know.
Report_2_Narrative: At the conclusion of a maintenance flight from ZZZ1 to ZZZ; the disarming of the doors was not verified. During approach brief; I briefed that the L1 door needed to be disarmed before anyone tried to open the door from the outside. We parked the aircraft; shut down the engines and did the parking checklist. Upon reaching the door verification; I stated 'to go' because we had to disarm the doors ourselves. We got up and I went to the back and disarmed L2 and R2; leaving the front doors to the First Officer. As I returned to the flight deck; I double checked L1 to make sure it was disarmed. I then returned to the flight deck and shut down the aircraft. I did not re-verify that the parking checklist was completed. I was informed yesterday that a slide had deployed after our flight. I did not verify the doors disarmed; to finish the parking checklist. I also should have double checked both front doors; after disarming the back.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Crew reported an evacuation slide deployed after parking aircraft.

Report_1_Narrative: Normal day; normal passenger operations; on Aircraft X; performing ZZZ to ZZZ1 flight. With APU being under MEL; started engine number one at the gate according to normal checklist. Cleared to push out of the gate; to the blue line. The initial push back was mostly smooth. Aircraft pushed on a slant angle on the green line and stopped. Tow truck driver contacted the flight deck; stating that he will pull us to the blue line. Since then; the mild tensions and sounds were sensible as if it felt that the angle of pulling forward to the blue line was kind of steep. I; personally; could not see the tow truck from the right seat. Shortly after; we heard a bigger noise and aircraft started to move forward that followed immediately by the driver asking us to set the brake in a rushed voice; Captain acted promptly; and we stopped the aircraft on time and smoothly. I personally did not feel any impact. We stopped with an angle on the blue line. The driver mentioned that the tow bar broke and he is going to disconnect and contact the ramp safety. We communicated with the Ramp; Operations and MX (Maintenance) Control. Captain communicated with the flight attendants and made an announcement to the passengers informing them about the nature of problem. Within 10 minutes or so; with the supervision of our MX personnel on the ground; a new tow truck; new tow bar and a new driver towed us back to the same gate. This time it was very smooth. We found out that a scratch line and a shallow dent exist on the lower right-hand side of the aircraft. It happened by the shallow impact of the fuselage with the roof of the tow truck. Captain wrote up the damage in MX logbook. Dispatch and Flight Operations have been informed. Everybody acted professional during and after the event. Don't know if the tow bar breaking happened because of the angle & the tension exposed to it; or it was the material failure. Tail swap happened shortly after; and we performed the same flight on ship (tail). If a tow truck driver is not happy with the location of the aircraft or if for some reason they are in a tight spot; or any other unusual issue; they can always consider us as a team and communicate any unease with us; so we all figure out how to get out of it. My assumption is that if we were unhooked from the tow bar on the green line; the entire event could have been avoided. It could only cost me a simple radio call to the ramp; I guess.
Report_2_Narrative: These are my recollections as I remember them: We were operating Aircraft X operating out of gate X. Aircraft X was operating with MEL APU Inoperative applied. We complied with procedures for engine start with external pneumatic air source & completed the appropriate normal checklists. Ramp tower assigned us a push back onto the blue line. The push back seemed normal with the exception that the AC (aircraft) was at an odd angle. I attributed this to the push crew having to avoid the construction adjacent to N11. The tug driver announced that he would get us over to the blue line & proceeded to turn the jet that direction. At this point I could sense some stress on the tug/towbar combination but nothing that seemed abnormal. As the driver proceeded towards the blue line the noise the towbar was making got louder until we heard what I'd describe as a pop or snap. At this point the jet rolled forward due to forward momentum & the driver or wing walker said set the brakes. I estimate the jet moved forward about 10 feet as I was applying the brakes. We verified that there were no injuries to any of the push back crew & were informed that everyone on the ramp was safe. I stopped the jet as judicially as I could; taking into account that the FA's (flight attendants) were probably standing; conducting their safety demonstration. The driver announced he needed to have the Ramp Safety Supervisor conduct an inspection & we called Line Maintenance to survey the situation. We called the cabin to verify there were no injuries to guests or crew & subsequently a PA was made by me to inform the guests of our situation. Line Maintenance asked us if we could taxi the jet back to gate under power which I declined; not knowing the extent of any possible damage. A new towbar & tug was connected to the jet & we were towed back to gate. After the checklists were completed I proceeded to do a visual inspection; where I found an approximately 5 foot scrape on the underside of the fuselage; outboard of the right side nose gear door. I made another PA from the L1 door area informing the guests that there would be a tail swap & what our new gate was; then made an AC logbook entry describing the damage I observed. The flight proceeded as normal to ZZZ1 after a 2 hour delay to get everything ready on the jet we swapped into. Not sure if time was a big factor or not. The ramp personnel did not seem rushed but we did push back several minutes after departure time due to the jet being fueled late. Parking an A-321 at [this] gate with the current construction process ongoing may present a challenge to the push back crew due to the longer fuselage & trying to avoid the construction area adjacent to gate. My biggest suggestion would be for the push back crew to communicate any difficulty they may be having with any ground operation. In this circumstance we could have easily stopped the jet; set the parking brakes; & requested a taxi from our current position. We strive to comply with directions given; however; sometimes we need to ask to amend those instructions to meet the current situation.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight crew flying A321 aircraft report contact with tow tug during pushback.

Report_1_Narrative: After a successful CAT III landing; we had crossed the two inboard runways and were taxiing north on taxiway towards gate. The FO; who was on the first trip back after one month off; did the after landing flow and confirmed our gate with operations. I thought we were cleared into the gate via spot; but this was not the case.As we were rounding the corner for spot and passing Aircraft Y that was on the line just south of spot; I confirmed with the FO that we were indeed cleared in as I had been distracted switching from low vis taxi diagrams to normal taxi diagrams as the vis was very good; shutting down the Number 2 engine; in addition to the fact that the FO was a soft spoken person. I only mention this as I wasn't surprised I hadn't heard them confirm our clearance to taxi into the gate as I was busy concentrating on the other threats just discussed.As rampers were visible from spot and were marshaling us into the gate; we pulled into the gate normally. Approximately 20 feet short of our final parking spot ground reminded us to contact ramp. We immediately contacted ramp; who was understandably very unhappy with us and we apologized for our error.Needless to say; I take complete responsibility for this incident and am embarrassed I allowed it to happen. I have learned a couple of things from this incident- first; that I need to be extra vigilant when some crew members don't have a lot of recent experience; secondly; when we had discussed that the ground ops were our biggest threat for this CAT III approach; I need to truly take it to heart and be extra cautious to help mitigate the threats present during this segment of our flight.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported being distracted and not contacting the ramp before taxiing to the gate.

Report_1_Narrative: During boarding as I was walking the cabin to do a compliance check and exit seat briefing a passenger stopped me and questioned why she was seated next to a person she did not know.  I told her I would check and see if there was another seat she could move to.  At this time I did not see any open row that has no other people in it. I was going to send a flight family message to alert the Gate Agent. I walked up a row or two and another lady questioned me about why her seat would not recline (she was in front of the exit row). I explained to her why her seat would not recline and told her I would check with the agent about reseating them.  I then walked to the aft jump seat to send the flight family request. The agent then came down and we had a short conversation about rebooking the one lady and the other passengers who wanted a seat that reclined. There were no other seats to move the recline passenger to and the other passenger was given the option to take a later flight with no guarantee that she would have a seat by herself.  I informed all passengers involved. We took off and it was not till about mid flight that I realized that I had not ok'ed my exit seats. I proceeded right away to the exit row and briefed both passengers and they both were ok to sit in an exit row. The lady passenger did say that she noticed I had not briefed them before the flight. [The cause was] work overload.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Attendant reported inadvertently not briefing exit row passengers due to other passengers making special seating requests.

Report_1_Narrative: I was assigned to accomplish a de-preservation of the APU on Aircraft X that has been in storage.  The documentation for the aircraft stated that the aircraft had been in storage for XXX days and the APU needs to be de-preserved before XXX+1 days. The APU will need more work accomplished if it is de-preserved after the XXX+1 day mark than if it is de-preserved before the XXX+1 day mark.  The issue is that the APU had a placard attached that stated the preservation was good until date and after the APU compartment was opened there was a different tag that stated the APU preservation was valid until date+4 days.  So there were two different dates documented for the APU for the XXX+1 day mark.   The question is when is this XXX+1 day mark?  The date that the APU was actually preserved or the date for the preservation / storage of the aircraft.
Report_1_Synopsis: Technician reported confusing dates relating to work that needed to be performed on an aircraft that had been in storage.

Report_1_Narrative: On date I had scheduled an evening flight for dinner. My original aircraft was still out past the time it would be back due to a checkride. The scheduler working offered me a different airplane that would return a little bit sooner than my originally assigned aircraft. The CFI in the new plane I was assigned told me all that was needed was fuel; therefore I topped it off after my preflight and departed ZZZ2. I flew an uneventful flight to ZZZ1 to pick up. Following that; we also had an uneventful flight into ZZZ followed by a normal and smooth landing. On the end of rollout; the engine quit and propeller stopped turning. After that; I attempted a Cessna hot start technique for a fuel injected engine. It did not start back up so I asked Tower for assistance and a tow back to the FBO. I called ZZZ2's mechanic and he flew out to me and got it restarted. We swapped airplanes and went home. He advised me that my plane may have over flown the 100 hour check. The 100 hour inspection was scheduled for the next day. It was crossed out for the next day on the schedule for the next day; but not for the day I rented.
Report_1_Synopsis: Private pilot flying C-172 reported engine failure during landing rollout.

Report_1_Narrative: On DATE; Company Maintenance Technicians had replaced the existing OEM Taxi Light Installation with Whelen Aerospace Technologies Boom Beam Taxi light System IAW STC# ST02893AT on G-550 X. I was intermittently involved in the installation and had inspected the completed installation by request of the installing technician. I was notified on DATE1 of the intent to fly the aircraft in the evening so the pilots could observe the performance of the new lights. On the day of the flight I had been working on other projects and was preparing to depart for the day when the pilots arrived and asked if we had completed our maintenance pre-flight inspection. I discovered that the preflight had not been completed and proceeded to perform the preflight with the installing technician. Part of our preflight includes a review of the maintenance records and after reviewing the documents in Gulfstream's Computerized Maintenance Program (CMP) determined that there were no outstanding maintenance items. I asked the installing technician if the 337 had been completed and he responded with 'It's on Mechanic's (the Certifying IA) Desk' which I assumed to mean that it was complete.I signed the maintenance release and preflight form and departed for the day. The aircraft flew under part 91 rules that evening without incident.On DATE2 I spoke with Mechanic and discovered that although he had completed the inspection and all other associated paperwork before the flight; he had not signed the IA block of the 337 until the evening of the DATE3.Overall there were no unsafe conditions; only an oversight in paperwork. Upon discovery of the documentation error I self reported to my Supervisor and filed this report. An internal investigation has been initiated by my supervisor.
Report_1_Synopsis: Technician reported an aircraft operation in Part 91 flight without all documents signed and the log book update correctly.

Report_1_Narrative: Ground Control cleared Flight AB on local IFR flight plan; Flight AB requested own navigation to VOR for full procedure at 2;000 feet. The MVA throughout most of ZZZ airspace is 2;400 feet and normal practice is to clear all IFR aircraft above the MVA. Ground Control did not coordinate the abnormal altitude with Local Control. I did not catch the altitude and due to traffic Flight AB could not get own navigation on departure. I issued a departure heading to Flight AB to avoid traffic that put Flight AB into a MVA of 2;400 feet.Ground Control should only issue IFR aircraft altitudes at or above MVA.
Report_2_Narrative: Flight AB was assigned 2;000 feet from the Clearance Delivery position on a local IFR flight plan. The request was to fly their own navigation for full VOR Runway XX circle to Runway X approach. Flight AB was assigned a 080 heading on departure that goes into a 2;400 foot MVA area. The weather at the airport was 10 miles/CLR. I climbed the aircraft to 3;000 feet to get them above the MVA and started the process of getting him on course to the VOR for their approach. There was training on Local Control taking place and social distancing guidelines make it difficult for the OJTI to review the strip marking. The 080 heading is near 180 degrees off what the Departure Controller would expect. The Local Controller should coordinate aircraft that are that far out range of their flight plan. Review of strips prior to sending it the approach would help all controllers be on the same page.
Report_1_Synopsis: TRACON Controllers reported social distancing; during the training period; may have contributed to an incorrect altitude assigned to the aircraft.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Workload; Time Pressure; Situational Awareness; Communication Breakdown
