The Tower Controller re-confirmed that it was 'apparent' to him that the right main gear appeared to be fully extended while the nose and left had retracted.
Report_1_Synopsis: HS-125 Captain reported right main landing gear failed to retract resulted in return to departure airport.

Report_1_Narrative: The issue arose when I was taxiing from the northernmost T hangars to Ramp C at DWH to perform a run-up before a VFR departure for a local flight. Several corporate jets were parked on Ramp C and upon entering my aircraft I could hear a jet engine running; but I couldn't tell which aircraft it was. Ramp C is where run-ups are performed on the north end of DWH; and I needed to taxi to the south end of Ramp C in order to access an open spot for run-up; however the way I was familiar with was blocked by a pickup-truck. I then elected to turn right on N and taxi north then turn left on Ramp C. There is normally room to taxi behind aircraft parked on that ramp; but because one of the jets was running at least one engine; it wasn't safe to taxi behind them. I then elected to taxi south on Ramp C in front of the parked jets; and as I did so I saw that there were people walking in front of them; and also a vehicle approaching them from the south; so I swung out wide to give plenty of clearance; proceeded to an empty spot; and performed a run-up. On my initial taxi out for the run-up I didn't see the white boundary line of Ramp C; and assumed that I was safely inside of it; based on my previous study of the Jeppesen airport diagram. However Ramp C does not extend out as far toward Taxiway P as it appeared on the diagram. This was only my second time operating out of the north side of the airport; and my first time taking this route at the north end of Ramp C; and unfamiliarity was a factor. I chose this route instead of taxiing around the south end of Ramp C because the way was blocked by a pickup truck. The area is very congested; and the airport is poorly marked. Many of the ground markings; taxi lines; etc. are faded. Additionally; many ground vehicles; such as the airport vehicle; fuel trucks; golf carts; and other vehicles for pilots; passengers; employees; and residents that live on the field routinely drive on some of the ramp and taxiways without communicating on the radio; blurring the lines between the movement and non-movement areas. Specifically fuel trucks and the official airport vehicle (marked with signage on the doors) operate on taxiway P without making radio calls. Though I didn't realize it at the time; it was when I swung wide while heading south on Ramp C that I feel I may have encroached into taxiway P. It was upon completion of the flight when taxiing back to the hangar via taxiways E and P that I was able to see the faded white line that designates the border of Ramp C and realized that I may have made an incursion onto taxiway P at the beginning of the flight. The next day I sought out a highly experienced instructor who has operated out of DWH for over forty years and asked him about Ramp C; the faded white line; and the boundary between Ramp C and Taxiway P. He informed me that the area is tighter than I realized; and that anything west of the white line is a movement area requiring a clearance. Most importantly; I should not have assumed; and simply called Ground and coordinated with them; that way there would not have been an issue. Additionally DWH has a reputation for being poorly marked and I should have sought out more help becoming familiar with an airport that is new to me. My perception based on looking at the airport diagram was erroneous; and it was poor judgment to not call Ground and simply get cleared into the movement area; instead of trying to squeeze along the edge inside of Ramp C. I'm comfortable talking to controllers; I thought I could safely and legally do it and didn't want to 'bother them'. The reality is that's what they are there for; and I am sure the controllers would have preferred a call if there was any doubt.  The biggest factor affecting performance was the difficulty to see the faded border line of Ramp C. Additional factors were a reluctance to bother ATC; and the movement of road vehicles all around that gave a false perception that the non-movement area was larger than it really is. Unfamiliarity with the airport; especially when operating out of the north end was also a factor. The major inaction was failing to contact ATC.
Report_1_Synopsis: A pilot reported they failed to contact ATC for taxi instructions. The pilot reported that while avoiding congestion on the ramp they had a taxiway incursion.

Report_1_Narrative: Following a weather brief ( winds 130/03) and unicom radio check (in which we were confirmed to be 'loud and clear' by the FBO dispatcher); my student and I declared on the CTAF frequency that we were taxiing from the FBO tie downs to the run-up area for runway 5. Prior to entering the taxiway from the tiedowns; both my student and I cleared left and right for traffic on the taxiway. After our engine run-up; we announced that we were taxiing from the run-up area to runway 5. Prior to takeoff; we heard another pilot announce that he was landing on runway 5. While holding short of 5; we cleared the approach end for 5 and 24 and announced that we were departing runway 5. There were no additional radio calls from time of  taxi to takeoff; other than 1 inaudible transmission. Shortly after departure (I assume around a couple hundred feet); an airplane approached head-on from the opposite runway then quickly veered off to the right (left of our course). After review of the time stamp (ADSB out); it is to my knowledge that both aircrafts had departed from opposite runways.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Instructor reported at take off seeing opposite direction traffic resulted in evasive action.

Report_1_Narrative: I was working Approach; it was south flow. I cleared Aircraft X; a heavy B7XX RNAV approach then switched him to tower. Then; tower called me said that Aircraft X was going around and they issued him 185 heading climbing to 5000 ft. Then; Aircraft X came on my frequency; I radar identified him; told him to climb to 7000 ft.; because there was a 6300 ft. MIA block to the east. Once he was level at 7000 ft.; he was about 14 miles southwest; I issued him a 030 heading; then a 350 heading vector for RNAV approach. There was a 11000 ft. MIA block east of the 6300 ft. MIA block; but the distance from Aircraft X's position when he made the turn to the boundary of the 11000 ft. MIA block was about 5.6 miles. I thought that was enough space for him to make the turn. However; Aircraft X took an unexpected very wide U turn and clipped the corner of the 11000 ft. MIA block; he clipped the corner of 11000 ft. MIA for about 3 seconds while turning to the north; the MSAW alert was triggered; I issued him a low altitude alert. The aircraft then exited the 11000 ft. MIA back into the 6300 ft. MIA safely.
Report_1_Synopsis: TRACON Controller reported issuing a late vector resulting in air carrier entering higher MIA.

Report_1_Narrative: When I arrived at work for my XB00-XJ00 shift there was a CIC on the Supervisor desk. The area was still combined at the mid sector (XX) except for sector XY which sits 4 inches from sector XX. Sector XY was open and staffed by a Supervisor not wearing a face covering over any part of his face other than his neck. This Supervisor has been repeatedly told to do so; but most of the time doesn't do so. The adjacent airspace was ATC zero for a positive COVID case that had been reported the previous afternoon. This Supervisor often opens this sector between XA00 and XC00 am to avoid going to stand up and also avoid any sort of volume or complexity in the airspace. I understand normally it's not an issue besides that it's an awkward configuration that confuses everyone in and around the area; but today it was much more than that. Today marked ZZZ's X confirmed positive COVID case in X days' time and X [number] in X weeks. This supervisor not wearing a mask and opening the sector to get time was not only dangerous but just plain rude as the controllers sitting next to him were forced to work the other sectors while properly adhering to mask wearing guidance. I wish this was the end of this report however the day progressed to be even worse. During the morning the contingency plan was abandoned and we were told we could go through the sterilized airspace however far 'we felt comfortable.' In fact we were told it would be OK to give IFR clearances off the ground in the sterilized airspace as well. I don't think this is a safe idea. One person's comfort level could be more than a different person's. We don't know how far frequency coverage goes into the sterilized airspace and this could result in NORDO aircraft in conflict in the airspace with no way to resolve the confliction. To add further to this; later in the day a D-side trainee was brought to the area to give an over the shoulder for the resumption of training. 4 people were plugged in to one sector while the same Supervisor still wore his mask around his neck. This put 3 more controllers at risk unnecessarily during the middle of a facility outbreak. This D-side trainee is now fully certified again on all the area D-sides after working a total of 1 week in the past 7 months which presents even more risk both to proficiency and also to proper social distancing measures. After this certification was complete he was used throughout the day and told to 'pick a D-side' at the instruction of the Supervisor further combating any social distancing guidelines that have been set in place by state health officials; NATCA; and facility management.If this is how ZZZ center is going to continue to operate this is only the tip of the iceberg with how much crossing paths there is since the return of normal schedules and staffing. Supervisors do not need sector currency.
Report_1_Synopsis: Center Controller reported a facility Supervisor continually does not follow state and NATCA guidelines regarding face mask policy.

Report_1_Narrative: After pushing back from the gate the aircraft was deiced using Type 1 fluid to remove excessive ice buildup.  The aircraft had been RON for nearly 10 hours and spent most of its time exposed to FZRA (freezing rain) and -FZRA.  The deice crew completed spraying/decontaminating the aircraft and called 'aircraft deicing complete'.  At this point; I still could not even see out of the co-pilots number 3 window due to excessive ice buildup.  This made the Captain and I suspicious (identified a threat) and asked the ground crew to spray the window and to be sure that they observed a clean airplane.  They resprayed and said the aircraft was clean.  To be sure; I performed a 'wing check' prior to engine start and noticed the wings were completely saturated with at least a quarter inch of ice.  We called them back and asked for a complete re-do explaining how difficult it may be to remove the ice.  They completed a second total deice and stated the aircraft was clean.  We elected to perform another 'wing check' and noticed that nothing had changed.  In fact; on one side of the aircraft we were unable to view the wing from any of the passenger windows due to ice buildup.  At this point neither one of us felt confident in the aircraft's condition and the Captain elected to return to the gate to perform both a walk around as well as conference with all ground personnel.  His communication was effective.  As a note; during the walk around noticed icicles hanging from the leading edges and the upper wing surface was completely saturated with ice.  We pushed a 3rd time; deiced by a different crew member; performed a 'wing check' and were satisfied the wings and control surfaces were clear.  Departed nearly 4 hours late.  An unsuspecting crew could have very easily departed with an aircraft completely covered in ice.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported failure of deicing crew to properly deice aircraft; resulted in multiple efforts to get deiced

Report_1_Narrative: The Flight Attendant (FA) in charge advised that passenger in XX10 would not wear mask and was becoming belligerent changing seats at will while disregarding FA instructions to wear his mask and return to his seat. Dispatch [was] notified. We decided to have personnel meet aircraft in ZZZ and advised that this passenger should be denied boarding on next leg to ZZZ1.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported a passenger would not comply with face mask policy and became belligerent with the Flight Attendant in Charge.

Report_1_Narrative: IOE (initial operating) student was attempting a flaps 22 landing. During the approach; gusty winds from outer bands of an approaching hurricane contributed to an unstable approach and generating two glide slope EGPWS annunciations. We initiated a missed approach and were put in sequence to reattempt the approach. The vectors from the second approach brought us in above the glideslope. We engaged the vs (vertical speed) mode initially at 1;200 feet per minute (per GOM) and then 1;000 feet per minute as we closed in on the glide slope and stabilized approach criteria. The student had NAV armed; not APP; which as PM (pilot monitoring) I should have caught. My attention was briefly diverted to reassessing our fuel; which was 200 pounds over final divert at the final approach fix. At 1;000; instruments cross checked; the GS (glideslope) was exact (though not captured). At this point; we had been in visual conditions for several minutes. The runway did not have visual guidance (PAPI nor VASI); I looked out the window to verify the runway was clear; of which I annunciated. At approximately 700 feet AGL; we fell below the glide slope; generating additional glide slope EGPWS annunciations. Due to the winds; fuel nature; incoming weather; and diversion airport expecting similar conditions; I used my command authority to take control of the airplane; reestablish ourselves on the glide path; and land without further incident.
Report_1_Synopsis: EMB-145 Captain reported an unstabilized approach due to gusty conditions.

Report_1_Narrative: ATC had given us a series of headings to avoid an active MOA. After the headings; they gave us direct CULAB then DIESL for the DRLLR5 arrival into IAH. I was writing the clearance while the captain put the change in the FMS. I copied the correct clearance (direct CULAB; DEISL then the DRILR5) and the captain input direct CULAB then DIESL for the MSCOT4; our originally assigned arrival. A proper cross check was not applied and the change was CONFIRMED. The MSCOT4 and DRLLR5 are very similar coming from that direction and both start at DIESL so upon looking at the first page of the FMS all seemed correct to me. It was not until later in the arrival were we/nor ATC aware we were on the wrong arrival into IAH until around the SUUNR intersection on the MSCOT4. Proper cross checking was not implemented on the arrival change. We did confirm the route change to CULAB then DIESL. A more thorough cross check of the arrival change would have caught the issue. Neither of us caught it and continued the flight to IAH on the MSCOT4; even fully briefing it. ATC said 'no worries' and left us on the MSCOT4 all the way into IAH.
Report_1_Synopsis: First Officer reported flying the originally assigned Arrival procedure into IAH after acknowledging an ATC clearance for a different STAR.

Report_1_Narrative: During a VFR climb to 4;500 feet; I encountered what I believe to be a powered parachute at about 4;000 feet. I made a slight right turn to avoid the hazard and continued the trip without incident. The parachutist was in Class E airspace in VMC conditions and appears to have been complying with regulations. But it seems dangerous to have such slow-moving traffic in such busy airspace without ADS-B.
Report_1_Synopsis: Pilot reported an NMAC with a powered parachute resulted in taking evasive action.

Report_1_Narrative: I was acting as an instructor to a CPL who was new to flying the Aircraft X Type. He had spent all of his time up to this point flying the Aircraft Y Type; so I was helping him familiarize himself with the different aircraft. We were doing pattern work while several other aircraft were in the pattern.  Upon getting abeam the numbers and beginning our descent; there was an aircraft on long final (roughly 2-2.5 miles) that we did not hear on the radio.  We continued with our base; and final. The CPL whom I was instructing did not speak very strong english; and was having some trouble with the radio calls in the pattern; and occasionally neglecting to make them. In this instance; he neglected to call his base; and also neglected to call final.  I noticed this only after him turning final without saying anything; and immediately announced our one mile final. This set up a situation where a near miss occurred between us and the other aircraft who was on long final. The aircraft that was on a long final did not call an extended downwind; or a base.  They called final and neglected to give any mileage to indicate they had flown a much larger pattern than usual for a light general aviation plane. The other aircraft noticed us only because I called our final; and immediately broke off his final leg to avoid collision.  I spoke with their pilot after this incident and he said we were slightly above them and cut them off. I believe this incident was caused by a number of factors mentioned above; and could have been avoided with better radio work on the part of my aircraft and the other one on final.  I had a high workload at the moment; which caused my attention to lapse when the CPL turned base without making the call.  However; the pilot on the other aircraft also did not specify that he was purposely flying a large pattern with an extended downwind/base/final.  His failure and mine to accurately give position reports caused the incident.   I also believe that often pilots become complacent and fly a pattern which is far too large at this airport.  There are several times in a week where I have to extend my pattern to a point where I would not be able to make the runway in the event of an engine failure.  Routinely; general aviation aircraft at the airport fly a 2+ mile final; which should be considered a 'long' final.  Like in the incident mentioned; this can cause confusion when someone joins flying a smaller; more appropriate pattern.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Instructor reported a NMAC of final resulted in Evasive action.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Situational Awareness; Workload; Communication Breakdown; Distraction
Report_1_Narrative: On our enroute descent 30 miles west of ZZZ; ZZZ Center had to cancel our IFR flight plan due the ZZZ1 Center COVID related airspace closures.  There was a miscommunication when we checked in with ZZZ Approach Control with us being VFR with the airport in sight.  We picked up an IFR clearance with a Visual approach to the airport.  We continued our arrival and landed uneventfully.The cause was that ZZZ1 airspace closed and there was a communication gap between ZZZ Center and ZZZ Approach.No suggestions; as our required cancellation of our IFR enroute with ZZZ Center and our subsequent picking up of our IFR with a visual approach from ZZZ Approach is what was required due to the ZZZ1 Airspace closures.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported the flight's IFR flight plan was canceled near the destination airport because the ATC Center had airspace closures due to COVID-19.

Report_1_Narrative: Unanticipated GPWS warning on approach requiring crew action. We were flying the freighter (tail); second leg ZZZ-ZZZ1 (1.5 hr delayed at start of day); 5-6 hours into the flight duty period (~XA:00 pm local time). Night IMC w/moderate to heavy rain showers in vicinity. I was Pilot Flying PF (Captain).Clearance was ZZZ...ZZZ1. On the ground at ZZZ we planned and briefed the departure and RNAV (RNP) Rwy XX from the ZZZZZ1 transition. De-iced; taxied; departed; climbed to cruise at FL280.Enroute to ZZZZZ1 at cruise; Center warned of areas of moderate to extreme precipitation from ZZZZZ1 fix to the airport and advised of better weather to the Northeast. After discussing a change to the arrival; we both agreed to request radar vectors to the approach segment from ZZZZZ (IAF). Center agreed to vector us around and down to put us on the published portion of the arrival with the stated intention of joining us to the approach path at ZZZZZ2. FO (First Officer) made the changes in the FMS and we briefed and then ran the Decent Checklist Change Triangles.Radar vectors included a descent and vectors resulting in established on published segment near ZZZZZ2 at 5000 and given approach clearance from center (I had directed PM to reset FMS Cruise Alt to 8;000 feet when we were on vectors). Once established near ZZZZZ2 at 5;000 cleared us for the approach. I engaged LNAV/VNAV and set airport elevation; but was high on the vertical path. I continued to slow to final configuration (gear down; Flaps 40) by ZZZZZ1; stable; but still 1;400 feet above the path in VNAV SPD (vertical navigation speed). After the turn at ZZZZZ1 I set 1;600 feet in the MCP ALT window (FAP 1;600 MSL) and at approximately 2;300 MSL; engaged Vertical Speed down in order to regain the VNAV Path before the FAP. As I approached the path; I reset MCP altitude to airfield elevation and engaged VNAV while pitch mode was in ALT ACQ (altitude acquire); resulting in an unrecognized mode change to V/S (2;100 ft/min) and projected vertical path well before the airport. It was at this point; we received a GPWS 'Caution Terrain' followed shortly by GPWS Warning 'Terrain Fly UP.'  I immediately executed an escape maneuver/go-around; climbing and flying the go-around flight path to ZZZ2 and mistakenly climbed to 5;000 MSL (missed approach alt 3;000 MSL); entering the hold as published. I requested and was given a descent to 3;000 MSL in holding.We then built and briefed the RNAV (RNP) Rwy XX from ZZZ2; ran the Descent Change Triangles; received our approach clearance; and executed the approach to landing uneventfully. The FO and I thoroughly debriefed the events of the flight. I then called the Duty Pilot and DISPATCH to report the incident. I should have requested radar vectors ZZZZZ1 for the best opportunity to acquire the VNAV path. I allowed the Controller to compress and to keep me high on my approach; and reducing my situational awareness. I configured very early; but it still wasn't enough to regain the VNAV path. In the future; I will not allow the ATC Controller to dictate the terms of my energy management and will give myself the Flight Handbook recommended 3 miles per 1;000 descent planning as a minimum starting point.Because we compressed our arrival and ended up high above the VNAV path I attempted to use the Vertical Speed method on LNAV/VNAV Approach rules to regain VNAV path prior to the FAP. Had I cross-checked my FMA after selecting VNAV; I would have noticed the V/S mode and perhaps executed an uneventful go-around. In the future; I will make sure to always verify my FMA mode on the PFD after making a selection on the MCP.Lastly; after fully configuring and still not descending to the path; I might have been able to acquire VNAV path prior to the FAP using Speed Intervention. There was chance we were light enough (low Ref Speed) to accelerate the idle pitch descent to regain the path; ensuring the pitch FMA remained in VNAV and avoiding the unrecognized and inadvertent V/S mode descent that caused the GPWS Warning. Recommend expanding the understanding of VNAV speed during initial and continuing qualification training in the B737.
Report_2_Narrative: Escape Maneuver occurred at approximately (time) local time on (date). Flight conditions at the time were night; IMC; rain; light turbulence.Leg 2 of a planned 4 leg day. Leg 1 was delayed 1 hours due to cargo loading. The flight was uneventful. Deiced in ZZZ after aircraft pushback. Filed route was ZZZ...ZZZ1. We planned and briefed the RNAV Rwy XX from ZZZZZ. Cruise was at FL280. PF (pilot flying) MFD was in WX Radar mode due to significant weather in the area. PM (pilot monitoring) was in TERR (terrain) mode with VSD (vertical speed) displayed. Cruise was at dusk. Shortly after starting the descent; ATC notified us that he saw an area of Moderate to Extreme precipitation ahead of us. ATC said it looked clearer to the north and asked if we would like vectors to the north for an approach via ZZZZZ1. We responded yes and he started vectoring us north. PF flew while PM loaded the arrival from ZZZZZ1 (via IAF ZZZZZ1). PM briefed the new approach and called for change triangles; which we accomplished. ATC had us do intermediate level-offs at 8;000 feet; then 7;000 feet. PF asked PM to reset the cruise altitude to provide an accurate flight path. In anticipation of being high on flight path; PF configured early to flaps 40. PM was actively monitoring the VSD and flight path; and requested lower when able from ATC. ATC said he would give us lower in a few miles. He then gave us a short vector prior to ZZZZZ2 with a descent to 6;500 feet. At approx 0.5 miles before ZZZZZ2 at 6;500 feet; ATC cleared us 'to cross ZZZZZ2 at or above 5;000 feet; cleared RNAV Rwy XX at ZZZ1'. When cleared for the approach over ZZZZZ2; PF dialed in field elevation in the MCP and descended towards the flight path. Flight conditions were night; IMC; rain; light turbulence. Approximately 1 mile prior to ZZZZZ3; we were still high on flight path so PF verbalized and set Vertical Speed down and reset MCP to 1;600 feet. PM saw the downward vector on the VSD and monitored it for approaching the flight path. Almost immediately thereafter; we received a 'Caution; Terrain' and the depicted island terrain went yellow on PM's MFD. This was quickly followed by a 'Terrain; Pull up' and the depicted terrain on the MFD went red. PF called for go-around and executed the escape maneuver. After aircraft was climbing; PF asked PM to reset MCP for missed approach altitude of 3;000 feet. PF initially had difficulty verifying the missed approach altitude on the EFB due to turbulence; transition to nighttime; and prioritizing monitoring the aircraft state while performing aircraft cleanup. PF put and verbalized 5;000 feet in the MCP window; thinking 5;000 feet was better in case 3;000 feet was incorrect. PMs intent was to devote more brain cells to performing the aircraft cleanup items and monitoring the safe aircraft state as we climbed. Aircraft was cleaned up; leveled at 5;000 feet and continued to holding at ZZZ2. We then queried ATC for a descent to 3;000 feet; setup the RNAV Rwy XX from ZZZ2. Approach was briefed by Captain; flown; and landed uneventfully. Once the aircraft reached parking and shutdown at ZZZ1; Captain and FO debriefed the events. Captain called and briefed Duty Officer; who approved continuing to the remaining 2 destinations. Captain also called and spoke with Dispatch. The remaining flights to were flown with minimal changes. Post flight; the Captain called Quality Assurance to see what they could tell us; so that we could learn further from this experience.Stay on the magenta line; and if vectored off; get back on it as early as possible. Even though the controller had plans to vector us back onto the RNP approach; a better outcome likely would have resulted if we started at the IAP. This way we would have been able to descend on a normal flight path; with adequate time and pacing; vs. having to stay higher due to the controllers higher vectoring altitudes. Request the IAP next time.At nighttime in IMC; I need to have a faster response timecalling for the escape maneuver/go-around. I should clarify this maneuver more; particularly the triggers. I should have been the first to call for it since the Captain was the PF. Instead of trying to salvage a bad or difficult approach; make the decision to go-around earlier. Memorize the missed approach altitude prior to each approach; or ensure my EFB chart is not zoomed-in so far that I cannot see it without a quick glance.Clarify various 'what-if scenarios' on RNP approaches; Escape Maneuvers; Go-Arounds. If I haven't flown as much recently; spend extra time clarifying. Communicate with Center that 6;500 feet at ZZZZZ2 creates a very difficult approach to accomplish. Recommend to them that vectoring to the IAF is likely a better option.
Report_1_Synopsis: B737-700 flight crew reported executing an escape maneuver due to a CFIT event resulting from a compressed approach clearance. Crew completed subsequent approach in an uneventful landing.

Report_1_Narrative: On departure at about 300 ft. the left T-handle light illuminated. I immediately ran my memory items; checklist; set a timer; and continued my climb. I completed my climb checklist. At about 15 seconds; the light was still illuminated so I began preparing for an air return. At 20 seconds; it was still illuminated; this was at about 4500 ft. I informed departure that I needed an immediate return for a possible engine fire; [requested priority handling]. I was cleared for the Visual Approach; and switched to tower; and was cleared to land. I completed the rest of my checklists for landing; including single engine; because the left engine was still pulled to idle and ITT (Interstage Turbine Temperature) was stable. Landed without incident. As I pulled off the runway; the T-handle light extinguished.At about 300 ft. on my climb the t-handle was illuminated. Maintenance believes that the sensors/wiring had a malfunction. They were cleaned and returned to service. I ran my checklists. I stayed ahead of the plane by choosing to do them ahead of time; anticipating that the light might not go out. I communicated with ATC immediately; and decided the safest choice was to not be in the air should things continue to escalate.I don't really have control over this event happening again; however; you can always learn something to do differently or better. Now that I have an idea of what this type of event looks like; I would have also have done a precautionary engine shut down and had them send me on a downwind instead of a 180 into the runway I just departed.
Report_1_Synopsis: C99 Captain reported false engine fire warning after takeoff.

Report_1_Narrative: A gentleman walked on the aircraft without a mask; I nicely asked him if he had a mask and if not; I would supply one for him. He said he did have a mask; but just needed to find it. He made his way to his seat in X6 and was putting his seatbelt on. I told him since he was in the bulkhead he'd have to stow his bags above him in the overhead bin. He is now moving around; bending down close to the gentleman beside him; who clearly looked uncomfortable. I then handed him a mask and told him he needed to put it on. He said once again; he has one. My B-FA then comes up and I inform him of the situation. B FA says to the gentleman he needs to put his mask on and the man loudly and rudely says; 'Oh would you just shut your mouth!!' Now; I inform our Captain on what is happening in the back and he said; 'He can't talk to you guys like that; get him off.' So I tell the gate agent; she gets her manager and the security coordinator and the man is escorted off.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Flight Attendant in Charge reported a passenger became belligerent about the face mask policy and was removed from the flight.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Communication Breakdown; Distraction; Workload; Situational Awareness
Report_1_Narrative: Passenger seated on X4 continued to disregard our request for him to keep his facial covering on at all times. We asked him several times (FA's # A; B & C) but continued to disregard our request. I even gave him a face mask but still; no compliance. Passenger seated nearby in X6 was very disturbed by it.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Attendant reported a passenger would not comply with the face mask policy.

Report_1_Narrative: Passenger X that was escorted off previous flight for acting erratically and refusing to wear his mask was then given a boarding pass to fly on the flight I was working. Agent never informed Captain or crew of this passenger's history. The only way we found out was by Captain asking agent when she came to close the flight about the information of this certain passenger!  I had to ask this passenger numerous times to follow the mask policy. Communication on the agents behalf would be a good start and for the company to actually follow through with the mask policy! I am risking my health and safety every time I come to work; it would be nice if my company would actually start to act like they care. Working on an aircraft has become a dangerous place to be. I'm begging the company to pull their head out of the sand and start taking my overall health and safety seriously!
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Attendant reported a passenger; whom had acted erratically and refused to wear a face mask on a previous flight; was allowed to board the flight.

Report_1_Narrative: I was moving a lift to do a door lube.  When done with the R2 door I moved the lift while looking to the rear; I did not realize that the lift was in drive not reverse.  While looking over my shoulder I felt the tug go forward I hit the brakes.  I did not feel it strike the aircraft. I then moved the lift to the L2 door and completed the lube on the L2 door and then moved the lift back to the parking area.  I did not know that I had contacted the aircraft until notified by the Senior Manager.  The lighting was poor and I had never done a door lube on this type of aircraft.  I also had just came back from almost three weeks off from being quarantined for COVID-19.  I was not used to night and was very tired.When selecting the lift to Reverse it inadvertently ended up in Drive.  Some of our lifts have drive forward on the gear selector and some have drive in the back of the gear selector.  Shifters are not lit and some go forward to go forward and some go forward to go aft.I really have no idea [for suggestions] other than making sure all lifts have the gear selectors the same way.  Gear selector levers should be lit at night so they can be observed.
Report_1_Synopsis: Technician reported making contact with an aircraft after moving a lift in the wrong direction.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Training / Qualification; Time Pressure; Situational Awareness
Report_1_Narrative: Upon landing the student was going too fast to make a 90 degree turn on to the taxiway. The instructor did not have enough time to correct the rudder input. If the instructor had pushed on the rudder to correct the aircraft would have tipped. So the instructor kept the aircraft going straight once it was aimed off the runway. We went into the dirt and on to a taxiway. The aircraft did not hit any lights or signs. The aircraft did not appear to sustain any damage. The engine appeared to be fine. Taxi the aircraft everything seemed to be normal.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Instructor reported student attempted to exit the runway too fast resulting in a runway excursion.

Report_1_Narrative: Due to the COVID-19 slow down our department has flown our aircraft every X weeks to keep the plane and crew flight ready for our corporation.  On this particular flight I the Captain; and the Second in Command were briefing the approach into ZZZ airport.  While briefing we were headed direct to ZZZZZ intersection for the ZZZZZ6 arrival.  The plane had not flown for two weeks and due to a cancelled trip I had not flown for 56 days.  The Second in Command had flown a trip 2 weeks prior to this flight.  On receiving the ATIS the approach advertised was different than what was usual and anticipated.  So we as a crew briefed the approach thoroughly (it was noted it had some updated information).  During this briefing I noticed we were below 10;000 feet; around 8;000 feet and traveling at 270 knots indicated airspeed.  Upon this observation I slowed the aircraft to below 250 knots.  The Controller never mentioned anything and there was no traffic noted on the TCAS or visually.  The procedure I should have done differently/better was to transfer control or to have the Second in Command brief the approach.
Report_1_Synopsis: Corporate Captain reported a speed deviation and cited lack of flying during the COVID-19 pandemic as a contributing factor.

Report_1_Narrative: Good VFR weather and Forecast for destination; enroute; and return.  Morning flight to destination was uneventful.  Afternoon return flight at 6;500 feet; and 80 NM to destination an overcast layer developed.  Obtained weather reports which indicated ceilings of 2;500 feet tapering to 900 feet at destination (forecast for improvement).  Overcast conditions about 2;000 feet thick.  Since it would be getting dark by the time I got to the destination; I elected to stay on top. Temperature at 6;500 feet was 45F (although I was flying North and knew it would decrease); surface temperatures around freezing. Obtained IFR clearance and completed ILS approach.  Entered tops at 4;500 feet MSL and broke out at 2;800 feet MSL (1;400 foot ceiling).  As soon as I entered the clouds the temperature dropped to freezing.  Picked up about 1/8 inch of ice on the horizontal stabilizer; with less on the main wing.  Windshield was warm enough and didn't have any ice.Best option would have been to land and stay overnight--while this is always a hassle; COVID pandemic has made this even less appealing.  Flying underneath a deteriorating ceiling; I believe would have been a bad option; especially at night.  The weather and temperatures of the upper Midwest limit the use of an airplane without deicing equipment for six months of the year.  Anything other than local flights; always plan an option for a rental car; or overnight stays; and utilize those options.
Report_1_Synopsis: GA pilot reported that; due to deteriorating weather; an overnight at a location other than the destination would have been a better idea than continuing the flight. But the COVID pandemic made the intermediate stop unappealing.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Time Pressure; Situational Awareness; Fatigue; Distraction; Confusion
Report_1_Narrative: Runway XXR was NOTAMed closed for 2 hours due to a crane on the departure end of the runway. Runway XXL was in use. Aircraft inbound from the west was given a right downwind entry for Runway XXL. The aircraft was sequenced to follow multiple aircraft ahead. On short final; I noticed that he appeared to be lined up for the closed runway (Runway XXR). I instructed the pilot to go-around and re-enter right traffic Runway XXL and emphasized to the pilot that Runway XXR is closed. When I cleared him to land Runway XXL; he again appeared to be lined up for XXR. I verified if he was lined up for the correct runway and on very short final; he appeared to maneuver for the correct runway.Background: all controllers at ZZZ have been on 6 day work week for the last few months due to a shortage in staffing. Our facility has also been experiencing roughly a 20% increase in traffic volume compared to last year. In September; our traffic count index has reached the numbers for us to qualify for a level 8 upgrade. If we sustain our traffic numbers for the next couple of months; level 8 at ZZZ will become a reality once it gets approved by the National Validation Team.We are all fatigued from the increase in traffic and the amount of overtime we have all been working. This is no doubt affecting our performance on position. Morale is down and controllers are becoming more and more impatient with pilots as a result of being over-worked. I worry that this will impact safety by increasing the possibility of human error.I felt noticeably fatigued towards the end of my work week. If I had not been as fatigued; I may have been able to recognize the aircraft lined up for the incorrect runway sooner. Thankfully; I recognized it at the last second; but it was very close.Yesterday; I was working CIC combined with GC. Traffic was busy. A Controller who was finishing an overlap in the back of the cab was on the phone with someone and relayed information to me. I was in the middle of working a lot of traffic on ground and what I thought I heard was to have the pilot of an Aircraft X with an XXXXX tail number call the airport manager when he lands. It turned out that the airport manager wanted us to call him when the aircraft landed.  Had we had more staffing and CIC was de-combined; this information would have been properly relayed to me. I would have been able to figure out that we had to call the airport manager and not have the pilot call. Again; my lapse in judgement may have also been due to fatigue from prolonged 6 day work weeks.For the safe of safety; the agency needs to take our staffing situation seriously. In the midst of the pandemic; our tower hours have changed to XC:00am to XO:00pm. Even though we have a staffing issue; due to the compressed tour hours; there is a good amount of overlap between controllers so we can keep LC split into 2 positions. In a little over a week; we will be going back to our normal hours which are XA:00am until XQ:00pm. This means the staffing will be spread out and during peak work hours; we may be forced to combine the LC position. As busy as it has been; it is very unsafe to work the volume of traffic we have been working with a combined LC position. This will result in 2 hour holdovers for many of us on top of the 6 day work weeks we have already been working.We have been begging for better staffing for years. There has been word that the higher ups in our region are finally taking the situation seriously. I hope this is true and we get more staffing numbers to alleviate this serious issue.
Report_1_Synopsis: ATC Controller reported fatigue and safety concerns due to 6 day a week shifts and short staffing related to the COVID-19 pandemic.

Report_1_Narrative: The VFR Aircraft; Aircraft X; was cleared on the [published VFR route] to maintain 5;500 feet. He was southbound and converging over the VOR with Aircraft Y who was IFR and descended to 5;000 feet and told about the 5;500 feet traffic that was at the time 4 miles north of the VOR. Everything was fine and it was a normal everyday situation. I was cleaning up some loose ends giving headings to other aircraft and traffic advisories; many traffic advisories. I had an aircraft report getting an RA but its resolution told him to stay where they were because there were just so many VFR's. Then I hear the Traffic Alert start which isn't uncommon for aircraft 500 feet apart in this airspace and as I look up the Aircraft Y tells me he's responding to an RA and his voice is clearly strained.I incorrectly said what I was thinking which was 'Aircraft X what are you doing! Climb immediately to 5;500' as I'm watching him descend through 5;200 feet right on top of Aircraft Y. He responds that he 'thought they were on a collision course'. To which I informed him that his actions caused the collision course. He also turned right which would have been fine if that's all he had done and stayed at 5;500 feet; but the descent made it a near or for sure mid-air if Aircraft Y hadn't taken evasive action. I issued a Brasher Warning to the pilot of Aircraft X because he 100% cause a perfectly separated situation to become a very ugly situation. Both aircraft were in the Class Bravo airspace and the VFR aircraft had no right or reason to descend at all.Over the top of LA is just a busy place where aircraft are routinely separated by 500 feet; that's just life. If they move the VFR areas where Special Flight Rules is to somewhere else then we would definitely have more altitudes to use to separate people by greater than 500 feet. but; until that happens it's just going to be what it's going to be.
Report_2_Narrative: While on a Class B clearance through the Class Bravo airspace on published VFR Route southbound at 5;500 feet; I received a traffic notification from Approach for traffic at 11 o'clock; opposite direction; at 5;000 MSL a conflict for traffic that was approaching nearly head-on. I continued to visually scan for the traffic in front of me; and when I finally spotted the oncoming traffic it was at my 11 o'clock to 11:30 position in my windscreen; at eye level. I was unable to discern any relative motion of the target relative to my windscreen. The only change I could see in the target was that it was getting larger in my field of view; and that it appeared to be some type of small jet aircraft. I immediately initiated a turn to my right in order to avoid the oncoming traffic. The turn that I initiated was done very quickly; and was probably on the order of a 30 to 35 degree angle of bank. As a result of this turn; I lost approximately 250 feet of altitude from my cruising altitude of 5;500 feet. My change in heading was approximately 45 degrees; and once my turn was completed I was able to discern relative motion of the target with respect to my windscreen and left side window. The traffic was now moving to my left; and the separation between the two of us was increasing.The opposite directly traffic passed well behind me. At that point the TRACON Controller called me and admonished me for deviating from my assigned heading and altitude. I responded to the controller with an apology; and explained that the opposite direction traffic appeared to be on a collision course with me; and it required me to take evasive action. The controller provided me with a toll-free number to call after I landed. After landing I called the toll-free number and spoke to an individual at SOCAL who asked me to describe the occurrence from my perspective. I described the occurrence in an identical manner to what I have written here. The individual was very courteous and listened carefully to my explanation; and thanked me for calling. The call ended with no indication to me that any further action would be forthcoming.It is extremely difficult to estimate lateral and vertical separation of traffic; especially when a target has no apparent relative motion and is approaching head-on. Any vertical separation that does exist between two aircraft in this situation will not be perceptible until the aircraft are very close together; when there is very little time to take evasive action if it is required. In this particular case; the opposite direction traffic was probably traveling at least twice as fast as my aircraft; resulting in an effective rate of closure of at least 400 MPH. A vertical separation of 500 feet is very small; and when possible sources of altitude error are included; it is possible that the actual vertical separation between our two aircraft was less than 500 feet.  Approximately ten minutes after this occurrence; I was in the vicinity of another airport and was in contact with another sector of the TRACON. This Controller provided me with a traffic advisory regarding jet traffic inbound from the west at 5;000 feet; and gave me instructions to climb and maintain 6;000 feet for separation purposes. I initiated the climb and leveled off at 6;000 feet; and observed the jet traffic passed well below me. After the jet traffic had crossed my flight path; the Controller cleared me back down to 5;500 feet. I have included a description of this action on the part of Approach as an example of prudent traffic management.In summary; I should have been more diligent in maintaining my assigned altitude of 5;500 feet during my turn to avoid the oncoming traffic. However; it was my belief that there was insufficient separation between the flight paths of our two aircraft; and seeing no relative motion of a target that was at eye-level in my windscreen; as pilot-in-command of the aircraft I took evasive action in the interest of collision avoidance.

Report_1_Narrative: The reason I am writing this is for safety. I would like to shine a light on the technique that I have used for years. That technique recently was cited as the reason for a one minute delay. In fact; it was not the reason we were late. The DGS system and a slightly delayed ramp clearance to push were the real cause. We were ready and the brakes were released a minute early. These delays are useless and mean nothing when an agent would have never entered it had no delay been incurred. However; the multiple events that occur after door closure still doesn't preclude the agent for coding the delay incorrectly. I would also like to point out I was contacted by my supervisor who was only interested in my holding the 1L door open versus the actual cause of the delay. I continued to be harassed by various phone calls during my layover trying to get me to see the light. All over one minute. It felt like pilot pushing to me.Company has always claimed Safety to be the number one goal. Schedule will never come before safety. It appears in this instance that schedule may be first which is sparking my desire to revisit this very important subject.Company has shown videos during recurrent training cycles highlighting the technique I use. The aircraft was at a foreign station. It was parked at the gate. The cargo doors were open. The Captain allowed the agent to close the 1L door early while cargo doors were still open. The jet bridge was pulled. Slides are armed. The aircraft begins to fill with smoke. The decision is made to evacuate. The 1L door is no longer available; nor is the slide since the jet bridge prevents it's inflation and proper position. The usable exits are opened and slides inflated. Passengers evacuate via the slides. Injuries occur. The working Captain in hindsight wishes he had not allowed the entry door to be closed so early. It would have allowed for a safe and orderly deplaning via the 1L door. After all; the aircraft isn't moving until cargo is loaded and the doors are closed. These seeds were planted during FAA approved recurrent training cycles. I listened. I agreed. My supervisor now tells me I'm out of line. It's a technique that isn't allowed. It's not in the FOM. It's also not in the FOM preventing me from doing this. Captains Authority allows me to address issues that don't exist in any manual.I've been flying airplanes for XX years. I've never had an accident or incident. I operate with safety as my number one goal. I intend on leaving here with that streak intact.I implore all that read this to come to the conclusion that I have. It makes no sense to close and block the 1L door while in the chocks with cargo being loaded. Did we not already learn this the hard way? I could have left 5 mins early but would have still been late due to routing around Tropical Storm Zeta. This is about safety. It's about the talk and the walk being in lock step.Supervisor putting schedule ahead of safety.Let Captains be Captains.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported disagreement with current policy of the timing of door closure.

Report_1_Narrative: Was advised inflight by ZZZZZ controllers that they were unable to contact ZZZ Approach controllers. In addition to there being no NOTAM; ZZZ had also failed to 'release' the airspace over to the Center before going home. As a result; ZZZZZ could not clear us for an approach into the airspace. We were issued holding instructions until someone in ZZZ returned to the airport to release the airspace. Initially; ZZZZZ seemed unsure if ZZZ was even open or not. I told them that they had indeed closed based off of the remarks section of the AWOS. I knew that ZZZ closed at XA00 local based on recent flights. Plus; the airport itself (Runways and taxiways) would close later due to the construction that takes place at night. However; because there were no NOTAMs for either closure this time; I thought that they would be open. We had no alternate; as the weather was good; and as such had limited time to hold. Fortunately; we eventually got clearance to proceed into ZZZ.ZZZ ATC failed to release the airspace to ZZZZZ prior to signing off for the night. As a result; we were held until the airspace could be released. In addition; there were no NOTAMs noting the early closure of the ATC facilities at ZZZ.

Report_1_Narrative: I experienced a near midair collision while flying a glider south of the ZZZ airport. Purpose of the flight was currency since the soaring season is mostly over apart from mountain wave flying. Typically; I take a tow into the mountains to connect with the excellent soaring conditions. The plan was to stay close to the airport and perform a short pattern flight. Before the flight; I thought about the extra vigilance required due to the flight in congested airspace. Flying in the mountains presents it's own set of challenges; but from a traffic perspective it's much less stressful than flying close to the ZZZ airport. Takeoff and climbout were normal; and we were established on an easterly heading in the 'glider box' climbing through 7;200 feet when I released from the tow plane. Normal release procedure is to clear right; release from tow; and perform a slight climbing right turn to deconflict from the tow plane while the towplane performs a descending left turn. This was accomplished; and I kept the turn going to a 270 heading. Once rolling wings level at 270; I was presented with the image of a blue and white Piper Cherokee rapidly filling my windscreen head on. Time from recognition to action was within a second and I dumped the nose to build airspeed/separation and rolled right to deconflict. The Cherokee seemed to pick me up at the last minute; and I observed him making a slightly delayed climbing right turn. I estimated separation at between 100 and 200 feet. It was too close! If I remained on tow on an easterly heading; there is a very good chance the Cherokee would have flown directly into me at my 6 o'clock. Very similar to a fatal midair accident that happened 10 years ago at ZZZ between a towplane; glider; and Cirrus transitioning the area. I was on the ZZZ CTAF with the tow plane; and neither me or the tow pilot heard the Cherokee making position calls. The Cherokee continued it's flight eastbound and I made an announcement about the near miss and called his position to anyone else on frequency. Technically; nobody did anything wrong. The Cherokee was not required to make position calls. However; in the busy airspace around ZZZ this is common sense. See and avoid worked; but just barely. I was squawking 1202 (glider transponder code per Letter Of Agreement with TRACON) with a Mode S transponder. I confirmed the transponder was on during my before takeoff checklist and directly following the incident. I had a FLARM collision avoidance system installed in the glider. This picks up Mode C; Mode S; and other Flarm traffic. In the event of a conflict; there is an audible warning and the screen on the S100 variometer displays the clock position; distance; and altitude above/below of conflicting traffic. Very similar to a TCAS. It does not display resolution advisory/vertical speed required for deconfliction. The FLARM alarm did not activate; and I didn't even look at the instrument. My eyes were outside the whole time and I was very lucky they were. This comes down to solid training and a good scan. The World War II pilots had it right. 'Keep your head on a swivel'. Don't trust your traffic avoidance system to show or alert you to everything out there. TCAS; ADS-B; TIS; FLARM; etc. all offer an absolutely incredible advantage in situational awareness and safety. However; it's not a 100% solution. Many gliders and older powered aircraft don't have transponders; and a traffic avoidance system won't pick up something they can't see. You still need to look outside the cockpit.The FLARM/S100 system has certain configurations that can be set by the pilot on when to audibly and visually alert on a potential conflict. Due to flying in close proximity to the tow plane on tow; I believe it's a possible setting to inhibit warnings while on tow. Since this happened within seconds of release; it's possible that is the reason I didn't receive an alert. I'll need to do some reading of the manual and also investigatethe configuration of the S100/FLARM system installed on Aircraft X to further understand this logic. It's very possible this is my fault; and by configuring the system differently I could have avoided a slice of swiss cheese or two from lining up. It's not the people talking on the radio that will hit you; it's the people that aren't. A good scan is critical. Keep that head on a swivel and outside. When releasing from tow in the future; I'll start clearing not only my 3 to 4 o'clock but all the way to my 6 o'clock. It's unlikely I would have spotted the traffic doing that due to the headrest blocking my view directly backwards; but it's a good idea none the less. The local terrain and airspace setup cause a bottleneck between the mountains to the west and the Class B to the east. You have a lot of airplanes flying VFR in a fairly small corridor. That ups the chances for these types of incidents occurring. More education for pilots that not all traffic will be presented or presented accurately on their traffic displays. This is a perfect example. Many pilots think everything out there that can hit them will show up on Foreflight; TCAS; etc. That's absolutely not the case. Better education about the 'glider box' at ZZZ. There is a note about it on the ZZZ airport website; and in the Chart Supplement. It's buried; and realistically not many pilots read those materials for airports they will overfly. There should be a note on the Sectional about the specific dimensions/locations of the ZZZ glider box.Even better; the FAA should make a database of this type of airspace and it's dimensions and allow it to be displayed as an overlay on tools like Foreflight. Just like they do with TFRs. While the Chart Supplement is an awesome resource; my honest experience is nobody looks at it unless they are taking a checkride. Everyone uses Foreflight these days. By presenting this type of airspace as a graphical overlay on these types of moving maps/apps; you have a much higher likelihood of awareness and compliance from the pilot population. This would increase safety tremendously! This wasn't a causal factor in this incident; but easily could be in a future one. All gliders should be required to have transponders. There are plenty of people flying gliders at 17;999 feet. In busy terminal arrival and departure corridors without a transponder. The battery technology exists for this to not be a problem anymore. I can fly all day with my transponder; radio; electronic variometer; and two moving map displays without running out of battery power.
Report_1_Synopsis: A Glider pilot reported a NMAC with a fixed wing aircraft while in a published glider flying area that is close to a busy airport on one side and a mountain range on the other.

Report_1_Narrative: We were returning from a local flight. We were using Runway XXL & R which is not our normal pattern. Therefore; instead of flying closer to the airport; we were maneuvering to a XX landing pattern. We had called the tower 15 miles Southeast to obtain a clearance to enter the D space. We were given a squawk code and told by the tower operator we were observed now at 8 miles Southeast and told to 'fly present heading to avoid traffic'. We were doing so and a minute or two later saw what appeared to be Aircraft Y at our 12:00 position lightly lower and noticed a rapid close rate. He initiated a rapid turn to his left; east. We turned rapidly to our left; west; and avoided contact. The tower called at about that time and instructed us to dive immediately. It was a close call. The tower asked me to call him after we landed. We discussed the event from the point at which he gave us the beacon code. I am not sure if he was talking to Aircraft Y traffic or not. We were able to see and avoid the traffic so it worked out. The operator and I agreed we were closer than we would have liked to be.

Report_1_Narrative: I was instructed by the ZZZ1 Tower after taking off on Runway XR to follow another small aircraft who had taken off before me before turning right downwind to depart to the north east. I was expecting to get clearance through the [ZZZ] Class B because the Tower had indicated so. The aircraft I was following never turned crosswind; so I initiated my turn and was a little faster than normal climb because I was trying to stay below 1;800 feet which was the bottom of the Class B airspace straight ahead. In turning right to depart to the east; I clipped the corner of the Class B surrounding ZZZ2 just to the north of ZZZ1. The Tower asked if I was familiar with the airspace around ZZZ1 and I stated that I am and that I had clipped the corner of the Class B and was expediting turning south. I thought the bottom at that point was 1;800 feet and I remained below 1;800 feet before getting south of that corner; however; after landing at home ZZZ3; I checked my actual track and saw that at that point where I briefly went in to the Class B it exists from ground to 10;000 feet; not 1;800  feet to 10;0000 as I had thought. In this particular area the Class B just to the west of me showed 1;800 feet to 10;000 feet which is what I saw on my chart. Tower thanked me for getting out quickly and handed me off to ZZZ Departure who gave me an unrestricted climb to 10;500 feet; my filed encounter altitude. Departure never specifically cleared me through the Class B to the east which has a base of 4;800 feet and top of 10;000 feet; but they did give me an unrestricted climb to 10;500. It's possible that I was above 4;800 feet; on my climbout which also would have been flight in to the Class B without a specific clearance which I failed to ask for.I have flown down to ZZZ1 3 times in the past few months and because of the reduced traffic during COVID I've been cleared through the Class B and even offered it by ATC without asking; which is unusual. ATC is very pleasant in that area; but I thought I should report this to help others with this type of potential confusion. ZZZ1 gets a lot of local flights and the Tower issues quite a few follow another aircraft instructions as well as 'stay south of highway XXX that only locals would know; I presume to stay away from the nearby Class B airspace from the ground to 10;000 feet.

Report_1_Narrative: This event was a complex setup with numerous contributing factors that led to a slight and uneventful course deviation on a flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1. Having spent 30+ years in the part of the US I was quite familiar with the dynamics of the environment. In preparing the flight; I ran a prelim flight plan which recommended a route I would expect; a SID that meshed with the ZZZZZ3 arrival to ZZZ1. For arrivals from the south into ZZZ1 it is customary and without exception have flown the ZZZZZ3 which runs with the arrivals and departures to several airports. There were numerous TFR's along and around the route of flight this day. I filed a flight plan using app which recommended a different route; a SID to Victor airways; no STAR into ZZZ1. It was presumed this route was preferred to accommodate the numerous TFR's. I know for certain in the app I had selected FL230 as I wanted to either be rerouted as necessary for the TFRs or be above as the TFRs were below FL180. These issues were disclosed; briefed between the two pilots prior to filing flight plan; discussed verbally in the takeoff briefing; and even added extra fuel for possible reroute. When our clearance was obtained to depart ZZZ; it was for the SID and Victor airways as filed with app; further reinforcing the presumption that it was ATC preferred due to the TFR's. The final altitude cleared was 17;000 feet due to the Victor airways chosen; not FL230 as was desired.As we began our taxi; we were expecting Runway XX for departure which was a fairly long taxi. Traffic was light; and Ground Control stated Runway XXC was available which we accepted. This now being a very short taxi. I stated to the copilot would taxi slowly to allow time to load new departure runway in FMS; the SID chart was retrieved; compared to the FMS; and the takeoff briefing verbally amended accordingly. In doing these things; we verified only page one of the flight plan in the FMS. At this point we were not aware that in reloading the departure RW; the FMS had on the second page not only inserted a discontinuity; but had deleted two waypoints; the last one on the SID and first point on the filed Victor airway.As we were flying the departure and level at 15;000 feet; we crossed the second to last waypoint on the SID. At this point when the FMS sequenced; the discontinuity appeared on page one. This FMS has known issues and several Service Information Letters (SIL's) from the manufacturer regarding runway changes with SIDs and STARs. Having seen the occurrence a vast number of times for arrivals when changing or loading the arrival runway after the STAR; the resolve had always been to delete the discontinuity as no waypoints had ever been seen deleted and verify altitude/speed restrictions. When the discontinuity appeared on page one of the FMS flight plan; it was simply deleted without verifying the fix meshed with the filed route. As two waypoints had also been deleted; this created the issue at hand. Soon after we crossed the waypoint in question; ATC asked if we were beginning our RH turn. This exchange revealed the error at hand and we were given a vector. Believe it was just prior to that waypoint that ATC asked if we could join the ZZZZZ3 arrival; to which we stated yes. The Controller stated this will be vectors to join the ZZZZZ3 and cleared us to 17;000 feet. At this point we inserted the missing waypoints and queried ATC to confirm our currently assigned route. ATC again stated expect the ZZZZZ3 without confirming assigned route; and did not provide an expect to waypoint to join the ZZZZZ3. A level of uncertainty remained as the ZZZZZ3 has six (6) transitions into the arrival. We briefed and had STAR displayed to deal with the coming short notice for the join waypoint as the fixes along this arrival are close together with several altitude and speed restrictions. Throughout this event; we could hear ATC transmitting to other aircraft; but never heard other aircraft respond; thus the controller was obviously working multiple frequencies/sectors with a resulting high workload likely contributing to not providing and expect to waypoint. This also presented a certain level of distraction on our part. Once we were cleared to a waypoint on the ZZZZZ3; and with a descend via clearance; the remainder of the flight was uneventful. The slight deviation actually took us further away from the TFRs; no restricted airspace was encroached; and there were no traffic conflicts.
Report_1_Synopsis: Corporate Captain reported a track heading deviation during departure and cited ATC workload as a contributing factor.

Report_1_Narrative: Pressurized brakes...It did it again. It was not even X years ago that I landed a Piper Malibu on a short runway only to notice upon touchdown that one complete side of the brake system was completely inoperative. Now; just last week; it happened again. Here's the story; and Piper needs to fix to the design problem...The Malibu has inverted master brake cylinders on the rudder pedals like many Pipers. Normally; the brakes work and there are no problems. Yet an insidious problem will develop. There are 3 O-rings on each master cylinder and these O-rings will leak. Yet; they will not leak brake fluid out of the system; they will and do let air into the system. The Malibu is pressurized; and when flown with a differential cabin pressure; the pressure is pushing air in to the brakes system thru the brake master cylinders. The cabin air which is under pressure is flowing to any opening in the cabin which to escape. When the O-rings in the brake system allows the cabin air to enter the braking system; the brakes stop working. If allowed to persist; the air in the system renders the brakes on the affected side or both sides ineffective...or even non-existent.Upside-down brake master cylinders...As you would expect; the air migrates upwards and enters the brake lines even so insidiously and it doesn`t take much air to make the brakes disabled. Here's the issue; Malibu brake failures are common on flights where the brakes worked perfectly on run-up and pre flight checks. The problem does not reveal itself until the brakes are used on landing.Although the checklist in the Malibu clearly states to check the brakes prior to takeoff. How do you check the brakes in flight prior to landing?If either side of the braking system is weak or non-existent; perform a go-around and consider your options. Pilot might want to fly to an airport with a longer runway if they have fuel. They may want to fly an approach a little slower and maybe plan to touch down as early as practicable on the runway. They might want to call for safety vehicles to be ready in case there is a landing over run issue and notify the FAA. In any case; you do not want to touch down on the runway and then realize you've got a brake problem. Many Piper pilots and passengers are in danger when this occurs.
Report_1_Synopsis: PA-46 Malibu pilot reported brake failure during landing rollout; citing a possible design flaw in the braking system.

Report_1_Narrative: We landed 31R in DAL and exited runway at M5; Ground issued B to D to the gate. We made turn onto M. Ground caught the error and issued new clearance 'M B5 ramp'. There was an Operations vehicle on the frequency and Ground asked him to look at the signage at M/M5 intersection; Ground stated we were the fourth aircraft to make the same error and he didn't want to file a deviation if it was a signage issue.
