Report_1_Narrative: I deferred a defect for the VHF Comm broken knobs on the observer audio panel for Aircraft X. I used MEL 23-XX-XX-XX. I incorrectly interpreted this MEL for the observer audio panel when the MEL states that 2 Communications Systems (VHF) are installed. So the assumption is that the observer audio panel is excluded from this and it only applies to the Captain and First Officer. The Aircraft had accomplished one flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1. I had discovered the error a few hours after. The MEL is confusing for my level of experience; and suggest that this MEL be reviewed and changes made to it.
Report_2_Narrative: During the deferral process; I was working with [Name] to sign off the discrepancy using an MEL for the audio control panel for the observer side. When talking with [Name]; he said he had deferred the item already in TRAX and called to give me the information and walk me through the sign off. I went with the MEL number that he gave me. After I finished the MEL with him I finished closing he work order on Aircraft X to get it ready for the flight. I did not double check the MEL number he gave me and later he called me to tell me he gave me the wrong MEL number. I fixed it on the paperwork that I had.  I will need to make sure I double check any MEL Maintenance Control gives me to make sure it is the correct one and they we all agree.
Report_1_Synopsis: Technician reported applying the wrong MEL and the aircraft flew in service.

Report_1_Narrative: I was training in Aircraft X; doing pattern work; and while on final to [Runway] 7R; I was looking out to my left and saw an Aircraft Y starting his turn from downwind to final for 7L. We originally were offset to the right as a precaution for traffic on 7L. As I was getting closer to the runway; I looked back again and saw that the Aircraft Y overshot his base to final turn and was on path to hit us (noticed him about 200-300 feet away). I took evasive action and went full power and a sharp turn to the right to get out of his path. About 3 seconds later he intercepted our path and if not for evasive maneuver; we would've had a mid-air collision.
Report_1_Synopsis: Student pilot reported an NMAC with an aerobatic aircraft in the pattern at LVK airport.

Report_1_Narrative: [We] departed AUO to complete a Commercial Pilot Stage Check. The objective was to complete a practice ILS approach to Runway 36 at AUO; with simulated vectors to the final approach course. The private; instrument rated pilot was the pilot flying (PF). He was wearing view limiting 'foggles'. The aircraft is equipped with an ADS-B traffic awareness system; displayed on the MFD. We were established on the localizer for Runway 36 at approximately 9 miles from the runway. The PF made his initial radio call on CTAF that we were 9 mile south on the ILS Runway 36. There was one other aircraft approximately 3 miles ahead of us; on final; on the ILS as well. We were approximately a 6 mile final when [Aircraft Y] reported 10 miles straight in for Runway 36. We subsequently made another distance call to alert the Aircraft Y of our location. By this time; we had the aircraft on the ADS-B display. That aircraft was at a higher altitude but substantially faster than our final approach speed of 90 KIAS. We had no visual contact with the Aircraft Y; our only reference was the track on our MFD. When he called 5 mile final; I asked over CTAF if he intended to overfly us on final. The response was; 'we will sidestep to the left'. When the ADS-B showed +300 and very close behind us; I stated to the student 'I have the flight controls' and descended and banked right. The pilot of the jet stated that he had us in sight no factor. We then saw the Aircraft Y slightly below and to our left as he passed by. The other aircraft ahead of us called low approach only and went around. We sidestepped to the right and climbed back to pattern altitude on an upwind leg. The Aircraft Y landed without further incident.
Report_1_Synopsis: Instructor pilot reported an NMAC on approach to AUO airport.

Report_1_Narrative: I was told by our company Chief Pilot; my 61.58 check-ride had lapsed after I had been flying PIC for several flights in our aircraft under Part 91. I was told I had operated the aircraft as PIC outside of my 61.58 requirements. I had received a check-ride which I was told was for my PIC currency under 61.58 with our Chief Pilot/Check Airman. My company says they have no record of a signoff of my completion of the 61.58 flight during my 2 month COVID-19 SFAR put forth by the FAA. I was told by my Chief Pilot I am illegally operating as PIC 3 months after I had been evaluated after the check-ride. My usual check-ride month is X; and fell under the SFAR time period and our training facility was essentially closed due to COVID-19; so an in-house check-ride to satisfy my 61.58 requirements was performed; within the SFAR grace period specifications. Apparently my company never logged/lost the flight training records and put me in a situation where I am in violation of 61.58. In the near future my company is going to perform another in-house check-ride with the same Chief Pilot/Check Airman to satisfy my 61.58 requirements. In the meantime I will not be performing any PIC duties going forward until my new signoff is complete.I had understood my 61.58 requirements were to be met that day; so I continued to operate our aircraft as PIC under normal circumstances. It wasn't until I was to be contracted out by my company to ferry an aircraft that this clerical error was discovered in my records. I have a log book entry of this flight occurring and there is company records of this flight occurring as well as a training flight. My company should be held accountable for any issues that arise from this in the future as I performed the check-ride to satisfaction and was under the false assumption that my Check Airman followed through with his paperwork for company records. Going forward; I will now require a copy of my training record for my own personal files.
Report_1_Synopsis: Corporate pilot reported the company lost or misplaced SFAR (Special Federal Aviation Regulation) records of the pilot's completed check ride during this pandemic period.

Report_1_Narrative: I am writing this report to report a near miss situation in the standard traffic pattern for Runway 27L at Gillespie Field. My student and I were practicing traffic pattern operations at SEE. After checking upwind ; crosswind; downwind; clear we made a left turn into the pattern for Runway 27L. When my student looked to check the distance from aircraft to [the] runway; he also looked back and noticed that there was another aircraft right on our tail - same altitude; less than 100 feet behind us - same altitude. Tower advised that [he] was too close to us and told them to offset to the south for spacing. Aircraft Y offset to the south towards our 5 o'clock position and we got cleared to land #2 for Runway 27L.
Report_1_Synopsis: Instructor pilot reported an NMAC in the pattern at SEE airport.

Report_1_Narrative: I was with my student in initial climb out for Runway 21. We were roughly 1200 feet MSL. We made all the proper calls. Winds were favoring Runway 21. When we were 1200 feet MSL; a Piper made a short final call for Runway 3. The Piper did not make any calls before that. We had to turn to avoid them. It was a really really close encounter.
Report_1_Synopsis: Instructor pilot reported an NMAC in the pattern at EYE airport.

Report_1_Narrative: Aircraft X [flight] got handed off from ZLC they passed along that they were low fuel. Aircraft X was a flight of 6. With the weather being poor and the visibility being 4 miles an instrument approach is what they were requesting. That being said; their TACAN and ILS were both out of service. The only way they were getting in was a visual to [Runway] XXR. So I vectored the flight behind the [civilian] aircraft coming from the south. Giving them block altitudes above the MVA so they had proper spacing amongst themselves. As I was stepping Aircraft X down they kept wanting lower and lower in order to get the visual approach. I stepped them down to 5000 and they descended to 4800; I gave them an LOA (low altitude alert). Then after fixing that issue I gave them 4500 once they were in the 4500 MVA. Turned them to final and I noticed that they dropped below 4500. So I gave them another LOA and told them to maintain 4500. I asked them numerous times if they had the airport in sight. They said no so I climbed them to 8000 and told them to fly heading 100. Aircraft X flight 2-5 reported the field in sight and at that point I cleared them for the visual. Aircraft X 6 didn't get the airport so I turned him away from the mountains and climbed them. After that I gave him a new squawk code and split Aircraft X 1 and Aircraft X 6 up. After clearing Aircraft X 6 to ZZZ and verifying his altitude I sequenced the two flights to get the visual behind another arrival. When we have airplanes that are low fuel and have no approaches we need to get those approaches fixed. Tech ops or who ever was fixing them need to understand the situation on hand.
Report_1_Synopsis: TRACON Controller reported having to break up a flight of 6 fighters to get them to land.

Report_1_Narrative: Aircraft X was on heading 360 and instructed to descend to 6;000 ft.  I observed Aircraft X descend through 6;000 and at 5;800 I issued a low altitude alert; the MVA was 5;600.  Aircraft X did not respond and kept descending.  I issued another low altitude alert; climb and maintain 6;000 immediately and when their data block displayed 5;100 they reported level at 6;000.  I told them altitude indicates 5;100; they asked to verify altimeter 30.25 and I gave them the current altimeter 29.24.  After a couple miles they showed a climb and climbed to 6;000.It was apparent watching the replay that Aircraft X check on indicating 12;100 and reporting level at 13;000.  For some reason I did not catch it.  I even descended them to 8;000 and they leveled at an indicated 7;000 and I did not notice.  I think this is because 7;000 is a normal altitude that I would descend them to at that location but I had left them a little higher.  When I descended them to 6;000 and they indicated lower it was apparent something was wrong and I was immediately concerned about the MVA so I issued a low altitude alert before they went below the MVA and a climb to 6;000.A snowstorm had just blown through the airspace and there was still stiff winds out of the west gusting to 30 kts.  I had a sequence developing for ZZZ and Aircraft X was near the front of it.  I recall planning ahead; looking at strips; using the STARS (Standard Terminal Automation Replacement System) to determine how much the wind was pushing the vectors.  Also ZZZ had many taxiways closed from the snow so I was vectoring for much greater distance than usual (10 miles on final).  I must not have looked at Aircraft X's altitude when they checked on and just used the reported altitude.  While I am happy I got a low altitude alert out when they were near terrain; I wish that I had caught it on check-on.I found it strange that their altitude in STARS was accurate but not in the cockpit.  I thought the altimeter setting would change what STARS reported. I have to be diligent to verify altitudes when the aircraft check on; so altimeter discrepancies can be caught early.
Report_2_Narrative: Descending into ZZZ through FL 180 we completed the Approach Checklist and verified 30.24 altimeter setting. On vectors to final as we were leveling off; Approach Control asked us to climb to 6;000 ft. We were indicating 6;300 at that time; so the clearance just sounded odd. The Approach Controller said that we were at 5;200 and for us to climb to 6;000 and turn to a heading of 030. I immediately clicked the autopilot/auto-throttles off and started my turn towards 030 heading and started climbing; as my Pilot Monitoring verbalized that we had the wrong altimeter setting of 30.24 instead of 29.24. We leveled off at 6;000 on a 030 heading; and at that time I engaged the autopilot and auto-throttles. We got vectored for approach and landed uneventfully on Runway XX. We were asked to contact TRACON on landline by the Ground Controller as we taxied to the gate. We realized that we had unintentionally set altimeter setting of 30.24 in error instead of 29.24 which directly led to the altitude deviation. We failed to catch our error during crosschecks as we ran the checklist due to expectation bias. Lack of digital ATIS was also a contributing factor; however; we should have trapped this error as we updated the new weather. We needed to be more vigilant to trap these kind of errors.
Report_1_Synopsis: TRACON Controller and the pilots of aircraft reported setting the wrong altimeter in the aircraft which led to low altitude alerts on final approach.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Workload; Confusion; Situational Awareness; Time Pressure
Report_1_Narrative: I was in bed sleeping at XA:05am.  My scheduled shift for the day was supposed to begin at XE:00L.  I received a phone call at XA:05 from my operations manager.  He said that this phone call was not a joke and that he needed me to report to work ASAP because the Tower was being evacuated due to a COVID-19 case and the 'need for secondary cleaning.'  I was aware of the fellow colleague who had been out on quarantine. The colleague had last worked a shift on [date] in the Tower.  Apparently managers above me had become aware that this colleague had contracted the virus.  A telcon had been convened in the earlier hours of the morning and during that telcon it was determined that cleaning the Tower was necessary due to the COVID case of an employee who hadn't worked in the Tower in over XX days.  It was determined that this cleaning needed to take place ASAP.  No regard was given to the fact that the employee hadn't worked for XX days and that controllers had worked in the permanent Tower for close to two weeks. Even more frustrating was the fact that this cleaning would take place during the busiest and most complex traffic times of the facility.  There was no pre-planning for this transition to take place.  From the time I was awakened; I was on the phone communicating and preparing for a very complex transition to a temporary Tower.  As this was early in the morning; there were almost no resources available to prepare for and to facilitate this transition.In my opinion; those that made this decision were extremely short-sighted and negligent in considering the impact to the safety of the operation and to those working in the operation.  With the help of the ZZZ Airport Manager on Duty and my Operations Manager; I reported alone to a contingency Tower at the terminal at with two portable radios.  Prior to leaving the permanent Tower I met with one of the two controllers on duty for the graveyard shift and explained to them the transition.  These two controllers stayed beyond the end of their shifts to facilitate the transition.  Their actions were exemplary. By XF:00 am all X controllers who were scheduled to work the day shift were with me in the temporary Tower.  I had coordinated with the TRACON to have the Developmental Controller on shift stay in the TRACON to work flight data.  The actions of the controllers that morning were heroic.  Working with 3 radios; two telephones; and a few pads of paper and pens.  The controllers on shift safely moved the three busiest traffic banks of the day while the permanent Tower was cleaned.  I was in awe of their professionalism and commitment to safety.  Their expertise was truly heroic.At XH:00 am Local; the cleaning was completed and we were able to transition to the permanent Tower.  As a team we were proud of what we had accomplished in spite of very difficult circumstance.The timing of this event was horrific.  Those who demanded the cleaning take place took no regard for operational safety.  There is no reason that after XX days of working in the permanent Tower under possible exposure that it would not have hurt to delay the cleaning until the operation was in a better position to support cleaning.  This cleaning should have happened on a mid shift and the facility should have been closed for the duration of the cleaning.  I am aware of multiple enroute centers that have been closed for cleaning.  The cleaning is always done overnight and there is sufficient traffic management support and communication to the users about the event.  This decision to clean the Tower was made in the early hours of the morning and as the one who facilitated the transition I am aware of no support or awareness that come from outside the facility.  In this event I am not aware of any communications to the users that we were in a temporary Tower.  This event was mitigated by the expertise of air traffic controllers who have been heroically working for months through thispandemic.  They are already working short staffed in less than ideal conditions.  Instead of recognizing these circumstances; those on the telcon who mandated the cleaning ignored the safety of the operation.
Report_1_Synopsis: Tower Controller reported safety concerns while transitioning to a temporary contingency tower while the permanent tower underwent COVID-19 cleaning procedures during a busy traffic time of day.

Report_1_Narrative: As the pandemic is surging to record levels again; I feel compelled to highlight an ongoing and now seemingly institutionally entrenched intentional violation of basic company safety policy regarding mask wear in the ZZZ base pilot lounge.  According to the policy letter from management; employees are required to wear face coverings in crew bases whenever not actively eating; drinking; or taking medicine.  This does not occur with the vast majority of employees I observe regularly regardless of time of day; number of occupants; lack or not of social distancing; and is an ongoing situation.  I have even heard some say they spend more time in the lounge these days in order to avoid the gate/terminal areas where other work group members might express the need for compliance.  The ZZZ base pilot lounge is seen by nearly everyone as a 'safe space' to willfully flaunt company face covering policy and could easily end up being a major source of COVID-19 transmission; resulting in increased sick calls; company health expenses; or even employee deaths.This starts at the top.  I can't speak about other bases; but there is no messaging; signage; or even leadership by good example by base leadership for this simplest and most effective of pandemic mitigations.  If company policy is meant to actually have a positive effect and not be simply lip service; leadership needs to inform and demand compliance and show leadership by demonstrating compliance.  This needs to be standard across ALL employee work spaces and leadership must be held accountable.  I refuse to spend any more time than absolutely necessary in my company workspace of the pilot lounge because it jeopardizes my health and that of my co-workers and family.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier pilot reported that many employees in the pilot lounge do not comply with company face mask policy.

Report_1_Narrative: I contacted First Officer X to notify him of my desire to wear masks on the flight deck. The FO replied that he did not want to wear a mask in the cockpit. As per policy we both agreed to contact the Union. The Union notified me that they would contact me. They called me to give me the option to remove myself from the trip either with or without pay. I was informed that I could be removed from the trip by using my vacation time thereby retaining my pay. The other option was to be removed from the trip without pay and suffer no other adverse consequences. Although I did not believe that the offers to remove myself from the trip were fair; I felt compelled to drop the trip because of my desire to protect myself from potentially being exposed to COVID-19 on the flight deck. The practice of offering crew members the option of taking vacation time is not sustainable. Considering the variables of the extended time COVID-19 may be affecting operations as well as personal choice to refuse mask wearing; one's vacation time could potentially be quickly exhausted. The company mandates pilots that masks be worn in all public places upon reporting to work to include the employee bus; the terminal; and the cabin to protect ourselves and others. This leads me to question why; when COVID-19 cases among pilots are growing; there is no direction strongly encouraging the wearing of masks even when it is not currently FAA directed.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported the First Officer did not want to wear a mask in the cockpit. The Captain decided due to concerns about exposure to COVID-19; to take the only option given of dropping the trip.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Human-Machine Interface; Situational Awareness; Confusion; Distraction
Report_1_Narrative: Leaving MMMX on OMPUT departure; chart 10-3 shows a speed constraint of 200 knots until D6 MEX. No other speed constraints are mentioned on chart; or 10-7 pages. Out of 10;000 feet we wondered why FMGC speed stayed at 250 knots and were prepared to intervene with a higher speed but didn't. Passing 18;000 the speed jumped up to a normal climb; and we remained in Managed Speed. Turns out there are other speed constraints out of MMMX; but they are only found on the 10-1R Radar Minimum Altitudes chart; which isn't something we'd normally look for on an RNAV departure. That chart shows 200 knots to D10 or 10;500 feet and 250 knots to D30 or 18;000 feet. Once again; neither are referenced on any departure; or other publication. Since the 200 knot to D6 speed limit is on the 10-3 departures page; it lends a false sense of security that this is the only speed constraint that applies. Thankfully the FMGC knew; and we remained in compliance.
Report_1_Synopsis: An Air Carrier Captain reported confusion due to the aircraft complying with altitude and speed restrictions which were not published on their chart.

Report_1_Narrative: Forgot to submit my COVID assessment prior to the first leg in the morning.  I did the assessment and became distracted through my preparation to begin my day and forgot to submit my COVID assessment.  I submitted my assessment once the first flight segment was completed.[Cause was being] distracted and not following personal reminding procedures.  Maybe there is a way that we can acknowledge that we have performed the COVID assessment in the same way we acknowledge that we are FIT for Duty.  This would make a normal part of the procedures we already have in place.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported forgetting to submit the COVID assessment form prior to the first leg.

Report_1_Narrative: The Captain and I made a go around on our second attempt to landing. The first approach was discontinued due to RVR being reported below the minimums for the approach outside the final approach fix. Due to a glideslope anomaly on Runway 23. The glideslope a few hundred feet from reaching minimums made a quick movement towards half scale deflection down. The aircraft was on a constant rate of descent; airspeed and proper configuration; hand flown below 1700 feet per approach plate. At the point that I called runway in sight the Captain and I noticed that the aircraft was not going to touch down in the prescribed TDZ and accomplished the go around procedure. While being vectored for a 3rd attempt at landing; the Captain and I briefed that if the anomaly happened again; we would accomplished another go around. Before the 3rd approach; another flight was able to land on their first attempt. After requesting a PIREP from the crew; they said they were able to see the runway right at minimums. We were able to obtain visual reference with the runway right at minimums and complete a successful landing. In the hotel van with the other crew we asked them if they had issues with the glideslope and mentioned they did. They said it acted very similarly to our situation. It seems that this has been a recurring theme at CRW in the past as well. The cause of the second go-around was due to an inaccurate indication of the glideslope that put the crew in a situation where a landing would have been made outside of the TDZ. I think the FAA needs to take a deeper dive in what is causing glideslope anomalies for the ILS 23 into CRW. Especially coming into the winter months in mountainous areas where weather can deteriorate rapidly.
Report_1_Synopsis: An Air Carrier First Officer reported having to initiate a go around on their second approach attempt due to the glideslope fluctuating. The pilot reports this is a recurring issue on this approach and other crews also reported the glideslope fluctuating.

Report_1_Narrative: We were cleared for the visual approach Runway 17 into Asheville. We were at 6000 feet coming in from the southeast and we had the GPS runway 17 loaded in the FMS. The Captain set 4000 ft in the Altitude Selector and we looked at the GPS plate confirmed 4000 ft at FAF and saw the highest obstacle of 4368 ft to our right in the distance.  We were VMC at night and we saw the higher terrain to the right of us and we saw [lower] terrain in front of us. We both thought we could get through with the [lower] terrain ahead. As we crossed over the [lower] terrain we got the GPWS 'terrain' and pull up. The Captain quickly clicked off the autopilot and arrested the descent at 4700 ft MSL. No limitations were exceeded as we were at Flap 8.  We continued on the approach and landed without further incident. We saw the higher terrain to our left which I pointed out and we both agreed we could set the FAF altitude and descend. The Captain even slowed his descent to 0.9 from 1.5 as we crossed the terrain. We may have been too focused on the highest obstacle and higher terrain. We clicked off the autopilot and I called out the altitude we were at cleared his FD. We continued since we arrested the descent and no further incident took place. Next time I will suggest to wait until we cross over the terrain before descending from 6000 feet.
Report_1_Synopsis: CRJ First Officer reported receiving a GPWS Terrain warning on a night visual approach to AVL.

Person_2_Human_Factors: Situational Awareness; Communication Breakdown; Confusion; Distraction
Report_1_Narrative: We briefed the route and departure; to include the [engine failure] procedures. We confirmed the route in the FMS. After being cleared for takeoff and reaching 400 AGL; We turned to heading 189 and hit moderate or greater turbulence and mountain waves; which significantly affected us. I had trouble communicating with ATC and performing cockpit duties due to turbulence. Just before reaching 1;000 AGL; Tower said switch to departure. Upon contacting departure we were told 'upon reaching 8;000; proceed direct to a fix'; but the radio quality of the transmission was poor and we couldn't clearly hear the name of the fix. I realized the mountain was on our path and for an immediate left turn to avoid terrain. The Spokane Departure Controller cleared us direct to a fix by name but not the identifier or phonetic spelling; which I couldn't understand due to significant turbulence and poor radio quality. We continued normal flap retraction callouts and takeoff profile. We were given heading a 120; to which we turned; and it took several radio calls between the Captain and ATC to get clarification on the identifier to which we were cleared. This was due to scratchy radios; the turbulence; and some possible confusion on the part of the controller who was talking with us and another company aircraft. We were mistakenly trying to navigate to ENY VOR which caused us to be confused and task saturated. Once we got the correct identifier for HIA and entered into the FMS; we proceeded on course as cleared. However this delay resulted in us temporarily deviating from the charted procedure. This caused the controller to get a low altitude alert although we did not receive any terrain avoidance warnings from our aircraft. In retrospect; the controller admitted on our phone conversation afterwards that this situation is very common. There are a lot of risks and stressors associated with this MZULA.MSO RWY12 and I feel like our outside resources did not help the flight crew. We accept full responsibility for allowing this situation to develop; but changes to this procedure will greatly increase safety in the future.First our Jeppesen charts had no verbal narrative and left us needing FAA charts to understand the procedure. It would be a great help if the procedure could be simplified or the controller's expectations that are outside the procedure could be communicated before we hit significant turbulence. The controller was clearly frustrated with us which only made our situation worse by trying to give us a phone number during a high stress and high workload phase of flight in significant turbulence. This shows the controllers are not fully aware of what human factors the flight crews have and how to help safety of flight. Having poor radio transmission quality was also a significant factor.
Report_2_Narrative: I was the First Officer and Pilot Flying departing MSO. I received and read back the clearance from ATC which included the MZULA5 Departure MSO transition. I programmed this into our FMS and the Captain and I thoroughly reviewed the route in the FMS and on our Jeppesen plates. We also briefed the procedure for engine failure departure. In my takeoff briefing I again described the departure we were assigned. After being cleared for takeoff and reaching 400 AGL; I turned to heading 189 as charted. Immediately we began to encounter moderate turbulence. Just before reaching 1;000 ft AGL; Tower said switch to Departure. Upon contacting Departure we were told 'upon reaching 8;000; proceed direct to ________ ' but it was very turbulent and we did not clearly hear the name of the fix. I immediately realized the flight director was not commanding a left turn in accordance with the charted procedure. The Captain asked to say again the fix; and the controller said the name but not the identifier or phonetic spelling. At 1;000 ft AGL; I called out 'flight level change'; followed by the normal flap retraction callouts and told him we needed a left turn since I knew from the charted SID that's what we were supposed to do. Meanwhile the Captain was trying to get clarification on the fix to which we were to proceed. We knew it would be a left turn so he asked for a left turn and we were given heading 120; to which we turned. During this entire time it was very turbulent and took a lot of effort and concentration to focus on safe flying. It took several radio calls between the Captain and ATC to get clarification on the identifier to which we were cleared. This was due to scratchy radios; the turbulence; and some possible confusion on the part of the controller who was talking with us and another company aircraft. Once we got the correct identifier and entered it into the FMS; we proceeded on course as cleared. However; this delay resulted in us temporarily deviating from the charted procedure. During this time; we had terrain radar displayed on our MFD and were well aware of our surroundings and the location of rising terrain; and at no time did we ever get a terrain caution or warning.Although the SID was correctly programmed into the FMS; for unknown reasons the Flight Director did not command the left turn to intercept the MSO 159 radial. The extreme turbulence and difficulty understanding ATC instructions caused a delay in turning to the assigned fix; resulting in a course deviation. First of all; given our route of flight; it would have made much more sense if; in the pre-departure clearance; we would have been given the Salmon transition. This fact was even stated by the ATC supervisor on the phone when I called him after we landed. He further stated they have had frequent problems with pilots and aircraft not following the procedure we were assigned. Second; I could have anticipated a potential issue; and tuned the MSO VOR in NAV 1 and 2; along with the radial to intercept prior to takeoff. If I return to MSO in the future; I will definitely do that as a backup in case this kind of thing should happen again. I realized we were supposed to be turning left; which is why we asked for a left turn in the interim while trying to get the identifier for the fix and get that loaded in the FMS. The significant turbulence and the communication difficulties with ATC were definitely contributing factors in this temporary deviation. Nonetheless; as a pilot it is my responsibility to safely and correctly fly the plane; so I will ensure I have a backup navigation source programmed and ready in the future. And if I go back there again and get assigned that same SID; I will ask for the Salmon transition rather than the MSO transition; as suggested by the ATC supervisor. Finally I will brief my Captain on what happened previously so we can be vigilant and prepared.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight crew reported receiving a low altitude alert from ATC departing MSO when they had a track deviation following communication difficulties.

Report_1_Narrative: While approaching ITH from the south; we had a visual on the airport and were cleared for the visual. I turned away from the FAF which was our last point of direct navigation as assigned by ATC. I slowed the airplane and configured for flaps 9. As we got closer I was heading for a 4 to 5 mile intercept of the final approach course and began a slow descent from 4000 ft to 3000 ft; the final approach [fix] altitude. I set 3000 ft and began a 500 fpm descent. As we approached 3200 ft we got an EGPWS warning 'Terrain'. I disconnected the autopilot then added max thrust and began a climb; I climbed to MSA for the area; 3700 ft. The First Officer and I felt that we were still in a position to continue the visual into ITH and did so. All precautions were taken; the flight operations quality alert and terrain were discussed both on the departure briefing and the arrival briefing. We briefed the tallest obstacles; their location and the rising terrain. We were slowed to 180 kts flaps 9 and used a slow descent rate to avoid such alerts. Performed the escape maneuver and leveled at MSA. Next time I will ask to just begin the approach from OCCIE fix rather than attempting the visual.
Report_2_Narrative: During visual approach on RWY 32 Pilot Flying (PF) turned away from FAF .The airplane [was] slowed and configured for flaps 9. The airplane was on left base about 5 miles before intercepting the final approach segment. [Captain] began slow descent from 4000 ft to 3000 ft with VS 500 fpm. At 3200 ft we gotten EGPWS warning 'Terrain '. PF immediately followed escape maneuver for EGPWS and climbed to 3700 ft. After that we continued visual for landing. During departure briefing and approach briefing we following all SOP's. During approach we briefed for tallest obstacles. We used slow descent rate to avoid such alert.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight crew reported receiving an EGPWS Terrain warning on a night visual approach to ITH.

Report_1_Narrative: We had just switched on to approach frequency and were given a heading and altitude for the visual approach. We both heard the altitude clearance as 5;000 ft. and the PM read back 5;000 ft. A few min after we had leveled off at 5;000 ft. ATC asked us to confirm altitude and gave us the altimeter. We responded with 5;000 ft. and verified we had the correct altimeter. ATC then responded the minimum vectoring altitude was 5;300 ft. for that area. As the PM (Pilot Monitoring) attempted to clarify we read back 5000 ft. in the initial clearance; I started a climb to 5;300 ft. ATC then asked if we had the field in sight which we did and then we were cleared for the visual approach using the GPS 14 approach plate as guidance. We landed normally.The cause of this event was a miscommunication with ATC. We both heard 5;000 ft. in the initial clearance not 5;300 ft. The PM read back 5;000 ft. and we didn't hear a correction from ATC. A contributing factor in my opinion was the fact that we were experiencing light to occasional moderate turbulence for most of the flight including the descent and that could have caused us to miss hear the original clearance and potentially the read back was hard for ATC to hear due to the PM's mic being jostled.In cases such as this we could have requested clarification if the altitude didn't sound correct but in my estimation the clearance seemed to make sense based on our position and the airport elevation and the location of obstacles and terrain which were not a factor from the direction we were arriving and they also seemed to be similar to the altitudes we would expect if on the GPS approach we were using as a backup. But it would be prudent in the future especially in turbulence to verify clearances considering the effect turbulence could have on radio transmissions.
Report_2_Narrative: We had just checked in with approach and they gave use a heading to turn to for vectors and an altitude to descend to. I thought I had remembered reading backing 5;000 ft. as the captain who was the PF put 5;000 ft. in the FMA and we both confirmed the 5;000 ft. once set. After reaching 5;000 ft. the controller asked us to verify our altitude and I read back 5;000 ft. The controlled returned with 'the MDA is 5;300 in that sector do you have the field in sight?' We had the field in sight but the question led us to believe we descended to the wrong altitude. The controller didn't clarify the altitude at this point and said were cleared for the visual using the RNAV GPS 14 approach plate for guidance.The cause of the event was a miscommunication with ATC and I could have possibly read back a different altitude and thought that 5;000 ft. was what he said instead; after we had set 5000 ft. Also; we were in light to moderate turbulence during the entire flight and it might have caused me to mishear the controller or misread the altitude.I should have asked for clarification from the controller after we had set the altitude in the FMA. From where we were; the altitude of 5000 ft. made sense so it did not cue me to ask for clarification. We had briefed the approach plate as well and the higher rising terrain was on the other side of the field and we determined it would not be a factor for the altitude of 5000 ft. Where we were seemed to coincide with the altitudes on the approach plate as well.
Report_1_Synopsis: CRJ900 flight crew reported descending below minimum altitude for the area due to a misunderstanding of assigned altitude.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Workload; Distraction; Physiological - Other; Situational Awareness
Report_1_Narrative: On a relatively calm and clear day at ZZZ1; I departed southbound toward ZZZ. The takeoff was uneventful; I contacted Approach for flight following. Throughout the climb to 9;500 ft.; there was constant light to moderate turbulence; typical for this segment of flight throughout this area. Upon reaching cruise the severity increased to consistent moderate turbulence; again not abnormal for the route of flight; the aircraft was slowed. I reported the ride conditions to Approach; and they stated that a Cessna 208 had reported similar conditions and opted for lower. The airplane began to experience downdrafts; exceeding over 1000 fpm and airspeed fluctuations of +/- 20 knots. I elected to descend to 7;500 ft. based on the ride conditions reported by the aircraft in front of me. At 7;500 ft. I experienced consistent moderate to severe turbulence; with consistent up and downdrafts; accompanied by fluctuations in airspeed. Occasionally; I nearly hit my head on the ceiling of the airplane. I queried [ATC] and they stated that the aircraft had reported a better ride at 6000 ft.; at that time I descended to 6000 ft. At 6000 ft. the ride was much more manageable; and I was able to make it to ZZZ safely. I made the decision that the airplane did in fact fly through severe conditions and required an inspection. I wrote the airplane up and contacted Maintenance Control. The unstable nature of the valley I was flying over and the absence of weather reporting in the valley make it difficult to gauge the ride conditions. I should have slowed the airplane down; and descended to more manageable flight conditions.A solution would have been flying the airplane above the valley to avoid possible severe turbulence. I talked with my pilot supervisor and he advised that flying at 15;500 ft. over the valley is a viable option. This particular route is very abnormal; with respect to mitigating risk. This is a prime example of how quickly things can change when flying. The more we can do to try to mitigate these risks as a whole; the safer it will become.
Report_1_Synopsis: Beechcraft 99 pilot reported flying through severe turbulence.

Report_1_Narrative: After passing waypoint GILLL on the LINKK1 arrival into IAH; we were cleared runway 27 ILS approach. The next waypoint on the flight was RDFSH then GEYGR. GEYGR was to be passed at 3000' while we were around 3600'. Being cleared the ILS approach; we were to comply with crossing restrictions that were still in place on the approach. The restriction was noted on the approach as a small note; and we announced it too late. The approach controller alerted us high on the crossing restriction and we were then able to comply with the rest of the crossing restrictions. After being swapped runways late in an arrival; we should still review all notes and restrictions applicable to the approach. The note indications are easy to miss; but I am well aware now of specific crossing restrictions instead of waypoint floors on an approach. I believe it would be beneficial to have these notes and restrictions in different colors or noted right below the waypoint name to make it more obvious to the pilots. The constant change in runway assignments late in arrival makes it easy to miss small annotations on approach plates that are important for traffic separation.
Report_1_Synopsis: Captain reported missing a required crossing altitude on LINKK ONE STAR and ILS runway 27 into IAH.

Report_1_Narrative: I arrived at the aircraft as relief pilot an hour before takeoff for a cargo flight to ZZZZ. The FO was at the aircraft and had completed much of the cockpit preflight. Because it was a cargo flight I went through the cabin and secured the overhead bins and many of the storage /catering carts. The Captain arrived and we went through the standard cockpit flight preparation prior to departure. After we pushed from the gate and initiated the engine start; I realized I had not done the Pre-Fight Walk Around Inspection. I asked the FO if he had completed it and he said he had not. He thought I was doing that when I was actually securing the cabin for departure. I told the Captain I forgot to do the walk around. The Captain got clearance and we turned around on the ramp and went back into the gate. The Agent came back; hooked up the jet bridge and I went out and completed the walk around inspection. We re-accomplished all the pre-departure checks and ended up departing to ZZZZ about XX minutes late. Most of the delay was a result of getting personnel back to park us and recalling another push crew.I think that because it was a cargo flight; I was possibly distracted by some non-standard items in the cabin and got out of my habit pattern. Like most of us; I haven't been flying too much but the bottom line is that I simply forgot to do the walk around preflight and realized it after the push.In the future I will report to the FO that the walk around has been completed and as the FO I will verify with the relief pilot that it has been complete. I have been flying airplanes for XX years and have never forgotten to do a walk around inspection.
Report_2_Narrative: During the pushback from the gate; the flight crew realized a communication error occurred resulting in the non completion of the pre-flight walk around duties by a pilot. A return to a gate commenced to complete the required tasks. Contributing factors may have been one crew member being newly experienced to three-four pilot crew tasks combined with a multi month period of not working. Making the crew cross information in this specific area a mandatory portion of any preflight operations area briefing; crew text preflight contact; or aircraft boarding process.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Relief Pilot and Captain reported forgetting to do the pre-flight walkaround and cited communication; distraction and lack of recent flying as contributing factors.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Distraction; Situational Awareness; Workload; Time Pressure
Person_2_Human_Factors: Workload; Distraction; Situational Awareness; Time Pressure
Report_1_Narrative: After a diversion to our planned alternate we had a routine enroute and descent phase. We contacted Tower on about a 10 mile final. We were approximately 5 miles in trail of a B737; and we heard them check in as well. I overheard tower tell them about a Medevac helicopter who was operating to the east of the airport and transiting to the west. Once we were on about a 5 mile final; tower provided us with a traffic call for the same helicopter. The first call we received was traffic at our 10 o'clock and about three miles; and that the traffic had us in sight and was maintaining visual separation. Due to the lights of the city; I did not see the traffic; and it was not yet showing up on our TCAS.Inside of a 4 mile final; at approximately 1200 ft. we received a Traffic Alert for the traffic. On TCAS it showed him at 200 ft. above us and inside a mile. I immediately saw the traffic visually and told the first officer that I had the traffic in sight. Based on the traffic's track and altitude; I very quickly suspected that we might receive an RA. I instructed the first officer to go slightly below the glide slope to increase our separation. Very shortly after that; at 1050 ft. we received a 'DESCEND DESCEND' TCAS Resolution Alert. The First Officer followed the TCAS guidance and I informed ATC. Due to the switch at 1000 ft. to Traffic Alert only we never received a clear of conflict; but we were able to visually identify that we were clear of conflict at about 800 ft. We were one dot low on the glide slope but correcting and all other approach criteria were stable so I quickly asked the First Officer if he felt stable. He responded that he did; so we agreed that we were okay to continue the approach. At our closest point; the helicopter was directly above us and approximately 200 ft. above; leading to a significantly reduced margin of separation.This event was caused by several factors. The helicopter pilot had us in sight and was maintaining visual separation; but in our opinion; the separation provided was not adequate. I was not able to visually identify the traffic until the Traffic Alert occurred; and at that point there was very little we could do to avoid a loss of separation. I do not believe we should have been sequenced by air traffic control to pass directly underneath the medevac's flight path. After landing I communicated my concerns to tower and he said that once the helicopter reported maintaining Visual Separation; he had no further responsibility to separate us. If that is correct; I believe it is a fundamentally unsafe procedure. In this event it led to us receiving a descending RA at 1000 ft. leaving us with very little maneuvering room. I should have made more of an effort to find the traffic prior to receiving a Traffic Alert; but with the city lights it was difficult. This was at the end of a very high workload; 3 hour blocked flight with significant weather; holding; a diversion; and fuel considerations. I believe that this type of event could have been prevented with better planning from air traffic control. There was clearly a difference in expectations between the helicopter pilot and us; and the helicopter pilot may have been comfortable with 200 ft. of separation; but we were not.
Report_2_Narrative: We diverted due to weather. On final approach we received a TCAS Resolution Alert due to a medical helicopter crossing the final approach. I was Pilot Flying for the approach. When we received the Traffic Alert; I initially assumed it was an aircraft on a parallel approach. The Pilot Monitoring reported the aircraft in sight. The helicopter had also reported us in sight. Only moments before the Resolution Alert did I realize the aircraft was going to cross directly in front. We received a descending Resolution Alert. I complied with the Resolution Alert. The helicopter passed approximately 200 ft. above. I don't recall ever hearing a clear of conflict call. We descended below 1000 ft. and the TCAS went into Traffic Alert Only mode.A medical helicopter was crossing approximately 3 mile final at approximately 1200 ft. while we were on approach. I was manually flying a challenging approach due to high winds and did not recognize the threat until a few seconds before the Resolution Alert.
Report_1_Synopsis: CRJ900 flight crew reported 200 ft. of separation with a helicopter on approach.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Workload; Confusion; Training / Qualification; Distraction; Situational Awareness
Report_1_Narrative: Let me say to begin I am not familiar with Flight Check. By this I mean I never came across it in any of my FAA materials or non-FAA reading; online; or video materials. It was not on any of my private; instrument; or commercial FAA exams. It was never brought up to me on any flight checks or check rides. I have never seen anything written about it in any online materials. No CFI or CFII ever mentioned it to me. I have never seen Flight Check aircraft at my home airport or any other airport I've ever flown into. Yesterday I experienced a conflict with a Flight Check aircraft. Just after I made my routine call for my pattern entry '...6 miles to the northeast inbound for a left downwind...'; a Flight Check aircraft made the call they were on an approach to the same runway as me and that they would need to drive inbound on the final until just short of the approach end for on an obstacle check. We're looking for inbound traffic. Other calls by various aircraft as well as Flight Check and my aircraft were made. One of the flight check calls was stepped on however and was therefore not audible. What is important to note too; is that there was an aircraft 2 to 3 miles behind me following me in. Because Flight Check and I were on an entry for the same runway in opposite directions I felt the situation was beginning to become dangerous; I considered doing a 360 turn at 6 miles out just to give spacing to the Flight Check aircraft coming in from the wrong direction. However; I did not do this because there was an aircraft directly behind me and I felt a 360 might put me into him. Therefore; for safety reasons I decided against it. I felt the safest course of action was to proceed on because I felt a King Air at 6 miles out was going to arrive much sooner than I was at 6 miles out because of his faster speed and because he was doing a straight in and I was doing a standard approach. Additionally; he said he was not going to land but instead 'break off just short of the approach end...'. Lastly; he said he was 'looking for inbound aircraft' which I felt meant he was aware of me and would divert if needed. I also briefly considered the option of extending my downwind but felt that to be unsafe because other aircraft were in the area and I had lost track of exactly where everybody was due to the constant traffic chatter both for ZZZ and other nearby airports. It was becoming stressful and my goal was to fly the aircraft; look out the window; and either land or see and avoid this other aircraft. As our approaches proceeded and I turned final I could see an oncoming aircraft above me ascending and turning south as I was descending to land. As I was about 50 feet off the runway I received a tongue lashing from the Flight Check aircraft and my landing was hard and it took several moments for me to calm myself after parking. Only after going into the Fixed Base Operator and asking about what a Flight Check aircraft was did I understand what had just happened. I now understand; after I did my own investigation; what Flight Check is and what I should do if I encounter a Flight Check aircraft in the future. I will now avoid Flight Check if I ever encounter one. I will advise other pilots of what Flight Check is and to avoid them. What caused the problem and what can be done to prevent a recurrence or correct the problem.The problem was caused by me not knowing what Flight Check is and that they have the authority to fly wherever they want and however they want. I will stay away from all Flight Check aircraft in the future. Flight Checks should be included in NOTAMS. I checked NOTAMS prior to my departure and there existed no such NOTAM regarding Flight Check aircraft that day. ATC; such as Approach did not advise me of any Flight Check aircraft. Flight Check pilots should include such wording as; 'This is the Federal Aviation Administration advising all aircraft to avoid (airport name) until (time).' This should be repeated over the appropriate frequency every 1 to 2 minutes until Flight Check is clear of the area. Include Flight Check information in FAA teaching materials. Include Flight Check information in FAA testing materials. Flight Check pilots should avoid berating pilots on frequency especially just prior to them landing as this can cause an unsafe distraction.
Report_1_Synopsis: A General Aviation pilot landing at a non towered airport reported a Flight Check aircraft which the pilot was aware of had to take evasive action to avoid them on short final.

Person_2_Human_Factors: Confusion; Distraction; Situational Awareness; Training / Qualification
Report_1_Narrative: I am a flight instructor I was on the ground observing the traffic pattern. I had just sent my student on his first solo flight. There were three Citabrias in the pattern; all same company. My solo student was Aircraft X. Aircraft Z was on ½ mile final. Aircraft Y was on an extended downwind. My student; Aircraft X; was abeam midfield in the downwind. All traffic was in a left pattern. Tower called and told my student 'traffic to follow ahead in the downwind'. My student replied with 'traffic in sight'. My student had mistaken Aircraft Z on final as the traffic he was following; instead and of seeing and following Aircraft Y in the downwind. Tower proceeded to clear my student 'follow that traffic; clear to land Runway XX'. Because my student was following the wrong aircraft; he turned base (about a half mile) in front of Aircraft Y and cut him off. Aircraft Y was on a 1 mile final at the time. Aircraft Y saw the error and made appropriate maneuvers. Tower noticed when Aircraft X had turned final in front of Aircraft Y and proceeded to tell both aircraft to go around. No further events took place. The pilot in Aircraft X did not see or follow the correct traffic and turned base accordingly. He unintentionally deviated from the ATC clearance. The plot of Aircraft Y noticed and took evasive actions as necessary. I was on the ground and all distances are highly estimated.
Report_2_Narrative: I was given traffic information by ATC while on downwind leg of pattern; a Aircraft X in the pattern ahead and to my left. I saw an aircraft matching ATC description on short final approach and responded that I had the traffic in sight. ATC gave landing clearance with instructions to follow that aircraft; so when I had sufficient distance behind I began my turn to the base leg of the pattern. Upon turning I spotted another aircraft ahead and to my right at about 500 feet clearance on final approach. I took a hard left turn to evade and was told by ATC to go around and that the aircraft I flew in front of was the traffic I was originally advised of and that I had cut them off. I continued in the traffic pattern and landed without further incident.
Report_1_Synopsis: A Flight Instructor observing from the ground and their student reported the student turned base leg and followed the wrong aircraft causing a subsequent aircraft to take evasive action.

Report_1_Narrative: My student and I were cleared for the RNAV 18 from Tower we were told to report the FAF. At this point we were roughly on a 13 or so mile final. I hear Tower talking to another aircraft that was VFR wanting to practice approaches and also shoot the RNAV 18. Tower then told this aircraft to also report the FAF and advised them there is a Warrior on a 9 or 10 mile final and to look for us. The pilot responded that he does not have us in sight yet. I advised Tower that we are still in fact farther away than 9 miles. We had a strong headwind so our ground speed was pretty slow. Tower said we were still cleared for the option and to still report the FAF at this point we were at the fix half way between the FAF and the IAF. Tower again advised the other traffic that we were an 8 or less mile final and to report and he has us in sight. The Cessna still responded he didn't have us in sight so Tower told them to do a right 360. I then reported that we are .5 away from the FAF. At this point I got a traffic notification and I looked up [to see] the Cessna is at the same altitude off my right nose and passed right in front of me at the same altitude. I then took the controls; banked right and pushed the nose forward. The other pilot [said] 'holy crap I see them now' and I let Tower know we were going off course and low. Tower didn't seem like they were paying attention. Or seem to ask about it. We then continued on with the approach and went missed and Tower didn't ask us about it. When I reported going missed we didn't hear back from Tower till after several calls.
Report_1_Synopsis: Piper Warrior instructor pilot reported an NMAC with another light aircraft on final approach at LSE.

Report_1_Narrative: After completing a flight with a passenger and entering the flight into my logbook; I realized I had only 2 takeoffs and landings within the last 90 days and was not compliant with FAR 61.57(a).  Prior to the flight that included 2 landings on [date]; I had not been flying since March 2020.  I think lack of recency led to the mistake.  I had not thought of the requirement until after the flight was completed and I was making the logbook entry.  As a corrective action for myself; I made a checklist to use before every flight that includes currency requirements to carry passengers in VFR day and VFR night.
Report_1_Synopsis: GA pilot reported flying with a passenger; but not being current for takeoffs and landings to do so.

Report_1_Narrative: My instructor and I were on downwind approach for landing. Meanwhile a C-172 had just performed a go-around. We were told they came around at a faster velocity than us; but at nearly our same altitude/path. We later were told (I believe the C-172 instructor told my instructor) that the C-172 was only 100 feet away from us; I believe from above. We had no concrete idea about any of this at the time. We proceeded to land. Afterward; my instructor asked me if I was aware that we were almost in a mid air collision. He had just spoken with the other pilot near the fuel pump. We then looked at radar tracking website to see the activity but we only saw our airplane and not theirs. Pilot from C-172 came into the office to get water (Instructor I believe) and saw us looking at the radar map but didn't seem too concerned about the incident. That's all the information I have.
Report_1_Synopsis: C-150 pilot reported an NMAC with another light aircraft in the vicinity of an airport.

Report_1_Narrative: We have a family ranch which I normally patrol every other day; usually in the evenings; checking for things like bulls; cows; baby calves; horses; stray animals; escaped animals; distressed animals; fences; gates; water; feed; weeds; any vehicles; tractors or implements; and trespassers.  This evening; I was checking fences along the freeway; when I was shocked to see a powered parachute go by below me off to the right.  I do not know how close; it was far enough away that collision was not possible; nor was my wake turbulence likely to hit it; but it seemed big.  That is why I estimated 100 ft. over and 100 ft. down as being the closest it could have been; it could have been further but not closer.  I had not noticed it before because it was below me; with terrain as the background as shadows had fallen with the sun going behind the ridge to the west; and it had no lights and had made no radio announcements.  Its speed was likely no more than 20 MPH; and mine was 60 MPH; so closing speed was 40 MPH.  It is likely that due to the parallel positions of the two aircraft; my aircraft's nose covered it as I got closer; until I passed it.  I was not able to observe it long enough to determine his course before or after the miss; since as soon as it came into view it passed backward (relatively) on my right at a likely relative speed of 40 MPH; and I turned left.
Report_1_Synopsis: PA-12 pilot reported an NMAC with a powered parachute while he was on livestock patrol.

Report_1_Narrative: While flying with a student on an IFR flight plan; we departed Camarillo on an assigned heading of 270 and told to expect vectors to the VNY VOR.Whle climbing; Camarillo Tower handed us off to Mugu Approach. I looked and changed the frequency. Before being able to transmit; I saw a very close aircraft on the G-530 traffic awareness warning; which I announced and told my student to turn right. I could not see traffic and told the student to continue his turn.After nearly 180 degrees of turn; the traffic (a Bonanza) descended past us on the right. I instructed my student to maintain his heading and contacted Point Mugu. The controller asked us if we were on an IFR flight plan; which we confirmed. He told us to fly a (Heading) 070 vector for VNY without further discussion; and we completed our flight.
Report_1_Synopsis: PA-28 instructor pilot reported an NMAC with another light aircraft in the vicinity of CMA airport.

Report_1_Narrative: In non-tower airport PRB; when exiting Runway 31 to Taxiway B; announced on CTAF intentions to exit runway; taxi on (Taxiway) B; cross Runway 1-19; then turn to Taxiway A. To do so; I had to turn my right hindquarters to the approach path of Runway 19; not realizing that a small plane was actually landing on Runway 19. I was unable to see the landing traffic from behind the right wing; and I never heard this plane on radio or made a radio contact. Thanks to prompt warning from a passenger; I was able to stop on Taxiway B short of the Runway 19. It was daytime; clear sky; and unrestricted visibility.
Report_1_Synopsis: C172 reported his passenger alerted him to an aircraft landing on a runway he was preparing to taxi across.

Report_1_Narrative: On an IFR flight plan; departing CMA; we were instructed to fly heading 270 for vectors to the VNY VOR. On climb out; we were instructed to contact Mugu Approach. I looked inside and changed frequencies; and noticed a traffic alert on the G530 that was close. I announced it to the student; and he started a right turn.I could not see the traffic; and told him to continue his turn. I instructed him to to roll out on about a 050 heading. The aircraft passed off of our right side in a descent. We contacted Mugu Approach; who asked if we were on an IFR flight plan; which we confirmed. He instructed us to fly a 070 heading. We continued with flight to ZZZ without further incident.The incident occurred very quickly; and we were unable to query Tower due to the early frequency change. In retrospect; I would not have looked inside the cockpit at such a low altitude with a student.
Report_1_Synopsis: PA-28 instructor pilot reported an NMAC with another aircraft in the vicinity  of CMA airport.

Report_1_Narrative: I was training on the X Scope and traffic volume was fairly high compared to the previous several weeks.  ZZZ was landing Runway X and ZZZ1 Runway Y Right; making for a complex approach pattern.  Aircraft Y was NW bound toward ZZZZZ; the South fix for RNAV X approach at ZZZ level at 030.  Aircraft X was on the Localizer Y Right approach at ZZZ1 east of ZZZZZ1; descending out of 030 for 020; not cleared for the approach.  The close proximity was recognized as Aircraft X (now at 025; still descending) was established on the localizer and Aircraft Y (still level at 030) was approximately 1 NM away from ZZZZZ; the situation was recognized just as 3 mile separation was lost.  I turned Aircraft X to a 180 HDG as they were out of 022 for 020 to avoid a further loss of separation.Aircraft X was slow to descend and I did not recognize the altitude in sufficient time.  Training has been intermittent for a long time due to the COVID situation.  Also; unusually frequent storms and bad weather had kept traffic volume low for the past few weeks; keeping training complexity low as well.  Today presented lots of training and volume; I was getting tired due to not being conditioned for constant traffic and lost focus.  I would [recommend that I] recognize my own fatigue and ask for training or to work a slower or less complex position for a mid day break or to change things up.
Report_1_Synopsis: TRACON Developmental reported a loss of separation and cited lack of training in high traffic volume as a contributing factor.

Report_1_Narrative: BUF ILS 05. Note 1 at the bottom of the page states 'RVR (Runway Visual Range) 18 with Flight Directors and Autopilot......'. Note 3 in the briefing strip note section states 'Autopilot coupled approach not authorized.' Remove the 'Flight Directors and Autopilot' from Note 1.  While a fresh crew might be expected to catch this; at the end of a long day; a tired crew might not; so why not make it easier for them.
Report_1_Synopsis: Reporter reported conflicting guidance on the BUF ILS 05 instrument approach chart referencing autopilot use.

Report_1_Narrative: In an effort to depart the gate early; I released the brakes and gave the ground crew permission to push the aircraft off the gate. Immediately after; I realized that we had not yet received our final Dangerous Goods report. After the pushback was completed; a request was sent to the station operations to send the report. The final Dangerous Goods report was sent within minutes.
Report_2_Narrative: Both Captain and First Officer took note of needing the final Dangerous Goods summary prior to push back; xxx pushed back without the document. The error was noted immediately as the push commenced. An additional written item (Final Dangerous Goods summary) will be added to the list of other items I currently look at before departure.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight crew reported flight pushed off gate without required Hazmat documents. After a minimal delay documents were received; flight complete an uneventful flight.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Human-Machine Interface; Distraction; Communication Breakdown; Situational Awareness
Report_1_Narrative: We exceeded 250 knots below 10;000 and were on speed by 9;600. I (PM) was looking at weather and the STAR and when I went to monitor the aircraft displays I noticed we were doing 300 knots at about 9;760 feet. I said check speed and the PF disengaged the autopilot; reduced power; deployed speed brakes; and leveled off. He had the speed window open and we both failed to monitor the speed window. He is very good about VVM (Verbalize; Verify; Monitor) and not doing something without informing the PM; so I feel I'm just as much responsible for the incident. I believe the speed window was open from a previous instruction from a Controller.
Report_2_Narrative: On the ZZZZZX south of ZZZZZ [Intersection]; we exceeded 250 knots below 10;000 feet.ATC had originally asked us to cross ZZZZZ at 15;000 feet leaving us high for the next restriction (ZZZZZ1 at 8;000 feet and 250 knots). I was using speed intervene (300 knots) and flight spoilers to make the anticipated restrictions at ZZZZZ1 while descending from 15;000 feet. The FMA switched from VNAV SPD to VNAV PATH at approximately 12;500 feet. At this point; I began focusing more attention on small build-ups and ensuring the flight attendants were seated. Upon crossing 10;000 feet; the PM called out 'speed' and we quickly corrected to 250 knots by 9;650 feet. ATC passed us off to Approach without commenting about the speed deviation.The FO did a great job as the PM. However; we did debrief that; despite verbalizing the use of speed intervene; we ended up below 10;000 feet above 250 knots. The error is mine and I own that; but recency of experience may have been contributory as well.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported a speed violation below 10;000 feet.

Report_1_Narrative: On an early evening flight to IAH we were descending via the DRLLR 5 RNAV arrival being set up and briefed for the RNAV Y 26R with our altitude set to 6000'. When checking on with the approach controller we were told to expect the runway 26L transition. We selected the new runway in the FMS but failed to reset our altitude selector to 7;000' at that time. As we neared ZOEEE Drag Required appeared on the FMS scratchpad and the Captain said; 'Careful not to be too hot at ZOEEE'. I deployed the speed brakes and slowed us to 210kts and checked the FMA and we were still in VNAV PATH. Shortly after passing ZOEEE; I noticed the FMA showed VNAV SPEED as we were leveling at 6;000' and I no longer showed SKLER as a waypoint on the screen. I then looked more closely at the DRLLR 5 chart and noticed the point we'd briefed as the lowest altitude on the arrival had (Runway 26R) beside it and thought we should've stopped at 7;000'. I brought it to the attention of the captain who then queried ATC. The ATC response was that we were ok and to now descend to 5;000'. We started the descent and shortly after were told by what sounded like a different voice on the radio to maintain 6;000'. We reversed the approximately 200' descent and returned to 6000'.The rest of the approach and landing were uneventful and the flight ended safely at the destination. I believe we should've stopped at 7;000' but am unsure since the controller didn't have a problem with us being at 6;000' so I listed the event as a possible altitude deviation.
Report_1_Synopsis: B-737 pilot reported neglecting to change the descent altitude after receiving a change in assigned runway from ATC late in the Arrival procedure.

Report_1_Narrative: As the flight progressed; I was made aware that two particular passengers; seated XX5 and XX6; were repeatedly not in compliance with the mask policy.  I made the announcement encouraging everyone to wear their masks.  Subsequently; the passengers XX5 and XX6; failed to comply and attempted to use 'Active eating and drinking' as an excuse not to wear the mask.  The purser advised me that they were non-compliant for most of the X+ hour flight; so I forwarded their names and seat numbers to Dispatch to support the flight attendants and to document the passengers' non-compliance so that company can evaluate whether they be allowed future travel.  The customers were met by Customer Service representatives upon arrival in ZZZ.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported two passengers were not complaint with face mask policy during flight.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Situational Awareness; Training / Qualification; Communication Breakdown; Confusion
Report_1_Narrative: Upon arrival to Gate X in ZZZ we were asked to call OPS. The Captain called them and we were reminded that we should call ramp before entering the ramp next time. I couldn't believe that I had made such a mistake after over XXXXX hours on the fleet and almost XX years of flying at the company with many many ZZZ arrivals. I looked at the Captain and I said; 'I am sorry I have no excuse;' which is how I felt. I then called the ramp and apologized. I called them on the frequency that I had set on stby at Comm 2 prior to the top of descend when I was setting up for our arrival to ZZZ. As we debriefed I started questioning the why of my mistake and I realize that I am taking for granted my lack of situational awareness as a result of my 7 month absence from flying.When I went to ZZZ1 I was very serious about it; during my OE trip I was still very conscious of my weaknesses because of my lack of recency but now as I am finishing my second trip after OE I feel that 'I am back' which obviously I am not. There were a few other threats that contributed to my mistake. We had thoroughly briefed a [Runway] XXL arrival and taxi in but had spent way less time discussing [Runway] XYR. Our set up for XYR and execution was great but created a distraction and increased the workload. We cleared XYR on Taxiway 1; were given instruction to cross XYL on 1 and call Ground. Both myself and the Captain were anticipating taxi via 1; but when I called Ground we were told 'Taxi via 2; 3 hold short of 4 and at the half way point on November call Ground at XXX.YY.' A lot of information to digest especially if you aren't very familiar with the airport; you have been out for a long time (this is the Captain's first trip after RQ (Recurrent Qualification) training and OE). We were both expecting to go straight on Taxiway 1.I told the Captain to stop. Which he very nicely did as he was also figuring out that we were not suppose to continue on 1. The Captain taxied as instructed; I called Ground Control and was told to taxi via 3; 4 to the gate. After making the turn on 4 we were instructed to give way to opposite direction traffic on 4 that was turning on 5. We then were told to turn right on 5 and continue via 6 to the gate. As I am debriefing this I realized that ZZZ unlike ZZZ1 or ZZZ2 doesn't instruct you to contact ramp. They simply say taxi to the gate/ramp. Finally as we were approaching the gate area I was trying to time my APU start so it is running when we come to a full stop; and I also noticed that there was a lot of vehicle traffic traveling parallel to us and I was a little concerned on whether or not they will stop at X7 for our turn. There was no traffic in the alley and we taxied to Gate X uneventfully.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported not contacting the ramp before entering and cited as contributing factors a lack of recent flying and ATC not instructing them to contact ramp.

Report_1_Narrative: At trip report I looked at the pilot bulletin for temperature check instructions at ZZZ. Trip report time was XA:00L and according to the bulletin it would be accomplished at the departure gate for the time frame. I proceeded to the departure gate and upon arrival asked the gate agent about getting a temperature check. The agent said no one was there to do it and they don't do it. I was unable to get a temperature check.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported not being able to get a temperature check at the departure gate.

Report_1_Narrative: The procedure for screening crewmembers at ZZZ KCM [Known Crew Members] allows for social distancing; if the crewmembers follow it; right up to the actual point of screening.  There are 2 screeners/podiums; which is great and efficient; but they are located within inches of each other.  The screeners keep waving people forward to move the line; but this requires standing within a few inches of the person you were just trying to distance from.When I mentioned this to the screener he offered to send me back into the line; which I declined.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported social distancing concerns during TSA screening.

Report_1_Narrative: I was originally told by the company none of my sick time would be used if I needed [it] due [to] contraction [of] COVID.  My sick time has not been replenished.  Due to this policy now; there has been talk in our breakroom that if someone contracts COVID [they] will not inform the company and will come to work potentially infecting coworkers.  So the possibility of our work area becoming a safety hazard is dangerously probable.  The company should do the right [thing] during this pandemic and do their part to keep employees and customers safe.
Report_1_Synopsis: Ground employee reported concerns with COVID-19 sick leave related policies.

Report_1_Narrative: We were assigned the ZZZZZX RNAV departure off Runway X at ZZZ.  The clearance was to climb via the SID; top altitude of FL230 was set in the MCP. All the fixes and altitude restrictions were correct in the FMC; I was the PM; the airplane was light; so we had a good climb rate. The PF was hand flying as we approached the first fix which has a crossing restriction of at or below 10;000. LNAV/VNAV and VNAV PTH was selected. Close to the first fix the PF called for the autopilot as the airplane started its turn to cross the fix that placed the sun directly into our face which affected our visibility. As I turned my head to get my sunshade; ATC asked if we were going to stop at 10;000 feet; we got as high as 10;300 the PF turned the autopilot off and went down to 10;000.  In this situation I think turning the autopilot on earlier would have helped. Also anticipating the sun and take steps earlier to mitigate the effects of the sun would have helped us to maintain better situational awareness.
Report_2_Narrative: Our departure SID was the ZZZZZX.  Our departure plan was for Runway YYR per the ATIS.  During taxiout our runway assignment was changed to Runway X with the same SID.  My First Officer ran the runway change checklist and briefed me on the changes to the SID departing Runway X.  During the climbout I called for the autopilot sometime prior to 10;000 feet.  There is a fix named ZZZZZ that has a crossing altitude of 10;000 or below.  Our automation level was LNAV/VNAV with the autopilot engaged.  Approaching 10;000 feet I noticed that the FMA went to VNAV PTH.  About that time; I also got a face full of morning sunrise.  It briefly made it hard to see and I had not deployed my sunshade or put on my sunglasses yet.  When my vision adjusted to the glare of the sun I noticed that the aircraft did not level at 10;000 feet.  It overshot the altitude by 300 feet.  I disengaged the autopilot and returned to 10;000 feet.  The Controller did query us on our altitude during the overshoot.  One other piece of useful information is that the aircraft was very light.  I'm wondering if the system was respecting a G-Load vs. an altitude because I have no other explanation as to why it did not level at 10;000 feet.  Factors that I feel contributed to this event were the runway change on the ground; high airport elevation; sunrise; fatigue and maybe our light weight.  Next time I will not accept the immediate line up and wait from ATC.  Instead I would re-brief the SID so that my situational awareness would be better.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported an altitude deviation during departure.

Report_1_Narrative: ATC cleared us for a visual approach to Runway 16R into Denver after turning us on to a right base approximately 5 miles from MERYN intersection on the ILS 16R. After being cleared for the visual approach the First Officer (FO) selected the approach mode and a selected a slower speed.
