The FO was slow to turn towards MERYN and over shot the final approach course. I instructed to FO to turn immediately toward the runway and then back to the final approach course. The approach controller asked if we need a vector and I declined. The FO had previously briefed the ILS to 35R. During the approach briefing we discussed threats that included high elevation; an MEL that restricted RNAV approaches; and that we were tired. The flight was cleared to descend via the TBARR 1 RNAV Arrival with the Runway 16R transition. The transition ends at CLFFF intersection at 11;000' with a speed of 210 knots. ATC was informed that we could not accept an RNAV approach and we were told to expect a visual approach; which we backed up with the ILS approach. The flight was turned to a right base heading at 210 knots. While turning the FO requested a slower speed which ATC approved. ATC asked if we had the airport insight. When I replied that we had the runway insight we were cleared for the visual approach. The FO selected the approach mode. As the FO was selecting a slower speed I mentioned that she should turn toward MERYN intersection. She slowly selected a heading toward MERYN and over shot the final approach course. I think this was due to the angle in which the course was intercepted. I would suggest adding a discussion about accepting visual approaches to the approach briefing; as a possible threat.
Report_1_Synopsis: Captain reported overshooting final approach course on a visual approach into Denver.

Report_1_Narrative: Approximately 8 hours into our flight; my ears started to block. I swallowed to clear them; but it came back repeatedly. I spoke with 3 other flight attendants and they said they had the same symptoms. I called the cockpit and talked with the flight crew about the situation. They informed me that everything checked out all right. We were informed about a 'PAC' being 'out' during the Captain to crew; pre-flight briefing.  I questioned  flight crew if this had anything to do with our ears being blocked. Captain told me that the PAC that was out was like having a 'spare tire.' I questioned him because he informed the crew that the temperature in the cabin might be a problem. I asked him if the PAC situation had anything to do with air circulation or filtration; due to COVID transmittal. He said it was not going to affect the pressurization; air circulation or filtration. The ear blockage lasted for 15-20 minutes and didn't return the rest of the flight. Captain asked if we needed MedLink and we declined.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Attendant reported having ear blockage problems during flight and questioned if it had to do with one Pack being 'out.'

Person_1_Human_Factors: Situational Awareness; Communication Breakdown; Distraction; Workload
Report_1_Narrative: Passenger in seat X failed to comply with crew member instructions on wearing a facial covering at all times in flight; other than eating or drinking. Passenger created a disturbance around him and made fellow passengers extremely uncomfortable.  All passengers and myself were and are concerned about COVID exposure.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Attendant reported a passenger was not compliant with face mask policy.

Report_1_Narrative: I worked a task card on Aircraft X which consisted of applying locktite to both ENG (Engine) start knobs on the overhead panel. This task card only has one block to sign for which caused me to be confused. The task card only had one space to sign off for removal and one for installation. This task card needs to be re-written and a space for a SECOND AMT (Aviation Maintenance Technician) needs to be added to prevent any future potential ETOPS violations.
Report_2_Narrative: I was assigned to work task card ETOPS. The task card states that the knobs are to be removed from the start switch and Loctite applied then install knobs and tighten set screws. I asked my lead for clarification since I had never completed this task. On the task card there is one line for an AMT (Aviation Maintenance Technician) signature and one line for an EV number. I completed the task card and signed the paperwork after calling Maintenance Control and receiving my EV number. I was informed by my supervisor via email that the task required 2 mechanics therefore I had incorrectly completed the task. If the task card was written correctly to include a space for 2 EV numbers and 2 AMT signatures I believe this could have been prevented.
Report_1_Synopsis: Maintenance Technician reported that a Task Card is missing a second Signature Block.

Report_1_Narrative: After [working] on Aircraft X; returned to shop to research history on item. Upon return to aircraft ramp had removed the crew stairs from Gate X to Gate Y for next inbound flight. After arrival of inbound Flight ABB Gate Y; could not return to Flight CBBD; Gate X; until crew stairs were returned.Need to have 2 crew stairs so AMT is not split between gates. Normal staffing is 2 AMT's for shift; but one AMT was out sick with COVID-19. Operations could have allowed more ground time by tail swapping aircraft.
Report_1_Synopsis: Technician reported not having enough air stairs and having to wait to accomplish a task.

Report_1_Narrative: I began the drone flight to inspect the subject property roof thinking I had the automated FAA authorization to fly in the Class D ZZZ airspace. After realizing that I had not written down the authorization on my work order I immediately discontinued the flight and landed the drone. I then tried to obtain the automated approval through the Airmap application. Per the Airmap application; approvals up to 400 feet could be obtained; however; the application stated that the approval was not available on an automated basis at that time. Flight was discontinued. The max height the drone climbed to was 110 feet without approval for a period less than a couple of minutes. Pilot error was not obtaining approval before flight. The pilot thought the approval was already obtained which was the reason the drone flight was started. Future corrective action is to include the approval verification in the preflight checklist.
Report_1_Synopsis: UAV pilot reported pilot error in not obtaining authorization for the flight.

Report_1_Narrative: I had just descended through IMC and was worried about the potential icing and high winds. I hand flew the approach and due in part to lack of recent experience (rustiness due to 2020/COVID); I inadvertently descended to ~2;100 feet MSL between ZZZZZ (IF) and ZZZZZ1 (FAF) on the RNAV XX approach into ZZZ; about 200 feet lower than the 2;300 feet minimums. I recognized my error and climbed back to 2;300 feet by ZZZZZ1 then continued to an uneventful landing. I should not have hand flown the approach given my rustiness--despite having done well in an IPC (Instrument Proficiency Check) a week or so ago--as I was preoccupied with studying wings for evidence of icing in the fast approaching twilight/dusk; and I was fighting strong winds that had me watching airspeed more than altitude.  All in all; it was 100% my fault and reemphasized to me that currency does not equal proficiency.
Report_1_Synopsis: GA pilot reported an altitude excursion during approach and cited lack of recent flying as a contributing factor.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Workload; Communication Breakdown; Confusion; Time Pressure
Report_1_Narrative: ZZZ was going ATC zero for a cleaning due to coronavirus.  We had aircraft still in our airspace at the time of the scheduled cleaning.   We were advised by management to terminate radar and to flash the aircraft to the next facility or sector that they would be entering next.  Fellow controllers later told us that we couldn't do this; but no official guidance from the FAA has been given to us on what the proper way was to handle this.
Report_1_Synopsis: Center Controller reported there was no official FAA guidance regarding how to handle traffic in the airspace when the facility went ATC zero for COVID-19 cleaning.

Report_1_Narrative: I had been off from flying since [Month] due to the Covid19 slowdown and my leave over the summer. This was my OE after completing training to get me refreshed and up to speed with line flying. I was definitely a currency and recency of experience threat that was discussed in the cockpit and prior to the top of descent going into ZZZ. After being cleared for the ILS approach to XXR; we were using VNAV and either LOC or LNAV to track the approach course to the runway. There was a lot of haze and smoke from the fires in the area that was obscuring our ability to see the runway.  We flew the approach and eventually selected APPR mode on the MCP with approx 5 miles until touch down. Approach told us to contact tower around the Final Approach Fix. I was almost exclusively focused on flying and failed to cross-check the Captain to make sure he contacted Tower for our landing clearance. Even at the 1;000 foot call; I thought we were most likely cleared to land; and I was so focused flying that I didn't suggest the Captain query ATC. Poor workload management on my behalf. I felt very compressed as the work load increased. I flew a stabilized SOP ILS approach and landed uneventfully on XXR. Upon contacting Ground Control we realized that Tower was never contacted and clearance to land was never received. Ground Control made no mention of this failure and cleared us to our gate.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported that the crew landed without a clearance after forgetting to contact Tower. The First Officer cited poor workload management and lack of recent flying as contributing factors.

Report_1_Narrative: The break-room had dividers poorly installed on the round lunch tables; they were just set on the tables and move around freely. The dividers also have many sharp edges on them and someone will end up being injured and or cut on these sharp edges. Along with moving around; our department has actual man-sized employees here and the room that is being given to us to sit and have lunch is the size [for children].If this ridiculousness continues I feel that the training room needs dividers between all the computers and the break-room computers as well. There also needs to be dividers installed in between the seats along the wall as we cannot afford to remove any of these seats since our break-room is already too small for our size of group.I also feel that our vans and trucks need dividers that we move our employees in since masks are clearly not enough for this very 'deadly disease.'
Report_2_Narrative: As I came to the break-room for lunch I noticed that dividers were installed on our break room tables well after this supposed 'pandemic' hit us. Someone with obviously way too much time on their hands thought it prudent to install clear dividers on the tables. If this 'pandemic' is so very deadly as the media portrays it to be I suggest very strongly that we need to install these unnecessary dividers in our Super Tugs since we sit much closer in the cab of that than in a break-room for a few minutes while we eat lunch. Anything less than putting dividers is Unacceptable and will show that our lives do not matter to this company and prove that you can put a price on our safety.
Report_1_Synopsis: Ground employees reported concerns regarding social distancing protections in their work environment.

Report_1_Narrative: On approach into ROA; we were at 4;000 feet. and cleared for the visual approach just south of PROSE but before HIBAN; minimum altitude was 3;700 feet. The FO (First Officer) was PF (Pilot Flying) and began a turn towards the runway but due to the radar altimeter registering rising terrain during the bank; we got a momentary EGPWS caution. We knew our position on approach was above the minimum altitude for that sector and could verify visually we were not in conflict with any of the terrain so we continued with the approach while paying attention to our position; FPA (Flight Path Angle); and the PAPIs. Conditions during event were day VFR.[The] bank over terrain triggered EGPWS. Continued visually. We had discussed the terrain as a threat numerous times before attempting the approach.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported a momentary EGPWS warning on visual approach to ROA airport over terrain.

Report_1_Narrative: While departing ZZZ we were cleared up to 7;000 feet and receiving vectors. The First Officer was hand flying and we received a TA alerting us to a crossing aircraft on the arrival that was leveling at 8;000 feet. I told the First Officer I had the traffic in sight; it was no factor and he had already begun leveling off. Due to our light aircraft and high rate of climb an RA was triggered. Since the First Officer was already hand flying and in the process of leveling off we complied with the RA and continued the flight uneventfully.Due to a light aircraft and dense air there was a high rate of climb. The First Officer was hand-flying and slowly leveling off while not busting altitude and triggered an RA.
Report_2_Narrative: While departing ZZZ for ZZZ1 we received a TCAS RA.  I; the First Officer; was hand-flying and cleared to 7;000 feet MSL. The Captain called traffic in sight as the system said 'traffic;' so I began to level off; while doing so we received 'monitor vertical speed' which I was already doing. This RA was likely triggered due to our light GTOW and high rate of climb. We continued the flight uneventfully.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier flight crew reported receiving a TCAS RA during departure.  The TCAS RA was reportedly due to the aircraft's high rate of climb as a result of having a light gross takeoff weight.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Situational Awareness; Training / Qualification; Distraction; Fatigue
Report_1_Narrative: I was PF and the Captain was PM. We had winds gusting to 190/22G40 knots and low-level wind shear advisories in effect. Around 500 feet or so; I was task saturated just trying to fly the plane and I did not see the altitude. We got a wind shear caution. I said 'continuing' and the Captain agreed. He later mentioned he was watching the altitude and we were continuously trending up. We should have used the wind shear escape maneuver according to the SOP. We had wind shear advisories on the first two approaches; had reviewed the SOPs and briefed that with a caution we may choose to continue or perform the wind shear escape maneuver.  A warning and we would be getting out of there. We briefed the entire maneuver to ensure it was fresh for both of us and we were clear on our individual roles. Since we briefed on the approach that we would decide with a Caution; it was fresh in our minds. The Captain mentioned in cruise that we should have performed the wind shear escape maneuver because we were departing. Contributing causes; last leg of 4 flying around weather; moderate turbulence all day; almost diverted and had to hold due to weather on last leg; wind shear on approach and flying at night. I am relatively low time ~120 hours in 7 months; an average of 17 hours a month; which has led to poor consolidation of knowledge.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier First Officer reported not following Standard Operating Procedures in a wind shear situation during departure and cited fatigue; weather; and low flight time in the last several months as contributing factors.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Workload; Time Pressure; Distraction; Situational Awareness
Report_1_Narrative: This flight was designated as a quick turn. Once cleaners were off the aircraft flight attendants boarded and less than 30 seconds later three members of management were asking the crew if we can board the customers that were shoulder to shoulder with poor ventilation and no signs of social distancing on the jet bridge. I understand that safety checks must be done before door closure. It is extremely difficult to do safety checks during the boarding process of a full X type aircraft with the added pressure of the three members of management standing outside the boarding door. An in-flight Supervisor was standing in front of the flight attendant jump-seat; at door one left during the boarding; to have a look at the boarding process and kept asking how the overhead bins looked. As the A Flight Attendant; I discussed this matter with CS and would contact them when bins were getting full. To complicate things; we had an extra pilot doing a check ride so we had a total of three; we also had a maintenance issue with the aircraft and at one time I was pressed against the door at one right; as we had three pilots three mechanics two flight attendants and one in-flight Supervisor standing in the forward part of the plane along with customers boarding .  It was clear that everything that happened during the boarding process showed we need to do a better job during this COVID-19 pandemic and the quick turn needs to be updated to reflect that.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Attendant reported social distancing problems/concerns involving passengers; crew and maintenance personnel during boarding on a quick turn flight.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Communication Breakdown; Training / Qualification; Workload; Confusion
Report_1_Narrative: Aircraft X had a BTB for a Captain pitot static amber EICAS warning. We quickly determined it was a probe. We have an FAK with a R/H probe in inventory. We needed an LH probe. We were able to get one from company; we installed the probe; Ops checked probe; accomplished the paperwork. Had multiple conversations with Tech and [Maintenance Control]. Deferred the aerodynamic sealant with a 767 desk. No mention in B767 MM 34-11-01 OF RII . ETOPS was noted for ice/rain (mm 30-31). When I awoke this AM; I had a friend look up in GMM ATA 34 FOR RII and then notified [Maintenance Control] of a possible situation my next step was my report. There was 1 mechanic at ZZZ that was ETOPS qualified; me who accomplished task; [and] we had another who was RII but not ETOPS.
Report_1_Synopsis: Technician reported not having correct qualifications to perform and sign off the log book for a Captain's Pitot Probe replacement.

Report_1_Narrative: Aircraft X was climbing out of 5;000 feet for 10;000 feet. Aircraft Y was 25 NM NW and level at 9;000 feet SE bound. The sectors were combined and busy with a full workload including practice approaches on the north side of the sector configuration; with multiple in-bounds as well as terminal arrival and departure traffic. Aircraft X initially had a good climb rate which declined with altitude; and became traffic for Aircraft Y. The two aircraft were opposite directions and at around 7 miles apart Aircraft X was only at 8;300 feet and climbing and would not top Aircraft Y at 9;000 feet. Traffic alert was issued to Aircraft X and given a 30 degree turn to the right and a descent to 8;000 feet. Traffic was issued to Aircraft Y and a climb to 10;000 feet. Aircraft Y reported Aircraft X in sight and was instructed to maintain visual separation and to climb and maintain 10;000 feet. To my knowledge separation was never lost but was close.Due to very short staffing; along with COVID-19 scheduling this makes it hard to mitigate busy traffic by splitting sectors in the optimal efficiency of running the NAS. Other issues that could have been preventive; would be the presence of a Supervisor to staff the area when a Supervisor was scheduled for work; however; the Supervisor was on break and a Controller in Charge took the position which greatly hurts the staffing of able bodies to the operation.
Report_1_Synopsis: Center Controller reported a possible loss of separation and cited COVID-19 related staffing issues as a contributing factor.

Report_1_Narrative: I was paged back to work the D side on Sector X to assist the Radar Controller. The previous evening we were told that we had to take over ZZZ TRACON airspace because they had too many COVID cases to staff it properly. We have been working without any clear guidelines and it feels like every shift when we come in we get new information about what we're gonna do and how to work aircraft in and out of this airspace without any training.  While having to work Sector X and ZZZ TRACON airspace; he got request from Aircraft X to do a flyby at Park X and University X. He then started getting requests from Aircraft Y and Aircraft Z to also do those without any flight plans. Controller Y was working a light to moderate workload until all of these requests came in. Because we had no information about the flybys; (there was actual information offered to ZZZ TRACON; but they did not share it until we complained). This session became extremely confusing. I was attempting to coordinate with ZZZ Tower about them coming in bound; but they were staying above their space.  Our side kept giving them communication changes over to the Tower and then they were being sent back. Luckily no incident occurred but this made for an extremely high workload and high stress scenario. Because of the confusion at the sector I had a very difficult time even being able to help from the D side. The more information we have ahead of time the better. But having zero information was really difficult to manage with the increased workload of our own airspace and TRACON's as well.The coordination between TRACON and our Center requiring that we take over this airspace for two weeks has been very poor. The supervisors and operation manager on duty have attempted to coordinate for us; but with every day I walk in; we get new information about how we have to change what we had done the day before or what we were doing was wrong. This also leads to controllers in charge being responsible for the area much more this week than normal. We needed the support of our airspace and procedures staff to step in and get some coordination done to give us clear guidance as to what we should be doing because our LOA with TRACON does not clearly cover how we take over their space. There's been confusion all week as to whether they are Class C surface area or a Class D. Also; they have a waiver to be within 1 mile of a restricted airspace RXXXX while fixed wing aircraft are in the space. They've been in there operating all week long while we've been doing mostly visual approaches but sometimes IFR approaches. But apparently some of the IFR approaches are not separated from the restricted airspace. Which creates a very unsafe situation for us to take over the space with no training. We also need any of the flyby information passed to us. We now have that information; but we didn't until date; one week after taking over their airspace. If we had the information about the flyover; the session would not have been nearly as stressful and confusing. And my XX years here I've never been so confused on sector. Luckily; he was not overwhelmingly busy with his other traffic.
Report_1_Synopsis: Center Controller reported confusion with taking over a TRACON's airspace and difficulty with coordination with Tower on how to handle some flights.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Distraction; Human-Machine Interface; Situational Awareness; Training / Qualification; Confusion; Communication Breakdown
Report_1_Narrative: I was training my trainee at Sector X only.  We had all of the airspace combined as well due to COVID traffic (normal).  My trainee pointed out Aircraft Y to Sector Y in ZZZZ center.  They were combined with Sector Z as well.  They approved the point out on Aircraft Y and then started a hand off on an aircraft we did not know about or see yet (Aircraft X).    Neither of us said anything because we did not know what aircraft [in] Sector Y was talking about.   After about 3; 4 seconds of silence from my trainee; Sector Y said 'disregard.'  So we never took the hand off.  A couple minutes later; Aircraft X checked on out of about 160 for FL230.  Sector A airspace was hot FL180 - FL230 with 4 drones delaying.  There was no data block displayed; but we eventually found the limited data block and pulled it up and stole track control and immediately my trainee told Aircraft X to descend and maintain 170 to miss the airspace. Prior to stealing the track; the status of who had track control was listed 'Unknown.'  My trainee said it was OK if he was already above 170; but to descend anyways.  He was climbing really well and got up to about 185 before starting back down.  Aircraft X may have clipped the Sector A airspace for a hit or two while descending.  Safety was never compromised because we had clear radar on all 4 other type aircraft and the closest one was well south of where Aircraft X was 15-20 miles.  I would have intervened if safety was at risk and vectored the aircraft away from danger.Just [need] better coordination and more timely hand off from the north.  Maybe a heads up prior to departure on ZZZZ departures entering our airspace due to proximity to our airspace.
Report_1_Synopsis: Center Controller reported a hand off issue with adjacent airspace resulting in an airspace violation.

Report_1_Narrative: Had HAZMAT (hazardous material) added to flight; received the NOTAC (notice to Captain) form; signed a copy and gave it to the Ops Agent; forgot to amend the Release and add the HAZMAT notation to the Release. Dispatch contacted us en route; at that time we both remembered the new policy that HAZMAT must be noted on the Dispatch Release.
Report_1_Synopsis: B737-700 Captain reported flight departure without amended Dispatch release stating Hazmat cargo on board.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Workload; Communication Breakdown; Confusion; Physiological - Other
Report_1_Narrative: Captain's window opened and detached from aircraft during climbout. All checklists were completed; perhaps they were not completed in normal sequence due to severe noise associated with window detachment. Aircraft configuration was fulfilled after much consternation due to nearly nil communication due to wind noise and headset loss.
Report_1_Synopsis: B737 Captain reported that the Captain's side window opened and became detached during climbout.

Report_1_Narrative: There was a line of storms crossing ZZZ.  We were told to expect holding at ZZZZZ.  We ended up holding.  We did one turn and then we got sent back on the arrival.  We ultimately got vectors from ZZZZZ1 and were following one Company aircraft.  The plan was to fly northeast about 30 miles at 5;000 ft to go around the weather and then come back south to land.  We couldn't get in front of it or through it.  Company turned around to try to get around the weather from the other direction.  We did the same thing.  We got a 270 heading and a descent to 4;000 ft and an assigned speed of 170 knots.  On that vector; I noticed airspeed decreasing and added some power.  Then the airspeed dropped to approximately 140 knots and the autopilot and autothrottles were disconnected.  I announced to the PM (Pilot Monitoring) that we were in windshear and I added power and started a climbing turn to the left.  The aircraft started accelerating and climbing; and we retracted the flaps.  The highest speed I saw during the recovery was 220 knots.  During this period; airspeed; pitch attitude and altitude was very difficult to control and we encountered what we believed to be severe turbulence.  The PM told ATC that we had severe turbulence and windshear and that we were turning to the left and climbing.  We tried to level at 5;000 ft and flew southwest.  ATC told us to climb to 6;000 ft for traffic.  I added power and the aircraft responded poorly.  Eventually; we got a climb going; but we were unable to stop the climb at 6;000 ft.  The aircraft continued to about 6;450 ft and ATC asked us what altitude we were going to.  PM told them that we were trying to get to 6;000 ft but were having a difficult time maintaining altitude with the turbulence.  On our way back down to 6;000 ft we got a TCAS TA for traffic at our 1-2 o'clock at 700-800 ft above us.  I continued down to about 5;800 ft to make sure we avoided that traffic.  We continued southwest and diverted to ZZZ1. If we had asked to stay in holding until we saw that the line had passed even further northeast of the field; it would have prevented this.  We had about 13.0 of fuel when we entered holding; so we had the time. [We were] unable to maintain assigned altitude; heading; and airspeed due to windshear and severe turbulence.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported the flight encountered wind shear and severe turbulence associated with a line of storms resulting in altitude/airspeed excursions; a conflict and a divert.

Report_1_Narrative: The ramp light post lights are extremely bright; causing a high amount of glare. The ramp lights are angled such that they shine directly into the flight deck. The gate is equipped with a DGS (Docking Guidance System). The DGS at gate X is mounted high and close to the ramp lights. Trying to use the DGS system in the glare was very difficult. Looking at the high mounted DGS while also looking up at the bright ramp lights blocked out all peripheral vision of the ramp on approach to the parking spot. In order cut the glare I had to deploy the flight deck sun visor.The ramp lights in the D terminal gates are too bright. Gate X DGS system is mounted high; causing the pilot to look up into the glare of the very bright ramp lights.[I suggest to] lower the lumens of the ramp lights; angle them better (more of a down angle); and mount the DGS systems lower so the pilot does not have to look up into the bright ramp lights while using the DGS.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Captain reported that both position and brightness of ramp lights at gate in CLT impacted ability to see Docking Guidance System.

Report_1_Narrative: I was notified by the Specialist that they had received word from the ramp that they had a piece of undeclared ADG [Accessible Dangerous Goods] that was not listed on the DG manifest. Its my understanding that ZZZ had a 5 piece shipment of FLAMMABLE LIQUID that was to be bumped from the flight however 1 piece was actually loaded into the ADG/FFO ULD [DG Container]. Ops was informed when the aircraft was on short final; at approximately FL020. I was never in contact with the crew; nor the Ramp regarding this issue. [Suggest] better verification process and tracking of all HAZMAT (hazardous material) shipments by the ramp.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Dispatcher reported undocumented Hazmat cargo was mistakenly transported.

Report_1_Narrative: Pushed back from gate at CLT. Ramp cleared us to spot X; approaching X I switched us to ground on 121.8 as directed and then we were cleared to proceed to Runway 36C via Golf; right turn onto (closed) Runway 5; hold short of Bravo. Instead of proceeding onto Golf we made a slight left onto Taxiway Romeo to join Runway 5. It was dark outside and the taxiway sign for Golf was not illuminated; we had seen the illuminated taxiway directional sign for Golf sitting to the right of Runway 5. Due to the nature of spot X being in between taxiways Romeo and Golf and the fact that the taxiway sign was not illuminated we mistook Romeo for Golf and contacted Ground to clarify new routing. The rest of the taxi and flight concluded normally.
Report_2_Narrative: We pushed back from gate in CLT; started engine 1 and began to taxi out to spot X. Before reaching X; to stay ahead of other traffic calls; the FO (First Officer) called Ground of our approaching location. Ground had told us to 'taxi via G; Runway 5; and hold short of B; and contact 121.8.' Having not made the turn yet I had seen a lit up Golf sign in front of me I began to continue forward thinking it was Golf. It was not until being in the middle of R that I realized that all other Golf lights were out and the Golf we had seen was actually a turn-off sign for Runway 23/5; not the actual taxiway we were on. I queried with Ground that we may have taken taken the wrong taxiway and that we were on Romeo instead of Golf. 121.8 had simply responded to 'continue on to Runway 5; left turn E and taxi to Runway 36C.' The taxi to the runway and the flight continued without incident.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported taxiway signage not illuminated at CLT contributed to a taxiway incursion.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Situational Awareness; Distraction; Communication Breakdown; Other / Unknown
Report_1_Narrative: During boarding; I was standing in an exit row scanning passengers for meeting the selection criteria to sit there. There was a lot going on in the exit row and I was preoccupied with confirming that two younger passengers met the age requirement and whether another passenger was willing to assist. One of the last passengers to board was holding a really small dog in front of her face and I was concerned with whether or not she was wearing a mask with a valve on it. After she sat in the exit row and I determined she had a mask with a valve and needed to get her a disposable mask; I failed to realize that her dog disqualified her from sitting there because I was distracted by her mask and addressing the other passengers' needs to meet exit seat criteria. I did confirm the other passengers' eligibility and briefed the exit row passengers; but during cruise; the B Flight Attendant notified me there was a passenger with a dog in the exit row. I was shocked to realize my mistake and immediately moved the passenger to an empty seat behind the exit row; so the passengers met the exit seat criteria for final descent.Focus my attention on scanning each passenger again for selection criteria prior to briefing and really check on their laps and under their seats for pets. Have the B or D Flight Attendant cross check exit row passenger selection criteria after boarding is complete. Ensure the operations agent gives out disposable masks to passengers with valves prior to boarding; so flight attendants can focus more on other safety precautions. Have operations agent notify any passengers with pets that they cannot occupy an exit seat as they scan their boarding pass.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Attendant reported a passenger with a dog was seated in the exit row; however; the flight attendant did not recognize this due to being distracted with the passenger's face mask non-compliance.

Report_1_Narrative: I have been having severe headaches after flying lately.  Being masked on an airplane and duty day that are now on average 10-15 hours a day.  I had a deadhead recently and wore an oxygen sensor from start to finish.  My oxygen in the hotel was 99/98 on the pulse oximeter.  During the flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1 I wore it the whole time.  My oxygen was between 89 and 94 the whole way until landing.  It then was back up to 98; 20 minutes after landing.  It is a fact that extra oxygen is pumped into hospital rooms during long surgeries because the doctors are masked.  I feel this shows that lack of oxygen; just on 1 flight is proving how I'm getting my headaches; let alone being masked as well.  I have never felt more unsafe flying than I have since having to wear masks.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Attendant reported the requirement to wear a mask during flights is resulting in having low blood oxygen levels and associated headaches.

Report_1_Narrative: On a 1.5 mile final for ILS XX at ZZZ Aircraft Y turned to base right in front of us even though we had just made a radio call and he knew we were on a short final.  This caused the instructor to grab the controls and full throttle to go missed. Had we not done this we would have been within a hundred feet of Aircraft Y.  He knew where we were and disregarded our radio calls and cut us off.
Report_1_Synopsis: Pilot reported a NMAC on final approach.

Report_1_Narrative: Operation in violation of Certificate of Waiver issued for UAS flights of multiple aircraft. I was issued a part 107 waiver to operate multiple aircraft with one remote pilot. One of my waiver provisions is to issue a NOTAM 24 hrs in advance of my operation. I flew yesterday without a NOTAM issued. We had issued a NOTAM to close the runway at airport ZZZ in which our operations are taking place. I thought this NOTAM was sufficient to satisfy our requirements.  When reading the operational waiver again today I took note that provision X of my waiver was not satisfied by the issuance of a closed runway NOTAM [as follows]:Not less than 24 hours prior to conducting operations that are the subject of this waiver; a Notice to Airmen (NOTAM) must be filed. The NOTAM must include location; altitude; and/or operating area; time and nature of the activity; and number of sUA flying in the operating area; To correct my mistake I called to issue a NOTAM as soon as I discovered my error.
Report_1_Synopsis: UAS Pilot reported noncompliance of CFR part 107 waiver due to not issuing a NOTAM.

Report_1_Narrative: Catastrophic engine failure at 8500 ft. MSL. Uneventful landing at ZZZ.
Report_1_Synopsis: Pilot reported engine failure during cruise.

Report_1_Narrative: While conducting a IFR training flight with a student; we were on an IFR flight plan and on initial climb vectors from ATC when we noticed the Oil Pressure indication slowly; but consistently; dropping.  It triggered a CAS caution message for Low Oil Pressure; then the pressure reading slowly recovered.  As we discussed the potential causes of this indication change; the Oil Pressure reading decreased again causing another CAS message.  At this point we both decided to return to the departure airport ZZZ.  The student informed ATC of the issue and asked to return to the airport.  We were given vectors back to ZZZ and confirmed with ATC that we [would like priority handling] We ran the appropriate checklists as a crew. We were then cleared for a visual approach and landed uneventfully at ZZZ.  This event was a great learning experience for the student and myself.  Always leaning towards caution and returning to the airport was the right move.  It would have been easy to convince ourselves that the oil pressure indication was a sensor error and continue to our destination; but this would have been very poor ADM.
Report_2_Narrative: While on an IFR flight plan and on initial climb vectors from ATC; we noticed the oil pressure indication slowly; but consistently dropping. It triggered a CAS message for low oil pressure; then the pressure reading slowly recovered. As we discussed potential causes of this indication change; the oil pressure reading decreased again causing another CAS message. At this point we both decided to return to the departure airport ZZZ. I informed ATC of the issue and asked to return to the airport. We were given vectors back to ZZZ and confirmed with ATC that I would [request priority handling]. We ran the appropriate checklists. This likely could have been a sensor issue; but I always prefer to be more safe than sorry.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Instructor and student reported during climbout the engine oil pressure was slowly dropping and a oil pressure warning occurred. The crew made a precautionary air return.

Report_1_Narrative: I was transiting from ZZZ1 to ZZZ; VFR;  beneath Class B at 1000 ft and circumventing ZZZ2 [military] Class D airspace to the southeast; when I got a traffic alert.  I spotted a C130 to my right; about 500 feet above and 2000-3000 feet horizontally.  In watching him and turning out of his path; I inadvertently climbed to 1260 feet; into the Class B airspace.  I immediately descended back into unrestricted airspace.
Report_1_Synopsis: Single pilot reported an inadvertent airspace violation which maneuvering to avoid other traffic.

Report_1_Narrative: HNL ATIS [is] so long no one actually listens to it. For the last several years I have listened to HNL ATIS thousands of times. It is the worst and longest ATIS I have ever heard and the ultra-long; droning voice with redundant; useless information creates conditions under which a pilot can't listen to and understand the whole thing even if he tried. I have timed the ATIS broadcast several times and it's always over 2 minutes in length. This represents about 5 NM traveled in a small aircraft; and probably double that in an airliner. Additionally; most of the information is useless or suffers from poor quality control.Examples:-Listing all lighting inoperative for a runway that is closed; in the middle of the day.-Way too much time spent on taxiways out of service.-Duplication of information like 'LAHSO in effect' spoken twice.-'taxiway Relative Humidity out of service' referring to taxiway RH.-'men and equipment working all taxiways and runways' has always been on the ATIS.-'increased bird strike hazard all runways' has always been on the ATIS.Nobody listens to this. I have tried to pay attention to the whole thing and it's damn difficult even on the ground. Last year when there were more runway closures there were events where aircraft overran closed sections of runway and I believe ATIS was primarily to blame.Ideas to make this better:-Get a faster talking robot; or make a human record it (that will eliminate some errors).-Move information that's always on there (like the bird strike thing) to the chart supplement.-Consolidate groups of information; like 'Taxiways closed: B; D; F; RH; RB'.-Maybe make a separate frequency with a 'long ATIS' for out of towners who want to hear about how bad the bird strike hazard is getting.We have a 20 min leg from ZZZ. This ensures that 10% of the flight will be spent listening to HNL's ATIS. Please make the FAA fix this.
Report_1_Synopsis: Pilot reported the HNL ATIS as very lengthy; repetitive; outdated; and of poor quality.

Report_1_Narrative: While troubleshooting an audio squeal at the Captain's cockpit station; ZZZ AMT discovered the AMU in the E/E was overheated. After removing the unit and allowing it to cool off; the AMTs found the rack cooling plugs were filled with a rubber plug. Given that this aircraft was less than 2 weeks old; it was believed that the rack cooling holes were inadvertently left plugged. The ZZZ AMTs misread the plug configuration placard on the rack; and my department did as well. As the [Maintenance] Manager; I allowed the aircraft to depart with the plugs removed. Boeing confirmed on the following day that the plugs should have been installed. The aircraft operated one leg out of configuration before corrective actions were taken.
Report_1_Synopsis: Technicians reported misidentifying aircraft configuration; resulting in the removal of aircraft equipment rack cooling plugs and the aircraft flying misconfigured.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Human-Machine Interface; Communication Breakdown; Situational Awareness
Report_1_Narrative: I was working Position X with numerous runway restrictions. Due to taxiway and runway closures we were running 4-8 MIT (Mile in Trail) to our runways we utilize except for Runway XXL which was normal. Due to these restrictions; over feeding an arrival controller happens quickly unless you build space by vectoring and speed reductions. Although this is necessary almost every push now; you begin to get backed up and run out of airspace. ZZZ [TRACON] already does not have much airspace and when you vector almost an entire base leg that is entering the metroplex airspace it becomes congested rather quickly. I was utilizing Runway YYR for as many aircraft that I could from the ZZZ1 Center; Position Y sector. We have had issues getting our spacing from this sector so we have to start taking aircraft off of the arrivals and slow them to make it work. I had assigned Aircraft X; Runway XXC because he was too close to the proceeding aircraft to land Runway YYR. The Controller working Runway  XXC was already turning a 25 mile final so I vectored Aircraft X 130 [heading] down the Runway YYR final  descending to 5;000 to put them in the downwind. I was also feeding ZZZ2 downwind aircraft to Runway YYR if I had gaps. Aircraft Y was one of these aircraft and turned to a 310 descending to 060 for right downwind to Runway YYR. I kept working and noticed the CA on both aircraft and immediately intervened by climbing and turning away Aircraft X. Aircraft Y also got a descent to 4;000. Closest proximity was 500 FT and 1.7 miles. I was in my airspace the entire time but the controller working YYR was so busy that he did not see my aircraft descending to 5;000. Aircraft X was not in a good place to begin with. I usually stop these vectored aircraft at 7;000 so I assume the other Controller was just not expecting anyone there at 5;000. We have an incredible amount of traffic with very little staffing. We should certainly keep the staffing the way it is for COVID-19 for the safety of the facility personnel. The issue is the amount of concrete we have at ZZZ available to us. We are constantly doing things out of the norm that could potentially cause an error. I could have handled this better by stopping at 7;000 or 8;000.
Report_1_Synopsis: TRACON Controller reported a loss of separation and cited traffic volume and staffing issues as contributing factors.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Training / Qualification; Situational Awareness; Communication Breakdown
Report_1_Narrative: I was working Ground Control and Controller in Charge position. I was over seeing the operation when I noticed the Cessna on landing roll when the RV was almost over the threshold on the same runway. I ordered the Local Controller to send the landing RV around. The Local Controller refused. I again ordered the Local Controller to send the RV around because there was not 3;000 feet between the Cessna on landing roll and the landing RV. Again the Local Controller refused.  Runway separation was lost and a runway incursion occurred.This is a controller judgment issue not a system issue. This controller continuously puts aircraft under his control and other controllers aircraft in danger on a daily basis. Nothing is being done about it. I recommend decertification.
Report_1_Synopsis: An ATC Controller in Charger reported the Local Controller refused their instructions to send an arrival around due to insufficient runway spacing between subsequent arrivals.

Report_1_Narrative: I was working all positions combined in RADAR. Traffic started to pick up far more than what we have had over the past few months due to COVID. Aircraft Y was level at 10k westbound and Aircraft X was east; inbound ZZZ out of 11 for 2500. I saw the traffic and turned Aircraft X 15 degrees left to maintain separation from Aircraft Y. I thought the turn would have been enough for 3 miles and degrees of divergence but ended up not being so. At the closest point I had 2.87 laterally and 800 ft. We went from a slow COVID season to busier than normal with a lot of crossing traffic.
Report_1_Synopsis: TRACON Controller reported a loss of separation.

Report_1_Narrative: I was operating flight to ZZZ. The weather was good and after detecting inadequate fuel planning and requesting additional fuel we departed on time and flew the filed flight plan. We were clear direct to ZZZZZ. Our ATIS was showing that we were expecting to land on Runway XX left.Knowing it was early in the morning we did anticipate a possible runway opening of either XX right or XY. When we were about three minutes from ZZZZZ; We were given the instructions to depart ZZZZZ on a heading to intercept the XY localizer. Although we had planned for the possibility of XY; this was a fairly abrupt and last-minute instruction from ATC. As briefed; this falls under the 'slam dunk' which was is always a threat; as I briefed for departure.We departed ZZZZZ on the assigned heading and began to set up for the intercept of the XY localizer. We were given a descent to 9000; then very quickly a decent to 6000; then a speed reduction to 170 and then briefly after that another speed reduction to 160 (until 5 out). All of this seem to happen in [a] very quick sequence. I was set up to intercept; set up to descend and began to slow down According to our instructions.We established our self on the ILS [Runway] XY without incident but when I realized that we needed to slow down; I called for flaps 22 'out of sequence.' (Typically flaps 22 is called with 'Gear Down'). I had already called for flaps nine; and just naturally called for flaps 22 knowing I needed to slow down.My First Officer (FO) followed the command and put in flaps 22. I naturally look down and scanned my instruments as I always do after a change command and I immediately realized that we were above the 200 knot threshold. I immediately took action - I pressed in the TCS (Control Steering) button; pitched up and began to slow down. As quickly and as safely as I could I brought the aircraft under the 200 knot limitation and completed the rest of the flight without incident.Upon landing I called my dispatcher; explained what happened; maintenance came out; they completed a full inspection and downloaded the information from the airplanes computer. We swapped airplanes so that the inspection could be completed and by the time we landed in ZZZ1; I had heard back from the maintenance supervisor. He told me that the inspection was completed no defects were found and the airplane was returned to service.I detected the problem. I always do a brief scan during critical phases of flight to confirm that the command and input was followed. So I did my scan after calling for Flaps 22 and immediately realized the error. I did not alert FO; as it was not necessary and I simply made the adjustments to the pitch and speed by using the TCS button. I feel there were 2 factors contributing cause to this event. The first was the additional time we had to spend on considering our planned fuel situation. This was definitely an added concern that both FO and I collaborated on before we even left the gate. Then; as Runway XY was opened and we received the 'Slam Dunk' vectors onto the ILS XY; was a second major contributor to this situation. My suggestion as to how to avoid this situation is to simply avoid the 'slam dunk' vectors. Had I asked for better vectors; I'm certain that this situation could and would have been avoided.
Report_1_Synopsis: Captain reported a flap speed was exceeded when the Captain called for an early flap extension to slow after ATC gave them a series of rapid descents and airspeed reductions.

Report_1_Narrative: The flight from ZZZ1 to ZZZ was dispatched under our new fuel management program. The 1 hour and 25 minute flight was dispatched with planned fuel of 5830 lbs. The FO and I both noticed and mentioned that the landing fuel numbers were very low for our standard operation. The NAV Log section of the release showed 1;829 lbs. which is planned fuel minus taxi and fuel burn. But the fuel calculation section showed 1;660 lbs. This concerned both the FO and I; as such a long flight with very little fuel to be landing with. We both discussed that the airplane was [under] fueled by at least 200 lbs. Therefore we both felt landing with 2;000 lbs. or worst case scenario 1;800 lbs. was low but a safer and acceptable number. The performance manual shows around 1;700 lbs. at 5;000 ft. is around 45 minutes of fuel. Knowing our fuel was tight; we did what we could to help conserve fuel by delaying the second engine start as long as possible; and we attempted a Flight Level Change climb by several and normal intermediate level off altitudes with only 7 miles in the opposite direction. We continued to monitor our fuel burn. Upon our initial descent; we noticed we had burned more than planned; but we had received a shortcut and still calculated landing with around 1;800 lbs. On a few turns before final; the right fuel gauge began to flash amber at us then continued to flash in and out as fuel moved around throughout the final approach. Upon landing; we had around 1;800 lbs. of fuel. I feel this margin of safety is extremely low for a safety conscious airline and program. The fuel management program should be providing us with more fuel not less fuel. We were [under] fueled and received no undue delays and were proactive in managing and conserving fuel. Our end result was landing with 1;800 lbs. of fuel. In a medium case scenario; if the airport shuts down for an aircraft emergency or anything else; a go around diversion to the closest company destination (ZZZ2 is 78 miles away); say 25 to 30 minutes at 8;000 ft. (1;100 lbs.); would have me landing with 400 lbs. of fuel and I would have had to make that decision immediately. ZZZ3 is the next closest at 117 miles. That is also if those stations both have personnel staffed to service the aircraft. While legal; and probably acceptable; this practice seems to create an unreasonable reduced margin of safety standards with the trade-off being cost savings. In addition; as a Check Airmen and experienced pilot; I have more wherewithal to be neurotically monitoring developing situations; and weather. I can see an average pilot easily being forced into a no-win situation or very unsafe situation with dire outcome.[We] detected and attempted to manage [the issue] upon review of the release and even with proactive measures; the aircraft still landed with an uncomfortable amount of fuel. [We] took proactive fuel burn reductions with no changes in landing fuel. The airline's new fuel management program and a lack of safety margins created by the program [were contributing factors].I suggest changing the standard practice of providing 45 minutes of cruise fuel from flight level altitudes and provide the crew with an accurate and manageable 45 minutes of fuel near 10;000 ft. which is where most people will need that extra fuel in the case of holding; delays; reroutes and diversions which more likely occur below the flight levels. Add fuel and increase the amount of minimum fuel required to be on the airplane for dispatch.
Report_1_Synopsis: An air carrier Captain reported receiving a low fuel indication during final approach and suggested that the company's fuel management program did not allow enough fuel for adequate safety margins.

Report_1_Narrative: Approximately 3 hours into flight a group of 3 passengers would not comply with the Flight Attendant instructions regarding wearing their face masks.  She notified us and we told Dispatch of the situation and their seat location.  Shortly after; they became belligerent to the flight attendants and continued [with] non-compliance.  Now they were using foul language and disrupting other passengers.  The Captain asked one of the foreign language speaking flight attendants to go try and deescalate the situation but that only made things worse.  We looked in the Flight Operations manual and technically this was a threat level 1.  We discussed whether should we notify Dispatch and we agreed by the definition it was; but we did not really think this was anything other than a couple of intoxicated passengers.  The Captain got on the PA and addressed the cabin of the importance of wearing the mask.  After this announcement we had no further trouble with these passengers. They apologized to the Flight Attendant as they exited the plane in ZZZ.Mask requirements in cabin; possible intoxication; lack of respect for airline rules. As soon as the Captain made the announcement this problem went away.  Maybe we should have tried that sooner.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier First Officer reported 3 passengers would not comply with the face mask policy during flight and became belligerent toward the flight attendants.

Report_1_Narrative: On approach into ZZZ Runway XXR; the Captain called for Flaps 1. The slats extended as expected. Shortly thereafter Captain called for Flaps 2. An ECAM message appeared and flaps had not moved at all. We followed ECAM procedures to no avail. Several miles out; we went around to diagnose the problem with the aircraft and requested priority handling. We ran the ECAM [procedure] and landing data as required then flew a zero-flap approach to an uneventful landing and roll out. The Captain notified Operations and filled out the logbook as required. Two weeks later I received a call from the gatekeeper looking for information on the event. I turns out Maintenance said they could not find a problem and signed off the logbook. The next day the following crew had the same issue flying into ZZZ1 according to the gatekeeper.
Report_1_Synopsis: An air carrier First Officer reported the flaps did not extend during final approach and a zero flaps landing was performed.

Report_1_Narrative: After getting on the aircraft to fly; I did all my pre-flight duties including putting my personal luggage away and doing my safety checks. Just before we were ready to board; the flight crew including myself; was notified that someone had tested positive for COVID-19 from the inbound flight. We were later told that it was a passenger who tested positive for COVID-19. After waiting and many phone calls by the ground management as well as the pilots; it was decided ground personnel would clean the area where the customer had sat more thoroughly than just the tray table areas. The passenger was said to have been sitting in row X that tested positive. The cleaning personnel who wipe down the areas cleaned row X and the surrounding 6 rows behind it as a precaution. They then did it again because the cleaning solution being used says on the directions that it must sit for at least XX minutes on the surfaces being cleaned to properly be effective. Once the cleaning process was finished and completed; we boarded the flight and went on our way.The safety concern here is that there is no protocol for this exact situation and possible exposure. Our whole working crew and whatever ground personnel who entered the plane post flight are possibly exposed to this virus. I personally work in the affected area of the row. I sat in the row waiting for answers as to the protocols on what we were to do next. I touched all overhead bins around row X; the bathroom; bulkhead working station; and all surrounding areas that all could have been affected by this customer who tested positive. It's also not known if this customer had affected any other parts of the cabin and if this virus is on surfaces of the plane in more than just row X and the area of the aircraft that all the crew had to walk on to get on the aircraft.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Attendant reported possible COVID-19 exposure from a passenger on the inbound flight. The crew used the same aircraft outbound after being notified of the positive test.

Report_1_Narrative: Engine oil pressure maxed out during flight. Requested ATC to direct me to nearest airport. ATC sent me to ZZZ1. I landed safely. In light of this event; I believe the FAA should not exempt club aircraft from the same maintenance schedules required by training/school aircraft. A law should be implemented that aircraft for rent; for example; through a club; should require the exact same maintenance requirements as training/school aircraft. In talking with the owner of the plane; owner and his son both knew there was an engine oil pressure [gauge] issue; but allowed me to rent his plane and fly it. I noticed [gauge] was slightly high during run-up. The needle went full deflection after reaching cruise. I believe this situation could have been avoided if the [club] came down harder on aircraft owners to maintain their planes. It should be mandated to impose stricter maintenance schedules on club planes for rent. The airplane owners in the club have very little incentive to spend the money to keep the planes properly maintained; beyond the annual inspections. Pilots suffer due to owner thriftiness.
Report_1_Synopsis: Single pilot reported that engine oil pressure exceeded operating limits resulting in a divert and successful precautionary landing.

Report_1_Narrative: I was planning to fly from the ZZZ airport to my home on the lake a distance of approximately 5 NM. I was solo; and did a weight and balance and determined I needed 45 pounds of ballast in the nose anchor compartment; and confirmed it was there. The winds were very light out of the south and I took off on Runway XX and turned towards my home. I went to do a 'splash and dash' on the lake before going to the house so after climbing to about 500 ft. I reduced power and did my pre-water landing checklist. On touchdown I immediately did a water loop with no injury to me or any other property; and minor damage to the plane. I must have let the nose get too low; and possibly was hit by an unnoticed boat wake. Since I had lake specific recurrency training on [Date] and [Date1]; have done [Number] water landings; [Number1] in the last year and [Number2] in the last 90 days I do not know what else I should have done.I did notify the tower that I had a problem and was heading back on the water to the seaplane ramp. They called the fire department and asked them to launch a boat to assist if needed. When I got to the seaplane ramp their launch vehicle; trailer; and boat were on the left side of the ramp. I tried to call the tower to ask them to have the equipment moved; but could not raise them. I then tried to get up the right side of the ramp; and the right main gear went off the ramp and was damaged. I feel personnel should not block runways; taxiways; or seaplane ramps when trying to help.
Report_1_Synopsis: Seaplane pilot reported that during touchdown; the plane did a water loop; possibly as a result of the nose getting too low.

Report_1_Narrative: At ZZZ; an uncontrolled airport; my student and I had just landed. We cleared the runway and taxied to Runway XX for another lap in the pattern. Making appropriate radio calls; we searched for traffic and then lined up on Runway XX. To our surprise; there was an aircraft on the runway at the other end. It was too late to move by the time we realized the aircraft; some type of business jet; was taking off. We heard no radio calls from this aircraft either before or after the event. We knew that we were on the correct frequency because we heard comments from the other aircraft also waiting to depart Runway XX. The departing aircraft flew directly over us as we sat in position at the numbers XX.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Instructor reported that after lining up on the runway; another aircraft was departing from the opposite end and had made no radio calls of their intentions.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Workload; Communication Breakdown; Distraction; Situational Awareness; Confusion
Report_1_Narrative: I signed in to work; and went to get the person out of positions at Sector X.  The CPC who was working had just gotten someone else out 5 minutes earlier; which added to the confusion in my opinion.  During all of this; I was not wearing my eyeglasses because they fog up badly when I wear a mask for COVID.  I received a quick briefing; and during the briefing; I vaguely heard Sector Y tell the Controller who was working to 'start the Aircraft X down to FL310.'  Then I recall hearing a straight descent to FL310.  I was unable to really scan accurately because I could not see any data blocks.  Anyways; the briefing completes; and I sit down and put my glasses on and start working and scanning.  I answer a landline call or two; issue a few clearances; then look at Aircraft X who was now FL390 for FL310.  I notice that it looks like it will be close with an aircraft level at FL350; so I call Sector Y and asked them what they want me to do with the two planes and that I had just sat down.  After some back and forth; they told me to stop the guy at FL360.Well; the first Controller at Sector X should have never given a pilot's discretion clearance to FL250.  Secondly; we're supposed to comply with the SOP with ZZZ Center Sector Y; which would have the Aircraft X crossing the boundary AOB FL310; this was never done.I believe all of the relief briefings had a part to play with the lack of communication in this scenario.  Another aspect which compounded this all is that I wasn't able to wear my glasses due to the fogging up issue.  I wasn't able to properly scan before I really sat down because I trust the members on my crew.
Report_1_Synopsis: Center Controller reported a near loss of separation and cited fogged up glasses due to wearing a face mask and poor coordination during a controller switch contributed to the event.

Report_1_Narrative: This is a general safety concern. We landed and departed during a time of limited visibility which; for us; was a period of approximately 3 hours. First off; the Tower controllers did an excellent job but it was obvious they were task-saturated. A single Controller was working Tower/Ground/Clearance frequencies with an inability to visually see aircraft on approach and while taxiing. The weather conditions were simply too overwhelming for one Controller to safely keep track of arriving/departing aircraft as well deconflicting taxiing aircraft. Again; phenomenal job by the controllers; however; was the risk necessary to continue the single Controller operation of the airport? In my opinion; no; and it would be unfair to blame the Controller if an incident had occurred.Forecasted poor weather should mean extra manning of ATC facilities. One Controller [was] working Tower/Ground/Clearance during low visibility operations.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported that one Controller was working combined frequencies during low visibility conditions at the airport. Reporter stated safety concerns with the situation.

Report_1_Narrative: Climbing out of ZZZ; at approximately 18;500 feet; we heard a muffled bang and felt yaw. The engine instruments indicated the number two engine EGT was near zero; and it was no longer producing thrust. I asked the FO to tell ATC we required a level off at FL190; and requested priority handling. I then directed the FO to read the QRH Engine Failure or Shutdown checklist.We asked ATC for return vectors to ZZZ. The landing runway was Runway XX; and strong; gusty winds favored this choice. We relayed number of souls onboard and fuel remaining to ATC.After the Engine Failure checklist was complete and the engine was secured; I spoke with the FAs; immediately followed by a brief PA to the passengers. I told them the number two engine has failed; we're returning to ZZZ; and we should be on the ground in 10 to 15 minutes.The remaining 'clean-up' checklists went well; and to my knowledge all steps were completed. We were a bit rushed due to our proximity to ZZZ. In hindsight we should have asked for slightly extended vectors to give us more time; as the approach brief was glossed over. Although it was clear VMC and we were familiar with the airport; it would have been best to do a standard brief. Also; I should have considered restarting the engine; as there was no abnormal vibration; but just occasional slight buffet. We made an uneventful; under max weight; Flaps 15 landing.The rescue trucks met us with one on Taxiway 1; north of the far end of Runway XX; and another group; I believe on the Apron near the fire station. We easily exited the runway on Taxiway 2X; and we told them we did not need any assistance; but to follow us to the gate. ATC and Crash Rescue were flawless. They were helpful; did not interfere; and followed up where necessary.Other agencies also contacted us in a professional manner; and we spoke to them in turn: Dispatch; Maintenance; Operations team; Chief Pilot; and [other] Management.
Report_2_Narrative: Preflight and takeoff were without incident until climb through 18;000 feet. As the aircraft was climbing through 18;000 feet. I felt an abnormal airframe vibration along with thumping sound that seemed to come from the right side of the airplane (lasting a few seconds). Within a few seconds the #2 Eng Fail indication appeared accompanied with a roll back and aircraft yaw. Almost immediately the 'A' Flight Attendant called up and inquired if everything was okay. I informed her we lost the #2 engine; and we would call her back. The Captain told me to call ATC [and advise them] and get vectors back to ZZZ. We accomplished the Engine Fire or Engine Severe Damage or Separation Checklist as we began our descent back into ZZZ. The Captain briefed the Flight Attendants and informed the Passengers about our situation. During our descent; we encountered occasional airframe vibrations. We also completed the One Engine Inoperative Landing Checklist on the way into ZZZ. The Captain flew a visual approach backed up with the ILS to Runway XX. After landing we taxied to the gate (IAW Brake Cooling).
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported an engine failure occurred during climbout which resulted in an air return.

Report_1_Narrative: 150;000 pounds at pushback. Pushed straight back off Gate XX. Started both engines. Did checklist and released brakes for taxi. Plane wouldn't move. Added power; no movement. Increased N1 to 40%; plane would not move. Figured we were chocked or brake stuck. Had Ramp Agents come out and check if we were chocked. They believed mains were below the lip of ramp. They suggested to add more power. I shut both motors down and had them go get a Tug. They discovered both mains were in storm drains. We pushed plane back 10 more feet. Started up and taxied out.Suggestion - Have ramp in ZZZ be aware of storm drains.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported that after pushback both main wheels became stuck in storm drains requiring a tug to free the aircraft.

Report_1_Narrative: BNA is in desperate need of a Ramp Controller. On this flight; we had four airplanes pushback simultaneously; unnecessarily crowding the alleyway. I wish I had paid closer attention to which gates had pushed; but we pushed; in essence; tail 'NW at a 45' from Gate XX; another aircraft pushed from the opposite side of the alley effectively blocking us in; and then two aircraft pushed off the end of the terminal effectively blocking the both of us in. All this while there was an aircraft waiting on the south side of the terminal trying to get into the alleyway. We are setting ourselves up for failure (late pushes; delayed departures) or worse yet; an incident or accident. And this was day VMC. Add a few additive conditions and we are in trouble.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported that four aircraft pushed back simultaneously; causing some of them to be blocked in the alley at BNA airport.

Report_1_Narrative: Arrived at appropriate report time. Flight planned and then proceeded to COVID test site. Test extremely unpleasant. Results took XX minutes. Had to call Operations and delay the flight; fortunately a cargo flight today; so no passenger connection issues. Departure was XY minutes late. This could result in crews rushing in the future. Please have someone review testing procedures and timeliness of receiving results. Forward as you see fit.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Captain reported the time required for the COVID-19 test delayed the departure of their flight.

Report_1_Narrative: After I aligned the aircraft with the gate; I noticed the chocks were in position.  I then transferred my attention to the Marshaller providing positive guidance.  Smoothly and slowly approaching the Marshaller's stop signal; I felt a slight bump - after that the Marshaller gave me abrupt opposite direction guidance and then simply the stop guidance; and shook his head.  I spoke to the Gate Agent in the jetbridge who concurred with my description of the event and informed me that he saw the right portion of my nose gear hit the chocks.  FO inspected the nose gear and did not notice any damage; I called Maintenance Control to report a precautionary discrepancy (because I could not enter it myself at the point).  I described to them what happened.
Report_1_Synopsis: A320 Captain reported that while being marshalled into the gate; the aircraft nose gear hit the chocks.

Report_1_Narrative: We are supposed to run our [specific equipment] to reduce COVID exposure; yet I was flight planned with [specific equipment] inoperative. When I queried the Dispatcher why it was dispatched that way; his response was 'I don't know.'  I refused the aircraft.After refusing the airplane the Dispatcher stated [I] was to speak to Flight Operations. The Dispatcher also had me talk to Maintenance to confirm I 'understood the nature of the MEL.' This sounds a lot like pilot pushing to me.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Captain refused the aircraft due to a specific equipment MELed inoperative; which is reportedly used to reduce COVID exposure.

Report_1_Narrative: During my third flight back after a 7 month absence (first flight back into ZZZ); I forgot to call the ramp prior to parking at Gate XXX; one of the exterior gates. I believe ground control cleared us 'taxi to the gate' or a similar clearance; and I simply forgot that I was supposed to call Ramp Tower.
Report_2_Narrative: Taxed into gate without ramp clearance. The self park was green with wing walkers. It is a short taxi from Runway XXR.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier flight crew reported a ramp incursion and cited lack of flying as a contributing factor.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Situational Awareness; Communication Breakdown; Training / Qualification
Report_1_Narrative: Climbing out of ZZZ on the ZZZZZ2 RNAV Departure. The departure lists the fix ZZZZZ as cross at or below. As monitoring pilot I was waiting for the hand off from Tower to Departure. Tower was busy handling other aircraft; and sometimes they hang on to you a little longer than normal. My mind was fixed on listening for the hand off; and wondering why we didn't get it. Not to mention I am brand new to the aircraft and have not flown much in the last several months. I finally decided to switch to Departure on my own and about that time I noticed the autothrottles retarding. I realized what had happened; the flying pilot had overlooked the level off and we crossed the fix 600-700 feet high. I contacted Departure and we continued the flight without further incident.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier First Officer reported an altitude deviation during departure and cited poor CRM and lack of flying as contributing factors.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Other / Unknown; Situational Awareness; Physiological - Other
Report_1_Narrative: On [date] two ramp employees came into the breakroom; neither had a mask on...they both stood close to me.
Report_1_Synopsis: Ground employee reported two ramp employees entered the breakroom without wearing a mask.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Situational Awareness; Time Pressure; Communication Breakdown
Report_1_Narrative: Aircraft X apparently hit a set of stairs on pushback with their right wing tip unbeknownst to the crew or Marshaller. A ground crew member saw it and called it in to his supervisor; who called it in to the Ops (Airport Operations). The plane at this point was on takeoff roll and wasn't in contact with Ops via radio anymore. After getting airborne; Ops took it into their own hands and called Tower and told them to have the flight return to field. I received an message from the crew asking why the return to field; which is when I started to make calls. This happened while the crew was at 3;000 feet and turning around. Crew landed uneventfully and the plane was taken out of service with visible damage to the right wingtip. No request was issued for a return to field as I felt in the short time frame; and with how busy the crew would have been setting up an unexpected approach; that it would have been unsafe to add more to their workload. Operations staff need to be fully aware of their limitations in regards to operational control of flights. Perhaps there needs to be a rapid communication procedure for the ground personnel; as they had to make several calls to get the information to someone who could have made a difference quicker.
Report_2_Narrative: After we took off and checked on with ZZZ Departure Control we were advised by the controller that Company wanted us to return to the airport. Upon questioning; the controller did not know the reason. I sent an ACARS message to our Dispatcher advising of an air turn back and asked why. His response was that he didn't know but would find out. We set up for the return to ZZZ and landed uneventfully and taxied to parking. Upon aircraft shutdown and secure a ZZZ maintenance representative met us inside the cockpit to advise us that the right wingtip possibly came into contact with a set of crew stairs during block out. We took a look at the wing and there was some minor damage to the right outboard leading edge slat just inside the right navigation light. At all times during the block out we were under the guidance and direction of the marshaller. Appropriate logbook entry made and reports submitted by both myself and First Officer. Reflecting upon blocking out; after engine start we cleared the mechanic and ascertained immediate area left and right were clear; I signaled the marshaller across the ramp and on the nose that we were ready to taxi out. We were marshaled straight out into the alley and given the signal for a left turn into the alley followed by a wave-off and salute. During the initial block out taxi roll; the First Officer mentioned the crew stairs seemed close; but from my position the stairs did not appear to be encroaching on the taxi lane and I continued to follow the marshaller's instructions. All marshaling signals were consistent with the aircraft being clear of any obstacles; and at no time did the marshaller give us a stop signal during the taxi out; nor did we feel any bump from the right wingtip possibly making contact with the crew stairs. I do not know if there was a wing-walker on the right wing due proximity of ground equipment between our aircraft and the aircraft to our right. I do recall a white ramp vehicle was encroached in the clear area to our right as we were blocking out; but the vehicle backed up out of the way. Recommendations: wing-walkers; all ground equipment clear; equipment safe boxes painted on the ground around the aircraft like in ZZZ1.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier flight crew and Dispatcher reported that the aircraft wingtip hit a set of stairs during pushback but that it was not communicated to the flight crew until after departure. An uneventful air return was made.

Report_1_Narrative: We got our IFR clearance from ZZZ Tower about 30 minutes prior to departure. We were surprised that ZZZ Tower closed shortly after getting our clearance; at XB:00 p.m. we taxied to the runway and made position announcements on the CTAF. After takeoff we contacted ZZZ Approach at about 1;500 feet AGL. Approach informed us that we should have gotten an IFR release from them on the ground.  We need to remember to get an IFR release for departure from Approach Control if the Tower closes after issuing our clearance.
Report_2_Narrative: In ZZZ; I called ZZZ Clearance and received our IFR clearance to ZZZ1 at approximately XA:30 p.m. local time. After a slight ramp delay; we pushed back around XB:10 p.m. The Tower at ZZZ closes at XB:00. We made all our CTAF calls and took off in clear VFR conditions. I checked in with departure at 1;400 feet. At that time Departure let us know we did not get our IFR release on the ground.I recommend once a Tower closes; even with a clearance received prior to closing; always contact Departure on the ground prior to departing and pick up your IFR release to destination. The cause was some confusion with already receiving the clearance and picking up the release after the Tower closed. Lesson learned is as described above; once Tower closes you need to pick up your clearance from Departure prior to taking off.
