Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier flight crew reported obtaining an IFR clearance before Tower closed; however; they departed after Tower closed and did not obtain an IFR release for departure.

Report_1_Narrative: During climb after departing ZZZ; we experienced light clear icing; which began around 12;000 ft and ended around 20;000 ft. During this time; we noted STALL PROT ICE SPEED status message displayed; as well as the WING and both ENG BLEED VALVE OPEN advisory messages displayed. Roughly around 24;000 feet and still climbing; we experienced a master warning EICAS message (A-I WING 1 LEAK). The FO was flying; so I asked him to maintain control of the airplane; and to handle the radios while I ran the QRH checklist. The checklist drove us to press the wing ice protection button out; which we did. Almost immediately the EICAS message disappeared from view. I brought up the ice protection schematic on my MFD; and verified the wing valves were closed. We continued and completed the checklist.We exited icing conditions around 20;000 feet; and it appeared that clear skies were ahead and above us. We decided to continue the flight and landed safely at ZZZ1.We decided that icing conditions were not forecast or reported on our WSI app along our route of flight. We also could not see any apparent icing conditions ahead. With this in mind; ultimately I decided that we could continue the flight safely to ZZZ1. I also did not feel that this warranted an in-flight call to Dispatch and Maintenance; however; I did call maintenance control after we reached the gate at ZZZ1. I informed the controller what we experienced; and we both agreed that a discrepancy no longer existed and therefore did not make an AML entry. At the end of our day; I made the next Captain aware of our event verbally when we got to ZZZ2.I wish that I had taken a picture after the wing valves were closed on the ice protection schematic on my MFD. I think we handled the situation well as a crew; and we both agreed that we could continue the flight safely.
Report_1_Synopsis: EMB-175 Captain reported that the wing bleed air system malfunctioned while the aircraft was experiencing icing during climbout.

Report_1_Narrative: Upon arriving at MSO airport on [Date] at approximately XA:00 the winds were not favorable to execute the ILS to RWY (Runway) 12. The weather conditions to perform the RNAV GPS D were alternating between ceiling and visibility going below minimum conditions. We were communicating with Dispatch along the way and were discussing diverting to our first alternate; which [was] Billings (BIL). The ceiling and visibility at MSO was above minimums at time of arrival. We started the RNAV approach with a circle to land on RWY 30. After crossing the final approach fix at 6;800 ft.; and descending to our MDA of 4;700 ft.; we started to have some ground contact. The FO (First Officer) said that he saw the PAPI lights to the right of us. The approach did not allow for us to circle to land northeast of RWY 12/30. The only way to commence the circle was to fly over the airport and circle around to the west. We briefly discussed circling to the west and quickly decided that it would be unsafe to circle around the airport at night in low visibility with LLWS (Low Level Wind Shear) conditions in mountainous terrain. During the decision making phase I had inadvertently disconnected the auto throttle. We continued to the missed approach point. As we went around I had realized that the MAP fix was not in the box. As we looked at the approach plate and quickly made a climbing left turn on a heading of about 340. We asked ATC for a heading while we headed in the proper direction. Once WENKE was back in the box we realized we were right on course.At approximately 8;000 ft. we were back in radar contact and was giving a vector off the final approach course. ATC asked us if we wanted to commence another approach or divert to a different airport. After discussing the conditions that we saw and weather forecast to be deteriorating; we unanimously decided that it would be unsafe to conduct a circle to land night approach based on the current weather and forecasted conditions.We then told ATC that we were going to divert to BIL. We sent ACARS message to Dispatch telling them we were diverting as well. After landing at BIL; Dispatch told us that we were to refuel and proceed back to MSO. Dispatch then said the weather was not good enough to go back and was delaying our departure. After waiting about an hour Dispatch said the winds were improving and we should be able to do the ILS RWY 12 back into MSO. We departed BIL for MSO with BIL as our alternate if we could not get in. We executed the ILS to RWY 12. While in Billings we contacted ATC and they told us at that time that they did not have radar until about 8;000 ft. The controller said that he was not working at that time but discussed with the previous controller that we were right where we were supposed to be and we said we just were at a high work load and wanted to verify with them that we were on course.High workload with low ceilings; LLWS; at night in mountainous terrain. Having to circle with visibility below what was projected and inadvertently disconnected auto throttles to land.I feel like this approach is not a safe approach to do at night. I spoke with several carriers that land at this airport and this approach is not authorized.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported difficulties while conducting a circle-to-land approach at night in mountainous terrain in low visibility conditions followed by an improperly executed missed approach.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Troubleshooting; Confusion; Time Pressure; Communication Breakdown
Report_1_Narrative: Please read MEL 24-XX-XX and apply (O) action #2. This morning on a first flight of the day at XA15 we received paper work for Flight XXXX ZZZ to ZZZ1. I reviewed the paper work and noted 2 MELs. One for the coffee pot and the other for a TRU (Transformer Rectifier Unit). I reviewed the log book and noted that everything had MCNs and appeared correct. I then proceeded with the acceptance inspection. Once the acceptance was complete I looked up the MELs to familiarize my self with them. The coffee pot MEL was complied with correctly. The TRU MEL was complied with correctly as well. After reviewing the MEL with my First Officer we then proceeded with the rest of the gate work; checklist; and departed. While en route I decided to re-read the MEL and learn a bit more about the write in the log book. I came to the conclusion that the MEL did not apply to the write up. The write up said 'DC Service Bus still shows powered when no power is applied to the aircraft. Nav Lights are still on; Placarded and Placed on MEL.' The MEL (24-XX-XX) was applied and the service TRU was MEL'd. When the (O) action #2 was applied per the MEL however the Essential Tie is closed manually and DC Service Bus was re-energized via the Essential TRU2. This did not solve the problem stated in the write up. Once we landed in ZZZ1; I contacted Dispatch and Maintenance and we all agreed that the MEL was inappropriate for the discrepancy in the log book and the aircraft was taken out of service. The complexity of the electrical system and the rarity of MELs used on it played a factor in missing this at the gate as well as the early morning and pressure to get out on time.
Report_1_Synopsis: Pilot reported a misapplied MEL was used and the aircraft flew in revenue service.

Report_1_Narrative: First flight in Aircraft X. We programmed the FMS with the intended runway for departure. Upon taxi clearance; we had a runway change of [Runway] XX. When we changed the runway the FMS deleted our fixes in between our departure and arrival. We proceeded to program the FMS again with all fixes and found no further issues. Next issue was our following flight from ZZZ1 to ZZZ2. We programmed landing into ZZZ RNAV Y XXL. Instead of showing the landing runway on FMS and MFD; it showed the missed approach point of ZZZZZ. Once reaching that point; two EICAS messages displayed. Vertical mode off and lateral mode off appeared with no FMA modes active. We also lost guidance from ZZZZZZ to the runway. We are unsure if in a missed approach guidance would be active if needed. Once we landed the EICAS messages went away and no further issue. Programming the FMS [for the next flight]; performance data showed us landing with 4;100 lbs of fuel. Once we started engine 2; we received a message to check fuel reserve with indicated landing fuel of 2;500 lbs. We stopped at hold short line of Runway XXL to further diagnose. We found the climb page showing us climbing at a speed of 138 knots (V2) to TOC (top of climb). This showed us taking a total of 43 minutes to TOC; which should have been 20 minutes. We tried to program the climb speed and switch to manual to see if it would recalculate but it did not work. We were above our planned fuel and calculated our fuel burn manually to find we would be safe to begin the flight. Once we advanced our power; it recalculated our landing fuel to our projected 4;100 lbs. No other issues came of this flight.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Crew flying EMB175 aircraft reported multiple issues with the Flight Management System.

Report_1_Narrative: Near top of climb we had an intermittent ENG 1 OIL LO PR Amber Caution message which became a steady RED Warning message. I performed the ECAM (Electronic Centralized Aircraft Monitor) actions and follow up for the message which included shutting down the engine. The Captain [advised ATC]. We landed without further incident.I don't know what caused the indication but we had multiple indications which led us to believe it was not an erroneous indication and resulted ultimately in the engine shutdown per the ECAM.I believe it was a mechanical issue but I was unable to find a clear procedure for what to do for an intermittent (or even steady) ENG 1 OIL LO PR Amber Caution message with other supporting indications. Having a discussion in training about unusual/non standard situations would be helpful insight. ATC was very accommodating and we found it helpful to have ATC provide us a separate frequency to communicate with Tower and ARFF (Aircraft Rescue Fire Fighting) simultaneously. ARFF was very responsive and communication was excellent. It was a seamless process on final approach with our requests.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Flight Crew flying A-321 aircraft reported low engine oil pressure inflight.

Person_2_Human_Factors: Workload; Time Pressure; Confusion; Distraction; Human-Machine Interface
Report_1_Narrative: Crew was descending into ZZZ Airport at about [night] time. Weather revealed winds 350 with good visibility and MVFR conditions. With the higher winds out of the north; the crew elected to fly the RNP Approach which requires the PAPI to be operational to fly the approach. A review of the NOTAMs revealed this would not be an issue; though the REIL was out of service to this runway. Icing conditions on the approach prompted to crew to conduct a flap full landing with ice numbers. Additionally; Tower mentioned that they would be closing just prior to our arrival. The Captain; myself; briefed the autothrottles would be disconnected on the arrival; with the autopilot off once established inbound. I disconnected the autothrottles and left the autopilot on as briefed. We continued to configure through the landing checklist and saw the runway on the approach. Once we rounded out on final; I disconnected the autopilot and began slowing to our approach speed when the lights at the airport clicked off. I briefly shallowed the descent anticipating the possibility of a go-around and had my First Officer turn the lights to high which failed to bring the PAPI back online. Being VMC and within required company parameters for a safe approach; I inquired to my First Officer if he was comfortable with continuing under the conditions which he was. I corrected descent angle and the flight landed without any further incident.This was the flight crew's first time flying this approach; my first RNP approach in a while; and my fourth night landing in about 2.5 months. This RNP Approach requires the PAPI to be operational to use. With there being no PAPI NOTAM; it was determined that it would be appropriate to fly it. After we had landed we found that the Tower; attempting to enable the pilot controlled lighting; had inadvertently switched all lights off. This was corrected with my First Officer turning the lights back on but the action failed to turn the PAPI on. The ATIS had called for gusty winds out of the north but; once we were established on final; I noticed we had a quartering tailwind at 15 kt. which caused me some confusion. The light issue and shifting winds prompted me to shallow out the approach due to the possibility of a go-around. However; with the airport lights on minus the PAPI and in VMC conditions; I figured the safest course of action was to continue given the fact that we were within parameters required to continue the approach and land. My thinking was a go-around late at night; in mountainous terrain and icing conditions with a possible changing weather pattern; may not be the best idea given we were still within tailwind parameters and touchdown requirements for landing. To me; this incident illustrates how important it is to appropriately manage [non-forecasted] distractions; especially during high workload phases. Additionally; it's imperative that we strive to remain current even during prolonged periods of stagnation.When weather is in vicinity; ensure [that] the most accurate weather is obtained from Tower if necessary. Relay concerns of airport issues to ATC or go-around. Be wary of Tower closures near arrivals to airports. A reminder that higher elevation airports present unique challenges which must be reviewed and briefed prior to flying into them. A reminder to chair fly approaches to destination airports; especially if the approaches you intend to follow are unfamiliar. The importance of maintaining appropriate approach currency. Speed management and adequate monitoring during all flight phases. A reminder to fly the airplane first and; if mounting distractions cause confusion; go-around.
Report_2_Narrative: I briefed the descent and approach with Captain; Captain as pilot flying. Reviewed FMS approach briefing card. Verified all NOTAMs and approach requirements per the chart and current ATIS. Both First Officer and Captain acknowledged Runway End Identifier Lights were inoperative; [but was not] not required for approach clearance. Received approach clearance from Approach. Tower closed while just outside the FAF with acknowledgment from Tower on Tower frequency of no traffic in the area on frequency and no issues to report from the last reported ATIS. Broke out from IMC to VMC conditions before the FAF. Acknowledged 'runway' by First Officer and 'landing' by Captain. Clicked the CTAF frequency 5 times by [the] First Officer to assure lights would remain illuminated while on final; [as] requested by [the] Captain. Runway lights removed from view while just past the FAF.Then; [the] First Officer clicked 5 times on CTAF frequency again; after [the] Captain asked about the runway lights turning off; both runway lights illuminated again. Moments later we both acknowledged that we didn't see the PAPI to the left. CA (Captain) asked if I found the circumstances to land safe versus a missed approach late at night and snow in the forecast. [We] agreed it would be safe to land given the real time circumstances. Upon landing with no issue; Tower Controller got on CTAF frequency to apologize that they configured the runway lighting incorrectly; which is why it turned off momentarily. The First Officer reported the PAPI was also not working when lights returned. [The] ATC Controller reported on CTAF; 'That is weird;' and would be reporting it to airport operations. Great example in how reality and goal for safety require pilot judgment.
Report_1_Synopsis: E175 flight crew reported that as the Tower Controller was closing up the Tower; had inadvertently turned off the runway lights; resulting in a non-functional PAPI lighting system while the crew was on approach.

Report_1_Narrative: We were navigating between coordinates at FL410 and M.80 assigned.  We received a CPDLC clearance that said; 'Resume normal speed'.  We reviewed the Europe Jeppesen Airway Manual section entitled 'Operations Without an Assigned Speed' to review this relatively new procedure. After agreeing on what it meant we accelerated to M.83 and advised ATC at XA:03z via CPDLC 'Present speed .83'.  ATC responded at XA:13z with 'Do you want M.83'.  We responded; 'Received normal speed CLNC and advising our speed is .83'.  At XA:17z ATC sent; 'You may want to read up on that. Resume normal speed means plus or minus mach .01 from cleared mach.'  We immediately changed speed to Mach .81 and replied; 'Roger speed now is .81 requesting M.83' (XA:18z). At XA:19z ATC sent 'Maintain .83M'. All communications were done via CPDLC. The rest of the flight was uneventful.  We disagree with the controller's interpretation of the 'Resume normal speed' clearance and request clarification from the company. Page 668 of the Jeppesen Airway Manual (Europe) says; 'If the aircraft then receives RESUME NORMAL SPEED (via CPDLC or Voice); the flight crew no longer needs to comply with a previously issued Mach. However; the flight crew shall advise ATC if; as the result of the RESUME NORMAL SPEED message; they intend to adjust their speed by plus or minus Mach 0.02 or more from their last assigned speed.'  Furthermore; in the operational example given on page 688 it says; '...message RESUME NORMAL SPEED will be sent.  The flight crew no longer needs to comply with a previously issued Mach. However; the flight crew shall advise ATC if; as the result of the RESUME NORMAL SPEED message; they intend to adjust their speed by plus or minus Mach 0.02 or more from their last assigned speed. In this case; with a previously assigned speed of .81; they must inform ATC if the flight either slows to M.79 or less or speeds up to M.83 or more.'  Finally; in the North America Jeppesen Airway Manual it says; ' When adherence to an assigned 'MACH' setting is no longer required; pilots will receive a controller-pilot data link communications (CPDLC) message to 'RESUME NORMAL SPEED;' at which point the flight crew can continue at their cost index. Refer to aeronautical information circular (AIC) 1/20 Operations Without an Assigned Fixed Speed (OWAFS) in the North Atlantic for more details.'  In looking at the ICAO NAT OPS Bulletin (2019_001); the text mimics what is published in the Jeppesen Airway Manual. In conclusion; I believe we were in full compliance with the 'Resume normal speed' clearance when we accelerated to M.83 and advised ATC but since the controller has a different understanding of the situation I would like to get clarification from the company.
Report_1_Synopsis: Medium Large Transport Captain received CPDLC speed clearance from Gander Control which created procedural confusion between ATC; Jeppesen manual; and company policy.

Report_1_Narrative: It was the Captain's leg on a return flight from ZZZ when we were given the ZZZZZ3 SID. We were given a standard take off clearance from Runway XXL (no heading; altitude; or fix to fly) and I; as the pilot monitoring; engaged the autopilot modes as directed. When I engaged the NAV mode; it did not arm FMS but instead HDG mode. After double-checking I correctly engaged NAV mode; we were still in HDG with the only white needle navigation being from ZZZZZ to ZZZZZ1 and then on the rest of the departure. Since we were still in HDG mode with what I remember was runway heading bugged; we were heading directly for the terrain off of the departure end of XXL. We received hasty instructions from ATC to turn left immediately to get away from the terrain; which we complied with. We were in VMC and could clearly see the terrain; which we had already climbed above when the instructions from ATC came through to start the immediate turn. We never received a GPWS terrain alert. Once established heading back to ZZZZZ on the departure; the Captain had disengaged and reengaged the NAV button to finally arm FMS mode. ATC then advised us to resume the departure and continue our assigned climb altitude to 17;000 feet. No further communications between us and ATC about what had happened. The rest of the flight went on normally and without incident. Really make sure on RNAV departures that when you select the NAV button that the FMS mode activates and if needed spin the heading bug to the headings provided on the charts to avoid conflicts like this.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier First Officer flying CRJ-900 aircraft reported flying toward terrain on departure.

Report_1_Narrative: The crew departed ZZZ on time after calling maintenance to reset a Rudder Trim Limiter ECAM malfunction. Pushback; start; taxi; takeoff and climb out were uneventful. Passing FL260 for a cruise altitude of FL270 the First Officer (Pilot Monitoring) identified a flashing oil quantity advisory reading and a low oil pressure indication on the #1 engine system display. Due to the aircraft's momentum and vertical rate of climb the Captain (Pilot Flying) elected to level off at FL270 as planned. Initially the zero oil quantity and low 60 PSI pressure indication were not accompanied by an ECAM message and system status indicated normal. Within a couple of minutes a series of intermittent ECAM cautions and warnings occurred leading to an engine shutdown condition. The amber ENG 1 OIL LO PR Caution illuminated first on the ECAM display. The crew responded by initiating the company non-normal checklist strategy. The Captain announced 'my aircraft' then the First Officer verified that the ECAM was not a Quick Action or ECAM exception item. The Captain elected to remain flying and also took control of the radio. It was a crew awareness only caution so the FO (First Officer) then checked the QRH for follow up items. This Caution does not direct the crew to adjust thrust settings. During this process the caution [message] cleared itself without any inputs from the crew but the zero oil quantity and 60 PSI indications remained. At this point the ECAM display was clear and system status indicated normal. Shortly thereafter the red ENG 1 LO PR warning illuminated on the ECAM display. This occurred intermittently 3 times and then cleared itself each time resulting in a normal system status display on the ECAM. Oil quantity remained at zero and pressure was now steady at 40 PSI on the system display. These intermittent ECAM warnings lasted for approximately 2-3 seconds and then cleared to a normal status for roughly the same amount of time. The next time the ECAM warning illuminated it remained steady and the crew followed the ENG 1 LO PR warning procedures and shutdown the engine. The crew notified Center and requested a radar vector descent to final for the engine out approach at ZZZ1. The non-normal indications initially occurred just prior to the ETP (equal time point) between ZZZ and ZZZ1. However by the time the ECAM directed engine shutdown the flight had progressed passed the ETP and was at a normal descent point for ZZZ1. Dispatch was called using the iPad crew phone and notified of the nature of the emergency and decision to land at ZZZ1. The flight attendants and passengers were briefed about the Precautionary Landing at ZZZ1 and the possibility of airport fire vehicles near the aircraft. After shutting down the engine and notifying ATC; the crew requested and was given a vector and descent direct to a left 10 NM base at ZZZ1. Descent and approach were very stable and normal. The Captain flew the descent and approach with both the autopilot and auto thrust on. Crew requested ARFF (airport rescue fire department) for the landing and cleared the runway for a brief inspection of the engine. On request of the crew the fire department followed the aircraft to the gate. Shutdown at the gate and passenger deplaning were normal. Note: ATC handling by ZZZ Center; ZZZ1 Approach and Tower were outstanding. Handoff from Tower to ARFF at ZZZ1 was seamless and well coordinated. Flight Attendant performance was also outstanding and the passengers remained well informed throughout the emergency. Although oil fault indications were somewhat intermittent and erratic the fact that multiple independent sensors indicated a problem caused the crew to shutdown the #1 engine when directed by the ENG LO PR Warning ECAM. After the flight; maintenance personnel initially reported normal engine oil quantity on a sight gauge even though the engine instrument remained at zero. Initially crew suspects a partial blockage or pump failure in the system without oil loss. The engine oil quantity and pressure indications were initially both alarming and confusing. As the adrenaline level increased for the crew due to the perception there would be an engine shutdown there was also a level of doubt that the indications were accurate. Low oil pressure on the engine instrument should be accompanied by a Low Pressure ECAM Caution or Warning. Why did the pressure remain steady in the amber range with zero on the quantity? This is an uncomfortable situation because our training does not address multiple oil failures without ECAM warnings. It puts the flight crew into one of those gray areas where a Captain is expected to make a decision based on the information he has on hand in a situation not covered in training. The natural instinct of a pilot is to shutdown an engine before complete oil loss to prevent a catastrophic failure. In this occurrence engine indications identified a problem well in advance of ECAM warnings. Yet crew training and aircraft procedures generally do not address engine shutdown without ECAM warning checklist direction. Should crews be given shutdown discretion in the absence of ECAM warnings and checklist? In this situation the Captain elected to continue as the Pilot Flying while the crew worked through the non-normal checklist strategy. Even though most aspects of company's non-normal strategy were performed correctly the overall pace and structure were hampered by the Captain continuing to fly. In this case the checklist strategy would have been better managed if the Captain had delegated flying to the FO. For example; when the ECAM directed the 'Engine Master Switch-Off' both pilots confirmed it was the #1 engine but the Captain positioned it to off. Procedure dictates that the non-flying pilot position the switch to off.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Captain flying A321 aircraft reports low engine oil pressure inflight.

Report_1_Narrative: Captain came out to brief FAs. Told us [the] FO was not going to wear [a] mask in cockpit; anyone [have] a problem. I said I did. And would prefer to have him wearing [one] when we [are] in the cockpit. Captain continued to look for another FA to go in the cockpit.My take: If there is no courtesy to me or any of my flight attendants; why should we have to go in the cockpit? When I said I had a problem; he should have backed off. Yet; now he was telling us; he had no problem wearing a mask; but the FO had. Then; later; [the] FO comes out of cockpit not wearing a mask; and proceeds to talk (very close) to a FA standing near him; with no mask on. I reminded him; to go out; he had to wear a mask. He put his mask on.I have a problem with a pilot who does not care about our well being. Our health; our ability to work and stay healthy to support our families; and all that comes with us exposing ourselves. It is not acceptable and it should not be tolerated to continue to ask for a FA to go inside the cockpit when the FO was not going to wear a mask.Today; we had an XX:59 minutes duty day + hour before and hour after wearing a mask.  The least he could do is wearing a mask for 5 minutes when one of us goes inside to relieve them. It's intimidating; it's a disregard of others and disrespectful to all FA group; as if we do not matter.This is not company policy and someone should speak with him about caring for his coworkers; or anyone for that matter. Because I bet he is not wearing a mask where he goes. Just unacceptable. I have a problem with a pilot refusing to wear a mask when a FA goes in the cockpit; and whoever is reading this; should too.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Attendant reported refusing to be in the cockpit to provide break relief because the First Officer would not wear a face mask. The Flight Attendant reported that the Captain asked for other flight attendants who would be willing to provide break relief under those conditions.

As per MM 71-00-00-800-804-f00; [it] will require boroscope due to temp going into area C of chart. I did not notice that the APU bleed was left on and I did not pull ignition circuit breakers. [I] had 2 techs clearing around engine.

Report_1_Narrative: With the COVID-19 pandemic; technicians are concerned about proper safety with the removal and disposal of HEPA filters. The procedures are consistent with all of company fleet types; including both Manufacturer X and Manufacturer Y aircraft types. All of the AMM procedures include a list of the necessary PPE as well as Disposal requirements.DescriptionSTD-XXXX Coveralls - Hooded STD-XXXY Goggles - Safety; Non Vented STD-XXXZ Respirator - Particulate; meets NIOSH 42 CFR 84 Class N95; N99; N100 The question here is; what qualifications (if any) are needed and where can we find the company policy. The main item is the use of the respirator Class N95 as is called out for in the AMM procedures [for several aircraft types].The second question concerns proper disposal of used HEPA filters and used PPE. Obey the airline policy; local health department and law enforcement regulations when you discard this material. Obey these instructions to prevent injuries to personnel.

Report_1_Narrative: I was working enroute Center for two hours and 20 minutes with heavy to moderate traffic without the help of a D side. Sector XX.  Normally this would not be a problem but during the coronavirus situation there is a skeleton crew of controllers in the area and we are short staffed. Training in the area was also underway.  Also; we had no management in the area acting as a Supervisor.  We had a Controller-in-Charge position staffed by one of the FPLs in the area.  After working 2 hours of heavy traffic I began to tire and was transposing callsigns and missing check-ins.I asked one of the controllers working another less busy sector to swap positions with me.  I just could not work that volume of traffic anymore. The Controller was kind enough to swap with me. I was mentally drained. The culture does not generally allow for complaints of this type.  After my break (which I am on right now) I will do it all over again.  If this continues the risk grows of a Controller contributing to error within the airspace. This is normally not necessary.  This is a very busy time of the year and it is unbelievable that the FAA would allow this lack of staffing and allow the normal flow of traffic.  This situation routinely happens at ZZZ (Center) in Area X; I am not sure about the other areas; but I have heard similar things from other controllers.
Report_1_Synopsis: Center Controller reported becoming fatigued due to working heavy traffic for an extended period of time and cited low staffing levels as a contributing factor.

Report_1_Narrative: Our aircraft had just landed at ZZZ when a single-seat aerobatic biplane began to do low-level aerobatics (hammerheads and rolls) opposite normal traffic in the pattern. A Cessna 150 entered left downwind Runway XX; well spaced from the biplane; which was in a modified right downwind/base; when the biplane crossed the field and entered a midfield left crosswind-to-downwind behind the 150. The 150 continued downwind; turned base then final; when the biplane banked hard from downwind directly to final abeam the 150 and approximately 25 feet above. The 150 initiated a go-around and the biplane did the same; nearly colliding which each other. The 150 eventually landed on a second go-around while the biplane continued to execute high speed low passes over the runway at about 50 feet AGL. The problem likely arose because the biplane; which was NORDO; was engaged in a low level acrobatics display for a group of onlookers in the tiedown area and was not scanning for conflicting traffic. The 150 likely saw the biplane traffic near the airport; but the biplane's erratic behavior and rapid altitude and direction changes would have complicated efforts to maintain separation. The conflict could have been resolved if the biplane pilot refrained from low-level aerobatics in the vicinity of the traffic pattern; was visually scanning for traffic; and vacated the traffic pattern area when other traffic was inbound to land.
Report_1_Synopsis: Pilot observer reported a near mid air collision between two airplanes in airport traffic pattern.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Communication Breakdown; Physiological - Other; Situational Awareness; Time Pressure
Report_1_Narrative: During a Medevac flight to ZZZ1 from ZZZ I initiated an approach with less than the required RVR to do so. Our return flight had been delayed by 4 hours because the patient was very difficult to stabilize. I had checked the weather before departing ZZZ and it was above the minimums that were required for the approach. While enroute to ZZZ1; I acquired the ATIS and found that visibility had decreased to 1/8 mile. The situation at the two nearest options that would allow me to get the hospital was the same. I chose to go to ZZZ2 because it was near enough that we could get the patient to ZZZ1 and the automated weather was well above minimums for the approach. After two attempts at landing in ZZZ2; I realized that the weather was worse than reported there. While I had been maneuvering I was monitoring the conditions at ZZZ1 and they seemed to vary minute by minute. I decided to divert to ZZZ3 since the medic told me we had no time to waste with another approach as he was running low on medication for the patient. When I requested the change to ZZZ3; the controller asked me if I wanted to attempt an approach to ZZZ1. After two go around and working on my fifth backup plan; I was desperate to get the plane on the ground and the patient to the hospital. I accepted the clearance and started the approach. I saw the runway lights at 400 ft AGL and the runway at 200 ft AGL. I decided to land. As I was rolling out I noticed that ground visibility was very low and I realized I had landed with less than the required 2400 RVR that I was supposed to have. Contributing factors: I had the weather and forecast from when I left ZZZ1 6 hours prior printed out. I should have reviewed the forecast more thoroughly rather than just checking present conditions before returning to ZZZ1. I did not realize that night that I was getting sick. During the climb out I was queasy and I attributed this to a lack of horizon at night. The next day I had full flu like symptoms that precluded me from working. What I would do differently: I should have asked the medical team where they wanted to go if ZZZ1 did not work out. If I had that we could have all been prepared to go to a different hospital if the ZZZ1 airport did not work.
Report_1_Synopsis: Captain flying a C90 aircraft reported landing below minimums.
