They provided the partition on the customer service side and failed to do the one on the employee's side which as a result expose the sitting employee to more virus.
Report_1_Synopsis: Ground employee wrote that maintenance failed to complete a barrier between employees to help prevent the spread of COVID-19.

Report_1_Narrative: During cruise flight at 40;000 ft. in the vicinity of ZZZ we began to smell an electrical type smoke. Moments later the A Flight Attendant called the flight deck to report smoke in the cabin. Simultaneously the master caution came on for ELEC and the TRU (transformer rectifier unit) light illuminated on the overhead panel. I as Captain was Pilot Flying and initially transferred control to the First Officer for me to chase down the TRU checklist. I accomplished the checklist; noting that approach mode with the flight directors would be unavailable... At this point the smoke was getting thicker; and we decided to accomplish the smoke/fire/fumes memory items. After communications were established we notified ATC and asked for a left turn direct to ZZZ1. We considered ZZZ2 but figured in terms of time we were about the same distance away due to our altitude; and that with a straight line to ZZZ1 we would be able to keep both our heads in the game running through checklists and monitoring the aircraft vs a circling descent into mountainous terrain. It was at this point that the First Officer made me aware that all his flight and NAV displays had failed. He thus transferred control back to me as the Pilot Flying and he took over the smoke/fire/fumes checklist in the QRH.ATC told us to expect one of the north runways into ZZZ1; but we told them we wanted [Runway] XXL as we were just on the north side of the airport so that was closest. We requested direct ZZZZZ on the ILS to backup our visual approach; and used our emergency authority to proceed at about 320 knots in order to expedite landing. At this point the First Officer discontinued the smoke/fire/fumes checklist at step 20; having noted at step 16 that we should not delay landing in order to complete the checklist. We then briefed and ran a descent and approach checklist. I asked the First Officer to call ZZZ1 OPS to let them know we were coming and for them to relay the info to Dispatch but at that point the #2 radio and comm panel had failed and the ACARS was no comm. It was with the master caution recall on the descent checklist that we realized how many issues were piling up beyond the TRU and smoke. Looking up after being prompted by the recall we saw a solid portion of the overhead panel was lit.With the glare from the smoke and setting sun we were only able to pickup the airport just outside of ZZZZZ. I disconnected the autopilot and proceeded to fly a visual approach backed up by the LNAV track for the ILS XXL. I quickly realized that electric trim was inoperative and proceeded to trim manually. With the landing checklist we also discovered that the auto speed brake would not arm; so I asked the First Officer to back me up for the manual deployment. We landed in the touchdown zone and exited at gate without incident where CFR was waiting. We stopped in order for CFR (crash fire rescue) to do a quick external inspection. As it was pretty quickly obvious the smoke was inside the aircraft and they weren't seeing anything outside; we asked them to get out of the way so we could get to a gate and let our passengers stop breathing fumes.After shutting down the engines the APU appeared to be supplying only partial power and the ground call horn sounded constantly. Due to this issue the cabin was already dark; and knowing we were dealing with an electrical issue we opted to remove all power from the aircraft and performed the secure checklist. Then we took a breath and asked each other (at the same time) 'well; how'd that go'. Of course sitting on the ground I feel like I can armchair quarterback the situation and nitpick some of the decisions; but overall I feel like we handled the situation well. We had good crew coordination given the circumstances (on O2) and the First Officer did a great job of running the checklists as well as keeping an eye on my flying once we had to transfer controls back to me. It did feel weird turning away from ZZZ2 since it was practically right below us; but I still feel like it was the correct decision given the circumstances and the amount of time it would take to descend; and how much of a distraction an orbiting descent into mountainous terrain would be while trying to deal with smoke.One thing I would do differently has to do with after the situation was over on the ground. I ended up talking with the Chief Pilot; then the firefighters; then the mechanic outside the aircraft on the ramp. By the time I got back inside I couldn't find the flight attendants to debrief and see how they were doing. Upon opening the flight deck door the A had told me that they were all fine; but I would have liked to make sure and check in with them individually. I called scheduling to try and get them to transfer me in order to at least talk with them on the phone; who then transferred me to the scheduling desk where I waited on hold until it disconnected. I still hope to talk with them at some point to learn how things went in the back and find out what we could have done better for them.

Moments later the A Flight Attendant called the flight deck to report smoke in the cabin. Simultaneously; the Master Caution came on for ELEC and the TR (transformer rectifier unit) light illuminated on the overhead panel. The Captain was Pilot Flying; and initially transferred control to me; in order to run the TR checklist. It was at this point that I noticed all my flight/nav displays and radios had failed as well as ACARS No Comm" being displayed on the FMS.  I immediately notified the Captain and said that it might be better if he flew.  He agreed and took control back as the Pilot Flying and I took over the smoke/fire/ fumes checklist in the QRH. A short time later I advised the Captain that I'd like to discontinue the smoke/fire/fumes checklist at step 20 since I had reached a decision point in the QRH; and it appeared I would most likely be heads down for almost all of the rest of the flight into ZZZ1 with this exhaustive checklist; and not be able to properly; and safely perform my duties as a PM.  I came to this decision based on the fact that step 16 states we should not delay landing in order to complete the checklist. He agreed.  We then briefed and ran a descent and approach checklist. The Captain asked me to call ZZZ1 OPS to let them know we were coming and for them to relay the info to Dispatch; but I reminded him that the #2 radio and comm panel had failed and the ACARS was no comm. It was with the Master Caution recall on the descent checklist that we realized how many issues were piling up beyond the TR and smoke. Looking up after being prompted by the recall we saw a solid portion of the overhead panel was lit. With the glare from the smoke and setting sun we were only able to pickup the airport just outside of ZZZZZ. The Captain disconnected the autopilot and proceeded to fly a visual approach backed up by the LNAV track for the ILS 17L. I noticed during the approach that the Captain had to trim manually; which led me to believe that we had obviously lost electrical control.  With the landing checklist we also discovered that the auto speed brake would not arm; so the Captain asked me to back him up for the manual deployment. We landed in the touchdown zone and exited at gate without incident; where CFR (crash fire rescue) was waiting. We stopped in order for CFR to do a quick external inspection. As it was pretty quickly obvious the smoke was inside the aircraft and they weren't seeing anything outside; we asked them to get out of the way so we could get to a gate and let our pax stop breathing fumes. After shutting down the engines the APU appeared to be supplying only partial power and the ground call horn sounded constantly. Due to this issue the cabin was already dark; and knowing we were dealing with an electrical issue we opted to remove all power from the aircraft and performed the secure checklist. A short time later; CFR  and a maintenance person were able to find the cause of the TR failure and pulled one of the TR boxes out of the E&E bay (electronics & engineering); which showed significant electrical fire damage. Lesson learned: maintain awareness of the type of emergency and aircraft state; compared to how long QRH steps could take you out of the critical Pilot Monitoring role. This checklist taught me to bring my head back up and get a grasp on the fact that we were in a rapid descent; over mountains; with half of our displays and comms out and I was only half aware of some of the radio calls and aircraft state. This was more concerning to me."
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier flight crew reported an uneventful divert due to a fume event during cruise.

Report_1_Narrative: I entered the ramp from Taxiway E5; established on the center line. Traveling parallel; same direction; in the designated vehicle lane to my left was a large fuel truck. Rate of travel was approximately 10 - 15 mph with my aircraft overtaking. As I approached where the vehicle lane has a T intersection and runs across the taxi line to the parking ramp; the fuel truck took the turn without stopping. As soon as I noticed the vehicle taking the turn; I immediately initiated a stop with foot brake and full engine reverse. The driver noticed my aircraft as soon as he made the turn and also stopped. The fuel truck then reversed to provide wing tip clearance so I could proceed. If I had taken evasive action that involved any turn away from the fuel truck; it is likely that the left wing tip would have been close to; if not impacting the front area of the fuel truck. There was little to no margin. After parking and securing the aircraft; I did talk to the fuel truck driver. He admitted that he did not see my aircraft and that the large fuel trucks have a blind spot on the right hand side; which is where I was in relationship to him. However; he acknowledged that he did not stop to clear the turn. This vehicle roadway and subsequent T intersection does not have any mandatory vehicle stop markings before traveling across the ramp center line. It may be suggested to add markings to reinforce the practice of stopping to clear the turn. I would also suggest that [the truck operator] add larger mirrors or combination of mirrors to address the blind spot issue if they haven't already. Finally; this underscores the necessity of reasonably slow travel speeds for both aircraft and service vehicles for ALL operators. Had either fuel truck or my aircraft been traveling faster; which has been observed in the past; it is very likely a collision would have occurred despite the evasive action taken.
Report_1_Synopsis: Small Transport pilot reported a near-collision with a fuel truck while taxiing at PDX.

Report_1_Narrative: Lost SA partially on arrival. Approach gave us a 240 heading and asked us to call the field. I had selected managed speed out of 10;000 and was configuring. Extended gear descending through 9;200; so we could continue to slow. Aircraft wasn't slowing. Captured LOC; but overshot a bit. Glide slope didn't capture. Once I saw the PAPI I saw I was low I leveled; continued to configure and slow. Leveled at 1;000 feet AFL momentarily to rejoin glideslope and ensure configured for stabilized approach. Had runway in sight the whole time after turning final; met gates at 1;000 feet AFL and 500 feet AFL; but felt behind and should have gone around. Maintenance delay; unfamiliar airport; late runway change; long day (nearly 9 hours of flying); no approach control (ZZZ Center handling approach due to COVID outage).I should have asked for vectors onto the approach rather than accepting visual. ZZZ is surrounded by high terrain; I was unfamiliar even though I felt I had prepared carefully; vectors would have provided a less dynamic environment. Also; if I were in a similar situation; I would go-around and ensure I don't press when I feel at all like I have lost SA. Also; the high altitude made slowing the aircraft down more difficult. I didn't include that in my briefing. I know better; but after the long day I failed to consider that as a factor.
Report_2_Narrative: ATC gave us a 90 degree plus vector for Runway XXR and asked us to call the field. We had it in sight and were cleared for the visual. We were above the glideslope; with flaps 1; put the gear down to slow down; and used managed speed. The approach was armed; caught; but overshot the localizer because the aircraft wasn't slowing down. The glideslope didn't capture and we were then low on the glide slope as we passed through it from above. We leveled off; slowed down and finished configuring. We were within stable criteria at 1;000 and 500 feet; but it was a messy approach.Cause - Long duty day; extended due to maintenance. Bad vector from ATC and pressure to go visual. Approach was closed and Denver center was handling approach.Don't be pressured into accepting a visual at night with mountainous terrain. Go-around if an approach is feeling uncomfortable. Slow down earlier when at a higher elevation airport.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported an unstabilized approach into an unfamiliar airport.

Report_1_Narrative: The airplane was released with Auxiliary Power Unit (APU) deferred; thus required air-cart start procedures in the gate.  Preflight; airplane setup; briefings; checklists; crew duties; paperwork; ground interactions were all normal; and (Minimum Equipment Lists) MELs were complied with.  Normal air-cart start and subsequent pushback were all normal.  After clearing the ground crew off the headset; the Right; Number 1 Inner Tank Fuel Pump faulted.  We complied with the instruction to turn off the pump; and contacted Ramp Control and Maintenance on separate radios.The Captain worked with Maintenance while the First Officer worked with Ramp Control.   The Captain discussed the need to do a deferral and the First Officer received instructions for us to taxi to spot for off the gate maintenance; or something to that effect.  Neither of us had ever heard of such a thing; and I told the First Officer to say; 'No; we're not doing that.'I called on my cell phone and told them about the situation; and we began discussing the need for a maintenance deferral; and whether or not we had enough fuel under the circumstances.  I suggested we look at deleting the alternate from the flight plan if it would be legal to do so.  The Dispatcher said he'd begin working on it.  It was about this time that Maintenance suggested we go to a designated spot for hot refueling.  I again said we wouldn't do that and that the best plan should we need fuel would be to just taxi into the gate we just left; shut down; get fuel; and have Maintenance sign off the fuel pump.  Maintenance told me that that wasn't the best idea because if we did that we'd have a long delay and have to do the paperwork over again.  I called Dispatch back and he said there was no way we could just do the deferral and that we'd need to go back for fuel; and I said fine we will do that.  As a note; Dispatch told me that he had also never heard of hot refueling. At that point I told Maintenance what we were going to go back into the gate.  Maintenance proceeded to explain that the hot refuel was done all the time and that the FAA and that Company Safety had approved of the procedure.  He was adamant that the hot fuel was the best way to proceed.  Ramp also confirmed the procedure; so after discussing it as a crew; we agreed it sounded like a legitimate request; and we agreed to go to the spot and proceed with the fueling there.  When we arrived; we were stopped by a pickup truck pulling close to the airplane that made me stop.  There was no further guidance from Ramp; other than to ask us to pull the tail clear of a taxi lane.  A second vehicle with built-in airstairs arrived at the airplane.  He began giving us hand signals that made little sense; and eventually hooked up to the intercom system; and asked us to shut down the engines.  I suggested that was not a very good idea and that we could have done that in the gate and that we were there for hot fueling.  He then said to just shut down engine number two and to open the door so he could give us a fuel slip.  I asked the First Officer to do an after landing flow to make sure we were caught up; and then to open the door after disarming the slides.We received fuel; a fuel slip; coordinated hand signals; ran appropriate checklists; did a cross-bleed start to get engine number two back on line; accomplished the after-start checklist; and taxied via Ramp's instructions.  The First Officer made adjustments to the aircraft performance data and we ran a new performance briefing; noting a two knot increase in the new V speeds; and feeling comfortable that we had returned to safely normal operations. We proceeded to taxi and takeoff with normal operations.At cruise we received a message from Dispatch that we didn't do a new weight and balance.  He asked for our fuel onboard; we sent them. Either an ill conceived procedure or a lack of adequate resources for flight crews to safely conduct this procedure.The Pilot in Command shouldhave stuck to his first decision.  And from a more proactive approach; a checklist should be developed and added to the QRH.  The maintenance deferral flowchart should mention the need to revisit weight and balance. requirements and anything else we might have missed.  Additionally; I would highly encourage a module during simulator training that runs crews through this exercise and the use of new flow charts and a checklist.
Report_2_Narrative: The flight blocked out and then had a maintenance problem.  Right Inner Tank Inoperative. This not a flagged item; so the decision was made to put the aircraft in a maintenance area on the ramp. The Minimum Equipment List (MEL) requires 8800 lb penalty fuel and adjust fuel for FL200. Fueling is allowed in the maintenance area.  Since it was not a block turnback; a new release was not required. We did the prescribed procedure with Maintenance and I then sent a mini flight plan showing the new numbers with fuel penalties. After fueling was finished; I sent an ACARS asking for the new fuel breakdown so the hub could send a new Weight and Balance. However; the plane had already blocked and departed without an up to date to the weight and balance. I informed the Duty Officer and then tried to send the new weight and balance. The new weight and balance never showed up in the crew's ACARS messages although it showed up in the playback screen in ACARS. So I copied and pasted and sent the information; but did not notice that the information in the weight and balance that the hub sent was the information from the original block out. Even though we had received the correct fuel breakdown from the crew enroute.  The flight landed at its destination and I talked with the crew and passed them on to the Duty Officer. The initial problem was caused by crew departing without an updated weight and balance. I suggest following procedures when an aircraft blocks back to a maintenance area
Report_1_Synopsis: A Flight Crew and Dispatcher reported the flight departed with incorrect weight and balance information due to being distracted after issues refueling on the ramp with an engine running. The flight crew was not familiar with refueling with an engine running and could not find any guidance or published procedures that allowed this.

Report_1_Narrative: While crew was preparing for departure in the aircraft; an ACARS was sent from Captain to Dispatch notifying that there was dry ice in the lower forward compartment and this was not reflected on the release. I was not notified by the ramp agent that there was any dry ice on the aircraft. I calculated the required overburn and forwarded the information to the crew via ACARS. I phoned Ramp Agent to inform that I was not notified of any dry ice in the lower compartment of this 777 aircraft. The response was [the] agent not aware that Dispatch should be notified of dry ice in the lower compartments. Agent assumed a very defensive tone and I terminated the call. I explained the situation briefly to Flight Coordination. The response was that agent was never aware of any requirement to inform Dispatch in this situation also. My concern is that these two ramp agents are relatively senior company ramp agents and neither one claims to be aware of this essential procedure.  The cause was two senior ZZZ ramp agents claim to be completely unaware of an essential procedure to notify Dispatch in the event there is dry ice in the lower compartments of a 777 aircraft. I suggest remedial training for any or all ZZZ ramp agents to familiarize them with their required function in this instance.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Dispatcher reported a communications breakdown between Dispatch and Ramp personnel regarding Dispatch notification of DG handling.

Report_1_Narrative: It was night. We were on the ground taxiing to the runway.  We had a jumpseater in the cockpit as well. We were cleared across one runway and to taxi to our assigned runway. After crossing I called for the Before Takeoff checklist. The First Officer proceeded to accomplish those duties which included contacting the cabin crew. While the First Officer was communicating with the cabin we were cleared for take off.  When the First Officer was done with the cabin notification I informed him that we were cleared for takeoff. The First Officer ran the checklist. As I was taxiing to the runway there were a lot of lights due to the proximity [of] two runways beginning in about the same location. It was a little confusing and I verbalized my confusion by saying 'Is this the right runway' meaning the one I was about to taxi onto. The jumpseater piped in and said it was a different runway. I was referring to the one in front of me he was referring to the one to my left. So; I proceeded forward crossing the runway we were cleared to takeoff on looking for the entrance to my runway and stopped on the other side realizing I had been on the correct runway. Tower saw what happened and canceled our takeoff clearance. We were in fact on the correct runway; I just wasn't sure that we were. We never lined up for takeoff on any runway. We just proceeded across the one [we] were cleared to take off on. The cause was partly due to my limited use of that runway in the past and especially at night. There was a degree of unfamiliarity with that runway. Another factor was my accepting a takeoff clearance before the First Officer was back fully engaged with me and feeling a little rushed. On my part; I could have declined takeoff clearance until we were finished with the 'before takeoff checklist' and both of us of us could have been fully engaged in only taxiing.
Report_2_Narrative: Pilots were not familiar with the runway configuration at night. Confused assigned runway with an intersecting runway.  We taxied through approach end after being cleared for takeoff. Tower said to cancel takeoff clearance and turn around taxi back and hold short of the runway. We complied. We reviewed our taxi charts and realized our error. The Captain and First Officer were not familiar with the runway configuration at night. From our perspective it seemed the runway lights to 35 may have been turned down and due to that it could've been mistaken for 32 as we expected the lights for an active runway to be brighter. It would have also been helpful to have moving maps on taxi charts. We would have realized immediately where we were. As it stood the lights being turned down confused the unfamiliar crew into thinking they had to taxi further to Runway 35. From our perspective it seemed the runway lights may have been turned down and due to that we could've been mistaken our runway as we expected the lights for an active runway to be brighter. It would have also been helpful to have moving maps on taxi charts. We would have realized immediately where we were. As it stood the lights being turned down confused the unfamiliar crew into thinking they had to taxi further to the runway.
Report_1_Synopsis: An Air Carrier crew reported they taxied across the assigned runway for takeoff due to confusion about the runway configuration at night.

Report_1_Narrative: Approximately 3 hours into our flight from ZZZZ-ZZZ; Flight Attendant X told me that his daughter had tested positive for COVID-19 the previous day.   Flight Attendant X said that he contacted Airline when he learned of his child's positive test result and was advised to continue with his pairing; despite his immediate family member receiving a positive COVID test result.  It made me extremely uncomfortable to hear that Flight Attendant X was directly exposed and that he chose to continue to work; possibly endangering the health and safety of others.   Flight Attendant X also mentioned that he is a [Medical Professional] and exposed to COVID positive patients regularly at his other job.  While Flight Attendant X may not have received the support from the company in line with our responsibility to keep one another as safe as possible during the global pandemic; common sense and personal ethos would dictate that one would remove them self from flying until they had a negative test result and quarantine period of 14 days.  I contacted ZZZ Supervisor upon landing in ZZZ and expressed my concerns.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Attendant reported concerns with another Flight Attendant showing up for work after a family member had tested positive for COVID-19 the day before.

Report_1_Narrative: Passenger X boarded the aircraft and proceeded to self-upgrade himself to a better seat.  When he was asked about this by another FA; he held his ground.  Apparently; out in the gate area; he was quite belligerent.  So; a member of the ground staff had to come on board and move him back to his assigned seat.  He said that he was fine.  After takeoff and constantly throughout the flight; I had to ask him to put his mask on.  It happened several times.  He was not happy that I kept asking him.  I guess he felt that he was exempt from the wearing of masks.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Attendant reported a passenger was not compliant with face mask policy and also moved to a better seat without asking FAs.

Report_1_Narrative: A party of 3 came on just as we were to close the flight; the agents stated he was exempt from wearing a mask; to which we questioned what he was told he was going to be able to do for the flight; which was not to wear his mask.  The crew on the whole questioned what the Agent was saying; the Purser approached the Captain who said he would ask ZZZ operations; in the meantime the Lead came down and agreed with the crew that there were no exceptions to our mask policy; with debate and talking to the passenger we all looked to find it in black and white; while waiting for ZZZ to call back; the gate agents closed the door and pulled the jet bridge.  The Purser explained to the passenger from [seat number] that he and one of his guests could move to seat area X to keep them separated from the majority of our guests; during the flight I have to say I had to tell his friend to keep his mask on more; I chatted to them prior to landing and informed them they would have to wear their mask for their trip itinerary as there were no exceptions...that they had been miss informed prior to our flight.  They actually seemed nice.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Attendant reported having to explain to a passenger that there were no exemptions to having to wear a face mask.  Passenger and two others traveling with him were not compliant during the flight.

Report_1_Narrative: I was [the] Purser on Aircraft X. When we boarded I noticed the entire phone was missing from XLR Jumpseat. The cockpit also informed me it was missing and that it was okay to go. I said that used to be a 'no go' item. I have no way of notifying the cockpit if there was any emergency- be it evacuation; a threat level; a medical emergency; etc. I asked if there was another plane that we could take. I notified the system that we were checking within maintenance on an issue before we board. We still had 15 minutes left to board. I was told that I was to refer to the Flight Attendant Manual regarding other means of communicating. I'm not sure if you've worn a mask and spoken through a megaphone; but that's not really a reliable means of communication with a mask on. And it still does not allow me to communicate with the cockpit. We were on a type X aircraft where the other FAs are backwards facing and would not know if a situation were to arise up front. We were also advised that it was to be a bumpy flight and we might need to remain seated for the duration of the flight. An in-flight Supervisor met the aircraft. Captain said he would refuse the aircraft if I was uncomfortable. I said that decision should not solely rely on me. However; this was the second flight in a row where the forward intercom was broken. This one happened to be completely missing a phone. The one prior was hanging off a screw. A Mechanic also came up during boarding to see what the problem was. I said this should be a 'no go' item referring to the missing phone. He said he deferred it that morning and that the part was awaiting the aircraft in ZZZ. So the aircraft had flown two previous legs before mine in this condition. I believe that a PA INOP is 'not' a no-go. A missing intercom should be a no-go item.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Attendant reported the phone by a jumpseat was missing and requested the aircraft be swapped due possible communication issues in case of an emergency.

Report_1_Narrative: Two passengers; traveling together; in seats; X1 and X2; were wearing non-compliant masks. FA C noticed the non-complaint masks in main cabin when I was beginning the safety announcement. From the front of plane; I could see the couple arguing with FA C and refusing to put the company provided masks that Flight Attendant was offering. I approached passengers; with FA C still present; and asked them to wear the compliant masks; and they initially refused me as well. I then asked them to make a decision to wear the compliant masks; or we would be required to return the plane to the gate. They complied. We took off. Once at cruise phase; the gentleman in X1 stopped me and started to engage me as to how he has been allowed to wear those masks on previous flights and that they were safer masks. I responded that he could reach out to customer care and write to the FAA about the masks they were wearing.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Attendant reported two passengers traveling together were wearing non-compliant face masks and initially refused to wear company supplied compliant face masks.

Report_1_Narrative: Bus overcrowding every day. The lack of buses and social distance is not followed.  We have told the company numerous of times regarding to inability to social distance. Their response is 'do not take the bus; wait for the other bus.'
Report_1_Synopsis: Technician reported social distancing concerns in overcrowded buses.

Report_1_Narrative: What happened: Aircraft Y was given a take off clearance for a runway that was occupied by a helicopter that had landed on the opposite end and was awaiting taxi instructions.What led to this:  The helicopter was coming in from the east and requested to land on the western side of the airport.  The active runways at the time were south to north (XXL and XXR).  The Tower cleared the helicopter to land on the numbers of an inactive runway XY; which would keep the helicopter on the eastern side of the airport; away from the flow of fixed wing traffic. About 5 minutes elapsed between the time the helicopter landed and Aircraft Y flew over the helicopter.During that time I believe the Controller may have been distracted by pattern traffic; Aircraft Z arrival (this was a factor prior to the helicopter landing which resulted in the controller deciding to keep the helicopter on the eastern side of the airport); a change in Aircraft Y IFR clearance; and by a pilot of an airplane who mistakenly made a final approach to the wrong parallel runway.Starting from the point at which the helicopter lands; the following exchanges were heard.Aircraft A was cleared for touch and go #2 behind Aircraft Z for runway XXL.Aircraft B was cleared to Land runway XXR.A few seconds after Aircraft B acknowledged the landing clearance the tower issue a taxi instruction to the airborne Aircraft B 'hold short of runway XXR I am going to have a departure off runway XZ.'Aircraft B responded 'I am in the air.'The tower replied 'Disregard; Land and hold short of runway XZ; land and hold short of runway XZ.'Aircraft B responded that this was their intention and would be parking in an area that would not put them at risk of crossing into runway XZ.The tower approved a request to taxi back to parking after Aircraft B completed a 180 degree turn on the runway after landing.30 seconds later the tower controller said to Aircraft B; 'Disregard the land and hold short clearance. I won't have that departure.  He will be holding in place; though.'The tower instructed Aircraft Y to line up and wait on runway XZ.The 737 had already landed on XXL and the tower cleared a Cessna for takeoff runway XXL.20 seconds later Aircraft B realized he was about to land on top of Aircraft A who had just been cleared for takeoff and asked the tower if he should go around.  There was no response.  Aircraft B hailed the tower again.  I observed Aircraft B descend below 100 ft AGL before deciding to go around.  40 seconds elapsed between the 1st and 3rd time Aircraft B called the tower.The tower gave the departing Aircraft A; a mixed up call starting with 'line up and- cancel take off- cleared for takeoff runway XXL'The tower then gave Aircraft B instructions to remain in the upwind; he would give him a crosswind instruction to follow.Aircraft B apologized for lining up to land on the wrong runway.As soon as the frequency congestion allowed; knowing there was a jet on the opposite side of my runway; I made a call 'Tower; Helicopter (call-sign) holding position on the numbers of [Runway] XY ready to taxi to (name of ramp)'.  The call was not acknowledged and 55 seconds later an amended departure clearance; combined with a takeoff clearance; was given to the waiting Aircraft Y.   I did not hear the departure clearance and Aircraft Y began racing towards us.  Ironically; I may have turned to my student and said to keep an eye on Aircraft Y.  As it rushed overhead I made an aggressive maneuver off of the numbers and onto the closest available vacant spot beyond the runway safety area.Previous experiences at this airport have made it clear when a helicopter accepts a landing clearance to a spot; taxiway; intersection; or helipad; they are expected to remain there until given a clearance to taxi.  Quite often the controllers will vector an arriving helicopter far around the approach or departure center lines of the active runways and restrict them to altitudes below 600 MSL instead of accommodating a flight path crossing the active runways at a higher safe altitude. Less often are we allowed to land as in the case above in a place safely away from the departing/arriving aircraft; and in a position where we can easily air taxi at a moment's notice.  A helicopter is highly maneuverable and this aspect should be used to the utmost advantage when minimizing delays to arriving or departing airplanes.  As mentioned earlier the helicopter's arrival was prior to Aircraft Z checking in with the tower.  There was Aircraft A on a half-mile final to runway XXL ahead of Aircraft Z.  With several miles of spacing between Aircraft Z and Aircraft A; the tower began to ask the helicopter to pass behind the landing Aircraft A.  We accepted.  The tower immediately reversed their decision due to Aircraft Z scheduled arrival and cleared us to land on the numbers of [Runway] XY with the restriction 'remain north of XX'. We accepted the clearance to land.  It is very likely that a helicopter crossing the approach end of XXL shortly after the landing Aircraft A would have had little to no effect on any of the other present arriving or departing aircraft.
Report_1_Synopsis: Helicopter pilot reported that after landing; another aircraft was cleared for takeoff from the opposite end of the same runway; resulting in the helicopter taking evasive action. Pilot reported that several other aircraft and confusing ATC radio communications were part of the overall situation.

Report_1_Narrative: On date I was conducting training in an R22 Helicopter departing out of ZZZ at XA:45 local time to ZZZ1. Winds were predominantly out of the west at around 10 kts and we joined left closed traffic for RWY 26 at ZZZ1. There was high training volume and I estimate 7 aircraft were on the ground waiting to depart or actively in the Right Closed Traffic for RWY XX plus our Helicopter. At around XB:10 local time a Jet taxied to the active with no Radio (or no radio communication was made) as we were on a left downwind for [Runway] XX. Local pilots made calls on the radio so all would be aware of his departure and be vigilant/use caution. The jet took off without incident and departed to the North. As pilots worked together to sequence traffic we made our base and final leg before again departing XX to rejoin left closed traffic. At approximately XB:15 local time on the upwind of XX roughly 300ft AGL without warning the jet made a low pass on runway XY at very high speed. I would estimate the pilot was 300ft off our starboard side and about 100ft below our current altitude. I was able to track his flight after the incident to find his Ground Speed was in excess of 330mph. The Jet than proceeded back out to the North again and ended up circling to land on RWY XY this time to a full stop. (The following is my personal opinion) I believe this pilot does not have any remorse for his action. He has an attitude that the FAA can't/won't get him in trouble for this reckless behavior. He wasn't breaking any REG by operating without a radio in an ECHO airspace but his speed certainly was in violation of FAR 91.117(a) and given the high training volume being conducted on this day the pilot showed a clear disregard for other pilots or even his/her own safety.
Report_1_Synopsis: Helicopter pilot reported an NMAC in the traffic pattern when a jet trainer made an unannounced high-speed low pass over the runway next to the helicopter.

Report_1_Narrative: Flight was from ZZZ to ZZZ2 with a stop to pick up a passenger at ZZZ1. ZZZ Approach provided flight following all the way to ZZZ1 as I was unfamiliar with the airport and had difficulty identifying it from the air. After overflying the field at 2;000 ft (Approach assigned flight following altitude) a frequency change to the CTAF was approved and made. I descended to pattern altitude and crossed midfield before entering downwind leg for runway XX. Crossing midfield; turning to downwind; base and final; position reports were made on the CTAF. No other aircraft operating at ZZZ1 were heard on frequency. Landing XX; proceeded to back taxi to the end of the runway. At the XY threshold; my passenger saw me and began approaching the aircraft. So as to not create an undue hazard to my passenger; I exited the runway onto the available taxiway and turned parallel to XY. At this point; my left wingtip was impinging on the runway.I continued to hear no other aircraft on frequency as I performed a safety briefing for my passenger and ensured he was ready to fly. Shortly thereafter; another aircraft landed on runway 19. This aircraft proceeded to back taxi on XY and then made contact on CTAF. The other aircraft pilot reported to have been making calls on CTAF and attempting to reach me prior to landing; but I did not hear him. The other aircraft pilot reported landing left of center due to the runway incursion. On resuming flight towards ZZZ2 another aerodrome on the same CTAF frequency performed a radio check with me and assured that they could receive me loud and clear.
Report_1_Synopsis: Pilot reported that after exiting the runway their wing tip remained over the runway while another aircraft landed off centerline due to the runway incursion. Pilot reported not hearing any communication from the landing aircraft.

Report_1_Narrative: In a left turn to intercept final approach course for RWY (Runway) XX at ZZZ. Altitude 1;800 ft. Received RA to descend and complied. Traffic had been previously unannounced by Approach. (If they did announce; we neither heard nor replied).We did not see traffic prior to RA. Cloud; haze; and rain were factors. Our assumption is that the Cessna dropped below clouds to maintain VFR.Complied with RA. Observed traffic passing above right wing. Approximately 400-500 ft.
Report_1_Synopsis: HA4T Captain reported an RA resulted in taking evasive action.

Report_1_Narrative: On [Date]; I was acting as Pilot in Command (PIC) of a UH-60 L Army National Guard Helicopter conducting a round-trip air movement of crew and passengers from ZZZ1 to ZZZ. I was sitting left seat; my Co-pilot (PI) sat right seat. I had two crewmembers in the gunner's seats (Row 2); and one passenger in Row 3. Total: 5 souls on board.Earlier in the day; we had flown IFR from ZZZ1 to ZZZ2 for a fuel stop before heading to ZZZ. We had received a military weather briefing and were aware of an AIRMET Zulu for moderate icing along the route. We monitored PIREPS and determined as a crew that the risk of anything beyond moderate icing was minimal; as the few PIREPS observed were for light rime ice at flight levels above our planned flight altitude.The conditions observed on the flight from ZZZ2 to ZZZ were very stable. There was a stratiform cloud layer; approximately 1;000 to 2;000 ft. thick; that we either flew below or above the cloud layer the entire way to ZZZ. We observed no icing.We were on the ground for approximately two hours after landing at ZZZ. I continued to monitor weather conditions; and it appeared they had not changed from the time we landed. I observed the same AIRMET Zulu and a couple of PIREPS reporting light rime above our planned flight level.Prior to departure; my crew and I conducted de-ice checks in accordance with our aircraft's technical manual; which all passed.After an uneventful climb to our requested flight level of 7;000 ft. MSL; we leveled off. At this time the annunciator panel gave us a warning of 'MR ICE DETECTED'. We had discussed this as an expected possibility; acknowledged the caution; and monitored our ice rate meter; which read 'Light Icing Detected'.At this time; I asked ATC if they knew where the cloud tops were. We were informed that they were at approximately 8;000 ft. MSL. Faced with the decision to climb approximately 1;000 ft. through visible moisture; or descend approximately 4;000 ft. through visible moisture; I requested to climb to 10;000 ft. MSL. ATC gave a clearance to 9;000 ft. MSL. We began our climb.In approximately 1.5 minutes; our icing condition worsened. Our ice rate meter pegged out at its maximum indication of severe icing. The helicopter began to shake; and we lost a dangerous amount of our main rotor RPM (a true [anomaly]). I immediately pressed down on the collective to preserve our rotor RPM; took the controls from my co-pilot; [advised ATC] by announcing 'PAN PAN PAN' on ZZZ Approach frequency. I asked the controller to help me get out of the icing situation and was ultimately cleared down to 2;500 ft. MSL.My crew and I flew the helicopter well; in a level attitude at approximately 2;500 ft. per minute. We maintained 100% rotor RPM during our decent and exited the cloud layer at approximately 3;000 ft. MSL. I tested the controls as we got closer to the surface to ensure I would be able to arrest the helicopter's rate of decent. Upon exiting the clouds; the icing condition improved; and the rest of the flight home was uneventful and under VFR conditions.Chain Of Events:How the problem arose: The problem arose from the unexpected encounter into severe icing.How it was discovered: The severe icing was detected by on the on-board ice detection system; severe vibrations were felt by the crew; and the low rotor warning alarm sounded.Corrective actions: The Good: The crew responded to the [situation] well by manipulating the flight controls to preserve rotor RPM; communicating the [anomaly] to ATC; and flying the aircraft out of the icing conditions.The Bad: The crew did not respond correctly to the initial 'ICE DETECTED' caution. In accordance with the UH-60 Operators Manual; 'The ice rate meter activates the ICE DETECTED caution when the BLADE DE-ICE POWER switch is turned off; informing the pilot of the requirement to turn on the system'. Contributing Factors:Neither the UH-60 Operating Manual or checklist clearly emphasizes the immediatememory item actions required in the event of an icing [situation].An updated -1 weather brief was not obtained from the Air Force Operational Weather Squadron by the Pilot in Command.Human Performance Considerations:The perception of the Pilot in Command that the 'AUTO' function on the ice rate meter meant that the system will 'automatically operate upon detection of ice' was incorrect.The perception of the Pilot in Command that the weather conditions would be the same on the return flight as they were on the first portion was incorrect.The actions of both the Pilot in Command and Co-pilot ultimately saved the lives of the crew; however their inaction to turn the de-ice system on was detrimental to the safe operation of the aircraft.Factors affecting the quality of human performance:Neither the Pilot or Co-pilot complained of fatigue or other exogenous factors prior the flight. Both had a good night's rest and were well within the confines of their duty day at the time of the incident.Recommendations:Ensure aircrew are intimately familiar with the de-ice equipment and capabilities on their aircraft. Recommend that changes be made to the UH-60 Operator's Manual and checklist to emphasize the seriousness of an icing [situation] and the immediate response required. This should be an underlined step. Once the ICE DETECTED caution appears; the immediate action required is for the blade de-ice switch to be turned ON.
Report_1_Synopsis: UH-60 Pilot reported encountered icing; received accumulation warning; but failed to understand and activate the rotor ice protection system. Pilot reference UH-60 Operator's Manual suggestion.

Report_1_Narrative: On a flight from ZZZ to MPR; I flew a practice approach into MPR (RNAV 18) visually in VFR conditions with no view limiting device. As I was touching down on Runway 18 at MPR; I observed another aircraft taking off from the grass Runway 8. The other aircraft crossed in front of me about 400 feet ahead of me and was about 100 feet above me and climbing. I had made a number of radio calls including a 10 mile straight-in final; 5 mile final; 2 mile final and short final. I never heard the other aircraft make any calls. Upon landing; I realized that although I had plugged the MPR CTAF frequency into my radio; I never flipped that frequency to active. Therefore; I had been transmitting on and listening to the incorrect frequency (departure Tower frequency). I take full responsibility for not having the correct frequency active in my radio and will use this as a learning opportunity and a reminder to be more vigilant about confirming proper frequencies. I am surprised that the ZZZ Tower did not hear my 10 mile; 5 mile; 2 mile and short final calls and inform me that I was on the incorrect frequency.
Report_1_Synopsis: Pilot reported landing after broadcasting on the wrong CTAF frequency for MPR airport resulting in a conflict with another aircraft taking off on a crossing runway.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Training / Qualification; Situational Awareness; Confusion; Communication Breakdown
Report_1_Narrative: Early morning at roughly XA:30; Aircraft X flew from the west into ZZZ for pattern work. At the time Aircraft X was the only aircraft that was currently in ZZZ's airspace at the time of the event. Initially Aircraft X made a call to ZZZ Tower asking for pattern work. Since the aircraft was positioned over the mountains the response for ZZZ Tower came in weak. Clarification was requested by pilot flying and stated that the Air Traffic Control Tower was closed. The pilot flying treated the airport as a non-towered airport and switched frequency to XYY.Z. From that point the pilot flying used non-towered airport call outs to announce position. After completing three laps in the pattern an airport operations vehicle flagged down the pilot in command. The pilot in command then preceded to reject the takeoff and continue to the run up area. Airport operations advised the pilot to contact Tower at XXZ.A where the pilot was advised that he could continue pattern work yet had to take a phone number down. Pilot took down phone number and contacted Tower staff after the flight.Due to COVID-19 many ATC facilities are having to temporary close down due to cleaning. ZZZ has also been changing hours of ATC operation in the last ninety days. Pilots from ZZZ1 have also run into the problem of not properly reaching Air Traffic Control due to altered non-posted hours.The pilot in command flying was a student pilot that had recently soloed. When contacted by an airport operations vehicle; [they] only asked for intentions which the pilot responded that he was doing pattern work. At the time it could not be depicted if the airport operations vehicle told on XYY.Z to contact Tower on XXZ.A. In the future [if] airport operations could do this it would help. At the time the pilot thought the airport operations vehicle was attempting to do a FOD patrol of the runway since it was the early morning. The aircraft has been in the past known to have radio issues at random times.The student pilot will go over procedures with Class Delta airports with a flight instructor to mitigate problems in the future.
Report_1_Synopsis: GA student pilot reported frequency communications issues while flying to an airport whose Tower services were not in use.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Situational Awareness; Human-Machine Interface; Confusion; Communication Breakdown
Report_1_Narrative: The incident with Aircraft X can best be described as the perfect storm where in this case the R-side Controller working [two sectors] was very busy and on top of that had numerous aircraft that departed ZZZ Approach level at 160 in his airspace without communication. Prior to me sitting on his position he reached out to the Supervisor to request a D-side along with advising that ZZZ Approach was not shipping aircraft in a timely manner. One aircraft he had was Aircraft Y who was 53 miles into his airspace level at 160 still not on frequency and Aircraft Z; 23 miles into his airspace with the same issue. I mention this because I believe this was the biggest contributing factor to the event with Aircraft X. Aircraft A was at 160 and he descended the aircraft to 10;000 thinking he was a ZZZ1/ZZZ2 arrival and to alleviate all potential traffic conflicts. The main problem was as soon as I sat down and signed in; the R-side was too busy to give me a brief but I was eager to help and to catch up on anything. As I was beginning my scan I noticed Aircraft X getting close to the ZZZ1 Approach airspace at 10;000 without a hand-off and I immediately jumped on the line to coordinate with the ZZZ1 Approach Controller. I began to try to APREQ the aircraft at 10;000 but the ZZZ1 Controller realizing he had an arrival to ZZZZZ [Intersection] already at 10;000 he instructed me to descend Aircraft X to 080; the R-side complied. There was no loss of separation between any aircraft; however; I have decided to report this event because I was talked to by management because of it. I advised my Supervisor in the X area that I did the best I could given I had just sat down and had just noticed the aircraft not handed off to ZZZ1 Approach. Given the coordination could have been done in a more efficient and timely manner I had to work with what I had.According to the safety board's review of the event there was an airspace violation as a result of this coordination. In my opinion this happened because the ZZZ1 Controller and his uncertainty of what needed to be done. I offered to descend Aircraft X to 080; but he advised me to just leave him at 10;000 and then instructed another aircraft to descend below the Aircraft X flight. This back and forth coordination and being reluctant to take the hand off is what resulted in Aircraft X entering his airspace without a hand off. I would like to add that overflights are not allowed over ZZZ NAVAID per our LOA; however the situation dictated a different solution. I would also like to emphasize that as the D-side Controller in this situation had I not immediately gotten on the line with the ZZZ1 Controller this would have been a much different and ultimately worse issue. I am almost certain a loss of separation would have occurred. My Supervisor agreed and the R-side backed me up on it. I have chosen to report this event because even though management advised me this was not disciplinary in any way shape or form; I would still like to bring this up to the safety council's attention.Because of COVID; staffing has been an issue and the traffic volume was high. We had staffing later in the day that helped tremendously but this particular situation we were at minimum. I would also like to receive guidance as to what I could have done better given I was forced into a bad situation and I did my best to separate aircraft and coordinate what I could before an incident may have occurred.
Report_1_Synopsis: Center Controller reported an airspace violation due aircraft hand-off issues with a TRACON facility.

Report_1_Narrative: Aircraft X was advised of airport conditions as well as the work in progress on the runway and was cleared for the VOR 26 approach and told to change to advisory frequency and report cancellation on the frequency.  About 15-20 minutes later the pilot called and informed me he was in the hold over ADQ VOR at 2;000 ft but had not completed the approach or the missed approach.  I double checked the approach plate and immediately issued a climb to 3;700 ft.  Once the aircraft reported reaching 3;700 ft I issued a holding clearance as depicted on the approach plate for the missed approach holding pattern with an EFC and probed for more information which he provided.  The aircraft eventually ended up diverting back to ZZZ due to the poor runway conditions. The pilot needed to inform us of his intentions prior to entering the hold he was not authorized.
Report_1_Synopsis: ZAN Controller reported aircraft was below the MVA during missed approach hold. Controller reported incorrectly aircraft cleared VOR approach executing MA was not authorized holding.

Report_1_Narrative: Aircraft X was handed off at 4;000 feet direct to the initial approach fix. The weather was good for a visual approach so I queried the pilot if he would prefer a visual approach and offered a 6 mile straight in. The pilot concurred and I initiated a descent to 2;100 feet. I did not check the (minimum vectoring area (MVA) map and believed with the descent the pilot would enter the 2;100 foot MVA west of the airport. As the aircraft left 2;600 feet the adjacent facility Controller advised me of a low altitude alert. I was not receiving an alert and mistakenly believed they were getting a false alert due to rate of descent. Shortly after I checked the MVA map and noticed the aircraft was just leaving a 3;000 foot MVA area level at 2;100 feet. Three things contributed to this; two directly under my control: I believed the edge of the 3;000 foot MVA shelf was further north than it was. I should have rechecked the MVA map before issuing a descent. Having had false low altitude alerts before; I believed the other Controller was getting a false alarm. I should have immediately went to the MVA map. And we never received a low altitude alert.
Report_1_Synopsis: FAY TRACON Controller reported they descended an aircraft to an altitude below the Minimum Vectoring Altitude.

Report_1_Narrative: Working in a north flow; with arrivals coming in on the downwind; spacing not really an issue; and I had just been in a rhythm bringing the arrivals in for visual approaches. My general method is to give a descent to 9;000 feet which is the downwind Minimum Vectoring Altitude (MVA) when clear of traffic; then slow to 180 knots 2 miles from the base turn; then turn to a 070 heading; then when the first turn is observed and they are now crossing the 9;000 foot MVA line into the 8;000 foot MVA; give a descent to 7;000 feet; then call the airport; then clear them for an approach with a turn to final. This sequence requires 5 or 6 transmissions per plane; but I feel like it is an expeditious way to safely get aircraft in with such a high MVA on the downwind. After having worked many aircraft in without issue and rather monotonously; Aircraft X checked on and was one of the last aircraft in the bank. I descended them to 9;000 feet; slowed to 180 knots at the normal place; then got distracted by something going on with another sector; I can't remember what; but I returned my focus to Aircraft X; incorrectly thinking that I had already given the base turn; and I was watching for the target to start a turn to the east. I saw the target move and started the transmission to descend. The pilot read it back; but I soon could tell that they were not in the turn and were not leaving the higher MVA for lower terrain. I asked the pilot if they were in the right turn heading 070 yet; and they responded that they were turning to 070 degrees; but in reality I had not yet issued it and didn't realize that until reviewing it afterward. The aircraft was soon in the base turn leaving the higher MVA; I called the airport and the pilot responded in sight; and I issued a visual approach clearance. It was my mistake that I did not catch it earlier. I will practice more vigilance in ensuring a complete turn out of the MVA before issuing the descent.
Report_1_Synopsis: S56 TRACON Controller reported they forgot to issue a heading to an aircraft for the base leg and the aircraft flew below the Minimum Vectoring Altitude.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Training / Qualification; Time Pressure; Situational Awareness; Confusion; Distraction
Report_1_Narrative: Aircraft requested IFR clearance airborne. I proceeded to find the flight plan and issue a clearance when pilot was out of 2;900 feet when the MIA was 3;000.  This was my first day back in the facility in 4 months due to COVID. Prior to that I worked straight mid shifts for the preceding months. I haven't seen any day/evening traffic since month (8 months). This session appeared complex for me due to my absence. I was told I would have this 1 single day to OJT and then I must get an Over The Shoulder.  Jumping immediately into the job made me overthink a lot and I rushed the clearance without thinking of the MIA.Provide more than 8 hours of OJT prior to forcing people to re-certify. This would make the transition back a little smoother.
Report_1_Synopsis: Center Controller reported having an aircraft below the Minimum IFR Altitude.

Report_1_Narrative: High speed abort.Captain at controls.Cleared for takeoff and Tower advised aircraft on 5 mile final as we approached the RWY (Runway). Approximately 1/4 way down runway into our takeoff roll; Challenger announced going around left side. At approximately 1/2 way down runway into our takeoff roll; Tower directed us to abort our takeoff. We were in the high-speed regime at approximately 115 kts. I could see the jet going around on our left abeam; in my peripheral vision as we were aborting.Maximum reverse application w/ maximum brakes. Uneventful abort; cleared runway onto Taxiway F and brought jet to a stop. Manually held brakes while running all applicable checklists. 2 MLG (Main Landing Gear) trucks reached 610 C; others approximately 590 C. Brake temp cooling chart referenced 35 mins used; brakes took approximately 50 min to cool to 270 C. In the meantime; ZZZ Fire-Rescue examined MLG. No evidence of overheat. Conferred with [Maintenance Control] for any further guidance. Later; Maintenance came to the jet; examined MLG per [Maintenance Control] guidance and gave us a thumbs up.In the meantime; we had a conference call with Flight Ops Management and ZZZ Station Ops. Both gave us the ok to continue'.Maintenance Control sent us a new maintenance release; Dispatch sent Release 3. Brake temp left main was the highest temp; at approximately 240 C when we began taxi. No noticeable increases.We departed ZZZ; kept gear down for approximately 5 minutes til all MLG brakes were below 200 C and decreasing. Retracted gear and continued to ZZZ1 via the flight plan.As a side-note; we received an ACARS message at approximately 7;000 ft.; on climbout; directing us to return to gate for another check. We leveled at 9;000 ft.; called Dispatch for clarification. He talked to Maintenance Control and surmised the return to gate message was an old message and may have been caught up in the ACARS system somehow and decided to transmit to us after takeoff roll. Anyhow; message was deemed as received in error and we got a thumbs up to continue OPS (Operations) normal to ZZZ1. I'm not sure if this is something systemic to Company 2 ACARS interface or not; but this issue might need to be examined."
Report_2_Narrative: Cleared takeoff at ZZZ with aircraft on 5 nm final. As we began our roll I heard the aircraft on final say they were initiating a go-around. Around 115 KIAS the Tower directed us to reject which we accomplished. We told the passengers to remain seated and we taxied clear to find a place to cool our brakes; get Maintenance to inspect our brakes/tires; and coordinate for a new maintenance release and Dispatch release while re-initializing our FMC. We accomplished all pre-flight; before push and before takeoff checklists again and accomplished an uneventful takeoff over an hour later and landing uneventfully in ZZZ1.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported a runway confliction resulted in an ATC directed high speed RTO. Captain also report a late ACARS message conflict.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Communication Breakdown; Distraction; Workload; Situational Awareness
Report_1_Narrative: The foreign City X flights are a big problem with the issue of a large number of the passengers refusing to wear their mask from after boarding and throughout the entire duration of the flight. The flight attendants are nonstop in the processes of enforcing the mask requirement and a constant barrage of calls to the cockpit; in addition they are being verbally abused and disrespected by the non-compliant passengers . Company needs to find a way to strongly inform the passengers of the requirement and the seriousness of the lack of respect to the crew and fellow passengers. This is becoming such a problem that I as Captain of the aircraft am going to be forced to land the aircraft at the nearest suitable airport along our route and deplane the instigators.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported many passengers refuse to wear face masks during flights to a specific international destination.

Report_1_Narrative: I unknowingly rode in a van with; and flew with a Flight Attendant who had exhibited COVID symptoms the day prior to our flight.  On [date 1]; the Flight Attendant reported from ZZZ that she had been vomiting and had a temperature above 100.  She reportedly called in sick at that time; but still flew the next day with us ZZZ-ZZZ1.  That day she also rode with us in the van; a 15 minute ride from the hotel.   Only once airborne; from ZZZ-ZZZ1; was I made aware of the Flight Attendant's situation; and reported it immediately.  I must not have all the information; because it appears that she called in sick on [date 1] with COVID symptoms; but was allowed to fly the [to] ZZZ1; then was on sick list again when she got to ZZZ1.  Because I was in close proximity to the Flight Attendant with COVID symptoms for more than 15 minutes; I called in sick for the remainder of my trip.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported concerns with being in close contact with a Flight Attendant that had called in sick the day before for COVID-19 like symptoms.

Report_1_Narrative: Hand flying on climbout when ATC asks us about icing and temperature. We respond with light rime and the SAT. This happened just before reaching FL210. I looked down at EICAS for temperature and in the process climbed through FL210 by 400 feet; but immediately corrected. ATC did call us on it but we were back at FL210. At no time was there any traffic conflict or separation issue. Being new to the airplane; I was hand flying to get a better feel for the airplane. Might be worth mentioning that plane was light and was climbing like a rocket ship but previous to this event; we had complied with correctly with all other altitude assignments.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported an altitude deviation during climbout.

Report_1_Narrative: HKG Runway 7L/25R is closed for construction; but there is no NOTAM for this condition. It does show on the ATIS. I'm told this condition has been ongoing for a while; and I'm also told that it's been previously reported. Why is there no NOTAM for a runway closure? If the local authority will not issue a NOTAM; then our company should issue an internal NOTAM. This runway closure makes HKG a single-runway airport with diversion options that are limited and/or undesirable.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier First Officer reported a runway at this location is out of service and there are no NOTAMs.

Report_1_Narrative: New FO updating arrival waypoints mistakenly deleted route in legs 1 at XA:40Z.  CAand FO immediately reinstated route in legs 2.  CA sent position reports to ATC at XA:50Z and XB:17 Z.  CA counseled FO.FO familiar with Manufacturer X aircraft type and not Manufacturer Y aircraft type. Unable to fly after training due to virus.[I suggest] more training.
Report_1_Synopsis: Captain reported the First Officer mistakenly deleted the route in legs 1.

Report_1_Narrative: While taxiing out to Runway XR at ZZZ I might have failed to hold short at the hold short line. The FO and I recognized the error at the same time. He yelled stop as I hit the brakes. Looking out at the line; it was difficult to tell if the nose of the aircraft had crossed over the line. The Tower was informed immediately. The Tower then cleared us for takeoff. No other issues. Both the FO and I had reviewed the bulletin for ZZZ about this problem and it still may have bitten us.  Other issues that may have affected our situational awareness was a last minute weight and balance issue that required us to stop on the taxiway to move passengers and get our numbers. Another issue is that I and the FO are starting to fly again after three months. It is taking time to re-acclimate to line operations. Even being aware of this and taking our time to get it done right; we may have still gotten bit by the error.
Report_2_Narrative: Approaching Runway XR hold line Captain began to apply brakes; so I thought he was coming to a stop. I looked down to bring up the legs page on my FMC and when I looked up again it was apparent he was not going to stop short of the hold line. I told him to stop and he brought the plane to an immediate stop. We had crossed the line by a few feet. Captain told the Tower we may have crossed the hold line and they asked if we could take an immediate takeoff; we said yes and proceeded to takeoff on XR without incident.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported a runway incursion.

Report_1_Narrative: Aircraft X. ARD had previous write-up about compressor stalls on #3 Engine. Maintenance said the morning crew rejected the takeoff for compressor stalls; we read the write-up and maintenance action in detail and discussed the issue. We identified this as a potential threat to our flight. On push back; while starting #1 Engine; we got ENG 1 FADEC ALTN alert; we referred to the QRH; it also identified 'action code' as SW. After engine start; the Captain said we could recycle the switch and asked if I was okay with that; I replied if he was okay; I was okay. We selected FADEC ALTN; then selected it again to the normal function; the alert went away. Later as we taxied out; I thought about the PDM process and not consulting maintenance; but the Captain's action corrected the alert to the proper configuration without any alerts and without an AML write-up; so I resolved my dilemma internally. Prior to taking the runway; the Captain announced he was gonna run-up all the engines a bit higher than usual while holding the brakes to ensure #3 Engine was operating correctly; I replied it was a good idea. It was my take-off (hand flown as briefed) and everything went normal up to about 700 ft. AGL.About 700 ft. AGL; with the gear up and flaps extended; we heard loud bangs associated with a compressor stall (I only heard this before in the sim) and a jolting in the plane; there were no differing indications on any of the engine instruments (all three N1; EGT; and N2 indications were identical). Around 1;000 ft. AGL; the Captain said he was gonna shut the engine down; I said okay with the bias of the previous write-up in the ARD; also thinking we'd go thru the process of 'Throttle-Idle; Fuel Shutoff Switch-Off' (I admit this wasn't the calm and rehearsed engine failure problem in the sim; and I was a bit anxious about the actual compressor stall). About that time; Tower called us and said we had intermittent flames shooting out of the left side (#1 Engine); the Captain said 'left side; I shut down [Engine] #3' (paraphrase). I looked down and noticed 0 fuel flow and the engine N2 decreasing while the banging continued. I exclaimed 'Let's start it back up' thinking #3 wasn't the problem and we definitely needed it if we had to shut down #1! The Captain quickly returned the fuel cutoff switch to on and I saw the N2 increase. I turned the autopilot on (as briefed if we had a problem) and announced I was disconnecting the auto throttles while the Captain told Tower we were returning to the field for compressor stalls and advised ATC. Tower told us to turn left downwind for [Runway] XX and I told the Captain 'I got the plane and the radios' and I replied to Tower. With the autopilot on and above 1;000 ft. AGL; the plane accelerated above Vf and I asked Tower if 2;000 ft. MSL was okay to level off; Tower replied yes. As I started the heading guided turn to the left; I adjusted the altitude to 2;000 ft. and manually retarded all the throttles for level off then selected airspeed 200 knots. With the throttles out of take-off power; the banging went away; I believe Tower said the flames stopped. While flying downwind abeam the field; I began to setup for the approach [Runway] XX; adjusted the minimums (already had it preselected); and announced I was moving the flaps to 15 degrees since they were still extended. Tower asked if we had the field insight; I replied yes and Tower cleared us the visual approach [Runway] XX and cleared to land; I repeated the clearance but said we were gonna fly out a bit to get our normal visual glidepath. After the Captain programmed the FMS and inserted the ILS frequency into the NavRad page; I called for the approach check and turned base to final; on dogleg; I began the descent on glidepath before intercepting the localizer and called for the gear down and before landing check. With the final configuration and checklist complete; I asked the Captain if he wanted the landing since we were an emergency; he took control of the plane with the autopilot on while I briefed him of the FMAs. Landing was uneventful.  We taxied clear onto taxiway XX and waited for the fire truck's inspection. With the all clear (no fire); we terminated the emergency and taxied to parking.Engine compressor stall.Some missteps between the crew while successfully resolving an engine compressor stall. Better crew coordination would simplify resolution.
Report_2_Narrative: Alerted that Aircraft X might be returning to ZZZ due to problem with #1 Engine. I immediately contacted ZZZ Tower. I was told; right after flight was wheels up controllers in tower saw sparks/flames coming from left engine and also heard 3 to 4 loud booms. Flight returned to airport and landed without issue on Runway XX. I talked to the Captain. He said that right after takeoff; there was compressor stall #1 Engine. They advised ATC and returned to ZZZ. The aircraft was met by the Fire Department. The Captain said he did not know what caused the loss of the #1 Engine. He also said the maintenance told him there was damage to the engine.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Crew reported compressor stalls on the Number 1 Engine and inadvertently shut down the Number 3 Engine.

Report_1_Narrative: Air Carrier Ground Agent 1 in ZZZ called coworker and stated that some MISC HAZMAT (hazardous material) had been placed in position 6R. Apparently this had been loaded into this can 2 days prior; and they didn't realize this until the aircraft had already taken off.   I then talked to Agent 1 about the situation and had him to send me the HAZMAT paperwork. Called the Director of Operations and informed of the situation; and also informed the crew of what had happened. As showing on the paperwork; it was Class 9; MISC; 804KG - position 6R. The cause was with the holiday; it caused the ramp to lose track of the can where this HAZMAT was and the paperwork that needed to be with the HAZMAT material. I suggest when there is a holiday; the ramp needs to make sure that they are extra careful about where the HAZMAT is and the [related] paperwork is.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Dispatcher reported Hazmat cargo was inadvertently left on aircraft over the holiday weekend without appropriate Hazmat documentation.

Report_1_Narrative: Arriving at security at XA:00pm; we found all security check points and KCM [Known Crew Member] closed.  We were directed to security for airport employees in another terminal.  After setting off the alarm; I was instructed to start removing various articles of clothing.  With a line of airport employees behind me; I asked for a private search.  I was taken to yet another terminal and told to enter a room the size of an average walk in closest.  Two security personnel crammed in behind me.  There was poor ventilation and no possibility of distancing ourselves.  We all stood within a foot of each other.  I would suggest in this time of COVID; TSA like every other organization must adapt procedures and protocols to prevent the spread of COVID-19.  Utilizing KCM decreases the time and contact between security personnel and flight crews; two groups exposed to more human interaction than most.  Increasing the hours of KCM operation and relaxing constraints within the program to facilitate secure social distancing is a reasonable adaptation to help mitigate the spread of COVID among both essential workers and the public at large.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported concerns with security checks in the terminal area that do not allow for proper social distancing.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Confusion; Situational Awareness; Time Pressure; Training / Qualification
Report_1_Narrative: Upon executing a missed approach; the aircraft was leveled off early. The error was recognized and the aircraft put back into a climb to reach its target altitude for the missed approach. Pilot flying became disoriented after the acceleration and climb on the go-around in IMC. The aircraft was light and the majority of experience was on the Y series. It had been 15 days since the last flight; and 76 days since flying in an X [series] for the pilot flying. The PF reaction to the increased pitch attitude and acceleration was to level the plane prematurely.[Need] Review of SOP procedures for go-around; and mental preparation for pitch attitude changes from the Y to X series on the X type aircraft on takeoff and go-around configurations.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier First Officer reported not following SOP's during a missed approach and stated that an extended period of time off was a contributing factor.

Report_1_Narrative: Being vectored onto the final approach course 26R; we had a brief encounter with a wake turbulence. And then again during the landing flare to the point where it was becoming a problem to maintain a stabilized approach path above the runway in ground effect. Did not have time to notify air traffic control that this happened. I don't know if we were behind a heavy previous arrival. But we were getting really close to having to go around from the landing flare. The roll motion was becoming such a problem with keeping the aircraft stabilized; and aligned with the runway. I was actually shocked that we touchdown as smooth as we did. I asked the pilot flying if he thought that was a bit unusual his statement was 'I was just one more jolt away from going around'. Wake turbulence encounters in Atlanta are becoming an every week problem; more like almost every inbound leg into Atlanta problem. Also it seems there is little consideration given to the fact that we may be departing behind something that might be a threat as well. I'm beginning to think that there's nothing much going to be done about it until something serious happens. Often the wake encounter threats are not much of a problem if there's sufficient crosswind push the wake away from trailing aircraft; from my experience it does not take much to all. However I've learned that this is still a problem at some point on the arrival or departure procedure. For example a crosswind on the departure runways will clear you of the wake threat for takeoff; but might present a very real problem in trail of a heavy navigating to a point; to the same on that departure or arrival. Especially if it's a direct head; or tailwind now.
Report_1_Synopsis: CRJ-900 Captain reported encountering wake turbulence on final approach into ATL.

Report_1_Narrative: The aircraft was late arriving. There were fumes and a very strong smell coming out of door 1L from the sanitizing spray while we were standing out on the jetway. The training that all FAs are required to complete; states we must wait at least XX minutes before entering the aircraft after spraying is completed. The agents started boarding while we were still on jetway and the customers told the agents. So the gate agents came down to ask what the problem was and we stated the fumes are too strong for us to board. We were pressured to start boarding as to not cause a delay!
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Attendant reported the gate agents tried to board the passengers right after the aircraft was sanitized; disregarding the mandatory wait time.

Report_1_Narrative: As Passenger A boarded our flight; I asked her to please make sure that her mask was on over both her mouth and nose.  She did not comply.
