AFE (Above Field Elevation) with advancement in override thrust. Subsequently received windshear caution. After selecting TOGA and pitch up flew flight director. No windshear escape guidance provided as the windshear was not sustained. Thrust was advanced to GA (Go-Around) RSV as a precaution. Stable in the missed approach maneuver with no caution windshear; PF called Flaps 4 due to flaps full configured. Gear retracted at a safe altitude with positive climb rate. Flew ATC assigned runway heading with missed approach climb profile. Subsequent approach flown to the ILS profile with Flaps 5. Flew the glide slope to RWY [Runway] XXR. No windshear event occurred. Received wind report with gust factor 28 kts. Selected manual speeds to increase approach sped until 4-5 kts. until after passing 500 ft. AFE 'stable' call the target speed was reduced. Maintained visual descent rate with visual cues and instrumentation of the ILS. During round out to flare automation set the aural 'sink rate' message. FO (First Officer) announced correcting due to the aural call and confirmed with a cross check the sink rate was induced by maintaining descent rate with the descent maneuver to coupled round out pitch rate simultaneously for the landing maneuver; not due to windshear as the speed was stable. FO and CA (Captain) on debrief both acknowledged the aural alert at post flight and both agreed with given conditions the approach to landing was stable given the conditions. Touchdown was within LTP (Landing Threshold Point) distance.Second approach with Flaps 5 configuration allowed for a higher approach speed and acknowledging the wind factor with increase in target speed for gusty conditions allowed for less susceptibility for the same condition. Automation with sensor inputs from other automated systems is subject to its own set design limitations and may not reflect positive confirmation of the event with pilot judgment of the same situation monitoring the same event. Such as automation latencies detecting the windshear event prior to the windshear caution; or sink rate alert while the pilot is initiating real time assertive maneuvers in turbulent conditions. Inertial vertical speed descent rates measure acceleration as it filters out noise of turbulence conditions causing a lag as opposed to real time judgment of the flight crew.
Report_2_Narrative: Approach into ZZZ on our 1st attempt we conducted a missed approach due to wind shear. On the 2nd approach in the flare we briefly went to a sink rate of 1;100 [ft. per minute] the FO (First Officer) was already correcting and we received a 'sink rate' aural tone just prior to touchdown.
Report_1_Synopsis: E-175 flight crew reported executing a missed approach due windshear during final approach. Subsequently flight crew executed an uneventful landing.

Report_1_Narrative: Enroute to ZZZ1 we failed to set altimeters to 29.92 when climbing through 18;000 feet. Due to the very high altimeter setting at our departure field; it lead to us inadvertently leveling off 300 feet below our assigned altitude. ATC queried our altimeter setting and we immediately corrected. Inconsistent scheduling and continued ongoing stress from the organization's uncertain future lead to a flight deck environment prime for small errors such as this one.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported not setting the correct altimeter and leveling off below their assigned altitude.

Report_1_Narrative: On a visual approach to Runway X; the FO was flying; he started the approach a little high but managed to get back on a 3 degree glide to the runway. By the time I noticed we were at 500 feet and his airspeed was still about 20 knots above Vref. The airspeed managed to get down to Vapp with the engines spooled before touchdown. I hadn't flown in a month so my situational awareness was not on a level it should have been and I should have called a go-around.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported an unstabilized approach and stated they should have executed a go-around.

Report_1_Narrative: After landing at CBF the airport manager approached and asked about turning on the PCL [Pilot Controlled Lighting] lighting. Airport manager stated that it was very expensive for airport lights to be turned on and asked if local pilots and flight instructors could be coached on not turning the lights on so much during the day and at night when not necessary. It was explained to airport manager that turning on the lights is at the pilots discretion and a potential safety issue and asking them to try to monitor turning runway lights on and off to help airport control their electric expenses seemed as counter to safe operations of aircraft.
Report_1_Synopsis: Pilot reported Airport Manager's request to ask pilots to avoid using pilot controlled lighting due to cost.

Report_1_Narrative: When loading Cargo Compartment the Loading Supervisor noticed that there was no DG (Dangerous Goods) info for this ULD (Unit Load Devise) in the Load Platform Program.He contacted the Load Controller who then contacted Cargo for the information and the DG info was then updated in Load Platform Program.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Ramp Agent reported required Hazmat load documents missing from Load report. Dispatch notified; Load report corrected prior to departure.

Report_1_Narrative: VFR traffic failed to level when instructed by ATC. I had to drop 500 feet and bank had while accelerating to avoid a mid air collision. We only got one small heading change from ATC that made us more of a factor.
Report_1_Synopsis: Diamond DA20 pilot reported taking evasive action to avoid traffic.

Report_1_Narrative: Working a slow but steady local session with Supervisor working GC/CD combined. Very low staffing due to COVID. Steady traffic all day; I wouldn't call it too busy though. Very last transmission of my shift was to Aircraft X.Aircraft X called on about a 7 mile final (new pilot). I cleared it to land on Runway XX right and then started my position relief briefing within seconds of my transmission.Finished the brief and my 2 minute overlap; said bye to my fellow coworkers and left. Aircraft X was probably on a 2 mile final by then.I was paged at the bottom of elevator and Supervisor asked 'Did you give Aircraft X Runway XX right or Runway XX left'? I told him I didn't remember.Turned out aircraft landed on Runway XX left instead of Runway XX right. No separation issues luckily.All they said was 'cleared to land' I didn't even realize it at the time.I was distracted; ready for the briefing to be done after a long; busy day with a skeleton crew.Expectation bias all the way; I just assumed they said XX right in their transmission.All controllers tend to get complacent in this job when everything goes right for some time; I need to stay vigilant and listen to every transmission. If I would've just listened to that pilot's readback instead of thinking about getting off position and being done for the day; I would've noticed it and I would've got verification that she was cleared to land on runway XX right and all would've been good.
Report_1_Synopsis: Tower Controller reported communication issues with an aircraft resulted in a wrong runway landing.

Report_1_Narrative: Training on combined sectors; moderate traffic; two practice approach aircraft in satellite airspace all other traffic in departure sectors.Aircraft X came off ZZZ on the published missed approach for the RNAV RWY XX approach; he checked in and was radar identified while in the published left turn towards the missed approach fix; ZZZZZ.  The trainee subsequently verified the pilot's previous request to return to ZZZ1 on an IFR clearance.  The trainee cleared Aircraft X direct ZZZ and instructed the aircraft to maintain 2;000'.  At the time; the aircraft was within a 2;000' MVA [Minimum Vectoring Altitude].  I believe both the trainee and I anticipated that the pilot would make a right turn direct to ZZZ1; not recognizing that a continued left turn may be more appropriate because the aircraft was already in the published left turn on the missed approach.  With the anticipation of a right turn in mind and the aircraft in a 2;000' MVA my attention as the OJTI turned to the other departure traffic; which was going to require the trainee to merge and weave multiple departures off multiple airports (ZZZ2/ZZZ3/ZZZ4) to get them on course and through our airspace.  This was an area the trainee had shown struggles in in previous sessions as well as earlier in this training session; so I was attempting to stay ahead and have a plan of my own if needed.  Upon reviewing the incident; I became aware that in the moments following Aircraft X's clearance I was suggesting an alternative course of action for one of the trainee's departures in an effort to illustrate a way to expedite getting a departure on course which also got them out of the way of succeeding departures quicker.  Unfortunately; this conversation kept my focus on the departure traffic as opposed to the continued turn that Aircraft X made into the higher MVA.  Aircraft X subsequently continued a left turn towards ZZZ1 and entered a 2;500' MVA at his assigned altitude of 2;000'.  The trainee was aware of the incident almost immediately.  The trainee issued a climb to 2;500' to Aircraft X when the aircraft was only a third or a half a mile inside the 2;000' MVA.  I was not aware of the situation until I heard the trainee issue the climb to Aircraft X.  I subsequently requested that we be relieved.  The trainee and I debriefed; after which I informed management of the incident when I requested time for myself and the trainee to review the incident and fill out our report.  To my knowledge; Aircraft X climbed to the MVA and subsequently landed at ZZZ1 without further incident.Numerous things could have prevented this occurrence.  Had the trainee climbed Aircraft X to 3;000' instead of descending them to 2;000' they would have been above the MVA.  Had the trainee left the aircraft on the published missed approach for even a few miles they would have climbed above the MVA and a subsequent clearance may have included a more appropriate altitude.  Had the aircraft made the anticipated right turn instead of continuing in a left turn they would have remained in the 2;000' MVA.  Had the trainee issued the clearance to ZZZ1 via radar vectors; I believe they would have assigned a vector that would have remained within the 2;000' MVA and avoided the situation.
Report_2_Narrative: Recertification time on [positions] (departures) and Article 67 training on[positions](south satellite). Aircraft X departed ZZZ on the published missed from the RNV runway XX  approach. Requested clearance to ZZZ1 airport. I observed Aircraft X in a 2;000ft MVA [Minimum Vectoring Altitude] and told pilot to maintain 2;000' and proceed direct ZZZ1; which is north east of ZZZ. A direct flight path would have kept the aircraft away from the 2500ft MVA east of their position. Pilot was in a left hand turn though; and continued a left hand turn direct ZZZ1. I was expecting a right hand turn direct. The left hand turn put the aircraft 2-3 miles further east than planned and inside the 2;500ft MVA. I climbed the aircraft to 2;500ft and let them continue on course. I; as the controller should have been more aware of the chance the aircraft could have entered higher MVA. I should have climbed Aircraft X to 2;500ft before sending direct ZZZ1 to account for a left or right turn.
Report_1_Synopsis: Instructor and Re-certification Controller reported a MVA [Minimum Vectoring Altitude] violation when an aircraft under their control turned the wrong anticipated direction leading to the violation.

Report_1_Narrative: Planned flight as normal; no limiting MELs were attached to the aircraft at any point during planning.  I received a call from the crew at asking for clarification that MEL XX-XX-X-1 meant that center tank fuel was unusable; I confirmed this was the case; that this MEL means that both center pumps are INOP and that any fuel in the center is trapped; I thought it was a generic question and didn't question the MEL on this specific flight.  I was advised by Dispatcher X that he believed the flight departed below minimum fuel; I brought up the [planning] and the fuel I had planned it with was below the level at which fuel is added to the center tank; this immediately raised flags and I attempted to contact ZZZ Tower to stop the aircraft from taking off; however they said clearance had already been given and the aircraft was rolling.  I believe the aircraft departed with approx 24.7 usable fuel with a MIN TAKEOFF fuel of 27.0.  After takeoff and at a safe altitude; I ACARSed the crew asking them to confirm the fuel available in their main tanks only; I determined this fuel was not sufficient to make it to RFD and advised the dispatch lead.  The crew agreed that a tech stop was in the best interest of safety and it was decided that ZZZ1 was a suitable gateway for this; the flight was diverted to ZZZ1 to add fuel.  Unfortunately; at no point during the pre-planning or planning stage of this flight; did I receive a call from Maintenance Control advising the MEL was being added; nor did the crew request an amended release before blockout advising that the MEL was not on their paperwork and thus not considered for the flight.  The call was a routine call in which I thought the crew was just asking for interpretation of a MEL.I would suggest to Maintenance Control that they advise all dispatchers that have that tail assigned of any MELs being added; unfortunately we don't always have the aircraft on its previous leg and thus when they advise one dispatcher of an MEL being added; the next dispatcher does not receive this information.
Report_1_Synopsis: Dispatcher reported that a flight departed without the minimum required fuel due to a miscommunication about an MEL.

Report_1_Narrative: Upon arrival into the terminal environment at MGM; flight crew was informed of a portion of runway lighting reported as inoperative. Information was not published in NOTAMs and Dispatch was not aware. During the time spent in researching suitability of the given conditions; the flight crew observed Rwy 28 with VMC conditions. The crew determined that the runway lighting that was visible was suitable to execute a safe landing. Some factors to take into account: filed alternate was ZZZ. Crew knew that the weather to get back to ZZZ was not ideal. Having experience occasional moderate turbulence; and 30 knots more headwind than planned. Extended taxi time leaving ZZZ; and stair-stepped altitude climb out had us approximately 300 pounds behind on fuel. Having had a same day previous min fuel declaration; we determined ZZZ was not best action. In our judgement at the time; landing at Montgomery was the safest course of action. Unreported facility malfunctions.Safest decision was madeBuy more time. Request vectors; or holding to further coordinate airfield suitability with all available resources.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Captain reported the runway lights at this location were inoperative and there were no published NOTAMs.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Situational Awareness; Distraction; Confusion; Time Pressure
Report_1_Narrative: When I arrived at the airplane for departure I was informed that the FA X had called in sick.  Apparently he had been exposed [to] COVID-19. I discussed the need for a new general declaration with the agent once they had found a replacement. About 30 minutes before push back they gave me the new declaration with all positions filled; and I signed it. About 20 minutes before pushing the agent returned and told me that they had pulled the new crew member off for another flight; and asked me if we could go with XX [number] of FAs. Not catching my error I said yes and asked for a new general declaration; it arrived just before departure time I signed it and we departed shortly thereafter.This was my first flight in over nine months with passengers; I had a discussion with the Lead FA about the FA that had called in sick; and wanted to be sure none of the other FAs had been exposed to him; apparently none had. We also discussed the fact that we would be getting a replacement. I just missed the fact that our duty time would require XY [number of] FAs.For myself having been on leave and away from flying for so long; I need to slow everything down; take a little more time.
Report_2_Narrative: Last minute flight attendant sick call and another reassignment. Misunderstood flight attendant minimum requirements. Was unaware that requirements were based on duty day and not flight time. Departed 1 flight attendant undermanned.Last minute changes at a critical time. COVID-19 concerns and maximum limit of XX passengers. We should seek waiver for restricted load passenger flights. Need assistance from dispatch; flight attendants and load to help watch for errors in manning requirements.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported inadvertently departing with one less Flight Attendant than required for the flight.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Communication Breakdown; Confusion; Situational Awareness; Workload
Report_1_Narrative: On descent into CLT; open descent; 6;000 selected in the altitude window. Approaching AAIRE on the JONZE 2; I asked the FO to verify our descent clearance as it didn't feel right being cleared to 6;000 with departures at CLT coming off of 18C. As I asked this; I disconnected the autopilot and arrested the descent at 8;820. The frequency was quite congested (CLT Approach) so the FO was unable to get a word in. However; as I continued the climb from 8;820 to 9;000; CLT Approach did ask us to climb and maintain 9;000. To my knowledge; there were no traffic conflicts; however it was a very uncomfortable situation.Flying into CLT has become problematic with the CDA arrivals. The CHESLY has become legendary for altitude busts; and the JONZE 2 isn't much better. The scenario goes something like this; you check in with Atlanta Center and receive a 'descend via' clearance. Not long after; you are turned off of the arrival and given a 'descend to and maintain' clearance. This process usually repeats itself a couple of times (either with Atlanta Center or Charlotte Approach) before you are assigned a final descent clearance. This system makes it very difficult to fly the arrival. Please know that this isn't pointing blame; but pointing out a problem. As PIC; the responsibility ultimately falls on me. However; a smoother process would be helpful.Eliminate the CDA arrivals into CLT. We rarely fly them as published.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported an altitude deviation during approach to CLT while on the JONZE 2 RNAV Arrival.  Captain stated the CDA arrivals to CLT are allegedly problematic and should be eliminated or a 'smoother process' should be implemented.

Report_1_Narrative: During the boarding process of Aircraft X at Gate; a passenger in her assigned seat was holding her carry-on bag on her lap. The carry-on had a vape charger inside the bag and the batteries started to smoke and meltdown. There was smoke and fumes in the cabin. An unknown passenger ran towards the front of the aircraft yelling that there was a fire in the back of the aircraft and for everyone to get off. The flight attendants made an announcement and commenced the Emergency Deplaning at the Gate procedure (which we had discussed in my pre-bridging brief to the FA's (Flight Attendants)). The Purser asked what to do and I told him to continue the process they had started; which was going very well with passengers calmly deplaning up the jet way. The First Officer alerted emergency response and got up from his seat to assist. I was then told by an unknown person; that the smoking bag had been removed from the aircraft by a dead-heading pilot. I ran the Emergency Evacuation checklist to secure the aircraft; grabbed the fire extinguisher (not needed) and stood at the door directing the passengers to continue up the jetway; 'do not take bags or stand in the jetway; and to proceed to the terminal.' I directed the First Officer to go to terminal. There were a few passengers slowing the process trying to grab their carry-on bag; but were directed to stop and continue to the terminal. Once all passengers were off; I directed the FA's to go to the terminal while I swept the aircraft to be sure all crew and passengers were off. I then proceeded to the terminal. At the terminal I found the crew and deadheading crew members at the door; several passengers and agents and the smoking bag lying on the floor next to the ticket counter. I then directed all persons to leave the area; and requested Law enforcement with/dogs and fire and rescue to the bag. Asked the gate agent to call medical assistance and found the affected passenger sitting in the terminal; which I directed Medical to her location. At that point I was alarmed that the threat had followed us to the terminal and was concerned as to its contents. I then briefed fire and rescue; Maintenance as well as corporate security and law enforcement. I directed the deadheading crewmember who had carried the bag to seek medical attention. We coordinated for the FA's to stay nearby to facilitate the eventual allowing of 5 passengers at a time to go back to the secured aircraft to get their belongings. The First Officer was having chest pain and went to the hospital. I declined medical treatment. And met the ZZZ Chief Pilot who assisted me in the process remaining. There were burns on the owner of the smoking bag; and she also went to the hospital. There were no other injuries or incidents associated with the emergency deplaning procedure...but there was some uncertainty among the many constituents affected by the procedure; gate; ground; maintenance. etc. I was relieved from duty with 'p' for the remaining duration of the trip. I received follow up calls from ZZZ Chief Pilot on multiple occasions and was grateful for his support. I also contacted directly Union Safety and spoke with [Representative] who provided assistance and guidance during and after the event. Overall the procedure works; but should be expanded to a joint training scenario. I was most alarmed to learn. That the (brave) deadheading crew member had carried the smoking bag with him during the deplaning and it eventually ended up in the terminal with no oversight. The direction was to deplane away from the threat; not take it with us.The cause was allowing of the charging device and vape apparatus onboard the aircraft as a carry-on. The positive outcome was due to emergency deplaning at the gate procedure and pre-briefing. Well trained and professional back-end crew was outstanding. First Officer reverted to training and promptly called fire and rescue. However once passengers were off; there was confusion and potential danger which needs to be mitigated for future events. Communication and full understanding and procedures associated are necessary.I suggest the need to continue the use of and to training of the 'Emergency Deplaning at the Gate Procedure'. Would recommend suggested briefings for the crew. Also believe joint training would be very beneficial to role play these scenarios...there is a lot going on and many potential pitfalls. This affects all constituents of the normal process; but also many others. Being released from duty by the Chief Pilot was appreciated; however as a reserve pilot; working to get my time for the month; Pay - No Credit does not help in any way. In fact it prevented me from flying another 4 day trip I could have held; and subsequently puts me at zero(0) hours going into the middle of the month.
Report_2_Narrative: It was the first leg of the start of the sequence. I had just met the CA (Captain); for the first time; that afternoon. Along with the first time working with the FA's (Flight Attendants). Boarding started as normal; the CA and myself went about our preflight duties. We had finished all our checklists and were just waiting for the Gate Agent to inform us of boarding being complete. As we sat waiting to close up FA-1 shouts up to us 'We have a fire in the cabin'. In the time that it took the CA and I to get over the initial shock factor; the FA's immediately began an 'Emergency Deplaning' of the aircraft. From my advantage point I had no clue how bad the fire was in the cabin. I did not hear any call for an 'Evacuation'; or see any doors and slides deploying; so I assumed that the FA's were just doing the 'Emergency Deplaning'.The CA went to the QRH immediately. I got on the radio to ops and told them of our situation. That we had a fire onboard the aircraft; we were 'Emergency Deplaning' into the terminal; and we needed ARF (Airport Rescue and Fire Fighting).The CA and I had completed everything we could think of to help the FA's with the situation in the back. Still not knowing how bad things were in the cabin the CA instructed me to exit the airplane. I did so and then followed my 'evacuation' duties when outside the aircraft. As I exited the flight deck I found a clog of passengers not moving out the door. I made my way through them to find a group of passengers have congregated on the jetway. I instructed them to move and get in the terminal building. This helped the flow of passengers off the aircraft. I found one passenger in visible distress on the jetway. I did a quick assessment of the passenger and then asked if they were OK. The passenger complained of burns on their arm. It did not look bad so I asked if they could walk. The passenger said yes. So I got the assistance of another passenger to help them into the terminal. I also instructed them to take the bag that the hurt passenger said was theirs and was standing next to. Later I would find out this was the bag that was smoking. It was not smoking when I was on the jetway and I was unaware this was the threat on the aircraft. I never would have thought that the threat would be off the aircraft in the direction the passengers were going. Or taken off and left unattended.After the passengers were off the aircraft the FA's were coming off and then asked where the bag was. I asked 'What bag? The one on the ground in the jetway?' They responded Yes; that was the one that was smoking. At that point I realized that I sent it inside the terminal. I remembered what passenger had it and told the supervisor; that was on the jetway; that I could identify them to find that bag.The CA completed his final check of the aircraft and we proceeded into the terminal. The bag has been cordoned off at the gate and people were being kept away. The CA remained at the gate until ARF arrived. I took the FA's and proceeded to an unused gate to keep us together and away from the situation.The incident started with a passenger's bag there was no control over the problem. There was some confusion over what procedures were started and what roles the flight deck crew had in an 'Emergency Deplaning'.It was also confusing how and why the fire; smoking bag; was put onto the jetway. The use of the 'Emergency Deplaning' was very appropriate to this situation and did exactly what it was intended to do. However there is not a clear signal; that we knew of; that signals to the flight deck that an 'Emergency Deplaning' is in progress. There was also not an immediate action item; QRC; or QRH procedure to reference for an event like this for us on the flight deck to help. It felt as if we were making it up as we went along. Merging our evacuation checklist and duties into the 'Emergency Deplaning'.There is also no defined plan for fighting an onboard fire at the gate; that at least theflight deck is aware of. Just so we know what to expect. Example; that if we are to expect the fire or threat to be taken off the aircraft mid-deplaning.The event was a success; it was extremely helpful that the flight deck knows about 'Emergency Deplaning'. However there seems to still be confusion on roles; how to help with and execute an 'Emergency Deplaning'.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight crew reported a fume event during boarding caused by a 'vape charging device' meltdown in a carry-on bag.  An orderly passenger deplaning was executed and necessary emergency responders notified.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Human-Machine Interface; Situational Awareness; Time Pressure; Workload; Distraction
Report_1_Narrative: Upon descent on the RNAV arrival; the aircraft ahead advised 'moderate turbulence at 10;000 ft.… We as a crew evaluated the deviations options and concluded to stay on route and cross the next fix at 9;000 ft. The area north and south of course on the radar were shaded with darker colors. The current inflight night visibility was zero with moderate to heavy rain lightning and St Elmo's fire. Upon crossing the fix we begin to encounter moderate turbulence. The autopilot was engaged; 250 kts. speed selected. After passing the fix and right about when the smart turn over another fix began we received an immediate CLIMB RESOLUTION ADVISORY and a RED traffic appeared on the Multi-Function Display (MFD) in the 11 o'clock position.I; the Pilot Flying; began the TCAS TA/RA actions and call-outs disconnecting the autopilot; complying with the RA climb instructions. The Captain turned off the Flight Directors as per company procedures. Due to moderate turbulence the aircraft began to rapidly slow below the selected 250 kts.; so I; the Pilot Flying; selected TOGA (Take Off/Go Around) to equalize the descending energy and avoid a stall or near stall condition. With the lack of Flight Director (FD) lateral guidance the MFD became primary for lateral guidance for the turn over the fix; the red threat traffic appeared between us and turning left to rejoin the arrival. As we began to level off and reestablish vertical and lateral guidance ATC queried us. The Captain; who was Pilot Monitoring; was tasked with selecting the Flight Directors ON and selecting the desired modes to return us to course and altitude in a rather bumpy erratic flight condition. I; the Pilot Flying; with hands on a push to talk advised ATC of complying with a TCAS RA. As we began to turn back to course the previous red threat traffic reappeared yellow and a 'TRAFFIC; TRAFFIC' was heard; so we remained leveled off and slow turned towards the course. After establishing guidance; and positively managing the aircraft's speed and energy we began a turn towards the next fix. We as a crew were task saturated controlling the aircraft in moderate turbulence and complying with the TCAS RA and were merely queried by ATC; never advised of traffic by ATC or given any lateral guidance after stating we were complying with a TCAS RA. It was only several moments after we were reestablishing on course avoiding the traffic that ATC assigned a heading. Most disturbing during the irregularities of moderate turbulence; TCAS RA with traffic conflicting the turn; and turbulence induced energy state beyond authority of the auto thrust; ATC tries to immediately give us a phone number to call instead of any assistance in weather or traffic guidance.The portion of the RNAV arrival; during the event; has 6.5 miles to descend up to 2;000 ft.; slow 40 kts.; and smart turn 51 degrees; coupled with a very changing tailwind of 150 kts. at 20;000 [ft.] slowing to 36 kts. at 10;000 [ft.] and the aircraft's FMS plotting the deceleration to approach mode between fixes thus requiring manual speed selected management; it is a very busy part of the arrival.Casual factors were night with St. Elmo's fire; lightning causing a very dark outside and requiring bright instrumentation that is difficult for the eye to follow in moderate turbulence. Possible other factors of AUTO FLT FCU 1 FAIL immediately after the event. ATC was extremely busy. I think another big factor was ATC confusion of what we were experiencing; due to the fact we were both task saturated controlling the aircraft and avoiding a mid-air collision ATC communication became a lower priority. With reduced traffic separation ATC becomes an integral part of every flight; if the manuals would include 'advise ATC' as a step; and clear guidance on priority of traffic avoidance in relationship to lateral guidance and where it is seen or sourced this could help."
Report_1_Synopsis: An Air Carrier pilot on an RNAV STAR at night in moderate turbulence and heavy rain reported taking evasive maneuvers to comply with a TCAS/RA advisory for conflicting traffic. They received no traffic advisory from ATC.

Report_1_Narrative: While we were on base leg on the RNP Y Runway 2 approach to MGGT [airport]; someone on the ground pointed a green laser and it flashed in the cockpit a few times; twice hitting me on the right eye. We were in between GT504 and GT503 with the aircraft fully configured; I was PM and since it was my first time flying into MGGT; I was looking outside to get a mental picture for future reference and situational awareness; trying to identify the runway;  when I saw a green laser beam being pointed at the aircraft; I called it out to the Captain and he kept his head down but I was hit twice on the right eye before I could go head down. I reported it to the Tower (in Spanish). The Captain asked me if I was OK; and I just mentioned that my eye felt drier than normal. (I've had the misfortune of being hit by a laser while flying before; so I knew the sensation). We continued to approach and landing without any further incident.Unfortunately; these types of events are almost impossible to stop; unless we wear protective eye gear; there is nothing we can do but lower our heads if a beam is being pointed to the aircraft.
Report_2_Narrative: While on approach; circling left arc to final; RNV Y 02; MGGT; about 145 knots and 2;000 feet AGL; FO (Non-Flying Pilot) observed a green laser coming from the low 10 o'clock position.  We continued approach to landing. FO reported it to ATC; giving them location; and Controller said it's been happening more often now and that they'll report it to authorities. I asked FO if he was OK and he said his eyes were drier than normal.Suggestions - Patrol the terminal area in vicinity of airport more often. Make area more sterile. Prosecute those who attempt to lase airplanes as they land at airports.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported a laser strike during approach to MGGT airport.

Report_1_Narrative: I was PF; hand-flying.  On departure; we were cleared to 10;000 feet.  Northbound on the SID; climbing through approximately 7;500; I increased pitch to avoid a small build-up off the nose.  Climbing thru approximately 8;800 feet; I realized that I was going to have a difficult time leveling off by 10;000 feet.  I asked the CA to advise ATC of the potential altitude excursion and aggressively; but smoothly; reduced pitch to level off.  I exceeded our assigned altitude by 450 feet; and promptly descended back to 10;000 feet.  ATC did not seem concerned by our deviation and cleared us to 16;000 feet.This was one of my first sequences after a 6-month leave of absence.  The CA is new to the airplane and new to the seat.  These factors contributed to our poor altitude SA and slow cross-check.Our threat-forward briefing focused on our lack of recent flying.  We needed to be even more vigilant to trap decision and execution errors.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported overshooting an assigned altitude during departure.

Report_1_Narrative: After landing in ZZZZ airport personnel took our temperatures with an ear thermometer.  He did not replace the tip with a new one nor did he clean it after each person.  This is unhealthy and unsanitary.  Use only a forehead thermometer.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported that a person checked their temperature after landing with an ear thermometer and did not replace the tip between checks.

Report_1_Narrative: We were given taxi instructions from the gate at GSO to Runway 23L via Kilo; K6; with expected delays due to traffic into ZZZ. We taxied down Kilo; but the sign for K6 was located 'after' the intersection of Kilo and K6 (not before); so we continued past the intersection; and then saw the late sign for K6. We stopped and asked ATC if we had in fact gone past K6; which they confirmed but said 'no problem'. We asked and received permission to taxi forward on Kilo and execute a 180 degree turn at the taxiway near the entrance to the cargo ramp; which GSO Ground approved; then taxied down Kilo again to K6; and waited for our flow time to ZZZ. The problem could have been easily avoided if the taxi intersection sign had been placed ahead of the K6 intersection (facing towards K5 vs. the cargo ramp); instead of after the intersection.I would suggest that the taxiway K6 sign be placed 'before' the intersection of Kilo and K6; so that a pilot taxiing down Kilo and looking for K6 would actually see it. Where it sits currently; past the actual K6 intersection; does no good to anyone; and is conducive to other pilots missing this intersection. A sign is cheap; compared to the potential problems.
Report_2_Narrative: During taxi at GSO we were taxiing to Runway 23L from the terminal via J3; K; and K6. We had passed taxiway K6 and continued straight on taxiway K. During the time we passed it; I was running the before takeoff checklist where I tried being outside of the airplane but the entire checklist is verifying the inside components are set and completed. The sun was also glaring in from my right side due to its position where I was partially blinded through the whole taxi even with sunglasses on. When I completed the checklist I looked up and saw the approach light systems for Runway 23L and looked behind and saw we missed K6. I advised Ground that we missed K6 and asked if we'd be able to make the turnaround we told them we'd have to wait until we were at the end and the Captain said we were able to so they said continue back K to K6 hold short Runway 23L. The Captain told me the sign for K6 is also after the taxiway and if you don't see that there isn't a taxiway past the sign it's already too late because you have to continue straight on K. When we taxied back; I wasn't able to confirm what sign was before K6 intersection. [Causes of the incident include] running the before takeoff checklist; sun glare on my side of cockpit; and the possibility that the K6 sign is after the taxiway. This was the last leg of a 4 day trip.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported the positioning and location of a taxiway sign K/K6 was confusing; which resulted in a taxiway incursion at GSO airport.

Report_1_Narrative: I have witnessed a potential for aircraft spoiler damage during flap rigging. When rig boards are installed on aircraft for a mechanical flap rigging the outboard flap rigging task requires you to turn on hydraulics. Even though the manual tells you to keep the spoiler lever at zero; I have witnessed them deploy if the aircraft has been powered up recently during its self-BITE (Built-in Test Equipment) checks. This can cause the spoiler to hit the rig board if installed. The manual does not tell you to pull circuit breakers for the spoilers during rigging; just to put a placard saying not to operate spoilers; but aircraft cannot read placards.[I suggest] a page that requires you to pull and lock out the spoiler circuit breakers. This will prevent any accidental deployment.
Report_1_Synopsis: Maintenance Technician reported potential for CRJ-700 aircraft spoiler damage during flap rigging.

Report_1_Narrative: We were given a recovery trip from PBI to ZZZ1. Upon arriving at the aircraft we had to defer the Nav database and the Jeppessen charts. We did just that which made us unable to do RNAV STARS; SIDS; routes etc. When the First Officer tried to get the clearance they gave us a RNAV SID and an AR route as that is what had been filed. The First Officer advised them we were unable to accept the route as we weren't able RNAV SIDS; STARS; routes etc. they informed us that our suffix indicated we were RNAV capable so we would have to refile correctly for us to go without using an RNAV SID. I called dispatch and explained it to the dispatcher and asked for it to be refiled with an appropriate route and suffix. It was refiled with a different route but the suffix still showed us as RNAV capable so clearance still wouldn't issue it. I called dispatch again and asked for it to be corrected and filed again. I made sure the third flight plan did come through with a different suffix before turning my attention to the passengers as they had now shown up. I greeted the owners and got them loaded and made sure the bags were loaded. During the baggage loading it became apparent I would have to increase the weight to match the weight of bags for the trip. I adjusted the weight in the waypoint app and waited for a valid release. The First Officer had briefed the passengers and we got into the cockpit and got ready to go while we waited for the release. We waited quite a while for the release as we began making phone calls and sending messages to try and see if the release was coming. Once I finally got through to the dispatcher on the phone and asked if the new release was coming soon. He responded 'what do you mean? You're in the air already.' I informed him that no we weren't we were still waiting on a valid release due to the weight change. Shortly after that we received a release from a different dispatcher which we verified the suffix was still the same as the last release and made our way to depart. A short time into the flight they gave us a reroute to a couple RNAV fixes and different route. We advised them we weren't RNAV and would like to remain on our route navigating by ground based navigation. It was at this point that I started to wonder if the suffix still wasn't correct for the airplanes condition. We continued without further issues. The entire process was truly exhausting having to review and keep straight in my head four releases and make sure they were done correctly; even if it wasn't already a new airplane as well as a recovery at the end of what was now becoming a long day. The last two releases being issued after the passengers were already onboard the airplane.
Report_1_Synopsis: Captain reported difficulty with dispatch getting the correct aircraft suffix filed on the flight plan.

Report_1_Narrative: While flying a VFR flight to LOM; I may have entered the Philadelphia Bravo airspace without clearance. I was communicating with PHL ATC on 124.35 for flight following. I was told to climb from 3;000 to 3;500 to avoid a TFR but don't remember specifically being cleared into the bravo airspace. Normally I would verify with ATC before entering the bravo if I was unsure. However; on this flight; my GPS equipment lost the GPS signal near Wilmington and I got distracted troubleshooting it. I was a few miles into the Bravo airspace when I realized I had not double checked the clearance. I was still talking with PHL ATC and they did not express any concerns with my location.
Report_1_Synopsis: GA pilot reported inadvertently entering PHL Class B airspace without a clearance due to distraction from having to troubleshoot the GPS system on the aircraft.

Report_1_Narrative: Randall Airport; 06N; in Middletown New York has often been a decent place to train. Runway 8 is noted as having a substantial displaced threshold and the winds on that day favored it. At 150 feet AGL my student elected to go-around and when I questioned why they said; 'I cannot read any of the runway markings nor see the displaced threshold.' They were right to do what they did. The runway is in a sad state of repairs with large cracks and areas of heaving. But worse; the paint is so faded that an unsafe landing could be made without even knowing it on the displaced threshold(s) especially on Runway 8. I implore the appropriate people be contacted so the owner/operator of this field can do some maintenance on this field to keep it open; safe; and operational.
Report_1_Synopsis: Instructor pilot reported the runway and runway numbers are faded and difficult to see at 06N airport.

Report_1_Narrative: I decided to do some practice approaches with my safety pilot. I got gas at ZZZ1 and it was a direct line from there for the approach into ZZZ so I did that one first. I got the weather; which was favoring the opposite direction; and changed to the advisory frequency. Another airplane announced that it was on the the approach for Runway XX but was farther out than we were. I announced that I was on the approach for Runway XY and would break off early. There was a lot of chatter on the radio both at ZZZ and at other airports that shared that frequency. We heard someone else mention Runway XX but couldn't make out what they were doing. I broke off the approach at about 800 ft. and 2 miles from the end of the runway as I knew I'd be far from the aircraft on the opposite approach. That's when my safety pilot saw the near miss plane that had departed Runway XX at some point. We never heard them announce taking off or on upwind and they did not show up on ADS-B (Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast). We immediately turned left for the missed but were past them by that point. After we passed them and announced the missed; the pilot of the other aircraft said something on the radio that I couldn't make out.Contributing factors were me continuing an approach in the wrong direction longer than I should have given the heavy chatter on the radio. The other aircraft was also not announcing enough or not announcing correctly or getting stepped on by other chatter or otherwise unintelligible. Another contributing factor was the other aircraft not having ADS-B Out installed. It wasn't required there but it would have greatly helped avoid the near miss. Given that we did hear another mention of Runway XX; I should have asked for their position since I didn't hear it the first time. In the future; I will break off opposite direction approaches much sooner when there is other traffic in the vicinity.
Report_1_Synopsis: A pilot on final approach to a non towered airport reported a near miss with an aircraft departing the opposite direction runway.

Report_1_Narrative: To keep current; I try to fly at least one hour a month. I confirmed that there was 15 gallons in each tank which would allow for 3 hours for an anticipated flight of less than 2. I did 8 landings at 3 airports and was on my last 10 mile leg to home base. About 1.5 hours. Because of failure to change the fuel selector to both; the engine died during low level cruise. I [selected and checked] carburetor heat; mags and gas but the engine did not start for unknown reasons. I landed in a farm field with no injuries; property damage and no damage to the airplane as determined by the club mechanic.  Lack of experience in type. This the only plane that requires leaving the fuel on right only that I have flown. I was interrupted during the preflight; I should have stated over again. I should practice emergency procedures more often.
Report_1_Synopsis: Cessna pilot reported landing in a field following an engine failure related to fuel mismanagement.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Situational Awareness; Time Pressure; Communication Breakdown; Distraction
Report_1_Narrative: I departed 52F from runway 35 for a straight out VFR climb enroute to ZZZ for pattern work. After departure; and during the initial climb; I visually observed a powered parachute maneuvering at approximately 1;200 feet MSL on the extended straight out departure path from 52F.  I then observed a second powered parachute operating at my current altitude of 1;500 feet MSL directly in my flight path (altitudes later crosschecked from my ForeFlight flight path replay). Since the second powered parachute was head-on I did not see him until the last minute.  I was forced to make an abrupt maneuver to the left (west) to avoid a midair collision.  I have since learned from other pilots based at 52F that this is a frequent occurrence in all areas around 52F; and at times powered parachutes have operated within the lateral and vertical traffic pattern boundaries of 52F; which seems to be contrary to 14 CFR part 103.13(a) and (b).  In addition; this type of operation is prohibited at 52F per the remarks section of the A/FD.  These types of operations are less regulated than drones and drone operators.  I am concerned that if allowed to continue without some type of mitigation or FAA intervention that it is only a matter of time before there is an accident. I would suggest either requiring some kind of formal training/testing/checking for powered parachutes or prohibiting these operations under (not just within) the all Class B airspace.
Report_1_Synopsis: GA pilot reported a NMAC with a powered parachute at 52F airport. Reportedly; this is a common occurrence around this airport.

Report_1_Narrative: While in the cruise portion of my flight on an IFR flight plan I was alerted by ATC of traffic converging same altitude. I was on a NE (northeast) heading but was instructed by ATC to fly at 6;000 ft. The traffic was on a SE (southeast) heading also at 6;000 ft. descending for ZZZ. Due to me being on an IFR flight plan I did not deviate altitude or heading. The traffic descending was descending apparently at a very slow rate. ATC provided traffic alert but did not suggest new heading or altitude. When I had the traffic in sight about 200 ft. below me and very close I elected to climb based on my traffic message from my G1000 avionics with TIS-B (Traffic Information Service - Broadcast). At my altitude of 6;200 ft. the traffic passed below me by 500 ft. ATC was very busy but I should [have] queried them for vectors [or] altitude change earlier so I would not have to take action on my own. ATC did not complain about my momentary altitude deviation.
Report_1_Synopsis: SR22 pilot on an IFR flight plan reported taking evasive action to avoid another aircraft that was 500 feet below him.

Report_1_Narrative: At XA:28Z; Aircraft X checked on the frequency asking for VFR flight following in the vicinity of ZZZ. He was given a beacon code and I displayed a data block on the radar scope; waiting for it to track up. After a minute I told the pilot that I did not have radar contact; and I didn't have a target in the area he stated. I verified his code and location; and had him reset his transponder after another minute went by. At XA:31Z I told him it might be necessary for him to climb before I could establish radar contact. He reported that he was starting a climb to 7;000 feet.One minute after he started his climb; at XA:32Z; I picked up a primary target in the area the pilot reported. I tried to verify the position of the primary target; but the pilot just responded that he was showing zero oil pressure and having electrical issues. As he was saying this; the data block correlated to the code and I radar identified Aircraft X and verified his location. My standard practice; something that I did less than ten minutes prior; is to radar identify; verify location and altitude; and give altimeter. I do it every time; and in that order. When I radar identified Aircraft X; there was no Mode C data; so I asked him to report his altitude. He reported that he was climbing to 7;000 feet and asked for help to get into ZZZ; he was showing zero on his oil pressure. I didn't circle back to the altimeter at this time.I issued Aircraft X a heading to set him up for a pattern into ZZZ. If his engine was about to quit; I wanted him lined up for an airport; not guessing what was below him. I told the CIC I was working a special aircraft; and the OM was quickly in the area. I didn't feel it was in good judgement to add on to the pilot's stress level by pointing out that he was experiencing an urgent situation. It was being handled as such.He asked as he rolled out if he was on the correct heading. I advised that he was 20 degrees off course; and that he should correct. He told me he was using his backup compass; due to electrical failure. That information made a lot of sense at that moment. The backup compass is a magnetic compass. It's one that bounces around as you turn it. The magnetic compass will continue to turn past the heading and then bounce back and correct as the airplane levels off and the compass stabilizes. This is something that an IFR rated pilot would be more knowledgeable about. No gyro turns; or turns with only the backup compass were part of my IFR certificate training. Due to this; I decided to give him small turns that would create an arc to final; and help him maintain better control and orientation.I told him to descend to 5;000 ft. and that I should still have radar contact at that altitude. He responded that believed he'd be able to poke through. I knew it would be minimal conditions; I still believed getting the aircraft set up for a runway was the safest places. As I gave him a turn to the left he stated that he was going to get into the clouds. I asked if he and the aircraft were IFR qualified. He said they were not. I asked if he could maintain VFR conditions. It sounded like he was trying; but didn't seem sure that he would.I told Aircraft X that he could continue down to 4;000 feet and gave him a heading to get him turned more toward the airport. About that time at XA:39Z; just eleven minutes into the situation; an aircraft inbound for ZZZ1 checked on. I issued the ZZZ1 altimeter. This aircraft would end up being held out for the [situation]. I then told Aircraft X he could descend at his discretion to 3;900 feet; but that was the minimum enroute altitude in the area; and the lowest I was comfortable advising him. He said he was starting to poke through at 4;100 feet. I gave him the position and distance of ZZZ1. He responded that he could see some ground.I had him continue his gradual left turn but saw a much more aggressive turn on the radar. I asked if he was circling down to stay in VFR conditions. He said he saw bases at 3;800 feet and it was an unintentional 360. Based on what the radar showed; it was not a controlled maneuver; and probably resulted from an unusual attitude due to spatial disorientation. I asked him to regain level flight; as to maintain control of the aircraft and not get into another unusual attitude. I asked him his altitude; he responded 3;680 [feet]. Up until this uncontrolled maneuver; every report was that he was in marginal conditions; but always seemed to have some visual capabilities. At this point the inability to maintain VFR was imminent.The aircraft showed a northeast heading; I asked him to make a slow turn. Being an IFR rated pilot myself; and seeing how easily he became disoriented already; I wanted to avoid a stall; spin or turning over the aircraft. In the clouds a turn can make your body feel like you are descending; and a climb can make your body think you are turning. A more abrupt climb or turn only magnifies this effect. At XA:43Z as I maintained focus on keeping the pilot's wings level; I offered the option of climbing back up into VFR conditions. He was in favor of the idea. He added that the engine had been running fine; and believed the zero oil pressure reading to be due to electrical issue; not engine issues. With that information I immediately reassessed the IFR conditions to be the most hazardous conditions in the situation.I saw the aircraft again start a west turn that seemed to increase in rate. I gave the aircraft his location and his observed turn. I advised that he level off and focus on flying straight and level. He did not respond. The maneuver seemed unstable and I tried to relay that he needed to get wings level; then start climbing slowly. Anything aggressive would cause greater disorientation. He said the engine was running fine now; no longer a concern. I told him that we believed it to be clear in ZZZ2; ZZZ3; and ZZZ4. He said that sounds nice. I wanted to get him into ZZZ3 if it was in fact clear. It was much closer; and based on his workload; fatigue due to stress; and equipment issues; I wanted him in the air the least amount of time possible. The CIC or the OM; I don't remember which; went up to the weather desk to get the most complete weather information available. Other controllers were also pulling weather at surrounding airports. I was focused on getting Aircraft X oriented and into VMC.I told him to fly his present heading and start a climb; advising that there was no traffic ahead. He responded that he was having trouble keeping his wings level. I advised back to straight and level and asked his altitude. The climb was giving him a sensation of turning and he was having trouble overcoming that. I should have advised him to focus on the instruments over his own sensations; but I did not think of it at the time.He said he was at 4;020 feet. I said give me level straight flight and then we'll start a slow climb. I wanted him to remain calm and know that we were going to work through it. He did not answer. Seeing what appeared to be straight flight on the radar scope I advised a shallow climb. He said he was trying to keep the wings level. At that point a VFR aircraft departing ZZZ1 was checking in. I called the traffic to that aircraft; advised the altitude was unknown; and asked Aircraft X to say his altitude. He did not immediately answer. Instead another aircraft keyed up; saying the other aircraft didn't look good on his TCAS and he needed to level his wings. Aircraft X then responded; he pulled into a stall; but was starting back up. I advised him to take it slow. At that point Aircraft Y verified ZZZ2 to be clear. I asked if Aircraft X was staying level. He said yes; 5;000 feet and seeing sunlight. I saw another turn on radar and had him level his wings once again. A minute later he reported on top of clouds and level. I told him maintain level flight; catch his breath; and if there were any airports he wanted to try to get to; we would get the weather for him. In my experience; it was best to remind him that he could exhale. He still needed to have the ability to fly the rest of his flight with electrical issues. I also offered him the opportunity to request an alternate airport. He had equipment that most likely needed to be repaired or replaced. I didn't want to send him somewhere that he'd get stuck. Aircraft X was maintaining a southeast heading and I asked him his altitude. He responded; 5;860 feet. I offered again; ZZZ2; ZZZ3; and ZZZ4. The pilot was happy with ZZZ2 because it was reported clear. I gave a heading for him to fly that would get him started turning more towards either airport as I waited for the weather information. I recommended going to ZZZ3 because it was the closest. The pilot agreed that ZZZ3 would be his first choice; then ZZZ2. Immediately as he said that; the information was back from the weather desk and I relayed it to the pilot. He said he wanted to shoot for ZZZ2 because it was clear and ZZZ3 was overcast. I gave a few more heading changes and turns to get him direct to ZZZ2. I also lost radar contact on him a minute later as well. I received another report that he should expect to be clear of the west edge of the moving weather some time before ZZZ2; and passed that along. I advised him that he appeared right on course; and I was relieved at XB:08Z.Ten minutes later; while talking to the relieving controller; the pilot thanked us all for the help he received and said he was feeling the love. He even asked to get a forwarding address to send me a bottle of good scotch. Additionally; when calling the facility from the ground; the pilot was very thankful for the services he received. He informed the OM that he had to change pants when he landed; and again wanted to send a thank you bottle for getting him to safety. It was not apparent at the beginning of the situation that the engine oil reading was due to an electrical issue. It was possible that it could have been a number of different factors; but I knew that he could lose his engine at any moment; and it may not sound rough right away. I wanted him to get lined up for a runway as safely and quickly as possible. I gave him the option to get down below the bases; but should have emphasized to maintain VFR; even though it is the pilot's responsibility. During a stressful [situation]; that would be a good reminder to give the pilot. Once the pilot gained confidence that the engine was running properly; I did everything in my power; and with all of my flight experience to keep the pilot focused on not getting into an unrecoverable condition; while maneuvering safely into VMC.During an imminent [hazard]; controllers have to make judgement calls on what is the most prudent and time critical course of action. Access to checklists during these situations would ensure that all services are provided. Controllers could check that they had provided all of the information possible without taking as much attention away from the imminent safety issue. An easier to use weather reporting system would ensure more weather reports are forwarded along from controllers. The current GI method can be tedious and the tie up keyboard use during busier sessions. ERIDS (En Route Information Display System) offers weather reporting by tapping on the information and hitting send. Using this system would increase the efficiency and result in more weather reports being available. Even just having paper weather slips that controllers can hand to a supervisor would improve efficiency.A working knowledge of flight instruments and factors of flight would allow better assistance to pilots in [hazardous] situations. Recurrent training that focuses on best practices during imminent situations would enhance controllers on seldom used skills.
Report_1_Synopsis: Center Controller reported an aircraft that was having equipment problems; a VFR pilot in IMC and how the controller helped the aircraft get on the ground safely.

Report_1_Narrative: On the Arrival into ONT SoCal Approach assigned vectors to sequence behind a 747. We were vectored directly behind and above the preceding 747 for 26L when we were cleared for the visual approach to 26R. ATC advised to maintain visual separation. At that point; due to concerns of descending behind the heavy aircraft; I offset right of course and attempted to parallel the 747. My intention was to remain clear of the 747's wake vortices. As we continued the approach and began to converge with the other aircraft; ONT Tower issued clearance to S-turn to the right if necessary. At that point we were too close to the runway to make any effective maneuvers and still maintain a stabilized approach. We then received a 'Descend' RA and continued descending on the visual approach to 26R while the adjacent aircraft executed a climb and go-around from 26L. In retrospect I believe a better course of action would have been to discontinue the visual approach or ask for delay vectors to increase separation from the heavy aircraft. ATC should have issued more realistic vectors to sequence us further behind the 747.
Report_2_Narrative: Descending on the Arrival into ONT; SoCal Approach Control gave a maintain current HDG [instruction]. We visually acquired a 747 at our 12 o'clock position approximately 5 NMs. SoCal then gave us a right turn to a 140 HDG; then subsequently a 170 HDG that placed us at the 6 o'clock position of the 747 approximately 5 NMs behind. Once established on the 170 HDG; SoCal cleared us and the 747 visual approaches; 747 to Runway 26L and us to 26R and told us 'Caution wake turbulence and maintain visual separation with the 747'. The Captain did not want to be in a position to be at a 45 degree angle behind the 747; which would've increased the chances of getting into the wake of the 747; so as we were descending for the approach we received a descend RA and Aircraft Y executed a go-around for a climb RA. When we noticed that it would be challenging to do the approach and simultaneously staying out if the heavy aircraft's wake turbulence; should've asked the Controller for a vector or turn before starting the final portion of the approach.
Report_1_Synopsis: B737 flight crew reported receiving an RA on approach.

Report_1_Narrative: I was the Pilot Flying. On climb-out I noticed my electric trim was not working. The First Officer's electric trim was also inoperative. We leveled off to assess the situation and complete the QRH checklist. We elected to return to ZZZ.
