Report_1_Narrative: Our alternate was ZZZ2 exactly because ZZZ3; ZZZ4; ZZZ5; and ZZZ6 were not suitable weather-wise. The original flight plan had fuel to fly ZZZ-ZZZ1; go-around and fly to our alternate of ZZZ2 landing with a fairly standard REMF; as I recall; certainly not enough fuel to shoot a second approach in ZZZ1 and comfortably divert to ZZZ2.This was our third and final leg of the day; following a ZZZ-ZZZ7 turn. It was our second day of a three-day trip and we felt reasonably alert. If we had to divert to ZZZ2; I suspect we would have been close to timing out in our block time; from a passenger standpoint; ZZZ2 made a lot of sense with the ability to re-crew in a base. By the time we blocked in ZZZ1 we had completed 7:30 actual flight time. I know I was tired at the end of the day. Time compression in ZZZ between second and third leg.1. The flight plan for our final leg was not yet available for downloading and consideration before top of descent ZZZ7-ZZZ (leg #2). Flight planning on the ground felt very time compressed.2. We were switching aircraft in ZZZ.3. We were supposed to have been boarded crew meals for our second leg (ZZZ7-ZZZ) but for some odd reason; the FO's hot meal was boarded and I was offered a hodge-podge of a snack box; beef jerky; a cookie; three dried apricots and a packet of honey. I snacked on that offering but needed to find a real meal back in ZZZ between flights.4. Please appreciate the 64 minutes on the ground is from parking brake set on Flight number; (inbound flight); complete the parking checklist; collect our belongings;  traipse over to a different gate (thankfully; the gates were close); download and review: Flight Number's OFP; NOTAMs; and aircraft maintenance and history; review weather on WSI iPad app; pre-flight a new aircraft; load and check the FMC; brief flight attendants especially on the weather conditions; receive an ATC clearance; departure brief between pilots; accomplish both the pre-flight checklist and before push checklist; and then release the parking brake for push-back.Given the lower ceilings and reduced visibility with snow-rain mix and strong direct gusty crosswinds in the TAF I felt it prudent to add contingency fuel. I called our dispatcher at the gate in ZZZ and we agreed to add approximately 30 minutes of fuel; specifically; 3;000 pounds. I had hoped that our dispatcher was cognizant the conditions forecast in ZZZ1 warranted more consideration than a milk-run; day; VFR landing; but truthfully; I had a whisper of uneasy misgivings. Perhaps I felt this was the fuel plan SABRE popped out and there could have been more... more human QA to it... perhaps. Then again; maybe it was nothing... yet the voice in the back of my mind wasn't letting up. Something felt unsettled. Was our dispatcher a little susceptible to Automation and Anchoring Bias... was our dispatcher's Situational Awareness appropriately elevated? Was her Review/Monitor/Predict loop firing on all cylinders? I decided: 'I'll set it aside for now--relax; captain--it's probably nothing.' (spoiler alert: it turned out to be nothing but the ambiguity of whether it was or not; before and during the flight was distracting.)I do not have the ATIS but I did reconstruct the conditions from a historical AWOS archive01 XA:51Z: 330/19G26 6SM -RASN BR BKN009 OVC016 02/01 A29.60 PK WND 3303301 XB:51Z: 330/18G27 3SM -SN BR BKN008 OVC013 02/01 A29.61 PK WND 3203201 XC:06Z: 330/16G29 3SM -SN BR BKN010 OVC015 02/00 A29.61 PK WND 3202901 XC:14Z: 320/16G24 2-1/2SM -SN BR BKN008 OVC 013 02/00 A29.61 PK WND 3202901 XC:23Z: 320/14G28 1-3/4SM -SN BR OVC010 01/00 A29.61 PK WND 3202901 XC:30Z: 330/18G22 1-3/4SM -SN BR BKN008 OVC012 01/00 A 29.61 PK WND 32029The ATIS stated ILS RWY XXL and RCC (Runway Condition Code) 5/5/5 at XJ:00Z; XXR/YYL and XY/YX CLSD; and variousCLSD taxiways. The RCC time stamp of XJ:Z caught my attention as being roughly 16+ hours old.[Aircraft type] landing crosswind component 'guidelines' in the Flight Manual Limitations Chapter:RCC 5 and 6: 40 knotsRCC 4: 35 knotsRCC 3: 25 knots'NOTE: The crosswind guidelines presented...... The use of these guidelines should be based on the current weather conditions and thepilot's ability and experience level.'Even with the recent uptick in flying the overwhelming majority of us are feeling 'rusty'. Generally; with my XX+ years flying experience it seems to come back fairly quickly but I definitely don't feel the same high level of finesse as I did a year ago. I'm aware of it; very aware. I'm working diligently to trap the errors and as minor as they seem there are more of them.Actively seeking and countering threats; setting the right tone on the flight deck; and ensuring we are working well with dispatch these are some of the best tools we have. Overconfidence bias especially in challenging conditions while none of us are flying as much as we usually do is probably at the top of the list. Going the extra step of resolving seemingly small ambiguities seems especially appropriate right now. Plan continuation bias; expectancy bias; and optimism bias creep into the mix a little more insidiously than usual. The ever-present threat of complacency has absolutely not waned. I wonder is Dispatch in the same boat? I suspect so. I want to be cognizant and understanding of that likelihood--we are a team and we need to lift each other up.A little over an hour prior to touchdown we began planning our ILS runway XX approach and landing with the most current conditions at the time. We reviewed the NOTAMs; assiduously marking up the myriad of closed taxiways on our -9 pages. We pulled landing performance data and reviewed it intently. With the strong direct and gusty crosswinds we might have preferred a flaps 40 landing on Runway YX but it was closed.I felt the RCC 5/5/5 at XJ:00Z (16+ hours old) was a remnant and if we just encouraged dispatch to make a call to ZZZ1 Tower; we could get something much more useful; more akin to an hourly observation. Actively countering the ambiguity of a very stale RCC given the worsening weather conditions. Making allowance that Dispatch is planning and monitoring somewhere between several and a small slew of flights they aren't going to catch everything. The ACARS reply from 'X Dispatch' for an updated RCC:'ZZZ1 CITY OPS SAYS 5/5/5.THEY WON'T UPDATE THE NOTAM/FICON UNTIL THERE IS SOMETHING SIGNIFICANT TO UPDATE.'Ambiguity not resolved. Concern we were being led down a path... heightened.With time for more nuanced decision points running out; I replied to X Dispatch:'Name; JUST WANT US ALL TO HAVE THE SAME UNDERSTANDING ABOUT HOW CRITICAL I VIEW A CURRENT AND ACCURATE FICON* WITH THE GUSTY DIRECT CROSSWIND TEMP/DP 02/01... I WILL NOT ATTEMPT A LANDING WITHOUT IT. IS THE 5/5/5 FROM XJ:00Z OR HAVE THEY MEASURED IT MORE RECENTLY... I WILL NOT ALLOW A GREEN BAY OFF THE ENDCOMPLACENCY FROM ZZZ1 CITY OPS TO SUFFICE. PLS INFO FODM OF THIS'(*FICON; I should have used 'RCC' instead)X Dispatch reply:'OKAY.I GOT THE [Flight Operations Manager] IN ON A CALL TO ZZZ1 TOWER. FODM IS UP TO SPEED ON THE CONCERN. THEY REPORTED: RWY XXL AT XS:54Z. 5/5/5. 100 PCT WET.AGAIN; THEY DO NOT ANTICIPATE TO UPDATE UNLESS THERE IS AN ACCUMULATION ON THE RUNWAY OR ANOTHER CHANGE IN CONDITION.'Did I feel like we were pushing a rope? Yes. Yes; I did. I felt like we were being dismissed and my confidence in X Dispatch was significantly diminished. I felt like X Dispatch was not proactively leaning forward in the saddle and was content to accept whatever ZZZ1 City Ops said. Rather than feeling supported; rather than feeling like the increased risk was being adequately considered and mitigated; I felt a certain inappropriate nonchalance had insidiously permeated. I feel like Ihad to kick up a ruckus to finally get an RCC 5/5/5 at XC:00Z--as the XS:54Z RCC was still 7-ish hours old... DURING a RASN event. Finally; I feel like the fact that nothing bad happened adds to the confirmation bias that it was much ado about nothing... right up until it's not nothing. And 'Not Nothing' happens in a blazingly fast moment.What could I have done differently and more effectively?I should have called X Dispatch from ZZZ7 on leg #2; asking her to work up our leg #3 early--I could have alleviated the time compression I felt on the ground in ZZZ.In retrospect; I wish I had noted the XJ:00Z RCC from the ATIS available in either FD Pro X or just pulled the ZZZ1 ATIS on ACARS before pushing and added resolving the stale RCC to the fuel increase phone call with X Dispatch.I should have used 'X' words in the ACARS messages with dispatch to convey the level of my unease.I should have started descent planning and landing in those conditions at Top of Climb (TOC) to allow more time to get 'the ball rolling'.I should have taken the time to call after the flight; to debrief with our dispatcher... really wish I had done that.Ongoing concerns/questionsX Dispatch:1. How early can I ask for a flight to be planned?2. What fuel contingency plan is appropriate in these meteorological conditions for delayed arrival (E.G.; holding while treating the runway) or the preceding aircraft doesn't clear the runway in a timely manner or a gusty wind event causes an unstabilized approach condition? To name but a few possibilities...3. What could I have done differently from X Dispatch's perspective? I would like the feedback to make me a better Captain.ATC:1. How long before an RCC gets updated? Is there an upper number of hours? 2 hours? 36 hours?2. In these particular conditions of strong gusty crosswinds and rain snow mix; what is an appropriate update interval to give us 'end-users' a reasonable level of confidence in the data?3. How are RCCs actually determined?I am going to end this unusual report with a few words from a recently would-have-been furloughed-but-took-advantage-of-voluntary-separation-program and much-liked coworker. It's important to recognize that Name was an administrative co-worker. He's not a pilot himself but he certainly recognized how important his part in the team mattered. We could all profit from his example. 'I made it my goal to make sure every pilot left the flight planning area with a clear head. No matter what issue they had coming in the door; when they went out to fly that issue was taken care of or they knew that I would do my best to take care of it and follow up with them on itsoutcome. I did not want to be the one to cause a distraction. I was proud to be the one who cleaned up the distractions.''...cleaned up distractions' ... Indeed.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported weather and associated planning issues at many airports and in particular one that was an alternate for the flight.

Report_1_Narrative: After landing on Runway 31 we exited at taxiway Tango. We told Ground Control we were going to gate. Ground Control instructed us to 'turn left on Bravo; right on Lima; taxi to the gate.' I have a lot of experience operating out of LGA; however; I have not landed there since the new terminal was built. I taxied south on Bravo and I identified taxiway Lima. It was dark and the new terminal is very bright. I made the right turn on Lima and saw gate straight ahead. I taxied toward the gate and suddenly; out of the darkness in front of me I noticed multiple; 2-3 foot tall; UNLIGHTED taxiway edge posts. I immediately stopped the aircraft and was able to make a hard left turn to barely avoid hitting the posts. It immediately became apparent that taxiway Lima is actually on about a 45 degree angle from off of taxiway Bravo vs what I thought was a 90 degree right turn. For whatever reason; there is an UNLIGHTED; 'false island' between Taxiway Lima and the ramp. Due to the conditions of darkness; a very bright new terminal and gate area; and unlighted taxiway edge posts; it was very easy for me to turn right onto taxiway Lima and then focus on taxiing straight ahead to gate right through the 'island.'
Report_1_Synopsis: Captain reported on night taxi to gate; crew nearly hit unlit taxiway edge posts which are difficult to see due to bright terminal lights at LGA airport.

Report_1_Narrative: I am writing this report due to the potential this type of incident has to distract aircrew; particularly the pilots.   I believe Purser X; was attempting to implement her own personal mask policy with respect to eating and drinking.  Even though I complied with her excessive demands after our first encounter; she immediately escalated the issue and contacted the flight crew (because I asked her name); thereby creating a potential distraction to the flight crew.Summary of events follows:  A couple of minutes after being served a drink; I was actively drinking and had my mask down.  Purser X; came by only a few minutes later and said I had to put my mask up.  I told her I was actively drinking and I had actually just set the cup down.  She said my mask had to be replaced between each sip.  I identified myself as an employee and told her I disagreed with her interpretation of the policy.  Of note; I have never had a Flight Attendant make such an assertion before.  I told her I was actively drinking and she said; that what I was doing was not allowed and reiterated; I had to put my mask up between sips.  She also immediately threatened to 'Go to the pilots' when I challenged her interpretation. I complied with her dictate; though I believed it to be errant; and put my mask up; dropping it only between sips of my drink thereafter.  Of note; the Flight Attendant deadheading adjacent to me left his mask down for long periods of time while eating and drinking; so it appears he had the same opinion as I did.  Afterwards; when she passed back by; I asked her if she would give me her name as I felt I needed to report this incident; since she threatened to go to the pilots and I considered her interpretation of the policy to be errant.  She refused to give me her name and said she was ' Going to the pilots' now; because I asked her name.   If Airline X intended her rule to be the standard; then I'm certain Airline X would specifically state that mask must be replaced between sips and bites as opposed to actively drinking or eating.  I reread the policy and I still believe her interpretation is errant.  I also checked with the ZZZ Chief Pilot office and they also believe there is nothing to support her interpretation of the mask policy.In summary; I believe her actions; specifically developing her own policy and her abrasive engagement has the high potential of creating additional conflicts with passengers and unnecessary distractions to the cockpit.
Report_1_Synopsis: First Officer who was deadheading reported a disagreement with a Flight Attendant regarding interpretation of mask policy.

Report_1_Narrative: I inadvertently pushed back from the gate without a final Dangerous Goods summary because I mistook a secondary planned summary to indicate that no Hazmat was loaded. Another reason that I hastily made my assumption was because we don't ever receive secondary planned DG summaries. We only get a final summary after the initial planned summary. Thankfully; due to ramp congestion; we did receive a final Dangerous Goods summary prior to taxi.There are a couple of key notes added into the software log stating that a ramp scanner deleted the Hazmat at close out.
Report_1_Synopsis: B-757 Captain reported pushback from departure gate without required Hazmat Final DG Summary. DG Summary was received during pushback traffic delay.

Report_1_Narrative: Gate agent was ready for early push. Planned Dangerous Goods was printed and noted. Cabin was secured and ground crew ready to push 10 mins early. Checklist completed and push back clearance received; as the IRO I was checking all the documents as many were being printed as we began push. I noticed that we had not received the final DG. The Captain stopped the push and we called operations. Final DG showed up right away and continued push with out further issues.
Report_2_Narrative: Gate agent came up early said they were ready for push. I think that we were caught off guard by the agent saying they were ready that early. We pushed early. The IRO was cleaning up the paperwork and noticed we did not have the final DG summary. We had only pushed a few yards; the Captain stopped the push. We notified ground and called ops to ask about the final DG Summary. As we were talking to ops; the final DG Summary printed out. We called ground and continued the push without incident.
Report_1_Synopsis: B-787 First Officer reported pushback initiated from gate without required Final Dangerous Goods Report. Documents received after momentary delay.

Report_1_Narrative: Arrived at the airport at XA:45. The station representative met us advising he had just received an email further pushing our departure back to XE:00. He also advised they were unsure as to whether there were even parts on hand to repair the aircraft correctly and wondered if it would even depart that day. We settled in the crew rest area to wait and see. At XC:51; I received a call from a Company A representative asking how we felt and if we were still good to fly. They said Maintenance advised they would have the plane fixed in about an hour. We advised we were good to go. I then called Dispatch to advise and keep them in the loop. The Dispatcher emailed us release revision 2. We reviewed it and headed out to the aircraft. As we arrived outside the aircraft; Maintenance was still aboard working on the aircraft. At XD:35; Maintenance finished with the aircraft. We then boarded the aircraft to find it on battery power and the GPU (Ground Power Unit) running but the over voltage warning light indicator on. We flagged down personnel to get a new GPU. At XD:45 the APU (Auxiliary Power Unit) was started. The replacement GPU arrived as the APU completed powering up. We then began our preflight. At XE:20; the preflight was finished. At XE:35; Maintenance finished the logbook and maintenance brief. We then blocked out. During this time I became aware of Company A Maintenance Control pressuring the on-site Company B maintenance personnel to 'line out' the other maintenance personnel's write-up stating 'Undocumented speed tape found concealing stripped and unsecured mounting screw to extruded MCD (Main Cabin Door) Manual Vent Door Drive (Pressure Vessel) cover panel'. This was found in Aircraft X's logbook. Maintenance Control wanted this done so as not to draw scrutiny to it by the FAA. Thankfully and appreciatively the Company B Mechanic refused to assist in this cover-up.This is the consistent behavior I have observed from the pressure Company C exerts on this operation to dispatch the aircraft on time at all costs. In the past several years I have submitted safety reports and FCRs (Flight Crew Reports) observing willful and wanton disregard of DDG (Dispatch Deviation Guide) procedures plainly written out. I've listened to Maintenance Control; on speakerphone; tell an on-site mechanic to 'Write whatever the hell makes the pilot happy to get that damn thing out of there.' I've had Maintenance Control denigrate me for not immediately pulling back into the gate with a problem but instead I followed procedure and called Dispatch for a three-way call with the problem. I've observed on numerous occasions and numerous stations Company B mechanics back-dooring the fuel sheets to make the numbers work instead of obtaining the fuel density to compute the numbers correctly to check the accuracy of the fueling process. I've had Company B mechanics on my jump seat share experiences of Maintenance Control telling them to check good" a system without actually testing the system. Thankfully as well; those mechanics told Maintenance Control their tickets were more important to them than their jobs. Both of those mechanics have since left Company B for more ethical workplace environments.My observation is the attitude in Maintenance Control is a mixture of arrogance and fear-driven to kowtow to this pressure. The pressure is passed down the chain from Company C to the executive level to the middle managers to the line supervisors to the line workers. This culture is a very dangerous one. It severely erodes the necessary safety and trust in the process required for it to work as it is designed. I have personally had so many of these instances where I have found incorrectly complied with DDG procedures both by blatant disregard and ignorance. I and several of my colleagues have experienced an extreme increase in time and concern when reviewing the log and maintenance procedures. I personally am not trained as a mechanic. The amount of items that we can see and have found greatly concerns us. Our concern is the amount of Maintenance egregious violations and errors we can see are so numerous and regular; how safe; complete; and compliant is the work; like the heavy checks and line maintenance behind the panels and cowlings that we cannot see. Our fear is this is going to lead to injuries; loss of life; and more aircraft damage and hull losses. The solution is straight forward and already established. Enforce strict adherence to maintaining the aircraft and equipment as directed by our FAA-approved maintenance program."
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Captain reported non-adherence to proper aircraft maintenance procedures.

Report_1_Narrative: I have been on more than one flight scheduled to DH to ZZZZ.  Of the X # of DH FA crewmembers NOT ONE of them was aware of the required Country X medical tracking system to come and help the FA crew get the system installed and the form completed.  On the other flights; [the FA department] failed to respond to our request. As a result; the other pilots and I had to take time to instruct the flight attendants on the process.  The time we took to do this took away from the time we had to do our flight duties and resulted in a flight departure delay.  The set up and function of this program does not allow it to be downloaded and permission for entry obtained while in-flight.  I have heard everything from 'I don't think we need that;' 'I will just do it inflight;' and the best 'I don't read the email messages.' (This from the FA who was detained). In any case it is not the job of the flight deck crew to instruct the FA group something of this nature.   If a crewmember is caught without this tracking system; it exposes the whole crew to medical detention. The in-flight group needs to take responsibility for ensuring the FA group has the proper tools and is following the proper guidelines.  I believe for the immediate future a station manager needs to meet each departing crew and ensure that they have the tracking system on a device and it has been properly filled out. They also need to ensure the FA group is aware of the requirement of a daily health submission. Those who fail to comply with this Country's government procedure jeopardizes our right to operate in this Country.  The hotel hands out a form which in part states that if you are caught outside your allowed radius of operation; your airline may lose its right to fly to this Country. The same rule applies to not having the tracking system on arrive or not submitting a daily health check.Cause - Lack of oversight and education from the inflight group.  Lack of following procedures from FA group.  I have to wonder if this important item is missed; what else are they missing?Each DH crew should be met at the gate by an in-flight Supervisor who ensures that the app is installed and a health check complete.  Failure to comply should result in being sent home without pay. Individual FA who do not read company Email messages should be put on a monitor system to ensure the start reading messages and complying with company procedures.  I would like a response; other than the usual thanks for the report; it has been accepted we are looking into it.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier pilot reported problems flying into a specific country relating to COVID-19.

Report_1_Narrative: I take full responsibility for this altitude deviation.  We were in the chocks at ZZZ and there was a slight reroute to ZZZZ.  The FO X said it would not load in the FMC; but FO loaded manually.  FO said the same thing happened on the last flight also into ZZZZ.   I had flown down to ZZZ1 in Month X and had the same reroute.   The FO had over 40 hours total time with XX landings.  I have not flown in over 60 days.  So in the chocks the Departure Briefing I briefed CA designates PF PM states concerns and threats PF states concerns and threats taxi; takeoff/reject departure.  The FO said low time and I said my over 60 days off.  FO is rock solid; what an excellent stick.  You know when you meet someone for the first time; it's going to be a fun flight.  Every time I see FO X's name on the crew list; it will be a fun flight.  For over 40 hours and XX landings FO flew real well.  Talking to ZZZ Center of frequencies XYZ.Z and XYA.B and we're climbing to FL230 and they ask Aircraft X we just want to confirm the route.  FO asks this is a reroute you want me to put on the autopilot?  If I had said yes; I would not be writing the report.  The fault is all mine.  My thinking was this is the same reroute we got in the chocks easy-peasy.  And it was the same route but took three or four minutes to get everything done. ZZZ Center then cleared us ZZZZZ JXXX ZZZ1 as filed.  I spelt ZZZZZ wrong and it was not accepted in the FMC.  Right then the Altitude Deviation warning came on.  ZZZ Center told us switch over to XYZ.Z and I reported FL240 we were at FL238 and our clearance was FL230.  Center than cleared me to climb to FL400.Lots of areas to hit on.  Even though I haven't flown in over 60 days do Company work on most days; I read all the changes; FD Pro X; Airline Pilots; WSI Pilotbrief; and Outlook.  On any day to read all this it takes 45 minutes to and hour and a half.  For this ZZZZ flight; I checked it three days in a row.  What was the routing; did it go over ZZZZ1 Country; and the weather?  FO is an excellent pilot.  Low time like FO is the autopilot should have been on.  The mistake is on me; no excuse; I messed up.It pains me to have made this mistake; I can't remember my last report.
Report_2_Narrative: New on the aircraft; I had briefed the Captain I wanted to hand fly the aircraft; which he agreed was a good idea. We departed ZZZ on XXL and was cleared on the ZZZZZ1 4 RNAV SID.  In our turn towards ZZZZZ1 we received clearance to ZZZZZ2 on frequency XYA.B. When we checked in to XYZ.Z we received a clearance to FL230 and to fly direct to ZZZZZ. ZZZZZ is not on the SID or depicted anywhere on the SID. The Captain was unfamiliar but I was because I flew the same Flight the day before and we received the same clearance. I believe I spelt the fix out to the Captain and asked if I should I put the Autopilot on; which he responded 'no it's okay'. Just as he was typing it in and he executed it we heard the altitude alert caution and we were at 23;580 feet. I quickly reacted and proceeded back towards FL230 at the same time the Captain called ATC and stated 'Aircraft X at FL240'. ATC then cleared us to FL310 or FL330. The deviation occurred at XA:22Z.I should not have asked the Captain if I should put the autopilot on; I should have just done it. We were obviously both needed to navigate. I should have put the autopilot on while the Captain was trying to figure out and insert a fix that was not on the SID. Having the autopilot on would have prevented us from flying through our assigned altitude while we were navigating the new clearance.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported an altitude excursion during climbout.

Report_1_Narrative: Aircraft X.  Ground Service personal brought Hazardous Cargo paperwork to the cockpit about dry ice being loaded in the aft cargo compartment and live animals being loaded in the forward cargo compartment.Normally live animals are loaded in the aft or bulk cargo compartments which are heated by engine bleed air. If carrying animals in the aft cargo compartments we make sure the cargo heat switches are in the high position which will warm and maintain the compartment temperature between 65F and 75F.  Due to the dry ice being loaded in the aft we are not allowed to have animals and dry ice in the same compartment.I was told by the ground service worker that they load live animals in the forward cargo compartment and do this regularly because the forward cargo compartment is heated. I explained that it is heated with cabin air that has flowed through the E & E compartments equipment ventilation system to cool the electronics and exhausted into the forward cargo compartment. We have no way of knowing what the temperature is in the forward cargo compartment is and no way of knowing if it is suitable for live animals.  We do have aft and bulk cargo compartment temperature indications on our air synoptic located in the cockpit. I asked Ground Personnel to swap the locations of the dry ice and live animals so that the animals could be kept warm for the flight in the aft cargo compartment.  I was told that this would be difficult to do because the dry ice would need to be moved to another canister and this would take time.  I asked to speak with the Ramp Supervisor and I spoke with the Station Manager. She explained that their ROM (Ramp Operations Manual) authorizes the loading of live animals in the Forward Cargo Compartment of the 777.  I explained that our Aircraft Operations Manual authorizes the loading of live animals in our aft or bulk cargo compartments only.  She explained that they have done this before and that I was not the first Captain to question this practice.I called the Dispatcher for the flight and discussed the situation with her thinking that she had seen this situation before and she had not.  She did some investigation and spoke with a mechanic and he told her that the forward cargo was heated. I explained to her what our manual stated and where live animals were to be transported.  The Station Manager directed the ramp personal to move the dry ice to the forward cargo compartment and move the live animals to the aft cargo compartment as per our operating manual.  I thanked her for her help and cooperation and explained that both of our manuals not being in agreement is a problem and that I would write this up so that we can get this discrepancy rectified so that we are all on the same page. The Ramp Operating Manual and the Aircraft Operating Manual not being in agreement on where live animals are to be transported caused a waste of time and effort.  Also; the animal's lives might have been in danger if the temperature was too low for the extended period of time of this flight. Both manuals (Ramp Operating Manual and Aircraft Operating manual) being in agreement would alleviate this problem.  Ramp Services and Flight [Operations] should get together and clarify the procedures for this subject.
Report_1_Synopsis: B777 Captain reported a discrepancy between FOM and Ramp Operations Manual regarding loading dry ice and live animals in cargo compartments. The specific incident was rectified but the conflict between the manuals requires a revision.

Report_1_Narrative: While on the RNAVM XX in ZZZ1 we encountered a GPWS event. At the beginning of the approach we had a tailwind and the descent angle of the approach caused us to be a little fast starting the approach. As the pilot monitoring I should have caught this issue sooner and brought it to the attention of the PF (Pilot Flying). Because of the speed the PF disconnected the autopilot/auto throttles and slowed the plane to the proper approach speed. During the turn onto final the PF was visual with the runway and let the nose drop which caused a momentary don't sink. He corrected and the warning went away. Still with the airport visual he tried to correct on the VASI and received another momentary don't sink call at around 700 ft. We continued the approach and the landing was normal. I don't have anything to add for [this report].I have learned many lessons from this very short flight. I haven't had much ZZZ experience and my FO (First Officer) who was PF has had very little. We tried to mitigate the possible issues by having a slow cruise speed of 210 kts. and trying to get ready for the approach early. We briefed the 3.4 GP and felt we were in a good position for the approach. With the unfamiliarity of the situation and the weather in ZZZ this day I missed the strong tailwind that was making our situation worse. This put us behind and we had to play catch up. It was turbulent the whole flight and when he disconnected the AP/AT my [situational awareness] went down because I was worried about his flight path at that time. As I look back at the event and if I could do this again I would have us discontinue the approach early and come around to try again. Once we continued and got out of the [weather] and had the runway visually climbing back into it in that terrain did not seem the safest option. But if we had bailed early it would have made the situation easier the second time.
Report_1_Synopsis: B737 Captain reported an uneventful landing after two GPWS alerts during approach due primary weather conditions.

Report_1_Narrative: While flying into Burbank at night PF (Pilot Flying) / PIC (Pilot-in-Command) elected to do visual to [Runway] 15. Clearance was granted around JANNY [and] PF took a course that meant we would intercept the final approach course from the left of centerline. PM (Pilot Monitoring) noted that we were left of centerline and that there was terrain in the area. We crossed over the ridge line at the standard 5;500 ft. but thereafter while still left of centerline the PF started a descent. PM had terrain display up on MFD and was watching; there was never a yellow or red terrain ahead of the aircraft at anytime. Yet PM noticed that the radio altimeter was showing a reading while still left of centerline. The radio altimeter reading went below 1;000 ft. and got to around 800 ft. The PM called out the altitudes as soon as they were decreasing below 1;000 ft. and the PF took evasive action by disconnecting the auto pilot and stopping the descent. Almost immediately after the radio altimeter reading went away and we continued a normal descent to landing on [Runway] 15. Taking a visual to [Runway] 15 at night is unnecessarily risky. With margins very tight on the left side of the approach course; situational awareness is reduced at night. The benefits certainly do not outweigh the risks. We never received a GPWS yet we came within below 1;000 ft. of terrain on around an 8 mile final. It is easy to become complacent with your surroundings when you can not see them; so don't bother putting yourself in this situation... The company needs to put into writing that visuals to [Runway] 15 should not be allowed at night. As PM I should have called an immediate go-around the second I saw the radio altimeter go below 1;000 ft.
Report_2_Narrative: High terrain in the form of a mountain ridge exists just north of BUR. The BUR airport is located at the east end of the San Fernando Valley. Additional mountains are present just to the east of BUR.Discontinue night visual approaches to BUR Runway 15.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier flight crew reported flying uncomfortably close to terrain on a night visual approach to Runway 15 at BUR; and suggested that the procedure be restricted to daytime operations.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Confusion; Situational Awareness; Distraction; Communication Breakdown
Report_1_Narrative: Upon deplaning a gentleman complained to the Purser and I; regarding another gentleman passenger.  He said the man sitting near him was coughing and sneezing the whole flight and that he was not wearing a mask.  He pointed his finger at us and sternly said you two did nothing about it.  The Purser responded to the gentleman about the situation.  My work position was in the First Class galley.  There was no complaint brought to my attention during the entire flight.  At no time did I observe any of this behavior.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Attendant reported a passenger complained about another passenger coughing and sneezing on the flight and not wearing a face mask.

Report_1_Narrative: Passenger A had to be told several times to please wear his mask.  The last time I asked him; he was playing with his cell phone; was NOT chewing anything and shook an empty chip bag at me; telling me twice that he was eating.  Well; he was not.  I learned later he had connected that day from ZZZ; a hot zone.  I guess Passenger A felt that he was exempt from wearing a mask on board.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Attendant reported a passenger would not comply with face mask policy.

Report_1_Narrative: While doing my countdown/brief down; there was a passenger in [seat] XX1 complaining about the passengers in [seat] YY3 and [seat] YY4 that were not being compliant about the mask being over their nose and mouth. I immediately told the passengers in YY3 and YY4 to place their mask over their nose and mouth; which they complied. While I was waiting for the pilots to finish up the last of the paperwork; so I can close the main cabin door; the passenger from XX1 came up to me to complain about the passengers again in YY3 and YY4 that were not being compliant about wearing their masks. The passenger from XX1 proceeded to ask me what the consequences were for people who don't comply with wearing their masks so I told him that I would speak to the Captain. I told the Captain to make an announcement about wearing the masks over their nose and mouth for the duration of the flight and in the next few seconds the Captain made the announcement and everyone was in compliance. It was then time to close the main cabin door and begin the safety announcement. I started the beginning of the safety announcement and the passenger from XX1 walked right up to me to complain yet again about the passengers in YY3 and YY4. I told the passenger that I am doing the safety announcement and I have to do my Flight Attendant duties but I will come to address the issue. The passenger was not pleased with my response because he wanted me to address the issue right at that moment; but I only have a finite amount of time to do the safety announcement and do the last of my Flight Attendant duties before takeoff. After the safety announcement was complete; I went to the passengers in YY3 and YY4 and told them to keep their masks over their nose and mouth. One of the passengers said that he was drinking his beverage so he forgot to put the mask back on. I reminded both passengers to keep their masks on and comply with the policy in order to avoid any issues in the future. Both passengers made some remarks and was upset that the passenger from XX1 was complaining about them so much. I even offered to give them additional masks because the face covering that they had on was sliding off their faces. The passengers refused to receive the additional masks and said that they would comply. In the end; both passengers from YY3 and YY4 complied so that we could depart safely. While inflight; I made several announcements about all passengers keeping their masks on for the duration of the flight and that everyone had to comply with this policy. The passenger from XX1 did not come to me to complain at all during flight or after taxi. I assumed that he was satisfied with the results of what happened and the passengers in YY3 and YY4 remained compliant with the mask policy.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Attendant reported two passengers would not initially comply with face mask policy. Both passengers complied after another passenger began complaining about them.

Report_1_Narrative: During taxi FA-B and I (FA-C) smelled a glue/stinky sock odor.Then we got headaches; Dizzy; Light headed; Confusion.FA-B called FA-A asked if she noticed any smell of felt ok. She didn't notice a smell but didn't feel well.Symptoms weren't going away so FA-B called the flight deck to notify.We went back to gate. Deplaned and once the PAX.Then we stepped off we did as well to get fresh air and air in the jetway; due to feeling weak and queasy.Hours later we all went to the ER to seek medical attention that should have been advised to do so immediately.  Wasn't feeling fit to operate due to the inhalation of hazardous fumes.I think that there need to be a procedure set in place for our management and CSAs to deal these types of serious situations like air quality because the people who are experiencing air quality problems aren't in the right state of mind to make first responder decisions for ourselves. There should be a training and also a checklist; such as if the ones who are felling two symptoms or more should be urged to go to the doctor and the paramedics should meet the flight without question.
Report_2_Narrative: All three crew members experienced an odor in galleys and cabin that smelled like glue and dirty socks during taxi out; after de-icing and before take-off. With Communication among each other we all started experiencing symptoms of feeling ill; dizzy; light headed; tingling sweaty hands; nausea; and confusion. We contacted the pilots to let them know of odor and illness. They Captain made the decision to go back to gate. We deplaned the passengers and were met by supervisors. We were told med-link would be contacted but they were not. The airport police (just one officer/ EMT) spoke with us and took our oxygen levels which were safe but low. We were not met by any paramedics. We were not given any oxygen. We should have put our selves on it; but we were fatigued; confused and not in correct state of mind to be making first responder decisions for ourselves. We drank water in crew room for a couple hours. We all three went to the ER fives hours later still feeling bad; to get blood tested and oxygen for dizziness. Symptoms lasted for about 11 hours. Toxic fume inhalation from air quality issue in cabin caused confusion for crews state of mind during taxi out and deplaning. We safely disarmed our doors at gate to deplane but may have made a lack of announcements and we I'll during the process. Training for CSA and Supervisors for consistency in protocol for Air Quality issues when meeting crew that reports problem. Always contact me slink and paramedics for crew just as we would passengers. It was not helpful to be down playing the situation to calm us; we needed help and we being asked what to do for ourselves; when we had been in wrong state of mind to make first responder decisions..
Report_1_Synopsis: B737-700 flight attendants reported a 'glue and dirty socks' odor during taxi-out resulting in health issues. The crew returned to the gate.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Physiological - Other; Time Pressure; Communication Breakdown

Person_2_Human_Factors: Training / Qualification; Troubleshooting; Workload; Communication Breakdown
Report_1_Narrative: We had walked into the hanger that morning and found out that we were doing an engine change. The engine had already been removed and needed to be installed. My Supervisor was the one in charge of the operation and he had wanted us hang the engine on the FWD top mount first then the AFT mount and then the bottom FWD mount. The task has you install the AFT mount 1st and then the 2 FWD mount; but since I had worked with him before on engine installs I just followed his lead. We had got the 1st mount installed on the aircraft we ran into some trouble on the AFT mount. We had ended up damaging both the upper and lower cowling and 2 hinge fitting panels. Later I had found out that the 2 panels were supposed to be removed before the engine ever can off the plane. We ended up pulling the engine back off aircraft and on removal the engine had snapped down and had made a small nick on the FWD mount. My other Supervisor (who was working with us the whole time) was trying to tell me that the damage was no big deal when I knew that the FWD mount had no damage limits. I had ended up writing up the damage to all 3 parts that got damaged.I believe that the damage to the aircraft could have been prevented if the 2 panels had been removed and we had followed the task in order. There should also be note in the task stating that the AFT mount needs to go in 1st. I also believe that supervisors shouldn't be doing the work of the mechanics. They seem to have a time ordinated mentally over a safety one.
Report_2_Narrative: On DATE on first shift at the ZZZ maintenance hangar; the right engine of aircraft X was being installed by the first shift maintenance crew. The individuals who performed and assisted in the task and include; myself (NAME2 RII Inspector); NAME (Maintenance Supervisor); NAME1 (Maintenance Supervisor); NAME3 (Maintenance Lead); NAME4 (Maintenance Technician); NAME5 (Maintenance Technician); NAME6 (Maintenance Technician); and NAME7 (Maintenance Technician). NAME8; Assistance Chief Inspector was also a witness to some portions of the task being performed. During the installation of the right engine the upper trans cowling 443AT; the lower trans cowling 443AB; and the upper and lower rear thrust reverser hinge line fairings 443BT and 443BB were damaged. Also there was damage to the forward engine mount on the pylon side. NAME (Maintenance Supervisor) was taking the lead on the job and operating the heavy duty forklift. Of the employees performing the task NAME had the most experience in doing this specific engine CF34-8C5 installation. NAME6 was the only technician besides NAME who had performed the specific installation task before and he had only performed it one time. Before the job started there was a safety meeting to discuss the possible dangers of the job. Everyone was assigned a position on the lifts; on the aircraft pylon; or on the ground. NAME8 present at the safety meeting and shortly thereafter I saw him from a distance talking to NAME about the task giving him some advice on how to install the engine and to make sure the task was followed exactly. Since I was on the lift and carrying out other duties I did not hear much of the conversation but it seemed more like an argument. NAME8 left the job site and we began to hoist the engine in place. NAME directed the mechanics to install the forward engine mount first because it was easier. NAME mentioned to us all that he had done at least five successful engine changes this way with no issues. At this point no one made an objection this. The two mechanics on the engine pylon; NAME4 and NAME5 aligned the forward engine thrust mount into place and torqued and safetied the nuts and bolts. They then attempted to align and fit into place the aft thrust mount. After a few minutes of trying the aft thrust mount would not fit into place. At that point myself and NAME6 double checked the manual instructions which we had on hand on the lift. We mentioned to all that the aft thrust mount should have been installed first according to the instructions the manual laid out. NAME stated that it should not matter and they proceeded to try again to fit the aft thrust mount into place. NAME3 kept saying that he thought some thing was binding where he was in the front side of the engine pylon. He mentioned this several times but because we were all in different positions around the engine we could not see was he was talking about. NAME3 asked NAME specifically if the panel 443BT is supposed to come off because it seemed like it was in the way. NAME replied that he had never seen that panel come off in his experience. They proceeded for another few minutes and then decided to remove the engine from the aircraft and put it on the stand to double check if anything was wrong with the engine mounts on the engine side. After the engine was secured on the stand. We found the above mentioned aircraft damage. A few minutes after the damage was discovered we did some more research. We found that the technicians that removed the engine the day before on second shift failed to remove panels 443BT and 443BB that are specifically mentioned in the removal task. We believe that this was the cause of the damage to the aircraft. With the panels installed there was not enough room to position the engine in place correctly. As an R.I.I. I rejected the installation in the maintenance software program and the maintenance staff asked for engineering relief for the damage. NAME then refused to sign the AMM task even though he took the lead on the job and operated the engine lift thereby performing undocumented maintenance on the aircraft.There were many factors that contributed to this incident. One was a serious lack of experience with this specific task. At other airlines they have an engine installation and removal team the handles all engine changes because of the complexity of the task and the teamwork it takes to do the job with five or more individuals. Most of the tasks frequently performed at ZZZ are done individually or with one helper. Only one technician on the job had performed the task more than one time. The complexity of the task meant that all involved had to read and understand a greater amount of technical data in a short period of time. Also the order of installation instructions were not followed because the most experienced technician claimed it was easier to perform the instructions out of order safely. Human factors also was a cause of this incident. The supervisor taking the lead on the job; NAME; has a reputation at ZZZ for being cocky and having a know it all 'one up you' personality. I have noticed that he has a condescending leadership style and likes to be condescending to his employees to make himself look good. Rather than train his people and build his employees up he would rather tear them down to make himself look better. I have been at Company almost six years and unfortunately Company management is full of people like NAME. I believe this creates a work environment that is intimidating and detrimental to open communication. People like NAME create a 'shame' environment where people are afraid to speak up when something is done wrong or doesn't look right to them. This creates and enhances human error.  Failure to read and understand the entire task and remove all the panels on the list for the removal task CRJ 900 AMM 71-00-00-000-801-A02-PSA led to the 2nd shift mechanics failing to actually remove the required panels. Failure to follow the installation order of specified steps in the task may have led to error also.More training by experienced technicians on more complex and team oriented task to train inexperienced technicians. In the manuals special notes to identify where the order of installation is a must and cannot be deviated from.(example: Note - Aft Thrust mount MUST BE INSTALLED prior to forward engine mount to avoid damage to aircraft and engine.) Better Leadership training for Supervisors with less than 3 years experience to avoid the cocky and condescending 'know it all' leadership culture. Make Maintenance Supervision and leadership responsible and accountable for the maintenance they perform on all Company aircraft. No running away and only making the mechanics on the floor sign something off when the job is not done right and something is broken.
Report_1_Synopsis: Technicians reported that appropriate AMM references were overridden by Supervisor and the engine mounts and access panels were damaged.

Report_1_Narrative: I was the PNF and the First Officer on this flight to ZZZ. On our approach into ZZZ we were slightly high on vectors and then cleared for the visual approach. The Captain PF was at a speed of 230 knots indicated airspeed (KIAS) and was trying to descend and slow to land. He was unable to slow to 200 KIAS as we were entering the Class C airspace and we determined the approach was unstable and executed a go-around. We entered the traffic pattern and landed successfully. I believe the cause is a decrease in proficiency due to reduced flying during the pandemic. We were doing 220-230 KIAS while entering the Class C airspace.
Report_1_Synopsis: Corporate First Officer reported an unstable approach occurred and cited lack of flying as a contributing factor.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Distraction; Workload; Time Pressure; Confusion; Communication Breakdown
Report_1_Narrative: I went into the control room to relieve the RX2 Controller at XA00Z.  I received a position relief briefing and there was nothing out of the ordinary that was given to me.  There were a couple of frequency notes given to me with ZZZ1 [Center]; but other than that there was nothing different from normal.All during this time apparently ZZZ2 [Center] was ATC-0 and we in Area X were never told about this going on.  When I came in that evening there was no notice; and no one was told that a Zero event was going to be taking place.  The Controller on RX2 that I relieved was never briefed about ZZZ2 [Center] being ATC-0.  When I took control of the position I had Aircraft X on frequency and he was turning towards ZZZ [VOR]..ZZZ [Airport].  This is the routing that per the LOA we give to ZZZ2 [Center].  The aircraft was level at FL340.  After a few minutes I gave the aircraft a crossing restriction to cross ZZZ [VOR] at 100; what we give these aircraft again per the LOA.  His route of flight was going to clip Airspace X if the aircraft stayed up high before meeting the restriction.  I placed a PVD [Plan View Display] on Airspace Y that auto-directed to Airspace Z as normal for that time of night.  When the aircraft started to descend the point out had still not been accepted; so I called to the sector and got no answer.  I tried a few times to no avail.  I then tried to call ZZZ2 [Center] Airspace X and got no answer from anyone.The Controller on the low side RX1 said the Shout Lines with ZZZ [Approach] were down; maybe the ZZZ2 [Center] lines were down as well.  By this time I had hollered for the FLM to come down and explain if they knew what was going on; and it was then I was told that ZZZ2 [Center] was ATC-0.  At this time the aircraft had already entered ZZZ2 [Center] airspace without approval; and my main focus was to handle the aircraft towards ZZZ [Airport] approach.  We pulled up the approach plate at ZZZ [Airport] and I told Aircraft X to maintain 110 to not enter approach's airspace and gave the aircraft I think XYZ.AB to switch over.  Not two minutes later; ZZZ2 [Center] comes back up and helps me with necessitating the hand-off.  Not at any time was anyone working traffic aware of this issue with ZZZ2 [Center].  After this aircraft handling was done; I called Area B controllers and asked if they knew about the ZZZ2 [Center] Zero event and they said no that they had not heard anything.  Area B also is adjacent to ZZZ2 [Center] airspace.Later the FLM came back down to let us know the ZZZ [Approach] lines were back up and running.  This makes this Zero event even more frustrating to us in Area A since the routing and altitude that we give ZZZ2 [Center] aircraft going to ZZZ1 Approach requires us to call ZZZ Approach for a Point out.  So during this Zero event; we had no clue that we were actually in it; and then if we did know we would have had to do extra work just to get the procedure to work with ZZZ Approach.Another part of this is that the controller on RX1 never knew about this event as well because he had a ZZZ [Airport] departure at FL230 during this time as well; and according to the ATC-0 procedures we are to Radar Identify the aircraft when they come over to us.  I cannot be sure that this was done.  This aircraft... I don't recall the numbers or where he was headed.   Communication is a big deal in what we do.  It is highly irresponsible to not be told about something as important as an ATC-0 event in the facility.  All I needed was to know was who and when and we could have handled this situation the correct way.  We have routing for this exact situation; we have the procedures posted in the area; but if no one tells me what is happening then this type of event will continue to happen.
Report_1_Synopsis: Center Controller reported an ATC Zero event at another Center facility resulted in communication issues and an airspace violation.

Report_1_Narrative: In the upwind after VFR departure; Aircraft X advised that he wanted to return to the field. I immediately asked if he needed any help and he replied no. I told him to make left traffic. As he didn't indicate an [urgent problem]; I treated him like a regular aircraft who decided to return to the field. We get this all the time for all sorts of reasons. It was nothing out of the ordinary at that point. He was going to be next to land just as soon as I departed the waiting IFR Aircraft Y. In order to depart Aircraft Y I had to first turn two pattern aircraft out of the way early. As soon as the second aircraft - a touch-and-go aircraft- passed the threshold; I told Aircraft Y to LUAW (Line Up and Wait); which he read back and did. I informed Aircraft X (who at this point was approaching the midfield left downwind) that I would give him a base turn and landing in just a moment as traffic was in position. He again acknowledged without issue. I then told the first aircraft (a stop-and-go aircraft) to turn an early left crosswind when able and waited to tell the second aircraft (a touch-and-go aircraft) the same once he was safely established in the upwind. At that point; Aircraft X suddenly announced that he was turning base right now and had to land. I acknowledged the base turn and immediately told the upwind [touch-and-go aircraft] to start his early crosswind now; which he did and then went right to the Aircraft Y and cleared him for 'immediate' takeoff; which he didn't even acknowledge. I asked Aircraft Y if he'd started his roll; knowing Aircraft X was essentially now in a short approach. The Aircraft Y responded by saying he was 'holding position.' At this point I knew he hadn't been paying attention and there was no moving him out of the way in time. I told Aircraft Y to cancel his takeoff clearance and hold in position because any movement would have increased the likelihood of his being in the way of the inbound behind him. He acknowledged; 'hold position.' I then went right to Aircraft X and advised that I couldn't give a landing clearance because traffic was on the runway. He acknowledged but repeated that he had engine trouble and was coming in to land. I gave him the traffic on the runway and informed him that Aircraft Y wasn't moving. He responded that he would side-step around the jet and land in front of it. I repeated again to Aircraft Y to hold position and informed the pilot what was happening to help his situational awareness; telling him that a 'Aircraft X' would be coming around to land on the runway in front of him. He acknowledged and didn't move. Aircraft X landed without further incident and rolled out to the taxiway exit where he was taxied by Ground Control and met by Operations vehicles. If a pilot's aircraft indicates any sort of malfunction whatsoever on takeoff that prompts a request to return to the field; it should be required that the controller be made aware of this for priority and for a sterile runway. Otherwise we will just fit them right back into the pattern and treat them as any other inbound. This return to the field is a very common occurrence for all sorts of [non-priority] reasons. Barriers which might serve to deter pilots from declaring [urgency] or requesting priority should be removed so they can feel free to request the help they might need without repercussions. Additionally; changes should be made on both the controller and pilot sides in the event neither has time to [advise ATC]. When seconds allow for only the transmission of control instruction to prevent collision; neither party should be held liable for not having wasted precious time saying pointless words in that moment. The actions being taken alone speak to the [situation] without having to necessarily say as much.
Report_1_Synopsis: Tower Controller reported a departing aircraft had to return to the airport with an equipment problem.  Aircraft landed over traffic that was in position and holding on the runway.

Report_1_Narrative: Aircraft X was the only aircraft on frequency due to issues with the normal frequency. They attempted to check in on the missed approach off of a satellite airport but were stepped on by multiple other aircraft. Including Aircraft Y that sounded like a similar call sign at the time. Due to the frequency congestion; I answered who I could hear and asked all aircraft to standby until I called on them. When I did hear Aircraft X check on; they told me they responded to an RA and I saw a target near them squawking 1200 at a similar altitude. I identified Aircraft X and issued instructions to approve their further requests. Upon watching the replay; I saw that the 1200 code had departed the satellite airport ahead of Aircraft X but do not know if the Tower issued the traffic. I did have another controller working my assist during the frequency congestion which lasted about 5 minutes.Continue scanning airspace and keep more aircraft on the same frequency so they can hear each other.
Report_1_Synopsis: A TRACON Controller reported they were distracted with radio and communications problems and did not notice an aircraft conducting a missed approach had conflicting traffic that the missed approach aircraft received a TCAS/RA for.

Report_1_Narrative: The Ops Agent arrived in the cockpit just prior to push time and provided me with a NOTAC (Notice to Captain) to sign. I looked over the NOTAC. Everything looked appropriate; the correct flight number and city pair and date. What I failed to do was to call Dispatch and amend/add HAZMAT (hazardous material)/ COMAT (company material)-ONBOARD to the release. I realized my error upon arrival in ZZZ1; at which point I contacted my Dispatcher.
Report_1_Synopsis: B-737 Captain reported departure without amended Release for late COMAT Hazmat addition.

Report_1_Narrative: The purpose of this report is to point out a possible safety issue in regards to the no fly zones going to South America. Flying over South America there are two no fly zones; one in the Peruvian Airspace and the second one extends from south of Peru across the Andes mountains all the way down to the south of Chile. Those areas where depicted in our old paper navigational charts and every no fly zones had waypoints. Those waypoints where depicted; for example the no fly zone over Peruvian airspace had the following waypoints depicted on the old paper navigational chart as follows: NFZ01; NFZ02; etc.; up to NFZ06. Those way points are still on our Nav (Navigation) Database and can be still used for safety awareness by building the no fly zones on the secondary flight plan. When we switch to Electronic Flight Bag you can still see the no fly zones but the way points are taken away. Based on my experience; about 80% of the times that we fly to South America; the iPad loses his own ship due to lack of signal and you cannot use the electronic chart for reference to make sure that you are not getting over any of the no fly zones; especially when we are deviating from weather. The only place that we can find those no fly zones way points is in the diversion guide page XX. I always put those way points on the secondary flight plan so I can see them on the Nav Display just in case we have to deviate due to weather and the iPad loose the signal. On my last flight to Lima we had to deviate due to weather over the shore line and because we had those no fly zones on the secondary flight plan; we were able to stay away from that area. I been flying into South America for over XX years in different fleets and we always had use that procedure and the information was everywhere. Now we have lost that information when we switch from paper to electronic nav charts. We also are getting new pilots from other bases that never been in those routes before and the majority are not even aware of those way points; and have no clue how to find them and use them. I believe that in the name of safety; those way points should be inserted into the electronic navigational charts and the company should provide more information about those way points.If you need any additional information please don't hesitate to contact me.Thank you for your time and attention to towards this matter.Experience flying this division.As I mentioned before; I believe that in the name of safety; those way points should be inserted into the electronic navigational charts and the company should provide more information about those way points.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported the waypoints that marked no fly zones in South America on the old paper charts are no longer available in the electronic charts.

Report_1_Narrative: While climbing to our cruise altitude the Captain and I began to hear a noise coming from the cabin that sounded to us like a pressurization leak in the airplane. Shortly thereafter the Captain received a call from the cabin crew; I believe notifying him about the same noise we were hearing. We then asked ATC for a lower altitude in hopes of the noise stopping. Shortly after that the Captain received another call from the cabin crew; when he hung up the phone he told me we were returning to our departure airport ZZZ due to claims of smoke or fumes in the cabin. I then donned my oxygen mask and notified ATC with our intentions to return to ZZZ. We were then given a lower altitude and vectors. We conducted the smoke/fumes checklist. We also decided ZZZ1 airport would be closer and notified ATC we would be landing there. We landed in ZZZ1 without incident where we had the ARFF (airport rescue firefighters) search our aircraft for any hot spots while still on the runway. After no hot spots were found we taxied to the gate where we deplaned normally. The pressurization leak that caused a loud noise and I never heard what the cabin crew smelled in the cabin. I really can't come up with any suggestions that would have prevented this event without knowing what caused the leak and what caused the smell.
Report_1_Synopsis: A321 First Officer reported a cabin fumes event during climb and cruise level off resulting in a diversion. The fumes were reportedly caused by a pressurization leak.

Report_1_Narrative: I took over this flight at shift change and outgoing Dispatcher advised they had just received information about undeclared HAZMAT (hazardous material) being on the aircraft.  Service recovery advised that there were 98 packages of lithium batteries in position 2R; which was located too close to ADG (accessible dangerous goods) loaded in position 1L.  At this point; flight was about 3 hours out of ZZZ; notified crew of issue via ACARS; and after service recovery consulted with Duty Officer; determined no immediate safety issue existed; so flight continued to ZZZ1. I do not know what caused the issue; aircraft was already in the air when I found out about it and the error was with the loading of the dangerous goods and lithium batteries; anyway.  You would need to contact hub to find out the cause.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Dispatcher reported aircraft en route with Hazmat cargo was incorrectly loaded at departure. Flight continued to destination since no immediate safety issue existed.

Report_1_Narrative: The 'Before Takeoff' Checklist was not performed.  The Captain did not call for the Checklist and I did not catch the error.  The Aircraft was properly configured and the Takeoff occurred normally without incident.We were both focused on properly performing the ZZZ Noise Abatement procedure.  We pushed back from Gate X (very close to the departure end of Runway XXR).  During the pre-departure takeoff briefing neither of us discussed the Threat of the very short Taxi to the Runway.  We did discuss that ZZZ was a bit of a 'Ghost Town;' with minimal activity compared to the times we'd previously been to the airport (for both of us it was during the 'Pre-COVID' era).  Within a short period of time after Departure; I mentioned we'd forgotten to perform the Before Takeoff Checklist.  We both discussed our expectation that there would have been wait during Taxi; which is part of the 'Normal' routine.  In this case; we did perform the Runway/Performance Change items after push-back with the Parking Brake set - we were then cleared to Taxi; instructed to switch to Tower; and then Cleared for Takeoff.  The delay we were anticipating never occurred.  The Captain called the Cabin after we were out of the sterile flight deck period and learned that the Aft Flight Attendant (FA) was seated; the Forward FA stated he was standing in the Galley during Takeoff.  Both FA's indicated that all passengers were seated.Suggestions - 1.  Brief the Flight Attendants that the Taxi Time is ZZZ is very short; and to be seated prior the call for 'Cabin Secure'.  2. At ZZZ; include the short Taxi time; close proximity of the Gates and Runways as a Threat during the takeoff briefing.  3.  Perform both the Runway/Performance Change items and Before Takeoff checklists prior to beginning Taxi for Takeoff.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported they did not perform the Before Takeoff Checklist.

Report_1_Narrative: Turned in closer to final than anticipated after receiving vectors to final.  Cleared for the approach and wasn't quite to ZZZZZ [Intersection] before descending to the final altitude.  Received a low altitude alert from ATC.  Called up ATC and discussed the situation; didn't lose any separation or any other problems.Turned in closer to final than anticipated.  Cleared for the approach and wasn't quite to ZZZZZ [Intersection] before descending to the final altitude. Create a clear path for the descent and verify the DME.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported descending too soon while on approach and receiving a low altitude alert from ATC.

Report_1_Narrative: I was complying with a functional check of the aileron cable tension in the forward cargo area. With this task you must remove the forward bulk head right hand panel and cargo area floor boards. After the aileron cable tension checks; I completed the job card signing off all the tasks including the completion of the bulk head blow out panel and floor boards. I failed to secure the floor boards and the bulk head panel resulting in the aircraft flying in an unsafe condition in which could of resulted in a catastrophic result. As a maintainer it is my responsibility to make the sure any and all aircraft is it a 100% airworthy. In the future; any task that is not completed will not be signed to make sure it is completed to ensure the aircraft is airworthy.
Report_1_Synopsis: Maintenance Technician reported failing to secure the floor boards and bulkhead panel after completing a functional check.

Report_1_Narrative: Passenger started complaining that he was extremely hot and was grabbing at the collar of his shirt. The vents were open and the aircraft was chilly not warm. I could see that he was sweating and he asked if he could have some water.  I went to the back galley to get him water and some iced cloth folds to put on his neck.  When I turned around to head out with his items; [his condition had deteriorated].  I immediately called the pilots and we paged for medical assistance.  We had a few nurses onboard that assisted us with the passenger.  He stated he needed to get to the restroom.  I helped the nurse get the passenger to his feet and the passenger went into the lav.  He was vomiting for several minutes.I spoke with the Supervisors the next day and advised them if my concerns regarding the fact that this passenger seemed to be exhibiting COVID symptoms.  I was advised there was nothing that could be done regarding the possible exposure and that I should just self monitor while continuing to fly.  I feel that more precautions should be taken when a passenger shows symptoms of COVID mid flight.  I think we should carry a thermometer onboard and when a passenger shows COVID symptoms especially when it results in a call to medical. More precautions should be taken to protect crew members proactively instead of retroactively.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Attendant reported possible COVID-19 exposure from an ill passenger and expressed concern the company did not have a plan for the exposed working crew.

Report_1_Narrative: C Flight Attendant positioned behind the exit row on Aircraft X. Family boarded with 2 small children; one of whom would occupy a car seat. I believe car seat may have had blankets over it during boarding so it was difficult to tell that it was a car seat. It was also difficult to see what was going on in front of the exit row when I was behind it due to multiple passengers; seats; and distance in the way. We also became distracted at the end of boarding by a high maintenance passenger traveling with 2 dogs that attempted to sit in the exit row that took some time to relocate. It was getting close to our departure time; so C needed to brief the exit row passengers and get to the front. Due to the above factors; it was missed that the family with the car seat was one row in front of the exit row. This was not noticed until A flight attendant did the final walkthrough shortly prior to being cleared for departure. At that point; the plane was in motion; the seatbelt sign was on; and every row was occupied. There was not somewhere we could realistically move a family of 4.We could have more specific instructions for the D Flight Attendant during boarding; to position on an opposing part of the exit rows from the C on the 800 to be able to see what is going on all around the exit row. The 737-800's exit row is 3 entire rows; and it is difficult to see what is going on all around it with just one person located there. Additionally; the D positioned in the exit row during boarding would keep the exit row monitored during potential distractions; like having to relocate a passenger from the exit row.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Attendant reported a family with a car seat sat in an unapproved location.

Report_1_Narrative: Today I used new temperature check system. Recommend adding hand sanitizer in this area as the touch pad is a touch point every employee must touch if the bar code doesn't work. Presently no hand sanitizer dispenser is available.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Attendant reported a hand sanitizing dispenser is necessary when the temperature check system with a touch pad is used.

Report_1_Narrative: Passengers bag was too large to fit in overhead bin; I advised bag needed to be checked. I noticed the face mask was down and asked her to cover her nose and mouth. She said that her mask just fell down when she sat in her seat. I advised her that her mask had been down since she tried to stow the bag. She started yelling at me and ask if I was the mask police? I said no; but if your mask doesn't fit; I can provide you another mask; she declined. I told the Captain and forward Flight Attendant because the passenger would not comply. Forward Flight Attendant asked passenger if she needed another mask; she complied wearing her own mask. I had to ask the passenger to pull up her mask a second time.  When deplaning; passenger had mask down again.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Attendant reported a passenger would not comply with face mask policy.

Report_1_Narrative: Three passengers boarded with their masks down. I asked them to pull them up. When collecting trash; before door closure; I noticed passenger in XX4 mask down again.  I asked her again to pull up mask and advised of policy; she laughed at me; then mocked what I had said. I asked again if she would pull up mask. Then advised the Captain of the interaction since I had to speak to her twice while on ground. Passenger in YY3 had mask down for second time in cruise when I collected trash after service.  He claimed he was forgetful. XX4 passenger played the peek aboo game where she had mask down but each time I approached; before I reached her; would pulled it up. ZZ4 passenger asked me how many times I was going to ask him to pull up his mask. When deplaning; had mask down.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Attendant reported three passengers would not comply with face mask policy.
