Report_1_Narrative: Incident / Discovery: Maintenance work light / flash light found in the the nose landing gear wheel well which resulted in an air return of the aircraft.Aircraft location: Aircraft X B737-800 was located in the parking area at ZZZ Airport.Work Conditions: Night time; outside; no spot lighting or ambient lighting. Sky conditions clear. Temperature 30(s) Fahrenheit.On the night; Coworker and I were assigned to troubleshoot log X 'Unable to access APU bite' Per previous log entry of being suspect; I replaced the R735 relay in the J20 box; took us some time to locate the J20 box and the relay because the WDM and IPC were not clear on the exact location. 2-3 hours to locate on aircraft. This junction box is located behind the L/H rear pressure panel of the nose landing gear box structure. However; access was difficult to the box from the nose landing gear area due to the angle of access and aircraft height. In turn; I climbed into the E/E bay with a blue hand light; head lamp and a No. 2 Philips screw driver; maneuvered/positioned myself over the flight deck air supply duct along the left side of the nose wheel box structure to get better access to the J20 cover; Relay 735 and associated cannon plug for troubleshooting purposes. Coworker was in support from the nose landing gear wheel well to hand me various items I needed to work through the access structure.As documented in the log; the relay did not correct the issue so we continued to troubleshoot which required continuous access to the J20 box. I was mainly working from inside the E/E bay; not from the nose landing gear wheel well.As the night progressed and not finding any faults with the physical wiring; we reported to our lead where we were at. Was told that the aircraft is needed for a flight; document where we were at and close up the aircraft.We headed back out to the aircraft. When we got back to Aircraft X; I double checked the APU ECU security; checked the aft cargo bay for equipment and tools; closed the aft cargo bay door. I then proceeded into the E/E bay to secure the J20 box cover and check for security and check for tools and equipment. As I was doing this; Coworker was securing the nose landing gear wheel well pressure panel.After Coworker finished installing the panel; I went inside the flight deck to re-engage two circuit breakers and to pressurize the aircraft for the leak check of the pressure panel. Once pressurized; Lead performed the leak check of the pressure panel. When leak check was satisfactory; I depressurized the aircraft; powered down; closed the main cabin door and pulled the air stairs. Shortly after we met in the vehicle we had and began going over paper work.Coworker and I are somewhat new to avionics and have a lot to learn about the various differences between our fleet types and associated details of each. We are very capable of doing the work but would feel more comfortable to be paired with someone who is well seasoned in the avionics shop. It should be this way for anyone that is new. Since I have been in the shop; I have been paired mainly with inexperienced technicians who are learning the same way as I am; learn as you go. Common sense would dictate to pair a very experienced tech with a inexperienced tech; this promotes growth; development and prevents mistakes.I'm sorry that this unfortunate mistake took place and is an oversight I strive to never let happen; unfortunately it did. I will be much more vigilant in the future about tooling and equipment used for aircraft maintenance to make sure this will never happen on my end again.
Report_2_Narrative: My co-worker and I received our assignment to work on the Aircraft X located [in parking]; a remote maintenance area (ZZZ). I remember on that day I was closing up a pressure panel at the nose landing gear wheel well and the battery of the octagon light died on me and so I had to use my flash light. Because we have been outside for so long; I was in the rush to get back to the office; which in the process I left the light in the nose wheel well and also I forgot to double check all my tools and I take full responsibility for my actions. Co-worker and I are new to this bid area and every day we are been paired with new people to figure things out on our own. On the day of the event; the working area was pitch black; it was very cold outside; the AMM (Aircraft Maintenance Manual) was a little confusing; trying to locate this J20 box to change a relay. and when the relay didn't fix the problem; we had to follow the wiring diagram. Everything was overwhelming. But all that been said; I still take a full responsibility for my action and I hope this will not repeat itself again. Thank you.
Report_1_Synopsis: Technicians reported leaving a flashlight in the nose wheel well after maintenance; causing the nose landing gear to not retract; causing an Air Turn Back and precautionary landing.

Report_1_Narrative: I experienced a loss of full engine power during initial climbout from RWY 32 at ZZZ. I had the student notify Tower we wanted to return for landing. We were still able to climb and engine was running smoothly so I wanted to keep as low key as possible. When asked by tower we did not request assistance and did not require priority handling. We climbed to approximately 1;000 feet AGL as we entered left downwind. Just past abeam approach end of RWY 32 while on downwind engine experienced further reduction in power without moving throttle. I told Tower we were turning base at that time; added 10 degrees flaps and aimed for the approach end of RWY 32. As we rolled onto final there was a business jet in position for takeoff on the runway. I heard the Tower clear him for an immediate takeoff; then tell him to abort and hold position. The Controller then advised me they could not issue a landing clearance. I responded that I had to land and Controller told me about the jet in position. I replied that I observed the traffic and would maneuver to pass to the right so I would not overfly the jet; and come in around and land in front of him. I flew a few hundred feet to the right at approximately 300 feet AGL; did not fly over the jet and passed well clear of him holding in position. I then slipped the aircraft into the left crosswind; lined up and landed on Runway 32 about 1;500 feet down the runway. The engine was generating enough power to taxi and I utilized Taxiway XX and called ground control when instructed for taxi back to ramp. When I reviewed the event; I believe I incorrectly assumed that the tower controller was providing me priority handling; when in fact the Controller was not fully aware of my situation. I should have just requested priority handling either prior to or as I turned downwind so Controller knew not to have the jet line up and wait on the runway before me.
Report_1_Synopsis: C172 flight instructor reported an engine malfunction after takeoff resulting in a return to field.

Report_1_Narrative: Practicing landings and flight pattern. As practicing the landing I was told to pull quickly for the flare process of the plane and caused a miscommunication as to pull on the yolk quicker. With the miscommunication caused the airplane to balloon and land on the nose wheel hard and causing internal damage to the nose wheel internals; ripping almost all the screws off the nose wheel screws keeping it attached to the plane. After the incident the instructor took control of the plane and went on a go-around and landed the plane with the nose being as high off ground as possible.
Report_2_Narrative: I was instructing my student on landing; focusing on the timing of flaring. He flared too much; which made him balloon. And to correct for it; he pushed down on the control to bring the nose down and landed nose first. The process was too quick for me to intervene. I heard a cracking sound as the nose wheel touched down on the runway. I executed a go around and made a soft field landing; wheelbarrowing the plane all the way down to the taxiway connected to our flight school's entrance. When I exited the plane; I visibly verified that the nose strut was sitting abnormally. I alerted our maintenance tech; who has verified that the nose strut was damaged.
Report_1_Synopsis: C172 student and instructor pilots reported a hard landing.

Report_1_Narrative: After landing when I requested that I be able to keep the same squawk for convenience as I was dropping two people off and continuing on VFR; the Tower Controller ask if I heard him calling us. I said no; due to Approach Controller keeping us on their frequency. As we are a helicopter and we are given clearances like 'landing at the ramp is at own risk' it can be confusing as to a clearance to land. I thought I was given a clearance to land. I'm not sure if it is due to COVID and staffing issues but it seems like I hear more ATC frequencies managed by one person; so this could have led to confusion during frequency changes.
Report_1_Synopsis: Helicopter pilot reported a communication issue with ATC resulted in a landing without a clearance.  Pilot stated the Tower Controller was working multiple frequencies; which may have contributed to the event.

Report_1_Narrative: Many of our fellow pilots have said to me that many pilots and others have been affected by COVID in one way or another; either necessitating quarantine or even hospitalization. Further; and in particularly our fleet; there is a disruption to the training schedules due to a lack of instructors; hence little; if any continuity. Have the Union and the Company considered shutting down for another month as the surge upon surge rages? There's no need to rush training if pilots will go non-current without the additional flying. Plus an additional month might get us to the beginning of a vaccination.I don't know if I have missed communications or not from the Union or the Company; but what is the plan for vaccinating pilots or other front line employees? Is there a timetable? Where do we stand in the national 'Phase 1' rollout? Has an update to the memorandum on pay during COVID sick leave been considered? Specifically; what happens to the pilot who receives round 1 or 2 of the vaccination and has to call in sick due to side effects. What happens to a pilot who has adverse side effects which lead to LTD? Could this pilot apply for the new LTD benefits and not wait until month X? Is a pilot required to take the vaccination? If yes; what happens if he declines? Where will pilots get the vaccination? Does a pilot have to wait until the Company procures the vaccine? What has FAA medical said about any of this?
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Captain reported concerns regarding company COVID-19 related plans pertaining to sick leave; vaccinations; training schedules; etc.

Report_1_Narrative: Briefed the ILS 26L IAH prior to top of descent (DRLLR 5). Center delayed our descent due to traffic. When descent clearance was given; told to maintain 310 kts. or greater. We were already over 6;000 ft. above descent profile. We were able to get back on profile just prior to approach handoff. When switched to Approach Control; they told us to expect RNAV Y 26R. After positive aircraft transfer control; I loaded the RNAV 26R and briefed the approach. We were expecting vectors to final RNAV Y 26R. I became PF (Pilot Flying) again. We were still descending on the arrival passing through approximately 8;000 ft. and 6 miles from SKLER when approach cleared us the RNAV Y 26R approach. We then realized the RNAV approach started at SKLER and included an arc segment to final. The Captain reloaded the approach with the SKLER transition. As we approached SKLER; everything looked good as we accomplished approach procedures. Autopilot was still engaged. Approaching DRKAR; we were expecting the aircraft to start a right hand turn on the arc. It didn't turn as we continued straight ahead. Captain said we need to turn as I selected HDG SEL (Heading Select) to start a right hand turn on the arc. We were a couple seconds late to start the turn. At this time ATC said we were late on the turn and gave us vectors to intercept visual [Runway] 26R. Visual approach and landing were uneventful. We debriefed after block in and recreated load the FMC. Although the arc portion showed on the route; there was also a vectors line after DRKAR. We think this is why the aircraft didn't turn on the arc and maybe we needed to sequence the FMC.
Report_1_Synopsis: First Officer reported not verifying the correct waypoint sequencing on RNAV approach due to a late clearance change from ATC.

Please review cameras to see the amount of people in the same area.

At the kiosk I realized that it was around 200 people and only 2 agents were scheduled to work that area.  I was very concerned about safety and health of myself and others because there was no social distancing and not following CDC guidelines. I hope you will be able to see the cameras in order to understand the horrible situation.I think all the authorities including health department will be concerned about this very important issue.
Report_1_Synopsis: Customer Service employees reported social distancing concerns at the airport lobby due to it being overcrowded.

Report_1_Narrative: ZZZ based Flight Attendant (FA) A was coughing during pre-flight and during the flight commenting about a sinus/cold issues. She accomplished her boarding / pre-departure duties. FA E advised that FA A was feeling ill due to cold; sinus; headache and now running a fever. (unverified) and that the FA A had taken a cabin seat and was attempting to rest. Dispatcher was notified via SATCOM and advised that FA A was feeling ill; running fever and that I was requesting a Manager meet the flight. I inquired if COVID (rapid) testing was available (due to current world events) for FA A upon arrival at ZZZ. Dispatcher respond that ZZZ did not have rapid testing and Customer Service Manager (CSR) would meet the flight. Upon arrival; the flight was met by 2 CSRs and they were briefed. I also spoke with the ZZZ Chief Pilot on the phone; post flight.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Captain reported a Flight Attendant on the crew became ill and there was concern regarding exposure to COVID-19.

Report_1_Narrative: We were cleared for takeoff. We set takeoff power and started our takeoff roll. At around 80 KTS the center runway red warning lights came on indicating another plane was on the runway. We queried ATC and they aborted our takeoff.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported the Runway Status lights indicated traffic on the runway and after asking Tower about it Tower cancelled their takeoff clearance.

Report_1_Narrative: Have more of a warning from ATC of the turbulence expected to encounter. We did not know of the severity of the turbulence until we were in it ourselves. Experienced continuous moderate turbulence between 8;000 feet to 3;000 feet on descent on the RNAV arrival. We landed without incident.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported unexpected moderate turbulence during descent.

Report_1_Narrative: Please thank the Customer Service helpers for arriving immediately. 10 minutes prior to departure; the lead Flight Attendant (FA) informed us there was a female passenger who was dizzy and had vomited. The FA was concerned about the passenger's fitness to fly and requested we call for the Customer Service helpers. They arrived and immediately removed the passenger. I suggested to the Gate Agents that they consider calling for Medical Assistance. I discussed the situation with the lead FA and First Officer. The lead FA said the passenger had described a history of kidney illness. We all agreed we had not received any information that would cause us to suspect COVID-19 illness. We departed on time. I described the event to our Dispatcher via ACARS. After arrival; I called the Duty Officer and the Chief Pilot on Duty and reported the event to them.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Captain reported a ill passenger was removed from the flight before departure.

Report_1_Narrative: After landing and during rollout on RW (Runway) XXR; we were instructed to 'make left turn if able and hold short of [Runway] XXL; then notify if gate was open'. As PF (Pilot Flying); I had already briefed during approach briefing that we would likely make left turn on [Taxiway] XX then hold short of [Runway] XXL to await further taxi instructions. As we decelerated and approached [Taxiway] XX; we noticed another airplane on Taxiway XY (around [Taxiway] XZ) facing east. We were initially uncertain if it was holding or continuing east so we were going to skip [Taxiway] XX and make next left. ATC stated that they were holding for us; so we made the turn on [Taxiway] XX. As we exited the RW (Runway); the CA (Captain) continued taxiing to cross RW (Runway) XXL even though we had been told to hold short. We were across the hold short lines when I queried him about holding short; but I was late in warning him to avoid the confusion and mistake of going so far. At same time; an airplane had rotated for takeoff on RW (Runway) XXL just prior to our position making it a more serious event. ATC never said anything to us as the event happened or immediately after; so I asked them if we should continue across RW (Runway) XXL. They replied in the affirmative and to contact Ground Control after exiting on other side. At no time did ATC comment on the event. We continued to the gate without further incident.Contributing factors were the confusion about the intention of the aircraft on Taxiway XY near the [Taxiway] XX exit we were instructed to use; the short distance between the parallel runways; and lack of coordinated and deliberate attention to the immediate situation we were in. I failed to give the CA a reminder we had been instructed to hold short of RW (Runway) XXL prior to him crossing the hold short lines. Neither of us confirmed both directions were clear prior to crossing even though it is SOP to do so and we had consistently been doing that up to that point. He said during our debrief he had momentarily looked down at his taxi diagram to confirm location of the potential crossing taxiways we might use before realizing too late we had taxied over the lines. I had also momentarily diverted my attention to try to contact ramp (per ATC's request about our gate availability); while assuming the CA had heard the hold short instructions and would comply. Again; we had already briefed this likelihood of taxi route and necessity of holding short of and eventual crossing of RW (Runway) XXL during the arrival/approach briefing during descent into ZZZ area. I had never received a query from ATC about gate availability in ZZZ; even though it's common procedure at other airports. Therefore; it affected my normal after-landing expectations and flow. That's not an excuse; but was definitely a factor.Weather was not a factor; nor was the lighting due to being midday. I don't believe fatigue or other physiological factors contributed either.
Report_2_Narrative: CAVU. RNAV [Runway] XXR. FO (First Officer) was PF (Pilot Flying). Upon landing standard transfer of controls on roll out. I planned on exiting [Taxiway] XZ to [Taxiway] XY to get behind a Airbus on [Taxiway] XY. ATC states 'exit [Taxiway] XX hold short of [Runway] XXL on [Taxiway] XX' (and gate status I think). The Airbus on [Taxiway] XY held short of [Taxiway] XX as directed by ATC. As we were in front of the Airbus as directed (on [Taxiway] XX) I was looking at chart and outside to see which way [Taxiway] XX veered (it looks like it veers left or right and is a wide taxiway). I was quickly comparing real life view to the chart diagram. As I was at that point we had already passed the hold short line. It then realized it and stopped. My FO asked 'if it's okay to cross [Runway] XXL'; ATC cleared us across [Runway] XXL at [Taxiway] XX left on [Taxiway] XA. All the while ATC communication was busy with the changing of our exiting directions to switching to ground. I have been to ZZZ multiple times before although I was unclear of how [Taxiway] XX is setup and viewed in real life. I was shocked what I had accidentally allowed to happen. I deviated from my exiting plan and slightly rushed thus missed seeing the HS (Hold Short) line and my situational awareness. I am at 100% fault in not continuing to [Taxiway] XZ as planned; taking on the slightly rushed exit; and most certainly not stopping as directed. I am still criticizing myself as I write this. I can guarantee that I will be more diligent and aware of actual versus chart of my location at all times.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported a runway incursion after landing.

Report_1_Narrative: While unloading Aircraft X a BE-1900C in ZZZ1; I discovered HAZMAT that had not been declared to the crew. The HAZMAT was a 'Battery; wet filled with acid' UN2794; class 8. The HAZMAT had the appropriate paperwork; but the pilot notification paperwork was not completed; nor was the crew notified. Appropriate company management personnel were notified and a SMS was completed.
Report_1_Synopsis: Beech 1900 Captain reported undeclared Hazmat had been transported to destination. Flight crew notification procedures were not completed at departure airport.

Report_1_Narrative: While in the downwind leg of the pattern working with a student; Tower cleared our aircraft number one for touch and go on. They also directed an RV9 to enter left base. The RV9 was asked to report us in sight. After several moments; they reported us in sight and Tower cleared them number two to land. We then turned base and the RV9 turned base inside of us. When we rolled our wings level; tower called the RV9 to tell them they had turned inside of our turn. The RV9 was then cleared to land number one; however; he had already entered an evasive 180 degree turn to his right and when I gained visual contact again; he was directly above us with less than 200 feet separation. We were unable to maneuver evasively at our low altitude but he was able to pass over us with no further conflict.
Report_1_Synopsis: C172 instructor pilot on short final reported an NMAC.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Communication Breakdown; Confusion; Distraction; Situational Awareness; Time Pressure; Workload
Report_1_Narrative: Volume during this session was not particularly high; but complexity and workload changed quickly; and a sequence of events took my attention away from aircraft that didn't need much of it; including the aircraft in question. Aircraft X descending into ZZZ. My initial descent clearance was to 15;000 ft. An eastbound departure was potentially in conflict with 3 other aircraft; including Aircraft X. Deconflicting this aircraft took much of my attention during this time. Aircraft X ended up being no factor. Once clear of all other aircraft; I gave Aircraft X descent clearance to 11;000 ft. Read back was not as clear as I thought; but I had other things to worry about; including two aircraft simultaneously calling for VFR flight following and a conflict alert between VFR aircraft I was providing flight following to and a Mode-C intruder which took much of my attention because they were tracking to pass about 1 mile apart and the Mode-C intruder was climbing into the other VFR aircraft. Once that situation cleared up and as Aircraft X was descending through 12;000 ft. I received a call from FSS (Flight Service Station) which I decided to answer on the assumption that it would be a faster phone call than it turned out to be.Their request was for a Special VFR departure (SVFR). I had to take time to verify that SVFR was possible from this airport and since SVFR is a very rare request in my area of specialization I then had to look up the phraseology to give the clearance. By the time the clearance was delivered and read back; at least 2 minutes had passed. As I disconnected the FSS call; Low Altitude Alert showed Aircraft X at 7;900 ft.; descending below the MIA (Minimum IFR Altitude) of 8;000 ft. I immediately issued a low altitude alert with a clearance to climb to 10;000 ft. immediately. After the pilot responded I advised the pilot that his descent clearance had been to 11;000 ft. and asked if he had ZZZ in sight. Pilot responded that he had the field in sight. I cleared Aircraft X for a visual approach and gave instructions to contact Tower. It did not appear that he observed the climb clearance that accompanied the Low Altitude Alert; and the aircraft was at 7;300 ft. when I cleared Aircraft X for a visual approach.It is difficult to recommend any actions or changes to prevent re occurrence. This particular sector is quite complex; with high terrain; military airspace; two approach control facilities; arrivals to and departures from ZZZ1 in all directions. Convergence between ZZZ arrivals/departures to the south of ZZZ and ZZZ1 arrivals/departures to the southeast of ZZZ1. Also ZZZ2 arrivals and departures to the northwest of ZZZ2 all come together in the vicinity of ZZZ3. Also several satellite airports where pilots cannot reach us on the ground resulting in FSS relays. 11 adjacent sectors adjusted for typical sector configuration with multiple combined but the actual number of individual adjacent sectors is much higher and a relatively heavy VFR workload. It can unexpectedly become quite busy; even with a small number of aircraft in the sector. When this happens; it usually entails coordination calls from one or both of the approach control facilities; the military controlling agency; FSS; and one of the 11 adjacent sectors; and often includes aircraft that require a higher-than-normal workload. The timing of these factors is not controllable; so when several things happen at once; it usually can't be predicted; it can become difficult to manage; and it's often over before a D-side (Radar Assist) can make it to the sector to help.
Report_1_Synopsis: Center Controller reported they were distracted by a high workload and missed an erroneous read back of a descent clearance and the aircraft descended below the Minimum IFR Altitude.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Time Pressure; Workload; Confusion; Distraction; Human-Machine Interface; Situational Awareness
Report_1_Narrative: Aircraft X entered a terrain area at 7;200 ft. with a Minimum IFR Altitude (MIA) of 7;400 ft. Aircraft X was cleared for the RNAV [Runway] XX approach. Aircraft X executed the missed approach. Aircraft X requested vectors for the RNAV [Runway] XX Approach. I issued a turn 30 degrees left when able direct to the Initial Approach Fix (IAF) and notify me when he was direct. Aircraft X reported they were ready for the approach clearance. I issued '[Aircraft X] maintain seven thousand until established. Cleared RNAV approach Runway XX at ZZZ.' Aircraft X read back the correct clearance.Aircraft X continued on their heading past the IAF without beginning a procedure turn for the approach. I was busy with multiple requests from other aircraft and fighters departing a military base for active Warning Areas. And didn't notice Aircraft X missed the fix. I was giving a relief briefing and noticed Aircraft X was not on his cleared route. I asked him where he was heading. Aircraft X stated he was waiting for vectors to the approach. I pulled up the MIA's and noticed he was about to enter a 7;400 ft. MIA block. I issued a safety alert for the terrain and climbed Aircraft X to 8;000 ft.In my scan I knew that Aircraft X was out of position but assumed he was unfamiliar with how to execute the procedure turn at the IAF and was going to get back on a correct course soon. Every time I checked back in my scan he was a bit further off course. The workload was high. Frequency congestion was causing a lot of missed and stepped on clearances further increasing workload. I had requested help from the Controller-in-Charge twice prior to this happening. I needed assistance with a flight break up flight plan and to notify the surrounding facilities the Special Use Airspace went cold. A dedicated D-side (Radar Assist) would have helped notice the aircraft off course.
Report_1_Synopsis: Center Controller reported frequency congestion and a high workload caused them to not detect an erroneous altitude read back and an aircraft flew below the Minimum IFR Altitude.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Distraction; Communication Breakdown; Human-Machine Interface; Situational Awareness; Confusion
Report_1_Narrative: There was some confusion going into work as I was notified at XA:00 pm for my XA:30 shift  and told not to report to work until XD:45 due to Level 3 cleaning that was taking place. When we arrived at work the control floor was empty and ZAU ARTCC resumed operations at XD:55am with no briefings at all. I was working the MID configuration which includes the following sectors (sector numbers removed) along with the following approach controls (ZZZ1/ZZZ2/ZZZ3/ZZZ4/ZZZ5). During my stint which started at XF:00 am and ending at XI:00 am around XX:50 ZULU I spoke with Aircraft X looking for the ILS to Runway X at ZZZ2. I asked the pilot if he had the current weather at the field along with the NOTAMs and the pilot responded with a yes to the weather and that he had read the NOTAMs yesterday. I then read what I thought was all the pertinent NOTAMs to the aircraft. I vectored Aircraft X for the ILS at ZZZ2 and cleared the aircraft in for the approach. I switched the aircraft to advisories and requested a timely cancellation due to a second aircraft being vectored for the same approach. Aircraft X soon cancelled his IFR and reported a down time along with the condition of the runway and that the ramp area was in a much worse condition. I inadvertently missed the snow removal NOTAM and was later on informed by management that Aircraft X had landed on a runway with snow removal equipment on it. Any usage of the active runway should require call to either the facility or on frequency to prevent any confusion on what is going on at the airport. Any and all NOTAMs that directly effect the runways should be better identified. ZZZ2 had over 15 NOTAMs listed at the airfield which all look identical; if the ones like snow removal were BOLD or even a different color it may help the next person avoid the same mistake I made.
Report_2_Narrative: I was notified today upon arrival to work that Aircraft X had landed on a runway occupied by snow removal equipment at the time. I was unaware that this had happened. I was working the assist position when the aircraft was cleared for the visual approach. The Radar Controller had issued the weather and read the NOTAMs to the aircraft and neither of us were aware that snow removal was taking place at the airport. The aircraft canceled IFR prior to landing. I was not made aware of the hazardous situation until the following work shift. This is the third report that I have written on this type of event at this airport! Several years ago; I myself had an aircraft execute a missed approach due to snow removal equipment on the same runway. I of course submitted a report detailing the situation and offered recommendations to prevent the situation from occurring again. I received no feedback. I told my Operations Manager; who was aware of the incident; and was dismissed. I then took it to the local safety council who actually looked into it. However; after some time I was informed that the current procedures would remain in effect. No definite reason was given. If a runway is possibly occupied by snow removal equipment; an aircraft should not be cleared for an approach. Having an aircraft switch frequencies to contact the snow removal crew themselves to land obviously has many drawbacks. The snow removal crew should simply notify the control facility prior to entering the runway. ATC could then close the runway until notified that the snow removal crew has exited the runway. This could be done by radio or phone; thus preventing the situations that have previously occurred.
Report_1_Synopsis: Center Controllers reported an aircraft landed on a closed runway due to snow removal equipment and not being able to identify the correct NOTAM for the runway closure..

Person_1_Human_Factors: Confusion; Communication Breakdown; Situational Awareness; Distraction
Report_1_Narrative: ATC assigned a vector '[Heading] 140 and maintain 3;000 ft. until established on localizer....' As Pilot Monitoring I heard the vector and maintain 2;000 ft. until established. Captain heard 2;000 ft. as well and entered 2;000 ft. I read back 2;000 ft. to the controller. The Captain briefed and all checklist items were briefed prior to this event. The Captain flew through the localizer due to his failure to move the localizer frequency from Standby to Primary. He quickly recognized it and visually maneuvered aircraft back toward course. We received a Terrain Alert and we discussed to shallow our intercept angle. The course was intercepted safely. The controller transmitted that the altitude was 3;000 ft. until established. We were at approximately 2;000 ft. at that time. I transmitted that we had heard '2;000 ft. until established' and read that back to him earlier. We maintained 2;000 ft. until glideslope intercept. We landed uneventfully.
Report_2_Narrative: Beautiful day; 30 mile visibility; clear skies; airport in sight 30 miles away. Routine departure from ZZZ. At altitude; we were given direct to a fix and descend to 3;000 ft. Approaching the fix estimating 5;000 ft. altitude ATC gave us a clearance: 'Left turn of (EST) about 30 degrees and intercept localizer' which was inside of the fix 'and descend to 2;000 ft.' The First Officer clearly repeated to ATC '2;000 ft.' and no ATC correction was said. I set 2;000 ft. in the altitude alerter and pointed at it until the First Officer repeated '2;000 ft. A slight north wind caused my track just slightly south of center line of final; well within reason; estimate one dot right. As I was correcting and back on centerline the GPWS (Ground Proximity Warning) sounded; when back on center line the GPWS stopped. The hill was always in sight and we were never left of center line; never was there any danger. At that moment ATC asked if we had the airport in sight and we said yes. ATC cleared us for a visual approach to the runway and said our clearance was only to 3;000 ft. Uneventful landing. I clearly heard and after discussion; the First Officer also clearly heard '2;000 ft.""
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Crew reported they read back to ATC descend to 2000 feet when ATC meant 3000 feet and then flew through the localizer and received a Ground Proximity Warning.

Report_1_Narrative: I notified my lead before departure that there was low visibility due to the jet bridge placement. He asked me if he wanted me to push or if he wanted me to push it. I told him I would wing walk. Once he gave us the clear to push signal; he almost immediately began to push the plane before the wing walker opposite to me could make sure traffic was stopped. A pick up truck with a plow was going; probably too fast; down the vehicle service road. The opposite wing walker was waving his hands and wands to get the trucks attention. The plow got stopped finally nearly once he got to the line of the envelope. The back of the truck went up in the air as he stopped due to how fast he was going and how fast he stopped. By the time the truck stopped the entire tail of the aircraft was in the vehicle service road.
Report_1_Synopsis: A Ramp Service worker reported an aircraft was pushed back too far extending over a vehicle service road and into conflict with a snowplow.

Report_1_Narrative: Aircraft X arrived. As reported before; this aircraft's aft cargo pit mechanical loading system is inoperative; causing the ramp crews assigned to have to manually unload thousands of pounds of cargo loaded onto pallets that the equipment is specifically designed to move. This continues to create an unsafe environment as the crews are moving individual pallets weighing thousands of pounds; up to one piece listed at 9427 lbs. These loads were never meant to be muscled by ramp service employees while inside the aircraft. It's irresponsible to continue to use this aircraft and expect people to put themselves in danger. The danger; as always; lies in requiring employees to manually move thousands of pounds they were NEVER intended to move that exposes them to injury in multiple ways. The very floor of the cargo pit isn't specifically designed for walking and moving loads as they have MANY trip hazards opening employees up to MORE injury. Again; it's VERY irresponsible to continue to use this broken aircraft. It NEEDS to be removed from service.
Report_1_Synopsis: A Ramp Service employee reported the same aircraft's mechanical cargo loading system has been inoperative and the ramp workers have to continually manually move thousands of pounds of cargo from the aircraft.

Report_1_Narrative: During initial taxi out and under the direction of the marshaller our right main landing gear departed the paved surface and became stuck in the grass. The airport diagram does not accurately depict the taxiway layout and I did not realize how close the landing gear was to the edge of the pavement after push back. It was very dark and perhaps the marshaller could not see that either. I followed marshaling signals up until the event took place.
Report_2_Narrative: During initial taxi after push back; we were being directed by marshaller and our right main departed the paved surface and was stuck in the grass. I believe the cause of the event was being pushed back to close to the edge of the taxiway; very dark ramp and the airport diagram doesn't accurately depict layout. I could not see how close to the edge of the taxiway we were and possibly the ground crew either. In the future; I will be more vigilant to dark areas and better lighting on the ramp will assist.
Report_1_Synopsis: Pilots reported during push-back from the gate the aircraft left the pavement.

Report_1_Narrative: Air return to ZZZ due to strong odor and haze entering the cockpit and cabin through the air system. This occurred right after takeoff. After running the appropriate checklists; were vectored back around and landed and taxied without incident back to the gate. We were deiced prior to the flight. Caused by fumes entering the cockpit and cabin.
Report_1_Synopsis: CRJ-900 Captain reported a fumes event during initial climb resulting in a return to the departure airport.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Confusion; Distraction; Situational Awareness; Workload; Communication Breakdown
Report_1_Narrative: Aircraft X was leaving late. Four Company aircraft were leaving DTW around the same time with very similar call signs. To be exact; Company; Aircraft Y; Aircraft Z; and Aircraft A were also leaving. Meanwhile; the controller working Tower was also working Ground frequency. More than once; aircraft were taking frequency changes for other aircraft. While no serious deviations occurred; my First Officer remarked that both the high workload of the controller and the similarity of call signs could be a number of threats that on a worse day could lead to a serious safety concern. I do agree with him. I think Company has been aware of the issue of similar call signs leaving and arriving at hubs at the same time for a while; but it would require too much work to actually re-work the system to better avoid this issue. I fear that we will have to wait for some serious incidents to have the impetus to actually change this feature of our dispatching. Flight Planning presumably has a reason for making the flight numbers a particular way.
Report_1_Synopsis: An Air Carrier pilot reported their company had four flights with similar sounding call signs departing within a ten minute time period.  The reporter states this problem occurs at all their hubs.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Distraction; Confusion; Communication Breakdown; Situational Awareness
Person_2_Human_Factors: Situational Awareness; Distraction; Confusion; Communication Breakdown
Report_1_Narrative: The timing of the situation was ripe for a mistake; as a similar-sounding call sign received the exact type of clearance we would have expected as we approached the end of the runway while I was task saturated with completing the required checklist. Ideally; I would not have misheard the call sign; but ultimately I should have realized my attention had been entirely focused on the checklist; not the radio; and asked Tower for a short delay; clarification; or repeated clearance. We were operating the second leg of the day as Aircraft X from ZZZ to ZZZ1. We were given a short taxi from the terminal to Runway XXR. Approaching the departure end of XXR I switched to Tower frequency while still completing the Before Takeoff Checklist. As we made the turn from B onto B5 and while still finishing the last few steps of the checklist; Tower cleared another aircraft with a similar-sounding call sign; to line up and wait on XXC. I mistakenly thought the line up and wait clearance was for us and read back a clearance to line up and wait on Runway] XXR. Tower did not acknowledge my call; and while the Captain and I both saw an aircraft on final for [Runway] XXR; it appeared there was adequate spacing for the line up and wait clearance to be reasonable. As our aircraft passed the hold short line; Tower cleared the similar call sign for takeoff on XXC. The Captain and I simultaneously realized there had been a possible mix up of call signs. We advised tower we had read back the line up and wait clearance and asked for confirmation that it had been for us. Tower advised that it had not been for us; but cleared us for an immediate takeoff to accommodate the aircraft on final for [Runway] XXR. We immediately transitioned to a rolling takeoff and were able to get airborne before any go-around or other action was required by the aircraft on final.
Report_2_Narrative: It did not sound right to me when the Tower said to line up and wait; but after the First Officer read back the instructions and the Tower did not correct us we pressed on. Next time I am in a situation that does not feel right; I will stop what I am doing and verify the instructions before taking the runway.We were taxiing to Runway XXR in ZZZ. As we were approaching the hold short line we heard the instruction to line up and wait. The First Officer read back 'Aircraft X line up and wait XXR.' Both of us looked at final approach and saw an  aircraft on approximately a 5 mile final; I verified this with my MFD. As we turned on to the runway the Tower cleared an aircraft for takeoff that had a very similar call sign as ours. At this point; I verified our instructions to lineup and wait. Tower said that he did not clear us to line up and wait. The Controller immediately cleared us for takeoff and so we took off.
Report_1_Synopsis: A320 flight crew reported runway incursion.

Report_1_Narrative: We taxied out single engine.  There was some distraction/discussion on taxi out regarding a large brush fire burning to the east of the airport.  Upon turning north to Runway XXL we noticed Aircraft Y holding short of the runway. There was some discussion of the aircraft as we had a similar setup the day prior in ZZZ and it changed up the departure sequence and we had to maneuver around that aircraft.  As we neared the runway the Tower then cleared as for departure without delay as there was another aircraft on final.  We lined up on the runway and as I added power I noted the asymmetrical thrust. I rejected the takeoff and advised Tower. After clearing the runway we started the second engine and completed the takeoff without incident.In my opinion we developed some expectation coupled with distraction that it may be a bit before we departed. This must have pulled my mind from the task at hand (starting the second engine).  With the Tower then expediting our departed we switched into a rushed sequence that resulted in the error of not starting the second engine.  The other aircraft and the aircraft on final also pulled my eyes and attention outside the aircraft more than usual.In hindsight and trying to examine why this happened I have also had some personal distractions that could have been a casual factor in contributing to my lack of focus.  This was my first trip after recovery from a moderate case of COVID as well as an [another personal issue.]  While I can say these weren't outwardly conveyed or discussed they were heavy on my mind.
Report_2_Narrative: We taxied out to XXL from the gate single engine. On the way we noticed a big smoke plume and also saw a fire truck spraying water on field which was unrelated. When we turned on bravo away from view of the smoke we noticed Aircraft Y awaiting takeoff similar to yesterday at what appeared to be the end of the runway. We couldn't tell they were at the intersection prior until we were upon them.  I was looking at them when Tower cleared us onto the runway. I read the line up and wait back and instinctively started my before takeoff flows. Notifying the flight attendants; transponder and to config. As I read that checklist ATC interrupted and said cleared for takeoff. I read that back then restarted the checklist and finished it. The captain added power and immediately rejected. We notified ATC and exited the runway. We then started the engine and ran the checklists from there and resumed the flight.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier pilot reported asymmetrical thrust on start of takeoff roll resulting in a rejected takeoff.

Report_1_Narrative: Enroute we heard a company flight with a very similar callsign on same frequency. Center notified us that the company these two similar callsigns on the same route at the same exact time every day. Similar callsigns increase workload unnecessarily. No deviations happened as a result of similar callsigns.Company should review similar callsigns and assign [different] numbers during forecasted conflicts like before.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported his company regularly dispatches two flights with similar call signs at the same time every day.

Report_1_Narrative: From Captain X - 'When I approached the gate for my flight the boarding agent was talking on the phone.  As a courtesy I waited until he was off the phone to identify myself (as working crew).  I overheard his side of the conversation and clearly heard him state that he was (now) aware that the first four rows of coach class could not be occupied due to weight and balance and that he would re-seat the passengers that were booked in those seats.  During my FA briefing I said nothing about those seats because there was no mention in my flight release that the first four rows of coach should not be occupied.  During pre-flight in the cockpit I called my Dispatcher to ask for additional fuel and an alternate and during this conversation nothing was said about the first four rows of coach not being occupied.  We pushed at XA:15Z and got airborne eight minutes later.  The closeout had a note about the first four rows not being occupied; but since I recalled the agent saying that he would re-seat the passengers in those rows I did not pursue it any further.  After climbing out of ten thousand I called the #1 FA and told him to make sure that no passenger changed their seats to the first 4 rows of coach during the flight and was then told that there were 3 passengers sitting in the first 4 rows of coach.  I called my Dispatcher to make sure we were restricted and was told we were.  I asked Dispatch to find out why those seats were assigned by the gate agent after I heard the agent acknowledge over the phone that those seats were restricted due to weight and balance and should not be used.  I also asked my FA to re-seat the 3 passengers and make sure the first four rows of coach remained unoccupied for the duration of the flight. I don't know why the agent who said he was going to re-seat the passengers didn't do it.  The passenger manifest clearly showed that at least one of those 3 passengers was assigned a seat in the first 4 rows of coach by the agent during our boarding process.'   To tag along with what Captain X said; the TPS did not have any weight and balance information about seat restrictions. The closeout did; but since Captain X knew that the gate agent knew about it already; we figured no one would be assigned those seats. For some reason; those passengers got assigned those seats; I assume because they were non revs and the gate agent was under pressure to get the flight out so they probably forgot about the restriction. Time pressure; gate agents are under a lot of pressure; and seem understaffed during COVID. Due to this; they should be commended for doing the work that they are. They should be thanked for making sure non revs make it on. The intense amount of pressure agents work under day in and day out; adds up and a mistake is bound to happen. This mistake; although a procedural mistake; was not one of extreme error. The margin of error built into weight and balance is wide. If weight and balance is truly as tight as 3 passengers; the FAA would make sure we weighed every single bag individually and get true cargo weights instead of averaging bag weights. We would also weigh passengers instead of simply assuming there are average summer and winter weights per passenger. The flight was completed successfully; transporting XX or so people across the country.Don't work gate agents so hard. Give them the tools they need to succeed and ease up on micromanaging. Let agents make real decisions and they will feel empowered to complete their tasks; like making sure 4 rows are empty on a flight. I could place the blame on the agent and make a bunch of suggestions and punishments up; but I'm tired of the culture of pitting work group against work group here. This is the only airline I've worked for where this practice is known and visible. We are all working toward the same goal of trying to save the airline industry. Let the agent know of the mistake and move on. We need to work together now more than ever.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported that the first four rows of the aircraft were to be left unoccupied for weight and balance reasons; but found out when airborne some of the seats were occupied.

Report_1_Narrative: After takeoff we delayed our Tower assigned turn to 120 until reaching1;000 ft. per the company Ops pages. We received a RA (TCAS resolution advisory) at about 1;000-1200 ft. We responded to the RA. Informed the Tower immediately; they did not acknowledge our report and switched us to Departure. After we were cleared of the conflict we noticed an aircraft on the MFD 400 ft. above us. The Tower Controller cleared us for take off with a turn to 120 before we reached the runway; suspect the departure corridor was not clear. Better communication between flight crew and ATC; about traffic awareness in the vicinity of the airport.
Report_2_Narrative: Departed RWY XXR ZZZ; per company pages started right turn to heading 120 assigned by ATC. Immediately received an RA 'monitor vertical speed' we were climbing at about 1500'/min and v/s (Vertical Speed) tape showed we needed to limit climb to about 200'/min. We pitched over immediately; shortly thereafter we got 'clear of conflict'. All this happened between about 1;500 feet AGL and 3;000 feet. After the RA was complete I noticed traffic on the ND (Navigation Display) about 400 feet above us and slightly behind us. During the event Tower handed us off to Departure; we told him we were responding to an RA. Without any comment he repeated the hand-off to Departure.We were following our assigned clearance.  We do not know who the other aircraft was or if they had deviated from their clearance. It all happened very fast at a busy phase of flight. Pull the [Quality Assurance] data for this flight and ATC records to see what caused this event. I believe we got close to this other aircraft but I don't know why. I think it's worth investigating.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Captain Flying A321 aircraft reported NMAC after takeoff.

Report_1_Narrative: About 2 hours into the flight; I received a call from A Flight Attendant that a passenger was told on 5 occasions to properly wear face mask and would not comply.  The situation never escalated to heated verbal exchanges or threats.  I informed the flight attendant to pass on to the passenger that the Captain will have law enforcement meet the aircraft upon gate arrival if he does not comply with policy on wearing of a face mask.  The passenger complied for the duration of the flight which had approximately 1 hour remaining.  I called ahead to have a Customer Service Agent meet the aircraft at gate arrival and talk with the passenger; which was done.Some passengers believe that certain policies regarding flying do not pertain to them.Keep backing up the flight crew when passenger disregard airline and FAA policy when on board an aircraft.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported a passenger was not compliant with face mask policy.

Person_1_Function: Dispatcher; First Officer; Pilot Not Flying
Report_1_Narrative: Prior to block-out of Aircraft X; ZZZ airport Tower and Approach Control closed due to a COVID cleaning. Dispatch informed the flight crew to remain in the gate and not block until a new flight release could be sent with an alternate. Additionally; a non-tower operation worksheet was needed which includes approval from the manager and flight operations duty officer. Once the crew signed the new release and had a copy of the approved non-tower ops worksheet; the aircraft blocked out and operated to ZZZ.  Later that night; the captain called the Flight Operations Duty Officer around XA:15pm to inform the Duty Officer that when he landed the aircraft in ZZZ; the airport lighting was not operational. However; the flight crew was able to safely land the aircraft in ZZZ because the moonlight was bright. There were no NOTAMs indicating the airport lighting was INOP. Additionally; Dispatch was never notified by the crew that the lighting was INOP. Dispatch was only notified by the Duty Officer four hours after the aircraft blocked in at ZZZ. I called the airport Tower after it reopened; and the controller stated he wasn't aware of any lighting issues and the lighting was operating normal.Even though this was a short flight; communication from the flight crew to dispatch was poor. They're several things Dispatch could have helped with prior to the outcome; including calling airport operations to inquire about the lighting issues and suggesting diverting to the alternate airport.
Report_2_Narrative: Just before we were ready to pushback ground ops messaged us to let us know that ZZZ was going to non-towered ops for COVID cleaning. After we reviewed the FOM to ensure that we collected all the required documents and procedures.  We had all the required items per the FOM. With that we departed 1hour and 8 minutes late. We knew that Tower and Approach would be closed upon arrival. We were being vectored in by ZZZ Center. We requested to come in between ZZZZZ and ZZZZZ1. We requested the visual into Runway XX at ZZZ the weather was VMC.   On the base leg I has a visual on the PAPI and the captain intercepted final around 8 miles out and was flying the glideslope towards the runway. We were cleared the visual and switched to CTAF frequency.  We made multiple calls on final reporting our position. We also tried to activate the lights on the field 3 times with no success (there was nothing on the approach plate indicating it would be pilot controlled. But we hoped that it being listed as the CTAF would give us control). Around ZZZZZ the runway was clearly coming into view. By 1;000 feet we could clearly see the runway and all the markings. The Captain then proceeded to land and we taxied into parking. The landing occurred at XA15z which was in the twilight hours. At no point did we feel that we were in danger or unsafe. We mistakenly used the takeoff lighting requirements. After landing we looked everything up in the FOM to double check ourselves. We do feel it would have been dangerous to go around in a CFIT moderate environment with minimal coverage from Center. This was my second flight in ZZZ with the Captain this week. We were comfortable with the approach leading into Runway XX.The event was caused by ZZZ Tower not leaving the lights on when they closed and us as a crew using the takeoff lighting requirements vs landing requirements for CATI table.We could have delayed longer out of ZZZ1 to arrive when ZZZ was definitely going to be open. We could also call the Tower before departure to ensure that they leave the lights on. We could also plan to shoot the ILS all the way from the initial approach fix.
Report_1_Synopsis: Dispatcher and flight crew reported a night landing without runway lighting.

Report_1_Narrative: ZZZZ hub failed to notify us (Dispatch ZZZ) of Dry Ice being loaded in aft belly of aircraft. Required fuel over burn not included on release as a result.Failure of the ZZZZ hub to notify Dispatch ZZZ of Dry Ice being carried in forward or aft belly of a 777.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Dispatcher [at main base] reported Hub Dispatch neglected to provide Dry Ice cargo information to main Dispatch resulting in no  'over burn fuel' on Flight Release..

Report_1_Narrative: Alerted to passenger with continuous cough throughout flight.  Passenger in [seat] X3 had spent the last year in [foreign country] and reported that she had the cough for a week and had been taking medicine for 2 days. Flight Attendant witnessed her taking cough medicine during flight. No other COVID symptoms reported. Dispatch and Medlink consulted. Passenger was relocated to aft of aircraft to isolate; per recommendation of Medlink doctor. She was also given an N95 mask. Paramedics met aircraft. Passenger's temperature was taken by EMS and was normal. She refused to answer any further questions and treatment. All 3 flight attendants [were] exposed to this passenger.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported having a passenger who was coughing throughout the flight.

Report_1_Narrative: While flying the ZZZZZ RNAV departure this morning; ATC asked us if we were assigned a heading from the last Controller. The PM replied stating we were direct ZZZZZ1; with ZZZZZ behind us on the FMS legs page. This made us look closely at our legs page and moving map on our iPads; which showed us off course. ATC replied with 'roger.' Shortly following that; we were handed off to the next controller. When we checked in we mentioned our box input error and he said; 'No problem; proceed direct ZZZ1. How's that?' No further discussion with ATC. I immediately knew what happened and why. The FMS would not download our flight plan (not uncommon) so I built in manually. As I looked at the clearance I noticed the departure and selected it; but failed to assign the ZZZZZ1 transition. ZZZZZ1 appeared on our route packet as a different fix; not part of the departure and I fell for it. I had a lot of fixes and airways to type in so I focused on getting them correct and failed to notice how I had loaded the departure; without the transition. Ultimately we were missing 4 fixes in the legs page. I checked the first 5 fixes in the legs page to confirm the altitude restrictions since we were cleared to climb Via. Normally I check all the fixes but the other contributing factors today were no coffee or breakfast at this point. I wanted to get setup and ready so I could get coffee. Due to COVID; food and coffee was not available at the hotel so we catered it for our morning departure. Additionally; the pax showed up XX minutes early which squashed my plans to eat before we took off. Additionally; the lead pax birth date was incorrect on our brief so we were further distracted.Human error. I caused this event during the FMS setup. The pre-flight distractions becoming more and more common place with passenger related issues of catering and name details; today it got me. Another potential cause could be how the flight plan route is displayed on our packets. I'm used to seeing something like 'ZZZZZ.ZZZZZ1 ZZZ2; etc.;' as the FMS shows; but the filed route on our flight plan shows 'ZZZZZ ZZZZZ1 ZZZ2; etc.' Seeing it with the period would have drawn my attention to the ZZZZZ1 transition. Suggestions - For me; all things being the same again; if the filed route on our flight plan packet showed 'ZZZZZ.ZZZZZ1' this deviation wouldn't have happened today. Regardless of this and the distractions; I need to be more careful.
Report_2_Narrative: Clearance was ZZZZZ departure ZZZZZ1 transition; data link would not download flight plan. Flight plan was manually entered by PF loaded ZZZZZ departure to ZZZZZ then direct ZZZZZ1.  When verifying flight plan off filed route page neither of us caught this manual entry error.  When asked if on heading by ATC we started wondering why so checked departure and GPS position and found our error.  Asked ATC if we needed to correct error and they said no and cleared us farther down line on clearance.  Possible contributing factor were passengers showed XX minutes early; the way ARINC flight plan filed route shows on first page.  Things could do to correct this issue on future.  Verify and check each fix on the departure and also check mark each fix on lat long pages in flight plan compared to what is in the box.The way filed route showed on ARINC page; not loading transition properly when manually entering flight plan.Cross check each leg of the departure versus the plate.  Also check mark each way point matches the lag/long pages in the ARINC flight plan.  Any time having to manually enter information verify everything a couple times.
Report_1_Synopsis: Corporate flight crew reported a track heading deviation due to loading an incorrect transition fix in the FMS.
