Report_1_Narrative: During arrival to HAN; I was a jumpseat observer. We were at 2;000 ft. on the localizer; cleared for the ILS [Runway] 11 Left approach. Just outside the Final Approach Fix; I heard the Captain (Pilot Flying); say glideslope captured; and he set the missed approach altitude of 5;000 ft. in the altitude alerter. I was confused; because looking at the FO's (First Officer's) PFD (Primary Flight Display); I could see that we were below the glideslope; and it was no captured. I could not see the Captain's PFD to verify whether or not the glideslope was captured. The aircraft started descent from 2;000 ft.; even though we were not on the glideslope. I called out to check the glideslope and/or altitude. I did not have a hot mike; and maybe they weren't hearing me. The aircraft passed the Final Approach Fix approximately 500 ft. low. I called out the glideslope deviation again. The other jumpseat observer was also telling them to climb; and I yelled 'Go Around'. Then we got a GS caution with a line strike through the FMA on the PFD. At approximately 1;200 ft.; the go around was finally initiated with full scale deflection indicated on FO's PFD.During the surprise go around; we were instructed to maintain heading and climb to 5;000 ft. At some point the autopilot was disconnected; and situational awareness was deteriorating. The aircraft was veering to the right of track; 20 degrees nose up; and not following the flight director commands of 10 degrees nose up. I called out something like 'Who's flying the airplane; fly the airplane!' The flying pilot then steered back toward the flight director; regained control and the autopilot was re-engaged. After reaching 5;000 ft. we were vectored back for another approach to Runway 11 Left.Also of note; there was runway/taxiway construction at HAN airport that could have possibly created a glideslope anomaly. Though I could not see the Captain's flight instruments; it is possible there may have been a loss of glideslope indication at the start of the event. On the FO's PFD; I could see that the ILS was identified; and localizer/glideslope were displayed at all times.The Pilot Monitoring should have noticed on his instruments that the aircraft was not on glideslope; and should have called out the deviation immediately. When I saw the deviation; I was trying to alert the crew to fix the situation. I should have called out go around immediately.
Report_2_Narrative: While inbound on the localizer for RNWY (Runway) 11L; the glideslope was captured and the 'G/S' FMA was active. Shortly after capturing the glideslope; the 'G/S' FMA blinked and had a yellow strikethrough. The glideslope then started to fall beneath us; while the autopilot tried to increase the rate of descent. The Pilot Flying switched to V/S [Vertical Speed]; and rolled in more V/S down to stay on glideslope with a more than normal descent rate. I instructed to 'level off; level off' followed by 'climb back to 2;000 ft. It was then I noticed the glideslope dot had blinked and reappeared at two dots high; indicating we were low. The Captain in the observer seat then said 'Go Around; Go Around'. The Pilot Flying initiated the go around with the 'TOGA' [Takeoff Go-Around] switches and sometime thereafter turned off the autopilot. He then hand flew the go around to 5;000 ft. and present heading. After notifying Tower of our missed approach; we were told to contact Approach frequency. During this event; with my seat position; I was only able to observe the Captain's PFD [Primary Flight Display]. After landing safely and gathering all facts observed between crewmembers; it was apparent that the autopilot tried to capture a false glideslope and failed; thus giving us the yellow strikethrough the 'G/S' FMA."
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Flight Crew reported un-stabilized approach.

Report_1_Narrative: Upon doing cockpit pre-flight to ferry Aircraft X out of long-term storage from ZZZ to ZZZ1; I noticed the aircraft was fueled improperly. The wing tanks were not full and were imbalanced; there was no fuel in the center tank and there was fuel in the ACT (auxiliary) fuel tanks. This is not the proper configuration for fueling the aircraft. The wing tanks must be full before there can be any fuel in the center tank and certainly there cannot be fuel in the ACT tanks in this scenario. We notified the mechanics onboard who were assisting us to make sure everything was good prior to departure. What ensued was a three-hour debacle trying to figure out how to drain the fuel from the ACT tanks and ensure the only fuel was in the wing tanks. Planned release fuel was 25k; which in this scenario should result in fuel only in the wing tanks. After the fueling issue was finally resolved; we received two separate ECAMS after engine start. Shut down the engines and called the mechanics back to fix the new issues. SMOKE DET Fault and ANTI ICE STBY L STAT. MX fixed those two issues and we finally departed over four hours late.Someone in ZZZ is not making sure [aircraft company] aircraft coming out of storage are fueled properly. This is the second time I have caught a problem. Someone less vigilant may miss the problem.This is the second fueling issue I have had with an aircraft coming out of storage from ZZZ in the past two weeks.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported having an aircraft that was fueled incorrectly for a ferry flight.

Report_1_Narrative: Just after departing ZZZ; heard F/A's on cabin inter phone complaining of an odor in the cabin.  About that same time; the FO and myself noticed an electrical/plastic melting odor in the cockpit.  Performed Avionics Smoke procedure in the QRH.  Smell dissipated after selecting Blower and Exhaust fans to override and turning off cabin fans and galley equip. Confirmed odor was dissipating with the cabin crew; so after some discussion; we decided to continue to ZZZ1.  Talked with dispatch and Maintenance Control; filed out fume event report.  We [advised ATC] to minimize delay getting into ZZZ1 and as we begun defending thru 10;000 ft; the fumes returned.  FO and myself both donned out oxygen masks and got the a/c on the ground in ZZZ1 as quickly as possible.No casual factors involved. About a serious event as can be!Unsure where the actual source of fumes came from.
Report_2_Narrative: After departing ZZZ; heard F/A's on cabin inter phone complaining of an odor in the cabin.  About that same time; the CA and myself noticed an electrical/plastic melting odor in the cockpit.  Performed Avionics Smoke procedure in the QRH.  Smell dissipated after following QRH and selecting Blower and Exhaust fans and turning off cabin fans and galley equip. Confirmed odor was dissipating with the cabin crew; so after some discussion and already having ZZZ1 as nearest suitable airport; we decided to continue to ZZZ1.  Talked with Dispatch and Maintenance Control; filled out fume event report.  We [advised ATC] to minimize delay getting into ZZZ1 and as we begun defending thru 10;000 ft; the fumes returned.  Both crewmembers donned oxygen masks and got the a/c on the ground as quickly as possible.'
Report_1_Synopsis: A320 flight crew reported an uneventful landing at destination after experiencing a fumes event noticed throughout the aircraft.

Report_1_Narrative: I as Pilot Flying; was initially on a stable approach descending to 3;500 ft. on base for [landing]. I had briefed a Flaps 22 landing. As I was turning base to final (a left turn) and starting further descent; the winds shifted and resulted in a loss of tailwind; and my airspeed increased in the turn. At that same time Tower told us to turn 10 degrees right I believe due to traffic. Through all of this; my approach became unstable with too steep a descent; and got [we] a GPWS sink rate alert. I immediately executed a go around. ATC issued a new clearance and we came back and landed without incident. Suggest some more insight; and different scenarios taught on Flaps 22 landings possibly during training. Because of the higher airspeed vs. Flaps 45; it seems there is an increased chance of unstable approaches; especially if the winds shift as in my case. I carried too much power on this approach and also got distracted with the instruction from Tower to turn opposite of my base to final turn.
Report_1_Synopsis: EMB-135 First Officer reported executing a go-around after receiving a GPWS 'Sink Rate' alert on a visual approach associated with a wind shift.

Report_1_Narrative: I went into the cockpit for a bathroom break at XA:30pm.   Neither pilot was wearing a mask.   I asked; 'please put on a mask;' and pointed to mine as I entered and saw they weren't wearing masks.   The First Officer reached for his mask and put it on as I paused upon entering and pointed to my mask.   I again asked the Captain to put his mask on; once again pointing to my mask with both hands this time.   The Captain just turned and looked forward out the window in front of him.  He would not verbally reply nor put on a mask.   He refused to follow company policy.   We did not speak the entire time I was up there for their break - he looked out the window; I stood silently by the door.     I had to stand there in the cockpit and potentially be exposed to COVID-19 and the serious consequences that could ensue.   It is my understanding that COVID policies apply to everyone!    When the First Officer swapped out; I said something to him about the captain refusing to comply with policies and procedures and being disrespectful.   The First Officer chose not to comment on the Captain's inconsiderate and dangerous behavior; although the First Officer was wearing a mask at that time and he kept it on while I was in the cockpit.I chose not to go up again; so a colleague said he'd help with the meals in 20 minutes.   At the time the colleague handed the meals up; the person taking them from him didn't have a mask on.   The Captain did not wear a mask when others went into the cockpit to help.  Several crew members chose not to go up there at all; several were offended and uncomfortable but chose not to say anything; and one said they didn't care that much.  Fortunately; we only flew one leg with the Captain.The Captain's behavior was inappropriate; disrespectful; non-compliant with company policy; and potentially quite dangerous.  His behavior was unsafe and unacceptable on all fronts.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Attendant reported that the Captain did not wear a face mask while flight attendants were in the cockpit and was non-compliant with face mask policy.

Report_1_Narrative: During Takeoff a strong odor of chemical/burning plastic filled the cabin and all-call was made to confirm everyone else also smelled the same odor. It lasted for about 15 minutes.  Pilots also confirmed the smell; along with some passengers and non-rev crew members. During descent and approach the same smell came back through to landing; 15 minutes; the chemical burning odor.  The Flight Attendants felt symptoms (coughing; watery eyes; sore throat; lightheaded; headache) from this odor and had Medical meet us at the gate.  The First Officer also had Medical check him as well.  We did not feel well enough to continue on for our next segment of our trip.  Due to the pandemic of COVID-19 and the short time frame of a fume event needed for bloodwork; the risk to go to a hospital is too high for both ourselves and others.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Attendant reported a cabin fumes event during departure and again during descent resulting in health issues. Flight Attendant described the odor as 'chemical/burning plastic.'

Report_1_Narrative: Captain reported that the CPDLC [Controller-Pilot Data Link Communications] accept and reject buttons were switched; this caused 2 occasions of erroneous reject responses being sent to ATC. On arrival switches were confirmed in the wrong place (IPC (Illustrated Parts Catalog) 31-10-51-02) and switched back (SWPM (Standard Wiring Practices Manual) 20-84-13). This report is to raise awareness that these switches can be inadvertently transposed.
Report_1_Synopsis: Maintenance reported that CPDLC buttons were reversed.

Report_1_Narrative: A near midair collision occurred while in the traffic pattern. I was cleared to take off after [a] Cessna and was told to follow traffic. I took off and turned to John Wayne's standard 15 degree offset heading while climbing to TPA. Around 500 feet AGL I realized I no longer had traffic to follow in sight. I heard the Cessna request a short approach and ATC approved [him] for a short approach and clearance to land [Runway] 20L; after this I assumed that the traffic to follow was downwind and that I would have visual contact if I turned towards crosswind and downwind. As I was in the turn ATC asked me if I had traffic to follow in sight still. I reported back that I no longer had traffic in sight. ATC then told me to just fly a wide downwind for spacing. At this point the Cessna reported that [they] needed to make a right turn to avoid me. This whole time the Cessna was not in my visual; so they must have been beneath us and out of line-of-sight. I can only speculate on how exactly we converged as I had zero visual reference at this point with the Cessna. The Cessna and I continued flying the pattern together with no further incident but I did notice this Cessna was not flying the standard 15 degree offset on upwind and seemingly a little lower than TPA. I am unsure if this was an attributing factor to the loss of separation we encountered.
Report_1_Synopsis: PA28 Instructor Pilot reported an NMAC in the traffic pattern at SNA airport.

Report_1_Narrative: During a tailwheel transition training flight; the aircraft departed the runway surface on landing. The winds upon time of landing favored Runway XX and a right-crosswind component of about 10 knots was present at the time of the occurrence. No other traffic was in the pattern and the approach was stable throughout. The touchdown was in a three point attitude and did not bounce. On the rollout; the student improperly managed rudder control and the aircraft rapidly developed a significant turn to the left. As Instructor; I took control of the aircraft and stopped the ground loop from further developing. The aircraft departed the hard surface of the runway at roughly a 10 degree angle at a fairly slow speed and came to rest in the grass about 20 feet from the edge of the runway. Upon shutting the airplane down; both the student and I exited the airplane to assess the situation. No signage or lighting was hit nor was there any damage present on the airplane. The grass was smooth and no holes were present.The situation developed from a normal crosswind landing to a runway excursion quickly. The cause was an improper control input by the student that was not caught in time by me; the instructor. Despite not reacting in time to prevent the excursion; the aircraft did not ground loop and no damage was sustained by the airplane. Any corrective action would be on my part as the Instructor; to take control sooner before such a significant turn could develop.
Report_1_Synopsis: PA-12 Instructor Pilot reported his student lost directional control on the landing roll resulting in a runway excursion.

Report_1_Narrative: I was entering the traffic pattern at 45 degrees for a downwind entry for RWY14 at FIT. I had previously announced my intentions and location on the 122.7 CTAF. I did not see or hear the conflicting traffic during its go around and climb out from RWY14.  I was alerted to the traffic by an ADS B traffic alert on my iPad. At this point I could not see the traffic in my field of view. I turned 45 to downwind and added power to get away from the traffic.  Earlier I had heard the conflicting aircraft on the CTAF advising it was on the RNAV20 approach and would be breaking off the approach for a straight in to RWY14. Calls to the conflicting traffic before and after ADS B alert we're not answered.It all happened very quickly and I only glanced at the ADS B display; figuring my attention should be outside the airplane looking for the traffic. But the combination of repeated ADS B traffic warnings and not being able to visually see and avoid the traffic was quite stressful.  Today; I was able to get the conflicting traffic's flight path from flight aware and compare it to my own from Garmin Pilot. It appears the conflicting traffic did a low approach to RWY14 and a go around; making a left climbing turn close to my own flight path. From the flight paths; the time stamps; and the fact that I never made visual contact with the conflicting aircraft; I think it passed behind me; and estimate it may have gotten as close as 500 ft.Being more vigilant to visually identify and track what I thought was landing traffic; would likely have avoided this dangerous conflict. The fact that the conflicting traffic never responded to my radio calls should also have raised a red flag.
Report_1_Synopsis: M20 pilot reported experiencing an NMAC in the pattern at FIT airport.

Report_1_Narrative: I was on the ramp at the FBO which is located at the end of the taxiway. I had received my IFR clearance for departure on Runway 7 on the clearance frequency. I then switched to the ground frequency and requested taxi clearance. (It was now well after sunset) I was told to taxi to Runway 7 via Foxtrot. I left the ramp and made an immediate left. Upon reaching Foxtrot 2; I realized that I wasn't actually on Taxiway Foxtrot; but was on a parallel road which was intended for vehicle traffic; not aircraft. I stopped at Foxtrot 2 and notified Ground control what had happened. I informed them that I could make a right onto Foxtrot 2 to get on the Foxtrot Taxiway. The controller notified me to hold my position and that he would send an Ops (Airport Operations) vehicle out. About 5 minutes later the Ops vehicle arrived behind me. The ground controller notified the Ops vehicle that I had stated that I could make the turn onto Foxtrot 2. The Ops vehicle approved that which I did and I made the right onto Foxtrot 2 and then left onto Taxiway Foxtrot and proceeded to the hold line for Runway 7 without further incident.After making the wrong turn on what I thought was Taxiway Foxtrot I did see a sign with an F on it with a black background on my right which is why I thought I was on Taxiway F. As I proceeded towards Runway 7. I commented to my passenger that there were several dips in the pavement which was unusual. As I approached F2; I saw a red sign past F2 indicating no entry. That's what was literally the red flag. Fortunately; I was in a high wing aircraft which cleared all lights and signs. This may not have been the case in a low wing aircraft. This second road was not shown on my airport taxi diagram which might have helped. I don't know if anyone else had ever made this same mistake; but I think better signage would have helped. Perhaps a sign coming out of the ramp on F1 indicating 2nd left to Foxtrot or a red no enter sign like the one at F2 might have might have also helped. I had not flown into this airport in over 15 years. I did not request progressive taxi instructions because the route appeared to be very simple. I will be more vigilant during night operations at unfamiliar airports.
Report_1_Synopsis: GA pilot reported unknowingly taxiing on a vehicle roadway at ROC airport; thinking it was the taxiway.

Report_1_Narrative: Flying the published missed with autopilot in NAV and VS ALT to capture 4;000 [feet] as assigned by ATC. I was instructed to fly heading 070. After setting the heading bug to 070 I forgot to switch AP from NAV to HDG mode. The autopilot then started into the hold turning right to 161. [ATC] asked where I was going and at that point lost control trying to turn too steeply back to 070. In an unusual attitude I was trying to recover. Eventually; [I] hit the straight and level button on the autopilot and climbed above the cloud deck; got reoriented and rejoined the approach and landed without further problems.
Report_1_Synopsis: SR22 pilot reported experiencing inflight loss of control while trying to correct to the proper track during a go-around.

Report_1_Narrative: When I arrived at DUY there was another aircraft parked in the ramp area and it began to taxi out before I vacated the runway. The previous aircraft had offloaded cargo in the center of the ramp but I failed to see it due to the ramp being unlighted and the difficulty of seeing over the engine cowling. The aircraft's taxi light is also located in one wing and doesn't illuminate objects on the other side of the aircraft very well.While taxiing onto the ramp; the propeller contacted a cardboard box from the previous aircraft's cargo. There was no damage to anything outside of the cardboard box and there were no injuries involved.The ramp area at Kongiganak is very constricted and requires a lot of effort to operate safely in the best of circumstances. I feel that this episode might not have happened had the previous aircraft unloaded its cargo in a less hazardous location. At DUY the runway is lighted but the ramp is unlighted. If the ramp area had better lighting; then this unfortunate episode might have been avoided.
Report_1_Synopsis: Pilot reported hitting cargo during taxi on an unlighted ramp at DUY airport.

Report_1_Narrative: My Recommendation: Because there is what I believe to be a low but uncertain chance that the primary pressure vessel of the Aircraft X has a current active failure; the aircraft should be immediately grounded; and an investigation be initiated into whether this issue is just a classification and engineering oversight; or indeed a failure to the aircraft's primary structure. Aircraft X (Boeing-767-300) is potentially operating on an inapplicable airworthiness sign off and may fly (already has flown) with a possible serious defect to the aircraft's primary structure (pressure vessel). Aircraft X arrived at ZZZ station December 2020. Upon arrival the following defect was found and recorded into the maintenance log book:Discrepancy: Undocumented Speed tape found concealing stripped & unsecured mounting screw to extruded Main Cargo Door (MCD) Manual Vent Door Drive (Pressure Vessel) cover panel.I notified Maintenance Control of the defect and submitted via email a proposal for a temp repair utilizing non-standard substitution parts available on-hand at our station that I hoped would allow for a timely repair keeping the aircraft on scheduled revenue flights despite the need for an Engineering Order (EO) and additional authorizations. After an appropriate time; an outline of maintenance action to be completed was submitted to our station for a yet unapproved EO numbered: XXXXXXXX; that was a substantial deviation from my own earlier proposed temp repair. This EO after performing a Detailed Visual Inspection (DVI) merely called for reattaching the panel in place with RTV-106 sealant; no hardware; and a covering of multiple layers of aluminum speed tape. Knowing that an external application of tape over a hole in the primary pressure vessel of an aircraft did not meet the basic criteria for acceptable maintenance standards; I contacted maintenance Control to inform them that we (aircraft technicians under my purview) at ZZZ would not be able to comply with the EO maintenance instructions as they were currently written because of the safety implications.After expressing my unwillingness to press forward with the draft EO I began receiving pressuring communications from various maintenance controllers; maintenance duty managers; and Company management; saying everything from 'just do it;' to 'it'll be fine.' Additionally; it was overheard in background talk on more than one phone call with maintenance controllers that they did not believe the panel in question was actually a primary pressure vessel fitting as I had asserted in multiple emails and phone conversations; and was merely a weather seal. Worried that I had somehow made an egregious mistake about the panel in-fact being a pressure hull seal; I enlisted both additional night shift mechanics to assist with a cabin pressurization leak check (referencing AMM 05-51-24-782-001) with the damaged MCD Manual Drive cover panel removed. As I operated the cabin pressure manually; utilizing APU bleed source; the two assisting technicians reported a strong; unrestricted flow of air emanating from the uncovered hole; while I was observing only 1 PSI indicated differential cabin pressure. Believing that this observation adequately supported my previous assertation; I terminated the test; returned the aircraft to its previous configuration; and felt confident that my continued refusal to repair the aircraft as outlined in the draft EO to be a safe and correct judgment call.The scheduled departure of the aircraft was altered from XA:15z to XE:00z. At XB:16z I received an email asking me to 'please call In to Maintenance Control to advise on current status of approved EO compliance;' (no approved EO had been received or transmitted to anyone at ZZZ station). Given the ongoing pressure from phone calls and condescending emails to comply with an EO I had yet to see; I advised [the] maintenance controllers that I would not be complying with the EO and to direct all future communications to be in writing. I then suggested at that point that they 'just AOG (aircraft on ground) ship the required parts necessary to return this defect to its original condition;' with the observation 'that the original undocumented speed tape repair has already been proven to fail;' as my own justification for non-compliance with an EO that called for doing the same thing; only with more tape.At XD:50z we received the first approved copy of the EO XXXXXXXX via email from the Maintenance Manager; which upon review was consistent with the advised sealant and tape repair already rejected. The scheduled aircraft departure was once again pushed back to XG:00z; well after the scheduled arrival of the oncoming maintenance day shift. At XE:15z I received a phone call from my Company Regional Manager asking me why I was not complying with the EO and then; regarding taping over a hole in the pressure vessel; to 'explain how this is a safety concern?' After briefly elaborating to him about how the loss of cabin pressure makes flight crews go to sleep and planes to become lawn-darts; he said that I would 'have coverage in terms of liability because the engineer signed off on three layers of speed tape.' After mutually disagreeing; he proceeded to switch the subject to asking me which maintenance technicians were coming in on day shift; then; seeming unsatisfied; continued to ask me about the status of other technicians not scheduled for shift. Several minutes after hanging up; another call was received from a subordinate technician; not scheduled to come in; inquiring as to what was going on and why the Regional Manager was asking him to come into work on his weekend and 'override' us. At the advice of another technician overhearing the conversations; I took a written note of the above quotes from the calls.With continued inquiries for resolution on the aircraft; the oncoming day shift Lead informed Maintenance Control that the EO was still unworkable as it was and reiterated that the original temp repair proposal forwarded to Maintenance Control that included substituted hardware installation would be a fix deemed acceptable and believed conforming with standard practices that we would still be willing to sign off on. Giving in; the Maintenance Controller agreed to get the hardware installation added to a revised version of the EO along with an additional step for a cabin pressurization check that the day shift Lead smartly felt necessary for repairs performed on the pressurized structure of an aircraft. With assurances that the revised EO would include the agreed upon amendments; the day shift Lead and myself expedited the repair to the aircraft in an effort to make the scheduled departure pending timely receipt of the revised EO. The cabin pressure leak check of the repair was then successfully accomplished with only a small movement observed in the repair at a peak indicated differential pressure of 4.5 PSI; and no leaks or excessive loss rates noted. Upon departing the aircraft to accomplish paperwork closeout we were greeted by the oncoming flight crew; who had apparently been kept apprised of the ongoing situation and wanted to personally thank us for looking out for their safety.At XF:18z we received the approved EO XXXXXXXX Revision 1. Required paperwork was completed; signed log pages were sent; flight crew was briefed; and the aircraft was returned to green status at XG:10z. The aircraft subsequently blocked out of the gate at XG:39z for a delay from scheduled departure of 39 minutes. Why is this a safety concern? Upon later realization and review; I have found several possible deviations to Federal Aviation Regulations (FARs); the airline General Maintenance Manual; and uncertainty to the validity of the accomplished repair that should be investigated immediately as it may represent a serious safety issue to the aircraft. Having been so narrowly focused on getting the point across to the necessary parties involved in the tribulations of Dec Xth that the damaged part was indeed part of the pressure vessel of the aircraft and that a workable repair would have to be tailored to the additional physics involved with that part of the structure; I failed to realize the broader implications of what a repair to the pressurized structure of an aircraft entailed in terms of adherence to regulations; maintenance policy; and accepted practices. The FARs define 'Primary Structure: is that structure which carries flight; ground; or pressurization loads; and whose failure would reduce the structural integrity of the airplane.' Even though steps were added to Revision 1 of the EO to conform the repair to acceptable practices 'equal to its original or properly altered condition;' because the installation hardware was a reasonably close approximation of the original parts; the additional step of adding three layers of overlapping speed tape is in direct contradiction to the airline General Maintenance Manual policy for its use:          -HIGH SPEED ALUMINUM TAPE-          High speed tape is a convenient material for use as an interim repair for          non-structural materials. Under no circumstances will it be used on primary          aircraft structure. A Log Book entry is required when high speed tape is           applied unless instructed to do so by an EO with DER approval.Under this policy; the use of speed tape in this manner is strictly forbidden and forgiveness when it comes to doing the maintenance under the provision of an EO only absolves the requirement of a log book entry for its use. However; even though agreement was made in Revision 1 of the EO for addition of attachment hardware and an added cabin pressurization leak check; the EO creator did not alter the original classification of the repair to acknowledge that the repair was in-fact being accomplished on an aircraft primary structure:          'The Main Deck Cargo Door Manual Vent Door Drive Cover is considered secondary          structure. The time limited repair per this EO is minor; and the temporary           repair per Part 1 does not affect the fit; form or function of the skin.'I would imagine this to be an oversight; and if it is; then an additional revision needs to be made which would at a minimum alter the category of the defect deferral and its associated time-limited re-inspections and permanent repair due date/cycles. If this is not an oversight; however; as this EO has been twice over reviewed and approved; and the MCD Manual Vent Door Drive Cover is indeed a secondary structure; then the original investigative cabin pressure leak test failed for a reason other than indicated (i.e. there is an existing failure of the primary pressure vessel somewhere internal to the Main Cargo Door). Which would in turn mean that a damaged secondary structure is now fulfilling the function of a primary structure pressure seal. I do not believe this to be the case; but; as the MCD is a modification from the original aircraft structure; the existing reference material available for my use to confirm the hypothesis that the cover plate is indeed a primary structure component is vague and uncertain. Tech Engineering likely has additional references not available at a line station that could perhaps shed light on the issue.Since issuing equivalent versions of the above safety report to both Airline and Company on [the next day]; Aircraft X has remained on a regular flight schedule with recurrent re-inspects per Part 2 of EO XXXXXXXX Rev 1; until receiving Part 3 Permanent Repair [4 days later]. I can currently find no record that any further investigation has been conducted.
Report_1_Synopsis: Lead Technician reported refusing to sign an Engineering Order due to compliance issues.

Report_1_Narrative: During a Flight Attendant crew change and passenger boarding; our Flight Attendant B advised Flight Attendant A and myself; Captain; that she received a call from her personal Physician that she had a positive result for COVID-19 test resulting from a pre-surgery screening. A Flight Attendant immediately advised B Flight Attendant to contact Crew Scheduling and request to be removed and replaced for the flight. The Captain immediately advised Operations Agent to discontinue boarding and have passengers in jet-bridge return to boarding area in terminal building; while B Flight Attendant gathered her belongings and removed herself from the aircraft.I then requested the Operations Agent to call Flight Attendant crew lounge to see if a Reserve Flight Attendant was available to assume vacant position. The Flight was originally advised of a 30 minute delay for inbound Flight Attendant from another flight. After approximately 10 minutes; we were advised that a Reserve Flight Attendant was enroute from the crew lounge to cover flight. The Flight took a 17 minute delay due to the Flight Attendant exchange.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Captain reported during passenger boarding one of the flight attendants received a call from a physician reporting a positive COVID-19 test result.

Report_1_Narrative: We were at FL410 in continuous light chop. The seat belt sign was on before we entered the known area of turbulence and remained on till we passed the turbulence. ATC [was] reporting light chop for the next 150 miles. I had the speed intervene window open. The N1 was set for turbulence penetration. The speed was Mach .76. Within a matter of seconds we were in severe mountain wave. The speed increased to Mach .80 and we were in the over speed band. The over speed clacker went off right away. We began losing altitude. I immediately reduced thrust which was ineffective so pulled the speed brake. The speed slowed to Mach .76. We lost 300 ft. quickly. Then the second wave hit and we climbed rapidly back to altitude then 200 ft. above the assigned altitude. The aircraft returned to FL410. The event was probably 30 to 45 seconds. During the event I had the FO (First Officer) seat the flight attendants immediately. I had the FO ask for a descent to FL390. We were given the descent. The FO reported the mountain wave and the trends to ATC. There was no traffic in the area on TCAS and none was reported by ATC. We reached FL390 with no further wave but the light turbulence continued. I checked the flight attendants in and they reported no one was up during the event. I reported the event to Maintenance as severe mountain wave and over speed. I reported the event to Dispatch as well. In my 25 years of flying I have never seen mountain wave this bad.
Report_1_Synopsis: B737 Captain reported encountering severe mountain wave activity that resulted in altitude excursion.

Report_1_Narrative: After getting clearance to push from both Towers to the 'Y' I initiated the pushback. As soon as I started my turn into the taxiway the pilot notified me of a jet speeding in our direction. I immediately braked and pulled back toward the gate. The pilot stated again that we had the clearance and the jet should have stopped. It did not stop and sped right by.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier tug driver reported a near collision with another air carrier aircraft during pushback procedure.

Report_1_Narrative: While driving the bridge to the aircraft the 737-900 door was opened prior to the bridge docking or the required two knocks by myself. While driving I don't expect to see the door get popped which is extremely distracting while I am moving heavy equipment towards an aircraft. If the slide had been deployed it could have caused me serious harm or even death. I file an average of 3 or 4 [safety reports] on this exact issue every single week. This has got to stop.
Report_1_Synopsis: Jetbridge driver reported the B737 cabin door was popped open during the docking maneuver.

Report_1_Narrative: Aircraft X was showing out of the gate when the ramp tried to final. Once I finished working another flight I saw I had 5 Weight and Balance Check messages showing Hazmat not secure w/15 bags for flight Aircraft X. I called ZZZ Operations at first the zone controller did not want to be bothered said ramp will call me. After the ramp tried to final another 5 times the Lead [Ramp Supervisor] then decided to call the Load Planner. When he called he at first stated the Hazmat was below the line; which I corrected him and said nothing was ever below the line because the flight was not weight restricted. That line isn't what got my blood boiling; the lead then stated on a recorded called all of the Hazmat was no show and wanted me to hold it off. I refused because I couldn't understand why if it were a no show he would attempt to finalize the Manifest 10 times before calling me. When I asked him that question he hung up the phone. The lead then attempted another 6 time to finalize the Manifest with no bags in the pit; afterwards he called back to say the plane is going to have to come back because the Hazmat is onboard. If I would have been one of those push over load planners I would have simply held off the Hazmat taking the lead at his word and we would have had a plane takeoff with Hazmat onboard; not secured; and no pilot paperwork. That really irks me the fact that he lied on a recorded line to have me hold off Hazmat that he knew he loaded on the aircraft.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Ramp personnel reported Load Planner pressured Ramp Agent to falsify Hazmat departure documents to reflect initial Hazmat loading configuration error had been rectified.

Report_1_Narrative: There was no disinfectant or sanitation spray in the lobby today.  This is not what has been promised to us to protect us from COVID.
Report_1_Synopsis: Customer Service employee reported lack of sanitizing spray in the airport lobby.

Report_1_Narrative: ATIS was advising ILS approaches in use. We requested the RNAV Y for pilot proficiency reasons. The request was approved by the final approach controller. At the end of the RNAV arrival; we were put on the published heading and told to expect vectors onto final for the RNAV Y approach by the final approach controller. We requested but were denied direct both initial approach fixes to start the approach. We were given 2 vectors; the last being [Heading] 290 and the clearance to fly heading 290 maintain 4;300 ft. until established on the final approach course cleared for the RNAV Y approach as we were vectored toward the course between the initial approach fixes. The approach became challenging at that point because the final approach course and glidepath anticipation cues were not visible and therefore we were unable to arm the approach. Additionally; the 4;300 ft. restriction left us high rather than leave us in a position to descend to 2;900 ft. in the space between the initial approach fixes because the width of the lateral course at that point is much narrower than a localizer signal. The IMC and terrain rich environment added to the concerns at this point. I feel that part of this challenge was created by the technique US air traffic controllers are using to get aircraft onto RNAV approaches. Rather that clear an aircraft to a fix on the approach; they are trying to vector them onto final as they would for an aircraft flying an ILS approach. My first safety concern is that there is not final approach course to intercept when flying an RNAV approach such as the localizer transmitting out bound from the runway for many miles. Rather there seems to be courses from one fix to the next all the way down the published approach. When ATC says 'fly heading xxx until established on the final approach' there isn't a final approach to intercept. I question whether a clearance of that wording is procedurally correct on RNAV approach. There are no examples I can find in company manuals or the Airman Information Manual the depicts starting an RNAV approach at anywhere other than a fix on the approach. I have had this type of vector onto final clearance for an RNAV approach for RNAV approaches in other U.S. destinations also so I feel the safety threat posed by this type of RNAV clearance is widespread in the USA. I have never received a clearance like that outside of the USA. Outside the USA; I have always been cleared to fix to start the RNAV approach. My second safety concern is that if that type of RNAV approach clearance is correct; we do not train that at any point during initial or recurrent training. All of our simulator training clears the aircraft to a fix on the approach when cleared for an RNAV approach. If the type of ATC clearance we got is procedurally correct we never see it in training.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier pilot reported ATC issued a vector to intercept the final approach course for an RNAV approach which does not have a final approach course. The reporter stated this type of clearance is issued routinely by U.S. ATC but overseas they are always issued direct to a fix to begin the approach.

Report_1_Narrative: During passenger boarding I started the APU to cool the aircraft. I selected the APU bleed on and immediately began to smell a foul pungent odor. I turned the bleed off and waited a couple minutes. I tried the APU bleed again and encountered the same pungent odor. I waited a minute to see if it was a temporary smell but it persisted. I turned the bleed off and wrote up the airplane in the maintenance logbook. The smell was predominantly in the flight deck and forward galley however passengers deplaning from the rear of the aircraft were inquiring about the odor. Maintenance checked to see if the APU was possibly over serviced. The APU checked out normal. Maintenance continued their work and eventually cleared the write up. When we returned to the aircraft to get ready to board all crew members again smelled the same smell. Although it was not as strong as before it was still there and seemed to get slightly worse if we turned the Number 1 Pack off. I again wrote the aircraft up in the maintenance logbook. No medical attention was requested or required for crew or passengers.As for the probable cause; no causal factors that I can think of. Maintenance said it could have been the fumes from an aircraft starting upwind of us however that wouldn't explain why we smelled it the second time hours later.
Report_2_Narrative: APU was started in preparation for departure; upon turning on the APU bleed to begin cooling the aircraft there immediately was a strong fume that made my nose and eyes begin to burn. I told the CA (Captain) that was the bad fume smell we need to be careful about and said I was leaving the flight deck to stand on the jet bridge. The bleed was turned off and I left for fresh air. After multiple retries by MX (Maintenance) who agreed the smell was there the passengers and remaining crew were deplaned. Later the MX personnel had done nothing other than run the packs using the external air cart and were ready to sign the plane back into service; but simply walking into the galley every single crew member could still smell the fumes. We tried to isolate the problem pack by switching packs and the fumes became worse again. We then left the aircraft again. This is an ongoing problem worldwide in the industry. The potentially disastrous health consequences of this type of pyrolization should be addressed before more crew members and passengers are impacted.
Report_1_Synopsis: A321 flight crew reported a fumes event during passenger boarding resulting in maintenance action.

Report_1_Narrative: The Captain and I met at the airplane in the morning and the first topic of discussion was the automated parking guidance procedure as neither of us had used the system yet and they appeared to be operating. We referenced the flight manual as well as the local notes concerning the system and still felt that we were not sure exactly what we were supposed to do approaching the gate. We asked rampers prior to departing and their explanation; which did not help much. We departed and further discussed our plan for approaching the gate in our briefing for the return leg. As we approached the gate 3 rampers were present and the guidance panel worked well and was intuitive. We found a Ramp Supervisor and he discussed the details with us and answered questions we had. The guidance in the flight manual is inadequate as it does not address definitively whether or not marshallers are required to be at the spot. It does not specify the procedure for requesting assistance from ramp personnel if required It does not address what to do in the event that equipment is in the safety zone. Finally; the guidance as to when the screen symbology is required references 'the nose of the aircraft passing the jet bridge' which does not apply to the Aircraft X in where the system is active. My interpretation and common sense answers to these questions are likely to create a safe operation but safe and compliant are not always the same thing.  We entered the gate area in compliance with the flight manual to the best of my knowledge and interpretation; however I feel that the guidance in the manual was inadequate. Part of the information we used to determine a plan for parking came from talking with rampers. They obviously have good insight but their word does not meet acceptable standards for determining compliance with a procedure. I would recommend a simple update to the manual that goes beyond description of the guidance panel and sets definitive procedures for entering the gate.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier pilot recommends changes to flight manual guidance concerning operations using the automated parking guidance system.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Distraction; Communication Breakdown; Workload; Situational Awareness; Physiological - Other
Report_1_Narrative: There was a break before the next flight to ZZZ.  Flight attendants left the aircraft.  First Officer (FO) left the aircraft.  Captain left the aircraft as one of the FAs came back to the aircraft.  Captain came back to the aircraft.  Both FAs and FO were on board.  Also a Ramp Agent (RA) was on board sitting in the back of the plane resting.  One of the flight Attendants told the Captain she was concerned that the RA did not complete the security search.  From her perspective it seemed as if the security check was not complete.  Captain went back and asked the RA if he had completed the security search.  He said yes.  Captain asked what was involved with the search and he described that it was a visual search and where he looked.  Captain told the Flight Attendant that the Ramp Agent said he did it.  Flight Attendant was not sure because the RA hadn't lifted up the seat cushions and looked behind them or put the tray tables down as the FA had seen done in previous security searches.  Captain asked the RA if he could do the security check again and that there was a concern that it was not complete.  The RA started doing another security check lifting up the seat cushions in the first couple rows.  Captain went to the flight deck to prepare for the flight.  Captain assumed that the security check got completed the second round and all was good to go.  Flight departs for ZZZ; Captain and FO review the security section of Flight Ops Manual (FOM).  After arrival in ZZZ; the Captain goes to review the security section with FAs.  It is then that he hears that the Ramp Agent did not go completely through the cabin on the second time and check seat cushions and tray tables at ZZZ1.  The RA talked with another RA and then told the Flight Attendants that the search had happened and it was complete.  The Captain called the Duty Officer and had a discussion about the situation and the wording in the FOM.  Duty Officer told the Captain that he would call back after a few minutes while he made a call to find out what the Ramp manual says to do.  After the Duty officer called back to the Captain he referenced the Services Manual about aircraft search to and from ZZZZ; wording was not the same as what is in the FOM.  The Duty officer agreed that there is room for some confusion between the wording in the two manuals.  Captain decided to stop the operation and have ZZZ ramp agents do a Full Search before continuing on to ZZZ2.  A Big thank you to ZZZ RAs in knocking out a Full Search.         My thoughts (Captain) there is some confusion in how the FOM describes a cabin search and what a visual inspection actually is on the security form.Pay closer attention to details.  Don't assume anything; make sure everyone is on the same page in understanding of what's happening.  Ask questions; try and understand the full picture.  It's been awhile since our airplanes have made ZZZZ trips and it was the first time for our crew the other day since prior to COVID-19.  We need to show each other respect; and give grace in this super stressful time.  After talking with the Duty Officer; I more fully aware of the staffing issues with ramp; COVID-19 cases and just under staffing in different areas which has been extremely difficult.  I also see a value in debriefing the crew at the end of the trip or after abnormal situations as a learning time for all as we grow as professionals.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported the aircraft security check may have been improperly conducted and cited confusion between the wording in two manuals as a contributing factor.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Situational Awareness; Time Pressure; Communication Breakdown; Confusion; Distraction
Report_1_Narrative: We were fully boarded; with checklist Before Start To The Line complete. Flight Attendant B reported passenger submitted; when Flight Attendant A reported the ramp agents requested we contact Station Ops.  Operations informed us Flight Attendant B was being replaced on the trip by a reserve. I assisted Flight Attendant B off loading bags; and advised them to catch a breath and gather all effects. The pressure of the last minute situation and the ramp; and the timeline; needed to be ignored at that moment. The replacement flight attendant arrived; I assisted loading bags; verified ID and returned to the flight deck. Weight and performance numbers came up and the Captain stated ready for door closure. The main cabin door and cockpit door secured; weights entered and verified on FMS. Without communication from ramp agents; they re-opened the main cabin door. Flight Attendant A knocked on the cockpit door; which we opened. Flight Attendant A stated the First Officer was now also being replaced on the trip. I queried Crew Scheduling and was told name ordered me off the trip with no further information given. The replacement First Officer arrived and I offloaded the bags. The Captain was astonished that such an action would take place without communication; consult; or apparent consideration for safety of flight.Passengers expressed surprise; and some measure of concern and alarm. The main cabin door being opened without the crew's awareness is not a procedure I have seen before. Replacing crew members who are not ill at the last minute affects our morale and pocketbook; and creates unnecessary concern for the revenue passengers. Safety of flight is inevitably affected by this kind of turmoil; and it falls on the Company to alleviate stress and safety rather than contribute to it. The Company exercised authority in contradiction to common sense and safety of flight. The timeline; already compressed; became distressingly so given the apparent chaos this action caused in view of passengers. Ordering the ramp to open the main cabin door without communicating first to the crew is an extraordinary act of harassment and intimidation. If a pilot needs to be replaced on a trip for administrative reasons; surely that can wait until after a short turn is completed. This action requires the crew; the new crew; to re-brief and reinitialize a flight under stress; delays our passengers; compromises our timeline; and potentially costs us our bonuses. It should be taken only under extraordinary circumstances; which apparently do not exist. The Company should be an asset to safety of flight rather than a liability.
Report_1_Synopsis: An Air Carrier First Officer reported ramp agents opened the main cabin door without coordinating with the crew and ordered the First Officer and B Flight Attendant off the aircraft.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Other / Unknown; Physiological - Other; Situational Awareness; Workload
Report_1_Narrative: During boarding Family A was sent down to aircraft not wearing face covering. Passengers were asked the age of the child at the entry door and stated 3 years old. Passenger stated at the doorway she had the child's mask in her purse and would put it on at their seat location; I apologized and stated the mask would need to be on the child before boarding the aircraft. Family A then stepped out on the Jetway; pulled the mask out and said it would be difficult getting the child to wear and keep the mask on. I wanted to have the passengers go back up and speak with customer service; but thought they would comply. As other passengers were boarding; Family A followed behind; I did not notice they had not put the mask on the child.After we completed the safety briefing and doing the walk through; Family A were sitting with the child; had not placed the mask on the child; mother had placed the mask back in her purse. I apologized again and stated she would need to put the mask on child. Captain had signaled for takeoff. I also mentioned to the parents the Captain wanted to go back to the gate and I told them I did not want to go back to the gate. The mother tried to put the mask on the child; the father tried; then stated he wanted to give her some medicine that would make her go to sleep. I informed the Captain what was going on and of our progress; Captain made the call to go back to the gate. Several managers met the aircraft. Family A was asked to deplane.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Flight Attendant reported a family was removed from the flight because their 3 year old child would not wear a face mask.

Report_1_Narrative: I came to my gate early to work my next flight. A flight was still there and boarding. I watched as passenger after passenger scanned their boarding pass or mobile device across the gate reader. I even watched as one gentleman sneezed with his boarding pass in hand. The reader was never wiped down with sanitizer between scans. I believe we should be wiping down gate readers before and after each flight.
Report_1_Synopsis: Gate Agent reported the electronic boarding pass readers at the gate need to be sanitized after each flight.

Report_1_Narrative: Due to COVID-19 the following statements need to be remove or change for the Technician performing the task.task# XX(A) put the mask-regulator unit on your head and your face.task# XX1Breathe through the mask-regulator unit with dilution control lever set to N (normal) and when it is at the 100% position.Remove or make an amendment to skip the step; it's also on the Y type aircraft manual.
Report_1_Synopsis: Maintenance Technician reported wording in maintenance instructions needs to be changed to accommodate for COVID-19 policy.

Report_1_Narrative: On [Date 1]; I was reviewing paperwork on the current Aircraft X in the [Maintenance Visit] in ZZZ and noticed that a robbed transponder on Aircraft X was installed the previous night and did not get a signoff in the logbook releasing the aircraft for RVSM (Reduced Vertical Separation Minimum) operation. This aircraft was still scheduled to be in the [Maintenance Visit] for another 5 days so I just had the nightshift avionics tech complete the entry the next day. But I knew that the avionics tech that forgot the RVSM signoff on the [Maintenance Visit] also replaced a transponder on Aircraft Y during the overnight on [Date 2]. I pulled the paperwork from the night of [Date 2] and found that the #2 Transponder was changed to clear a MEL (Minimum Equipment List); but a RVSM release was not done in the logbook. I called Maintenance Control and told them what happened and Aircraft Y was inbound to ZZZ1 at the time so when it landed in ZZZ1; Maintenance went out and deferred the RVSM. The ZZZ Avionics tech that replaced the transponder is [Name].Found during paperwork reviewShould of; but did not realize the transponder is RVSMCalled Maintenance Control and had the system deferred (RVSM)[Parts Document] lists the PN (Part Number) of the transponders that go on our aircraft that are post ADS-B (Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast) mod. This PN [XXX] is not listed in the aircraft IPC (Illustrated Parts Catalog); so there is no statement (RVSM Critical Item) like all the other transponder PN's listed in the IPC. This statement (RVSM Critical Item) should be added to the [Parts Document]; to bring attention to it like the PN's listed in the aircraft IPC.
Report_2_Narrative: On [Date 2] I was assigned to clear a Transponder #2 MEL (Minimum Equipment List) on Aircraft Y. I determined it needed a new transponder; however; we did not have the proper transponder in stock required for ADS-B (Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast) mod aircraft. I was directed to rob the transponder from Aircraft X which was the [Maintenance Visit]; after robbing (from Aircraft X) and installing (on Aircraft Y) the transponder; I went through the operation checks and everything was good. I went to sign off the paperwork and seen; from the beginning of Chapter 34 in the AMM (Aircraft Maintenance Manual); that it was not CAT II (Category 2). I forgot that RVSM (Reduced Vertical Separation Minimum) isn't included in the beginning of ATA (Air Transport Association) chapters and since I picked the part number based on [Number] I didn't see the RVSM reminder note seen in the AIPC (Aircraft Illustrated Parts Catalog). I went to open the GMM (General Maintenance Manual) on the tech computer I was using and it wouldn't open. It was known within the base that PDF's can act up on the 2 provided tech computers. My ignorance of not remembering that RVSM wasn't included in the beginnings of ATA chapters; and not going into AIPC; and assuming that since RVSM wasn't downgraded it wasn't an RVSM component; along with my laziness of not confirming with a lead or Supervisor on their computers contributed to missing the RVSM release sign off. The plane made at least one flight with out having the RVSM release. The next night I installed new transponder in Aircraft X and Operations checked everything and since I assumed it wasn't RVSM the day before I repeated my mistake for the [Maintenance Visit on Aircraft X]; and didn't write up a RVSM release sign off. It was caught before the aircraft left and the other avionics technician went through the operation checks again and provided the RVSM release sign off.The day shift Supervisor caught the [Maintenance Visit] not having the release and knew that I did the aircraft the night before and seen that I didn't release that one either and took corrective action.I didn't put max effort into looking into seeing if the component was RVSM critical. I went off of a handful of assumptions and didn't double check with my leads or Supervisor. The [Number] didn't reiterate it was an RVSM critical item; the GMM PDF didn't want to load on the tech computers; RVSM isn't located at the beginning of ATA chapters like CAT II and RII (Required Inspection Item) are.Put RVSM in beginning ATA chapters like CAT II and RII. Add a reminder in [Number] that the transponder is RVSM critical component. Remove old transponders from stock that can't be used with ADS-B aircraft seeing that our whole fleet has ADS-B mod. Leadership verified wrong part number in stock the night before contributing to this issue being on 2 aircraft due to robbery. Update/upgrade/fix tech computers so we can open the files we need.
Report_1_Synopsis: Aircraft Maintenance Technician reports that component was installed on aircraft without proper signoff.

Report_1_Narrative: On a training flight with a student; we had alternator failure an hour into our lesson. I did not notice the ammeter reading negative until the transponder began to flicker on and off. When I was troubleshooting; I asked the student to look at the ammeter; since it was on his side; and he told me that it was showing a negative reading; and that there was a red light. I immediately turned towards ZZZ1 and began to reduce the electrical load; hoping to lengthen the amount of time that we would have a working radio. At this point I checked into our traffic avoidance system; and noticed that there was heavy traffic at my airport of intended landing. I queued up Approach and told them the nature of my situation. I told them I wasn't sure if I would have enough battery to safely make calls to get into the traffic pattern; considering my transponder was dying. A few minutes later; right after they transferred us to Tower; who quickly cleared us to land; we lost all ability to communicate. We were unable to use our electric flaps on the landing. I taxied back to the ramp and gave Tower a call to see if I needed to fill out any paperwork; and they told me that they had taken care of it. In retrospect; I should have caught the failed alternator sooner. My student had noticed the light; but did not know what it meant; and his yoke was in the way for me to notice it. During our cruise checklist; that is one of the items that we check; and I did not notice anything wrong when we did the checklist 20 minutes prior. Additionally; after noticing the issue I could have just completely turned off the master switch and used pilotage to get us close to [the airport]; after which I could have turned the master back on and then used my radio. I had never had this happen before; so I was trying to make quick; confident decisions.
Report_1_Synopsis: C172 Instructor Pilot reported returning to departure airport after experiencing alternator failure.

Report_1_Narrative: After doing 5 touch and goes on runway 28R; I received clearance to land. I did a wheel landing; let the tail come down; and when the aircraft was traveling slowly at about 15 kts or less; I started turning left to aim for the taxiway exit; and the aircraft kept turning to the left and did a complete 360 ground loop on the runway. The aircraft did not suffer any damage or touch any part of the aircraft to the runway; except the wheels of course; and I did not leave the runway. Due to this unexpected delay the aircraft landing behind me had to go around. I attribute this ground loop to unexpected strong crosswind; and the fact that we just put air in the tires and the aircraft was a lot more responsive to rudder control inputs that on my previous flight. She just got away from me for a moment.
Report_1_Synopsis: J3 Cub pilot reported loss of directional control and a ground loop on the runway during a crosswind landing.

Report_1_Narrative: This was my first flight at the controls of a tail wheel aircraft. I was in the left seat receiving flight instruction from the CFI in the right seat. A thorough pre-takeoff briefing including experience levels and positive transfer of controls was accomplished before departure.As we approached ZZZ; we briefed the fact there was a right crosswind with gusts and the appropriate actions to take regarding this. The approach was stabilized. A normal wheel landing was accomplished and the tail was successfully lowered to the ground. The left main tire failed; at which point the instructor stated 'my airplane' and I released the controls. The resulting swerve was not controllable and the airplane ground looped approximately 150 degrees; coming to rest on the runway. We immediately shut down the aircraft and exited. No propeller or wingtip contact with the runway occurred. The aircraft remained on the runway. No injuries occurred.
Report_2_Narrative: The mission was to fly with 2 friends and give them tail wheel instruction. There was a crosswind from the right and we discussed crosswind correction and the plan. [The pilot flying] conducted the wheel landing and shortly after putting the tail down; the airplane started shaking violently. I thought this may have initially been a tail wheel shimmy; which was odd since it didn't shimmy since the tail wheel springs were replaced in month; but the airplane started veering to the left so I announced 'my controls' and corrected it with right rudder. The shaking got worse and the plane then swung around to the right and ground looped. The wings did not contact the surface and there was no prop strike. The airplane was then towed to the hangar where I worked with a mechanic to change the wheel and tire so that the plane could be moved while inside the hangar. I did identify some contributing factors. There was a strong right crosswind; it was my student's first landing; and I had previous issues with my tires slipping on grooved runways. They are 8.50 oversize tires. I do believe the left main tire went flat on landing; and with the strong crosswind and delay of taking the controls from my student; it was unrecoverable. I'm filling out this report to detail human factors issues that contributed to damage to my precious airplane; and as the investigation unfolds it will determine if there is need for additional caution when using larger tires.
Report_1_Synopsis: Cessna 170 student pilot and instructor reported the aircraft experienced a flat tire upon landing and ground looped.

Report_1_Narrative: After takeoff Runway X on the ZZZZZ3 departure ZZZZZ transition; the Pilot Flying called for clean wing configuration; Climb Power and VNAV.  Pilot Monitoring failed to properly select and verify the selected vertical command.  PF flying did not receive the correct level off climb guidance.  Human error focused on initially to cross ZZZZZ1 above 7;000 feet NOT at or below 7;000 feet. ATC immediately instructed aircraft to 'STOP CLIMB' and level off in which we complied with.Contributing factors:Pandemic and lack of flying time in last 6 months.Unfamiliar airport operations.
Report_2_Narrative: At departure called for clean wing; CLB; VNAV. PM cleaned wing and selected VNAV;CLB. I as PF failed to verify new VCLB mode on PFD. Contributing factor: - on initial brief i misread SID as cross ZZZZZ above 7;000 feet. The SID requires a cross ZZZZZ below 7;000 feet. - last flight was July 2020.
Report_1_Synopsis: Corporate flight crew reported an altitude deviation during departure and cited lack of flying as a contributing factor.

Report_1_Narrative: Took off from ZZZ in VFR and picked up IFR plan and was given clearance to 190. After passing through a thin layer I encountered a very large build up and the base was lower than the MEA. I was concerned for the safety of flight and descended below the MEA in order to clear the buildup. I did this without calling center. Center was very upset and canceled my flight plan. After clearing the buildup I began my climb again and was reissued my clearance.
Report_1_Synopsis: TBM pilot reported deviating below MEA to avoid weather.

Report_1_Narrative: I was working two radar sectors combined with a trainee and trainer as my coordinator. The traffic volume was high with the normal arrivals; departures; overflights; and practice instrument approaches. The complexity was high due to a 10 minute notice of a flight check aircraft that needed to check an opposite direction approach. Once the flight check aircraft started his opposite direction approach I started briefing the relieving controller in training for a sector split. As the flight check aircraft had just finished with the opposite direction approach and continuing to brief the relieving controller for the split; I radar identified the flight check aircraft and turned him on course for the next approach. As all that was happening; I was descending and vectoring Aircraft X for the ILS approach to a different airport. Aircraft X was the second aircraft in the sequence of three for the ILS approach. As Aircraft X crossed 2 miles north of a satellite airport; Aircraft Y was departing VFR north bound climbing to 3;000 ft. without any communication with me. I called the traffic as soon as I saw the issue and Aircraft Y reported that he was maneuvering to avoid collision. A few seconds later Aircraft Y called VFR looking to pick up his IFR flight plan. Also the weather at each facility within the airspace was overcast or broken around 2;200 ft.
Report_1_Synopsis: TRACON Controller reported they were distracted by splitting a combined sector and a flight check aircraft and did not notice two aircraft in confliction which resulted in a NMAC.

Report_1_Narrative: I signed Dangerous Goods Form for wet battery HAZMAT; only later did I realize that there needed to be a HAZMAT on board notation from Dispatch on the Dispatch Release notes section. This notation was missing. This notation is a recent change to the Dangerous Goods Form procedure.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Captain reported required Hazmat notice on Flight Release missing while reviewing flight documents during cruise.

Report_1_Narrative: During pushback a Flight Attendant called and informed me that a passenger was refusing to wear their face mask.  I asked if she wished to have the passenger removed for non-compliance to which she responded in the affirmative.  I had the push crew pull us backed to the gate and requested a Supervisor from operations.  Arriving at the gate; the Flight Attendant informed me that she made four attempts to have the customer replace his mask over his nose to which he refused or was otherwise non-compliant.  The Gate Agent boarded the plane and was unable to get the customer to wear the mask appropriately so he was removed.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Captain reported a passenger would not comply with face mask policy and was removed from the flight.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Situational Awareness; Time Pressure; Confusion; Communication Breakdown
Report_1_Narrative: Aircraft being pushed back from gate XX in ZZZ. Just prior to our pushback; another company had started to tow a type X aircraft from gate XX1 to XX2 (I didn't see which gate specifically as I was the wing-walker). The crew towing the type X aircraft cut across the ramp when they had plenty of room to maneuver around our flight and in the process give us plenty of room. The other company tow team's action forced me to motion to our pushback driver to stop the push ASAP. We stopped our push and the other company continued to their gate. Our crew then continued our push back and dispatched the flight normally. The X gates are being used for RON aircraft due to ongoing COVID-19 flight reductions.
Report_1_Synopsis: Ground wing-walker reported ramp safety concerns because of the unusual aircraft parking areas needed during the COVID-19 reductions.

Report_1_Narrative: While in cruise flight Flight Attendant (FA) A called the flight deck.  The First Officer answered the call.  He told me the FA had a non-compliant passenger with the mask.  He reported that she was tapping him trying to waken the passenger and he pushed her arm away.  We transferred control and I called her back and asked it everything was OK and to repeat what happened.  We ACARS Dispatch to have a Supervisor at gate.  We were in range when we received the call and elected to continue to ZZZ. The passenger was mask non-compliant.  He was told to cover his nose with the mask.  He was sleeping when mask slid down.  FA woke passenger with a tap; it may have startled him; but he pushed her hand away and swore.I believe the company has to make sure the passengers are aware of the seriousness of non-compliance.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Captain reported a passenger was not complying with face mask policy during flight while sleeping.

Report_1_Narrative: We noticed when we were doing the in-flight service that passing out the bottle of water/snack bag first; meant that all the passengers had their masks off as we were serving them from the bar cart. It would be safer for passengers and crew to serve the beverages first; then the snack bags as the amount of time the masks were off would be shorter. This would also limit our exposure time while passengers have their face masks off.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Attendant reported there should be a change to the in-flight beverage/snack service to limit exposure time to Flight Attendants while passengers have their masks off.

Report_1_Narrative: Passengers were sitting in seats across from the jump-seat. There was not 6 feet between us. We were face-to-face! Our knees were touching. I'm concerned about the safety of not socially distancing between Crew jump-seats and passenger seating.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Attendant reported there is not enough room to social distance between the FA jump-seat and passenger seats.

Report_1_Narrative: Upon boarding [Passenger X] was noted to have a valve connected to his mask board. As Flight Attendant A was able to ask the valve be covered with one of the on board masks or swapped at his discretion due to the company not permitting direct exhaust valves. He indicated his mask had filters on the interior and was disappointed he could not use his preferred mask.  After discussing with crew we agreed the valve at least needed to be covered or swapped out. Mask was swapped prior to departure. Advised I had asked for a Supervisor to ensure we were on the same page regarding masks and valves noting it was not my intent to single him out or pick on him; but wanted to ensure we were on the same page for policy. The passenger thanked me and we departed for ZZZ1.Enforce policy at gate.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Attendant reported a passenger that had a valve on their mask was asked to replace the mask or cover the valve.

Person_2_Human_Factors: Troubleshooting; Workload; Communication Breakdown; Training / Qualification
Report_1_Narrative: During accomplishment of portable water system disinfect done by using ozone cart; as instructed by fellow mechanic assigned as support; (name unknown). I might have improperly connected the water supply line. This happened at ZZZ [Gate] around XA:00 [Date]. As soon as I noticed water coming out of the aft fuselage drain holes; I immediately stopped the re circulation process; notified crew chef; dumped over serviced wasted and requested for assistance form tech crew personnel.Lack of work experience with this specific task on my part; lack of assigned training; inability to complete work interdependently due to not having D1 endorsement and being able to drive on airport premises and move around with equipment and tools. Hostile work environment.Assigned training required to completed before being assigned to perform ozone cards; different diameter or tread pattern on water fill line attainment port preventing from improper installation; picture diagrams included in revised work card; hands on ozone unit classroom training; ZZZ ramp driving credentials; hangar access in below freezing conditions; better gate illumination; larger port markings allowing to differentiate between both ports housed only 3 ft. apart.
Report_2_Narrative: I was assigned to drive new transfer AMT's around since none of them had their DR1/3. One group required the 'blue cart' for water servicing; and the tech responsible for the job asked me questions about it. I gave him a basic description of the job; helped hooked the FILL line to the FILL nipple; and showed him the correct adapter for the job and threaded it in to show it was the right fit. After which I left to move other techs around. When I came back to the gate; that's when the results of the improper servicing occurred. The event occurred at [Gate] at roughly XA:00 on [Date] during the cycling phase of the disinfect.
Report_1_Synopsis: Technicians reported not connecting potable water disinfection equipment to aircraft correctly; causing the aircraft to flood the lower areas.

Report_1_Narrative: This submission is not to report and accident; rather a serious incident under FAA and NTSB definitions. The day before the flight; my wife and I planned to attend a meeting in ZZZ1. I moved the helicopter out of the hangar and had it fueled to the 1/2 full point. We contacted the church where we were going and obtained permission and authorization to land on the property. Early the morning of the flight; I opened ForeFlight and briefed weather; winds; and the anticipated location; and sent a screenshot of the map and location to my rotorcraft instructor. He and I then had a conversation about the steps and procedures to assess the location once I arrived; and we discussed how to set up for the landing. At XA:00 my wife and I met our friends at the ZZZ airport; performed the preflight; calculated a weight and balance; loaded up in the helicopter and headed for ZZZ1. The weather was excellent with good visibility and cool temperatures in the 50's to 60's. After the 20 min flight; upon arriving at our landing zone; I circled twice as a part of our reconnaissance and did our steps of the 600 ft. recon: size; surrounding; surface; slope; safety and then the 300 ft. recon: wind; wires; way in; way out; where to auto. The landing was normal and I secured the helicopter and we attended the meeting and luncheon. After the luncheon; I went out to the helicopter and started my preflight. During my walk around; I walked out to the road next to the church and looked in all directions. I observed wires to the north across the highway; to the east I observed wires; the church building was to our south; and I cleared the area to the west visually; and saw it was open and unobstructed; the wind was from the west. Once the preflight was complete; I recalculated the weight and balance; all was good; we were more than 200 lbs. under the gross weight limit; and with the temperature in the mid 60s; performance showed to be real good; so we loaded back in the helicopter. After going over the passenger briefing and seeing that all passengers were buckled up and ready I started the helicopter. After all checklist items were completed; and the warmup was accomplished; I lifted into a stable hover; maneuvered up and out toward the highway. Once again I looked for any traffic; and noted that the intended flight path was into the wind; and to the west; was clear and unobstructed.
