The Captain as the pilot flying had properly briefed the visual approach; to include the obstacles in the vicinity and highest obstacle on the approach plate. On right base; the Captain turned autopilot off with flaps 3 and gear down. I announced visual contact/no factor on the highest obstacles out the right window - a set of towers. We continued to slow and configure for landing and maintain an altitude of more than 1;000 ft. AGL. We received a caution from the GPWS; followed by a PULL UP verbal command. The Captain took the appropriate actions and immediately increased the airplane's altitude. We were in daytime visual conditions; and in accordance with company policy; determined we were still in a safe position to stabilize and conduct a safe landing after clearing the obstacle. We finished the turn to final; configured the aircraft for flaps 5 landing; completed the before landing checklist; were fully stable by 1;000 ft. and in a safe position to land the aircraft. Upon landing; we debriefed the situation; reviewing the approach plate for any obstacles. At more than 1;000 ft. AGL and no visual contact with an obstacle; we were unsure why the GPWS gave us the PULL UP command; but agreed that it was the most appropriate and safest action to respond to the command as we didGPWS PULL UP verbal command resulted in appropriate action of increasing aircraft altitude.A visual traffic pattern is one of the most difficult approaches we fly. I would suggest additional training during initial and recurrent training on distances and altitudes for different types of visual traffic patterns. I will personally work to improve my awareness as the pilot flying to ensure 1;500 ft. AGL on downwind and the 3:1 descent path ratio throughout the visual traffic pattern. I will review my flying skills to ensure I am flying this way as well. While I believe we took the appropriate action both during the event and after in the debrief; I will use this as a learning experience to ensure I am always a safe and skilled pilot.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported receiving a GPWS 'Pull Up' warning on a visual approach to XNA.

Report_1_Narrative: I departed ZZZ with the intent to ferry it to ZZZ1.  At the time of departure; weather was reported as overcast at 1;800 feet; visibility 10SM.  Field elevation is 2;500 feet.  Highest obstacle of the enroute corridor was indicated as 3;325 feet; per ForeFlight profile.  Reported weather allowed for a 1;000 foot clearance of the highest obstacle.  Upon departing and climbing to 3;200 feet; I could clearly see over all the hill tops along my intended flight path.  Approximately 10 minutes into the flight; clouds started to form and spill over from hill tops to the north and west into the adjoining valleys.  I executed a turn to avoid the clouds.  I decided I would return to ZZZ.  Suddenly; clouds started to form all around me.  The area around me was mountainous covered with thick forest. I felt that IMC was imminent so I initiated the IMC procedure.  I leveled the aircraft and started a climb; after adjusted power & airspeed settings.  I passed through the bottoms of 2 clouds as I started to set up the GPS for an instrument approach into ZZZ.  A moment later I was in a pocket clear of clouds with a large field next to a residence below me.  I decided it better to land VFR in the field than to continue IFR back to ZZZ.  I performed a descending orbit towards the field to get a clear picture of any/all possible obstacles.  A safe landing was performed without incident.  Notifications were made to Center.  After waiting approximately 2 hours; I was able to safely complete the ferry flight. Become IFR current within company.
Report_1_Synopsis: Helicopter Pilot reported being VFR in IMC and making a precautionary landing in a field.

Report_1_Narrative: Aircraft ahead failed to exit landing runway in timely fashion. ATC instructed us to execute a go-around; Runway 34 right. Simultaneous departing traffic on 35 left was offset and behind. We were than instructed to turn right heading of 105. Almost immediately we got a proximity warning. We were then instructed shortly after to fly runway heading and climb maintain 9;000 ft. ATC came back after giving us vectors for Runway 35R; informing us they had a mix up in call signs. Their intent was to turn the aircraft heading 105 departing off of Runway 35L. It seemed that air traffic control had a high workload at the time of our go around and I assume the controller was fatigued. Suggest continued use of good situational awareness about surrounding air traffic environment during high workload for air traffic control.
Report_1_Synopsis: Regional Jet pilot reported experiencing an airborne conflict with an aircraft taking off from a parallel runway during an ATC directed go-around.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Communication Breakdown; Distraction; Situational Awareness; Time Pressure; Workload
Person_2_Human_Factors: Workload; Situational Awareness; Distraction; Communication Breakdown; Time Pressure
Report_1_Narrative: While I did perform a visual inspection of the flight deck in accordance with FOM requirements on all flights departing the US to Country X; I never received or completed a search form. I realized this about halfway to our destination. I called the flight attendants and asked them if they'd performed a visual inspection during their pre-flight; to which they responded in the affirmative. I also called ground handlers in ZZZ when I got to ZZZZ. The gentleman confirmed with me something along the lines of; 'the cleaners perform the search of the cabin while they're cleaning and disinfecting the aircraft.'This was a 'turn around' with maintenance items that needed addressing and [aircraft] disinfection that needed accomplishing; so some task saturation. Furthermore; my normal routine is typically to trade the Gate Agent's paperwork with my completed security sheet. With the auto passenger count closeout; that moment is no longer consistently there. I think we could benefit a lot from some more standardization (pilots; flight attendants; and Customer Service) regarding the completion of the security sheet. With the new below wing ground handling and the new procedures in ZZZ; there are changes in the way aircraft are turned and the people I interact with. I will most likely remind myself and my crew about the security sheet during my Pre-flight Briefing when I mention passports. This way; verifying the paperwork is received and goes out the door can be a collaborative effort.
Report_2_Narrative: When airborne on our flight to ZZZZ the Captain realized that he didn't receive; fill out; and return the paperwork saying that he did the security sweep of the aircraft. He did perform the sweep when we first arrived at the aircraft and asked the Flight Attendants to see if they did their sweep as well. They also performed the sweep. When we landed in ZZZZ my Captain called the ground handlers and explained the situation and confirmed that he did the sweep.Our plane arrived late into ZZZ. We had to do a quick turn and wait for cleaning to [sanitize] the aircraft before our crew and passengers could get on the plane. Maintenance had to be performed on the aircraft. A lot had to be done in a short time.On the quick turns everyone needs to slow down and make sure they are doing things correctly even if it means we won't get out on time. If the Gate Agent; Flight Attendants or Pilots took time to remember the security sheet then it would have been filled out and given back to be filed.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier flight crew reported failing to complete the security sheet due to pre-flight work overload that now includes the added task of ensuring the aircraft was sanitized.

Report_1_Narrative: In ZZZZ loading was taking too long so I stopped our duty day because at our arrival point we would be over our legal XX hours.  I asked the company for hotel rooms for the crew.  The Handler informed us we would need to stay in a government designated hotel and undergo COVID-19 testing or stay on the airplane.  We chose the hotel.  The handler and a [company representative] informed us the immigration service of foreign country denied our crew entry into the country and we were not permitted to leave the airplane.  I asked the Directors of Operations; Safety; and Standards; and the Chief Pilots if this would be legal Rest for our upcoming Part 121 assignment and got no response from any of them prior to our new (after minimum rest time) departure time; so I asked my crew if they felt safe to fly and they all said yes; we departed.  We were in a foreign country subject to our Handler's communication with local immigration officials and them informing us what we could or could not do.  We were even warned not to leave the aircraft by the handler to walk over to our other company airplane on the ramp as it could subject us to serious consequences if we were detected by Immigration.   When we realized we had no alternate other than to obtain our Rest on board the aircraftA lack of planning on company Operations part in terms of how the Crew would be provided with normal hotel rest facilities should they get stuck in this location as we did.  Even if you book a hotel if Immigration won't let you leave to go to it it is of no use.I kept my crew 100 percent in the loop as to all communications and any of them were free to decline the 121 assignment after we obtained Rest on the airplane.  All of them told me they felt safe and were ready to fly.Plan for more than adequate time to load an airplane at this location.  X.X hours were allocated obviously that was not nearly enough.
Report_2_Narrative: Though we were as a flight crew rested; alert and fully capable of conducting the flight safely; local authorities had denied our entry into the country. We were forced to obtain rest prior this leg in the aircraft. Again; to restate; we had no choice other than to stay in the aircraft during our rest period. Our choice was originally to be tested for COVID-19 and risk quarantine to obtain adequate rest in the hotel. I personally witnessed company's efforts to get us into a suitable hotel. Those efforts were denied by local officials as relayed through emails from our handler.We were aware prior to the flight that it would be necessary to depart after resting in the aircraft.1) Mechanical delay departing ZZZZ on previous leg. 2) Failure of our handler to obtain rights to enter the country to ensure proper rest facility.All attempts were made to complete the flight within the originally scheduled duty day. We even suggested a shorter flight time to a different destination for a crew change. All efforts made by the crew were denied by the handler.Explain to the customer / handler that it will be necessary to obtain permission for the crew to stop enroute for a crew change if the loading is delayed. Please note here that the load being stopped and the crew departing within the appropriate duty day was an option given to the handler. The choice was made to continue with the full loading of the aircraft.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported that they had to get their required rest on the aircraft instead of at a hotel. The flight crew stated that although they had agreed to take a COVID-19 test to stay at the hotel; the foreign country's immigration service did not allow them to leave the aircraft.

Report_1_Narrative: Prior to entering the ZZZ Center airspace; during cruise at FL330; I had just returned back to my seat as 'as pilot monitoring' after using the rest room.  As a matter of practice; I read aloud the FMA parameters (which all appeared normal); upon taking my seat and assuming the role as 'pilot monitoring.'  Immediately after that; the Captain had also returned back to his seat as 'pilot flying' from his rest break; and exchanged his position with the IRO who had been occupying the captain's seat as the 'pilot flying' during the captain's break. At that time the Captain noticed that the aircraft had momentarily climbed to and leveled off at an indicated altitude of 33;500. The Captain immediately commenced a descent and returned the aircraft back to its original altitude of FL330; without any further consequence.We had become aware of the altitude when the Captain brought it to our attention In the cockpit. However; it was on the following day in ZZZ1 during my deadhead trip; that the captain recollected the event details and informed me that we had a deviation that may warrant the filing of a report. I believe that the aircraft may have climbed 500 feet and leveled off by the inadvertent touching of the altitude selector knob; either by the handling of the clipboard or by using disinfectant wipes in close proximity to the FCP; by one of the crew members; while getting in and out of the seats.  None of the crew members is sure of what caused the movement of the altitude selector knob and the gain in altitude.  The Captain immediately commenced a descent and returned the aircraft back to its original altitude of FL330; without any further consequence. As crew members; we were all equally surprised by the inadvertent deviation in altitude. Exercising greater level of situational awareness by all crew members; increased monitoring of the FMA; especially during the exchange of pilot seats and exchange of pilot roles while commencing and ending of crew rest periods.  Exercising extreme care during handling of clipboard and using disinfectant wipes in vicinity of FCP during flight.
Report_2_Narrative: Aircraft wandered off of assigned altitude in excess of 300 feet in cruise flight. [It was identified] when the Captain pointed it out. Mountain waves and or FO accidentally bumping the VSI or altitude pre-select while cleaning/sanitizing the FCP [may have caused it].I confirmed that the altitude was off the assigned; and needed to be corrected immediately. Advise all flight crews to use extreme caution when moving things around or cleaning the FCP inflight.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported an altitude deviation after the altitude selector knob was inadvertently moved. The flight crew stated the use of disinfectant wipes on the control panel may have been a contributing factor.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Troubleshooting; Time Pressure; Confusion; Communication Breakdown
Report_1_Narrative: We began our duty day at XA30 Z on date in ZZZZ; for a flight to ZZZZ1; continuing to ZZZ.  Upon arriving in ZZZZ1 the ground handlers removed existing pallets and started loading the outbound cargo; before fueling started. Approximately 30 - 45 minutes later we had about a 16 ton imbalance with all of the fuel in the left wing tanks and center tank; and fuel was venting overboard; after the fuel spill clean up the fueling process resumed and again stopped due to the mechanic onboard the flight was not experienced on the aircraft type; and could not figure out how to operate the valves and transfer fuel to the right wing tanks. With us as the flight crew not allowed to exit the aircraft in foreign country; had no other option but calling [company]; and keep them in the loop. At this time we are approaching our duty limit for the day in order to reach ZZZ; and we all agree to extend our day by X hours to get the job done; as described in the FARs. Numerous calls are being made to Dispatch; Maintenance Control in order to find help for the Mechanic who is outside supervising the fueling. Again we are approaching our duty limit; and calls are being made to Director of Operations Control; who hung up the phone on the Captain and to the Duty Officer who hung up the phone twice. What we were trying to accomplish was if the company had a contingency plan; or a plan B for us. As we had discussed this earlier; and rather sleeping on the aircraft; we were thinking more like proceeding to either ZZZZ2 or fly back to ZZZZ to rest; which was denied by the Duty Officer. We ended up spending the night on the aircraft; and after the curfew was lifted in ZZZZ1 we were able to get the required paperwork and fuel for departure. Finally arrived in ZZZ with no issues almost XX hours after the duty day had originally started. Would like to add that ALL phone conversations to operations control; maintenance control; Director of operations control and Duty Officer were made using speaker phone and was heard by the entire crew on the aircraft.[Caused by] inexperienced Mechanic operating and supervising the fueling process. The company needs to have a contingency plan; and plan B.By changing the scheduling procedures; have a dedicated crew fly between ZZZZ - ZZZZ; and use heavy crews for the rest; and provide better training for maintenance personnel in order to understand the aircraft type refueling process.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported that a ground delay caused by fueling imbalance resulted in the crew approaching duty time limits. Due to the foreign country's COVID-19 restrictions and company procedures; the crew had to remain on the aircraft for required rest.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Confusion; Physiological - Other; Communication Breakdown; Time Pressure; Situational Awareness
Report_1_Narrative: My duty day started in ZZZZ.  I was part of a 2-man crew; scheduled to operate ZZZZ-ZZZZ1-ZZZZ.  At the time I left ZZZZ; the TAF for ZZZZ had a small period of low visibility in the forecast; which was to occur while I was on the ground in ZZZZ1; and the weather was forecasted to improve to be above CAT I minimums prior to my arrival back into ZZZZ.  While on the ground in ZZZZ1; I was checking the ZZZZ weather and found out that the ceilings were WELL below CAT I minimums.  I called Flight Operations for a briefing and was told the same thing.  I decided to delay the flight for an hour to watch the ZZZZ weather and to 'time' my arrival into ZZZZ to coincide with the forecasted lifting of the weather.  Flight Operations then called me back and asked for me to delay another 30 minutes so we would arrive 30 minutes after the period of low weather in ZZZZ - I agreed; as it was a good idea.  I also knew that I was currently at an outstation where I really have zero options for adequate rest if we got stuck there since we can't deplane the aircraft without mandatory COVID tests and quarantine until test results come back negative.  So; in reality; flying to ZZZZ1 is really a gamble in the first place but; for sure; I knew that staying there wasn't even an option. I eventually departed ZZZZ1 at the newly determined departure time and flew towards ZZZZ.Through the use of ACARS ATIS updates as well as messages to/from the company - it was determined that the weather in ZZZZ had not cooperated with the forecast.  Visibility was 125 meters to 225 meters - well below CAT I minimums.  I talked with my First Officer and we decided to enter high altitude holding and set a 'bingo' fuel number for us to know when it was time to have to go to the alternate airport; ZZZZ2. We burned through our holding fuel and were forced to divert to our published alternate airport. That's where the real fun began.  This is the point where we found out that an alternate that looks good on paper doesn't always work in actual practice.  We landed; parked in spot XX; and sat; and waited; and sat; and waited some more.  It took almost an hour just to get a set of stairs brought to the aircraft - and took an equally long amount of time to get a GPU and wheel choked so I could release the parking brake. At this point; I became doubtful that we would have the duty time to allow us to continue to ZZZZ1 - and that feeling was mirrored back to me by Flight Operations on my first phone call to them.   A plan for crew hotels was then started; as well as the continued effort to contact our 'handler' there in ZZZZ2.  Next came the biggest issue...Customs.  The handler first started telling me that we can't stay there because we can't clear customs 'in their country'.  I reminded him that we were scheduled to land in ZZZZ; which is the same country - but he didn't care.  Clearly; the thought of a crew having to get rest at this published alternate airport hasn't been approached before?   Finally; after 4 hours on the ground; the handler comes to the aircraft; asks me to shut it down so he can take us to a hotel close to the airport.  I complied; and as soon as I carried my personal items downstairs; I was told by that same handler that it would be another hour before customs can clear us and to please wait on the aircraft - which was now shut down.  I opened the aircraft again and that's where we waited for almost 2 more hours before the handler came back to tell us that there is 100% no way we were gonna clear customs there at that airport.  At this point; we had absolutely no choice but to stay on the aircraft.  After talking it over with my crew; we decided that the only option would be to depart ZZZZ2 as soon as we were legally able to do so - even though sitting on the aircraft isn't actually 'rest' - we had no other options.  I talked with Flight Operations and they told me that we could depart at XA:00Z; which was another 3 hours from then.  Out of lack of betterideas; we agreed; got the plane ready; and blocked out at XA:01Z for ZZZZ.   The real point in this report is to illustrate that so many of our flight plans might look OK on paper; but when it comes time to actually put contingencies into practice; the plan immediately dissolves - leaving crews stranded without the ability to legally continue operating; and without the ability to obtain legal rest.  Vetting of our 'approved alternates' certainly needs to take place.Not properly vetting filed; 'approved;' alternate airports to facilitate crew egress between aircraft and legal rest facilities.Worked tirelessly with the ZZZZ2 handler to try to secure rest facilities for my crew.  When that failed; I worked with my crew and with Flight Operations to determine when we could 'legally' leave.Time and manpower needs to be put forth in this company to actually find out what processes would need to take place at alternate airports or at intermediate stops to allow crew members a place to get safe; legal rest when needed.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Captain reported a delay due to weather at an international location resulted in crew rest issues.  The Captain also stated they decided to not deplane the aircraft during the delay due to the requirement of having to take a COVID-19 test if they left the aircraft.

Report_1_Narrative: On pushback from gate; ground crew asked me to set brake because they had an issue with the tow bar. It was difficult to understand what they were saying outside of normal communication procedures because the tug operator spoke poor English. The ground crew was in the process of switching tow bars when I selected the external horn and informed the crew to remove all equipment and provide me a wing walker for the turnout as I had plenty of room to accomplish the taxi out. I watched the upper ECAM and waited for the 'NW STRG DISC' message to extinguish as confirmation of pin being removed. I also received a 'wand up with pin flag in hand' signal/salute. Taxi out was normal. On climbout; Center called and said the ground crew asked them to inform me that the nose wheel steering disconnect pin was still in the nose gear. I immediately knew this was false as I had confirmed before taxi out that it was removed and also the aircraft would not be able to be taxied with the pin installed. I contacted ops on company frequency and informed them that no pin was in the nose wheel. Again; I had a hard time understanding them as their English was poor.  I then received a message from Dispatch and my understanding was they had lost the pin; assumed it was on the nose gear and then later found the pin. As a precaution; on arrival; I inspected the nose wheel and found no discrepancies. As a side note; it appeared that the tow bar being used was much smaller than normal. The tow bar they were going to swap it with was much larger.Cause - Poor English and communication.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported communication issues with the pushback crew resulted in the flight crew being advised during flight there was confusion as to whether or not the tow bar pin had been left in. It was later determined the ground crew had lost the pin after removal.

Report_1_Narrative: On departure climbing in icing conditions with engine and airfoil anti-ice on the Captain airspeed and altitude alerted to 40 feet [difference] from First Officer and airspeed 30 kts. [difference]. After a few minutes; alert cleared; and everything was normal up to cruise altitude. Flight continued normal until we descend into icing conditions. Radar showed scattered precipitation and ATC reported turbulence ahead. At 14;000 feet we got into heavy rime ice. Captain airspeed indicator went to zero; autopilot disconnected; FADEC went to alternate all 3 engines; LSAS (Longitudinal Stability Augmentation System) all failed. I started hand flying checking FO (First Officer) and standby instruments; First Officer notified ATC of the failure of our airspeed and altitude due to ice. The First Officer instructions looked to be reliable compared to the standby; so I transferred control of the aircraft to the First Officer and assumed Pilot Not Flying duties doing the checklist. After about 10 minutes Captain airspeed and altitude started working again. We were given a speed restriction of 260 kts. or less and to cross intersection ZZZZZ at 14;000 feet and then cross ZZZZZ1 at 12;000 feet. The incident happened just after ZZZZZ. We were not able to make the restriction at ZZZZZ2. I told the FO to stop descent until we were sure of the instrument readings while we were communicating with ATC telling them of our situation. We cross ZZZZZ2 at 13;800 feet about 280 kts. I took control of the aircraft back from the First Officer and continued the arrival and approach via ATC instructions.We were immediately aware of the malfunction. There were multiple alerts and warnings going off when it happened.After landing the mechanics did a CFDS (Centralized Fault Display System) check which showed a MSC (Miscellaneous Systems Controller) failure. Look like the Captain pitot tube was not being heated properly and descending into the icing conditions cause it to become blocked. Immediate corrective action was taken by both me and my First Officer to fly the airplane and contact ATC.
Report_1_Synopsis: Captain reported that while flying in heavy icing conditions the autopilot disconnected and the airspeed indicator went to zero. Subsequent maintenance inspection determined that a pitot tube was not heating properly and had become blocked.

Report_1_Narrative: After being notified by Management & Safety about Aircraft X air return was due to a (new) nose gear down lock safety pin installed and 5 each (normal equipment) were found in E&E (electronics bay) equipment stowage. The ETOPS inspection was performed with no need for the use of 5 each landing gear down lock safety pins. At no time was red streamer visible during ETOPS inspection.
Report_1_Synopsis: Technician reported a B767 air turnback was caused by an additional NLG safety pin left installed.

Report_1_Narrative: I was cruising VFR at 7;500 ft.; without flight following; but monitoring Center. My ADS-B (Automatic Dependent Surveillance - Broadcast) showed traffic 500 ft. below me; 12 miles out at my 1:30 position. This caught my attention because this condition indicates we will pass laterally very close. I heard Center alert the other aircraft about the traffic (my aircraft); but he was unable to get a visual. Center indicated my altitude was 7;200 ft. I turned on my taxi and landing lights to make my aircraft more visible to the other aircraft. We passed with 500 ft. vertical and about 150 ft. lateral separation. The other pilot called me on the phone later that day because he was concerned about a near miss (although he did get a visual on my aircraft just before we passed). His ADS-B indicated 150 ft. separation. My flights showed my ADS-B altitude 350 ft. lower than what it actually was; which was the cause for the other pilot's concern. I am reporting this to my avionics shop for repair; and in the future will pick up flight following earlier in the flight for better communication.
Report_1_Synopsis: GA pilot reported a NMAC and later discovered that separation from the other aircraft was less than originally thought due to the reporter's ADS-B equipment not indicating the correctly.

Report_1_Narrative: I landed on Runway XX and my airspeed was approximately 76 knots. As soon as I touched ground; I slowed down in order to follow Controller directions. The Controller asked if I could make Taxiway Alpha X. By that point; I had already passed the taxiway and responded to the Controller in which I stated negative. The Controller's commands were to make a left turn at Taxiway Golf. I then proceeded to slow down and pulled back on the yoke to the turn left onto Taxiway Golf. Before fully exiting the runway; the tires of the plane became stuck on the snow ground and I was not able to move forward. The Controller questioned me and asked if I was able to move forward. I replied that I was unable to and that I was stuck in the snow. The Controller responded back and said hold tight; ground operations was on their way. As ground operations came; I shut off the plane and aided the ground operations staff in pushing the plane backwards. We successfully pushed the plane out of the snow.I started the plane back up and I was then able to make a U-turn back onto the Runway XX and taxi onto Alpha Y. The sign for Bravo (B) was not visible and I exited off of Alpha Y; made the left turn for Alpha and then right turn for Bravo.This experience taught me to avoid any taxiways that appear to have ice or snow on them. I also learned that I must make the judgement as being the pilot in command. As the pilot in command; I have the ability to deny requests made by Air Traffic Controller if I cannot adhere to their request promptly. I must note that it is important that all parties involved must remain safe; since safety is a priority of mine.
Report_1_Synopsis: GA pilot reported a taxiway excursion and getting stuck on the ground snow/ice.

Report_1_Narrative: Prior to taking off I checked the UAS FM (facility maps) and observed that I could not exceed 50 feet AGL as I was in ZZZ Class B airspace. In an error; I did not file a flight plan and instead flew the drone; keeping it at an altitude of 50 feet AGL or below. After ending my flight I realized my error and immediately contacted my company UAS coordinator. In the future I shall always remember to file a flight plan and receive authorization before flying in controlled airspace.
Report_1_Synopsis: UAS pilot reported inadvertently flying in Class B controlled airspace without authorization.

Report_1_Narrative: I was flying right seat. After landing; Runway XX and exiting at [Taxiway] XX1; Tower radioed; 'taxi to ramp; this frequency.' PF (Pilot flying) proceeded to taxi south on Taxiway XX; and then turned right onto Taxiway XX4; into the FBO's ramp.I noticed Aircraft Y; parked close to our taxiway (on our right side); and asked PF to slow down; which he did. I then asked PF to come left (away from the aircraft) which he did. This put us left of the taxiway centerline (away from the aircraft). In the dim light; it looked as if we would clear the aircraft wingtip; particularly since we had come so far left. Unfortunately; the wingtips made contact.We then taxied to parking to deplane our passengers. After our passengers departed; I informed the FBO. PF walked to Taxiway XX4 and measured the distance from taxiway centerline to the wingtip of Aircraft Y. The distance measured 32 feet 8 inches. There was a cone under the wingtip. The wingtip did not have a static wick cover on it.
Report_2_Narrative: Taxiing into ramp on center line we were turning into the FBO ramp and clipped the wingtip of Aircraft Y. The wingspan of our aircraft make/model is 69 feet 6 inches and from Center line to the edge of Aircraft Y was 32 feet. The PIC (Pilot in Command) who was in the right seat told me to adjust over some and I did. He then thought we were clear of Aircraft Y. While taxiing by the tips met by a few inches. It only scratched the winglet of [our aircraft]; but bent the wingtip of Aircraft Y.
Report_1_Synopsis: Corporate flight crew reported misjudging clearance with a parked aircraft while taxiing into parking; resulting in contacting and damaging the wingtips of both aircraft.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Workload; Time Pressure; Situational Awareness; Communication Breakdown
Report_1_Narrative: I was Instructor Pilot; low time student pilot was in the left seat. We were practicing ground reference maneuvers; specifically S-turns across a road. Except we used the river as a 'road.' My thinking was that no traffic should be near us if we are 1;000 feet AGL (1;200MSL) at that location. Boy; was I wrong.My student had completed a few S-turns across the river and was just turning westbound to cross the river again when I noticed a target on our ADS-B (Automatic Dependent Surveillance - Broadcast) in display less than a mile to our right (north) -- actually; much less than a mile -- showing 100 feet below us; coming straight toward our right rear quarter. It looked like a 90-degree track compared to ours; meaning the offending aircraft was heading roughly 190 while we were heading approximately 270 (all magnetic). I took control immediately; raised the right wing; and looked intently to our right rear and all other parts of our right side in an effort to make visual contact. Alas; no joy.Since the ADS-B track showed he was likely to pass behind us; I went full throttle in order to give the other aircraft the best chance of doing so. That appeared to work; but we only knew that when the target (after what seemed like an eternity) moved to our left rear on its same heading. Finally; we were diverging. We both looked in the direction of the target; still no joy. Never saw the guy. Thank goodness for ADS-B in this case.Let me add that I was scanning for traffic the whole time my student was S-turning. Whenever he banked left; I took the opportunity to look under the raised (right) wing. When he turned right; the other raised wing. Nonetheless; no joy whatsoever.We were not monitoring any radio frequency at the time since we were not close to an airport traffic pattern nor in a designated practice area (the 'west practice area' near there is several miles west of our position). Now this: Thanks again to ADS-B; I was able to find both our flight tracks on FlightRadar24 (FR24). I identified the other aircraft's N-number; looked it up in the FAA database; found the owner's information; and called him. Nice; retired fellow on this third Cirrus; based at the airport 3 NM to our north-northeast; ZZZ. He had just departed ZZZ Runway XX and was climbing; per the FlightRadar24 track; via track 235 degrees at a ground speed of 132 knots. Our track at the time; per FlightRadar24; was 283 degrees with a ground speed of 71 knots. So roughly 50 degrees different in ground tracks; not 90 as estimated above.I asked the owner; who was the pilot in the Cirrus; if he saw us either visually or on ADS-B. He said he did not recall seeing us on either and that he did not get a traffic alert on his ADS-B device. I think we received an alert; but not positive in retrospect. I am just glad I glanced at the display when I did.The Cirrus pilot said that he always announces his takeoffs from ZZZ on the CTAF; which is Multicom 122.9. I admitted that I should have been monitoring that frequency for traffic awareness.I mentioned as gently as possible to him that the FAA recommends (via AC 90-66B; Non-Towered Airport Flight Operations) that airplanes departing a non-towered airport should fly straight out until reaching pattern altitude; then continue straight out or turn 45 degrees in the direction of the traffic pattern for that runway. This gentleman did neither. His FR24 shows that he went straight out off Runway XX for less than a mile; then turned 65 degrees!! To his right!! Even though Runway XX is a left-traffic runway. He did not seem impressed when I mentioned that to him; he was more eager to repeat that I should have been monitoring CTAF so we would have known he was departing.The upshot of our conversation for me was to guard the nearby CTAF whether or not I am in a location where I 'shouldn't' need to do so; and to realize that pilots operating at quiet; non-towered airports will do whatever they darned well please regardless ofany FAA guidance.Lastly; I offered to do his next flight review or IPC for free since I have never been in a Cirrus and would be eager to be his 'passenger.' Scolding him will not do any good; but perhaps by instructing him; should he decide to take me up on my offer; I may be able to remind him of proper non-towered airport procedures.
Report_1_Synopsis: Instructor Pilot reported a NMAC.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Troubleshooting; Workload; Situational Awareness; Time Pressure
Report_1_Narrative: I departed ZZZ on an IFR flight plan to ZZZ1. The aircraft had sat for roughly 3 days over the weekend before this flight and was difficult to start that morning (battery seemed weak). 40 minutes into the flight; the first symptoms of an electrical malfunction began to show up. I was roughly 15 nm from the IAF for the RNAV XX approach into ZZZ1 at 8;000 feet MSL; in actual IMC with light to moderate rime icing. I had just switched from ZZZ2 Center to the CTAF for the ZZZ1 airport when the auto-pilot for the aircraft unexpectedly disconnected. All of the lights on the autopilot control panel went dark; and the autopilot would not turn back on. Initially; I decided to continue the approach by hand and have maintenance check the autopilot malfunction on the ground. After briefly troubleshooting the autopilot; I returned to my instrument scan. At first glance; my HSI indicated that I was on Heading/Course. Needles were centered and heading bug was situated at the top of the instrument. But when I looked over at the Garmin 430 GPS; it indicated that I was off heading by 20-30 degrees. By the time I looked back towards my HSI; there was a 'HDG' flag starting to flicker in the top right hand corner. I looked across the panel at the co-pilot's instrument cluster and noted that the co-pilot's artificial horizon was flopped over; indicating a 45* right bank and 20* nose up attitude. The co-pilot's side DG was also off by 90* from my magnetic compass. As I looked back towards the pilot's side instrument cluster; my HSI began spinning around and around like a top.At this point; I had obviously determined that several of my gyroscopic instruments had failed; and I had difficulty determining which instruments were trustworthy and which were not. From this point on; I did my best to maintain straight and level flight with my remaining instruments and the Garmin 430 GPS ground track. I looked out the window at my wings (I was still in IMC and light to moderate icing [at] this point) and saw that during my troubleshooting I had enough ice accumulation that small 'horns' of rime ice were begging to grow on the leading edges and my de-ice boots were mostly white with a layer of ice. When I pressed the switch on the overhead panel to activate my de-ice boots; nothing happened. I immediately switched back to ZZZ2 Center and [received priority]; advising them that I had gyroscopic instrument failures and inoperative anti-icing equipment. I requested an immediate climb in an attempt to escape the icing conditions and find visual flight conditions before my remaining instrumentation failed; along with vectors back to ZZZ (which I knew had good VFR weather conditions...ZZZ1 conditions appeared to be worsening when I had last listened to the automated weather). ATC was extremely helpful and professional. Immediately offering any assistance they could; giving me no-gyro vectors towards ZZZ and approving a climb to 12;000 feet MSL. I had difficulty maintaining a heading and climb pitch-attitude initially; but got vaguely stabilized within a few minutes. Once stabilized; I noticed that the left alternator light was on; I attempted to re-cycle the alternator master switch twice without success. I then began to load-shed all electrical equipment which was not absolutely necessary for the continuation of the flight; and I advised ATC that I had experienced an alternator failure. 	I initially broke out of the top of the cloud layer and entered VMC around 10;000 feet roughly 15 minutes after the first indication of electrical failure. I had to request a higher altitude shortly thereafter as the tops of the clouds sloped higher towards ZZZ. ATC cleared me for a block altitude 8;000 feet to 12;000 feet; then eventually up to 14;000 feet; and authorized any course deviations necessary for me to remain in VFR conditions.Upon leveling off; I was initially concerned about what appeared to be a fairly significant performance loss. My first assumption was that it was due to ice build up on the wings/tail. In a level flight attitude; at 38 of manifold pressure and 2400 rpm (typical climb power) I was only getting 120 knots indicated airspeed. 160 knots to 170 knots indicated is more typical during cruise flight at a much lower power setting (30'/2300rpm). I alerted ATC that I was seeing abnormally low air speeds. But after a quick glance at my GPS (which was showing a 230 knots ground speed) I realized that the airspeed discrepancy was most likely due to pitot icing. ATC confirmed that they were showing me with a ground speed in the high 220's. By this point; the aircraft was out of icing conditions and flying just fine in VMC. So most of the potential danger had past. The last thing I had to do was search around for a hole in the clouds so that I could get back into ZZZ (there was an overcast layer between my aircraft and the ground). With the help of ZZZ3 Approach; ZZZ Tower; and several other aircraft in the area giving pilot reports; I found an opening near ZZZ4 and circled down for a visual approach into Runway XXL at ZZZ. The vast majority of the ice which had accumulated on the aircraft came off in the decent due to higher airspeeds and increasing temperatures. I landed without further incident; parked the aircraft; and immediately took down notes regarding the order of events while they were still fresh in my mind. I then called the Chief Pilot to relay what happened."
Report_1_Synopsis: Single air taxi pilot in IMC and icing conditions reported an alternator failure.

Report_1_Narrative: While conducting RNAV Runway 15 approach into ESN; received a low altitude alert from Easton Tower while at our MDA of 440 ft. MSL. We immediately climbed to 550 ft. MSL and conducted a missed approach once at the MAP. My assumption is that the aircraft descended too rapidly; causing us to be below glide slope as indicated by the PAPI's.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight instructor reported executing a missed approach from an instrument approach after descending below minimums.

Report_1_Narrative: While entering the downwind via the 45 for Runway XX; right traffic at ZZZ; we were following a Cessna. I was sitting in the passenger seat as the NFP (Non-Flying Pilot)/Safety Pilot observing my friends landing. We completed our landing checks and continued following the Cessna. As the Cessna reached our four o'clock position I told the PF (Pilot Flying) that he was clear to turn base leg behind the Cessna. We made our radio call; and turned to base leg. After we made another radio call to final; a young woman flying some sort of low wing canopy glass cockpit airplane turned directly in front of us and cut us off in the pattern. She did make a radio call announcing her turn to base. Approaching her turn to final she then queried 'how many airplanes are in the pattern and where are you'. I am sure she was completely unaware of our position. Out of the turn we were approximately less than a quarter of a mile at her seven o'clock position. Clearly she had no idea that she had just cut us off and was now on a simultaneous approach with another aircraft. The PF did not have the conflicting aircraft in sight until late after turning final. In the interest of safety; I took control of the airplane and elected to fly a parallel to her track. I passed by her left wing approximately 400 feet lateral distance and nearly level with her aircraft. Once I knew we were safely passed her aircraft I executed missed approach. We then came around for another successful landing to a full stop.
Report_2_Narrative: As background; ZZZ was heavily congested with training and weekend aviators. The approach to the downwind leg was reported via UNICOM as 4NM southeast to enter a 45 - downwind entry. We coordinated spacing with another crosswind aircraft to follow us for spacing in the pattern. Our aircraft was operating with LED strobe lights and all landing lights for visibility to other aircraft.Reported downwind; uneventfully. And recognized the aircraft we were to follow and mimicked their pattern to minimize spacing conflicts. Reported our base turn to UNICOM; uneventfully. Our track on base leg was approximately 2 NM from the end of the runway. At no time was our location questioned by the conflicting near miss aircraft.Reported a base-to-final turn; uneventfully and unquestioned. Upon the completion of the turn to final; I focused on vertical alignment to the runway and did not see the conflicting near miss aircraft. The PNF (Pilot Not Flying); in a radio call questioned the conflicting near miss aircraft to determine her position upon hearing the UNICOM base report. After it was determined the conflicting aircraft turned inside of our location; resulting in cutting us off placing our aircraft in a hazardous flight profile; PNF took control of the aircraft in a professionally coordinated manner. At this time; the conflicting near miss aircraft was well within 1/4 NM and somewhat above our altitude; which was approximately 300 ft. AGL. Because of her proximity to us; and her apparently being unaware of our location; the resolution was complex. Keep in mind in her base to final turn (Right Hand pattern) with a low wing aircraft she would have then been unable to locate us visually. In a UNICOM radio call; the conflicting near miss aircraft questioned 'how many aircraft are in the pattern and where are you'; indicating her further lack of awareness to traffic as she was a close in final; an inappropriate time to establish traffic.Suspecting her unpredictable actions; we were prevented from a turn to side step since it would have blocked our ability to monitor her activities. Our inter-cockpit discussion created the point; given our closure rate; that our only recourse; in the interest of safety; was to parallel her path; fly past her which would have given her awareness of our location; then when ahead of the conflicting aircraft; we could safely initiate a missed approach; which we did.We remained in the pattern for another approach and full stop landing; uneventfully.
Report_1_Synopsis: Pilot on final approach reports a near miss with another aircraft.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Workload; Time Pressure; Situational Awareness; Communication Breakdown
Report_1_Narrative: After two right 360s we were told to extend downwind for runway X; and look for helicopter traffic (Aircraft Y) three miles west of the field at 700 feet. We called out traffic in sight; and continued. After Aircraft Y didn't respond to two radio calls; we were told to do another 360. Rolling out of the 360 we were told to look for Aircraft Y one mile ahead at 900 feet orbiting. We called traffic in sight; and began a climb to 1;300 feet. It appeared as though Aircraft Y was still climbing as they passed in front from our left to right. After a controller change; Tower called our position to Aircraft Y; they did not respond. Shortly after that call; Aircraft Y made a sharp climbing right turn directly into our flight path. To avoid a collision; I took the controls and made a climbing left turn as sharp as I could. Shortly after I started that turn; Aircraft Y banked sharply to their right to avoid us. I can't put an exact number on the distance between us; but it was close enough that I felt the need to bank sharply towards traffic on final; and Aircraft Y banked hard enough for us to see the bottom of their helicopter. Once a safe distance away; we turned to rejoin downwind; and began a descent back to pattern altitude. After that; Aircraft Y asked tower to keep aircraft away from that area while they followed a pursuit. Hearing other aircraft have difficulty with separation; we departed the pattern to ZZZ1 to avoid a similar situation.It is normal for us to fly over helicopter operations at 500-600 feet while in the pattern at 1;100 feet. It is not normal to fly the pattern with unpredictable traffic at the same altitude.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Instructor reported a NMAC with a helicopter.

Report_1_Narrative: R-side working Columbus/Pike/Parkersburg airspace; Charleston Approach and Columbus Approach airspace at the same time. Having little effective contigency plan for approach controls shutting down. Working multiple aircraft into unfamiliar airspace with unfamiliar approaches to three airports all within 15-20 miles of each other; while managing holding aircraft; other enroute aircraft and aircraft wanting approaches to airports where we provide approach services. A laser event also occured around the ZZV VOR while this was occuring; with a green laser hitting an aircraft. Luckily no injuries were reported. Have a baseline contingency plan that includes aides for the controller; including LOAs between facilities; suggestions like establishing holding stacks; downstream speed reductions; local best practices used by respective approach controllers; etc. Also; try not to shut down an entire approach control facility during peak traffic times; especially on one of the busiest travel holiday weekends of the year.
Report_1_Synopsis: ZID Controller reported working two approach airspaces without proper contingency plan or established procedures resulted in airspace and MVA violations.

Report_1_Narrative: Aircraft X departure ZZZ IFR enroute to ZZZ1. I released the aircraft with a heading of 130 degrees & 2;000 ft. off Runway ZZ. This is a fairly standard procedure for releasing IFR aircraft off ZZZ when the metroplex is in a north flow. This keeps the aircraft away from the ZZZ2 finals which are just a few miles to the west of ZZZ. At the time; ZZZ2 was in the middle of an arrival push. Once the aircraft became airborne & I established communication with him I called ZZZ Tower & requested control so I could turn the aircraft back to the west across the ZZZ airspace. I turned Aircraft X westbound toward ZZZ1 & pointed him out to the appropriate ZZZ2 arrival sectors & handed him off to ZZZ TRACON. My plan was to keep Aircraft X low (2;000 ft. MSL) below the ZZZ2 finals where all the arrivals would be at 3;000 ft. MSL. A couple minutes later I noticed an aircraft in very close proximity to Aircraft X on a similar course. I called traffic but Aircraft X couldn't locate the aircraft. Due to the ZZZ2 traffic I couldn't climb Aircraft X for the traffic nor could I descend him due to the MVA of 2;000 ft. I again called traffic to see if Aircraft X could acquire the target visually. He still couldn't & the courses were converging while Aircraft X was overtaking the target. I called ZZZ Tower to see if they were talking to him or see if they knew what he was doing. They told me they thought he was heading to ZZZ3 which is very close to ZZZ1. The target had just departed ZZZ. I vectored Aircraft X to the north to in an attempt to increase the distance between him & the unidentified target. I then turned Aircraft X back to the southwest to go behind & to the left of the target to try & increase the separation even more. Once I was satisfied the two targets were safely separated I transferred communications of Aircraft X to ZZZ TRACON. I believe Aircraft X was on a heading of either 250 or 260 degrees at the time. It was brought to my attention later that while Aircraft X was on the heading I gave him when I transferred communications that he clipped a 2;100 ft. MVA while still at 2;000 ft. MSL. This occurred before the ZZZ TRACON controller was able to turn the aircraft. I didn't realize the heading would allow Aircraft X to clip the MVA. The MVA is a very small area; approx. 1-2nm wide 'shelf' of a larger MVA. I would not have given the aircraft a shortcut by taking him under the ZZZ2 finals. I was attempting to be as efficient as possible. However; with the amount of traffic in the area at the time I should have just taken him to the south off ZZZ & then westbound from there. This would've added approximately 30-40nm to his route but would've prevented this from happening. In the future I would also ask ZZZ Tower if they have anyone departing to the west who would be in conflict with this aircraft when I asked for control for a westbound turn. This also would've impacted my decision making.
Report_1_Synopsis: TRACON Controller reported communications transfer to late to prevent aircraft from entering a higher MVA.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Workload; Training / Qualification; Time Pressure; Situational Awareness
Report_1_Narrative: Prior to top of descent we briefed the NNCEE 1 RNAV Arrival into IAH.  The arrival says to plan on flying the RWY 8R transition.  So we briefed the ILS RWY 8R approach.  Houston Approach Control then told us to fly the RNAV (RNP) Y RWY 9 approach.  The CA was the PM and told the FO he would change the approach in the FMC.  After selecting the new approach the CA told the FO that there was a discontinuity at HOWLN.  By selecting the HOWLN transition two separate HOWLN fixes were created separated by a discontinuity.  The discontinuity appeared at the top of page two in the legs page of the FMC.  So the CA brought up the second HOWLN fix and entered it into the discontinuity boxes and assumed that this action closed the discontinuity.  But he never went back to page one to verify that the discontinuity was closed and he did not ask the FO to verify it as the FO was busy managing the descent.  The MCP displayed LNAV and VNAV were engaged and so did the FMAs.  Approach Control then said at HOWLN you are cleared the RNAV (RNP) Y RWY 9 approach.  So the CA set FAF altitude of 2;000 in the MCP.  The FO went through LAVSFT and at HOWLN (IAF) had me set TDZE of 100.  Then we both said why isn't the airplane turning?  Tower immediately cancelled our approach clearance and vectored us for the ILS RWY 9 approach.  The CA was on a larger scale than the FO and noticed that the magenta line showed both the RF leg turn inbound but also extended beyond HOWLN as well and said I think I did not clean up the discontinuity correctly.  The contributing factors were both pilots did not verify the legs page after the Captain cleaned up the discontinuity and the high workload environment in IMC.  Additionally it was the FO's first trip in over a month.
Report_2_Narrative: I briefed the ILS 8R per listed as the runway for flying the NNCEE1 Arrival.  During our descent when checking in with Houston approach we were given a new runaway RNAV Y runway 9.  The captain put the new runway into the FMS and Verbalized he was cleaning it for the RF.  I was reviewing the approach plate and didn't verify his FMS inputs.  The CA noticed right away that the plane should be starting to turn for the RF; which ATC cancelled our approach and told to fly a heading.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported a track deviation on the mid-approach segment due to a high workload environment coupled with the First Officer's extended period of time off.

Report_1_Narrative: On the arrival into ZZZ on the ZZZZZ1X arrival; we were told to maintain 250 knots to ZZZZZ; cleared the approach; ILS DME X rwy XXR. We had LNAV and VNAV engaged; I recommended the FAF altitude of 1300 feet be set in the MCP altitude window; the PF; F/O agreed and I set it. The controller told us to slow to 190 knots followed by a slow now call; the F/O (first flight from a long break; several months) was a little hesitant to get it done; so I told him he could hand fly bringing the nose up to slow aside from the speed brakes that he was using; or he could use vertical speed and decrease the descent rate VNAV was currently giving him. He opted to use the vertical speed. I got a call to switch to the Tower; as I did; I got distracted from resetting the MCP altitude of 2000 feet for the mandatory fix altitude at ZZZZZ1. We crossed ZZZZZ1 at approximately 1700 feet. Recognizing this; I had him climb back up to 2000 feet until we intercepted the glide path. We were visual with the runway the entire time and the aircraft in front of us; that is perhaps the reason I wasn't giving due diligence to my approach plate.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Captain reported an altitude deviation.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Time Pressure; Training / Qualification; Situational Awareness; Distraction; Communication Breakdown
Report_1_Narrative: We were descending via the ZZZZZX arrival with the Autopilot off - on profile and speed. FO decided to hand fly the remainder of the approach and landing and disconnected both the Autopilot and Autothrust near ZZZZZ1 intersection. A minute later I looked away and when I looked again; I noticed the FO was high on profile and I mentioned that we needed to cross ZZZZZ1 level at 6;000 feet. The FO increased the rate of descent and crossed ZZZZZ1 level at 6;000 but then continued to descend to approximately 5;900 feet and around 250 knots - with accelerating trend. I verbalized both altitude and speed; and the FO quickly recovered both. We were soon level at 6;000 feet - 240 knots...and soon to slow to 210 knots by ZZZZZ2. There was very light traffic in the terminal area and ATC made no mention of conflicts of any kind. We then proceeded to land uneventfully on Runway XX. The main contributing factor was the FO being new as well as not having flown much for the last several months. We fully debriefed everything; including what to improve on; once at the gate when duties permitted.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported an altitude and airspeed deviation during arrival.  Captain cited the First Officer's lack of flying time in the last several months as a contributing factor.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Troubleshooting; Time Pressure; Situational Awareness; Confusion
Report_1_Narrative: I am concerned about having to wear a mask at cruise altitude while a Flight Attendant is on the Flight Deck. I feel we are putting Flight Attendant mask concerns over safety of flight concerns. If we experience a Rapid Decompression at FL 390; time of useful consciousness is measured in single digit seconds. A Rapid Decompression would be stressful; disconcerting and confusing. Now we would also have to waste a precious second or two to remove the cloth mask. If it is OK for the pilots to be mask-less in the cockpit when no Flight Attendant is present; why put the safety of the flight at risk solely for the comfort of flight attendants?
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Captain reported the requirement of wearing a face mask with a Flight Attendant on the Flight Deck is a safety concern; especially if there is an event such as a rapid decompression.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Troubleshooting; Time Pressure; Communication Breakdown; Other / Unknown
Report_1_Narrative: Two back to back flights had people scheduled to work type X Aircraft gates with no (zero) type X Aircraft experience.  The flight out of [Gate] XX1 at ZZZ had several maintenance items at the gate.  Two or three mechanics wasted their time and our time due to lack of type X Aircraft experience.  A fourth mechanic got us out of town after someone tracked him down at a different gate.  Another flight took a half hour delay because no one on the ramp had ever worked a type X Aircraft.  30 extra minutes to load bags after someone that had worked a type X Aircraft showed up to help.  Worse yet; no delay information was available without the cockpit being proactive.  Zero communication via the gate screen in front of the aircraft (at one point it changed to the next flight on that gate); nothing in the companies message updates; no updated flight service form; no call from Local Control.  Each posted delay (and there were several) was initiated by the pilot contacts.  The Local Control seemed to be the last to know and blamed the delay on the baggage system. The tug driver told us it was that the employees scheduled to work that gate had no experience on the type X Aircraft.  With all of the cutbacks and furloughs; we need to make sure that each gate is staffed with people that know the type of aircraft that will be parked there.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Captain reported maintenance and ground personnel with no experience on specific aircraft types are being utilized due to staffing cutbacks.

Report_1_Narrative: Captain had been off for 6 months.  Flying First Officer new on aircraft 3 months. I was Relief Pilot #1 in corner seat.  Initial clearance to climb to 3;000 feet.  Then cleared to climb higher.  Around 4;000 feet after flaps up; plane was in a descent and ATC asked if we were going to climb?   FO put on autopilot; plane was still not climbing.  Power was nowhere near full power. The other Relief Pilot #2 talked FO into moving power up by hand (manually).  After quite some time we realized plane was in ALTITUDE hold.  Altitude knob pushed; plane entered VNAV climb mode.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Relief Pilot reported the Captain and flying First Officer were not climbing as instructed by ATC due to inadvertently being in altitude hold during departure.

Report_1_Narrative: I was the Relief Pilot on Aircraft X and during the briefing; I requested that masks be worn while I was in the flight deck because my wife has a condition that will require surgery and I am trying to protect her and my family. I explained that I was okay with masks being off if we were eating and drinking. The Captain's response was that 'It is too long of a flight and that I should have not come to work.'  This set the tone. He then stated I should remove myself from the trip. I attempted to contact company but was unable to reach anyone. I then called the flight operations management and requested to be removed from the trip. I was removed from the trip with a significant reduction in pay. Safety was never mentioned as a concern just the inconvenience of wearing a mask for a long period of time.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Relief Pilot reported removing himself from a flight due to a disagreement with the Captain about wearing masks in the flight deck.

Report_1_Narrative: Every day for at least the last 2 months there has been a huge lack/deficiency of staffing Customer Service Representatives in the Lobby.  Even when staffing looks good at the beginning of a shift; Lobby agents will be moved by to gates; Customer Service Counters; Baggage; etc.   Management operates the lobby everyday below number of agents and moving agents to other areas just compounds this huge safety debacle!  Management continues to open Kiosks for check in and also keeps all kiosks open which does not allow for the CDC recommended 6 foot distancing as these kiosks are not 6 feet apart!!!   As our Customers check-in with their families and fellow travelers there are groups of people standing too close to each other!  Lack of agents has many times created safety issues as passengers/groups checking in line up in bunches too close to the passenger currently using a kiosk.  Also due to the continuing lack of staffing passengers are touching; grabbing and pulling agents to the kiosk they are at and need help checking in.
Report_1_Synopsis: Customer Service employee reported there is a lack of proper staffing in the lobby; which makes it difficult to follow CDC social distancing recommendations as passengers bunch up in groups while waiting in line.

Report_1_Narrative: The scanner radio room is located in a busy hallway at [location] on the X-Concourse. During peak times; many employees are accessing the scanner radio room for equipment needed for their shift. Recently a temperature check station was installed near the scanner radio room in an already busy hallway where many employees are accessing for various areas. The added temperature check station is creating congestion where six feet of spacing for COVID is not able to happen. As much; many lead kits taken from the scanner radio room are being taken off the counter and coming close to hitting people in the hallway when congestion is high during peak times.
Report_1_Synopsis: Ground employee reported that the addition of a temperature check station nearby an equipment room creates congestion; making it difficult to social distance during busy times when many people are in the hallway.

Report_1_Narrative: Seconds after takeoff from ZZZ we smelled a burning-rubber like odor. It was strong and acrid within seconds. Passing through 2;400 ft. we made the decision to level off at 3;000 ft. and put our O2 mask on. I instructed the jumpseater to don his mask as well. I advised ATC as the First Officer was pilot flying. I coordinated an air return to the same runway we took off from and asked the tower to call our dispatch to notify of the diversion. Approach and landing was normal. I had Airport Rescue and Fire Fighting approach and inspect the plane before taxiing back to the ramp. Our mask were on until that point; but the fumes had subsided. The First Officer; did an amazing job; and I am grateful to have had such a professional with me at the time. We were only airborne for a total of 8 minutes. For hours after the event; I was short of breath and felt chest discomfort; a slight headache and inability to process thought. I elected to get checked out at the company provided medical center close by; escorted by Assistant Chief Pilot and was released. I am still not feeling 'normal' but hope to be by tomorrow. I feel as though I definitely took in some of the fumes; although it also seems that it was not for very long as I got my O2 mask on so quickly.
Report_2_Narrative: After takeoff we had a strong burning smell. We advised ATC; leveled off at 3;000 ft. Donned O2 masks.   Remained VMC. Vectors for Runway XX. Same as departing runway.   Landing uneventful.
Report_1_Synopsis: MD-11 flight crew reported smelling a 'burning-rubber' like odor immediately after takeoff resulting in a return to the departure airport.
