Person_2_Human_Factors: Distraction; Time Pressure; Situational Awareness; Communication Breakdown; Confusion; Workload
Report_1_Narrative: Leaving ZZZ; we turned left on Taxiway XX out of FBO to taxi to [Runway] XXR. When we turned left; ground told us to expect 15 minute delay due to departures on the center runway. We therefore proceeded to wait to do the taxi checklist until we were holding short. Approaching [Runway] XXR; I switched to Tower; and within a matter of seconds we hear Company Traffic is on a 4 mile final; and from there I do not recall what I heard. I do not recall because we were then doing the taxi and before takeoff checklist. I remember going up and hitting all of the lights on; which in my mind I must have thought that we were cleared for takeoff; and not line up and wait. We both verified the runway; did all the checklists; took the runway and took off. We never got corrected by ATC to abort takeoff because we weren't cleared. Everything seemed normal; we then got handed off to Departure; and a few minutes later we got asked to copy down a phone number for a possible pilot deviation. At this point both my partner and I looked at each other confused; not knowing what we did. We arrive in ZZZ1; we call the number; they said if they needed us they would call us; they then called us on the Monday after the incident and told us that we took off without clearance. Apparently; I did read line up and wait correctly; though I do not remember what I said due to the last minute high work load. We were called the morning of Monday [Date] from the supervisor telling us what we did. I then told him our side of it. He told me he had to do a report; I told him we would do the same on our end.This occurred because of task saturation. We went from a very calm and slow environment; to a very fast; high workload and task saturated environment. Part of doing the checklists requires a lot of talking between the flight crew. Having to do two checklists; the end of a briefing; as well as listen to ATC all last minute; we clearly didn't hear/comprehend the full ATC instruction. Which; led to us taking off without a clearance. The fact that neither of us caught it; and still didn't know what happened until we got a call; just shows to me how fast we were working. That is a pure reminder to remember to take things slower to make sure this does not happen again.Both my partner and I immediately started doing a report from the incident; when we found out what we did. We made sure that we timely called the ATC facility on the day of the incident as instructed.This occurred because of task saturation. We were thrown off guard getting a clearance 10 minutes before we were expecting to; and were rushing to complete everything. Rushing is never a good thing. We should have stated that we need a minute to finish some checklists and not agreed to the clearance; and if there was ever a doubt in our mind that we didn't understand a clearance we should have double checked with the Tower.
Report_2_Narrative: We were given taxi instructions from FBO via [Taxiway] XX to Runway XXR and told to expect a 15 minute wait at the end of the runway. I was Pilot Flying and made the decision to hold the taxi checklist until we got to the runway due to the short taxi and long wait for takeoff. Once we arrived at [Runway] XXR we switched to Tower and immediately was given clearance onto the runway. Due to the rush to get through the taxi checklist and before takeoff checklist; remember hearing traffic on four mile final and all lights being turned on; I thought we were cleared for takeoff. Once all checklists were done I preceded to takeoff. I do not recall hearing the lineup and wait instructions as my mind was rushed to complete both checklists. Looking back I clearly should have denied instructions to take the runway and take my time to complete checklists.We were notified after takeoff of a possible deviation and even at that time we did not know what we did. We called ATC after landing in ZZZ1. They didn't tell us what the possible deviation was and that they would call us back if needed. They called morning of [Date].I allowed myself to be rushed and became task saturated at a critical phase of flight by trying to rush through two checklists before takeoff and knowing traffic was inside a four mile final behind us. This prevented me in clearly hearing our instructions from the tower which was line-up and wait; not cleared for takeoff.Completed report after speaking with ATC on the morning of [Date]I allowed myself to be rushed and task saturated; trying to run two check lists after ATC instructions at the runway hold short line. Even though we had a short taxi and an expected 15 minute wait; I should have still ran the taxi checklist on the taxiway enroute to [Runway] XXR. If we had to wait the entire 15 minutes; I could've reviewed the taxi checklist again if needed. At the hold short once we were given instructions by ATC; I should have denied instructions to allow sufficient time to run the taxi checklist.
Report_1_Synopsis: EMB-505 / Phenom 300 flight crew reported taking off without a clearance.

Report_1_Narrative: We were given descent from 12;000 feet to 4;000 feet. As we approached 9;700 feet; ATC amended the altitude to 7;000 feet for traffic. A minute later they advised us of traffic climbing to 6;500 feet VFR. At this point we were still at about 9;000 feet and descending. The TCAS popped up and an unknown traffic was spotted approaching us; we could not locate it; and it was not the traffic ATC advised us of. Moments before the RA; ATC advised us of unknown traffic approaching us and to turn to a right heading of 310 as we were currently on a west heading of 270. As ATC was talking TCAS yelled 'traffic traffic' as we were in the right turn. The First Officer immediately disengaged autopilot and continued turning right; added max thrust and began climbing. I caught the traffic on TCAS as close as 300 feet and approaching and we were at about 8;500 feet and descending. After we were clear of conflict we were told to descend to 4;000 feet on heading 270 and continue for Visual [Runway] 13. At this point I refused any visual responsibility and requested the ILS. The aircraft was way; way; way too close! Way too close!
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported an NMAC with a VFR aircraft on descent into CRP.

Report_1_Narrative: This was a rapid pressurization. After single engine start; I asked the FO (First Officer) to accomplish the single engine after start checklist. We received taxi clearance to Runway XXL. I began taxiing about 50 feet and the aircraft began pressurizing immediately. Everyone on the aircraft began feeling their heads squeezed together.  Immediately the EICAS gave a 'PRESN AUTO FAIL' caution. What would you do? Are you going to let the airplane keep pressurizing until it reaches 14;500 ft while simultaneously running the QRH and then aircraft drops masks mid checklist? I used my instincts and immediately stopped the aircraft; set the parking brake and pressed the 'dump' button near the pressurization panel to dump the pressurized air. I only knew to immediately do this because I've personally thought of this scenario plenty of times in situations where the boarding door was closed and external air condition was hooked up. I always thought to myself if the door couldn't open quick enough then I'd need to dump the air; so my instincts reacted as such when this actually occurred. This is not something I was taught; this is not something the company teaches; however it should certainly be a point of emphasis. Moving along; after I dumped the air; the aircraft began depressurizing as expected just enough for about 3 seconds and then immediately began pressurizing again. I unpressed the 'dump' button and pressed it again. Nothing happened. I did this instantly. Afterwards I pressed the manual pressurization button; and rotated it to 11 o'clock position and waited 2 seconds; nothing happened; I then rotated full clockwise but the aircraft kept pressurizing and I wasn't going to wait to run the checklist as the aircraft altitude kept climbing. I have read this checklist before and ran through this procedure on my own time once or twice due to curiosity; so I knew what to do personally. I then pressed the EMER CALL button to the flight attendant; and told him to immediately open the galley door. Keep in mind all of this happened within 15 seconds. I also told him the galley door because I didn't want passengers to panic and run out the boarding door thinking their heads were going to explode. This is how it felt. When the flight attendant opened the door; it slammed open; as expected; despite the pressurization knob fully rotated to the right. Then I ran the QRH. Keep in mind we were not losing pressurization; we were rapidly pressurizing; oxygen masks were not my immediate thought on the ground. The checklist says to don oxygen masks during rapid decompression. I made the PIC authority to open the galley door once the pressure would not dump properly because I knew it would completely depressurize the aircraft. After I ran the QRH; I called Maintenance and they wanted to MEL the Auto Pressurization; and have me continue with the aircraft to ZZZ; an airport with a field elevation of 3200 plus/minus 100 feet. One; I've never controlled pressurization manually in flight; and secondly I've never been to ZZZ; a high elevation airport. So I refused. Nonetheless; we went through the QRH; I ran through the proper steps from instruction from the book; and Maintenance. I did what the QRH said; which I actually did myself already; then I personally went to go close the galley door myself; in case it didn't properly pressurize. I at least considered running through the proper MEL procedure; however I was still not sold on taking the airplane. Once I closed the door; the same thing happened; aircraft began over pressurizing. I immediately opened the door again. I went back on the phone with Maintenance; after a quick discussion with my First Officer & flight attendant; I told Maintenance Control 'I will not take this aircraft.' He said ok; we ended the conversation; then I began coordinating with OPS for a gate return. I did not want to taxi with the galley door open; nor did I feel it was safe to close the door as well; so I simply turned off the #2 engine; the only one running; and asked to be towed back to the gate. I sent an ACARS message to Dispatch 'returning to gate; need new aircraft.' They responded 'copy.'  After a few minutes a tug came; we were towed; I blocked in and I then I called Dispatch and explained to him the situation. He said he'd call me back. In a few minutes he did; he said he spoke to Maintenance and they wanted to MEL the issue and keep the same aircraft; I refused again. The aircraft was not safe to fly. No one knew what the actual issue was; and unless you felt your head being squeezed in an airplane uncontrollably on the ground; you wouldn't know how that felt. I can't imagine what it would have felt like if we were flying at 3;000 feet and the aircraft wanted to over pressurize to a higher altitude and the dump feature didn't work properly; because opening the door inflight; is obviously not an option. A few minutes later Dispatch called and said they'd reach out to the Duty Manager and call me back.  The Duty Manager then called me; he said the same thing the Dispatcher said; to MEL the aircraft; and continue on the same plane. I respectfully refused again. The aircraft was not safe to fly. The Duty Manager then coordinated a new aircraft and I swapped to one about 30 minutes later. I must repeat; if you were not on the aircraft; you do not know how it felt. The crew was light headed; myself included; and the passengers had to have been as well. As a crew I felt we made the right decision; despite pressure to take out the same aircraft. About an hour later; when my new aircraft was being boarded; the previous aircraft was adjacent to us being worked on by Maintenance. In other words; it was not a simple MEL procedure. The aircraft was not safe to fly. Our new plane was just fine; we boarded; and proceeded to ZZZ safely and landed about 2 hours late. The QRH procedure is for inflight; and mainly focused on cabin depressurization; we were being over pressurized.  There wasn't enough time to run a QRH all while solving the issue as the aircraft continued pressurizing on the ground. I wasn't sure how much time I would have. There were children on board; I immediately thought about everybody; and since I knew opening the door would solve the issue; I made the decision to open. I didn't know of any other checklist action item would actually stop exactly what was happening. There isn't even a tab here for cabin over pressuring. You had to be there.
Report_1_Synopsis: Captain reported returning to the gate and refusing an aircraft that had an uncontrollable cabin pressure issue.

Report_1_Narrative: We were cleared to descend from FL180 to FL050. We ran the descent checklist and approach checklist as necessary. During descent ATC advised of a VFR target approaching our descent path at our roughly ten to eleven o' clock position. We scanned visually for traffic as well as verified the target on TCAS. ATC then advised us to descend to a higher altitude of FL070 to avoid the traffic. We amended altitude; visually scanned as the target got closer in vertical and horizontal path. As we began to approach the TCAS advised with a 'traffic; traffic' alert. Our altitude to the best of my memory was roughly between 10;000 feet and 9;000 feet. We scanned for traffic appearing to be around the 12 o' clock position of the aircraft. ATC issued a vector turning northeast bound which we complied with; however the TCAS RA went off immediately with a 'climb; climb' resolution. I disconnected the autopilot; put the thrust levers into the maximum position and adjusted the aircraft pitch to the vertical speed resolution. I believe we were about 9;000-8;700 feet before completing the RA TCAS. The separation showed about 300 feet. We climbed until clear of conflict to 9;500 feet and continued the ATC vector. After the 'clear of conflict' we leveled the aircraft; advised ATC of the TCAS RA and returned back to new given ATC clearance. We continued the flight to land safely at ZZZ. This was a huge learning experience to maintain separation and situational awareness of other aircraft and ATC instructions.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier First Officer reports multiple TCAS RAs during descent to airport.

Report_1_Narrative: We were descending via the DRLLR5 arrival for Runway 26R transition and we had everything briefed and ready to go. At a point ATC changed the runway on us from [Runway] 26R to 26L so we reloaded correct runway and its respective ILS approach procedure to back up the approach. We rebriefed the approach and reloaded all frequencies again so we were ready once again for the approach. At the end of the arrival there's a fix named ZOEEE; right upon crossing that fixed; my First Officer selected HDG sync; immediately follow by HDG mode. And just like that; we were auto sequenced for the approach. ATC then came to us with right turn for a right base followed by another right turn turn intercept the localizer for Runway 26L. At that point the FO (First Officer) armed APP and we confirmed APP1 was armed. So we continue with the approach but the airplane didn't intercept the LOC but instead it continued. Before we reached the final approach course I told my First Officer 'Be careful I don't think it's going to intercept' (he didn't acknowledge) right when we reached the course I told my First Officer 'turn now...turn now!' But he didn't; so at that point I said 'I have the flight controls' and I hand flown the airplane back the final approach course. At that point ATC came to us to let us know we were showing left of course to what my First Officer responded 'We are correcting. This happened like at about 3000 ft. AGL. After I restablished the airplane on it's final approach course I asked my First Officer if he wanted the controls back and he said YES. So I transferred the controls back to him. Then I quickly checked the information and I verified that the FMS was loaded with the ILS26L; we had a good preview with right identifier IJYV and we were showing an inbound course of 267 and APP 1 was armed. So I had to reach the FMS and I activated vectors then I forced V/L on the Pilot Flying side after asking the flying pilot if he agreed with every single step. Then the airplane's automation 'woke up' and the First Officer followed the FD all the way. We were stable at 1000 ft. and we continued to landing. I think the new FMS program has a glitch or something. Apparently it doesn't auto sequence the approach the same way. This happened in another aircraft which has the latest FMS update. From now on I'm not going to trust the auto sequence on the new loads and I am going to manually sequence it from a fix on the final approach fix. This should prevent the same issue from happening again."
Report_1_Synopsis: B-737 Captain reported failure of the FMS to capture final approach course following a vector to final.

Report_1_Narrative: While turning from base to final on a visual approach to Runway 13; Tower informed us that we had triggered a terrain alert. Around the time of the transmission I noticed we were between on the PAPIs to slightly low on the PAPIs. We acknowledged the transmission and said we were visual with the runway. We proceeded to get established on final and land. On board EGPWS equipment was never activated.Flying a fairly tight base to final turn that necessitated a continuous descent in the final turn.Extending downwind would have allowed a higher altitude for the base to final turn and possibly a more level turn to final that would not have triggered the alert.
Report_2_Narrative: While flying a visual approach on base to Runway 13 at DSM; ATC Tower gave us a low altitude alert; and said to 'check altitude.' We confirmed that we were above visual glide slope in reference to the PAPI; and continued onto final; where we intercepted and maintained ILS glideslope indications to an uneventful landing.Base turn to final approach inside FAF for ILS approach.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported receiving a terrain alert form ATC during approach to DSM airport.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Workload; Time Pressure; Distraction; Situational Awareness; Communication Breakdown
Report_1_Narrative: Typical peak afternoon departure.  Estimated 1hr late with 2 MELs; one unfamiliar. Flap system inoperative. About 25 minutes after show time finally got notice and it showed aircraft nearly fully loaded with 1 can to go. Went to aircraft and still pushed late.  After engine start got ECAM flaps extended.  Since flaps should have been fixed in the closed position I believed it was a problem.  Maintenance believed it was an expected spurious ECAM due to the MEL.  It took over 40 minutes to taxi to maintenance area; make calls to duty officer; and attempt calls to 2 tech pilots to finally have Maintenance on ground visually confirm that the notch flap on the left wing was not retracted and the ECAM warning was real.  Returned to gate; tail swapped and blocked out in just under 2 hours.  Nice job by everyone involved.  Flight to ZZZ was uneventful until approach control informed us the Tower was closed due to COVID.  We flew a box pattern while simultaneously looking at ZZZ1 as alternate (we could get there with 10;000 pounds of fuel due to Captain added fuel) and FO working ACARS to get non-Tower approval.  We briefed the details and flew an instrument approach in VFR conditions to an uneventful landing and block in at destination airport.  After block in I studied the events and our crew response and believed we did an excellent job under the conditions but noted the newest FOM revision required an alternate to operate to a non-towered airport; which we did not have.  The following morning; further study showed that the normally 24 hour Tower may have been closed due to COVID; but there was indeed a NOTAM for the closure which both I and the Dispatcher missed.The confusing MEL language refers to 'appropriate AFM performance restrictions are applied' led to longer than necessary hunt for those in the AFM when the only restrictions I could find are in the QRH.  The time I spent trying to make sure I didn't miss any restrictions could have been better spent studying the NOTAMs.  The closure NOTAM was found using the iPad app. which sorted the airport closure first; while company's provided NOTAMs sorted the closure near the end next to the airport inop lighting.  The requirement for the alternate seems to be a change in this week's FOM.The missing NOTAM closure is high workload human error sorting through pages of NOTAMs.  Lowering the workload by changing the MEL to point to the restrictions rather than creating a lengthy search would have helped. Company NOTAMs should be sorted more like the iPad app.
Report_2_Narrative: Flight was scheduled out and conducted a return to gate. An aircraft swap ensued and then departed. I took the flight over from Dispatcher #1 at shift change. I am unsure if the crew was given any NON-TOWER OPS info before departure. The following NOTAM came into play upon arrival: Air Traffic Control and Air Traffic Control Procedures------------------------------------------------------ZZZ APTZZZ SVC TWR CLOSED CTC CTAF XXY.Z DLYZZZ APTZZZ SVC TWR CLOSED CLASS D SERVICE NOT AVBL CTC ZZZ3ARTCC .4 PRACTICE INSTR APCH NOT AVBL DLYDid not know if the crew or the releasing Dispatcher #1 saw the NOTAM for the Tower closure due to the aircraft swap and delay that occurred.  Which delayed the flight where the NOTAM became an issue.Double check NOTAM closures when flights are delayed for an extended period of time.Checked NOTAMs to verify Tower was closed. ACARSed the crew a non-tower operations worksheet and informed the crew to contact ZZZ Center for arrival procedures.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier flight crew and Dispatcher reported missing a NOTAM alerting that the destination ATC Tower was closed due to COVID-19.

Report_1_Narrative: Air Carrier Dispatcher reported Aircraft X ZZZ-ZZZ1 advised ATC after doing a go around.The ZZZ1 ramp agent called to say that Aircraft X was doing a go around. I contacted the ZZZ1 Tower and they said the crew was talking to Approach Control. I asked our ATC coordinator to contact them and he confirmed the crew had advised ATC. I informed the Supervisor; the Duty Officer and the Recovery Specialist. I printed up the DG manifest and faxed it to the ZZZ1 Aircraft Rescue and Fire Fighting and gave a copy to Supervisor. The Captain called and confirmed the requested priority handling. He said that on approach they experienced a flap issue and a slat issue as well. They completed a go around so they could set up an approach for Runway 33L. No further issues.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Dispatcher reported sending DG report to destination Airport Rescue and Fire Fighting due to the fact that aircraft landing with a flap issue. Aircraft competed an uneventful landing.

Report_1_Narrative: While descending on the DRLLR5 into IAH; I asked the Captain a question regarding the flight and we began to converse about the topic. I continued to monitor the descent and we were on speed and on altitude all the way through MPORT. The Captain had the bottom altitude of MPORT (16;000 ft.) in the altitude selector and once past MPORT it was not changed to the bottom altitude of DRLLR (13;000 ft.). Since the altitude selector was still at 16;000 ft.; it looked as if we would be fine with the restriction at DRLLR according to the vertical guidance. 5 miles from DRLLR I noticed we were actually high and told the Captain we needed to increase the vertical descent. He increased the vertical descent while maintaining the speed restriction but we passed DRLLR 400-500 feet above the restriction. The flight continued normally and we continued on the arrival into the visual on 26R. This event was caused by a discussion about the flight leading to a monitoring breakdown. As Pilot Monitoring; I lost focus of the descent path and did not realize the bottom altitude of DRLLR was not set. By the time I realized and queried the Captain to increase the descent rate it was too late. I should have waited to ask a question until we were on the ground considering we were already on the arrival. This would have allowed me to monitor the descent rate more accurately and avoid being high at DRLLR. I also probably would have caught the altitude still being set to MPORT.
Report_1_Synopsis: First Officer reported missing a crossing altitude on the DRLLR FIVE Arrival into IAH.

Report_1_Narrative: I was assigned to and present aboard a deadhead flight. I opted to occupy the center jumpseat of the cockpit for taxi and takeoff. The push-back and start-up from the parking spot at ZZZ were uneventful.After completion of the Before-Taxi Checklist; the Captain began a taxi to the southwest; along the ramp; in accordance with marshaller's instructions. At the southwest end of the ramp was a wing-walker with lighted-wands; and several other employees. As the plane approached the southwest end of the ramp; the wing-walker and other ground personnel passed out of my field-of-view and were not visible to me for the duration of the taxi; due to the visibility limitations of the jumpseat.The Captain then began the 180-degree right turn denoted by the ramp taxiway centerline. At the Captain's request; the First Officer monitored the right wing during the turn. Upon completion of the 180-degree turn; the aircraft appeared (from the jumpseat view) to be located on or near the centerline of the ramp taxiway. The Captain then requested the First Officer verify that the right wing was clear of obstacles. The First Officer turned his head far enough to the right to see the wingtip of the aircraft. He responded that the wing was clear; and that he had the wing-walker in sight.The Captain then began a left turn towards Taxiway F. The Captain's focus was on the turn. The First Officer monitored the aircraft which was giving way to us; as we [exited] the ramp. (The aircraft was approaching from the opposite direction; with its taxi-lights on; however; it had been stationary for several minutes prior to this point.) Passing through 20 degrees of left turn; a shudder was felt in the cockpit; similar to heavy braking.The Captain immediately brought the aircraft to a stop. All three of us in the cockpit made a visual inspection of the aircraft (from the cockpit.) The cause of the shudder was not readily apparent. At my request; the Captain checked the Main Body Gear Steering indications on the EICAS; to verify it was not the cause of the shudder. At that moment; (deadheading) Captain [Name] entered the cockpit and advised us that the right wingtip had separated from the aircraft.The Captain proceeded to start the APU; shut-down the engines; configure the aircraft for towing; and make contact with the ground crew. After the damage was inspected by ground [personnel]; a tow vehicle was connected. The aircraft was towed back to the parking spot; where the cargo was off loaded and the aircraft turned over to maintenance [personnel] for inspection.Immediately following the events described above; the right wingtip was discovered on the ground; adjacent to a ramp lighting tower located on the southwest end of the ramp. (This tower had passed off the right wing during the right 180-degree turn required to exit the ramp.) Ground personnel reported that the Tower appeared to have damage; in addition to the aircraft's own damage.Shudder notice after contact with obstacle.Inadequate ramp space/clearance from obstacles.Ramp space and access points need to be verified for sufficient obstacle clearance prior to operating at such location.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Jump Seating Pilot reported the aircraft hit a light pole while exiting the ramp area.

Report_1_Narrative: There was a family in exit row. They were not compliant with mask policy. We asked for a Supervisor to come on board to talk with them because it is an X hour flight.  We were close to push when the Sup came on.  I forgot to brief the exit row.I realized it when we were going up in the air.  The Captain dinged us at 10;000 [feet].  I made sure it was safe and A made her announcement.  I got up and briefed the exit row.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Attendant reported that they forgot to brief the exit row because the passengers were not compliant with face mask policy and a Supervisor had to speak to them.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Time Pressure; Training / Qualification; Situational Awareness
Report_1_Narrative: Due to the COVID pandemic; I have not been able to fly as much but had ample time in full motion jet simulators within the preceding month. That day I was working at the airport when I was contacted to help move planes around in the area for a business because their main pilot did not show up. I was told I was to be flown to an airport and to pick up a plane from a local airport and to fly to another airport. I got to the airplane and was able to fly the airplane to ZZZ. Upon arrival at the airport; the person I was following then asked for a ride back to the origin airport on the plane I was in. I accepted and flew without incident to the airport and made a safe landing. Upon landing; I realized that I had not been passenger current for single-engine aircraft. I would not say there was a lack of proficiency; just a lack of currency. I have been in and out of simulators for jets and had no worries that I could not fly and land the aircraft safely. I was just not able to fly as often as I'd like. I think some of the main causes of this was the fact that this was sprung on me with little warning and no clear plan and I had not flown with this group of people before. It was a major complacency incident on my part and lack of proper flight planning.
Report_1_Synopsis: GA pilot reported flying with a passenger while not being passenger current for single-engine aircraft.

Report_1_Narrative: After takeoff [I] started after takeoff checklist. ATC instructed me to contact North Tower. I changed frequency before completing after takeoff checklist. During that time TCAS voice message [announced] 'traffic.' I got confused because TCAS is inoperative and placarded. I started right turn 2;150 feet MSL. ATC called me and gave me instruction for upwind. At that time; I was at 2;400 feet MSL; saw the aircraft left and below me. I told ATC 'aircraft in sight; climbing to avoid traffic.' ATC gave instructions to enter right downwind which I acknowledged. To avoid traffic I had climbed to 2;750 feet MSL then descended to TPA and landed safely.
Report_1_Synopsis: Pilot reported an NMAC in the pattern at FFZ airport.

Report_1_Narrative: There was moderate turbulence all altitudes. I asked the prior controller to let me know when turbulence had lessened at higher altitudes so I could climb as I was at FL280. The next Controller cleared me to Flight Level 400. I confirmed the climb to 400. At about 36;600 feet I was asked by that Controller on frequency XYY.Z whether I wanted FL400 or FL360 or similar words. I remarked back that I was already cleared to FL400. He didn't respond. This Controller was very busy because everyone was asking for a different altitude. I confirmed the altitude assignment and before he even cleared me there he asked if I wanted that altitude. It was the only smooth altitude at that time.I think the best way to correct this is for the Government to get back to work and live with COVID. They were short staffed.
Report_1_Synopsis: High Performance Aircraft Single pilot reported receiving confusing instructions from the Controller and believes COVID-19 ATC staffing issues were a factor.

Report_1_Narrative: I was conducting a private flight in my aircraft.  I had utilized VFR flight following and was handed off to Tower.   I heard numerous bangs in quick succession. They were alarming and my wife whom was in the front passenger seat abruptly turned to me and exclaimed in a concerned tone; 'what was that'? I too was extremely concerned and began checking all aircraft systems. Fortunately; all systems were functioning and I continued the approach to an uneventful landing. Upon examination of the aircraft post-landing; I noted damage to the fairing protruding from the underwing of the right main landing gear. Although I did not see what caused the damage; I am certain the damage was not present before the return flight due to my preflight inspection. I surmise the aircraft was struck by an unmanned aerial system as there were no signs of blood or feathers consistent with a bird strike.
Report_1_Synopsis: A General Aviation pilot reported hearing banging noises on final approach and upon inspecting the aircraft after landing saw damage and believes it was caused by colliding with a UAV.

Report_1_Narrative: I was the Controller in Charge position (CIC) listening to Local (LC); Ground Control (GC); and Clearance Delivery (CD). The Local Controller (LC) was located on the south side of the tower; I was on the opposite side of the tower watching LC's sequence via the STARs radar display.  The sun was directly in our face at the time which makes it difficult to visually acquire aircraft on final; especially small aircraft. Aircraft X was told to land on Runway 34R; Aircraft X acknowledged his clearance to land Runway 34R. Aircraft Y was cleared to land Runway 34L. Aircraft Y acknowledged his clearance to land Runway 34L. Aircraft X was ahead of Aircraft Y for the parallel runway. Aircraft Y initiated a go-around; as I went to do the paper work and find out why Aircraft Y went around; the LC and I noticed that Aircraft X had exited the runway and was in between Runway 34L and 34R indicating that he had landed on Runway 34L (the wrong runway). I called NORCAL to verify that was the reason Aircraft Y initiated a go-around; and it was. I suggest that all aircraft be required to turn on their landing lights during periods of difficult visual condition to include sun glare.
Report_1_Synopsis: RNO Tower Controller in Charge; CIC; reported due to sun glare blocking controller's view of final; traffic landed on wrong runway resulted in traffic executing a go around.

Report_1_Narrative: We landed on Runway 4 and due to the snow removal operations that were occurring at the time as the front had just cleared the city; with numerous taxiways closed or impassable; we were instructed to exit onto Runway 13/31 and taxi to hold short of Lima. We were then cleared onto Lima; Alpha to the gate; but it turned out that there was on outbound Company coming out of the alley. We then were told to hold short of Bravo on Lima. We did and then I heard Ground give the outbound Company aircraft instructions to taxi Lima; Bravo.  I said to my FO (First Officer) that I didn't think we had room for him to clear us. As he came past Spot X I was concerned. As he started onto Lima I said 'I think this is too tight.' As he started his turn onto Lima I knew it was unsafe and I instructed him three times on Ground frequency to stop. He did. We were staring at his right winglet very close to us. I then coordinated with Company and Ground to get a tug out to us. Because we were inbound; I had the Ground Crew push us back towards Runway 13/31 on Lima to allow [the Company aircraft] to continue his taxi. We then continued to the gate. I have since talked to and debriefed the other Captain to get his view of what occurred and to talk about the safety concerns that I had. No metal was bent; but it would have if we hadn't both realized his close proximity to our aircraft. There were parallax concerns from Ground's view and the other crew's view. Speaking up is critical when things don't look right. The substantial numbers of snow removal trucks and plows along with closed taxiways that were constantly changing made it even more challenging.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported a near collison during taxi in LGA.

Report_1_Narrative: I don't know what to make of the most recent bulletin about pilot mask usage and COVID-19. To date there is no concrete directive about mask usage in the cockpit. My own policy as Captain is to direct mask usage at all times possible while in the cockpit other than while eating or drinking or obviously in an emergency while using oxygen. I believe this to be congruent with CDC guidance for when someone needs to be in close contact with someone else who does not live with that person. This procedure is not perfect but the best I can come up with outside of pre-departure rapid COVID testing. As pilots we usually fly with new coworkers on every new trip and to date there is no way to determine that the person you are flying with is not an asymptomatic carrier of the virus.This whole situation is a failure of:The pilot group as a whole: We should do better than thisUnion: Our pilots are more at risk from death or injury from COVID than any other operational threatAirline: The safety protocol enforced outside the cockpit should extend inside as well; no exceptionsFAA: If none of the above will take action the FAA needs to step inMy First Officer on the flight associated with this report agreed in the briefing phase to comply with my directives for mask usage. During the flight I detected a problem though. I generally try to be friendly and conversational not only to pass the time in pleasant way but also to provide a comfortable environment to empower my First Officer to be a helpful partner in the flight.This wasn't to be on that flight and it culminated in my FO intentionally removing his mask on descent into ZZZ. Stating when asked about it that 'It is interfering with my duties.' The interference he was referring to was that I didn't hear the altitude ATC assigned and I asked him to ask ATC to confirm. I don't know how his mask interfered with ATC transmissions.I honestly think he was looking for an opportunity to remove his mask in defiance.I asked him to replace his mask and offered to work the radios if it's a problem.Later at the hotel I restated my objection to flying with someone who refuses to wear a mask and asked if that would be a problem in tomorrow's flight. He stated it would not.  There were no mask issues on that flight; however it was not the most pleasant environment; quite sterile.Mask-less cockpits are dangerous.Unfortunately this is not my first time experiencing the mask resistance in the cockpit.The current guidance on this is weak and shows a lack of leadership on all involved.My experience is that a surgical type mask does not interfere with my duties; is easily and quickly removed if necessary; and by medical consensus prevents contagious droplets from dispersing to a great extent.Please enforce mask usage and prevent the sickness or death of our brothers or sisters in the cockpit.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain expressed a need for a concrete directive about face mask usage in the cockpit.

Report_1_Narrative: Before push checklist and Ramp tower clearance to push were completed / obtained per procedures. Following standard pushback verbiage from the ground crew; I released the brakes. Pushback and No 2 engine start proceeded without incident. Ground crew instructed to 'Set Brakes' - at this time I read back 'Parking brake set; pressure normal' while the FO (First Officer) and I visually checked the red parking brake indicator for illumination and Brake Press gauge for 2800 PSI. Ground crew then announced 'Aircraft disconnected by-pass pin removed' to which I replied 'Disconnect headset.'Shortly after this statement the aircraft appeared to move forward unexpectedly. The ramp agent came back on headset with 'Set brakes set brakes' to which I applied brakes.Apparently the parking brake was not set; as we had intended and thought; and an uncommanded aircraft movement had occurred. The ramp agent came on the interphone and indicated that all was fine on the ground; and standard signals were given for ramp departure. Upon crew debrief; one of the threats that we identified was the sun shining into the cockpit; making the red parking brake light less apparent to the crew. Another threat was the general distraction of normalcy and not blocking out the sunlight's glare to verify aircraft condition.We are glad no one on the ground was injured and will learn from this experience.
Report_2_Narrative: Before push checklist was completed. Received our push back clearance and the Captain communicated with the ground crew standard tow bar less pushback clearance and released the brakes appropriately. Pushback was completed uneventfully and during so we were cleared for engine start after which the Captain had me start the No. 2 engine. The ground crew instructed to 'Set Brakes.' I saw good brake pressure - 2800 psi; and what I believed to be the red Parking Brake light illuminated so I continued my duties of setting the packs appropriately.The ground crew announced 'aircraft disconnected - bypass pin removed' and I heard the Captain respond with 'Disconnect Headset.' Shortly after this the aircraft began an uncommanded movement forward; ground crew came on headset Immediately saying 'Set Brakes Set Brakes' to which brakes were applied and the aircraft stopped the slow roll and the Parking Brake was appropriately verified engaged at this time. The ramp crew came back on the inter phone and indicated all was fine on the ground; and standard signals were given for departure. Apparently our parking brake was not set after all when we initially thought; and upon debrief we both agreed the threats encountered were the glare of the sun on the parking brake light illuminating it more red than usual; as well as the general distraction associated with starting engines and push back tasks in general. We did not properly block the sun's glare and we should have been more vigilant to ensure it was set properly. We are both thankful nobody on the ground was injured and we will learn from this experience in order to prevent it from happening again.
Report_1_Synopsis: B737 flight crew reported uncommanded aircraft movement occurred following pushback without brakes set.

Report_1_Narrative: Aircraft was out of balance at start of my shift. It required the last row to be blocked. I sent a message to ZZZZ to do so and they did. At about 10 minutes before departure aircraft went out of balance again and I determined that the last 3 rows now needed to be blocked. ZZZZ called to find out why weights weren't generating and I advised that last 3 rows now needed to be blocked. He advised that aircraft was already out so I said I would handle it with Captain. I sent Captain that info via ACARS to block last 3 rows; but when I went back to double check the Load Program (LP) to verify that in fact the additional 2 rows needed to be moved and blocked; this time LP indicated that no rows needed to be blocked. I checked it 1 or 2 more times because it didn't seem right to me. LP again indicated no rows now needed to be blocked. So now I quickly sent Captain an ACARS to disregard moving the additional 2 rows of people as that would now be an unnecessary waste of time since no longer needed. I sent the disregard message and then released weights. Departure [load] control now did not indicate to block any rows-although row XX had been blocked from the beginning. As I thought about why LP would show 3 rows needed to be blocked; and then it indicated that we now didn't need to LP any rows; I checked the seat map (aircraft was airborne by then) and sure enough; Operations had gone in and shown last 3 rows blocked but never spoke with the crew. They should not have touched the seat map since they did not physically move anyone. And since they are not supposed to do that; it didn't occur to me that they had. But that is why LP did not show I needed to block rows; it was reading that the rows were already empty. I called Dispatch and asked them to find out from crew exactly which rows were blocked on take-off. The answer was just row 34-the last row. I verified with ZZZ; and they advised that they had not told crew to move anyone; they just showed passengers moved out of last 3 rows. I advised ZZZ never to indicate passengers moved seats unless they have physically accomplished the move. They understand now.
Report_1_Synopsis: Load Planner reported aircraft departed with blocked rows being occupied by passengers; contrary to the weight and balance report.

Report_1_Narrative: I was working Aircraft X ZZZ-ZZZZ1 at gate and had planned the flight according to the [Manifest]. One of my agents connected a cart of freight going to ZZZ2 to a string of carts that was going to ZZZZ1 unbeknownst to me. Since all of the carts were together; I scanned all of the carts for the flight going to ZZZZ1. The last cart of freight was a pallet going to ZZZ2. At first I had no idea that it was going to ZZZ2 so I scanned it just like I scanned the other cart before it since it was DG for ZZZZ1. When I scanned the cart for ZZZ2 the barcode wouldn't scan so I had to enter it manually. I did and confirmed the weight. I did not get an error message stating this was freight for ZZZ2 the scanner allowed me to add it to my flight for ZZZZ1 and I continued on my work.  I was moving from AFT to FWD of the aircraft to ensure the operation runs smoothly on my gate. I am the Lead. I instructed my agent in the back to load up a cart of bags and a cart of DG (freight) and to surround the DG with 15 bags. I went to the front of the plane to check on the crew working there. When I returned to the rear of the plane all three carts were loaded including the freight for ZZZ2. When it became time to close the flight on the scanner the scanner asked me to confirm if everything was loaded and again no error message was displayed and since everything was in fact loaded; I confirmed that everything was loaded. Still nothing on the scanner told me that I had freight for another destination; in this case ZZZ2 going to ZZZZ1. I didn't realize I had loaded the ZZZ2 freight to ZZZZ1 until the plane was already gone and I was already working the next flight on my gate and the cargo coordinator questioned me about the freight that it was missing from the gate. I notified my supervisor and spoke with safety to file a Report and the Cargo Dispatcher regarding the incident.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Load Controller reported inadvertent transport of Hazmat cargo to wrong destination.

Report_1_Narrative: I was Pilot Monitoring on flight [on] DRLLR 5 RNAV STAR to IAH. Aircraft X had one MEL for right FMS inoperative. Single FMS operation. We entered the STAR during preflight and 26R runway per the DRLLR 5 STAR. ATC instructed us to change to 26L just prior to MPORT. This changes the final point on the STAR from SKLER to ZOEEE. I entered the new runway and verified that no duplicate waypoints existed. I also verified and noted that the waypoint sequence on the MFD looked correct; noting the large gap between ZOEEE and BOZZZ on the 26L approach. I also noted the line on the MFD depicted from DOMNO to ZOEEE. For unknown reasons the airplane approached DOMNO; overflew DOMNO; and the autopilot went immediately into ROL mode and continued flying straight. It did not sequence to ZOEEE as expected. We noticed the change immediately; selected heading mode to start the turn to ZOEEE; and then re-engaged LNAV after verifying the FMS was sequencing properly to ZOEEE. As we started to sort out the flight path error; I was distracted when ATC issued heading calls and pilot deviation calls; which removed my attention from assisting the pilot flying. No other deviation occurred that we were aware of. Both pilots were fully engaged in managing the flight. We acted as fast as we could to regain flight path control. [I] suggest verifying the integrity of the FMS arrivals into IAH. Delay pilot deviation calls until on the ground and the airplane has been secured.
Report_2_Narrative: We were on the DRLLR 5 arrival and planning for Runway 26R. We had checked the route for no double waypoints and all altitudes were correct. We were assigned Runway 26L and made the appropriate checks of waypoints and altitudes. At DOMNO the plane went into Roll mode and continued south. We saw it right away and began left turn as ATC told us to turn left and gave us a heading (070 I think). A few minutes later the controller gave us a phone number to call about a possible deviation. This plane had the #2 FMS MEL'd which may have contributed since we don't often operate with 1 FMS. Better planning for operations with one FMS. Closer attention while passing DOMNO; which has known issues. However we had no duplicate waypoints so this may be a new issue.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight crew reported experiencing an unplanned autopilot/FMS mode shift causing a tract deviation during the DRLLR 5 STAR into IAH. Flight crew cited a runway assignment change; plus one FMS being inoperative as causal factors.

Report_1_Narrative: Descending on the DSNEE 4 arrival from EMLLD; we became aware of congested airport environment with two different TCAS traffic alerts very close by. Approach had us at 190 knots departing DSNEE; and we were expecting the visual to runway 20R. We had gone to flaps 2 configuration. We were handed off late to the final controller; and when we switched over we heard a company call sign with nearly identical numeric as ours; cleared for the RNAV (RNP) Z runway 20R. We heard the other aircraft read back the clearance; we knew a VERY similar call sign was on frequency. We thought we might be cleared for the same approach. We checked in and asked if we were going to get the RNAV approach; and the controller said no; we were going to get a visual unless we asked for the approach. Shortly after; the controller cleared an aircraft to descend to 3000'; but neither of us were sure that it was our call sign. The First Officer (FO) attempted to clarify; but the controller was very busy and talking nonstop. We flew a few more miles; and before we could clarify he repeated the clearance to descend to 3000' and asked if we had the airport in sight. We called the airport; and said we were high. He cleared us to fly through final approach course and intercept from the right. FO read back the clearance; and we both agreed it was going to be tight. I immediately called for gear down and got the flaps to full; I also used the speed brakes as long as safely practical. We switched over to tower control; and I made the glideslope at approx. 1400' AGL; but we were still 40kts fast. I told the FO we were going to do a 'Soft Go'. At 1000' AGL I called for 'Go Around; Takeoff/around (TOGA)' and advanced the thrust levers to TOGA. I then called 'climb' as I brought the thrust levers back to what I thought was the climb position; but was actually the Maximum Continuous Thrust (MCT) detent. The tower initially held us to 2000'; so I reduced our climb rate - we were accelerating rapidly. As we cleaned up and were cleared to 3000'; the FO recognized that we were in MCT detent and brought it to my attention. By then we were clean and rapidly approaching 250 KIAS. I brought the thrust levers back to idle as we passed 260; and we saw a maximum speed of about 280 before we began to slow down again. I selected speed mode and set 220 KIAS; positioned the thrust levers in the climb detent and re-engaged auto thrust. We slowed and turned back into a right downwind for an uneventful visual approach and landing at SNA.Causes(1)	Late clearance to descend. SNA is challenging even when on a normal profile; and a few miles made all the difference.(2)	Task saturation. The L.A basin is one of the busiest airspaces in the world. Two Traffic Alerts and nonstop chatter from the approach controller indicated that he was task saturated; as well.(3)	Call sign confusion. The scheduling shop should never have had two call signs separated by one digit arriving at the same airport at the same time.(4)	Approach expectations. We were going to do a visual; and changed our setup and expectations when we heard preceding traffic approach clearance.(5)	Fatigue. Our FAR 117 duty day limit was 10 hours. We had been awake since 3.5 hours earlier to make sign-in; and were at 9:00 of our 10:00 limit when we arrived at SNA. When we knew we were too high to likely make a successful approach; we could have asked for a vector and more time/distance to descend. Flight scheduling needs to de-conflict call signs so very similar ones are not scheduled to arrive at the same airport at the same time. The ATC controllers seemed very busy; perhaps a few more controllers on-shift would help divide the workload better. Crew scheduling could alleviate fatigue factors by avoiding sequence builds that have crews flying into airports at the back end of their duty periods that are known to present unusual challenges (even if they aren't officially 'special qualification' airports).
Report_1_Synopsis: Airbus First officer reported a go-around caused by late clearance to descend and confusion caused by a similar call sign for an aircraft preceding them.

Report_1_Narrative: During the baggage loading phase I loaded a small box containing approximately 6 small bottles of recreational Oxygen. We departed ZZZ with a final destination of ZZZ1 and the flight proceeded uneventfully. Upon arrival all baggage was unloaded and the First Officer questioned me after the passengers left regarding the contents of the box. At no time up to this point did I consider the possibility of this being HAZMAT or anything not authorized to be carried by us. Upon further research I felt compelled to reach out to the Chief Pilot for guidance. I suggest a more thorough training of company policies; procedures; and specifically HAZMAT information. Access to more detailed information regarding Hazmat material.
Report_2_Narrative: The owner and family arrived to the airplane ramp side. I went to open the exterior baggage compartment; to load the luggage. While loading bags the line personal were bringing me; I saw the Captain was also loading bags/backpacks etc. inside the cabin of the airplane. After the the baggage was loaded in the exterior baggage compartment of the airplane; I walked into the airplane greeted the owner and family and sat down in my flight deck seat to preform the rest of the pre-takeoff duties for the flight to intermediate stop to pick up two passengers and then finally on to final ZZZ1; our final destination. All flights were uneventful. When we landed at ZZZ1 while unloading the baggage; I noticed the box contained portable Oxygen containers which the Captain had loaded at our initial departure airport. After the passengers were on their way; I mentioned to the Captain about the box and it's contents. I said I don't think that was something we could carry; as it may be considered Hazmat. We further discussed this and performed research of company FOM and HAZMAT. The Chief Pilot was contacted to get clarification and guidance on this issue. I suggest more specific HAZMAT guidance and possibly more comprehensive HAZMAT training. Also a more detailed description of carry and non carry items would be helpful.
Report_1_Synopsis: G-200 flight crew reported inadvertent transport of undeclared Hazmat material.

Report_1_Narrative: On Aircraft X from ZZZ to ZZZ1 while boarding passenger seated in seat XX4 came on that aircraft with his mask below his nose and between his lips. I told that passenger his mask must come over his nose and mouth. He responded 'He will try.' I then offered him a company approved surgical mask that were provided by the company. He responded 'No thanks.' That was the first time of me asking him to put his mask on properly. During my compliant check before doing the safety demo; the mask was down again. I told him once again about the mask. That was the second time. During cabin service the mask was down again and I had to remind him once more. Once cabin service was over and passengers were given time to eat and drink; I then went around to collect trash and he was asleep with his mask down. I called out to him and he opened his eyes and I told him for the third time about his mask. Once we got to the final descent his mask was down and I reminded him once again for the fourth time. Once I told him this time he just looked at me and shook his head. This passenger and his wife; were both sick. They were both coughing without covering their cough. The couple kept coughing during takeoff; throughout the flight and landing. The coughing drew the attention of other passengers to look. People are very scared and when they hear coughing and other passengers not wearing mask properly they worry.  Many verbal warnings were given.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight attendant reported two passengers were coughing throughout the flight and not adhering to face mask policy.

Report_1_Narrative: On Day 5; the crew desk called me to assign me to a trip on Day 6 with a XA:40 report time.  I called in fatigued on Day 6 at approximately [3 hours prior]. I had just finished a 4 day trip from Day 2 to Day 5; with each day requiring subsequently later report times and the last 2 days requiring late or all night flying.  Additionally; even though this trip spanned 4 calendar days; it only included 2 sleep cycles.The previous 4 day trip created a significant cumulative sleep debt; as tracked my my Apple Watch. Day 1-Day 2; 6:38 of sleep at home prior to reporting for my 4 day trip. Day 2-Day 3; 8:44 of sleep in the ZZZ hotel. Day 3-Day 4; 5:26 of sleep after landing in ZZZ1; but I woke up at XA:00 am local time and had a XR:59 departure that night.  I attempted to take a nap prior to reporting for duty but I couldn't fall asleep and was awake for about 18 hours prior to flying a redeye. Day 3-Day 4; No sleep due to redeye.  I flew a redeye.  Extremely tired during the flight and took a 25 minute nap during cruise.  When I returned home; I slept from approximately XA:45 until the crew desk woke me from deep sleep shortly after XG:00.  After the crew desk woke me; I packed my bags and prepared for the new trip.  I attempted to go back to bed at XK:00 but could not fall asleep.  I realized that it was not safe for me to attempt to fly my 3rd transcontinental trip in 2 days so I called in fatigued. Day 5-Day 6; No sleep due to crew desk interrupting my recovery sleep from the previous redeye.Of note; my previous trip involved a significant cumulative clockwise circadian rhythm disruption in which every day required a later report time and each day flew later into the night.  Clockwise disruptions such as this are generally easier to tolerate compared to counter-clockwise disruptions.  However; this 4 day trip also was engineered to accumulate sleep debt.  Day 1 was 11 hours of duty and 20.5 hours of rest; which equates to a 31.5 hour long duty/sleep cycle.  Day 2 of my 4 day was 7:15 of duty and nearly 25 hours of rest; which was a 32 hour duty/sleep cycle.  Combined with each day's later duty periods; it was generally easy to fall asleep at the beginning of the rest periods.  However; it was not realistic nor possible to achieve 2 circadian rests or resets during the layovers; which meant that each day I would be awake for a longer period of time prior to reporting for late night flights.  This culminated when I reported for my redeye after being awake for 18 hours.  Upon landing I was absolutely exhausted and needed to catch up on the previous 4 days of missed sleep.  Unfortunately the crew desk interrupted this much-needed sleep and assigned me the new trip on Day 6.  In other words; the crew desk expected me to shift from my previous XM:00 pm and XS:00 pm local report times to a XA:40 am report time after disrupting my rest and being awake for over 12 hours.  Furthermore; the crew desk did not consider the larger picture of the 4 day trip and subsequent 2 day trip as a single 6 day long physiological marathon.  Considering the operational design of my previous 4 day trip; combined with a back-to-back 2 day trip; I do not think it's physiological possible or safe for anyone to endure such a disruptive 6 day period especially after the crew desk wakes you up in the middle of a much needed restorative sleep period.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier First Officer reported they called in fatigued due to not being able to get sufficient rest from the previous four days flying schedule.

Report_1_Narrative: Arriving DEN on the CLASH2 arrival from the southeast; I planned and briefed an easterly flow arrival to land 17R. ATIS advertised 17R; 16L; 16R ILS; visual and RNAV Z approaches. I briefed for the RNAV RNP Z 17R. The final point for the arrival was QWIKE intersection and I left a discontinuity between that QWIKE and the QWIKE point starting the RNAV RNP Z 17R. Denver Center gave us a clearance to descend via the CLASH2 arrival landing south.The PM (Pilot Monitoring) and I confirmed that that was what we briefed and the FMC was properly programmed. The PM checked on with DEN Approach and we were told to expect RNAV Z to 16R. The PM installed that approach and I briefed the new arrival points and crossing restrictions on the CLASH2 that coincided with that runway; which were now a west downwind; the final fix being CLFFF. I briefed the approach as well. We did the same thing; leaving a discontinuity between CLFFF on the arrival and CLFFF as the IAF on the approach. The PM pulled the landing data for 16R and we briefed the changes on the engine-out missed approach which was slightly different then 17R. Approximately EVRLY intersection as we were descending through FL180; DEN Approach then said runway change; expect visual or ILS (I can't remember) to 16L. I remember it was at FL180 because it coincided with the altimeter change and the need to verify that VNAV is still able to maintain. The PM installed runway 16L and I did a briefing for the ILS 16L. This changed the FMC to an east downwind; the same fixes as for runway 17R but I did not note the changes in arrival fixes. As we were approaching JURKY intersection; I noticed on the FMC that the next waypoint was not what I was expecting. I had in my mind that we would be on a west downwind for the 16 runways. I said to the PM; it's not the correct fix next for runway 16R. The PM then asked DEN Approach to verify the runway assignment.Approach responded with a frequency change but did not respond to the request for runway clarification. This was at the point where we needed to go left or right depending on the runway. I thought it was 16R; so I went to the next fix for that runway; ROOTZ. As soon as the PM checked on with the next frequency; the Controller asked our runway assignment. The PM said we were trying to clarify. Approach then gave us 16R as a runway assignment. In fact; the previous clearance was for runway 16L. And that runway is an east downwind; not a west downwind even though the runway is on the west side of the airfield. This was absolutely my responsibility to ensure the correct runway and corresponding waypoints for the arrival. Going forward my personal correction will be to write down the runway assignment given by ATC each time it changes; whether on the yoke clip notepaper or on the iPad graphic. I also got complacent after doing 2 full briefings into DEN on a clear day. With the 3rd briefing; I did an abbreviated briefing. A full briefing; stepping through every arrival point would have caught it earlier. Additionally; as suggested by the Jump Seater; instead of clarifying the runway and having to verify the points quickly; I will ask ATC for the next waypoint they are expecting in order to give myself some time to figure out any ambiguities between the FMC and the chart. If we are adding to the data for DEN arrival deviations though...I didn't think this could happen to me. We briefed the threat of runway changes going into DEN. But DEN giving runway changes that impact arrival points without sufficient time for us to properly program and confirm was a contributing factor. Its 11.4 miles from EVRLY where we got the change to JURKY where the arrival splits. To reprogram; confirm; brief; get landing data and brief the engine-out profile changes while monitoring the descent is challenging.
Report_2_Narrative: CLASH2 RNAV into DEN we initially planned for a Visual Approach to 17R backed up by the ILS. Initial Controller told us to expect 16R so we loaded RNAV/RNP 16R with the CLFFF transition to the approach; per ATIS. Cleared to descend via the CLASH2 arrival so we set 11;000 feet in the MCP (Mode Control Panel). ATC then advised us to expect Visual Approach to 16L. I then loaded the 16L ILS in the box and the Captain continued the descent on the arrival around the JURKEY fix. When the Captain started to brief the new arrival she noticed the arrival fixes did not match up with the new runway.I asked ATC to verify our runway assignment as all 3 of us in the cockpit were unclear at that point. After a pause; ATC gave us a new frequency instead of answering my query regarding which runway. At that point the Captain manually entered the ROOTZ fix. We changed our altitude in the MCP to correspond to the 13;000 feet minimum at ROOTZ while we checked in with the final Controller. Upon checking in the Controller asked us which runway we were planning on. I asked again which runway as we were not certain at that point. He then stated Visual Approach 16R. I updated the box AGAIN to the ILS 16R and; we were then given a heading and new altitude. The rest of the arrival and approach were uneventful.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported they deviated from the assigned route due to last minute runway changes and incomplete communications from ATC during arrival to DEN airport.

Report_1_Narrative: I was reassigned from a deadhead to ZZZ to flying a turn to ZZZ1 because the copilot called in sick with suspected symptoms of COVID-19. Reportedly he had lost his sense of smell and had a severe headache. He had already flown with Captain X that morning potentially exposing Captain to the virus.  Now I am assigned to fly with Captain X potentially exposing me to the virus. I called the flight operations management; explained my concerns; he explained CDC guidelines; I told him I was uncomfortable with the situation; he told he would call me back. I got no such call. We are flooded with cautious bulletins; emails and other communications from our company about COVID-19 yet when faced with getting a flight out it would seem that's all thrown out the window.  Regardless of CDC guidelines; it would seem prudent to remove anyone who is knowingly exposed to the virus from duty until verified negative or positive.Please note; I was not trying to get out of the trip; I was trying to get out of being needlessly exposed to COVID-19. I'm exceptionally disappointed with how this was handled.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported being assigned to fly with a Captain whose previous First Officer co-pilot called in sick with COVID-19 symptoms.  Reporter described concerns with management's handling of the situation stating it goes against all the guidelines delineated by the company.

Report_1_Narrative: Departing Runway XXR ZZZ we were filed ZZZ1 Departure ZZZ transition then ZZZZZ [fix].  Upon receipt of CPDLC clearance there was a route modification that was obtained that had us routed via the ZZZZA3 ZZZZZ.  I loaded the flight plan per the CDU prompt and accepted the clearance and printed it out.  There was plenty of time as loading was delayed.  When I reviewed the loaded clearance it came up ZZZZA3 ZZZZA ZZZZZ.  I then went back to the DEP/ARR page and checked the runway and SID which I had previously selected to ensure it was still in the FMC.  I did notice that the routing had us now going south to ZZZZZ and thought the ZZZZA ZZZZZ was a short cut ATC wanted due to light traffic and time of day.  I also looked at the printout and didn't see the period between ZZZZA3 and ZZZZZ as in ZZZZA3 DZZZZZ verses ZZZZA3.ZZZZZ meaning that ZZZZZ was the transition.  Once we were airborne ATC cleared us directly to 12;000 which we were initially given 7;000 in the clearance.  ATC then came back and said maintain 12;000 unrestricted which in my mind validated the shortcut because usually you get the phraseology 'Climb via the SID except maintain XXX'. ATC then informed us our deviate and asked us if we were on the SID.  I said affirmative except from ZZZZA we were direct to ZZZZZ which was incorrect according to the clearance.  After getting to cruise the Captain and I discussed the situation looking at both the clearance; the FOM and the loaded routing from the CPDLC.  We realized that two errors were made.  When I loaded the SID I did not reselect the runway and SID with the ZZZZZ transition because when I checked it was in the box and because we both missed the period in the printout and ZZZZZ was on the regular routing I thought ATC wanted us to cut that part of the SID off because of low traffic volume.   It was pilot error and it's a difficult lesson.  I am fully aware that a period means a transition but I missed it on the printout and assumed ATC wanted a shorter routing which has become the norm is so many ATC environments with COVID.  I also realize that I will always double check every period on the CDU against the printout copy as it's easier to see.  In addition I will ensure that every modification in the future requires an input of both the runway and SID even when uploading clearances from CPDLC which I'm aware to do but I didn't see the period on the printout.  I take full responsibility for this mistake and I feel really bad I missed such a small but signification part of the clearance.   I know better so there's no excuses for this missed detail.
Report_2_Narrative: First leg (and only leg) with FO; blocked XX mins late for loading; so not rushed. Filed FP was ZZZ1 ZZZ transition; ZZZ [VOR]; ZZZZZ; RXXX ....CPDLC had 'route change' (I was doing exterior prefect when it came): cleared ZZZZA3 ZZZZZ; RXXX ... climb via SID except maintain 7;000 feet. The actual printout was 'ZZZZA3. ZZZZZ'; which means the ZZZZZ transition with the 'dot' in between. We missed that dot. We both assumed the clearance was direct from ZZZZA to ZZZZZ. The ZZZ1 does not have ZZZZZ as a transition; yet it was on our filed flight plan. To add some justification for our assumption; the ZZZ1 goes way north and west before heading west. The ZZZZA SID went south of ZZZ [airport] and more direct west on course. Add that is was [early] in the morning (very light traffic plus Covid19 low traffic) we assumed we were cleared a more direct routing south of ZZZ [airport]. And the Controller gave us climb unrestricted to 12;000 which also made sense for the Direct ZZZZZ we had in the FMC. And then climb to FL340 but then stopped us at 15;000. But we were wrong. He questioned us and we discovered the actual clearance was the entire transition out to ZZZZZ. At that point he cleared us to ZZZZZ and to climb to FL340 again. No TCAS or other traffic was in the area. This was a crew error. We both were very disappointed with the mistake. We reviewed the FOM and saw our mistake. We have both done this correctly many times but the 'ZZZZZ' on the filed route threw us off. No other excuse. And as the Captain I take responsibility.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported a track deviation occurred due to misreading a changed departure clearance.

Report_1_Narrative: A vibration / rumble was noticed during the No.2 engine start.   During taxi the Captain performed his flight controls check so fast that I was unable to keep up with the call outs. It had been this way the whole trip; in fact I had insisted that it be repeated on the 1st leg so I could correctly check the control position.  Whilst holding short of Runway XXL the Captain indicated he would turn the anti-ice off on taking the runway. I pointed out that the published ATIS reported runway conditions of 3;3;3 with 50% compacted snow; 50% compacted snow; 75% compacted snow. He was still inclined to turn off the anti-ice so I tried again suggesting should anything happen any investigation would focus on this. Reluctantly the anti-ice remained on and having lined up it was obvious that the runway was still significantly impacted by snow.  On departure I chose to call for autopilot 2 at approx 100 ft in case the controller was busy. This allowed me to notice during the initial turn towards / at ZZZZZ that on the E / WD the title Engine" was flashing as well as "N1 VIB" was flashing green 9.9. An increase in noise and vibration was perceived from the right engine. Anti-ice was reapplied and after a short while the indication reduced to 8.2. The indication returned to 9.9 after the anti-ice was turned off during climb and it remained this way until the engines were at idle during the descent. During cruise I suggested the possibility of a bad sensor; the Captain's opinion was that we had a vibration. Later during the leg I commented on the vibration and now the Captain's opinion was that we may have a bad sensor. We were initially cleared to FL360. As we approached level off the Captain requested a climb to FL380 earlier than the flight plan fix of ZZZZZ1. On reaching cruise I reduced then increased managed Mach by 0.01 to investigate the potential of a harmonic vibration. Once established at the new speeds there was no difference in the indicated vibration so I returned to the managed speed with the intent to divert should the situation deteriorate. The Captain took out his QRH and referenced the High Engine Vibration procedure. It was given to read and after a discussion the Captain elected not to follow it as it would require descending from cruise altitude. For the remainder of cruise the Captain returned to reading his magazine. I monitored the indications; changed assigned radio frequencies and from time to time closed my eyes to concentrate on feeling whether the vibration had changed or the ambient sound had changed. We began flying the arrival. During the descent; Approach instructed us to increase speed to 310 kts or better. I felt that this was a bad idea and expressed this by saying ' I don't want to do that ' and 'I am uncomfortable with that'.  'So what it's only 20 kts' was the reply and seeing no intent to inform Approach of our situation; I felt that I had pushed as far as I could and increased speed. The Captain gleefully declared that the vibration had dropped to 2.2. I countered stating that the engines were now at idle as the aircraft attempted to stay on the profile at a higher speed. It was at this point that I decided to reach out  and have myself removed from the trip. ZZZ1 was landing north with reported winds of 160/6 so a landing approach calculation was performed for the tail wind landing. On short final the Captain elected to increase Vapp unilaterally leading to a long float during landing. A new landing approach calculation for the new numbers was not performed. On landing I briefly deployed reverse thrust and quickly closed down the right engine before it could spool up and exacerbate the vibration problem. I moderated the thrust from the left engine and relied mainly on wheel braking to slow the aircraft. Control was passed back to the Captain at approx 60 kts for the taxi to the gate."
Report_1_Synopsis: First Officer reported asking to be removed from the flight after disagreement with Captain over correct actions to be taken after excessive vibrations on an engine were not followed.

Report_1_Narrative: I went to retrieve a pressure gauge for the Aircraft X oxygen system and went into supply. The drawer I opened was in location cabinet XYZ for the pressure gauge. I found the gauge I needed and when I went to close the drawer I saw another gauge there that is used for the hydraulic reservoir cap with gauge attached in the same location as a gauge we use for oxygen. This is a major safety concern with petroleum products like hydraulic fluid being near oxygen tooling and equipment can cause combustion in the right conditions.The oxygen equipment needs to be segregated from ANY hydraulic or petroleum product at all times.
Report_1_Synopsis: Technician reported discovering oxygen  gauges intermixed with hydraulic gauges in the company tool room in the same drawer.

Report_1_Narrative: While working Aircraft X ZZZ-ZZZ1; I became concerned for the health and well-being of my flying partner.  She displayed numerous symptoms of severe illness including: persistent coughing; sneezing; shortness of breath; weakness; and sweating profusely.  Prior to starting the service; I witnessed [flying partner] remove her tote bag from the galley cart and take several pills.  [Flying partner] then had difficulty pushing and pulling the beverage cart with assistance.  It strained her and seemed very difficult for her to speak with customers; so I had prepared a sign in blue marker that read; 'What do you want to drink?' and listed beverages.  After picking up trash; [flying partner] repeatedly placed her used gloves on top of the galley counter.  Upon descent into ZZZ1; I noticed the orange strap at door 2R was not attached and reminded her to affix it.  At that time; she was coughing and was no longer wearing a mask at all.  I expressed genuine concern for her well-being and was uncomfortable flying with someone who appeared so unwell.
