Report_1_Narrative: Today I taxied to the ZZZ strip with ATIS weather to ZZZ Runway XX. I noticed 4 or 3 maybe snow removal vehicles working around but not yet on the runway. I called in to the Tower and I introduced my airplane numbers and request for takeoff. The Tower asked me to repeat my call sign and I did.  The Tower told me to wait. I heard quite a bit (of half) the Tower radio traffic communication.  The Tower then told me I was cleared for takeoff and I confirmed.  I noticed that the snow removal vehicles all had backed off and so I took off successfully; without incident.  One of the snow removal drivers called into the Tower and told them I took off the strip.  I verified this and was told to call into the Tower later.  I called in and told the Tower how it happen from my prospective after my flight. They say they are passing the incident on. There was a southeast wind and in reflection; the Tower may have told me I was clear to take off southeast; which is from the lake; not the strip.  I should have reiterated my position on the runway when he asked me to repeat my tail numbers.  I do not believe I called for a southeast take off; but there was a southeast wind that I was in my mind.  I was also watching the snow removal equipment but believed he must have told them to back off on a different frequency. There was no other radio traffic until I was 8 to 10 miles away. The lake was empty and the Southeast water lane; frozen; is right in front of the Tower. He could have helped the situation if he said he could not see me. He did not see me take off at all. It was the snow worker that saw me. When I returned about an hour later the ATIS changed to MIKE and the strip was closed.  I had no issue landing on the lake to the southeast. I have flown out of ZZZ since I was a training pilot. I use the lake in the summer and occasionally in the winter. I regret this happened today; regardless that all was safe and there was no chance of any collision with truck or another plane.  It was my intention to follow ATC control; I am sorry if I heard/misinterpreted; or even possibly asked for the incorrect runway. I will certainly talk more to the Tower when they are short and listen more acutely.  I will be more certain of the runway as well and add it to my checklist as I am with wheels and skis. I have caught miscommunication from the Tower in the past coming in on floats but was able to talk it out.
Report_1_Synopsis: A pilot departing from an airport with a hard surface runway and water lanes reported he took off from the runway but found out ATC had cleared him for takeoff from the water lane as the runway was closed for snow removal.

Report_1_Narrative: The incident occurred while on the initial climb from runway 25 at Orlando Executive Airport (ORL). The probable cause appears to be communication and pilot error. Our aircraft was a Aircraft X. The student and I were remaining in the pattern practicing touch and go landings. An Aircraft Y [faster aircraft] was following us throughout the pattern. Our call sign was occasionally [mis-stated] which contributed to the confusion. During our pattern practice we were told to extend our downwind and that Tower would call our base. While we were in the right downwind and extended right downwind for Runway 25; Aircraft Y was noticeably gaining on us as shown on our MFD's traffic feature. Our base was approved and we were number 1 cleared for a touch and go Runway 25. [Aircraft Y] was cleared for a touched and go number 2 behind us. While on short final; it was noticeable once again on the MFD that Aircraft Y was gaining on us significantly. Our approach speed in the Aircraft X is 65 kts. With the headwind component that day our ground speed was undoubtedly slower than 65kts. Aircraft Y was told by Tower to do an s-turn on final for spacing as it was apparent they were getting close. The problem arose on the initial climb out following the touch and go; Aircraft Y overtook our aircraft while on the departure leg at approximately 800 feet; resulting in a near miss.The traffic we were following was told to extend upwind and we were expecting to receive a similar instruction for ourselves. The confusion seems to have begun when Executive Tower radioed for Aircraft Y to continue in the upwind and that they would call their crosswind. We did not respond to this call; as we assumed it was intended for Aircraft Y.  Aircraft Y responded confirming to extend their upwind until their crosswind was called. This transmission must have stepped on the Tower's transmission because as soon as Aircraft Y was finished broadcasting; the end of tower's transmission came through with the only audible portion being '...end upwind.' (Most likely 'extend upwind.')  This stepped-on call was most likely a follow up to [us]; but Aircraft Y then responded to continue their upwind for a 2nd time. Tower then called for Aircraft Y to extend their upwind. At this point the instructor in Aircraft Y; clearly confused; read back the extend upwind instruction for the 3rd time. We realized that the extend upwind call to [callsign] was most likely for us and we continued the upwind as instructed with the traffic ahead of and behind us being on extended upwinds.During this time; we again noticed Aircraft Y gaining on us on the MFD traffic. We continued in our upwind climb as Tower called for Aircraft Y to follow traffic ahead to the right (us). They responded that they had us in sight as they continued climbing and closing in on our left hand side. This is the approximate time that [we] was overtaken by Aircraft Y at approximately 800 feet MSL. Aircraft Y passed by us at roughly 200 feet off of our left wing; while both of us were still climbing to pattern altitude in the upwind leg.
Report_1_Synopsis: Instructor Pilot reported an NMAC on takeoff from ORL airport.

Report_1_Narrative: I was approaching F70 from the southeast after a personal flight while making radio calls every few miles as I noticed on my ADS-B in several targets circling around the airport due to intense student activity.Someone made a radio call a few minutes before I was in the vicinity of another aircraft cutting them off on downwind too and I prepared myself for heavy traffic in the pattern and trying to find an opening so I could join the downwind.Upon entering the 45 for downwind I noticed visually an aircraft on the upwind taking off and repeatedly asked his intentions and if he could see me.There was no answer and seeing him proceed on runway heading I continued on the 45 for downwind being confident he wouldn't start a turn to crosswind until he reached close to pattern altitude as is recommended for the noise abatement procedure out of F70 for departures from Runway 18.Then I saw him maneuver for the crosswind maybe 500 feet below my altitude which was at pattern and make a radio call in that regards. At this point I had contacted him several times regarding his intentions and whether he could see me but without any answer.Seeing him turn and put me on the direct collision course with me although 300 ft. below me I decided to execute a 360 degree turn saw him coming extremely near me. Finally he acknowledged my presence in a subsequent radio call.I continued the full turn and reentered downwind.F70 was extremely busy that day with several schools on the field and at one point I saw no less than 5 aircraft in the traffic pattern. Needless to say a Tower is badly needed in that field for the safety of flight as the indiscriminate addition of several aircraft from several schools without any sort of coordination between those schools makes this urgently needed.A bit of courtesy goes a long way too and someone was nice enough to extend their downwind for me earlier in the day so I could depart as I had to hold short of the active runway at least 10 minutes as one aircraft after another was landing with no end in sight.On my side I should have waited outside the pattern on a hold in a safe area until there was no aircraft on upwind and the downwind leg would be fully opened; with adequate radio communications ensuring everyone in the pattern has knowledge of any other traffic with acknowledgement for all.This was my first experience with this field with that many aircraft in the pattern and the lesson learned here is to stay outside an uncontrolled field until there is fewer than a set limit of aircraft that one can set as personal limit.Such a personal limit is not taught at all as part of any training curriculum nor in the AIM in my knowledge.Most uncontrolled field are uncontrolled because of very low traffic but some reach levels just below the threshold needed for a tower and F70 seems to be in that category.Also the schools on the field could coordinate some kind of schedule among themselves so not everyone is up in the air at the same time. Poisson's law dictates things happen in bursts unless there is coordination to avert it.
Report_1_Synopsis: GA pilot reported an NMAC in the pattern at F70 airport.

Person_1_Function: Single Pilot; Flight Engineer / Second Officer
Report_1_Narrative: We were flying east at 3;500 VFR and Aircraft X was 3;500 Westbound. We noticed the Aircraft X at very close range and made a turn to the right to avoid the aircraft. We had ADS-B and did not see the traffic and believe there is no coverage in this area. No ATC services were requested at the time.
Report_1_Synopsis: A VFR Pilot reported they performed evasive maneuvers to avoid an opposite direction VFR aircraft flying at a wrong altitude for their direction of flight. The aircraft did not appear on their ADS-B.

Report_1_Narrative: Post flight the aircraft was parked at the unmanned self-service fuel station to be refueled before returning it to the hanger. After the aircraft was refueled the parking brake was checked; the throttle was set; and the aircraft was hand prop started; this aircraft has no electrical system. The throttle setting was too high; over powered the brakes; and the aircraft began to roll quickly. An attempt was made to redirect the aircraft away from the building (FBO) and in doing so was looped back at the fuel station where it struck steel/concrete poles; and the fuel pay kiosk. The prop and engine directly struck one pole while the leading edge of the right wing tip stuck the other.I believe human factors were the cause. An additional check of the throttle setting; additional wheel chocking; or anchor the tail wheel would have likely prevented this.There were no injuries; also there were no passengers or crew aboard.
Report_1_Synopsis: Pilot reported aircraft began moving during a hand prop start and struck object before regaining control.

Report_1_Narrative: I have been working for a Part XXX operator this year.  At the beginning of the season; when I was hired; I noted aggressive corrosion in multiple areas of the aircraft.  I also noted that some components were missing documentation from the logbooks; and other components were 'time expired.'When I made mention of these items to the certificate holder; I was told that the aircraft is 'public use' and that the airworthiness requirements do not apply.I was also told that if I don't like the way they operate; I can find a different job.  Well; I left a good job to come to this operation and it is too difficult to find decent jobs with the COVID employment downturn in general aviation; so I was stuck.I still refused to sign off an annual inspection so the operator had a different Inspector Authority (IA) sign it off.  The other IA never inspected the aircraft...just signed the logbooks.The aircraft operated all season in this condition.Now that the season is over; I was again told to do an annual inspection; so that it is ready for next season.  Instead; I turned in my notice.  I don't feel the aircraft is necessarily a danger to the public; however I also don't feel the aircraft is necessarily 'legal.'Maybe all this is acceptable in the Part XXX world.
Report_1_Synopsis: Maintenance Inspector reported concerns with company signing off of annual inspections of aircraft with several known maintenance issues and discrepancies.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Communication Breakdown; Distraction; Training / Qualification; Confusion
Report_1_Narrative: I was working everything in the Tower combined. Aircraft Y checked in on a GPS Runway XX approach and I cleared him for the option. A few minutes later Aircraft X called for taxi and I gave him the normal taxi instructions with a crossing at Runway XX; forgetting that I had cleared an aircraft for that runway. While I was making an amendment to a flight plan I hear Aircraft Y ask why there is an aircraft on his runway. He had come to a complete stop on the runway while Aircraft X was crossing. I told him to hold position and once it was clear I cleared him for takeoff from present position. We're reduced staffing due to COVID-19; and having to train forces us to combine positions to accomplish the numbers that management is pushing for.
Report_1_Synopsis: Tower Controller reported a ground conflict and cited reduced staffing due to COVID-19 and training at combined positions as contributing factors.

Report_1_Narrative: I departed Aircraft X for takeoff. Once approved separation was anticipated I cleared Aircraft Y for takeoff. Once airborne I noticed the departures in a closer proximity than anticipated but I was providing visual separation. I verified that I had appropriate separation on the radar display. In my judgment speed and spacing was adequate and I switched both aircraft [to] departure. Not long after I was called by the Departure Controller that they needed more space between departures because I had less than three miles between Aircraft X and Aircraft Y. This is not typical of my best practices to ensure separation. A possible factor could be aircraft performance. I wasn't anticipating the trailing aircraft to be so much faster or the lead aircraft to under perform like it did. Both aircraft were similar types. Another factor could be that I had been medically decertified due to a COVID-19 exposure at the facility. I was not sick but I was only notified the day before this incident that my medical had been reinstated and that I was to report to work the next day. [It] was quite a surprise to me and didn't give me any time to mentally prepare to conduct air traffic duties after [several] weeks away from work.The only recommendation would be a more advanced notification of a return to air traffic duties after a long time off. It allows controllers to be more mentally prepared to preform safety related duties.
Report_1_Synopsis: Tower Controller reported a loss of separation between two departures and cited aircraft performance differences as a possible contributing factor.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Time Pressure; Communication Breakdown; Workload; Confusion
Report_1_Narrative: This aircraft called asking for lower; they were no longer on my scope; I did not know who was calling.  The sector was completely out of control; we had a tracker; and D side.  The level of traffic at the same time was unheard of; uncalled for and completely irresponsible. There was no in trail spacing for ZZZ1 and ZZZ2 arrivals; the departures out of ZZZ2; ZZZ3; And ZZZ1 were not stopped.   The sector was not split.   I do not belief we had the staffing to split the sector.   Supervisors did not do enough to slow the sector down; TMU did not do enough to slow the sector down. This is one of the worst situations I have been put in in my XX years as a controller.  People should be held responsible for the out of control sector.  This event should not have happened.  This event was damaging to my health.  I think something like this should never be allowed to happened again;  and there should be an investigation into how so many airplanes can be allowed in a sector that was already overloaded with traffic.  I often asked for a couple minutes to stop the traffic and let me catch up.  I several times asked for help from the D side and the Tracker neither one seemed to have any idea what was happening. There should be national flow initiatives to slow the traffic down to these saturated airports.  Planes should have to wait safely on the ground.  This can not be that hard to figure out.  They can safely flow planes to all the ZZZ4 airports; they sure as hell can figure out how to do it to South ZZZ5 airports.  Staffing needs to be returned to normal ASAP.  TMU needs to get their act together.  If the chief of the facility gets this; he does not need to look any further then this session to see that TMU is broken in this building.
Report_2_Narrative: I was flying Aircraft X; at this time. During our arrival into ZZZ6 we were on the ZZZZZ STAR talking to ZZZ Center. The controller was very busy and I would say over loaded. He instructed us to descend to 10;000 ft. so we did as we were approaching the inner 10 mile ring on the TFR we radioed many times asking for lower and waiting to be handed off to ZZZ7 Approach. When he finally handed us off we apparently entered the 10 mile ring just as ZZZ7 approach replied to us. We were instructed to turn right I believe to a 250 heading and descend to 8;000 ft. As I started the turn I got a RA and was told I was being followed by the Aircraft Y. I was then asked to descend to 5;000 ft. and he radioed the fighter that he now had radio contact with me and was released. He continued to vector us to land at ZZZ6 and told me to call Phone Number. When I parked the aircraft I called and told him what had happened. I then had a interview with the government agency and told them what had happened. We were in and out of the clouds on the arrival and with as busy as the controller was he never gave us the hand off until it was to late. Knowing we were close to the TFR and the airspace and controller was saturated we could not make any abrupt turns to avoid the situation and could not get the controller to answer us in time to get properly vectored around.
Report_1_Synopsis: Captain reported due to ATC workload and failed communications; Captain entered TFR.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Human-Machine Interface; Situational Awareness; Confusion; Distraction
Report_1_Narrative: Aircraft X was on the RNAV Z approach for Runway 22L. The aircraft had been cleared to land. The approach naturally brings aircraft in on a slight angle to the runway. Aircraft X appeared to be coming in at an angle on short final; but aligned with the runway prior to crossing the threshold. However; an ASDE alert triggered with Taxiway Y; which is parallel to Runway 22L. I instructed the aircraft to go-around. The aircraft went around and later landed without incident.This approach is likely to be problematic in the future because the angle it brings in aircraft on lines up with Taxiway Y until the last minute. It might be best this approach not be used if it can be avoided.
Report_1_Synopsis: MDW Tower Controller reported an unsafe situation when an aircraft lined up with a taxiway instead of the runway.  Controller reported this approach is likely to be problematic because the angle it brings in aircraft on; lines up with Taxiway Y; until the last minute.

Report_1_Narrative: Initially coming in on the IAH LINKK1 Arrival expecting 27 but then just before descent; we were switched to NNCEE arrival expecting 8R (parking north side). Once with 2nd approach controller we were given change to RNAV 9. We asked if they could please work out 8R; a few minutes later cleared RNAV 9. Started setting it up; reprogrammed the box and reconfigured the aircraft. We then received 'maintain 200 until advised; level 6;000MSL at HOWLN'. Came out of box to open MCP speed window for 200 (FMC VNAV speed would be 210 per the arrival). Looked back down and saw us going through TEXXN where the ARC was supposed to commence.I immediately clicked off autopilot and started 30 degree turn to get back on ARC. Halfway through the turn (past HHOOG) received call from ATC stating he saw that we went past TEXXN and to turn left to 300 but we were already 45 off from runway (base). ATC asked if we had runway in sight; we confirmed and were then cleared visual Runway 9. Visual approach was executed and landing was normal. We programmed FMS to perform RNAV 9 from HOWLN but don't think it closed the loop automatically like it does on LINKK1 to 27 approach and that's why the aircraft continued past ARC point.
Report_1_Synopsis: Captain reported  to complete FMS setup for the last of three approach clearances from ATC.

Report_1_Narrative: Initial setup and brief was LINKK arrival; with visual ILS 27. Weather was clear; with excellent visibility. At TOD IAH changed to East flow; and we were given the NNCEE arrival. Approach control said expect RNP Y 9. We requested 8R since our parking gate was on the north side. Were told 'standby; we'll see'. Frequency change; and no reference to 8R request. Then cleared RNAVP Y 9 via HOWLN; maintain 200 knots. I observed Pilot Flying choose RNAV Y 9; with HOWLN transition. Other radio calls and congestion and nonstandard speed change prevented from looking into the LEGS page to see it tie into the HOWLN we were proceeding toward. Immediately after TEXXN we realized it did not turn and turned the aircraft with heading select.Approach queried about being outside the turn as our actual heading turned through approximately 330. Approach control said maintain current heading'. I immediately asked what heading do you want; we are currently in the turn. First response was 260 heading. We initiated a turn reversal; then approach said; I see you are in the turn; turn right 060; descend 3000; cleared the visual runway 9. I acknowledged. Soon thereafter were given 'maintain 6000; turn heading 100.' Responded with climbing back to 6000. Controller asked if we were still visual with 9. (It was perfectly clear; with unusual 30+ mile visibility). Responded yes; still visual. Re-cleared the visual runway 9. Flew the visual to an uneventful landing."
Report_1_Synopsis: First Officer reported failure to complete FMS setup following three approach clearance changes.

Report_1_Narrative: Landed Runway 35R and was instructed by DFW tower to taxi Q - Z hold short of Runway 35C. Approaching Runway 35C DFW Tower instructed us to cross 35C at Z landing traffic will land and hold short. As we began to proceed across Runway 35C; after crossing the hold short line; the Runway Entry Lights (REL's) illuminated red. Landing traffic was still airborne on approach to Runway 35C. Since we were already moving; I determined it would be safer to continue across the runway and exit rather than stop in the runway environment. Notified Tower Controller once clear of the Runway that the REL's illuminated as we crossed Runway 35C. The Controller apologized and stated that was not supposed to happen since they were in Land and Hold short (LAHSO) operations.Possible ground equipment failure or programming error.Not certain. Perhaps a question for DFW Tower.
Report_2_Narrative: Landed Runway 35R and was instructed by DFW Tower to 'taxi Q-Z; hold short of 35C.' Approaching 35C tower instructed us to cross 35C at Z; landing traffic will land and hold short. As we began to cross 35C; the runway entry lights illuminated red. Landing traffic was still airborne on approach and we were already across the hold short line; so we decided it was safest to continue and exit the runway. The Captain notified the Controller that the REL's had illuminated; and the controller apologized and said that shouldn't have happened.Possible equipment malfunction. I don't have any suggestions other than checking the operation of the equipment.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported the REL [Runway Entry Lights] activated as they started to taxi across Runway 35 center following ATC's instructions.

Report_1_Narrative: We were conducting Aircraft X at night into ABE; vectored from the north; and then given a clearance for a Visual Approach. As always; we had an approach set up; ILS 24; and while descending from the north side of the airport from 3;000 feet; the vectored altitude; to 2;400 feet; at an altitude of about 2;650 feet we received a one time (only 1) 'Terrain' warning from the TAWS (Terrain Alert Warning System); while descending very gently at about 300 feet per minute. We leveled off for a moment; there was no other terrain warning and never a 'Terrain; Pull Up' command; then as we intercepted the final; we continued to the 2;400 feet glideslope intercept altitude. There was a ridgeline north of the ILS course; which we had briefed on; but it did not show an altitude greater than 1;000 feet; so we did not think it would be a problem to start a shallow descent from 3;000 to 2;400 feet; especially at a shallow rate. This is a potential problem at night; as there are no obstacle lights on the ridge line; so I believe Approach should simply provide vectors to the ILS approach instead of just giving a 'visual.'  A little more work for ATC but a safer way of operating. Caused by ATC clearing crew to do a night visual instead of providing vectors; knowing that there are unmarked; unlit; terrain ridge lines to the north of the airport. Also caused by crew not requesting full vectors to the ILS at night. Most ATC facilities in small airports don't want to work that hard. Suggest that crews start asking ATC at small airports to provide vectors to the Approach being used to back up the Visual when in night VMC conditions; as a means to improve the level of safety; even if it means that ATC might have to work a bit more.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain descending on a Visual Approach to ABE reported they received a Terrain Alert.

Report_1_Narrative: We were descending on the JANNY5 Arrival.  At the KOPLE waypoint; we were given 'Direct JANNY at 8;000' by ATC.  We began our descent with Joshua Approach.  Around the JANNY waypoint; we were transferred to SoCal Approach for terminal instructions to Burbank airport. The controller initially gave us a 'descend 7;000' instruction which was followed shortly thereafter with a 'descend 5;000' this descent was well prior to the usual instructions given to Aircraft X from this location.  The crew complied with all instructions from ATC.  We were receiving vectors to intercept the ILS-Z Runway 8 Approach into Burbank.  We became aware that the controller was vectoring us to intercept the localizer between the SILEX and BUDDE intersection.  While approaching from the north at 5;000 ft MSL; we were heading over one of the small mountains northwest of Burbank Airport.  We were vectored near the highest point on that hill which is charted at 3;734 ft.  While going over the hill the aircraft gave us a 'TERRAIN; TERRAIN; PULL UP.' I looked at the RA as the first 'TERRAIN' was enunciated; and saw the RA indicator show around 1;500 feet; then jumped immediately to 2;500 feet.  The warning was only given once by the aircraft.  The PF (Pilot Flying); Captain; reported not seeing any altitude indication on the RA.  We continued the approach and the remainder of the flight was uneventful.  We aren't sure whether it was an erroneous aircraft indication or if ATC may have descended us a little too low for that sector. Clarify with ATC on altitude assigned and whether assigned altitude is appropriate for sector.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported a GPWS alarm while flying into the Burbank airport.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Troubleshooting; Workload; Situational Awareness; Distraction; Communication Breakdown
Report_1_Narrative: The flight departed the from Gate X in ZZZ1 at XA:10z and proceed to flight level 200 to ZZZZZ intersection to join the arrival into ZZZ without incidence. At approximately XB:10Z while descending through 8;000 MSL for 7;000 MSL in IMC conditions with heavy rain and continuous light and occasionally moderate turbulence we received a single chime and an ELT ON Master Caution message was displayed on the EICAS primary page. Approximately one to two seconds later a very loud ELT signal began sounding through the flight deck intercom system. I notified ATC that we had an indication that our ELT had activated and that it was in error and could be disregarded. I further advised them that the ELT tone was sounding on the flight deck and it was making radio communication and flight deck communication very difficult. I turned the number two comm radio off of the guard frequency and reduced the volume; but it did not have any effect on the volume of the ELT. The First Officer (FO) began to attempt to find a resolution [in] the QRH and we attempted QRH procedure several times to try to silence the tone without success. The noise was deafening and flight deck communication and air to ground communication was very difficult.  At 4;000 MSL we were given a heading of 360 degrees then descended to 3;000 MSL and turned to a heading of 085 degrees and instructed to join the localizer for Runway X. At this time both aircraft localizers failed; and a red LOC indication was displayed on both PFD's.  We advised ATC and asked if there was a problem with the localizer.  ATC queried several other aircraft and all advised they were receiving the localizer.  We broke off of the approach per ATC instruction and attempted to set up for the ILS to Runway YL but could not receive any ILS signal.  I advised ATC that we would need a GPS approach and we were instructed to prepare for the GPS YL.  After having set up the GPS YL ATC advised that the wind had shifted and were now from 275 degrees gusting to 25 kts. We were further advised that the airport was now in a west flow.  We requested RNAV YY and began preparing that approach. We received radar vectors to RNAV GPS YY and completed the approach without incidence.Due to extreme flight deck noise from the ELT throughout the event communication on the flight deck and with ATC was very difficult. The noise and inability to communicate throughout added a high level of stress and complexity.  Continuous turbulence and instrument meteorological conditions were present throughout; with ceilings and visibility at or near minimums on arrival at the runway.  The double failure event coupled with the inability to sync the two MFD's due to a previously existing MEL added complexity and were additional threats. To mitigate these factors myself and my FO followed SOP to the extent that we were able. We resisted the urge to rush and after preparing the RNAV approach we briefed the approach; and the runway change items in an attempt to slow down the process and bring the flight back into the normal envelope as much as possible. In hindsight I wish that I would have tried the EMER function on the RCP (Remote Compensation Panel). I don't know if it would have helped but the noise made concentration and communication very difficult and it was very fatiguing. Overall I was satisfied with my actions and those of my FO given the circumstances and without the benefit of hindsight I thought that we met or exceeded expectations.
Report_1_Synopsis: CRJ-900 Captain reported a turbulent flight; with an airport configuration change and an ELT alarm that was making it very difficult to hear ATC.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Troubleshooting; Workload; Communication Breakdown; Confusion; Situational Awareness
Report_1_Narrative: On the Visual [Runway] XXR approach into ZZZ. Cleared for the approach about 5 miles out; and given a heading 090 to join the localizer. We joined the localizer and got a TA and noticed another RJ (Regional Jet) headed around 150 degrees to join the localizer for [Runway] XXL; which wasn't going to be a factor. We were never left of the [Runway] XXR localizer at any point. We caught the glide slope and headed down while configuring. At this point we received a RA that the [Runway] XXL RJ had blown through the localizer and was right over the top of us; about 300 feet of vertical separation. Captain was flying; he disconnected the AP (Autopilot) and flew the breakout procedure. I told ZZZ Tower we had a RA and he was swamped today so he initially wanted us to go around; to which I said we had flown the breakout and were established on the approach - going around and flying his instructions would've led to a second RA since we were instructed to climb right into that jet that just flew over the top of us. Tower changed his mind and gave us [Runway] XXR landing clearance. ZZZ ATC workload was extremely high and the [Runway] XXL RJ didn't intercept the localizer at all; nor were they aware of the traffic around them (us).High ATC workload and neighboring jet on the other approach had low SA (Situational Awareness).ZZZ workload review and talk to the crew who blew through the [Runway] XXL localizer and crossed into us.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported flying the breakout procedure in response to an RA triggered by an aircraft on approach on the parallel runway that had overshot the localizer and was directly overhead.

Report_1_Narrative: I operated Aircraft X. When I had shown up to the aircraft the FO (First Officer) was already at the aircraft. The FO had the aircraft powered up and had started the preflight duties. During the before start checklist it was acknowledged that the preflight was completed. The FO did not indicate that anything appeared abnormal during the preflight. Before the pushback the ground personnel said all secure below; FOD walk complete; steering disengaged; standing by for parking brake. The ground personnel did not report any panels that were open. Some point above sterile we heard a thump noise. We then called the flight attendant to ask if everyone was okay. The flight attendant indicated everything was fine. We checked the EICAS and all the engine instruments were in the green. We then checked the MFD pages and everything was normal. We preceded onto the destination as there was nothing to indicate any abnormality. We have no way of knowing if this was related to the latches underneath the engine coming open. When we had arrived to the gate the ground personnel had told us that there was two latches underneath the engine hanging down. The two doors open underneath Engine Number 1 was the engine oil service door and the air turbine starter access panel. Me and the FO proceeded outside during the walk around to look at the access panels underneath the engine and relayed the information to Maintenance. The access panels had also caused holes in the engine cowling.The cause was the access panels underneath Engine Number 1 came open during the flight. During the preflight during before departure nothing was noticed abnormal.A thorough preflight was done before the flight. Nothing out of the abnormal was indicated by the FO or the ground crew. A thorough preflight was accomplished and should before every flight. No other suggestions at this time.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported that the access panels underneath one of the engines came open during the flight. Postflight inspection revealed that the open panels had made holes in the engine cowling.

Report_1_Narrative: Assigned DRLLR 5 arrival into IAH. We were planning 26R RNAV Y. We were cleared to descend via the DRLLR 5. 6000 was set in altitude window and aircraft was in LNAV/VNAV. Runway was not assigned so approaching SKLER; Captain queried ATC. ATC advised ILS 26R. Crew discussed ensuring proceeding straight after SKLER. Captain as Pilot Monitoring began to change the approach in the FMC; in the process the aircraft leveled off at 7000; rather continuing the decent to 6000. We recognize this a couple miles from SKLER but before we were able to notify ATC that we might be high at SKLER; ATC assigned us a descent to 5000. We proceeded to descend to the new altitude and land uneventfully.
Report_1_Synopsis: First Officer reported leveling off high while they attempted to reprogram the FMC following a late runway assignment on the DRLLR FIVE STAR into IAH.

Report_1_Narrative: 45 minutes into the flight we received a Dispatch message that Passenger X in seat X5 has tested positive for COVID. Passenger X was traveling with 3 others which all were in row X. I contacted medlink and was disconnected. I asked my entire crew if they had any experience with this which none of them had and I hadn't either. I asked Dispatch for the name of the passenger and protocol to follow. I retried medlink and followed their instructions to minimize contact with Passenger X and get row X off before all others. We asked for priority handling. Dispatch informed us the station will meet us at the gate. Before getting to the gate we asked all passengers to stay seated with seat belts on at gate arrival for a medical situation. I opened the cockpit door to make sure everyone was complying and only Passenger Y wasn't. I said 'Please everyone stay seated' and he sat back down. Later he made a rude comment deplaning and complained to Customer Service. We deplaned row X only and met them and Customer Service in the jet way to assess Passenger X. Passenger X was a young woman that had COVID a few months ago and was 100% healthy. Customer Service followed them to baggage claim for another test. Customer Service cleared us to deplane so I made a PA explaining the situation. Customer Service informed me many people that have had COVID in the past test a false positive.
Report_2_Narrative: Received Dispatch message indicating passenger in [seat] X5 received an airport COVID test that came back positive. We were located about 1 hour from ZZZ.  Continued towards ZZZ; declared a medical issue on board indicating positive COVID passenger. ATC turned us into a priority handling.  Coordination through medlink provided some guidance and we were met at the gate by appropriate personnel to evaluate the passenger.  Passengers were informed of the medical issue and told of the possible positive test at the gate. ZZZ supervisors cleared us to continue our trip.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported a passenger who had tested positive for COVID-19 was on the flight.

Report_1_Narrative: We started out vectored off our arrival by ZZZ Center to the southwest with several step down altitudes.  30 miles from the airport we found ourselves at 20;000 MSL which is about 10;000 feet higher than usual for a normal descent.  ATC; specifically ZZZ Center; was overloaded with aircraft going into south State X.  The Controller brought us around and eventually around 10;000 MSL he told us to go direct to the ZZZ airport.  At that time; we were about 15-18 miles away at just under 10;000 MSL.  A few minutes later the Controller asked if we had the field in sight to which we replied that we did; but we needed a vector because we were too high to safely attempt the visual approach.  We were given a left 360 degree turn and cleared down to 3;000 MSL also while given direct to the ZZZ airport.  Upon leveling off at 3;000 MSL we were in a cloud layer and couldn't see the field.  We requested lower and were given 1;500 MSL.  Once we reach that altitude; we could see the field and was cleared the visual approach to Runway X and to switch to Tower.On final; after fully configuring the aircraft; Tower told us to turn right to a heading of 180.  Very confused; we asked him to repeat the instructions at which point we executed a missed approach for a disabled aircraft on the runway.  Tower never actually told us to go-around.  We were given heading 180 and a climb to 4;000 MSL.  Following the level off we were instructed to hold present position however the aircraft will not hold present position on HDG mode.  It can only PPOS HOLD while on and active FMS leg with less than .25 NM cross track.  Knowing this; we told the Controller we needed a fix to hold and we were given the ZZZ2 NDB which doesn't exist in the database.  We instead requested the missed approach fix for the RNAV X approach.We weren't sure or told how long the runway was going to be shut down so the crew started to discuss diverting options which ZZZ1 was the only real viable option.  The FMS indicated it would take about 3;500 lbs of fuel and we had about 2;300lbs of reserve fuel on board.  From my quick calculation; I had to make a decision fairly soon considering the following:  we had about 5;700lbs on fuel on board; unknown runway closure; time; FMS calculation of 3;500 lbs of fuel required to ZZZ1; high volume of ZZZ Center traffic and high controller work load.  I sent a message to Dispatch informing them we would attempt one more approach and if unable to make it in we would divert to ZZZ1.We notified ZZZ Center Controller we needed to attempt another approach or we would soon have need to divert.  We were given vectors around and cleared for the visual to Runway X once again.  As the pilot flying; I opted to proceed direct to the FAF of the RNAV X and continue the visual approach.  At about the base leg portion I turned off the autopilot and turned towards the runway.  I believe that a slight turn inside of the FAF did not sequence the approach nor the glide path information which led to a position above the glide path.  I flew down to correct the glide path all while in and out of 1;000 FPM VVI.  I acknowledged the momentary deviations of descent and quickly corrected as I was now on the visual indications from the PAPI's.  On short final; a thermal briefly interrupted our descent and with a quick correction back to glide path I corrected the path for a safe landing.I believe the accumulation of all factors above could have led to a critically low fuel situation much quicker than expected.  I believe the saturation of airspace on a very busy travel day could have been underestimated in the current climate of understaffed controllers.  ZZZ Center controllers were so saturated with aircraft that any chance to hand an aircraft off to a visual approach whether it was really safe to do so or not was attempted.  Unsure about divert fuel and runway state created a high-importance; high stress moment of deciding when a divert should occur without having proper data supporting it.  Lastly; in a heightened sense of urgency with a tight turn inbound to the runway and sub-sequence 'Cutting the corner' led to the aircraft being in a position higher than the glide path.I would suggest the following for operations into ZZZ Captain only approach and landing.  I believe most captains take it upon themselves to make the approach and landing due to the short runway as it is.  There should be more 'hip pocket' information whether in the form of a bulletin or some other format that provides rough numbers of divert options; fuel required; routing; etc when a formal alternate is not filed.  I also suggest fuel planning take into account busy travel days and add as much fuel as practical for contingencies even on days with VMC conditions that does not preclude landing due to being over max landing weight.  I also believe during all forms of training (initial; recurrent; etc) special authorization airports and airports such as ZZZ are discussed. It is my suggestion that ZZZ be a mandatory training event.  I can tell you everything you need to know about flying to ZZZ2 yet we don't actually go there in the aircraft.  However; airports such as ZZZ are rarely mentioned when we fly there every week.  I suggest more 'hangar flying' where scenarios are discussed (such as this one) in a classroom/training environment to get captains to start thinking about scenarios such as these.  I'd also like to recommend that one or two approaches from ZZZ3 be included in our Jeppesen charts or company pages.  Should ZZZ be shut down for any reason and there is not enough divert fuel to safely make it back to the mainland there will be a 10;000 foot runway available; especially in IMC conditions.  Lastly; I suggest that pilots refrain from attempting to cut corners while approaching the runway from greater than 90 degrees.  Instead; they should fly the published approach in its entirety including glide slopes or glide paths so that they maintain a safe; stable approach to the runway.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported a disabled aircraft on intended landing runway resulted in their flight being vectored away from their approach path.  The additional vectoring caused them to be concerned with their fuel state and made a request to be cleared as soon as possible.  The crew was cleared for another approach and landing and reported being unstable/high before safely landing the aircraft.

Report_1_Narrative: We were flying a parcel of contaminated blood. The box had the UN1845 on it as well as the Dangerous Goods Form. I thought about it and felt it was correct. Later that evening after signing off duty and the next day I was thinking that the parcel should have also had a UN3373 as well as a category B bio substance label. I only saw the Dangerous Goods Form and parcel that was labeled UN1845.I saw the parcel and inspected it and it's associated paperwork during preflight.Possible incomplete labeling of HAZMAT.At the time I looked the information up in the Dangerous Goods manual as well as online and determined in the short time we had that it only needed the UN1845 and nothing else. The more I thought about it however; I feel that it may should have had the UN3373 and cat B bio labels as well.[More correct procedure];verify with the manuals and if still not sure; discuss it with Dispatch or the Chief Pilot.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier First Officer reported the transport of Hazmat cargo with incomplete required Hazmat labeling.

Report_1_Narrative: Reflecting back on this flight today; I fear we may not have obtained verbal landing clearance from Tower before touchdown on Runway X at ZZZ. This was my first flight in over two months; and was assigned with another Captain as my First Officer; with no one else present on the flight deck. I had also been on leave earlier in the year. Before we flew; I briefed that two captains flying together as a two-pilot crew complement is a threat; as it does not happen often; and there is an operational bias for the acting First Officer (co-Captain). During the descent; Air Traffic Control vectored us to a close-in base leg to Runway X. Approach Control asked us if we had the field in sight; and I elected to continue with a visual approach; which I believe now was not the best choice for myself. My acting First Officer momentarily lost sight of the field during my turn from base to final; however I had it acquired visually the entire time. I pointed out the field to assist; and the pilot monitoring re-acquired it. This should have resulted in a go-around to rejoin the approach; as this is a team environment; and a two-pilot airplane. I know I did switch the nose-wheel landing light to 'on' during the final approach leg; as that is SOP after being cleared to land; according to FOM. I was focused on flying the plane; slowing down early; and ensuring a stabilized approach.  I was not completely in tune with what my co-captain was or was not doing. Stabilized approaches are a topic often discussed in training; so it weighed heavily in my priorities on this day. My co-Captain (pilot monitoring) may not have switched to Tower as it was somewhat a high workload environment and unusual operation; at least to me.I should have recognized the threat of two captains flying together; along with my low state of landing currency; would lead to a chain reaction easily. I should have requested the full ILS to Runway X; or at least a longer final approach leg. I would recommend after a Captain returns to the line after a lengthy vacation; and in my case leave earlier in the year as well; to not pair up with another Captain; but only a highly current First Officer. Although everything was completely my responsibility; this would have eliminated the threat. I recognize that sound aeronautical decision making as it relates to all phases of duty; is the number one factor influencing safety; and it must be practiced even in high-workload environments.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Captain reported landing without a clearance and attributes the event to lack of flying and complacency while flying with another Captain as the First Officer in this flight.

Report_1_Narrative: While preparing the aircraft for departure from ZZZZ to ZZZ I made contact with our Dispatcher to address a minor deferred maintenance item. While I was on the phone I learned we were getting new paperwork due to the ZZZ1 ATC Center shutting down for sterilization. The Dispatcher was still working on the details due to severe weather to the east of ZZZ1 and indicated that it would be sent to me and the normal station location when it was finished.The Load Master came in wanting me to complete the weight and balance so he could leave. I notified him that we needed new flight release paperwork and told him it should be sitting on his printer and to look for revision 1 at the top of the front page.The Load Master came in again later and indicated that he wanted to do the weight and balance paperwork. I told him I wanted to wait till I had the new paperwork in hand and reviewed. Eventually the paperwork showed up and once we reviewed and did a few more items to finalize the preparation I turned around to notify the Load Master that I was ready for the cross check. The person said that they were not doing the cross check at that station due to COVID-19. I was surprised by his answer and said something like 'REALLY?' And he repeated his original statement. I told him I had not been notified of this situation and he said it was to reduce exposure on the flight deck.I gave him the paperwork that was completed but did not have the check marks related to the normal cross check process with the Load Master. In hindsight; I am skeptical about the answer I received and decided I should make this report to make sure that this situation is truly their process. If it turns out to be accurate we should possibly notify any crews that will be going into ZZZZ.This flight was already scheduled later than normal due to crew rest requirements and due to the delay in receiving the hard copy of the amended flight release it was running approximately 10 minutes later than the newly scheduled time. It was obvious that they were under pressure to get us moving and I was attempting to keep things standard and attempt to not introduce the opportunity to have errors.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported a weight and balance change was not cross-checked due to COVID-19 company guidelines as cited by the Load Master.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Communication Breakdown; Confusion; Distraction; Situational Awareness
Report_1_Narrative: As I am greeting passengers and handing out wipes; Passenger X seated in X; boards the aircraft with mask barely covering his nose or mouth; him and his family. I gently as them to please cover nose and mouth to board; they comply. Keep in mind even kids barely have mask. They all boarded with mask on chin. When they get to their seats they still have it on. Now after pilots inform us that we are departing; Passenger X completely takes off his mask; passengers around him are looking uncomfortably anxious and he is looking to see if I am can see him.  Although the lights are dim in the cabin I can still see him and he sees me. I do a friendly gesture so he can put it on. He completely ignores me. Then when I get the 10;000 I get up to kindly ask him to place mask over nose and mouth; he complies and then as I walk away he takes it off. I let him know one more time announcements say. He doesn't comply and wife [has] her mask off too; to tell me why don't I leave him alone. At this point I head towards forward to inform pilots and they let me know to let him know one last time. When I informed him I spoke to the pilots and then finally after three gentle reminder; he and wife and kids comply.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Attendant reported a passenger was not compliant with face mask policy.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Situational Awareness; Training / Qualification; Communication Breakdown; Confusion; Distraction
Report_1_Narrative: During boarding; the gentleman in [seat] XX1 got my attention to ask if he was in the right seat; so I looked and tapped on each person in the row to confirm for him. That is how I noticed the X Family was a party of 4. The mother was holding the child and I asked if the child was a seat or a lap as I didn't have her as a lap child in my list; but in her own seat. She said she has her own seat. And I asked if she was over 2 years. The mother said yes. I asked if they had a mask for the child reminding them of our policy and also reiterated that the child would need to be in her own seat for takeoff (FAR); landing and whenever the seat belt sign was on. The father stated that she's only two. I said yes; she's over two that's why she's required to have and be in her own seat. The father also said they were traveling internationally. (I believed they were traveling internationally when we got to ZZZ; but later in this situation the Supervisor who spoke to the family ascertained that they had come in from ZZZZ on Aircraft Y; where apparently the situation was not addressed on that flight).I offered to bring a mask and did. I informed the Purser and cockpit that there was both issues. While I was closing bins I walked past the family and they had made no attempt to rectify the situation. I also had to remind the father twice to fix his own mask. When there was no attempt to address the non masked child by the family I chat text for a Supervisor to address the situation since the door was open. The first Supervisor went to the seat and was there for a few seconds; I was concerned that it didn't appear the situation was addressed by the reaction of the family. The child still didn't have a mask on and no motion to attempt. I approached the Supervisor and asked him about it. He said he told the family. I informed him that I walked by their row and the child wasn't wearing a mask nor was there any attempt to get the child to wear one. The purser also spoke to the family.Another Supervisor came; and spoke to the family. I stayed at the front of the cabin to let them deal with the situation. Supervisor 2; Inflight supervisor came as we were now taking a delay.Supervisor 2 said that they could make an exception to the mask policy.I; as an employee who is required to be masked with verbalized and written termination warning from my company if I do not remained masked at work; is now telling me that exceptions can be made onboard the aircraft for passengers. I have never heard of this and am not aware of documentation of this.The passenger knows the child isn't allowed to be a lap child and they know that anyone over two is required to be masked.While I realize it's difficult for a young child I also acknowledge that Airline chose to pick this age for mask requirement likely to coincide with the FAA mandated age seat requirement. There is ample notification for these policies (during booking and check in); passengers personal responsibility is a choice. As is proactive parenting. After more than two decades of flying there are quite frankly cultural differences/ beliefs of non-compliance and this presents itself as complete lack of acknowledgment of our policies (or FAR's). I completely acknowledge that the flying public is a challenge at times; most follow the rules. This includes me; especially at work. While I'm completely capable of sympathy; compassion and compromise... I'm absolutely not when it comes to safety.I applaud Airline for enforcing the mask policy. I would encourage them to strive for consistency on a multitude of other safety issues that appear at times to go by the wayside in favor of on time departures and convenience. It is this mentality that creates inconsistencies and quite frankly makes my job harder to do.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Attendant reported issues with a family of four who had a 2 year old who did not want to wear a face mask.

Report_1_Narrative: My flight began at ZZZ1 with the intent to fly direct to ZZZ for touch and goes and return to ZZZ1. I have flown this particular airplane multiple times with no issues. The start; taxi; and run-up were normal and no different than any other time; except that the strobe lights were blinking slower than usual but working as expected.The airplane was flown earlier; and no issues were reported; hence there was no reason to suspect a problem. I did two take-offs and landings before departing to ZZZ; I had no issues. During a normal approach to landing at ZZZ; all-electric equipment failed at an altitude of 300 feet from touching down on Runway XX. I was forced to immediately clear the runway and exit onto the first taxiway I saw; Taxiway XX; I had a disabled radio; transponder; and ADS-B.Although clear from the tower for a touch and go; I could not continue the flight safely with disabled equipment; therefore a go-around was not an option. Luckily; I have a handheld radio and was able to contact the control tower to explain what happened; and request directions to the parking area. I had to deviate from the touch and go clearance since I dint know what else was wrong with the airplane and continuing the flight would have been unwise.After arriving at the parking area; I talked to the mechanic who was only available by phone and asked me to go through my checklist again to troubleshoot the issue. I made multiple attempts to restart the airplane; loud cabin speaker noises could be heard as the power switch was turned on as if there was a short circuit in the system; but all fuses were okay and there was no power to start the engine. The mechanic determined that I had a dead battery and it could only mean that the airplane suffered an alternator failure on landing; grounding the airplane immediately.The flight club from which I rented the airplane has multiple airplanes of the same make and model and provided me with one so I could fly back to ZZZ1. The return flight was uneventful.
Report_1_Synopsis: PA28 pilot reported that on final approach all electrical equipment failed. After a successful landing; it was determined that the battery was dead.

Report_1_Narrative: Pre-flight planning with ForeFlight didn't show icing conditions where I encountered them in flight. The ZZZ1 live weather cams looked promising too. I should've used multiple resources instead of just ForeFlight. Years of multiple flights on this route gave me a false sense security. I was aware of a small storm moving in. I pushed my limits; trying to arrive before the storm while taking advantage of tail winds.These are all examples of what lead up to my problem. I encountered MVFR conditions over the mountains approximately 40 miles southwest of ZZZ2 at approximately 14;500 ft. I noticed light rime icing; air temp -20c. I climbed and notified ATC I would return to ZZZ due to weather. This was a safe decision. While Heading back at 17;500 ft.; it appeared I could make it safely over the top of the weather. I planned to overfly ZZZ2 and look for a safe opening in the weather. I had done this many times before and was still feeling complacent and confident. I informed ATC of my plans to turn around. This was NOT a safe or intelligent decision and caused my problem. I should have acknowledged my original weather concerns and continued back home. While close to ZZZ2 clouds built up vertically rapidly. I started icing up and informed ATC of my situation and needed to climb to FL 18;500 ft. I was at my service ceiling; with few options. Despite pitot heat and MVFR; my pitot tube froze up. I lost all primary instruments; switched to secondary steam gauges; also my O2 tank malfunctioned. This all happened in a matter of minutes. Lack of practice on partial instrument panel failures did not help my situation. I informed ATC I was unable to copy IFR clearances at this time.Maneuvering around building IMC icing conditions; on steam gauges; at my service ceiling; without O2; and now fighting headwinds was very challenging. Flying the plane had to be my sole focus and ATC understood. ATC made me a priority aircraft for me due to my unwillingness to copy my IFR clearance. As I headed southwest my instruments came back online and the weather improved. I subsequently picked up an IFR clearance. I requested lower; plus cancellation of IFR from ZZZ Center. ZZZ Center asked if I was still in distress. I assured ATC everything was fine now. I was no longer considered an aircraft in a priority handling situation. As a preventative safety measure; planes without deicing equipment should not fly near icing conditions even in VMC. Traditional VFR cloud separation rules; while legal are not always safe; especially when potentially hazardous conditions exist. A good preventative measure would have been not to fly at all that day.
Report_1_Synopsis: GA pilot reported inadvertent VFR flight into IMC that resulted in an airspace incursion.

Report_1_Narrative: We were delayed yesterday because of ATC issues. By the time we took off it was dark and we had been up for 12 hours. As we flew east off the coast of State X we encountered moderate turbulence and precipitation. The Captain got distracted and as we leveled off at 7;000 feet his speed began to increase. I called out 'Speed' and he did not acknowledge so again I said 'Watch your speed.' By this time we were doing around 275 knots and I don't why but he thought we should continue the climb so he used the autopilot to begin to climb the plane. I immediately told him to maintain 7;000 and reduce his speed. The initiated climb resulted in an altitude gain of 400 feet and the Controller told us to maintain 7;000 feet. We returned to 7;000 with no other issues and slowed. I was told our delay was a result of staffing issues at ZZZ center because of COVID-19. This is by far the longest ATC delay I have experienced and I definitely know fatigue was a factor hear. Do I think we were unsafe? No; I do not. That being said I don't think we were the tip of the spear that late in the day. ATC was super busy on the radios and we tried calling several times to request higher to get out of the weather we were in to no avail. Under staffing; busy airspace; delays; fatigue; and weather all combined would be the problem in my opinion. As well as pressure to get the job done.
Report_1_Synopsis: First Officer reported a speed and altitude deviation during departure and cited fatigue from a lengthy ATC COVID-19 related delay as contributing factor.

Report_1_Narrative: Passenger in [seat X] refused to wear mask. He was addressed by passengers and flight attendants. He was issued the mask card in regards to not following company's mask policy. The flight attendants did not inform me until after parking about the situation even though it happened during the flight and other passengers were complaining. The station manager at ZZZ was able to find the passenger after deplaning and had a conversation with him in regards to company's policy.  During my welcome aboard announcement I did reiterate [the] company's mask policy.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported that after the flight the Flight Attendant stated that a passenger had been non-compliant with mask policy during the flight and that other passengers had been complaining.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Communication Breakdown; Time Pressure; Troubleshooting; Workload; Situational Awareness
Report_1_Narrative: On RNAV to Runway XX due to GS being inop on the ILS; winds; and airport conditions.  Outside FAF; attempted to extend Landing Gear and got only the 3 red UNLOCKED lights.  No landing gear operation.  Our airspeed was around 165 KIAS.  We attempted to recycle the gear and got exact same thing.  We executed a missed approach; [advised ATC]; and attempted to contact Dispatch on ACARS.  We tried several frequencies but could not make voice contact.  ZZZ1 airspace was undergoing some sort of COVID cleaning so not sure if that had anything to do with ARINC in that vicinity.  We just used the ACARS to communicate as best we could.  Dispatch texted that the only thing he was showing was LANDING GEAR NOT DOWN LOCKED (same as us) but had no other system malfunctions that he could see.  We followed the ECAM which instructed us to use the gravity extend.  We did; it worked; and we landed safely.  We texted Dispatch once on the ground that we made it safely; Maintenance came with the tug and towed us to the gate.  Passengers and flight attendants were informed in the air and on the ground as to what was happening.
Report_2_Narrative: Just after midnight; outside the FAF to Runway XX at ZZZ; I was the PM and was asked to extend the landing gear. The gear failed to extend. Landing gear not down-locked. Recycled landing gear. No joy. Told Tower we needed to go-around to troubleshoot. Requested priority handling and then transferred controls; I was now PF while the Captain ran the ECAM and coordinated with Dispatch/Maintenance Control/FAs. I requested vectors away from the weather and near the approach so we could quickly join final when complete; requested they roll the trucks; and advised ATC we would need a tow off the runway. The Captain had difficulties talking with Dispatch and Maintenance over ARINC due to our low altitude (3;000) but was able to exchange some messages over ACARS with both. He ran the landing gear gravity extension checklist as directed by the ECAM. Landing gear came down. Captain updated FAs and made a PA to the passengers. We transferred controls and I was then PM for the final approach; visibility was poor due to a weather system. Rough winds and conditions but great landing by the Captain. Full stop on the runway. Crash truck circled and checked the plane out. Tow arrived and we shutdown motors and were towed to the gate.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported an unsafe landing gear indication. ATC communications were also reported possibly due to a COVID-19 ATC Zero event.

Report_1_Narrative: To my surprise we now deice at the FBO in the 'Deice Pad GA'; vs the deice pad at the end of [Runway] 28R. 1. The area is not that large. It's sized for general aviation.2. As configured this day; a 180 degree turn was required.3. As you might guess there is snow on the ground. So most markings are not visible and it's slippery. 4. The vendor prepositions their two trucks in the small area.  So when you enter the pad; you are taxing the aircraft towards one truck with a guideman in the bucket and there is another truck off your left wing. Both trucks are moving also. Then you swing a left 180 making sure you are not skidding; not going to hit a truck with your right wing and then stop the jet so you run into the truck that is not positioned in front of you. Whoever evaluated this as a viable procedure did not take into account the size and conditions (snow) as well as the truck positions.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported that the new area being used for de-icing presented several safety hazards; including a slippery surface and a small area for maneuvering the aircraft.

Report_1_Narrative: Deice in PIT is unsafeDeice in PIT done by [the FBO] on the general aviation deice pad near taxiways N and N5. Deice for other[s]; that I could see; was done by another vendor on either deice pad E or C.The short story is that the deice pad we are expected to use is just big enough to park [our aircraft] only if the pad was clear and unobstructed. When we arrived; the pad was unplowed; with no markings available. Lighting is poor. There were two deice trucks; one facing east and one west; with what appeared to be perhaps 125% of our wingspan between them. It's difficult to judge distance at night in the snow on a poorly lit ramp with lights facing us - but it was WAY too close. There is no specified aircraft operation zone. Were the vehicles in that zone? Who knows? Add that braking values on the ATIS were 3/3/3; and the ramp appears to slope slightly downward to the north.We did get the east-facing truck to back up so we could get parked; to do this I had to make a 120 degree turn (roughly from N5 into the ramp; I was able to widen out a bit) on this snow-covered; unplowed (and therefore unmarked) ramp. There are NO WINGWALKERS provided here - it's all on your own with only the driver and sprayer in the truck on duty as far as we could see. With a corporate jet; the building; and then a fence all within less than a wingspan this is simply unacceptable.To leave this deice pad; I had to add power to get through the unplowed snow. Notice that there was a building less than 150 feet behind me; and possibly the corporate jet there too although I think we got turned enough to not endanger them.While the folks in the deice truck were very professional; we did have to prompt them for the fluid type; etc. On the initial call to let us know they were done they only told us that the deice and anti-ice steps started 'x' minutes ago.We got it done. I'm only moderately sure in hindsight that it was safe enough. I can't be sure that when we got deiced we were completely off the taxiways. I am certain that if this setup continues someone will hit something. Why we don't use the vendor that *others* use is beyond me.
Report_1_Synopsis: Captain reported that the deicing location had several safety hazards; including no wing-walkers; poor lighting and unplowed snow on the surface.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Workload; Human-Machine Interface; Troubleshooting; Communication Breakdown
Report_1_Narrative: After Takeoff on our climb up 2;500 ft. out of ZZZ; we lost the use of both VHF radios com1 and com2. We leveled off at 2;500 ft. worked the problem and the Captain was able to get com1 back by using the ALT switch. All the communications on the First Officer side of the plane had died I could not use the hot mic or communicate with ATC on my side I tired different headsets and nothing worked. We then decided to return to ZZZ since we were going out over the water on our way to ZZZ1. WE had to burn 14;000 lbs. of fuel to get under max landing weight. We ended up holding over ZZZ VOR since the weather in the area was raining and turbulent and ZZZ VOR was in the clear and smooth. We worked the Flight Attendant; Dispatch; Maintenance Control; and ATC; till we had burned off enough fuel to return to land in ZZZ. We kept the passengers informed of what was going on as much as we could during the entire event.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported that both VHF radios stopped working during departure; resulting in a diversion.

Report_1_Narrative: Descending on LINKK 1 arrival ATC cleared us at some point (think above 10.000 feet) for the ILS 27 approach. Pilot Monitoring re-selected the ILS 27 connecting the transition from RDFSH (which was not done on initial FMC setup). Our altitude was set at 6000 passed RDFSH. We never set FAF altitude to keep the descent.Houston approach checked if we were cleared for the approach. After that; I realized we were supposed to descend via the transition. No further ATC communication was received however after the crew debrief and looking at the approach plate again; the altitudes were mandatory altitude restrictions and we don't think we made GEYGR and/ or SYYKO.
Report_2_Narrative: I was the First Officer and pilot monitoring on this flight IAH. We were cleared to descend via the LINKK1 arrival except maintain 300 knots. Then; 320 knots. Then; as fast as practical until LINKK. Then we were cleared for the approach from RDFSH and maintain 210 knots until FESTA. We had 6000 feet in the MCP window as this was the bottom altitude for the STAR. After being cleared the approach; I failed to set a lower altitude. Shortly after RDFSH (and level at 6000') ATC asked if we were descending on the approach. We were immediately aware of our mistake and the captain began descending. GEYGR and SYYKO (the next two fixes on the approach after RDFSH) had mandatory altitudes of 4000' and 3000'; respectively. Because of our delayed descent after RDFSH; we were high at both of those fixes. The multiple airspeed changes on the arrival caused a distraction and I failed to notice that I hadn't set a lower altitude to continue the approach after RDFSH. That being the case; it was still my job as pilot monitoring to set the lower altitude and I failed to do it.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight crew reported that following multiple speed adjustments per ATC's request; they misprogrammed the aircraft; which resulted in not satisfying the mandatory crossing altitudes.

Report_1_Narrative: On taxi out of parking; contacted Ground for taxi clearance. Was given instructions to taxi [Taxiway] A; B1; Z; S2 for Runway 10L. On Taxiway Zulu; Ground asked us about the B1 signage. We told him that we saw the [Taxiway] B1 sign and proceeded B1 to [Taxiway] Zulu. After talking with Ground; we looked at the Jepps (Jeppesen) 10-9 taxi page and saw that after [Taxiway] A; the Taxiway B1 turns left to the northwest (approx. a 45 degree angle/ jog) to join [Taxiway] Zulu; where as we turned slightly to the left proceeding north to join [Taxiway] Zulu. The [Taxiway] B1 sign on Taxiway Alpha did not show any kind of directional arrow of the Taxiway B1 like many other airports that have similar offset taxiways. Talking with Ground Control; I am led to believe that we were not the only aircraft to make such a mistake on this given day as Runway 10L/R is not our normal runways for departure and taxi out is different that normal. My recommendation is to change the [Taxiway] B1 sign to add the directional arrow to show turn or to rename the 2nd half of the angle/jog of Taxiway B1 to emphasize the direction of taxi that Ground wants us to take.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Captain reported turning the wrong way to join a taxiway and cited confusing signage as a contributing factor.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Training / Qualification; Workload; Communication Breakdown; Distraction; Situational Awareness
Report_1_Narrative: On final; Runway XXL; ZZZ; Night; 1000 foot ceiling; Me (Captain) flying; gusty winds; very light load; FO low currency- only 150 hrs in type since hired 1 year ago; and has not been flying much. I was hand flying at 2;000 feet on normal ILS. Called for gear down; flaps 15 at approximately 2;000 feet and flaps 30 landing; check at about 1500 feet. FO ran check list; while I hand flew the approach. The winds were gusty; our target was +15 ref and it was night.  I saw flap refs change on airspeed tape; and glanced at gear lights when FO ran checklist; but I did not have full attention to FO duties since it was dark and gusty. We broke out at 1;000 feet; I called clear to land and set missed approach altitude. At 500 feet we simultaneously got the 500 auto call out and Too Low Flaps. I simultaneously; started a Go-Around (finger to toga button) and looked at flap gauge - which was at 25. But I hesitated on the go-around when I saw why we got the GPWS. I commanded flaps set to 30; which the FO immediately did. We were then about 350-400 feet and stable; and I continued to a normal landing. After landing I realized; even though there was adequate time to set the flaps to 30; I should have gone around. We debriefed after parking. The FO said he just missed the flaps in setting and checking on the checklist; most likely due to being low time in aircraft and rusty from time off. I missed his wrong setting; due to the dark and the gusty winds requiring my attention. I said I should have gone around; and that he as well should have told me to. I am confident if I had not immediately recognized why we got the too low flaps and immediately corrected it; I would not have continued.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Captain reported a TOO LOW FLAPS warning and an Unstabilized Approach.

Report_1_Narrative: While doing preflight walk around; I noticed the fueler was using the pressure refueling when they shouldn't have been because it was MEL'd. I approached her and let her know that she shouldn't have been using it because it was MEL'd. She was aware of the MEL because she was touching the sticker in the fueling panel as she was fueling. Her response to me was 'I'm almost done and it seems to be working fine.' I told her that it doesn't matter if it seemed to be working fine because we had to follow the MEL and she told me she was only 200 lbs. from being done. So I went and let the Captain know and he called Operations to report the fuel truck and called Maintenance to make sure we were okay to fly. Just before closing main cabin door we noticed someone open up the fuel panel again. He was in a white truck and an orange vest. When we got to ZZZ1 on the post flight walk around my Captain asked me to check and make sure the MEL placard was still there and that's when we saw it had been removed and I got a new placard from the Captain and placed it back in the refueling panel. Placed new placard for MEL.Emphasis on compliance of fuelers with SOPs.
Report_2_Narrative: First Officer came in after preflight and said [the] fueler had used pressure refueling port to fuel; she was almost done fueling by the time he saw and was able to say something. At this point the fueling panel was MEL'd with a placard on the panel. Called Maintenance to see if there was anything to do in regards to fuel or the panel and they said they didn't have time to clear the MEL; if we had the appropriate amount of gas we were good to go. I called Ops (Operations) to mention the fueler had used a panel that was MEL'd and shouldn't have; gave Ops the truck number. Just before closing the main cabin door; I noticed the fueling panel open and we saw a white pickup truck next to the aircraft as well as someone in an orange vest at the fueling port. The fueling panel was then closed; we departed without incident. Upon arriving in ZZZ1; I asked the First Officer to check the fueling panel on his post flight and he said the placard was gone. We replaced the placard and left the aircraft for our overnight. Post flight inspection revealed the placard was missing. Replaced the placard on the fuel panel. Emphasize Fuelers compliance with SOP's.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported that the aircraft fueler was using pressure refueling port although it was not useable due to an MEL.
