Report_1_Narrative: Captain (CA) was PF and First Officer (FO) was PM. We had a crew alert action of AUTOFLT FCU1 failure not far from our initial descent for the STAR. CA was working the crew alert issue and Center called saying what the CA heard was 'Flight ABC'; Direct ZZZZZ descend via ZZZZZ1' (CA was in the QRH; reading about or looking for the crew alert issue).  After talking with the FO on the ground in ZZZ; after the event; the FO thought the read back something like 'Flight ABC direct ZZZZZ for the ZZZZZ1.'  Then; PM made sure PF was inserting the bottom altitude of STAR in the FCU (Meaning PM understood the clearance to descend via the ZZZZZ1).  PF did insert the bottom altitude. Then; shortly afterwards; we hit some moderate turbulence and PF decided to start descend early because he could not read the QRH; hoping to get into some clear air.  Then we were told we descended and there may have been a flight deviation.  I did not think so at the time because of the clearance I understood.I believe there were several causal factors on this event. 1) Pilot Inexperience.  The FO was on the Type X aircraft and in March was awarded the Type Y aircraft.  But from March through December; all the FO did was go to Type Y training; and IOE.  This was the FO's first flight since IOE. The FO was going very slow making sure no mistakes were made. The PF was also going very slow to ensure all FO tasks were completed.  2) Task saturation (crew alert event; pilot inexperience; turbulence and clearance understanding). Combined; this put both pilots in a 'caution situation.'  The PF; was trying for something like this would not happen from the moment the flight started by making sure he was slow and deliberate on all his thoughts and actions. 3) Turbulence event. We descended early because PF had a hard time reading the QRH. 4) PF flying and completing crew alert actions.  In this case; it may have made a difference; but; I do not believe it would have made a difference; because the PM understood the clearance from Center was a clearance to descend Via;   and when the turbulence started; the person working the crew alert action would have said descend to get out of the turbulence the QRH could be read. The same outcome would have happened.Suggestions - Verify the clearance; no matter the circumstances...In this particular event; the PF should have verified the clearance knowing the proficiency of the other pilot may not have been 100%.  A pilot may be 'Current' with regards to the official written documents approved by the FAA; but they may have not been proficient...(I do not know how this can be fixed...)
Report_2_Narrative: In preparation for descent; Status Page showed an inoperative system the CA/PF noticed. CA was in the process of investigating the crew alert message that caused it. We had a seasoned CA in the Jump Seat who was assisting in the lookup for the crew alert actions; if any; and the code was send to Maintenance. In that time; we received a call from Center to proceed 'direct to ZZZZZ for the ZZZZZ1.' I read the clearance back 'direct ZZZZZ for the ZZZZZ1 arrival'. I then conveyed to the CA/Pilot Flying 'direct to ZZZZZ; we can descend via the ZZZZZ1' and I backed CA up to set direct ZZZZZ in the FMS and dialed in the lowest altitude in the arrival for south landings. We verified the altitude. While inbound to ZZZZZ; we were at FL390 and encountered some occasions of moderate turbulence and continuous light chop. The CA/PF commenced a descent to avoid remaining in the turbulent conditions. I contacted the Center to let them know we were descending out of FL390. They called back to ask what was the reason for the descent. I stated we had encountered moderate to light turbulence and needed to descend to avoid it. They called back asking me to confirm the reason for descent was turbulence. I confirmed. Then; before we were handed off to the next frequency; the controller asked us to contact a number for possible altitude deviation. There was a misunderstanding; on my part; of the vertical clearance in the call with Center with the initial clearance for ZZZZZ1 and I passed that misinterpretation on to the CA/PF.It was my first flight in over a month; preceded only by sim events way back in September and just prior to OE. This was a threat up front. Hadn't flown in this environment in over 18 months. We had multiple distractions due to the crew alert and system loss being addressed; icing conditions and turbulence. The ATC frequency was covering high traffic volume so there was a significant amount of talking on the frequency. We had both been up very early in order to be ready at report time. My expectation bias led me to believe we were cleared to 'descend via' when we were cleared only laterally for the approach.We could have briefed the arrival prior to addressing the crew alert and done a transfer of control of the aircraft and radios. I could have had ATC repeat the clearance; once the PF was back with me; so that they could communicate directly what the intended clearance was. I could have stated the clearance exactly as it was read back to eliminate any 'single point' of interpretation; or misinterpretation.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported an altitude deviation and cited the First Officer's lack of flying as a contributing factor.

Report_1_Narrative: This flight is part of the second trip to be on a landing currency waiver. Landings expired [Date]. Waivers issued for the next two pilot trips. I have stated plainly to the training desk I want to regain my currency vs flying not current on waivers. One area of safety concern arose prior to this flight due to being non-current. Scheduling called the CA the morning of the flight asking to crew the leg ZZZ to ZZZ1 with just 2 pilots (CA and myself) because they could not find a replacement FO for the trip. CA agreed after checking with union contracts. Safety Issue: CA was unaware I would be arriving for work on a waiver. The CA should be notified well in advance instead of at sign in that a non-qualified pilot would be on their flight. The only way the CA found out I was on a waiver is when I notified him. To be clear: I was never assigned FO in the system. The situation was resolved without ever assigning me as FO. The safety issue is with the PIC being unaware they will have a non-qualified crew member.Issuance of this waiver is only made known to the non-current pilot. Other crew members are un-aware until sign in.This waiver should be rarely used vs the recent expanded use and it needs to be depicted plainly in schedules being visible to all crew.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier First Officer reported having a status as flying on a special wavier that was not reported by the company to the Captain before the flight.

Report_1_Narrative: After we were clear for takeoff on the Runway XX; at ZZZ airport. The Captain applied power; he waited for the engine to stabilize; then he pressed TOGA. As the plane started moving; it suddenly started veering to the right. He tried to correct it by pressing the left rudder; but the aircraft did not respond right away. After a few seconds; the plane veer back to the left; but it only went about 45 degrees to the left. After that; the Captain pressed the right rudder and was able to bring it back to control. Furthermore; we stopped at the runway; then; I called the tower to abort the takeoff. Finally; we were able to taxi off the runway and went back to the gate.
Report_2_Narrative: Cleared for takeoff Runway XX. Engines spooled up 'taxiing' up to takeoff point on Runway XX. With engines at 40% N1 pushed TOGA button and throttles advanced. We observed the white arcs advancing but the plane didn't seem to be accelerating normally. As I glanced inside to ensure the auto throttles were engaged (they were) the aircraft started to drift right. I tried to correct back with the rudder as we always do but it had no effect. As the right drift continued I rejected the take off and had to use almost full nose wheel tiller to correct back to centerline. We smelled burning rubber; so we taxied clear of the runway and had ARFF (Airport Rescue Firefighting) come inspect the gear and wheels. No problems found by ARFF. Tower had the runway inspected. Nothing found. I had ARFF follow us to the gate where we made an AML entry and had a lengthy discussion with Maintenance. During the takeoff roll the throttles never made it to Takeoff Thrust and I was looking outside the whole time; but the speed achieved was well below 80 kts. Probably around 40-45 kts. In addition; on taxi out when brakes were applied to stop in line they often 'chattered.'We suspected a brake problem or asymmetric thrust.I'm not sure why it happened. I've seen asymmetric thrust before and it is easily corrected with rudder to steer back to centerline. This plane was very difficult to get turning back to the left.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported the takeoff was rejected after the aircraft drifted to the right and was not responding to rudder inputs.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Situational Awareness; Training / Qualification; Communication Breakdown; Physiological - Other
Report_1_Narrative: I was the flying pilot; we were kept high the whole time. Then we were given [Runway] XXR GPS Y; as we turned; the turn was inside the approach fix; it was tight.  I turned to final and we looked high and I wasn't comfortable; so we asked for a go-around. I initiated TOGA; we were approximately 2;200 feet when we did the go-around; and began the go-around process and around 2;500 feet. ATC asked to maintain 3;000 feet. We got extremely busy and by the time we realized it we were at 3;500 feet.  We descended to 3;000 feet and we asked to extend the downwind.I had been out for a year and half; and since I gotten back; I did not fly that much; also was off last month and half of this month due to COVID-19; but also I should have asked for extended downwind in the airport; should not [have] allowed the Controller to rush us and I have learned a lesson.Don't accept any arrival that I am not comfortable with.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier First officer reported an unstablized approach and an altitude deviation during a go-around.  First Officer cited lack of flying as a contributing factor.

Report_1_Narrative: I was acting as pilot flying on the flight to ZZZ. While flying on our assigned course direct to the ZZZ airport; approximately 100 miles from our destination; while conducting the arrival and approach briefings; ATC Center assigned us to turn left 10 degrees; which I complied with by selecting heading mode on the FCP; and selecting the desired heading with the heading bug. Several minutes later; the Controller; again; assigned us to proceed direct to the ZZZ airport. I selected in the FMS direct to the ZZZ airport; confirmed the selection with my captain; and executed the flight plan modification. However; I had neglected to select NAV mode; which resulted in the aircraft continuing on its previously assigned heading for several minutes while I finished the arrival briefing; resulting in the course to show a full-scale deflection to the left (south). Upon finishing the briefing; I realized the missed step; and immediately turned back toward the course and armed NAV mode. Having recently switched over to ZZZ approach; within several minutes the controlled queried us about our position; informing us we were left of course. We notified the controller that we were rejoining the course. The controller then assigned us to proceed direct to the ZZZ airport again; which we selected in the FMS; confirmed; and executed; this time ensuring NAV mode was engaged. The flight continued without issue.This event was caused by lack of recent flight experience; as well as momentary task-saturation.This has not been a reoccurring trend for me during training or during revenue operations. I plan to continue to maintain a high level of situational awareness in the cockpit to trap threats before they become errors. I also plan to ensure I am making appropriate FCP selections when I am making an adjustment to our course.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier First Officer reported a heading deviation and cited lack of recent flight experience and task saturation as contributing factors.

Report_1_Narrative: During passenger boarding there were many people not wearing their face mask. I was also spending time finding room for bags. It was a busy time and I forgot to brief my exit row passengers.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Attendant reported forgetting to brief the exit row passengers due to distraction from having to remind boarding passengers of the face mask policy.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Situational Awareness; Physiological - Other; Communication Breakdown; Troubleshooting
Report_1_Narrative: Crew stepped off aircraft and was on jetbridge. When I looked at my handheld it said we were boarding. So I replied back we had not been cleaned or sprayed yet so we were not boarding. About 3 to 4 minutes later 2 cleaners came up the airstairs and boarded. One had an electric vacuum in hand the other had [a] trash bag in hand. Shortly after a 3rd cleaner came on board with a bag of supplies and boarded the aircraft and put [the] bag down by the First Class Lavatory. About 5 minutes later another cleaner (gentleman with nothing in his hands) came up the airstairs and boarded the aircraft. Within 10 to 15 seconds the first 2 cleaners came off the aircraft and right after them the other gentleman came off the aircraft saying 'we are good to go.' One of my crewmember's asked him was the aircraft sprayed. He repeated 'we were good to go' and proceeded to exit the jetbridge door and down the airstairs. I and the other crew member both said I don't think the aircraft was sprayed as neither of us saw the cone being put in place nor did we see the sprayer. At this time the last cleaner with the bag with supplies came off. I asked her has this aircraft been sprayed? She said what did he say; I said he said yes; she proceeded to exit the aircraft.  I said can you please show me what you have in that bag; because if there is no sprayer in there; then there is no way our aircraft has been sprayed. She then said 'I will tell him to come back.' At this time the Gate Agent came down to see if we were ready to board. I explained the situation to the Agent and she said 'oh no I am so sorry; that's not right.' The Captain was on the jetbridge with us and we were all in agreement that we needed to be sprayed before we could start boarding. The previous gentleman came back up the airstairs with sprayer in hand and sprayed aircraft. When he was done; without further delay; we boarded and departed. The Gate Agent was very apologetic about the incident.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Attendant reported a cleaning crew had to be reminded to properly sanitize the aircraft prior to passenger boarding.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Troubleshooting; Physiological - Other; Situational Awareness; Confusion
Report_1_Narrative: The hand sanitizer installed on this aircraft is in a dangerous location. Several times I have hit my back center spine and also hit my arm on it. With the addition of the X row of seats on this plane the bulkhead wall is already pushed forward. With the addition of the sanitizer it makes the work space even smaller. Someone is going to get seriously injured in turbulence or any sudden movement of the aircraft as the bottom part that sticks out; is a thin edge. The catch dish was missing on this aircraft; so any liquid was falling on the floor creating a slip hazard. Whomever is putting the bottles in the holder; they are not securing it in place. The flight attendants have not been shown how to secure the bottle in place.Why are we taking space away from an emergency exit that has already been encroached on by the wall being pushed forward; to add an X row of seats?
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Attendant reported concerns with the placement of the hand sanitizer installed on the aircraft.

Report_1_Narrative: Uneventful 3 hour VFR flight from ZZZ1 at 16;500 feet.  Just after starting my VFR descent for SRQ was advised by ZJX Center that TPA Approach would not take the hand-off and told to squawk 1200. I switched to TPA Approach for SRQ airport and monitored frequency as I continued VFR descent to 8;500 feet - above the top of Class B.  After monitoring approach frequency for 5 minutes as I continued my VFR descent to 4;500 feet - above the top of the SRQ Class C; it was evident that the TPA Approach Controller was saturated so I switched to SRQ Tower.  I advised Tower that I would fly west beyond the Class C and descend to 1;100 feet - below the floor; before turning back to SRQ for VFR approach and landing. Tower worked me in perfectly on intersecting Runway 4.Although 121 traffic is down considerably; FAA now needs to assess the current flight activity - which for ZZZ Approach certainly exceeded the ability of 1 Controller to control all sectors; and add back controllers before someone gets hurt.
Report_1_Synopsis: Pilot reported the flight was not accepted by TPA Approach Control due to staffing/workload issues. The Captain circumnavigated the area and proceeded VFR.

Report_1_Narrative: The landing was excellent; Rollout of the aircraft was straight and smooth. When reaching for the toe brakes; I had a left brake but no right break. The toe brakes are little round pads on the top outsides of each rudder and are not easily identified with your toes even with soft sole shoes which I wear to fly in. I did not realize my foot had slipped off or was not on it properly until it was too late. The aircraft took a left direction as I was wishing to slow down. I let go of the left brake and caught it/straightened it with the right rudder. Right after I had it straight; I removed my right foot to lift it higher up to engage the right brake. The aircraft took a sharp left direction went onto the grass which with then full right rudder and the right brake did not help. The slope away from the runway is very steep and the aircraft was not able to be brought back up onto the runway; so I kept it straight and aimed at the taxiway; With the airplane tailwheel not willing to provide steering since it was on grass and the slope was still steep; the aircraft slid over the other side of the taxiway. The aircraft refused to turn right with all my efforts; so my next choice was to hit trees and or a building; so I choose to ground loop the airplane to avoid the trees and building. NO damage was done to any property including taxi signs or even lights. The aircraft came to a stop 180 degrees to the landing direction. No one was hurt in any manner since the speed was not very fast. The right gear leg collapsed as it stopped and the prop hit the grass and broke one of the tips. The engine was shut down and everything was turned off. The Runway XX is a challenging runway since there is zero room for error.
Report_1_Synopsis: Private pilot did not have proper foot placement and lost control of the aircraft during the landing rollout. The aircraft  had a prop strike and right main gear failure.

Report_1_Narrative: I was on a instrument approach to CID talking with Chicago Center and picking up ice. Chicago asked me to cancel IFR clearance as early as possible because a (Company) plane was landing behind me. I changed to the CTAF frequency and made a 10 miles out announcement. I broke out around 2;000 ft msl/1;200 ft. AGL and change back to Chicago Center and cancelled my IFR clearance with ATC. I switched the comm back to CTAF and continued the approach; however; the button push failed to change to CTAF and stayed on Chicago Center and I missed that. During the approach I was stunned to see a vehicle pull out onto the approach end of the runway and stop at the very end just beyond the runway end lighting. I was still approximately 1-1 1/2 miles out. I had to make a decision to land or go back up into the icing. As the runway was 8;000 ft. long I elected to extend and land in the 2nd half of the runway as opposed to risk picking up excessive ice and endangering my aircraft.
Report_1_Synopsis: Pilot was flying instrument approach after having ice build up on aircraft. During landing a vehicle entered the  runway. Instead of going around; pilot chose to land long instead of returning to icing conditions.

Report_1_Narrative: As background; ZZZ was heavily congested with training and weekend aviators. The approach to the downwind leg was reported via UNICOM as 4nm SE to enter a 45 - downwind entry. We coordinated spacing with another crosswind aircraft to follow us for spacing in the pattern.Reported downwind uneventfully and recognized the aircraft we were to follow and minimized their pattern to minimize spacing conflicts. Reported [our] base turn to UNICOM; uneventfully. Our track on base leg was approximately 2 nm from the end of the runway. At no time was our location questioned by the conflicting near miss aircraft.Reported a base to final turn; uneventfully and unquestioned. Upon the completion of the turn to final; I focused on vertical alignment to the runway and did not see the conflicting near miss aircraft. The PNF (Pilot Not Flying); in a radio call questioned the conflicting near miss aircraft to determine the position upon hearing the UNICOM base report. For clarification; the safety pilot - PNF; is a seasoned 121 CA (Captain) and highly experienced in the PA24-250 with close to 2;000 hours in type. After it was determined the conflicting aircraft turned inside of our location; resulting in cutting us off placing our aircraft in a hazardous flight profile; PNF took control of the aircraft in a professionally coordinated manner.At this time; the conflicting near miss aircraft was well within 1/4 NM and somewhat above our altitude; which was approximately 300 ft AGL. Because of the proximity to us; and apparently being unaware of our location; the resolution was complex. Keep in mind in their base to final turn (RH pattern) with a low wing aircraft [they] would have then been unable to locate us.Additionally; as we both rolled out on final we were both nearly lined up on the centerline; the closure rate was approximately 42 FPS and without evasive action; contact would have occurred in about 30 seconds; short of the runway; all due to the difference in V-ref and approach speeds. The PNF recognized this before I had visual contact with the conflicting traffic and they took control of the aircraft and became the PF.The evasive maneuver was complex in that [the other aircraft's] intentions seemed unpredictable and we did not want to initiate a go-around with the associated high deck angle; which would interrupt visual conflict with the conflicting traffic. Communication from their aircraft was weak and seemed confused as they; on short final; radioed 'how many aircraft are in the pattern and where are you located'. We discussed the possibility that they may begin a go around and that would worsen the conflict since we may have lost visual contact and keep in mind... at this time we were behind their location and out of view.In the interest of safety; we chose to sidestep slightly left and to pass them on the level and then after we cleared the aircraft to begin a go around. The point we were trying to achieve was to maintain visual contact with the conflicting aircraft until we passed clear of their position.
Report_1_Synopsis: GA pilot reported a NMAC in traffic pattern occurred when another aircraft turned in front of them requiring an evasive maneuver and go around.

Report_1_Narrative: Aircraft X was landing HHR on an IFR flight plan. There were multiple weather cells in the airspace and LAX Aircraft were deviating around the final to the north. I had DYNR/EAFR combined and was quite busy handling the coordination for the deviations with STAR/ZUMR and figuring out the sequence for dependent simultaneous ILS's. I advised Aircraft X of some weather; but did not issue a heavy precipitation on the route to HHR. I asked Aircraft X if they could advise HHR in sight because the HHR weather was reporting BKN045 and LAX Aircraft could not get the visual. We also did not have staffing available in the facility to open up parallel monitors for independent simultaneous approaches. Aircraft X responded HHR in sight and I cleared them for the visual approach. Traffic for LAX was increasing and frequency congestion was becoming a problem. Aircraft x did have delays with their read backs/understanding as well. Aircraft X went down to 1100 ft. in a 2000 ft. MVA and I issued a low altitude alert. Aircraft X responded with; 'correcting'. Then Aircraft X kept heading toward the LAX finals and I asked them once or twice if they still see HHR. Then the HHR weather deteriorated to IFR and I advised Aircraft X that they'd need the localizer approach. I told the CIC (Controller in Charge) to open up monitors; they were trying to find staffing at the time already. I then got Aircraft X above the MVA and vectored them for the approach while continuing to deal with LAX deviations. After clearing Aircraft X for the localizer runway 25; I switched them to HHR tower; monitors had opened at this time. Aircraft X then proceeded to do a left turn southbound on about a 7 mile final without notification to me from HHR tower. Monitor 1 then called HHR and asked what was going on. Aircraft X then checked back on frequency with me heading 160; no coordination. I climbed Aircraft X above the MVA and vectored them for another approach. I also asked the pilot if he could accept the approach and they agreed they could. I was then relieved.[We need] staffing. We have more than enough people on a shift to facilitate monitors being open. So many coworkers are worried about their long breaks and getting done early that we are leaving the operational floor short between shifts.
Report_1_Synopsis: SCT Approach Controller reported inability to manage aircraft due to staffing issues.

Report_1_Narrative: Aircraft Y had taxied into parking via Taxiway A and was pulling into his parking spot on the ramp. Aircraft X was doing a touch and go on Runway 14L which is directly west of the ramp. During the touch and go Aircraft X was directly behind the Aircraft Y and was hit with jet blast on his left wing from Aircraft Y while they were still under power; idle or taxi power unknown.This happens here often enough and some of us to issue cautionary jet blast calls to Runway 14L traffic. I do not know if the pilot was told or not.We could put a message on the ATIS; create another Hot Spot or at least post it in the Airport Directory.
Report_1_Synopsis: Local Controller reported that a small aircraft was hit with jet blast while on the runway at BFI airport. Controller stated that this happens frequently and suggested adding a message on the ATIS.

Report_1_Narrative: Aircraft X took off RIL climbing to 15;000 feet; at around 10;000 feet; Aircraft X informed me he was having a landing gear issue; could not climb further and needed to return to RIL right away. I sent him direct to RIL. He had good sight of the terrain and once he got the visual he was cleared the visual approach. Aircraft Y was another aircraft going into RIL north of the airport level at 14;000 feet with no approach clearance. Aircraft X appeared to be circling to the runway so I did not clear Aircraft Y into the airport. Aircraft X then popped back on the frequency saying they cannot land at RIL and need to go to [another airport]. Aircraft X at this point was 8;000 feet climbing eastbound still in priority handling status. I re-radar identified Aircraft X and had them climb to 13;000 feet to try to maintain positive Minimum IFR Altitudes. They affirmed they had good sight of the terrain. I called the traffic to both Aircraft Y and Aircraft X hoping to apply visual separation. Neither saw one another so they both remained 13;000 feet (Aircraft X) and 14;000 feet (Aircraft Y).Once able; I vectored Aircraft X south to get him away from high Minimum IFR Altitudes and the RIL approach corridor. I asked Aircraft Y 'if I turn you direct to RIL; do you think you can get a visual with the airport?' Aircraft Y responded he could. I then said 'Aircraft Y; cleared direct RIL' I then went back to Aircraft X and asked fuel remaining; souls on board; what altitude they could climb to; and then explained why 15;000 feet was not feasible. I offered GJT etc. While discussing options with Aircraft X; I noticed Aircraft Y leave 14;000 feet and begin their descent while still 3 to 4 miles from Aircraft X. I gave a traffic alert to Aircraft Y and told them to climb back to 14;000 feet immediately. I then gave the traffic alert to Aircraft X. Aircraft Y climbed back up; I gained the 5 miles and climbed Aircraft X up and gave Aircraft Y the visual approach to RIL. I issued Aircraft Y advisories.In this session I had two separate situations. A pilot deviation; an arrival rush; a handful of ornery pilots on the ground at RIL clogging the frequency looking for releases off the ground. Had RIL sector been separated out through our split frequency procedures; this may not have occurred. There was a lot of frequency congestion between the sector's two frequencies which blocked transmissions to the priority handling aircraft. We used to do this procedure and have been recently barred from doing it again. This procedure could have helped!
Report_1_Synopsis: ZDV Center Controller reported an aircraft that had deviated from their assigned altitude and descended towards another aircraft that was in a priority handling condition resulting in a loss of separation.

Report_1_Narrative: While on the ZZZZZX Arrival we were at FL350. We were given a descent to FL330 and to cross ZZZZZ at FL240. I set FL24000 in the MCP and the Captain set cruise in the FMC to FL330 and we started down. I looked at the ND display and saw FL240 next to ZZZZZ and a Top of Descent point and thought we were set up correctly. In reality the FMC was still loaded with FL240; At or Above; which is the altitude loaded with the ZZZZZ1 arrival. We noticed the error and made the changes and started the descent; however we were too high at that point to make the crossing at FL240; I think we were about 2;000 feet high. The Controller did not say anything to us and handed us off to the next Controller. You can say there may be some currency issues in that I have only flown about 9 flights since March; and this was 3rd time at the controls in the last 30 days. However I have been on the aircraft for almost X years and I know what it's supposed to do. I just misread the ND display and didn't see the A (At or Above) next to FL240.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier First Officer reported an altitude deviation during descent and cited lack of recent flight experience as a contributing factor.

Report_1_Narrative: Directed to fly NNCEE arrival. Directed to descend to FL300 and then via NNCEE; subsequently ATC issued a late descent to 10 miles east of LINKK at 17000 feet. Programmed FMS and determined unable to meet restriction without relief from ATC.ATC provided relief; I flew a fast descent; and met altitude restriction. We were then switched to follow-on ATC controller. ATC controller questioned our descent while inbound NNCEE (at or below 12000 feet). We informed him we obtained relief from previous controller and he responded 'no problem'. We continued with 'descend via'.
Report_2_Narrative: I was the Pilot Monitoring during this flight. IAH center assigned the following descent. Descend to cross 10 East of LINKK at 17000!The issue with this clearance is that it was assigned late. The aircraft was already at the top of descent as planned by the FMC for a LINKK crossing between 17000 and 20000 at 280KTS. I immediately informed the center controller that we would need relief from this clearance. The controller responded that relief was granted but try to make the 17000 crossing 10 miles east of LINKK and it was okay if we were fast at the intersection.At LINKK we did make the 17000 and were approximately 320KTS and slowing. We were given a frequency change to IAH approach. This controller asked what our altitude and airspeed where. Then asked what our clearance was. I responded that the previous controller gave the flight 10 mile east of LINKK at 17000 but also provided relief. I also confirmed with this new controlled that we were still cleared to continue descent via the NNCEE 1 transition to runway 9; which he confirmed.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight crew reported requesting relief from Center; after receiving a late descent clearance. Approach controller later queried about the previously issued clearance.

Report_1_Narrative: While taxiing into the gate X noticed a tug pulling a baggage cart stop after the stop sign/line on a roadway to the right of the airplane. I then noticed the vehicle backing up and it appeared to be close to the stop line; I looked forward and looked back to my right and noticed the vehicle proceeding what appeared to be underneath the scimitar and the wing walker still giving the all clear. I told the Captain to stop which he did; the vehicle cleared the wing/scimitar and continued; we then continued on to the gate safely.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported while taxiing to the gate at ORD; a ground service vehicle drove underneath the wing.

Report_1_Narrative: We were cleared via the Mustang 5 departure. This DP (Departure Procedure) is for [Runways] 9L/27R. The Draggin 5 departure is also for [Runways] 9L/27R. However; there is major construction on that runway and it is closed indefinitely. We were assigned [Runway] 27L for departure. We had to query Clearance Delivery for departure instructions for that particular runway. They said it was the same for both runways on the Mustang 5 departure.It seems like Jeppessen should update the chart to include routing instructions for both runways.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Captain reports Departure procedure does not specify correct departure runway.

Report_1_Narrative: This break-room at this location needs to be swept; mopped; tables wiped down; and disinfected. The location is extremely dirty. The cleaning crews only take out the trash and nothing else. Because of COVID-19; cleaning needs to be done on a regular schedule.  Nothing is being done to make improvements and keep this break-room clean.
