Report_1_Narrative: Upon coming to work to I witnessed about 30 people all crowded together on the kiosk machines. Social distancing was completely impossible.  ZZZ does not close every other machine; there are 2 rows of kiosks closed for the convenience of bag drop.  There were no stations set up to crowd control.
Report_1_Synopsis: Customer Service Representative reported crowding and social distancing issues near company provided kiosks in the terminal area.

Report_1_Narrative: Landed in ZZZ was normal. Visibility was 1/2 mile fog snow RVR 2;400 feet. Runway code was 3/3/3 and the previous landing reported fair braking. We landed flaps 30 auto brake 3. The airplane slowed down normal. Had to roll to the end due to taxiway closures. As we approached the end; I told my First Officer [we] needed to go slow in case it was slick. As we turned off [Runway] XXL the plane started to slide in the turn. Used left engine thrust reverse to help. Hit 3 taxi lights we did not leave the pavement. Taxied to the ramp notified ATC of the situation and was told we hit 3 taxi lights. Called and notified Dispatch and Maintenance Control. Made logbook entry. On walk around no aircraft damaged noted.
Report_2_Narrative: After an otherwise normal landing in ZZZ; the aircraft started to slide on a patch of ice as the Captain was turning off the runway and onto the taxiway. Although the aircraft never departed the paved surface; we were uncertain if the slide caused any damage to the taxiway lights. We informed ground control of the slide and the possibility of striking a taxiway light. Ground control notified the airport operations to have them take a look. They reported back that there were indeed 3 taxi lights down. Weather conditions at the time were 1/2 mile visibility with snow and fog. The [Runway] XXL runway condition code was reported as 3/3/3. We landed with auto brake 3 and the aircraft slowed normally. ATC requested a turnoff at the end of the runway due to numerous taxiway closures. It was at the end of the runway while turning off that the aircraft entered into the slide. No damage to the aircraft was found by either the flight crew or Maintenance upon inspection of the aircraft at the ramp.Unfortunately despite the rest of the runway having adequate braking; the runway end was incredibly slick. The only suggestion that could've prevented this would have been to make the turn at an even slower speed in order to possibly prevent the slide.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported loss of directional control while exiting the runway due to 'incredibly slick' conditions.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Distraction; Confusion; Communication Breakdown; Situational Awareness
Report_1_Narrative: ZZZ Center queried us about our routing. Apparently they expected us to go further east due to ZZZ1 Center having a limited number of operating frequencies. Our filed routing showed us [on one routing and our clearance was different] based on what we heard and read back. ZZZ Center was under the impression that we had received an amendment to our flight plan. At our departure airport we were unable to get our clearance through ACARS and had to receive clearance on the radio. The flight continued without any further anxiety.ZZZ1 Center connections with their remote receivers and transmitter antennas were not operational; or so we were told. If we had been able to get our clearance on ACARS we could verify the clearance and that nothing was missed on either our part or the Controller's.
Report_2_Narrative: During cruise; ZZZ Center queried us about our routing. It seems they expected us on a different route further east due to ZZZ1 Center having communication issues. We double checked our FMC and the clearance that we both copied [earlier] since we couldn't get it through the ACARS; and it was clear what our route was. ZZZ ATC thought we had received an amendment but we never did. He explained ZZZ1's situation and what potentially happened; re-cleared us and agreed that nothing wrong on our side had occurred; just ATC misunderstanding. We continued our flight and landed without any further issues.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported they flew a different route than expected and Center stated the mix-up was an ATC error.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Workload; Time Pressure; Human-Machine Interface; Communication Breakdown
Report_1_Narrative: [I] missed applying an MEL with a fuel penalty. Corrected the mistake and resent the [release] for the Captain to sign.I got to work 10 minutes early for an [early morning] shift. The license had expired for the Jeppesen chart viewer on my computer. I called the help desk. After trouble shooting for 10 minutes; I was told to find another machine. There were no more licenses available. My workload was 20 fights vs. a normal plan of 18. Seventeen of my flights were scheduled out in a one hour period. (Shift starts at XA:00. First flight due out at XC:00 and the 17th was due out at XD:00). I had a major snow storm out over the plains; frequency outage in the vicinity of ZZZ. I had to build around ZZZ and had a couple of transcontinental flights for good measure. After the computer delay of 30 minutes I went to work at XA:30 looking at weather and MELs and contacting ramps with restrictions. I have long advocated for a maximum of 18 flights on [this] desk. They were originally designed for this number (some dispute this claim). I have had discussions with numerous members of management; [supervisory dispatchers] and coworkers about why this should be the maximum. We have experienced and documented problems when the number of flights exceeds 18. When coupled with the compression (numerous departures in a short time period) it only makes these types of mistakes more likely. Today; it caused me to rush and miss a MEL item. I feel like I was setup to fail when I walked through the door. An inoperative computer system; excessive number of flights and a tight compression of departures. I realize that responsibility rests on me for my work; but these issues continue to be ignored time and time again. first release was generated at approx. XB:05. This particular flight had two MELs. The first was a broken lock and the other was a fuel penalty. I looked at the lock MEL first; called the ramp with the restrictions and then failed to go back and account for the fuel penalty.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Dispatcher reported that a heavy workload; inoperative computer; and difficult weather; contributed to a fuel miscalculation when preparing a flight release.

Report_1_Narrative: We were cleared for the ILS for Runway XXR in ZZZ. ZZZ at the time was CAT II minimums showing 3/4 mile visibly and 300 feet ceilings. We started getting a LOC flag prior to final approach fix. We broke off the approach and executed a missed approach. Knowing that there are many variables as to why we would not be getting reliable LOC information we elected to try a CAT II again but to a different runway. We go set up again for the ILS for Runway XXR. While intercepting we received a LOC flag again about 18 DME from the LOC. Again knowing that there are many variables that go into receiving a good signal we decided to give it a few more miles. We caught the LOC and GS and executed a CAT II to a landing. The only thing I can think that was improper about this circumstance was the continuation of a CAT II after receiving a LOC flag. It's being 18 miles out I believe we were in some gray area. At any rate we wrote up the LOC on the aircraft so that it could be ruled out as the cause. Perhaps the LOC on Runway XXR was not strong enough or there was interference from the proceeding aircraft causing the localizer. Or it was the aircraft itself. I think we did most everything right. It just felt weird to write up the LOC after a successful CAT II approach. I didn't see any reason we shouldn't try the CAT II we had plenty of fuel and had an alternate already specified.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported continuing with a Category II approach after receiving the LOC flag indication prior to localizer and glideslope intercept.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Situational Awareness; Workload; Distraction; Human-Machine Interface
Person_2_Human_Factors: Situational Awareness; Workload; Human-Machine Interface; Distraction
Report_1_Narrative: [We were] inbound to Ontario; CA. Prior to the descent the flight was brief following the [approach briefing]. Ontario was landing 8L and 8R; with good VFR weather and a light wind from the west. The crew descended on the Ziggy 7 arrival and was given a clearance to track outbound on 270 radial after Paradise VOR. There was a distraction trying to set up the tracking of a radial in the FMS by the pilot monitoring. As the pilot flying I decided to use the VOR and VOR mode to accomplish this. We complied with clearance and were cleared to 3;000 feet.After leveling at 3;000 feet a traffic report was issued for a helicopter at 1 o'clock and 4;000 feet. We were given a base leg heading of 320. After starting this turn an amber target showed up on the PFD (Primary Flight Display) at our altitude. I was looking out the window for traffic; in a matter of 2 seconds the Captain pushed forward on the controls; we got a TA/RA descend descend warning; I saw a small aircraft at 2 o'clock and 100 yards; I turned off the Autopilot and Autothrottle stopped the turn towards the small aircraft and descended to 2;500 feet. [We were] cleared to remain at 2;600 feet and received radar vectors to join the Localizer and landed 8L. The Captain was the pilot monitoring and the First Officer was the pilot flying. The ATC controller did make some kind of apology regarding the event. There was a minor distraction regarding the tuning of our radios. I had the VOR tuned and needed to make a switch to the ILS frequency. This took a matter of seconds to correct and we had the airport in sight the entire time.The Captain and I debriefed the event and felt we made all the correct decisions. The next day we confirmed how to track a radial using the FMS and LNAV mode. A note regarding small aircraft in vicinity might be a good idea. Knowing how to set up the FMS to track a radial would be helpful. Above all fly the airplane; keep your eyes outside; and expect the unexpected.
Report_2_Narrative: Descending on the ZIGGY ARRIVAL ATC gave clearance to fly the PDZ 270 radial after PDZ. PM (Pilot Monitoring) was unable to input the radial to fly in LNAV and the PF (Pilot Flying) flew the radial using raw data. ATC gave clearance to descend from 4;000 to 3;000 with a right turn to a heading of 340 for vectors to 08L. ATC advised traffic (helicopter) in the turn at 3;500 and gave clearance to continue turn to 020. Helicopter traffic was never observed. On TCAS PM saw a target which appeared to be at 3;000 feet on the 020 heading and advised PF to stop turn. TCAS aural warning TA 'traffic traffic' annunciated and PM saw traffic as TCAS aural alert advised an RA 'traffic descend now'. PF and PM both pushed controls forward as conflicting traffic continued to descend and turn into the jets path. PM advised ATC of the new heading altitude deviation due to the RA. Conflict was resolved at 2;300 feet; PF leveled off and started climb back up to 3;000. ATC advised stop climb at 2;600 and continue turn to 020 to intercept 08L LOC with an apology for conflict. PF intercepted GS inside NAROD (FAF 08L) due to ALT (Altitude) assignment by ATC of 2;600 feet. PF and PM had field in site and terrain in site during all phases. ATC reported 'helicopter' traffic at 3;500. Both PM and PF did not observe the traffic on TCAS at 3500 nor saw any helicopter traffic in the initial turn. Controller change during the descent from 4;000-3;000 feet. Weather was VMC daytime.The clearance received to fly the 270R outbound caused PM and PF to be distracted. PM could not get the radial to input in the FMC and therefore the PF flew raw data. This created additional threats which created additional distractions at the low ALT 2;600 with terrain all around. Having had to use RAW DATA the radio panel had mismatched frequencies and MCP had mismatched courses in the selectors which caused FD to give incorrect LOC info. PM was able to configure the MCP/radio panel and EFIS in time to capture LOC before crossing LOC. It caused the PM to be heads down instead of assisting PF in confirming the airport in sight for a visual backup. During debrief both pilots agreed that asking for a climb back to 3;000 may have helped with visual guidance to help with positional awareness. The following leg PM/PF practiced input of radials off VOR stations to create a less threatening environment for the 'next time.'
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported an airborne conflict during descent to landing at ONT.

Report_1_Narrative: Departing ZZZ1 for ZZZ2 I was the PM (Pilot Monitoring) and the CA (Captain) was the PF (Pilot Flying). We planned a low altitude flight due to the shortness of the leg. Some altitudes in the legs page were edited to allow the lower cruise altitude to be selected. The flaps 10 takeoff went as normal (LNAV/VNAV). The PF called for flaps 1 as near as I can recall. I believe this is the case as most if not all of our previous legs had been flaps 5 takeoffs. I was distracted with a radio call or frequency change and I moved the flaps to 1 and did not catch the error. Shortly after that; the FMC changed to the descent phase and the speed bug moved to the flaps 5 maneuver speed; and the A/T (Auto Throttle) mode went from N1 to FMC speed; which resulted in the flaps 5 maneuver speed being the A/T target. As; or just prior to this happening the PF called for flaps up. I moved the flap lever to the up position; and since we were no longer accelerating got a momentary stick shaker. The PF instinctively lowered the nose reducing the AOA (Angle Of Attack). I increased the speed in the MCP window to get the A/T to command acceleration. The remainder of the flight was normal.Suggest crews be alert for unusual mode reversions when using low altitudes for cruise. I would probably use non VNAV takeoff procedures in the future. The big lesson is not new; vigilance absolutely has to be maintained during the 'red' parts of the flight path. The PM job is challenging and can be intolerant of errors.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier flight crew reported a procedure error during flap retraction.

Report_1_Narrative: While performing task card Passenger Compartment Seat Installation in conjunction with the STA (Station) 540 slot sealant inspection seat row 12ABC was inadvertently reinstalled in the wrong seat row position. Although we do not remove seat row 13ABC for this inspection; somehow row 13ABC and 12ABC were in swapped positions as reported by an inflight crew member due to tray table operation being impaired due to the armrest tray table seat row being installed in the wrong seat row position. Although I know I verified part numbers and serial numbers of all rows of seats after they were removed to facilitate the STA 540 slot sealant inspection; I cannot be certain that I verified part number and serial number of seat row 12ABC after final installation as required per the task card step. Seat row 12ABC being swapped with 13ABC is an anomaly that I can not explain as we do not remove seat row 13ABC during this process. I understand that I could have possibly transposed part numbers during my inspection and let the incorrect part number get reinstalled in the wrong position if that seat row arrived in the wrong position which is the only way I can account for this seat row being in the incorrect position per the drawing as we never removed row 13ABC.
Report_1_Synopsis: Maintenance Technician reports that passenger seat row was installed in the wrong position.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Troubleshooting; Workload; Situational Awareness; Human-Machine Interface; Distraction
Report_1_Narrative: We were approximately 20 miles SE of the airport in the mountains on a sight-seeing flight. I was PIC (Pilot In Command) and the only pilot on board with 2 passengers. At 4;500 MSL the AWOS was intermittent because of the mountains. The MEF (Maximum Elevation Figure) on the sectional chart was 4;400 MSL and I was working my around some shorter hills. While experiencing some lighter bumps over a ridge; the 'GEAR IN TRANSIT' annunciator light lit up. I immediately checked to make sure I hadn't selected the gear handle down because we were too far away from the airport to have the gear down. The selector handle was still in the 'GEAR UP' position so my next instinct was to grab the emergency gear override and hold it in the 'UP' position to keep the gear from extending so far out. I checked the circuit breaker and everything seemed normal. I cycled the gear down and got 3 green lights and when cycled back up the green lights went away but the transit light never turned off. The AWOS suddenly kicked in and led me to decide on Runway 8 which meant I would cross the airport midfield and enter a tear drop for a left downwind to Runway 8. On the sectional I saw the altitude as 1;907 and decided to over fly the field at 2;500. In my mind 1;907 was pattern altitude and not the airport altitude. My mind was still on making sure my gear didn't fall down and create more drag for me that far away from the airport. About 1.5 miles to the south of the airport I once again communicated on the CTAF of my intentions to over fly the field at 2;500. One aircraft said they were back taxiing and going to depart Runway 8. As we approached the airport I felt like I was too low even though I was at 2;500 and then realized my mistake by how well I could see details on the ground. I quickly announced my intentions to climb up to traffic pattern altitude of 2;900 feet just before reaching the south side of the airport pattern which meant I was then climbing into the pattern instead of already being at the correct altitude. Directly over the runway we were back to 2;900 feet and I continued out to do a right hand turn and enter a tear drop to the left downwind. The gear came down fine and we landed safely. The combination of trying to troubleshoot an annunciator light while listening to incoming traffic and the intermittent AWOS left me to be distracted and mixing up proper altitudes for the pattern.Better self-briefing prior to arrival to an airport would have greatly reduced the chance of this occurring. Along with remembering that I had plenty of fuel and could have circled at a safe altitude to troubleshoot and then with a clearer mind come up with a plan to land at the airport normally.
Report_1_Synopsis: PA28 pilot reported entering airport traffic pattern at incorrect altitude.

Report_1_Narrative: I had taken position after coming down from the tower working Ground Control. A priority handling had been coordinated with Aircraft X with an engine out. This had been coordinated at least 45 minutes prior to the aircraft's arrival. It was briefed from the relieved controller that this aircraft had requested 'wide vectors for an ILS.' At the same time Aircraft Z was inbound on the RNAV arrival along with Aircraft Y call sign unknown. In my judgement as well as the relieved Controller both of these aircraft would have arrived easily before Aircraft X came in on the ILS. I cleared Aircraft Y for the Visual Approach to the right parallel runway and decided to change the Aircraft Y to the left after they requested the ILS. Aircraft X changed his mind for the Visual Approach which I approved. I asked Aircraft X if they could visually follow the Aircraft Y and they said they would not because of wake turbulence. Since I did not issue a 30 degree intercept we coordinated with the tower to issue a go-around to Aircraft Y. We decided not to send the Aircraft Y around because he was established on the ILS even though I had not issued a 30 degree intercept for Aircraft X. In my opinion wake turbulence to a priority handling aircraft was more of a factor than a parallel runway approach.Due to the busy nature of this session I think splitting the radar position may have been warranted. The relieved Controller had been on position for over 1 hour and 45 minutes. Aircraft X changing his mind mid sequence also caused a lot of problems. I was wary of issuing delay vectors to an aircraft that was a priority handling.
Report_1_Synopsis: GSO TRACON Controller reported improperly turning an aircraft onto final with another aircraft on approach to the parallel runway.

Report_1_Narrative: ZZZ1 Center had a positive COVID test from an individual in their building. The decision was made to go ATC-0 in the middle of the afternoon to perform a Level 3 cleaning.  I would completely understand the need to do the cleaning immediately; even if it was a high traffic time; if the individual had started not feeling well during that shift; or during the any shift in the previous 24 hours.  This was not the situation here. The positive test came from an individual that had not been in the building in X days!  Every Controller that had worked in the previous X days already had worked in a potentially contaminated area. There was zero benefit to go down at that time. The decision makers did nothing that was reasonable and responsible in this situation. Reasonable and responsible would have been to wait for a slower traffic period to get the clean accomplished. I had Aircraft X that had been in the air for 15+20 hours. I was forced to route him over an hour [out] of his way which put him in a minimum fuel situation.  We had MedEvac flights; on critical missions that were not allowed to pick up their patients.  I would hate to know how many passengers missed their connecting flights. We put our controllers; pilots; and flying public in an unnecessary unsafe situation.When an individual has not been in the building in the past 24 hours DO NOT CLEAN during a high traffic period.
Report_1_Synopsis: Center Controller reported an adjacent Center going to ATC Zero due to COVID-19 cleaning and having aircraft that were not allowed on filed routes.

Report_1_Narrative: We were cleared for the visual approach to Runway 35R at 9;000 feet. The DRUMM approach segment was to 9;000 feet; and we started down to 7;000 feet for FRONZ approach segment. ATC alerted us of a MVA altitude alert. We corrected up to the altitude of 7;500 feet as ATC said that altitude was needed for that segment. We were cleared for the visual and were following the step down altitudes.I contacted one of our managers here at the Company; and they followed up on it for me and there was no documentation noted by ATC of any issues or violations. Company Manager said that we might have touched the Class B airspace limit and that would trigger the same alert per DEN ATC. The rest of the flight was uneventful.
Report_2_Narrative: We were at 9;000 feet MSL approximately three miles east of DRUMM on the visual to Runway 35R. We had Runway 35R in sight and were cleared the visual. Abeam DRUMM we started a descent to 7;000 feet MSL. We leveled at 7;000 feet in between DRUMM and the FAF FRONZ. ATC informed us of a low altitude alert and advised the MVA was 7;500 feet. We were approximately 1;200 feet above the terrain and out of caution climbed up to 7;500 feet and intercept glidepath shortly later. No GPWS alerts occurred.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported receiving altitude alert from ATC on approach to DEN airport.

Report_1_Narrative: I was the pilot flying into ROA at night. We were at 6;000 abeam the airport on a left downwind for Runway 6. We were cleared for the visual approach and I asked for 3;000 feet to be set into the FCP (Flight Control Panel). I was aware there was a ridge we would need to cross on our left base turn; charted at 2;000 feet on the RNAV (GPS) Y approach plate. I planned to descend to 3;000 while turning base and turn onto final at HIVLU; charted at 2;700 on the vertical profile of the approach plate. I began a descent at 2;000 FPM just prior to turning base. On the base leg; I believe due to the rate of descent; a GPWS terrain warning occurred. I immediately increased the power; increased pitch; and arrested the descent. The warning stopped. The ridge was visible throughout the event and the aircraft did not descend below 3;000 until past the ridge and beginning a turn to intercept the final approach course. We continued and made a normal landing.Being unfamiliar with this approach I should have communicated my plan to the Captain and asked if he agreed. After landing we discussed the approach and he explained that we could have descended on downwind to 5;200; continued past the ridge; turned base at or just inside DIXXY; and then followed the descent profile on the approach plate. I agree with his assessment; that would have been a better course of action. In the future I will verbalize my intentions; particularly on approaches I am unfamiliar with; and have a discussion to collaboratively determine the best course of action.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported receiving GPWS alert during approach to land at ROA airport.

Report_1_Narrative: After landing on Runway 12R; Tower instructed us to exit the runway at Taxiway C3; hold short of Taxiway C (parallel taxiway) and contact ground on 121.7. As we approached Taxiway C3; I saw an Aircraft Y taxiing northwest on Taxiway C with moderate speed. The Aircraft Y was approaching Taxiway C3 and it appeared that we had been instructed to hold short of Taxiway C so the Aircraft Y could pass in front of us right to left. As the CA (Captain) made the ninety-degree left turn to exit the runway onto Taxiway C3; I switched to ground control frequency 121.7 as instructed. The CA then stopped with the nose of our aircraft near the runway holding position marking on Taxiway C3. This left the aft end of our aircraft on the runway. The Aircraft Y then stopped short of Taxiway C3. As I was about to ask for clarifying instructions after switching frequencies; Ground Control instructed the Aircraft Y to continue taxiing and then asked if we were on his frequency. I responded that we were and then Ground Control instructed us to turn right on Taxiway C (behind the Aircraft Y that had by this point passed through the intersection) and then left on Taxiway B4 to our gate. As we taxied southeast on Taxiway C Ground Control advised us that we had created a dangerous situation by not fully exiting the runway. He informed us that a light general aviation aircraft had taken off while part of our aircraft was still on the runway. At the time it happened; I agreed with the CA's decision to stop the aircraft since we were unaware of the Aircraft Y's taxi instructions (we had just switched to Ground); and the appearance that the Aircraft Y may taxi through the intersection due to its rate of speed and remaining distance to C3. I also wondered why tower control had cleared an aircraft to take off while we still occupied the runway. On the taxi out for our return leg; we observed that there was a taxiway hold short line further ahead on C3 that would have allowed us to pull further forward; but our tail would still likely have been over the runway hold short line.Limited distance between the runway and Taxiway C. Lack of communication at a critical juncture: we were unaware of the Aircraft Y's taxi instructions as we had just switched to ground; and Tower didn't advise us of them when issuing us our initial taxi instructions (ie '... Aircraft Y will hold short.') The Tower Controller cleared an aircraft to take off while part of our aircraft was still within the boundary of the runway. The Ground Controller did not instruct the Aircraft Y to continue taxiing with a sense of urgency. Better communication from ATC. Better awareness of the location of taxiway hold short lines (of possible runway turn-offs) as a part of our approach brief.
Report_2_Narrative: After landing on Runway 12R; tower instructed us to exit the runway at Taxiway C3; hold short of Taxiway C (parallel taxiway) and contact Ground on 121.7. As we approached Taxiway C3; I observed an Aircraft Y taxiing northwest on Taxiway C with moderate speed. The Aircraft Y was approaching Taxiway C3 and it appeared that we had been instructed to hold short of Taxiway C so the Aircraft Y could pass in front of us right to left. As I made the ninety-degree left turn to exit the runway onto Taxiway C3 at less than 12 knots of ground speed; the FO switched to ground control frequency 121.7 as instructed. I stopped with the nose of our aircraft near the runway holding position marking on Taxiway C3 because of the short distance to Taxiway C in front of us. This left the aft end of our aircraft on the runway. The Aircraft Y then stopped short of Taxiway C3. Ground Control instructed the Aircraft Y to continue taxiing. After the Aircraft Y passed Taxiway C3; Ground Control asked if we were on his frequency. When the FO responded in the affirmative; ground control instructed us to turn right on Taxiway C then left on Taxiway B4 to our gate. As we taxied southeast on Taxiway C Ground Control advised us that we had created a dangerous situation by not fully exiting the runway. He told us that a light general aviation aircraft had taken off while part of our aircraft was still on the runway. At the time; I felt that I could not have fully exited the runway considering the limited distance available to me on Taxiway C3. I also wondered why Tower Control had cleared an aircraft to take off while we still occupied the runway. On the next flight; we taxied out on Taxiway C. As we passed Taxiway C3 I noticed a taxiway holding position marking on Taxiway C3 that I had not observed on the inbound flight. Although the taxiway holding position marking appeared too close to Taxiway C; I could have taxied farther onto Taxiway C3 after exiting the runway on the inbound flight. If I had taxied to what I considered a safe distance from Taxiway C; our tail probably would not have been within the lateral boundaries of the runway; but it would have been on the runway side of the runway holding position marking on Taxiway C3. Limited distance between the runway and Taxiway C prevented us from fully vacating the runway while complying with the instruction to hold short of Taxiway C. The Tower Controller cleared an aircraft to take off while part of our aircraft was still within the boundary of the runway. The Ground Controller did not instruct the Aircraft Y to continue taxiing with a sense of urgency. When instructed to hold short of a taxiway after vacating a runway; stop the aircraft as close as safely possible to the restricting taxiway. Even if your aircraft is not completely clear of the runway; risk will be diminished by reducing the amount of your aircraft remaining within the runway boundary.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported lack of communication from ATC during taxi at MMUN airport resulted in a ground conflict.

Report_1_Narrative: Cleared for visual approach to Runway XXL on modified downwind; at 3;000 feet. Maneuvered aircraft to arrive at ZZZZZ at 3;000 to intercept LOC/ Glideslope simultaneously. Thought I was going to be above glideslope at ZZZZZ; asked FO to set 2;000 feet acquired Localizer inside of ZZZZZ; still at flaps 3. Drove into glideslope; selected flaps full. Radio altimeter briefly showed 800 feet due to terrain variation. Broke SOP of being fully configured by 1;000 feet.I accepted a night visual approach after a 12 hour; three leg duty day. Fatigue was a contributor. Hurried visual; should have intercepted final at IAF vs. FAF. My currency was spotty due to reduced flying on reserve.Never accept short visual approaches at end of long duty day.
Report_2_Narrative: I was acting as PM. Approaching ZZZ at night from the SW with a high overcast layer above. ATC had us on a downwind leg for [Runway] XXL at 4;000. The autopilot and auto thrust were engaged. Approximately abeam the end of the runway; ATC asked us if we had the field in sight. The CA/PF says he does; so I reported the field in sight. ATC then cleared us for the visual XXL. The PF then set 3;000 in the FCU and I confirmed and referenced the plate showing the FAF ZZZZZ at 3000. I believe the PF went open descent to 3;000 from 4;000. The PF then began his base leg turn. The intercept angle initially looked like it was going to join the final just outside of the FAF. As we approached 3;000 the PF continued the turn in. He asked me to set 2;000 into the FCU and set 1;000 v/s down. I complied as it appeared to me that the PF was trying to intercept the course and I assumed he was going to join inside of ZZZZZ/FAF. He readjusted his intercept to join the final at ZZZZZ or just outside it. By that time I began to realize we were getting low on the profile. I still had visual contact with the runway. At approximately that time; the airplane leveled at 2000 just inside of ZZZZZ and ZZZ tower advised us of a low altitude alert and to check our altitude with the current altimeter setting. I replied with our call sign. We continued at 2;000 until intercepting the glideslope and landed safely. We were approaching the end of a long duty day and it was a non eventful and quiet flight; so fatigue was a possible factor. I am also familiar with operating into ZZZ; so I was a bit complacent; as well as being in VFR conditions and being able to see the runway. Having both pilots confirm and verify any further altitude changes in the FCU after the setting of the lowest charted altitudes for the approach used.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported an unstablized approach and cited fatigue; time pressure and reduced flying as contributing factors.

Report_1_Narrative: On the taxiway contacted Tower.  After check in we thought we heard 'clear for takeoff;' but neither of us were sure so I asked the First Officer to confirm if we were cleared for takeoff. The First Officer asked this question and the very clear reply was 'affirmative.'  We entered the runway and were subsequently told while finishing our line up on centerline to stop and hold position.  After a delay we were told of 'pilot deviation' and then cleared for takeoff.I allowed an 'affirmative' reply by Tower to suffice for a query on were we cleared for takeoff.  That is the root cause.  'Affirmative' is not the correct response and in retrospect I believe Tower perhaps misunderstood our query.  Choice of words and insistence on clarification.  I should have asked the First Officer to say 'Tower say again.'  Tower would then have repeated all instructions.  Looking back the word 'Affirmative' is not enough.  I allowed my leeway on foreign controllers English and accents to accept 'affirmative' for a cleared for takeoff query rather than insisting on hearing the entire standard 'cleared for takeoff' verbiage. The Tower could have easily misunderstood us and replied 'Affirmative' to what Tower believed was the question.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported confusing communications regarding the takeoff clearance resulted in ATC advising them they departed RCTP airport without a takeoff clearance.

Report_1_Narrative: The incident occurred during an otherwise uneventful reposition flight from ZZZ - ZZZ1. The PIC was acting as Pilot Monitoring; and the FO as Pilot Flying. The filed altitude was FL200; but the flight had requested and received FL220 approximately 45 minutes to an hour prior to the incident to escape some moderate turbulence.  At the time of the incident; the conditions were IMC with intermittent patches of VMC; light turbulence; and trace to light icing at about -23 deg C. The aircraft was on the western edge of the occluded segment of a frontal low. The first indication was the De-Ice Boots CAS. The FO remained Pilot Flying; and PIC attempted to troubleshoot the problem with the QRH. In addition; the QRH checklist was cross checked by the FO. Unfortunately; the problem did not reset; so the crew determined that it was not safe to remain in icing conditions without wing De-ice capability. The crew then examined alternates; eventually deciding on ZZZ2 due to the availability of a runway greater than 10;000 feet in length; its position behind (west) the front; and the prevailing conditions of unrestricted visibility and a 900 foot ceiling. The PM then informed ARTCC of the need to divert and received a vector for the ILS XX. During the descent; the PM calculated the required landing distance for the Flaps 0 deg Boot Fail scenario; the approach was set up and briefed; and the appropriate checklists were run. Due to the failure of the De-ice Boots; some mixed icing on the leading edge; clear runback ice on inside third of the upper surface; and rime on the underside of the airfoil accumulated during descent and approach.  The crew monitored the accumulation visually and by referencing the trim indicators to ensure that abnormal force was not required to control the aircraft. The approach and landing was conducted at Flaps 0 deg and in accordance with procedure for landing with inoperative boots.
Report_1_Synopsis: PC-12 Captain reported an uneventful mechanical diversion due to Ice & Rain Protection system malfunction during icing conditions.

Report_1_Narrative: About 10 minutes prior to scheduled passenger flight pushback at ZZZ; received a HAZMAT NOTOC (hazardous material notice to Captain).  There were 6 lines of HAZMAT of which 5 were normal but one stood out with lithium metal batteries; ERG (emergency response guidebook) code 12FG.  I queried the messenger about them; he said he could take a picture of the box to show me.  While he went to do that I discussed the situation with the FO (First Officer).  The battery weight was.15 kg or just a bit over 5 ounces and contained in equipment.  That size battery is similar in weight to our iPad batteries.  12FG code is risk of fire/heat/smoke with the additional risk Z 'aircraft cargo fire suppression system may not extinguish or contain the fire.  Consider landing immediately'.  When carried in our cargo hold; with passengers on board; that sort of risk gets my attention.  When the messenger returned with the picture I queried him about carrying that cargo in the cockpit or passenger compartment where we at least have our BCB battery containment bag; in case something went wrong.  He said they didn't know which box batteries were in so that wasn't possible.  It was almost push time so I called and discussed the situation with Dispatch.  They agreed with my concern and said they weren't experts on HAZMAT but could research who was or we could just remove the batteries in the interest of expediency.  We then opted for removing the lithium batteries for simplicity and timeliness.  After this was accomplished; we got a revised load closeout and were on our way about 20-30 minutes late.  The rest of our flight was uneventful.  Having reviewed FOM guidance on this issue previously; I consider it somewhat vague.  While the likelihood for these batteries to start burning is slim; the impact would be catastrophic and the ERG  code even warns us of this.  This could easily be mitigated by having an item like this in the passenger cabin or cockpit where FAs (flight attendants) or pilots could at least deal with the threat with the BCBs which are provided for an unlikely event such as this.  FOM  deal[s] with this and state or imply that these types of things should not be in the cargo compartment.  FOM addresses HAZMAT codes but really gives no guidance other than inspecting NOTOC paperwork for date; tail number etc.I've been involved in carrying lots of hazardous materials in aircraft over my career and believe I'm well versed on the risk vs reward of it.  While technically the NOTOC I received was legal per our FOM; the risk of these batteries also noted on the NOTOC; didn't appear to make sense from a risk management or an SMS (safety management systems) standpoint.  Thus my questions about better potential options.  If we are intentionally doing something like this; I; Dispatch; other pilots etc would probably be better served with more of a heads up on the decision process and other options sooner in the departure process.  Were we just doing the minimum legal or is there a more appropriate way in hindsight?  It certainly seemed like pushback time induced pressure discouraged discussion/questions about this sort of thing.
Report_1_Synopsis: B737-800 Captain reported refusing Hazmat cargo due to vague FOM guidance as well as lack of definitive Dispatch information regarding the risk of transporting Hazmat cargo.

Report_1_Narrative: While on a visual approach to [Runway] XXR; I was the PF. I hadn't flown in a month and a half or so; and the weather was conducive to trying to practice skills; so I turned off the AP/AT/FD. While over the ZZZ1 area; we received an RA directing me to level off. After complying with the RA; I began to descend to catch up to the approach; but at the altitude I was at; and the descent rate required to get back on the approach; I would not have been able to do so within stabilized approach criteria; so I conducted a go-around.The go-around was not smooth; and left room for improvement; but all call outs were made; and the checklists were accomplished. After passing through about 1;300 feet or so; we were assigned an altitude of 2;000 feet. The FO selected 2;000 feet and made the comment that we were about 700 feet away. We were climbing at a high rate as we were in TOGA (Still no AP/AT); and I was trying to get the plane slowed down; and arresting the climb rate; the FD began to turn to follow the missed approach for the ILS; as we had loaded it as the backup. We had yet received instruction as to what direction to turn; since we were assigned the visual approach. Between the FD turning and leveling off; it was at this point that I was focused on wanting the aircraft to continue straight on runway heading; and I flew through the 2;000 feet restriction; to my recollection by about 300 feet. The PM attempted to get some sort of instruction from ATC as to what they would like us to do; but struggled to get a word in on the radio. Finally they called and assigned us a vector. They also said since we went past 2;000; to level off at 2;500 feet. At this point; we had a moment; and was able to match up the information on the PFD with what I was wanting; and was able to add back in the AP/AT.This event felt like a culmination of a few problems. The root cause is that I; as the Captain; wasn't as prepared as I should have been. Having flown so little the last few months after upgrade sign off in month; I have been limited to just XX hours of total flying since month; my skill upkeep has been mainly book studying. While this is important; it does not replace being behind the controls of an aircraft.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported an unstabilized approach leading to a go-around; which then resulted in an altitude deviation. The Captain cited lack of flying as a contributing factor.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Workload; Troubleshooting; Time Pressure; Physiological - Other; Communication Breakdown; Distraction
Report_1_Narrative: Operating at FL190. After cruise checklist was completed; cabin altitude was indicating approximate 10;000 feet. After 5 to 10 minutes' elapsed; I felt a change in pressure inside the aircraft. When I crosschecked the cabin altitude climb was indicating 4;000 feet climbing; a minute later; the cabin altitude warning illuminated. This was followed by aircraft memory item and checklist. I pulled O2 knob located left upper just left of the external power switch and as I pulled the mask I placed the O2 mask on emergency mode and no oxygen was flowing. I placed it back on normal operation and nothing happened. I switched the mic to the O2 mask and advised ATC for urgent descent 10;000 feet. I discovered that ATC was unable to hear me at all.  I looked over and the switch for the microphone was placed on oxygen mask and nothing seemed to fix the problem. The cabin altitude was indicating roughly about 20;000 to 21;000 feet from what I recall. I switched again to my headset and requested '...priority; need to descend now to 10;000 feet pressurization problems.' As soon as I talked to ATC; I started immediate descent memory item and checklist; while descending; I took the First Officer mask to see for O2 flow and no O2 was flowing; I double checked the O2 handle.  I pulled both located on the Captain left hand side upper and lower; and nothing resulted for O2 function. Since I was indicating 60 miles from my departure airport; I decided to return since for my judgment it was unsafe to continue the flight without O2 flow; no O2 mask microphone and pressurization problems. Upon reaching 10;000 feet the cabin stabilized and the cabin altitude indicator was no longer illuminated with a cabin altitude about 9;000 feet.ATC gave me instructions to descend to 5;000 feet and while at it; the cabin altitude started to jump 5;500 feet up followed by a descent to 4;000 feet and this continued all the way to 3;000 feet. At that moment; I was feeling uncomfortable since my ears where hurting and I knew I was not feeling 100%. At 3;000 feet; I turned off my bleed air and flew the aircraft unpressurized. Why ? I had 'ears popping' several times at this time and I wanted to make the little time left comfortable in order to make a safe landing; since this constant climb and descend from the cabin was making me feel really weak. Landed the aircraft successfully without any major issues. After landing Maintenance and Station manager met me at the airplane.  I took  time at the crew van to see if I felt better and I did.  This resulted in a maintenance write up for 3 items.  Unable to control cabin altitude; O2 Mask Mic not operating; O2 not flowing properly.
Report_1_Synopsis: BE1900 pilot reported aircraft lost pressurization; oxygen masks; and oxygen masks microphone failed during cruise resulting in a return to departure airport.

Report_1_Narrative: Onboard the aircraft was a piece of Hazmat which I was unaware of.  The company manifest did not disclose it and I was not notified by any company personnel.  I am unsure of when the piece was loaded; if it was during the preload process or while I was present.  Upon finding the Hazmat during aircraft unloading; I reported it to Dispatch.
Report_1_Synopsis: Captain reported the transport of undocumented Hazmat package.

Report_1_Narrative: A Flight Attendant in my recurrent class notified the company on [date] that they tested positive for COVID-19. Company notified me [10 days later].  That is 10 days after Company was notified which I find to be completely unacceptable. I had a trip and could have exposed hundreds of passengers plus my crew.  I should also add that I exposed my family and I am a caregiver for my XX year old father and YY year old mother.  I find this to be an egregious safety concern in delay of notification since I shared a classroom and training aids to include donning the PBE and POB (Portable Oxygen Bottle) with someone who has since been confirmed positive.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Attendant reported being notified by company 10 days after another Flight Attendant tested positive for COVID-19.

Report_1_Narrative: VFR flight from ZZZ1 towards ZZZ2 and return with no specific route. Tablet GPS lost connection with autopilot and I lost situational awareness trying to get the GPS reconnected (using AVARE app). When I finally abandoned the effort and looked at the GPS I realized I was in ZZZ Class B airspace at approximately 3;200 MSL instead of below the 3;000 MSL floor as I usually am. Corrected altitude immediately and left the Class B; went home and landed.I should have had the GPS completely set up before departure and should also have stayed at my usual altitude of 2;500 MSL for local flights.  I really don't have an excuse for losing situational awareness. Problem was exacerbated by opening a 2nd app (Naviator) at which point I didn't know which app might have been trying to control the autopilot.  I will certainly not make that mistake again! Had not flown at all from 5 months so I am admittedly not as proficient as I would like to be. Will be correcting that situation shortly also!
Report_1_Synopsis: GA pilot reported losing GPS connection on tablet resulting in a Class B airspace incursion.

Report_1_Narrative: After having sent 2 test balloons (party balloons with helium) to check winds and finding they both showed no more than 7 knots of wind and practically went straight up as far as I could see them. Only clouds in the visible area were small white cumulus approximately 10;000 feet high. I chose to launch my hot air balloon near in a dirt lot with no obstruction down wind and more than enough room to move around in case of wind gusts. Knowing I might experience some gusts of wind due to only one local airport having seen gusts up to 14 knots. During my entire set up and inflation; I hadn't experienced any gusts more than 10 knot. After inflating the balloon to an upright position and the balloon maintaining its usual shape and taking pressure as normal I asked the passengers to load into the balloon basket. I was still tied to the van with a 5/8' polyester yacht braided rope and started heating the balloon with a fuel tank only used for the purpose of inflation to buoyancy.Before I could heat the balloon to buoyancy the wind hit the balloon from the opposite direction pushing me toward the passenger van westbound. Then hit me again heading east at an estimated 30 knots while dragging the balloon to the end of the tie down rope. The rope then broke and the balloon began to drag across the large lot. I gave full power to the burners trying to heat the balloon into flight knowing I wouldn't be able to stop the balloon on the ground in that speed of wind before hitting something. We started to lift off the ground approximately 10 to 15 feet off the ground and the balloon started descending again toward a chain link fence. Once hitting the fence was inevitable I started opening the deflation port. It took an additional acre of land for the balloon to come to a complete stop on another chain link fence.After this was all over the wind had completely stopped; and had relatively calm winds the rest of the evening. All of the small cumulus clouds were completely gone after this incident with clear skies. Making me assume those clouds had dissipated causing outflow gusts of at least 30 knots. In total hitting 3 chain-link fences. All passengers and myself were unharmed with no injuries and no damage to the balloon to cause it to be unairworthy.
Report_1_Synopsis: A Balloon pilot preparing for departure reported unexpected gusts of wind blew the balloon across the ground uncontrolled. The pilot became airborne for a short period before coming to rest against a chain link fence with no injuries or damage to the balloon.

Report_1_Narrative: I had heard that the FAA had suspended/extended GA compliance regulation deadlines due to COVID-19. I have operated an aircraft outside of my normal deadline date for medical and BFR requirements.  In the last two days I have found that this might not be the case. I purchased an additional aircraft and I don't know if the deadline for registering the plane has also been extended or not.I shouldn't be making assumptions or go by information that I am hearing from the airport/other pilots or online. No additional flights will be made until I verify that I am in compliance with the proper FAA office.
Report_1_Synopsis: Pilot reported not being sure of General Aviation Compliance regulation deadlines.

Report_1_Narrative: This was a second flight of the night shift; and was unusually busy; because the hospital we are associated with is understaffed because of COVID. We got the call to go to ZZZ; and the weather was marginal; but good enough to get in. We accepted the trip; and flew the RNAV approach to Runway XX. Later; I looked at the approach chart; and it said that the approach was not authorized at night. I think that being busy after a long period of hardly flying contributed to the error; and also that it was XA:00 in the morning. Also; due to COVID-induced rules; we had to wear masks flying; and it fogs up my glasses; making it harder to see. I need to make sure that I check all the notes on an approach before accepting a trip.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Taxi Captain reported flying an RNAV Approach which was not authorized at night.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Time Pressure; Situational Awareness; Training / Qualification
Report_1_Narrative: The weather enroute to ZZZ1 wasn't too bad. I would characterize the clouds as scattered around 9;000 to 1;0000 feet with periodic cells of precipitation. Low temperatures meant icing conditions so we avoided all precipitation. Preflight planning weather briefing was in agreement with what we were observing; and we listened to each Automated Weather of the airports we passed.The area was nearly clear skies. Few clouds if any and no observed precipitation within 20 miles. Winds and clouds were moving east; following a cold front which passed the day prior. We encountered one broken cell at 10;000 feet off our left and few clouds off our right. We climbed to 11500 feet and passed above and well clear of that cell within a short period of time.We stayed VFR; away from known icing conditions and moisture. The ride was uneventful. On the ride back; I expected the same weather. Conditions at my destination were VFR with scattered clouds up high; and a nearby airport was reporting the same. I did not check one of the airports enroute.  Radar returns on the map showed the same few cells scattered without only light precipitation. In the same region we encountered what I believed to the be the same cell we crossed over in the previous flight. We took note of precipitation left; right and ahead to the left. With a large enough gap of scattered clouds ahead to the right. We continued; and I made the decision to climb up to 10;500 feet to determine the height of the clouds. The clouds which were still only 500 feet in height; were now based around 10;500 feet.I made the decision then to climb to 12;500 feet to cross over them. I knew we were less than 30 minutes from an area which previously was nearly clear skies. Upon reaching 12;500 feet; I started the timer and we continued to cross well above the layer. I would describe this layer to be 6/8 to 7/8 as there were often breaks where we could see ground and see that the layer was not very thick in height. Roughly 10 to 15 miles; 5 to 8 minutes we noticed the clouds were becoming higher altitude; and we were losing spacing from them. We maneuvered around them as best we could; but would need to climb to stay above them and away from icing conditions. I absolutely knew that we would not be putting the airplane into known icing conditions. At this point; turning back didn't seem to be any more promising than continuing on course. We had confidence that the weather in the area was better beyond this cell; and we just witnessed the weather make a change of heart behind us.At this point; I knew that things could turn worse. As contingency; we began direct course for an airport with good weather. In the event that we reached 30 minutes above 12;500 feet or encountered any ice; we would immediately descend through the nearest break and land the airplane.As we continued; the clouds continued to rise. Still broken and overcast beneath us; we were faced with few options. Climb higher; enter known icing; or drop through a break and hope there is not precipitation around which would become ice.Entering icing conditions was not an option; or if anything a very last resort. Hypoxia was our biggest threat at altitude; and we were well aware and cautious of any symptoms. Luckily; I have had the experience of an altitude chamber and know my symptoms and signs. But we had to climb higher to avoid the icing conditions. We climbed up to 14;500 feet briefly and descended back down when able. Then the weather cleared up; the clouds became scattered; and we were able to descend back down to 8;500 feet. A total time of 24 minutes was observed above 12;500 feet. I would estimate that only 2-3 minutes were spent above 14;000 feet. No signs or symptoms of hypoxia were observed. The remainder of the flight was VFR and uneventful.The challenge was the lack of weather reporting equipment to determine the weather enroute; but this is not an excuse. I will exercise more resources such as a phone briefing or additional charts next time. I will also remember to never expect the weather to remain the same. Next time I will remember my favorite motto; Plan for the worst; and hope for the best.
Report_1_Synopsis: A flight instructor on a VFR flight reported encountering unexpected IMC weather and momentarily climbed to 14;500 feet to avoid clouds without oxygen.

Report_1_Narrative: Aircraft X was an arrival into PVU airport. He came to my sector from the northwest.  I had to vector the aircraft to get him in trail of SLC arrivals. I turned the aircraft in trail of a SLC B752.  As I turned the aircraft further north so final turn wasn't so tight; the pilot called the airport in sight. PVU was advertising Visual Approach Runway 13. I cleared the aircraft for the Visual Approach. They turned towards the airport; I shipped them to the Tower approximately 10 miles out when I saw them turning towards the airport. Almost immediately the aircraft started turning further south towards a 8;900 foot Minimum Vectoring Altitude descending out of 8000 feet. I called PVU and they said they were talking to him. I asked what they were doing and was advised the pilot stated they were making S turns or something. The aircraft descended to 5;100 feet 7 miles from the airport; elevation 4;497 feet.  At that point PVU called stating the pilot had lost the airport and was climbing to 9;000 feet. The pilot checked in with me heading 180 and climbing to 9;000 feet. I said roger. They then asked for vectors to an ILS and I stated I would when they were at Minimum Vectoring Altitudes. I vectored for the ILS with no further complications. I don't really have recommendations on my end. PVU after this incident continued to advertise Visual Approaches. My Supervisor did not want to fill out any paperwork on the incident; so they said nobody did anything wrong and to leave it at that. I felt like this should be reported somehow. The pilot was extremely low a long distance from the airport trying to scud run the Visual Approach. I knew visuals were iffy because when I descended the aircraft to 9;000 feet they were IMC; I turned them and descended them to 8;000 feet (also telling them to expect the ILS) and they called the airport. It's not surprising they were able to call the airport in sight at that point; the mountain sits below and often they can descend slightly and get the airport in sight. What's surprising is the pilot accepted the approach if clouds were that bad; that we didn't 'declare an emergency' for the aircraft when they lost the airport at 5;100 feet in an 8;900 foot Minimum Vectoring Altitude MVA; and that the supervisor wouldn't at least want to follow up with the pilot. I truly don't know why we wouldn't want to look at this further.
Report_1_Synopsis: A TRACON Controller reported an aircraft cleared for a Visual Approach turned away from the airport due to losing sight of the airport and flew below the Minimum Vectoring Altitude.

Report_1_Narrative: The rides were bad and Aircraft X asked to descend. My D-side called and requested control; but neglected to point the aircraft out to the underlying sector. I forgot about the shelf as well so I never double checked my D-side's work and I descended the aircraft. There is really no recommendations. The issues are a lack of competency on everyone's part. The D-side barely works as is; and I myself do not get enough quality time anymore because of the lack of traffic. Combined with a constant changing of sector configurations led to this issue.
Report_1_Synopsis: Center Controller reported descending an aircraft into another Controller's airspace; thinking the D-Side had pointed the aircraft out.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Training / Qualification; Workload; Time Pressure; Situational Awareness; Troubleshooting; Communication Breakdown; Confusion; Distraction
Report_1_Narrative: First day back after being off for two weeks for COVID-19 quarantine; we don't even have half of our normal staffing which is already low due to COVID.  Total number of CPC's for the day is only 6 when normally it would be at least XX.I get put on the LC1 position with no assist or LC2; I was told that there was a CFR [Call For Release] in effect for ZZZ.  It ended being super busy and it seemed like there was no flow put in place; we were pretty much operating business as usual.  I did not receive much spacing on final and I even had to send an aircraft around because of an overtake and lack of runway separation.  Approach also sent in an uncoordinated early turn IFR jet from the north east; I had to adjust his flight path to de conflict him from the [aircraft in the] traffic pattern and from a departure I had rolling on [Runway] XXR.  This created another conflict with another arrival they had doing 180 kts that they never slowed down.It was pretty overwhelming to work that volume/complexity of traffic after two weeks off and not being able to ease back into the work flow; especially when we have limited staffing/positions open and with TRACON not following the LOA's and traffic flow directives.We are going to be operating in this limited capacity working 6 days a week 10 hours a day for the next week.  There needs to be better communication and an understanding of the unfortunate circumstances that we will be working under for the next week.  It is completely unsafe to operate business as usual and I'm hoping there will be better coordination going forward.
Report_1_Synopsis: Tower Controller reported an airborne conflict resulting in an aircraft having to execute a go-around. Controller cited staffing and traffic volume as a contributing factors.

Report_1_Narrative: We were two hours late due to ATC closure (ZZZ Center). After discussing with Dispatch that we would be very close to Crew day; we launched from ZZZ to ZZZ1. Landed approximately two hours late and took off from ZZZ1 in time to land back at ZZZ within Crew day; however; upon landing (with 20 minutes to spare) there were approximately 10 aircraft waiting for a gate. I sent Dispatch an ACARS telling them that we were going to exceed our 13-hour Crew day. I was told by ZZZ Ops and Dispatch that gates were being issued 'first-come; first-serve.' We waited approximately 45 minutes before making it to a gate. Total day was approximately 30 minutes over allowed hours.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported being two hours late due to ATC COVID Center Closure and going over daily allowed work hours.

Report_1_Narrative: During boarding [I] was notified by Lead Flight Attendant and Customer Service Agent that passengers in row X123 traveling together were loud; intoxicated; disruptive; not adhering to mask policy and one was vaping in his seat. Customer service agent was in the process of removing them when one of them decided to make a display of his anger in the forward part of the aircraft near first class. I was making a cup of coffee and he directed his anger and profanity towards me. I tried to get him to step into the jetway where the other two companions were and hoped he would follow. He mentioned something about getting his jacket and passport but the companions already had them. All three people continued their verbal tirade and protest while the agent called for law enforcement. Subsequent check of their row found two cans of open alcohol containers which they brought on board. Remaining customers seated nearby told the flight attendants they were drinking and loud in the boarding area. Another nearby passenger had been 'egging' them on and also difficult with the agent at check in but he immediately complied with flight attendant instructions; apologized; and said he would not cause any trouble. I discussed this with the customer service agent and told him it was his call whether this passenger be removed as well. Based on his cooperation and lack of evidence of intoxication; he traveled uneventfully on the flight.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported that several intoxicated passengers were being disruptive and not complying with face mask policy. The Captain stated that while one passenger was being removed from the aircraft; he became angry at the Captain and used profanity.

Report_1_Narrative: The DEN NIIXX1 arrival [now NIIXX2] has two similar sounding fixes consecutive to each other; BSTON (pronounced 'Boston') and BOSSS; that could be easily confused/misheard.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported similar sounding fixes on the NIIXX 1 [now NIIXX 2] arrival into Denver which might be confused or misheard.

Report_1_Narrative: After V1 the First Officer and I noticed an odor that smelled wet; damp; musky; wet sock type of smell. This odor did not clear and remained strong throughout the duration of the flight. When we reached a safe altitude on departure; I contacted the Flight Attendant and asked if she smelled any odor or fumes. She replied positively. The FO and I requested priority handling and landed back in ZZZ. After landing; we taxied back to the gate. Speaking with the FA more after the emergency; she told us that there had been an odor during taxi and takeoff; with it increasing strongly on takeoff. The FA thought it was just her that smelled it and did not say anything; but confirmed she smelled the same odor mostly in the front to row 2A [I initially noticed] smell of fumes in cockpit and cabin. Requested priority handling; donned O2 mask; and landed in ZZZ. [My] suggestion is to emphasize in training to flight attendants if anything is out of the ordinary or unknown fumes are present to speak up and not be afraid to contact the flight deck in sterile if it may be a safety of flight issue.
Report_1_Synopsis: EMB-145 Captain reported a strong 'wet sock' type smell during takeoff resulting in a return to the departure airport.

Report_1_Narrative: It was an uncontrolled airfield; visual approach; left traffic to Runway 17. Daylight calm winds and ceiling and visibility unlimited. Terrain factors were discussed on our briefing. We built the escape maneuver on the secondary flight plan. On the UNICOM frequency we were aware of a (Air Carrier) jet that was north of the field landing south on 17. They decided to slow so we could go first. We made a shorter approach than usual and while turning towards the final approach fix and putting out flaps 3; we descended away from the terrain as it sloped down hill and we got a terrain warning and reacted appropriately. We were very aware of the terrain and were completely surprised that the GPWS sounded off. We continued the approach and landed normally.We should have just extended our downwind leg and went number 2 to the runway.Maybe a little better understanding of the normal traffic patterns on the company pages.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported GPWS alert during approach to land to MTJ airport.

Report_1_Narrative: Passing FL230 in VNAV Climb FMC airspeed was set at 310 KIAS. As airspeed approached Vmo; power was reduced but the airspeed briefly passed Vmo by about 5 knots and for 3-5 seconds. Pilot flying was new to airplane and neither of us are flying much.  Pay closer attention to FMC inputs; fly more!
Report_2_Narrative: Entered climb speed in FMS of 310. Previous Econ climb was 257/.81.  I failed to enter .81 after 310/. As the aircraft climbed speed approached MMO at FL 230. Adjusted speed in FMS but the aircraft was empty and continued to accelerate. I manually reduced the throttles; but not enough we exceeded about 5 knots before we slowed down.New to the aircraft. I had not flown since OE ended. Fly more. But we all know the environment.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported an over speed during departure and cited lack of flying as a contributing factor.
