Person_2_Human_Factors: Situational Awareness; Communication Breakdown; Time Pressure
Report_1_Narrative: In cruise I messaged Dispatch and asked the RVR for [Runway] XXR.  They told me 1400 for [Runway] XXR.  About 30 minutes from arrival we started our brief. We briefed the arrival and the approach plate for [Runway]. We then briefed the CAT2 checklist. We both put 705 feet in our DH and verified it. We did the decent check and verified it again. Did the approach check and was getting vectors to [Runway] XXR. Gear down flaps 45 before the marker.  I called 1;000 feet cleared to land when I knew something was wrong. I couldn't grasp why we only had 300 feet left to go missed. Told the First Officer something wasn't right. We hit minimums at 705 feet AGL and I called the missed. Did the missed approach; cleaned up aircraft and did the checklist. Didn't take me long to figure out what I did. The RA for [Runway] XXR is 116 feet. We put the new DH in and took our time to get set up for approach.  We got vectors on the LOC and shot the approach to a landing.We both missed the right number for the DH. I knew the approach would be to minimums so I was looking at chart in cruise so I wouldn't miss anything.  Ended up on a go around at 700 feet AGL because we had the MDA in. It was first flight of day we both felt good. Just the low visibility at destination caused a threat.Even after the lengthy briefing and checklist usage the DH was still put in there wrong. What I have learned over my career is not to get upset at the moment you realize you did something wrong.  Great training over the years and good CRM has trained me to fly the airplane. Run the appropriate checklists and then discuss what happened at a safe time later.
Report_2_Narrative: We incorrectly set the 705 feet in the DH for a CAT 2 approach and logically got the mins aural alert more than 500 feet early. We executed a go-around; set up the DH properly and flew the second approach normally.
Report_1_Synopsis: CRJ--900 flight crew reported setting the wrong DH for the approach and executing a missed earlier than required.

Report_1_Narrative: A little while after reaching cruise altitude; the flight attendants contacted us to let us know that there was a passenger who was not complying with the mask policy.  They were handling it per their guidance and keeping us informed.  Later in the flight there had been some other problems that they had informed us about. The First Officer and I had completed a bathroom rotation just before starting down into ZZZ when we got a call from the flight attendants informing us they were [having problems with this passenger]. They just wanted to be sure we knew this. I asked them to let us know if there were any problems.  Several minutes later; we received a call that this passenger had not taken kindly to the warning and had become 'verbally combative.'  I thanked them for letting us know; and asked if everyone was okay.  They replied yes; they were.  I asked them to keep us informed if there were any changes of if anything escalated; they said they would.  At this point we had begun the descent on the arrival into ZZZ; the First Officer had been flying the whole leg.  He had been managing the radios as well while I was talking to the flight attendants.  I considered that while the situation currently was Level 1; I felt it was most prudent to get the aircraft on the ground to protect my crew and the other passengers.  Additionally; felt it would reduce my workload as well as my First Officer's if we requested priority handling.  I told the First Officer what I was considering and why; and asked if he had any considerations.  He agreed that was a good choice.  I then requested priority handling with ZZZ approach and informed them of SOB and fuel remaining.  I had sent an ACARS message to Dispatch informing them of our situation.  I called ZZZ ops and informed them of the same.  I then checked in with the flight attendants to ensure things were okay; which they were.  I informed them we were accepting priority handling and would be on the ground as soon as possible.  As we passed through 10;000 feet we kept the speed up around 315 knots to expedite our arrival.  We were given radar vectors to a visual Runway X and landed uneventfully.  We had to wait a few minutes for our gate as it was occupied.  We pulled into the gate.  The passenger disembarked and the situation was over.  There were no injuries.  After the plane was empty the crew got together in the front of the airplane for a debrief of the situation.  At the end of the debrief I asked the flight attendants if they were okay and would be comfortable with continuing.  They all felt that they were okay to continue.  When the First Officer and I debriefed; I asked him the same and he was good.  I took a moment to assess myself and determined I was good to continue as well.It is worth noting that the flight attendants did a very good job of keeping us informed as to the status of the situation.  This was helpful and good crew CRM.  They were clear in their communication; calm and professional.  My First Officer also was a model of CRM and performed exceptionally to include his aircraft handling to expedite our arrival.
Report_2_Narrative: Passenger wasn't complying with mask usage after being repeatedly requested to by flight attendants. Flight attendants issued warning after which passenger became verbally aggressive.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported a passenger misconduct incident during flight that initiated due to non-compliance with face mask policy.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Situational Awareness; Time Pressure; Distraction; Physiological - Other
Report_1_Narrative: On approach to ZZZ; Initially the weather report was 3/4 SM visibility; so I informed the controller that I needed 1SM to shoot the approach due to my high minimums status. The Controller gave me direct ZZZ VOR and Hold northeast as published at 6;000 feet. I began heading direct to the VOR; when the controller came back and gave me the updated visibility at 1SM. So I accepted vectors to the approach. As I neared the FAF; I knew that I would need to be able to see the approach lights and runway in a low visibility situation; so I attempted to move the sun visor back to its stowed position. The visor became stuck; which is normal for these airplanes so I pushed harder. As I did that; the visor suddenly released itself and hit me in the face; causing a dull pain and immediate swelling. I touched the area and came back with a lot of blood on my hand; so I concentrated on flying the approach using standard procedures and call-outs and getting back on the ground. Unfortunately; I reached mins and did not see the runway environment; so I called out 'minimums; missed approach' and began the missed approach procedure according to standard procedures and call-outs. The controller attempted to give me a hold over the ZZZ VOR; but as I was bleeding and didn't know how long I would need to hold I chose to divert back to ZZZ1. I confirmed this decision after reaching cruise and having center call company Dispatch. Center informed me that I was a [priority] aircraft and would be treated as such as I had initially requested paramedics upon arrival. Upon reaching cruise however; I used my phone (which was off) as a mirror and concluded that I did not need medical assistance. So I informed Center of this change. I completed the flight back to ZZZ1 with no further issues. Paramedics met me at the ramp anyway; along with Airport OPS. They did not request my information and sent me on my way after cleaning the blood off of my face and neck. I then called dispatch and the Chief Pilots office to inform them of the situation.When the sun visor hit me in the face and I found blood on my hand. The sun visor in this airplane is in poor condition and gets stuck on the rail constantly. This in addition to the fact that I was very task saturated and didn't realize that the bleeding wasn't as bad as I had initially thought. I made the division to divert as I was performing a missed approach and wasn't aware of how severe the injury was. I knew the other airports in the vicinity were not suitable so I decided to go back to ZZZ1 as I knew it was 800-1000 foot OVC and I would have no issues. If I had moved the sun visor earlier that would have been beneficial; aside from that it could definitely use some TLC.
Report_1_Synopsis: Beech-1900 pilot reported trying to move a sun shade during an IMC approach and causing an injury to the pilot's head.

Report_1_Narrative: Controller had to have had a mask on as his communications were muffled and thus hard to understand.  We read back clearance to FL230 and as we were passing through 22;500 he said we were only cleared to FL220. He said to just continue to FL230 and that is what we did. No conflict was noted.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported an altitude deviation during climbout and cited communication problems with a Center Controller due to the Controller possibly wearing a face mask.

Person_1_Function: Flight Attendant (On Duty); Flight Attendant In Charge
Report_1_Narrative: I was the AFA (A Flight Attendant). Every part of the flight (boarding; climb; cruise; etc.) seemed to be going fine and seemed standard. When the pilots told us to prepare the cabin for arrival; I decided to look over the PAX (Passenger) manifest before tossing it. I had used it during the flight but only looked at part of it. To be honest; I didn't read over it before we departed. When I read over it toward the end of the flight; I noticed that one PAX was listed as a Special Assistance Passenger. This PAX was listed as needing a wheelchair and as blind. At no point was I aware that we had a PAX with a visual impairment. The PAX was boarded first and the person who pushed his wheelchair stowed the PAX's luggage. When interacting with the PAX on boarding; I handed him a sanitizing wipe and he seemed to have no trouble getting the wipe from me or getting to his seat; although I didn't really watch him go to his seat. At no point did the gate agent inform us that we had a PAX with a visual impairment nor did the person who pushed the wheelchair. When the B Flight Attendant asked the gate agent if we had any specials (for the PAX count form) the gate agent said we had one wheelchair. There was no mention of a PAX with a visual impairment.We did the standard briefings (announcements and safety demo); but neither of us provided a one-on-one briefing with the PAX. We were unaware of his visual impairment. After I realized our mistake on descent; I wasn't sure what to do. I had a brief conversation with the PAX; and he seemed to look me in the eye for the conversation. After I played the final descent announcement; I showed the B Flight Attendant the manifest and how it showed a PAX listed as blind. She was surprised to see it. We discussed our situation in regard to the PAX and the possibility of writing a  report.After we landed; the PAX gathered his belongings and deplaned without help. He also told the person waiting with the wheelchair that he didn't need it. He was traveling alone and without the assistance of a service animal. He only used a simple walking cane; not a red and white cane frequently used by people with visual impairments. He gave me no reason to think that he was visually impaired; but I understand that some disabilities are not apparent. When all the PAX had deplaned; I informed the Captain of what had happened and asked for advice. He said to fill out an report because we didn't do a required briefing. The B Flight Attendant and I knew that one-on-one briefings are required; we didn't know the PAX was visually impaired.I am concerned and upset that we potentially caused a safety incident with a PAX with a visual impairment. This is unacceptable. I hope to use this as a learning experience and pay closer attention to the PAX manifest before shutting the boarding door and proactively asking all gate agents about special assist PAX that we may have onboard. I say this with caution; though. We don't always receive the correct manifest; we sometimes receive incomplete manifests with no PAX information; and sometimes we don't even receive a manifest at all. While in the end; it was my responsibility to confirm with the gate agent about special assist PAX; I feel like there was a breakdown of communication between the gate agent and me. I wonder if the gate agent knew there was a visually impaired PAX on the flight. Perhaps there could be strengthened training for gate agents and flight attendants for recognizing special assist PAX. For flight attendants; also what to do if a special assist PAX is discovered during flight and certain briefings did not occur; as in our case. As stated before; I didn't know what to do in regard to the PAX.I understand the severe safety hazards not providing a one-on-one briefing could have caused if something went wrong during flight. I hope to use this as a lesson learned and not solely rely on being informed of all special assist PAX by a gate agent. In other words; I need to be more proactive; and I need to use my resources more wisely. My hope is that this can be used as a lesson for all flight attendants so that incidents like this don't happen again. We are first and foremost a safety industry; and we failed to keep to our safety standards.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Attendant reported not performing safety briefing for blind passenger.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Workload; Training / Qualification; Communication Breakdown; Confusion
Report_1_Narrative: While executing the ILS to [Runway] XXR at ZZZ; ATC informed us that we were following a heavy and instructed us to slow to 170kts. The Captain and I saw the other aircraft on TCAS and judged the distance to be six or seven miles. We discussed the possibility of wake turbulence but we didn't think the spacing was an issue. Then; after switching the tower; at around 3;000 feet; we were instructed to start slowing to our final approach speed. We then configured the aircraft for landing and started running the landing checklist. While listening and responding to the Captain's checklist callouts; I thought I heard someone say 'approach clearance canceled; maintain 3;000'; but I was unsure of the call sign. This was partly because the Captain and I were in the middle of running a checklist and partly because there was another aircraft on frequency that had a very similar call sign. We were Company X Callsign ABBC and the aircraft ahead of the heavy was Company X Callsign ADDC (there were at least three instances during the arrival where an instruction was given and we weren't 100% sure who it was for). I interrupted the Captain and told him that I thought tower had just canceled someone's approach clearance and asked him to query ATC to see if it was for us. The controller responded with a very urgent tone and said 'That is affirm; Callsign ABBC your approach clearance is canceled; maintain present heading and climb to 3;000. I'll have a turn for you in just a second.' As the captain was responding to ATC; I pressed the heading button to maintain our present heading as instructed; but I was confused as to what to do next. At this point we were around 2;400 feet (about 2;000 feet AFE); so a hard go-around using the TO/GA button was not required. I was not really mentally prepared for the go-around and was having trouble deciding what to do next; but ATC sounded like they wanted me to start climbing immediately to 3;000 feet; which was already set in the altitude window; so I reacted to his instruction by hitting FLCH. This caused the aircraft to apply full throttle and pitch up to maintain our current approach speed of about 145kts. We maintain this climb for several seconds until I was able to dial the speed up and get the aircraft accelerating. With everything happening so fast; and not really being mentally prepared for a go-around; I called gear up while the flaps were still at 5 which caused the landing gear warning to sound. It was a very sloppy go-around but I don't think the aircraft was ever in an unsafe state.This was my first go-around in the actual aircraft. However; I have mentally rehearsed and practiced enough hard go-arounds in sim training that the procedure is pretty much automatic and I can execute it without much thinking required. However; I can only recall doing a soft go-around once during FTD training and; as I recall; in that scenario we were not yet configured for landing and the altitude assigned was below us; so it was a simple matter of stopping the descent and flying the assigned heading. We also discussed soft go-arounds vs hard go-arounds in training and I had recalled that using TO/GA was optional but not really preferred during a soft-go around. I think there needs to be more training on soft go-arounds and the SOP should give more guidance as to preferred methods in various scenarios. Currently; the SOP does not give much guidance on the subject other than reminding the pilot to retract flaps at the F-bug or XX knots above green dot. After landing; the Captain and I discussed what I could have done better. He suggested; and I agreed; that the best course of action would have been to press ALT to stop the descent and then start accelerating before starting our climb. However; after replaying it in my head all night; I came to the conclusion that; given the fact that ATC wanted me to climb; it would have been perfectly acceptable to switch to heading mode and then press TO/GA and execute my normalgo-around actions and callouts; even though we were well above 1;000 feet AFE. This would ensure the aircraft was maintaining a safe speed while we began to reconfigure the aircraft and would have eliminated a lot of confusion that I created while I pondered what technique I should use to get us to 3;000 feet while also cleaning up the aircraft. Perhaps this should be the preferred method to execute a soft-go around when fully configured for landing and a climb is required. But perhaps there's another aspect of it that I'm not considering. The technique of pressing ALT and accelerating aircraft prior to starting the climb also seems like it would work in most situations. That's why I think the SOP should give more guidance on the subject. If there were a preferred method spelled out in the SOP; then it would eliminate a lot of the confusion and both pilots would be on the same page instead of debating on a technique for a procedure that is rarely used when there isn't really time to stop and think about it.This experience has also taught me to be prepared for a go-around at all times; not just when below 1;000 feet on an approach. Although; the spacing behind the heavy looked good to us; we should have been more prepared for the possibility that ATC would call for a go-around unexpectedly.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported having to do an unexpected go-around on final approach that may not have been correctly executed and cited confusing communications and unclear SOP procedures as contributing factors.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Troubleshooting; Physiological - Other; Communication Breakdown; Fatigue
Report_1_Narrative: Ever since we began wearing masks I am fearful of my job. I am getting headaches and at times migraines. When I get a headache; I am cranky so not always nice to passengers. I cannot communicate properly with my [coworkers]; my customers; the agents; etc. In an evacuation; how are we to hear one another? We are in a metal tube with little oxygen already. What our company is spraying on the aircraft can be damaging to the human body.Neurologically speaking and hard to pinpoint.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Attendant reported experiencing health issues since the wearing of a face mask began and the use of sanitizing spray in the aircraft.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Situational Awareness; Physiological - Other; Other / Unknown; Communication Breakdown
Report_1_Narrative: I took the insert of the food catered for the pilots up to the flight deck prior to passenger boarding. The Captain asked me to set it on the jump-seat behind him.  During boarding; the Captain came out and told us that the First Officer does not wear a mask in the flight deck and asked if either Flight Attendant A or myself would be willing to come up to the flight deck if the Captain needed a lavatory break in flight.  We both said that we would not be comfortable with coming up there if the First Officer was not wearing a mask.  Upon landing; I realized that the insert of flight deck food remained in the flight deck until after landing.Better CRM between flight deck and flight attendants if this situation comes up.  I honestly don't think that anyone even thought about it.  Flight Attendant A and I just knew that we were not going to put ourselves into the flight deck if the First Officer wasn't wearing a mask; which we would have had to in order to grab the insert.  But it absolutely was not intentionally left on the flight deck for takeoff and landing on our part.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Attendant reported the FA crew were unwilling to enter the flight deck because the First Officer would not wear a face mask.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Communication Breakdown; Distraction; Physiological - Other; Situational Awareness; Workload
Report_1_Narrative: I was working the FWD cabin and Flight Attendant (FA) B was working the AFT. During the flight FA B approached the galley and states to me that she was going to give Passenger X a face mask warning; because he was having a hard time complying to keeping the mask over his nose and she asked on numerous occasions before pushback; taxing out to the runway; and during the flight to keep his mask over his nose. I called flight deck to inform the Captain what was about to happen. So FA B gave the written policy to Passenger X and he stated he didn't want to see it. FA B informs me what happened and I call the flight deck. I tell the Captain she gave the warning and Passenger X refuses to hear it. The Captain states we'll just call for supervisors to meet us at the gate. FA B and I both say 'okay.' I decide to do a walk through in the cabin and notice Passenger X has his mask on covering his nose and mouth. I inform FA B and the Captain. Captain states that's great; but so there's no further issues with Passenger X we'll still have the Supervisor meet us. I say 'fine.' I guess noticing that FA B and myself are talking to the Captain inflight; Passenger X states to FA B he now wants to read the policy. Once seeing the policy and reading it Passenger X states to FA B that he's sorry. FA B then calls the Captain to let him know Passenger X has a change of heart. Captain still states he'll have the Supervisor meet the aircraft at the gate. We say 'okay.' Once at the gate; I open the main door and the supervisors are there. They wait for Passenger X to deplane to talk to him. The supervisors also state they will inform his connecting flight.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Attendant reported a passenger would not comply with face mask policy and was met at the arrival gate by supervisors.

Report_1_Narrative: On [Date] I was given the work assignment of running the #1 engine on Aircraft X for a BUG (Back-Up Generator) operational and leak check by my lead mechanic; ref log page. I knew that there was a fuel leak in the pylon for the #1 engine as I had written it up the day before; ref log page. At this time the left wing had 30;000 lbs of fuel in it to help find the leak source into the pylon. I declined to run the engine to verify the operation of the relatively minor repair of the BUG replacement compared to the danger of fire from an active fuel leak into the #1 engine's pylon. I explained my reasoning to the pair of shift foreman. They went away and returned with the directive to 'Run the Engine' regardless of the fuel leak or my concerns. The foreman said the Operating Manager had directed this.  At this point I decided to run the engine as they ordered me to do rather than risk losing my job. I ran the engine with an eye for protecting my work partners and the aircraft as much as possible given the situation management forced me into. As the days have gone by since this happened it has bothered me more and more until I felt I had to reach out to the [Aviation Safety Action Program] and Ground Safety committees. Please take note of [Company] Engine Run Policy [Number].'At no time will safety be compromised for operational reasons'.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Maintenance Technician reports Management pressure to ignore safety concerns.

Report_1_Narrative: I was in contact with Chicago Center on our flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1 on a direct flight plan at FL290. We were talking with Chicago Center when he transferred us to another Chicago Center frequency. I tried 3 times to contact the Controller as he was quite busy. The third time he said 'unless it is pertinent to the safety of flight; maintain radio silence.' I complied with his instructions. During this time I was working on other items pertaining to the flight. Some time had passed and I realized I have not talked to a controller in some time and the radio calls I was hearing were getting fainter. I called the Controller and asked if I needed to be transferred and was told that he did not have me on his list and was unsure of what frequency I needed to contact. I tried to go back to the previous frequency I was on but was not getting what I needed there. I then looked at my route and found that the closest larger airport was ZZZ2 and called their Controller asking for a correct frequency for Center and he asked for my position; squawk code; and tail number again. I gave him the information he requested and afterwards he recommended a new frequency to me. I contacted the Controller on the recommended frequency I was given and he was also unsure of who I was. He requested our altitude; tail number; and squawk code. I complied and he advised I contact the next control frequency he had. This next Controller was Cleveland Center. He seemed to have somewhat of a better idea of who we were but recommended the next Controller on Cleveland Center as well on a new frequency. As soon as I contacted this new Controller he knew who I was and kept me on the same altitude and course I had been on. Again; we were direct from ZZZ to ZZZ1 at FL290 and had not modified our course and ATC had not advised us of any course or altitude changes. Before we were switched to Potomac Center nearing our destination I was asked to take down a number and call it on the ground for a 'possible pilot deviation.' I complied and we were able to continue and land without any further incident. On the ground I called the number I was given and talked to ATC about the situation. They took my information and we talked about what happened. They advised me that in the future it is always a good idea to go back to your previous frequency if needed. I agreed with their advice and they said that I may be contacted in the near future about this incident. I said that is no problem and am more than willing to talk to whomever about it.To correct situations like this in the future I believe there are a couple things that can happen. For myself as a pilot that if I am ever unsure of who I need to be talking to that I can check in more often and make sure that we are all on the same page. The suggestion I would offer for the controller side would be that if anyone is in a NORDO aircraft situation that all the controllers in the area know of that tail number and are able to direct the aircraft to the correct frequency quickly rather than searching around.
Report_1_Synopsis: Small transport pilot reported a breakdown in communication with ATC.

Report_1_Narrative: Aircraft X came to an abrupt stop on Runway XX at ZZZ due to snow on the runway. We were the only occupants of the craft. Neither of us were injured; nor was the plane damage. There was no damage to any other persons or property.A low approach was made to assess the condition of the runway before attempting a soft field approach and landing. We decided to make an approach to land after judging that the snow looked to be at or less than 2 inches. It looks like two layers of very thin snow. We could see tracks from another tricycle gear airplane. What we didn't realize was that that plane had landed in much shallower snow and that it had then snowed more on top. Being able to see grass protruding through the snow also gave the notion that the snow was not deep. I briefed my student on precautions to take with landing on snow before we made the approach.When we landed; the plane's mains and nose wheel sunk in causing us to come to an abrupt halt. We were able to taxi the aircraft most of the way up the runway. We agreed to attempt a soft field take off back down our tracks; which didn't get very far.Chief; Assistant Chief; Owner; and Lead Pilot were notified. We contacted the Airport Manager; who was able to come to our aid with a backhoe. We took off from the county road next to the runway as decided between myself; the Student and Chief Pilot; and as advised by the Airport Manager. A successful short field takeoff and climb out was performed by myself; the instructor and my student and I returned to ZZZ1.14 CFR 91.103; Pre-flight preparation; was not observed or fulfilled to its fullest. I will not get into the possible reasoning behind this; aside from that we decided to go to #X# during taxi.Lessons learned are abundant by our main takeaways that [we] I discussed were as follows:-New or unfamiliar airports need better preparation and scrutiny.-Snow depth should not be judged from the air. Until properly equipped and properly trained; no approach and landing should be made to a snowy runway that one is not sure they could take off from again.-I now have a new example of things not to do to use as a teaching tool with my students.We were extremely lucky pilots today. but we as pilots do not want to rely on luck. Lessons learned.
Report_1_Synopsis: Small aircraft instructor pilot reports landing on contaminated runway of unknown snow depth resulted in abrupt stop and being stuck.

Report_1_Narrative: I was working Approach Control and received a call over the landline from ZNY Center about an emergency aircraft that was diverting that had an engine failure and was going to be landing. They checked on normally with me and said they were expecting a normal approach and landing at the airport and were getting set up to receive the approach clearance. They were given vectors to help them descend and they advised when they were ready to accept the approach clearance for the ILS approach. They then flew the approach and landed safely. Emergency vehicles were standing by; but not needed. It was brought to my attention that the ILS approach was not authorized in the NOTAMs. I had been briefed that changes were made to the approach plates for the ILS approach and was informed that the changes went into effect four days prior. It was not clear and I was not aware that the ILS approach was not authorized at the time the emergency aircraft used the approach.Clearer guidance is needed from the FAA once changes are made to approach plates.
Report_1_Synopsis: Approach Controller reported issuing a clearance for the ILS approach; only to discover later that ILS approaches were not authorized per the NOTAMs.

Report_1_Narrative: Prior to the event; I came up from break and took a LC (Local Control) position that controls a satellite Class D airport with a gravel strip and water lanes. This position was combined with both CIC and Clearance Delivery/FD. This was never trained as a standard; but some work crews have made this a normal practice when staffing is short. Quickly after taking position; and before the event occurred; I did call up someone to split off the position but I should not have allowed it to remain de-combined in the interim. LC and GC (Ground Control) were de-combined; and while working I heard GC bring a potential conflict to LCs attention (good tower teamwork from GC). As I examined the situation I saw the same conflict- a heavy aircraft had taxied into departure position (Runway 33) with a large aircraft arriving behind on a non-intersecting runway (Runway 7L). With the spacing of the aircraft it did not appear that there was enough space to ensure compliance with our facility order. Our facility order details spacing required with aircraft arriving Runways 7R/L and departing Runway 33. I advised the LC that I did not believe adequate spacing would exist and suggested; but did not instruct; alternate courses of action to avoid a situation where the arriving aircraft might encounter jet blast. The LC insisted it would work and did not take any action. With the proximity of the aircraft; I don't believe a safety issue existed; however lack of compliance with facility guidelines with no standard for separation is an unacceptable risk to the users of the system.This event highlights many issues.As CIC during the event; I take responsibility for my own personal performance. I should not have taken CIC combined with an LC position. I should have had more engagement in the operation - if this situation had been detected earlier there may have been more time to correct it. I also should have given the LC instruction instead of suggestion when I saw action was not going to be taken.1. Lack of staffing. Perpetual lack of staffing leads this facility down the path of using what should be contingency practices into day to day practices. Positions are too often combined and because this has become the norm; controllers do not understand that they are providing a reduced level of service.2. Lack of safety culture. LC had two controllers address concern over this action and did not appear to consider an alternate course of action. This is not a behavior to this specific Controller but throughout this facility.3. Lack of training. The training culture and training at this facility has fallen short on ensuring that the staff of the facility have a thorough understanding of the rules we are expected to apply.4. Lack of supervision. Much like our Controller workforce; our supervisory staff is frequently understaffed and asked to do an excessive amount of duties that take them away from the operation. There was not a supervisor present at the time of the incident.5. Bad procedures. The facility; and region as a whole have done a poor job at creating procedures that are not easily followed by pilots or controllers. Many of these procedures don't have reasonable 'outs'; which put pilots and controllers in dangerous situations in a recovery situation.Consider revising ANC jet blast procedures.Provide clear expectations to CPCs on services we are expected to provide pilots.Provide adequate staffing to accomplish existing goals.
Report_1_Synopsis: ANC Tower Controller reported Local Controller failed to follow facility policy nor take action to comply. Reporter states facility policies are unclear and difficult to follow.

Report_1_Narrative: I was notified about a report of a wrong surface landing. I was the Controller on the midnight shift.  I cleared Aircraft X for Runway XXC; but the Aircraft landed Runway XXR. Approach switched the aircraft on an extended base for the visual approach [to] Runway XXC. The pilot checked on the frequency for Runway XXC. I cleared the aircraft to land for Runway XXC. After I cleared the plane to land the janitorial guy comes to the Tower cab to vacuum the Tower and empty the trash. I usually go opposite of him so we can keep our space (we had our mask on) for social distancing. When he finished cleaning the Local 3 position I recognized the aircraft was short final to Runway XXR. I knew the runway had no vehicles on it because my strip bay showed no vehicle above Runway XXR bay header. I let the aircraft land Runway XXR due to the critical phase in flight. I taxied the aircraft to the ramp after the aircraft landed safely. In the past Approach would call me on the shout line to remind me that this aircraft is set up on the wrong approach. By me not being at the position walking around the Tower cab I did not recognize the aircraft on approach for the wrong runway.The recommendations I would use to prevent this wrong surface landing is to observe an aircraft turn onto the right approach for the right runway. If that pilot makes a mistake turning on to the wrong approach I can either send the aircraft around or correct the aircraft to land on the proper runway; or I can help the pilot get visual for the runway the pilot is lined up for and clear the plane to land for that runway. The key is catching the aircraft turning on the approach early enough so I can correct the pilot.
Report_1_Synopsis: ATC Tower Controller reported an aircraft landed on the wrong runway and cited social distancing distraction during a janitorial service in the Tower as a contributing factor.

Report_1_Narrative: Climbing out on the ZZZZZ2 RNAV Departure off [Runway] XX in ZZZ. We did a precautionary takeoff for LLWS reported on the ATIS. It was a light aircraft. We climbed at a high rate and got distracted with doing the Climb Checklist. Also we were accelerating to 250 knots; which masked the level off prompt on the PF FD display. We did not honor the 10;000 foot hold-down at ZZZZZ Intersection. The PF was hand flying and climbed to 10;400 feet before noticing the hold-down symbol on the MFD maps display route. The PF immediately began a descent to 10;000 feet. Upon which ATC queried if we were climbing via the ZZZZZ2 Departure. We acknowledged our mistake and corrected.Enhanced pilot monitoring; higher situational awareness climbing with a light aircraft and notice that things are moving fast and hold off on Climb Checklist until higher altitude with autopilot on [would help prevent this type of event].

Report_1_Narrative: I did not declare an emergency with ATC. We were already near Top of Descent with no traffic ahead. Getting medical attention was not time critical. The greatest risk was in the deplaning of our other passengers.While enroute to ZZZ; I was notified that 'A man in [seat] XX1 had declared that he had a high fever prior to boarding; and that he now felt very ill.' Once I got this additional information and spelling of the man's name; I sent the message and spoke with Medical and Dispatch in attendance. In the meantime; I got another call indicating the man now said that he just had high blood pressure and would be okay. The load was light and we agreed to move the man to the back row and to move other passengers forward. The Flight Attendant's temperature strip was inconclusive. This information was passed to Medical. We issued the man an N-95 mask; and he wore it. The advice from Medical was to provide Tylenol and continue to ZZZ. Paramedics would meet us at the gate.IMPORTANT; it was then that FA called back to say there was an identity mistake. The actual seat assignment was XX6; not XX1. This meant that the passenger's name was incorrect during the Dispatch/Medical call. The incorrect passenger name is omitted to avoid confusion. I sent the correct name to Dispatch via ACARS.On approach to ZZZ; the man aspirated on the carpet and floor next to the last row and could not wear a mask. FA's notified me of this on taxi-in.Because of the concern for COVID-19; we made the decision that we would have passengers deplane quickly; then allow either the paramedics to the passenger; or allow the man to deplane. Inflight Supervisor and Customer Service Supervisor were at gate and aware of the de-boarding plan. The paramedic overruled the plan and rushed aboard. He proceeded to escort the man passed all the economy passengers and then blocked the jet-way several moments to get him into a wheelchair. I ordered the First Class cabin to deplane after the paramedic passed on his way to the back. I'm glad I did.The aircraft was towed away for disinfection. I checked in with Flight Ops enroute prior to landing and told a call would not be required. Checked in with Chief Pilot on the day after to determine COVID-19 result. There was no answer as of this writing.

Report_1_Narrative: We were assigned the RNAV Rwy 35; and given direct MEYRS.  We briefed the approach and confirmed altitudes in the FMS.  ATC gave us the clearance 'Cross MEYRS at or above 14;000 [feet]; cleared for the RNAV 35.'  I was the Pilot Monitoring; and I dialed 14;000 into to the autopilot pre-select.  The Pilot Flying entered 14000 in the FMS at MEYRS and executed a direct VNAV descent to MEYRS.  This caused the altitude to turn yellow in the FMS because the next altitude on the approach; at YARUB; was 14;800 [feet].  We discussed this for a moment and I deleted the 14;800 from the FMS.  The Pilot Flying then stated; and I agreed; that we should follow the charted altitudes and we entered 15;000 for MEYRS so that we would be above the published MEA of 14800 between MEYRS and YARUB.  With my intention being to put the YARUB altitude back into the FMS; I referenced the chart and then entered 12000 for YURUB (which was an error).  After crossing MEYRS at 15;000 [feet] we began a slow VNAV descent for 12;000 [feet]; but we should have been level at 14;800 [feet] all the way to YARUB.  While cross checking our position between the map display and the Jepp chart; I began to suspect that we had made an error.  Passing about 13;000 [feet]; I asked the Pilot Flying to level off; which he did; and then I stated that we were not at the correct altitude and that we should climb.  At that moment we received a GPWS caution that gave us a one time audible alert; and the Pilot Flying began a climb.  Shortly afterwards we passed the YARUB fix; and the MEA was now 12;000 so we continued the descent.While monitoring our progress on the approach; I noticed that our altitude was below the charted MEA.  I was confused for a minute while I tried to determine if we had made an error and then realized that I had deleted an altitude; and then re-enter it; but had in fact programmed the incorrect altitude.  Looking back I can't quite explain my thought process; and after the fact my mistake seems very obvious and amateur.  I did reference the chart for the YARUB altitude; and looking at it again '12;000' is written very close to YARUB; and that's my only explanation for how I matched that altitude to that fix; but of course 12;000 is the altitude after YARUB.  While I was monitoring our progress I remember thinking that something didn't seem quite right; and it took me a minute to piece together the ATC clearance; our ensuing actions; and to come to the conclusion that I had made a mistake.  The ATC clearance to an altitude that was already below a charted MEA caused a moment of confusion and second guessing.  I removed an altitude from the FMS that was auto loaded with the approach.  A few minutes later; when I realized I had made an error; I attempted to correct it but I put the wrong altitude back in the FMS after incorrectly reading the chart.  I asked the Pilot Flying to level off while I cross checked the chart and; FMS; and our position.  I then stated that we should climb; which we did.I should not have been so quick to delete an altitude from the FMS which was loaded by selecting the approach.  Also; when entering an altitude into the FMS I need to be more careful while referencing the chart and also confirm with the Pilot Flying that I am entering the correct altitude.
Report_2_Narrative: While descending into MJT we were cleared by ATC to pass over MEYRS at or above 14;000 feet and cleared the RNAV 35 approach. We had already briefed the approach and checked the altitudes in the FMS. The first segment between MEYRS and the next point on the approach YARUB is 14;800 feet. Just before reaching MEYRS we decided to stop our descent to pass over MEYRS at 14;000 [feet]and hold at 15;000 [feet]. After YARUB the next step down is 12;000 feet. We had been descending in VNAV to make the cross at Myers. My First Officer put 12;000 feet at YARUB and I confirmed it. In VNAV we then started a slow descent to pass over YARUB at 12;000 feet. This was a mistake on my part. We realized at about 12;700 we where wrong and below a published minimum. I stopped the descent and started a climb. We did get a momentary GPWS terrain and responded according. We climbed about 20 feet and it was gone. We had already stopped descending when we got the GPWS. Realizing we where doing the wrong thing by descending in VNAV to cross YARUB at 12;000 [feet].Allowing the Pilot Monitoring to put 12000 feet n the FMS at YARUB. Immediate once we realized our mistake.. Autopilot off. Start a climb. We never did get to 14;800 [feet] because of how we where close to YARUB. I realized that we where low but also safe and never in any danger. I feel like I should have queried ATC about the descent clearance. I should have been more vigilant with the cross at YARUB.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air taxi flight crew reported confusing ATC clearance; automation mismanagement; and MEA confusion resulted in a GPWS warning.

Report_1_Narrative: I was pilot monitoring on the initial climbout from ZZZ when I noticed my FO (First Officer) was nose high and banking to the right approximately 40 degrees with airspeed decreasing from 95 KTS to 85 KTS. I asked why he was turning as were supposed to be climbing left to ZZZZZ. He seemed confused by my question and I realized that he had lost situational awareness. I declared 'My Plane' at which point he gave a positive transfer of controls. I leveled the wings and regained a positive rate of climb before turning back onto course. After regaining stable flight I offered the controls back to my FO. He refused controls and I continued to fly. I told him he had the radios and told him to check in with departure. Center asked us why we had turned to the right off of our expected heading and my FO was honest with the Controller; informing him that he had lost control of the aircraft and heading had diverged prior to me regaining control of the aircraft. The Controller acknowledged and told us to climb according to our planned route. After reaching cruising altitude I debriefed my FO and we discussed what went wrong. We ultimately determined that the loss of control was due to deficiencies in his scan as a result of his inexperience with analog instruments.

Report_1_Narrative: I was soloing a new student pilot at ZZZ. After completing several warm-up laps in the pattern dual; I informed Tower that my student was about to solo and had my student drop me off in the non-movement area of the east ramp. On my student's first attempt at a landing; he flared high and initiated a go-around. On his second attempt he landed; stopped; and then initiated a takeoff roll. I realized that my student had mistaken the command 'Cleared to Land' for 'Cleared Stop-And-Go.' I used a handheld radio to call out my student by name and told him to discontinue the takeoff. He stopped on the runway; and he was switched to Ground for taxi instructions. I asked Ground to instruct my student to return to my location and discontinue the flight. While taxiing back to my location on south end of the east ramp; my student missed a left turn from A to F; stopped; and was directed by Ground to complete a 180 turn and return to his original taxi instructions. If had continued forward there was the possibility of crossing Runway XX-XY and committing a runway incursion.There were several contributing factors to both of these new runway incursions/violations.1) My student's confusion about ATC clearances. We had previously been issued 'stop-and-go' and 'cleared to land' clearances earlier that morning; but I did not confirm that my student understood the difference.2) Poor Aeronautical Decision-Making: My student informed me after the flight that he had only slept four hours the night before. I believe this contributed to both errors he made during his solo.3) Unfamiliarity/Lack of Training on Towered Airport Operations: We had one previous flight at ZZZ; but it did not involve extensive taxi instructions or various ATC clearances. Even that morning my student had the same repetitive taxi clearance after each of our landings completed together.Corrective Actions (To be completed with this student and future students).1) My student and I are going to have an extensive ground covering various ATC clearances; communication procedures; and possible taxi instructions at unfamiliar airports. I will require my student to complete a FAASafety.gov course on runway incursions.2) While I have my students use an ADM (Aeronautical Decision Making) checklist before each flight; I will audibly confirm the 'IMSAFE' checklist is complete before each flight.3) We will conduct another dual flight or two and ask for various different taxi instructions to diversify my student's experience.
Report_2_Narrative: I made a call on the downwind 'Full Stop Touch and Go' and was cleared for landing. Did not correctly understand that Cleared For Landing does not allow for 'Touch and Go' unless given that prompt. Also missed a taxi-way.Not properly understanding 'Cleared for Landing' in full. After given Instructor not to take off; I missed my taxi-way; thus entering a different taxiway from Instructor. Unfamiliar with map + going too fast; missed the taxiway. Ultimately; challenged with receiving tower communications at their rate of communications.My Instructor realized I was not stopping and told me to not take off. I saw that I was about to cross a runway and realized I was missing something. I realized it and then was given Instructor to 180. My Instructor told me to not take off so I didn't take off. We exited the lesson and went back to our home airport. Need to slow down on taxiways. Mostly just incorrect decisions on incorrect understanding of definition 'cleared to land'. Will role-play / simulate communications and different scenarios to ensure I'm understanding and communicating properly with the tower.

Report_1_Narrative: DEN ground instructed us to taxi to RWY 17L from E4 via mike; hold short of ED. Once on Mike northbound Ground instructed us to turn right at ED and hold short of the approach end of Runway 17R. The FO (First Officer) was in the process of completing his delayed engine start flow as I started the turn on ED. At this point I noticed traffic on short final to Runway 17R and thinking to myself that it didn't seem right to turn on ED. I stopped the aircraft as soon as it was straight and pointed east on ED. I asked the FO if he saw a sign or hold short line on his side. I saw no signage in front of us and now felt extremely uncomfortable with our proximity to the Runway 17R approach path. At this point the Ground Controller told us we were supposed to stop 50 ft. further back. I looked behind us and noticed the left wing tip was over the east edge of Taxiway Mike. I could not see a hold line below the wing. We were switched to Tower. The Tower Controller gave us a number to call for a possible pilot deviation. Shortly after writing down the number we were cleared for takeoff. As we rolled down the runway I realized we failed to complete the final items.I spoke to the Tower supervisor later that day and explained the events as they occurred. He admitted that this hot spot is an ongoing issue; the hold area is not well marked and the Controller's intent was to have us pointed east to help move aircraft through the Runway 17R approach path faster. Unfortunately the Tower had to send around the landing traffic I was distracted with during the turn because they were not sure if we would stop. I have flown in and out of DEN since the day it opened and have never been issued a clearance like this. I have always been instructed to hold short of ED when aircraft are landing Runway 17R. I believe this type of clearance should be avoided; specially in an area that is a hot spot. The aircraft behind us which received the same clearance had to confirm the clearance and the intent to hold short immediately after turning.
Report_2_Narrative: We had a leg planned for DEN-ZZZ with Runways 17L; 17R; and 8 being used for departure.  Going westbound; I programmed and planned and briefed a 17R departure. The captain briefed a single-engine taxi.  After block out we were advised of a 17L departure.  For me that is several threats; a runway change requiring FMC programming; retrieving new performance; single-engine taxi ( increased workload; 2 engine-start flows etc); and unavoidable time when only the Captains eyes are outside the cockpit during FO single-engine duties during hi intensity ground operations @ DEN. On taxi out we were instructed to taxi to Runway 17L via Taxiway M and hold short of ED.  At some point northbound on Taxiway M with a hold short instruction in hand;  I initiated start of ENG 1.   During the engine start; the ground controller gave an additional instruction to turn right on to ED and hold short of the Runway 17R approach area.  Due to my required duties during an engine start which aren't easily paused/stopped; I could not write down the instruction; nor could I refer to my taxi diagram so that I could act as a backup-another set of eyes in the cockpit; I was only able to say-back the instruction and nothing else. The captain had a response to me that conveyed that he heard and understood the instruction.  I pressed on completing the engine-start.   I was heads down completing my duties during our expected right hand turn onto ED.  Shortly thereafter I heard the captain make a comment about an aircraft landing on Runway 17R and he brought the airplane to stop.  It was several moments before the ground controller came on the radio to say that we were to hold short of the approach area which was now behind us.  We were then instructed to continue taxi; switched over to tower; given a phone number and cleared for takeoff.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Pilot Crew reported Ground Control instructions and the charted version of this Hotspot at DEN airport are confusing.

Report_1_Narrative: We all have been complying with mask use at ZZZ to 'Stop the spread' and for public image. Yes; if we are unable to maintain social distance; we should also be wearing a covering outside of public area.  What this does not address is the long term health effects of wearing a face covering every day of the week for hours at a time.  Extended mask use can cause and is not limited to:1.Shortness of Breath and Light headedness2. Headaches3. Dermatitis4. A weakened Immune System ( your body is unable to rid toxic cell normally because they wind up staying in your face covering which causes bacteria to stay in your mouth. Having bacteria stay in your mouth leads to health issues such as dental issues (root canals; infections; etc.) Healthy oral hygiene is a necessity for heart health and overall health.5.Chronic Respiratory Issues
Report_1_Synopsis: Customer Service Representative reported health related concerns with wearing face masks at work for extended periods of time.
