Report_1_Narrative: During the arrival; we were given a vector and then a direct to DSNEE. As we were still in the high teens; I suggested opening the speed window at 280 KIAS (assigned speed) and then spinning it down below 250 passing around 12-13000' (due to the Captain's relative inexperience). Sometime below 15000'; SoCal Arrival asked if we wanted the SNA 20R RNAV Z. We had already setup and briefed for the ILS but we discussed any benefits to switching and decided against it. I informed SoCal of our desire for the ILS and crosschecked my instruments and noticed we were descending through approximately 8700' still doing 280 KIAS. I gave a corrective command and immediately pressed ALT HOLD (Altitude Hold); spun back the speed to below 250 KIAS; and deployed the speed brakes. I did not say; 'My Aircraft' but time was of the essence. We slowed and continued the arrival and landing uneventfully: there was no communication from SoCal referencing the deviation.Using SPD INTV (Speed Intervene); without its protection; coupled with the distraction of SoCal's request set us up for the deviation. Additionally; the Captain is new to both the seat and the airplane.[I] suggest using all available automation to the maximum extent. We could have instead entered speeds into the CDU at the abeam waypoints and allowed the aircraft to gradually decelerate on its own (or the DESCENT page speed).
Report_2_Narrative: I was flying. Received a vector off the arrival. Chose to use speed intervene; 280kts. Just before I went to reduce speed to 250kts for 10;000; ATC asked if we wanted the Required Navigation Performance (RNP) Z. We had set up and briefed the ILS as I had been refused the RNP Z on a prior flight. First Officer (FO) and I got distracted discussing the pros and cons of accepting the RNP Z; descended below 10;000 ft. doing 280kt. The FO caught it. We leveled off; used speed brakes; got below 250kts; and continued decent. I am a new Captain. About 150 hours on the 737; which I haven't flown. I haven't flown in the last 2 months. These factors mainly contributed to a narrowing of the big picture. Additionally; I was tired. It was night. Last leg of 3 day pairing. More than anything; don't use speed intervene without a lot of extra caution. Putting the speed in the FMC is the better way to go; it only takes a couple of seconds longer.
Report_1_Synopsis: B737 flight crew reported exceeding 250 knots below 10;000 feet after planning to slow from an assigned 280 knots several thousand feet above 10;000 feet to accommodate the Captain's relative inexperience.

Report_1_Narrative: Better monitor FO actions. Increase awareness of calculating descent points using distance from the runway to approximate a 3 degree descent path to the runway in order to avoid unnecessary and lengthy low level segments.  Flying at 3;000 feet about 15 miles WSW of IND direct to BIGRD on the RNAV Y 5R. Approach asked if we had the field in sight; we responded that we did; and then we were given a left turn pretty much direct to HUUPS; which is the final approach fix on the RNAV Y 5R; and cleared for the visual approach. Tower then handed us off to Tower. During this time while I was switching to Tower I became task saturated with my PM flying duties from the frequency change; getting a landing clearance; and the FO requesting flap configuration changes. After we were cleared to land I noticed we were just about to level off at 2;100 feet. Well below a 3 degree descent path given our current position to the runway. I had not noticed the FO had set 2;100 feet; which is the altitude at HUUPS; and started a descent as soon as we were cleared for the approach. We leveled off at 2;100 feet and continued for some time before reaching HUUPS and continuing the descent for the runway. We were level at approximately 1;300' feet AGL for a while before descending for landing. I don't think this was technically illegal or in violation of an FAR; as we were cleared for the visual and in the process of making a descent for landing; but I do feel it's not a good technique to simply set the FAF altitude; dive and drive to that altitude; level off for several miles; then continue descent once over the FAF. We were not on a published portion of an approach; and well below a 3 degree descent path to the runway. This wasn't an issue for this particular approach; but it could become an issue at night in mountainous terrain or if there are obstacles in the area.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported getting too low while on a visual approach to IND airport.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Situational Awareness; Training / Qualification; Confusion; Distraction; Communication Breakdown
Report_1_Narrative: When arriving at gate for our ZZZ-ZZZ1 flight; the Purser told the CS agent we needed a few minutes so we could do our required Safety duties (FA briefing which is required per safety checklist. Safety checks (which company says can be done during boarding which isn't the safest during COVID time); be at the boarding door after putting our bags away; get customer wipes for customers company's COVID safety protocol. The agent was told by inflight Supervisor X;  ZZZ; to begin boarding  on top of the flight attendants boarding the plane. When questioning Supervisor X about not giving us time to do our required safety duties Supervisor X's answer was 'We can't hold boarding on a quick turn.'  I understand we all want an on-time operation but that shouldn't come at the cost of safety.  Even the Captain was amazed that we were not given time to do our safety duties.I would like to know if flight attendants are required to brief as stated on the safety checklist or not; and if we are required to brief why are we not given the time to brief when we ask for 2 minutes. If we are not required to brief then please alter the safety checklist.What happened to safety is our top priority?
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Attendant reported concerns with completing safety checks while passengers are boarding.

Report_1_Narrative: The flight crew received our flight release indicating the MEL for the RH EEC. When the crew arrived on the aircraft maintenance was already on and working numerous issues on the aircraft. The flight crew was informed that a bite test showed no errors with the EEC and and at the time it was operating normally. It was believed a ground air start error was what caused the EEC to trip off. The MEL was signed off and the release amended to show its removal. A ground air start was conducted at the gate with no issues; and the aircraft was pushed back. After a cross bleed start and concurrent with the tug disconnecting the RH EEC tripped offline. The crew ran the appropriate EEC QRH checklist directing both EECs to be selected off. Since we had previously reviewed the MEL we elected to continue. During the takeoff it was noted that the auto throttles were not responding and takeoff thrust was set manually. During climb and initial cruise it was noted by both crew members that the left engine EGT was fluctuating 30-50 degrees but stabilized with cruise power set. After approximately an hour of cruise at FL390 and 0.78 Mach the aircraft passed a front causing the airspeed to increase above the assigned speed. Power was gradually reduced to allow the speed to decrease to the assigned value. As the power was increased back to maintain Mach speed it was noted that the left engine was stuck at flight idle and was not responding to thrust lever movements. The thrust lever was positioned to the firewall with no response. As the airspeed was deteriorating rapidly the aircraft offset from the airway and began a descent while a revised clearance was received from New York via HF to return to JFK. ATC issued a revised clearance to JFK and approved the initial descent to FL360. At approximately FL370 the engine again began responding to thrust lever movement. Further descent was not considered necessary at this point and we continued to JFK since we couldn't guarantee that the engine would not stop responding again. After getting the aircraft stabilized; [we] notified via phone patch and the flight attendants and passengers were briefed on the situation and decision to return to JFK. No emergency was declared nor any emergency services requested. The flight continued normally to JFK and accomplished a normal approach and landing to runway 31R with no further incidents. Upon shutdown the crew briefed on site maintenance along with [Operations and Maintenance Control]. The issues were also written up in the log book.
Report_1_Synopsis: B767 First Officer reported electronic engine control and throttle malfunction resulted in a return to departure airport.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Confusion; Communication Breakdown; Distraction; Situational Awareness; Workload
Report_1_Narrative: I left ZZZ VFR to ZZZ1.  I requested flight following from the Ground and was informed they are 'Not allowed' to do this. (This in itself is part of a BIG problem).  So I called [TRACON] Departure and requested the flight following -no problem - standby.   After 10 minutes of standing by they come back and say ....oops - you're out of my airspace; ask the next ATC Controller.  So I did; and they replied 'No services available; ask the next Controller.'I am TRYING to get thru the X VFR route which is at 5;500.  There is a 5K bravo shelf right before it.  I stay at 4;500 until I make two-way contact with the Bravo.   It's incredibly busy - can't get a word in....I finally do and I was told 'Cleared thru the Bravo; climb to 5;500' - I repeat it back.   Then 3 minutes later; I hear my call sign again and was told 'State your request' - very confused at this point; I say I want the X route and I'm told.....'You better make a left 360 because you're about to enter Bravo and I haven't cleared you.'   Still very very confused; I make a left 360 - then he states; 'Make a right 360 - huh??  Then he says; ok - I see you're already making a left 360; stay with that.   Well; all that turning and confusion put me at around 5;200 (I was already climbing because I thought I was cleared).   So I'm pretty sure I went into that Bravo space just above 5;000 and I immediately dropped as fast as I could back down to 4;500.  1/2 way thru my turn I was cleared the Bravo and X route.Guys - I'm not a novice pilot - I've done these VFR routes many times.  I don't know what's going on with ZZZ Center.Here's what I think happened.....maybe someone was on UHF that I couldn't hear and that is who the Controller cleared through the Bravo - or maybe it was a similar tail number.I asked for clearance; heard it given to me; confirmed it back.  I'm super curious as to what exactly happened.We are trained - if you don't know - ask.  Well...that's only possible if you CAN ask and get into the frequency - I couldn't.   I would never have entered the Bravo but for the Controller telling me 'cleared thru the Bravo and climb to 5;500) - or at least I thought that was for me.If you're going to have VFR corridors - make them accessible - otherwise; just close them all down until you can staff them.  Had I known up front it wasn't available; I would have just climbed to 10;500 and flown over.As for me - I'm just going to go IFR unless I can get flight following from the Ground.  This is very dangerous - it's too busy and you're going to see an accident sometime soon.
Report_1_Synopsis: GA pilot reported communication issues with ATC while attempting to receive a Class Bravo clearance.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Communication Breakdown; Situational Awareness; Training / Qualification
Report_1_Narrative: I was flying with a student pilot; practicing simulated engine failure emergency procedures. Student selected Frazier Lake airport (1C9) as the landing point. We positioned the airplane directly towards 1C9 for runway 5 which is a grass runway. I scanned the area in front and right of us to make sure there was no other traffic nearby. We descended towards runway 5 and ended the practice by going around above runway 5 at about 800 ft AGL. The next day we received a phone call from another pilot who was operating in traffic pattern at 1C9 attempting to land on the hard surface taxiway parallel to runway 5. He told us that he saw us on final flying next to him only approximately 200 ft above. He made few radio calls trying to reach us but no response; because we were not on 1C9 CTAF at the time. What have caused this event was that the student was busy performing the maneuver; forgot to change frequency to 1C9 CTAF and announce our intention. I was too focused on the training but overlooked the safety aspect of the flight. The corrective action is I should have changed frequency to 1C9 CTAF and monitor it when the student decided to head over there.
Report_1_Synopsis: C152 Instructor reported failure to utilize CTAF resulted in a NMAC on final.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Workload; Time Pressure; Situational Awareness; Human-Machine Interface; Communication Breakdown; Confusion; Distraction
Report_1_Narrative: Aircraft X departed Runway 30 on an assigned 270 heading. Shortly after switching the aircraft to departure; I scanned the radar and saw Aircraft X turning through a 270 heading and continuing a left turn to the east directly into the arrival corridor for aircraft landing Runways 1L and 1C. At that moment; a controller at PCT; I think Departure Control contacted me. My initial thought was that Aircraft X had misunderstood my assigned heading and had not switched to Departure Control and was still on my frequency. While the controller was speaking to me other aircraft were talking on the frequency. The cross-talk prevented me from clearly understanding the information that was being relayed in the coordination. I heard the controller say climb the aircraft to 3;000 ft.; and turn him to the west immediately.Because I did not clearly hear the call sign of the aircraft he was referencing my mind jumped to Aircraft X as the aircraft needing the instructions. I immediately issued a climb and turn to Aircraft X and began issuing traffic alerts. Midway through issuing the traffic alerts I recognized that Aircraft X was descending and turning to join final for Runway 1L. In that instance I recognized what Departure Control was trying to coordinate and I sent Flight Number X around and vectored him away from Aircraft X and issued a traffic alert.Aircraft X checked onto my frequency on a mile final. I cleared him to land. Immediately after clearing him to land; the ASDE-X alerted with a taxiway proximity alert. It appeared to me that Aircraft X was correcting back toward Runway 1L. I asked the pilot if they requested priority handling. The pilot said no. The aircraft appeared aligned with the runway and the pilot confirmed they were; but because he was not a priority. I sent the plane around as required by the 7110.65. Coordination would have been easier and clearer had the radar data tag scratchpad entry for Aircraft X been changed to '01L' which would have indicated that he was inbound to land. The scratchpad showed the SID he filed; which contributed to my initial thinking that he was off course and not a priority. Additionally; had Departure Control requested priority handling in the coordination; I believe I would have immediately keyed onto the fact that Aircraft X was returning.The Airport Surface Detection Equipment (ASDE-X) ASDE Taxiway Arrival Prediction Software (ATAP) has had five alerts since its implementation on Date. In every case; the aircraft have been properly aligned with the runway and the alerts have been the result of poorly designed taxiway capture zones. The ATAP enhancement should be temporarily disabled and a full review of the ATAP system should occur.
Report_1_Synopsis: A Tower Local Controller reported a departure deviated from its clearance and turned back to the airport to land and into confliction with an arrival on final approach.The Tower received an alert from an automated system (ASDE X ATAP) warning that the aircraft was aligned with a taxiway and not the runway although the aircraft had corrected back to course. The reporter states that false alerts from the ASDE X ATAP (Airport Surface Detection Equipment Taxiway Arrival Prediction Software) is a recurring issue.

Report_1_Narrative: I was working LC/GC (Local Control/Ground Control) combined during LADP (Local Airport De-Icing Plan) operations. An aircraft called ready for departure on Runway 6 and was instructed to hold short for traffic landing Runway 33. Several Airport-Operations vehicles were on the frequency at the time and one of them stated on the frequency that Runway 33 was closed. The landing aircraft was issued go-around instructions on a two-mile final and subsequently landed on Runway 6. The Tower CIC (Controller in Charge) checked the NOTAMs and verified that Runway 33 had been closed for approximately 30 minutes. No notification had been received from Airport Operations that Runway 33 was closed.Similar incidents of this nature have happened in the past. Coordination via automation; or recorded landline; may help prevent these situations from happening in the future.
Report_1_Synopsis: BDL Air Traffic Controller reported confusion of runway status due to poor communications with airport operations resulted in a go-around.

Report_1_Narrative: Working Radar East at ZZZ. I had approximately 14 aircraft. Aircraft X was on an arrival to ZZZ. I had many other over flights and 3 more arrivals into ZZZ. I got caught watching a separation of ZZZ also Traffic near another airport. I had based Aircraft X. I missed the turn to final. I tried to turn the Aircraft X back to ZZZ and was late in seeing Aircraft Y that was being vectored south of ZZZ to a nearby airport. When I saw Aircraft Y; I told Aircraft X to give me a tight turn to heading 020; if unable I'll need to turn to the south. I called traffic and the aircraft were really close. Aircraft X reported Aircraft Y insight and was climbing. They didn't report and RA at the time. Aircraft Y was also called traffic and told to maintain visual separation after they reported Aircraft X insight.Aircraft X was cleared for visual approach shortly afterwards.Due to the COVID staffing my crew continues to work short staffed. I allowed another controller to allow a VFR aircraft to be flying to conflict with my arrivals that drew attention away from the final at the time. I also should have handed off the arrivals to the West Controller that also had the finals at the time. The West Controller was the one that allowed the VFR traffic that I was watching in conflict with the arrival into ZZZ conflict.
Report_1_Synopsis: TRACON Controller reported an unsafe operation between an IFR carrier and a VFR aircraft resulting in an airborne conflict.

Report_1_Narrative: Aircraft X was issued a heading on departure to avoid VFR traffic in the area by my trainee; NW bound. Turn NW bound without a climb was not enough of a turn to completely avoid the MVA in area and the aircraft 'Rode the boundary' of the 2;500 MVA at 2;000 for 2 miles before a climb was issued.  Climb the aircraft earlier or turn out further west to avoid the MVA.
Report_1_Synopsis: RSW radar Instructor reported developmental failed to climb traffic resulted in entering a higher MVA.

Report_1_Narrative: Aircraft X was IFR inbound to CNO on RNAV RWY 26R. At about 6 miles out when he contacted me; there was traffic at his 1 o'clock and 1-2 miles same altitude Aircraft Y. Aircraft Y was not on my frequency and was just outside the Delta airspace just about 5 miles east. I gave numerous traffic calls for Aircraft Y. At about a mile and half separation; I issued the IFR to descend which led him to continue on the approach with an early descent. Aircraft Y passed behind and about 400 higher than Aircraft X. Just as Aircraft Y passed behind Aircraft X; said he had the traffic in sight and said that was scary. due to the pilot saying it was scary an NMAC would be done. Since I wasn't talking to the transitioning aircraft who was last talked to by ONT with just one traffic call then a frequency change; I was never talking to Aircraft Y.Extend the Class Delta more east so aircraft would be forced to contact CNO. have better traffic calls for aircraft from previous facility to eliminate NMAC or having ONT give the aircraft a frequency change to CNO Tower to have better control and communication with all aircraft.
Report_1_Synopsis: CNO Tower Controller reported issuing inbound IFR a descent to avoid NORDO traffic resulted in a NMAC.

Report_1_Narrative: SNA Tower cleared us for takeoff on 20R but changed our clearance altitude from 5;000 feet to 3;000 feet for crossing traffic. We were very light and the max power setting gave us a very very high climb rate. We had a LEVEL OFF RA at 2;800 feet MSL which was the easy part. We complied and did not go above 3;000 feet as a light aircraft passed directly overhead. I believe the separation was 400 feet. Complicating this situation; and the real reason for this report; was the fact that we were given a 3;000 feet clearance and our performance was so high; we got ALT ACQ around 1;000 feet. Our automation did not provide proper guidance as the speed reverted to flaps up speed (15) and the autothrottles wanted to go to max power (takeoff power 100.6%). Also; the cutback N1 was 26% less than takeoff power! My FO had to disconnect the Autothrottles to prevent them from surging back to max power after he set them to cutback and flight directors were commanding a climb well above 10-15 degrees even though my speed was below the shark tooth. I had to fly out of the situation and my FO gave great communication as he kept our SA in focus. I am not 100% sure what happened with the automation but I believe the ALT ACQ at such a low altitude caused some serious issues. This would not have happened with a normal 5;000 feet clearance; or if we were heavy with less performance or we were doing a normal takeoff profile.However; I am concerned that with a few more variables or a crew that did not work as effectively as we did today this could have been a much worse outcome. I am wondering if we should be given 3;000 feet clearances with crossing traffic. With a normal takeoff profile it would have been fine but the max power setting and with the large power cutback for noise abatement this was a tricky situation. Compliments to my FO who took action on the autothrottles to prevent an automated max thrust climb after he pulled for cutback by disengaging them and clearly communicating that part of the problem.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported an NMAC during takeoff from SNA airport.  Captain cited a high climb rate due to the aircraft being light in weight and a last minute lowered altitude crossing restriction contributed to the event.

Report_1_Narrative: Early in the boarding process the Purser notified me of a family that was being defiant about wearing masks in compliance with company policy.  After speaking with the family; the Purser still felt uneasy about the family. I then asked for a Customer Service Supervisor to meet the airplane.  While discussing the issue with the supervisors and FAs; a separate family came forward to note their concern over the behavior of the first family. Two of the second family quickly began tearing up.  Additionally; there was a passenger in the vicinity of the problem family who had health issues. At this point; I decided to have the problem family removed.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported that during boarding a family was not compliant with face mask policy. After other passengers expressed concern; the Captain had the family removed from the flight.

Report_1_Narrative: We arrived in ZZZ at XA:00 local time. The aircraft was to remain overnight and we were asked to leave the APU up and packs on due to cold overnight temperatures. This method was used by the ground personnel in lieu of a ground heat cart since one was not available. We left the APU running as requested and left the airport. Upon returning to the airplane the next day we found the left wing tank which the APU was being feed from only containing 200 pounds of fuel. This is a concern as there is no one on the aircraft overnight to monitor the fuel low pressure lights. If there was a delay or other situation this aircraft would have run the left tank dry causing the APU to shut down. Most importantly there would be an unmonitored low pressure fuel low pressure light. The other concern for this configuration was the outflow valve was closed manually with the APU and packs on. I understand this configuration with an external air cart on the aircraft; but not certain it is appropriate for the APU configuration. If the main cabin door were to be closed this would pressurize the aircraft completely making it impossible to access unless the fire handle is pulled in the wheel well to shut down the APU.
Report_1_Synopsis: B737 Captain reported ground personnel requested APU on overnight; but failed to monitor low fuel pressure.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Communication Breakdown; Human-Machine Interface; Distraction; Workload; Confusion; Situational Awareness
Report_1_Narrative: On pushback the towbar broke. When I heard the noise I looked down and saw that the brakes were still set. I had failed to verify that they were released. Fortunately; maintenance found no damage on the inspection. The flight continued normally after we received a new release.There were numerous contributing factors that led to this place. This was my first international trip in quite some time. There were many issues related to COVID-19 and catering. Chief of which was no ice being available. I tried to coordinate with the station to get some even asking if the terminal restaurants had some they would spare. No luck. There was also a discussion between myself and the First Officer regarding the rarely used method to obtain the ATC clearance in ZZZZ.The First Officer said he wanted to get home early and I believe he initiated the call to ground for the push before I was ready. I hadn't yet removed my mask. I did not have my audio panel properly configured and my mask was blocking my view of those switches. Ground Control gave us a push clearance then added a last minute query as to which runway we wanted which the First Officer and I discussed and verified.I either missed the pushback crew saying they were ready or they did not initiate the standard sequence so I had to verify that they were ready. Ground then told us to hold our push and that stopped me from releasing the brakes at that point when I normally might have done so. There was also confusion with the pushback location. I could not locate it on the charts. We were also using a gate in a part of the terminal neither myself or the First Officer had been at before.As I was re-configuring my audio panel my watch flashed a [personal message.] Although I did not read it; I noticed it. That took my out of my routine and although I felt my legs relax after I thought I hit the pedals to release the brakes; they were still set.Although I have been with the company many years; I have also not been flying much lately; 4 legs in the last 90 days or so. I also don't know why my watch flashed a message when my phone was off.In the end it was a failure to verify the status of the parking brakes. I will redouble my efforts to ensure a verification that the brakes indicate they are released in the appropriate sequence going forward.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported not releasing the brakes before pushback resulting in a broken tow bar.  The Captain cited multiple distractions and lack of flying as contributing factors.

Report_1_Narrative: When we were turning into the parking space on hardstand; the ground personnel had the wrong lead in sign lit up; and that is the one we lined up with.  The Captain did a good job and was taxiing very slow cause it didn't look 100 percent; but the ground personnel just stood and watched us.  This led us to believe that we were parking where they wanted us to.  As we moved closer; a bus on the left side looked too close (but was behind the line) and that is when the Captain stopped the plane to wait for ground personnel to double check.  At that point they realized we were not on the line to the right where they actually wanted us.  A tug was brought over to push us back and line us up with the correct line and lead-in sign.  Even when we docked; the correct taxi-in guidance was never turned on.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported almost hitting a bus while parking at EGLL airport and cited communication issues with ground personnel as a contributing factor.

Report_1_Narrative: The Captain briefed that he would fly the ZZZ ILS 27R. On the arrival abeam the FAF we called the airport in sight and were subsequently cleared #1 for the visual approach. In the turn towards the final approach I lost sight of the runway. I was expecting the Captain to maneuver the aircraft to align the airplane with the approach course prior to; or at; the FAF. He turned well inside the FAF to intercept a 3 mile final. I was not expecting this and felt behind the aircraft. While on the base leg we received a radio call from Tower 'low altitude alert; below minimum vectoring altitude.' This left me even more uneasy during the approach. I expressed my concern to the Captain. The Captain was able to re-cage my situational awareness and continued the visual approach. We rolled out on final; stabilized on glide path and made an uneventful landing. We thoroughly debriefed the flight; with much attention on the approach.
Report_2_Narrative: The FO (First Officer) had never been into ZZZ; and I hadn't been there for years. Briefing the approach; I handled the terrain" item by saying something silly like "I don't know of any." In fact there was no high terrain; but there were close-in obstacles. I mentioned that we might well get a slam dunk visual but I did not communicate to the FO my idea of normally being comfortable joining the final on visual approaches inside the FAF; about 3 miles out at 1;000 feet AGL. If I had done that fuller briefing; he would not have been surprised when I later pointed the aircraft inside the FAF. Descending on the arrival; we noted that the procedure put us on a long final for the ILS to 27R; but we both got the impression that we would be #1 to the airport and slam dunked. On downwind abeam the airport we were descended to 3;000 feet and then cleared for the visual approach. I headed over toward the ILS FAF and descended toward its crossing altitude; 2;100 feet; while I evaluated the position and energy. I saw that we were in a position to join a 3-mile final in a stabilized condition. Focusing visually on the right base leg and the airport; we were at about 1;700 feet on about a three mile base. At this time ATC transmitted; "Low altitude alert; minimum vectoring altitude is 2;100 feet." Our path looked clear ahead and on final to the right; and I did not consider ATC's radar vectoring altitude to exactly apply to our operation. Still; they were trying to tell us something! I looked to the left and saw downtown; laterally closer than desired but certainly more than 2;000 feet horizontally. I shallowed the descent as much as I could without going too high to be stabilized on final. We joined the final and landed normally.By inadequately studying and briefing the airport's visual flying environment; I did a night visual approach that was safe but that (1) concerned ATC; (2) concerned my flying partner; and (3) worst of all; surprised me about our proximity to downtown because I had not identified the high buildings as a threat."
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier flight crew reported crew communication breakdown during approach resulted in a CFTT event.

Report_1_Narrative: Aircraft X had been blocked out for 12 mins at the time when they received an ACARS from load planning stating that 'Captain we have a ramp loading error with DG and need you to return to the gate. Zooming in on ZZZ in [Software] I could see Aircraft X was taking the runway. I immediately called the tower and asked them to tell him to come back to the gate as well as copy and pasted the message from load planning to him in another ACARS message. At that point it seemed like he had got the message and turned off the runway. The Load Planner also called me to inform me of the situation but at this point the plane had already turned off the runway. The issue is not load planning; the issue is ramp. This was a ramp directed loading flight and load planners didn't receive the information until it was almost too late. If the crew missed the ACARS or maybe if it were to have been rejected; they could have been airborne with the DG loaded improperly. Not only is this incredibly dangerous but happens entirely too often."
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Load Planner reported notifying flight crew to return to departure gated due to a DG load configuration error detected as aircraft about to takeoff

Report_1_Narrative: Failed to add an alternate on the flight when required by FOM.All of my other flights inbound to ZZZ1 had ZZZ2 listed as an alternate.  It was simply a missed step on this one.  This was one of the earlier departures on my desk and I was still dealing with a full outbound as well as a complicated swap between Aircraft X/Aircraft Y.  While OJT was not being conducted at my desk; the Recovery Specialist was conducting OJT in the other chair.  Overall and simply put; additional focus by myself or the Captain would have solved this issue.  There is also an issue of our airline running behind schedule due to COVID-19 and those flights that would normally be airborne are now departing causing additional distraction.  I would suggest that management take at least a temporary look at better matching our flights with the scheduled workload.
Report_1_Synopsis: Dispatcher reported not adding an alternate to a flight.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Situational Awareness; Communication Breakdown; Confusion; Distraction
Report_1_Narrative: The event occurred because ZZZ is working a busy airport with one Controller utilizing all three frequencies. This is a major safety of flight issue as multiple links in the safety chain were broken that day. If the sharpness of the crews from Aircraft Y and Aircraft Z had not utilized full four ear policy and patience it could have been an issue. The actions taken by the ATC operation in ZZZ are uncalled for and unsafe. If this is overlooked there could be fatal consequences in the future. There are a few local airports in the area of ZZZ that are non-towered. If the Tower Controller delayed any further for us to be handed over to Departure; we could have had a collision or RA with an unknown aircraft all due to the unsafe actions of one Controller handling a workload bound for a minimum of two personal.On the morning of date; I was in command of flight Aircraft X; ZZZ to ZZZ1. The ZZZ Tower had one Controller working all three frequencies: clearance; ground; and Tower. This day was a busy morning with Aircraft A bound for ZZZ1; Aircraft Y to ZZZ3; Aircraft Z to ZZZ4; and us to ZZZ1 all departing at roughly the same time.When we called for our clearance on the delivery frequency; we noticed there was some bleed over as the Controller was issuing takeoff clearances. We had to repeat our request for a clearance but were given it with no issues.I released the brakes and we called for push shortly after. Aircraft Y also called for push after us. In the middle of our push back the Controller called on the ground frequency to inform Aircraft A of a delay to ZZZ2 for them.  The two began to have a conversation on ground of a game plan to be made. As their conversation occurred our Ramp crew disconnected the tow bar and gave the wave off for an all clear to a taxi.I noticed Aircraft Y had pushed off gate X and we were pushed off of X+1 with our nose in the direction of travel to only exit at [intersection] with a head on collision. First Officer and I finished our 'After Start Checklist' and cleared the area to begin our taxi. I switched on our taxi and nose lights to noticed Aircraft Y did the same. With the Controller and Aircraft A conversation occurring to what was now a clearance being given with a read back to follow there was no way for me or Aircraft Y to have confirmation one was waiting for the other.There was dense fog and low visibility on the ramp that morning. Tower does not control the ramp and a courtesy call is requested. The weather was so bad we had a takeoff alternate of ZZZ5 that morning.It was a frustrating situation as Aircraft Y and I could barely make out the 2nd half of each other's aircraft; so it was a game of chicken. I tried to call over the radio and speak over the clearance being given but it did not work.Ultimately; I turned off my lights to give Aircraft Y the right of way. As we began our taxi to Runway X Aircraft Z called clearance to get their clearance to ZZZ4 and that now was being broadcast over the ground frequency adding to the safety issue that no one moving on the aircraft surface could talk to each other.The Tower issued Aircraft Y their takeoff clearance and told us we were next. After we got our takeoff clearance; we began the takeoff roll with no issues. As we continued our takeoff climb Aircraft Z called the Controller over the ground frequency. All we heard was the Controller responding over the Tower frequency meaning he was working all three frequencies still. This delayed our hand-off to departure and made us uneasy as the Tower radar could not see our path beyond a certain mileage. As we checked in with ZZZ Departure we were given an instruction to contact ZZZ3 Center as our time had been too long and radar services with ZZZ could not be utilized further.This told me the ZZZ airport Controller took too long to hand us off and impeded the Departure Controller from doing their job properly. We did not have sufficient air traffic control separation all due to the unsafe practices of the ZZZ airport and Air Traffic Control operation at the airport of ZZZ.ZZZ needs to hire another Controller! There must be at least one person working Ground and Delivery while another separate Controller works Tower. The operation in ZZZ has been compromised and it is scary to think that the unsafe actions are acceptable to those working in the ATC system.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported Air Traffic Controller was working Local; Ground; and Clearance Delivery on one frequency resulting in communication issues and a delayed hand-off to Departure Control.

Report_1_Narrative: On flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1 'smoke-like' smell present in both cockpit and cabin. FA (Flight Attendants) investigated to determine source; but were unable to locate anything of note. Smell dissipated and generally disappeared in cockpit; whilst simultaneously continued in the cabin and became more present. Smell when present in cockpit was identified as smelling like burn off from automobile exhaust piping when road water is splashed on the piping. Maybe even an oil burn off smell. Definitely not the same smell as deicing fluid. FAs reported the smell was similar to the burning smell of an overheated hair dryer.On continued investigation while still climbing; FAs noticed a strong smell of fuel in the aft cabin. One FA reported development of nauseous feelings and also a strong headache. As CA (Captain) I determined that continuation was a poor choice and elected to divert to ZZZ2 as it was at our approximate 4 o'clock position and was a good Airport Rescue and Fire Fighting location should fire be present.ATC notified of our intentions and diversion was begun.No indications on EICAS; no hydraulic or fuel losses. No additional identifications from the FAs except that the odors were continually present in descent and approach and taxi and were strong. Odor returned to cockpit but only slightly.  FO (First Officer) did not report noticing it again; CA noticed only slightly.ATC requested fuel remaining and souls on board. Priority handling never declared by CA; FO never heard requested priority handling status; but it is believed that we became priority handling status. Landed opposite direction in ZZZ2 and met by Airport Rescue and Fire Fighting.Landed XR; exited runway and parked on taxiway. Airport Rescue and Fire Fighting did a drive around for any abnormalities or indications of smoke or fire and found none. Taxied to gate XX with ARFF following. Taxied behind a 777 and experienced exhaust fumes. Only reason for note of this is that the exhaust fume odor was distinctly different than the odor noticed during the flight.Parked at gate. Did not start the APU having concerns that it may have been the culprit in regards to the possible odor and\or with the potential to be a source of fire and\or smoke at parking. Ground power connected and normal shutdown and parking.Airport Rescue and Fire Fighting personnel met the aircraft as jetbridge attached. Forward FA was the reporting FA for the feelings of nausea and headache and was removed from the aircraft first. As CA I assumed her position for overseeing of the passenger. FO continued to monitor radios.FA reported the fresh air provided relief; but not complete. Was released by the EMTs and also cleared by MedLink to the hotel for rest.Passengers deplaned approximately 5 minutes after door opening. Smoke like smell in the cockpit and cabin and also fuel smell in the cabin. Diversion to ZZZ2.
Report_1_Synopsis: EMB-175 Captain reported a fumes event during initial climb resulting in a diversion to a suitable airport.

Report_1_Narrative: While in cruise flight (FL370) we were cleared to cross the ZZZZZ intersection at FL330.  The FO entered the new altitude and I confirmed it.  We agreed to start down at the TOD.  ATIS indicated that we could be landing either [Runway] XXC or XXR.  I noticed the runway condition was 555 and total runway distance for Runway XXR was 7500 feet; which required a non-standard landing assessment.  I started entering the numbers in the landing app; when I decided to look back at our progress.  I immediately noticed that we had overflown the TOD.  I alerted the FO and he selected 'OPEN DESCENT!  I knew this would be insufficient and called out 'My aircraft;' he acknowledged and I attempted to make the restriction.  I quickly realized there was no chance of making the restriction; so as I stabilized the descent; I instructed the FO to inform ATC would be unable to make the restriction (we would be high).  After that I called for 'autopilot 2 and we transferred control of the aircraft back to the FO.  ATC acknowledged the transmission and we proceeded to the destination airport without further incident.  I decided not to debrief until we were at the gate; so to avoid any further incidents.In an effort to stay ahead of the; all too often; last minute approach changes and subsequent rushed approach briefings at low altitude; I as the non-flying pilot; elected to proactively run the landing numbers and review the XXR approach plate.  The obvious problem with that is; that the check and balance system for aircraft control is compromised when both pilots are not concentrating on the more immediate task at hand. It should be noted that the FO had just come from a training event to restore currency after almost 3 months off.  My FO did list that as a threat on our very first flight of the day. As such; I had been trying to complete tasks earlier than usual; not only to avoid the problems associated with operations at ZZZ1 but also so I could more closely monitor him; but in this case it backfired.According to the report home page altitude deviations are the number one reported event; so I don't really know what could effectively prevent this type of event. Possibly; the best we could hope for is to reduce the frequency.  For my part in reducing the frequency of which this event occurs; I will not address any other actions until the descent is begun and the altitude clearance is assured.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported not making a crossing restriction after realizing they had overflown the top of descent.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Communication Breakdown; Situational Awareness; Distraction; Workload
Report_1_Narrative: Inbound to ZZZZ on ZZZZZ Star.  Taken off STAR early and cleared direct to ZZZZ1 VOR.  We were instantly 1;800 feet above the path.  Proactively used speed brakes and planned to slow and extend flaps when below 20;000 feet; but were then told to keep speed at 250 KTS.  Lowered landing gear shortly after passing ZZZZ1 to get back on profile.  Was able to regain the VNAV path just prior to ZZZZZ1 and at Vref +10 per procedure.  Flaps were at 25. Frequency was very busy and sky hazy. Very late hand off to Tower.  Localizer did not correctly ID until just prior to FAF.  FO was very busy with frequency changes; configuration changes and checklist.  Tower did not clear us to land; but instructed us to continue as an aircraft was in position on our Runway; XXR. Another aircraft was holding short of XXR waiting to cross.  At 1;000 feet I was at approach speed and called 'stable;' but was distracted by no landing clearance and aircraft on runway.  Aircraft in position was cleared for immediate takeoff; we were cleared to land; and other aircraft was given clearance to cross XXR.  Departing aircraft was slow to accelerate.  Passing 500 feet FO made 'stable' call.  Shortly after we received an aural alert indicating we did not have landing flaps selected.  Flaps indicator showed flaps at 25 degrees verses the planned and briefed of 30 degrees.  I realized I had not asked for flaps 30 and was now below 400 feet. Elected not to make a configuration change to 30 degrees below 1;000 feet per procedure.  Hesitant to go-around per procedure because I wasn't sure if the crossing aircraft had not just departed the inboard parallel Runway XXL; and the late departing XXR aircraft had just rotated.  With the very hazy sky I was concerned about a conflict and /or overtaking the other aircraft during the go-around to increase speed to Vref+10 and land with flaps 25. Landing and rollout were normal.Despite adequate and recent experience into ZZZZ; these particular controllers were hard to understand.  FO had to ask for clarification a few times in the last 1;500 feet FAF. FO had just returned from 7 months of leave; was called out on reserve; and had only flown once earlier; and 4 times in the last 7 months.  I briefed the arrival and approach thoroughly and early; but it was a Max effort with the direct clearance.  I believe he got distracted from completing the checklist when the localizer did not ID until just before the FAF.  I was distracted from not calling for final flaps with the aircraft on the runway and the hazy conditions; and the late localizer ID.Add to the note of being at Vref +10 by the ZZZZZ1 fix; to be at final landing flaps. This may have helped me if I had a goal to complete that by the fix.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported an unstable approach and cited it was difficult to understand the controllers at this foreign location.

Report_1_Narrative: Noticed slight airframe vibration in the climb.   At FL300 it was much worse. Getting even more vibration as speed increased.  Called up the flight control page and saw the R FLPRN was almost all the way up with the L in a normal position.  The control column was 2 degrees right wing down.  Called Operations Control and discussed.  Had the Tech Pilot on the phone also.  All agreed it was not normal.  Decision was to return to ZZZ.  Had to dump fuel.  Did this in coordination with Center.  Arrival was normal until landing flaps were selected.  When flaps started past 20 the airplane shook violently and rolled to the R.  Re-selected flaps to 25 and added 15 knots.  At the gate the maintenance tech could see the Number 6 spoiler was up.  Wrote up the discrepancies and debriefed the mechanic.  Crew did a phenomenal job.  Great back up.Cause - Spoiler float not locked down.
Report_2_Narrative: Aircraft X did a block turn back for a spoiler issues when I first sat down.  After nearly 5 hours on the ground; we received a duty extension and the flight departed. (XA16z) At approximately XA55z crew sent ACARS message:...ALT AIRFRAME VIBL ENG 1.0  R ENG .9R FLPRN IS UPVIBWORSE AT HIGHER SPD.I spoke with the crew on the SATCOM for over an hour bringing in Operations; Tech Pilot; Maintenance Control and Maintenance Control talked to mechanics that did the spoiler work.  We determined it was odd behavior for B777 controls and this aircraft usually flies straight. Determination was made to bring the flight back to ZZZ as this may not be an easy fix.
Report_1_Synopsis: B777 flight crew and the flight Dispatcher reported airframe vibrations during climbout which worsened as the speed increased.  The crew contacted the company and decided to return to their departure airport.  Reportedly; the cause of the issue was a spoiler float was not locked down.

Report_1_Narrative: Prior to Final approach in ZZZ; approach vectored us very close to the final approach course with a 30 kt tailwind on base and at 4;000 ft just outside ZZZZZ for the ILS XXR; assigned 190 kts. As we intercepted the course the autopilot flew past the localizer at close to half scale deflection; as it would not correct course timely. We also had to descend and slow down to configure for final approach within 3 miles of final approach fix. As the autopilot was correcting for that we set 3;000 ft for the missed approach altitude. A CAS MISCOMP status message appeared and the altitude alerter came on would not stop ringing. When we changed navigation source to green needles; the localizer would not capture with the autopilot; therefore the glide slope would also not capture. During the navigation source change; my flight director on the first officer's side became erratic and I lost the localizer transmission. We decided to execute a missed approach due to being unstable along with the flight instrument errors. Tower assigned us a heading and altitude and we reconfigured the aircraft for the go around all while the altitude alerter was blaring. During straight and level flight; we decided to reassign the FCP to heading and altitude. Once established; we turned the autopilot on and all instruments worked correctly. The altitude alert ringer was still buzzing so we decided to silence using Data Control Unit (DCU) audio buttons to declutter the situation. After completing proper checklists; we decided to continue on with another ILS XXR and executed approach and landing normally. After shutdown the altitude alerter still continued to ring until AC power was switched from the APU GEN to EXT AC. We wrote up the problem and notified maintenance.ATC giving us tight vectors with a tailwind on base along with our equipment malfunctions. The altitude alerter sounding loudly along our flight directors being erratic caused task saturation to the captain who was PF. As PM I helped the captain de clutter the situation and to reminded him to just fly the airplane which he did well as we tracked the localizer and conducted the go around. Once we silenced the altitude alerter it became much easier to fly the aircraft and we were able to conduct the next approach successfully.Possibly asking for a slower intercept speed or lower from ATC. The equipment malfunctions lead to the approach to become unstable and that's why we conducted a go around. I could have possibly contacted tower a few seconds earlier to ask for a vector and altitude but it was quite difficult with the task saturation being as high as it was; especially with the altitude alerter loudly sounding. Overall it was a great lesson in always being able to maintain control and fly the aircraft regardless of the state of automation it is in which I thought we did a great job of despite the system malfunctions during a high work load environment.
Report_1_Synopsis: CRJ-200 First Officer reported experiencing a high workload during final approach and cited poor ATC vectors; the autopilot failing to capture the localizer and a continual altitude alerter sounding as contributing.

Person_2_Human_Factors: Confusion; Workload; Time Pressure; Communication Breakdown; Human-Machine Interface
Report_1_Narrative: In preparation for our arrival into DEN we briefed for the CLASH 3 RNAV arrival and the ILS to 35R as this was the expected runway from our direction of arrival. We also included in our brief the threat in DEN of runway changes and how we'd handle that especially during the descent phase on the arrival. About 20 NM from the waypoint CLASH on the arrival ATC informed us to expect runway 35L. We then re-set up for that runway and re-briefed. There was still plenty of time for this and there was little time compression. One point of confusion; however; was that the CLASH 3 has a transition for RWY 35R; but doesn't for 35L; which only has a point at which to expect vectors. We spent some time studying the arrival and approach plates to ensure that was the case to make sure we weren't missing something. I asked my F/O to double check as he was the PM and I wanted to concentrate on the descent as the PF. This has always been confusing as some arrivals and approaches have transition points and some don't. There should be some consistency. This was the beginning of some of the time compression which would later result in some workload management issues.Some point after this ATC broke us off of the arrival and instructed us to descend to 9000 feet and gave us a heading. They then assigned us to RWY 35R. We related that we'd just been assigned 35L and they reiterated we were now reassigned to 35R. This resulted in a very rushed set up for 35R as we were now pretty close in to the approach environment. I asked the F/O to set it all up so that I could continue to fly. I quickly dialed in what I thought was the 35R LOC; but it turned out not to be. I could see that he was struggling and tried to help him out. In hindsight; this was a mistake in workload management because I should have let the F/O do all of the set up. I verbalized that we didn't need to re-brief for 35R as we'd already briefed it and so had a plan. Again; in hindsight; I'm not sure this was a correct call; but we literally did not have time to brief at that point.Shortly after this we were cleared the visual approach to 35R.  We were roughly 7 miles from FRONZ and discussed not descending too quickly so as not to bust the floor of the Class B airspace. At about the same time ATC asked us to slow to approach speed for traffic ahead of us for 35R. After slowing we ended up just about 2.5 miles in trail.  At this point we were apprised of traffic for 35L and received a TCAS TA because of the assigned heading we were given to intercept the LOC for 35R. We both saw the traffic and I decided to hand fly from this point on as we had an overshooting crosswind and given our heading there would have been a good chance of an overshoot of the LOC.At FRONZ I asked for gear down and flaps 15. At about this point I noticed that neither the LOC or GS were engaging but I had the runway and the PAPI and decided to continue as we had been cleared for the visual. The FO asked if I'd like him to try and dial in the correct LOC and I said yes if he had the bandwidth to do so. Soon after we passed through 1;000 feet and we both missed the call out as I think he was still trying to dial in the LOC frequency. Also we never accomplished the Landing Checklist as we never got to final flaps. We got to 500 feet and we made those call outs. At around 400 feet AFL we received a Too Low Flaps GPWS warning and my knee jerk reaction was to call for FLAP 30 once I realized we were still at FLAPS 15. I don't know if the FO ever selected them; however. I quickly realize this was the wrong call and called for us to go around and the FO called for it at about the same time. We executed the missed approach with no issues and were vectored expeditiously for a second approach and landing without further incident.The FO is not submitting a report as far as I'm aware as we had no ATC deviations or non-compliance with FARS.
Report_2_Narrative: This is a report regarding Flight X ZZZ-DEN regarding the changes and ATC clearances we received during our descent and approach to land in DEN.When we reviewed the flight plan in ZZZ we loaded the CLASH3 STAR with runway 35R being our selected landing runway. The flight plan had 17R; but DEN was landing North so that was the only change made to the plan on our part versus what dispatch had planned.Prior to TOD the CA fully reviewed and briefed the STAR and approach that we were expecting. We were fully prepared to execute this plan. Upon checking in with a close in DEN center controller we were advised to expect runway 35L with the EBBLR transition. There was some discussion regarding the EBBLR transition by myself and the CA as we were attempting to figure out if the transition and how the transition linked up with the approach. However; we did this again prior to TOD and were able to be prepared for the new arrival transition and approach. As we descended into Denver; we were handed off to DEN APP. This controller changed our runway back to 35R. We were well into the descent at this point and fairly close to the airport. The CA instructed me to load up the new approach and as I was attempting to do so ATC took us off the arrival for vectors and speed changes. At this point we were South of DEN but still fairly close in. I was still working on getting the FMC setup when ATC vectored us due West and then turned us on to final for 35R. The vector was vey poorly planned by the controller and both the CA and I could see that we were going to blow through the localizer if we allowed the A/P to handle the intercept. The CA disengaged the A/P and made a manual turn to join the localizer. At this point we could both see that the vector had us close in behind another airplane in final. ATC requested that we slow to 160 knots. The CA asked for me to deploy the gear and the flaps to down and 15. Shortly after ATC then requested us to slow to the slowest possible speed. Both the CA and I were closely monitoring the separation between us and the preceding aircraft. At this point I noticed there was a message on the FMC scratchpad that I had not seen before and did not recognize. I don't remember exactly what the message was but it did indicate that there was a conflict between the FMC selected approach and what the VHF radios were tuned to. I was rapidly trying to get the correct frequency on the NAV radios but my JEPP app on the iPad was not responding quickly as I was attempting to zoom in to view the frequency box. At this point we were somewhere around 1;000 feet AGL. The CA announced that he had the runway and the PAPIs in sight and was going to land and just disregard the FMC He was busy attempting to slow and again we were both concerned about the separation between us the preceding aircraft. That was what are focus was on at this point. I cannot recall if either the 1;000 ft or the 500 ft call outs were made. We were both totally task saturated at this time. At some altitude below 500 ft we received a warning message 'too low-flaps'. We both looked at the flap position and realized we were still at flaps 15. The CA called for flaps 30 and I monetarily selected flaps 30 before advocating that we needed to go around. The CA also realized we had to go around at almost the same instant I was stating that we needed to go around. So we executed the go around. We did have the 10;000 ft foot missed approach altitude selected in the MCP so we were climbing to that altitude. However; while just climbing through 7;000 the tower told us to maintain 7;000. I advised tower that we were at 7;200. Tower instructed us to maintain 7;100. We descended back to 7;100 feet and flew runway heading and completed the rest of the go around profile. Tower asked us for the reason for the GA and I replied 'configuration'. They handed us off to approach and we were vectored back around for another ILS to runway 35R. We ensured everything was properly setup and landed without further incident.Some comments about this incident. Both the CA and I had discussed the threat of Denver and how they often make changes to arrivals and approaches during cruise. In fact the CA had been reading in the flight ops newsletter on his iPad about the problems we have been having with arrivals into Denver. We were both fully aware that Denver presented a threat and thought that we had planned and were prepared for our arrival. Had we been cleared as planned per our original plan we would have been fine. Even after the first change to runway 35L we had time to plan and brief. It was only after the final switch back to 35R that we both began to become task saturated with the speed changes; the off route vectors; the FMC programming; the NAV radios; the poor vector to join final; and finally the separation between us and the preceding aircraft and the speed changes made while on final in regards to that aircraft. The amount of items needed to be accomplished while this was occurring in the terminal area was long and complex. We both became so overcome that we must have failed to accomplish the landing checklist; which would have had both of us realizing that we were not in the landing configuration.We made errors along the way; failing to get some of the call outs accomplished; FMC programming; and NAV radio frequency selection among some of the errors. However; many of these errors were driven by the nature of the changes being made by ATC in regards to arrival vectors; speed changes; runway and approach changes among other demands being made by ATC in a very time compressed period while flying within (or near) the terminal area.One more note about the runway changes in Denver. I know Denver and am aware of its threat even on departure. So while we were getting ready to depart and head to ZZZ2 I asked the ramp controller which runway was in use for the ZZZZZ SID. He stated XXR. Yet; when we received our push clearance 15-20 minutes later he told us to expect runway XY. I don't know if he was given bad information by the ATC tower or what happened; but yet again here we are in a high workload situation having to make changes to the FMC and request new TO data.Because of our short turn time in Denver the CA decided to debrief the entire arrival event into Denver while in cruise flying back to ZZZ2. We spent a good 30-40 minutes discussing the flight. Threat and errors were discussed; we used the briefing cards and identified what had occurred on the flight. I am not going to make excuses for the errors that we made; even if they occurred during a task saturated situation. However; a couple of my observations from this event were that we had talked about Denver ATC being a threat. We thought that we had addressed this threat by a good solid brief for the originally planned arrival; even after the change to the 35L arrival; we had time to plan and brief. We were ready; but ATC in Denver threw us some many changes and curve balls that we both were task saturated to the point leading to an undesired aircraft state. Fortunately; both the CA and I followed our training and SOP. safely executed a missed approach; and subsequently landed safely and uneventfully on the next approach.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported a high workload environment on approach into DEN airport; which included several runway changes; confusion over arrival procedures; and an unstable approach resulted in a go-around.

Report_1_Narrative: After landing in ZZZZ I was advised by the charter rep that no cabin cleaning had been arranged.  The flight had come in with passengers onboard.  This resulted in the flight attendants cleaning the aircraft and with no ability for proper COVID mitigation.I queried Dispatch but nobody ever got back to me.  Meanwhile the charter representative assured me that the cleaning they did was all that any Ground Personnel would do.  He also wiped the bathrooms with clorox wipes and then assured me that the aircraft was fit to be boarded.The flight attendants on this crew went above and beyond the call of duty - especially considering that we were already over two hours late on a long duty day due to previous delays from late aircraft and snow storm in ZZZZ1.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported no ground crew was available to sanitize the aircraft resulting in the crew having to clean the aircraft prior to departure.

Report_1_Narrative: Sink rate EGPWS below 1;000 feet / spoilers used below 1;000. TRK Tower cleared us for the visual Runway 29.  Due to the strict noise abatement procedures and high terrain; the maneuver had to be performed within a shorter radius of the Runway 29.  PF and PM briefed the possible sink rate and usage of the spoilers due to the possible increase of descend rate.  The aircraft was stabilized by 300 feet; on speed.Cause - The peculiarity of the airport location.Suggestion - Request Runway 11; or waiver from the noise abatement community for less strict noise procedures.
Report_1_Synopsis: Corporate pilot reported experiencing a sink rate EGPWS event while on the Runway 29 visual approach to TRK airport. Reporter cited high terrain and 'strict' noise abatement procedures contributed to the event.

Report_1_Narrative: Flight Attendant was removed from flight due to COVID exposure. Pre-flight complete with review of AML. Airplane swap from a Type 1 to a Type 0; due too no FA replacement. Running behind schedule. Pre-flighted aircraft and apparently did not verify AML which was left behind and in Maintenance hands. Could have sworn both First Officer and I had hands on! Departed to ZZZ1 without AML.Rushed.I always turn around and confirm that AML is on board at the stage of the checklist when it's announced. Obviously a lack of attention on my part. Still can't believe it happened.
Report_2_Narrative: During pre-flight the CA and I conducted our respective preflight duties; including the Before Start Checklist. At the line item AML and flight forms; we both verified that the AML was on the aircraft. The CA then placed it in the CA side bin. At XA:25 I was notified by the Duty Chief that Maintenance reported the AML for aircraft and XXX was left in ZZZ.Unknown; as we do not know how the AML was left behind. In the future I will be more vigilant in checking that the AML is onboard once the flight deck door is closed.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported departing without the Aircraft Maintenance Logbook (AML) onboard.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Situational Awareness; Confusion; Fatigue; Physiological - Other
Report_1_Narrative: While waiting for the airplane to be towed to the departure gate; I ate a heavy breakfast and did not consume any coffee as this was an Air Carrier X operation and I anticipated coffee being readily available on the plane.  In spite of my request; the FA never made any coffee.  ATC issued a 15 degree heading change for traffic.  I made the heading change without incident.  Subsequently; I began to feel a bit drowsy.  After approximately 5 minutes; ATC issued 'Direct SUNED' fix.  I selected direct SUNED in the FMS and activated after PM confirmed the change.  I forgot to select the NAV mode on guidance panel and we continued on the previous heading for 3 more minutes.  I snapped to attention ATC reissued the Direct SUNED clearance and after a moment of confusion as to why the clearance was reissued; I realized that the guidance panel was still set to HDG mode.  The proper NAV mode was engaged and we proceeded direct to SUNED without incident or any further mention of the issue by ATC. Driven by adrenaline; I remained mentally aroused and vigilant for the remainder of the flight.Cause - PF's Postprandial lassitude caused by failure to ingest a suitable amount of caffeine following heavy breakfast.  PM inattention/distraction was also a factor.Ensure personal availability of postprandial drowsiness countermeasures (aka Coffee) and remember to verify changes on flight mode annunciator.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported a track heading deviation during departure from SLC airport.  First Officer cited feeling drowsy due to not consuming caffeine after a big breakfast may have contributed to the event.

Report_1_Narrative: I was acting as PIC (Pilot in Command) and PF (Pilot Flying). On taxi out from maintenance facility; ATC Instructions were 'cleared to taxi Mike; Alpha cleared to cross runway 14.'Just prior to reaching the intersection of Mike taxiway and runway 14 ATC Instructions heard was 'clear to cross runway 14' The PM (Pilot Monitoring) read back; 'cleared to cross runway 14.'At the point just past the hold short lines and the runway ATC asked if we were holding short. A short exchange was made between us and ATC as ATC stated we were to hold short. An aircraft was held in position on runway 14 and ATC instructed us to proceed and cross runway 14.This flight was an test flight as the day before we had a number 2 engine failure. During taxi out a series of checklist items are accomplished in addition to the normal SOP line flight checklist items. Due to the preceding day's events and root cause of the engine failure information obtained; I ran additional thrust settings changes while on taxi to induce multiple pneumatic pressure bumps and fuel flow oscillations to further test the engine performance. Both the PF and the PM have an abundance of items to accomplish during taxi out on a test flight; I heard two separate clearances to cross runway 14; repeated the clearance verbally to the PM while physically scanning the approach end to my left stating 'cleared to cross 14; clear on final.'While conducting test flights the 'normal everyday expected clearances' and communications exchanges with ATC are handled quickly while simultaneously running additional checks pertinent to specific tasks.
Report_2_Narrative: I was acting as the pilot monitoring on flight.  The day prior we had a block turn back due to an engine shut down during taxi out for the test flight.On an FCF flight taxi time is quite busy. We have many checks to perform; sometimes with very little taxi time to do it. Report_1_Narrative: Flight started out of ZZZ1 with an extended duty period that included X days 'on the road' (unknown to the crew at the time).  I did not verify the aircraft records to see when the next maintenance inspection was due.I usually always look at the aircraft book to see this information.  I did 'open' the aircraft book to retrieve the aircraft keys but did not check the numbers.
