Report_1_Narrative: As we turned on to the lead in line at gate X; we noticed self-park guidance indicated STOP in red letters. We stopped. We noticed two ramp service agents on both wing tips and a marshaller under the unit. We decided that we were expected to taxi down the lead in line with marshaller hand signal guidance and ignore the self-park guidance STOP signal. We parked without incident. On debriefing we (me and the FO) both agreed that taxiing down the lead in line with a marshaller issuing hand signals in the face of a self-park guidance STOP indication is a normalization of deviance that has crept into the culture at ZZZ and should not be accepted at company.During the debriefing the FO encouraged me to consider setting the parking brake; shutting down the engines and politely and professionally request a tow in. It should not come to that.It is lazy and sloppy. It is; of or pertaining to; an organization that because of COVID; layoffs; displacements; cash burn; disappointments; you name it; has taken their eye off the ball. It goes against the pilot culture of never accepting RED. e.g. flight deck indications; Runway Status lights; VASI/PAPI; Runway Stop Bars; REIL; PWS; yet on this occasion; I'm just expected; in the course of normal operations; to taxi to [gate] X at ZZZ with a self-park guidance red STOP indication.This is the second report on such an occurrence at ZZZ.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported taxiing into a gate with the use of a Marshall; while the self-parking guidance system was indicating STOP.

Report_1_Narrative: Ops normal from pushback to takeoff roll.  I was flying pilot; [the] Captain non-flying pilot.   Power was set and autothrottles and FMAs all had normal indications. At approximately 60 knots there was a loud bang and the jet swerved to the right.   I steered the jet back to centerline with rudder and the Captain initiated the abort.  We stopped quickly on the runway and told ATC we'd aborted and instructed the passengers to remain seated.  After quickly assessing the risk; and talking with the Lead Flight Attendant; Captain determined it was safe to taxi clear of Runway XX and we stopped on the parallel taxiway. We requested assistance from [the] Fire Department to look at the landing gear to ensure we hadn't blown a tire or had smoke/fire coming off the brakes.   After getting the all-clear; we coordinated with Operations/Tech Ops to return to Gate X.  We closely monitored brake temp indications during the taxi back and saw that they were all decreasing in normal fashion as expected.  We were met by many company personnel at the gate and Maintenance was able to quickly determine we had an Engine Number 2 compressor stall during takeoff roll.  Passengers deplaned in normal fashion through Door 1L; and the flight crew was then escorted up to ZZZ Flight Ops to discuss our readiness and ability to continue flying the trip.  Captain and I then proceeded to fly as scheduled.
Report_2_Narrative: During takeoff roll; heard a loud bang and aircraft swerved to the right.  Executed rejected takeoff procedure.  Exited runway.  Personnel inspected aircraft externally.  No visible damage and no fires were detected.  Returned to gate.  Maintenance data showed engine stall on Number 2 Engine. My compliments to the First Officer and Flight Attendants for their professionalism during this unexpected event.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported that an engine compressor stall occurred during takeoff roll; causing the aircraft to swerve and the crew to reject the takeoff.

Report_1_Narrative: Ramp called to unlock flight will add ballast. Flight did not have 15 bags minimum to secure DG (Dangerous Goods). Unlocked flight waiting for cargo to add DG in software. Once ballast was added (by ramp) I locked the flight. DG can go thru the locks therefore I was not notified when the DG was added. At departure and ramp finals I realized ballast is loaded with 14 bags but software did not indicate as DG. Cargo Specialist confirmed DG radioactive. Invalid flight but it did not go thru ACARS as invalid all this happened with 4 minutes of from OUT.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Load Planner reported a communications breakdown between Load Planner and Ramp personnel resulting in aircraft departure with incorrect Hazmat documentation.

Report_1_Narrative: Descent and approach were briefed with expectation of [Runway] XXL at ZZZ. ATC advised during descent to expect Runway XYR. ATC was advised that we were a 747-8 and a request for [Runway] XXL was made. ATC advised that Runway XXL was not available unless operationally required. Runway change checklist was performed and performance obtained for [Runway] XYR. Captain briefed that a right turn [off] [Runway] XYR was not allowed except for Taxiway E. However we did not expect to make this exit so he briefed a left turn at [Taxiway] K or roll to the end. Arrival and landing were normal; after slowing through 60 kts. we were past [Taxiway] E and the Captain stated that he would be exiting left on [Taxiway] K. As we began our left turn toward the high speed taxiway I noticed a line of lights on the ground marking the taxiway closed. These were very dim and low to the ground. Very hard to see. I said very affirmatively; STOP; STOP Barrier. The Captain [stopped] the aircraft and then corrected taxi course. The aircraft did encroach on the first few feet of Taxiway K but not far enough that he couldn't correct back onto the runway. On our rollout ATC did issue an invalid taxi clearance that was a distraction. The taxi clearance was corrected after our [query] and the remainder of the taxi was uneventful. Post flight review of NOTAMS (Notice to Airman) and ATIS (Automated Terminal Information Service) revealed that the taxiway was NOTAM closed and was missed on our part. The poor lighting of the taxiway closure barrier was a large factor in us not seeing it sooner.
Report_2_Narrative: Prior to top of descent we briefed and prepared to fly the ILS (Instrument Landing System) approach to Runway XXL at ZZZ. Our airport briefing page does say that arrivals between XA:00 and XB:00 should expect Runway XYR for landing; but goes on to state that 747-8 aircraft should expect XXL. Upon check in with ZZZ Approach; we were told to expect [Runway] XYR. I reminded the controller of our aircraft type and queried whether [Runway] XXL was available. We were told that due to noise abatement procedures at that time of day that we could only use [Runway] XXL if it was due to operational necessity. After a quick discussion with the Captain; we decided that due to our light gross weight; we could accept [Runway] XYR. We quickly reprogrammed the FMS (Flight Management System) and briefed the new approach; to include the many 747-8 taxi restrictions and the fact that taxi to parking was likely to be somewhat complex. We decided that a left turn off the runway on Taxiway Kilo was the most likely scenario. While we did these things quickly; I felt that we had covered all of our bases and did not feel rushed or that the workload was too high. What both the Captain and I missed however; was the fact that [Taxiway] Kilo was closed. We had both reviewed the NOTAMs (Notice To Airmen) and ATIS (Automated Terminal Information Service); but since we were planning on landing on [Runway] 8L; I believe we both simply failed to register the Taxiway Kilo closure; as it did not apply to our original taxi plan. The approach and landing were uneventful and both the Captain and I were focused on identifying Taxiway Kilo in order to vacate the runway. At no point during our approach or rollout did Tower relay any instructions on how we could expect to vacate the runway. As we began to make the turn for [Runway] Kilo; the IRO (International Relief Officer) forcefully stated 'Stop! Stop'. He had managed to pick up the extremely dimly lit barricades that marked the closure. The Captain managed to get the airplane stopped before we were committed to Taxiway Kilo. Around the time we stopped; Tower transmitted that [Taxiway] Kilo was; in fact closed; and that we could expect to make a right turn off the runway at Taxiway Charlie. This was an invalid clearance; as the -8 is restricted from using that portion of [Taxiway] Charlie. As we were about to query Tower; I believe he realized our aircraft type and issued a clearance to taxi clear of the runway at the end. The rest of the taxi was uneventful. I think there are several take-aways from this incident. First; the IRO was worth his weight in gold this morning. Had he not spoken out in a timely and forceful manner; I think there was a very good chance we would have impacted the barriers or at the very least been unable to continue our taxi. The IRO was the last link in the error chain and that link held strong. Second; I think both ZZZ Approach and the Tower Controller were both unaccustomed to a 747-8 arriving at that time of morning. Landing on [Runway] 4R presents a number of taxi challenges to a -8; and perhaps the best practice may be for -8 crews to declare 'operational necessity' and request [Runways] 8L or 8R unless there are other extenuating circumstances. In the event we must land on [Runway] 4R; a simple 'plan to vacate the runway at X' from Tower would be extremely helpful. Finally; while I do believe the way our situation evolved created somewhat of a setup regarding the closure of Taxiway Kilo; the information was in fact available in the NOTAMs and via ATIS. I overlooked that information largely due to an incorrect expectation bias. I am aware of my ultimate responsibility to digest that information and will make an effort in the future to pay more attention to the 'Plan B' options in addition to the expected one.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Flight Crew taxiing 747-8 aircraft reported taxiway incursion on closed taxiway.

Report_1_Narrative: Landing [Runway] XXL on final; aircraft in front of us reported a 10 knot loss. The FO was pilot flying at the time and over corrected for the wind; causing us to descend below glideslope very quickly on short final.  As soon as I was calling go-around the GS aural warning came on.  The FO executed a go-around. Because of the difficult wind conditions and seeing we were already at 2;100-2;200 LBS; I decided that I would land the second attempt as I did not want to get into a fuel situation. We were in agreement with this.  On short final for the second attempt; with me as pilot flying; at about 150 feet; we had the wind-shear caution alert and proceeded to execute our second go-around. ATC gave us instructions to set up for [Runway] XXR but due to fuel concerns I said 'Unable' and declared min fuel. Also; I added that if we did have to take any delays we would be declaring emergency fuel. ATC set us up immediately for a close pattern for [Runway] XXL. On this attempt; I stayed slightly high as the wind shear seem to be the worse right at the tree line at about 150 feet.  On this third attempt; we landed successfully and taxied back to the gate.Unstable approach recognized by me and a wind shear caution message for the second attempt.Inexperienced FO who had only flown once since May 2020 and challenging weather conditions with wind shear.Two go-arounds and declared min-fuel.Have pilots who have been out a while receive more recurrent training.  It was evident due to lack of recency the FO was struggling with the conditions that day.  Also; be vigilant on [Runway] XXL as I have had issues on windy days before where the tree line ends and the field begins. With the second attempt we had a 15 knot increase with the wind shear caution message.
Report_2_Narrative: I was the Pilot Flying. The Wind shear changes in combination with the amount of time since I've been flying in the airplane were contributing factors. There were changes of +/- 15kts and on short approach I went slightly below glide slope and then the Wind shear happened which caused the Glideslope aural warning to sound. The Captain called for a Go-Around which we executed. Once we were at a safe altitude and being vectored back for another approach the we exchanged controls and the Captain became the Pilot Flying. As we were coming in on short approach the Wind shear Aural Caution message sounded so we executed a second go-around. ATC told us that they were going to vector us around for Runway XXR; but were now low on fuel and declared min fuel. They instead kept us close pattern for Runway XXL and we landed safely. Upon landing we had 1;450 LBS of fuel. We taxied to the gate with no issues.Glideslope Aural Warning System on first attempt and Wind shear warning system on second attempt.Wind shear affecting experience level.Go-Around executed twice.Keep crews more recent on flying or more time in simulator if it's been a while.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported experiencing wind shear on final resulting in a go-around. Captain made reference to the First Officer's lack of flying as a contributing factor.

Report_1_Narrative: Aircraft X; ZZZ1-ZZZ did a block-turn-back for maintenance and transload. Due to delay; flight ended up arriving in ZZZ when Tower was closed. I knew ZZZ Tower was closing due to staffing/COVID cleaning and because of the block-turn-back; I simply forgot to add Non-Tower Ops worksheet.Airport towers are constantly closing early due to COVID cleaning or staffing and just need to pay attention to them. Suggest going ahead and sending crew via email Non-Tower Ops Worksheet just in case of delay.
Report_1_Synopsis: Dispatcher forgot to include Non-Tower Operations worksheet with the aircraft paperwork.

Report_1_Narrative: At the start of our flight there were thru passengers; one of which was a family of 4. Their small child was not wearing her mask correctly; so I ask that they use the child mask that the previous crew left for them. They were compliant and not a problem. During boarding; another family of 4 boarded with a child that had his own seat and was clearly not under 2. He had no mask at all; I told the Mom that he needed to have a mask on before boarding the plane. She said she told the Gate Agent that he was under 2. I let her board and called down the agent who said that even though he had a purchased seat there was no way other than to take her word for it. During the flight his sister came up and spoke to us about her vacation and told us that she had a baby brother who is 3. This being the same kid that was questioned. My problem with us not having a policy to check for birth dates is that it essentially creates a problem with compliance. How can I be expected to enforce the mask policy to the family that was honest about their child's age while the family that lies does not have to comply. If this was done when the ticket was purchased; then it makes it fair for everyone.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Attendant reported a child was not wearing a face mask on the flight and questioned how flight attendants could enforce a child to wear a mask.

Report_1_Narrative: I was the least involved crew member. Passenger X was assigned to seat XX2 but upgraded herself to YY6; an exit row seat next to her friend. The A [FA] gave her a mask when she boarded because she only had a scarf. Passenger X had food in front of her for much of the flight so that she wouldn't have to wear a mask. I picked up her food trash about 1 1/2 hours into flight and advised Passenger X that she needed to wear a mask. Fellow FAs had told her that she needed to wear a mask previously while not eating. She stated; 'I won't' very clearly.Suggestion - Have a National Policy on mask wearing and ban passengers that fail to comply. This passenger told my coworkers that she didn't intend to fly our airline again. A coordinated policy might have more teeth; and since these passengers are failing to comply with crew member instructions; consider a permanent ban.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Attendant reported a passenger was not compliant with face mask policy.

Report_1_Narrative: I departed ZZZ at ZA:10 local on an IFR flight plan to ZZZ1 in [a rented aircraft]. A preflight inspection at ZZZ revealed no items of concern; and the brakes responded as expected when I tested them upon first movement from the tie down spot and throughout my taxi. The weather was VMC for the duration of the flight; and the weather I picked up on the ZZZ1 ATIS 15 minutes prior to arrival was winds 320@7kts; 9SM visibility; sky clear. I informed ZZZ Approach I would take the visual approach to Runway XX; at which point they cleared me for the visual approach and handed me off to ZZZ1 Tower. Tower requested me to continue on course to fly a left base for Runway XX and report three miles west of the field. Upon my reporting three miles west of the field; they cleared me to land runway XX. Upon nearing the extended centerline; I turned 90 degrees left and aligned myself on an approximately three mile final for Runway XX while at approximately 1;200 feet MSL and 90 KIAS. I completed my final approach and before-landing checks; including pumping the brakes to check for pressure; and crossed the runway threshold at approximately 65 KIAS with 30 degrees of flaps. Immediately upon touching down; the aircraft yawed violently to the left. I applied full right rudder deflection; which somewhat arrested the left yawing and increased the radius of the turn. However; the left main wheel by that time had entered the grass adjoining the runway; further aggravating left yaw. The aircraft continued to rotate about the left wheel until it came to a stop facing approximately due east approximately 75 feet from the west edge of the runway. After ensuring there was no immediate danger of fire or structural damage; I checked the main gear tires out the windows to see if one had blown; but they appeared to be OK. I advised Tower I would try to taxi back to the runway and proceed to the ramp. Upon applying throttle; the aircraft pivoted about its pitch axis into a slight nose-down attitude; which ceased upon decreasing throttle. I tried twice more to increase throttle to induce forward movement; but the aircraft continued to pitch forward when throttle was increased and pitch backward when throttle was decreased. At that point; I informed Tower I would need a tug. An airport crew came with a tug and attached a towbar to the aircraft. Upon attempting to pull the aircraft forward; the tug was not able to move it and subsequently became stuck in the ground. The airport crew then tried using a pickup truck to pull the tug while the tug pulled the aircraft; but the pickup truck became stuck. A 4wd pickup truck came and was able to remove the tug and the first pickup truck back to the runway. The airport crew used a shovel to dig the front wheel of the aircraft out of the ground; as it had become stuck during the previous attempts to taxi back onto the runway. They then attached the towbar to the 4wd pickup truck and were able to get the aircraft moving and onto the runway. I was then able to taxi the aircraft to the ramp under its own power; but noticed it had difficulty tracking in a straight line without additional brake inputs. Upon reaching the ramp; I did a quick inspection of the brake assemblies and discovered a metal-on-metal scraping noise when moving the aircraft back and forth by hand and no movement of the calipers when the toe brakes were actuated. At this point; I felt it was unsafe to continue operating the aircraft and arranged for a mechanic to inspect it the following morning. I called the owner; and he told me; 'that is why you shouldn't take that airplane places on a [weekend] afternoon - no one is around to fix it.' The mechanic inspected the brakes and found that the caliper slider pins were void of lubricant and rusted frozen; one brake lining was missing its rivets due to them rusting away; and several fasteners were loose. He replaced the linings on both slides; lubricated the assemblies; and torqued all the fasteners. I visually inspected the brakes; tested them on the ramp and during runup; and was satisfied that the aircraft was safe to operate. I departed ZZZ1 and had an uneventful IFR flight and landing back at ZZZ.In the future; I will add more thorough visual inspection of the brake assemblies to my preflight inspections; along with checking to make sure the calipers move when the brakes are actuated. I will also land prepared for a problem such as stuck brake; blown tire; or FOD and be more ready to immediately lift back off if safe to do so.
Report_1_Synopsis: GA pilot reported that during touchdown the aircraft yawed violently; departed the runway; and became stuck in the grass. Subsequent maintenance inspection found that the wheel brake assembly was rusted and had missing parts.

Report_1_Narrative: I was working the Operational Supervisor Desk when a controller told me there was an aircraft that had not [requested priority handling]; but was trying to figure out a technical difficulty. The aircraft [requested priority handling] with an engine malfunction; and requested to land at [a] Naval Air Base immediately. There was a layer of clouds over the field. The airport lies within a Restricted Area that was hot. We had already coordinated direct to the airport with the Military Radar Unit for the [priority situation]. The pilot asked what the MVA was in the area he was at because he needed to get down to land and was on top of a cloud. The controller issued the MVA. I instructed the controller to issue the aircraft a short range IFR clearance to get him down. I made the decision as a safety of flight due to [a priority] situation. There was a disagreement as to if it was legal. Our LOA (Letter of Agreement) on controlling in the Restricted Area Complex allows us to issue short range clearances when aircraft in the complex encounters IMC conditions.
Report_1_Synopsis: An ATC Supervisor reported instructing a controller to issue an IFR clearance through a Restricted Area due to priority situation.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Situational Awareness; Confusion; Communication Breakdown; Workload; Time Pressure
Report_1_Narrative: Aircraft X checked on and I climbed the aircraft to 23;000 feet; and gave them normal speed leaving 13;000 feet. A little bit later; Aircraft X and an aircraft on another frequency of mine transmitted at the same time. I responded to the other aircraft first; and when I went to look at Aircraft Xs data block; they were squawking XXXX. They requested to level at 12;000 feet and fly a 360 heading. I immediately assigned it to them. I called Departure; requested control and told them they were a priority handling. I went back to Aircraft X and they requested a 090 heading. I assigned that to them; notified my Controller in Charge; and began to collect the information. I asked for the nature of their situation; which they told me there was high vibration in their left engine.I also gathered that they wanted to return. It was difficult to understand the pilot due to a language barrier; but finally I understood how many souls on board there were and that there was more than 10 hours of fuel remaining. I then called Departure to forward the information and ask them for a heading and altitude I could turn the aircraft to. They gave me a 160 heading and 12;000 feet; as well as a frequency. After going back to the pilot; I called Departure back to ensure he was radar contact with them. Departure said yes; and asked if he needed to hold. I told them I had not asked. I then shipped the aircraft to TRACON. By the time the aircraft had turned back and I had shipped the aircraft; the aircraft did fly through and leave the southern tip of an adjacent Approach's airspace. However; I did not have a chance to call them as I was busy coordinating with the other TRACON and trying to get information from the pilot. I also never cleared the aircraft back to its departure airport. I simply turned the aircraft to a 160 heading and shipped the aircraft to Departure.I don't believe there was much I could do to prevent this situation. If I had the chance; I could have called TRACON; but in this scenario I didn't have any time to call due to the high workload.
Report_1_Synopsis: A Center Controller reported they vectored an aircraft under priority handling and requested clearance to return to the departure airport through a TRACON's airspace without a point out.

Person_2_Human_Factors: Situational Awareness; Human-Machine Interface; Distraction; Communication Breakdown
Report_1_Narrative: On flight XX; ZZZ to ZZZZ FO pre- loaded FMC with arrival ZZZZZ XA with Runway XXR.  Before descent checklist (6 hours) later briefed STAR and arrival into ZZZZ for both XXL and XXR. ZZZZ ATIS stated both XXL and XXR were in use. Obtained landing data for both runways. Approaching ZZZZZ we got vectors to ZZZZZ1 with expect XXL. On descent ATIS was calling for gusty winds on final from moderate to severe broken clouds at 2;500 feet. We talked about the winds and before we got to ZZZZ1 we got vectors and a decent to XXL we talked about the winds and forgot to change the FMC to XXL. On vectors to XXL with the approach mode armed we intercepted the LOC to XXR. We still were not aware of the error until the controller told us we were lined up for XXR and wanted to give us a heading of 160. We knew traffic was very light so asked if we could continue to XXR and was cleared to continue and land XXR. Landed without incident.
Report_2_Narrative: Upon returning to the flight deck from break; I was briefed on the ZZZZZ XA arrival and ILS XXL approach. ZZZZ ATIS broadcast that both XXL and XXR were in use. Runway data for both XXL and XXR were had been obtained earlier. Prior to descent we completed the descent checklist. At the FMC's; radios; item on the descent checklist; I intended to check the FMC to verify the approach and checked the item complete; but was interrupted by a radio call and never completed it. I did not catch the error that the FMC had ILS XXR programmed instead of ILS XXL; which had been briefed and anticipated. On the descent we were cleared the ZZZZZ XA Arrival to ILS XXL. Having briefed the ILS XXL; and believing we had ILS XXL programmed; no changes were made to the FMC. We did not catch the error until receiving radar vectors to the final approach. We were given a base leg and shortly after a vector to intercept. The turn to final seemed late and the aircraft but captured and lined up on the centerline. At that point; ATC gave us a 'right turn to 160' and then stated we were lined up for XXR and that we had been cleared for ILS XXL. He said there was no traffic for XXR and asked if we wanted to continue. We were at least 4 miles from the FAF so we accepted the approach clearance. We were able to review the approach noting the LOC identifier; changing the minimums and reviewed the Missed Approach procedure prior to descent on the GS. A stable approach was flown from the FAF to the runway for landing and was uneventful; as was the rollout and taxi-in.On the ATIS; gusty winds were noted and moderate; possibly greater; turbulence mentioned. This was a topic of discussion during the briefing and after. We briefed the cabin crew to have the cabin secured early and to take their seats as soon as possible after the chimes for the sterile cockpit notification. The aircraft was slowed early and we had begun configuring early as well so as to be stable early. The discussion was possibly an additional distraction during the briefing and Descent checklist.While we were able to comfortably get set up for the approach that was incorrectly loaded in and able to fly a stable approach; we should have asked for vectors to a new approach in order to properly brief prior to the initiation of the approach phase. We were lucky there was no traffic conflicts as there was little if any traffic due to time of day and the current state of airline traffic due to COVID.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported loading the wrong approach in the FMC and received clearance to land on the selected runway because of light traffic due to COVID.

Report_1_Narrative: I took the plane out to practice maneuvers etc. and was out for about an hour and a half.  There were a lot of planes in the area when I returned from the north and was asked to fly down the east side of the valley to enter a right downwind for Runway XX and to report midfield.  I repeated the instruction and entered the right downwind for Runway XX.  As I was about to report at mid-field; the controller stated that he saw me and cleared me to land on Runway XX.  A couple of minutes later; I believe he also stated that a plane was holding short for takeoff until I landed.I passed around the back of the landmark; made the right turn to the runway heading and saw the runway.  I then finished my landing checklist and proceeded to land on what I thought was Runway XX. Just as I was about two feet off the runway a second or so before the wheels touched; I heard the tower say to 'go-around' just as my wheels touched the ground. This was immediately followed by the tower stating-- [aircraft call sign] cleared to land Runway XX.I have no one to blame; nor any condition to blame for my mistake--I was shocked beyond belief that I had landed on the wrong runway and as many times as I've heard other pilots talk about it happening to them; I honestly thought it would never happen to me; as I have not had a single incident in 10 years of flying.  I have only one possible answer for my error and that is the 'confirmation bias' I've read about and heard discussed in the FAA courses and webinars I've taken.I take full responsibility for my error.  To say I'm embarrassed is an understatement; but one good thing has come of this:  I'm now acutely aware of the reality of confirmation bias from this first-hand experience and will definitely be intensely focused on confirming and reconfirming my runway prior to landing forever more.
Report_1_Synopsis: GA pilot reported landing on the wrong runway and not being aware of doing so until the Tower Controller instructed the pilot to go-around.

Report_1_Narrative: I had the idea in my head from somewhere in my training about what medicals were due for what type of operation. And if you are not confronted with it you don't really look into it. You feel you know the answer. In the course of running my business I got a database to track currencies; compliance; inspections and flight and engine times. While I was loading the database and setting up alerts and warnings I noticed that I may have; in the past; been flying commercially on a third class for a couple of short periods. I am not sure since I do not have all my old medicals to check. And by the past I am talking about 4 to 5 years ago. Remembering exactly what happened is difficult. Because of this incident I am super vigilant now about medicals; although because of COVID; I had to use an extension on my last medical. My database now warns me when I am getting close to my medical due date. I have gotten the idea out of my head that I can let a second class turn into a third class.
Report_1_Synopsis: Reporter reported possibly flying commercially with a third class physical several years ago.

Report_1_Narrative: We had planned on doing a touch and go at 33V on Runway 22. After we had touched down we raised the flaps and began to add power. While we were rolling at about 65 mph; a pickup truck with a snow plow on the front of it pulled out onto the runway; and started coming down Runway 4 head at us. I didn't believe we had enough room to stop; so I kept the throttle in for full power and tried to get airborne so we could side step the runway. The airplane was not able to break ground effect due to the high density altitude. The vehicle drove off the side of the runway and we were able to continue down the runway for takeoff. We had made standard radio calls on the CTAF frequency.
Report_1_Synopsis: GA instructor pilot reported that as they started the takeoff roll a truck began driving toward them from the opposite end of the runway. Pilot elected to continue takeoff and truck drove off the runway; allowing plane to continue.

Report_1_Narrative: This flight started the night prior when my normal First Officer had flown someone a few days earlier who contracted COVID-19.  That night; I was left trying to find a new First Officer for the next morning's flight at XA:00am.  I found an FO who has not flown in a while.  Our flight to ZZZ was uneventful.  On climbout from ZZZ the Tower Controller had issued a speed of 230 kts and a climb to and maintain 10;000 feet.  I asked the FO to run the climb checklist. While doing so; the Controller issued us instructions.  My FO was caught off guard and looked at me as if to say; 'I didn't hear that.'  I thought I heard and understood the instructions to be 'Normal speed and climb 12;000 feet and I read back 'Normal speed; climb 12;000 Aircraft X'.  I then began to climb.  This put me into conflict with Aircraft Y that was in the downwind for ZZZ; I never got a TCAS or TA/RA alert from my TCAS system.I know that after the instruction to proceed with normal speed; there was another instruction after that statement.  I just cannot remember what it was.  The crew change and heavy workload contributed to the misunderstanding.  I do not know what could have been done differently to avoid this in the future.  I do wonder why ATC would have pilots turn left towards another aircraft even if they were planning to keep the aircraft separated by 2;000 feet. I have flown this departure from ZZZ many times in the past and the point where we were issued normal speed was completely normal from past experience.  I really wish that ATC would issue a climb straight ahead until the departing aircraft is no longer in a position to potentially interfere with other aircraft."
Report_1_Synopsis: Corporate Captain reported an incorrect read back for altitude which caused their aircraft to climb an additional 2;000 feet resulting in an airborne conflict with another aircraft.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Time Pressure; Situational Awareness; Human-Machine Interface; Troubleshooting; Communication Breakdown; Confusion
Report_1_Narrative: There was a recent change with how our the Military Operating Area (MOA) has been handled in conjunction with ZZZ1. For the years past the MOA has been handled as an autonomous airspace which Center cleared [aircraft] in and out of. The decision has been made to have the ZZZ1 control the aircraft in and out of this airspace by designating a new control area. This week was the first time [new control area] has been in operation since its development and we expected issues; and encountered numerous airspace violations and automation issues throughout the day. The event I am reporting was only one of the numerous issues I encountered during this 1.5 hour session; and there will be numerous reports regarding this airspace from other controllers.The situation that caused the most alarm was [Aircraft X; Aircraft Y] which is a flight of 2. We received a call from [new control area] giving us the 5 minute notice that [Aircraft X; Aircraft Y] is ready to leave the airspace. This is the procedure that is published in the Letter of Agreement and following this call [new control area] will initiate an automated radar hand-off. For [Aircraft X; Aircraft Y]; there was no hand-off initiated and [Aircraft X; Aircraft Y] called Center stating they were at 25;000 ft. descending to 13;000 ft. I look in the airspace and search the 5 limited targets and do not see [Aircraft X; Aircraft Y]'s beacon code. I then notice a beacon code 5 to 10 miles outside the airspace at 25;000 ft. which is heading back to ZZZ1 and towards some ZZZ arrivals. I quickly pair the data blocks and establish communication with [Aircraft X; Aircraft Y]. Thankfully this time the traffic into ZZZ was far enough away that this was not an immediate issue. This area [Aircraft X; Aircraft Y] was in is a very heavy area for military traffic; ZZZ arrivals; ZZZ Departures; ZZZZ1 Arrivals; ZZZZ2 Departures; and ZZZZ3 Departures. If this issue happens again during a busier session this could very well end in a TCAS/RA event or even worse due to the speed of the exiting [aircraft] speeds. Either better training on the procedures for the ZZZ1 Controllers and the [aircraft] fighter squadron; or amendments to the [new control area] procedures.
Report_1_Synopsis: A Center Controller reported a flight of two military aircraft exited a Military Operating Area and began descending from 25000 feet without communications or a radar handoff from the military controlling agency. The reporter states there is a new military controlling facility and procedures which have been violated many times since the new procedures were implemented.

Report_1_Narrative: Consulting team was on Aircraft X to ZZZ1. It was a miss communication with the team. They did not properly review flight information; the aircraft was being loaded with other employees. When I arrived and did not verify all Dangerous Goods cargo was loaded also consulting team prevention team did not show up or help in anyway when they showed up it was 5 to 10 minuets before departure and they did not verify that dangerous goods were on board the aircraft. These teams were put here to help and verify and locate freight mail and other items and fail to do so.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Ramp Lead reported a communication breakdown between company ramp personnel and other ground personnel [consulting group] regarding Hazmat cargo load.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Workload; Communication Breakdown; Distraction; Situational Awareness; Time Pressure
Report_1_Narrative: Please reference ZZZ [airport]; ZZZZZ 4 RNAV SID.  We were assigned the ZZZZZ 4 RNAV SID and departed Runway XXR at ZZZ.  After checking in with Departure Control the FO (pilot flying) called for the After TO Checklist.  This is when several things happened at once.   Before finishing the checklist the Departure Controller told us to climb to 10;000 feet and said we were clear ZZZZZ1 [Intersection] then ZZZZZ2 [Intersection].  At the same time we received an ECAM alert for a #1 Pressure Regulator Fault.  By the time I set the altitude in the FCP; read back the clearance; re-visited and completed the after TO checklist and trying to diagnose what the ECAM was telling me we were over ZZZZZ1 [Intersection] and the aircraft was starting to turn to the next point on the SID which was ZZZZZ3 [Intersection].  The FO put turned the auto pilot on and placed the aircraft in heading mode and started a turn to ZZZZZ2 [Intersection].  We got the aircraft navigating to ZZZZZ2 [Intersection] but apparently it was not quick enough for the controller.  He chimed in and gave us a heading for ZZZZZ2 [Intersection].  We told him we were in the turn and navigating to ZZZZZ2 [Intersection] at that time.  Probably not a big deal.  No conflict with other aircraft or terrain.  No airspeed or altitude violations.  Just a lot of things happening at once during a busy phase of flight.  The result was we were a few seconds late to make our turn when our departure instructions were changed from what was given to us on the PDC.We complied with the ATC instructions as soon as we could.  It was a busy phase of flight and we were task saturated at the time. Getting an ECAM message for a pressurization fault was an added distraction.   I have been off work for almost a month due to COVID leave and this was my second trip since returning.   I was a little slow to respond but I've been off work almost X weeks and I'm still shaking off the cobwebs.Not pointing fingers; but a change to our SID would have been nice to know BEFORE we took off so we could expect; brief; and build the change into the FMS.  When taking off on [Runway] XXR via the ZZZZZ 4 RNAV SID you are over the first point; ZZZZZ1 [Intersection]; seconds after TO.   Having a change to the SID when approaching ZZZZZ1 [Intersection] only gave us a few seconds to react.  Trying to read back and amend the departure clearance in the FMS; clean up the airplane; finish the after takeoff checklist; and diagnose an ECAM caution made for a lot of balls to juggle.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported a track heading deviation during departure. Captain cited distraction dealing with an ECAM alert and lack of flying contributed to the event.

Report_1_Narrative: Company Duty Officer informed CA (Captain) and FO (First Officer) (me) via company email that after block-in of a revenue flight from ZZZ-ZZZ1 that ZZZ1 offload crew discovered Aircraft X had unmanifested ADG in position 12L. The container at 12L was labeled as international box volume; but actually contained 321 pieces of flammable gas (this info provided via Duty Officer in same company email). It was my understanding based on standardized DG (Dangerous Goods) procedures pre-flight that Aircraft X did not have any DG loaded.The cause of Hazmat violation was improper tracking of DG materials. DG unmanifested in non-DG labeled container.I suggest more vigilance and thoroughness when handling; tracking; and loading DG.
Report_1_Synopsis: First Officer reported undocumented transport of Hazmat cargo due to improper DG tracking.

Report_1_Narrative: Coming to ZZZ on the ILS [Runway] XXR; we were continually slowed by ATC for spacing of traffic ahead and behind.  At about 1;200 MSL on glide path still IMC Tower told us to go-around.  I was PF and hit GA button and advanced power levers.  We went through missed approach procedure; but as flight guidance was attempting to be set the aircraft was also capturing the level off of 2;000 MSL so took a little longer to complete.  Meanwhile we were a little late on turning to 195 heading.  ATC queried us as we were in the turn.  We had also climbed to 2;180 feet before stopping and returning back to 2;000 immediately.  After we got settled ATC vectored us back to ILS with no further issues.  ATC told us they had to send us around because aircraft on final for parallel Runway XXL behind us had gotten .99 miles from us.  Spacing needed to stay a min of 1 mile.I should have paid more attention to altitude and started turn to 195 even if flight guidance wasn't quite set yet.  Also pulled back power sooner or not add as much to avoid going through altitude.
Report_2_Narrative: During our arrival into ZZZ; when told to run base (heading approximately toward ZZZZZ [Intersection]); we were slowed to 170 KIAS.  We were maintaining 4;000 feet throughout base turn and intercept turn onto final.  Once established on final (approximately 20 NM from ZZZZZ1 [Intersection]) we were slowed further to 160 KIAS; with traffic approximately 4 NM in front of us.  Once we intercepted the glideslope; we maintained approximately 1;000 feet above the preceding traffic; but gained to within 3 NM distance.  Meanwhile; ATC vectored a airline flight onto final for [Runway] XXL close behind us.I told the First Officer (PF) to potentially fly a half-dot high on the glide slope to avoid any potential wake from the preceding aircraft.  Once we reached approximately 10 NM from ZZZZZ1 [Intersection] we were slowed further to 150 KIAS.As we continued down the approach; the TCAS showed us to be approximately 2.5 NM from the preceding traffic; with the traffic behind us close in trail (unable to tell the specific distance).  At approximately 600 AGL; ZZZ Tower issued a Go-Around; with nonstandard missed approach instructions (Right turn heading 195; climb and maintain 2;000).  The First Officer initiated the Go-Around and the Captain (PM) proceeded to re-program the Flight Guidance.Due to the light passenger load; the subsequent climb rate caused the Flight Guidance to immediately switch from a Climb indication to an Altitude Capturing indication; which caught the Captain off-guard; and he tried to re-configure the Flight Guidance back to a Climb indication.  The Flight Guidance again sequenced to an Altitude Capture indication.  At this point; the Captain (PM) noticed the aircraft was off course to the left approximately 35 degrees and was rapidly approaching 2;000 feet.  The Captain brought this to the attention of the First Officer while also simultaneously acknowledging ATC stating 'Turn right heading 195.'  The Captain also prompted the First Officer to reduce the power setting; as the airspeed was approaching maximum flap speeds.  The missed approach up to leveling off at 2;000 feet was all hand-flown (i.e. not with the autopilot).Once the aircraft was established on the appropriate heading; altitude; and configuration; ZZZ Approach vectored the flight around for a second attempt at the ILS 16R; which occurred without further incident.  In researching the First Officer's seniority; he has been here less than X years (Date).  After debriefing the flight; he stated that that was his first Missed Approach / Go-Around in the actual aircraft EVER.Since we had been slowed down significantly early during the approach; we knew we could expect to be sandwiched in between other aircraft.  However; we did not know that ATC needed only 1 mile separation between aircraft on parallel ILS approaches (told to us by ATC during our second attempt).  There was no mention of spacing requirements on our first approach.Due to 'COVID loads;' the aircraft type climb rates are very good; requiring steeper than normal attitudes so as to not exceed flap speeds.  This factor; combined with the First Officer's relative inexperience with missed approaches; caused a momentary loss of situational awareness by the First Officer.This required the CA to not only re-configure the flight guidance for a missed approach; but also ensure the First Officer did not over speed the flaps; communicate with ATC; and ensure the aircraft was following appropriate flight guidance (which was a non-standard missed approach).Also contributing to the loss in situational awareness was the altitude at which ATC issued the Go-Around:  600 AGL.  This caused a significant startle factor in both the Captain and First Officer.  Had ATC mentioned anything about a potential missed approach; we would have been much more prepared.Last-minute ATC-issued Go Around instructions (below 1;000 AFE); caused by inadequate spacing with simultaneous parallel approach aircraft.RECOMMENDATIONS:1.  ATC NEEDS to let crews know 'be ready for a missed approach' if there is potential for a spacing issue.  We were given our Go-Around instructions at 600 AGL.  This is a very high-risk area to issue a Go-Around; when spacing throughout the entire approach was tight.  Some sort of notification to us would have primed for a potential Missed Approach and therefore could have avoided any loss of situational awareness and subsequent heading / altitude deviation.2.  STOP ISSUING NON-STANDARD MISSED APPROACH INSTRUCTIONS.  The ILS [Runway] XXR's Standard Missed Approach instructions are to fly runway heading to 900 feet; then climb on heading 195 to intercept the ZZZ 210 degree radial; maintain 2;000 feet.  This is VERY similar to what we were assigned (heading 195; climb to 2;000 feet).  However; when we're given nonstandard missed approach instructions; not only do we have to interpret what it is ATC actually told us; but also program that into the Flight Guidance.  This programming is CONTRADICTORY to what our normal Flight Guidance programming procedures are.  Had ATC simply said 'fly the published missed approach;' that could've aided in our appropriate handling of the aircraft.LESSONS LEARNED:Don't trust ZZZ ATC to not screw up.  If spacing looks tight; brief a missed approach; even if it's done on the Final Approach Course.  Also; do not trust your fellow crew member to fly a perfect Missed Approach.  Watch them like a hawk for course; airspeed; and altitude management; and IMMEDIATELY speak up if there is even a minor deviation.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported executing a go-around due to ATC spacing with another aircraft on final. The flight crew overshot their altitude during the go-around and cited the aircraft light weight as a contributing factor.

Report_1_Narrative: Tower was very busy with a single Controller working Ground and Tower. On initial climbout we wanted to confirm our initial altitude but had a difficult time getting in contact with ATC. While this was occurring; I missed PIC call for autothrottles; and he did not recognize that I had failed to engage them. We momentarily exceeded 250 knots below 1;000 feet; accelerating to ~290 knots. After clarifying with ATC we both noticed the speed; PIC noticed speed and made adjustments to pitch and power and then I engaged autotrottles. Flight continued normally.Recency of experience due to COVID-19; early morning fatigue may have played a role.
Report_1_Synopsis: Corporate Captain reported a speed deviation during climbout. Captain referenced distraction while trying to communicate with a busy ATC and lack of flying contributed to the event.

Report_1_Narrative: A passenger wore a mask that looked like it had holes in it; he was irate when I told him it was not allowed onboard. He had a kid with him and to make things easier I grabbed him a mask from the galley. When I got to his seat he had another face covering but I still offered him the mask. He took it but and threw in the seat back pocket. He told his kid he didn't wanna make a fuss; it wasn't necessarily a non-compliance but it is definitely worth reporting my point of view.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Attendant reported a passenger boarded the aircraft with a mask that had holes.

Report_1_Narrative: We landed on Taxiway 1 at ZZZ in front of the FBO hangar. We then began to hover taxi to parking at approximately a 3 foot skid height above the ground. A tug pulling a cargo container was approaching from the south traveling north on the service road. As I neared the service road to cross it; the tug just kept traveling towards us and refused to stop. I had to abruptly stop my taxi and let the tug proceed but; in the process; he passed directly in front of the helicopter and underneath the rotor disk. I reported this incident to my manager and county airport personnel. This is the 5th incident with personnel in the same location within the last 3 months. The others were all very similar. Basically; the tug drivers refuse to give way to moving aircraft.
Report_1_Synopsis: Helicopter pilot reported that while they were hover taxiing a tug pulling a cargo container passed directly in front of the helicopter under the rotor disk.

Report_1_Narrative: The problem arose when I went to log the flight and found out that I was not current. Contributing factors (beside my inattention) could be that with COVID; both in general and having had it; I have not flown the amount that I normally would. However; I should have been more alert to my 'currency.' I file IFR for every trip whether VMC or IFR and so I filed IFR; again without checking for currency. For corrective actions I have set dates in my calendar quarterly to make sure I am on track for currency.Concerning my medical currency; I have two years 'under my belt' with Basic Med. I went in for my annual physical and gave the forms to my doctor. However; when it was discovered that I was not under Basic Med; I called the Doctor's office and his response was that he remembers the conversation but not filling out any forms. He had done my last Basic Med so I left it in his hands to complete. I understand that it was/is my responsibility to follow up on this; but I did not. Again; I have placed a reminder in my calendar both to renew my Basic Med in two years and then a week later to follow up with my doctor.
Report_1_Synopsis: GA pilot reported inadvertently flying without a current medical.

Report_1_Narrative: I was instructing on a training flight; and departed from ZZZ; while climbing out and making a crosswind departure to the east. The student was flying while I was making radio calls. Upon reaching approximately 2;300 feet MSL; I caught a plane performing a steep left turn bank towards us. I took flight controls from the student and descended around 500 feet approximately 1;000 feet AGL to avoid the other traffic. I made radio calls on CTAF at the local airport and the other aircraft was not on frequency. I proceeded to warn an aircraft behind us on CTAF performing a low approach with a departure to the east as well about an aircraft performing unpredictable maneuvers on the departure end at a low altitude. Once on the ground we were able to review the flight data and track logs of the other aircraft. My assumption is the other aircraft was unaware of their proximity to the airport and performing steep turns. Another contributing factor could have been the difference in altimeter settings between the two local airports and change from departure of approximately .11 in/hg. The maneuvers were being performed outside the local practice area box. Panel mounted ADS-B-In could have assisted with our situational awareness of the aircraft location. We had a portable receiver but did not have an tablet out as we were practicing crosswind landings so we had no traffic advisory until after corrective action. Once corrective action was taken; and tablet was consulted; we still had traffic above and turning towards us from the opposite side. We maintained a low altitude until well clear of the aircraft. Which leads me to believe he was unaware of us and their proximity to other aircraft and airport.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Instructor reported an NMAC occurred nearby the departure airport when another aircraft maneuvered directly into their flight path requiring evasive action. The other aircraft was not on CTAF and appeared to not be aware of their proximity to the airport.

Report_1_Narrative: In being given instruction to taxi from Ramp 1 to Runway 7R; the instructions were to enter Delta taxiway to [Taxiway] D4 then to C3 and hold short. Taxiway Delta is a newly constructed taxiway with a vehicle roadway just prior to Taxiway Delta. In executing the turn; the vehicle access road was mistaken for Taxiway Delta. Immediately upon realizing this error; I contacted DVT Ground Control and advised them of the situation. I was given the choice of remaining where I was and be re-positioned by ground personnel or taxi around to the north side of the airport via the vehicle access road and proceed normally from the north runway (Runway 7L). While I was deciding; the Ground Controller stated that aircraft had been previously towed on this very road in the past. Bearing this in mind; I chose to taxi around the vehicle access road; ultimately discovering it to be too narrow and resulting to the necessity of ground personnel having to dismantle all the remaining signs; so as to allow me to complete this route and arrive at the [Runway] 7L run-up area; after which I was given instructions to proceed normally to the hangar area on the south field; which occurred without further incident.It should be noted that in reviewing this incident; that the vehicle access road and Taxiway Delta are immediately adjacent to each other and if additional signage were present to further clarify this potential hazard; it would be an important addition to improve safe taxi at this airport.
Report_1_Synopsis: Light aircraft pilot reported confusing signage at DVT airport led to a taxi deviation down a vehicle roadway.

Report_1_Narrative: I was sitting front seat; doing my tail wheel training in the Citabria practicing touch and goes. I was practicing my second ever short field landing in this aircraft and as I was applying breaking to the aircraft I heard my instructor telling me to press harder on the brakes; as we were nearing the end of the landing. I then applied brakes to the point of the tail wheel rising up and then the propeller struck the runway.
Report_2_Narrative: We were practicing short field landings for training. After landing the student started applying brakes very lightly. I prompted the student to increase braking action and the student suddenly applied aggressive braking action. The tail began to rise and I applied full aft elevator to help slow the rise but was unable to prevent the prop from striking the runway. From the time aggressive brakes were applied until the prop struck the ground was less than .5 seconds. I had previously briefed with the student what the appropriate short field landing and braking action should look like on the ground and in flight just before the demonstration. I then demonstrated how the maneuver was to be performed before allowing the student to execute the maneuver. Total distance covered from the time the prop impacted the runway was only approximately 5 feet. After the aircraft came to a stop I shut everything down besides the radio; made a radio call to traffic in the area to temporarily close the runway and then had the student monitor the radios while I contacted airport management to notam the runway closed and get assistance with the aircraft. A preliminary inspection revealed damage to the prop; spinner; and lower cowling. No injuries were incurred and not further damage is known at this time.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight instructor and student reported that during landing practice in a Citabria tailwheel aircraft; the student applied aggressive braking which caused the tail to rise resulting in a propeller strike.

Report_1_Narrative: After filing IFR; I got an email (Foreflight) stating 'Expected Route Received' of 'BFI TAOMA J5 SUMMA J54 BKE BYI BEARR5 ZZZ. BFI clearance delivery gave me a verbal clearance of NRVNA1 TAOMA fly 135; climb via SID. The SID has a climb limit of 2;000 feet. Tower cleared me for takeoff and (I believe)135 heading. After takeoff; I checked in with Seattle Departure and a few seconds later; they asked me what my heading was. I replied 135 then direct NRVNA which is what the SID says. They asked me again and now I was SURE I was not doing what I was supposed to be doing. They gave me a 30deg LEFT turn followed shortly by a climb; so I believe I flew farther to the west than what they expected of me. I am still confused by what I would term a sort of 'hybrid' clearance. Was I cleared to fly the NRVNA SID or was I supposed to maintain 135 deg heading until further notice. It was the combination of 'fly 135' and 'climb via SID' that seemed contradictory. I should have been more forceful in querying the controller; but the freq was very busy. A simple solution; in my opinion; would have been for Tower to say 'Fly 135; climb and maintain 2;000 feet; cleared for takeoff'. Then it would have been clear to me that the NRVNA SID was not expected right after takeoff.
Report_1_Synopsis: Pilot reported a heading deviation after takeoff that was caused by confusing pre-takeoff clearance instructions.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Workload; Distraction; Situational Awareness; Time Pressure
Report_1_Narrative: [Aircraft X] was being vectored for an ILS approach into BFI RWY (Runway) 14R by the Arrival West (1W); Arrival East (1E); Boeing Arrival (1D); and Paine (1P) sectors combined. As [Aircraft X] was being vectored traffic was issued for two VFR aircraft on 1200 codes transitioning both north and south through the localizer for Runway 14R. Due to this traffic I left [Aircraft X] at 3;000 ft. and obtained a point-out with SEA Final (1F). Despite this altitude; [Aircraft X] responded to a TCAS RA and; in an effort to protect the sea final approach course; I turned [Aircraft X] right to a heading 220. As [Aircraft X] turned southbound I observed a C172; [Aircraft Y]; being vectored for the ILS Runway 20 approach into PWT. I turned [Aircraft X] further right to a northwest heading; and measured the distance between [Aircraft X] and [Aircraft Y]. I observed approximately 3.3 miles between the two and since I had already issued the turn; I judged that sufficient separation and attempted to continue working to not fall further behind. [Aircraft X] turned slower than anticipated and caused a separation error between themselves and [Aircraft Y]. The root of this issue is the continual constant conflict between IFR jets into BFI and VFR aircraft transitioning through the localizer in both north and south flow. It is a well-known; persistent issue that has been thoroughly reported for several years. Several solutions have been proposed; but none have been adapted.The only fix for this issue is a restructuring of the Seattle Class B airspace to protect the finals in both directions at BFI. I have personally submitted redesigns for this issue that both protect BFI; and in doing so protect SEA; and allow VFR operations in and out of BFI; and are not unduly hindering to the general aviation community. If safety is truly the priority of the FAA and the Seattle region; changes will be initiated immediately. I understand the process for airspace changes take time; however; the changes will never take place if the process is not started. When the inevitable aircraft incident finally occurs; I hope that no one dies and I am not on position.
Report_2_Narrative: [Aircraft Y] was on vector; at 2;500 ft.; to ILS Runway 20 approach at PWT. [Aircraft X]; controlled by W Sector; was on final to Runway 14R at BFI and experienced a TCAS RA with an uncontrolled VFR aircraft. The W Controller was already at a high level of complexity and volume as sectors were combined. The BFI Runway 14R final is in close proximity to PWT 20 mile final and is also underneath the Runway 16 finals at SEA. With limited options [Aircraft X] was turned to the southwest towards [Aircraft Y] with only 500 ft. between them. There are many factors that lead to this situation. These include airport proximities; sector overload; traffic complexity. There is also the issue of lack of controlled and protected airspace in and out of BFI. This is an issue controllers have been bringing to local management for years. The workforce is metaphorically beating our heads against a wall as we are asking for help and are given zero assistance in return. The final to BFI is underneath the SEA finals so we are forced to descend large; fast turbojet aircraft out of Class Bravo airspace into a very high VFR traffic area. This leads numerous TCAS situations. Many suggestions have been brought up through established reporting procedures so I will not waste my time typing them out again. The feeling of a lack of support for change is disheartening. There needs to be change made into airspace and procedures for aircraft landing at BFI; and this should be done for both arrival directions at BFI.
Report_1_Synopsis: Two S46 Approach controllers reported an aircraft on an ILS Approach to BFI had to be vectored away from two conflicting VFR aircraft not in communication with ATC which resulted with the BFI aircraft losing separation with a fourth aircraft on an ILS approach to another airport. Both reporters emphasized these situations are a recurring issue due to the insufficient Class B protected airspace in the SEA/S46 airspace.

Report_1_Narrative: A person came to work and his wife had COVID. He was among several of coworkers in a Kiosk. I went with co-worker Y to Manager's office and explained the situation because we were in the Kiosk with him. We asked if the Kiosk could be cleaned right away before anyone else entered. She said she sent the Supervisor to wipe things down and that the cleaning service would clean/spray it tonight. Co-worker Y said the Supervisor did not wipe it down. This is a potential risk of spreading COVID to many people at work and their families. I gave co-worker Y my own personal can of LYSOL spray to use in the KIOSK.
Report_1_Synopsis: Customer service representative reported that a kiosk was used by an employee whose wife had COVID. Reporter was advised the kiosk was cleaned; but another employee stated the kiosk was never cleaned.

Report_1_Narrative: On climb out of ZZZ [airport] we received an ACARS message from Dispatch saying that the TRACON was closing and that we should ask ATC if we could do Tower enroute to get into ZZZ1 [airport]. It also said if we couldn't return to ZZZ. We were still climbing on the SID out of ZZZ and I was still running the after Takeoff checklist. I finished the checklist up and consulted the FO. We were both confused by this message. I went ahead and asked ZZZ Departure if they knew anything about it. They did not know anything then handed us off to ZZZ Center. I checked in with ZZZ [Center]. I responded to Dispatch asking which facility it was that was closing. They replied with ZZZ1 TRACON and that it was to be closed from XA:30 to XB:30z. After getting this response. I asked ZZZ Center if they had any information on it. They checked with their managers and didn't know anything about TRACON in ZZZ1 shutting down. I messaged Dispatch saying that we wanted to continue and see how things progress since ZZZ [Center] said they didn't know anything. The reply we received was a strong negative. Dispatch wanted us to turn back to ZZZ [airport] right away. At this point in the flight; we were half way to ZZZ1 [airport]. We were estimated to arrive in the ZZZ1 [airport] area around XB:00z and had enough fuel onboard the aircraft to hold for a while before having to go to an alternate that we would have added. ZZZ2 [airport] was close and had good weather. Dispatch didn't give us any time to explore other alternatives; so we complied with their demand to return to ZZZ [airport]. The entire time; my FO and I were trying to figure out why we were returning to the airport. The workload was high on the return. The risk for making mistakes was pretty high on both our parts. Thankfully; ZZZ [airport] wasn't busy and was able to cut down a lot of our workload by giving us a descent and direct a fix on the approach. Once on the ground I was able to call Dispatch and talk. They closed the TRACON for COVID cleaning and only gave about 20 minute notice. It sounded like the dispatcher knee jerk reacted to it and wanted us on the ground as soon as possible. That's why she didn't want us to continue. I complied because it was a safe course of action to return and because I couldn't get Dispatch to agree to continue. So this was the safest course of action that was mutually agreeable.Suggest going over delay options inflight with dispatch and to not make the decisions for the flight crew. Dispatch should seek the advice of other dispatchers and most importantly of the crew to come up with many options and narrow it down the best one in a non-time critical situation as this. Freaking out and demanding an air return is not a normal way to run an operation. Dispatch should be made aware that there are many options available to crews to stay in the air longer while saving fuel. We could have easily slowed down and held until TRACON opened again or we could have diverted to ZZZ2 [airport] and picked up some more fuel if we needed to. Both would have been faster options of keeping the operations going while being safe.
Report_2_Narrative: After departing ZZZ we received an ACARS message from Dispatch informing us that ZZZ1 TRACON would be closed upon our arrival.  Shortly after we received another message instructing us to return to ZZZ.We received an ACARS message from Dispatch.The flight return to ZZZ per Dispatch request due to ZZZ1 TRACON closed prior to us landing.We returned to ZZZ and the Captain contacted Dispatch after returning to the gate.Suggestion - If possible; comply with Dispatch instructions.  Coordinate with Dispatch for clarification via ACARS or after returning to the gate.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported receiving a message from Dispatch during climbout that destination TRACON was closing before arrival.  Dispatch told crew to return to departure airport.

Report_1_Narrative: I recently completed the B737 Max training. I found the training to be good but do have concern for the Airspeed unreliable when the stick shaker is going continually. The loudness contributes to a continued distraction and ability to clearly communicate. This all for an erroneous warning. The ability is there to disable the erroneous stick shaker via pulling the offending circuit breaker. This is somewhat analogous to not silencing the fire bell until the fire is out and you're on the ground. Additionally; with the distraction; auto throttles off while running the QRH; the opportunity presents itself for masking a real stick shaker if in low speed event. Would you recognize the other stick shaker going off if the pilot monitoring was not on the controls? One additional step in the QRH after identifying the erroneous side would take a significant distraction out of the equation. Other than the initial stick shaker and identifying the erroneous airspeed indication; I feel the continuous stick shaker is the greatest threat in this situation. By taking away the erroneous stick shaker distraction you can eliminate one of the 'holes in the cheese'.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Captain reported while in a 737 MAX Simulator; with an airspeed unreliable situation; the unreliable airspeed indicator with associated stick shaker warning is too loud and makes communication difficult.

Report_1_Narrative: While conducting a FAR 91 reposition flight from ZZZZ to ZZZ; we were cleared to maintain a cruising altitude of Flight Level 260. Approximately three hours into our cruise; the Central Advisory and Warning System (CAWS) triggered a master caution and the LH FUEL PUMP and RH FUEL PUMP green indicator lights illuminated. About 10 seconds later they extinguished; only for another master caution to sound and the same lights to return; indicating a low fuel pressure situation. We ran the emergency procedure checklist for low fuel pressure. After completing the low fuel pressure checklist; we were unable to rectify the low fuel pressure condition and [advised] ZZZ Center. Per the low fuel pressure checklist; we diverted to the nearest suitable airfield. ZZZZ1 was the nearest suitable airfield. Center informed us that all nearby airports; including ZZZZ1; were closed at sunset and personnel were being contacted by ZZZZ Approach to turn the lights on at ZZZZ1. We conducted the RNAV RWY XX Approach to a visual landing at ZZZZ1 and parked the aircraft without further incident. The aircraft was then grounded. Lack of guidance in emergency checklist on time frame for both rate of descent to warmer air; as well as restoring boost pump switches to AUTO after descent to warmer air.
Report_2_Narrative: [Report narrative contained no additional information.]
Report_1_Synopsis: Air taxi flight crew reported that they got a fuel pump warning followed by a low fuel pressure warning and were able to divert without further incident.

Report_1_Narrative: I was scheduled to fly out of ZZZZ to ZZZZ1. While in cruise; I noticed the rudder pedals on the pilot side didn't mobilize as they should when pressed on to engage the brakes. I asked my SIC to perform the same checks on his side and he noted the pedals felt operational. We decided to continue our flight to ZZZZ1 and land taking into consideration that we might not have brake pressure and would have to perform a go-around and diversion to a longer runway. Rain had just ended in our destination and the runway was slightly wet. After touchdown; I try to engage the brakes to verify their status. Brakes started engaging on and off while we rolled on the runway. We decided to go-around. Before diverting to ZZZZ2 we acknowledge the fact that the runway was slightly wet and decided to try landing again. This second landing was firmer than the first one; I; as pilot flying; applied the brakes once more and this time around; no braking action was noticed therefore we decided to perform a go-around and divert to ZZZZ2. After touching down in ZZZZ2; brakes didn't engage appropriately; they were intermittent. After shutting down at the main ramp in ZZZZ2; deplaning and sending the passengers to a lounge; I talked to our mechanic on the phone and we both noted the brake fluid was lower than usual. The company flew another aircraft with a mechanic which happens to be also a pilot. He inspected the brakes visually and noted that the system looks fine. With that assessment; we accepted a ferry permit to fly back to base ZZZZ without passengers; for proper maintenance action. After touchdown in ZZZZ RWY XX and noting the fact that my 'now' SIC is a mechanic; I pushed on the rudder pedals to engage the brakes and try to assess what the issue was. This prompted no braking action. I communicated this to my SIC/Mechanic; and I increased pressure on the rudder pedals trying to note a response from the system with no luck. Eventually; after I kept applying pressure to the rudder pedals; the left and right main gear tires deflated disabling our aircraft in the runway. After this happened; we notified ATC (ZZZZ Tower) and shut down on the runway.
Report_1_Synopsis: Pilot reported that the brakes did not show any braking action during several landing attempts. Pilot diverted and while attempting to brake upon landing; both main gear tires deflated.

Report_1_Narrative: After making the turn at ZZZZZ intersection at FL300; we had a bleed 1 leak caution message. We ran the QRH and isolated system 1 and after a few minutes the message returned forcing us to continue the checklist through the descent portion. As we were waiting the three minutes before the descent; I initiated contact with AIRINC to reach dispatch as our ACARS had just lost coms most likely to it transitioning from one frequency to another. However with the need for a descent arising we lost communication with AIRINC before establishing any plan with dispatch. We requested priority handling with ZZZ Center and initiated a turn towards ZZZ as the thought of continuing towards ZZZZ or ZZZZ1 was the longest stretch of open water on the route and worst case scenario we were 60-80 miles north of the coast and ZZZZ2 was the closest [authorized] airport around if we had to continue the checklist and shut down the engine. As we got closer to ZZZZ2 while still 130 miles from ZZZ we were able to get an ACARS connection and get dispatch caught up on the situation. They did not realize how bad the situation was and thought we were closer to ZZZZ and ZZZZ1 than we actually were. As the aircraft was stable and the bleed temp of system 1 was around 50C; the system still held almost 70psi throughout the flight indicating one of the valves was still open and not properly closed; we confirmed with dispatch that it was safe to continue beyond ZZZ to ZZZ1 for an uneventful landing. Throughout the communication black out center was very professional and extremely helpful. I hope our thanks and appreciation for their work can be passed on to the controllers working with us.
Report_2_Narrative: Prior to ZZZZZ1 [fix]; flight sent an ACARS message stating a Bleed Leak. Flight followed the QRH and three minutes later the message returned requiring a diversion to nearest suitable. There was quite a bit confusion going on because the flight also attempted to contact us via ARINC. The ARINC call failed; and the flight seemed to be in an ACARS dead spot as well. A few minutes later; I received multiple ACARS messages stating the flight was diverting to ZZZ. Per the flight's location; ZZZZ1 seemed like the closer; more suitable option and would've had the flight avoid going EOW (Extended Over Water) at 10;000 [with priority handling]. After running numbers for ZZZZ1; flight informed me over ACARS that ZZZ or ZZZ1 was closer. Although [our equipment] showed the flight over ZZZZ1; in reality the flight was 250 nm to the east; indeed much closer to ZZZ or ZZZ1. With that information; we decided ZZZ1 was a more suitable airport. In addition to runway length; ZZZ ops informed us that pax would not be allowed off the aircraft due to customs issues. Flight landed and blocked in.While I was certainly caught off guard and should've opened the QRH a few minutes faster; I was seriously hampered by our lack of equipment accuracy; ACARS dead spots; and ARINC being unable to raise the flight. It's hard to have an accurate; timely discussion over ACARS when both sides of the situation are working quickly on fixing the problems. If this were being done via remote dispatching; I do not wish to imagine the consequences. In the future; I will remind myself to remain calm and follow step-by-step actions to reach a quicker; less confusing end.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier pilot and Dispatcher reported confusion over diversion airports due to communication difficulties after bleed air leak.

Report_1_Narrative: We flew to ZZZ on aircraft X. We then were scheduled to fly same aircraft from ZZZ to ZZZ1 with a new flight attendant crew. When the flight attendants did their pre-flight; I was notified that the emergency equipment in the AFT bins were in the incorrect bins. They were in the opposite bins as depicted in the 737 diagram and the flight attendant manual. Apparently they were installed that way back in month when the modification was complete. The stickers that were on the bins depicting what emergency equipment was correct but the emergency equipment was on the incorrect side. I called dispatch who connected me to maintenance and they said couldn't find any diagram that would place emergency equipment where it was. ZZZ maintenance agreed that emergency equipment was installed incorrectly. The aircraft was taken out of service.The equipment was installed wrong. In is my understanding this airplane flew around since April like this. More emphasis on flight attendants checking proper locations of emergency equipment.More checks to make sure when there is an interior modification that it's installed correctly
Report_2_Narrative: Upon arrival a ZZZ; we received a new cabin crew for the flight to ZZZ1. ZZZ to ZZZ1 was to be the flight deck crew's second flight using the same aircraft.   During the pre-flight; the aft cabin crew called the flight deck and advised us that the emergency equipment that is stowed in the two most aft overhead compartments were not located in their proper location.  TO fully understand; I also went aft to see for myself.  The FA showed me in her manual; the proper location and orientation of the equipment.  I went back to the flight deck; verified the same information in the aircraft operating handbook.  I advised the Captain of the discrepancy.  Maintenance was called.   This discrepancy was found on the second leg of the day; while utilizing the same aircraft.  The location of the equipment was inverted in its actual location vs. the location as stated in the manuals.Cabin crew may have not been facing forward in the cabin when pre-flighting the emergency equipment.  While the equipment was stowed in an overhead bin correctly; with the proper associated placards; the actual location of the equipment did not match the location stated in the manual.  As an example Oxygen is to be in the port side overhead.  Its actual location was starboard.  It is possible that during a pre-flight that a crew member facing aft will simply associate that the oxygen is 'on my left side'   This aircraft also had new overheads and added capacity within the last year. During that change; the equipment may have been installed incorrectly. Cabin crew may need to have greater situational awareness as to the actual right and left side of the aircraft; regardless of their orientation within the cabin.
