Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier FIrst Officer reported that Flight Attendants discovered Emergency Equipment was not reinstalled in the correct locations after an interior modification.

Report_1_Narrative: During my leg while cruising at FL350 to from ZZZ to ZZZ1 with the autopilot engaged. multiple caution messages popped out; suggesting some electrical issue with the #2 IDG/BUS. there was not a lot of communication in between the pilots but the Captain grabbed the Quick Reference Handbook and began working; So I decided to keep flying and work the radios. I kept monitoring the Captains body actions because I know that moving the wrong electrical switch could lead to further electrical issues. During the troubleshoot I confirmed that he could touch the Integrated Drive Generator 2. when he mentioned he was going to turn on the APU I reacted and say no; he asked me Why I did not want APU; so I advised that we were above the maximum altitude for APU start; so he understood and agreed to wait. advised descending; to which he agreed. I requested 29;000 ft. from ATC; and descended to 29;000 ft. When I suggested we were at an altitude where we could; he asked me to turn on the APU. When attempted to start APU about 4 screens went black momentarily and the autopilot and auto throttles disconnected. I announced I had the flight controls; and the throttles. The Captain re-engaged the autopilot without asking me but voiced it over and I monitored the correct engagement. Given the autopilot was responding correctly I decided to leave it engaged and monitor it. Given the APU caused appeared to cause the distruption for the APU I did not attempt turning it on again. Captain kept working Quick Reference Handbook; and coordinated with Dispatch and flight attendants. Captain decided to do the approach and landing; we briefed and landing at ZZZ1 without incident. No request for priority handling was declared.Multiple electrical failures.While we seemed to reach each other fairly well; I feel like the threat was treated like a no-time threat rather than a time threat. However; the outcome was positive.
Report_1_Synopsis: First Officer reported multiple electrical failures after the #2 IDG failed in flight.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Situational Awareness; Time Pressure; Physiological - Other; Communication Breakdown; Distraction
Report_1_Narrative: Arrival process and COVID screening under new ZZZZ guidelines contribute to extreme fatigue; physiological and psychological concerns. The entire process takes more than several hours. The arrival screeners are unprepared for each flight adding time to the process. The crew is sequestered within the airport during the process without access to toilet; food; or water. Cell phone contact with the company or union is prohibited during the testing phase. The threat of a possible positive test result and subsequent 14 day quarantine in an unknown government facility causes great psychological stress to the crew member.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported COVID-19 screening in foreign country contributes to fatigue; physiological; and psychological concerns.

Report_1_Narrative: Parking at stand X in MZBZ; we taxied into the parking spot. The Marshaller was giving guidance and was very slow with the stop signal. I was unsure of the command and proceeded to move forward; but quickly realized I was past the stop mark. I brought the plane to a stop and set the brake. The ramp agent informed me that a ground worker approached the aircraft and was almost run over. I told the managing agent the aircraft never came to a stop intermittently and did not stop until I brought it to a stop and set the brakes.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported almost hitting a ground employee while taxiing to their parking spot at MZBZ airport.  Captain cited communication issues with ramp personnel as a contributing factor.

Report_1_Narrative: While approaching to land in ROA Runway 24 we were being vector by ATC for a straight in approach. At 4;000 feet in level flight.  The aircraft was approximately 3.0 NM southeast of the final approach fix of HIBAN. ATC issued us a turn 'To a heading of 290 to intercept the GPS course. Cleared for the GPS Y Runway 24 approach.' Shortly afterwards the aircraft GPWS system activated with 'TERRIN TERRAIN PULL-UP.' Pilot flying disconnect the autopilot and climbed to approximately 4;700 feet. Then turn to the assigned heading and intercepted the GPS course and continued the decent to land into ROA. On the approach flight crew verified altitude and position and told what had occurred. ATC verified that the aircraft was at the appropriate altitude and position. They also added that their minimum vector altitude in the area that the aircraft was at was 4;000 feet. The flight continued the approach and landed safely on Runway 24.Still unsure on what the cause of the GPWS.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported a CFTT event while on the GPS Y Runway 24 approach to ROA.

Report_1_Narrative: Prior to initiating descent to ZZZZ1; the flight crew contacted ZZZZ Center and advised that we were unable to accept RNP-1 (Required Navigation Performance) arrival procedures. At this point; Center instructed the flight crew to fly an RNP-1 arrival despite having been informed of the incapability and the flight crew reiterated the fact they were unable to accept the arrival. Instead; the flight crew requested to fly direct to ZZZZZ waypoint for the start of the RNP RWY (Runway) XX approach. However; Center ignored this request and instructed the flight crew to fly direct to ZZZZ1 VOR and expect the VOR-A approach (Jeppesen Plate [Page]). When the crew once again requested to fly direct to ZZZZZ for the RNP RWY XX; Center repeated the instruction to fly direct to ZZZZ1 and expect the VOR-A approach without further acknowledgement or explanation of denial. The flight crew speculated that Center's refusal to assign the RNP approach was due to misinterpretation of the flight crew's inability to accept the RNP arrival; and efforts to clarify this case were also ignored by Center. The Captain (Pilot Monitoring) selected the VOR-A approach in the MCDU (Multi-Purpose Control Display Unit) and verified the route information while the First Officer (Pilot Flying) briefed the approach plate. At this time; both crew members observed what appeared to be inconsistencies between the MCDU approach database and the Jeppesen approach chart; specifically that the waypoint on Chart X did not match the waypoint shown in the MCDU routing; nor did the MCDU approach procedure indicate the required procedure turn under routing [FLP page] or Procedure Turn Info page [NAV - Page 2 - Patterns - Procedure Turn]. As the workload for the flight crew increased due to the inconsistency between chart and MCDU database; Center's refusal to assign a more effective approach; continuing descent towards mountainous terrain; and multiple segmented and non-standard clearances from Center that threatened to interrupt critical flight deck operations (notably the approach briefing); the flight crew elected to fly the VOR-A approach under raw data (green needles). All elements of the planned approach thus far mentioned became void after the flight crew received the hand-off to Approach Control who instructed them to fly direct to the airfield and complete a visual left-hand traffic pattern from overhead the runway.This flight crew highly recommends that an investigation be conducted into inconsistencies observed between the Jeppesen approach plate for the ZZZZ1 VOR-A Approach [Chart] and the MCDU database for the EJET fleet; namely the incorrectly labeled waypoint identified as ZZZZZ1 on the chart. This flight crew also highly recommends that effective communications be made between [Company] Flight Operations and the [Country] Air Traffic Control agency to ensure better understanding of which procedures [Company] flights are able to conduct and which procedures they are not; specifically the differences between RNP-1 'Arrivals' and RNP Approaches.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Flight Crew flying EMB-175 aircraft report inconsistencies between Navigation database and approach chart.

Report_1_Narrative: After I briefed the A Flight Attendant; she asked if I would be wearing a mask whenever they came in the cockpit for a lavatory break.  I informed her as per our protocol I am not required and for operational safety reasons I do not wear my mask in the cockpit. She then informed me that they would not enter to give us a break unless I wore a mask.  I then initiated calls to Dispatch and Operations to inform them of this problem.  I understand their concerns and respect their decision.   Yet; I do not understand why they would take issue with cockpit members facing forward and unmasked when they are continuously exposed to passengers in the cabin who have their mask off while eating or drinking as well as children who are not required to have a mask.On a recent flight my First Officer and I had a hard time understanding the ATC Controller due to the muffled sound because they were wearing a mask.  It is also difficult understanding a First Officer who is wearing a mask in the loud cockpit environment.  Safety of flight is my priority followed by mission and passengers.  I regret the inconvenience this brought to passengers and company alike but this difference in protocol needs to be resolved without imposing non safety operational constraints on the cockpit.   I realize this is a novel disease and the information from the CDC and NIH [National Institutes of Health] is at times confusing and conflicting but believe that we should not take information to extremes and compromise operational safety.Lack of cohesive policy between Cockpit and Flight Attendant protocols that plays between personal concerns over operational safety.  I also feel misinformation or agenda also play a role on differences regarding relative issues.Keep the current Pilot protocol which works well and imposes minimal restrictions regarding operational safety.  Clarify Flight Attendant protocols so they do not conflict with the cockpit.   To each individual this pandemic is relative and emotional.  Any preconceived or personal perception cannot be satisfied by one fits all protocols; so I believe individuals overly concerned should be required to get the vaccine.  I will at the earliest opportunity get vaccinated for myself; family and coworkers.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported a Flight Attendant stated they would not enter the cockpit for pilot break unless pilots were wearing a face mask. Captain described some the communication issues related to wearing a face mask.

Report_1_Narrative: Bleeds off TO. After starting engines; I turned off APU switch - IAW Normal after start flow. I should have left APU switch on IAW OM XXX.6 (Bleeds off/APU on TO). We did; however; carefully configure bleeds/packs IAW OM XXX.6. We did not subsequently catch that APU switch was off before takeoff. After departure; First Officer reconfigured bleeds/packs IAW with XXX.6 and continued normal flight to ZZZ.This was the 4th line trip I've flown at airline since April 2020. A lack of recency flying into ZZZZ1 and a reliance on the muscle memory/normal after start flows contributed to my error in turning the APU off prematurely. Both the First Officer and I were very aware of the bleeds/packs configuration as we had previously emphasized this TO briefing item at the gate prior to departure. Ultimately; by accurately following the pre-briefed OM 120.6 to reintroduce bleeds/packs after TO we trapped my error and the threat was mitigated.We received ACARS msg and SELCAL warning bleeds/packs off on climbout as First Officer was restoring the bleeds/packs per OM XXX.6. The SELCAL was a helpful reminder/backup to the crew.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported a lack of recency flying and a reliance on the muscle memory/normal after start flows contributed to an error in turning the APU off prematurely.

Report_1_Narrative: We were entering the terminal area with given heading descending from 11;000 feet down to 4;000 feet from the South west of the airport for RNAV 28. Passing through 5;000 feet we called the 'airport insight' and received the clearance for the visual approach for Runway 28. By the time we were abeam the airport flap 1 was down and altitude was 2;400 feet descending to 2;200 feet which was final approach segment altitude. Even though I was fully aware of the presence of obstacle (1;687 feet) on the path of our downwind I was confident that 500 feet margin and few thousand feet right of the course would give us good margin for safety. As we were getting close to the tower crane 'terrain' aural message came and after 2-3 second later 'terrain! pull up!' message came. I applied immediate max power and established pitch between 15-20. The message lasted few seconds and we climbed about 2;700 feet. After the conflict was resolved I intercepted the final course and follow the PAPI to the runway as normal operation.When we have received the visual clearance about 20 miles away I bugged the altitude down to 2;200 feet assuming within the 10 mile radius to the airport there cannot be anything that can pose threat to our path. Even though I was aware of the Tower; I didn't mention it during my briefing and considered it a big threat. When the Captain brought me an attention about the Tower once we were getting closer to it and asking me to turn inside the final approach point I delayed his suggestion wanting to intercept the final course outside the FAP. I could have been clear to ask him his intention or worries as we are nearing the obstacle and get the concurrence from both of us that 500 feet is enough or not.1. Better understanding of EGPWS logic could have given me the conservative altitude margins. 2. Detailed briefing; I could have planned better plan by flying higher or going around the tower instead of over flying it. 3. Rushing; I could have gone further out and fly higher to intercept instead of tightening my base turn to join right at the FAP.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported an obstacle related CFTT event requiring a pull up maneuver during approach to ALB airport.

Report_1_Narrative: The above pairing or trip is built with a tag after an all-night flight and I feel it is not safe for the employees and passengers. We check in at XA:X5 for an all-night flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1. After arriving in ZZZ1 exhausted from working all night the crew has to sit 3 hours at a hub where it would be easy to crew the next flight from ZZZ1 to ZZZ2 with a fresh crew that has slept. Instead a crew that has been up all night has to board and work a 2 hour flight. This I feel is not safe or healthy for the employees and lowers our immunity making us more apt to catch COVID; or some other sickness also not safe for passengers traveling with a crew that is exhausted.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Attendant reported after flying an all-nighter; they had to wait 3 hours in the crew lounge to make an additional two hour flight.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Situational Awareness; Communication Breakdown; Time Pressure
Report_1_Narrative: I was on the ground at JNX with my student pilot getting ready for a soft field takeoff. The pattern was very congested with 5 aircraft in the pattern in various places. An aircraft had just landed; and there were a few other aircraft on downwind. A downwind aircraft stated that they were extending their downwind for departing traffic. I told my student that after the landing aircraft had exited the runway to be ready for immediate departure. The exiting aircraft called clear at this point and I told my student to make the radio call and take us out. As we were taxing out the aircraft that had said they were extending downwind was now on a 1.5 mile final. I told the student to accelerate and a radio call over the CTAF said go-around. I took the controls from my student to avoid a confliction with the aircraft going around. The aircraft going around side stepped to the right to avoid conflict. At no time was a G1000 traffic advisory issued; and no aircraft came close to contact. The overpopulated pattern with 4 aircraft doing stop and goes and my aircraft trying to find a spot to get out was a contributing factor to this issue. After the aircraft sidestepped; they immediately departed the pattern; and we continued our takeoff and entered left closed traffic to continue landing practice.
Report_2_Narrative: Myself and a student who is currently working toward his CFI certificate went out for a training flight. After an hour of practicing maneuvers we approached JNX to practice takeoffs and landings. During our final approach into landing on Runway 21 at JNX my student made a call to let the other traffic in the pattern know of our position and our intentions; shortly after this call another plane pulled out on to the runway in frontof us. We made the decision to go-around and commenced a turn to the west so not to be on a collision course with the downwind traffic. We then proceeded to climb and leave the area.
Report_1_Synopsis: GA instructors on different aircraft reported conflicting with each other at JNX non-towered airport.  Reportedly; one of the instructor's aircraft took the runway for takeoff as the other was on final prompting a go-around and sidestep to avoid a possible collision.  Traffic volume at the uncontrolled airfield was cited as a contributing factor.

Report_1_Narrative: I departed ZZZ East ramp in [a] R22 with a private pilot student for pre-solo training at ZZZ1. We practiced emergency procedures en-route. After listening to ZZZ1 ASOS we determined to set up to enter the traffic pattern for Runway XX. 8 miles west from ZZZ1 we announced our location on CTAF and identified there were two airplanes in the pattern. We entered a 45 degree left downwind for Runway XX at ZZZ1 at 1;100 ft. and 75 kts. We announced and turned left base for Runway XX at 900 ft. and 60 kts. during which I could see Aircraft Y in a close left downwind. We announced turning final and turned final on Runway XX rolling out at 300 ft. AGL (900 ft. MSL) and 60 kts. I instructed the student to perform a normal approach to the approach end of Runway XX and terminate to a 3 ft. hover directly over the numbers (just as would be required during solo or a check ride). The student initiated his normal approach at the normal 10 degree angle required. I then heard Aircraft Y announce he was on final for Runway XX and had the helicopter in sight. I assumed the airplane had misjudged his spacing in the traffic pattern would either adjust his airspeed; perform turns for spacing; or go around. This is not uncommon and simple courtesy to the lower aircraft. On short final for Runway XX I looked out the left rear of the helicopter and could see Aircraft Y on short final right behind us. Aircraft Y asked me my intentions on CTAF. I replied that I intended to complete a landing to a hover at the approach end of Runway XX and then conduct a normal takeoff. Three things were on my mind. First; an aircraft on final and at a lower altitude always has the right of way. Second; I wanted the student to have the opportunity to conduct a normal approach to a hover just as he will be required to do during upcoming solo flight and his PPL checkride. Third; I need to access the student's ability to terminate the landing to a stationary hover. I asked Aircraft Y if he intended to 'go around' as it was clear either we would have to rush off the runaway; before completing the landing; or Aircraft Y could go-around. Aircraft X immediately replied with a complaint over CTAF stating that 'you little black helicopters are hogging the runways here and as a local pilot I can tell you that we are sick of you'. Just as I decelerated to a 3 ft. hover over the numbers for Runway XX I heard the sound of an airplane at high rpm overhead. I looked up to see Aircraft X directly over my helicopter about 20-30 ft. As he overflew me; he stated; 'he intended to report me to the FAA' and requested my name. I provided my tail number for his use as I did not want to provide my name over CTAF. I then contacted Aircraft Y over CTAF and requested that he not over fly my aircraft (for fear of collision) and that I will work with him to gain proper spacing in the pattern. Aircraft Y insulted me over CTAF and challenged me to a physical altercation. I instructed the student hover taxi to the parallel taxiway for Runway XX. I then noticed a pickup truck [surveying] our helicopter. I instructed the student to land on a nearby taxiway intersection near parking and go to idle. I exited the helicopter and approach the truck. I greeted the driver of the white truck with a handshake; introduced myself; and asked if there was an issue. I was told by the driver that they are reporting me to the FAA and they are just 'sick of our little helicopters that are difficult to see and tie up the runways for airplanes.' I sympathized with the driver but told him this is a public airport and that we have a right to conduct flight training here just as much as anyone; provided we all adhere to the rules. Furthermore; I told him that the airplane made an error in spacing by turning downwind; base; and final too quickly and essentially attempted to push me off the runway while conducting a landing. I told the driver that I am sorry this happened; but I feel the airplane did not adhere to Part 91 Right of Way rules to a lower aircraft on final. I gave the driver my number and told him I'd be more than happy to work with him on any future issues. We shook hands and went separate ways. I returned to the helicopter and returned directly to ZZZ. My chief concern with this incident is that the airplane should not have rushed or crowded another aircraft on final approach. A change in speed; turns for spacing; or a go-around were all options for the airplane pilot. Furthermore; executed a go around directly over and in close proximity to another aircraft is dangerous. What if I had directed the student to execute a go around or immediate takeoff (because we were being rushed on final and had climbed up into the airplane. As a military aviator and civilian helicopter and airplane pilot of over XX years I had always striven to fly with the utmost safety and friendliness. I preach this to my students; and I hope that all Aviators practice this as well. My goal is simply to encourage friendly; smart; and safe flying by all pilots at both ZZZ and ZZZ1.
Report_1_Synopsis: R22 Instructor reported that during a training flight while hovering over the runway numbers an aircraft in the pattern flew directly overhead them and made threatening comments over CTAF.

Report_1_Narrative: Personal training flight. Weather clear. Wind 05 at 120. Had flown east about 10 miles to the training area East of Morse Lake. I was flying at 2;600 feet. Cleared area. Flew S turns; turns around point; when I saw a plan approach on ADS-B (I was using a Dynon ADS-B receiver and wifi to my cell) Airplane approached close to me from the East. I noticed; since the plane's symbol turned orange - meaning it was 'close' I continued my training. The plane approached closer; and his symbol turned red. I looked to my left where he should have been viewable; but was unable to make contact. I turned away; to the right; and during my turn noticed a Aircraft Y above me; about 300 feet. I ID'd the plane on my ADS-B (Aircraft Y). I immediately pulled power and lowered to 2;100 feet. I turned course to Morse Lake; and the Aircraft Y followed me; above approximately 300 feet. I was able to see it; since my plane has a 'greenhouse' roof; and I was able to simply look up. The ADS-B signal was now one single red dot on my screen. The plane followed me right/left across Morse Lake.... We had NO Prior agreement to fly in formation. I had no way to contact this plane during my flight. The operator of Aircraft Y was obviously following my plane. My opinion; they were playing a weird cat and mouse. This behavior is contrary to proper airmanship. My major concern in writing this report is the fact such an act is now very easy. Any plane equipped with ADS-B can easily follow/shadow another --- and keep the signal on top of another. I have concerns this may be a new way for pilots to play cat and mouse - it is a very dangerous maneuver and against the FAR's separation guide.
Report_1_Synopsis: GA pilot reported an NMAC near 5I4 non-towered airport and questioned the airmanship of the other aircraft's pilot.

Report_1_Narrative: We had departed ZZZ1 to the south; when Tower was shut down due to COVID-19; VFR to pick up IFR clearance over ZZZ2. After passing under the [ZZZ] Class B to clear it; we contacted ATC. After giving us the clearance; the Controller gave the Captain a phone number to call (which he did later after landing); and advised of a report; that we had strayed into [ZZZ] Class B airspace.
Report_2_Narrative: ZZZ airport Tower was closed for to Coronavirus. [ZZZ is] a busy airport with mixed high speed and low speed aircraft.I departed VFR to pick up IFR clearance over ZZZ2 for arrival into ZZZ3.ATC; as always was very busy in that congested area and it took several attempts to make contact with ZZZ Approach.Very busy in cockpit looking for traffic; etc. May have clipped Class B airspace.ZZZ Approach advised; I may have entered Class B airspace and to copy phone a phone number.I replied: thank you; what altitude and heading would you like? The Controlled replied: 'continue; there is no traffic and then handed us off to ZZZ Center.I followed up with a phone call and thanked them for the wonderful service and protection they provide.I have been flying there for years. I have thousands of hours in general aviation and XX years flying airliners.The controllers do an unbelievable job working with an airspace system that does not work. The way it is designed doesn't work for the controllers or the pilots. At times the controllers are at max effort to keep up with the congested radio traffic.I am sure just they have their distractions with the maximum workload and have their own mistakes to sort out.That airspace configuration needs a good look at for something that works better for high speed aircraft. Get them out up and out of the way as fast as possible.It's a poor system to have jet aircraft level off at 1600 feet right after takeoff for normal operation under IFR conditions. In the cockpit of a jet aircraft you are very busy during this time.There needs to be change even if it slows down the current operations.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight crew reported a Class Bravo airspace violation due to the Tower being closed for COVID-19 issues.

Report_1_Narrative: Holding short of Runway XX at ZZZ; our aircraft was given a departure clearance void time of 60 seconds from ZZZ Center. We initiated an immediate departure on Runway XX. After climbing via the obstacle departure procedure; we proceeded enroute and contacted ZZZ Center again. We then heard another aircraft call back to ZZZ Center; and stated they were forced to initiate a go-around as they were on final approach to Runway XX. It is my guess that our departure is what caused that aircraft to go-around. I however; do not recall seeing the aircraft on final approach; or hearing a radio call that the aircraft was on final approach. Conditions were VFR at the airport; but IFR traffic load was heavy. I do not recall ATC advising us of the aircraft on final approach. It again is responsibility of us as a crew to ensure the approach/runway was clear for takeoff. If this incident was caused by our departure; we should have more clearly made sure it was safe for takeoff; and will do so in the future.
Report_1_Synopsis: First Officer reported another aircraft conducted a go-around after his aircraft took the runway for takeoff to beat a clearance void time.

Report_1_Narrative: I was conducting a training flight with a student and entered the pattern at PWT on the 45 for a full stop landing on Runway 20; making all radio calls in the pattern. As I was on short final (100 ft. AGL); the aircraft holding short makes a radio call that he is 'taking the active [Runway] 20'. He did not move his aircraft and continued holding short as I crossed the threshold; at which point I assumed he saw me as I passed right in front of his windshield in my roundout. I could not make any radio calls within those few seconds due to other traffic making calls in the pattern. As I am completing my landing roll to exit on taxiway A3; I hear a plane takeoff right on top of me. I asked on CTAF if he took off while I was still on the runway; to which 3 different aircraft concurred that he did. After a few minutes; as I'm departing the airspace; the aircraft in the pattern (along with myself) were discussing the events that transpired over radio. At that point; the pilot in question keyed up saying 'I'm still on frequency guys; what's the problem?'. I told him that he took off while I was still on the runway; to which he replied 'yeah; what's the problem with that?'. Another pilot noted that immediately after lift-off; he executed a steep right turn and exited the airspace at low level. In my professional opinion; the actions of the PIC of Aircraft X is a textbook example of a reckless operation; and a clear demonstration of several different hazardous attitudes. He obviously showed no remorse for his actions; believing that they were considered 'normal' things to do. There was absolutely nothing I could have done to prevent this from happening; because it is clearly all happening from the other guy's end. If I had to execute a go-around; it would almost definitely have resulted in a midair collision. The only way to prevent something like this from happening again is remedial training for this guy; or even a reevaluation of his certificate; because the way he operates his aircraft is clearly without regard for anyone's safety.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Instructor reported that during the landing rollout another aircraft took off from the same runway and flew directly over them. While the flight instructor was discussing the event over the radio with other aircraft in the traffic pattern; the departing aircraft asked 'what the problem was' with his departure.

Report_1_Narrative: During heavy traffic with inbound and outbound traffic Aircraft X was on short final. Aircraft Y was in line with several other aircraft for a [Runway] 28 departure. Aircraft X was calling position inbound for [Runway] 28. When Aircraft Y was number one in line to depart; the aircraft advanced on to the Runway 28 without any radio traffic and departed. This caused Aircraft X to go missed to avoid a collision. Aircraft Y never responded to any radio traffic.
Report_2_Narrative: Event happened at Yampa Valley Colorado. Contributing factors were a weather pause for both incoming and outgoing traffic. As we were trying to take off Denver Center was trying to sequence arrivals and departures. The aircraft in front of us was cleared to take off by Denver Center. We were asked if we could take off and be airborne within 90 seconds due to an inbound aircraft. We had an aircraft in sight and believed that to be the aircraft which we were cleared in front of. Contributing factor was Pilot in command was on ATC frequency but not on CTAF frequency. First officer was on both frequencies; but VFR aircraft was not transmitting position in pattern. As we took the runway and began our takeoff roll; chatter on the CTAF frequency alerted us to the traffic conflict. First Officer began giving vectors to Pilot Flying to avoid possible conflict. Due to being on takeoff roll we did not have visual on conflict aircraft. After getting airborne and getting in a safe flight configuration we took a slight left turn to displace ourselves from the TCAS information. We did not receive an RA likely because we were too low.Situational Awareness of Pilot Flying was increased dramatically once on both frequencies. Both pilots were under the impression clearance to depart was given with the aircraft we had in view to be the called traffic.
Report_1_Synopsis: Pilot and ground employee reported that an aircraft did not communicate their intentions on CTAF; taxied onto the runway and departed in front of an inbound aircraft causing that aircraft to go-around.

Person_1_Function: Single Pilot; Pilot Flying; Flight Engineer / Second Officer
Report_1_Narrative: I was on top of scattered clouds at 5;500 ft. arriving at HAF from the south. Weather reports from the airport all indicated the airport was VFR. As I approached the IF for the approach I had to decide between coordinating a pop up approach with Approach Control or descending through a large opening in the cloud layer and flying up the beach. I chose to remain VFR and fly up the coast due to the fact that it was getting dark and I had no idea how long it would take Approach Control to coordinate an approach. I descended uneventfully below the clouds and proceeded to the airport at between 1;000 and 1;500 ft. over hills that vary from 100 ft. to 300 ft. high. Apparently there is some drone operator who operates off a hill that gets upset when aircraft fly over at low altitude. He called me right after I had landed. He told me he 'I can not enforce this but I am requesting that we not fly over his drone operation'. I never saw a drone and am not sure if he was operating one at the time. Talking to other pilots it appears he calls every pilot he sees fly over at 1;500 ft. or below. I typically fly higher but on days when the ceilings are 1;500 to 2;000 ft. it is unavoidable to fly low. I am concerned about the drone operator calling pilots and possibly influencing their decisions when sacrificing safety of flight of the aircraft vs. inconvenience of the drone operator.
Report_1_Synopsis: A pilot reported a concerned citizen called them after landing to request that they do not fly over the citizens' 'drone operation'. The reporter stated other pilots who fly into this airport have also received phone calls from the same person.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Communication Breakdown; Confusion; Distraction; Situational Awareness; Time Pressure
Report_1_Narrative: During this incident I was on a checkride and we ran a partial panel VOR Runway X approach with a circle to Runway XY. This is normally a Class D airspace but the Tower at ZZZ is currently closed due to COVID and this has presented some challenges to the arriving and departing process given we share the airport with airline operations. We made it to the left downwind for XY and there was a carrier aircraft holding short of XY getting ready to take the runway and they requested over CTAF for us to extend our downwind so they could takeoff. We extended our downwind about a mile or so and decided to turn base. About the time we were turning base there was another carrier that called a 10 mile final for XY. With the position report given; we were under the impression we had the appropriate spacing for us to get on the ground and off the runway before they reached the field. We continued and turned in for final and the carrier taking off was on the roll. I made position reports and heard nothing back that would indicate an issue. When we were on short final carrier made a 6 mile final call. I then made a position call for short final and we were within a half mile of landing. About the time I was roughly 100 feet over the runway threshold; the carrier aircraft called and stated; 'Aircraft on short final; we are going around and will be flying above you.' We landed safely and had to extend our ground roll down the runway to exit because another carrier aircraft was taxiing to Runway XY via Taxiway A and we had to taxi beyond where they were. That concludes the incident. I do not know how accurate the position reports were from carrier or their speed but there didn't appear to be an issue on spacing and if they knew they were catching us that fast they could have let us know and I would have executed a go-around. This was not a near-miss event and we never saw the aircraft near us on ADS-B radar or receive any traffic notification. It seems to be more lack of communication in a non-towered environment with busy airspace as a root cause. I think they were well aware of our location in front of them and didn't speak up to let us know how quick they were catching us. I feel like there should be some additional measures in place when a tower is closed at an airport like this with heavier volume and many different types and sizes of aircraft operating. Sharing an airport between GA and airline ops in a non-towered environment is setting the stage for incidents like this to happen and truly presents some added challenges and hazards.
Report_1_Synopsis: GA pilot reported CTAF communication challenges at an airport that normally would have a working Tower facility; but was closed due to COVID-19.

Report_1_Narrative: I flew into ACT to see our son. This was a night flight and upon entering the ACT airspace it was very difficult to see the runway lighting. The runway lights were very dim and indistinguishable from surrounding city lights. When I asked the tower to turn up the runway lights; the Tower Controller stated they haven't been able to control the runway lights for 9 months due to a lightning strike. They have filed numerous maintenance requests; but none have been acted upon. This is unacceptable and a safety of flight issue. I request the runway lights be fixed as soon as possible to allow the tower and pilots to control the lighting intensity.
Report_1_Synopsis: Pilot reports low intensity runway lighting and that ATC cannot control runway lights for 9 months after a lightning strike.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Workload; Situational Awareness; Troubleshooting; Human-Machine Interface; Distraction; Confusion; Communication Breakdown
Report_1_Narrative: Enroute at 2;000 feet when I received a message on GPS and EFIS saying RNAV signal is lost; ADS-B is lost. iPad does not show correct location. No problem because VMC and not going anywhere. No navigation and no traffic. I called Approach Control to ask if they knew of any GPS outages. They said they hadn't and nobody else was having a problem. After landing; about 20 minutes later the system was back to normal. Another pilot had the same experience. Called Approach Control again on the landline and they advised that they had gotten several reports but they had no prior record of it and they should have been advised that Navy was doing testing offshore. There were no local NOTAMs and when I went back to look; there was a NOTAM for the outage lasting for about a week at various times for Center. Send [a] NOTAM to all Approach Controls that underlie testing area and also to local airports so that flights that never touch overlying airspace are aware of possible outage. They should also be sent to EFB providers so they can include it in their system. Had this occurred in IMC it would have spiked the workload considerably and only VHF navigation would have worked.
Report_1_Synopsis: A Pilot reported GPS interference.

Report_1_Narrative: I was approaching L52 from the north/west to enter a left downwind for Runway 29. As I was crossing the shoreline at 1;000 AGL (one mile out) and decelerating; my passenger and I spotted two powered gliders crossing the departure end of 29 at approximately 900 feet AGL.They seemed to be transitioning from the southern part of the dunes to the norther part of the dunes through the upwind part of the traffic pattern. I veered the aircraft slightly more to the south to avoid them when I spotted another powered glider transitioning from the south to the north by intersection the downwind leg of the left pattern to 29. He was coming directly toward my aircraft in the opposite direction of traffic pattern. I then had to veer slightly to the left (north/east) to avoid that vehicle. I then landed without incident on 29.When parked at transient space we witnessed another powered glider takeoff from the tarmac and join the other gliders.  They continued to overfly the airport at pattern altitude and not seem to adhere by any observable pattern.
Report_1_Synopsis: GA pilot reported an NMAC with powered gliders during approach to L52 non-towered airport. Reporter stated the gliders were not following pattern procedures.

Report_1_Narrative: I released Aircraft X for departure from BFI in a south flow. Aircraft X reported climbing to 2;000 ft. on the NIRVANA1 SID. I radar identified Aircraft X and climbed them to 6;000 ft.. As Aircraft X was climbing through 1;800 ft. I noticed that Aircraft X appeared to be making a right turn towards the SEA VOR and not following the NIRVANA SID. I instructed Aircraft X to 'turn left immediately; left turn heading 130.' At this point; Aircraft X was starting to converge with Aircraft Y who was on final approach into SEA descending through 1;100 ft. on the ILS Approach to Runway 16R. Aircraft X was about 1.5 miles laterally separated and 700 ft. vertically separated from Aircraft Y and converging. I observed Aircraft X achieve vertical separation from Aircraft Y; then saw the turn to heading 130 start occurring. I gave Aircraft X the Brasher statement. The pilot of Aircraft X stated that it 'looks like the activation for the autopilot for the NIRVANA1 did not take place.'I honestly don't know how to fix this problem; but it is a recurring; systemic issue. This is not my first event with almost identical circumstances; and many of my co-workers have had very similar events. Attempts have already been made to alter the SID; or issue an initial heading for aircraft departing BFI; but these events still occur. The typical issue is that pilots are filing SEA.J5 and though BFI is issuing the NIRVANA1 SID and a Preferred Departure Route that would join J5 from TAOMA or SUMMA; pilot error including unchecked autopilot actions that result in a turn to SEA VOR will immediately cause convergence at the same altitude as aircraft inbound to SEA within the final approach fix; as well as any aircraft departing SEA during that time. There is very little and very subtle warning; and immediate action is necessary to recover separation and end the rapidly worsening danger of the situation. I believe in most cases it is a result of an individualized pilot deviation; and I don't know how to end those completely. The only other solution I can think of would be to completely remove/decommission the SEA VOR.
Report_1_Synopsis: A TRACON Controller reported an aircraft departing an airport deviated from their SID and into confliction with an air carrier on final approach to an adjacent airport. The reporter stated pilot deviations on this particular SID are a recurring issue.

Report_1_Narrative: It was toward [the] end of the rush; I was working the low side and had all of my aircraft slowing to 170 kts. Controller Y plugged in for a relief briefing after working as the main arrival coordinator. As I was going through the position relief checklist Controller Y noticed something was off. At first I thought Controller Y was looking at the spacing on final; which was perfect. But then I saw Aircraft X on a 180 heading racing towards the Runway XL final. My first reaction was to turn Aircraft X right to a 330 heading but then Controller Y suggested a left turn to continue eastbound away from final. I issued a left turn 090 and then a climb to 050 to get above the traffic on final approach.It was clear that Aircraft X took the left turn to 180. Aircraft Y had turn to a 180 heading at his appropriate time.If it wasn't for the fast acting from Controller Y the issue could have worsen.In this new world of 'COVID Traffic' pilots need to do a better job of listening to control instructions especially when the volume is high.
Report_1_Synopsis: TRACON Controller reported clearance communication issues with an aircraft resulted in a conflict which was saved by another attentive Controller who offered a different heading to avoid further separation issues.

Report_1_Narrative: In ZZZ we attempted to start number two engine using APU air and it spooled up abnormally slowly; and I noticed that the EGT seemed to lag. At 45% N2 the start stagnated and decayed until a 2.5% N2 decrease and Engine Fail indication on the ECAM. We stopped the start; then following guidance in our paperwork; we started number one (which also stagnated a little bit but then started normally) and then attempted a second start on number two using cross-bleed from the number one engine. We allowed the engine to spool up to 25.7% N2; then added fuel. At starter cutout; the engine hung again; dropping to about 43.2% N2 and hanging there before slowly spooling up to about 43.8% N2 when it timed out for the start and Engine Fail was indicated on ECAM again. Our Quick Reference Handbook said we could attempt a second start after the first hung start; but that maintenance action was required if the second start failed. At that point we requested a tug and BTB to our parking space. This is where Maintenance Control got involved. At first they suggested that we defer the APU bleed; however it was obvious to me that the air was not the problem (we used a separate source for each start); so I told him the APU bleed deferral was not sufficient. Then he suggested that a problem with the Integrated Drive Generator might be causing the hung start and suggested we defer that; and I agreed it could be tried. As part of the maintenance action during start the Inetgrated Drive Generator was disconnected and deferred; and the Airworthiness Release in the log book was signed off; then we continued getting the jet started and were on our way. During the flight the APU was running as required by the deferral; and at 36;000 ft. it automatically shut down. I attempted to start the APU; and on the second try; it started. I requested and descended to a lower altitude of 30;000 ft. and the APU operated normally for the rest of the flight. If I had not been able to start it; I would have had to advise ATC and divert. I wrote up the APU under a P code for momentary or transitory malfunction. In ZZZ1; maintenance checked the APU for any failure codes; did the repetitive inspection for oil quantity for the Integrated Drive Generator deferral; and signed off the APU. The FO (First Officer) and I discussed the situation and agreed that the APU was not malfunctioning and may have had a momentary problem with operating at high altitude. We accepted the jet for the leg to ZZZ2. With a fresh Airworthiness Release in the log book; we started the number one engine first; then started number two using cross-bleed at the request of maintenance. The number two engine came close to exceeding time limits; but did eventually spool up. We were filed for 33;000 ft.; and at that altitude the APU did the same thing--it shut down--and we were able to get it started again on the second try. We requested and descended to 29;000 ft. for the remainder of the flight. Again; the APU operated normally from there on; and again; I wrote it up with a P code for the shut down. I also made a comment in the logbook about the number two engine start; even though our flight paperwork said that comments for a successful start were not needed. There I made a note that the EGT from fuel introduction to the point where the start stagnated; then started to spool up; seemed abnormally low and was at least 50 degrees cooler at 45% N2 than the other engine. The stagnated start was evident from fuel introduction until after started cutout when it became apparent that the engine was not ready to continue the start on its own. The Integrated Drive Generator has nothing to do with the EGT during start. I suspect something else is going on here; perhaps a Electronic Engine Control problem with the fuel mixture at high altitude; or a sensor malfunction. On further reflection; I feel that the deferral of the Integrated Drive Generator was inappropriate for the problem we had; and I should not have accepted it. It created a problem where we could have been forced to request priority handling and divert. It is likely that whatever is wrong with our engine starts does not pose a safety of flight risk once we get the engine going; so it makes no sense to do a deferral that could compromise safety. Until this is figured out; the guidance needs to be specific and it needs to go out to everyone in the maintenance and crew pipelines and it should be operations friendly. My recommendation is that everything in the fuel system be checked in case it is causing the starting problem for cold engines at high altitude. I think that the bleed system is less likely to be the issue because of the low EGT I saw during all four start attempts on that engine. I also recommend that maintenance be able to attempt at least one more start before the aircraft is taken out of service; and that crew get more guidance concerning the problem. 'Maintenance action' is not enough to let a Captain know what to expect or what to accept. I also have felt for a long time that our systems manual has been scrubbed of a lot of detail about systems with which we do not directly interact; so we are less able to make informed decisions and instead have to rely on experience. That will not always save us from making the wrong call. Everyone in this situation acted in good faith; and I am not writing this report to cast any doubt on anyone. I only want to point out a safety issue that we can avoid in the future.
Report_1_Synopsis: Pilot reported application of the wrong MEL complicated the flights unnecessarily.

Report_1_Narrative: On climb out after 5 min. for approximately 15 min. FA (Flight Attendants) 3 and 4 reported smelling sweet glue like odor that went away in about 15 min. About 35 min. into flight FA 3 reported a headache and FA 4 reported headache and nausea. FA 2 reported the smell was faint but did smell it but felt OK. FA 1 and flight deck did not smell odor. The odor was noted from Row 10 to aft of aircraft. The FA 4 reported feeling worse at 35 min. into flight so we elected to return to ZZZ. 1 passenger in 13A reported slight irritation in nose and slight headache. On return to ZZZ as a [prioritized] aircraft on descent through 10;000 ft. flight deck and cabin noticed a distinct odor like Elmer's Glue. Uneventful landing with flight deck on O2 and cabin use of 4 portable O2 bottles. FA 4 went to hospital remaining crew felt fine and continued on new aircraft to ZZZ1 as rescheduled.The probable cause was possible oil leak but no indications in flight deck.Dependent on maintenance findings.
Report_1_Synopsis: A321 Captain reported a cabin fumes event during initial climb resulting in a return to the departure airport.

Report_1_Narrative: After takeoff during initial climb out we received a ACARS message. The message informed us of dangerous goods being carried and to expect a NOTOC (Notification to Captain) prior to gate departure.Suggestion - It would be preferable to have a system in place that would ensure a NOTOC was presented to the flight crew prior to closing the boarding door.
Report_1_Synopsis: A-321 Captain reported uneventful flight completion after receiving airborne ACARS notification of undocumented Hazmat cargo on board.

Report_1_Narrative: Upon landing at their destination of ZZZZ1 and looking at the W/B (Weight and Balance) for the next flight ZZZZ1-ZZZZ2; I noticed the W/B had Dry Ice loaded in the lower forward compartment. I checked the W/B for the ZZZZ-ZZZZ1 leg; and ZZZZ had loaded Dry Ice in the lower forward compartment and did not notify me; thus no 0.4% overburn had been applied. Flight crew did not say anything to me as well. Dispatcher suggested better ramp training for them to be aware of need to inform Dispatcher if Dry Ice will be loaded in lower compartments of 777. Also; suggest programming [Software] to trigger an alert to the Dispatcher anytime Dry Ice gets loaded in a lower compartment of a 777. I made this suggestion previously to [Name] in an email sent on [Date].
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Dispatcher reported unmanifested Dry Ice had been transported to destination.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Physiological - Other; Communication Breakdown; Confusion; Situational Awareness; Troubleshooting
Report_1_Narrative: I believe complacency played a role in this error. I am always checking and double checking my work but unfortunately I missed an important piece of information on the Center of Gravity (CG) and Passenger Count (PC) data. Next time I will slow down and thoroughly check my work without rushing and recognize my complacency.We arrived to our aircraft in the morning to perform our duties for the first leg out of two for the day. Boarding was complete and I received the cargo sheet and CG/PC Data from the gate agent. As I plugged the numbers in for departure I noticed the passenger count seemed low.  Thinking that it was due to the slow season and COVID I continued to run the numbers for our takeoff data. With the low passenger count I figured we were going to also need a ZFW reset from the dispatcher. I confirmed with the Captain and went ahead and contacted Dispatch with our new ZFW and confirmation of our CG. New numbers were sent back and we took off uneventfully.While in cruise the Captain requested a lavatory break. Upon his returned; he voiced his concern with the passenger count from what he saw in the cabin while checking our CG/PC. That is when we realized that the incorrect CG/PC was given to us. As we were starting our decent; the Captain transferred the controls to me while he referenced the COM and tables to calculate our correct weight along with the landing data and Vapp. As a precaution we also added few knots to the Vapp. The Captain completed the tasks and I confirmed that all the information was correct and within safe parameters for a safe landing.  We had sufficient runway and the field was VMC at the time of landing. The landing was uneventfully and we continued to the gate.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier First Officer reported the pilot crew realized; in cruise; the weight and balance data were incorrect. The pilots did not question the small passenger load; which is common during the COVID-19 pandemic; before takeoff.

Report_1_Narrative: During initial climb out (400 or 500 ft.) we heard a call from Medical saying that 'something's burning'. I looked behind and noticed the cabin was beginning to fill with a smokey hazy layer. The temperature in the airplane had increased and now the smoke was reaching the cockpit. I reset both bleed air valves in case we had a stuck valve; but this did not change anything. I told FO (First Officer) to turn off all fans in case that is the cause. I looked back again and I could visible see the smoke rising out of the rear right wall panel. We stopped the climb at 2;500 ft.; [advised ATC] and I made the decision to return back to ZZZ. I assumed control of the airplane and radios while FO completed checklist and set us up on the approach and calculated the weight of the airplane. He advised me that we were currently 500 lbs. overweight; I made the decision to still continue to the airport as I did not know the cause of the smoke and did not want to waste any time burning off extra fuel. We ultimately made a safe left base visual approach and landed 300 lbs. overweight. We were able to taxi into the ramp and shutdown and safely exited the airplane. We followed checklist and [Company] SOP.
Report_1_Synopsis: Learjet-35 Captain reported a fumes event during climb resulting in a return to the departure airport.

Report_1_Narrative: At [Gate] at ZZZ; the First Officer said he saw [Package] near the aircraft; I had just received the cargo load report; so I asked the tug driver over the headset if [Package] was loaded onto the aircraft; he said he would double check and asked someone. He got back to us with that there was no [Package] onboard. I also specifically asked about the presence of dry ice (Dangerous Goods); and the answer I got was that there was not. So neither of those were marked on the cargo load sheet; and neither were onboard according the verbal response I received. I assumed it was coming off our aircraft from the previous flight or destined for another flight. The First Officer during the post flight at [Gate1] at ZZZ1 saw [Package] in our cargo compartment waiting to be unloaded. I do not know if there was any dry ice with it.
Report_1_Synopsis: EMB-175 Captain reported undocumented Hazmat transported due to a communications breakdown between flight crew and Ramp personnel during preflight.

Report_1_Narrative: I was notified of my reserve assignment at XA:00 by Crew Scheduling. They stated when they called me to pack a bag because I might not be home as the airplane we were to repo back to ZZZ was still broken. They assigned me a XB:00 showtime on the phone. I however noticed later my show time was modified to XC:00. Either way I arrived at the airport and sat down at the gate that was on my schedule. The First Officer texted me and stated the hotel van was just pulling up. At XC:00 when no gate agent was around the gate area at [Gate] I called my Dispatcher at [the] desk. I asked if he could get someone to let us down to the plane. After placing me on hold he stated we would be originating from the maintenance hangar. He asked the maintenance department where we needed to go to be picked up. They stated [Gate1]. He then started to fill me in that we would be hauling two mechanics; their tools and few other miscellaneous items. We met the maintenance personnel at [Gate1] and was transported to the airplane near the maintenance hangar. Upon arriving we noticed a 5 gallon bucket of Skydrol hydraulic fluid in front of the airplane along with what appeared to be a hydraulic pump and some hoses that were located in an open top box. The maintenance personnel stated that Maintenance Control okayed this being transported onboard the airplane. The FO (First Officer) went up to the flight deck and stowed her bags. I called the pilot on duty to get some direction on this 5 gallon container and was also hoping he could put me in touch with the hazardous materials specialist. The pilot on duty tracked him down and he okayed it based on being less than 5 gallons and it was in a sealed container. The box with the pump; hoses and other miscellaneous items was also OK. I question that now based on the [Operations Manual]. The last bullet point is my question. While I was inspecting the cabin's emergency equipment the FO notified me that the maintenance personnel stated that there was a substantial amount of items loaded in the forward cargo bay accumulating to about 300 lbs. I asked if the items happened to get weighed as they went on. The answer was they did not and someone was going to come out with a scale to unload and weigh the items. I called the pilot on duty to confirm needing this information. The maintenance personnel did provide the information after unloading and reloading the cargo bay. During this time the 5 gallons of Skydrol was brought into the cabin and placed between two first class seats. The box with the pump also was. I called the scheduling and asked to speak to the manager on duty. I was connected. After explaining the situation to him he stated he would call me back. The maintenance personnel placed the Skydrol in a first class seat and placed a seatbelt around the container. Sometime after this they place an orange ratchet strap around this bucket also. After some time Duty Officer called me back. At this time Maintenance removed the Skydrol and the pump from the aircraft and stated we would be going without it. He stated they would remove it and place it below and secure it. He instructed us not to leave if it was placed below and not secured. At some point after this call with Duty Office crew scheduling called me questioning where I was at and why we have not departed yet. I explained to them we were on the airplane and attempting to safely depart after everything was in order. I called the Dispatcher and inquired about a new release because our release was timing out. We decided to add fuel to the airplane at that time because the APU has been running for along time now. While waiting for the fuel truck to arrive the maintenance personnel drove back up to the plane and loaded the Skydrol and the pump into the forward cargo bay. I went to look at how these items were secured. They were just sitting in boxes and not secured. I took a few pictures to send to Duty Office and the maintenance personnel asked me if this was OK. I stated I was told it had to be secured and that I was send this pictures to my manager. The maintenance personnel stated they would remove it from the plane and we could depart. The items were removed. While waiting for the fuel truck we also inquired with scheduling on what hotel we would be staying at in ZZZ1. They stated that we would be flying back because the 14 hours from our reserve availability period only was restricted to passenger flying and since this was Part 91 flying we were good for 16 hours. We were told we would have to call off if we didn't want to work the flight back. The fuel truck arrived and we departed soon after. The remainder of the flight was uneventful. We concluded the flight in ZZZ1 at XD:00.We were sent to the hotel and was scheduled for a min rest overnight. We called when we reached the hotel and had the show time adjusted to allow us 10 hours.
Report_1_Synopsis: EMB-170 Captain reported a Hazmat configuration violation during preflight of a ferry flight. Completed an uneventful flight after Hazmat cargo was removed.

Report_1_Narrative: Flying C172 on an IFR flight from ZZZ to ZZZ. Was flying a RNAV approach to ZZZ. Soon after hand off to ZZZ Approach; I disconnected the autopilot when the aircraft was at about 4;000 feet AGL. At that time ATC advised to turn left to 220 heading to intercept initial approach fix. Right after disconnecting the auto pilot; the aircraft banked left steeply to about 60 degrees roll and started descending while the ATC keep advising to turn left and cleared me for the RNAV approach. The conditions were IMC and aircraft was hard to control. It took a few minutes to get the aircraft under control. The ATC workload obviously increased while not knowing the exact situation and even doubted at one point if the pilot (me) was IFR rated and current. Once I was finally able to get the aircraft stabilized; I informed ATC that I was having trouble with the controls and apologized. The flight ended safely after all at ZZZ. The probable cause was having an iPad mounted on the yoke. Will never mount the iPad on the yoke again.
Report_1_Synopsis: C-172 pilot reported experiencing aircraft control difficulty caused by the yoke-mounted iPad.

Report_1_Narrative: I wish to report a near mid-air collision.  We were operating Aircraft X; ZZZ-ZZZ1; on a 737-900ER. The FO (First Officer) was the PF (Pilot Flying). I was the PM (Pilot Monitoring). Our IFR clearance was [SID]. Upon takeoff clearance from Runway XXR; we were given a heading of 290 with a initial climb limit of 3;000 [feet]. We received no notification of any traffic that we should be looking for upon takeoff clearance or during our initial climbout. As we were climbing out and cleaning up the aircraft; we received a TA at out 1 to 2 o'clock and high. I stopped my PM duties to search for source of the TA. As I searched; we got the altitude alert for the level off. I found the aircraft. He was not moving in relationship to our direction of travel. I told the PF to stop his climb. As I was saying that; we received the RA. The PF lowered the nose the slow the climb; as he was doing that the TCAS annunciated 'monitor vertical speed.' I glanced at the MFD to see the aircraft was only +200 feet above us. I was still on the 5 mile range and the symbol was inside the 2.5 mile tick mark at our 1 o'clock. The PF executed the RA escape maneuver to comply with the RA. I then told ZZZ Departure that I had the GA aircraft in sight; as we still hadn't been given any traffic alerts. The TCAS announced 'clear of conflict' and we resumed the climb uneventfully.
Report_2_Narrative: Aircraft X; ZZZ-ZZZ1 I was the PF (Pilot Flying). Our clearance was [SID]...off Runway XXR heading of 290 with a initial climb limit of 3;000 [feet]. We received a TA at about 2;200 [feet]. There was an aircraft approximately 2;500 feet. No notification from ATC about the traffic. TCAS told us monitor our vertical speed which I did. I performed an RA escape maneuver and TCAS said clear of conflict. We notified approach about the traffic and TCAS RA. It seemed as if there was something going on at ZZZ or surrounding airport with an emergency at the time...rest of the trip was without incident.
Report_1_Synopsis: B737-900 flight crew reported taking evasive action after receiving a TA and RA.

Report_1_Narrative: For the ILS Runway 04R at ZZZ; performance numbers were run for a Flaps 30 landing with a good stopping margin at Autobrakes 3. ATIS winds were calling approximately 070/13 - no gusts. Upon switching to Tower at ZZZZZ on the localizer course and tracking the glideslope; Tower cleared us to land with winds now gusting to 20. As PF (Pilot Flying); I elected to add 4 knots to the Vtarget and as an added Safety measure at ZZZ; I selected Autobrakes MAX to compensate for a slightly increased approach speed. The PM (Pilot Monitoring) attempted to quickly re-run the performance data; but the gusts were not yet accounted for in the METAR. Rather than going heads down any longer inside 1;000 feet AGL; we agreed a 4-5 knot addition to VTarget and using Autobrakes MAX would be more than sufficient to account for the gust factor.At approximately 500 feet AGL; we received a GPWS Too Low Flaps Alert. The PM immediately called for the go-around and it was initiated. A quick scan of the flap handle and I realized that I had neglected to call for Flaps 30 from a Flaps 15 setting; and the Before Landing Checklist was not run. We were quickly vectored around for another uneventful ILS. The minor distraction of adding a gust factor and changing the Autobrakes setting sent me out of a normal approach configuration sequence and we ended up both missing the final flap setting and subsequent checklist.With the normal ZZZ procedure of not contacting (and often not switching to) Tower until reaching the fix at about a 5-mile final; it's possible for us to miss out on cues to changing weather on the ground. We were number 3 or 4 in a sequence of landings on 04R. Had we switched to Tower five or more miles sooner; we may have caught the gusting winds earlier and had more time to type in the adjusted winds and send away for the performance numbers prior to 1;000 feet AGL. This was another series of events combined with mild fatigue that led to poor task prioritization on our parts.
Report_2_Narrative: The short version is that we got 'Too Low; Flaps' at 500 feet because we were at Flaps 15. We went around. Planned winds were 070/7. Tower winds were 070/12G20. I re-ran the performance landing numbers at 1;500 feet; but did not override the METAR and got back the numbers for 070/7. The PF (Pilot Flying) chose to add 5 knots to VTarget and we agreed to go from Medium to Max braking and continue.There is no guidance I am aware of as to when we would be required to re-run our landing numbers. I should not have tried to re-run the landing numbers at that point. That would have eliminated the distraction that led to not selecting our planned final flaps or running the Before Landing Checklist.
Report_1_Synopsis: B737-800 flight crew reported executing a go-around due to improper flap setting on short final.

Report_1_Narrative: Over last few days; there is indication that certain aviation companies are looking into making the COVID vaccine mandatory for their employees. I strongly believe that this is a potential security risk; due to the fact that if an individual is forced to do something against their will; they might fight back. In the aviation industry; as history has shown so well; there is a strong possibility that airplane safety might be compromised; especially by individuals that have direct access to the unsecured aircraft; such as gate agents; operations personnel; mechanics; and ground handlers.Due to the significant safety concerns; I strongly urge the FAA to prohibit mandatory vaccinations.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Captain reported concerns with airlines possibly making it mandatory for employees to get the COVID-19 vaccine.

Report_1_Narrative: With about 4 hours to go before landing; I had just emerged from the crew rest bunk when Lead Flight Attendant asked me if I could have the flight deck crew wear a face mask when a Flight Attendant was in the cockpit in flight. I told her no for the safety of flight reasons. I did not add anything further.I personally was not going to wear a face mask in the cockpit since I would be in the cockpit for the rest of the flight. I am required by the FAA on my medical 'Must wear corrective lenses; possess glasses for near/intermediate vision.' Since my glasses fog up every time I wear any type of face mask I know that wearing a mask at my flight deck seat is a safety of flight issue. About two hours later when the Lead came to in to give us a restroom break we; First Officer and I; offered her an N95 mask to wear for her safety and set it on the pedestal for her. She did not put it on and chose to wear what appeared to be a non-N95 certified black cloth mask.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Captain reported telling the Lead Flight Attendant that he would not be wearing a face mask in the flight deck due to safety of flight reason as his glasses fog up when wearing a face mask.

Report_1_Narrative: While in line for takeoff on Taxiway for XXR; we received a notification from the flight attendants that the cabin was filling up with smoke which was coupled with a foul odor akin to burning rubber. We smelled the odor at the same time the flight attendants notified us of the smoke. I asked them if it was thick enough to block view of the back of the aircraft and if they thought we needed to evacuate right away. They answered no to both questions. I then told them that we would be moving to a cargo ramp to run a QRH and if they thought at any point we would need to evacuate while moving to call me back and we would stop immediately. I also informed them that the next time we stopped would be the last time we would move without calling them and that once stopped; if they felt the need to evacuate; they were to do it. We taxied to the cargo ramp just south of taxiway after alerting ATC that we were [requesting priority handling] and would be pulling off to the side to run a QRH and to have the fire trucks standby. We ran the entirety of the smoke fire fumes QRH; which had us deactivate the PACs (Air Conditioning Packs) and close the bleed valves. We elected to not drop pass O2 or go on O2 ourselves as we were not having any adverse reactions; but just dealing with an unpleasant smell in the flight deck. We called the flight attendants at this time and asked about the passengers' condition and they stated that everyone was fine. The smoke slowly dissipated throughout the rest of the event. At this point; we decided to go back to the gate as the smoke was no longer producing from the vents and the passengers were not complaining about any issues when asked. We cancelled [priority handling] but requested that crash rescue follow us to the gate. Once arriving at the gate with the aircraft shut down and the flight deck door open and main cabin door; we had one woman reportedly having bronchitis coughing to a large extent. She was the first off. I was not aware she had an adverse reaction until pulling into the gate. We deplaned everyone as quickly as possible and had Maintenance confirm that PAC 2 was the culprit. To my knowledge; all passengers refused medical attention. We later got another aircraft and had all passengers board.The probable cause was something happened with the Right PAC as we were single engine no APU taxiing to XXR with Engine 2 running.
Report_1_Synopsis: CRJ-900 Captain reported a fumes event during taxi-out resulting in a return to the gate.

Report_1_Narrative: TCAS RA on arrival into ZZZ [airport]. Assigned descent to 7;000 feet and vectors to final by ZZZ Approach. We reached 7;000 feet and noted approach was extremely busy where the Controller was being stepped on seemingly more than half of her transmissions. While level at 7;000 feet the TCAS noted a proximate target converging from 1 o'clock; 400 feet below. We attempted to contact Approach but there was zero opportunity to get a word in due to the sheer amount of communication on frequency. I advised the Captain PF to 'get ready' while we attempted to locate the aircraft visually. A few seconds later the TCAS noted traffic and ordered a very shallow climb. I announced to ZZZ Approach that we were responding to an RA; but I believe I was blocked; the frequency still jammed with constant communication. A very short time later the controller issued traffic to us and I again advised 'Climbing on RA.' Controller replied 'Roger' I believe and the event was over shortly after. We returned to 7;000 feet and were vectored for the visual; but the controller still had to vector us around multiple VFR targets on our way to the runway. Most significantly we were cleared for the visual approach; but were restricted to flying and intercepting between 5 and 7 NM from the airport due to area traffic. This caused a perceived limitation that pilots are not used to. The CA/PF then overflew the Localizer slightly attempting to maintain these limitations. The aircraft was clearly stable by 1000 feet and we continued in to land; but this was following an incident due to the same cause.Cause was due to the intense level of traffic in ZZZ Approach's airspace. I spoke with a contact at ZZZ [Approach] later who noted the Controller had 15 active aircraft not including the VFR targets attempting to get clearance from the closed airspace; Practice IFR traffic; and VFR flight following requests. The Controller was doing an excellent job and maintained a very professional demeanor throughout. There was just no reasonable way for Controller to maintain communications with the volume of aircraft. I am not sure; but this could have been a result of reduced staffing due to COVID. Maybe there was an East and West ZZZ [Approach] sector available; but no staffing to accommodate. My suggestions would be to either split ZZZ Approach or to draw a new arrival for ZZZ airport to reduce the amount of communications and possible routes needed for the controllers.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier First Officer reported an RA event and blocked ATC communications due to possible COVID-19 ATC staffing issues.

Report_1_Narrative: Flew ZONNA1 arrival to TUS. I was PF (Pilot Flying) and did the arrival briefing prior to descent which included terrain hazards and the MSA. Both pilots had terrain selected. Approach control gave us a clearance to turn right to 270 and descend to 10;000' for sequencing. Soon after this clearance we entered IMC. Passing north and abeam Mt Lemmon at about 10;300'; we got an EGPWS TERRAIN PULL UP warning. I executed the EGPWS Recovery Action. Almost immediately we went VMC. After passing the MSA of 10;700 and visually verifying terrain clearance; I resumed normal flight; leveled at 11;000' and informed ATC that we had responded to a GPWS terrain warning. They acknowledged and gave us a descent to 9000'. Remainder of flight was uneventful.Either the Terrain system gave us a false alert or we were given a clearance to descend below the radar minimum altitude. We never got any indication on the Terrain display. STAR page showed us north of Mt Lemmon and the terrain depicted around it. While we had good terrain awareness; I should have queried Approach about an IMC descent below the Sector MSA.I recommend a Radar Minimum Altitudes chart be included in the Jeppesen pages for TUS.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported receiving a EGPWS warning while being vectored for approach to TUS airport.
