Report_1_Narrative: ATC turned us onto the approach while still at 4;000. Told us to 'maintain 3;000 till established cleared ILS [Runway] XXL. FO (First Officer) put in 3;000 in the altitude selector and I acknowledged it. Once established; instead of selecting 2;700 feet for the FAF altitude he rolled the altitude selector to 3;300 and started a slow descent. Stated he was going to just control the altitude himself. I thought that was strange; but let him do it figuring it was just a technique he liked to do.As we approached 2;700 feet; he was still descending at ~700 FPM; so I realized he was going to blow through the altitude. I told him he needed to stop descending and return to the FAF altitude until we intercepted the GS. The first time I said this he seemed confused and didn't really do much. I said more sternly that we needed to climb back to the proper altitude. This time he initiated a climb back to the proper altitude and we were still stabilized and fully configured by 1;000 feet AGL. ATC did issue us a low altitude alert as we were climbing back to the proper altitude and we got a single 'Glideslope' callout from the aircraft.The cause was the FO's improper use of the altitude selector and VS (Vertical Speed) mode. Contributing was me allowing him to do the method he did instead of asking him to just put the FAF altitude in the altitude selector till GS intercept.I should have insisted that the FO put the FAF altitude in the altitude selector; especially in IMC. I also told him afterword's that he could have just stayed at 3;000 once established and intercepted the GS from there since at that point we were already close to GS intercept.
Report_2_Narrative: Cleared ILS [Runway] XXL; we were given an intercept heading and told to maintain 3;000 feet. The Controller kept us close and fairly high before clearing us for the approach. We were at 4;000 feet when cleared. Captain was PM (Pilot Monitoring); First Officer was PF (Pilot Flying). Once established; PF started down with vertical speed to capture glide slope by 2;700 feet at ZZZZZ. PF moved altitude knob up to 3;300 feet from 3;000 feet instead of to 2;700 feet causing us to go below published altitude by almost 500 feet. Was immediately corrected and aircraft was stabilized. Given a close proximity intercept; task saturation was high with intercepting; radio communications; and configuring aircraft. Should have cross checked better and stated intentions more clearly (PF to PM).If crew starts to feel rushed or task saturation is high; ask for longer final or a more stable intercept from ATC. Never let cross checking suffer due to task saturation; should always come first. PM should state approach intention more clearly while getting established. Don't have tunnel vision (Example Focusing on getting configured and not having correct altitude set).
Report_1_Synopsis: CRJ-900 flight crew reported receiving a Low Altitude Alert from ATC after they descended below the glideslope intercept altitude.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Confusion; Communication Breakdown; Physiological - Other; Situational Awareness
Report_1_Narrative: Operating flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1. After landing on Runway XX; exited on Taxiway A and turned left on Taxiway C; and believing that Tower had actually cleared us to taxi to the gate; we started to slowly taxi; when Tower called us and asked that we call Ground. We called Ground and he stated 'You started to taxi without calling us; and crossed Runway XX; which is an active runway'. We had barely started to taxi on C. We had read the NOTAMs; and in fact; Runway XX was 'NOTAMed CLOSED'; so it could not be an 'Active' at all. Regardless; we asked Ground for taxi clearance to the gate; and received clearance to the gate via 'C.' We did not want to argue with the Ground Controller; but we do know that Runway XX is Closed at ZZZ1; so it's not Active in any way. We asked the Ground Controller if we should 'expect any paperwork'; and he said 'no'. I do not believe we did anything wrong; but it's better to be safe and proactive; and learn from our possible mistakes.We had flown into ZZZ1 previously (a few days before) and due to controller shortages or consolidation of ATC positions (During COVID-19 times); the Tower normally gives us the taxi instruction after we cleared the landing runway. This time; we cleared the runway and thought we had heard the Tower tell us to 'taxi to the gate' (as they have been doing recently). We started to slowly taxi on Taxiway C and that's when Tower asked us to 'call ground for taxi;' something they had not done in the past 3-6 times we had landed there recently. So; probably I was expecting the same ATC procedures to happen; but regardless; in the future; will come to a stop on the taxiway and not move until further taxi clearance is received.I would suggest to avoid being complacent; and instead of expecting the same type of ATC handling from small airports as we may be getting every day during COVID-19 (combined controller positions; where there is perhaps combined Tower and Ground; or even Approach/Tower/Ground Controller); and instead treat it just like a busy airport.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Captain reported a taxiway/runway incursion and cited ATC staffing; local ATC procedure change and confusion over a NOTAM contributed to the deviation.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Troubleshooting; Communication Breakdown; Situational Awareness; Physiological - Other
Report_1_Narrative: Aircraft X was assigned to the hangar midnight crew for the 'A' check.  The first contact that technicians had with the aircraft occurred at approximately XA00 local time.  Avionics technicians; including myself; began the night with completing operational checks within the aircraft in preparation for the rest of the crew to perform their assigned tasks. Later technicians began to migrate in and out of the flight deck; cabin; galleys; lavs; etc.; to their assigned tasks.  All technicians were in compliance with the mask policy.Approximately 4 hours later; the Lead Technician and Supervisor alerted everyone on board that the aircraft had not gone through its disinfecting process which usually occurs at the gate upon arrival.  The aircraft was cleared and the Lead performed the disinfecting procedures.Concerns were raised from this event.  The potential of an infected passenger being on board and the potential of technicians being exposed to COVID.The protocol for traveling to ZZZ is to have a COVID test within an XX hour period of departure time.  However; once you are tested there are no guarantees that the individual will quarantine or shelter in place prior to boarding the aircraft for departure. The cleaners finally arrived for the disinfecting process at midnight. I asked the supervisor what the protocol is for an event such as this and he was unaware of one in place.This aircraft originated from ZZZ1.
Report_1_Synopsis: Technician reported the maintenance crew was advised the aircraft had not been disinfected after the inspection and repairs were already in progress.

Report_1_Narrative: I returned to work after a 3 month absence. I am still qualified on the module. I was assigned as the trainer to Mechanic Y. I was training him on the stator case assembly. I demonstrated how to tighten each vane segment foot bolts. The procedure that I was taught; and which had been in use as long as I can remember; was to slide the case and vane assembly; so that approximately one third of it overhung the table surface. Then the bolts were tightened from below with a ratchet with a socket and long extension; repositioning the case and vane assembly as necessary until all bolts were tightened. At the time of the incident; I was not in the work area; having gone to the restroom.Support the case with a hoist and sling before tightening the bolts. This should be added to the job card.
Report_2_Narrative: One week after return from 3 months off and being the first time working on this unit as a trainee.On Graveyard shift I was working on the module and order # XXXX. I was tightening the bolts of the vanes. The bolts are tighten from the bottom while the case sits on the table. To access the bolts part of the case is moved slightly beyond the edge of the table. I was sitting in a chair with rollers while I was tightening the bolts. The chair moved; the wrench and its extension did come off the bolt head causing the case to slide off the table and fall to the floor approximately 30 inches.There was no visible damage to the case because it fell directly on my arm and that cushioned the fall. Inspection will be called to inspect the unit.I would add to the job card to support the case with a hoist before tightening the bolts. Or developing a fixture that would allow to reach the bolts from the bottom without having to move part of the case off the edge of the table.
Report_1_Synopsis: Maintenance Instructor and Trainee reported a training mistake during a training session and both cited being off for an extended time contributed to the event.

Report_1_Narrative: I was performing a functional test of the stall protection computer. On step XX; the task tells you to put the aircraft in the weight off wheels configuration. On the first page of the task for putting the aircraft in the weight off wheel configuration you are told to pull and tag Circuit Breakers (CB): CB P-1; A12; A13; A14; G14; & CB P-1 lower U7. On the second page to pull and tag CB P-1 lower T7; T8; T9; CB P2; N6; H8; CB P2 lower S1; V5 and CB P-5; B10.I pulled the circuit breaker on the first page but failed to pull the circuit breakers on the second page of the task. On the next step on the functional test of the stall protection computer you are told to set the air data test set to 90 kts and the altitude to 18;000 feet. During this step is when we noticed smoke coming from the left pitot probe. I ran out to check the pitot probe and saw that I melted the pitot probe test head to the pitot probe. I quickly removed heat from the pitot probe.To pay more attention to the Aircraft Maintenance Manual and to double check all the correct circuit breakers are pulled.
Report_2_Narrative: While performing a functional check of stall protection system we were required to put aircraft in weight off wheels and put aircraft at 18;000 feet and 90 kts using pitot static test set. During the test; the test head on the LH (Left Hand) pitot static probe was melted to the probe.While performing the test I looked up and saw smoke coming from LH side of nose.My partner found the task in the AMM (Aircraft Maintenance Manual) and pulled breakers but failed to read far enough down and only pulled the breakers for the RH pitot static probe. Causing the heat to still be on to the LH probe.We quickly removed heat from probe.Pay more attention to AMM task and I should have double checked the CBs my partner pulled.
Report_1_Synopsis: Aircraft technicians reported the pitot probe test head melted onto the pitot probe while performing a test of the stall protection computer.

Report_1_Narrative: While descending into LRU airport; I heard ATC call to another aircraft (Aircraft Y) that was also inbound. I was arriving from the west; and Aircraft Y from the north; North West area. I could see him on ADS-B. While Aircraft Y was behind me; he was much faster; however ABQ (Albuquerque) center had him climb and then hold as I continued my descent. Leveling off at my assigned altitude; I was still unable to see the airfield; despite the field reports of better weather. I was; however; still several miles away. At about the same time; Aircraft Y called in; cancelling his IFR stating that he had the airport in sight. ATC cancelled his IFR as he stated he was now in VMC. I then asked ATC for a report from the Aircraft Y; as he was able to see the field and I was not; despite me being at a lower altitude. (I asked hoping I would break out of the clouds soon; or find an area where I could; such as where Aircraft Y came from). Quickly after; I did get the airport insight below me and was able to descend VFR. I also cancelled my IFR at that time.Being almost over the airport; I extended away from it and then I called entering the Left downwind for runway 26. (The winds at the time were reported as being 240 at 22 - 27; making runway 22 or 26 the best options.) I then called a base turn; and then final. At that time I also heard Aircraft Y call in for the RNAV for runway 12. Being as he cancelled IFR with no mention of practicing approaches; I anticipated his landing before me; with no conflict. As I came on short final for runway 26; I heard Aircraft Y call out that he was going missed from 12; which would then be intersecting my landing path. At that moment I looked up and saw Aircraft Y just ahead and to my right; above me; but very close. I would estimate within 200-300 feet. Already being close to the ground; no evasion action could have been taken. I landed and taxied into the ramp. Shortly after; Aircraft Y landed on a different runway and parked as well. I called the center to report the incident and express my concern and safety issue that had occurred.
Report_1_Synopsis: Pilot reported an NMAC after both aircraft had been cleared for the visual approach into LRU.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Distraction; Situational Awareness; Workload; Communication Breakdown
Report_1_Narrative: With a pre-checkride PPL (Private Pilot License) student; we were discussing pre-takeoff briefings and engine out after takeoff procedures. For our flight that day; I decided it would be good practical experience to get the student thinking about emergency landing options after an engine failure on takeoff. I believed it would be beneficial to see in reality what the landing options would look like with engine loss shortly after takeoff.The student performed a normal takeoff. Shortly after handoff from Tower Controller to Departure Controller (estimated 550 [feet.] AGL); I reduced the throttle to idle and instructed the student to pitch for best glide. I asked the student where an attempted landing might be possible based on our altitude and glide. I then asked if a 180 degree turn back to the departure runway seemed possible. After asking these two questions; I pushed the throttle back to full power and resumed normal climb. We continued to discuss procedures for engine failure on takeoff.Shortly after this; I noticed that our heading had deviated from the assigned runway heading by about 40 degrees to the south. Before I was able to correct; the Departure Controller assigned us an on-course heading. A few minutes later; Departure Controller asked if we had experienced an issue or needed assistance. I did not think much of it at the time and responded that we didn't need assistance.I later learned (from a phone call from Tower Controller to the flight school) that the Tower Controller had heard the engine power reduction and had seen the turn; and assumed an engine failure. I am not fully aware of what was experienced on the Tower Controller's end; but it is clear that my decision to practice an engine out procedure on takeoff caused a distraction to the Tower Controller that may have ended up impacting safety.Additionally; the fact that I did not notice the aircraft had turned 40 degrees to the south indicates that practicing that maneuver caused me to become more distracted that I had realized; or expected to be.Remedy:-Notify or request to Tower/ATC of my intention to practice any sort of maneuvers/procedures that are out of the ordinary from what is expected.-Be more aware of the probability of distraction while practicing any sort of maneuver during a high workload phase of flight.-Consider making engine out on takeoff procedures a ground instruction maneuver rather than in-flight.Human performance/Judgement:Ultimately; I made a bad judgement call by practicing an unusual/unexpected maneuver in controlled airspace. I did not expect or anticipate any disruption to the tower procedures; but I should have been more aware and given more thought to how my maneuvers would affect ATC.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Instructor reported a track heading deviation while demonstrating an engine out after takeoff with student.

Report_1_Narrative: I was working the entire area combined.  The evening west departure push was going on along with other aircraft throughout the airspace.  I was pretty busy on a small scale and multiple frequencies.I descended Aircraft X to 16;000 and verified he had the weather at ZZZ [airport] and what approach he wanted.  I cleared him for the LOC/DME [Runway] XX at ZZZ [airport].  I started to hand the aircraft off to ZZZ [Approach] and took it back thinking ZZZ [Approach] had gone home for the evening and we had the airspace.  Another Controller had sat down to help but didn't yet get a briefing.  ZZZ [Approach] called to give up the airspace and I just went 'Crap.'Apparently Aircraft X had gone over to Approach on his own and the controller had been watching him.I made a mistake thinking it was later than it was and that ZZZ Approach had gone home for the night.Since the COVID started everything has been off.  We are combine sectors too much and too early.  The scale and number of frequencies we are required to work is not helpful.  We get a lot of EA [Excused Absence] and are just not as proficient as we use to be.  I would like to see sectors de combined more often or not combined as early.  There are a few that push to combine and we just accept it and work through it.  It is really not safe or comfortable to work.   Mistakes are being made.
Report_1_Synopsis: Center Controller reported thinking it was later than it was and did not transfer communication to underlying TRACON; assuming the Center already had their airspace.

Report_1_Narrative: As I was leaving the flight deck approximately 6.5 hours into the flight for my break the Captain informed me the Purser had spoken to him about mask usage on the flight deck.  Upon returning from my break I was informed there was further conversation with the flight attendants.  Not much detail was discussed as we began the preparation for descent into ZZZ.  I never spoke to any FAs about the issue nor did they speak to me about it.I am aware the Captain chose not to wear a mask for safety of flight reasons concerning his glasses while on the flight deck.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported the Captain chose not to wear a mask for safety of flight concerns while wearing glasses.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Situational Awareness; Troubleshooting; Other / Unknown; Physiological - Other
Report_1_Narrative: I was deadheading on Aircraft X. I identified myself to the A Flight Attendant (FA) (as I always do) as a safety and security asset.The flight was nearly full.  During boarding a man who I later learned was Mr. X approached my seat.  He was wearing a camo gaiter around his neck which was partially covering his mouth but was not covering his nose. As he approached; I identified myself as a crew member and politely asked him to pull his mask up over his nose.  He complied but said that I should pinch my mask tight over my nose.  I didn't quite hear what he said so I queried him.  He said; 'You should pinch down on your nose to close the gap at the top of your mask.'   My mask was an NP95 which had no gaps anywhere around my face.  It was my sense that the man was being sarcastic and antagonistic.  I said nothing further to him.I advised the FA A what happened before we pushed back.  She told me that the man had boarded without his face covered and was told to cover his face.  Thus he had pulled his face covering off his face between the time he boarded (when he was told to put it on) and the time he approached me; which was no more than thirty seconds. He clearly had no intention of complying with the mask policy.  FA A asked me to brief the Captain about the incident and asked if I would talk to the CSR agent whom she wanted to speak with Mr. X. I agreed.  Before departure I walked into the jet bridge and spoke with FA A and the CSR.  I briefly explained what I observed and what he said to me then I went back onto the airplane and took my seat.  A short time later I observed Mr. X walk back down the aisle past me.Sometime during the flight FA A advised me that Mr. X had been [violating other regulations].  She advised me that Mr. X demanded to know the crews names (including mine) but that she did not give him any names. She was clearly concerned about this and I could see how his actions were distracting to the flight crew and were thus interfering with their duties.  She told me that she was going to have CS meet the aircraft and asked me to stay as a witness.  FA A as well as the rest of the inflight crew were nothing but polite and professional the entire flight; when I observed her dealing with Mr. X or otherwise.After leaving the aircraft I was standing in the jet bridge and spoke with a CS Supervisor.  Mr. X walked by me and said in an aggressive and hostile tone; 'I want your name.'  I told him that I could not give it to him and that I could not speak with him about this matter.  He again demanded my name and moved closer to me.  I backed up.  He then raised his camera and said; 'I'm taking your picture.'  I stated; 'Do not take my picture.'  He said; I'm taking your picture.'  I quickly turned around and walked around the jet bridge corner toward the aircraft door.   I do not know if he took my photograph or not but felt that his forcing his camera in my face was one of belligerence; hostility; and aggression.  I felt threatened.  All of this simply because he was asked to properly wear his mask.  After the CSR Supervisor and Mr. X walked into the terminal; I remained in the jet bridge as I did not want to encounter Mr. X again.When the CSR Supervisor walked back onto the jet bridge; I explained to her that I could not have my photograph taken and suggested that if he loitered around the terminal waiting for me that she please call law enforcement.  I asked her if she felt he was being hostile and or belligerent.  She agreed that he was.  After some time; Mr. X left the area; and I departed the terminal.Based on his behavior and actions I would strongly urge that Mr. X is not allowed to fly on our airline in the future.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain deadheading on a company flight reported a passenger would not conform to the face mask policy and was hostile; aggressive; belligerent towards the flight attendants.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Physiological - Other; Communication Breakdown; Situational Awareness; Confusion
Report_1_Narrative: The Lead Flight Attendant had apparently talked to the Captain or First Officer about masks.  They said something to me about it after my break along the lines that she was upset and combative. I was surprised; as I wore my mask (a KN95 on the ground and a solid multi-layer cloth one in the air) all times outside of the flight deck and in the flight deck if a Flight Attendant was present.  Additionally; the other First Officer did as well. The Captain wears glasses that fog easily with a mask on. He wore a mask on the ground; he did not airborne because it would greatly interfere with his duties both because he wouldn't be able to see and could not communicate. This was our 4th leg together and we had no issues with masks among ourselves or other flight attendants.  Additionally; both the Captain and other First Officer already had COVID which they had gotten from people they knew at home; not in the workplace. Before our next rest room break I got out a new unused N95 mask for the Flight Attendant that would be in the flight deck while I was in the bathroom. When I called back and ask for the break she ordered me that the pilot remaining in the flight deck should wear the crew oxygen mask.  I said that was not something that we did anymore-the practice stopped months ago because of COVID.   I offered her the N95 for extra protection because the Captain can't wear a mask and do his job.  She refused it.  Instead continuing to wear what appeared to be a single layer stretchy black cloth mask. Additionally the flight attendant blocking the cart was wearing a KN95 but the Lead FA did not send her into the flight deck. I found the flight attendant to not be willing to exercise self-help and any wearing of an N95 and apparent multiple complaints to be a distraction from my flight duties. This was not good for crew CRM. While the single pilot on the flight deck; I was distracted from monitoring the airplane by her distress and complaints.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier First Officer reported poor CRM with the Lead FA regarding the company face mask policy on the Flight Deck.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Physiological - Other; Situational Awareness; Communication Breakdown; Confusion; Other / Unknown
Report_1_Narrative: We were met at the hotel by the van to be transported to ZZZZ [airport]. The driver wasn't wearing a mask when he loaded the bags. He finished loading and sat down in his seat without a mask. I said something to the effect of; 'You aren't wearing a mask?' He didn't really say anything. After a few seconds; I said; 'Since you aren't wearing a mask; we will need fresh air.' I assumed that after seeing the 4 pilots with masks on and me saying something; he would put his mask on. He never did.Instead; he started fumbling with the AC controls. I told him that without a mask; we would need the front windows opened in order to ensure ventilation in the van. He eventually complied. We then drove 30 minutes to ZZZZ with the windows open with the OAT ~ 34 degrees. We were freezing cold.We were all upset; cold; and potentially distracted for our flight. This is a safety of flight issue. We used our CRM skills to identify this threat and deal with it. But; the bottom line is that we shouldn't have had to deal with this easily avoidable threat in the first place.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Captain reported the van driver from the hotel to the airport would not wear a face mask.

Report_1_Narrative: It wasn't supposed to be a very long leg or a long day. The plan was to fly from ZZZ to ZZZ1; grab a quick snack and go to ZZZ2 for the overnight and good food. But; that wasn't what happened.  Snow flurries forced us into unplanned deicing. Bad alternates required reworking and refueling. In the middle of deicing; a sudden snow squall sent visibility plummeting and negating any holdover times. New takeoff alternates then had to be amended onto the paperwork; and re-validating required new paperwork. To describe our departure out of ZZZ as a struggle would be an understatement. But; ever so slowly and methodically; we did eventually depart to ZZZ1. It was on arrival that we were notified that our overnight had changed and to contact scheduling on the ground. So; you can imagine that when we landed in ZZZ1; we were mentally bruised; hungry; tired; and on edge. The landing was normal; as was the taxi to our planned gate. What confused us is what we saw upon turning to face south; looking at [Gate X]. There was nothing. No rampers; or wands or even lights. It was a completely empty and dark. I set the parking brake and asked my FO (First Officer) to send another in range report and commented that we should probably call ZZZ1 OPS and see if they had changed our gate. FO dutifully called OPS on the number two radio so I dialed the north ramp frequency into radio one to monitor. At that exact moment the ACARS message returned as my FO was repeating what OPS had just said; gate change to [Gate Y]! I released the parking brake and began a slow turn to the right when I realized I wasn't at an outstation in the middle of nowhere or on an uncontrolled ramp. I had lost all situational awareness and was in the middle of ZZZ1 moving without permission! I immediately stopped the aircraft and called North Ramp with the gate change. He replied yea there was a gate change and 'did i just do a 180?' I don't recall saying much before he asked 'and are you still moving???' I immediately replied we were not moving. At that point I was told I should never; ever do that and that he had numerous aircraft with beacons on trying to push. I should have apologized right then but instead fumbled though the gate change and having the pushing aircraft in sight. I still can't believe I would make such stupid mistake. I can't believe I didn't apologize. I was just beat up and wanting desperately to just take a five minute brake. Instead I let my guard and awareness down which led me to make a very stupid move.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported taxiing on ramp without clearance and stated they had lost situational awareness as a result of a long and fatiguing day.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Workload; Training / Qualification; Time Pressure; Human-Machine Interface; Situational Awareness; Distraction; Confusion
Report_1_Narrative: I was cleared on the RNAV departure to maintain 3;000 feet. When loading the departure an additional fix not noted on the chart was loaded in. I reloaded the departure to ensure I had the proper transition and the fix appeared again. This fix is not on the RNAV departure. I later realized that this is how the G1000 creates additional heading legs; but at the time I did not realize this and so I deleted the extraneous fix to have the flight plan reflect the proper departure.  After reaching 1;000 feet the departure states to turn left heading 295; which I had briefed. I began turning right and was adjusting the heading bug and noted it was taking a long time to reach 295 before I realized that I was turning the wrong direction. I corrected and initiated the turn back to the left heading 295. I was about 20 to 30 degrees off from the heading when ATC called and asked if I was VFR or IFR. I responded with that I was IFR and turning left to 295.There are a few contributing factors that lead to my error. First was my general lack of recency with the G1000. In the last 120 days I had amassed a total of only 6.7 hours in the aircraft. Additionally I only have a total of 24 hours in the aircraft since my check-ride last summer. This lack of familiarity; currency and comfort in the aircraft contributed to the error.  After passing 1;000 feet the G1000 was showing a magenta line to the right which is probably partially why I turned the wrong direction. An additional contributing factor was that I was operating single pilot IFR in icing conditions with little experience in the aircraft. This was a Part 91 flight and the 100 hour rule for commuter passenger operations did not apply.   While the General Operations Manual has a dual qualification policy it does not adequately address low time pilots. When a pilot is only qualified in one aircraft type they are afforded an opportunity immediately after completing their check-ride and Operational Experience to gain significant flight time and consolidate their knowledge and skills in the aircraft over the course of a few months.  In my scenario I have accumulated only 9 hours since the completion of Operational Experience. I am in full compliance with the policy and have been active in ensuring I fly the aircraft within the 90 days and make an effort to coordinate a flight when I haven't flown in over 30 days. As is evidenced by my low hours recently this does not afford a pilot new in the aircraft any significant flight time; nor the ability to consolidate their knowledge. While all aircraft are of the general purpose multi-engine variety this aircraft is the only Technically Advanced Aircraft (TAA) in the fleet. This adds a significant amount of complexity to it's operation.I would suggest that when a pilot is qualified on any aircraft we afford them the necessary time and hours to consolidate their knowledge and skills. Part 121 recognizes this issue and has the requirement for consolidation of knowledge and skills in new type aircraft. While again our aircraft are of the same type I feel with dramatic difference in this aircraft particularly; being a TAA; there should be a similar effort. Under Part 121 a pilot would be required to obtain 100 hours within 120 days of becoming qualified in the aircraft. I think we should model a policy to have similar protections. Consolidation was identified in a joint government/industry task force in 1993 to be of concern. One primary reason was 'in recent years manufacturers have introduced a greater number of new aircraft containing more equipment and systems variations within type. Pilots must not only learn different aircraft handling characteristics but they must also be able to work with a variety of aircraft equipment such as automated flight control and flight management systems.' (Federal Register Vol 60 No 81). As this aircraft aligns closely with the concerns listed here that resulted in the regulatory change (advanced aircraft systems)I think a policy to ensure a similar amount of experience is obtained in each aircraft a pilot is qualified in. This would not be to change the dual qualification policy; however; it would most often be triggered and impact pilots who are dual qualified. If a pilot were unable to accomplish the consolidation of knowledge and skills then I think it would be best to enter them into a recurrent training program. As a direct result of this deviation and review of my recent experience I have requested a training event from the flight training department to ensure that I have the requisite proficiency and after that I will make a concerted effort to add shifts to ensure I can achieve my consolidation of knowledge and skills.
Report_1_Synopsis: Pilot reported they turned the wrong direction on a SID due to unfamiliarity and lack of proficiency with the navigation equipment in their aircraft.

Person_2_Human_Factors: Time Pressure; Distraction; Confusion; Communication Breakdown
Report_1_Narrative: We departed on time for a XX minute flight. Climbing through 10;000 feet I chimed the flight attendants and we continued our climb to 21;000 feet. Center was telling me to expect bad rides all the way to our destination. So when we leveled off at 21;000 feet. I made an announcement stating that the ride was going to be rough and that I would keep the seat belt sign of the entire flight. I also asked the flight attendants to remain seated for the duration of the flight as well or so I thought. The ride was not good. Continuous light occasionally moderate turbulence. The arrival is challenging on a good day and today was no exception. We were dealing with a complex arrival; turbulence; icing and multiple changes to speed and altitude. We were cleared to descend via the arrival with no speed restrictions with about a 90 knot tailwind.We would be early. Around the time that we started our descent I noticed that someone was trying to use the door code to gain access to the cockpit. I immediately declined it and made sure door was locked. The Pilot Flying and I both thought that was strange so I tried calling back to a Flight Attendant to see what was going on. That was the first indication something was wrong. When I turned on the speaker for the cabin I could hear an audible cycling noise. When I tried to chime the flight attendants I couldn't hear the chime and I could not hear any voices on the interphone. I tried to make a quick announcement but nothing was coming out back in the cabin. As the Pilot Flying and I were extremely busy managing the descent and approach we heard a knock at the door and could faintly hear a voice. Pilot Flying turned around and saw a note on the ground that said INTERPHONE INOP.I wanted to get up and grab the note to try and write something back but we were too busy. A few minutes passed. The cockpit door lock code was entered again and I denied it a second time. I tried to yell as loud as I could that we got the message. I think they must have heard that time because they stopped knocking on the door. We landed and began our taxi to the gate. After clearing the active runways I had Pilot Flying call maintenance and inform them that our Cabin Interphone and Public Address system was inoperative. We taxied to the gate and shutdown. After the shutdown checklist was complete and before the forward door was opened I got up to check on the A Flight Attendant and see if everything was OK. He was visibly upset. After the passengers got off the other two Flight Attendant's joined us up in first class to discuss what had happened. A Flight Attendant said that it was the scariest flight of his life. He said that after we had hit a rough patch of turbulence the cabin lights in the plane started to cycle on and off. They were still doing it after I went back to talk to them. He then had tried to call me to see if everything was OK but couldn't reach me. He thought that maybe we had lost pressurization and that we might have been incapacitated. He tried the door code to maybe get a peek inside to see if we were OK. He left a note under the door in hopes that we would grab it and write back. Only after the last time that he tried the door lock and I denied it did he hear me yell through the door. The other two flight attendants were also upset that they couldn't communicate with me. I spent at least 15 minutes with them trying to explain why I couldn't respond to them even though I wanted to.Trying to unlock the cockpit door without my authorization put me on high alert. This is not something I expected. If this had been a different flight with more time I would have taken their note and responded to it and sent it back. That would have been the best way. I tried yelling through the door; but it is loud in the cockpit and only on the second time did they hear me. If we had lost pressurization the masks in the back would have dropped and they would have felt it in their ears. The first time I denied his access to the cockpit door he should have known we were OK. I cannot just open the cockpit door without knowing who is behind it. My first priority is to fly the aircraft. I just didn't have enough time to respond to them the way they wanted me to.I tried to address all of their concerns and I did understand that they were upset. I wrote up the Public Address system as well as the Interphone system with their input to give the mechanics all they needed to fix the system. Maintenance came on board and reset the system. I tested the PA and both forward and aft intercoms with the Flight Attendants and in front of maintenance to make sure everything worked. Maintenance signed off the system and we than headed back. After our initial conversation about what had transpired I thought all Flight Attendants were OK just a little rattled but good enough to continue. If I had known they still had reservations about what had happened I would have immediately responded to them. My crew always comes first.
Report_2_Narrative: During our descent on the arrival we heard a knock on the cockpit door. We turned around and saw a note that was slid under the door stating that the interphone was inoperative and there were lights flashing in the cabin. We heard the Flight Attendant said that he was trying to get a hold of us. We never heard him prior to that as this was a 30 minutes or so flight and we were busy from wheels up. The Captain told him we were landing soon. When we landed Maintenance was contacted. Upon arrival at the gate the Captain met with the flight attendants to discuss the event. I went to do the walkaround. The mechanic came and fixed the problem. The interphone and Public Address system was tested before we left the gate and they worked.
Report_1_Synopsis: A319 flight crew reported while experiencing turbulence they were initially unaware their PA System and interphone warnings to the cabin were not heard due to the system malfunctioning resulting in frightened and angry flight attendants.

Report_1_Narrative: My first attempt at writing this portion did not save so I will attempt it again. We had an A321 sharklet. Every portion of the beginning of the flight leg from gate departure; takeoff and climb up to the fume event was normal and routine. At sometime above 10;000 ft. we got a call from our #1 FA (Flight Attendant) telling us that the FAs in Economy Class more towards the rear of the aircraft were smelling a sweat odor and a more robust glue type odor. I believe from my prospective that the odor came from the back from the wings black wards because we did not smell anything in the flight deck and no one smelled anything in first class; #1 FA or forward section of the cabin behind 1st class section. Captain began trouble shooting the problem with the QRH guidelines and the FAs that was smelling the odors. One of the FAs was feeling ill from the fume which was strong in the area they were working. Passenger in that area smelled the odors as well. Captain asked if she can continue or do we need to get back to the gate in ZZZ so she can seek medical attention. She was not sure if she wanted to continue on toward ZZZZ1 or return. Captain asked the #1 FA to monitor the FA's condition and if she worsened we will return to ZZZ. While we were discussing the QRH fume trouble shooting pages and making plans to return to ZZZ or another airport that may be closer to our position if we continued to fly farther away from ZZZ; the #1 FA called and told us the FA that was feeling ill was on O2 and was not getting better. So we notified ATC that we will be returning to ZZZ which was the best option to land. We [were given priority handling] to expedite our return to ZZZ and so the FA can get the medical attention she needed. As we began to descend into ZZZ I remember it was below FL180 and through landing that the odors began to infiltrate the flight deck and the #1 FA and passengers began smelling it too. We donned our O2 masks. It was a sweaty smell and it also had an Elmer's glue order to us. The odors continued until we arrived to the gate. The FA that was really ill went to the hospital and the remaining flight crew continued with us to ZZZZ1 with a replacement FA.I don't know of any causal factors that would cause a fume event other than fixing the problem of the source that caused the fumes from escaping and preventing and future leaks from going into the cabin.The only thing that would prevent this from happening would be a complete redesign of the airplane systems that keeps the cabin ventilation isolated from any possible fume leaking into the cabin.
Report_1_Synopsis: A321 First Officer reported a fumes event during departure climb resulting in a return to the departure airport.

Report_1_Narrative: We were waiting to take off. The aircraft that took off ahead of us reported hitting birds on take off. The controller asked if they hit the birds directly over the runway; the crew confirmed it was. We were next for takeoff when the controller asked if we had heard the report from the aircraft ahead. We said we did. Tower then delivered a caution about possible FOD (Foreign Object Debris) and birds on the runway and cleared us for takeoff. We refused the clearance and asked that the runway be inspected. We were then informed that it would take a long time for an inspection; we said we will wait. This seemed to aggravate the controller. Tower continued to give takeoff clearances until eventually no one wanted to go until the runway was inspected. This seemed to expedite the runway getting inspected. Once it was deemed safe and free from FOD; takeoffs resumed.I then reached out to an airport authority and their ATC group. They informed me that they have an agreement between the ATC and the Airport Authority about such events. If at their airport that same report was made on takeoff they stated the runway would have been closed for an inspection. They also stated it takes less than 5 minutes At DFW I waited longer than that due to refusing the takeoff clearance.I then took the question to the APA National Safety Committee and asked what they knew about procedure when this happens. Coincidentally; on that call was another pilot that had the same thing happened to them at a different airport. As we have been researching this we are finding there is no standardization from airport to airport on this. Some airports have written agreements between ATC and Airport Authorities and others don't. Does this infer that certain airports take safety more seriously than another? It is factual that the Captain will always have final authority. But shouldn't ATC procedures across the system be uniform with regard to concerns with the runway condition? To give a takeoff clearance with no attempt to inspect the runway in order to keep traffic moving seems at odds with a culture of safety.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier pilot reported they refused a takeoff clearance after the preceding departure reported a bird strike over the runway.

Report_1_Narrative: Taxing from the device pad for departure we came very close to coming in contact with Aircraft Y. Aircraft Y had been given clearance to taxi to the runway while we were still finishing up de-ice and neither the Captain or myself as First Officer gave it much thought. When we finished the de-ice process I called for taxi and we were given clearance to taxi. The Runway Visual Range was being reported at the time of 1;000 ft. so the visibility was obviously a contributing factor in the described events. As we were on Taxiway A approaching an intersection; I began to notice some lights on the right hand side of the airplane. I assumed that I was seeing hangar lights as they did not appear to be moving. Looking back this was due to the fact that ourselves and Aircraft Y had roughly the same ground speed and therefore the lights were staying in the same position on my window.As we got closer the Captain and I both realized at about the same time that what we were seeing was Aircraft Y. Aircraft Y must have seen us about the same time because we both came to a stop. When we stopped on the slick taxiway we were probably no more then 20 or 30 ft. away from Aircraft Y. We began to taxi away and as we did I asked ground to verify that we were in fact cleared to taxi to the runway. They stated that we were. Aircraft Y then asked the same thing and ground replied that they as well were cleared to taxi to the same runway. Due to the 1;000 ft. Runway Visual Range I know that Tower could not see where either of us were. I think that the normal low visual procedures of reporting when passing certain points would have saved this from happening. I think that Ground thought that Aircraft Y was already at the end of the runway when we were cleared for taxi and for some reason Aircraft Y was delayed.
Report_2_Narrative: We were departing. ATIS prevailing visibility was 1/4 mile in freezing fog. After start we went to device pad 1 and completed Type I and Type IV deicing. Ground gave us taxi instructions and to hold short the ILS critical area. Taxi was uneventful until reaching an intersection. Aircraft Y had been cleared to taxi to the same runway and we nearly met at the intersection. We both applied brakes. Aircraft Y told Ground they would 'give way to...' us. After starting to taxi we called Ground to confirm our taxi instructions. Aircraft Y did the same. We were both cleared all the way to Runway 12. Aircraft Y was cleared to taxi before us and either taxied slow or delayed their start. Ground could have confirmed their position before clearing us to taxi.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier flight crew reported they stopped their taxiing when they observed another aircraft taxiing into the same intersection.

Report_1_Narrative: On private lesson I took off and went to practice area and went through all maneuvers with no problems. I then flew back to the airport and did two successful landings and one takeoff. On my last takeoff I was preparing to do a short field takeoff. I rolled onto [the] runway with the yoke all the way back once getting lined up with the center of the runway I put in full power and started my takeoff. As I was rolling down the runway I added right rudder to keep down the center line. The plane left the ground and instantly turned to the left. I tried adding more right rudder to get the plane going straight. The plane continued to go to the left as it gained altitude. After I felt the plane was not going to recover I tried to put the plane down as softly as possible in the field left of the runway. I touched down in the field and rolled to a stop. I then went through engine shutdown procedure to turn the plane off. After the plane was turned off I waited for help and got out of the plane.
Report_1_Synopsis: PA-28 student pilot reported landing in a field after having directional control difficulties while attempting a practice short field takeoff.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Communication Breakdown; Confusion; Troubleshooting; Training / Qualification; Situational Awareness; Physiological - Other
Report_1_Narrative: While enroute at FL280; I noticed the radio frequency was very quiet. Since COVID has impacted US aviation; frequency congestion has decreased significantly; which makes longer periods of radio silence a new sense of normalcy.  My last handoff to ZZZ Center was eight minutes prior at which I made positive radio contact on frequency XYZ.AB. I was using COM 1 as primary radio and monitoring XYX.B on COM 2 with the proper audio panel selections to hear both radios simultaneously. After time passed by and I realized I was not hearing anyone; I transmitted my N number on COM 1 to ZZZ Center and did not receive a response. I selected microphone to COM 2 and reached out to ZZZ Center on XYX.B; no response. I switched the microphone back to COM 1 and tried XYZ.AB again; no response. I switched the microphone back to COM 2 and announced; 'All stations on guard; radio check.' After the second attempt; ZZZ1 Center answered and gave me a new frequency; XXC.DY. A Controller replied 'Aircraft X; possible pilot deviation; I have a number for you; advise when ready to copy.' I was extremely shocked at the situation as I was unaware the radio issue had escalated to that extent. I continued my flight to ZZZZ and called as soon as practical after landing. I spoke with a Controller. Controller said NORDO is a common issue but mine was excessive. I have no deviations on my record and strive to maintain a clean record. Going forward; I will be more diligent in recognizing radio silence and will reach out more frequently if I assume the silent period is excessive.
Report_1_Synopsis: GA pilot reported becoming NORDO enroute and thinking because of the COVID-19 pandemic the radio just had less communication traffic.

Report_1_Narrative: Was working these two sectors combined. It needed a D side or to be split. Sector volume was high and complex. Two CPC's [Certified Professional Controller] had been held over on OT to supplement our 5 CPC count for the night shift. They were relieved to go home as they hit their limits. That left 5 CPC's working 5 sectors. No sector could be combined up to free up a controller to help on a D side. There was extensive military training aircraft working sector X at ZZZ1; ZZZ2; ZZZ3. I told the supervisor they needed to tell those aircraft to return to base so X and Y sectors could be recombined to free up a CPC. He got that process started and eventually sectors Z and A were able to combine as well. We have been working short staffed on our 5 day rotations for too long. I am beyond frustrated working combined R/D positions with busy traffic. I have lost my patience and work angry. These sessions are unsafe and on the cusp of causing a safety incident to occur (loss of separation; etc). Our traffic levels are; in my opinion; back to pre-COVID levels. We need to transition back to normal schedules. If not; management needs to place traffic restrictions on the military training flights that routinely come out of ZZZ4; ZZZ5; ZZZ6; ZZZ7; ZZZ8;and etc. I'd say no more than 3 total aircraft allowed to work practice approaches at the ZZZ1 area and no more than 1 at a time at the ZZZ9 area until we can get back to normal schedules and staffing levels.
Report_1_Synopsis: Center Controller reported an understaffed shift with high traffic volume and offered recommendations to remedy the situation.

Report_1_Narrative: On approach to IAH; just prior to FESTA on the Runway 27 ILS being flown in VFR conditions;  we were notified by IAH Approach Control of VFR / no com traffic as we were receiving a TA and almost immediately an RA for that traffic at 400 feet below our path.  As the controller was handing us off to the Tower; I advised him that we were responding to an RA.  Another voice acknowledged this; and we were then switched to IAH Tower.  The visual approach continued without further incident.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported an NMAC during initial approach to IAH airport when an aircraft not in communication with ATC flew below them.

Report_1_Narrative: After takeoff at acceleration altitude I called for 'flaps 0; climb checks; pitch mode.' The PM (Pilot Monitoring) began the duties; however at the same time we were told to immediately turn right and level off at 3;000 feet as there was an aircraft that was not communicating with Tower headed straight for us. This diverted our attention from the task at hand. I suspect the PM omitted retracting the flaps accidentally and I failed to notice. Once we were clear of the traffic we were handed off to another frequency on which we were told to look for yet another aircraft in close proximity. By the time we were clear we were through 10;000 feet and due to the distractions we forgot to complete the climb check. I initially began accelerating and reached about 265 knots before I decided to slow to complete the second part of the ice test. Once the test was complete (at around 18;000 feet) I began accelerating and again reached about 265 knots before we realized the flaps were still set to 9. We slowed; retracted the flaps; contacted Maintenance and continued the flight without further incident.No real suggestions. It was human error on my part. I should have been more vigilant and will be in the future.
Report_1_Synopsis: EMB-145 Captain reported the crew oversped the flaps during climbout when they were distracted by ATC traffic calls.

Report_1_Narrative: In our initial climb to 6;000 feet we were instructed by Departure to turn off course and given a fix to fly to. I confirmed the fix with the CA (Captain) and pressed Nav Mode on the FMS. I looked over to my PFD to set the new altitude assigned by Departure and the CA looked away at the same time. Shortly thereafter; Departure called and asked us if we were turning on course. We both looked up and realized that the Nav mode had not captured the course. I immediately turned the heading bug towards the course line on the display; while the CA notified the Controller that we were correcting and turning on course.While compensating for winds and flying via the heading bug; we started to analyze the problem. Shortly after changing the AP to the CA's side; we were able to correct the Nav issue; as the AP was functioning properly on the CA's side; I continued as the pilot flying. About 45 minutes out; the CA left the flight deck to use the LAV. As he returned; he noticed that we had about 8 status messages that popped up sometime after he had left the flight deck. I was engaged with a short conversation with the FA (Flight Attendant) and did not notice the display of messages until he returned. The status messages were flight control related; noting flight spoilers; rudder; etc. The CA referred to the QRH for landing data as a precautionary measure; in the event of a total system failure to those systems. The CA Then notified ATC of our potential systems status and requested deleting the LAHSO restrictions. ATC was unable to comply.Later; as we were given an intercept angle to intercept the final approach course; I selected the NAV button and was waiting for the intercept. We had a [heavy aircraft] on our left and we were paying close attention to that traffic; when we noticed that the aircraft had blown through the center line and was deviating right. The CA then asked me what was going on and while trying to process the information; I replied; 'I have no idea.' At that time Tower called to query our actions; It was as if the aircraft had a mind of its own and before I was able to kick off the autopilot; the CA then asked for the flight controls. We landed without incident and all flight control systems were operational throughout the landing phase; as all the spoilers had deployed. The AP had remained on the CA's side throughout the entire approach.Hindsight; I told the CA; that the one course of action we could have taken at the onset of discovering that the AP/Nav was not recognizing my side; we should have changed roles and allowed him to be the Pilot Flying. With the unexpected behavior of the FMS during the critical phase of flight; I was in total agreement with the CA's actions and decisions; I believe his actions were appropriate and timely while operating in the essence of safety for the passengers and crew.
Report_1_Synopsis: CRJ-900 First Officer reported track deviations resulted when the aircraft's autoflight systems became unreliable.

Report_1_Narrative: I checked in with the gate agent prior to my flight to ZZZZ.  I don't recall if any passengers were boarded but there were no passengers that I remember waiting to check in because it was still pretty early.  As I walked down the jet bridge I noticed a Flight Attendant walking the opposite direction.  I had not met her prior as I had not been to the aircraft yet.  She told me she was trying to get better cellular reception so she could complete her COVID-19 form which is required for entry into ZZZZ.  When I boarded the aircraft; I met the other two FAs.  At no time did I notice any passengers boarding or on our aircraft.  After checking the aircraft maintenance log; flight documents; etc. I briefed the A FA.  I only briefed the A FA as passengers were now being boarded.  I assumed the other two flight attendants were on board.  I was completely unaware that we didn't have minimum crew while boarding.  Approximately 10-15 minutes prior to departure; the A1 FA informed me that she was informed that we had boarded without minimum crew.  I think the COVID-19 online form (for ZZZZ) was the reason that caused this problem.  I fly this trip nearly every week and it's generally always a bit of a scramble at the last minute to get the form completed by all crew members prior to departure.  In addition it is a very difficult form to electronically fill out for the first time.  I believe the FA was only trying her best to complete the form prior to boarding. Perhaps a reminder to both cockpit and cabin crew that a COVID-19 declaration form is required for entry into ZZZZ.  And that the form takes a while to complete as it NOT intuitive and can take a few attempts to complete it and requires sufficient WiFi or cellular signal.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier pilot reported the aircraft was boarded without minimum FA crew because the FAs were late completing COVID-19 declaration form.

Report_1_Narrative: I work the #X position regularly on the aircraft. Personal observation of the close proximity in which #Z and #X [Flight Attendants] sit; facing each other; is of grave concern to me; due to COVID-19. While occupying the jump seats at XX; true social distancing isn't possible. Depending on height it can be a challenge to sit without our knees touching or without adjusting our feet under the jump seat. All a non-issue; pre-pandemic.The #X flight attendant does not have a door arming or disarming responsibility. There's no reason for the #X's preflight; inflight; or boarding duties to change. I'm suggesting for safety and health reasons the #X Flight Attendant is temporarily relocated to an unoccupied jump seat at door Y for takeoff and landing.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Attendant reported concerns with the close proximity of occupied jump seats during takeoff and landing.

Report_1_Narrative: On Date aircraft XXX had fumes/smoke in the cockpit smell noticed by the flight crew.The event occurred due to a razor blade that was left inside CBP1 possibly during a visit to ZZZ for the ADS-B modification in the middle of month of 2019 and I could have possibly left it there during the installation of breaker CBP1-XX during the mod. Due to the length of time between when possibly leaving a razor blade and when it was discovered I cannot recall whether or not I used a razor blade in the area. But; typically; when I do wiring work I don't use razor blades to cut tape or remove wiring insulation. As we usually have the equipment to remove fiberglass tape (a wire spoon and flush cutters or just peeling it off by hand;) and wiring insulation (standard wire strippers and the twisted pair stripping tool). Reflecting on the experience I would hope that even during the crunch time of the push to finish the ADS-B modifications on all our aircraft before the deadline that I would have continued to practice strict FOD control.My suggestion is to not use lose razor blades when doing work on wires unless absolutely necessary; and to practice strict FOD control and to perform detailed FOD inspections before every panel close-up.
Report_2_Narrative: On date the crew of Aircraft X reported fumes in the cockpit. An AMT discovered a loose razor blade located behind circuit breaker panel 1. Records indicate that panel had work done inside on date. This event has been brought to my attention due to my participation in ADSB mod which the work was completed. Due to the length of time from when the work was accomplished until now; unfortunately I can not provide details on exact situation. I can say that I was the RII In the process and I understand the seriousness of the situation and would not have allowed a loose razor blade to be left in the circuit breaker panel. I did not see a razor blade in the panel when it was closed. AMT found razor blade after fumes noted in cockpit. The event was caused by a Razor blade left in CBP-1.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Lead Technicians reported being notified that they may have inadvertently contributed to a fume event by leaving FOD on an aircraft they repaired.

Report_1_Narrative: Took off from FPR approximately XA:40. Told to watch out for Aircraft Y. Had aircraft in sight. At about 1;000 feet; lost sight of Aircraft Y; he was below me at time of losing visual contact. I was closing on his aircraft. I took evasive action by turning right and climbing to 1;400 feet where I could see sky was clear of aircraft. At this time my radios started to have a lot of static; could not hear anything. We proceeded out of area to ZZZ; landed to see if radios could be fixed by changing headsets. Changing intercom helped a little.
Report_1_Synopsis: GA pilot reported an airborne conflict during departure from FPR airport after losing sight of another aircraft resulting in evasive action.

Report_1_Narrative: The issue is [the] extreme limit of CPC (Certified Professional Controllers). We were working with 3 CPC's on a shift that a year ago any less than 9 CPC's on a shift would have been unacceptable. The facility is combining 2 and 3 positions to one controller during very busy and complex traffic. All because a lack of CPC controllers due to COVID issues and minimum staffing due to the agency not hiring any more controllers for our facility. This whole COVID issue has caused all the rules and agreements to go out the window. It is unacceptable for the safety of the NAS! We are just treated like robots like we always have been. There is no empathy for the stresses in our lives outside of work. This year has created A LOT of stress due to all the COVID uncertainty and constantly changing ideas about how to deal with it. Also all the political stress that has gone on all year. As much as we try to push out personal issues and feelings when we work; we are still human. We are not robots. And some days all the crap going on in society added to an unacceptable over taxed work load just gets to a person. We need more controllers at ZZZ TOWER! Also the positions need to be de-combined when traffic is busy. Combining 3 positions to one controller puts that controller at risk of missing something. And that is not fair to that controller or the flying public. The flying public deserves better than this.
Report_1_Synopsis: Tower Controller reported low staffing levels during periods of complex traffic combined with undue outside pressures have created an unsafe situation.

Report_1_Narrative: Aircraft X was on an ILS Approach to Runway 16L. A VFR aircraft was skirting around AFW's Class D airspace; not in communication with AFW or D10. The VFR aircraft was eastbound then turned north and crossed over WIGZU the FAF for ILS RWY 16L at 2;600 FT MSL. Aircraft X was at the same altitude. The Local Controller called the traffic and Aircraft X reported the traffic in sight. Aircraft X reported that they had to turn off the ILS then turn back once they were clear of the traffic. The two aircraft were less than 1/2 mile apart at the same altitude head on to each other. This area is dangerous and this continues to be an issue. The airspace design is outdated. AFW airport has grown and is continuing to grow. The facility has recently been upgraded from a Level 5 Tower to a Level 6 Tower. In the last year three new air carriers have all started operating at AFW.  A contractor for the US military has relocated their maintenance base to AFW. Aerospace company X has also begun construction at their new facility here as well. Both runways were extended from 9;000 feet to 11;000 feet in the last few years. Everything at this airport has been growing and expanding except the airspace. The Class Bravo airspace should be expanded to include WIGZU the FAF for RWY 16L. This would allow us the ability to talk to VFR aircraft that constantly cross this area around 2;500 feet. We have conducted pilot outreach at surrounding airports. It has not been successful. We just want the ability to talk to these VFR aircraft to provide traffic advisories. The airspace needs to be updated.
Report_1_Synopsis: AFW Tower Controller reported an airborne conflict and cited airspace design as a contributing factor.

Report_1_Narrative: Today was a very busy day and on top of that our area was short staffed. At the time of the event; all 5 people staffed for the day were working; we needed to have 6 sectors open but couldn't due to staffing issues. We were told that TMU (Traffic Management Unit) was to slow traffic to help alleviate some of the pressure on our area; and we were also told that they could not call for overtime because of the COVID situation at hand. Today was a completely unsafe and unhealthy situation to have been in without any support from management and TMU. What is more important to the NAS; safety or COVID?  At the time of the event; I had been on position for just over an hour and it was after two other sessions that I had been working for well over 2 hours with a 20-30 minute break in between. I was definitely mentally fatigued at this time.  Aircraft Y was a departure from ZZZ flying west bound direct to ZZZZZ slow climbing from FL260 to FL340. Aircraft X was a southbound ZZZ1 arrival initially on a heading to avoid other traffic and descending from FL350 to FL270. I had turned the Aircraft X back on course to ZZZZZ1 thinking they were clear of all other potential traffic. When Aircraft X established to ZZZZZ1 they 'flashed' with the Aircraft Y aircraft heading west bound near ZZZZZ1. I had already switched the Aircraft Y to [the adjacent ARTCC]. So I turned Aircraft X and called traffic. The turn helped but still didn't fix the situation. Ended with 4.5 miles and 300 feet. We need to have the support from not only our local management but also national level management. Volume needed to be slowed due to staffing. Regardless of what the airlines are pushing for or wanting from us. We have to be safe first.
Report_1_Synopsis: Center Controller reported an understaffed shift and multiple sessions on position resulted in mental fatigue leading to an airborne conflict.

Report_1_Narrative: A snow team had cleared snow from an intersecting runway and taxiway and had left snow on the runway. I asked the city vehicle about the snow on the runway and if it was safe for aircraft to depart. The city vehicle said the snow was 'just a dusting'. Two aircraft departed without incident. The snow team did another pass on the intersecting runway. After that; another aircraft started departure roll and then aborted the takeoff after hitting a snow bank. The pilot said it was about 2 feet deep and felt like hitting a herd of deer. The airport needs a vast improvement in their snow removal operation overall; and they need to be aware of snow that gets left on active runways.
Report_1_Synopsis: Tower Local Controller reported snow removal vehicles reported clearing the runway before a departing aircraft hit a snow bank and rejected takeoff.

Report_1_Narrative: During the DINGO 5 arrival into TUS; after waypoint MAVVA; I continued on the charted 075 degree heading passing through the Runway 11L localizer course; not complying with the textual instruction to intercept the I-TUS localizer course. ATC gave me vectors back around to re-intercept the localizer course; and a normal landing was made.The cause of the event was a failure to cross-check the textual instructions with what is displayed on the chart. Contributing factors were as follows: 1) A 'Descend Via' clearance was not issued. ATC instructed to 'Descend and maintain 8;000 feet; and EXPECT a visual approach.' I misinterpreted that to mean he would provide vectors to the final approach course; or clear me for a visual approach passing MAVVA.  2) I found the verbiage on the chart confusing where it states 'Runway 11L EXPECT approach clearance'. I interpreted that to mean once established on the 075 heading from MAVVA; not upon intercepting the localizer; as normally you would not intercept a localizer without ATC clearance or prior to accepting a visual approach.To avoid a recurrence of this event; a thorough briefing covering all noted and textual information should be conducted and cross checked prior to every landing. While my briefing did cover all of the information on the plan-view of the arrival; I missed a crucial piece of information solely located in the textual description that was not well depicted nor defined on the plan-view. It would have been helpful if ATC had offered us a visual approach earlier; directed us to intercept the localized after MAVVA and THEN expect approach clearance; or have the instruction to Intercept I-TUS localizer clearly printed on the plan view. It is worthy to note; the ATC controller stated 'Yeah; you're not the first airliner to do this' both over the frequency and on the telephone while speaking with him after landing. This leads me to believe that this could be a common mistake that could be corrected easily with a revised; emphasized; note on the arrival chart.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported a track heading deviation while on the DINGO 5 approach to TUS.  The reporter cited 'Descend Via' vs. 'Descend and maintain' phraseology and confusing chart verbiage contributed to event.

Report_1_Narrative: I was First Officer and pilot monitoring for a reposition flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1. When I arrived to the airplane; the Captain was already there with multiple maintenance technicians working through a dual inoperative GPS situation. The consensus was to defer both GPS units; along with the associated MEL items. After processing our 9 MELs during our pre-flight discussion we waited approximately two hours for a flight plan to be filed due to the issue with ADS-B being inoperative.During the after-start checklist; the CONT CAB ZONE TEMP fault appeared on Master Caution recall. We complied with the QRH and MEL and contacted Maintenance Control for deferral under the 'flight crew placard' option. The Captain and I discussed the phrase in the QRH; 'if the light extinguishes when Master Caution System is reset; no further action is required' - and he noted that this does not alleviate us from the need to defer the item per the MEL XX-XXY. Along the same time; the Captain noted that the 'dispatch alert' box was unchecked; so after the deferral was complete we resumed normal operations.After takeoff we experienced two additional master recall lights - 'Anti-Skid Inop' and the 'Reverser' on the overhead panel.Shortly after we leveled off at cruise altitude the dispatcher asked if we had added a new deferred item after pushback. We responded that we had; that it was XX-XXY. He advised us to fill out a report; despite the 'dispatch alert' box not being checked.The reposition flights after long-term storage lend themselves to multiple maintenance related issues and could be planned ahead to be operated by Functional Check Flight pilots.The filing of our flight plan took nearly two hours. Not knowing the exact cause of the issue; it would be helpful for future flights to review the process for filing flights with inoperative GPS and ADS-B to minimize future delays.
Report_2_Narrative: Aircraft X was a reposition flight for aircraft (tail) in storage several months.  The aircraft was dispatched with multiple MELs.  We waited over two hours for Dispatch to be able to get ATC to accept a flight plan into the system for a clearance.A Control Cab 'Zone Temp' light illuminated during Master Cation recall during the after-start checklist.  QRH procedures were followed and Maintenance control was contacted for a crew MEL (XX-XXY) before departure despite the misleading 'No further action required' guidance in the QRH.Two more master caution lights were encountered after takeoff (Master caution 'anti-skid and reverser.')Dispatch sent an ACARs message after level off advising us to submit a report for not getting an amended release for XX-XXY before departure.  We responded that a Dispatch alert is not required for XX-XXY.  Dispatch responded 'They give us a heads up anyway.'  We did not believe we violated any maintenance/dispatch procedures but were led to believe we had.Reposition flights from long term storage are a severely irregular operation and should be conducted by the Functional Check Flight department.
Report_1_Synopsis: Pilots reported equipment issues on a flight due to the aircraft having been in storage for several months.

Report_1_Narrative: Outlet circuit breakers tripped overnight so the planes battery and engine was cold. I placed the heater duct under the RH cowling of the aircraft into the engine compartment to warm it up and left the engine cover over it to keep the heat in. Prior to departure; I decided that I was going to need an assisted start regardless so I moved the heater from the engine to the copilot door to heat the cabin (this is where I believe the latches were initially left unlatched). I left the engine cover on not noticing the latches and walked away. Prior to departure; I removed the engine cover from the pilot side and removed the tail stand and chocks and started up. There was no sign of anything wrong until I was on takeoff roll and the cowling caught wind and came up into my view. I immediately aborted the takeoff roll and taxi back to parking. I normally check the cowling during my preflight and ensure it is latched; but the heater event happened after I completed my preflight inspection. I think that many factors contributed; but the main reason for me was that I had never done what I did with the heater like that before so my preflight routine was off. I also failed to notice the latches on my walk around because the engine cover was on while I was on that side of the plane; which I normally take it off before I even go inside to get my final manifest. I will make sure that I stick to my routine when it comes to the pre-startup walk around and be very vigilant and aware when something non-routine happens. Having this event permanently in my brain will also help me never do this again.
Report_1_Synopsis: Caravan pilot reported rejecting a takeoff due to a partially separated cowling.

Report_1_Narrative: Inadvertent Code 7500 message via Aircraft Communication Addressing and Reporting System (ACARS) message. During the flight the Captain was discussing with the First Officer about the data link pages in the Multi-Function Control Display Unit (MCDU). One of those pages is the covert declaration of aircraft hijacking or Code 7500. The Captain displayed the page and explained how to read the page and then exited out of the page without entering any information or sending the page. Shortly afterwards our flight received a query from ATC asking if the aircraft was squawking a special code to which the crew replied no and confirmed assigned transponder code. Upon parking; the flight crew was informed by dispatch that a message with the default information from the Code 7500 page had been received and asked if everything was ok. Airport Security Manager also confirmed with the crew of their status.
Report_2_Narrative: Inadvertent Code 7500 message via Aircraft Communication Addressing and Reporting System (ACARS) message. During the flight the Captain was discussing with the First Officer about the data link pages in the Multifunction Control Display Unit (MCDU). One of those pages is the covert declaration of aircraft hijacking or Code 7500. The Captain displayed the page and explained how to read the page and then exited out of the page without entering any information or sending the page. Shortly afterwards the flight received a query from ATC asking if the aircraft was squawking a special code to which the crew replied no and confirmed assigned transponder code. Upon parking at the gate the flight crew was informed by dispatch that a message; with the default information from the Code 7500 page had been received and asked if everything was ok. Airport Security Manager also confirmed with the crew of their status.
