Report_1_Narrative: ILS [Runway] 06 circle to land [Runway] 01 just after dark with gusty winds and windshear. Miscommunication in the cockpit dealing with 'programming' the airplane for the approach. Got distracted on the maneuver which got us close to the towers; then got a pull up prompt. Recovered and landed safely.[Cause was] Lack of cockpit communication.[Suggest] Training this approach with bad weather in simulator.
Report_2_Narrative: Clearance by Approach Control - Intercept the Runway 06 approach course and expect the Runway 06 ILS; circle Runway 01. Clearance by Tower - Cleared for visual approach Runway 06; at TORBY cleared to circle to land Runway 01. During the circle we received TAWS Aural Warning - ''Obstacle; Obstacle; Pull Up'. The pilot flying began a climb from 820 ft. MSL to approximately 1;300 ft. MSL. Message cleared and the approach was continued to a full stop landing. The aircraft was flown too close to obstructions during the circling to land approach. 2 contributing factors: Unfamiliarity with the procedure at TEB and reliance on autopilot.With the frequency that [our company] operates in and out of TEB; it may be advisable to add some type of briefing to the pilot [group]. This is a common procedure at TEB; but it doesn't occur frequently enough to build pilot confidence in the circle to land maneuver.
Report_1_Synopsis: Fractional jet flight crew reported receiving a TAWS obstacle warning on a circling approach to TEB Runway 01.

Report_1_Narrative: On rollout deployed reversers. Noticed left pull and used heavier braking on RH side. Aircraft tracked fine down centerline. Captain advised one reverser inop. Walk-around prior to flight revealed no indication that No. 2 reverser had been inadvertently locked out. On ground post-flight walk-around verified that reverser lockout pins on No. 2 engine were NOT extended showing red. Mechanic found hydraulics lockout in place after opening cowling. This would not be visible during an external walk-around inspection. This is a procedural issue. During maintenance there is probably a checklist for this and it was simply overlooked; perhaps due to fatigue.
Report_1_Synopsis: A321 First Officer reported that right engine reverser failed to deploy. Post-flight inspection revealed that the reverser was locked out in a manner that was not visible during preflight.

Report_1_Narrative: Prior to crossing [Runway] XX at Yankee; we did the pre takeoff checklist flow. Held the takeoff checklist until crossing Runway XX. After crossing XX at Yankee; we ran the before takeoff checklist. After the Takeoff checklist was complete; I noticed a small twin taxing from FBO East to Yankee. I brought this up to my FO (First Officer); because Ground had told him to give way to Aircraft Y but I wasn't sure he saw us. He stopped short of taxiway Yankee and asked Ground if he was to give way to Aircraft Y. Ground advised him to give way to Aircraft Y. Both my FO and I agreed we had room to taxi by since he was not interfered with taxiway Yankee. As we taxied by the twin; he told ground our wing passed over his cockpit. It was really a surprise to both my FO and me as we had saw him; discussed him and thought we had plenty of room.[Cause was] the twin pilot's lack of situational awareness during taxingIf there is any question; I should have stopped the airplane and coordinated with ground.
Report_1_Synopsis: B767 Captain reported that during taxi the aircraft's wing reportedly passed over the top of another aircraft. The flight crew stated they believed there had been adequate clearance.

Report_1_Narrative: While on a left downwind for the visual approach (Runway 23) into CRW; we received a GPWS Pullup alert. The lowest noted AGL altitude was around 1;100 feet during the approach. We were aware of the mountainous terrain; the Captain selected the FAF attitude in the altitude sector once we were cleared for the visual. Sloping terrain set off the GPWS alert as we descended roughly 1;000 FPM.Perhaps a note in company pages would be a good way to remind crews who are on the visual.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported receiving a GPWS 'Pull up' alert on a visual approach to CRW Runway 23.

Report_1_Narrative: While working Aircraft X for a large issue with side-stay play and being the third documented discrepancy; it was requested to inspected and identify if the L/H (Left Hand) and R/H (Right Hand) side stays were still usable. It was found that they were also worn out and required replacement. Senior management refused to accept that fact and still was pressuring me for 8 hours to install the identified and documented unserviceable MLG (Main Landing Gear) side-stay assemblies and remained relentless to try any motive of pressure to have them installed with disregard with what was documented causing large amounts of stress and frustration and distraction on correctly repairing the aircraft referencing the corrected documents. Direct Supervisor and Direct Shift Manager were only relaying what was being directed and are not responsible for any pressure added.The reason for the distractions and pressure to install the side-stay assemblies that were found in poor condition for wear; was because the two side stays that were ordered could not be used until engineering had approved use and the two serviceable assemblies were the only two in the system. Senior Management was made aware that the repairs for this aircraft were going to be lengthy and to export the aircraft next door the heavy maintenance department; the discretion was ignored and they basically buried themselves into what did turn out to be a large repair on the aircraft after no side-stay assemblies were usable during the event; pressure was applied to try brush the issue out by installing the unserviceable side stays and accomplishing a visual inspection with no reference to do a visual for wear and play while installed on the aircraft. Engineering concurred the side-stay assemblies are inspected with the CMM (Component Maintenance Manual) while removed. The amount of stress and frustration with my senior management not wanting to accept the fact of what were honest documented finds after being requested to do so.The local senior management in ZZZ will not accept the reality of what large repairs are and refuse to listen and force pressure and manipulation tactics to try to get supervisors; shift managers and mechanics sign a document or stamp a block in any form possible to get what they want. It creates large safety risks and is why many of our aircraft have repeat write-ups. Senior Management relies on myself as one of the people who know how the A320F works to a detailed engineering level; until it is not the answer they want to hear. The only way to avoid the occurance would be to stop harassing people on the floor and realize that sometimes; it is what it is after poor managerial decisions were made.
Report_1_Synopsis: Technician reported resisting pressure from management to install unserviceable side stays during a MLG strut change and refused the work.

Report_1_Narrative: I attended 737 Max class earlier in the week. This class has dwindled from an X-hour class to a Y-hour summary. There was virtually no discussions on the Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System (MCAS) other than it's non-deferrable. When I asked if there were any RIIs involved with MCAS maintenance; the instructor could only answer with; 'probably.' I feel the Y-hour Max class is insufficient for qualifications.
Report_1_Synopsis: Maintenance Technician reported that a training class on the B737 MAX was not long enough and did not adequately cover the Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System (MCAS).

Report_1_Narrative: Aircraft Y was flying through established practice areas at 7;500 feet; flying various heading changes affecting other aircraft in the area. we adjusted course to avoid the traffic accordingly and the aircraft then turned around to a heading that would lead to a converging conflict. Our aircraft was to the right and proceeded with caution keeping an eye on the aircraft in case they made yet another heading change; they did not. we started to alter course to the right in order to maintain our general direction of flight but also resolve the converging conflict. The aircraft was not transmitting on the local frequency and not responding to radio queries. The aircraft never deviated course at any point. Had we not seen the aircraft and taken evasive action the conflict would not have been resolved.
Report_1_Synopsis: GA pilot reported that another aircraft in the practice area was not transmitting on the local frequency and was making heading changes that required the pilot to take evasive action.

Report_1_Narrative: During deplaning at ZZZ airport; a passenger advised the lead flight attendant that either she may have been or was exposed to COVID-19. The affected passenger advised she was transferring to an international destination. This passenger would have had to disclose at check-in if she was possibly exposed; but passengers lie because they want to get home or travel to their destination. Also; on this flight I observed at least 10 passengers walk off the plane without any mask on and about 20 passengers walk off the plane with their mask only around their mouth. I see this type of activity on EVERY flight EVERY week. This is even with numerous PA's telling the passengers they must wear the mask around their mouth and nose. Many customers just don't care. I've had passengers completely remove this mask right in front of me. I've even experienced passengers telling me; '[profanity] the mask' right in my face as they walk off the plane mask less. This is the type of activity I see on every flight.
Report_1_Synopsis: Captain reported being advised that a passenger told the Flight Attendant they may have been exposed to COVID-19.

Report_1_Narrative: We were assigned and on the NAPAA4 Departure off Runway 19R at APC. During pre-flight and once again prior to departure we (as per SOP) confirmed the runway and SID was properly loaded into the Dual FMS. After takeoff; during the climb; I was 'heads down' as I was PNF and was just assigned a frequency change from the Tower to Departure Control while at the same time we encountered a TCAS for VFR traffic off the parallel runway (NOT DUE TO ANY NAVIGATIONAL ERROR IDENTIFIED IN THIS REPORT). During the scan for traffic and putting in the new frequency into the FMS; I noticed we were making a longer left turn than I anticipated. I said to the SIC (in left seat flying the aircraft) why is it turning so far and where are we going? We both looked at the SID displayed as well as the FMS and it was evident the FMS decided to sequence us to our next fix - SAC VOR and in doing so commenced a 'smart turn' in that direction.Upon contacting OAK departure; they verified our position/altitude and shortly thereafter contacted us and said 'Just so we are on the same page; you made a left turn after departing APC towards SAC and did not complete the SID.' I responded that yes; we were looking into the FMS turn as we had verified that the SID was loaded correctly in the FMS.Upon completing our day; we decided it was best to get both OAK and APC Tower on the phone to discuss. Both controllers appreciated us contacting them and mentioned that this was not the first time they have seen this happen with the NAPAA4 departure and they were going to look into it. Both controllers indicated since safety was not an issue; they were not interested in any action on us. In addition to the above discussion with ATC; I am also going to contact Collins and/or Jeppesen in regards to a possible issue with the database and/or SID for the NAPAA4 departure.
Report_1_Synopsis: Pilot reported an unexpected track heading deviation during departure from APC airport while on the NAAPA4 SID.  Reporter stated the SID was properly loaded in the FMS; yet the aircraft turned the wrong heading.
