Report_1_Narrative: While on an OE Refresher flight; I was the PM and my FO student was on his first PF leg in about 9 months due to being non-qualified during the COVID crisis.We were on a right down wind with a clearance to descend 2;000 feet. We were told to stop our descent and we leveled off at 2;600 feet. ATC alerted us to a helicopter crossing our path at 2;000 feet. We reported him in sight and ATC turned us for a right base. When we were clear of the traffic we were cleared to 2;000 feet and then for a visual approach with the airport in sight.  The FO called for gear down just outside the marker and managed the speed at the marker. We were at 170 knots at the time.  We had planned for a flaps 3 landing. With our encounter/interruption with the close traffic we didn't take into account that the marker was 3.4 miles from the runway and at 1;200 AGL. With the glide slope captured and a planned flaps 3 landing the airplane was having a hard time slowing down. I pulled the speed brakes to assist the aircraft and the FO was slowing the airplane down.  I pulled them just inside the marker and stowed them a few seconds later when the airspeed was near Vref. What I didn't realize was I had left them extended below 1;000 feet.  I think part of the issue is the approach seems a little nonstandard (standard: 5 NM; 1;500 feet AGL) and sneaks up on you with the marker at 3.4 NM from the runway at 1;200 feet.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Captain reported an unstable approach.

Report_1_Narrative: We encountered a significant unforecast mountain wave. Autothrottles were slow to react. I called out acceleration to Captain who was pilot flying. He acknowledged but did not react to the acceleration. We started to overspeed so I deployed the speed brakes and pulled back the throttles. Lost 500 feet in recovery. Reported altitude loss  and wave to ATC. Debriefed event and discovered pulling throttles back was counter to FM guidance. During debrief we also discussed late departure and long taxi with complications on ramp due to weather on departure as contributing to our reaction to this event due to being fatigued. Good debrief.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported an altitude excursion occurred when the flight encountered an unforecasted mountain wave.

Report_1_Narrative: Flight departing ELP. Flight crew input the flight data into FMS noticed that the RNAV and VOR approaches for Runway 26L was missing the last fix in the approach procedure (the runway); finding a discontinuity from MAF (waypoint in the RNAV) and the runway from WANUN and the Runway 26L; 0.7 DME. We were cleared for the Visual Approach into Runway 26L. We continued to use the RNAV Runway 26L data in the FMS as a reference to the final Approach Course in VMC conditions. All worked as predicted LNAV mode capture GP mode capture with coupled Auto Pilot. Prior to MAF the Autopilot was disconnected and a normal landing performed. No additional flags; or master caution alert nor altitude alert were observed. the flight proceeded normally to the gate. Upload database corrections to this software version.
Report_1_Synopsis: An air carrier pilot reported a fix missing in their FMS database for RNAV and VOR approaches to Runway 26L at ELP airport.

Report_1_Narrative: We operated Aircraft X from ZZZ to MDW; and the majority of the flight was uneventful. Mr. Y was my Captain and PF; and we had setup well in advance for the RNAV RNP Y approach for Runway 22L at MDW according to their latest ATIS. Later we received an ATIS update showing that the ILS for Runway 31C was active; so we re-configured and briefed that; still with plenty of time. We had discussed the possible need of diverting to ZZZ1 rather than our filed ALT1 of ZZZ2 and ALT2 of ZZZ3; but the visibility at MDW stayed above the minimums we needed for either the RNAV or ILS approaches to 22L/31C respectively.Fast forward to our first approach attempt: we're established on the ILS to 31C; fully configured well before the FAF and I was thinking we've got it made. We broke out at around 1;700 MSL and inflight visibility was not an issue and better than reported. From around 2;000 feet and down we experienced constant light and moderate turbulence; but no icing or precipitation. Captain had turned the autopilot and autothrottles off to help deal with the winds that were gusting from 260 degrees at 21 to 39 knots. We were also landing with stall protection ice speeds; adding 10 knots to our Vref and Vapp speeds.Everything was going great until somewhere between 1/2 to 1 mile from the approach end of 31C we got multiple 'WINDSHEAR' automated call outs from the airplane. Captain elected to go-around which we did; re-configuring as needed and I let MDW Tower know at around 400 feet AGL per the SOP. They gave us a heading and altitude to fly; asked us the reason for the go-around and handed us back off to Chicago Approach. We cleaned up the airplane and got vectored in for another ILS approach to 31C behind an Air Carrier Y.The second ILS approach was almost identical to the first; albeit with slightly less wind and turbulence. This time; even though we were ready for the conditions and knew more of what to expect; we managed to catch a gust of wind right in the flare and didn't touch down on Runway 31C until between the first third and the midpoint of the runway. Captain did a great job of thinking quick and performed a rejected landing; setting and calling 'TOGA' almost immediately after touchdown and off we went. We reconfigured again; got vectored around and handed off to Chicago Approach again and came around for a third attempt at Runway 31C.The third time Captain was able to land normally and well within the touchdown zone; but when he applied the brakes we found out that the '5/5/5' runway condition codes advertised for 31C were optimistic at best with the airplane noticeably sliding and skidding as we rolled out. We also noticed that there was blowing snow obscuring at least 50 percent of the runway surface. Captain advised MDW Tower of the braking action we experienced; calling it 'poor' and; to their credit; they immediately directed the broom and plow teams out to clear Runway 31C again. The rest of the flight was normal as we taxied into our gate.If there's anything I learned tonight; it's that just because you're on short final that doesn't mean you're going to land. Also: just because the Air Carrier Y flight that landed ahead of you reported 'braking action good' doesn't mean you will. I remember being on short final during our first ILS approach to 31C feeling complacent that we 'had it made' being on the ILS rather than RNAV RNP approach with its higher minimums and having broken out early at 1;700 feet. My go-around call outs also could have been crisper and more prompt; but that was mostly due to the 'startle' factor which was my own fault.My one suggestion would be for the airport operations crews at MDW to conduct their own braking action tests more often and with a more pessimistic eye. When the ATIS states RCCs are '5/5/5' the Air Carrier Y flight that landed ahead of you reports 'braking action good' and yet you experience significant wheel slip/skid due to icy runway surface conditions upon landing; thatindicates someone is being either dishonest or overly optimistic on their own braking action reports. If we or our Dispatch had known that the 'real' RCCs for 31C at MDW were actually 3/3/3 or even 2/2/2; we most likely would not have had the required landing performance numbers that we needed to land at MDW's shorter runways and would've gone to ZZZ1.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported having to go-around/missed approach several times due to weather at MDW airport.  When they finally landed the crew experienced some sliding and skidding due to braking action being 'poor' contrary to the reported 'good braking action.'

Report_1_Narrative: Descending via the NIIXX 2 arrival for the ILS Runway 35R in CAVOK conditions. Around the BSTON Intersection we were given a westerly to northwesterly radar vector and cleared to descend and maintain 10;000. As we got closer to the final approach course (somewhere between DEANE and DRUMM) we were cleared to descend and maintain 8;000 and cleared direct to the FRONZ Intersection (FAF for the ILS). The Controller asked if we had 35R in sight; after a pause; we had the runway in sight and advised ATC. We were then cleared for the visual approach to 35R. The FAF altitude at FRONZ is 7;000 so that is what we set in the MCP while descending through approximately 8;800 in FLCH. We had just gotten the '2;500' call from the Radio Altimeter and made our call outs. As we descended through 8;000 I noticed the Radio Altitude around 1;800 and descending. A quick look at JeppFD PRO showed our aircraft position just south and east of the DRUMM Intersection. I called out the altitude and the fact that we need to go back up to 8;000 (our last cleared altitude prior to the approach clearance) until we are north of DRUMM. I reset the MCP to 8;000 and verbalized that we need to climb back up. The Captain selected a V/S climb back to 8;000. We joined the approach course and followed the G/S and landed without incident.ATC never mentioned anything to us about violating airspace or going below the DEN Class B. Though it is nice to get directs; etc. However; I believe the direct to FRONZ clearance; if not really familiar with the DEN Class B; can set crews up to possibly violate airspace and even lead to an unstable approach.Once parked at the gate with all checklists complete; we debriefed and there certainly was some confusion as to exactly where we were when we descended below 8;000. We had a jump seat observer who thought we might have been a little low as he has a lot of General Aviation experience in the DEN area.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported an altitude deviation that may have put them below the Class B airspace during a visual approach to DEN airport.

Report_1_Narrative: As an LCA I was in the right seat and training a new B787 type aircraft Captain in the left seat. We had landed from on Runway  XXR in ZZZ and taxied to gate. Upon approaching the gate there was a marshaller and a wing walker on both sides. They were all giving us the all clear signal and marshalling us in to the gate. Gate X is a challenging gate because close proximity to other aircraft. We noticed tractors; baggage carts; containers; and container trailers all parked in the transgression zone on both sides of the entry path. We stopped the aircraft and attempted to contact Operations. As we waited the wing walker; especially on aircraft right; seemed to be frustrated and continued to try to get us to move forward. I witnessed a baggage tractor drive up and just push some of the baggage carts; not even taking time to hook up and pull them. Operations radioed back and told us they would call the ramp. A pickup truck showed up; presumably with a ramp supervisor. The person got out and started directing the removal of the equipment from the path of the aircraft. It was extremely hard for us to see the lines marking the transgression zone and we wanted to be able to rely on the ramp team; but it was more than obvious due to our experience with our aircraft; taxi training; and taxi experience; that we weren't safe to proceed. Finally they cleared all of the obstructions except for one container cart. Once that was cleared and could confirm that the transgression area was clear; we taxied in. What was most disturbing about this whole situation was the continued all clear signal from the wing walkers and the signal to continue the taxi from the marshaller.
Report_1_Synopsis: B787 Captain reported a ground conflict with ramp vehicles during taxi in and cited concerns with the ramp marshaller instructions to continue taxi without properly clearing the transgression zone area before continuing their taxi in.

Report_1_Narrative: Landed without incident. Took taxiway D. At a slow pace got 2/3 of the way up the taxiway and left brake froze up. Slid off to the left and stopped the aircraft. Throttled up a little to try to get centered again to no avail. Stopped engines. Airport personnel came and attempted to clear out the snow. Started engines and tried again to get centered. Slid even more to the left and stopped aircraft again. Left main ended up off the pavement. Called for maintenance to tug me in. Kept engines running for passenger comfort; heater; until tug showed up. Stopped engines and was tugged in. The cause was primarily due to 5 to 6 inches of snow on the ground; below freezing temps.
Report_1_Synopsis: C-402 Captain reported a taxiway excursion due to left brake failure due to freezing temperatures.

Report_1_Narrative: I do not believe jamming was a factor. I believe there was a failure of the HF antenna. If I am correct; there is only one antenna for the two HF radios. The observer pilot was at rest during the initial stages of the event and was not involved in the decision making process. An example of how [to] deal with dual HF failure and a reference to where the Chief Pilot was able to coordinate our continuation would be helpful in either the [Jeppesen] notes or some other searchable publication. I felt the Captain did a thorough job of putting safety and regulatory compliance first and operational reliability second. In the future; I will start to check the HF radios to ensure that they will tune prior to departure.
Report_2_Narrative: Second narrative contained no additional information.
Report_1_Synopsis: A Flight Crew reported they were unable to communicate via HF Radio and utilized CPDLC.

Report_1_Narrative: Coming in to ROA we were cleared for the visual approach for Runway 34; I was PM and Captain was PF. We were set up for a left base and kept our descent coming down to 4;000 feet. On the descent down we received a GPWS warning for terrain and Captain took immediate action and we climbed out of the terrain we were near. Captain and I both had our terrain mode on; but it was not showing up on the MFD for both sides. ATC also reported to us if we saw the terrain ahead before we received the GPWS.I believe this started from the beginning of our trip both Captain and I were deadheading from ZZZ to ZZZ1 and the aircraft had a hydraulic issue which made our flight delayed. Which got rid of 2 of our 3 flights that we were supposed to operate and made this flight our first flight of the day together. This was also my first time at ROA and Captain told me that he has been there a couple times before so I was unfamiliar with the airport and the surrounding terrain. With it also being a moonless night it was very hard to see the terrain in front of us and with terrain mode on but it wasn't showing us anything made it very difficult to determine exactly where we were at on the ILS approach plate when we were in VFR conditions. I also should have spoken up when I was looking on the approach plate that the highest terrain was 3;508 and Captain was setting the altitude bug to 4;000 feet. I believe our vertical speed was also a factor but I don't remember exactly what Captain had it set to. Captain and I also debriefed together to figure out what we did wrong and what we did right and learn from our mistakes.Add terrain photos or jepp plates on the 10-7 pages to help with situational awareness.
Report_2_Narrative: Cleared for ILS 34 on an extended left base and received the ground proximity warning for terrain on decent to the final approach fix altitude. Initially cleared to altitude on our route to 9;000 feet crossing Pulaski (PSK) [VOR]. After PSK on rout to ROA we were then given a decent down to 6;000 feet. Clear night we called airport in sight for the sight of the rotating beacon we set up for ILS 34. On an extended left base approach control gave us heading 090 and we were cleared for the visual to 34. After our clearance I gave a further turn to heading 100 and tried to widen out the base for Runway 34. With our clearance I descended down to 4;000 initially keeping in mind we had a tailwind until turning on final for Runway 34. On our descent to 4;000 we both switched to terrain mode on the PFD and saw nothing. Initially I was still on my legs page on my IPAD and my First Officer on the approach plate. We got a call from Approach asking us if we know the terrain around us and while he asked leveling at 4;000 we got a a TERRAIN TERRAIN PULL UP WARNING. We exercised the escape maneuver and leveled at 6;000. We replied to the approach that we exercised the escape maneuver and discussed that we thought we were south of the terrain further back. At night it is hard to distinguish that but exercised extreme caution until back on final.Cause - No initial knowledge of the area of terrain at night even in terrain mode on PFD. Cross reference with iPad to select altitude until final. Suggestion - I will hold the last cleared altitude at 6;000 feet and go further out towards the IAF before turning for final and descending to final altitude before glide slope capture.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported a CFTT event during a visual approach to ROA airport.  Reportedly; ATC advised the crew of the terrain right before they received a GPWS warning.  The crew exercised an escape maneuver.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Communication Breakdown; Situational Awareness; Time Pressure; Workload; Physiological - Other
Report_1_Narrative: The FO was on the very first leg of OE. The flight proceeded perfectly until arriving in the ZZZ1 [airport] terminal area. ZZZ Center descended us and never handed us over to the local [ZZZ] TRACON. Instead; we were told to expect holding instructions. It was clear the Center Controller was very busy (he was doing an exceptionally good job). Instead of issuing holding instructions we were asked where we wanted to hold. We told him we wanted to hold at ZZZZZ [Intersection]; the initial approach fix for the ILS Runway XX to ZZZ [airport]. He issued instructions to hold south. We asked if we could hold north inbound; right hand turns. He issued instructions 'cleared as requested' with no EFC. He asked how much fuel we had onboard and we replied 2 hours. I didn't push the EFC because it was clear he was saturated and we were holding at 11;000 feet above a lower layer in VFR conditions. ATC explained to other aircraft that ZZZ [TRACON] was ATC Zero and he was the only Controller handling all aircraft going into and out of 4 controlled fields. It was difficult to simply get a break on the frequency so I decided to just be patient.We had been sending ACARS messages to the company enroute and didn't get any responses; this is not that unusual; usually Dispatch will reply with 'OK' but not always. When we were issued holding instructions we sent Dispatch an ACARS message 'Holding at OM for Runway YY ZZZ; no reason given' and once again; we did not receive a reply. Incidentally; I instruct all my OE pilots; as I did in this instance; to look for the 'VHF IN PROGRESS' display after selecting SEND on an ACARS message to be certain the unit actually sent the message. In all cases it did.The airport pages indicated that ZZZ2 [airport] was just XX miles away and we knew they were not affected by this situation. The weather at ZZZ2 was also good. Our FMC fuel reserve was 4.0 since we had no alternate. At first I wanted to use 7.0 as a decision point on fuel. My thought it would probably take 20 minutes to get to ZZZ2 if needed and I wanted a cushion so I added 3.0 to the FMC fuel reserve to make my decision. If we hit 7.0 on the fuel it would be time to contact Dispatch and go to ZZZ2. While we were doing all this ATC was relying on us to contact aircraft going into and out of the airports below to issue instructions. Needless to say we were a bit busy. We were told to descend first to 8;000 feet in the hold; then to 6;000 feet. On several occasions VFR aircraft popped up on our TCAS (no alerts were issued) as we were holding in Class E airspace above the ZZZ Class D and the ZZZ1 Class C. We were keeping a keen eye outside. At one point ATC issued instructions to climb to 8;000 feet in the hold for traffic. Again; the Center Controller was doing an exceptionally good job. We were told on several occasions what our sequence was going into ZZZ; third; then second; then next.  Our intent; of course; was to get into ZZZ safely.ATC was issuing phone numbers for aircraft to call when on the ground. I was a bit confused as to why; I thought the towers were open; but paid it no mind. We heard the Controller mention COVID as the reason to another aircraft. Unfortunately; the aircraft landing ZZZ in front of us; Aircraft Y failed to call the phone number. This haunted ALL landings into all 4 airports. The Controller explained to another aircraft that his procedures precluded him from clearing any other aircraft for approaches into any of the four fields until had had a cancellation from the Aircraft Y. In fact; ATC had us attempt to call him on the frequency.I considered whether we could get in VFR but we could not get down into the class D with ZZZ Center and there was a layer between us and the field (I've forgotten where it was but probably about 3;000 feet). I then considered our fuel considerations; rather than using the 4.0 FMC fuel reserve I decided to use the actual FAR fuel reserve of roughly 3.6. The FO stayed on top of duties not only contacting other aircraft but complying with my requests as the flying pilot very well. Finally; when we reached 6;600 pounds of fuel remaining I asked the FO to contact Dispatch via ARINC phone patch. We had already looked at the ARINC Services page in the Jepps early on and determined that ARINC had a surface on ground frequency of XYX.XZ at ZZZ1; and we would be able to get a hold of them down low. I asked FO to come up with a diversion plan. FO worked with Dispatch who recommended ZZZ2 (of course) and said the fuel required would be 1;100 pounds at 10;000 feet. This seemed too low; I didn't see how we could climb to 10;000 feet; fly XY miles; and shoot an approach and landing on 1;100 pounds (and change) of fuel; so we declared minimum fuel and requested an immediate direct vector to ZZZ2. At no point did we use the words 'Mayday' or 'Emergency'. We were instructed to fly a heading (I believe it was 045 degrees) and issued climb instructions to 10;000 feet. We immediately complied and began to set up for an approach into ZZZ2.The FO did a great job juggling responsibilities; getting ATIS and setting up for the approach; contacting ZZZ1 local; etc. At one point ATC queried our fuel status and the FO initially used the word Emergency but then quickly corrected and said we had declared Minimum Fuel. We landed on ZZZ2 Runway XXL with 3.7 on the fuel. We pulled off the runway and asked ATC for a position where we could sit and call the company.We called Dispatch on the cell phone and were instructed to go to the 'Maintenance Ramp.' We complied and were met with a follow me car where we parked; right next to an aircraft with a full load of passengers (obviously there for the same reason; we were later joined by another aircraft). We were immediately met with a set of stairs and a representative who asked what we needed. Dispatch immediately gave us a field load and we ordered thirteen thousand pounds of fuel. We arranged for the proper fuel load. It took some time for the fuel truck to arrive.We then had to coordinate getting paperwork to the aircraft. While Dispatch and the team did a great job of getting that all set up; the young lady driving back and forth had to go quite a ways to get our paperwork which took a great deal of time.Once we had our paperwork we were able to depart for the short flight to ZZZ. We completed the legs without further incident.I am uncertain what drove ZZZ TRACON to close; whether it was a scheduled cleaning due to COVID or some type of emergency. We reviewed the ATC and FIR NOTAMs and did not have anything mentioning the closure. Clearly this was the beginning of the delay. Then; it was further exacerbated by the crew of Aircraft Y jet failing to call the phone number after landing. Had they called we were next to be cleared to land and we would not have diverted.Several suggestions: We need clear and concise ACARs policies in the FOM. Each and every time Dispatch receives a message from a crew inflight they should ALWAYS reply. Perhaps this is a policy with Dispatch; but since it is not in the FOM and once in a while we do not hear from them we have no idea and I was not concerned about not getting replies; until we mentioned holding to them and I got no reply. That's when we hopped on the ACARS Services chart and noted that ZZZ1 had a ground based frequency and we could reach them from our holding position (incidentally; many of our pilots don't even know that table exists). Second; It is not unusual for ACARs not to work. This needs to be cleaned up. We are constantly writing up aircraft for 'NO COMM' and ACARs failures and they don't work. Honestly; I'd say ACARS works correctly about 2/3 of the time; certainly not the spirit of FAR 121.99. Granted we have ARINC; but crews will rely on ACARS just to find out after the fact that dispatch never got anything from us. Next; if this was a scheduled COVID cleaning we should have known they were going ATC Zero before we arrived in the terminal area. Dispatch was even caught off guard about it. ATC must develop a means of communicating this so we don't find out so late in the game. They should also consider issuing a TFR. Perhaps the FAA should consider a new type of TFR for COVID. Frankly; I am a small aircraft owner and use it frequently. I don't want to be told I can't fly over class D airspace while in Class E airspace simply because they are cleaning TRACON. On a beautiful sunny day there are going to be aircraft all over. If I were flying GA in the area and knew the TRACON was down I'd probably stay away just because I don't want to get run over by a transport. Finally; the company should consider what paperwork we REALLY need at the aircraft. For instance; we can already get performance via ACARS. We can pull up our NOTAMS on our tablet. That would leave signing fit for duty and the release. Perhaps we could give Dispatch all the pertinent info (they already had the ZFW weight and balance) so all they needed was fuel onboard and they could simply give us the necessary numbers for departure. Next; send us an ACARS message for signatures - we could print 2 of them and leave one with the rep on the ramp. Had we been able to do that we would have been out about an hour earlier and would NOT have taken another delay. Incidentally; we obtained our PDC via ACARS in ZZZ2 correctly and it worked properly all the way back; including the summary page.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Captain reported the unannounced closure of a TRACON that was possibly due to an 'ATC Zero' event caused a divert for fuel. Captain reported there was only one ATC Controller working multiple positions.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Situational Awareness; Workload; Communication Breakdown; Distraction
Report_1_Narrative: We were flying into GUC in a non RNP aircraft. Winds were 250/11; SKC; elected to fly [Runway] 06 approach per ops pages; then enter downwind via Plato to GU24D. Used RNAV for SA (Situational Awareness); but did not Nav due to UNABLE RNAV RNP. When level at 9200 feet in valley on down wind; received 3 separate GPWS 'terrain; terrain' erroneous indications. There was no terrain and we were not descending. Additionally; there was no red GPWS indications on ND; just the aural cue one time with red warning light. I was the PF (Pilot Flying); and we both were perplexed by the indication. We continued the approach; as there was no reason to react to this partial warning. This event did make us question our flight path; but we also agreed that all was performed correctly. We didn't see any warnings about erroneous GPWS; and the Aircraft appeared to have no issues. We both also agreed that flying a Basic airplane that is not RNP capable into Gunnison was unsatisfactory. Are we to land with a 10 kt. tailwind to avoid indications such as this when performing the pattern as prescribed by the company?Flying a Basic; non-RNP AC into a challenging mountainous terrain airportOur original aircraft was swapped out for some reason. Non RNP airplanes should go to basic destinations.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Pilot reported 3 false terrain warnings on approach in a non-RNP aircraft.

Report_1_Narrative: Captain was pilot monitoring. FO (First Officer) was pilot flying. Passing through 4;000 feet MSL on climbout from ZZZ we noticed a fuel imbalance developing - right wing main tank fuel indication already 400 pounds lower than left wing. Right wing main tank fuel appeared to be feeding at approximately twice the rate of the left and it appeared that the center tank fuel was not feeding at all. Engine fuel flow readings appeared normal and equal. By 10;000 feet MSL the imbalance had increased to the point that the IMBAL alert was activated. We coordinated with ATC to level off at 12;000 feet MSL in order to reduce fuel flow and begin taking appropriate action. Upon leveling at 12;000 feet MSL we observed the right fuel tank quantity feed rate appear to normalize and then observed a 50 pound increase in right main tank fuel quantity. Fuel imbalance at that point was 1;100 pounds. We initiated the IMBAL checklist in the QRH. Observing what then appeared to be normal tank quantity indications for a crossfeed operation; we coordinated with ATC to continue our climb and proceed on course to the destination knowing we would also coordinate with Dispatch and maintenance promptly to determine if proceeding to ZZZ1 was advisable. As soon as we established climb fuel flow settings and pitch attitude; the right main tank quantity began to decrease again at what appeared to be the same abnormal rate observed during the initial climb. We then requested priority handling initiated the return to ZZZ (nearest airport) and started the APU as a precaution. I advised Dispatch; the cabin crew; and the passengers of the situation using SOP. As soon as we stopped the climb to initiate the return to ZZZ the right main fuel tank indication again stopped decreasing at an abnormal rate. We concluded the IMBAL checklist and for the remainder of the flight we observed no further indications of abnormal rate of decrease in right main wing tank fuel. During the descent; I spoke with the flight attendants and they confirmed that there were no visible indications of fuel leaks on either wing or engine. We landed uneventfully at ZZZ with a total imbalance of 1;220 pounds with 8;370 pounds in the left wing; 7;150 pounds in the right wing and 13;470 pounds in the center tank - 29;000 points total. The aircraft was below max landing weight at touchdown. ARFF (Airport Rescue and Firefighting) personnel were standing by as requested. After landing and before further taxi; ARFF personnel inspected the aircraft closely and reported no leaks; no visible damage; and no abnormalities. We shut down the number 2 engine as an additional precaution and requested that the ARFF vehicles follow us to our gate. Maintenance personnel were debriefed in person at the gate upon arrival.Captain suspects suspect faulty fuel crossfeed valve.Reporter recommends company consider revisiting the IMBAL checklist in light of this particular malfunction.
Report_1_Synopsis: B73-800 Captain reported an uneventful air return due to an airborne fuel system malfunction during initial climb.

Report_1_Narrative: After pushing off gate and starting 1 engine; we received an Elevator Servo Fault ECAM message. We went through all QRH procedures to resolve the problem to no avail. After calling ZZZ Operations to coordinate a return to the gate; we were informed that we were not allowed to return to the gate for a maintenance problem without Maintenance Control authorization. This seems to be in conflict with 14 CFR 121.533; 14 CFR 121.535 regarding Captain's Pilot in Command authority; as well as the MEL preamble which states that Maintenance Control's role is that of technical consultation (Not Command and Control). In any event; we eventually reached Maintenance Control via personal cellphone; and; eventually; Maintenance Control concurred that we should return to the gate. We returned to the gate; maintenance personnel troubleshot the problem to no avail; and the aircraft was taken out of service. My concern is that; in this scenario; the flight crew was forced to go through a Maintenance Control process that has 3 possible outcomes. First; Maintenance Control directs some off book procedure over the phone that 'fixes' the problem. Second; Maintenance Control directs us to flight crew placard the malfunction (which is not allowed by the MEL in any event). Neither one of those outcomes are acceptable with a primary flight control malfunction. The last possible outcome; and the only realistic outcome; is to return the aircraft to the gate; which we were frustrated from doing by this Maintenance Control permission regimen. I am concerned we are being pushed into possibly unsafe operation as our judgment is automatically questioned by a corporate policy that directly conflicts with Federal law.[Reporter stated the need for a revision of] company policy regarding maintenance troubleshooting.We [flight crews] need clearer understanding of the roles and responsibilities of Maintenance Control versus the PIC.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported ground gate return policy violates FARs in regards to Captain's Pilot in Command authority.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Troubleshooting; Confusion; Communication Breakdown; Time Pressure
Report_1_Narrative: We were working on Aircraft X. The task was to accomplish work order XX. We were told the new oxygen generators are in a box; in stores. After looking inside the box; I saw none of the paperwork was filled out. When I questioned the supervisor about this; he went to check on my issue. He came back and said he called inspection and they made one sheet to cover all these generators and we were good to go for install. After further review by the techs on my crew; none of these units in the box were usable for the Work Order and would have been expired prior to the run-out date listed on order XX. I did not ever see any blanket sheet for the box of oxygen generators. I have no idea how many of these were installed on the aircraft by the prior 2 shifts.
Report_2_Narrative: We are working Aircraft X performing the oxygen generator date check. We have conflicting dates on the oxygen generator service life. Work Order XX states the service life of the generators is XX years and makes no mention of the YY year units mentioned in MM XX. All oxygen generators we changed are the required type.
Report_1_Synopsis: Maintenance crew reported the required documentation for the replacement parts was incorrect.

Report_1_Narrative: C172 was established in the left hand traffic pattern [at] TRM; RWY (Runway) 35; performing touch and go training. Position reports were made in middle of left downwind and left base. CE560 entering a wide downwind circumnavigated [us] on its base leg. Upon noticing being circumnavigated; CE560 was inquired by [us] to confirm having the preceding traffic in sight. Visual contact was confirmed. Whilst established on a 2 mile final [we] were overtaken on the right side by CE560 having offset its final approach track to the right; subsequently cutting in front of [us]. Seconds later at a height of approximately 150 feet. [we] were caught in the jet's wake and a temporary low altitude loss of control was perceived (bank angles of 45 degrees were noticed without control authority in roll). A go-around was initiated and control over the aircraft regained. Subsequent calls addressed to CE560 to address the issue remained ignored.
Report_1_Synopsis: C172 instructor pilot reported encountering wake turbulence on approach to TRM from a CE560 jet that resulted in a low altitude upset.

Report_1_Narrative: Had a gear up incident. Landing gear would not go down. After manually trying to pump the gear down for over an hour I decided to belly land the plane at ZZZ. All precautions were taken and an emergency landing was made on Runway XXR. No injuries but plane has extensive damage.
Report_2_Narrative: My student and I took off in his airplane from ZZZ and flew to ZZZ1 where we added some fuel to the airplane. Then we took off and flew to ZZZ2 where we began an ILS practice approach. On final the gear would not extend. We went missed and flew around for an hour and forty five minutes trying to get the gear and flaps to extend. Only the nose gear came down. We decided to land at ZZZ2 so called approach for landing. They immediately turned us over to the tower where we explained our situation. WE then landed on [Runway] XXR on the nose wheel and the tail tiedown ring. It stayed on the tiedown ring until it was almost stopped then came to rest on the left wing. We departed the airplane with no issues. There was very minimal damage to the plane. Later we discovered the ELT battery was due for replacement 60 days earlier.
Report_1_Synopsis: C210 flight crew reported an uneventful planned gear up landing due to landing gear malfunction during training flight.

Report_1_Narrative: As I was pre-flighting the aircraft before the passengers were boarding; I noticed that ALL of the cleaners onboard the aircraft did not have a mask on around their nose and mouth.  Most of the cleaners had their mask only around their chin; some didn't have any mask on.  This is a federal mandate; and a company requirement to wear a mask; yet the rule is not being followed.  There's no enforcement.  Plus; there was no air connected to the aircraft; so there was stagnant air.  This was an unsafe environment.  I see this on just about every flight; which is 1-4 legs/day.  I'm also seeing at least 20% of the passengers in the boarding area or walking in the concourse not wearing any mask; and some are just wearing the mask around their mouth only.  There is no enforcement.  I'm seeing this at every airport I've been to in the domestic system.  This Federal Mask Mandate is a complete joke.  Airports are not safe if 20%+ of the passengers are not wearing masks.  These people are not drinking or eating; so there's no reason why they are not wearing a mask.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported observing a cleaning crew onboard an aircraft not wearing face masks correctly.  Pilot also reported people in terminal not wearing face masks correctly.

Report_1_Narrative: Description of Event: The aircraft with PIC as above and one passenger was returning to ZZZ from a 1-hour cross-country flight that originated at ZZZ1. The flight was uneventful in VFR weather; with altitude from 2;000 feet to 1;600 feet after takeoff and climbout until approach. Flight path was as depicted in the charted course; following VFR altitude restrictions as required within ZZZ2 Mode C airspace; and with ADS-B Out active on 1200 a required. Visibility was observed to be 10+ miles with a solid cloud cover (overcast) at 9;000-12;000 feet. Winds were variable 6-9 knots at approximately 230-260 degrees from surface to flight altitude. Within 10 nm on the approach to ZZZ on a vector of 220; while monitoring ZZZ voice radio on 123.00; little traffic within the airport operations area was observed or noted on the radio. At approximately 8 nm from ZZZ; an inbound aircraft was announced on my ForeFlight display through the ADS-B In signal at my 7 o'clock; 400 feet below and overtaking. That Cessna 152 pilot announced his intention for a straight-in approach to ZZZ runway XX. Communicated directly with that PIC and told him that we would slow down to distance behind him on my own straight-in approach to ZZZ runway XX; since he already had a 25+ mph speed advantage. Within 2 minutes; the Cessna 152 had passed us by on our left side and descended ahead of us to line up for Runway XX. In the process; I lost visual contact with that aircraft; and since there was no other traffic in the area; and ForeFlight did not show a blip for its position; I decided to perform a slight S-turn to the left to further delay our landing until the 152 announced he was clear of Runway XX. At approximately 4 nm from the threshold; with our speed down to 62 mph (58 mph Ground Speed); the Cessna 152 PIC announced 'clear of Runway  XX ZZZ'; after which I immediately announced a straight-in approach for Runway XX ZZZ and began to adjust our speed and trim to line up with the two VASI lights on the glide path. At approximately 2 nm; we were high (two white lights) but gradually settled to a nominal (white/red) glide slope on the final approach. We completed visual and verbal cockpit checks and I glanced outboard at the right Flaperon position (there being no flap setting indicator in this CH750 STOL; and no stall warning annunciation); but did not notice anything incorrect; even though I had earlier made a mental note that we would be making a flaps-up; standard landing instead of the full-flaps; STOL landings I usually make. We settled slightly low of nominal (two red lights) as we approached the threshold and at that moment; I made a mental 'flip' or attitude adjustment that we were about to land STOL; and I decreased power for a short-field landing. Our sink rate increased; but mentally; I still had confidence that the STOL nose-up attitude was safe; and did not add power but instead retarded it to idle as we crossed the threshold of Runway XX. Without flaps; our stall speed was 48 mph instead of 42 mph; and we stalled out at approximately 12' above the numbers and fell in a slightly nose-high attitude until impacting on the main and then nose gear. The aircraft bounced up and then impacted slightly nose-down; collapsing the nose strut; blowing out the nose tire; and stopping the engine as the fiberglass prop blades impacted and flexibly shattered.We immediately checked for fuel leaks even though the aircraft came to rest tail-high. I switched off the ignition and removed the key; exited the cockpit; checked again for fuel leaks (none); then shut down the avionics manually with the master switch; and turned the Fuel Selector valve to OFF. After ascertaining that the aircraft was not an immediate hazard and that both Pilot and Passenger were able to move about without difficulty; we called other airport residents; and cleared the CH750 from Runway XX.Conclusion: In summation; distracted flying due to traffic avoidance caused energy mismanagement resulting in a stall upon landing flare with flaps retracted and subsequent nose gear collapse without injuries.
Report_1_Synopsis: GA pilot reported losing control and stalling aircraft during landing.

Report_1_Narrative: I was providing instruction on new avionics for a client in Aircraft X. An IFR flight plan was filed by my client on his certificate. I briefed prior to engine start that he was PIC and that I was there to provide insight on the use of his new GTN 750. He had flown previously with this equipment; based on what he had told me. This was our first flight together in his aircraft.Prior to taxi; I reviewed with him how to load and activate approaches in his new GTN 750. He seemed familiar with its use and only asked a couple questions prior to departure. His knowledge of the features was adequate when I queried him on the unit.After takeoff from ZZZ Runway XXR; we were given a left turn to a heading of 070 and a climb to 3;000 feet. He engaged the autopilot at about 1;000 feet AGL. My client requested from ZZZ Approach the RNAV Y XXR but asked for a non-standard transition. He stated that he wanted the RNAV Y XXR to ZZZ 'via the ZZZZZ transition.' This is not a published transition and not what we briefed prior to departure. We had briefed previously that he would ask for vectors for the approach and he would repeat that same approach three times to increase familiarity with the equipment and its use in the approach environment. A short time later; we were given the instruction to climb to 3;000 feet and after that; to 'turn left direct ZZZZZ.' The autopilot began turning the aircraft to the right; presumably because he had switched from HDG mode to NAV mode without my knowledge. ATC queried and he once again read back the left turn. By the time I caught the erroneous turn direction and autopilot setting; the aircraft was well into the right turn. ATC then requested that we continue the right turn 'since we were already turning right and I have to keep you away from other traffic.'My client did as instructed and I queried ATC to confirm that we would overfly the ZZZZZ waypoint; then proceed outbound for the full approach. I apologized for the error on that same radio call. ATC responded in the affirmative; then cleared us for the approach. No further communication about the incorrect turn direction was made and the rest of the flight proceeded without incident.My client and I debriefed this issue and shared the lessons we learned. We both looked at this with an eye toward learning and future improvement.First; I reminded him of the importance of flying what we brief and that we will commit to always do so in the future. Second; as his flight instructor; it was my responsibility to catch the turn error and take control -- an effort I began but could not finish before ATC requested that he continue the right turn. Third; reliance on the autopilot worked against us and I suspect he switched from HDG to NAV mode without my noticing; initiating the right turn direct to ZZZZZ. Finally; business has been slow due to COVID and I have not been instructing as much as I normally would. I feel this last point is perhaps the most important one. As the pandemic has continued for nearly a year now; its effect on skills as pilots and flight instructors is being felt industry-wide.
Report_1_Synopsis: Instructor pilot reported a track heading deviation during a training flight with a student.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Communication Breakdown; Troubleshooting; Training / Qualification; Situational Awareness
Report_1_Narrative: On the downwind landing at ZZZ; I was #2 in the pattern when abeam the touchdown point. The plane that was #1 had just touched down; and around the same time my engine began stuttering and soon after failed. At that point; I had begun my descent and was at [approximately] 800 ft. AGL. I began to attempt to restart the engine and was unable to do so. I then decided to execute a power off 180 degree turn and land on the runway. Perhaps as a result of attempting to restart my engine and triggering the master on/off; I lost communication with ZZZ Tower (I had been previously communicating with them). The plane that was previously #1 was already quite far down the runway and not a factor. I ultimately ended up landing safely; although never received clear to land instructions from Tower due to communications failure. I attempted to advise ATC when the engine failed; however I don't believe this was communicated.Upon landing; I noticed that both of the fuel selector valves were turned off. I am not sure if these were inadvertently disabled when I was attempting to restart the engine; or perhaps I had accidentally turned both of them off before engine failure. I am skeptical that this would be the case; as I remember ensuring that they were both enabled as part of my descent checklist ~15 minutes before the engine failed. It is indeed possible that I may have turned both to the 'off' position accidentally during the descent checklist; but I do not believe the engine would have continued to operate for this long were they to be off.I do not have a clear recollection of what actions I took to restart the engine in the air as it is frankly quite a blur. After being on the ground; I enabled both fuel selector valves and attempted to restart my engine without success. I tried a second time; and it started and I taxied off the runway (at that point 2 fire trucks and a police car had arrived; and I taxied off in convoy with them).A takeaway for me is that; regardless of the cause of the engine failure; my previous flights had been in another model of airplane; and while I was very familiar with Aircraft X; I would say that I should have spent more time familiarizing myself with the emergency procedures checklist. Also; earlier in the day while pre-flighting; there were some irregularities with the communications systems in the plane; and also it was very difficult to start the engine. I did not feel that these issues were enough to warrant aborting the flight; but in hindsight perhaps I should not have flown that plane that day and had it serviced instead.
Report_1_Synopsis: Private Pilot reported engine failure on downwind that resulted in a successful power-off landing.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Confusion; Distraction; Situational Awareness; Human-Machine Interface
Report_1_Narrative: Landing Runway 26 Using Visual approach guidance from GTN 650(Garmin Navigation/Display). No glideslope guidance was provided by the GTN. I crossed what appeared to be the threshold with very faded marking in significant turbulence. I taxied to the ramp without incident. Only after reviewing the track log from foreflight on google earth did I realize I may have actually landed on the displaced threshold. I believe better markings on the displaced threshold would help prevent this in the future. In addition; a more positive identification of runway markings on my part and a go around would have prevented this event. Contributing was a runway change from our planned arrival to Runway 35R due to changing winds.
Report_1_Synopsis: A pilot reported they landed on the displaced threshold due to insufficient runway markings at HDO airport.

Report_1_Narrative: While departing ZZZ1 for a direct flight to ZZZ2; I inadvertently climbed into ZZZ Class C airspace while heading 280. My plan called for climbing to 3;500 feet for the short flight.  I completely forgot about the Class C airspace floor.  Contributing Factors include:- Not being VFR current due to winter weather; Coronavirus limitations.- The autopilot on the plane was placarded 'INOP'.  I typically set the altitude on the autopilot to 2;000 feet (100 feet below the floor) as a reminder for the airspace floor.- Air temperature was -X degrees C; which makes for great airplane climb performance.  The last time I had flown was October; and the weather was much warmer.  I was distracted by the great visibility and great climb rate.- This plane is part of a local flying club.  Planes are at X different local airports; only one of which is under the Class C veil.  It's sometimes hard to remember all the different nuances when you are flying different planes from different airports; and don't do it regularly.- I sometimes fly IFR.  This provides additional protection from this type of excursion because you are talking to ATC continuously.I just have to be more focused about airspace limitations when flying VFR from this airport.
Report_1_Synopsis: GA pilot reported entering Class C airspace without clearance.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Troubleshooting; Human-Machine Interface; Confusion; Communication Breakdown; Situational Awareness
Report_1_Narrative: This was my first time flying from PAO in this particular aircraft; and I had only been there twice before; in more modern aircraft.  Aircraft Y got clearance for a 'Right Dumbarton' departure; just ahead of me. The Controller explained the 'Dumbarton' departure to me and subsequently gave me clearance for a 'Left Dumbarton' departure; right behind Aircraft Y. Just after takeoff; as I was climbing out on runway heading; I noticed I was gaining quickly on the Aircraft Y; but I wasn't worried because I knew he would be turning right at the bridge.  Instead; he (or she) turned left instead of right.  I also turned left; and the Controller asked me if I had the traffic. I informed him that I did.  I was getting close to him but figured I would out-climb him and go above. My focus was on keeping Aircraft Y in my sight and avoiding the traffic.  I continued to climb.At the point we felt he was no longer a factor; I looked at my iPad screen and realized that something was wrong; and I could not figure out where I was. I spent several seconds trying to assess the problem; all the while still climbing.  I had full control of the aircraft; and I knew where I was visually; but I could not figure out where I was on the moving chart display; so that I could avoid airspace I shouldn't be in.Pretty quickly I figured out how to adjust my screen so that I knew my position; and at that point realized I had climbed into Class B airspace; or at least I think I did.  I had received no hand-off from PAO Tower and was so overwhelmed by that time; along with being very concerned about climbing into Bravo; I simply immediately put the nose down and descended below Bravo airspace.Here are the factors that precipitated this event: 1. I was flying an older aircraft with only one radio and an iPad with EFB for navigation. I was not as familiar with it as I am with the other aircraft I fly; which has a modern EFIS. I had not studied the airspace in my departure path from PAO; I thought I could rely on the iPad.  This was a mistake I'll not make again!  2. I've never flown in or out of an airport as busy as PAO.  I was very anxious about doing everything right; I wanted to be safe and not cause any issues or problems with the flow of traffic and the controllers.  The Aircraft Y's unexpected left turn and my focus on avoiding it became distracting factor that took me 'off my game'.In the future; I'm committed to more fully plan my flights; especially in congested airspace; and I will become more proficient in the use of my electronic flight aids.
Report_1_Synopsis: GA pilot reported overtaking a slower aircraft during departure from PAO airport resulting in an airborne conflict.  Reporter also reported an SFO Class B airspace violation after taking evasive action and losing situational awareness due to a problem with the iPad's moving map display.

Report_1_Narrative: I took off from ZZZ using Runway 18 with my destination to the north. I turned left crosswind then downwind; intending to depart from the area by maintaining a downwind heading until clear of the traffic pattern. During downwind abeam the runway; I continued to climb above traffic pattern altitude but did not announce the climb over CTAF.During upwind or crosswind; a Cessna (Aircraft Y) announced he was west of the airport and would be crossing midfield and entering into a downwind for [Runway] 18. He did not announce his altitude. I assumed he was at traffic pattern altitude and would be turning left and entering into the downwind. By midfield in the downwind myself; I was at about 1;800 ft. AGL and climbing. I did not see the Cessna until he was approximately 300 ft. directly ahead of me and 200 ft. above. I nosed over briefly to arrest my climb.I have since reviewed the AIM and AC 90-66B. I believe the Cessna intended to perform a descending teardrop turn to enter the downwind. This is a standard pattern entry. My own departure was nonstandard.I will use this experience to better judge traffic conflict and miscommunication risks.
Report_1_Synopsis: Pilot flying PA28 aircraft reports NMAC in airport traffic pattern.

Report_1_Narrative: While heading in to land at ZZZ; a black object was spotted approximately 1 mile from our nose at our altitude of 2;400 ft. Initial thought of both pilots was that it was a bird; then after noticing that it did not appear to be moving I determined it was most likely a drone that was heading straight toward us or hovering; so averted to the right at which point the drone flew past our left wing in the opposite direction approximately 500 to 750 ft. horizontal from our left wing at coaltitude (2;400 ft. AGL). The drone was determined to be a black quadcopter; approximately the size of a soccer ball; with a possible camera mounted underneath. ATC was notified; queried us for further information; and announced to all aircraft on frequency of drone activity in the vicinity of the airspace.
Report_1_Synopsis: A General Aviation pilot reported a NMAC with a Drone.

Report_1_Narrative: Initially; cruised at 7;000 ft.  From ZZZ to about the ZZZZZ intersection on V185; I was between layers.  ATC requested that I change altitude to an even thousand because I was now westward bound and gave me a choice of up or down.  Up would have put me in the clouds.  So; I requested down to 4;000 ft. because I knew that should be below the freezing level and below the ceiling as I progressed.  Upon reaching 6;000 ft.; I requested to stay at that altitude because I was still between layers and 4;000 ft. would have put me in the clouds for some time before reaching the higher ceilings.  Eventually; the layers merged and I was in the clouds at 6;000 ft.  A short time later; rime ice began to form.  In about a minute; I lost my airspeed indicator.  Just prior to a red X appearing over the G5's airspeed partition; the G5's airspeed tape quickly unwound and a stall indication began flashing.  Also; the GFC 500 autopilot had disengaged.  I told ATC I was in icing and received clearance to descend.The stall indication did not make sense.  But; I was confused by what was happening and pushed forward on the yoke so as to not take any chances. A recovery from a rapid descent and 180 degree turn was executed as I realized a stall was not happening and the auto pilot had disengaged.  ATC offered a 2;000 ft. altitude to get out of the clouds and in warmer temperatures.  I had turned on the pitot heat and the airspeed was functioning on both the airspeed steam gauge and the G5.  The plane was iced but flying without difficulty and the ice was melting rapidly. I turned back on course and continued without further incident below the clouds.  In retrospect; I should have descended to 4;000 ft. instead of stopping at 6;000 ft.  This would have put me in the clouds for awhile; but beneath the freezing level.
Report_1_Synopsis: Pilot flying C-172 aircraft reported inflight icing.

Report_1_Narrative: This narrative highlights two incorrect published crossing altitudes on two different arrivals that can lead to altitude deviations and aircraft overspeeds. The first is the PASLY 4 (10-2C) arrival to BNA at GROAT intersection. The crossing is depicted to cross GROAT at or below FL 230. It is always 1000 out of 1000 times given to cross GROAT at FL 220 usually by Memphis Center and has been for at least five years. Sometimes this occurs very late. This can lead to a situation where the aircraft was on the path; is now high; and the aircraft then pitches down at the last minute to meet the unpublished altitude of 22;000 ft. This pitchdown can lead to an overspeed and a situation that still does not meet the crossing. The second instance is on the ENDEE 6 Arrival into MDW (10-2). The fix in particular is KAMBL and the published crossing is between FL 270-FL 240. The unpublished crossing that is given; very late; is to cross KAMBL at 24;000 ft. Now the aircraft is in the same situation as the PASLY 4 Arrival; only you may have a 100 plus kt. tailwind to deal with as well. Both these situations persist but are preventable by simply changing the published altitude. Finally; there are several Pilots who are rusty from not flying; due to low utilization; whose situational awareness and lack of currency make this situation even more grave. Please fix these easy to remedy issues and trap the known errors. Thank you. We did not have a deviation. I am only reporting to highlight these issues.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier pilot reported ATC consistently issues a crossing restriction at a specific fix different than what is published and programmed causing difficulty complying with the clearance.
