Report_1_Narrative: On final [Runway] XXL ZZZ we were paired up with traffic on another runway in visual conditions. I thought the FO had selected TA on the transponder. After debriefing on the ground he told me that he was telling me to set TA on the transponder; but what I heard was transponder is set to TA. Inside ZZZZZ [Intersection] at about 1;200 feet we got an RA Climb. I verbalized 'We got to go.' I surmised that the TCAS RA would be followed by a go-around. My communication was unclear. The traffic was in sight throughout the approach. The FO continued the approach and landed uneventfully. We should have gone around; but after debriefing I understood that the FO thought it might be unsafe to climb and go-around with the other traffic so close.
Report_2_Narrative: With the A.P. and A.T. off; I was P.F. on the visual approach to Runway XX.  ATC calls out traffic at our 2 o'clock that will be close to us for another runway.  We call the Aircraft Y traffic in sight and proceed inbound.  Both the Captain and I are wearing masks (COVID); which I believe muffled my request to 'Set to TA only.'  The Captain later said he thought I said 'We're set to TA only.'  The approach continued normally with us going to managed speed; gear down; as we started down the glide slope inside the FAF.  Just after I called for flaps 3 around 1;400 feet AGL; I noted the Aircraft Y a little above us and the appropriate distance to the right joining up with us.  I was still slowing the aircraft at that moment; and the RA went off 'Climb; Climb.'  I asked the Captain 'We are not in TA only?'  He responded 'Well we are going to have to go.'  I momentarily considered going around; but thought continuing the approach was actually the safest course of action when the RA immediately stopped.  We continued the approach and landed uneventfully.  The RA happened the moment the Aircraft Y was joining the other localizer course.  What I should have done is gone around.  Following the RA is the right thing to do unless it is unsafe to do so.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier flight crew reported a communication misunderstanding between the pilots resulted in conflict during approach. The Captain stated they were both wearing face masks and that it may have contributed to the miscommunication as their voices were muffled.

Report_1_Narrative: On short final into SDF RWY 17R I noticed a shiny object slightly below and to the left of the aircraft on final. It was not directly in the flight path but close enough to be noticed. I noted that aircraft was 3 miles from the runway and 600 feet AGL. The drone was slightly below us (estimate 400 feet) and East of the extended centerline (estimate 2;500 feet). At first; I thought it might be a balloon; but recognized it as a drone as it passed abeam and behind us. The FO (First Officer) was flying and given the phase of flight and that I did not feel that it was an immediate threat; I elected to wait until we were clear of the runway to inform the FO and Ground Control.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported an airborne conflict with a drone during final approach to SDF airport.

Report_1_Narrative: We were on our way to hangar to pickup a plane; driving on Taxi way 1 driving empty tug with instruction clear all the way to the hangar via Zulu X; as we were approaching Yankee Y intersection; we heard a tower giving instruction to a plane just landed on runways XYC-YXC to take Yankee Z; Yankee short of taxiway Alpha; but that corporate jet enter on Yankee Y and took Zulu; I had to immediately take sharp right turn to a grass area to clear the taxiway Zulu to avoid a collusion; FAA was reported and was asked if we are OK and so we continue on Zulu to the hangar.
Report_1_Synopsis: Tug driver reported that while they were driving on a taxiway; an aircraft taxied onto the same taxiway caused the tug driver to take evasive action by driving onto the grass area.

Report_1_Narrative: While on approach to ZZZ in day VMC conditions; crew was instructed to fly direct 'ZZZZZ' - the FAF for ILS XX - for a visual approach to [Runway] XX. The crew had been left high by both Center and Approach; but was able to reach the 5;000 ft. and slow prior to intercept. The PIC/PF (Pilot Flying) briefed the SIC/PM (Pilot Monitoring) on speed/energy management and airspeed 'windows' prior to the approach. After reporting runway in sight and receiving the approach clearance; the PF initiated descent to 4;500 ft. (the FAF altitude) and began to lessen the intercept angle; and PM prompted gear down and flaps 22. Aircraft still slightly overshot the localizer but was able to capture both LOC and GS which happened simultaneously. 4;500 ft. is within 1;300 ft. AGL of field elevation; and due to the short distance both vertically to the runway and laterally (just outside 4 miles); the PM/PIC anticipated an unstable approach and called a go around. The PF pressed the TOGA (Takeoff Go-Around); disconnected the autopilot; and called 'check thrust flaps nine' and the PM set flaps 9 and checked the thrust to discover the PF had not yet increased thrust to detents. Concurrently with the 'check thrust flaps 9 actions'; and 'Sink Rate' EGPWS warning occurred; and momentary hesitation by PF prompted PM/PIC to take control and initiate the immediate action in response to the 'sink rate' AURAL as required for the EGPWS escape; with a 'Pull Up' Aural warning occurring concurrently with the initiation of the EGPWS escape procedure. (At the time of initiation the EGPWS escape; PIC noted an 1;800 fpm descent rate). Upon reaching a safe altitude; the aircraft configuration was cleaned up in line as normal; and flight continued back for ILS without further incident. One error was made during EGPWS escape; which was PIC only increasing thrust to detents and not to max. Upon completion of the flight; crew debriefed on a number of key items. These included energy management and the approach profile in the AOM; go around procedure and ensuring power is set concurrently with pitch and callout when conducting a missed; and the EGPWS escape maneuver.Crews should act very early to mitigate unstable approach situations; including in a situation like this requesting a lower altitude earlier and a vector out to the IAF in lieu of the FAF; this can alleviate the chances of an unstable approach long before the issue manifests. Missed approaches should be initiated immediately upon identification of an unstable approach. In the event of a missed approach; crews should ensure the action is taken decisively including the increase of power; and both pilots should remain involved in the process. Should a GPWS warning be received; decisive; immediate action should be taken - as per the AOM - superseding normal missed approach actions due to the time critical nature of high vertical speed close to the ground. Captains especially should keep a close eye on FOs conducting operations at outstations - in this situation; having approach offer a better vector to join or taking an actual ILS clearance may have prevented the situation from manifesting at all.
Report_1_Synopsis: EMB-XRJ Captain reported that while conducting a go-around from an unstabilized approach an EGPWS warning occurred.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Communication Breakdown; Time Pressure; Situational Awareness
Report_1_Narrative: During preflight in bitterly cold ZZZ; the FO (First Officer) completed the walk around as snow began to fall. The flaps were full down from the previous flight. She came to the cockpit and informed me that the flaps were clear of debris and asked if we should retract them for the deicing we would need after start. I agreed we should; and we did. Unbeknownst to us; the fueling of the aircraft began during this time and we didn't notice as we retracted the flaps. Just before pushback; ramp informed us that Maintenance was checking the refueling door on the wing; as it was damaged. This was our first indication that we may have damaged the door during flap retraction. Later on; maintenance personnel came to the flight deck and told us of the problem and that we would be swapping aircraft due to this.Cold weather operations; delayed fueling; miscommunication and worsening weather all contributed to this event.Don't touch the flap handle until all preflight items are complete before pushback regardless of weather conditions.
Report_1_Synopsis: A321 flight crew reported fueling door damaged during flight retraction at gate.

Report_1_Narrative: While instructing a student in the pattern at ZZZ; just before turning onto our base leg; we were advised to make a wide left 360 and re enter the pattern on the right downwind for Runway XX. As we began our turn to the left we noticed an incoming airplane on a left downwind flying at same altitude in our path. I took controls from my student and we rapidly began to descend. If wasn't for our quick reaction it surely would have been a mid air collision. The incoming traffic began a climb in order to avoid our path. The incoming traffic was out of our line of sight but ATC still made the call giving us clearance to turn after I voiced that we did not have the traffic behind us insight. This event was noticed by another controller and he promptly relieved his coworker and handled the situation. This controller has been known around flight schools operating at ZZZ to decrease safety in the sky. I felt it was imperative to report this event.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Instructor flying a C-172 reported a NMAC in the airport traffic pattern.

Report_1_Narrative: I received the second dose of vaccine against SARS-CoV-2 (virus that causes COVID). The vaccine is highly safe and effective; but clinical data show that many people have minor side effects like fatigue; muscle pains; headache; and flu-like symptoms. The FAA requires a 48 hour waiting period after administration of this vaccine for that reason.I had not reviewed the FAA circular. I concluded that it would take longer than the flight I had planned for any potential side effects to develop; so I launched on a 4 hour flight. Towards the end of this flight; I made an unscheduled fuel stop and started to develop a mild headache. Recognizing that these might be symptoms related to the vaccination; I grounded myself. Later that evening; I developed symptoms that were severe enough that they would have presented a safety issue; had I been operating an airplane.I neglected to review the FAA circular in advance of this flight. A 48 hour delay after vaccination would have prevented the possibility of experiencing symptoms that could present a danger during flight.
Report_1_Synopsis: GA pilot reported receiving the COVID-19 vaccine and flying before the 48 hour wait period requirement.  Pilot did not read the FAA circular regarding the vaccine and developed a headache during the flight.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Situational Awareness; Human-Machine Interface; Communication Breakdown; Distraction
Report_1_Narrative: Departed ZZZ1 and was given XXY.A departure frequency and after the fact it was XXY.B. I maintained VFR the whole time and was told I may have violated the Class Bravo airspace. Tower was closed at ZZZ1 due to COVID-19. A lot of confusion on the ground and with traffic in the air. I was VFR the whole time and contacted ATC when I landed in ZZZ2. Talked with Controller and explained my situation and filled out this report. No evasive action was taken.
Report_1_Synopsis: GA pilot reported entering Class B airspace without a clearance.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Distraction; Human-Machine Interface; Situational Awareness; Workload; Communication Breakdown
Person_2_Human_Factors: Workload; Situational Awareness; Fatigue; Distraction; Communication Breakdown
Report_1_Narrative: Arriving into ZZZ the altimeter setting was showing 0996 mb; so during our arrival brief we covered the VNAV limitation for altimeters lower than 29.70/1006 and put special emphasis on using FLCH (Flight Level Change) when transitioning. Transition level was FL070. ATC began descending us in small steps; they gave us a descend to FL070 but when we were passing FL080 they gave us a descend to 6;000 ft. then further lower to 5;000 ft.; during those step downs I missed switching the altimeter setting to the local 0996mb. Then when we leveled at 5;000 ft. ATC verified the altimeter setting stating that we were 400 ft. lower than we should have. I immediately realized my mistake; set the correct altimeter setting; took corrective action and called for the approach checklist. Since the airplane wasn't reacting as fast as I wanted; I disconnected the auto pilot; corrected the altitude and continued manual flying all the way until we landed. There is no excuse for missing an altimeter setting during transition. There were many factors/distractions that took place for this to happen and they all came pretty close together: long duty day; our bells to the flight attendants; re-route to a point not in our route; use of wing and Engine anti-ice; heavy rain during descent so continuous ignition was set; multiple small step downs from ATC; VNAV limitation; all of them occurring often simultaneously. We; as crew; came together and managed all threats that were thrown at us as best we could to bring the airplane safely to the ground.I will; from now on; better prioritize on the stuff that I delegate and ask my crew to keep an eye on me and remind me of things that could make us incur a deviation like this one. Even though we all had our hands full; I should have asked someone for some sort of reminder about the transition level.
Report_2_Narrative: At the conclusion of a long duty day and the second flight leg of the day; I was PM (Pilot Monitoring) en-route. This was my second leg as PM (6th leg as flight crew) in an international theater in nearly 3 years. Prior to descent and during the approach briefing as well as once the relief pilots entered the cockpit; we discussed the lower altimeter setting of 0996mb and the associated procedure per Company limitations from not using VNAV when transitioning from QNH (Height Above Sea Level) to QNE or QNE to QNH when below 1006mb. We felt very prepared for the arrival and descent into ZZZ. The transition altitude of 7;000 ft. was also briefed however as we proceeded; we encountered winter weather requiring extra vigilance (icing conditions and heavy precipitation). ATC descended us in multiple small increments below 10;000 ft. but the last prior to this event was a descent to 5;000 ft. With the added attention to the weather and ensuring proper use of FLCH instead of VNAV during what should have been the transition; both the pilot flying; and the pilot monitoring did not switch the altimeters at the proper time to the local setting of 0996mb. Upon level-off at 5;000 ft.; ATC came over the radio to verify local altimeter of 996mb and stating the observation of being 400 ft. low. I quickly realized my altimeter was incorrect and took corrective action and confirmed the pilot flying did so as well both with the altimeter and the flight path. One of the observer pilots also confirmed and stated the MSA for situational awareness. The pilot flying disconnected the auto pilot and continued to intercept the localizer path while returning to the cleared altitude. The aircraft was hand flown to landing with no further incident.Multiple links in the chain led up to this event and while we thought we had sufficiently briefed the several unique environments (low altimeter/Company limitation; winter weather) we also were distracted by being vectored to a point not on an arrival or the approach expected. It only goes to show that even with the best preparation and briefing that events can change and compound quickly and while attention to detail is most crucial during all phases of flight; extra vigilance is needed for approach and arrival; especially in areas that have not been flown to in recent months or years. Ultimately; the crew worked together to safely return the aircraft to the desired state and ensured a lesson learned for the future when operating in areas with differing transition altitudes.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Crew flying 767-300 aircraft reported not resetting altimeter during descent.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Human-Machine Interface; Situational Awareness; Training / Qualification; Workload; Distraction; Fatigue; Communication Breakdown
Report_1_Narrative: At 10;000 ft. cleared direct ZZZZZ and cleared visual RWY XXL ZZZ. We both agreed 8;000 ft. was a safe altitude due to terrain then 7;000 ft. after clearing the hills. Flying pilot; FO (First Officer); set 8;000 ft. then 7;000 ft. in the altitude window. It seemed we were high since we delayed the descent so we were trying to get down. I did not notice the altitude was set to 6;000 ft. Approaching ZZZZZ I realized we were low and told the FO to stop the descent. We climbed slightly and joined the Glideslope to continue the approach. We did not get any terrain warnings but it was concerning that we descended lower than anticipated at night into a high altitude airport.The FO was low time in the airplane and had just came back from a 5 year absence. I did not realize he was behind a bit on the automation. While I was trying to figure out what he was doing I lost situational awareness even though we had discussed safe altitudes. It was also the third leg we had flown that day so we were both tired.I was overly depending on the automation to help reduce the work load for both of us. The automation will only help if it is programed correctly so a person has to be very careful to cross check all available information. From now on I think it is best to request an instrument approach when it's dark going into airports you're not 100 percent familiar with. From now on I will at the very least request to join the visual further out on the instrument approach course in order to get more stabilized.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported descending too low while conducting an approach at night.

Report_1_Narrative: Performed a go-around on [Runway] 30R at MSP. We queried controller that we saw an aircraft sitting on runway while we were on short final approximately 900 feet. He told us to go around which we did - then thanked us for the query due to him being distracted or involved with a disabled aircraft on Runway 30L; this occurred during VFR conditions at night.
Report_1_Synopsis: Embraer pilot reported executing a go-around after spotting an aircraft stopped on the runway.

Report_1_Narrative: While on final approach into Seattle on a visual approach to [Runway] 16R; after Capturing glide path with the auto pilot; we were configuring the last of our flaps through 1;000 ft. and the Captain called for below the line; while running the checklist the Captain made the remark we were looking low. As I came up the plane was in the flight director; however for some reason the auto pilot had gotten knocked out of GS mode and defaulted to pitch hold. As the Captain started to correct back to the PAPIs we received a low alt alert from Tower; along with a glide slope warning from EGPWS. The Tower saw us correcting during the call however and noted disregard. As we were able to re established on glide path and were stable before 500 ft. we continued the approach to land. Not sure why the flight director disconnected from the glide slope and defaulted to pitch hold; and if was something we did while configuring; or if it was a fault of the plane or ground equipment.I was distracted by the running of the checklist and did not see the entities deviation from glide path; more why the autopilot changed modes. After returning to the displays I was getting conflicting information from the flight director and the glide slope indication. It would have been easier to just look outside and get the indications from the PAPI as to our current airplane state.
Report_2_Narrative: ILS [Runway] 16R into Seattle; visual conditions; LOC and GS captured with autopilot engaged. After aircraft configuration complete I felt like we were low. I saw that we were now in pitch hold and below glide path. LOC was still captured. I disconnected autopilot and leveled off; heard 'Glide-slope' as well. ATC was informing us about low altitude alert; then immediately said disregard. I regained glide-slope utilizing PAPI.Not sure why the GS disconnected; if it was something we did wrong or if it was a fluke or something to do with the system. I talked to the Captain taking the airplane about the event and suggested to use the ILS. Lesson learned; at all times monitor glide path and lat/vertical modes. The transition from GS to pitch hold was very subtle.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported that during final approach to SEA airport; the autopilot changed from glide slope mode to pitch hold causing the aircraft to descend below glide path. The crew regained control following a ground proximity warning and low altitude alert from air traffic control.

Report_1_Narrative: We discussed as a crew that in the future when we get pressured by time constraints and environmental pressures (i.e. raining hard during the walk around) that we won't allow ourselves to be hurried and in a rush. That is when things get missed.I missed the cowl latch key left in the Number One Engine on the preflight walk around. It was dark and raining hard and we were running a little bit late due to an excessively long line at the KCM (Known Crewmember) checkpoint.
Report_2_Narrative: We discussed as a crew that in the future give us more time to get to the airplane in ZZZ with the long train ride and busy departure time. And no matter never get caught rushing any procedure. Get down on your knees and check those cowl keys! Long line at KCM (Known Crewmember) Checkpoint and we were rushing to get the flight out on time. Rainy cloudy morning in ZZZ FO (First Officer) missed cowl latch key during walk around. Proper keys and pins located on the [Aircraft] during our interior cockpit preflight. Only informed of our mistake by the outbound crew in ZZZ1. Captain called Crew Scheduling to get my number.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Crew reported being informed that they missed the cowling door latch key still installed in the engine cowl latch and departed.

Report_1_Narrative: Upon reaching clearance for ILS XX circle Runway XY at ZZZ from Approach; we were switched over to ZZZ Tower frequency. Established on the approach between the IAF and FAF; I keyed the mic to establish contact with Tower inbound. The entire avionics turned off completely; losing intercom; transponder; GPS/Nav/Comm 1; and Nav/Comm 2. ZZZ was currently under IFR due to 2SM visibility; but we were in visual conditions on the approach course. I broke off from the approach and turned to the south; since we were no longer receiving navigational guidance along the approach; and I had no communications to contact Tower or Approach. I knew the weather towards the south was looking clearer so the plan was to continue south towards ZZZ1 or ZZZ2. We troubleshot the avionics; checking circuit breakers and cycling the avionics switch to no avail. No indications of ammeter discharge or low voltage illuminated; and the turn coordinator was still operable as well as engine instruments; so I presumed that the failure was based solely on avionics and not complete electrical failure. We descended lower; maintaining VFR so that we could receive cell signal; and I contacted ZZZ Tower via cellphone; since they gave us instructors their phone number another time when they had an ATC/instructor meeting. I told them we were okay; and had complete avionics failure. I asked for the phone number for ZZZ1 Tower so I could communicate with them if I decided to continue south to ZZZ1. At that time; the visibility and clouds around ZZZ began to clear up and we could start to see towards ZZZ. I asked ZZZ Tower if the field was still IFR; and they replied that it just went VFR. We proceeded inbound toward ZZZ; maintaining VFR; and were able to receive landing and taxi clearances for our aircraft through the cell phone. The aircraft was repaired; with the problem being a short-circuited avionics switch.
Report_1_Synopsis: C172 flight instructor reported a complete failure of communication and navigation equipment while on an instrument approach and in reduced visibility. The instructor broke off the approach; remaining in visual conditions; and was eventually able to contact ATC on a cell phone and make a successful approach and landing.

Report_1_Narrative: I had been delayed 1 day while performing a conditional inspection due to weather at the departure airport.  Once in the air; I transited through the congested ZZZ1 airspace to return to my home airport.  I contacted the ZZZ Control Tower once I exited the ZZZ1 airspace and read back instructions to make a downwind entry.  I monitored the radio for other traffic in the airspace and flew the pattern.  Once on the ground; I realized I might not have read back a landing clearance.Due to Coronavirus; I have been making limited flights; basically only to maintain currency.  Because of this; I pay more attention to flying the airplane; while radio work is handled habitually; and I wasn't letting each radio transaction sink in; nor ensuring I make all the necessary calls.  This leads to diminished piloting skills; and more practice is necessary to operate in congested airspace.
Report_1_Synopsis: Pilot reported a possible landing without a clearance and cited lack of flying as a contributing factor.

Report_1_Narrative: Based on unfamiliarity with the FAA's COVID relief policy regarding medical duration's; I acted as PIC between ZZZ and ZZZ1 on date in a type aircraft with an unknowingly expired 2nd class medical (issued date). The unfamiliarity came from reading headlines in several industry publication emails about the FAA extending medical certificate duration's during COVID.  I failed to follow up on these headlines to determine the extent of the extensions and therefore performed this flight under the assumption that medicals were extended indefinitely until COVID was over.I discovered my mistake after my coworker (in ground school) asked me about medical duration's in preparation for his private pilot written exam. I proceeded to search for his answer; and in the meantime recalled the COVID medical certification extension news.  Upon finding and reading FAA orders describing the extension details; I discovered my certificate was subject to a two-month extension and expired date.  Immediately I visited the FAA's AME directory and called several AME's because my AME has since closed their practice.  I found several AME's (including my previous AME) to be no longer practicing FAA exams (some for several years); however they were still listed in the FAA directory.  I finally found someone still in business and am in the process of scheduling an appointment with them at the earliest convenience.I have a flight today to/from ZZZ2 where I will sit the in the right seat only to provide an extra set of trained eyes and ears for the safety of the flight while not acting as PIC or SIC until my medical is renewed.
Report_1_Synopsis: Corporate pilot reported flying without a current medical.

Report_1_Narrative: This was my third solo XC (Cross Country). Flight planning was approved by the instructor. Weather and NOTAMs were reviewed by both myself and instructor and flight was deemed safe to proceed. There were no NOTAMs or field condition reports for the destination airport. One pattern was flown at departure airport with an instructor to update currency prior to departure of solo flight. Takeoff; climb; en route; and descent were uneventful. During a visual approach to Runway 02 at the uncontrolled airport; I noticed patchy snow on the runway. I noticed other aircraft had landed recently. I was expecting a normal landing to a touch and go. ASOS indicated the winds were from the northwest at 8 kts. I touched down on centerline at 67 kts. Before I set the nose down; the aircraft started veering to the left. I made the attempt to correct and the airplane continued to slide to the left. I believe due to the unresponsiveness of my control inputs; I was on ice. I made the decision to full stop and applied brakes. The aircraft continued to slide on the icy portion of the runway with no response to my braking or control inputs. The aircraft struck a snow bank on the left side of the runway. The aircraft tipped forward and to the right; resulting in damage to the propeller and the right wingtip. I'm not sure if this is a reportable incident/accident at this time. The following day; a NOTAM was issued for 30 PCT patchy snow and ice.	I believe I landed on a patch of ice. There were no NOTAMs published at the time of my departure. Had a NOTAM been published for wintery conditions; I would not have attempted a solo XC to this airport. I have not yet been trained to land in wintery conditions. Based on previous landing markings on the snow in the runway; I assumed it was safe to land. My relative inexperience resulted in not recognizing the ice under the snow. I should've gone around. In the future; I will take a harder look at my experience level and the conditions present in order to make a better decision. I have learned a valuable lesson to always err on the side of caution.
Report_1_Synopsis: Student Pilot reported on landing losing control due to ice; which resulted in loss of control; a runway excursion; and damage to the aircraft.

Report_1_Narrative: The single-engine taxi restriction from EWR Taxiway RG began around [Date] and I have observed minimal awareness and compliance since then. I believe a significant contributing factor to this un-intentional non-compliance is that the caution is located on the EWR  10-9D at the bottom in plain text. The ORD 10-7 for the same caution is significantly more visible immediately after the Safety Alert boxes and is in bold type.
Report_1_Synopsis: Captain reported violating the single engine taxi restriction due to the inconspicuous location of cautionary note as well as the plain text instead of bold type.

Report_1_Narrative: After arrival [at] ORD Flight Attendant advises door 2L has been disarmed but the slide armed light was still illuminated. ELB report of write up was sent and maintenance was verbally advised. Station operations and ramp control advised of irregular door situation. Jet bridge was unsuccessfully re-positioned to remove passengers via door 1L. Idea to taxi aircraft to [gate] was rejected after Captain consulted maintenance and MRD was broken therefore pushback unauthorized. Move team was called to tow aircraft. Duty Manager was contacted for authorization. Move team plugged headset into aircraft and plan was discussed on towing aircraft to [gate]. Pilots ran all normal checklists and consulted QRH tow in supplementary procedure. Move team advised pilots he would be providing all Ramp and ATC communications. He also stated that after he commanded the pilots to release parking brake he would need to disconnect headset with no further communications available until reaching [gate]. After parking aircraft at [gate] he would re plug in headset and advise pilot to set parking brake. As aircraft approached [gate] ramp area was covered with ice and snow. Digital sign read slippery conditions. Braking action appeared to be poor. Aircraft was brought to a stop. Captain was unsure if towing was complete; tug was sliding in slippery conditions or another white tug that was parked in front of aircraft was an obstruction. After a few seconds aircraft began to move forward again at the same feel; rate and speed as under tow. Soon mechanics were seen on both sides of the aircraft frantically giving the set parking brake signal. Both Captain and First Officer immediately and simultaneously pushed down brake pedals. Captain then set parking brake. Move team plugged in headset. Captain asked the question what happened? Move team replied they followed their correct procedures which was to chock main tires; disconnect tug; and they were in the process of chocking nose gear and plugging in headset when the aircraft jumped the main chocks and began uncommanded aircraft movement towards the terminal of approximately 10 ft forward lasting several seconds. Weight of aircraft was approximately 217;000 lbs. Aircraft made no contact with any person; jet bridge or equipment.
Report_2_Narrative: [Report narrative contained no additional information.]
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier flight crew reported while ground crew was repositioning aircraft in snow and ice; there was loss of aircraft control.

Report_1_Narrative: Enroute ZZZ-San Salvador at FL390 we were able to ascertain through ATC Control that Runway 25 was in use and that we could expect to proceed via CAT VOR and execute the ILS Y 25. The FO (First Officer) was the Pilot Flying and thoroughly briefed the approach and his expectations for altitudes; automation modes and aircraft configuration throughout the approach. We were turned over to San Salvador Approach approximately 70 miles from the airport descending to FL200. San Salvador Approach cleared us direct CAT VOR; cross VOR above 5;000 [ft.] cleared ILS Y Runway 25. Both pilots confirmed clearance; altitudes and automation as we proceeded. As we neared CAT we were around 8;000 [ft.] at 240 kts.; still on the VNAV path. Although the FMC appeared to like the profile we both agreed it was time to slow down to meet the briefed approach profile. The FO selected vertical speed and dialed the speed back in the MCP window. With the selected vertical speed we weren't slowing down so I recommended Level Change. We slowed; configured and continued the approach passing CAT VOR. I set 2;500 [ft.] in the altitude window to fly outbound from the VOR as we completed the landing checklist. Once crossing the fix at [8.0 nm] we turned inbound via LNAV and set the FAF crossing altitude of 1;600 [ft.]; approach mode selected. We were in VFR conditions with the airport in sight on my side of the aircraft. As we turned towards the airport and descended I noticed we seemed low since we were more than 8 miles away and below the glide path. I looked back at the FMC and noticed fix [7.8 nm] with a crossing altitude of 2;500 [ft]. Shortly afterwards ATC asked what our altitude was and I replied 1;600 [ft.]. At that point both the FO and I realized we had missed [7.8 nm] on the procedure and should have crossed it at 2;500 [ft.]. [7.8 nm] is not clearly depicted on the approach plate with a crossing altitude nor is there an altitude depicted for the turn inbound. Also; we flew the procedure properly if the automation was in VNAV; but it wasn't. Although it was nighttime we were in VFR conditions with the airport in sight throughout the procedure. No GPWS cautions. At no time did I feel the procedure unsafe.
Report_2_Narrative: I was the PF.  CENAMER approach cleared us to descend out of FL390 to FL 200.  We were expecting the ILSY Rwy 25.  We briefed the approach thoroughly and I explained I would stay in VNAV until lined up on final approach where I would select APP for the ILS.   Well above FL200; we were handed off to ElSal approach.  They told us to proceed to CAT VOR and cleared us for a full approach ILS Y Rwy 25 approach with procedure turn.  HOWEVER; we were high before arriving at CAT so I selected to use vertical speed and open the speed window to control speed.  The CAPT suggested I use LVL CHG instead since it would do a better job getting down and controlling speed.  I did so; while  flaps and gear helped slow us.  I was still well above 3500'; over the VOR beginning the procedure turn outbound to D8.0.  Still in LVL CHG; We were able to fully configure and be on the VNAV PATH at 2500' at D8.0.  We completed the LANDING CHECKLIST.  At this point we had the airport in sight and never lost contact the whole time.  We were both using TERR MODE for obstacle clearance.  After passing D8.0 I asked the CAPT to select the next lower altitude of 1600' as depicted on the approach chart; and he did so.  In my haste to get at the correct altitude; slow down and  configure for landing; I did not  realize I had not reselected VNAV.  The autopilot descended us to 1600' as we turned toward final.  We crossed D7.8 at 1600' vice 2500'..  There was no GPWS warning and we had the airport in sight the whole time.  On final approach I selected APP and we noticed we looked low and at the same time; the control tower queried us about our altitude.  That was when we noticed our error but were already capturing the glideslope at that time.  We continued the approach; landed safely and taxied to our gate without further incident.
Report_1_Synopsis: Captain reported a successful recovery of a CIFT event during approach as a result of temporary loss of Situational Awareness.

Report_1_Narrative: [Aircraft X] was a ZZZ1 flight and the ramp had already planned the loading and was ready to load. I checked the loading to see if the Hazmat was loaded correctly. There were a total of 3 pieces all planned in Pit 3. I noticed that two of the pieces; Items 3 and 5 can not go into the same pit they needed to be separated. One piece was Hazmat Class 5.1 and the other Hazmat Class 3. I contacted ZZZ Ops and advised them of it and to have the ramp lead call me. He called and Item 3 was held off due to not enough bags (15 bag minimum) to separate and load it into another pit. He also advised that Item 3 item did not have a bar code on the package to scan.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Ramp Personnel reported removing one of three Hazmat items during preflight due to Hazmat a loading violation.

Report_1_Narrative: We arrived at ZZZ after receiving minimum rest due to weather delays the previous duty period. Normal preflight; startup and taxi to Runway XX intersection X1 for takeoff. At approximately 90 knots; airspeed stagnation was noted and then airspeed increased. On climbout; we received the IAS Disagree caution. The Captain advised ATC. We leveled initially at 4;000 feet and the Captain took over the Pilot Flying role. I became Pilot Monitoring and worked with the jumpseater; who was an experienced B757 Captain; to run the checklists. Once checklists were completed and power settings were calculated. We requested vectors to the ILS at ZZZ. Approach vectored us and a successful landing was made. Upon return to the ramp; it was discovered that all four pitot covers were still installed.
Report_1_Synopsis: B757-200 First Officer reported IAS errors resulted in return to airport to find pitot covers still installed.

Report_1_Narrative: Cleared for Visual Runway 24 in UNV we descended to 3;400 feet. We were straight and level at 3;400 feet crossing the highest obstacle (approximately 2;400 feet MSL) to the southeast of the field. We got the 'terrain; terrain; too low pull up' GPWS warning.[We] climbed to 3;800 feet [and] leveled off; once passed terrain continued approach and landed uneventfully.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Captain reported during approach to UNV airport they received a GPWS alert while in VFR well above terrain resulted in taking corrective action.

Report_1_Narrative: During the crew briefing prior to commencing descent we discussed runway turnoff closures as listed in the NOTAMS and on the JFK ATIS. During the landing roll we noted that the green turnoff lights were illuminated for Taxiway WW; which was closed. After clearing the runway at Taxiway V we asked the Ground Controller if this was normal and she stated they had no control over individual turnoff lights. At other airports I have seen the taxiway lights turned off for closed exits and feel that pilots are expecting to see turnoff lights illuminated only for available taxiways. Since we had briefed the closures we had no issues exiting at the proper turnoff. I could see fatigue; poor visibility; and/or snow obstructed signs causing an incident. I feel that instituting individual runway lighting controls for the controllers at JFK would enhance safety.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Captain reported green turnoff lights were illuminated to a closed taxiway resulted in a pilot report to ATC.  Captain expressed a safety concern for possibility of confusion.

Report_1_Narrative: Cleared RNP 22 at MHLM. After landing Runway 22 and exiting at Taxiway B; Tower instructed us to taxi left (west) on Taxiway A; enter Runway 04 and backtrack down runway to Taxiway D. I advised Tower that we were entering runway at Taxiway A; whereupon tower instructed us to hold short of runway. I advised Tower that we had crossed the hold short line. Tower reiterated hold short instruction; 'For traffic.' CA (Captain) told the tower that an aircraft should not land on runway with us in our position. Tower said that aircraft was only doing a touch and go. After CA protested again; saying that it was unsafe for an aircraft to land on the runway; Tower said that aircraft would turn at the SAP VOR; which is on the approach (east) end of Runway 22. The aircraft; a yellow light twin engine; callsign Aircraft Y; completed its approach and made a low pass; flying the full length of the runway at 50 ft.; and passed in front of our nose. Tower then cleared us to backtrack on runway to Taxiway D. Remainder of flight without incident.Language; use of non-standard phraseology by ATC; lack of safety awareness (Tower).The tower seemed to think it was ok for an aircraft to land with another aircraft over the hold-short line.
Report_2_Narrative: [Report narrative contained no additional information.]
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported ATC violation of allowing aircraft to overfly them by 50 ft.

Report_1_Narrative: During the boarding of [Aircraft X] ZZZ - ZZZ1; I noticed a message on [Software] from the gate agent to station operations to inform the ramp personnel that there was a 'motorized wheelchair' on the jet bridge to be loaded onto the aircraft. I made a note to make sure we were provided notification of the wheel chair and when it did not come through the automated weight and balance data I asked the ramp lead. He just told me that it was 'very light' so he scanned it as a normal bag. I asked him if it was electric and if it had a battery and he said he did not know. He did not understand why I needed to know so after explaining that it was Dangerous Goods and required notification; he went to check it. I decided to go down with him to the cargo bin to make sure he knew what we needed. When he went in the cargo bin there was not a belt loader available so I was not able to also get in; and it was surrounded by bags so I was not able to see the base of it myself. He looked for several minutes; then informed me that it was 'not electric' and had 'no battery or electric parts' at all. I clarified this with him multiple times; both while standing at the cargo bin and also over the headset in the cockpit. After the flight was complete; we saw the agents in ZZZ1 unload it and the passenger get on it. I asked her if it was motorized and she said that it was. I asked her what type of battery it had and she said it was lithium ion and it was removable. She also showed me exactly where the battery was and how it could be removed. She also said that someone; it was unclear who and whether or not it was a [Company] employee; told her not to 'give too much information' during her check in process or she might have trouble flying with it. She couldn't remember if she had told the agent if it was a lithium ion battery. Regardless; multiple employees should have been able to figure out along the chain that it was motorized somehow; which meant it had to be electric.The cause was the ramp's misunderstanding of our DG (Dangerous Goods) policies and not being able to identify DG loaded on the aircraft; as well as possibly the passenger not reporting it as DG during check in.This is now the second time I have had an undeclared lithium ion wheelchair carried in the cargo bin in the past year and a half; which is indicative that this may be a larger issue than just one single missed item. Also; given that the ramp lead had no idea that electric wheelchair batteries had to be declared; it is impossible to know how many other events have happened where we simply didn't see the passenger after the flight.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported undocumented transport of Lithium Ion battery powered wheelchair.

Report_1_Narrative: While taxiing on Alpha Taxiway at a slower than usual rate for departure on Runway 33 and attempting to turn onto Alpha 1 to enter the runway; the aircraft continued sliding forward on Taxiway A. The right quartering tailwind combined with the icy taxiway caused the aircraft to depart the paved taxiway surface where the left main gear and nosewheel slipped off the paved surface onto the frozen ground. The right main gear remained on the paved surface. With the aircraft stopped we shut down the aircraft and arrangements were made with airport ground crews and maintenance personnel to have the airplane towed back onto the taxiway to the hangar where an inspection was made. No damage was found and the aircraft was deemed safe to fly. In addition no damage occurred to airport property.
Report_2_Narrative: [Report narrative contained no additional information.]
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Crew reported icy conditions; blowing snow; and gusty wind resulted in a taxiway excursion.

Report_1_Narrative: While flying a cross-country; I encountered strong mountain-wave action; making altitude difficult to hold. I asked for and received a 'block altitude'. The conditions were VMC all the way to the surface. The aircraft was on autopilot with altitude hold engaged. The autopilot called for 'trim up;' as the aircraft was descending I added power. I asked the other pilot to give it nose-up trim as he had done several times before. (The aircraft only has manual trim.) Suddenly; the aircraft nosed over. I immediately hit the autopilot disconnect button and pulled the circuit breaker. I noticed that the aircraft was very nose-heavy and I struggled to keep it from pitching down further. I called for more nose-up trim; but the problem got worse and I could barely slow the pitch-over even by pulling with both hands.During our descent; the controller queried us about our rapid descent. Given that I was extremely busy; I advised ATC. Finally; I told the other pilot to help me pull the nose up; whereupon the aircraft responded and I began adding nose-up trim and climbing back to altitude. We arrested the descent and leveled off and then I began the climb back to cruise altitude.I checked the aircraft for any control difficulties and determined that there were none; I advised ATC that I was climbing back to cruise altitude. Upon discussion with the other pilot; we determined that instead of adding nose-up trim; he was inadvertently adding nose-down. Because the autopilot had been engaged; we did not notice the wrong direction trim. We continued to our destination to get clear of the AIRMET for turbulence. Upon landing; an A&P inspected the aircraft and found no evidence of over-stressing the aircraft.
Report_1_Synopsis: PA32-300 Pilot reported mountain wave activity and improper operation of trim resulted in loss of aircraft control.

Report_1_Narrative: On reposition flight to ZZZ1; climbing through FL250; had Amber CABIN ALT CAS message followed shortly thereafter with Red CABIN ALT message. (Checked Pressurization gauges and abnormal checklist while descending). Leveled off and requested immediate descent which was approved. Rapid descent to 13;000 feet followed by return to ZZZ for maintenance on this aircraft. (Center provided priority handling; but we said it wasn't necessary).
Report_1_Synopsis: CE680 Captain reported a pressurization failure resulted in an expedited descent and a diversion.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Troubleshooting; Situational Awareness; Confusion; Communication Breakdown
Report_1_Narrative: While approaching MCO Gate XXX to park the aircraft; we noticed that the Marshaller had two wands that were flickering on/off.  A wand that is flickering on/off is not a properly working lighted wand.  The Marshaller needed to bang the wands individually to get them to operate.  Neither the left and right Wing Walker's had lighted wands.  I stopped the aircraft; set the parking brake; made a radio call to MCO Operations asking for six lighted wands (two for the Marshaller; two for the left Wing Walker; and two for the right Wing Walker).  We waited about 10 minutes while waiting for the MCO Ramp Supervisors to find six working wands from the surrounding gates.  One of the supervisors saw that the wands being used by the Marshaller were flickering on/off.  One of the Ramp Supervisors took one of the inoperative wands from the Marshaller and discarded it by throwing it across the ramp I spoke to the two Ramp Supervisors; and they explained the following:1. This situation happens all the time in MCO where the safety equipment (lighted wands) do not work properly at night.2. If we go to an adjacent gate to obtain wands; there is a 50/50 chance that we will find lighted wands that work (all the time; not just tonight).3. There is no manager on duty tonight.  All managers left for home earlier in the evening.  The managers do not preflight the equipment to ensure it is working properly and ensure that we have adequate numbers of lighted wands before the managers go home for the night (ongoing issue).  4. We have communicated the problems about the safety equipment not operating properly many times to our managers; and nothing ever happens to fix the problem.5. Other pilots have mentioned the same concern about lack of operating safety equipment to MCO Leadership and still nothing improves.6. One Ramp Supervisor explained that he has worked at four different (Company) Stations.  He said that MCO is by far the least prepared with ramp equipment; safety equipment; etc.  The (Company) VP of Ground Operations needs to ensure that all stations have adequate safety equipment and that it is used consistently when required.  The MCO Station Manager needs to get involved and ensure his/her (Company) Ground Operations Team has an adequate amount of properly working lighted wands every evening before the Ramp and Operations Managers retire for the evening.  The ramp agents need to be trained that the use of the lighted wands is mandatory to ensure the aircraft arriving at night can be safely parked in the safety zone.  No exceptions!
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Captain reported inoperative safety equipment used by the ground marshaling crew.

Report_1_Narrative: Air Carrier requested [taxi clearance] to deice [pad] after push to get the [Release] for this flight. After they deiced; Ramp Tower got a call concerning HAZMAT packing. The flight is now returning to the gate to deal with the HAZMAT.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Dispatcher reported aircraft on a ground gate return to correct a Hazmat loading irregularity.

Report_1_Narrative: Ground ops and takeoff were all nominal. During the climb phase passing approximately 18;000 feet MSL; we noticed a strong smoke odor with visible smoke and haze emanating from the courier area. The burning; smokey; smell was increasing. We requested priority handling with ZZZ center and stated the nature of our priority and our request to begin an immediate descent into ZZZ for Runway XXR. We ran the Smoke/Fumes checklist. The procedure cleared the smoke very quickly. An expeditious approach was conducted to ZZZ XXR. Crash/Fire/Rescue inspected the ac and followed us to parking without any further issues.
Report_2_Narrative: Captain was PM; First Officer was PF: Preflight; engine start; taxi and take off were all normal.  Climbing through roughly FL180 I noticed a slight burning smell which seemed to be intensifying in both smell and irritation level to eyes/throat.  Took a look behind me and noticed the light in the ceiling by the cockpit door shining down on a dense hazy smoke.  Mentioned to the Captain to take a look behind him and he noticed it as well.  We requested priority handling with ZZZ Center and requested an immediate return to ZZZ for a visual backed up by the ILS to Runway XXR.  As we began the turn and descent back towards ZZZ; the Captain ran the 'Non-Alert' Smoke/Fumes Removal Checklist.  At some point; approach control was notified of our intentions to be high speed below 10;000 feet.  After descending below 10;000 feet; the cabin was depressurized via the QRH procedure and the smoke/smell dissipated relatively quickly.  Flight Control was notified via Sat Phone of our intentions to return to ZZZ.  Approach and landing went smoothly.  After landing; we vacated the runway and came to a stop on the parallel taxiway so Airport Fire and Rescue services could take a look around at the exterior of the aircraft.  After getting the all-clear; we taxied back to the ramp and met with maintenance and eventually with EMS to get checked out.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported a flight deck fumes event during departure climb resulting in a return to the departure airport.

Report_1_Narrative: On an ILS approach to Runway 16L at HEF; at approximately 300-400 ft AGL; while scanning for approach lights; the crew observed two bright white steady burning lights located to the northwest of the approach lights to Runway 16L creating a momentary impression of REIL lights for Runway 16R.  The lights were shining directly into the approach path.  Crew continued the approach on localizer and glideslope; identified the MALSR for Runway 16L and landed normally.
Report_1_Synopsis: Captain of a training flight reported lights near HEF Airport caused confusion during an IFR approach.

Report_1_Narrative: I departed ZZZ after topping off my aircraft fuel tanks. I flew VFR in VMC conditions to PDK. The traffic pattern very congested so much so that several aircraft had difficulty obtaining clearance to enter the controlled airspace at PDK. After monitoring the tower frequency; I elected to call ATL Approach to request a VFR ILS to PDK for a full stop landing. This would help me to practice a VFR approach; setting up the approach; capturing the localizer and glide-slope; Because I was solo I remained alert to visually remain clear of all aircraft nearby.I contacted ATL Approach and received a discreet transponder code as well as VFR vectors for the approach; I was vectored through the ILS localizer for sequencing and then cleared for the approach just outside of the FAF CHAMB and was transferred to the PDK tower frequency.The radio traffic was so heavy that I was not able to transmit before the tower called my call sign and cleared me for landing number 2 behind jet traffic. Because I was cleared to land #2 behind the jet; this contributed to my understanding I would land on Runway 21L; the longer runway used by Jets. The parallel Runway 21R is shorter and primarily used by piston and training aircraft.I continued on approach on the Localizer and Glide slope until short final. When I was approximately over the Runway 21 L approach end I observed Aircraft Y fly over head at approximately 75 ft. at a faster speed. I immediately called the tower and reported the aircraft overhead while side stepping to the right to go around. The tower sequenced me to land on the parallel Runway 21R and I continue to a safe landingThe issue was I was cleared for the ILS by ATL approach and expected to land on Runway 21L. Also I was cleared initially by the tower to land #2 behind Jet traffic However; the tower said that they cleared me to land on [Runway] 21R.I have been flying from this airport for over XX years and I as well as many other pilots regularly receive runway landing changes often on short final. In this case I may have misunderstood or did not hear correctly the landing clearance and as a result had a near miss with another aircraft.Contributing factors was the radio frequency congestion as well as the high volume of aircraft in the airspace; and my expectation to land on the longer runway behind jet traffic. Also the Aircraft Y pilot did not see me as he approached from above and behind my aircraft; which also contributed to the near miss. I have on board Aircraft X an L3 active TCAS as well as ADSB traffic advisory. I do not believe I heard or saw a traffic alert on my avionics.
Report_1_Synopsis: Pilot reported ATC confusion and clearance resulted in a NMAC on short final to PDK airport.

Report_1_Narrative: We departed ZZZ on a part 91 day VFR local pleasure flight with one adult passenger in this 1979 Cessna 172N aircraft flying approximately east south east. The weather appeared to be six plus miles visibility with some cirrus clouds; winds under 10 kts. with what seemed to be an occasional thermal. Approximately ten to fifteen minutes into the flight; was at about 1;800 ft. and began a gradual turn to the right.As the yoke was first being moved clockwise; or perhaps shortly thereafter; a pop was felt; the yoke then had no resistance whatsoever with the control yoke ending up being all but fully deflected to the right where it remained at that moment. A vibration in the airframe began. It was a light though consistent somewhat disconcerting vibration. Even with the yoke as it was (all but fully clockwise at that time; in other words; the yoke was about 90 degrees clockwise from level) the aircraft was not banking right. The left rudder pedal may have been instinctively depressed to pick up the right wing after the snap occurred; but uncertain. The aircraft now appeared to not be entirely controllable as the yoke and inputs to it did not seem to be having the effect which they should have.Thereafter; if the yoke was moved counterclockwise; especially if moved past neutral to the left; a distinct buffet of unknown nature was felt; and the yoke was immediately returned to the position which resulted in the least vibration; about ninety degrees clockwise. Not being a mechanic there was significant uncertainty as to what actually was broken and what effect it could have on the flight characteristics of the aircraft. When a shallow climb was introduced or the pitch was increased; a distinct buffet of unknown nature was felt and the climb with the associated pitch and power increase was immediately discontinued and not attempted again. When a very shallow descent was introduced the ongoing vibration seemed to decrease or cease. When the engine rpm was decreased slightly the ongoing vibration also seemed to decrease. That said; no further attempts were made to bank or turn left or climb or increase the pitch or power. All turns thereafter; which were slight with little bank; to the right; were accomplished with slight rudder pressure.7700 was squawked and ATC was advised on guard. Center responded promptly to the call. Due to the limited and questionable control problem; along with the ongoing vibration and buffeting issues; the best course of action at the time appeared to be not to continue the flight back to the closest and seemingly most prudent airport as it would have required a flight directly over a densely populated area. The next closest airport considered potentially usable in the situation appeared to be ZZZ1. However; ZZZ1 was much further than ZZZ (about 18 NM vs. about 10 NM); although few homes along the route it required a flight over water which would have necessitated a climb and a left turn. Due to the buffet experienced during the prior attempted climb; local knowledge of many times there being turbulence where the water meets the land; the distance (would something else happen during that longer travel time?) and the buffet experienced when a left turn was attempted previously; ZZZ1 did not seem to be a good choice at that time.There was an acceptable looking farmer's field which required a slight turn to the right and was just prior to the populated area of ZZZ2 and ZZZ2; it seemed to be the best choice. The aircraft was maneuvered slightly right using slight rudder pressure. After the turn was completed a gradual descent at reduced power was begun. Communication with Center was lost due to the descent although an airliner relayed our communications with Center.During the descent at reduced airspeed a very minimal amount of flaps were introduced to see if any negative effect was experienced. No negative effect was experienced. The descent continued; doors were propped opened; fuel was turned off;mixture to idle cutoff; mags and master switch off which all then culminated in an uneventful though spirited landing on a farmer's field. The airplane came to rest seemingly undamaged. Aircraft was exited normally and moments later Center called to my cell phone in order to check status and get information. FSDO's and local law enforcement were notified and responded accordingly.
Report_1_Synopsis: C172 pilot reported a complete loss of aileron control that resulted in a forced landing.

Report_1_Narrative: While on approach into CHO we were being vectored by Potomac Approach on frequency 126.4. We were on a right downwind being vectored for the ILS Runway 03. It was IMC conditions with light to moderate rime ice accumulating on the aircraft. At 3;000 ft. MSL we were given a right turn; a base turn; toward the final for Runway 03. We were just outside; south of the fix WULDU. I noticed were getting close to the localizer course for the final approach; and Potomac had not issued a turn for us to intercept the approach. I prompted Potomac approach and tried to establish communication. There was no answer on 126.4. I prompted again; and still there was no answer from Potomac. At this time we crossed over the localizer course without a turn to intercept given from Potomac. I had guard (121.5) already tuned in on comm 2. I heard Potomac approach trying to hail us on 121.5 on guard and advised us to switch to frequency 132.85. I switched to 132.85 and they gave us an immediate turn to the right to reestablish us on the localizer course. The coverage on 126.4 for the area was lost and I confirmed that with Potomac that we were trying to contact them. Apparently a Learjet overheard us trying to transmit on 126.4 and relayed it to Potomac. Once we re-established communication; Potomac gave us that right turn to intercept but it was 'too late'; The aircraft GPWS detected terrain and gave us a 'Terrain; Terrain' 'PULL UP' audio warning. I directed the First Officer to Climb the aircraft and disregard the instruction from Potomac Approach. We climbed up to 3;500 ft. MSL and got the aircraft clear of the terrain. I advise Potomac what had happened and that we were unable to intercept the approach from the vector that they gave us. Potomac than gave us more vectors to get re-established on the approach. From there we landed with no further issues. I conversed with Potomac about the drop in radio coverage on frequency 126.4. They agreed and confirmed that they could not hear us and we could not hear them on 126.4.[Problem was identified by] flight crew scan. No communication from ATC have prompting them several times. Having Guard (121.5) on comm 2 and have our audio on to re-establish communication. Being aware of the terrain in the area and seeing the aircraft GPS position on The Jepp charts. [Cause was] loss of two-way communication on 126.4 between our aircraft and Potomac approach lead us to not receiving an instruction to intercept the localizer course. Without that instruction we continued on our heading and had to re-establish communication via guard and switch to a different frequency that has radio coverage in the area. All of this lead to vectors in an area with terrain and caused us to be in a position where the aircraft GPWS was activated. [We] contacted ATC. Followed the aircraft GWPS system and climbed to avoid terrain. Advised ATC that we were responding to a GWPS annunciation. [Suggest] better radio coverage equipment is needed for the area around CHO. Suggest the importance of ALWAYS monitoring 121.5 on Comm 2 for flight crews.
Report_1_Synopsis: EMB-145LR Captain reported communications loss ATC resulted in a GPWS warning requiring evasive action.

Report_1_Narrative: Upon entering the ramp (Taxiway Delta to Foxtrot) both of us noted that the Foxtrot taxiway centerline on the ramp and perpendicular to the gate centerline seemed too close to the southern edge of the taxiway on the ramp next to the grass. Recommend a site survey be conducted for heavy aircraft arriving/departing San Salvador to better understand how close taxiing on the Taxiway Foxtrot centerline will place the main wheels to the grass and edge of the taxiway. It appeared that taxiing on the Taxiway Foxtrot centerline would put our wheels very close to the grass or in it. We elected to deviate from centerline to keep us away from the edge of the grass and edge of the ramp taxiway.  It is possible that taxiway Foxtrot was measured and painted for B757 and smaller aircraft.  Conduct a site survey of MSLP to determine if the taxiway centerline is measured and painted for larger aircraft like Aircraft X. Publish guidance on the -7 pages describing the need for deviating from taxiway centerline on Taxiway F if it is found to be of sufficient distance from the edge.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier First Officer reported the taxi line at MSLP airport is too near the grass area for a large aircraft; creating a safety concern.

Report_1_Narrative: On the ZZZZZ6 we were told to level at 7;000 feet for traffic. This was my 3rd trip on IOE and was practicing hand flying the departure. It was turbulent and we were in and out of IMC. Since we were extremely light due to light loads we were climbing at an extremely fast vertical speed. Passing through 6;000 I announced that I was going to use TCS to reduce the rate of climb to about 1;000 since there was traffic above and I wanted to avoid a RA. I corrected the VS to about 1;000 ft/min. I was not quick enough to override and reduce the autothrottles to avoid increasing airspeed. The airspeed quickly and momentarily increased to 270 knots as we were leveling at 7;000 feet. I reduced the autothrottles too late and while reducing them altitude deviated by 140 feet high. Both deviations were short and immediately corrected. Nothing was mentioned by ATC. We were later given higher once the traffic passed. The combination of hand flying in turbulent conditions in IMC and leveling at a low altitude with light loads was a recipe for distraction and error to occur. I could have eliminated some of these variables by engaging autopilot earlier or reducing autothrottles quicker. The CA and I debriefed and talked through what led to the event and how to prevent it in the future.I learned that when possible reduce extra variables that could lead to an error. I am new to flying with the company and new procedures; was hand flying in turbulent conditions and IMC; light loads with good performance; and was given a low level off. That is a lot of variables at once and the ones that I could control are the earlier use of automation to help alleviation some of the task saturation. Hand flying in turbulent conditions and maintaining altitude can be difficult and the autopilot can alleviate and sometimes do a better job to avoid deviations. Additionally I learned not to lag on overriding the autothrottles when using in FLCH mode. From this experience I feel that I can better identify and evaluate a handful of risks in a certain situation and will take prompt action to reduce these risks in a timely manner. The CA and I had a productive debrief and agreed on what variables led to the deviation and how to prevent in the future.
Report_2_Narrative: Upon departure we exceeded the 250 knot speed limit in class B while leveling off. We sped to 265 knots for about 15 seconds while leveling off at 7000 feet.  Aircraft was very light and a great deal of convective weather in our vicinity.This was a training flight with a new first officer who was hand flying the departure. The rapid climb rate and early level off instructions caught the First Officer off guard. The First Officer recognized the issue and overrode the auto throttles to get the aircraft slowed to 250 knots.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier flight crew reported an airspeed and altitude deviation due to weather; hand flying and having an aircraft with a light passenger load.
