Report_1_Narrative: When we arrived and the door was opened we started to deplane the aircraft; a full flight; just as the first three first class passengers were deplaning ; the cleaning crew started to enter asking if they could board to clean first class to start. The first class wasn't even deplaned. Only three people had deplaned while others were trying to get their bag down and deplane. I said no not at this point; which in turn the first cleaner gave me serious attitude. The Gate Agent came down; no mask on; with an attitude about us not letting the cleaners enter to clean. They had 12 people to clean; usually they have a shortage of cleaners. But we hadn't even had first class passengers cleared and they started coming on. I asked not yet; let the passengers deplane and this flight is a full flight. This is becoming a serious issue at times and passengers getting upset they can't deplane and usually the cleaners keep cleaning and not moving in so they can deplane. Understand at this time with COVID the importance of cleaning but passengers complain at me about cleaners not clearing so the could deplane. It's stressful enough with all we are dealing with no food drinks and upset passengers about what they can't have. Our passengers were moving quick and not stalling getting off.  When they were off we couldn't get our bags and personal items together.  The flight deck wasn't able to exit. I understand there is time a limit and all but this rushing is going to seriously cause problems with safety of crew and passengers.  I was wrong possibly and maybe for which i will follow these memo's I forgot about from now on. Just trying to give our paying passengers a pleasant and safe flight including safe deplaning.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Attendant reported there was no social distancing by the aircraft cleaners during deplaning and also stated the Gate Agent was not wearing a face mask.

Report_1_Narrative: During taxi to Runway 31L; ground control told us to hold short of the approach end of Runway 22 at Taxiway Z. As another aircraft was landing; ground told us to cross Runway 22 In front of the aircraft on landing roll and told that aircraft to give way to us. As we began to cross in front of the aircraft on landing roll; there was no indication that the aircraft was slowing down to give way to us. So I stopped our aircraft and the aircraft on landing roll passed in front of us. Ground said that we shouldn't have stopped.This event was caused by ground control setting up a disaster scenario by wanting us to cross in front of the aircraft on landing roll. If anything went wrong; like brake failure of the landing aircraft; then there would have been a potentially catastrophic aircraft accident.In the future; ground shouldn't cross aircraft in front of other aircraft on landing roll unless they are positive that the aircraft on landing roll has slowed down sufficiently to be safe.
Report_2_Narrative: We were instructed to taxi from FBO to '[Runway] 31L via Zulu; hold short approach end [Runway] 22 at Zulu'. We exited the FBO ramp onto Zulu; turned left towards [Runway] 22 and noticed that [Taxiway] Zulu terminates before the approach end of [Runway] 22; and it becomes [Taxiway] Yankee. We discussed this on the flight deck that the taxi instructions should have been clearer because you can't really hold short of [Runway] 22 on Zulu; you would actually either hold short of [Runway] 22 approach on Yankee; or hold short of Yankee on Zulu. In any case; the Captain as PF (Pilot Flying) exercised some good judgement and decided to stop a bit back from Yankee; at least from the sign anyways. It's hard to figure where Zulu actually ended. That way we could respond to Ground if they modified their instructions to hold back further. Whatever is the case with Zulu or Yankee; we stopped and awaited further instructions. We noticed a bizjet (Aircraft Y) landing on [Runway] 4 so we suspected we were being held from crossing the approach end of [Runway] 22 (same as rollout end of [Runway] 4) due to the landing traffic. After a short wait; we heard ground instruct Aircraft Y which was now rolling out to 'give way to Aircraft X; he will be crossing at the end of the runway in front of you'. I cannot recall if the other aircraft acknowledged. The next thing we both heard was 'Aircraft X; cross Runway 22 and continue via Kilo'. I turned all the lights on and the Captain started to move forward. I looked right to clear and noticed the landing Aircraft Y was very close; it seemed to me he was past Bravo and Kilo 2 where I presumed he would have turned off; that his reversers were still deployed; and he was rolling very fast for so close to the end of the runway. I said 'STOP; we're not clear' or words to that effect and the Captain immediately stopped as he was now seeing Aircraft Y appear large in my windshield. It may have been hidden beside my windshield side pillar previously. We both agreed it would not have been pretty had we gone across the runway as it clearly appeared Aircraft Y was landing fast and rolling out long; and more importantly; evidently not giving way to us. After just a few seconds; Ground said 'Aircraft X; you're not moving' and we responded that it was not safe to do so. Ground replied; 'Aircraft Y is giving way to you' or words to that effect; and we replied that wasn't the case. After a few more seconds Aircraft Y exited onto Kilo in front of us; and Ground then instructed us to cross the runway and continue onto Kilo on our taxi to [Runway] 31L. Ground and Tower frequencies were combined per ATIS onto tower frequency 118.7; we were always using it; but when Aircraft Y cleared in front of us and we followed him until we turned left onto Charlie; we never heard him. Our subsequent taxi and departure was uneventful.The confusing or incorrect taxi instructions provided (i.e.; is it Zulu or Yankee to hold short) started us off with noticing ATC peculiarities as we spoke to Ground. The other aircraft not giving way to us; or appearing to do so; was the major cause of this averted conflict. Combining Tower and Ground on one frequency may also have caused some confusion; because the tower cab can hear everything but in the aircraft we can only actively hear the frequency we're currently using.First off; I think our alertness was the link in the chain that prevented an incident (or worse). I think that ATC made a procedural error in directing us to cross in front of the landing traffic without adequate time/distance to do so. I recommend [Company] request an official copy of the tape from the FAA if possible for review and development of lessons learned.
Report_1_Synopsis: CL-300 Flight Crew reported ATC created a runway incursion resulting in a critical ground conflict.

Report_1_Narrative: Cleared to descend via the ZZZZZ2 arrival except maintain 10;000 feet. Initially high; changed descent mode from managed to open and selected 300 knots to get to path with speed protection. However; due to distractions; failed to manage descent appropriately. A few miles from ZZZZZ with a constraint of 12;000 feet from FL190 I noticed we were approaching 12;000 feet rapidly. I asked the FO to request descent to 10;000 feet. We leveled off; but not in time and crossed ZZZZZ several hundred feet below 12;000 feet. ATC did not say anything however this was not safe and not professional airmanship.Distracted with conversation related to COVID and job security instead of flying the aircraft more attentively. Switched descent modes without alerting the PM. Failed to recheck altitude constraint early enough to discover error. Discontinue involved conversations prior to phase of flight changes.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Captain reported an altitude deviation during descent and cited being distracted due having a conversation about COVID-19 and job security.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Troubleshooting; Situational Awareness; Confusion; Communication Breakdown
Report_1_Narrative: Our flight departed from ZZZ enroute to EWY. Clearance was issued as follows: 'CLEARED TO EYW AIRPORT [via SID] FLY TOWER ASSIGNED HEADING THEN AS FILED MAINT 3000FT (ZZZ..ZZZZZ..MTH..EYW..KEYW)'. Established level at our cruise altitude of 14;000 ft. and on our cleared route we were handed off to MIA Center (ZMA). ZMA cleared us Direct to EYW and we proceeded on the new route. During our descent ZMA issued the cross a fix not on our route at 10;000 ft. We believed we heard GINGA as the controller pronunciation had the hard G sound. Looking at the chart the closest intersection with this sound was GIGIH. However; as we now know the fix was JANKA to the South. We requested clarification of the intersection 4 times from ZMA and received no response. Believing the clearance was to a GIGIH we started out turn to the West and continued our decent to meet the restriction. ZMA asked if we wanted to arrive from the North to EYW and we responded we had no preference. ZMA then issued at turn to heading 180 and we continued our descent to 10;000 ft. ZMA handed us off to Navy Key West Approach and the flight continued without incident. Upon landing and researching the charts in more detail we discovered the similar sounding intersections of GIGIH and JANKA in the EYW area; neither of which were on our flight plan. It is my opinion no violations occurred; and all altitude restriction were accomplished as published; however; the Safety of Flight is highest priority at our company and the crew felt this issue should be submitted as an ASAP report to further pilot education and professionalism. Similar sounding intersection names not on our flight plan. Controller pronunciation and being unable to confirm the waypoint.The ability to confirm the proper waypoint spelling with ATC.
Report_1_Synopsis: Small Transport Captain reported a track deviation due similar sounding waypoint names located in the same area.

Report_1_Narrative: On a descent into DEN; we were cleared to descend via the CLASH 3 Arrival. I confirmed that the final altitude was 9;000 ft. and selected it in the altitude window. About 10 miles from EVRLY; we experienced wake turbulence for about five seconds; and then experienced it again. I selected Vertical Speed and leveled off the descent to get above the wake turbulence. After we were clear of the wake turbulence; I selected a 2;000 FPM descent to get back on my vertical path. At that time; we were told to switch to Denver Approach. Upon checking in with Denver Approach they changed our runway to 35L. At this point I was concerned about changing the approach in the FMC. I forgot to re-engage the VNAV. Because I forgot to re-engage the VNAV; the aircraft did not slow down to 250 kts for EVRLY. The aircraft also continued a descent below 12;000 feet.; which was the lowest altitude at TWNSN. The aircraft continue to descend until I notice the deviation. By this time I was leveling at 10;000 feet. and was below the 11;000 feet. altitude required for PNBAL. ATC advised me to slow the 210 knots; and gave me a vector for the final approach to Runway 35L. They also gave me a descent to 9;000 feet. The rest of the arrival went as planned.
Report_1_Synopsis: B737 Captain reported distractions from a wake turbulence encounter on arrival into DEN contributed to altitude and speed deviations.

Report_1_Narrative: The deicing crew at ZZZ briefed myself and the First Officer (F/O) where the deicing was going to take place and we requested FULL AIRCRAFT DEICE with Type 1 and WINGS AND TAIL ANTI ICE with Type 4. After we pushed back and parking brake was set; the QRH was complied with for configuring the airplane for deicing as instructed by the deicing crew. The ice-truck drove past the nose to the left side and disappeared. Approximately; 15 minutes later; the truck rolled up from the right side and told us over the radio that the deicing was completed without giving us the pertinent data that we need like the type of fluid used for the deice and anti-ice. Moreover; we were not given the start time for the anti-icing. The first officer had to ask them for the information even to the point of getting clarification for the type 4 used in the anti-icing. This baffled us! As we tried to figure out what was going on; I asked my F/O if he had heard the sound of the spraying on the fuselage. He said no he really didn't hear it and I didn't hear it. So just to make sure; I asked the F/O to verbally ask if Type 1 was WHOLE FUSELAGE and TYPE 4 FOR WINGS AND TAIL; iceman said YES!  So we got the holdover time; and stated to taxi out but I had my doubt on what was done. As I was telling the F/O that we will need to pullover and do a pre-takeoff check by going in to the cabin to inspect at least the wings; we got a call from the flight attendants telling us that the windows were still glazed over with ice.I decided to return to the gate to do another walk around inspection. When we arrived at the gate at my F/O did the second walk around inspection; he came back angry and furious; and rightly so because the airplane was still ENCASED IN ICE! I too was very angry with the UNSAFE Job the iceman did for us and LIED about it. And please note that there was NO precipitation since we arrived at the airport.
Report_2_Narrative: During the night in ZZZ they had gotten freezing rain; so when we got to the airplane (10 minutes before departure due to the road conditions) we already knew that we had to deice; which my walk around affirmed that. At this point everything was pretty normal except for the fact we were late; (we did not rush nor did I feel rushed) and we had to deice. We ran all checklists and pushed back; we ran the QRH for de-icing and called OPS for deicing/ anti icing; and my exact verbiage was 'parking brake set aircraft configured for de-icing full body wings and tail Type I and wings and tail Type IV' when they were done which looking back; it didn't seem to have taken the usual amount of time; it was way shorter! We finished up with the QRH; started the engines; ran the checklists and started to taxi; to which we may have taxied 100 yards when the FAs (Flight Attendants) called and said that the windows in the back were covered in ice; the CA (Captain) was also listening to this; I than told ground that we needed to stop and work a problem; he stopped the airplane and we discussed the issue and both determined we CANNOT takeoff with ice on the airplane; we both made the decision to gate return and inspect the airplane; we got to the gate ran the parking checklist and they brought up the Jetway; I exited the airplane to do another walk around and discovered the airplane still covered in ice! When I returned to the Jetway the CA was talking to the station manager; I shared what I had seen on the walk around and returned to the flight deck and re-repaired the aircraft for departure; I was not part of the discussion with the station manager or the Chief Pilot; I was briefed by the CA as to what each had said; and the thing that gets me the most is that the Chief Pilot was making excuses for ZZZ Operations; as they 'don't do it very often'! Come to find out the person spraying our aircraft was the stations de-icing trainer!! After all the decisions and a call to dispatch for a new flight plan we pushed back again ran checklists; got property de-iced ( we think and hope) and departed about two and a half hours late for a uneventful rest of the flight.
Report_1_Synopsis: B737 flight crew reported a communications breakdown between flight crew and de-ice crew which created a potentially catastrophic situation.

Report_1_Narrative: We were being vectored from the northwest to the ILS approach and descending to 2;000 ft. when Tower asked if we had the airport in sight. This was my first time in ZZZ and although I thought I saw the airport I was not in a hurry to call it in sight; just to be sure. I verbalized that with the First Officer but he had been there before and was comfortable calling the airport in sight; so I did. Our initial vector would have taken us just outside the Final Approach Fix. However; when Tower issued clearance for the Visual Approach; the First Officer turned to a heading that would take us inside the Final Approach Fix. At the same time; he continued to descend while configuring with flaps (I think at either 10 or 15) and landing gear; and the speed brake extended. As the descent continued; Tower issued an 'Altitude Alert' and instructed us to adjust immediately. I cannot remember the exact verbiage; but there was a mention of our altitude being 1;200 ft. and perhaps something about 'minimum vectoring altitude.' The First Officer immediately adjusted his attitude to level off at around 1;200 ft. and continued to fly towards the runway center line. We were approximately abeam the Final Approach Fix at this point. He then asked for more flaps; ultimately Flaps 30; for the landing. I realized at about that point that he still had the speed brake extended and told him. He immediately stowed the speed brake and intercepted the visual glide path to the runway. I think he asked me at about that point if I was okay to continue. He was on the glide path and stabilized; so I said 'yes.'On landing rollout I noticed what sounded like an open microphone on the Tower frequency. Since there didn't seem to be any other aircraft on the frequency; I suspected it was coming from our aircraft. The Tower made a broadcast to all stations on the frequency that they were broadcasting on an active ATC radio frequency; and that they should cease immediately. When I made the '80 kts.' call out on landing roll; I heard myself over the radio. That confirmed that the First Officer was holding down the microphone button in his grip on the yoke. As soon as he loosened his grip; the transmission stopped.
Report_2_Narrative: I was the pilot flying. Based on the weather reported we briefed the RNAV Arrival to be followed by the ILS Approach. We made special note that we were not to utilize the Autothrottle for the approach due to MEL(Minimum Equipment List) restriction. The arrival went as planned until we were given a vector off the arrival and then direct to the Final Approach Fix and a descent to 2;000 ft. As we were a bit high and fast; the speed brake was being utilized to expedite descent. While proceeding to the Final Approach Fix; the weather was acceptable to proceed visually so we reported field in sight and were cleared for the Visual Approach. Due to the high intercept angle to the Final Approach Fix I turned to establish a more acceptable intercept angle to capture the localizer. My perception looking outside was that we were quite high so asked the Pilot Monitoring to set Touchdown Zone Elevation. I failed to engage Vertical Nav for better situational awareness in relation to my vertical path and relied solely on the visual sight picture until on final. While on a dogleg to final we received an ATC Altitude warning alert telling us that we were below the sector altitude. We were approximately 1;100 ft. just abeam of the Final Approach Fix on a dogleg to final. I then stopped the descent until approaching final approach course and engaging Approach mode for glideslope capture. Continued the Visual Approach to a landing.
Report_1_Synopsis: B737 Flight Crew reported after being cleared for a Visual Approach the Pilot Flying turned toward the airport inside the Final Approach Fix and received a low altitude alert from ATC.

Report_1_Narrative: Not realizing we were planning dangerous goods I requested pushback and in fact began the pushback without the final manifest.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported gate departure without required Hazmat documents.

Report_1_Narrative: We had been vectored off of the WAZKO1 RNAV Arrival toward the final approach course for the RNAV Runway 4 at ELP. We broke out of the overcast around 9;000 ft. and were approaching KANTR at 7;500 feet. There was a lot of ambient light from the city below and the reflection of that light from the overcast above as well as the fresh layer of snow on the surface. Approach cleared us for the approach and gave us 'Direct KANTR; Maintain 7;200 ft. until KANTR;' which I read back; with an emphasis on the '200'. The FO (PF) selected vertical speed mode after I set 7;200 ft. in the altitude preselector and called '7;200 ft. set!'. The published altitude at KANTR is 7;500 feet; which is located above terrain at 5;851 ft. We leveled at 7;200 ft. and she called for Flaps 18; and we joined the final approach course with the runway; and the terrain below in sight since descending out of 9;000 ft. Just then the GPWS System chimed in with 'Terrain! Pull Up!'. The FO dutifully disconnected the autopilot and I told her NOT to go around; as we were on a published segment of the final approach in good VMC (ELP was reporting 10 SM Vis) and I had the terrain in sight the whole time. We were not descending; and we had been level for some time. We landed without incident and taxied to our gate. Upon docking; I asked Ground for the phone number to the folks at approach control. The fellow who answered offered that he was indeed the Controller. I told him what had happened and he said that it was not at all uncommon; and that 7;200 ft. was their Minimum Vectoring Altitude in that sector. I told him that I would be filing a report with respect to the incident; for his own information.If there are other similar incidents here a communique should be distributed to the pilot group.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported GPWS Terrain warning while following ATC clearance at Minimum Vectoring Altitude during approach to ELP airport.

Report_1_Narrative: After deicing the aircraft we taxied to [Runway] 35L. Upon completion of all of our checklists we requested time on the runway to do a 30 second engine run-up for the A319. [Runway] 35L had just been plowed of snow before our taxi onto the runway. The Captain was the Pilot Flying and began to increase the thrust. At about 55% N1 the airplane began to slide and point away from centerline. The Captain tried to steer the airplane using the tiller with great difficulty. The aircraft rolled forward about 1;000-1;500 ft. I called Tower and notified them that we had a steering problem and requested to exit the runway. We decided to return to the gate to have the aircraft nose wheel inspected. The runway; although recently plowed; played a significant factor in our situation. Also; the recommended 70% N1 engine run-up per our [Operating Manual] is a lot of power to control in icing conditions on the ground. I think that the engine run-up procedure approved by Airbus can lead to very problem when operating on surfaces during icing conditions.
Report_2_Narrative: After deicing we were cleared to lineup and wait on 35L and to conduct our engine run up. I ran up both engines symmetrically to 70% N1 [following the SOP]. It was then that the right main gear lost traction and the aircraft turned aggressively to the left. I immediately retarded both throttles to idle and used nose wheel steering to regain the centerline. There was nose wheel scrubbing felt. I then cleared the runway and returned to the gate for a maintenance inspection of the nose wheel. The factors were the unprecedented DFW weather. Although the runway was freshly cleaned and we were the first aircraft to use it. There was obviously ice in spots that were hard to see at night. The light takeoff weight of 116;000 lbs coupled with the high power setting for the run up played roles in the incident. Although I had operated two previous flight in and out of DFW that day the runway conditions changed rapidly. I felt that the runway had been freshly cleaned moments before I took to the runway and that it would be suitable for the run up. I will continue to be vigilant in inclement weather conditions. I have gained a newer understanding for the power of the engine on an A319.
Report_1_Synopsis: A319 flight crew reported experiencing momentary loss of aircraft control during the initiation of takeoff roll due to ice on the runway.

Report_1_Narrative: Significant freezing rain event the day of this flight led to 1/4 to 1/2 inch clear ice covering the entire aircraft. There was no attempt to de-ice the aircraft prior to the crew arriving for preflight. The engine inlets needed to be de-iced prior to block out so that we could start the engines after block out. This de-icing of the inlets took a considerable amount of time due to the significant accumulation of ice in the bottom of the fan section of both engines. By the time we were able to block out (2h 39min late) and taxi to the remote de-ice pad A; a short distance from our ramp; the de-ice trucks had run out of fluid and trucks needed to also be refueled. Another significant delay ensued. Almost an hour after block out; de-icing began. The entire airplane was de-iced with Type I fluid since there was no precipitation falling. Aircraft was fully de-iced and inspected by the de-ice team. We then proceeded to our departure runway and prepared for takeoff. The reason for this safety report became clear as soon as we began the initial climb segment immediately after takeoff. We began shedding ice from the entire fuselage and this shedding continued through 12;000 ft.; approximately 7-10 minutes after takeoff. All four crew members could hear the ice departing the aircraft and felt the airframe vibrations as large chunks of ice tumbled down the length of the fuselage. All four crew members each have 20-30 years of aviation experience; and no one had ever experienced anything like it. In my 30 plus years of heavy transport category aircraft operation I have never experienced this kind of ice shedding event. I believe that the de-ice procedure was completely ineffective for this amount of clear ice that covered the entire aircraft. With that amount ice being shed from the aircraft for that long; we had a significant amount of Ice still adhering to the airframe when we took off. The engine vibration was well within limits even during the climb out and so the crew chose to continue the flight. I was concerned about airframe damage from that amount of ice departing the aircraft; and because of that concern; I recorded an AML entry asking that the aircraft be inspected for damage after arrival in ZZZZ. [Cause was] inadequate de-icing for the amount of clear ice that was adhering to the airframe. Also the de-ice crew was possibly unable to see the ice after de-icing; since it was clear ice and fully covering the aircraft; and the airplane was still wet from the de-icing fluid used. [Suggest] re-evaluate the process of de-icing when so much clear ice is adhering to the airframe.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Captain reported inadequate deicing procedures resulted in departure with significant airframe icing.

Report_1_Narrative: Upon completion of work on the aircraft; we boxed up our three pieces of tooling with no HAZMAT to return with us on the first ZZZ1 flight.  We attached the SLI (Shipper's Letter of Instructions) labels as required and moved them to the far left of the baggage cart that we were provided. We then moved the three hard containers with visible HAZMAT labels and no return paperwork on them to the far right of the baggage cart. We then took our escort over to the baggage cart and showed her the form and explained to her that the three boxes on the left of the cart with our tools and the SLI labels needed to be sent on the first ZZZ1 flight in the morning; and the three hard containers on the right side of the cart were labeled HAZMAT and needed to be sent through the freight house for HAZMAT shipping.  We then asked her if we needed to move the cart to a secure area and she said to leave it where it was.  We again; reiterated the importance of making sure the HAZMAT items were not shipped with our tooling; and asked her to make sure and leave a turnover if she was not going to be available in the morning. We still had to scan paperwork to Maintenance Control; and I failed to give her a copy of step 3A after confirmation from Maintenance Control that they received all documents.  After going through security in the morning we asked the Operations Agent on the ZZZ1 flight to confirm that our three boxes of tooling and only our three boxes of tooling were on the plane.  Due to TSA requirements; we are unable to go down to the ramp to confirm or review shipping procedures once we have been screened.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Contract Maintenance person reported improper shipment of Hazmat material due to a communication breakdown between maintenance and the shipping personnel.

Report_1_Narrative: This airport's rotating beacon is located 1.4 nm NE of the airport; well outside the airport boundary. Though very non-standard; it is not mentioned in the Flight Information Publication (FLIP) or depicted on the IPP plates. Even the Green Bay sectional could show the correct position; instead of the standard symbology which implies the beacon would be found on the airport.Only the Jeppesen instrument charts depict it accurately.This secret non-standard placement could result in disorientation and worse; at least give pilots a chance by publishing it.
Report_1_Synopsis: Pilot reported the rotating beacon located 1.4 NM NE of IMT airport is at a non-standard location and could potentially result in pilot disorientation.  Pilot also stated the beacon location is not mentioned in the Flight Information Publication; nor depicted in the IPP plates.

Report_1_Narrative: There are currently no NOTAMs published for N40.Upon landing I see that the runway is not plowed full width; and there are large snow piles on either side of the runway that could result in an impact with low wing aircraft. The taxi way snow piles are high enough that low wing aircraft will strike their wing on them.Also the AWOS-3 has been INOP for at least a year and I've never seen a NOTAM.Someone could easily strike a wing or flap on the snow piles during takeoff or landing and end up in an accident. The problem is caused by the airport management's ongoing failure to publish NOTAMs. N40 has forty (40) separate owners. which may lead to a 'if everyone is in charge; no one is in charge' situation. To prevent this in the future someone needs to tell N40 airport management to keep their NOTAMs up to date. If there are no plans to fix the AWOS then it needs to be removed from the chart.
Report_1_Synopsis: Pilot reported concerns with the lack of NOTAM publications at N40 airport for known issues. Pilot stated the AWOS-3 has been inoperable for at least a year and has never been NOTAMed.

Report_1_Narrative: There were snow drifts on the taxiway and runway.  Due to the snow; upon climb out; pilots side landing gear door would not close completely.  I cycled the gear several times to try and clear the snow to allow the gear to close fully.  We were unsuccessful getting the gear to close; so I decided to land and see if we could resolve the issue.  Feeling the departure airport was unsafe due to the runway conditions; I decided to divert to ZZZ1 to assess the situation.  I am familiar with the airport and they have a Tower and other facilities.  Roughly 20-30 minutes after ATC gave us our clearance to ZZZ1 (while we were at FL270); there was an explosion like sound and all cabin pressure immediately departed.  This blow out knocked off all of our headsets.  Understanding that we had a cabin de-presserization; I immediately pulled the power back to idle; dropped the landing gear and nosed the plane over for rapid descent.  Once we were going down; I changed our squawk to 7700 (knowing that this was our only form of communication with the outside world); set the autopilot to level off at 12;500 feet and re-engaged the autopilot in case I were to black out.  I didn't grab for my oxygen mask because at the time we were already coming down at a rate of over 8;000 ft/min and the wind/cold and just chaotic nature of the cabin; I didn't feel comfortable taking my hands off of the controls.  I also didn't go for my headset for similar reasons; as well as there being so much noise; I knew there would be no way for me to hear ATC let alone they be able to hear me. After we were able to level off at 12;500 feet; I looked for the closest airport (ZZZ2); brought up their weather and loaded the approach we wanted and turned to the appropriate heading.  I opened the inertial separator; turned on our landing and wigwag lights and decided to leave the gear down for the remainder of the flight.  I didn't want to accidentally add any other complications to our situation.  After what seemed like the longest approach in history; we finally touched down safely at ZZZ2; where I taxied the plane to the already waiting emergency vehicles.
Report_1_Synopsis: Lancair Evolution pilot reported landing gear door failed to close followed by pressurization failure resulting in emergency descent and landing.

Report_1_Narrative: Aircraft is non-electrical with no starter; and based at a private airpark home.  Aircraft was tied down at tail and triple chocked. Preflighted and prepared for a normal start and flight. Normal start; but as I was walking around wing to the cockpit engine power increased more quickly than expected after start. I was unable to reach the cockpit to shut the engine down before the chocks gave way followed by the tiedown stake pulling out of the ground. Aircraft traveled unoccupied down sloping yard and hit a ditch coming to rest on the taxiway; resulting in landing gear damage and propeller striking ground and pavement and engine shutdown. No injuries or property damage occurred. In retrospect I have always been careful to secure the aircraft for start correctly with triple chocks and tie down. It's possible; on this start; I may not have tightened the throttle friction lock fully which may have allowed the throttle position to travel partially forward after start. The chocks in front of all three tires started to strain; then failed and the aircraft rolled forward as I was moving around the wing. The last available restraint was a tiedown at the tailwheel position. Momentum and some slack in the tie down rope caused the tiedown stake to pull loose from the ground as the slack was taken up. The downhill slope of the yard added to the acceleration before impact with the ditch. I should have double checked the throttle setting and friction lock to make sure that throttle position would not change. The increase in power would not have happened.
Report_1_Synopsis: Pilot reported that after a prop start the aircraft jumped the chocks and separated from the single tiedown.

Report_1_Narrative: I am a CFI and I was flying a training mission with my client who is a licensed private pilot working on transition training to a new model aircraft (Aircraft X). This was my client's first flight in a Aircraft X. The lesson started with a detailed preflight; followed by a similarly detailed run-up. Once ready; we departed Palo Alto Airport for a familiarization flight in a practice area south and west of the airport. During our time in the practice area we maintained visual separation from another aircraft in the training area (each trying to stay in our own section of the training area; while we also maintained appropriate distances from scattered clouds in the area; and staying below the Bravo which starts at 4;000 in that area. During this time; we stayed in contact with the Tower having asked them for advisories during our training mission.After approximately 1 hour of Hobbs time (including the taxi and detailed run-up); we copied ATIS Quebec and informed the Tower that we would like to return to the field for the option; and closed traffic. We were instructed to fly over Stanford and enter the pattern for left traffic for Runway 31. We made our way as instructed and entered the left downwind for Runway 31. The Tower then told us that we were number 4 cleared to land; and that the traffic that we were following was roughly abeam us in the opposite downwind. We acknowledged the instruction and reported negative contact with the traffic to follow. Meanwhile; the Tower was very busy with numerous other traffic entering; leaving; and in the pattern. We were then told to extend our downwind; that we had extensive extensions into Moffett Field's airspace (it is very common for Palo Alto to have and use extensions into Moffett's airspace - this extension was even further than usual) and that the Tower would call our base. While extending; we saw our traffic to follow turn base and then final. But we continued downwind since the Tower said that they would call our base.Moments later; the Tower instructed us to fly 'straight towards the 31 numbers' which was a bit strange since we were so far from the runway (probably at least 3 miles at this point). But the frequency was very busy and it didn't seem to make sense (or even possible) to ask to verify the instruction. We turned left onto a long final and proceeded towards the runway. We were holding approximately 1;000 feet (+/- since my student was flying and this was their first time in the aircraft) this entire time on downwind; base and long final.Not too long after we turned long final; the Tower told us to climb 500 feet immediately for traffic. I immediately took the controls of the plane; quickly (re)checked nearby traffic on the G1000 MFD (with ADS-B traffic) and did a visual scan for traffic as I went full forward on the throttle; prop; and mixture and pitched the nose back for the climb. The quick scan of traffic (visual and ADS-B) did not indicate any traffic below or next to us; but it did indicate one aircraft above our altitude but not in the immediate vicinity. None-the-less; we tried to visually acquire the above traffic as we climbed.Moments later; the tower told us to stop our climb immediately and to turn right and fly directly towards Leslie Salt. Again; we immediately complied with the Tower's instructions as we continued to try to acquire and track any immediate threats visually. Just then; we saw another aircraft pass directly above us; slightly off to our left side; in very close proximity to our aircraft. The Tower then instructed us to make a right turn back to final for landing.I've been flying at PAO for nearly XX years; so I am familiar with how busy it can get. But even with that experience; it was particularly busy at this time. One of the things that I think was a factor in this situation was a partial callsign conflict. Our aircraft callsign ended in [--] while the callsign of another aircraft on frequency at the time ended in [--]. In fact; it is possible that the aircraft above us when we were instructed to climb; and the one that nearly collided with moments later; was the aircraft ending in [--]. My theory is that the instruction to climb was actually intended for Aircraft Y and not Aircraft X; and that the controller tried to stop our climb as soon as he noticed the error. Unfortunately; these problems were all compounded by the heavy radio traffic making it virtually impossible to verify instructions; especially in a timely fashion.My client and I replayed this whole incident both while still in the air; and during debrief on the ground; and we are both quite certain that we responded to our correct callsign and that this wasn't a case of us improperly (and unintentionally) responding to someone else's callsign. I wanted to use the G1000 PLAYback feature to check/verify the radio call; but; unfortunately; the radio traffic was so heavy that there was no way to use the replay feature successfully. I have replayed this entire situation a number of times trying to analyze what I could have / should have done differently to avoid getting this close to another aircraft. Unfortunately; I haven't really come up with a good answer given the details of the situation.Given that the only nearby traffic that I could observe at the time was the one above us; I could have held my attitude of 1;000 feet; in defiance of the Tower Controller's instruction; until I could verify that the climb instruction was for us; or until I could verify another nearby traffic threat. But this seems like a very bad idea. I have always operated that when ATC gives you an immediate traffic avoidance instruction that you follow that instruction immediately. There could have very well been another nearby aircraft that I was unaware of that was an even more of a threat that I was currently unaware of. Hence my immediate response as instructed.I believe that the similar sounding callsigns; heavy radio traffic; and large number of aircraft operating in the class Delta; all contributed to the confusion for all parties. I know that it made our task (mine and my client) much more difficult; and I believe that you could hear that in the voice and instructions of the Tower Controller and the other pilots. After landing; we opted to terminate rather than continue pattern operations. Once back in the flying club; we talked with another CFI and student who was flying (and returning to the airport) at the same time. I asked them if they heard the Tower 'trying kill us' and the CFIs response was 'yeah; the Tower Controller was clearly overwhelmed!' We asked him if he heard any indications that we responded to the wrong callsign. His response was 'no' and that; again; he thought that whole problem was that the Tower Controller was simply overwhelmed by the overall situation.I know that Palo Alto is an FAA Training Tower; and I'm fully understanding and supportive of that. But perhaps in this case maybe there should have been additional oversight of Tower operations; or at least a senior controller stepping in before the controller got too overwhelmed.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Instructor reported frequency congestion; ATC overwhelmed; similar call signs; resulted in a NMAC.

Report_1_Narrative: I reviewed the weather at approximately XA00 hours; including visibility; winds; and turbulence.  When I reviewed this weather; the winds forecast for the ZZZ airport was indicated to be 18-25 knots; and mild turbulence was indicated through both visual and graphical reviews using the ForeFlight products.  At 1 1/2 hours later; two passengers and I boarded our SF50 Vision Jet and rechecked the winds at the ZZZ airport.  The winds had held steady at the previous levels.  We decided that we continue with our planned trip; understanding that the winds were mainly straight down the direction of the runway.  We filed for an altitude en-route at 11;000 feet; believing that it would be high enough to prevent any issues that we've encountered on the numerous trips we've flown to ZZZ with respect to turbulence.  We've flown over 100 missions into the ZZZ area over the past six months.  The takeoff from ZZZ1 was routine and without incident.  We climbed up to 11;000 feet without incident and no issues with turbulence.  Our issues began when we transferred to the TRACON frequency. Twice during the turbulence; we attempted to review the weather using the GTC 2 system within the aircraft and were having a difficult time stabilizing our inputs with our fingers; even using the bezel to support our hands and use our thumbs to do so was challenging.  During one of the larger turbulent events; the autopilot disconnect was engaged by the second pilot in the right seat; which we were immediately able to re-engage as the buttons on the aircraft's autopilot is not electronic but tactile.  Once we had the autopilot back engaged; we referred back to the GTC 2 to re-engage the flight plan and selected the approach that was already listed on the display; which was the visual approach to Runway XXL; using the VOR as a descend and entrance point.  We had not noticed that the VNAV aspect of the approach had been selected when we re-engaged the auto-pilot; at which point we were now consistently in moderate to severe turbulence.  During this period; the TRACON controller called us and simply said 'Why are you descending.'   We told them about the visual approach being loaded in and began to describe what our corrective action would be -- however; in that split second; we hit the single most severe turbulence I've ever felt in an aircraft.  The turbulence threw the aircraft up; then aggressively left; which then dropped aggressively; throwing everybody to the header of the cabin.  My headset  (a Bose A20) was broken on the upper hinge; which struck the upper panel and broke loose my supplemental oxygen mask; breaking the clamp.   Objects in the cabin flew forward and up.  At this point; I immediately placed the aircraft in recovery mode; with full power; level wings and attempted to contact ATC to advise that I needed an emergency descent.  In VFR conditions; I noticed that I was over the mountain and switched to [next] frequency; and immediately advised the same and was given the approval to descend to 6;000 feet with a distinct heading.   I was then advised other aircraft were experiencing similar issues with turbulence and had gone missed into ZZZ. On the new heading and altitude; I began a full systems check of the aircraft; landing gear cycle; ailerons; flaps and review the fuel system.   I advised the TRACON controller that we were fine and that the oxygen masks had been deployed.   The controller provided be vectors; then cleared us for the VOR approach into ZZZ.  We flew the approach; we decided about three miles from the airport to abandon our approach and return to ZZZ1; in which we were given vectors and an approach back into the ZZZ1 airport without incident. Many things happened on this trip; almost in serial.  Without a doubt; the level of forecasted and reported turbulence was well above what we had seen using ForeFlight; or based on our prior experience.  When recovering from the several avionics disruptions (auto-pilot switch shut-offs; etc.); we had maintained a fairly vigilant response to restoring our programmed flight activity - until the turbulence began to get violent.   In a similar environment; I would ask for a 180-degree turn to remove myself and the aircraft from the events that led to deteriorating events with even lesser conditions.  Our corrective action after getting clearance for the emergency descent was sound; but it should have never been necessary if we had more carefully judged the degree of the turbulence; which had caused us not immediately to identify the VNAV programming into the GTC 2.  The three of us debriefed the flight in detail; including a review of the ForeFlight products to identify in greater clarity about Airmets (Tango) and how we could set up levels of automation that we could defer in order to maintain more positive control of the aircraft.   In reviewing our training materials; we reviewed the SF50 process on how to accept lower levels of automation during events that require higher pilot concentration and how this aids in the better situational awareness in events that we experienced on this date.
Report_1_Synopsis: SF-50 Vision Jet Pilot reported experiencing extreme turbulence resulted in loss of aircraft control.

Report_1_Narrative: A VFR flight was to be flown from BFL to ZZZ for the purpose of repositioning an aircraft for company business the following day. This flight was operated under Part 91 pursuant to all applicable FAR's and company SOP's. The intended route took the pilot from BFL to ZZZ2 to ZZZZZ to ZZZZZ1 then direct ZZZ at an altitude of 9;500. The pilot obtained a briefing via Foreflight at XA:21 local time for an intended departure time of XA:45. Upon reviewing the briefing; it was decided current conditions would allow for the safe operation of the flight. The pilot departed BFL at XA:45 local time and climbed straight out in VMC conditions to an altitude of 095. Cloud conditions in the valley were broken at various altitudes below 8;000 feet. As the flight progressed towards ZZZ2; the pilot then proceeded direct to ZZZ3. As the pilot approached the ZZZZZ2 intersection; traffic could be viewed on ADSB traveling opposite direction on the V197 (Northwest) at 10;500. This traffic was indicating a ground speed ranging from 50-70 knots confirming the PIC's suspicion of stronger than forecasted winds aloft. As the pilot continued southeast bound; it was apparent that the cloud conditions below and ahead were worsening and the PIC initiated a climb to 11;500 MSL. upon reaching 10;300 MSL just south of ZZZZZ3 intersection; the pilot turned east to avoid building clouds. During this moment; the pilot encountered a 2;000 FPM downdraft which they countered with a pitch up attitude to achieve Vy. Once established at Vy; the rate of descant had slowed to 700 FPM. Knowing conditions improved to the west; the PIC initiated a turn back to BFL and informed ATC of the intentions as well as the conditions. Upon receiving a handoff to BFL Approach; the pilot informed them of their intentions and that it may be necessary to notify ATC. As the ground speed began to drop below 45 knots still in a descent at Vy; the PIC saw a situation where the aircraft would not be able to stay above the cloud layer and safely away from rising terrain to the west. The PIC then informed ATC that they were turning southbound; notified ATC due to weather and squawked 7700. As this decision was made; the PIC was experiencing a severe downdraft where positive control of the aircraft's altitude was difficult to maintain. Upon descending to an altitude of 6;500' MSL; the pilot encountered a large updraft and used this to climb to an altitude of 12;00 MSL which allowed exceptional terrain separation. The pilot flew southbound; where it was visibly better weather and began to request PIREP's from ATC for a VFR field east of the terrain knowing that the area east offered high ceilings and lower terrain. ATC informed the pilot of a large hole in the cloud layer on a 090 heading and suggested the pilot land WJF. ATC then asked the pilot if they were able to accept a 090 heading and it was accepted. The pilot then sighted the large opening; measuring roughly 25-30 nm x. 5 nm and began a decent in VMC conditions. As the pilot descended below the surrounding cloud layer's bases (5;700 feet MSL); they verified ZZZ4 in sight and were given a handoff. Upon assessing the situation; the PIC decided against landing at ZZZ4 and determined an emergency declaration was no longer needed; relayed intentions to ATCT at ZZZ4 and were handed back to Joshua Approach. The declaration was canceled with them and the flight continued to ZZZ1 for a safe landing. Upon landing; the PIC contacted the Director of Safety for the company and informed them of the events that occurred. It was decided that the pilot made appropriate inflight decisions to ensure the maximum safety of flight. Further reviewing the events that took place; the pilot decided to reread the briefing to determine if any significant signs of these conditions were missed. No information was found to be omitted during the PIC's decision to conduct the flight. Numerous other aircraft had flown the same area throughout the day and encountered conditions well within the PIC's comfort; conditions were not reported outside of VFR regulations at departure; or at arrival. The only adverse weather reported was IFR at TSP to the north east of the intended route and winds aloft in that area in excess of 45 Knots. Going forward; the PIC will study material specific to the safe operation of a single engine aircraft over mountainous terrain to better be able to determine when such adverse conditions may be found and what to do differently when they are encountered. An action that could have been utilized by the PIC that was not was to request an IFR clearance east of the position where it encountered the first sign of severe downdrafts and flown via radar vectors to an area that was VMC away from rising terrain.
Report_1_Synopsis: General Aviation Pilot reported encountering turbulence and downdrafts which exceeded aircraft capability and controllability; resulted in emergency divert.

Report_1_Narrative: Upon pushback from ZZZ Gate 1; it was soon apparent the Pushback Crew was experiencing a problem. They said nothing but it was increasingly clear the Tug was sliding as well as the aircraft not proceeding in a direction I would expect. I tried asking the Driver if there was a problem but did not receive an answer via wireless headset. When his Tug was starting to jackknife; I decided to use my brakes to stop the aircraft. By this time; the Tug came very close to impacting the aircraft on my side. I later learned that his headset was working; but he was trying to talk to the other Ramp Agents instead and not me. I also believe he was cognitively overwhelmed with the unexpected situation as that same phenomena (not responding to me) continued later when we attempted to another push after re-attaching the tow bar/Tug. The First Officer was also adding his input; which was not helping the situation with communication. It was a communications mess. We called the station to inform them of the situation and eventually a Ramp Supervisor came out and took over. We then discussed the option of attempting to move the aircraft to another part of the ramp where it was known to be less than nil braking. Going back to the same gate would only have been to an area of known poor/nil control. We eventually got to an area where the Ramp Agents could safely walk and feel that the ramp was in better condition and where other aircraft were not experiencing any problems.When I landed approximately an hour prior in a different aircraft; my taxi to Gate 2 took me to an area where I lost all steering and braking control for about five seconds. We immediately notified this on Ops frequency; and at least one other Crew stated they experienced the same. Luckily; we slid to an area where I regained control and then carefully proceeded to the gate when the aircraft performed adequately. I then called Dispatch via my cell phone immediately after block in. He said he would pass it on to the supervisor; but I did not hear any apparent immediate concern. Instead; he said I needed to alert the Station; as it is their job to manage that info (I was really puzzled that our Dispatch gave me that answer). I eventually found the Ops Agent and wanted to make sure the Station had this information; as I was very concerned that others could experience worse.Q1: What does it take for a Pilot to state before any real concern is expressed by those managing our operation? Was poor or nil braking not a big enough concern?Q2: Why had nothing been done to correct the situation or at least alert other Crews that some areas were okay but others were NIL? Or stop the operation?Q3: Why would a Push Crew try to fix this problem without getting any other assistance or guidance? I could see they were guessing and even willing to just leave us there as they told us to try to taxi out of it. They even tried to tow us forward on the re-attempt with our engines running. They were completely overwhelmed; which gave me even greater concern.Q4: As Crews; we have no accurate resources (ZZZ is a joke as it is often old and/or inaccurate) to tell us real time conditions on other parts of the airport other than asking Ground Control (which I did). I was concerned that everything was starting to freeze over; and I did not want to the PIREP stating I was in NIL or off the taxiway later on. Without having routine freezing rain experience; how can I know how quickly conditions can go from good to bad?Q5: What does it take for a pause or stop in our operation? Damage? Injury? Taxiway departure? It seems like we just continue pushing with no apparent oversight. That is not a comforting feeling nor does it give me much confidence our system has mechanisms to protect me before getting in a terrible spot.I would appreciate answers to these questions and would like to know if anyone in Headquarters feels this situation was acceptable or not?
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported that during pushback the tug began sliding and the Captain applied brakes to stop the aircraft; avoiding a collision. Captain expressed concern that ramp conditions were poor and that company operations were not properly addressing the safety issues.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Troubleshooting; Confusion; Situational Awareness; Time Pressure
Report_1_Narrative: Jeppesen plate ILS 5 ORF. Note 3 towards top of page states: Glideslope unusable for coupled approaches below 744 ft. In minimums section box note 1 states: RVR 18 with Flight Director or Autopilot or HUD to DA. How can I use the Autopilot to DA when I'm not allowed to use the autopilot to DA!
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Captain reported confusion while looking at the special instructions for this approach.

Report_1_Narrative: Pushed away from gate. Started taxing in ZZZ alley when I got a call from #1 Flight Attendant; (FA); that there were First Class; FC; passengers that were not wearing face coverings after being told to wear them by the FAs. Stopped the aircraft and made a very 'To the point' PA that any non-compliance with Flight Attendant instructions; particularly pertaining to facial coverings; would have 'un-favorable' consequences. I had already made it clear that facial coverings were required while on-board during my 'welcome aboard' PA. Conferred with FAs that my second PA was successful; and we continued taxi and takeoff. Once established in cruise; the FAs informed me that they were having problems with FC passengers willfully being non-compliant regarding wearing a facial covering after being advised as such multiple times by at least 2 different FAs. My FAs had even switched working positions in order to try to de-escalate the situation and convince the passengers to comply. I commenced communication with Dispatch and relayed the situation with advisement to contact customer representatives. Shortly thereafter; due not only to non-mask wearing; but also; disruptive behavior by passengers requested to be re-seated in Main Cabin. I further relayed this information to Dispatch. It was at this point the FAs gave the notification of passenger misconduct warning. Shortly thereafter passenger started harassing my FAs with constant cornering them in the FC galley and demanding trivial items. At this point; even after a tremendous amount of patience; de-escalation attempts and warnings by the FAs; and with building harassment and aggressiveness being demonstrated by passengers; I notified Dispatch that we would be diverting to ZZZ1. We landed at ZZZ1 non-eventfully; without being overweight and without declaring an emergency. Passengers were removed from the aircraft. We departed ZZZ1 and arrived in ZZZZ uneventfully. Please allow me to acknowledge my FAs for their display of 'Consummate Professionalism' during this flight. They were tireless in their attempts to de-escalate the situation in hopes of precluding a diversion. I would also like to acknowledge the support of Dispatch and company as reflective of the number of communications that were made prior to our diversion. And last; but certainly not least; I would like to acknowledge the expert airmanship demonstrated by my First Officer during our extremely busy diversion as well as throughout the rest of a very long day. Should you need additional information from me regarding this diversion; please don't hesitate to contact me.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported passengers were unruly and not complying with face mask policy despite multiple warnings by the crew resulting in a diversion; and removal of the passengers.

Report_1_Narrative: On approach into MCO; the Captain identified a drone off our port side as we were landing [Runway] 18R. I was the pilot flying; had no visual on the drone; but was advised of it.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported an airborne conflict with a drone during approach to MCO airport.

Report_1_Narrative: A321 TOGA (takeoff/go-around switch) takeoff with APU on. Pouring rain. While climbing through approx 18;000 ft; first one; then other flight attendants called to say they smelled a burning rubber smell in cabin but could not see smoke. Passengers were also complaining. We smelled deice fluid in cockpit (plane had flown from ZZZ1 to ZZZ); but otherwise we kept talking with them to see if it would dissipate. While still discussing a return to ZZZ; first one; then two passengers had trouble breathing and the flight attendants made a PA for a doctor on board. At this point we felt we needed to return to ZZZ for an overweight landing. We notified and coordinated with ATC; Dispatch; and ZZZ OPS to return and have paramedics at the gate. The cause was unknown; but aircraft did have an MEL for avionics cooling extract fan that required it to remain in override. Perhaps this could have contributed to burning smell or a different load on air conditioning.
Report_2_Narrative: The Captain (CA) and I noticed a smell in the flight deck while in the climb; roughly around 10;000 feet.  The FAs (flight attendants) called climbing through flight level 180 stating they smell an odor in the cabin.  The FAs also stated some passengers were complaining about the odor.   The Captain requested the flight attendants to call back in 10 minutes and state if the smell is dissipating.  The FAs call back shortly stating several passengers are having difficulty breathing.  At that time the Captain made the decision to return to the ZZZ.  I took over as Pilot Flying and ATC communications. I requested to return to the ZZZ and notified ATC for an overweight landing.  At that time the aircraft weighed roughly 180;000 lbs.  The CA took over Pilot Flying on the arrival shortly before joining the approach to runway.  The aircraft weighed approximately 177;000 lbs on landing.  When we arrived at the gate paramedics attended to several passengers who were having difficulties breathing. [Possible cause or related issue]; we were relatively heavy; had a slight tailwind and the runway was wet.  The TPS (takeoff performance system) called for config 2; TOGO; APU OFF.  As a measure of safety the CA decided to leave the APU and APU bleeds on.  I concurred.  The aircraft's extract fan was also MEL'd (MEL 21-05a).  The CA and I both felt the odor mostly resembled anti-icing fluid.  Though we also discussed the possibly the inoperative extract fan or the APU usage on takeoff was the cause of the odor.  But mostly we thought it was anti-icing fluid.  Once we realized passengers and the cabin crew were being affected the decision was made to return to ZZZ which resulted in an overweight landing.
Report_1_Synopsis: A321 flight crew reported a fumes event during climb resulting in a return to the departure airport.

Report_1_Narrative: At 800 feet AGL; clicked autopilot off for a visual landing. At 500 ft.; FO called 'Stable; cleared to land Runway XX Center.' I replied 'Landing.' Between 500 and 400 feet AGL tried to make small lateral correction with aileron but aileron movement was limited. Used a touch of rudder for correction. Clicked autopilot button again and crossed checked then confirmed that 'Flight Director' was displayed in PFD. Landed uneventfully but elevator movement was very heavy in flare. After landing at taxi speed; I tried to move the yoke left and right and there was very limited movement. The First Officer tried as well with the same result. We checked the Flight Control and Hydraulic Displays and both were normal.I considered a go-around but quickly [determined] a go around would be extremely difficult with big power changes and limited flight control capability. The flight path was set up to touch down in the landing zone on speed so I elected to land.Unsure what caused the flight controls to be limited. After landing; I debriefed Maintenance in the cockpit and put a detailed write up in the logbook.
Report_1_Synopsis: B777-200 Captain reported aileron flight control stiff during landing and limited movement after landing.

Report_1_Narrative: On initial climbout of ZZZ off Runway XXC we experienced loss of power shortly after passing 400 feet and received the 'Landing gear' aural warning. I double checked the gear handle and verified gear position; then verified N1 rollback; momentarily thinking we had dual engine failure. FO exclaimed startle; I replied 'fly the plane'. FO disconnected auto throttle; brought the thrust back up to takeoff position. We momentarily lost altitude and airspeed as Startle and surprise delayed our recognition slightly. Timing of the event was before flap retraction so we were near flap over speed during recognition and recovery; I said 'watch the speed pitch up pitch up' until flaps were retracted. FO later indicated his flight director was not giving correct indications for phase of flight. FO was able to recognize and manually control the aircraft; resuming normal climb out. Once the aircraft was under control; auto pilot and auto throttle engaged normally and no further anomalies were experienced.Unknown; weather was stormy; with moderate turbulence and lightning flashes in vicinity; in full IMC.We teach hand on thrust levers at all times during arrival and landing phase; but not during takeoff...had the FO had physical contact with the thrust levers during the climb; the AT retarding would have been instantly detected. I recommend the same procedure is taught for takeoff as is for landing...one hand on the thrust levers.
Report_2_Narrative: After checking everything was normal we lined up on runway XXC in ZZZ. We verified our automation was in the correct mode including TO; ROLL; and FLCH were verified on our FMA as well as the crosshair flight director was up. As I advanced thrust the auto throttles took and the captain confirmed that ATTCS armed and we had normal TO thrust. at 80 knots while verifying the speed I saw the AT were in their normal HOLD mode. At this point everything was completely normal. When I went to rotate and was transitioning in the instruments I noticed that the FD had switched during the roll to the diamond mode which is supposed to happen at 1000'AGL. (Latter the captain confirmed that there's was normal). I had a normal rotation and pitched towards a normal takeoff attitude disregarding the flight director. At approximately 400 AGL the auto throttles commanded idle thrust suddenly. The startle and surprise nature of this took a second to process where we lost approximately 50 feet. At this point I disconnected the auto throttles and set climb power. The automation was still not working correctly including the flight director. Once we climbed through sterile we turned on the auto-throttles and they worked throughout the flight but we watched them very carefully and called Maintenance writing up the experience on the ground. The cause is unknown. before Takeoff we both verified we were in the correct automation modes. Once in cruise flight we verified all out take-off date and departure limits were set correctly and they were. Contributing factors to the loss of altitude was the thunderstorms in the vicinity; night; and moderate turbulence. More effective startle and surprise training in the sims. We are taught to keep both hands on the yoke throughout departure I think at 400 feet though 10;000 we should be guarding the thrust levers like we do on approach to landing.
Report_1_Synopsis: EMB 170/175 flight crew reported a momentary loss of control and altitude when the autothrottles (AT) went to idle thrust just after takeoff. The crew disconnected the AT; regained control; and continued the flight.

Report_1_Narrative: I was landing Runway XX at ZZZ.  It was a normal centerline approach to landing.  As I touched down; the nose gear seemed to touch before it should have; as if the nose gear strut was in an extended rather than a normal (compressed) position.  Within moments of touchdown; the aircraft darted quickly to the left of Runway XX;  I lost directional control of the aircraft. The aircraft came to an abrupt stop at the side of the runway. No one was injured in this incident.
Report_1_Synopsis: Commercial Single Pilot reported loss of directional control during landing.

Report_1_Narrative: After detailed pre-flight inspection according to manufacturer checklist; we noticed that both fuel tanks are full; samples from each fuel sump and sump under the engine are clear; we checked the color - blue color for 100LL; there was no water or other contaminants; oil level was in the operational limits for our airplane; and we decided that airplane is in the condition to make a safe flight. After listening the ATIS and getting all necessary information about the airport; we contacted Clearance Delivery requesting VFR Flight to NW (northwest) to our practice area; and after that Ground Control for taxi instruction.We completed the runup at the runup area next to Runway XX; as instructed by Ground Control; following every step on the checklist. During the runup we didn't find any issues with the airplane; magneto check was within the manufacturer limits; oil pressure and temperature were ''in green'; engine was working and responding normally like any other day. After completing runup; and agreeing that there is nothing wrong with the airplane; we decided to proceed with our flight. After contacting Tower; we departed NW to practice area. Student was flying the airplane and I was monitoring his and the airplane's performance. During takeoff roll we checked engine instruments; everything was normal; and we continued with liftoff and climb. When we arrived at [the] practice area we practiced Steep turns; S-Turns over the road; and turns around the point. During the time from takeoff; climb and during maneuvers; the engine was performing normally as well; without any issues. Once we completed the maneuvers we decided to go back to our airport. After gettingATIS information; [student] contacted the Tower and requested a full stop landing on Runway XY. We were told to proceed directly to the Airport.At that moment we were at around 1;700-1;800 feet and decided to slowly start our descent. Around 20-30 seconds after that we experienced engine roughness; loss of power and the airplane started shaking; and we started losing altitude. I took over the controls from [student] to try to troubleshoot and to find out what exactly could cause the airplane to behave like that. After checking the fuel selector (BOTH); mixture position (FULL RICH); carburetor heat (ON); primer (IN AND LOCKED) and ignition (BOTH); and noticing that everything is in position for normal operation; I started reducing the power to see how airplane will behave. With less power; shaking was reduced; but still present; and altitude losing was increased. After that I advanced power to maximum to see how the airplane will respond; but rough running increased again; shaking increased; and altitude loss was reduced but still present.At that moment we were at around 1;300-1;400 feet and descending; and I decided to contact the Tower again and to try to explain our situation. Tower asked me if we can come back; and after finding out that we are constantly descending regardless of our power setting; I acknowledge them that we are unable to do so. I decided to [follow] the [the] Expressway; to stay away from busy streets and populated areas; and to try to at least maintain the present altitude which was at that moment around 900 feet. They cleared us to land at any runway at any airport around; but not being able to maintain altitude using different power settings; I knew that we were not going to make a safe landing at any airport around; because we were getting too low; and airports were 8-10 NM far from us. At that moment we were at around 700 feet and descending; when I told the Tower that we will probably land somewhere around the Expressway. Having the populated area and narrow streets on our left side; [marsh] on our right side; and low altitude; I decided the best option will be to land on Highway; which; we were lucky; was not too busy. Having the wind from [the south] and traffic flow towards it; landing in the southbound lane was the best choice I could make at that moment. We touched down in the middle lane; and immediately started moving the airplane to the right side so traffic can keep moving. After noticing that we landed safely; without any injuries and damage to other persons and property; we secured and exited the airplane.
Report_1_Synopsis: C172 instructor pilot reported a power loss resulting in a landing off airport.

Report_1_Narrative: During cruise; a smoke smell was detected. We attempted to trace the smell and quickly found smoke to be coming out of the foot wells. We proceeded to descend to the nearest airport where we found oil spattered inside of the cowling. The local Mechanic traced the leak to the oil filter which was installed by a different Mechanic who we contracted for a pre-buy. The Mechanic in question had used a pair of pliers to torque the oil filter; punching a small hole in the exterior which started leaking in flight and dripping on the heater; creating the smoke. The local Mechanic fixed our issue with a new oil filter and we proceeded to our destination the following day.
Report_1_Synopsis: GA pilot reported the oil filter was installed improperly and caused smoke in the aircraft.

Report_1_Narrative: While descending on the CLASH Arrival just prior to EVRLY we encountered a wake turbulence event 2x in short succession with roll deviation. Autopilot disconnected; was immediately reconnected by the Captain (PF). He disconnected VNAV and initiated Vertical Speed mode to reset our descent path to be slightly above the previous aircraft path; to prevent a third event. About this time; ATC offered us a runway change from 35R to 35L; additionally they requested us to slow to 210 kts. The Captain went to reprogram the FMS for Runway 35L; I was confirming the Captain inputs at this time. The aircraft was still in Vert Speed rather than VNAV; neither of us noticed this and we descended below the STAR required altitude and did not slow to 210 kts. as directed. A query from ATC as to our speed brought us back to reviewing our flight path; at which point we leveled off and reduced speed. ATC made no further comments as to our flight path deviation and at that point broke us off from the STAR with a vector to intercept the LOC. No loss of ATC separation was reported to us.
Report_1_Synopsis: B737 First Officer reported speed and altitude deviations on arrival into DEN; citing distraction from a wake turbulence encounter as contributing.

Report_1_Narrative: Stores dropped DG (dangerous goods) paperwork to manifest without the freight. The Cargo team refused to manifest as the freight was not present. I received from the Store Supervisor that the team failed to manifest the shipment. I explain to him that we need to be able to check the DG label; checklist prior to manifesting.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Cargo personnel reported refusing Dangerous Goods paperwork to manifest Hazmat shipment without the accompanying Hazmat cargo.

Report_1_Narrative: I was the wing walker. As we were pushing back we noticed two aircraft coming on to the taxiway from another gate area. We got clearance and were already into the push. We passed the vehicle service road and the taxiing aircraft were getting closer. I told our driver to stop. We had wireless headsets; luckily. I tried to get the taxiing aircraft to stop by giving the stop signal with my lighted wands. I walked to the back of our aircraft to see if it would be too close and possibly hit our tail. I told our driver to start pulling back toward the gate. About 20 feet. when we got back to the gate after push was completed we found out the tower had made a mistake.
Report_2_Narrative: We got clearance from the tower to push. We were just passed the vehicle service road when there were two aircraft taxiing around the corner. Our wing walker gave the aircraft the stop signal and he did not slow. Luckily; we had wireless headsets and the pushback driver was told to stop. As the taxiing aircraft got closer the wing walker told the pushback driver to then start backing up or the taxiing aircraft could clip our tail. I called to inform them and they said the tower admitted it was their fault.
Report_1_Synopsis: A Ramp Wing Walker reported one of the wing walkers noticed two aircraft taxiing toward the same spot they were pushing back an aircraft to and instructed the tug driver to pull the aircraft back into the gate area.
