Report_1_Narrative: Once the aircraft door was opened and only a few passengers from first class deplaned; the cleaners were trying to come on. We asked them to wait just a bit; as we had 4 wheelchairs; and our first-class cabin was still getting off. The cleaners told us they are instructed to get on right away. The Captain said No; they needed to wait till most of the aircraft had deplaned. A few of the cleaners were still trying to argue with us; even after the Captain had said they had to wait. There are no quick turns; as our cleaning procedures during this pandemic are totally opposite of the term quick turn. This also is dangerous for the passengers and crew. There is no room for cleaners in the galleys or in the aisle as we safety try to deplaned using the company's policy of social distance; and deplaning a few rows at a time.In addition; the cleaners are getting in the way of the flight crew full filing our FARs responsibilities and safety obligations; post cabin sweeps. This is a safety hazard and needs to be addressed immediately.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Attendant reported; after gate arrival; the oncoming cleaning crew was interfering with passenger deplaning and social distance policy.

Report_1_Narrative: Before boarding.  They [Deice Crew] deiced the plane. Air Packs were open and fumes blew into cabin. Back to front.  We waited in gate area for 25 minutes until fumes were somewhat dissipated.  Then we boarded passengers. I had a sore throat and cough. During flight and at home.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Flight Attendant reported a fumes event during pre-flight due to a deviation of de-icing procedure.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Time Pressure; Situational Awareness; Workload; Confusion
Report_1_Narrative: I was enroute to ILM. As I began my descent into the Wilmington terminal area the ATIS and Approach Controller indicated ILS Runway 06Z was the approach in use. Weather was reported as 400 overcast and one mile visibility. Winds 030 degrees at 4 knots. A cold front and convective activity was approaching the airport and I requested a short vector to final. I was cleared for the approach and began my descent. I ended up too high on the approach and executed a missed approach at minimums. As I was being vectored back for another approach I was advised that the aircraft following me also executed a missed approach due to being too high. I looked at the wind vector on my PFD and realized that I had a 50 knot tailwind at 1;500 feet on my last approach. I advised the Controller about the strong winds at altitude and asked if Runway 6 was still the best runway.I also asked the Controller if he had any real time winds on the ground and was reminded that the Tower was closed; he would try to get me an update from the automatic reporting system. I was told that the automatic reporting system still indicated winds out of the NE (northeast) at 11 knots. I continued for a second approach but at 700 feet AGL my wind vector was showing a 50 knot tailwind and my groundspeed confirmed that. I deemed it unsafe to land and executed another missed approach.The Controller suggested ZZZ as an alternate. I began vectors to an approach to RNAV GPS Runway XX. I quickly realized that I would have the same 50 knot tailwind situation at ZZZ and began questioning the Controller about any real time wind information on the ground. He said the only info he had still indicated winds on the ground were out of the NE about 7 knot. He said the convective activity situation at Wilmington was improving and asked if I would like to go back for another approach. I was beginning vectors to another ILS Approach 06Z. I was still seeing the same 50 knot winds at altitude and began doubting the wind reports on the ground. I asked for an approach to Runway 24. I was cleared for the RNAV approach 24. As I was descending on final approach; I had a 50 knot head wind at 1;000 feet.When I reached minimums and began to go visual; I encountered a windshear. I increased power to MCT (Max Continuous Thrust) trying to climb out; but to no avail. As I was continuing to recover from the windshear; my landing gear contacted a treetop about 1/4 mile from the runway. At this point I deemed the safest course of action was to continue to land. I made a normal landing to a full stop; turned off the runway and taxied to the FBO. After exiting the airplane minor damage was noted. At this point the winds on the ground had shifted to the SW (southwest)) and were gusting to 35 kts indicating to me that I had landed during frontal passage.The biggest contributing factor to safety I noted; was the lack of any real time winds on the ground. If I had real time wind data from the Controller as I was conducting my approach; I would have been advised of the wind shift occurring; and might have been able to take preventive action before I encountered the windshear. My recommendation is to not have a system that solely relies on the automatic reporting system which is not real time. I would have each Approach Control have the ability to see and give real time winds just as an operating Tower would have.
Report_1_Synopsis: Pilot reported contacting tree tops during landing at ILM airport due to windshear.  Pilot stated there was no real time wind information.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Situational Awareness; Physiological - Other; Other / Unknown
Report_1_Narrative: I received the second dose of my Pfizer vaccine for COVID-19 yesterday at XA:00 AM. I was not feeling any immediate effects of the dose and had a flight lesson scheduled XE:00 AM and felt fine. It wasn't until this morning I was chatting with a mentor of mine and they had mentioned there being a 48 hour period of restriction for any flying for those that did receive the vaccine. I did some research of my own and found that this was indeed true. I did not feel like I was putting myself or my instructor in any immediate danger and could still perform my duties as a student pilot. Upon discovering the restriction; I scheduled my other lesson for after the 48 hours have passed.
Report_1_Synopsis: Student pilot reported taking a flight lesson prior to the 48 hour waiting period after receiving a COVID-19 vaccine.

Report_1_Narrative: I believe this aircraft had been parked due to COVID.  Apparently; when pulled out of parking; the FMS database was not updated.  During pre-flight we noticed that revision 'W' and 'X' were available; but revision 'Y' was now current.  I don't know how long this plane has flown without 'Y' database; but it is deferred now.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Captain reported the aircraft database was a few revisions 'out of date' and suspects the aircraft was 'parked' during the pandemic for an extended period of time.

Report_1_Narrative: We were in clear air above our altitude of FL410. we encountered unexpected continuous moderate turbulence and were unable to maintain altitude. We rapidly lost 1;000 feet of altitude.
Report_1_Synopsis: B737 First Officer reported temporarily losing altitude control due to continuous moderate turbulence.

Report_1_Narrative: On approach to ZZZ gear was selected down but normal gear indications did not appear and there were no associated noises such as gear extending into slipstream; etc. PF (Pilot Flying) executed a missed approach and while being vectored we tried to lower the gear normally with the same indications and we got the L/G Gear Not Down locked ECAM. Accomplishing ECAM led us to the L/G Gravity Extension QRH and after accomplishing checklist the gear safely extended. We (advised ATC) and coordinated with Flight Attendants and Dispatch and ZZZ for subsequent runway closure and tow to the gate.
Report_1_Synopsis: A320 Captain reported a landing gear malfunction.

Report_1_Narrative: Upon arrival at ZZZ Maintenance notified us that there were multiple damaged fan blades in the number 1 engine. While we do not know when or how this occurred; we can only guess that it was due to snow/ice ingestion on takeoff roll; improper de-icing and inspection of engine inlets prior to engine start; or de-icing prior to takeoff. While there was no active precipitation; upon arrival at the aircraft; the crew noted snow and ice on the aircraft to include in the engine inlets. Per [company] procedures; after the doors were closed; before blockout; the crew call Ramp to have engines cleared. The clearing crew showed up. The Tug Driver noted them moving around the aircraft and appeared to be clearing engines. They left shortly thereafter; and we confirmed with Ramp Tower that the clearing and inspection had been logged complete. After push back onto taxi; we noted that the taxi lane had not been completely plowed. There was a large snow berm; approximately 2 ft. high about 10 ft. left of centerline; which converged toward centerline all the way until Taxiway XX. After some discussion with Tower and the Pushback Crew; we opted to have plows come and clear an area in front of us; that they could pull us to clear of the berm before engine start to avoid ingestion. Engine start was slow; even for Pratt & Whitney; but no starter or engine limitations were exceeded. N1 started around 20-25%; well below the 40% limit. After engine start anti-ice was turned on due to temp/dew point spread. We taxied on cleared pavement to the de-ice area. The taxi took less than 15 minutes so no engine clearing was used. During de-ice we noticed B777 push back out of a gate on [taxiway XX]. It was pushed back through a berm of snow and ice. After de-ice we taxied and took off after this B777. It is possible that the B777 had some snow/ice on its trucks that was deposited on the runway on takeoff. From de-ice; we taxied to Runway XX. The turn from Taxiway XY onto Taxiway XZ could have been cleared of snow better; but the turn was made using minimal thrust. It is possible that some compact snow or ice was ingested here; however; once cleared for takeoff; we did a 30 second engine clearing procedure and all engine instruments appeared normal. After takeoff; the Captain mentioned a rumble; which sounded like it was coming from a pack. It was faint enough; that we didn't feel it was an issue; as all packs checked out normal. Later on climb out the number 3 engine EVM fluctuated up to 5.0; then back down to normal ranges only slightly above the other two engines. The captain sent a message to [Operations} asking about engine telemetry; and we were advised it was good; so we decided to press on.
Report_1_Synopsis: MD-11 First Officer reported after landing Maintenance notified them of damaged fan blades in one of the engines.

Report_1_Narrative: It happened when we were doing 45 degree maneuver to enter the left downwind at OBE.  We did radio call twice when we were maneuvering.  While we were almost at downwind; there was another aircraft using his high speed to bypass my left side. I had to do the 360 degree to avoid it.
Report_1_Synopsis: Small aircraft pilot reported an NMAC occurred while entering the OBE airport traffic pattern when another aircraft flew by them at high speed.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Human-Machine Interface; Situational Awareness; Communication Breakdown
Report_1_Narrative: We were transitioning in VFR conditions on the ZZZZZ3 arrival to the GPS approach to XXR. We loaded the approach into the FMS and set bottom attitude for the approach. I was in right seat flying and CA was in the left who is a CE510s rated pilot also. I was off auto pilot and hand flying with a different flight director display than normally used. The issue was when engaged the appr mode on flight director while still in Vnav instead of waiting until the GPS switched to LPV mode just outside of the final approach fix. The controller advised us that we had descended below the minimum vectoring altitude for that segment of the approach. The clear message here was that better crew coordination was needed.
Report_1_Synopsis: C501 pilot reported that while handflying an approach ATC advised them that they had descended below the MVA for the segment before the FAF.

Report_1_Narrative: After takeoff at ZZZ RW XXL; and at approximately 500 feet AGL; a slight haze was noticed in the cockpit by the flight crew. A few seconds later; the passengers also noticed this in cabin area of airplane. It was then we observed a slight pungent order typical of smoke. At this time we observed a 'baggage fire' alert on the crew alert system. Operating as a crew; we [advised ATC] at this time and made a downwind turn in the airport pattern for runway XXL. With the appropriate checklist for the indicated condition complete; we were cleared to land on runway XXL. The smoke that was observed previously had now dissipated we and turned base to final and made normal landing on runway XXL. After exiting runway XXL at intersection X; we shutdown the aircraft and executed an emergency evacuation using the appropriate checklist. Upon observation after landing no condition of heat; smoke or fire were observed. Internal engine component suspected problem.

Report_1_Narrative: We were flying from ZZZ to ZZZ1.We were at FL410 and given a descent to FL350. I was the PF and after the PM acknowledged the altitude and set it in the ALT selector I initiated a 1000fpm descent in vertical speed mode. At approximately 40;500 feet the aircraft pitch over 60-70 degrees and accelerated from Mach .80 to Mach .90+ in a matter of a few seconds. I turned off the auto throttles and pulled the throttles to idle while simultaneously canceling the auto pilot then extended the speed brakes. We were descending at such a high rate I had difficulty pulling back on the yoke; but was able to pull it back stopping out descent around 36;000 feet and after pulling back the aircraft climbed to almost 43;000 feet before I able to arrest the ascent and bleed our airspeed off. This entire event took place in the space of about 10-15 seconds. After bleeding the speed off and regain control of the aircraft I started our decent once again by hand and flew it down to a lower requested altitude. We were sure that our flight guidance computer was to blame and had it replaced.
Report_2_Narrative: We were flying from ZZZ to ZZZ1.We were at FL410 and given a descent to FL350. I was the PM and after the PFrequested the altitude change and set it in the ALT selector I initiated a descent of 1000 fpm in vertical speed mode. At approximately 40;500 feet the aircraft pitch was over 55-70 degrees and accelerated from Mach .80 to Mach .90+ in few seconds. the PF turned off the auto throttles and he's pulled the throttles to idle and simultaneously canceling the autopilot then extended the speed brakes. We were descending at such a high rate the PF had difficulty pulling back on the yoke; but he was able to pull it back stopping the descent at around 36;000 feet and after pulling back the aircraft climbed to almost 43;000 feet before the PF was able to arrest the ascent and bleed our airspeed off. This entire event took place in the space. After bleeding the speed off and regain control of the aircraft the PF started the decent by hand and flew it down to a lower requested altitude. We were sure that our flight guidance computer was to blame and had it replaced.
Report_1_Synopsis: Gulfstream flight crew reported that during descent the aircraft pitched over excessively and quickly accelerated. The flight crew disengaged aircraft automation and regained control. Crew reported that the flight guidance computer had malfunctioned and was subsequently replaced.

Report_1_Narrative: This safety concern occurred on two flights. Same aircraft and same exact routing and runways for departure (7L) and arrival (24R). The routing was the 7L.KEENS2.MESSI ESTWD.HLYWD1.24R. The First Officer briefed all of the points; speeds; and altitudes on the SID via the FMC CDU and I confirmed them on my EFB. We completed the Before Start Origination checklist; received performance takeoff data; and completed the Before Push checklist with no issues. After pushback and engine start; we started to taxi away and when I placed the LEGS Page up on my CDU there was now a discontinuity after the first departure point; and the next point. We corrected the situation by re-selecting the SID; transition; and departure Runway 7L; which removed the discontinuity. That situation by itself would be a little unusual; but as we flew back later on and the same issue occurred yet again it appears that there is a performance software issue that needs to be looked at. The Cost Index was 15 on Flight X and 5 on Flight Y. I unfortunately did not reference the FMC software version. We had no discontinuity on our flight; so the issue could be departure related; the SID related; or performance software related. Bottom line is that there is an issue that might cause pilots to take off and soon afterward encounter a discontinuity on the route; causing a potential navigation error.Flight Ops needs to work with Dispatch and Maintenance to determine if certain weights; Cost Indexes; FMC software versions; SIDS; airports; etc; are causing a discontinuity after receiving performance takeoff data in this fleet or solely this particular aircraft.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Captain reported a discontinuity on the FMC legs page; on the same route; in the same place; two consecutive times.

Report_1_Narrative: Aircraft X was uneventful leading up to the approach at ZZZ. We had been cleared for the approach to Runway XX and were established on the localizer and glideslope. The autopilot and autothrust had been disengaged earlier in the approach and the aircraft had been configured to Flaps 3 when Gear Down was requested. When the gear lever was selected down the three indicators on the landing gear panel indicated red UNLK (UNLOCKED); no noise from the landing gear doors opening was heard. Captain [Name] and I communicated and confirmed on the Landing Gear Systems page that the landing gear had not extended. We decided to level out at 6;000 feet MSL while we confirmed the situation and attempted to cycle the gear. We communicated to the tower we would be going around for a landing gear failure approximately 3mi prior to the runway. Tower provided vectors and a climb to 9;000 feet; we initiated a go around over the threshold per ATC instructions and cleaned up the aircraft per SOP. The autoflight was re-engaged after the go around. During this time after the failure of subsequent attempts to cycle the gear and with the lever still down; we eventually got the L/G GEAR NOT DOWNLOCKED ECAM. The ECAM was run according to SOP by Captain [Name] while I flew the aircraft and handled radio calls. We [received priority]; stated our intention to return to land on Runway XYR and requested CFR (Crash Fire Rescue Equipment). Gravity extension was successful and we were vectored to the approach. Approach and landing were normal with the exception of the gear doors remaining open. We landed with 8000 lbs. of fuel. We stopped on the runway and Operations was standing by to tow the aircraft back to the gate.
Report_1_Synopsis: First Officer reported a Go Around and precautionary  landing after landing gear lock problems.

Report_1_Narrative: We were on a Part 91 ferry flight. On climb out we noticed the ground idle annunciation light was illuminated which we concluded was not normal as the ground idle is on a squat switch and shouldn't be on in flight. We further discussed other system items which would possibly cause the issue. In addition we noticed that the takeoff V speeds were still showing on the airspeed indicator which should have been cleared out after takeoff. ATC cleared us up to FL390 and we were crossing our first fix. We tried cycling the ground idle switch during this time and were in the mid teens. The ground idle annunciation remained illuminated. Shortly after this the Captain noticed that our cabin was not pressurizing; as the cabin altitude was not increasing nor was the cabin rate increasing. He selected the cabin rate knob to high to try and get the cabin to pressurize. Shortly after; the cabin rate immediately went to approximately 6;000 fpm. He said lets get our oxygen masks on. We put them on and at this time we were at approximately FL220. Suddenly the master warning illuminated along with a cabin decompression annunciation. He disconnected the autopilot and leveled off and said lets advise ATC. I advised ATC and requested a return to our origin. ATC gave us a descent to 10;000 ft. with direct to the airport. Once we accomplished memory items for cabin decompression and emergency descent we ran the emergency checklist and returned with no further issues. I believe we handled the situation appropriately by advising ATC and going to a lower altitude and returning to our origin airport. Once we reached 10;000 ft. the cabin decompression annunciation extinguished and we landed with no further issues.
Report_1_Synopsis: Cessna V/Ultra Pilots reported a malfunction of the air/ground squat switch and unable to pressurize the aircraft.

Report_1_Narrative: After rotation PF (pilot flying) had difficulty turning left to HDG 330; I thought he was rusty. Had him hand fly to about FL180. When we put the auto pilot on we had the AP LWD Caution msg. We ran the QRH and noticed the aileron trim did not respond or move. ACARS Dispatch and they mentioned deferring the aileron trim. I then noticed the Aileron Trim circuit breaker was popped. I attempted to contact Dispatch through AIRINC prior to ZZZ. Dispatch could not hear me. We advised ATC for flight control malfunction. Test items ran no brace I briefed the passengers I did not have the go through planned diversion with passengers. I was very surprised that Dispatch had a known bad headset. She knowingly continued to act as a Dispatcher with a bad headset. I could not hear her on AIRINC and when I called on the phone I could not hear her. She said she knew it was bad and they needed a new one. If I knowingly operated an airplane with a bad headset I'd be in major trouble.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier check airman reported student difficulty with directional control after takeoff.  Discovered failure of aileron trim during climb. Returned to base and was concerned about communication with company personnel due their lack of adequate equipment.

Report_1_Narrative: We were given a NOTOC (NOtice TO Captain) with 2- 1.4S packages [explosives] and 1 lithium ion battery as COMAT (company materials).  In order to be fully aware of what we were carrying I called Cargo OPS.  The gentleman who helped me out to go over it realized that no two dangerous goods could go in one compartment and ask me to have the lithium battery removed. I requested the Crew Chief to accomplish the above request and was told that it was good and I should go. His goal was to be on time; and although I can understand his pressure; safety is our priority at all times.  I asked to get it removed and was told that they have been sending airplanes like this in the previous days with no issues and I should just push. I stated that what other flights have done; is not a matter of discussion regarding this flight; and that per Cargo OPS; HAZMAT it needed to be removed otherwise I would not be pushing until it was accomplished.  I was told that they were going to call the Chief Pilot on me. I'm not sure if that was a tool of intimidation or not but I told them to please have them call me.  A few minutes later I received the call from Chief Pilot. I explained the situation and understood what was happening. At one point the Crew Chief wanted to place both 1.4S packages on the aft cargo which I told him not to do so. Eventually they removed the 1.4S cargo from the fwd cargo leaving the lithium ion battery on the fwd cargo and one package of the 1.4S on the aft.   We departed and operated safely to ZZZ1. [Caused by] rushing to comply with departure times and not listening to what our priority is: Safety. I suggest training for our colleagues so their main focus is open communications for a safe environment so we can have a safer operation.
Report_1_Synopsis: A-321 Captain reported a successful resolution of a Hazmat cargo loading violation resulting in completing a safe transport of Hazmat cargo.

Report_1_Narrative: We had to reopen the Main Cabin Door and the jetbridge had to be pulled back to the plane due to a change in the release requiring more fuel. I'm unsure as to how the door was missed; as I thought we had pushed on it and checked it the second time we locked it and the flight attendant even said she gave it a pull after we locked it. However; on takeoff I heard a loud bang coming from behind me and I stayed focused on my takeoff. I'm not certain at what time the captain reclosed the door; but in cruise he did mention that he had to unlock the lock in order to re latch it and lock it. My memory serves that the door was locked when we did the checklist.We had flap gap seals damaged on the aircraft on initial walk around. Maintenance came out and was irritated at the captain for writing it up. I offered a printed flap aerodynamic seal inspection task given to me from previous A&P's to help him find a quick solution as that is what previous mechanics have used for write ups for the same seals . (I typically run into these particular seals being damaged at least once per trip). He got angry at me and told me its not my place to offer help. After putting an CDL on the plane that required a lower altitude on the release due to a performance hit he sent a message saying we were released at Time. We didn't actually receive the release until around Time. The mechanic had either forgotten or based on his demeanor intentionally delayed the flight to get under our skin. After being released; we did the before start checklist again and caught that the fuel needed to be added due to the new release. We waited again for fuel and a gate agent to come. Ultimately we were delayed about 51 minutes which likely played a role.My personal adjustment to this is to make sure I push on the door every time I read the below the line before start checklist as I believe the lights on the door lock corresponded to it being locked.
Report_1_Synopsis: First Officer reported cockpit door came open on takeoff and was closed and resecured by The Captain.

Report_1_Narrative: While on final approach the PF was having difficulty slowing the aircraft and continuing the descent. The headwind we had been fighting quickly turned to a crosswind. The PF elected to re-bug and use flaps 40 well above 1;000 feet. As the PF I selected the new flap setting in the FMC and verbally called out the Vref and target speeds. As we were slowing past our previous target speed the PF called for flaps 40. We had no amber band visible for flaps 40 placard speed; so I verified the placard; 162 knots; and selected the flaps seeing 158 knots and slowing on my tape. As I verified the speed brake was armed he again called for 40. The flaps were still at 30. At this point we were now below 1;000 feet but above 500 feet. We discussed the non-movement and load alleviation. As the PM; I suggested; pitch up and slow; the flaps moved to 40 as we suspected they would. The checklist was completed and we were able to be stable by 500 feet AGL; so we continued the landing. We did not observe any limitations being exceeded on the flaps or in procedure as the PM was able to manage the approach prior to the 500 foot gate.In discussing this event during our debrief we believe that we did meet our approach gate criteria. We were in our first 'heavy' approach in many months as the flight was full. The weight may have contributed. The wind was also a contributing factor as it shifted down the final enough that by the time we departed the traffic flow had reversed.Neither of us were averse to going around but it did not seem necessary in the moment as it seemed we met our criteria to continue. Having said that I'm certain eyes further from the instrument panel may have captured data we missed but I believe we trapped and corrected the situation.
Report_2_Narrative: While on final approach I; PF; called for final landing flap (flaps 40) and flaps did not move to commanded position (they were at 30); despite being slower than max speed for flaps 40. Since we were within a few knots of max flaps 40 speed; I slowed further and flaps extended to commanded position. I believe the flap extension occurred right around 500 feet.  The final approach speed was within stabilized approach criteria and the outcome of the approach and landing were not in doubt. Landing was uneventful.We have been flying mostly empty airplanes for almost a year and this flight was almost completely full. I believe the higher landing weight coupled with a significant loss of headwind on final contributed to the airplane taking a while to slow down to an acceptable speed for final flaps. When I called for final flaps; we were 3-4 knots below the max flaps speed and I believe the aircraft's safety system was restricting flap movement until I was a little slower. As we return to Pre-COVID passenger loads; I will have to adjust lead time for decelerating the jet. Today was a good reminder.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier flight crew reported the aircraft was carrying a pre-COVID passenger load and they were not prepared for the higher flap speeds required for a stable approach.

Report_1_Narrative: The Number 2 and 4 Flight Attendants (FA) called to report strong odor in aft galley. I continued boarding while the Number 1 FA went in to speak with the Captain. She returned and said we were to continue boarding. I could hear the aft FAs calling Captain while we stood in entry area. The Number 1 would go in to cockpit to get updates from the calls. A deadheading pilot then came from the back of plane and went to the cockpit to speak with the Captain. There was some question about it being a urine smell and perhaps the cleaning of the lavs. We had neared the end and I walked through closing bins; etc. As I got to row 25 I smelled a very strong and pungent dirty sock smell. I went to aft galley and told them it was a dirty sock smell and where I began smelling it. I asked them to relay that info up front. The Number 2 and 4 wanted the Captain to come and smell because they disagreed with that assertion. I had returned to the front of aircraft and the Number 1 and Captain went to the back. When he returned he seemed perturbed that the Number 1 was not immediately behind him and wanted to close up. I said I would close the remaining overhead bins. The Number 1 returned and we departed. First; I believe we should have stopped boarding and deplaned the passengers and crew until the cause/type/potency of odor could be established. Following the operating procedures for deplaning at the gate would have allowed a quicker review of the situation and the concerns for safety until a definitive answer could be established while removing passengers and crew from a potentially harmful exposure.
Report_2_Narrative: We commenced the boarding and Flight Attendant #2 and I walked to aft galley and both smelled a noxious odor. I called the Flight Attendant 1; three times and she in turn told the Captain. He said 'it is probably a leaky trash bag or rotten food.' Flight Attendant 2 called the Captain directly and he again blew us off. We had a deadheading pilot also go to cockpit to relay information and when he got back; he said the 'theory is that it is a leaky trash bag'. We had been on the aircraft for 4 hours prior to this event as we brought the aircraft in from ZZZ. The fumes were coming out of air vents in galley and aft lavs and was going into c zone. 33 minutes after we first notified Captain; at the end of boarding; he came to the back and said 'I don't smell anything; we are going to ZZZ1'. With that; he turned and walked back to the front. Yes; the fumes had just dissipated by that point; 33 minutes later. There was no interaction; NONE. He obviously did not care about the noxious fumes in the aft section of aircraft. For 33 minutes; he continued to disregard every attempt to tell him what was happening in the back. He's a Check Airman; really? He's supposed to be the best of the best. I felt like my safety was jeopardized and I would never feel safe flying with him again. What if I reported smoke; would he say it is stale cigarette smell on someone's shirt? The one important bit of information he might need might come from the most junior Flight Attendant or even a new hire. In this case he had 4 very senior Flight Attendants and disregarded all of us when we made 5 attempts to get his help in telling him about the noxious odors. Captain obviously needs some intense CRM training. Maybe giving a check ride to another pilot and trying to manage fume events are just too much for him. It obviously was.
Report_1_Synopsis: A321 flight attendants reported a communication breakdown with the Captain regarding cabin odor during boarding.

Report_1_Narrative: Aircraft X was an air return back into ZZZ; for the standby display cool fan malfunction causing the display screens to overheat. This aircraft was ferrying to ZZZ1 for a repair. During troubleshooting it was decided that the problem could be relays K7HK and K11HK in JB2. The relays were replaced per the AMM (Aircraft Maintenance Manual) CH24/ESPM (Electrical Standard Practices Manual) and did not fix the problem. The next likely part was the avionics cooling control panel; it was replaced per AMM CH21 and did fix the problem. Because I had removed JB2; a retest had to be performed per the AMM CH24. The first half of this complex task was done in the hangar. The second half requires the engines to be ran. Everything was checking out good per the AMM; until the final engine start. During the start sequence on the LH (Left Hand) engine everything seemed to be normal; then I received an APU Overtemp red warning message which distracted me from watching the LH engine parameters. After the APU Overtemp message cleared I noticed the LH engine ITT (Interstage Turbine Temperature) at 998 degrees. I immediately put the LH thrust lever to fuel cutoff and motored the engine until the ITT was below 120 degrees. The MDC (Maintenance Diagnostic Computer) engine exceedance history showed the LH engine to be at 1110 degrees for 10.6 seconds. This is the first time I have ever encountered 2 overtemp events or 2 red warning indications at the same time while working one of our aircraft. I was working hard to get this task done so the crew could move the aircraft yet that day; as they were standing by in the hangar to depart after repairs were completed. I must admit I did feel pressured and hurried; however I did complete the retest task per the AMM; with everything checking satisfactory. As for the engine hot start event; I really regret it happening. It seems like it was one of those situations that does not occur together all that often. I felt I was distracted and was task overloaded for maybe a second or two which played a factor in this unfortunate event.
Report_1_Synopsis: Technician reported APU over temperature and engine over temperature simultaneously during post maintenance engine run ups.

Report_1_Narrative: On initial approach to TRM I was announcing the arrival quite often and very diligently; in a descent of approximately 1;600 feet per minute another plane was observed on the ADS-B and was in sight. I continued the descent to fly well under the plane which was obviously VFR and as I approached the plane it turned into me with a sharp turn. The TCAS had a TA but not an RA as I had descended well below the other plane. The other plane must not have been monitoring the UNICOM or monitoring their traffic ADS-B.I realize now that I should have changed course at an earlier time; to give a much wider birth to the crossing plane. Also; I can not take into account other pilots listening to the CTAF or UNICOM frequency for area traffic. In addition; as I approached the airport to fly over and enter a left downwind; another plane was spotted that had just flown over the field with no announcements. VFR traffic in this area are not listening or announcing their intentions in the airport environment.
Report_1_Synopsis: GA pilot flying to non-towered TRM airport reported an NMAC with another aircraft in the pattern.

Report_1_Narrative: My student and I were conducting a dual pattern flight at ZZZ. We were cleared for the option number 2 for Runway XX. Number 1 was on final and number 3 was student pilot solo who was behind us in the downwind after going around after his first landing attempt. We turned based and then to final being number 1. On about a 3/4-mile final from the runway; the student pilot solo turned base and then proceeded to turn final right in front of us; and slightly below us. My best guess is that he thought he was following number 1 and that he was number 2. At best glance; they were probably 400 feet in front of us; and 200 feet below us on final. I took flight controls; queried Tower and initiated a go around left side. The student landed and was given a phone number to copy down. After we completed our lesson a few laps around the pattern later and taxied off the runway; Tower asked if we were okay with the go around. It was certainly a little close for comfort; but we had enough space to recognize the threat and execute a go around.
Report_2_Narrative: Was the 2nd solo flight in my pilot career. I had arrived back into ZZZ traffic pattern into Runway XX. While on downwind; I was cleared by Tower as number 3 and cleared to land on Runway XX. I had identified the traffic in front of me as number 2 without any doubt. I followed that traffic and landed safely. Once I called up ground; I was notified that I had cut off the actual number 2 traffic and that traffic was forced to go around. In reality; I had incorrectly identified the number 1 traffic as number 2 and failed to see any other traffic making me believe I had the correct number 2 in sight.When I am in a congested pattern like ZZZ; I will use my multi function flight display map page and make sure there are no planes I have failed to identify. I will also start counting out traffic to make sure I have accounted for all of them.
Report_1_Synopsis: GA flight instructor; a student on a solo flight; and the instructor of the solo student reported an NMAC in the traffic pattern during approach.

Report_1_Narrative: Training flight for a student who needed a 90 day solo endorsement. After doing maneuvers; I gave him a partial power loss and he decided to divert to ZZZ about 10 NM from our position. I had already checked NOTAMs and we got AWOS information twice on the way. Student announced every couple miles where we were and that we were inbound with a simulated loss of power for a straight in on Runway XX. I saw when we were about 2 NM away that the runway looked good but some of the taxiways were snowy and told my student we were not doing a full stop so we planned for a touch and go with a go-around possibility. About 1 NM away I saw a snowplow working on the taxiways. As we were in the flare; I saw the snowplow turning towards the runway. I put the flaps up and my student added power and as we climbed over the runway the snowplow turned onto the approach end of Runway XY and in our direction; we flew over the plow about 100-200 feet overhead.I believe the weather may have contributed as it was hazy on the ground; we could clearly see things on the ground but the haze may have affected the ability of the plow to see us.I think we could have made a safer decision to only do a low approach.I mostly think the situation would have not been an issue if there was any communication from the airport. There was no mention of work being done or the runway being closed in either NOTAMs or the AWOS; nor did the plow ever say anything on CTAF about their intentions. We were broadcasting our location and intentions regularly but heard no one else. We did a double check and volume was good; frequency was correct.
Report_1_Synopsis: C172 flight instructor reported snow plow on runway during landing maneuver.

Report_1_Narrative: ATC had assigned us an earlier timed descent to FL290 requiring a 2;000 FPM descent. Pilot Flying selected Vertical Speed mode to meet the descent. Prior to leveling; ATC revised the clearance to descent via the RNAV Arrival and delete the speeds. Both pilots confirmed the bottom altitude of the arrival at 13;000 feet; but failed to confirm the descent mode was in VNAV. Pilot Flying became distracted with updating the speeds on the arrival and did not see the aircraft was still descending in Vertical Speed mode. Upon passing 14;000 feet; the Pilot Flying realized the aircraft was below the arrival descent profile and began reversing the descent. About the same time ATC called to query our altitude as we had descended below their Minimum Vectoring Altitude. We were issued a climb back to 14;000 feet which we complied with and then a vector off the arrival to final and further descent. The rest of the arrival was without incident.
Report_2_Narrative: [Report narrative contained no additional information.]

Report_1_Narrative: On the morning of an international departure that was scheduled to depart later that evening; the Captain emailed and informed both FOs of how the flight would be conducted in regard to face masks.  During the pre-flight phase; the #2 FO challenged the decision and said he was walking off the trip unless the Captain agreed to wear a mask whenever he was on the Flight Deck.  In an effort to maximize safety and also to address the #2 FO's concerns; the Captain offered the solution that he would wear a mask during cruise; whenever the #2 was performing his relief duties; but; with safety concerns about glasses fogging and hindered communications during critical phases of flight; said that #2 could sit in the cabin rest seat during those phases if it would make him more comfortable (since masks would not be worn).  The Captain believed this was 'legal;' since an #2 actually wasn't required by the FARs on the planned 6 hour and XX minutes flight and was also the safest option since; if the #2 dropped the trip; the flight would likely be sent un-augmented with zero inflight rest periods then available to the 'flying' pilots. The #2 agreed with this solution and the flight departed.Prior to the later descent; the #2 stated that he believed that an FAR's had been violated by him not being in the cockpit for takeoff.  He said that he would be in the cockpit for descent and Captain said he was welcome to be there but reiterated that masks would not be worn during critical phases of flight.  The #2 did then come up for the descent and landing.After the aircraft was parked and debrief conducted; #2 said he would be submitting a report over his belief that an FAR was violated by him not being in the cockpit for takeoff and departure.The Captain and #1 FO are not aware of any 'violations' of FAR's in this instance but decided to report the incident in case there's something they are not aware of.
Report_2_Narrative: During takeoff; the #2 FO stayed in overhead flight crew rest area instead of on the Flight Deck.  Erroneously thinking his presence was not required on Flight Deck on takeoff. Captain and #2 chose that course of action; as #2 wasn't comfortable with staying on Flight Deck with the Captain who had a cough. Captain was unable to wear a mask due to fogging of glasses.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier flight crew reported they had an agreement between themselves regarding face mask policy on the flight deck and may have violated FAR/SOP policy.

Report_1_Narrative: Dispatch notified us that the release was not signed at cruise.   I immediately realized he was correct.  I added 2000 pounds operational fuel on the way to the airport and discussed this with the crew.  I planned on signing the release and talking with the Dispatch in Operations (Ops); because this is one of the last places internationally that we still go to Ops.  The van takes us through security then to Ops then to the bottom of the jetbridge.  All 3 of us had done this recently and knew of no change and in fact the 10-7 page states that we are not allowed to go through the terminal.  However; upon reaching the airport the driver brings us to the terminal; stating that this is the new procedure.  We verified on our iPads and even called Ops to verify this change.  Indeed; due to COVID; we go through the terminal.  The security was extensive; overly extensive and time consuming.  The walk to the gate is long and although we hustled; we still arrived at the jet later than desired.  I called Dispatch for the brief once arriving to the cockpit and received a standard brief which included a new release; release 2 due to ZFW increase.  I agree that was okay; but after the call; we realized the 2000 pounds I had added via app was not added; so I called the Dispatch back.  The Fueler arrived during this call and he agreed to add the extra 2000 pounds for us and I told Dispatch it was done so no new paperwork was needed.   I wondered why the Dispatcher had not included the 2000 pounds. In retrospect I should have realized something was amiss; for example; the release not being signed.  We then had discussions with Ops regarding the extra 2000 pounds; but it was all resolved.  During this time; the FO saw the dispatch release; stated it was #2; but neither of us noticed it said 'not signed' at the top; only noted that it was release 2 and that we were all fit for duty.  We had the Oceanic checklist out and looked through it; but missed the dispatch release on it.  I have been signing the release lately enroute from the hotel to the airport since we never go to Ops anymore due to COVID; except today; since this is one of the few places that we do go to Ops.  However; apparently; we don't.  A note in the 10-7; an Ops alert; or something stating this would have been helpful.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Captain reported a change in airport procedures; due to COVID-19; caused the flight crew to miss the required signing of the Flight Release.

Report_1_Narrative: Normal takeoff and climb out. We went to FL400 for cruise altitude. We got to cruise; made our PA turned off the seatbelt sign. I was Pilot Monitoring. FO (First Officer) said;'uh oh we have a light on the HYD overhead.' I looked up and ENG2 engine driven pump said low pressure. I canceled the master caution and got out the QRH. Simple checklist; select the HYD pump switch to off. End of checklist. We pulled up the hydraulic display on the center screen. B system 106%; normal pressure. We started a what if dialogue. We agreed it was OK to continue with present condition. We looked up Loss of System B in QRH; and discussed it. We looked at flight plan divert circles and discussed scenarios. After 5-10 min the system B quantity started to decrease; slowly at first. I asked ATC for a descent to FL 320. Now the System B started to decrease rapidly. We knew we were about to loose Hyd Sys B. We selected Autopilot A to fly the aircraft; still descending; we were now over Location X but before ZZZZZ fix. We texted Dispatch we were going to lose System B and wanted to confer if we should divert or continue; Note-Loss of SYS B checklist did not say land at nearest suitable airport. We were almost to FL 320 and the ELEC 1 low pressure light illuminated; as the system quantity reached 0 and system pressure was 0;pump switch off per checklist. We got a few more lights and confirmed we had a complete loss of system B. Unbelievably we now got an ENG 1 hyd low pressure light illuminate; pump switch off per checklist. ELEC 2 HYD pump only hydraulic pump now functioning. It held autopilot A. We looked at each other and said lets head to ZZZ1; we had previously talked about divert points and where to go if the situation had gotten worse which it did. During this time we noticed A HYD quantity decreasing from 90+% to low 80's(we thought we might loose A too)I requested a descent and a turn direct to ZZZ1 from Center for a hydraulic loss. He gave us a different heading and said to expect to hold for sequence. We were now clearer to the controller and requested priority handling. The lead FA dinged us and asked if everything was OK; I told her no; type of situation; and to prepare the cabin for a divert to ZZZ1; I asked her to have the cabin ready in 10 minutes; no evac prep necessary. We got direct from ZZZZ Center; reprogramed the FMC and let dispatch know we were diverting. We started in on the loss of System B checklist as we were making a dive for ZZZ1. We ended up taking a vector to lose altitude. We completed the loss of system B to the ALT Flap extension. I then called back to the FA confirmed TEST; no evac; trucks would be standing by; we might seem like we were landing faster. I made a PA to the passengers. The FO did an excellent job of flying the airplane first; great CRM working with me on the checklists; with ATC ; keeping me in the loop where we were when we were being pulled from so many directions (We were getting pulled from ATC; Dispatch; FA; PAX; checklists...). We completed the ALT Flap extension and then landing checklist. The landing was normal for a flaps 15 landing.After the parking checklist; we debriefed. ZZZ1 station manager entered the aircraft and said they might have an aircraft swap if we could fly to ZZZ2. Sent Maintenance report. I talked to the FO and cabin crew and they all wanted to continue and fly to ZZZ2. We called dispatch and he elaborated on the possibility of us flying to ZZZ2. All the crew members wanted to finish the flight to ZZZ2; so we started in on this plan. I spoke with the Operations Manager and the ZZZ2 Chief Pilot for clearance for all of us to continue to ZZZ2. We did have to also fill out a simple report and give copies of our licensed to the [local] authorities. We informed the passengers. The plan did come together and we did an aircraft swap and an uneventful continuation to ZZZ2.
Report_2_Narrative: In cruise; the System B Engine Pump 'Low Pressure' light illuminated. The Captain (non-flying pilot) accomplished the QRH checklist and the pump switch was deselected. Hydraulic quantity in the 'B' system was over 100%. Approximately 5 minutes later the 'B' system quantity starts to rapidly drop to zero. After reaching zero; the 'B' system Electric Hydraulic Pump unexpectedly illuminates 'Low Pressure.' We also receive the associated caution light for the flight control system. While the Captain was completing 'Loss of System B' checklist and we were discussing our options (ZZZ1 vs ZZZ2); we received another caution light for System 'A' Engine Pump 'Low Pressure.'We immediately decide to divert to ZZZ1. The Captain advised ATC; and notified the Dispatcher over ACARS. We completed the checklists; notified the Flight Attendants; and informed the passengers. There was a very clear division in the flight deck workload. The Captain worked the problems; communications with the company; and in cabin communications. I flew the aircraft and communicated with ATC. This workload division not only works well in the simulator but also in real life.We completed the 'Loss of System B' deferred items and Alternate Flap Extension procedure. We shot the ILS in ZZZ1 and landed without incident. Clearing the runway we taxied to the gate. The System 'A' Electric Pump continued to function and we fortunately had no other problems.This whole situation was extremely similar a recurrent training scenario that we had not that long ago. Having 'seen it before' was strangely reassuring.
Report_1_Synopsis: B737 flight crew reported a loss of B system hydraulic fluid; followed by the loss of multiple hydraulic pumps resulted in a diversion.

Report_1_Narrative: During descent on the arrival while speed brakes were deployed; the speed trim amber light illuminated. The master caution light also illuminated and a flight control light on the system annunciation panel also illuminated. Accomplished the QRH non-normal and proceeded to ZZZ with no further issues. Remained on auto pilot remainder of flight and successfully performed a CAT 2 auto land approach onto [Runway] 4L due to low visibility.
Report_1_Synopsis: B737 Captain reported that during arrival the Speed Trim Configuration Warning light illuminated and the QRH non-normal checklist was completed prior to landing.

Report_1_Narrative: TCAS RA on flight route from ZZZZ AFB to ZZZ. We were on Y52. We noticed two aircraft on TCAS and with audio in contact with Fukuoka ATC Control radio in front of us heading directly in front; 12 o'clock towards us head on. Altitude of two aircraft varied from below 1000 and to our altitude of 26000 ft. TCAS alerts were activated. One of the involved aircraft's call sign was Aircraft Y. Opposing aircraft now at our same altitude; 26000 ft.; closing fast.TCAS warning; 'Traffic-Traffic;' aural followed by TCAS RA and; 'Descend;' aural warning followed. Initiated evasive maneuver. I; the Captain; with minimum map scale on display could see opposing aircraft also now descending into our flight path. Initiated flight control input with verbal command that co-pilot continue to fly while I also inputted left lateral evasive maneuver to avoid collision. I noted our separation on TCAS was less than 100 ft. in red color. Increased separation was noted and aircraft flight was stabilized back to 26000 ft. No visual contact. Possible loss of 300 to 1000 ft. of altitude of our aircraft due to evasive maneuver. Cabin crew felt evasive maneuver with no injuries reported of passengers or crew.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported an NMAC with traffic from the opposite direction during cruise flight.

Report_1_Narrative: During our approach briefing we planned to exit the runway at Taxiway V near the far end of the runway to facilitate our taxi to parking. After landing on Runway 31R I followed the green leadoff lights to exit the runway at what I thought was Taxiway V and was already committed to continue onto the taxiway when Tower told us to exit at Taxiway V join [Taxiways] B and S to the ramp. The First Officer noticed that we had exited at Taxiway WW and asked the Tower if okay to exit there. The Tower then advised us that [Taxiway] WW was closed but no problem. We noticed that a couple of low and narrow snow berms across the taxiway that were left over from snowplows and we continued forward without any problem. I also noticed at the time that there were other aircraft tire tracks through the snow and did not appear to affect our progress. The taxi to parking was uneventful. During the landing rollout I tried to locate our position on the moving map airport diagram which I pre-positioned as much as possible at Taxiway V area; but could not ascertain exactly our current position. I saw the green leadoff lights; and thinking that we were at [Taxiway] V continued to follow them onto the taxiway. There was also another aircraft on short final behind us and it was my intention to exit the runway expeditiously so as not to complicate its arrival. I did not see a taxiway sign prior to the taxiway and determined that we must be exiting at [Taxiway] V. The Tower Controller did not seem to be phased by our encroachment onto a closed taxiway. We were already committed to Taxiway WW and there was no way to stop the aircraft and safely make a 180-degree turn to get back on the runway to exit at Taxiway V. There were not any cones or barricades with caution lights across Taxiway WW; and as it was not a construction area I felt that we could safely exit on [Taxiway] WW. To complicate matters; taxiway signage in that area is not sufficient as I did not see a WW sign prior to the taxiway - only the sign on the right side of the taxiway after entering [Taxiway] WW. Also of concern is that the green leadoff lights were illuminated allowing aircraft to taxi off the runway onto a closed taxiway. The lights should have been extinguished. I did not see any green leadoff lights at Taxiway V.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Captain reported after landing at JFK they turned onto a closed taxiway and cited signage issues as a contributing factor.

Report_1_Narrative: We were flying; from ZZZ to QRO (Queretaro; MX). During preflight inspection; the FMC database was current as well as both pilots' Electronic Flight Kits. While in-flight; the weather was reporting clouds at 1;200 feet 5 mile visibility and light winds. The runway in use was [Runway] 09. While in cruise flight; Mexico Center informed us to expect VOR DME 2 for RWY (Runway) 09 approach in QRO. The aircraft was set up; and the Pilot Flying (Captain) completed all briefings. While in cruise flight; Mexico Center gave us a late descent clearance which is very common on this flight that required LVL/CHG mode and speedbrakes to get back on path. While we were descending to our first cleared altitude (around 14;000 feet MSL); Mexico switched us to QRO Approach. Upon contact with QRO Approach about 15-20 miles out; they advised of a traffic on a ten mile final; and informed us to now expect the VOR DME 1 RWY 09 Approach. We were recleared direct to QRO VOR; provided another descent; and then shortly thereafter; Approach cleared us for the approach. The First Officer went into the FMC and configured it to fly direct to QRO VOR. After the aircraft was established on course to the VOR; the First Officer selected the QRO VOR fix in the FMC and inserted the VOR DME 1 RWY 09 approach after verification with the Captain. Because of the angle the aircraft was approaching the VOR (straight in Runway 09); and relative to the approach procedure (an outbound heading 292 followed by a left procedure turn inbound); an additional procedure turn was required just to begin the approach. The procedure turn would normally be done at the VOR. Due to the FMC not having a procedure turn at the VOR to begin the approach for arrivals from the west; it immediately started auto-sequencing fixes to fly the aircraft directly to the outbound procedure turn DME 10 from the QRO VOR. The First Officer had to re-enter the VOR into Direct To and build a holding pattern into the FMC. There was a missed approach holding pattern depicted on the approach chart; therefore; the First Officer built a hold based on the holding pattern published. The First Officer informed ATC that a procedure turn was required at the VOR and also notified approach that the aircraft would enter holding as published to begin the approach. ATC advised us to descend to 11;000 feet and cleared for the approach. ATC seemed confused as to what we were doing. It appears that they were expecting the aircraft to make a hard left after crossing the VOR (almost a 180 degree turn) into unprotected airspace that contained mountainous terrain. The minimum safe altitude for that sector is 12;800 feet and if the aircraft would have flown that; there could have been a CFIT event. Once the aircraft entered the holding pattern; making a procedure turn to enter the crew selected IMM EXIT and the aircraft completed the current holding pattern; just a procedure turn; and exited the hold to fly the entire approach as planned and expected. There seems to be an issue regarding the Jeppesen Charts; and FMC database for this specific approach. The FMC did not contain any proper procedure to join the approach legally. Also the FMC sequencing the approach could have presented multiple issues including CFIT; TCAS; or lost of Situational Awareness.
Report_2_Narrative: We were heading to MMQT to shoot the VOR 1 approach from the west. We were headed direct to the VOR with the approach loaded after that. Approximately 9 miles prior to the VOR the airplane started a left turn to join the outbound portion of the approach. This was not appropriate or legal. We turned the airplane back towards the VOR and realized there was nothing loaded to turn the airplane around to join the approach legally. There is also no procedure turn depicted on the chart. There was a holding pattern at the VOR and a missed approach procedure associated with the approach. We decided to enter the holding pattern at the proper altitude and told the controller we were doing that. That allowed the airplane to turn around and we were able to join and commence the approach that way. The rest of the approach was uneventful
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported they were cleared for a VOR approach which required a procedure turn. There was no procedure turn published on their charts or contained in the FMC.

Report_1_Narrative: This is a report to bring to light a potential issue with a NOTAM; no pilot deviation from ATC instructions or company procedures is believed to have occurred. References you will want: Approach Chart 11-3 ILS or LOC [Runway] 24 BHM; possibly the low IFR chart for that area; and NOTAM BHM A0233/21. This NOTAM has you take a turn to [heading] 219 to intercept the VUZ radial 067. This heading does not intercept that radial; I do not know how to fly this MAP (Missed Approach Procedure) legally. We caught this and requested amended MAP from ATC before commencing the LOC [Runway] 24.This is either due to me not understanding the NOTAM or it being written poorly.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported the missed approach procedure as described in the NOTAM; is in error.

Report_1_Narrative: After an uneventful approach and touchdown with Captain as Pilot Flying; the aircraft was decelerating normally with speed brakes and reversers deployed. The crew accomplished a normal exit of the runway when smoke could be seen in the flight deck and sirens sounded in the cabin. Purser was immediately contacted and told flight crew that there was smoke in the cabin and detectors going off. The Purser was asked to assess the situation in the cabin as simultaneous contact was made with the Tower. Cabin was asked for any signs of a fire or source of smoke and none were present. The Tower advised crew that a runway treatment had been used two days prior and that upon crew request no signs of smoke or fire were visible coming from aircraft. Crew determined it was safe to exit the runway taxiway due to smoke being from possible ingestion into the packs or reversers from chemicals in the runway area and proceed to the ramp with constant contact with the cabin to ensure no escalation or fire warnings.A short time later an evacuation message and siren was triggered in the flight deck. Once again we verified with cabin crew that no fire or source of smoke could be assessed. We requested that the emergency equipment be available and accompany the aircraft to the gate out of an abundance of caution and increasing warnings in the flight deck. A normal shut down was accomplished and the flight mechanic entered the flight deck and informed crew that he had inadvertently set off the evacuate warning while trying to cancel the smoke detectors in the cabin.Crew was met by local airport authorities and emergency personnel. During the interaction with crew we were informed that two compounds 'Sodium Formate' a liquid treatment and 'Potassium Acetate' mixed in with 'aviation grade sand' had been used two days prior and could possibly have been ingested by reverser system and packs leading to smoke. A giant smoke cloud could also be seen at the midpoint of the runway at least 200 feet tall but centered in one location; the possible site where chemicals interacted with the aircraft. Crew taking over the flight was briefed on the situation and Maintenance was in the process of examining the aircraft. By all logic with no indications of a fire and smoke being generated inside the aircraft an external source was deemed the most likely cause. The pebble sized compound that may have been present along runway edge and some portions of runway; even though runway appeared perfectly clean and clear were brought by airports OPS Crew after an inspection of touchdown and mid runway areas.With the compounds mentioned not being familiar to crews not much comment can be given; I would suggest familiarizing crews with this event to help discern an actual fire with a foreign contaminant causing indications of smoke and fire. I would also point out that procedures need to be followed in regards to on board mechanics response to dealing with abnormalities; rather than helping in trying to cancel an alarm after it was deemed non-threatening the issue was compounded which could have forced an evacuation had flight deck and cabin crew had poorer communication.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Captain reported smoke in the flight deck and cabin due to the reversers or packs ingesting chemicals that had been used to treat the runway surface.

Report_1_Narrative: On IFR flight plan I was cleared for an RNAV Approach. I was monitoring the CTAF while still with ATC.  There was someone ahead of me on the RNAV Approach; so I was second to land.  With the airport in sight; I canceled IFR and changed frequency; kept transponder number.  Another plane announced it would enter downwind and land after me.  Another plane announced in area and would be number four.  With each new plane arriving to the area; the Fixed Base Operator announced winds and preferred runway.  The plane ahead of me cleared the runway.  On short final; I saw a headlight at the far end of runway rapidly approaching. I announced that I was going around for plane on opposite side of runway. I climbed and turned slightly right.  The plane from the other direction was rolling on the ground and about midfield took off and turned slightly right. I then announced that I would be staying in the pattern.  I then landed uneventfully.  He came and found me to apologize. He said that he had keyed in the wrong frequency and had been announcing his intentions to land on the opposite direction runway.
Report_1_Synopsis: GA pilot on short final landing at a non-towered airport reported a conflict with an opposite direction arrival which had been transmitting their runway intentions on the wrong frequency.

Report_1_Narrative: Upon receiving taxi instructions to return to the ramp for parking; Student Pilot under my supervision did the taxi. At taxiway Charlie; by the wash racks we turned to left. Student got off the center line and I advise him to keep centerline and prepare to turn left again by reducing airspeed. At same time I finished giving student pilot those instructions; he added full power instead of reducing it. That action was faster than my reaction time to counteract. Immediately and simultaneously; I hit the brakes steering away from the hangar on the right that we were pointed at and pulled the throttle out. The right wingtip light hit the corner of hangar door. Wingtip lights were completely broken and there was a hole the size of a lime in the wingtip. The hangar door had a scratch on the corner where the wingtip hit. No other damages were found. Airplane was placed into maintenance. Student Pilot was instructed during the post flight on actions to avoid this situation of ever happening again. Chief pilot instructed CFI to enhance attention at all times; even when student is doing well.
Report_1_Synopsis: C172 flight instructor reported taxiing problems by the student which resulted in striking a hanger with a wingtip.

Report_1_Narrative: We landed in BTR. We were instructed to roll out to the end of the runway and exit left onto Taxiway Foxtrot. I remember seeing a NOTAM that B between Alpha and 4R was closed. Foxtrot was on the opposite side so we confirmed that Tower wanted us to exit left onto Foxtrot. They said affirmative left on Foxtrot and we complied. The CA (Captain) slowly steered us off Runway 13 and onto Taxiway Foxtrot. He was on centerline the entire time. At this point; I was getting the flaps up; clock started; APU started; and the rest of the after landing flow. Immediately after this; I called up ground for further taxi instructions. I felt a slight dip in the left side and we were unsure of the cause. The Captain said he added some power and the airplane continued to roll forward taxiing. I was focused on getting some complex taxi instructions from ground that were abnormal and a bit confusing. It took several calls for me to clarify the taxi instructions. When we parked at the gate; I went out to do my post flight walk around. The ground crew was already taking pictures and I could see dirt on the left side wheels. That's when it clicked that the left wheel had gone into the grass. I informed the Captain of the left wheel; and he called maintenance as well as informed Dispatch.Tower advised us to 'exit left at the end on taxiway Foxtrot' and to contact ground when off. We complied with their instructions. There is no mention of wingspan restrictions or weight limits for Taxiway Foxtrot. The company documentation does not make mention of any restrictions to Taxiway Foxtrot either. While the CA was on centerline; oversteering is needed for this taxiway - there is no mention of this on the 10-09.A note should be added prohibiting air carriers on Taxiway Foxtrot. At the very least; there should be wingspan restriction or weight restrictions. Additionally; tower should have instructed us to back taxi on the runway rather than tell us to exit on Taxiway Foxtrot.A note should be added prohibiting air carriers on Taxiway Foxtrot. At the very least; there should be wingspan restriction or weight restrictions. Additionally; tower should have instructed us to back taxi on the runway rather than tell us to exit on Taxiway Foxtrot.
Report_2_Narrative: Landed on Runway 13; rolled to the end; Tower gave instructions to turn left onto Taxiway F; I stopped the aircraft before turning asked the FO (First Officer) to query Tower if that was correct because I originally briefed that we would exit right and taxi towards the terminal located on the West side of the airport; the Tower Controller replied; yes; turn left and contact Ground Control for further taxi instructions. With my nose wheel on the centerline; I slowly and cautiously rounded the bend on Taxiway F; felt the left side of the airplane sink a little; maybe 3-4 inches; and added a little more thrust; 3/4 to a full knob of the left engine to keep rolling; after a few feet we were back on the asphalt. Once at the gate; I inspected the left gear and found dirt on the wheels; I then called Maintenance Control; filled out the LOG and contacted Dispatch.BTR ATC gave us the taxi instructions that caused this.Should have been allowed to exit right; then taxi via B; turn right on either Taxiway E or Runway 4R and then left on Runway 13/31; then left on Taxiway A into the terminal ramp.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier flight crew reported the aircraft left main landing gear left the taxiway while the aircraft was on the taxiway center line at BTR airport.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Confusion; Distraction; Situational Awareness; Communication Breakdown
Report_1_Narrative: Flight was all normal until we were cleared for a visual approach. Approach vectored us about 2 miles outside of the Final Approach Fix. When cleared for the a visual approach the First Officer turned inside of the Final Approach Fix. We had briefed the towers and their height and had them visually. The First Officer turned off the flight directors and turned directly towards the runway; about 20 degrees angle.  At 1;000 feet Tower called and asked if we had the towers in sight and said he had gotten an altitude alert.  At that point we were still visual with the towers and a half dot low on the glide slope. I directed the First Officer to come left and get on final. We continued the approach and landed. Found out afterwards this was the First Officer's first time to this airport and that he really didn't have a good visual on the runway. I felt his turning off the flight directors added to his lack of situational awareness. We discussed this approach afterwards and he felt I should have directed a go around. I believe he was waiting for me but I was in the green.  I didn't know he was lost. I explained to the First Officer that there is a reason we brief instrument approaches at night; to use them.  I shouldn't have allowed him to make the turn directly towards the runway but told him to intercept closer to the Final Approach Fix. The First Officer needed to communicate he wasn't in the green and execute a go around if he felt it was needed.
Report_2_Narrative: Cleared visual approach after I stated to the Captain that I had the beacon in sight. I turned toward the airfield and began my descent referencing the glideslope. I only saw the beacon; not the runway. Tower issued a low altitude alert as I flew too close to the towers west of the field. I had the towers in sight and the Captain gave me verbal commands to help me orient the runway. The landing and rollout were uneventful. I accepted a visual approach based on the beacon alone. I was also distracted by the airspeed going below the hook for reasons I didn't understand. After landing; the Captain and I thoroughly debriefed the approach and landing.
Report_1_Synopsis: A Flight Crew conducting a Visual Approach at night reported the Pilot Flying turned towards the runway prior to the Final Approach Fix and was issued a Low Altitude Alert from the Tower.

Report_1_Narrative: I was holding short of Runway 29R on Taxiway B2 at Stockton (SCK) in preparation for a VFR departure en route to ZZZ; waiting for a [Company] heavy aircraft to land and clear the runway. The prevailing conditions were night VFR; with unlimited visibility; clear skies; and minimal wind. Stockton Tower was closed; and traffic was coordinating via CTAF. After the heavy aircraft landed and cleared; I made my CTAF call indicating that I was taking Runway 29R for departure. The heavy aircraft crew acknowledged my transmission and noted that they were clear of all runways. While beginning my takeoff roll; a ground vehicle; self-identified as a tug; made a radio call on CTAF that they were crossing Runways 29L/29R en route to the cargo ramp. This was the first call the tug made on CTAF. I made another radio call noting that I was in my takeoff roll; and began visually searching for the tug. I reduced engine power to idle; and applied heavy braking. At that time I saw the tug's anti-collision lights cross in front of my aircraft. I stopped on the runway and made an additional radio call noting that I was aborting takeoff and returning to RWY (Runway) 29R. At no point did the tug acknowledge any of these radio calls or change behavior. I returned to RWY 29R and made an otherwise uneventful departure.Primary cause of the problem: runway incursion by airport tug vehicle that was broadcasting on; but possibly not monitoring; the CTAF frequency.Proximate causes of the problem: airport ops vehicles likely unused to operating on CTAF after-hours at normally tower-controlled airport. Night conditions may have made it difficult for the ops vehicle to see my aircraft on the runway; and made it more difficult for me to see the ops vehicle. Complacency: SCK is a cargo airport; and extremely quiet at night. It's possible that the ops vehicle crew was accustomed to only seeing large cargo aircraft operating at SCK at night; and so my comparatively smaller (and unscheduled) aircraft may have not been noticed/ignored. Finally; the airport operations staff may not have been aware that entering a runway - even several thousand feet down the runway from a takeoff aircraft - is still prohibited.Preventative measures: training for airport ops crews on proper radio use; importance of clearing runways prior to crossing; and runway incursion avoidance best-practices.
Report_1_Synopsis: Pilot reported on takeoff roll; a ground tug crossed the runway in use; resulted in aborted takeoff with evasive action.

Report_1_Narrative: Arriving at the aircraft and checking the logbook; I noticed that the last crew had written that the Takeoff Configuration light and horn activated on takeoff (speed of activation was not noted). I surmised that the crew rejected the takeoff and subsequently swapped out of the aircraft after returning to the gate and the aircraft was not flown afterwards. The corrective action was a check of the Takeoff Configuration Warning System with no faults noted. Since nothing was actually corrected; the Captain and I discussed the possibility of it activating again on our takeoff. We pushed late due to an unrelated finding of damage in the floor of the Forward Cargo Bin C. The bin was deferred and bags transferred to the aft bin. We were relatively full on this flight and our V1/VR speeds for Flaps 1 on Runway XXR were 125/135. The engine start and taxi out were uneventful with the throttle burst yielding no takeoff warning. On the takeoff roll at approximately 130 knot (5 knot after V1) the takeoff warning horn and light activated. We elected to continue the takeoff. The initial climb was normal and we discussed that we would be writing this up in ZZZ1. The Captain called for 'flaps up' at the appropriate speed and I moved the flap lever to UP. We had a few distractions from ATC due to hold-down altitude that was cancelled. Before I moved the landing gear handle to OFF; I checked the flap indicator and noticed that the flaps were still at 1 with the LE FLAP EXT green light illuminated. After confirming that the flap handle was up; I told the Captain the issue and that we need to keep our airspeed below 250 kts. and level off to handle the problem.After notifying ATC that we would need to level off; they gave us vectors for terrain while we ran the QRH for Trailing Edge Flap Disagree. Since the QRH doesn't really address the disagreement when attempting to RETRACT the flaps and only deals with setting the flaps for landing; we turned our attention to coordinating the air return. Dispatch was advised of the return as well as Station Ops in ZZZ. Our current gross weight was a little over 130;000 pounds so we extended the gear to add drag and burn off excess fuel for landing. The F/As (Flight Attendants) and passengers were notified of the return. Since this was a flight control issue; we [received priority handling] and notified ATC that we were requesting [Runway] XYL but would need time to reduce our landing weight to 128;000 pounds. We felt this was the safe option as time was not an issue. We then ran the QRH; ran the performance calculation for the Trailing Edge Flap Disagree QRH; and then the brake cooling module. The flaps extended normally with the Alternate Flap system to 15 degrees. The only slight issue was although I read the section directing the flap lever to be moved to the final flap position (15); we were sidetracked by discussing slowing during the extension and this was not done until after the QRH was completed. This allowed us to see our Flaps 15 maneuvering speed. After the delay vectors were complete and we were below the maximum landing weight; we made an uneventful landing on [Runway] XYL. Brake cooling allowed us to take right to the gate and the ARFF (Airport Rescue and Fire Fighting) trucks followed. No other issues occurred. We swapped into another aircraft and continued the pairing.
Report_2_Narrative: The aircraft was an originator. The previous day a takeoff had been rejected because of a spurious Takeoff Config Warning and the maintenance resolution was no faults noted.
