The F/O (First Officer) and I discussed possible reasons for a false warning lasting a few seconds; which refreshed our memories of the warning system and thankfully prepared us for a repeat occurrence. We pushed late due to an unrelated finding of damage in the floor of the forward cargo bin. The bin was deferred and bags transferred to the aft bin. On takeoff; approximately two seconds after the F/O's V1 call; the configuration light illuminated and the warning horn sounded. The F/O called VR; and we lifted off. The light went out and the horn stopped about the time the wheels left the ground. The F/O's performance and adhering to procedure during this event was flawless; which combined with our earlier discussion allowed the situation to be handled easily. We briefly mentioned writing the issue up again in ZZZ1. I called for Flaps Up; from their takeoff '1' setting. F/O moved the flap lever to Up; and then moments later told me the flaps didn't go up; and instructed me not to go over 250 [kts.]. We were still at about 200 knots; so no airspeed issues. I told F/O to tell ATC we needed to level off and maintain low airspeed. Initially we told ATC we would follow the SID and get back to them. ATC gave us a terrain clearance altitude. We confirmed the flaps were not up. I called for the QRH and we agreed that 'Flap Disagree' was the appropriate checklist. The checklist starts off by saying 'to prepare for landing' so we paused the checklist; agreed we were not going to ZZZ1 with flaps out; and I messaged Dispatch we were returning to ZZZ; told ATC; and received clearance to return to ZZZ. I notified the F/A (Flight Attendants) and told the passengers we were returning to ZZZ. We ran the QRH for Flaps Disagree; the procedure went mostly uneventfully. We were at 130;000 pounds; so we took delaying vectors to burn fuel to 128;000 [lbs.]. We checked the brake cooling for Autobrake 3; no issues. We did [receive priority handling]. We landed Flaps 15 and taxied to the gate. Positive takeaways. The CQT training from (year)?; (year)? that emphasized flap malfunctions prepared us well to handle the stuck flaps. Negative takeaways. The QRH for Flap Disagree was obviously written with a failure occurring during approach in mind. For our situation of failure on takeoff; the procedure kept us with the flap handle up until we had returned to ZZZ and were preparing to land; which meant we had flaps out; but no maneuvering speed. We know that Flaps 1 speed is 180 knots approximately; but it would have been one more item in our favor if we had moved the flap handle to match the flaps to give us the normal sight picture on the displays. While we were extending the flaps with the alternate switch; between watching the flap gauge and calls from ATC; we momentarily missed the instruction in the QRH to move the flap handle with the flap movement. We followed proper flap speeds as flaps were extending; but that that was because of our experience; not the display. The QRH should have the instruction to move flap handle with flaps before the actual instruction to move the flaps so that crews can discuss the handle in advance. We ran the brake cooling for Autobrake 3; and then tried to run again for Autobrake 2. The brake cooling module did not work the second time. We recalled a recent (Company communication piece) about Dispatch doing something to mess up performance calculation results; which could be rectified by requesting landing data again; but that did not work. Something in the performance calculations needs to be corrected so that brake cooling can be run more than once. Brake cooling was not an issue; even with Autobrake 3; so this was a small nuisance. Based on passenger comments; F/As did a great job. F/O's performance was excellent; our teamwork together allowed the situation to be handled easily.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Crew reported a repeat failure of the Take Off Warning System and a failure of trailing edge flaps to retract caused an Air Tun Back and a precautionary emergency landing.

Report_1_Narrative: At or near ZZZ VOR; I noticed the aircraft started to turn when on a direct clearance to fix ZZZ1. Followed quickly by an Unable RNP. I quickly went to heading mode and requested and was given a heading from ATC. Aircraft was about a mile left of course. Trouble shooting looked to be a GPS issue. Turned off GPS navigation and used IRS function and aircraft tracked courses normally. We changed flight plan with ATC to no GPS and continued on with a normal flight and approach and landing.
Report_1_Synopsis: B767-300 Captain reported having a GPS issue resulting in a track heading deviation.

Report_1_Narrative: Climbing out of ZZZ on the ZZZZZ TWO on our flight plan.  After a short delay ATC cleared us direct to the ZZZZZ1 Intersection followed by the ZZZZZ2 and ZZZZZ3 intersections which are on the ZZZZZ2 THREE departure.During the departure briefing both the FO identified our lack of recency experience as a threat. When the clearance was sent to the FMC with the new routing the FO was not aware of the LOAD FMC prompt so the new routing was never loaded. When I reviewed the print out of the PDC clearance I remember being confused by the clearance.I should of voiced my concern to the FO when I did not understand the clearance. Unfortunately; I got distracted and never resolved the discrepancy. There's no substitute for diligence when it comes to the route check.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported a track heading deviation.  Captain stated when the clearance was sent to the FMC with the new routing the FO was not aware of the LOAD FMC prompt so the new routing was never loaded.

Report_1_Narrative: While taxing to the gate and on the terminal ramp the 4th Flight Attendant called up and stated there was smoke in the cabin. She stated 'could be electrical'. I stopped the aircraft; I got a minor whiff of something but it dissipated immediately. FO (First Officer) smelled nothing. We reported smoke in the cabin to ground and requested Airport rescue and Fire Fighting. We considered running the Smoke/AVIONICS SMOKE/Fumes but needed more information; (global assessment). I called up the 1st and she stated she was unaware of what was going on. I called back to the rear of the aircraft and 2nd stated it had begun to dissipate. After a brief discussion with FO; I elected to taxi to the gate and have Airport Rescue and Fire Fighting follow us and access the situation. Aircraft deplaned normally. 1st was unaware there was an issue 4th thought it was an electrical odor 2nd stated there was an odor but not a burning odor. He noticed a lite haze in the reading lights. [The possible cause] was primarily due to the dark cabin; communications among cabin crew. In a perfect world; there would have been better communication between all of the flight attendants; prior to calling up the flight deck. A more concrete assessment could have made with all eyes on the situation. Then the degree of urgency; and solid information can be transmitted more efficiently to the Captain.
Report_2_Narrative: Taxiing to the gate on the terminal ramp we received a cabin call from the #4 FA (Flight Attendant) reporting smoke in the cabin. CA stopped the aircraft to assess the situation and asked if I smelled smoke or odor. I did not see or smell smoke or odor in the cockpit. CA said he sensed a brief odor but not burning. We called ground to request Airport Rescue and Fire Fighting due to the cabin smoke report. We discussed completing the Smoke/AVIONICS SMOKE/ Fumes checklist but after a follow up call to the FAs about the cabin environment the #1 said she didn't see or smell smoke or odor and #2 and #4 said the smoke/odor had dissipated. Due to close proximity to the gate CA decided to continue to the gate for further evaluation by the Airport Rescue and Fire Fighting personnel. The smoke report was entered in the AML and the fumes report [was] completed.
Report_1_Synopsis: A319 flight crew reported a fume/smoke event during arrival taxi to gate.

Report_1_Narrative: I was conducting a stage check for my student and we were practicing engine out approaches. On the first attempt a slip was attempted but the nose was too high and the airspeed dropped dangerously low. I took over and attempted to initiate a go around but the aircraft landed on all 3 gear to bounce sharply. I proceeded back to our base and the student and I attempted to get his power off approaches cleaned up and we did multiple touch and goes. After several landings we decided to end the lesson but I noticed that the left brake lost all authority when trying to stop. I took over and prevented a [runway] excursion and tried to slow down in a controlled manner. When I tried to exit [the] taxiway the wind pushed my tail around faster than expected and the plane skidded to a stop just before the hold short line with the nose gear and left main in the grass and snow. No damage to the plane or taxiway lights occurred. No injuries occurred.
Report_1_Synopsis: DA40 Instructor Pilot reported loss of directional control during landing roll.

Report_1_Narrative: During flight unexpected moderate rime ice was encountered. Upon encountering the ice I requested a higher altitude of 13;000 [feet] to attempt to escape the conditions which ATC approved. However; at that point; buildup had accrued and the aircraft was struggling to maintain 12;000 [feet]. I then requested 11;000 [feet]which Center also approved. The aircraft continued to have difficulty maintaining altitude and fell below the minimum IFR altitude for the area several times resulting in a terrain alert and several terrain vectors from ATC. An aircraft coming from the other direction advised that the area a couple miles ahead from the aircraft's current position was clear; so I elected to get to that area and the rest of the flight was completed normally. Lack of positive icing PIREPs in the vicinity of the route of flight informed that encountering icing would be unlikely. In the area where the icing occurred it seemed that the combination of location and temperature were contributing factors.
Report_1_Synopsis: C182 pilot reported receiving terrain alerts when his aircraft was unable to maintain safe altitude because of ice accumulation.

Report_1_Narrative: I departed from an airport which lies in a cutout from the adjacent airport Class C airspace. My desired on-course heading was 021. I knew that the adjacent airport Tower handled the nearby airspace; and I was comfortable contacting them and requesting clearance through Class C toward my destination.Immediately after lifting I established contact with Tower. Tower responded; and I requested clearance through Class C climbing to 3;500 feet. The Tower controller responded with the phraseology 'Cleared to operate in Class Charlie;' approved my course heading and told me that he only controlled to 2;500 feet. I took that as an altitude limitation; and continued north north eastward. About the time I was getting ready to level off at 2;500 feet; the Tower Controller cleared me to 3;500 feet; and handed me off to Approach.Upon establishing contact with Approach; that controller asked me if I was familiar with Class Charlie airspace and scolded me; telling me words to the effect of 'You can't just fly around here not talking to anyone.' I informed her that I had been in contact with Tower and he had handed me off to her however; I sensed that explanation didn't satisfy her. She then gave me a phone number that I could call later if I needed to talk with someone about it.At my next fuel stop; I contacted TRACON at the phone number that was given to me; and I was told that I had violated Class Charlie airspace. I explained to the gentleman on the phone that Tower had cleared me using the proper phraseology; 'Cleared to operate in Class Charlie.' The gentleman from TRACON went on to say that the Tower Controller shouldn't have done that. At this point; I didn't know what to do; and I certainly couldn't undo what I had done; so I thanked him for his time and told him I'd be filing a Report when I reached my destination.This airspace is remarkably busy with training aircraft. That is why I contacted Tower immediately with my request. If the Tower Controller didn't have the authority to grant me clearance then it's my opinion that he should have told me to remain clear of Class Charlie airspace; but he didn't do that. Instead; he specifically used the clearance phraseology that is taught in flight school and my company's recurrent training. Given those circumstances I proceeded in good faith with the clearance given to me by the tower controller. I believe that air traffic controller communications are recorded and stored. If so; I believe someone with the proper authority can verify this narrative and correct whatever caused this potentially dangerous situation.
Report_1_Synopsis: A Helicopter pilot reported they received clearance into Class C airspace from the Tower Controller and after handoff to TRACON the TRACON Controller accused them of entering the Class C airspace without authorization.

Report_1_Narrative: We were flying to ASE and I was the Pilot Monitoring. As we approached Aspen; we were given vectors to intercept LOC E into ASE. We accepted clearance to maintain 13;000 ft until established and clearance to execute LOC E approach. As we were intercepting LOC we picked up visual with the airport and commenced descent towards it while having visual reference with the airport and all the terrain around. In the midst of all things happening quickly and the excitement of having visual with the airport; I failed to communicate to ATC my intention of executing visual approach. At some point we lost the visual with the airport due to a cloud layer just ahead of us; but not the terrain. At the same time ATC issued an altitude alert to us due to us being lower than what LOC approach altitudes called for. I advised that we had terrain in sight but lost the visual with the airport and said that we would be going missed and starting a climb. We got another altitude alert from ATC. We advised we are in a climb and asked vectors; until we decide what to do. We proceeded to ZZZ airport afterwards.  At no time we were in IMC conditions and maintained visual clearance from all the terrain. My mistake in this case was deviating from ATC clearance and going visual without communicating that to ATC. And also; not staying on a LOC due to a cloud layer over the airport. At no time was the aircraft in IMC conditions and we were maintaining clearance with terrain at all times. By all means the aircraft was never put in any unsafe condition.  I did learn from this experience to clearly and concisely communicate any and all of my intentions with ATC; so there is no misunderstanding at any point of the flight.
Report_1_Synopsis: Corporate jet non-flying Captain reported diverting to an alternate airport after receiving a low altitude alert from ATC on approach to ASE airport.

Report_1_Narrative: I was doing my first solo for my CFI training so I was alone in the aircraft in the right seat. I was performing engine start up procedures and had to lean over to the complete left side of the flight deck to crank the ignition switch. As I was leaned over the engine started and my feet slipped off the brake pedals. The plane moved forward and as soon as I could react I moved the throttle to idle and my feet back to the brakes. I then taxied back into the parking spot; shut down the aircraft; and canceled the flight.
Report_1_Synopsis: SR20 pilot reported momentary loss of control following engine start from the right seat.

Report_1_Narrative: Runway was extremely slick. There was nothing on the METAR or the NOTAMs that indicated the braking action. The 210 overran the runway end by 8 feet. Local Airport Manager and his handyman helped push it aircraft onto the pavement. The maintenance personnel after looking at the airplane deemed nothing was wrong so [I] departed for destination airport.  No anomalies or problems found with gear; no prop strike occurred.
Report_1_Synopsis: C210 pilot reported running off the end of the slick runway after landing.

Report_1_Narrative: Was cleared visual approach [Runway] 23 / asked to turn short final inside of GS Intercept Altitude for traffic. Changed Alt Select from 2;300 feet to 1;500 feet and selected VS (Vertical Speed) descent of 700 rpm to get below GS. Descending below 1;800 feet or so; received Low Altitude Alert from ATC / Tower. Deactivated AutoPilot; added power and initiated climb to intercept GS.ATC Low Altitude Alert followed later (approximately 5-10 sec of 'Glideslope' call-out from GPWS.Two causal items: short turn to final / cleared for visual approach at altitude that would put us above glide slope; so selected lower altitude and initiated descent. Second causal item was over aggressive selection of Altitude Select to 1;500 feet . . . In retrospect should have selected something like 1;900-2;000 MSL given field elevation of 700 feet.De-selected AP and climbed to 2;000-2;100 feetWe actually discussed not accepting a short turn to final as part of approach briefing . . . When cleared for the visual; initially turned right to extend final leg; but then was asked by ATC to turn to a left heading given other arriving traffic behind us. In retrospect; could have indicate unable; but that seemed unnecessary given overall regime; weather; etc. Second suggestion would be to double-think / exercise caution in selecting an altitude above the DH but below the FAF / GS Intercept Altitude.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier F/O reported receiving a low altitude alert from ATC on approach to BUF.

Report_1_Narrative: The aircraft had several maintenance scheduled items that needed to be addressed before we could fly the aircraft. It was supposed to be the first revenue flight after long term storage. There was one maintenance schedule item X which needed to be accomplished before the aircraft can be used for revenue flight with passengers. The item was signed off on the completed items sheet and the aircraft was released for flight. When we were taxing; Dispatch notified us to hold. We called them and they said there was a maintenance schedule write off not signed off properly. So; we returned to the gate to have to addressed. The reason for this report is that you cannot leave the gate with passengers unless maintenance schedule item X had been signed off. Our paperwork showed it was signed of yet the electronic AML [Aircraft Maintenance Logbook] said it was not.  We returned to gate. We found out later that it was a clerical data entry error made by someone in maintenance and the maintenance schedule item sign off was entered incorrectly.The cause is easy to figure out. The only way to fix it is to have a computerized completed items sheet that only shows items cleared and then the computer copy and paper completed items sheet would always match!After items are cleared in computer; print out new completed items sheet for AML so paper and computer always match.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported a return to gate after Dispatch told them they had an improperly signed maintenance item.  The aircraft had several maintenance items that needed to be addressed before the flight due to it just coming out of long term storage.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Other / Unknown; Distraction; Physiological - Other; Workload
Report_1_Narrative: During the approach we were cleared direct down to 8000 feet from 12000 feet. During the descent Autopilot was engaged and following LNAV and VS we were encountering continuous light to moderate turbulence throughout the descent. As we passed through approximately 12000 feet and beginning to slow; we experienced severe turbulence mixed with continuous moderate [turbulence]. When we initially encountered the severe turbulence; the Autopilot disengaged; the aircraft was changing altitude and air speeds abruptly with several hundred feet of altitude change and at least plus or minus 20 to 30 knots airspeed changes. The Captain was thrown hard enough to hit the overhead panel with his head and we received a report one of our Flight Attendants had been hurt and several passengers had hit their heads. I as the Pilot Flying took manual control of the aircraft and flew the remainder of the descent and approach. The aircraft was extremely hard to control throughout most of the descent and approach as we continued to encounter continuous turbulence; strong crosswinds and wind shear. During the ensuing descent and approach the aircraft was extremely hard to control as we continued to experience moderate to severe turbulence; strong crosswind and wind shear throughout the approach. Once established inbound and cleared for the approach we were pushed several degrees off course and had some airspeed fluctuations of plus or minus 20 knots. We quickly discussed missed approach but prior to reaching 1000 feet we had regained the course; were on glide path and stabilized (properly configured) to continue the approach. We continued the approach while receiving some lower wind shear of plus or minus 10 knots down to approximately the 500 foot call. At 500 feet we were still stabilized and continued the approach to landing without further issue. Throughout the approach and landing; we had airspeed; altitude variations and heading deviations that were extremely hard to control due to the turbulence and wind shear events we were experiencing. I do not believe at any point we had any exceedances or violations; however; it was a very task saturated environment. There were no reports of the severity of the turbulence ahead of us and it was a very unexpected event.This was an example of good Crew Resource Management as the Captain and I maintained good communication throughout the event and helped to cross monitor the aircraft systems and instruments. As the pilot flying; I was entirely focused with aircraft control and the Captain doing the pilot monitoring was ensuring all the descent and approach tasks were completed. We kept good crew communication with what was happening with aircraft control and situational awareness. A recommendation is for pilots to ensure they continue to practice hand flying skills for situations like this. The autopilot was unusable; and I was thankful I constantly practice hand flying the airplane. It helped me with confidence to control the airplane to the best of my ability in a situation where the aircraft is being tossed around by turbulence.
Report_1_Synopsis: Pilot reported encountering a loss of control due to severe turbulence and wind shear on descent and approach into SEA.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Time Pressure; Physiological - Other; Human-Machine Interface; Situational Awareness
Person_2_Human_Factors: Human-Machine Interface; Physiological - Other; Situational Awareness
Report_1_Narrative: During our initial climb-out we noticed the rate of climb on the pressurization gauge was acting erratic with various climb and descent rates. As ATC continued to assign higher altitudes we both noticed that the cabin altitude was climbing but the differential rate needle was not increasing like normal. As we climbed through 10;000 feet the cabin altitude needle started to decrease and the differential rate needle started to increase. After leveling off at 23;000 feet everything appeared to be stable. The cabin altitude was decreasing below 9;000 feet after nearly getting up to 10;000 feet and the differential rate needle started to increase between 5 and 6 psi showing that cabin was pressuring like normal. After ATC clear us to 25;000 feet I then requested climb to 27;000 feet because of the moderate chop/turbulence at 25;000 feet. Once we reached 27;000 feet we proceeded with running the cruise checklist. Moments after completing the checklist our pressurization rate of needle showed a descent of 6;000 feet depressurizing the cabin; triggering the cabin high altitude annunciater and the master warning lights. At that time we both donned our oxygen mask; performed abnormal checklist and asked ATC for a lower altitude because of our depressurization issue. Once we reached a safe altitude we removed our oxygen masks and decided to return back to our departure airport.Although I believed this incident was handled safely; declaring an emergency would have been the right thing to do. Anytime an emergency checklist is used or a return to field situation arise should trigger one to declare an emergency regardless of the severity. By doing so helps the pilot in handling the emergency more effectively.
Report_2_Narrative: Upon initial climb out we felt our ears straining and popping so I as Pilot Monitoring looked at the pressurization gauge; and it was fluctuating between climbs and descents. We continued to monitor it and it stabilized acted as normal as we climbed through about 10;000 to 11;000 feet. The cabin needle stabilized just below 10;000 (cabin altitude) feet and started a slow descent down to 9;000 (cabin altitude) feet. As we climbed into the Flight levels up to our cleared altitude of 23;000 feet; it appeared stable at 9;000 feet; and the differential needle pushed to a higher differential as its design to do.ATC then cleared us to our filed altitude of 29;000 feet. As we continued the climb; the pressurization continued to operate normally; with the differential increasing and the cabin altitude slowly descending just below 9;000 feet. The Pilot in Command asked me to asked ATC for 25;000 feet as a level off altitude. We leveled there and were getting continuous moderate turbulence at 25;000 feet so we requested 27;000 feet as our final. We climbed up to 27;000 feet. We leveled off; and shortly after running the cruise checklist; we both felt high pressure in our ears; and I instantly saw the cabin needle jump up too a 6;000 foot a minute climb and then the Red Cabin above 10;000 foot annunciator illuminated and as well the master warning. We then both put on our mask and made sure oxygen was 100% and notified ATC that we were having an issue and needed to descend. The decision was made to return to our point of departure. ATC cleared us direct to the field and we descended down to 6;000 feet. We ran through the abnormal checklist for the cabin above 10;000 foot annunciator. Once were low enough to safely remove the oxygen masks we did. We did not declare an emergency. We continued without any further incident and landed safely.
Report_1_Synopsis: A Flight Crew reported a loss of pressurization then returned to their departure airport and landed safely.

Report_1_Narrative: In flying return flight from ZZZ1 to ZZZ2 at 3;000 feet; we were anticipating B clearance into the ZZZ 1;500 feet shelf northeast of ZZZ VOR. This expectation was due to the fact that clearance was received shortly before going the same route but opposite direction; and that ZZZ was landing Runway XX; so arrivals would not be a factor in receiving clearance.  We were receiving VFR flight following from ZZZ1 followed by ZZZ1 [TRACON]. Upon hand off to ZZZ Approach frequency from ZZZ1 [TRACON]; the frequency was extremely congested. We established two-way communication and made initial Bravo request with ZZZ around ZZZ [VOR]; but only received 'radar contact' in return with no further clearance. I queried the Controller at least two more times for clarification; but communication was blocked and the frequency was extremely congested. We initiated descent near ZZZZZ [Intersection] to avoid the 1;500 feet class B shelf; but may have penetrated the B airspace in the descent down to 1;400 feet MSL.  We remained below the floor of the Bravo and received no further communication from ZZZ until handoff to ZZZ2 Approach near ZZZZZ1 [Intersection].Contributing factors leading to this possible deviation are that the PF was the senior pilot on the flight and is very experienced in the area but may have been somewhat out of practice as COVID has significantly decreased flying. Also; the Controller seemed to be slightly overwhelmed; possibly working multiple frequencies; we weren't anticipating the business of the frequency although we should have known better. Additionally; the strong tailwind increased ground speed; although the descent was rapid; the ground covered during descent was greater than normal. Finally; as we just flew the same route the opposite direction; we were (falsely) anticipating the B clearance.While these factors are no excuse for possibly entering the airspace without clearance; the notion that business is picking up again means we all need to be more diligent in our planning and flight execution. As Captain; I should have anticipated not receiving the B clearance; and planned descent accordingly.
Report_1_Synopsis: Pilot reported a Class B airspace violation and cited ATC communication issues and the co-pilot's lack of recent flying as contributing factors.

Report_1_Narrative: Entering the traffic pattern for the airport I turned to enter final which positioned my aircraft directly into an extremely bright setting sun.  The sun then blinded me at that point and I lost visual contact with the airport and runway and altitude information.  After regaining sight from the sun and while establishing my position along with altitude in relation to the airport and runway I observed another aircraft that appeared to be flying in the opposite direction about 200 feet away.  I then took an evasive maneuver and cleared the traffic.  At that point I was no longer in position to continue the landing and I executed a VFR go around and re entered the traffic pattern and landed without further incident.  What caused this incident was turning on final directly into the extremely bright setting sun which blinded me. To prevent this from happening again I will use a runway if available that is not in line of sight with the sun or fly to an alternative airport without conflict with the setting sun or wait until sunset.
Report_1_Synopsis: A pilot reported after turning onto final at a non towered airport they were temporarily blinded by direct sunlight and had a NMAC with opposite direction traffic.

Report_1_Narrative: Cruise flight at FL 390. Smooth air while overlying thunderstorms and VFR conditions. ATC authorized deviations left and right. Captain (CA) made PA call to Flight Attendants (FA) and passengers to all be seated and fasten seat belts. As the aircraft approached the far end of storm; severe turbulence rocked the plane and stick shaker and high speed warning activated twice. CA corrected and re-established control each time; but lost approximately 600 feet in so doing. Pilot Monitoring (FO) called FA's and FA1 reported FA2 was injured. They found her on the floor. FA1 asked for help from medical personnel and they responded. Destination was only 25 minutes away so we continued heading there in case medical attention was needed. Reported injury to ATC. Below 10;000 feet personnel in back advised paramedics were needed. Called for them to meet us at gate and proceeded direct to airport with ATC approval. Emergency vehicles were at the gate; but no ramp personal. FA2 was conscious but confused. She was taken to hospital. Dispatch and Maintenance contacted. I (Captain) called hospital from hotel and spoke to FA2. She was coherent but had no memory of any events previous to people talking to her from the passenger seat.
Report_2_Narrative: Captain was Pilot Flying. Cruise at FL390 with smooth air flying over a thunderstorm. Deviations left and right approved. PA call to FA's (Flight Attendants) and passengers to all be seated and buckled. Far edge of storm was in sight. Severe turbulence; as published; was encountered. Stick shaker activated twice and Hi Speed aural warning twice. Both times; stick shaker stopped quickly before throttles were advanced to maximum thrust. Loss of altitude approximately 600 feet. Control was re-established. Called FA's and heard FA2 was injured. They found her on the floor. FA1 asked for help from medical personnel; two nurses and one flight attendant responded. Destination was only 25 minutes away so we continued heading there in case medical attention was needed. Reported injury to ATC. Below 10;000 feet; personnel in back advised paramedics were needed. Called for them to meet us at gate and proceeded direct to airport with ATC approval. Emergency vehicles were at the gate. FA2 was conscious but confused and in pain from a hip. She was taken to hospital. Dispatch and Maintenance contacted. I (Captain) called hospital from hotel and spoke to FA2. She was coherent but had no memory of any events previous to people talking to her from the passenger seat.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Pilots reported severe turbulence encountered and a Flight Attendant injured.

Report_1_Narrative: At Time ZZZ ramp loader [namd] walked on flight deck with Dangerous Goods Form showing Dry Ice was loaded in the forward compartment and stated he had loaded it himself in the rear. I asked him to correct the Dangerous Goods Form to show that it was loaded in the rear. We received an ACARS message from company at Time showing AUTODangerous Goods Form notification. The corrected Dangerous Goods Form was brought to the flight deck at approximately Time. We had a takeoff time slot of Time to ZZZ1. On taxi out we received our load close out that did not have the R/A (Restricted Article) Dry Ice on it. We contacted company via ACARS and Aircraft X replied at Time that Dry Ice of less than 5lbs will not show on close out and that our close out was good. We finished all takeoff checklists and lined up for takeoff and departed at Time. At Time some time during takeoff roll we received an ACARS message that said our load closeout had been cancelled. Then; multiple company messages that followed updating the load closeout and that it was determined to be 8 lbs of Dry Ice. The corrected load closeout was received at Time. The flight was operated to ZZZ1 uneventfully.[Situation was caused by] I believe that the casual factors are a communication disconnect between the ZZZ base and loaders to loads and planning in ZZZ2. Captain [recommends] a fix [to correct] the way we automate the communication of Hazardous Goods to Load Control & Dispatch.
Report_1_Synopsis: A-321 Captain reported a communications breakdown between flight crew and Dispatch regarding the correct amount of Hazmat cargo on the NOTOC. Hazmat cargo discrepancy corrected after aircraft departure.

Report_1_Narrative: When accepting the flight the Wx (Weather) report at base/sending hospital was 10 sm and clear. Wx at receiving hospital was 6 sm and clear. Although cameras showed haze down the mountain I was confident with the visibility reported and knew that the sun set made it look worse. Descending down the mountain the layer of haze did look more dense than forecasted and arrived at receiving hospital without issues. I checked all weather before return back to base and all were still reported the same. Now it was fully dark and cameras gave a clear view of the basin. I chose the return leg through ZZZ as this gives a good indication of visibility due to the lights up the mountain and all the way. Due to 0% moon there was no reference than the lights on the ground. I climbed to 8;000 ft. which provided proper clearance along that flight path. From ZZZ I could see the lights at the airport from about 10 sm. When I got to ZZZ1 valley the visibility rapidly decreased and within seconds we were IMC. I started my climb to about 9;000 ft. and because my crew did a fantastic job immediately giving me report on visibility left and right; I made a left turn which got us out of the clouds fairly quickly. My crew kept on briefing me their view/visibility on both sides which got us back on track on the north side of the lake. Here we could see the haze/fog/clouds spilling through and over the south mountain range. From that position we had a clear path to the airport and landed without further incident. Weather reporting in our area is spotty. We have wx reporting up in the mountain at the airport and down the mountain at two other locations. The weather 'out of control' factor here is the mountain ranges. There are several tools like cameras that supply information and you make your best judgment; but if the weather is very dynamic you can be caught by surprise like we did on this incident. The additional factor of 'no-moon illumination' added to the fact that we did not see the forecasted clouds rolling in. The 'in-control' weather factor here was that I could have been severely cautious and decline the flight on the haze shown on the cameras. Although I kept positive control over the aircraft when initiating IIMC [Inadvertent IMC] protocol I do want to mention that an autopilot would be a great tool in circumstances like this. When practicing the IIMC procedures in the SIM I am spoiled with the situational awareness and added 'second pilot' of the autopilot. Due to the fact that we are dealing with mountain obscuration and often weather that is not reported and can only be identified with visual cues; we should be first in line for a helicopter with these kind of capabilities.
Report_1_Synopsis: Medical transport helicopter pilot reported inadvertent IMC caused unforecast mountain obscuration.

Report_1_Narrative: On Aircraft X from ZZZ to ZZZ1 we had smoke in the aft cabin and diverted to ZZZ2. We were in cruise at 13;000 ft when the CA (Captain) saw the smoke. We descended to 10;000 ft right away and turned off the bleeds. The smoke in the aft cabin cleared. We landed in ZZZ2 with no further issues.[The first detection occurred] when the CA saw the smoke in the aft cabin.[Captain suspects] something in the Bleeds and/or Packs.
Report_1_Synopsis: SA-227 Captain reported a diversion due to smoke in the aft cabin during cruise.

Report_1_Narrative: Earlier in the day I wrote up the airplane for a pack 2 overheat. We were flying an airplane with an MEL on pack 2. We were cruising at FL250 about 90 miles north of our destination when we got a red 'bleed 1 leak' warning message on EICAS. I notified ATC that I wanted an immediate descent to 10;000 ft. for a bleed leak. The FO (First Officer) handed me the QRH and we began the descent and notified the FA (Flight Attendant) to take her seat because hot air was going somewhere it shouldn't and that we would call her back. I began to run the QRH. ATC gave us FL200 as the initial descent. He asked if I was requesting priority handling; I said YES. He asked for clarification on what a bleed leak meant for us and gave us 10;000 ft. subsequently. Our initial descent rate was about ~3500 fpm; faster than normal; to get out of the icing conditions and closer to a safer pressure altitude. I ran the QRH as written until I reached END. Once I finished running the QRH and put it back in the storage cubby; we began to breathe a sigh of relief that things are probably going to be okay. I directed the FO to slow the descent rate to ~1000 fpm. We were at about 16;000 ft. by this point. The FO then pointed out to me that cabin pressure dropping as indicated by the amber boxed Cabin Alt reading on the EICAS. Cabin altitude was at roughly 9;800 ft. and climbing. We elected to keep pace down to 10;000 ft. in order to get in front of the reducing cabin pressurization. The checklist list was not written with a pack 2 MEL in mind. I began to realize the ramifications of what I had just done by turning off Bleed 1; Pack 1; and closing the cross-bleed switch.The priority handling request with ATC and the events we had just gone through had my mind racing from adrenaline. I decided that 'worrying' about the pressurization system wasn't necessary. We were at 12;000 ft. and descending and if I recall correctly cabin pressure differential was about 2.2 psid. I decided to press dump on the cabin pressurization controller after looking over at the FO and mentioning that pressing the dump button wouldn't harm anything and that we weren't in dangerous territory as far as what happens if I press it. We felt a minor pressurization change as the airplane equalized. In hindsight; this was entirely unnecessary. I should have simply let the airplane depressurize on its own.I then began to evaluate how much fuel our descent to 10;000 ft. would burn instead of being at FL250. It took a minute for the FMS to catch up to the descent we had done. The initial fuel numbers it gave us led me to believe we would be very close to divert. I gave it some time and the numbers got more accurate for fuel calculations. I determined we had no need to divert on account of fuel. I notified dispatch; ATC; and the FA that the urgency was over and we would continue to our destination.Next; the airplane began to get hot and stuffy. One consideration was diverting to the nearest airfield. I didn't want to have a heat casualty in the back. The other was to get air into pack 1 so that it was useful in cooling the cabin. I looked at the overhead panel and discussed with my FO the notion of starting the APU to feed pack 1. This was a risky decision because if the leak was closer to pack 1 then feeding APU bleed air into the system would induce basically the same situation. I figured that I could simply turn the APU back off if that turned out to be the case. I figured the air and pressure coming from the number 2 bleed was hotter and higher pressure than the APU. The checklist had given me the steps to solve the problem perfectly if only my number 2 pack weren't MEL'd. I had a short mental struggle with my decision to do something that contradicted what the checklist had just made me do a few minutes earlier and really felt strange using Captain's authority to bypass it. I pride myself on checklist discipline and following the books as best I possibly can. In hindsight; I think alittle thermal discomfort and more rigidity with regards to the checklist would have been wise.I selected auto on the cross-bleed switch and turned on the APU and fed the number 1 pack. The airplane cooled down inside. I spoke with the flight attendant once more to ask about the faces of the passengers and if anyone knew about what just happened. She said they didn't have any idea and that we would keep it that way. We shot an ILS approach and landed normally.This situation was a learning experience of the highest caliber for me. I have since re-learned how the cross-bleed switch logic works. I have studied the layout and function of the bleed and pneumatic systems and learned much more about airplane pressurization. Pressing dump was not the right decision and I wouldn't do it that way again. Selecting the recirc fan off to bring in fresher air would have been a better choice than turning on the APU.
Report_1_Synopsis: EMB-XRJ Captain reported running QRH procedure of number 2 ACM failure.

Report_1_Narrative: Strong burning smell like hot wires shortly after departure. Since bleed air (heater) was on; my first step was to turn bleed air off assuming that is likely engine fumes. The switch would not turn off air; and hot air continued to enter and smell persisted. Thermostat control also would not change the air flow. Since the smell was abnormal and stronger than a common smell of TKS entering the engine (the TKS system was not used); I elected to return to ZZZ which had airport fire facilities and was only a few minutes away. In the event that were was a fire or something was about to catch fire; I elected to request priority handling and executed the in cabin fire checklist. Upon landing at ZZZ; no further indication of fire was present and I meet the airport fire on the ramp. Their investigation did not find anything that was or had been burning. Aircraft was secured on the ramp for inspection by a mechanic.
Report_1_Synopsis: C-208 Captain reported a burning odor during initial climb resulting in a return to the departure airport.

Report_1_Narrative: I was in command of Aircraft X schedule service from ZZZ to ZZZ1. We departed normally and were climbing to our assigned altitude of 32;000 ft. when just prior to level off our Flight Attendant called us in the cockpit to report that she had a smell of smoke in the cabin. We maintained communication with her as she said it seemed to be coming from Row 4 emanating from the lighting valance on the aircraft left side. We told her to monitor the situation and let us know if there was any sparking visible. She told us that she physically checked the valance and PSU's and they were very hot to the touch and that the smoke and heat was migrating rearward now from Rows 4 thru 10. I told the FA to get the PBE [Protective Breathing Equipment] out along with the fire extinguisher and prepare to fight a fire if one erupted. I then told the FO (First Officer) to notify ATC of our situation and that we needed to return to ZZZ. We were then cleared to return and given a decent clearance to 24;000 ft. Still not sure what type of smoke we had in the cabin I asked the FA to come forward so we could have the FO check the smoke for type of odor (electrical or engine based). FO advised me that the smoke odor seemed to have been not electrical. I then had him get the QRH out and run the procedure for SMOKE IN THE CABIN procedure. We accomplished the memory items and in coordination with ATC requested priority handling and were given an unrestricted decent to 8;000 ft. and vectors to a visual approach to Runway XX at ZZZ. The ARFF (Airport Rescue and Firefighting) trucks were standing by for our arrival. The QRH procedure was completed and the smoke seemed to dissipate a little according to the FA. We landed without incident and upon initiation of communication with the ARFF commander we were told there was no smoke evidence on the exterior of the aircraft. Since it appeared the internal situation was under control we decided to taxi to the gate for normal deplaning. Fire Dept. followed us to the gate and upon arrival ; they boarded the aircraft and I advised the commander of what had happened and where it had been located. The ARFF members then checked the aircraft over with their thermal heat locater and found no heat source in the Valance or PSU. They then left the aircraft. Dispatch and MX were notified of the situation. Aircraft passengers were deplaned without incident.
Report_1_Synopsis: Captain reported an uneventful diversion due to reported fumes of smoke in passenger cabin.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Physiological - Other; Communication Breakdown; Other / Unknown
Report_1_Narrative: Boarding a nearly full flight began at XA:30 AM. We had power (i.e. lights) but; we did not have any airflow (air conditioning). We were beginning to sweat profusely. I (FA) contacted the terminal Supervisor who patched me through to Agent; in the tower. I told him of our plight and passenger complaints and concerns. He said he would send someone immediately to turn on the air. This was approximately 20 minutes later. About 15-20 minutes later we still had no air. Passengers were getting very upset and many took their masks off. We made announcements stating that without airflow; it was even more important to keep their mask on since they could not social distance. I contacted the Supervisor again and insisted the passengers be let off the aircraft if we were not going to get airflow and we still didn't know anything about when the pilots would arrive. Approximately 10 minutes later the pilots boarded and stated we should never have begun boarding under those conditions. They got air up and we departed 15 minutes later. 1 hour and 10 minutes after boarding. I felt very; very unsafe in those conditions as did many passengers.We should never board without air conditioning during COVID. If the pilots are running late; a mechanic should be brought down to turn on the air. A few minutes would be acceptable but when the tower is contacted; something should be done in a timely manner. Flight attendants should be allowed to let passengers deplane under such extreme conditions where everyone's safety and health are put at risk.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Attendant reported passengers were boarded before the pilots arrived at the aircraft. No air conditioning was available and passengers began removing their face masks.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Training / Qualification; Confusion; Situational Awareness; Communication Breakdown
Report_1_Narrative: We were flying from ZZZ to ASE and I was the pilot flying. As we approached Aspen; which at that time was reporting VFR; we were given vectors to intercept LOC DME E into ASE. I looked over and noticed the LOC approach was not properly set up. I warned the monitoring pilot of this but at that point we made visual contact with the airport. We accepted clearance to maintain 13;000 ft until established and clearance to execute LOC DME E approach. Having visual contact with the airport we started our descent. A layer of clouds moved in below us as we made the final turn inbound. At the entire time we had full visual contact with all the terrain around. We lost sight of the airport due to the cloud layer; at the same time ATC issued an altitude alert. I emphasize that we were in full visual contact with all the terrain and that visibility at our flight level was unrestricted. The pilot monitoring advised that we had terrain but lost a visual with the airport and said that we would be going missed and starting a climb. We got another altitude alert from ATC. We advised we are in a climb and asked for vectors to give time to decide what to do. We proceeded to ZZZ1 airport afterwards. We were NOT in IMC conditions at any phase of the flight and we maintained visual clearance from all the terrain. The mistake was communication breakdown with ATC and in part CRM in regards to the intentions to execute a visual approach. At no time aircraft was in IMC conditions and we were maintaining clearance with terrain at all times. The aircraft was never put in any unsafe condition. I learned from this how CRM and communication has to be mastered the entire time.
Report_1_Synopsis: Learjet First Officer reported receiving a low altitude alert from ATC after descending early on a cleared instrument approach.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Time Pressure; Situational Awareness; Other / Unknown; Communication Breakdown; Workload
Report_1_Narrative: I was PF in the left seat and we were cleared for take off on Rwy XL.  As we were lining up on the runway; I heard the Tower clear a helicopter for an eastbound departure from the ramp; but I did not visually see the helicopter yet.  Once we were on the takeoff roll; I saw the helicopter lifting off from the ramp (ahead and to our left); but it appeared to be turning parallel to our runway to I diverted my attention back to the runway.  Right after initiating rotation; I saw the helicopter begin to cross over our runway; left to right; at approximately 200 feet AGL.  Because we were past V1 and already rotating on a short runway; I quickly determined an aborted takeoff was not an option so I continued our rotation.  During these few seconds; there were some communications between the Tower and the helicopter; but I did not comprehend them due to my focus on avoiding hitting the helicopter.  Shortly after liftoff (~100 feet AGL); I had to make an evasive maneuver to our left and reduce our climb rate for a few seconds to avoid hitting the helicopter.  Luckily; there was no terrain or obstacles to the left of our runway heading.  Once the helicopter passed off our right at what I estimate was 200-300 feet; I resumed a normal climb rate and a right turn back to our departure heading.  The Tower controller apologized and then handed us off to Departure.  Looking back on the scenario; I believe continuing the takeoff roll as we did was the right call; as we certainly would have had a runway excursion if we had attempted an abort at that point in the roll - passed V1 and already rotating.  Additionally; I am not sure how I could have anticipated the impending conflict earlier because helicopters maneuver on a dime and it was hard to tell its intending heading after liftoff.  After the event; I listened to the ATC recording on a publicly available website and it seems the controller tried to tell the helicopter pilot to remain north of the runway at all times; but that transmission was not acknowledged.
Report_1_Synopsis: Twin Engine Jet Pilot reported a NMAC with a helicopter during takeoff.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Situational Awareness; Training / Qualification; Communication Breakdown; Confusion; Human-Machine Interface
Report_1_Narrative: While performing a charter flight under FAR part 135 departing off of runway 25 at EGE we were assigned the BEEVR2 SID. After programming the FMS I noted that the FMS did not include the initial turn to a 206 heading; I told the Captain that he would need to use heading mode on the SID and he immediately dismissed it as incorrect; even after me bringing up the chart and the active legs page for him to review. This resulted in us not making the turn at the correct time and triggering a GPWS Warning accompanied with the 'Pull Up' 'Pull Up' annunciator to go off. Eventually he did disconnect the auto-pilot but went direct to the first fix instead of the 206 heading.
Report_1_Synopsis: Citation First Officer reported a delayed initial turn on the SID which resulted in a ground proximity warning.

Report_1_Narrative: Both the preflight check and weather were confirmed to meet solo flight requirements. During takeoff; and prior to rotation; the aircraft veered left and exited the runway. The aircraft struck a construction berm which caused it to veer further left where it struck a second construction berm parallel to the runway and damaged the nose and left gear. Emergency procedures were conducted and both power and fuel were cut off. I exited the aircraft and contacted emergency services. No one was injured.
Report_1_Synopsis: A student pilot reported losing control of the aircraft; during takeoff roll; which veered off the runway.

Report_1_Narrative: When reviewing my logbook on Date 6; I discovered that what I thought was a BFR completed on Date 2; was an IPC only. I did however complete a BFR on Date 1; eight months before the IPC. I made two flights after Date 3; one on Date 4 and the other on Date 5. I believed at the time that I made these flights that my last BFR was completed on Date 2; and thus that my next BFR was not due until Date 8.However; since I only completed an IPC on Date 2 (and not a BFR); even allowing for an extension provided by the SFAR in response to the COVID-19 health emergency; it appears that I made two flights after my previous BFR (the Date 1 BFR) expired.Upon discovering this inadvertent error; I immediately contacted my flight instructor and scheduled an appointment to complete a BFR with him today; literally one day after discovering my mistake.In order to prevent this from happening again; I have calendared the due date for my next BFR on an electronic calendar; with an automatic reminder set 30 days before my current BFR expires.
Report_1_Synopsis: GA pilot reported flying without proper certification.

Report_1_Narrative: I was 10 miles north of ZZZ and flying heading 220 at 1;500 ft. MSL and 105 knots in a Mooney inbound for a VFR traffic pattern entry on a right downwind to Runway XX. Three airplanes had just landed and I was maneuvering for the 45 degree entry to Runway XX. I heard the Cessna announce it was 4 miles ahead and also maneuvering for the same entry to Runway XX. The sun was setting to the west which made it difficult to spot aircraft to the southwest and west of my flight path. I announced on CTAF that I was 10 miles north and maneuvering for the 45 degree entry right downwind Runway XX. At 5 miles northwest of ZZZ; I announced that I was 5 miles northwest maneuvering for the 45 degree entry; right downwind; for Runway XX.At that point; I heard the Cessna was on the 45 entry to right downwind Runway XX. I turned to a heading of 180 at 1;300 ft. MSL; 113 knots; and remained 5 miles west of ZZZ; while visually scanning ahead; left and right; for the Cessna. It was very difficult to see southwest and west due to the sun setting. At 5 miles west of ZZZ; I announced Mooney is 5 miles west of ZZZ maneuvering for the 45 entry; right downwind; Runway XX".Within a minute; I spotted the Cessna approximately 100 ft. below and 400 ft. to the right. The CFI onboard called on the radio; and said "did you see us?" I responded; "Yes I just did. Would you like to go ahead of me or do you want me to proceed on the 45 entry?" He responded that they would continue the entry and go ahead of me. I continued to fly a heading of 180 and then executed a turn to the west followed by a 360 degree turn to the east to enter the pattern after the Cessna. I landed and did not see the Cessna on the ramp.Afterwards; I called the CFI in the Cessna; whom I've known for years. I listened to his remarks and explained that I had no intention of overtaking him in The Cessna. This is not something I would ever attempt nor have I ever done in 18 years of flying. He mentioned they had requested my position in the air (around 5 miles out) and I said that I never heard that request nor that they were in the Cessna. I was only monitoring CTAF and visually scanning for traffic. I heard they were already on the 45 degree entry to Runway XX. I believe that 1 or 2 of their position reports or requests for my position were not transmitted or heard because we may have both pressed the mic button at the same time to give or request position reports. One of the Cessna's communications may have been incomplete which could explain why I heard that the Cessna was on the 45 degree entry to Runway XX; as I was 5 miles west northwest of ZZZ."
Report_1_Synopsis: A single pilot reported a Near Mid-Air Collision (NMAC) with another aircraft entering the landing pattern. Sun position reportedly inhibited early visual contact.

Report_1_Narrative: Student pilot with instructor doing pattern work at 33N in crosswind leg. During turn to downwind in left traffic pattern Aircraft Y entered the pattern in crosswind leg and was operating dangerously close to my aircraft creating a collision hazard. Aircraft Y did not enter 33N left traffic pattern correctly and executed an unsafe maneuver putting myself and other aircraft in the pattern at risk.
Report_1_Synopsis: Aircraft reported that another aircraft entered the traffic pattern incorrectly; creating a conflict.

Report_1_Narrative: A flight of 2 helicopters called Ground Control on for VFR flight following. They were on a non controlled ramp. Ground Control issued departure frequency and squawk. No readback was heard. Generally; this is an issue with military helicopters; and they usually call up local shortly after; when ready to depart. I reached out several times on Ground Control; inquiring if they had the ATIS information; and if they wanted to taxi to a runway or a present position departure. They were non responsive.I passed the strip to Local Control; thinking they would call him. Moments later a Aircraft Y who had been in the pattern was departing and I saw the 2 helicopters departing the ramp; right in the path of Aircraft Y. I alerted Local Control and he had the Aircraft Y make an evasive left turn to avoid the traffic. Both Local Control and myself on Ground Control made multiple attempts on all frequencies to reach the Aircraft X flight. They both almost had a NMAC with the Aircraft Y. TRACON was calling on the shout line and I answered on Ground Control as Local Control was trying to move the Cessna to a safe position. The TRACON controller alerted me Aircraft X had called them and they mistakenly thought they were calling from a different airport so the TRACON controller gave them a departure clearance which resulted in the unauthorized departure from ZZZ and the NMAC. Once Aircraft Y was safe Local Control and Ground Control both advised TRACON to issue a brasher.Military helicopter pilots need better training on how to depart here and learn to give appropriate readbacks. TRACON should have verified where the helicopters were. Assuming they were at ZZZ1 created a dangerous situation. The VFR flight plan was in the system. TRACON Flight Data should have seen it originating from ZZZ.
Report_2_Narrative: Aircraft Y departed climbing to remain in closed traffic for stop and goes.  Aircraft X helicopters on a ramp near the departing Aircraft Y began to lift climbing in front of the Aircraft Y who did not have them in sight. Local Control issues immediate traffic for the Aircraft Y and told to turn left immediately. Local Control called out to Aircraft X on Local Control frequency several times and on guard frequency.  Aircraft X did not answer and continued to fly toward Aircraft Y which was maneuvering to avoid the helicopters. Aircraft Y made an inadvertent low altitude turn to avoid colliding with the helicopters. Coming out of the turn the Aircraft Y reported them in sight.Approach Control called Local Control in a panic about Aircraft X saying she gave permission for departure to the helicopters saying she thought they were at another airport nearby. She did not know they were actually located at this airport. Aircraft X continued toward the Aircraft Y and eventually called local control once they departed the airport.  Local Control told Aircraft X that they were not cleared by Local Control for departure and advised that they almost hit Aircraft Y that was climbing directly toward the helicopters.Aircraft X replied that Ground Control gave them the departure frequency.  In error Aircraft X thought that they needed to contact Approach for takeoff from the airport.  When Aircraft X called for VFR departure; Ground Control issued Aircraft X a squawk code and told them the departure procedure which is normal handling for VFR aircraft.  The next expected sequence of events is that the VFR aircraft then contacts Local Control for takeoff clearance. Aircraft X bypassed Local Control and went directly to Departure Control thinking that is who they needed for departure.My recommendation is that there is clarity made to pilots that their receipt of the departure frequency is not a directive to contact them to depart while the Tower is actively controlled by a Local Controller who is issuing control instructions and safety alerts.
Report_1_Synopsis: Tower Controllers reported a flight of two helicopters departed from the ramp without clearance from the tower and had a NMAC with a departing aircraft because Ground Control mistakenly issued them a TRACON frequency which cleared them to depart thinking they were at an adjacent airport.

Report_1_Narrative: Aircraft X was inside of a quarter mile final on the ILS Runway 31C approach. I turned around for a second to tell the supervisor about the visibility getting better on final when the supervisor noticed an airport vehicle going onto Runway 31C. At that point I issued a go around to the aircraft and to climb and maintain 3;000 ft. MSL and turn right to a heading of 110. I also let the aircraft know the reason of the go around. They were able to respond in time and were re-sequenced for another approach and landed without incident. I understand it was snowing and airport markers are difficult to see. I suggest airport vehicles be more vigilant of their position on the airport before moving anywhere. Driver refresher course recommended.
Report_1_Synopsis: ATC approach controller reported issuing a go-around clearance to an aircraft on short final due to a vehicle reported on the runway.

Report_1_Narrative: My second report regarding aircraft from the Palm Springs area performing erratic maneuvers in the face of IFR arrivals.  Aircraft Y departed Palm Springs and terminated services outside of the PSP Delta. They proceeded to fly just north of UDD and start performing aerobatic maneuvers between 050 and 060. This aircraft climbed right in front of Aircraft X; who was cleared for the RNAV visual 31L approach.  Traffic alert was issued to Aircraft X and while the pilot did not say 'near midair'; they did say 'he's right in front of us!' and the altitudes were the same.The pilot for Aircraft X said they had to respond to two RAs for that one aircraft.The pilot of Aircraft Y may have also been in violation of FAR Sec. 91.303 which prohibits aerobatic flight within 4 miles of a federal airway (V137) and over an area of congested population.I am requesting; again; for the PSP airspace to have a Charlie or Bravo airspace.  My colleagues and I deal with dangerous situations every day that could easily be avoided by having non-voluntary protected airspace.  This is the second event in one day where PSP Tower has terminated a VFR aircraft who ultimately got much too close to an IFR arrival. A Class C/B airspace and a requirement for Tower to hand off departures to approach; would allow the radar Controller to determine if a dangerous situation is imminent.As of now; the only controlled airspace in the Palm Springs valley is the Tower's Class D. Class E airspace exists around TRM; but only prohibits flight for poor weather. This airspace is a free-for-all with half of the aircraft talking to ATC and the other half are not; and just blasting through everyone else. This needs to change.Also; the local pilots should know better than to be flying in these congested areas doing aerobatics.  The safety culture of these pilots is questionable and should be discussed.
Report_1_Synopsis: SCT TRACON Controller reported re-occurring airborne conflicts between VFR aircraft executing aerobatic maneuvers and IFR arrivals into PSP.  Reporter advised they deal with these types of situations every day; which could be easily avoided by having non-voluntary protected airspace.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Confusion; Situational Awareness; Training / Qualification; Communication Breakdown
Person_2_Human_Factors: Communication Breakdown; Confusion; Situational Awareness; Training / Qualification; Workload
Report_1_Narrative: Training was in progress on Local control. Aircraft X was sequenced to follow Aircraft Y. Aircraft X had the wrong aircraft in sight and turned base early and at the same time as Aircraft Y. Aircraft Y had to maneuver off final to the north for spacing. Aircraft Y called the tower and spoke with me; the CIC (Controller in Charge); and said Aircraft X got as close as 50 ft. prior to him maneuvering. Aircraft X was also on his check ride.
Report_2_Narrative: I was training on the Local Control position. There were 4 VFR aircraft in the traffic pattern for RWY XX and 1 VFR aircraft on practice approach RWY YY. Aircraft Y was VFR in left traffic for RWY XX and given a sequence to follow Aircraft X. Aircraft X was VFR in right traffic for RWY XX. Aircraft Y was given a sequence of number 4; to follow Aircraft X on right downwind. Aircraft Y was extending their downwind until they had their traffic in sight. Aircraft Y asked if their traffic was turning final RWY XX. I visually scanned the traffic pattern to verify Aircraft X position. I saw Aircraft X on final for RWY XX. Aircraft X was the 3rd aircraft on final at the time and was on an approximately 4NM final. I cleared Aircraft Y to land RWY XX after my visual scan. Aircraft Y must have had the incorrect aircraft in sight; the aircraft preceding Aircraft X was an Piper. Aircraft Y flew into the flight path of Aircraft X; cutting them off. Aircraft Y had to make a quick turn north bound to avoid Aircraft X. Aircraft X saw Aircraft Y; after Aircraft Y turned to the north; and Aircraft X made a south turn to avoid Aircraft Y. At this time Aircraft X made a call to Local Control that he was making his north turn to avoid Aircraft Y. I did not see the two aircraft turning to avoid until Aircraft X made his call for the north turn. Aircraft Y rejoined the RWY XX final; in front of Aircraft Y; and was reissued a landing clearance for RWY XX. Aircraft Y was instructed to make a 270 degree turn back to final and rejoined RWY XX final behind Aircraft X. Aircraft X was reissued a landing clearance for RWY XX. Both aircraft landed without further incident. About 10 minutes after Aircraft X landed; the pilot called the tower to let us know that Aircraft Y was within close proximity to him and he would be filing a safety report.
Report_1_Synopsis: ATC Instructor and trainee reported misidentified aircraft in traffic pattern resulted in NMAC.

Report_1_Narrative: Aircraft X was on a visual approach about 1 NM north of WIGZU.  VFR Aicraft Y was 2 NM east of WIGZU tracking westbound.  I issued the traffic to Aircraft X and let them know where the traffic was; where it was headed; and that the aircraft was not in communication with ATC.  I issued the traffic again when Aircraft X was crossing WIGZU and the VFR aircraft was 1 NM east of WIGZU.  It appeared they must have seen Aircraft X because the VFR aircraft made a sharp northbound turn.  The CA alarm did sound between Aircraft X and Aircraft Y.I recommend a shelf or a key added to AFW Class Delta.  There are many; many instances where VFR aircraft are transitioning at WIGZU; at the same altitude as arrivals or departures; but are not in communication with ATC.
Report_1_Synopsis: AFW Tower Controller reported an unsafe event where a VFR aircraft is transitioning an arrival path for air carriers outside of Class Delta causing an airborne conflict.

Report_1_Narrative: I was working the Springs sector and noticed a high performance aircraft depart PSP and then the tower dropped them and they went to a 1200 code.  I kept my eye on them because we have had high performance aircraft interfere with arrivals/departures before. Over the next 30 minutes; the aircraft flew around the airspace; but it wasn't until around XA:45z that they started doing maneuvers around UDD.  I believe it was Aircraft X that was doing aerobatic maneuvers just east of the UDD airport.  The aircraft rapidly change altitude; turn very quickly; and all of this at a high rate of speed.  It's next to impossible to anticipate what their intentions are and makes it very difficult to keep other aircraft out of their way. These aircraft fly through the airspace; creating havoc; and then just call the tower for pattern entry; instead of calling approach for sequencing.  One of the aircraft was right next to a regional jet; but below; and keeping up with them; while they were trying to descend on a visual approach in to PSP.  This aircraft called the tower; instead of approach; and was sequenced by them.  I; however; was left focused on the situation; unsure what this aircraft was doing; and if they even saw [the regional jet].The lack of a mandatory controlled airspace in the PSP area makes it very difficult to make any sort of plan; since anyone who wants to can fly right down the final legally.  PSP tower is also terminating these high performance aircraft; right as they leave their Delta airspace; where they go on to get in the way of arrivals coming in PSP or other nearby airports.  These high performance aircraft are out every weekend; constantly getting in the way; and making the approach controllers bend to their will.  The workload on the Springs sector is already very high; but add in the lack of guaranteed controlled airspace makes everything much more difficult.  We are approach; departure and clearance delivery; all in one sector.  It is incredibly frustrating to make sense of all the aircraft criss crossing; formulate a plan; and then have someone who deems it not important to participate in the TRSA; blow up your entire plan; making you change everything.  While that did not happen exactly in this instance; it has happened many times before; and is what has brought me to file this report in hopes to prevent it from happening more.I recommend that we change the airspace around PSP to something that is mandatory controlled airspace.  The voluntary participation makes sequencing and separation difficult; and in the cases of these high performance aircraft; they are creating an unsafe situation; but still 'following the rules'.  Some sort of protection needs to be added to the area to help us ensure our separation and allow controllers to have a safe space to sequence.I would also request that someone look in to the legality of the aerobatic activities that these aircraft are doing in the Palm Springs valley.  Are they aware what they are doing is unsafe and potentially illegal?
Report_1_Synopsis: SoCal TRACON Controller reported an unsafe situation with VFR aircraft and IFR aircraft within close proximity to each other just outside the PSP Class Delta/TRSA.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Training / Qualification; Communication Breakdown; Situational Awareness
Report_1_Narrative: Aircraft X checked in for Runway XXC was told descend and maintain 040 and good rate down; leveled off at 050 while being vectored to final and told to parallel final on heading 350 and expedite down to 30; shortly after looking 1;000 feet at 2.7 miles he saw the field and was cleared.There was approximately 10 read back errors during this push due to the new mask mandate; control instructions had to be repeated to this pilot 2 times.  With the new mandate and tower restrictions forces us to land Runway XXC and XXR in IFR weather this operation is unsafe with the new altitude restrictions implemented by our supervisors.For the past 2 weeks management has told the arrival wall to not go below 4;000 feet until north of ZZZZZ (the dual fix) regardless of where the aircraft's flight path will be; this makes IFR operations very difficult to accomplish at ZZZ and is a very poor knee jerk reaction to a Controller making a simple mistake.  These type of rule changes mean that every single transmission on that wall need to be 100% clear and any read back error will cause an aircraft incident;  we cannot continue with frivolous rule changes and a mask mandate unless we would like a major incident or accident at ZZZ.Allow us to use judgment and common sense on where to turn our own airplane.  These unnecessary rule changes will cause more incidents than they will prevent.
Report_1_Synopsis: TRACON Controller reported communication issues with pilots due to having to wear a mask which is exacerbated when new procedural changes are introduced.

Report_1_Narrative: Aircraft X arrived from the south east at 110 where ZZZ has a MVA (Minimum Vectoring Altitude) at the highest point of 115. I do not know if ZZZ1 has the same or lower MVA in that area. Per the LOA with ZZZ1 any arrivals in this area 130 or lower; must be on an airway and verbally coordinated. There was no coordination from ZZZ1.  OJTI was being conducted at the Approach position; I was the OS in the TRACON. Due to COVID social distancing requirements the OJTI was working from the 'B' scope; the trainee was working from the 'A' scope and I was at the OS desk. There is no radar scope or secondary monitor available at the OS desk to observe traffic; so I was unable to see the altitude of the aircraft. A regional jet that was about to be switched to the Tower told approach that an aircraft was trying to call approach and at that point I was able to observe Aircraft X at the altitude below the MVA. Aircraft X eventually was able to reach approach on radio and landed without incident.-Review ZZZ1-ZZZ LOA-Add a non-certified radar display at the ZZZ TRACON OS desk-Check the MVAs to the south east of ZZZ to see if there are any discrepancies between ZZZ1 and ZZZ MVAs.
Report_2_Narrative: I am training the trainee on approach control. Three arrivals scheduled with close arrival times. Trainee accepted all three handoffs back to back well outside of our airspace boundary; further away than normal. He was not aware that Aircraft X was flying a wrong altitude for direction of flight as well as 500 feet below the MVA we have depicted on our maps until after accepting the handoff.  Neither of these two issues were coordinated between either facility. Aircraft landed without issue.We need to have matching MVA maps with ZZZ1. This could be a real issue in the future. That aircraft was 500 feet below our MVA and could not reach us on radio due to the terrain.
Report_1_Synopsis: Controllers reported an aircraft that they were not talking to was on an IFR flight plan; below the MVA and NORDO.

Report_1_Narrative: Recently we were told we had to wear masks while on sector. Following the rules I was wearing a mask; and multiple aircraft could not understand what I was saying. Multiple times I was told to 'Say again' until I pulled the mask down to give the aircraft the transmission. After I pulled the mask down they said they could understand me better. This is a safety issue. If the aircraft can't understand what we are saying and takes the wrong altitude this could be disastrous.Since Coronavirus started we were told we only had to wear masks when we couldn't be socially distanced. What has changed? Why do we have to wear masks all the time even if we are socially distanced?
Report_1_Synopsis: Center Controller reported communication issues with pilots while wearing a face mask.

Report_1_Narrative: With new guidelines for wearing mask on position. (With no one around) I am having multiple read back errors. Aircraft X miss read his restriction and frequency. The issue was corrected.When there is no one is close proximity controllers should not be made to wear mask.
Report_1_Synopsis: Center Controller reported multiple read back errors while wearing a mandated face mask.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Distraction; Situational Awareness; Time Pressure; Workload; Communication Breakdown
Report_1_Narrative: I was working Local Control and had four aircraft waiting to depart  with Aircraft X on short final to an intersecting runway and Aircraft Y still about 10 mile final for the same runway  on an instrument approach for a option back to radar pattern. There was also two VFR picture taking aircraft around the Tower airspace at 2700 feet. I asked Aircraft X if he could land to hold short of the intersecting runway. He said he could; though hesitantly. I cleared him for LAHSO(Land and Hold Short). I began to depart the other aircraft of the crossing runway with turns and to also have them stop at 2000 feet for the picture takers. When Aircraft Y checked on; I cleared him for the option. My biggest mistake was putting expeditiousness over safety. I overlooked Aircraft X in two important ways.  I had an expectation bias that he would exit the runway before the intersection and  even the I scanned the runway; I missed him sitting at the intersection. The color of the plane and the concrete made it difficult to notice him. Not until Aircraft X keyed up to talk did I remember he was there but by then Aircraft Y had touched down; saw the aircraft and was stopping to avoid.This situation very poignantly reminded me (because it was a very close call and so thankful it was not more serious) that safety is our number one priority. As a facility we need to have a clear reminder that a runway is occupied as opposed to one single light that carries multiple meanings.  We should clearly define a procedure for LAHSO as well.
Report_1_Synopsis: A tower local Controller reported they allowed a military aircraft to land with another aircraft stopped at an intersection on the runway.

Report_1_Narrative: Aircraft X on an IFR flight plan was being vectored for an ILS approach.
