I recognize that I need to work on still listening fully to Tower on this phase of flight if I will be rejoining the pattern; as it is importantto have a mental picture of where other aircraft are within the airspace.I also likely did start my crosswind turn early; as the data from FlightAware seems to pinpoint my turn as having started no further than 2.5 miles upwind. This is likely due to me misjudging my timing and distance in the aircraft after takeoff and is something I will need to also work on.With those in mind; the data from the PA28 also shows that it played a major factor in this event. After takeoff; the PA28 extended about 4.5 miles upwind while also drifting left of the runway. As such; their position report to Tower of being in the crosswind was likely when they just started their turn and the amount of time spent in the crosswind would be lengthened due to their drift left. The longer upwind extension would also explain how they ended up behind me once I turned onto the downwind leg. I am unsure if Tower recognized that the PA28 had drifted left and extended so far out; but I am assuming that they did not as no call was made informing me of their position or the potential for conflict.Overall; my own misjudgments of my timing and distance; mistake in missing calls for other aircraft to have an idea of what is going on big picture (as I would have been able to recognize that I would essentially be following an aircraft in the right traffic pattern); and the PA28's over extension and drift on the departure leg contributed to this event.
Report_1_Synopsis: Single Private Pilot reported a conflict in the traffic pattern.

Report_1_Narrative: Prior to the near-miss event; we made several CTAF calls with our intentions of entering the straight-in left downwind for Runway 32 from the north. An aircraft on the runway then announced their intentions to depart 32 to the north towards the Needles VOR. At this point; it is assumed he was going to make a straight-out departure to the north and climb since he did not specify. Instead; this aircraft initiated a left crosswind departure towards the west while we were entering the left downwind at approximately 1;700 MSL; while the aircraft was at around 1;400-1;500 MSL and crossed under us. My guess is that the other aircraft 'saw and avoided' and stopped his climb at approximately 1;500 MSL while we were at approximately 1;700 MSL. While the aircraft was on the left crosswind climb; I identified traffic and applied throttle; and climbed only approximately 100 feet or so to evade since I spotted the traffic sooner. No calls were exchanged after the near-miss event. In retrospect; I should asked the departing traffic for clarification on his departing direction and entered the pattern at a much higher altitude.
Report_1_Synopsis: Pilot reported taking evasive action to avoid a Near Mid Air Collision with a departing aircraft.

Report_1_Narrative: Moderate turbulence below 14;000 feet.  Heavy winds as well. 290/19 G29 on the ground.  Cleared Visual Approach 34L. Approach was normal; but Captain very busy dealing with speed fluctuations and turbulence.  I was double checking the winds with Tower. Watching terrain as well.  Adjusted REF speeds for gusts and prevailing winds. Captain called for flaps 30; I inadvertently moved flap handle to 25 and did not know it.  Everything was good until short final; we got Too Low Flaps" aural alert.  We executed go-around immediately. Need to look down and see if correct flap detention is selected."
Report_2_Narrative: On flight to RNO we received a Too Low Flaps warning from the GPWS around 500 feet AGL on an approach to Runway 34L. We had continuous moderate turbulence below 13;000 feet MSL on our approach and that was distracting. We were on a high right base leg because of the terrain. We were cleared for the visual on the right base leg. Also; on base we were gear down flaps 15; and near flaps 15 approach speed. I called for flaps 30 and the Before Landing checklist well above 1;000 feet AGL; because I wanted the extra drag. I did not notice the flaps were at position 25 during the Before Landing checklist. Our REF speed was plus 9 and then increased to plus 15 with the new Tower winds.  At about 500 feet AGL we received the Too Low Flaps warning and I did a go-round. We were vectored for another approach to Runway 34L and did a normal landing.I felt task loaded on the approach. I was concerned about the turbulence; terrain; and changing surface winds. I let these additive condition distract me while doing the Before Landing Check List.  I should have bought myself more time by asking for a longer down wind on the approach.
Report_1_Synopsis: B-737 flight crew reported executing a go-around upon receipt of a configuration GPWS warning.

Report_1_Narrative: Visual to 27 at SAN using RNAV Z. Ceiling was BKN015. Crew briefed visual procedures at altitude but was informed that ATIS had changed late in the descent; crew adjusted minimums to account for the updated ceiling. Earlier I had queried the Captain if he preferred flaps 40 for SAN and he said he wanted flaps 30. Vref was 141 knots; wind component added 6 knots for a VTARGET of 147 knots. Captain configured early and we were stable at 1;000 feet AGL with a slightly high VVI (Vertical Velocity Indicator) due to SAN Runway 27 3.5 degree approach and the high weight and subsequent high approach speed.  We were visual at that point; I think we broke out at 1;000-1;200 feet. Every time I crosschecked the speed and VVI; the Captain was stable; with the knowledge that the 3.5 degree approach and speed (as mentioned in the Safety Alert) would result in VVI rates over 1;000 feet. I was crosschecking radar altitudes and glideslope guidance more than I usually do; but this is my personal habit for SAN. As I did the normal 'in and out' visual crosscheck; nothing seemed amiss. Directly over or slightly after the parking deck on short final; the Captain slightly adjusted his visual aim point as is common technique at SAN. My eyes were outside at this point. We both heard a 'sink rate...'. I don't know what the second phrase was; as the Captain acknowledged the first sink rate forcefully and almost instantly. I quickly looked inside and I think I saw 'pull up' on the bottom of the PFD for what seemed like an instant. I can't be certain; however; and it can't be understated how fast it went away if indeed it was there. I looked back up and we were two red and two white on the PAPI; slightly fast; and Captain was in what looked like a good position to land. We made a safe landing and applied moderate braking and exited the runway. In the postflight; the Captain and I disagreed about what the second term was at the aural system annunciated. He thinks he heard 'sink rate; sink rate.' I actually don't know what the second term the aural system annunciated was; as I didn't hear it clearly due to the Captain's acknowledgment of it. I do think I saw a very fleeting 'pull up' on the PFD; but I can't be perfectly certain; and Captain is adamant that we didn't get the GPWS warning; only the sink rate caution. I want to be clear that I understand the limitation with regard to the warning annunciator. In hindsight; I can see now that a go-around could have been a prudent decision even though the aircraft appeared to be a safe and normal position for short final at SAN. I want to highlight this issue for a few reasons. It bears repeating that phase of flight; temporal distortion; and flight deck confusion can all conspire to create a situation where two trained and alert crew members can see different things. The other thing I want to highlight is how heavy -800's; going into SAN; can potentially be affected by a flaps 30 approach. I don't know why we don't have recommended flap settings for certain situations. We've all been flying light aircraft for almost a year now and perhaps it would help to remind crews about heavy aircraft with higher approach airspeeds and subsequently higher VVIs in higher altitude environments or steeper approaches like SAN.
Report_2_Narrative: On approach to SAN when transitioning outside; we briefly received a sink rate call. At the gate; the First Officer was unsure if it was just a sink rate call or sink rate pull up. I adjusted sink rate and landed normally.
Report_1_Synopsis: B737-800 Flight Crew reported on an unstable approach receiving two cautionary messages the were missed by flight crew.

Report_1_Narrative: After pushback in ZZZ; Dispatch notified us via ACARS that ZZZ Operations had contacted her and that 'you did not sign her [Dangerous Goods Form]'. However; only the Pilot's copy of the [Dangerous Goods Form] was provided to us by the A Flight Attendant. Prior to pushback; and at the same time the [Dangerous Goods Form] was delivered; we had an intoxicated Passenger removed from the aircraft. Once we reached our cruise altitude; we took pictures of the signed Pilot's copy of the [Dangerous Goods Form] and amended Release and emailed them to the Operations Center and the Dispatcher via the Company provided EFB.First of all; any time HAZMAT/COMAT is transported onboard; a face to face briefing with the Captain should be required. This will build a shared mental model and will allow the Captain the opportunity to efficiently and effectively bring Dispatch into the loop in accordance with the FOM. Personally; any time we carry HAZMAT/COMAT; I will review the FOM as this is not something I do every day; so I can back up the Captain more effectively. Finally; discussing actions to take if unruly Passengers pop up among the whole Crew can help prevent distractions when they do pop up.
Report_2_Narrative: After pushback; ACARS notification from our Dispatcher stated QUOTE 'You did not sign her NOTAC' ie; describing the Ops Agents copy of the NOTAC.  Apparently the Ops Agent only handed the 'Pilots Copy' of the NOTAC to the A Flight Attendant; and not directly handing it to the Captain.  No 'Ops Copy' was ever provided. Just when this occurred; a Passenger was being removed for behavior of what an intoxicated passenger would exhibit.  Once at cruise; photographs were taken of the 'Pilots Copy' of the NOTAC; and of an amended Release stating in the remarks section. Note: 'Raft on flight; refer to NOTAC' -- with our Dispatchers initials and the time of the amendment; and this was emailed to our Dispatcher and Chief Pilot in the Operations Center.  Confirmation was received on ACARS that Dispatch was in receipt of our email; sent via Company email on the Captains EFB.
Report_1_Synopsis: B737-700 First Officer reported a communication breakdown between flight crew and Dispatch regarding missing signed NOTOC document.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Communication Breakdown; Distraction; Situational Awareness; Time Pressure; Workload
Report_1_Narrative: This is a General Safety concern. No faults were committed by myself or the Captain. HOU ATC is constantly running 1 frequency to work Tower and Ground Control. This is causing an unsafe level of radio congestion. We could not get a push call in without blocking other aircraft or being blocked ourselves. Finally; once pushed; we had difficulty obtaining a taxi clearance. We finally were told to taxi and hold short of 13L. As we were holding short; we noted several aircraft attempting to push; taxi to and from runways; and obtain landing clearances. We noticed one corporate aircraft that could not obtain a landing clearance until short final; despite multiple attempts on their part; with no answer from Tower.HOU is a complex airport with multiple crossing runways; multiple taxi routes utilized; while also crossing runways. HOU ATC has been utilizing a single Controller for Ground and Tower Ops for most of the last 12 months; since the start of the slow down in air traffic. While this may have worked in the early days of this pandemic; it has turned into its own form of danger as air traffic has steadily increased; especially with the onset of Spring Break travel.I believe I am not alone in my concern that this could cause a serious incident at HOU; as there is no way a single Controller can safely manage traffic on the ground and in the air. I have been to far less complex; and less busy airports that utilize designated Ground and Tower Controllers. Please see to it; that this is not allowed to continue any longer. It poses a danger to our aircraft and our customers.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported not being able to communicate with ATC due to Controller working Tower and Ground Control combined at HOU airport.

Report_1_Narrative: While on a vector to a visual to Runway 35R at AUS we were awaiting a turn to the east for left base entry to the runway. At 3000'; and in a turn to 090 degrees we [got a] TA on TCAS less than one mile off our right or south course at the same altitude of 3000' and an urgent call from ATC to the traffic 'Whoever is off San Marcos;' to turn immediately to the south. We are convinced it was the traffic that suddenly appeared; and if we didn't make the immediate turn at 30 degrees of bank to 090 degrees would have resulted in a Resolution Advisory; RA; a near miss or very abrupt maneuver to avoid collision. We feel the extended downwind vector down towards San Marcos due to heavy traffic at AUS with one runway open; resulted in us being close to VFR traffic near San Marcos.
Report_1_Synopsis: Airline Captain reported a TA which resulted in evasive action to avoid worsening situation.

Report_1_Narrative: During climb out of SMF; everything was normal with some occasional light chop. We had asked the Flight Attendants to remain seated due to crossing the Sierra Mountains. We were climbing at approximately .76 Mach. Upon leveling at FL 370; we experienced moderate bordering on severe mountain wave. Our airspeed began decreasing rapidly and the F/O (First Officer) disconnected the autopilot; applied full thrust; and began a shallow descent to regain airspeed. The airspeed decayed to about .70 - .71. It was about a 30 knot decrease. I may be a little off on the Mach numbers. We descended about 500' and the airspeed began increasing.  I reported the encounter to ATC and we began climbing back to FL 370. The wave climbed us to FL 375; and at that time we requested a descent to FL 350. The Controller cleared us to descend to FL 350. We did not encounter any additional mountain wave and nothing more than a little light chop. We checked with the Flight Attendants to make sure everyone was alright; and the remainder of the flight was uneventful. I would like to add that the F/O did an excellent job of recognizing and reacting to the situation.
Report_2_Narrative: We had just leveled off at our cruise altitude of FL 370. (Filed for FL 390 but we were too heavy at that time.) During climb we had anticipated and encounter some light turbulence. Nothing more significant was encountered. WSI (Weather Service International) and Jeppesen weather showed areas of turbulence covering about the first 45 minutes of our flight. Our clearance was on the SCTWN 3 RNAV Departure. We were level at FL 370 when suddenly our airspeed had dropped from M.76 (250 KIAS) to 220 KIAS this was approximately 10-15 above the yellow maneuvering bar on the airspeed indicator and the green vector bar was indicating that the slowing was continuing and at a significant rate. I disconnected the autopilot and autothrottle and pitched down to keep airspeed. I also increased thrust to max and I was able to recover airspeed about 500' low at FL 365. In my attempt to climb back to FL 370 we started climbing at a significant rate and stopped the climb at approximately FL 376. The Captain reported to ATC that we were in MVA (mountain wave activity) and that we were unable to hold altitude. I continued to hand fly until I was sure we were passed the MVA and re-engaged the autopilot. The rest of the flight was uneventful.
Report_1_Synopsis: B737-700 flight crew reported encountering moderate to severe mountain wave for which led to a rapid decay of their airspeed.

Report_1_Narrative: This was me and the First Officer's first flight together.  He hadn't had a landing for approximately a month and hadn't been flying a lot recently.  It was a beautiful day in ZZZ and we were cleared for the visual to XXL at about 7;000 MSL.  We were established on the localizer as a backup and had the runway in sight holding around 210 knots.  Approach control handed us off to tower and I checked in.  We were cleared to land and told that there would be fighters departing out of ZZZ1; but they would stay below us.  The First Officer started too slow and I extended flaps to 2.  I started searching for the fighters and saw 2 of them takeoff.  I keep my eyes on them to make sure we were clear.  First Officer called for the gear and I extended it.  I noticed we were still at flaps 2 and we were too fast for flaps 3.  We were inside the FAF by this point and it was going to be close for a stabilized approach.  The first officer had previously selected the approach mode and we were on course about 300 feet high on the glide path and fast so not correcting.  I noticed the power on the engine instruments was not at idle which was strange because we had the approach selected in managed speed and the speed tape showed the target speed well below our current speed.  I pointed the power setting out to the first officer and it was also confusing to him why the power was still up.  We got to flaps 3 around 1;000 AGL and were still high on the glide path.  We leveled off a little to get the flaps to full and then started to correct to glidepath.  When we got to 500 feet we were still a good 200 feet high and 15-20 knots above our target speed.  The First Officer asked me if I wanted him to go around.  There was no traffic and the runway is 2 miles long so I said to continue.  We ended up touching down at target speed well within the touchdown zone and cleared the runway.  After getting to the gate and shutting down the engines we debriefed the approach.  The First Officer said that all along he thought he was setting himself up nicely for the approach and thought it would work.  I agreed and then I took myself out of the SA loop when I started searching for the fighters and didn't pay close enough attention to our energy status.  When I finally did get back into it I wasn't forceful enough to help.  When I pointed out the engines not being at idle I assumed he would disconnect the auto thrust and put the throttles at idle.  When he didn't I should have told him too and that alone would have probably made us stable as there was still some time.  At any rate I didn't and we were clearly unstable and we both knew it.  The only correct option was to execute a go-around.  Fuel was not an issue as we ended up landing with 6;500 pounds.  I told him that I should have told him to go-around but he should have just executed a go-around without asking.  That is the procedure.  You don't need permission from the other pilot and permission not to go-around is still wrong anyway.  We agreed that the biggest factor that got us going down this path in the first place was his recency of experience and that in order to fix that he should in the immediate future at least; slow down and configure earlier then he thinks he needs to.  Going back to our departure briefing I should have taken the first leg anyway since I knew he hadn't flown in a while.  This way he could have eased back into it.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported landing after an unstable approach when they should have gone around.

Report_1_Narrative: I flew the 737 Max aircraft for the first time and noticed an aircraft characteristic that I do not like. The altitude alerting system gives a loud buzz in the headset 900 ft. prior to level off MCP altitude. This buzz drowned out ATC communications twice during climbout due the timing of ATC communications. I was unable to determine what ATC was saying.
Report_1_Synopsis: B737 MAX Captain reported noise on headset when using air/ground communications systems.

Report_1_Narrative: I was working Aircraft X and was helping close the front cargo pit when hot scalding coffee came pouring down the front lavatory drain. I have lost count how many times this has happened while I was working a flight in the last few years. I notified the Captain what happen and he said he didn't know the lavatory sink drained right to the outside of the plane. He asked the Flight Attendant and she said she had a 'brain fart' and she was sorry? I'm so glad she was sorry and my face wasn't burned by this careless act!
Report_1_Synopsis: Ground employee reported nearly being scalded by coffee when it came pouring down the front lavatory drain; while aircraft was being serviced.

Report_1_Narrative: The above MEL required flying with no FMS; and navigation only by VOR.We tried for over an hour to get proper routing that would allow us to fly to ZZZ via acceptable routing that would allow for proper navigation via VOR/victor airways. Center would not allow acceptable routing. This made our release unreliable for time and fuel calculations. It also meant we did not have redundancy in our navigation. On multiple occasions ATC tried to re-route us and fly RNAV routing. A number of VOR's would not identify automatically and we needed to listen to the Morse code to identify each station. The autopilot would not track the victor airways properly. The autopilot would drift left and right of course. We resorted to using HDG mode and our [electronic tablets] for navigation.We do very little training flying a jet at 36;000 ft. flying solely on VOR navigation. The implications of not having an FMS; are not made very clear in the MEL. For example; no fuel planning; no vertical navigation; what VOR beacons are acceptable for high altitude operations; what does ATC actually go by (understand) versus what the MEL states.Resorted to using HDG mode; radar vectors; and our iPads to guide the aircraft. This report is primarily being done for pre-emptive measures for any deviations and to have the company not use antiquated technology for primary navigation.It should be company policy to not conduct revenue flights without two forms of navigation or without an FMS. It is hard to believe that there were no other available aircraft for use for our flight. ATC needs to be made more aware of when an aircraft is non-RNAV capable as we needed to tell each controller the situation.
Report_2_Narrative: [Report narrative contained no additional information.]
Report_1_Synopsis: CRJ flight crew reported that the MEL required flying without use of the FMS; so the flight was conducted using VOR and electronic tablets for navigation.

Report_1_Narrative: The flight operated from ZZZ to GRK following the the ZZZZZ departure to ZZZZZ1 Intersection and then direct to the airport. This route brings flights from the east to the airport just south of multiple restricted areas. At approximately 12-15 miles east of the GRK at 4;000 feet; We accepted a visual approach clearance for Runway 15. We noted the restricted areas to the north of the field and made a 'dogleg' downwind to base for the runway with a course correction to avoid restricted areas to the northeast; followed by a turn just inside the published ILS Runway 15 FAF for a normal landing. Upon touching down Supervisor wished to speak to our crew and or management to inquire about procedures into the airport.Based on my discussion with the ATC manager on duty at Gray Approach; there have been multiple occasions where other aircraft have penetrated restricted airspace and have had near miss collisions with military UAV's that took evasive action. In some cases the the restricted airspace is within 3 miles of the 15 runway east downwind. Per the traffic manager; controllers EXPECT crews to fly a traditional box pattern while executing visual approaches on left downwind legs to 15 at a rather close distance; or enter a midfield crosswind entry to a right downwind. There are no specific instructions from ATC at the time of a visual clearance to fly a specific pattern. I recommend additional coordination between company management; union; and Gray ATC to develop set of procedures and or additional guidance/recommendations for our flights that can incorporated into 10-7 station pages.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported an restricted airspace violation near GRK and was told this is a common occurrence; which sometimes results in conflicts with military drones.

Report_1_Narrative: Today I was contacted by my Chief Pilot and notified that there had been a report written about a flight I flew about a week ago. According to the report; 'DG/HM (Dangerous Goods/HazMat) COMAT (Company Materials) loaded on aircraft form received in ZZZ1 with no PIC (Pilot-in-Command) signature or flight information'. Prior to departure I (PIC) was not notified of any DG/HM onboard the aircraft. I am positive that I did not receive a DG/HM PNF (Pilot Notification Form). I am sure that I would have remembered seeing it since it is typically not common to receive them and they are designed to stand out with their chevron red border and bright yellow pilot instructions. In addition; whenever I receive these forms I keep my copy in my flight bag for quite some time and I don't have one for this flight.I am assuming the cause of this error was that the DG/HM was loaded onto the aircraft and then for some reason someone forgot to notify or provide me with the PNF. I feel that in the past the DG/HM procedures we use have worked well. The PNF stands out and requires us to send a spec command through ACARS which serves as confirmation of receiving the form. It also helps that typically the CLR will have comments that there is DG/HM on board. I guess if I had any suggestion it would be that whoever loads the COMAT should then come directly to the flight deck with the form so that there is no middle man; or no time to get distracted or forget about it.
Report_2_Narrative: The Captain and I performed a routine revenue flight. The ramp personnel loaded some COMAT [Company Materials] cargo without our knowing and we did not receive the proper paperwork for it. No negative outcomes from the flight or the cargo. Forgetting to bring paperwork to flight crew and making them aware of any COMAT cargo that we needed to sign for. Just remembering to bring the proper paperwork to the crew so we know about it.
Report_1_Synopsis: CRJ-200 Captain reported being notified that he neglected to sign required Hazmat documents while operating as PIC during the previous week. Reporter stated they did not receive any information or documents that DG cargo was loaded onboard.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Time Pressure; Workload; Communication Breakdown; Situational Awareness
Report_1_Narrative: We were being vectored to final for the visual to Runway XXR in ZZZ. Descending out of 9;000 feet in the right downwind of the ZZZZZ arrival we were then given a vector 'Turn right heading 030; descend and maintain 7;000 feet.' It was clear that the Controller was very busy and was working approach for three parallel landing runways with many inbound flights that morning. Our next instructions were; 'Turn right heading 090.' Shortly after the turn to the east we were assigned; 'Turn right heading 150 to join the [Runway] XXR LOC.' This last instruction was given a minute too late. It was already apparent that we were going to fly through the final approach course with parallel traffic joining up for [Runway] XXL. The Captain had been saying prior to this; 'Controller needs to gives us the turn... Controller needs to turn us already... we are going to fly through final.' Sure enough the turn was way too late and the aircraft automation was too slow to make the tight turn. The Captain immediately informed ATC that the vector was issued too late and that we would be flying through the final approach course and correcting west bound to rejoin. I disengaged the autopilot as the automation was not reacting fast enough to recapture the final approach course. ATC then issued us a 190 heading to rejoin the localizer and a traffic advisory to the aircraft that was flying the parallel; saying we were at their 3 o'clock same altitude and correcting west to rejoin [Runway] XXR LOC. Just seconds after the heading to rejoin was issued (We were already in the turn at this time) a TCAS Traffic Advisory went off due to the proximity of the aircraft on the [Runway] XXL parallel visual. Nothing further happened from this event. We were able to rejoin the [Runway] XXR LOC maintain 7000 feet until descent for landing was necessary and we completed a stabilized approach to landing.The cause of this event was due to task saturation for the Air Traffic Controller. Controller was working one approach frequency with dozens of aircraft needing vectors to final for the triple parallel visuals landing south at ZZZ. The automation lag didn't help when trying to join the LOC with the last second instructions however that was mostly mitigated by disconnecting the autopilot and hand flying a more abrupt turn to re-intercept and avoid further deviation.As a pilot (and never having been in to see a behind the scenes look at an ATC approach facility) I cannot tell you exactly what was going on or any; if at all; distractions may have existed behind the microphone at ZZZ Approach that morning. However; I can tell you based on my perception that the controller was talking non-stop with zero breaks between Controller and aircraft transmission and that Controller may have been overloaded during this event.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported the ATC Approach Controller seemed overloaded with arriving aircraft and gave the heading change for localizer intercept too late.

Report_1_Narrative: Flying from ZZZ-BUR we were in cruise assigned by ATC to start a descent from FL220 to FL180. Upon passing through FL215 ATC asked us to stop our descent at FL210; we complied and stopped at 210. Upon reaching 210 we received a TCAS TA. The FO and myself immediately looked at the TCAS screen and started to visually look for the traffic. He was getting closer to our six mile ring and he was still climbing; we saw him on our TCAS inside of our six mile ring and now at our same altitude. It was at this time the we received an RA. The FO immediately disconnected the autopilot and started to comply with the RA. At this time ATC told us to climb to FL230 I told him we were complying with an RA event and we could be unable to climb to 230. The RA initially gave us a command to descend at 3200 FPM and then the rate of descent was increased by the RA to 4500 FPM which was complied with. We leveled the aircraft off after the RA was complete at FL190. We asked ATC if he had any further instructions for us; he said to level at 190 and he would be back momentarily. He proceeded to give the other aircraft that caused the RA a phone number to contact center. The pilot sounded like he was possibly in distress in a potentially hypoxic situation from the tone and behavior of his radio calls and struggle to follow any ATC instructions at the time. We continued to descend into Burbank and now on SoCal Approach were given a heading of 150 and 5k feet which took us right over a mountain that gave us a terrain warning momentarily as we leveled at 5k feet. We cross this terrain at 5;000 often on a vector from ATC we happened to cross right over the very peak of this terrain and with the descent rate down we suspect that the rate of closure was too much for the GPWS.  Upon landing in Burbank on the ILS Z 8 we received on more TCAS TA/RA as we crossed over ZZZ1 traffic in the pattern below caused our TCAS to give us a 'Monitor vertical speed' we complied and landed at Burbank without further incident.All events that took place were as a result of other aircraft and ATC vectors. We as a crew exercised all appropriate training to comply with all events.
Report_2_Narrative: While operating ZZZ-BUR level at FL 220; LA center on 132.5; issued a descend and maintain from FL220 to FL190. Passing through FL21.5 ATC amended clearance with a limit of FL210. We leveled off at 210 without any deviation but noticed an aircraft rapidly approaching our guarded zone on TCAS. Momentarily after we noticed this; a traffic advisory was made by the TCAS system and followed by and immediate command for 'monitor vertical speed'. The vertical speed initially commanded was 3700 fpm. The target aircraft did not level off at their assigned altitude. After the autopilot was immediately disengaged and the descent was initiated to the commanded rate; the TCAS prompted 'increase vertical speed' commanding roughly a 4500 FPM decent rate. LA center was notified and after the aural clear of conflict was heard and agreed on the aircraft was level at FL190 and ATC issued a new clearance. With no further issues the flight continued through Joshua approach and then onto SoCal approach.  With SoCal approach upon completion of the JANNY5 arrival into BUR SoCal assigned a vector of hdg 190 and descend to 5;000 ft. Level at 5;000 feet we crossed over a mountain peak that was at 3;734 feet. This caused a terrain warning and a subsequent ' terrain terrain pull up'. The aircraft climbed roughly 100 ft since the conditions were VFR and clear. After the terrain clearance was accomplished; SoCal assigned a heading of 110 and 3000 till established and cleared for the ILS-z Runway 8 into BUR. Upon passing over ZZZ1 we received another traffic advisory and that was followed with a RA. The RA did not state any vertical speed as the target aircraft had already passed behind us. The flight landed at BUR on Runway 8 with no adverse issues or events after that point.Continue to follow SOPs and be a vigilante and proactive flight crew and practice good CRM techniques.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported that during arrival into BUR airport they had experienced an RA and later had a terrain warning caused by passing over a mountain peak at a high rate of descent.

Report_1_Narrative: On a vector to final; about 20 NM south of CLT; I observed the flight mode change from HDG to LNAV; then about 10 seconds later the flight director commanded a turn in the wrong direction. We were expecting all left turns to final; so when I saw the airplane starting to bank to the right; I immediately pressed the TCS button and leveled the wings.The first time that I saw this happen recently; I dismissed it as a fluke. But this has now happened to me 3 times at the same airport on different approaches. I would estimate this is happening on about 15% of all approaches to this airport now. It starts with a vector to the intermediate approach course; arming the LNAV mode; and shortly after switching modes the computer steers the airplane across the approach course; over-corrects back in the opposite direction; and then chases the CDI to a normal alignment.This error in navigation; even though semi-random in frequency; is of such concern that I have been briefing the risk of TCAS activations and NTZ [No Transgression Zone] incursions that could be caused by this computer glitch. At this airport; it is fair to assume that there is always traffic on the simultaneous parallel course. Today; I briefed this possibility with the pilot flying while at cruise; and his reaction when it happened; although not as fast as mine; was understandable. He thought the turn was at first a subtle deviation in the direction of the final course.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier pilot reported that the flight director commanded a turn in the wrong direction during approach to CLT airport.  Reporter advised; 'this has now happened to me 3 times at the same airport on different approaches.'

Report_1_Narrative: I had been furloughed and haven't worked the last 5 months. I got my first reserve trip as no 4. I worked my first leg; we were full to the capacity. It was hectic. When I was boarding my next leg; I realized I had not done exit row briefing on my first leg. I did everything I was supposed to; and absolutely have the knowledge of procedure; but having been out of work for 5 months; and working full flight with lots of bags; I think it slipped my mind. I regret forgetting exit row briefing. Had never happened and will never happen again.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Attendant reported forgetting to brief the exit row and cited not flying for five months as a contributing factor.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Distraction; Situational Awareness; Troubleshooting; Communication Breakdown
Report_1_Narrative: I was traveling from ZZZ to ZZZ1. I experienced radio and GPS problems when trying to activate the runway lights at ZZZ1 around XA:00 local. After 3 attempts to activate the runway lights; I contacted Tucson Approach to see if there were any other ideas to help get the runway lights on. They called the airport to see if Customs was there. As no one was there; I was reaching my personal fuel reserve of 1 hour. The radio I have installed is GNS 430W. I had also had intermittent GPS signal; which resulted in no ADSB. Tucson Approach offered ZZZ2 as an alternate; but the airport was closed for the night. I felt it was much safer to go to TUS; as it has a host of FBO's and services available 24/7. I estimate that my radio at that time had about a 5 mile range. I lost contact with Approach several times; but I was able to hear the transponder code.As I got closer; Approach advised me that I was to enter a Right Downwind for Runway 11L at 4;000 ft. or above; and that I was cleared to land. They also told me to expect light gun signals from the Tower. I was able to acknowledge that transmission and was handed off to Tower. Tower also had a hard time hearing me; describing it as broken and scratchy. I was receiving Tower just fine; as I was close enough to the airport. I landed on 11L without incident and was given progressive taxi to FBO. Once I arrived and shut down; I asked if they had Maintenance available; which they did not. I parked there overnight until I was able to get an Avionics Tech to look at the airplane the next day. The Technician noticed that the 430W was not seated completely due do the design of the radio stack. He was able to quickly solve the problem. We did radio checks with TUS Ground and listened to the ATIS both over the cabin speaker and headsets. This particular aircraft is new to me; and I had not noticed the issue before as I normally operate out of an uncontrolled field. Now I incorporate a visual inspection of the GNS 430W; the audio panel; and the transponder as part of my preflight inspection; specifically looking to make sure they are seated properly; not loose; and functioning as they should. I took for granted that they had been installed correctly from the previous aircraft owner. I trust Maintenance shops to do work and repairs correctly; but it is now a trust but verify as I am the one responsible for the operation of the aircraft and systems.
Report_1_Synopsis: Pilot reported experiencing radio and GPS problems when trying to activate the runway lights.

Report_1_Narrative: I was instructing student in Aircraft X. We were on right downwind Runway 16 at BDN at 4;500 MSL.Aircraft Y pilot made a position call with him being 'on a 3 mile 45 for right downwind 16.' Shortly after that radio call was heard; my student observed the plane being adjacent 50 feet (+/-20 feet) to me at an angle; forcing me to do an evasive dive.I made a radio call after I made the evasive maneuver; that I will slow down and he can turn downwind.
Report_1_Synopsis: GA flight instructor reported an NMAC during approach to BDN non-towered airport.

Report_1_Narrative: At around XA:00L time; my instructor and I were practicing engine out procedures per [the training] course. When we tried to complete the checklist for an engine air restart; the propeller failed to unfeather. Upon retrying the checklist; the engine would still not start. We then tried to troubleshoot the engine and nothing would make the propeller unfeather. My instructor made the decision to proceed back [to] the airport and request priority handling. We requested priority with ZZZ Tower requesting to land immediately. My instructor then took over controls; flew us back and landed safely. While he taxied us back; I completed the after landing checklist and we shut down on ZZZ's North ramp.
Report_2_Narrative: On a training flight in a PA-44-180 with (L)/IO-360-B1G6 engines installed I (MEI) was the PIC the student was acting PIC. At 6;000 ft MSL in the practice area north of ZZZ; I intentionally failed the left engine by bringing the left mixture to cut-off. The student performed his memory items and then checklist items for Engine Failure in flight checklist. He then performed the Troubleshoot checklist and then Engine Feathering and Securing checklist. We maneuvered with the left engine feathered for a few minutes; performing normal level turns using normal banking maneuvers. I then told the student to use the Air Start Procedure to restart the engine in flight. The student performed the checklist and upon completion of the checklist the left engine remained in the feathered position. We completed the Engine Feathering and Securing checklist again and after a few minutes attempted the Air Start Procedure again. After completing the Air Start Procedure a second time the left engine remained in the feathered position. We completed the Engine Feathering and Securing checklist again. The student continued to fly the airplane towards the nearest suitable airport ZZZ. I [requested priority handling] with ZZZ Tower about 10NM to the north. We were cleared straight in for Runway XXR; I handled the checklist and radios while the student flew us towards Runway XXR. At about 5nm from ZZZ I took the flight controls from the student and made a normal straight in approach and landing on XXR. I was able to taxi us to the maintenance facility where we parked and shut down. Maintenance is currently inspecting the aircraft to determine a cause. One thing I could have done differently was to call maintenance on the radio in-flight and explain to them what happened and what we see/hear and they could possibly troubleshoot the problem for us from the ground before advising ATC.
Report_1_Synopsis: Multi-engine flight instructor and student reported that during a simulated engine failure lesson they were unable to un-feather the propeller and returned to the departure airport for an uneventful landing. The flight Instructor stated they simulated the engine failure by moving the mixture control to idle cutoff.

Report_1_Narrative: I was working Sector X combined with Sector Y when I gave Aircraft X a descent clearance to FL300. I saw that Aircraft Y was potential traffic and though I had time to get back to monitoring the separation. I got caught up with other duties. The Controller at Sector Z mentioned that I may want to watch the Aircraft X and Aircraft Y.  When I looked back I increased the descent rate on Aircraft X through FL310 and turned Aircraft Y 20 degrees left. I forgot the Aircraft X turned slightly west at ZZZ VOR.  I should have given the Aircraft X a crossing restriction at ZZZ1 [VOR] and anticipated the turn to ZZZ [Airport] after ZZZ1 [VOR]. We are working very short in our area and having to keep sectors combined due to COVID-19 eliminating half our crew including our Supervisor. We now must run CIC and control and train.Get controllers vaccine shots so we can work together again and be back on a regular schedule so we can get used to busy sessions again.
Report_1_Synopsis: Center Controller reported an airborne conflict and cited staffing issues due to COVID-19 as a contributing factor.

Report_1_Narrative: I witnessed the Supervisor; who was working Local Control; Ground Contol and the Operations Desk combined have what I would call a near mid air. He had Aircraft X in the right pattern for the runway. Aircraft Y ready for IFR departure at the same runway. What I witnessed was Aircraft Y turning to avoid Aircraft X on the upwind. I heard the Supervisor tell Aircraft X if able turn your crosswind now (he wasn't even at the departure end of the runway; maybe 4;500 ft. down the runway) He then told Aircraft Y [that] Aircraft X was turning crosswind. Aircraft Y then corrected back and continued straight out. The Supervisor told Aircraft Y to start his 315 heading and contact departure. Aircraft Y did not turn until 2 1/2 miles upwind which at that point I had Aircraft Z on the upwind off an adjacent runway.I listened to the tapes because I initially thought Aircraft Y was departing a different runway however after reviewing the tapes he was cleared for takeoff on the same runway as Aircraft X. Aircraft X must have just touched down for his touch and go when he cleared Aircraft Y for takeoff. There was obviously no runway separation which is 6;000 ft. or turned to avoid when Aircraft Y started his takeoff roll. I also heard on the tapes what sounded like Aircraft Y stating he was deviating to avoid. And then later state 'I'm correcting back'. I tried to see the replay but wasn't able to log into the system. The reason I'm reporting this a few days later is because I wanted to review the tapes and was trying to get into the replay system to see if additional separation was lost with Aircraft Z and Aircraft Y after my days off.
Report_1_Synopsis: Controller reported the Local Controller cleared an aircraft for takeoff with insufficient spacing behind a previous slower departure which resulted in a NMAC.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Training / Qualification; Workload; Situational Awareness; Fatigue; Confusion
Report_1_Narrative: When I was assigned a Tower position I inquired as to working a different position as it was my 6th day working and my last round of the day. I was told no. When I got to the tower it appeared to me that Local Control and Ground Control had been on position for the same amount of time. I went to relieve Ground Control and the Supervisor told me 'no your not going to ground' when I inquired about the the time on position he told me that Local Control had been on position over 2 hours. I again asked if I could work Ground Control. The Supervisor did not answer and ordered me to go to Local Control.Another controller in the tower said the Local Controller had requested to go from a previous position to Local when he was relieved without a break. When I first assumed the position the Supervisor asked me if I wanted him to write some of the call signs on the strips. I declined since it did was not busy at the time. This session turned into a heavy arrival push with some departures and multiple crossings. There were numerous data tags constantly overlapping as well as approximately one half separation between several arrivals making it difficult not only to write down the aircraft call signs on the half strips used for this position but also to ensure the preceding arrival was off the runway prior to the succeeding aircraft crossing the landing threshold.The Supervisor stood at the Cab Coordinator position (which was not staffed) actively listening the entire time I was on position. The only coordination performed by the Supervisor was to tell me I could issue a 110 heading out of 1;500 feet which at the time was completely unnecessary as well as a distraction. Aircraft X had been cleared to land and hold short of taxiway whiskey for crossing traffic. I had an Aircraft Z that was going to do a missed approach with a 030 heading behind Aircraft X. Aircraft Y had previously called ready for departure I cleared Aircraft Y for departure then realizing it was not going to work when I did my 3 part scan I complete prior to every departure. I immediately went back to Aircraft Y and cancelled takeoff clearance and instructed them to hold short. The aircraft did not acknowledge; and even if a readback was accomplished and complied with; crossing the hold short line was inevitable. I chose to transmit to Aircraft X to get off the runway to prevent a possible departure creating a more dangerous situation. I have not had the opportunity to listen to the tape but I am almost positive Aircraft X exited the runway at an intersection. Aircraft Y was still northbound entering the runway when Aircraft X exited the runway. Aircraft Y was on the runway on an easterly heading and asked to verify if cleared for departure. I advised negative and instructed to hold in position to alleviate any further confusion on Aircraft Y part. After a short time went by I then cleared Aircraft Y for departure. At that point the Supervisor asked me if there was anything he needed to be looking into.I advised since he wasn't aware of what happened 'I didn't know' and then told him what is written above. I think it would be a good idea if a new Supervisor who may not be fully aware of the ins and outs of the facility during extreme pushes to have a Cab Coordinator opened. Also for whatever the reason; the Supervisor is unable to keep abreast of what is happening while actively listening with a headset standing 3 feet from the busiest position; then opening a Cab Coordinator would have been a good call. Perhaps a Cab Coordinator would have caught the situation not going to work prior to my clearing the aircraft for departure to begin with and would have definitely helped with the numerous crossings.
Report_1_Synopsis: A Local Controller reported they allowed an aircraft to taxi onto the runway for departure with insufficient spacing from a previous arriving aircraft.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Situational Awareness; Communication Breakdown; Confusion; Other / Unknown; Training / Qualification
Report_1_Narrative: Taxiing to Z10 in the Z concourse at ZZZ we entered the ramp area without checking in with Ramp Control due to our confusion with ground clearances instructions. We were waiting on Y Taxiway to taxi to our gate and instructed by Ground Control to 'follow an aircraft ahead into West (the ramp area leading to our gate).' Usually these instructions are followed by 'contact Ramp Control.' However today we did not get those instructions. We followed preceding aircraft into West. I stopped on the north taxi lane without pulling into our gate and instructed my FO to check in with Ramp Control to make sure were cleared in. They in turn informed us that we needed to get clearance to enter the ramp and 'that Company A has been entering the ramp without clearance all week.' Hopefully this report will stop a clearly recurring problem. Maybe our confusion with ground controls clearance isn't only unique to us. We operate at many airports with Ramp Control and I can attest that there are standard instructions that we as pilots look for as cues such as being told to 'contact ramp control' before entering ramp. Compounding my confusion is the non-standard operations at airports because of COVID where air traffic is down; and Ramp Control has been frequently out of service. I thought I did the right thing by stopping to query my instructions. I admit I'm still getting used to the Z concourse procedures at ZZZ having operated at ZZZ even before all the construction. I should have queried earlier right at the boundary of the ramp and relayed the instructions I was following. Also; we observed another Company A aircraft read back the wrong instructions going into the West Ramp Control. They were told to taxi Y to West. The pilots read back 'taxi to the gate.' Which is incorrect because they were told to taxi to the ramp area not straight to the gate. Not sure if they were able to follow the instructions correctly. I'm more aware and learned from this experience and will be more vigilant going into ZZZ in the future.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported entering the ramp without contacting ramp control and cited as contributing a confusing clearance and non-standard operations at airports where ramp control is frequently out of service due to COVID-19.

Report_1_Narrative: My Captain and I were ferrying an aircraft from ZZZ-ZZZ1. We were taking off Runway XX and after takeoff our lavatory smoke detector alarm started beeping. After direction from the Captain we [advised ATC] and made the decision to return to ZZZ. We requested direct ZZZ to hold and set up for our return. As we were entering the hold the alarm had stopped; we decided to still return to ZZZ as it was the safest decision and we could not verify that there was no fire. As we were holding we set the aircraft up to return; calling Company and following procedures for our return. After we finished setting ourselves up and getting ready we ran the checklists that we needed to; we requested vectors for to return to ZZZ and requested an ILS. We returned to ZZZ without any further issue and had fire trucks meet us on the runway to verify that there was no fire. After we verified there was no fire we taxied back to the ramp and shut down the aircraft. Lavatory fires or indications are handled by flight attendants; we did not have any on board so we treated this like a regular fire and returned to field in a safe and efficient manner.The Captain's workload was extremely busy; my recommendation/lesson learned is to help the Captain out sooner in any way possible including helping by offering to take flight controls and lessen the Captains workload. Another recommendation is having a procedure for pilots in the event of [lavatory] fire for pilots when no flight attendants are on board.
Report_1_Synopsis: Q400 First Officer reported the Lavatory Smoke alarm activated after takeoff resulting in a return to the departure airport.

Person_1_Function: Trainee; Pilot Not Flying; Single Pilot
Report_1_Narrative: In the VFR sectional chart issued Feb 25; 2021; the Danville VOR (DNV) has the wrong frequency listed. It should be 111.0. It is listed here as 110.0; which is the frequency for a nearby VOR CMI. I noticed while flight planning my student solo cross country flight.It seems plausible a NAVAID could be mistakenly tuned to the nearby one and be a safety factor. Hope it's fixed in the next issue.
Report_1_Synopsis: GA student pilot reported the wrong frequency is listed on the VFR sectional chart for the Danville (DNV) VOR.

Report_1_Narrative: My student and I were conducting a routine multi engine training flight. As part of this flight we had decided we would be doing a full engine shutdown; feather and in air restart. We shutdown and feathered the engine at 4;000 feet. About 1-2 minutes elapsed before we briefed and began to run through the engine restart procedure. When we engaged the start; we only got a half rotation from the propeller. We tried a couple different restart variations; priming; different throttle and mixture positions; but we still had the issue of not getting enough power to turn the engine over enough times to unfeather it. After 3-4 start attempts; all of the electrical components in the cockpit became inoperative. Avionics; intercom; transponder and transponder were all inoperative. After all the avionics and intercom shut off; we began to troubleshoot the issue. We recycled the avionics master; minimized electrical load and squawked 7600 in the event the transponder was still transmitting. I knew we needed to start back towards the airport regardless of whether we got the electrical system back up; because the likelihood of us getting the engine restarted with a clear electrical issue was slim to none; seeing as getting an engine out of feather takes a significant amount electrical power. Our next course of action was to get in touch with ATC. We did not have cell service at 4;000 ft.; (altitude at which the shutdown occurred) so we started a slow descending left turn (into the good engine) in hopes of getting service. I was not going to let us go below 3;000 [ft.]. At around 3;500 ft. I got enough cell service to call ZZZ Approach; using the Bluetooth on my headset and phone to talk with them. I told ZZZ Approach we had experienced an electrical failure and that we were also single engine. At this time I also [received priority]. Approach was able to give us a heading to fly to intercept final and during that time while we proceeded towards the airport; we ran through our engine securing checklist and single engine approach and landing checklist; we briefed the landing and determined I would fly the final approach and landing. With the checklist and briefing done; all that was left was to fly the approach. We got our landing clearance over the phone; got the gear down and established a final approach speed of 125 MPH. The landing on Runway XX was uneventful; with the aircraft touching down in the first 3rd of the runway. ARFF (Airport Rescue and Fire Fighting) units were on alert and followed us down the runway to where we exited at Taxiway XX. As we were coming to a stop on [Taxiway] XX all our avionics turned back on; so we were able to contact Ground to get our taxi clearance back to the [FBO]. An air guard fire personnel did a quick check of the aircraft; asked if we were ok and then we were able to taxi back to our flight school ramp without incident.
Report_1_Synopsis: PA-23 instructor pilot reported loss of all electrical power after shutting an engine down for air restart training; requiring a return to departure airport.

Report_1_Narrative: About one hour from landing; we started to smell a faint burning scent from the packs. It was very faint; but noticeable. It smelled like glycol or plastic burning. It remained constant until we initiated a descent from FL390-FL370. The smell became more pronounced. For lack of another checklist or procedure; we ran the smoke fire and fumes QRH. The smell was only in the cockpit and not the cabin. Since we could not determine the source. We deemed it appropriate to take the safest course of action to expedite getting the aircraft on the ground with no undue delay. We [advised ATC] and asked for CFR (Crash Fire Rescue) to meet us to check for anything out of the ordinary upon landing. We initiated a high speed descent and approach; and performed a safe landing. CFR met the aircraft and checked it over and we taxied to the gate.
Report_1_Synopsis: B737-800 First Officer reported a flight deck fumes event during cruise.  The crew ran the appropriate QRH checklist and continued to destination.

Report_1_Narrative: Prior to pushing; the outgoing Flight Attendant told me the air bag at [Seat] XXE was out. After some clarification she meant the life vest at [Seat] XXE was falling out. This distraction had us focusing on adding the MEL to the Release. We we're subsequently given the HAZMAT Dangerous Goods Form just prior to push and failed to verify that there was no remark on the Release regarding the HAZMAT.
Report_1_Synopsis: B737-800 First Officer reported Dispatch Release missing required Dangerous goods information.

Report_1_Narrative: Upon holding short of the runway in ZZZ; we experienced a burning odor in the cockpit during the pneumatic ice protection test. We contacted Maintenance and began troubleshooting. Both packs were individually giving us a burning odor. The flight attendant had called us to let us know that he smelled it too. We then returned to the gate. Once at the gate; we submitted 2 write-ups; one for the burning odor and one for a flickering Multi-Function Flight Displays screen that was progressively getting worse. I was informed later that this plane had the same issue the month prior. After our write up; maintenance could not reproduce the problem and signed the aircraft off. I later learned; from my flight attendant who was now with the new crew on the same plane; upon engine startup; they immediately began to smell burning fumes. This was following the sign-off from maintenance. Flight crew shut down packs and taxi back to the gate.Captain recommended replacing all duct work and packs as burning odor/fumes seems to be a common issue; or find out what is causing so many similar problems.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Captain reported a ground gate return due to a fume event during Pneumatic Ice Test while holding for departure.

Report_1_Narrative: While on descent into ZZZ on the ZZZZZ arrival we experienced a BLD 1 LEAK Master Warning with associated EICAS and red inscription messages. The FO (First Officer) proceeded to run the QRH; while I asked for immediate vectors to ZZZ along with a descent to exit IMC and icing conditions. ATC granted the descent; as well as direct ZZZ. The bleed leak warning was still occurring while the FO waited the requisite 3 minutes as per the QRH. This prompted me to [receive priority] as the eventual end of the QRH procedure is to secure the engine should the leak not extinguish. As we descended out of icing conditions; the BLD LEAK message extinguished; prompting no further action from the QRH. At this time I notified the FA (Flight Attendant) with a TEST briefing as to the nature of our [situation]; that the immediate threat had passed and we would be landing normally. I also made a PA to the passengers to inform them that they may see ARFF (Airport Rescue and Fire Fighting) vehicles around the aircraft on landing. We continued to a normal landing on XXL in ZZZ and taxied to the gate with no further assistance required.Master Warning bell with associated EICAS and red inscription messages.Unknown problem in bleed system caused a BLD 1 LEAK Master Warning. Aircraft had been written up 3 days prior for same issue with associated maintenance entry clearing the write up.QRH ran; ATC advised to clear icing conditions; proceeded to normal landing in ZZZ.Possibly more in-depth look at bleed system whenever a leak detection warning occurs beyond ops check good.
Report_2_Narrative: On the ZZZZZ arrival into ZZZ we descended into a cloud layer and encountered icing conditions. Within 30 seconds of the anti-ice system being turned on we received a 'Bleed 1 Leak' EICAS message. As Pilot Monitoring; I ran the respective QRH associated with that message. Still being in icing conditions we decided it would be best if we advised ATC to gain priority and also since we did not know how thick the icing cloud layer was. Upon waiting the 3 minutes as stated by the QRH we exited the icing conditions and within 30 seconds the bleed leak message and inscription went away thus ending the QRH procedure. We continued to ZZZ; landed and taxied to the gate normally.
Report_1_Synopsis: EMB-145 flight crew reported a BLEED 1 LEAK Master Warning on descent into IMC icing conditions and after descending out of icing; the warning discontinued.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Other / Unknown; Situational Awareness; Communication Breakdown; Confusion
Report_1_Narrative: Cleaners in ZZZ are not following policy for waiting for all passengers to leave aircraft before they board to clean; and not following crew instructions to remain off the aircraft. Cleaners must wait for all passengers to deplane prior to boarding the aircraft.Cleaners in ZZZ are aggressively pushing their way into the forward galley to remove trash from the carts during the deplaning process. This impedes the flow of deplaning passengers and obstructs the ability of flight attendants to manage the flow of passengers and maintain door and safety compliance. Cleaners are insisting that flight attendants leave the galley area so they can work; they say operations has told them to move the crew to accomplish the cleaning task. Allowing cleaners to pull carts and trash while flight attendants and passengers are deplaning creates safety hazards (bumps; trips; and impacts from trash removal) and does not allow for safe social distancing as per company policy.  Cleaners also leave bags on the floor posing a trip hazard for crew and passengers deplaning; as I was deplaning a cleaner had left a gray cleaning tote below a jump-seat and I tripped over it falling into the bulkhead.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Attendant reported the aircraft cleaners are not adhering to the social distancing policy.

Report_1_Narrative: I was in a Super Cub flying toward an uncontrolled airport. The pattern was very busy including some fast-moving aircraft so I veered off east of the airport planning to wait until the pattern cleared so that I could land my slow flying plane. I was just at 4NM from the airport.An instructional flight with a CFI and a student made a radio call that they were 'on the 45 to the left downwind for 23'. Shortly thereafter they passed underneath me from a blind spot behind me and to the right; east.The instructor was upset feeling that I was 'in the downwind' for 23 without making radio calls. At the time of the near miss; I was a few hundred feet inside the 4 NM airport area. From a visual perspective; I did not think that I was anywhere near the pattern; except for jets which I would have expected to be higher than my 2;300 feet.I was barely inside the 4 NM airport area and had not made any radio calls; intending to maneuver well east of the field to wait on traffic to quiet down.One contributing factor of the near miss was me not making a radio call that I was at the edge of the airport 4NM area. A contributing cause was a light aircraft at pattern altitude over 4 NM from the airport considering themselves to be in the pattern.I did contact the pilot of the other aircraft to 'debrief' the situation and I plan to discuss with the leadership of the flight school.
Report_1_Synopsis: Piper J3 Cub pilot reported an NMAC at an uncontrolled airport requiring evasive action.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Situational Awareness; Training / Qualification; Confusion; Human-Machine Interface
Report_1_Narrative: Got to location failed to research the airspace. Was relying on the manufacture's Geo fencing to guide me with airspace. Violation was discovered by company UAS coordinator. Violation was discussed and corrective action for further use is understood. We discussed and now understand the difference between Geo fencing and the NAS. I going further; will look up airspace before flights. I will not fly in controlled airspace without proper authorization.
Report_1_Synopsis: A UAS pilot reported an airspace violation.

Report_1_Narrative: The first 3;000 feet of Runway 14 has excessive dips and divots that are bottoming out our landing gear struts during landing rollout and during takeoff. On landing Runway 14; after touchdown with the thrust reversers deployed; we felt the main landing gear struts fully compress and the aircraft nearly bounce. The nose strut also bottomed out and we were pushed into our seats hard. This occurred around 80-100 knots and the dips continued down the runway fully compressing our struts each time. On departure from Runway 14; the same thing happened. We are concerned that without an immediate repair to the runway; that these dips and divots will grow and potentially cause harm to the aircraft landing gear and structure which would cause a landing or takeoff accident. It's that bad.
Report_1_Synopsis: Pilot reported runway condition at BLM airport could cause aircraft damage.

Person_2_Human_Factors: Troubleshooting; Workload; Situational Awareness; Distraction; Confusion
Report_1_Narrative: Aircraft X was on an LDA Approach. I had not cleared them for the approach because I was trying to descend the aircraft for the Visual Approach. Just leaving 9;000 feet; the aircraft took a hard left turn. I keyed up and turned them to a 010 heading to which they stated they were having autopilot problems. The aircraft started descending below 8000 feet. I issued a Low Altitude alert. Shortly after; the aircraft took another hard left turn. I did not reissue a low altitude alert but restated altitude and heading with immediately. Because of this; I broke the aircraft following him off the approach and re-sequenced him. Aircraft X landed without further incident.I'm not sure what else to do in this situation. Pilots need to learn to fly without their autopilot. Everyone is way too reliant on technology and need to get back to the basics.
Report_2_Narrative: While transitioning from the RNAV arrival to the LDA Approach; my autopilot malfunctioned and caused the airplane to deviate from the approach. I was below the cloud bases and in VMC. I attempted to fly the airplane without the autopilot and regain the appropriate heading and altitude; while troubleshooting the autopilot issue. I was given a vector and an altitude by the approach controller and I did not maintain that altitude during the trouble shooting efforts. I went below 8;000 feet which is below the minimum vectoring altitude in that area.My fixation on troubleshooting the autopilot and not devoting full attention to flying the airplane caused this issue. The fact that I was in VMC further added to my lack of focus; as I was clearly able to see and avoid any terrain in the area. Focusing solely on the task of flying the airplane would have prevented this issue from occurring.
Report_1_Synopsis: GA pilot and TRACON Controller reported the pilot flying a LDA Approach to SLC airport deviated from their course and altitude and flew below the Minimum Vectoring Altitude.

Report_1_Narrative: Aircraft X was on vector to RWY XX off the downwind. Ceiling was marginal; but I was confident I would get the airport in sight; at least by 070. I vectored Aircraft X in front of Aircraft Y on the straight-in. This situation happened less than 10 minutes prior to another report I just filed with a pilot deviation so I was already frazzled from that. I turned Aircraft X heading 090; they did not respond; immediately re-keyed 'Aircraft X; heading 080.' The pilot read back correctly. They were level 080. My vector had the aircraft practically straddling the 080/070 MVA line. My PTL (Projected Track Line) showed a left turn; I descended Aircraft X to 070. Almost immediately; the aircraft showed a right turn. I immediately corrected Aircraft X to a 070; realized I had given the descent and tried to stop at 080. The aircraft went to 075 in a 080 MVA. At this point; Aircraft Y is going to run them over; so I turn Aircraft X south at 080. I didn't have time to exchange traffic and he would pass about 2nm West. As Aircraft Y was approaching ZZZZZ; I cleared the aircraft for the approach even though they were not yet tail to tail because I knew the aircraft wouldn't descend quite yet. When I saw the aircraft side by side; I climbed Aircraft to 090 because 7nm south; Restricted Area XXXX was active to 090. Upon review; Aircraft X showed 081 and I was informed I had a LoSS [Loss of Separation Standards]  in addition to three separate pilot deviations.I guess I should have waited a second longer to climb Aircraft X; that would have prevented the LoSS; however; delaying any more could have put him in an unsafe situation with the Restricted Area where they are shooting artillery. I truly showed the aircraft side by side and waited as long as I could to climb to ensure I would clear Aircraft X; I thought I was legal. Choose the lesser of the evils. I truly thought I had crossing/diverging. I wish I wouldn't have descended the Aircraft X to 070 either; but he read back the turn; I saw the turn start with the PTL and pushed him down because I needed to with Aircraft Y coming fast behind; and already being extended from Aircraft Z I had to break off in the earlier situation. The fact I have two back-to-back pilot deviations; one go-around from it; and when I go on break and have to spend my break doing a report; to then be told I had a LoSS; rather than even giving me even a few seconds to get my bearings is why management in this facility is worthless. Back to back; high stress situations; and we would rather tell you that you [are no good] at your job rather than good job; or are you doing okay even. I'm not mad at them calling the LoSS; I take responsibility for observing my scope wrong since. I'm upset that rather than even attempting to care about their employees; they immediately try to make them feel worse.
Report_1_Synopsis: TRACON Controller reported a loss of separation occurred and one of the aircraft descended below the minimum altitude for the sector. Controller stated they had two pilot deviations shortly before this and the event caused added stress.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Other / Unknown; Situational Awareness; Communication Breakdown; Distraction
Report_1_Narrative: My D-side had reminded me about a pending confliction that I needed to resolve which I had put off. I was a little annoyed with myself and as such my resolution was perhaps a bit more aggressive than needed. Headings were issued to both aircraft and it worked out fine. I had intended to have Aircraft X on course before he neared the adjacent sector boundary but I didn't check on it quite soon enough. I remember thinking that it would work out fine but I was apparently slightly off in my estimation and the aircraft got within 2.5 miles of the adjacent sector boundary - without actually crossing the boundary - without a pointout; which my D-side also failed to notice.I never did notice the event; Management informed me later as they'd coincidentally been monitoring the sector.I had perhaps gotten a little complacent from the routine and experience. I'll be extra sure to follow up on any headings issued so as to ensure the aircraft involved perform as expected; and to be more vigilant in protecting my airspace boundaries.
Report_1_Synopsis: ARTCC Controller reported an airborne conflict due to a handoff issue.

Report_1_Narrative: Good VFR day; cleared departure out of ZZZ to TEHRU; then direct MTJ. Just prior to TEHRU we informed the DEN Center controller that we would be requesting the ILS [Runway] 17 and was expecting to be vectored to the localizer. Instead; we were given 'direct DIRDY; Cross DIRDY at or above 13;000 feet; cleared for the ILS 17.'Loaded that into the MCDU; which inserted the procedure turn depicted to the north; after BRUUK. As the track from GEJYU to BRUUK is 78 degrees off the localizer course we figured this was the only 'legal' way to fly it; based on our clearance; so wasn't surprised. (Coming from the west side of the localizer there is a DME arc with a lead-in radial depicted to account for that steep angle; but not from the east. Again; we assumed the procedure turn was the only legal way to turn onto the localizer.)Although the crossing altitude for GEJYU is 10;800 feet the initial procedure turn altitude is 12;500 feet so we crossed GEJYU somewhere above 13;000 feet on our descent to 12;500 feet. Unfortunately; when we visually picked up the airport this made us too high to ask for a visual approach so we decided to just fly the procedure turn; as planned.After becoming established in the procedure turn outbound; the Controller asked us what we were doing and said most flights just join the localizer and go directly toward the runway. After some back-and-forth about this; while we were in the turn back toward BRUUK; he said 'low altitude alert; climb and maintain 13;000 [feet]' (we were still at 12;500 [feet]; and VFR). We climbed to 13;000 feet; called the runway in sight; and were cleared for the visual approach.Long story short(er); there was obvious confusion on our part regarding how this approach was supposed to be flown; as well as; I believe; based on our conversation; the Controller's. After landing we looked over the chart for 5-10 minutes; looking at all the various notes; etc.; before finally noticing the 'NoPT' note depicted under the 9;000 feet MEA listed for the leg from GEJYU to BRUUK.I saw the altitude and NoPT but when looking at the routing in the FMS and the procedure turn altitude assumed it wasn't intended for flying the full approach. I also don't understand why we would expect to intercept a localizer from a 78-degree angle when; I believe; while being vectored to an intercept; the intercept heading given by ATC is required to be within 30 degrees of the localizer course. If we had flown the depicted track from GEJYU to BRUUK as apparently expected on this approach; I believe the airplane would have overshot the turn onto the localizer by at least 1-2 miles. As for the low altitude warning the airplane was flying the published procedure turn on altitude which would lead one to believe you were in protected airspace?
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier First Officer reported they misread the approach chart and did not fly the approach track correctly into MTJ airport. The crew was given a 'Low Altitude Alert' by ATC.

Report_1_Narrative: Near midair collision with a personal 'drone' remotely piloted aerial vehicle; roughly 18' square in size. Occurred on the SCBBY2 arrival; TAKOE TSN for RWY 26R; at 6;000 feet MSL; 3.5nm East of KALEA Intersection. FO (First Officer) was pilot flying and picked up tally off the nose inside .5 nm; low-hi; rapidly moving from right to left. Jumpseater also gained visual situational awareness at the left cockpit window #2. Both FO and Jumpseater estimate the drone passed less than 50 feet in elevation from the left wing and certainly within the lateral wingspan distance of the aircraft; which confirmed the visual ID of a drone vs. a bird. Captain was pilot monitoring and did not see the drone but reported location; altitude; time; and general description to SoCal Approach moments after the incident with the information FO passed to him. We continued the approach to land without incident.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported an NMAC with a UAV in SCT airspace.
