Person_2_Human_Factors: Confusion; Human-Machine Interface; Situational Awareness; Training / Qualification; Communication Breakdown
Report_1_Narrative: I operated Aircraft X from ZZZ1 to ZZZ. The weather was low; approximately 600 OVC at ZZZ and rain. I believe we had an alternate of ZZZ2. We planned to shoot the ILS to Runway 7 at ZZZ. I was the pilot flying. We operated the flight to ZZZ normally and got set up for the ILS to Runway 7. I was established on the approach and fully configured at approximately 1;000 feet when I noticed that both the localizer and glide slope were flagged. I was looking at the PFD (Primary Flight Display) and slightly startled by the lack of information. I then glanced to the First Officer's side and noticed his PFD looked normal. I never felt any erratic pitch attitudes but according to FOQA (Flight Operations Quality Assurance); we reached 12 degrees pitch down and up to 2700 FPM descent below 1;000 feet. I remember hearing the aural 'glide slope glide slope' The FO (First Officer) then questioned; 'should we go-around?' I responded yes and initiated a go around. We climbed up to 3;000 feet and requested radar vectors back around for the same approach. I then transferred the controls to the First Officer because his navigation equipment was operating normally. We continued on the approach. At approximately 600 feet I called runway in sight; and he responded landing. We drifted to the right of the approach course; due to the First Officer not reacting to the left crosswind. We were also a bit high on the glide slope. I told him to correct; and asked him if he was able to correct the flight path; he responded correcting. We ended up landing hard and fast. I taxied off normally. I forgot to write up the discrepancy that the airplane lost localizer and glide slope. I believe the cause of this event was due to the gradual failure of the glide slope and my reaction to that. It took us approximately 38 seconds from when the failure occurred until the missed approach was executed.  I don't think it would hurt to see this event repeated in a simulator so that I can see it again and understand how I could have reacted better.
Report_2_Narrative: I was Pilot Monitoring for an approach into ZZZ1. We were conducting the ILS to runway 7 at ZZZ1; and had just passed the final approach fix when the Captain's glideslope malfunctioned and presented a red 'GS' flag. My instruments appeared to continue to provide accurate glideslope indications; and the autopilot remained engaged; coupled to the Captain's side; and continued to fly the aircraft. I don't recall noticing which vertical mode took over in the absence of the GS. I suggested to the Captain that a go-around be made; she waited several seconds to see if the glideslope indications would return; then disconnected the autopilot to execute the go-around. The Captain applied TOGA (Takeoff/Go-around) power. Upon applying go-around power; the pitch attitude further decreased; and the vertical rate of descent correspondingly increased; causing a GPWS sink-rate warning. Visual ground contact was made briefly before the descent was arrested. We continued the climb straight out and contacted Approach for missed approach instructions. This event began with the malfunction of the Captain's side glideslope. This led to a breakdown in situational awareness and crew communication as the aircraft continued to descend in the absence of the glideslope until a go-around maneuver was executed. I believe additional training may be required; both on go-around procedures as well as on equipment malfunctions during approach.
Report_1_Synopsis: CRJ-200 flight crew reported glideslope failure on approach.

Report_1_Narrative: While boarding the ramp manager arrived to the flight deck with a NOTOC regarding 20 KG of dry ice being loaded onto the aircraft. The Ramp Manager informed the Captain that it was freight containing pharmaceuticals; not a UN3373. She also told the Captain that [this] was not an expedite item. Moments later the Dispatcher sent an ACARS to tell the Captain to verify that the package was an expedite item. The Ramp Manager again confirmed that it was NOT an expedite item. The Captain called the Dispatcher and they discussed that the package was not a expedite medical supply item or an expedite UN3373 and was therefore limited to 2.5KG per package. Because the package was 20 KG the Captain asked that it not be loaded. After swapping aircraft due to an unrelated Maintenance issue; the Captain went to look at the package and noted that it had a handwritten label saying it was the X Company Vaccine. The Captain noted that because it was not an expedite item it was not labeled normally; i.e.; it did not state 'Contains dangerous goods...' and did not have the dry ice placard. It also had a marking indicating that it contained no dangerous goods. When speaking with the Dispatcher again the Dispatcher told the Captain that we were indeed authorized to carry it citing the national state of emergency due to the pandemic. Captain read the FOM chapter pointing out that it was not an expedite medical supply item and not an expedite UN3373 and should therefore be limited to 2.5 kg of dry ice; but the Dispatcher assured the Captain that we could take it. The Captain confirmed that the package would not be able to fly on any other flight that day. After conferring with Dispatch; and the manager who brought up the NOTOC who confirmed the contents the package was loaded on to the aircraft. There were no further issues.Flight crew and Dispatch worked together to determine if the item was safe for transport.Speaking with Dispatch and the Ramp Manager; it became clear that each party agreed that the 20 kg of dry ice would normally exceed the limit for an individual package that is not an expedite medical supply item or expedite UN3373; it was; however; also agreed that this vaccine shipment was somehow excepted from that normal requirement. The cause would seem to be some confusion as to whether or not freight which is not an expedite item that contained medical supplies; specifically the Vaccine; were allowed. Perhaps a lack of guidelines specific to the transport of the vaccine was a possible cause (if such an exemption from policy exists). The Captain determined after speaking with the individual parties that it would be safe to transport.Better guidance; including up to date flow charts; to help navigate this issue. It is not entirely clear whether a medical supply needs to be an expedite item in order to be exempt from the individual limitations of 2.5 kg. Although both the Captain and the Dispatcher initially thought that it does need to be an expedite item to contain more than 2.5 KG; the chapter in the FOM does not expressly say either way. The exception to the limit of 2.5KG appears to be listed under the expedite item section on the maximum limits page of the FOM; but it then states; 'Dry Ice weight may exceed the 2.5 kg (5.5 lbs) limitation; if contained within the UN3373 expedite item or medical shipment.' The use of the word 'or' may indicate that a medical supply need not be an expedite item even though it is located under the expedite item section. This could use clarification. If a medical shipment can exceed 2.5 KG without being an expedite item; then it should be listed as a separate exception. Similarly; if the medical shipment MUST be an expedite item that should also be clearly stated. If there is some exception due to the pandemic for the COVID vaccine that should be conveyed. The current flow chart contained on our system could stand to be updated. Specially; it lists all limits in pounds; but the NOTOC is in KG; which in itself renders the tool useless. Also; the flow chart ask the question 'is dry ice in an expedite item?' This is a yes or no question; but the flow chart only has an option for 'YES.'
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported a hazardous material documentation issue while attempting to transport a vaccine.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Human-Machine Interface; Troubleshooting; Confusion; Distraction; Fatigue
Report_1_Narrative: Somewhere after Burns Flat (BFV) at 38;000 ft. and until ZUN VOR; we had encountered first an ATC Fault EICAS message. Oddly then on both transponders. First Officer was the Pilot Flying. So; we discussed and went into the QRH and complied. I had then though to ask ABQ ARTCC if they were able to see us on their radar scope. The controller had replied yes. So when I remarked of our issue; he knew right away that jamming was taking place. Now I didn't clarify if this was any kind of military exercise and if this was normal. He acted as though it was. Shortly after this; we started slowly seeing other EICAS messages. I can't remember the exact order though. I believe the next was EGPWS TERR or so. Then L GPS appeared not too far after this. Maybe R GPS as well; maybe. Eventually we saw UNABLE RNP. So we definitely knew GPS jamming was making sense. The RNP ANP scales on the Pilot Flying Display bottom was like RNP 2.00 ANP 2.93 in amber color. It was clear our GPS was in an inertial mode. I did select radio updating eventually per the QRH's procedural instructions. Center never seem too concerned as nothing else was said. The weather was quite good and while concerned; I had a good idea as we made our way towards ZZZ1; the start of the RNAV star; the GPS navigation would probably return to a normal state and it did. There wasn't any flight safety breaches or traffics conflicts as this event happened entered at cruise. Although; I did forget to make a maintenance log entry required by mandatory reports. I may have been more fatigued than I was aware. Sleep was fragmented in chunks of multiple 2 to 3 or so hrs. on this day. Intentional GPS jamming I suppose. I've never encountered this in my entire career here. Wondering if the military does these exercises; but I would expect we'd be notified via a NOTAM and on our [flight plan] if it was known. I suppose if we knew we could of had a different routing? I don't believe compromised safety as in this case was an issue. It never degraded to a more severe off course deviation and didn't cause traffic conflicts. Don't get me wrong we were concerned and a bit miffed. I will file a security report and read more on the subject of GPS jamming interference's.
Report_1_Synopsis: An air carrier pilot reported GPS jamming.

Report_1_Narrative: Trip began as Flight ABCD; 2-day ZZZ; daytime flying. On the XXth [Date]; crew brought in plane with flap issue. Took over one hour to resolve. Just prior to engine start; ground crew said fuel was leaking from Number 1 engine. Followed QRC; ended up doing engine run. Ground crew stated no leaks after engine run. Captain looked out window to see fuel streaming from number one engine. This was never resolved. We refused to fly aircraft. Were told by scheduling a new part was being flown in and we would Maintenance ferry jet home on the XXth [Date]; our scheduled day off.On XXth [Date]; discovered; at jet; no part had arrived but we were told to ferry jet to ZZZ1 and it would be fixed. After consultation with numerous agencies and several hours; we again refused jet. Nothing had been fixed. Worst engine leak I've ever seen. The directives Maintenance was following were for leaks in the range of 60 to 100 drops per minute of fuel. This became a steady stream the day prior. We refused to fly jet as nothing had been done.Took some time to get hotel; had to self-help. Arrived to hotel. Scheduled to deadhead home on XYth [Date]. Due to mix-up; transportation went to wrong hotel. We missed XA00 flight home. Rescheduled for XD:50 pm flight home. I had a ZZZ turn today; XZth [Date]; with a XA50 report. This was illegal crew rest so the crew desk did a mini-pack of my schedule; combined the now 4-day trip with 4 duty periods into a 5 day trip and 5 duty periods with near absolute minimum rest.I spent some time checking on the legality of what was done; with company. It turns out; this extremely onerous now 5 day pairing with very limited rest opportunity was legal. Legal doesn't mean smart or does it mean a pilot really has adequate rest.I gave every effort in an attempt to get adequate rest; but the pressure; once finally in bed; and reflection on the maintenance issues; the mental fatigue caused by the ever-changing schedule; flying into now two days off; and then paired with a trip packing with minimal rest caused sleep to be very difficult. Two-hour time difference; though seemingly minor; comes into play as I'd become acclimatized.I finally realized; as I was about to go to parking lot; I was not safe to fly nor could I certify FFD. I called fatigued.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported calling in fatigued due to several maintenance related delays and company scheduling techniques that push the limits of legal rest periods.

Report_1_Narrative: Descending into ZZZ; we received an RA from a VFR traffic crossing our path below us at approximately 5;500 ft. MSL. We were descending to initially 3;000 ft. MSL to setup for landing on Runway XX (VMC conditions prevailed and the ATIS advertised a visual to Runway XX); but then were told to maintain 6;000 ft. MSL by Center for VFR traffic she was not talking to in our path. Hearing and seeing this scenario develop we shallowed our descent rate to level at 6;000 ft. MSL in an attempt to mitigate a predictive RA scenario. Once level and seeing the traffic was continuing in our direction; we also attempted a turn to avoid the traffic prior to the RA; however the frequency was congested and the turn was too late. Once we received permission to turn and initiated it; we ended up receiving the RA. We complied with the RA; disengaged the autopilot; and also climbed to approximately 6;500 ft. MSL to avoid the traffic showing at one point 400 ft. below us and advised Center of the RA. We were given permission to climb and; once clear of the conflict; to proceed to ZZZ without further issue.The event occurred due to a few factors coming together. The main issue is that the VFR aircraft was maneuvering without talking to ATC so as to avoid traffic. It was also a beautiful day; so there was a lot of GA aircraft the Controller was working with causing the frequency to become very congested. Secondly; the Controller should have issued us a vector or higher altitude to maintain to avoid the traffic as we never had or called aircraft in sight. We could have tried to turn earlier; but the congestion on the frequency prevented this from happening as well.I feel that this issue could have been prevented had the Controller issued us a higher level off altitude; or given us a vector once it was determined that the VFR target could become an issue. I feel that we tried our best to avoid this scenario by shallowing our descent and even requesting a turn. It just came down to the VFR traffic had an unpredictable flight path; the frequency was very congested; and once we received our clearance to turn it was too late.
Report_1_Synopsis: First Officer of a CRJ-200 reported an RA while descending towards destination and cited the large amount of GA aircraft in the area as a contributing factor.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Workload; Troubleshooting; Confusion; Communication Breakdown; Time Pressure
Report_1_Narrative: We departed ZZZ on a Part 91 leg to ZZZ1. Reaching our initial assigned altitude from approach we were given a climb to 17;000 and that's when we lost EDC2 without making any changes to anything. We were caught totally by surprise. As a result there were several alarms and aural warnings sounding that could not be silenced. That's also when we realized that we could no longer communicate through the intercom and the First Officer had zero radio communication. We communicated through hand signals and loud talking. I was the Pilot Monitoring on this leg but I took controls at this point since I was the only one with radio communication. I pressed the autopilot disconnect button to ensure everything was disengaged and never made an attempt to reactivate it. I leveled at 14;000 and asked for a heading to troubleshoot and run the appropriate checklist. I announced that we had a failure of EDC2 and asked my First Officer to run the checklist. I couldn't hear any part of the checklist but he announced that the last step was to land as soon as practical.  I [requested priority handling] and asked for vectors back to ZZZ. I received a heading and a descent and [the] First Officer competed the appropriate checklists for descent and approach. On final approach during our before landing checklist we realized the gear did not indicate down. We aborted the landing and tried to see if the Tower controller could confirm if the gear was down or not. We made the first pass and he thought it was down but asked us to make one more pass with all the lights off in the Tower so they could try to get a better look. Again he said it looked like they were down. I considered calling for the emergency gear extension procedures but I felt a sense of urgency to get on the ground. There were several alarms sounding and we were still struggling to communicate. I was attempting to troubleshoot mentally but hand flying the airplane was my priority. At this point I realized I was getting overloaded and we still had no idea what had caused the failure in the first place. I was worried things could continue to get worse at any moment and I decided to land because so believed it was the safest thing to do. Just before touch down I recognized the gear was not down and I gently applied pressure on the power levers backwards against the flight idle stops to fully committed to the landing. At this point I knew a go around was dangerous. We touched down smoothly on centerline skidded down the runway. We finally came to a gentle halt just slightly off the runway in the grass. We ran the shutdown procedures and evacuated through the door where we were greeted by fire rescue. After walking away without even a scratch I discovered things were starting to come back to me that I couldn't seem to remember during flight. Details about the systems that I've learned in training that I could not dig out of my head while we were in flight. I've learned a lot about myself and how I react when the workload gets high and I know I can handle any future emergency better than this one. That being said; my First Officer and I were the only ones involved and we walked away completely unscathed.
Report_1_Synopsis: EMB-120 crew suffered multiple malfunctions in flight including inoperative communications making trouble shooting difficult. Discovering gear was not down when committed to landing; in spite of ATC confirmation that it appeared down; and under pressure of deteriorating unknown conditions a successful gear up landing was made that ended off the runway.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Situational Awareness; Training / Qualification; Communication Breakdown
Report_1_Narrative: My student and I were flying a C172 on the RNAV XY at ZZZ; planning to circle-to-land on Runway XX. We made radio calls on CTAF for 10 miles; 5 miles; 3 miles; and when starting to circle. We only heard calls from a plane on short final. During the circling procedure; before we were established on downwind; my iPad with ADS-B In (via Sentry) alerted that there was traffic 10 o'clock; less than a mile. Both my student and I observed the other aircraft; a C152; pass less than 200 feet above us and less than 500 feet horizontally away. I made another call on CTAF and the C152 finally made a radio call that they were performing a teardrop maneuver to the downwind. My student and I proceeded to do a touch-and-go and fly the missed approach procedure on the RNAV XY. We did not hear any more radio calls from the other plane.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Instructor with a student flying a Cessna 172 reported a NMAC on final approach.

Report_1_Narrative: After landing at MLB I turned off of Runway 9L at Taxiway Mike and was instructed to taxi Mike to the ramp. Due to it being dark and taxiway markings in poor condition. I got confused and accidentally taxied onto Taxiway Kilo. This was despite using a taxiway diagram and being very familiar with the airfield. I realized my mistake when I realized that Mike shouldn't have taxiway lights and turned off of Kilo as soon as possible. Luckily; due to the airport being empty at night; there were no aircraft on the taxiway at that point and I believe this reduced any immediate risk from the mistake; which I attempted to correct as soon as it was safe to do so. ATC did not mention my error to me. This means that either ATC did not notice my mistake or they did not think it was significant enough to mention. I was lucky that there wasn't an aircraft on the taxiway which could have resulted in a major situation. I believe it was a combination of fatigue (hour long night flight at the end of a day) and the dark conditions made it difficult to notice the proper taxiway markings. I believe having aircraft taxi on an unlit taxiway at night is risky as it could be easy to miss on a dark night especially next to a lit taxiway which would draw a pilot's visual attention. Additionally; due to it being my home airport I may have subconsciously paid less attention to the airport diagram than I would have at another airport. Going forward I will pay extra close attention to the airport diagram especially at night when I may have to taxi to an unlit portion of the airfield. This combined with verbally briefing the taxi route out loud could prevent an incident like this from happening again. It is easy to get distracted at night; especially if tired at the end of a flight; and make mistakes like this. So definitely; always use a diagram; double check the route and signs; airports should make sure markings are in good condition. More importantly than just using a diagram is actively reading it and understanding it no matter how familiar with the airport you are.
Report_1_Synopsis: Pilot reported a taxiway incursion at MLB airport and cited lighting and taxiway marking issues as contributing factors.

Report_1_Narrative: Upon landing at night from ILS Runway 16; we were given right turn onto H1 from Tower.  We saw the H1 Taxiway sign on the right and turned inadvertently onto Runway 11/29. Recommend this intersection be labeled a Hot Spot as it's difficult to see at night.
Report_1_Synopsis: Pilot reported a runway incursion at HPN airport and cited taxiway signage as a contributing factor.

Report_1_Narrative: On vectors from Houston Approach for the ILS 14 at GLS. Cleared to intercept the localizer from current heading maintain 2;000 feet. Tracking the localizer inbound at 2;000 feet was given a handoff to Tower. I wasn't cleared for the approach so I asked if I was cleared ILS. Was given clearance and switched to GLS Tower.The glideslope needle went active and I lowered the gear to follow the glide slope down. 400 feet later the glide slope needle flagged out and came in and out. I initiated a climb and realized I was outside of the final approach fix. This was a false glideslope.I climbed back to 1;800 feet and approached the FAF. The real glideslope came in and I completed the approach.I reported the issue via telephone to the Tower after landing.The late clearance from Center for the approach [was a contributing factor]. I didn't brief myself clearly enough on the minimum altitudes until the FAF. I had a big headwind so my internal timer felt right to be descending but the reduced ground speed I was still outside of the FAF.My reaction to realizing the issue was fast. I stopped my descent and started a climb quickly upon seeing the glideslope problems. I then identified the problem and what happened. Resumed the approach when everything was correct.
Report_1_Synopsis: Pilot reported glideslope problems while inbound to GLS airport.

Report_1_Narrative: Had a ground loop on landing rollout resulting in runway excursion.  No one was injured and there was no substantial damage to the aircraft. The winds were light and variable.
Report_1_Synopsis: Pilot flying S-7LS aircraft reported ground loop on landing rollout.

Report_1_Narrative: While enroute (cruise); an aircraft (C182 tail dragger) suddenly passed over and overtook us in our Piper Warrior at a distance that was close enough to almost cover the wind screen.  The student and I were discussing where we would land in the case of an emergency at the time of the incident.  We had ADS-B In via ForeFlight and did not see any aircraft around (electronically) just prior to the incident. Weather conditions were clear and we were scanning outside for traffic (visually). Evasive action was not taken as the aircraft passed over us at a slight angle and was to our left side by the time we were able to react.  The aircraft then turned to the left (south).  We were monitoring 122.9 (ZZZ uses 122.8 which is what I should have been monitoring at that time).  My fault in the incident was that I should have been monitoring and announcing on 122.8 instead of 122.9.  I do not believe that the Cessna saw us or even realized that we were sharing the same real estate.  In the future; I will be more attentive to local frequencies and stay at a higher altitude in that area.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Instructor flying Piper Warrior reported a NMAC in cruise.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Training / Qualification; Communication Breakdown; Situational Awareness
Report_1_Narrative: I was climbing out from Runway XX during a 'Go Around' turning from left crosswind to a left downwind at 800 ft. I heard another aircraft reporting entering a left downwind to the same runway. Right after entering downwind I broadcast in the blind looking for a position of aircraft and he told me I had just passed below his belly at about 200 ft. away from his aircraft. I apologized and told him I never saw him until after his call and he was about 1/2 mile off my left wing.A safer practice would have been if I sidestepped to the right during the initial phase of the go around and climbed to 1;000 ft. AGL before turning left into the crosswind. This action would have put me farther away from the airport and would give me a greater view of the area I was turning into.
Report_1_Synopsis: Pilot flying M20 aircraft reported a NMAC during initial climb.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Time Pressure; Situational Awareness; Other / Unknown
Report_1_Narrative: While on approach to landing in ZZZ; a gust of wind caused me to abort that landing. I was able to get enough altitude to take the gondola through the tops of trees just ahead of me. Once through the trees; I immediately saw power lines at eye level approximately 20 feet ahead of me. I immediately shut off the propane tank and turned off the burner; attempting to minimize any probable excessive explosion. After hearing the power line break; but not having an explosion and discovering that we were still aloft; I quickly assessed the state of passengers and equipment. Finding absolutely no damage; I turned on the propane tank and relit the burner. My ground team contacted me by radio and I informed them that we are okay and planning to land at the next available opportunity. I flew on and had a safe landing approximately 1/4 mile away. There was no aircraft damage and there were no injuries.
Report_1_Synopsis: Balloon Pilot reported encountering a gust of wind and colliding with power lines.

Report_1_Narrative: Aircraft X; cleared Visual Approach  off a downwind turn behind a Heavy. Aircraft X was pointed away and behind Heavy when cleared to follow the traffic and issued caution wake turbulence. The pilot turned to follow the Heavy at his discretion towards the traffic and the field to a dog leg at about 5.5 miles in trail of the Heavy. Aircraft X joined final approach behind the traffic and I; the Final Radar Controller; observed what looked like a quick radar track anomaly. Quickly followed was an observed turn and quick descent and climb by Aircraft X back towards the field. The pilot promptly advised of a 'complete upset' and that he was back on the turn towards the traffic and on the Visual Approach with out a chance for me to issue any instructions.Later to find out this verbiage meant the aircraft had been sent into a complete roll to the right in which the pilot continued to recover the aircraft. No official cause but I can only guess wake turbulence from the Heavy traffic sent him into an uncontrolled roll. I acknowledged; inquired if any assistance was required to which the pilot responded in the negative; and I continued to work the traffic to include breaking out a Heavy behind him to allow him to continue the Visual Approach. The aircraft continued on the approach and double confirmed that everything was okay and no assistance was required before sending him to the Tower for landing.No recommendation; but awareness for all pilots of potential wake turbulence induced events. I personally could have ensured the aircraft was at a higher altitude to possibly prevent the wake trajectory; but I was originally setting up Aircraft X for an ILS Approach to follow at the appropriate  wake turbulence minimums. Only after the pilot called traffic and field in sight was he given the Visual Approach clearance to follow. If the pilot did not feel comfortable with this; I did not know or could have recommended a different method of approach.
Report_1_Synopsis: A TRACON Controller reported a twin prop aircraft temporarily lost control when it was cleared for a Visual Approach and turned final behind a Heavy and encountered wake turbulence.

Report_1_Narrative: [This is] the same aircraft we took in to ZZZ and landed with MAIN PITCH TRIM INOP.  Upon landing; the FO thought he smelled an odor. During taxi; we both started to smell a roasting burning smell. We turned off pack 1 and it dissipated. When we arrived at the ramp; I smelled another burning smell. We turned off pack 2 and it went away again.  After troubleshooting with maintenance; we could not get it to reproduce. Captain recommended replacement all packs and ductwork or investigate more into why a burning smell is such a common issue.
Report_1_Synopsis: EMB-145 LR flight crew reported a burning smell event upon landing and taxi-in; which dissipated when the Pack 1 was turned off. Maintenance action was assigned.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Workload; Training / Qualification; Time Pressure; Situational Awareness; Distraction; Communication Breakdown; Human-Machine Interface
Person_2_Human_Factors: Training / Qualification; Workload; Time Pressure; Situational Awareness; Human-Machine Interface; Distraction; Communication Breakdown
Report_1_Narrative: Briefed low level level off at gate.  On taxi out; ship phone rang in cubby hole and I couldn't reach it.  Dispatch informed us that we needed to hold on the ground for a maintenance carry over item that would expire before the completion of the mission.  We waited ready for takeoff for almost an hour with several updates from Dispatch that sounded like we were going back to the gate.  Then suddenly told to go.  Briefed again the low level level off while waiting.  Took off and did not execute the maneuver as we briefed.  Got ATC call to switch to departure control right before ALT CAP.  Noticed the FMA was not matching the calls.  I switched my eyesight to the FO's hand on MCP.  Once correct; I returned to ADI and discovered altitude was approaching 2;500 feet.  Corrected pitch to return to 2;000 feet.   ATC then assigned us 5;000 feet.  No comment was made about the altitude deviation.  Cleaned up aircraft; engaged autopilot; no further incidents.Cause - Pilot flying distracted to monitoring.  Pilot monitor error in MCP.  Pilot proficiency played a role.  This was my first flight in 2 months and second in 5 months as pilot flying.Pitched down to correct altitude.  FO contacted departure and we got an immediate climb to 5;000 feet.The main thing that sticks out is pilot proficiency.
Report_2_Narrative: Briefed low altitude level off thoroughly. While taxiing; received phone call to hold for Maintenance waiver issue that affected later flights. Held for nearly 45 minutes at end of runway. Got the go ahead and proceeded to takeoff. Normal Takeoff until 'Alt Cap' called. VNAV was pushed initially then immediately corrected to Speed Mode and set 200 knots. Scanned back to instruments and noticed and called out altitude deviation. Pilot flying corrected immediately. Called departure with no further comments from ATC and rest of flight was uneventful. After MCP operation; noticed altitude deviation. Made deviation call out and pilot flying corrected immediately. Pilot flying became distracted with MCP operation. Pilot monitoring procedural error in MCP operation. Pilot proficiency. Time compression. Aggressively corrected and contacted departure. No comment from them and received immediate climb to 5;000 feet.Pilot proficiency should be maintained/bettered through flight/simulator scheduling efficiency.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported an altitude deviation during departure and cited lack of flying as a contributing factor.

Report_1_Narrative: Approximately 20 minutes after departure I received a call from the Flight Attendant that we had a couple passengers that weren't complying with the mask mandate and asked me to make our announcement reminding passengers of the Federal mask mandate. I made our announcement. Just prior to going through sterile flight deck period the Flight Attendant called again with passenger seat numbers X3 and YX4 and asked me to relay non mask compliance to the station. We made several attempts to contact Operations. After being unable to do so I sent an ACARS to Dispatch notifying them of mask non-compliance and asked them to have a CSR meet the aircraft. Being so close to the destination we elected to continue to the destination. After landing we tried several more times to contact Operations on taxi in and were unable to do so. Upon arriving at the gate the CSR came on board and informed me they had LEOs waiting at the counter and the TSA had been notified but she wasn't sure if they were sending a representative to speak with the passengers. She requested keeping the passengers on board for several minutes; so they could make sure everyone was prepared to receive the passengers. Given the all clear; the passengers disembarked without incident.The Flight Attendant mentioned she made multiple announcements and handed the passengers the information describing the penalties for non-compliance that are included in the packs of masks/alcohol wipes. It sounds like she made every available effort per SOP to have the passengers comply with the mask mandate. As states continue to withdraw mask mandates I foresee this becoming an increasingly widespread issue. I thought the idea of handing the passengers the information card was a very smart idea as seeing this in writing may carry more weight. Perhaps aircraft can be stocked with additional copies of these cards to hand out. Also our current guidance on the mask mandates in the flight crew memo make this policy sound like it is just per company policy. Updated guidance stating that this is a Federal mandate may make it more clear to the passengers that this is a serious federal violation. Every day we see passengers wearing masks that are not allowed on our flights and have to be given masks the meet standards; gate agents policing masks that required standard would also be helpful.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported passengers not conforming with face mask policy during flight and had personnel meet the aircraft on arrival.

Report_1_Narrative: North Little Rock regional airport; has commissioned an ATIS that is on the same frequency (123.77) as the DFW arrival ATIS.  This makes picking up the arrival ATIS at DFW difficult to impossible until 120-140 NM away; well into the arrival.Change ORK frequency.  Swap DFW arrival and departure ATIS frequencies (you can hear departure ATIS from FAR away and that's just not necessary - swapping the frequencies would fix it).  Get digital ATIS.  Allow access to the WiFi so airline pilots can use the Jepp's in the air to get digital ATIS (only resolves the problem if the plane has working WiFi).
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported it is difficult to receive the DFW ATIS due to ORK airport ATIS being on the same frequency.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Communication Breakdown; Situational Awareness; Training / Qualification
Report_1_Narrative: While descending to FL240 we were cleared to descended via the ZZZZZ X RNAV Arrival.  I selected 11;000 feet.  Approaching ZZZZZ Intersection I noticed that we were in open descent.  I disconnected the autopilot and leveled off at FL238 and then started a climb back to FL240.  Cause- While level at FL350 ATC cleared us to FL240 with a restriction to descend below FL310.  I selected open descent to meet the restriction.  After being cleared to descend via the arrival I did not select the managed mode.I need to increase vigilance when flying with people coming back from leaves for both PF and PM roles.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier flying pilot reported an altitude deviation during arrival and cited lack of flying as a contributing factor.

Report_1_Narrative: We were with ZZZ Center and I was having trouble understanding the Controller. I told him that he was coming in 3x5. The Controller proceeded to tell me that he had numerous complaints about being hard to understand and the reason was; that he was required to wear a mask while at work. I started thinking about this and realized that I was having trouble with other controllers throughout the country and never made the connection.  We never had an issue but the Controller had to repeat himself several times which seemed to clog the radio.Suggestion - Have the controllers not wear face masks that might make their transmission difficult to understand.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported the ATC Center Controller was difficult to understand because the individual was wearing a required face mask.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Distraction; Communication Breakdown; Situational Awareness; Workload; Training / Qualification
Report_1_Narrative: Turning for a 7 to 8 NM final from left base to Runway XX with aircraft configured flaps 20; PF established aircraft on ILS Runway XX GS and LOC for visual approach. PM made a VFR traffic call for an 8 NM final landing Runway XX. Another jet on the ground at ZZZ made multiple calls for a radio check and the PM responded he could hear the jet loud and clear. PF called autopilot off; and request the visual approach for Runway XX in the FMS. The PM entered the Runway XX visual approach into the FMS.  PM made a 5 NM final call on CTAF. The jet on the ground informed the PM they were taxiing on Runway XX and would clear the runway prior to aircraft landing and then engaged the PM in a conversation about their inability to contact ATC Clearance. PF called flaps 30 and flaps 45 and slowed the aircraft on speed and Glide Slope. PM read the before landing check and at the LANDING GEAR DOWN call both the PF and PM noted the lack of DOWN 3 GREEN on the display panel and then visually checked the gear handle and noted it was in the up position. This occurred at about 1;100 feet HAT and was follow by the gear horn going off. PF immediately began a go-around and made call outs PM preformed G/A TO actions and traffic calls. The aircraft descended to 900 to 1000 HAT before entering the upwind for Runway XX and performed an uneventful left traffic pattern landing on Runway XX.This was my first day back from a month of leave and my Captain had also recently returned from leave. Rust may have been a factor. Additionally; we were flying at a high altitude airport with terrain at night with no Tower. There was definitely a communication break down and I was tasked saturated and should have let the Captain know I was in the red; and I could have missed the gear call. The final distraction was the jet on the ground taxiing on Runway XX where they should not have been; and fixation on them clearing the runway and engaging in a conversation about contacting ATC to get their IFR clearance was also a factor taking my awareness outside the aircraft.In the future I need to be more aware of my saturation level and communicate this correctly to my captains and avoid engaging in extraneous ground communications with other aircraft. Also; I need to visually and verbally verify my actions and confirm call outs by myself and other pilots regardless if I am PM or PF and verbally verify ambiguous calls or situations.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier First Officer reported an unstibilized approach and cited not using SOPs and missing call outs from the Captain as contributing factors.

Report_1_Narrative: I was told by my Captain we are to expect two FAMs (Federal Air Marshalls) and one LEO on our flight. When boarding commenced; one of them showed his ID and asked me if he could check in with the Captain. After doing so; I asked him if he was aware of 'the other two.' He seemed confused. I told him we were supposed to have 'two FAMs and a LEO. Are you the LEO?' He said yes. I told him we have two FAMs too; but I'm not sure yet what seats they're in. He said OK and sat in seat. As he walked away; my Captain called me into the flight deck and said LEOs aren't supposed to know about the FAMs; but the FAMs are supposed to know about the LEOs. I was dumbfounded and anxious because I thought all armed persons are supposed to know about each other; with the exception of FBI agents; which is not in our manual anywhere; but was told to me when I inquired years ago at recurrent. I asked if ever someone can be armed on our plane and not have to tell us. The trainer answered FBI only. In flight; I looked it up in my manual because I hate not being sure of a rule; and I needed to read it to verify. I found two spots referencing FAM discretion; and to me; it says LEOS ARE supposed to be informed about the FAMs. All armed persons are informed about each other. Is our manual wrong? Am I interpreting it wrong? I informed my Captain what I had found. He said the Company gate agent was the one who told him LEOs aren't supposed to know about FAMs.My thought is; what if the FAM steps in to help us and pulls his gun out and the LEO shoots him. It could totally happen; because there would obviously be a commotion; the LEO thinks he's the only one on board with a gun; it's his job to help.Later that day; I asked a different company gate agent what their policy was. I wanted to verify. She said if the LEO asks if there is anyone else armed; she will answer 'yes; but they are not in your category;' but she will not disclose the seat number(s). If he or she (LEO) does not ask; she (gate agent) does not tell.Unless I'm reading my manual wrong; I think we have a policy discrepancy. Please let me know what's correct so I may comply in the future.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Attendant reported confusion relating to LEO's and FAM's onboard an aircraft and if they should know about each other.

Report_1_Narrative: Descending into ZZZ; I was keeping my speed below 250 knots while descending through 10;000 feet using speedbrakes (power at idle). As I was reaching my level off altitude in the descent; I retracted the speedbrakes and the aircraft speed increased to around 258 knots. Upon seeing this excess speed; I re-extended the speedbrakes and slowed the aircraft to below 250 knots. Cause - Not noticing the increasing airspeed was a rusty move on my part; I believe; due to lack of flying over the past few months. To prevent this from occurring again; I'll be more focused on the task at hand when changing configurations.
Report_1_Synopsis: Corporate Jet Captain reported exceeding the 250 knot speed restriction below 10;000 feet and cited lack of flying as a contributing factor.

Report_1_Narrative: I was working a Henderson departure on the SCAMR1 SID. The crossing restriction is 6;000 and he climbed well. The air carrier was departing Runway 19 at LAS and was climbing o the NIITZ1 SID. The crossing restriction is 7;000 over top of the SCAMR1; but 3 miles was lost and no divergence before the air carrier reached the crossing restriction.Move the flight paths away from each other as not to lose lateral separation. These are new routes for Metroplex and this was the first I've seen of these 2 departures at the same time.
Report_1_Synopsis: L30 TRACON Controller reported a loss of required separation between aircraft departing different airports on newly implemented RNAV SIDs which do not provide for procedural separation.

Report_1_Narrative: On approach at night extremely bright lights; said to be golf driving range over water (by local ATC) is to the north and west of the airport. Too bright for a normal approach.  This is causing a hazard to the arriving aircraft. During landing flare the lights were not a distraction.  On approach into RNO [Airport]; extremely bright lights presented a hazard.Maybe change the intensity of the lights; or no lights during north flow approach.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Captain reported bright lights beyond the airport at a golf range; are too bright and distracting while landing to the North at RNO airport.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Training / Qualification; Situational Awareness; Human-Machine Interface
Person_2_Human_Factors: Situational Awareness; Training / Qualification; Human-Machine Interface
Report_1_Narrative: We were cleared approach RNAV Z XXR.  I looked at the navigation display and saw a solid unbroken magenta line from our position to the runway.  LNAV and VNAV displayed in FMA's.  Prior to this we were given delete speeds and at some point; I think we were assigned 210 knots.  Weather was clear VMC.  We were looking for traffic.  At some point traffic was called to us.  I did not see the discontinuity at ZZZZZ in the MCDU.  Approaching ZZZZZ I felt the plane was not turning to follow the path as it should.  I disengaged the autopilot and hand flew the rest of the procedure.  ATC asked us if we were turning and then asked if we could land.In the 10 months preceding this incident; I have 18 hours of block time.  I have 2 hours of block time in the last 90 days.  I was an X type aircraft Captain but was retrained as a First Officer (FO).  I have 0 hours as an FO in this aircraft prior to training.  My training consisted of one 4-hour sim period and two OE legs.  I believe the Captain was just back from a medical issue; had done a short training course and this was his second trip on the line.
Report_2_Narrative: Arrival into ZZZ during daytime VFR conditions with excellent visibility. Our FMC was programmed for the arrival as well as the RNAV RNP Z to XXR with the transition at ZZZZZ intersection. Our primary error was that we did not close the FMC discontinuity between the arrival and the approach. The result was that we overflew ZZZZZ1 intersection and corrected immediately after recognizing that we were not turning at the appropriate time. In hindsight it appears that multiple distractions contributed to our failure to remove the discontinuity. The change in speed assignments as well as a request by the Controller to watch for Aircraft Y traffic on a parallel runway and the timing associated with the issuance of our approach clearance.We were able to visually identify the Aircraft Y parallel traffic and kept visual separation. Once established on the extended runway centerline we received TA/RA warnings associated with the proximity of the Aircraft Y on XXL.  Also; there was never any indication that our aircraft deviated laterally of the extended runway centerline that would have compromised separation.Immediately after arrival at the gate I called approach control to discuss the late turn on the approach. (I was not asked to call.) I requested to speak with a Supervisor and we had a 5-10 minute discussion. I was told there was 'nothing on their end' in the way of a complaint. We also had an additional discussion about the traffic advisories associated with our approach given the close proximity of parallel traffic.One of the challenges of flying into ZZZ is that we typically are issued our runway assignment; approach; and transition in the latter stage of our arrival. Also; once issued; it seems to be relatively common to be reassigned to yet another runway; approach and transition. It is also common to receive speed modifications on the arrival.We were prepared for the RNAV Z to XXR and per company procedure we had the default arrival transition programmed. In hindsight I believe that if our clearance to fly the approach had come earlier in the arrival phase (when we had less distractions) that we would have been more likely to close the link between the arrival and approach and avoid our error.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported a track heading deviation during approach and cited lack of flying as a contributing factor.

Report_1_Narrative: Landing 24 at night. Coming in over mountains in VMC. We knew we were fine however we got a terrain alert so we cleaned the aircraft up and went around and came back around landed on 34.Cleaned up and did a go around and decided to land on 34.At night when landing on 24 you need to go out further for the approach on 24 to avoid getting a terrain alert.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported terrain alert on approach resulting in a go-around.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Time Pressure; Workload; Communication Breakdown; Situational Awareness
Report_1_Narrative: I was made aware that our flight was flagged for a passenger location/count audit. Apparently; we sent two requests via ACARS for a manifest/performance numbers with the location/count of the second one being off from the first. I cannot recall the exact details of this flight but I believe what happened is that I was notified of passengers moving zones due to social distancing. When this happens; I request a manual location/count be completed by the flight attendants to ensure we have accurate zones for the takeoff data. I believe there was a count error that was missed by us or the cabin crew.Although every effort was made to ensure we had accurate zones for departure; we ended up with three extra passengers than what the final location/count included. We were doing our best to ensure we had accurate numbers before block-out and perhaps the final count was overlooked as we were pressured for time. I am often notified of these changes with only minutes to spare before departure; so I feel that letting the passengers move rushes us and exposes errors like this one.While I understand some peoples need to distance on an airplane; I think there should be a cutoff in time before departure for this to be allowed. This creates an unnecessary distraction for the crew; and could create potential discrepancies like this one for the location/count. I think it could easily be explained to a passenger that they are free to move at some point after departure.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Captain reported an error regarding passenger seating location and took off with an incorrect passenger count.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Communication Breakdown; Physiological - Other; Situational Awareness
Report_1_Narrative: I wouldn't mind to serve the passengers with our normal service any other time however with the national crisis still going on and only about 20% vaccination rates. With the new menu option; I feel that it is still too early to provide these options.At first; I noticed even with the menu placard; several people lower down their masks to order their drinks despite the numerous PA about the mask compliance. It is quite distracting and uncomfortable environment to other passengers who are sitting next to them and myself. Few people were chewing their food and talking to me without the mask.The second thing is that more people are traveling which I am happy for however the social distance is impossible already. After serving snacks they immediately remove their masks. By the time I bring my drinks to serve; I am exposed to all these passengers and passengers themselves while they are chewing and talking themselves.The third problem is that more drinks; more contacts. Almost everyone touched my hands when I served the drinks. And immediate contacts with them handing over the drinks; it makes some passengers quite uncomfortable and distracted events for the crews.The fourth problem is that WiFi is inadequate and lots of people ask how or where to find the menu; it may sound simple to do it but it's not something that generally people are familiar with our website and not many frequent fly members on board. It takes lots of crew time and distraction in fact.Lots of crew members are still not having the access of the vaccine yet. I feel that our company put our crews in great danger in our work environment. If we follow the federal guideline; I strongly believe that we are not ready for this; yet.Thank you for your consideration and help in advance.We must vaccinate the crews 100%. I believe it is the upmost important event the company needs to focus on and resume the service we normally do after. This extra menu service; is simple I understand; however it still too early to say we are safe.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Attendant reported it is too early to expand the inflight service. There are too many passengers with face masks down; talking with masks down; and social distancing issues during the inflight service.

Report_1_Narrative: While at 3;000 feet about 21 miles southwest of Deland (OMN) (and flying southwest enroute to LAL); I saw on my EFB a possible convergence between myself and two other aircraft. The first aircraft; a twin-engine; was at my five o'clock; slightly higher than me; flying southeast. The second aircraft; a single-engine high wing was at my ten o'clock; slightly below me; and flying southwest. I found myself in the middle of this impending convergence; so I turned right and behind the twin; knowing that the aircraft would safely pass me. In this position; I could observe the other two aircraft quickly converge. I could see they still had vertical separation during the convergence until I saw the high-wing perform a climbing left turn towards the twin's path. There was no collision; but I genuinely think neither aircraft saw each other considering the higher aircraft was a twin-engine low-wing and the lower aircraft was a high-wing. I estimate the aircraft were within 500 feet of each other.
Report_1_Synopsis: Pilot reports a NMAC in cruise flight.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Time Pressure; Workload; Communication Breakdown; Distraction; Human-Machine Interface; Situational Awareness
Report_1_Narrative: I departed Wings field while a TFR was active. Wings field has a cut-out for the TFR but I still got a discrete code and frequency from Philly ATC before departing. When I departed; there was one plane that had just done a go-around and another coming from the north to cross the field and enter the pattern. Rather than do a left turn out and add congestion to the left downwind; I decided to do a right turnout to stay away from the traffic in the downwind and provide room for the incoming traffic to enter the pattern. I announced my intentions on CTAF and the inbound plane acknowledged my intent. The runway I departed (24) headed directly at the TFR. My plan was to call Philly; turn into the TFR and get clearance through the Bravo airspace. As I climbed; the TFR was coming up very quickly. I was not at TPA (Traffic Pattern Altitude) but I was also not talking to Philly yet. I was concerned about entering the TFR without talking even though I was transmitting a discrete code. So; I made a hard turn to the right to stay out of the TFR but was anxious about calling Philly. I changed off CTAF and called Philly (but was still climbing to TPA). Just as I did; my traffic alert system started sounding an alarm. I could not hear what Philly was saying because the traffic alert system was extremely loud. I assumed it was alerting me to the traffic in the left downwind and I tried to silence it. As a result of trying to talk to Philly and trying to silence the traffic alert system; I got distracted and failed to keep my head outside the aircraft (failed to aviate above everything else). When I finally looked outside there was another plane crossing about fifty feet from me. I have asked several people; but it is still not clear to me whether I can enter the TFR while transmitting a discrete code but not talk to ATC until I reach a safe altitude clear from the traffic pattern at the airport. I would think that is the case; but I don't want to assume that. I also think more room should be given for airport cut-outs for TFRs. The TFR starts about .9 miles from the end of the runway which should be enough to get to TPA; but it still requires a pretty sharp U-turn to avoid the TFR.
Report_1_Synopsis: Pilot reports a NMAC during climb out after takeoff from LOM airport.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Time Pressure; Situational Awareness; Confusion; Workload
Report_1_Narrative: We were held down at 5;000 feet for traffic while essentially on a left downwind departure. After flying level at 5;000 feet for a couple of minutes we were cleared to climb to 16;000 feet. Once established in the climb and climbing out of 6;000 feet; we were climbing at a rather high rate. As we were established in climb; we received a TCAS TA on traffic at 1 o'clock; which appeared to be converging on us. No sooner than we noticed; we received a 'DESCEND; DESCEND' TCAS RA. I disconnected the autopilot and autothrottles while simultaneously idling the thrust levers and pitching down to comply with the RA. Essentially; we went from full climb thrust in a climb at 250 knots below 10;000 feet to needing to descend promptly. That's a pretty dramatic change of aircraft energy state. I saw from the corner of my eye that it appeared to be a twin turboprop. The conflict aircraft passed right over us; most certainly less than 500 feet.  As we were descending in our RA maneuver; ATC warned us to stop climb immediately. We informed him we were responding to TCAS RA already. After the threat aircraft was behind us; we resumed our climb and queried ATC as to why they didn't point out the traffic to us. The Controller said he 'didn't see him and wasn't talking to him.' I found that answer to be strange; but as it turned out; the top of the Class B airspace was below us. We reported the event to Dispatch and the Captain filed an incident report as per the policy. The question I have is whether the ATC can somehow remove VFR targets outside of their airspace band that are squawking VFR and wonder if that's what happened here. The threat aircraft was well within his rights to fly VFR above Class B airspace without talking to ATC; but without TCAS and without Controller pointing out traffic; because they may be 'squelching' VFR traffic outside of Class B; this could have ended really badly especially considering several cloud layers that we encountered. I recently flew an aircraft with TCAS MELed and I'm sure glad this happened when we actually had a functioning TCAS.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier pilot climbing on departure reported a NMAC with an unidentified VFR aircraft just above the Class B Airspace ceiling. ATC stated they 'did not see' the aircraft so did not issue traffic to the air carrier.

Report_1_Narrative: On the arrival in MGGT; winds were reported out of the south at 10 kts; so MGGT was landing Runway 20. Referencing WSI (Weather Services International); there were two active areas for volcanic ash; one for Pacaya and one for Agua. Both had plumes and ash clouds from the surface to 14;000 ft; and both were moving west. While selecting what approach we were planning; we looked at the different missed approaches and decided the VOR Z Runway 20 would be best in the event of a missed approach and avoid any ash cloud. The Missed Approach procedure for the VOR Z Runway 20 is AUR; 1 DME past the VOR; a slight left turn via the 169 radial to 17 DME and then hold at 11;000 ft with no special climb rates associated with it. Then our briefing turned to the Engine-Out (EO) Procedure. We immediately noticed the EO procedure splits the gap of the volcanos Pacaya and Agua; and right through the SIGMET area.We thought about what to do in the event of an engine-out missed approach. I decided; in this situation; the EO procedure would not be appropriate due to the active SIGMETs for volcanic ash; and I decided the missed approach for the VOR Z Runway 20 would be more appropriate and safer than the EO as published. We reviewed the terrain that shows on the EO procedure; terrain charts; and considered our landing weight. Landing was normal and no missed approach was accomplished. But planning for worse case revealed challenges to our procedures of following company EO procedures as published.Our training has us brief and setup EO procedures for missed approaches as well as takeoff; and fly them as published in the event of an engine-out event. This particular procedure; on this night; sets a crew up for a terrible scenario of going missed approach or takeoff; losing an engine; and flying directly into a volcanic ash cloud with one engine while these volcanoes are active.My suggestion would be to give the aircrews more options; have the EO procedure ready but review all the missed approaches as published and note whether we can fly them as a published engine-out. In this case; I believe we could have safely executed the missed approach for the VOR Z Runway 20; and possibly an engine-out scenario on initial takeoff; but I just don't have access to the information to confirm this. Blindly following EO procedures when other factors encroach on the procedures could result in a worse outcome.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported company policy for single engine missed approach would be through volcanic ash; unless flight crews plan for a different procedure.

Report_1_Narrative: Started APU shortly after arrival to cockpit and noticed a dusting of what we thought was debris coming from the ducts.  I asked the support crew to get in touch with maintenance to take a look.  Me and the crew continued with our duties and at some point we noticed an odor.  We felt it must be the COVID spray so we were not alarmed.  Spoke with maintenance about the dusting but language was a barrier.  Later alerted by the crew that smoke in the supernumerary was getting worse.  In the cockpit we had not noticed.  Maintenance came into the cockpit and told us to leave and shut down.  We vacated immediately.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Captain reported during pre-flight duties the crew noticed dusting in the air and believed it to be spray for COVID. Captain was told by Maintenance to shut down and vacate the aircraft.

Report_1_Narrative: While the loaders unloaded my plane in ZZZZ; a gust of wind blew over some boxes one of these was a Hazmat box that I had not been informed was put on my plane back in ZZZZ1.This loader and I have had problems with multiple times he'll not listen to what I want for Max loading so I have to watch him closely as well as tell him a lower number because if I look away he always goes between 50-100 over; and will wait to tell me the door weight until after he's finishes his paperwork so I have less time to do my paperwork when they finish. I've spoken to another pilot in base and they've had the same issues. I will have to be even more diligent when he loads my plane. I have informed the chief pilot of this issue.Recommend this company should develop a similiar paper to other freight operators that states if they are or are not loading Hazmat. That way in case the Hazmat is put in a bag or hidden behind a larger box I would be able to say this is missing.
Report_1_Synopsis: Captain reported undeclared Hazmat cargo discovered during unloading at destination.
