Report_1_Narrative: We; a C172S G1000; were flying to ZZZ under VFR radar vector with RNAV Y RWYXX for practice approach. While approaching to FAF; right after Approach told us to contact Tower; we found a Piper Cherokee on our 11 o'clock less than 500 feet horizontal above us and descending and approaching to us. We could not see them until last moment because they were above our wing 'blind spot.' Approach never mentioned about this traffic and our G1000 display never displayed its ADS-B location.  After I found the traffic; I took over the control from student who was under the hood and started descent in about 500-700 feet per minute. We reported to Approach after the traffic passed behind us. Approach responded that; it was showing 1;000 feet vertical separation with us so Approach did not mentioned that traffic. Also; that traffic was not talking to Approach; so Approach did not know their intention. After that; we continued the approach and landed at ZZZ.
Report_1_Synopsis: C172 flight crew reported NMAC on approach.

Report_1_Narrative: Winds were moderate; variable; and gusty; but within limits for the aircraft. In accordance with accepted technique; half the gust factor; approximately 6 knots; was added to the final approach and landing speeds. Just after touchdown on the centerline; with all three gears established on the runway; a gust was felt and corrected for. As the correction was made with what was perceived as moderate aileron and rudder input; the airplane veered sharply to the left. With the thought that over-controlling back to the right could lead to the left wingtip dipping and then digging into the runway resulting in the aircraft tumbling (worst case) or a ground loop at high energy (best case); I elected to input enough control to keep the aircraft tracking as straight ahead as possible. This resulted in departing the runway surface to the left of the runway. Once in the gravel that was lining the left side of the runway; my entire focus was on maintaining enough control not to hit obstacles or dig in gear or wingtips so as to cause tumbling. In the process of dissipating energy; I crossed two high-speed taxiways at almost a perpendicular angle and at a still relatively high-speed resulting in the aircraft becoming lighter on the struts. The struts compressed again on the other side of the taxiways resulting in enough energy depletion to safely steer back to the runway surface.Upon re-establishing safe contact with asphalt; the aircraft was taxied a short distance to parking. Upon the post-flight walk-around inspection; there was visible damage to two of three propeller blade tips (of composite material made by Hartzell) from contact with gravel likely occurring when the struts compressed after crossing the taxiways. No other visible damage to the aircraft was observed nor were fluids observed to be leaking. It is very likely the root cause of this event was the application of too much rudder for the capabilities of the aircraft in countering the cross-wind gust after landing.The PA-46 line of aircraft is known to have very sensitive nose wheel steering; especially at higher speeds; and while being aware of it and managing it were trained to extensively; it's entirely possible that too much rudder was applied as was appropriate for this aircraft type. Habit pattern transference is a likely contributing factor in that I have several thousand hours in other type aircraft; to include very recent and continued professional flying experience in the Pilatus PC-12; and all of which do not exhibit the level of sensitivity in nose wheel steering that the PA-46 does. In instinctively applying the crosswind gust correction I'm used to; it is very possible that I applied an amount that was too much for safe control of the PA-46 at the time of occurrence.I do not feel training was a contributing factor as I received very thorough Piper-authorized training and initial conditioning in the aircraft with a Piper-authorized instructor. However; overall low time in type is definitely a contributing factor. Up to the time of this event; I had logged 20 landings in the PA-46 and several of which were in gusty conditions and or crosswinds similar to what was experienced during this event. In the future; the biggest take away from the event for me for flying the PA-46 is to concentrate on keeping the nose wheel off the runway as long as possible as energy depletes so that when the nose wheel does contact the runway; it's at the lowest speed practical. During this event the nose wheel was centered upon initial contact with the runway; as was emphasized in training. Any application of nose wheel steering at higher speeds should always be done very lightly at first to ensure the aircraft remains under control.
Report_1_Synopsis: PA-46 pilot reported a runway excursion during the landing roll out.

Report_1_Narrative: During a normal takeoff; I announce my intentions to taxi to take off on Runway 32 since the wind was calm at the moment. Before reaching the runway's beginning; I announced I would enter the runway to take off. Before entering the runway; I announce myself one more time with a call sign and intentions for departure and direction of the turn. After turning into the runway; I notice at the other end of the runway; approximately 200 ft in the air; the landing lights of an aircraft taking off. At the moment; I see the airplane already beginning its right turn out at no time where both of the aircraft were in immediate danger or close to collusion. Still; neither of the aircraft realizes the intentions of the other aircraft or position. It is unknown if the other aircraft notice me on the opposite runway since they were on a climb and no radio call acknowledge me. As for my part; I did not hear any radio call or notice the aircraft until turning into the center of the runway and only notice due to the landing lights reflection.
Report_1_Synopsis: Pilot reported observing traffic on climb out opposite direction not on CTAF; resulted in pilot delaying departure.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Time Pressure; Situational Awareness; Other / Unknown; Communication Breakdown
Report_1_Narrative: Pilot on parallel Runway XXR lost his engine and made a return to my Runway XXL for [a priority] landing. I was given a lineup and wait clearance; followed by a clear for takeoff straight out on XXL. Upon establishing the aircraft on centerline I spotted the incoming aircraft and before I was able to bring it to Tower's attention they cleared us for takeoff. My student read back the clearance and initiated the takeoff. Shortly after our roll started I took the flight controls back and began a sharp right turn to exit XXL on taxiway Charlie as another aircraft had taken our place.We conducted the training flight as planned afterword.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Instructor reported taking evasive action to avoid an aircraft with loss of power returning to field.

Report_1_Narrative: While working [sector] X there were significant areas of weather that were impeding aircraft transitioning the sector.  One area in particular was south of ZZZ and it was causing large deviations for aircraft inbound to ZZZ.  Due to a recent Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) that drastically alters Controller's working conditions on sector; which mandates the wear of facial coverings due to COVID-19 communication began to break down with aircraft on frequency.  While trying to describe the precipitation to pilots the mask created interference and the pilots could not decipher what I was trying to relay; which was weather that would affect their route.  This was especially the case with a handful of aircraft inbound to ZZZ that needed information on the weather and on the other aircraft they would have to follow into their destination airport.  My only option was to remove the face covering so that I could communicate directly and effectively to the aircrews trying to navigate these storms.  I am simply trying to comply with the duty priority.  Management at this Center is more concerned with complying with the MOU regarding face coverings than they are about safely moving aircraft about the National Aerospace System. If I were to be seen without my face covering on sector I would undoubtedly be reprimanded for the 'face mask violation.'  Ironically enough; if I were to not be able to communicate with the aircrews effectively and they enter an area of severe turbulence associated with thunderstorms I would also be reprimanded by management.  We have now entered a situation where controllers are going to be forced to decide what is more important; the aircraft on frequency or the arbitrary rules being enforced by management due to a 'pandemic' that is now over a year old that has proven to represent little-to-no risk to the controlling workforce. By the end of the session I had several instances where separation errors almost occurred because of deviating aircraft and having to repeat transmissions to climbing/descending aircraft...this was even after I removed the face covering.I would recommend that someone in the Air Traffic Organization stand up for the safety of the system and issue some direction for controllers that need to communicate with aircrews.  It is unreasonable to expect controllers to day after day wear a face mask while on position that causes distractions and limits the ability to safely conduct air traffic control procedures.  There is currently no direction as to when a Controller can remove a face mask in order to promote safety.
Report_1_Synopsis: Center Controller reported having difficulty communicating with pilots while wearing a face mask and stated that the requirement to wear face masks causes distractions and limits the ability to safely conduct air traffic control procedures.

Report_1_Narrative: I had a civilian jet at 6;000 feet on a vector to miss ZZZ west airspace that was hot 6;000 feet and above. He was in ZZZ central that I was showing active 8;000 and above. Turns out ZZZ central was active 060 and above.Make sure airspace is coordinated correctly and is reflected in airspace status.
Report_2_Narrative: I walked into the aisle to split 3 sectors out to a different position but the current radar working it all/receiving the briefing from the shift leaving for the day said he needed a D-side now.  I sat on the D-side and was given a verbal briefing when he had time.  I did not know the previous shift changed to bottom limits of a MOA to an altitude that is usually reserved for summer dates; 8;000 feet; and is frequently displayed wrong because the default in the EDST is 080 not 060.  The Radar Controller cleared aircraft into the MOA/ATCAA with normal winter base limits of 6;000 feet.  I received a call from XX [Sector] asking if he can have control of a departure to climb to 7;000 feet and I questioned his request.  I asked the radar is the ZZZZZ airspace normal altitudes; he said yes and I explained to the controller that the base limits should be 6;000 feet not 8;000 feet.  I asked the XX [Sector] Controller if something else was coordinated from the day shift on a higher altitude limit and he said no.  I only assumed it was displayed incorrectly as 080 because it happens more often than not in winter time.  Come to find out; the day shift controllers did coordinate the base altitudes of 8;000 feet; that information was given to the Radar Controller I was working with as part of the briefing.  I was unaware of this information at the time this event happened.During the Summer months the MOA has a section of airspace with a base of 8;000 feet to allow for arrivals and departures out of a regional airport that sees most of its traffic during the summer.  In the winter time this base altitude is 6;000 feet.  In the EDST (Enroute Decision Support Tool) to activate the airspace; the default is 8;000 feet.Because the default is 8;000 feet; it is a REGULAR occurrence that 080 is incorrectly displayed.  Controllers open the airspace activation menu; change the Top altitude and hit enter.  There should be a procedure; an additional memory aid or something else that happens if we change the base altitudes outside of the normal because it cannot be relied upon during the winter months that it is accurate.  I questioned it because it happens all the time and in this situation; I was incorrect is saying the base was 6;000 feet.  In the X years I have worked here; this is the first time that during the winter months I have been incorrect when saying the base should show 6;000 feet; not 8;000 feet.
Report_1_Synopsis: ATC Controllers reported an airborne traffic conflict due to changes to the base altitude of the restricted airspace. A Controller stated it is difficult to keep informed of changes and stay proficient because controllers are working several different positions for short periods.

Report_1_Narrative: This is a very large sector that when worked on its own has 6 different VHF frequencies spread apart for coverage. In between these frequencies is a fairly large gap where aircraft below about 7;000 feet may have a brief period of no communication with ATC depending on how the Controller handles the frequency change. I received a handoff from Approach Control on Aircraft X which was level at 4;000 feet. An experienced Controller's first thoughts would be that this aircraft could not only go NORDO (No Radio) but also that the Minimum IFR Altitude (MIA) gradually increases to 5;100 feet to the western part of this sector. These thoughts came to my mind; and to be proactive; I issued a climb to 5;000 or 6;000 feet (don't recall which). Immediately after checking in; I realized this aircraft wouldn't need to be at 6;000 feet for a while and by then I'd be in communication with this aircraft on another frequency.Aircraft X requested to remain at 4;000 feet for better winds and flight conditions. I saw where the aircraft was landing; which was a few miles west of my sector; and measured from there to where I'd need the aircraft to be level at 5;000 feet. I instructed the aircraft to cross 120 miles east of the destination airport level at 5;000 feet and also to eventually check in on a different frequency when I was no longer coming in on the current frequency. Approximately 10 to 15 minutes later; MSAW (Minimum Safe Altitude Warning) was going off on this flight and flashing 4200 feet. It took a second for me to realize I made a mistake and overlooked a section of the MIA chart that was 4;200 feet. When MSAW flashed; the aircraft was beyond my frequency reach and we were unable to communicate.The aircraft was also just barely clipping the corner of this particular MIA section and then it was back to at or below 4;000 feet. Instead of trying to relay through an aircraft; I allowed the aircraft to fly through this corner since it was a 200 feet. difference we were talking about and it was such a brief time period. I was confident with my knowledge that although not ideal; this aircraft wasn't in danger. The Aircraft went on to meet my previous requirements of crossing at 5;000 feet at 120 miles from destination and checked in the next frequency and no further issues arose.I frequently skip a frequency that would likely work in between the check in frequency and the frequency at the western part of the sector. It's never been an issue because we very seldom allow an aircraft to make it that far west at 4;000 feet to begin with. I was confident I had been proactive and covered my bases when indeed I had not. I used a type of crossing restriction; at least for this purpose; that I never use and one that I had never used prior and I overlooked an important section of the MIA. I need to start using this intermediate frequency even if for a short time period. Pay more attention to detail when issuing a restriction of this kind. This was completely my fault.
Report_1_Synopsis: ZKC Center Controller reported an aircraft flew below a Minimum IFR Altitude that the Controller overlooked.

Report_1_Narrative: On a 14 mile final Runway 24R LAX Airport [at] 4300 MSL I spotted a drone approach another airplane at our 10:00 position on parallel final RWY 25R off their right wing.  Drone then turned and flew off of our left wing tip opposite direction at an estimated distance of 300 feet.  It appeared to be a silver quad propeller drone but not totally positive.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain noticed a drone within 300 feet of their flight path during final approach.

Report_1_Narrative: There were storms in the area; and we were given a reroute by ATC; to go south to the coast; and then follow the coast west to IAH. The FO (First Officer; Pilot Monitoring) had made a passenger announcement telling them that we were expecting storms along the route of flight; and that we were anticipating a bumpy ride. I; the CP (Captain; Pilot Flying); had advised the FA that it was going to be bumpy. In the climb out; we encountered light turbulence. Upon reaching cruising altitude of FL280; it was smooth; so we briefly let the passengers up. Upon reaching the coast; ATC advised us of multiple storms and cells along our route of flight; and had mentioned that several aircraft ahead of us had gone south of these storms; had stayed within 50 NM of the coast; and had reported nothing worse than light turbulence; and advised we do the same. After discussing with the FO; we agreed that flying south of our route; and staying within 50 NM of the coast; was our best option. At this time; I had my radar up; and the FO had his terrain map up. We advised the passengers and the FA to expect a few bumps; turned the seat belt sign back on; and to remain seated. We also decided to slow to turbulence penetration speed. We were painting multiple red and magenta cells which we were staying south of; and had a lot of green all over the radar. We were dodging and avoiding the cells to the north; while staying within the 50 NM range of the coast. We then must have hit an embedded cell that the radar did not pick up; as it was only reading green. Almost instantly; we went into severe turbulence; and lost approximately 400 feet. The aircraft did not go into any unusual or upset attitudes; and the Auto-Pilot remained on. During this turbulence; we also had a suspected lightning strike - we saw a flash of light all around us; heard a bang; and smelt the 'fireworks' smell that you usually smell associated with lightning. After being struck; we got a Stall Protection System advanced master caution message appear. It disappeared within 5 seconds of it showing. As quick as the severe turbulence hit us; it disappeared. ATC queried us regarding our loss of altitude; at which point the FO reported the severe turbulence and suspected lightning strike. ATC asked if we needed further assistance; to which we replied no. As previously mentioned; this happened very quickly. All in all; I would say it lasted no longer than 30 seconds; and closer to 20 seconds. Once we were back at FL280; we had completely exited all weather (which we had been in for a majority of the time upon reaching the coast); and were in clear blue skies. I spoke to the FA; and asked if she was OK; to which she replied she was. She then asked if it was OK for her to check on the passengers; which she did. There were no injuries; and the only thing she mentioned is that the passengers were staring at her wide eyed. ATC asked if there were any injuries onboard; we replied with none. The flight continued with no further incidents. Upon landing; both pilots thoroughly inspected the outside of the plane on the walk around; noting a black mark on the right side of the nose which may be the entry point to the suspected lightning strike; but with no damage seen. I wrote up the plane with 3 write ups - Severe turbulence; Lightning strike; and Lock out/Tag out installed.CRM was effectively utilized during this event; with the PF using the radar; and the PM using the terrain. With the information available to us at the time; with ATC advising us of going south of the cells; as opposed to north; the decision; at the time; to go south was the correct one. That being said; I think it would have been smarter to go north of the cells; but we did not have that information. Utilizing the radar was key during this event; by staying out of the red and magenta cells. However; the radar has its limitation; especially considering they are older pieces of equipment; and can not 100% accurately paint embedded cells; of which we hit. After the event; ATC began recommending to other aircraft to go north of the cells. Ultimately; I would say the crew were stuck between a rock and a hard place - staying within the 50 NM boundary of the coast; but staying as far south as possible of the mega cells to the north. Additionally; I would like to mention the extraordinary job that the company did after the incident. Upon reaching the gate; multiple members of both [safety teams] reached out to me and the crew; checking that we were OK; and that the passengers were OK. I feel our company truly encompassed themselves with the company values; of which we stand for; and has made me thoroughly proud and joyful to be a part of.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Captain reported encountering severe turbulence; loss of aircraft control and a lightning strike.

Report_1_Narrative: Turning final ZZZZ fully configured at 150 knots I armed the Localizer first than the Approach mode. First Officer inquired and received the landing clearance. I noticed that the glide slope didn't capture and that we were going above the path. I tried to descend in Vertical Speed; but it didn't come active; so it wouldn't work. Approach mode light still on. I disconnected the Autopilot; lowered the nose and started a descend using the VGSI (Visual Glideslope) path indicator and the outside PAPI (Precision Approach Path Indicator). During the descent we tried to reset the Approach/Glideslope unsuccessfully. The approach was pretty bumpy with some good downdrafts. The aircraft went below the glide slope and I started to correct back when the pull up warning came on then stopped right away. Then the glide slope warning followed. I was just under the path recovering and had 3 red lights and 1 white on the PAPI. Speed around 10 knots above Vref and decreasing toward Vref. I was very focused on the approach and continued to an uneventful normal landing.We were configured early; ready for approach; but the Glideslope not capturing and the uncertainty concerning the landing clearance created a distraction that put me behind the aircraft and I developed some tunnel vision trying to remedy the approach. I became fixated and continued when I should have discontinued the approach and gone around. After landing the First Officer said to me that she had mentioned going around; but it hadn't registered with me during the approach. I tell First Officers that there is no mission; but today I didn't follow my own advice. It's easy to become over focused without realizing it. When in doubt; go-around.
Report_2_Narrative: The event began while beginning the ILS Approach. The company notes on the approach dictate not to arm the ILS until reaching a certain position because of the possibility of false localizer signals. The Captain was the Pilot Flying and I was the Pilot Monitoring.  I remember thinking that the Pilot Flying armed the approach later than I would have since we were well beyond the designated point. My best guess on what happened is that because of the delay the localizer armed but the glideslope never captured because we were already too high. Whatever the reason for the automation not doing what we had expected; the result was that we realized that the Glideslope never captured and were trying to get the aircraft to come down.Not only were we distracted with being above the intended glide path; but we were handed over to tower late and I was busy with getting clearance to land while the Pilot Flying was flying the plane trying to get back to a stabilized approach. As the aircraft was getting back to a normal glide path (3 red; 1 white on PAPI) around the 500 foot mark I gave my stabilized approach callout and realizing we were slightly above speed and correcting; but the vertical speed exceeded what is acceptable. At this point I said 'I think we should go around'. I can't remember if it was just before or after I said this that we got a 'PULL UP' alert. The Captain elected to continue the landing. Later after discussion; I learned he may have had tunnel vision to the point where my go around call didn't register with him.My unfamiliarity with ZZZZ did not help our situational awareness as well as being distracted with getting switched over to tower (late) and attempting to get landing clearance around the same time we realized the automation did not perform as expected. As a FO/PM not being assertive enough when a go-around was needed.Abiding by company SOP to the letter. No matter what; at 500 feet if stabilized approach criteria aren't met; it's an automatic and firm 'GO AROUND'.
Report_1_Synopsis: B737 flight crew reported they descended below the glidepath on their approach resulting in an unstable approach and a  terrain warning but the flying pilot continued the approach and landed.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Communication Breakdown; Training / Qualification; Other / Unknown
