Report_1_Narrative: I was PM.  On initial climb passing 1;500 feet there was no power reduction as programmed on T/O page X.  I reached up and manually reduced power then checked T/O page X to find it was in fact still programmed properly. Passing 3;000 feet the speed bug did not bug up for flap retraction.  That is when I realized VNAV was not selected. I selected VNAV.  We retracted the flaps on schedule and continued the flight to destination.I have low experience with only 40 hours on the aircraft.  My Relief Pilot also was not yet consolidated and my FO just recently consolidated.  I must have incorrectly responded 'checked' to the 'MCP' challenge on the before Start checklist and missed that VNAV was not selected.Fly more often.  But hard to do under COVID. Be more deliberate in accomplishing checklist especially at the gate before airborne when stress and task demand is low.
Report_2_Narrative: Departing ZZZZ at 1;500 feet power did not reduce to climb power. The Captain checked the takeoff pg X for altitudes; they were correct. At 3;000 feet the speed bug did not bug up for cleanup; that's when the Captain realized VNAV was not engaged. He engaged VNAV and I called for flap retraction on schedule.Cause - Recency in right seat. Monitoring. Refrain from staying heads down in the checklist. Confirm selected items.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier flight crew reported not following SOPs during the takeoff and departure phase and forgetting to select VNAV mode resulting in a delayed flap retraction. Captain stated lack of flying contributed to the event.

Report_1_Narrative: Once established in descent just below FL180; we received a call from the Flight Attendants that there was an odor in the vicinity of row X. This odor was described by FA 'A' as something similar to fuel and/or oil; but not a burning or acrid smell. The odor was not detectable to any other passengers or crew on the aircraft except the passengers in row X; to whom it was very noticeable; which was also confirmed by FA 'B'; but only when they walked up to row X. There was no visible plume anywhere in the airplane. The pilots did not detect any irregular odor in flight.The FO was flying the airplane (PF) so they took the radios as the CA (PM) looked in the QRH checklist. The comment about a fuel smell drove the pilots to suspect a fuel leak; but after running through the fuel leak checklist; no fuel leak indications (per checklist) were confirmed (fuel imbalance normal/not increasing; both engine fuel flow rates equivalent; quantity as expected for phase of flight plan). CA then confirmed with FA 'A' that the smell was indeed still noticeable; but there was still no plume and the odor was still confined to row X.We continued descent into ZZZ1 on what looked to be a fairly expedited vector; while we requested ARFF to be on standby at time of arrival. However; after we received another vector away from an expedited intercept course; we quickly [advised ATC] to gain traffic priority; which ATC quickly accommodated; clearing other aircraft from our path. We were cleared to land and we confirmed with Tower that ARFF would be standing by. Tower indicated we would exit [Runway] XXR at Taxiway 1 for ARFF coordination.Upon exit at Taxiway 1; we were cleared to cross runway XXL; and brought the aircraft to a stop on Taxiway 1 clear of runway. We requested ARFF check/scan the exterior of the aircraft for leaks/heat/fire/abnormalities. CA made a PA to pax noting that ARFF would be approaching the aircraft as a precaution. After ARFF indicated no abnormalities; we taxied to the gate; making clear to Ops that as an extra precaution; we would not start the APU. After we had taxied into the gate and set the parking brake; we immediately shut down (left-hand-side) engine #1; confirmed good/stable AC external power connection; then shut down (right-hand-side) engine #2. Prior to departure from ZZZ; we were sprayed with both Type I 'Deice' and Type IV 'Anti-Ice' fluid; with engines running; at the X Pad.After landing; FA 'B' said passengers had complained that the odor became more noticeable after landing gear was extended on final approach. FO also said that after landing they briefly noticed an odor.We could have [advised ATC] earlier on in the event. This would have allowed us traffic priority earlier in the descent (and speeds above 250 KIAS once below 10;000); getting us on the ground sooner and reducing the overall time of pax/FA exposure to fumes.We flew the same airplane the following day; and the airplane was cleared by Maintenance with no defects found. Nothing was wrong with the airplane itself. Fumes remaining localized in a certain area of the cabin suggests internal point source emission rather than external ingestion or airplane system malfunction. However; at time of writing; we still do not know; definitively; what caused the fumes.The FAs are commended for their prompt notification and accurate description of the nature and extent of the fumes. FO is commended for flying the aircraft while coordinating with ATC and requesting ARFF; while the CA ran checklists and coordinated with the FAs; then flying the approach almost to minimums. Working together seamlessly is key in these situations; and the CA commends the crew for a job well done.
Report_2_Narrative: Prior to departure from ZZZ; we were sprayed with both Type I and Type IV fluid; with engines running; at the South De-Ice Pad.Once established in descent just below FL180; we received a call from the FA's. I (the FO) assumed it was the FA's notification that they were seated. Instead; they communicated to the CA that there was an odor in the vicinity of row x. This odor was described by FA 'A' as something similar to fuel and/or oil; but not a burning smell. The odor was not detectable to any other passengers or crew on the aircraft except the passengers in row x; to whom it was very noticeable. The pilots did not detect any irregular odor in flight.I (the FO) was flying the airplane (PF) so I took the radios as the CA (PM) looked in the QRH checklist. Since the CA was communicating with the FA's; I trusted his lead on necessary checklists to run; as he had the first hand information on the situation in the cabin. During this time; we had entered IMC conditions; and I was flying the airplane and working the radios; receiving several heading; altitude and speed changes during this time.The comment about a fuel smell drove us to suspect a fuel leak; but after running through the fuel leak checklist; no fuel leak indications (per checklist) were confirmed (fuel imbalance normal/not increasing; both engine fuel flow rates equivalent; quantity as expected for phase of flight plan). CA then confirmed with FA 'A' that the smell was indeed still noticeable; but there was still no plume and the odor was still confined to row X.We continued descent into ZZZ1 on what looked to be a fairly expedited vector; during which I requested ARFF to be on standby at time of arrival. However; after we received another vector away from an expedited intercept course; we quickly [advised ATC] to gain traffic priority; which ATC quickly accommodated. We were cleared to land and we confirmed with Tower that ARFF would be standing by. Tower indicated we would exit XXR at Taxiway 1 for ARFF coordination.Upon landing; I cracked the Thrust Reversers (TRs); and briefly noticed a smell in the flight deck. I then decided that the use of TRs may not be the safest procedure; as it was still unclear what was causing this smell. Thus; I immediately stowed the TRs and decelerated using only the brakes (long runway; good braking action).Upon exit at Taxiway 1; we were cleared to cross runway XXL; and brought the aircraft to a stop on Taxiway 1 clear of XXL. We requested ARFF check/scan the exterior of the aircraft for leaks/heat/fire/abnormalities. CA made a PA to pax noting that ARFF would be approaching the aircraft as a precaution. After ARFF indicated no abnormalities; we taxied to the gate; making clear to Ops that as an extra precaution; we would not start the APU. After we had taxied into the gate and set the parking brake; we immediately shut down engine #1; confirmed good/stable AC external power connection; then shut down engine #2.After landing; FA 'B' said passengers had complained that the odor became more noticeable after landing gear was extended on final approach. This was my 2nd precautionary ARFF event on 2 consecutive workdays (though separated by a period of leave). Having had the time to reflect upon the first event; I felt calmer and more prepared this time. I focused on making a successful approach (almost down to minimums).One error I made was to start configuring and thus slowing down too early. Due to several heading changes and an ATC request for us to slow down while the aircraft in front of us on the approach sped up to best forward speed; I had felt momentarily disoriented regarding our distance to the ZZZ1. Luckily; my brain was about 5 miles ahead of the airplane. Once I realized my error; I paused further configuration (which was gear down flaps 3 at that time) until closer to the ZZZ1.Considerations that were made were items for fire and emergency evacuation; should a fire develop after landing. Luckily; this was not the case.To my knowledge; it is still unclear what caused the smell. If it would have been more severe (filling the entire cabin and flight deck); then the checklist for smoke/fumes would have been appropriate.Overall; I feel that this event was handled well by everyone involved.
Report_1_Synopsis: EMB-175 flight crew reported a cabin fumes event during approach descent.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Communication Breakdown; Situational Awareness; Training / Qualification
Report_1_Narrative: I was assigned to work position Flight Attendant (FA) D on the aircraft and completely forgot my exit rows briefing duty the flight. I didn't realize my failure to brief exit row passengers the entire flight. It was during the boarding process of the second flight when I briefed those exit row passengers; that I became aware of what I overlooked on the first flight.I believe upon freshly returning to active duty; after almost an entire year being on extended leave of absence during COVID-19 schedule reductions; led to my lack of attention to flight steps in which years of routines were disrupted. To prevent this event from reoccurring; I need to refresh my memory and utilize my work manual in reviewing duties of each phases of flight.Realized mistake of skipped exit briefing for ZZZ-ZZZ1 flight while initiating exit briefing for the return flight ZZZ1-ZZZ.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Attendant reported after almost an entire year of being on extended leave of absence during COVID-19 schedule reductions; the disruption of routine led the FA to forget the safety briefing for the exit row passengers.

Report_1_Narrative: Aircraft ground-looped on landing damaging landing gear; prop and wingtip.
Report_1_Synopsis: Pilot of a biplane reported loss of directional control on landing that resulted in a ground loop and some aircraft damage.

Report_1_Narrative: Inbound to ZZZ from the south. Reported on CTAF 5 nm south of airport inbound for landing on Runway XX. A flight of 3 RVs reported taxiing out for XX. Approaching the airport RVs reported their takeoff roll; just prior to entering the downwind leg RVs reported they would be departing southbound. I then reported I was 2 minutes south. At that time; I observed the RVs over the departure end turning left. At this time; I could see them on a direct course toward me; they were climbing; I was level at pattern altitude (900 feet MSL). They were basically climbing or about to climb through my altitude; my best option was to descend underneath them; as they were climbing. At that point one of the RVs; I assume the leader reported seeing me headed underneath them. After we passed; I climbed back to pastern altitude and turned downwind; the RVs continued southbound.I saw the RVs from their x-wind turn. I thought they would make a standard 45 departure from the x-wind leg prior to turning southbound but they continued south. I should have been a little more to the East so that I joined the downwind at mid-field. They should have departed on a 45 to the x-wind. Fortunately; I was watching for them and saw them in time to avoid them. Everybody being on frequency was a positive.
Report_1_Synopsis: Pilot reported that during their approach to the airport; a flight of 3 aircraft departed and failed to use the correct pattern departure procedure; resulting in an NMAC. The inbound pilot had to descend in order to avoid the other aircraft.

Report_1_Narrative: I had just assumed responsibility of the position about a minute prior when the pilot of Aircraft X informed me that they were 'Over HOMAI; what do you want?' The previous controller; still observing the 2-minute overlap; confirmed what she stated in the relief briefing; that Aircraft X had been assigned direct HOMAI; which ties into their flight plan routing of the LNDHY1 STAR into OGG. I responded to the pilot that he should track outbound of HOMAI on the LNDHY1 arrival; which publishes a 204 degree track. The pilots were obviously confused; but began to correct. In the process of doing so; the aircraft may have clipped the boundary of a higher 6;300 ft. MVA. Aircraft X was level at 4;000 ft. in a 3;500 ft. MVA; and would have had no problems remaining so if they were established on the STAR. In an effort to salvage the situation; I asked the pilots if they had the airport in sight for a visual approach. They replied in the affirmative. Then I asked if they had traffic to follow in sight. They replied in the affirmative and I issued the visual approach clearance. The MSAW (Minimum Safe Altitude Warning) did not activate and I did not issue a low altitude alert. The pilots did not question the 'direct HOMAI' clearance they received from the previous controller until they were about a half mile past the fix. If there was any question about their routing; they should've clarified much earlier. But the confusion is not infrequent; and I have had pilots question the routing before. The published STAR clearly shows a 204 degree track after HOMAI on both the visual layout and written description. When I state this fact to querying pilots; the confusion is resolved. But the lack of a fix after HOMAI may cause pilots to ignore the track; or (as some controllers suspect) cause the track to drop out of the FMS when an approach is pre-loaded. My recommendation is for another fix to be added on the 204 degree track after HOMAI; to resolve the confusion; and to help ensure that aircraft don't fly on a free heading toward a higher MVA.My other recommendation is to look into how the LNDHY1 STAR is being programmed into FMS displays; and whether the addition of a (yet to be assigned) approach (e.g. RNAV Z RWY 2 from HOMAI) erases or otherwise obfuscates the 204 degree track outbound of HOMAI.
Report_1_Synopsis: HCF TRACON Air Traffic Controller reported an aircraft failed to track the STAR resulted in entering a higher MVA.

Report_1_Narrative: Aircraft X was released IFR off UDD; which off of RWY (Runway) 28 would be an immediate left turn (Southeast) to TRM; climbing to 4;000 feet. When they were released; there was no immediate traffic threat for the departure. By the time Aircraft X departed there was a target flying westbound (opposite direction) at 2;500 feet. On initial contact with Aircraft X; I told them about the traffic and asked if they could stop their climb at 2;000 feet (MVA in the area is 4;000 feet). They questioned the altitude initially; and I explained the situation to them. They agreed to stop at 2;000 feet. I issued a traffic alert; and Aircraft X eventually said they had to turn to avoid the traffic.I am recommending that there be some sort of real controlled airspace in the Palm Springs valley. The TRSA is not mandatory; and there are frequently aircraft (many high performance) that choose not to call the approach controllers and just go straight to the tower. The airspace in the months between September and May is extremely busy at times; and the controllers/pilots have no safe space in which to operate. It is called 'The Wild West' over there for a reason. Everything is shoot from the hip; because you have no idea what is about to happen next. We can not plan on anything; we can never assume anything. The most controlled airspace in the valley is the PSP Delta; which requires participation; while the approach controllers work 20x the traffic and have no 'safe space'.I ask that the airspace be reviewed and considered for a Class Bravo/Charlie airspace to avoid future NMACs or worse.
Report_1_Synopsis: ATC Tracon Controller reported this airspace needs a review and possible reclassification.

Report_1_Narrative: Aircraft X was southbound at 030 for a visual approach to Runway XX at ZZZ. I accepted a VFR point out from ZZZ1 facility on a XXXX code just a few miles east of ZZZZZ intersection going a few miles west of ZZZZZ to turn back to ZZZ1 airspace along the coastline at 015.  I did not tag up the point out because there was no traffic in that vicinity; and I was busy messing with my COVID mask. I was trying to put my mask on which I had in my pocket.  I cleared Aircraft X into Runway XX for the visual approach. I switched Aircraft X to the Tower when the point out aircraft was 7NM East of Aircraft X at 015. The tower controller issued traffic to Aircraft X three times. The first traffic call Aircraft X reported seeing the aircraft on TCAS. The third traffic call Aircraft X reported the traffic insight. No traffic alert was given to Aircraft X and no TCAS RA was performed. Aircraft X continued inbound and landed without further incident.  I lost track of the point out because when I took it I was working planes while trying to fix my COVID-19 mask.  When I decided to just work without one; I had moved on to other traffic and forgot to tag up the point out.The fact that I was more concerned with getting in trouble for not having my mask on rather than doing a completely efficient job is the FAA's fault.  The FAA is making us fear the repercussions of the mask mandate; so much its eroding the safety of the NAS...DO NOT REQUIRE MASK TO BE WORN ON POSITION IF WE ARE ALREADY SIX FEET APART; which we are based on the distance of scope to scope. Whether its distracting; [probably] muffles transmissions; the mask mandate on position is depleting the safety of the NAS.
Report_2_Narrative: I was working LC. Runway XX was the active Runway; advertising RNAVs.Aircraft X; checked on Tower frequency on an 11 mile final at an altitude of 1;700 feet.  I noticed a target moving east to west at a high rate of speed (240 knots) and was not tagged up.  I called traffic to Aircraft X at his 2 o'clock 3 to 4 miles moving westbound at 1;500 feet.  Aircraft X said he had it on his TCAS and he was looking for traffic.  I continued to watch the westbound traffic realizing it was going to potentially become a conflict for Aircraft X and continued to call traffic to them.  I advised Aircraft X to try and maintain 1;700 feet based on the fact the westbound traffic appeared to be holding 1;500 and Aircraft X was on an instrument approach.  I also told Aircraft X it appeared the traffic was going to pass underneath. Aircraft X reported the traffic in sight right as my Ground Control and I realized the target was making a hard 180 degree turn back to the east while climbing up into Aircraft X's flight path and altitude. I responded back to Aircraft X to maneuver at his discretion to avoid the aircraft. The target continued eastbound.  Aircraft X landed without incident.  I asked Aircraft X if he would give me a call so that I may ask questions.  I told him he was not in trouble; he obliged and I gave him the tower number.  I then attempted to call the Supervisor from our communications counsel to ask what was going on with the target to no avail; the Supervisor did not pick up. Once on break I was able to speak with the pilot: The Pilot said it was a [description].  He caught a glimpse of it while it passed underneath then Aircraft Y did the 180 degree turn back east and passed right off the nose of his aircraft at his altitude.  The pilot also mentioned that his passengers had asked about the aircraft; leading me to believe in fact Aircraft Y was extremely close and causing this to be a significant event.  The pilot said he was also going to file a report.I took the information down to my Supervisor.  My Supervisor called the ZZZ [TRACON] Supervisor who said he didn't know anything of the event and that he was too busy to look into at the moment.  Seeing as how Aircraft Y came from ZZZ's TRACON airspace; my Supervisor gave them a call to see if they knew anything about Aircraft Y and what it was doing.  ZZZ4 said they were talking to Aircraft Y and had coordinated with ZZZ with a point out; ZZZ accepted the point out on Aircraft Y.  There was never any coordination from ZZZ to myself on LC in reference to Aircraft Y.Note: I did not issue a Traffic Alert because I had no clue what Aircraft Y was doing; I was focused on calling the traffic from the beginning;  and with the 180 degree high speed turn I felt like giving the pilot discretion to maneuver as needed (since he had him in sight then) was the best course of action for the pilot to be able to keep his passengers alive.Note:  Aircraft Y was never tagged up on the scope.  They appeared to be VFR but I'm really unsure if they were.Events like this in the ZZZ [TRACON] airspace and ZZZ [Tower] environment in my opinion are a consistent problem.1.  ATC 101: coordination and positive control. ZZZ1 [TRACON] coordinated with ZZZ [TRACON] as a point out.  ZZZ [TRACON] accepting the point out.  In all reality both facilities should be monitoring what Aircraft Y was doing.  The original point out coordination was that Aircraft Y was going 6 miles west of the fix ZZZZZ.  Once Aircraft Y passed 6 miles there were 2 possible controllers to notice and do something about it.  ZZZ [TRACON] should have questioned ZZZ1 [TRACON] and myself reference Aircraft X; ZZZ1 [TRACON] should have reached out to Aircraft Y and ZZZ [TRACON].  Because no one did Aircraft Y was 15 miles west of ZZZZZ and crossing through the final of Runway XX at ZZZ.2. Take responsibility when you have accepted a point out by keeping an eye on the target as well as looking at your current traffic and what may be aconflict between the point out and current traffic. Do NOT lose track of your traffic and or point outs (which was the excuse of the ZZZ [TRACON] Controller). If you're busy do not accept the point out potentially causing yourself to 'lose track' of traffic.3.  CARE! This job is not a game.  There is not time to not care when human lives are at stake.For my side:1.  I have re-played this 1000 times over in my head.  I think maybe I could have called a traffic alert but what I can't see is what I would have suggested to Aircraft X.  I called the traffic early and continued too; once he got it I felt like the pilot knew how to fly that plane better than me; and could see what Aircraft Y was doing better than me as well.  If I had given him a suggestion based on how erratic Aircraft Y was I truly think it would have ended badly.   The pilot's RA never went off; and speaking to the pilot he wasn't sure why but he said it probably had no idea what to do based on what that Aircraft Y was doing.2.  Suggestion; call the pilot if able or the airport and question said pilot.  Potentially file a deviation or ask what was going on.3.Stop the 'holes in the swiss cheese'.  This was always my favorite CBI [Computer Based Instruction].  In order to not have the holes line up you have to be vigilant always.  I try and will continue to try. Maybe I could have even been more vigilant today?  Saw it coming earlier?4.  Encourage pilots to file reports so this information can be turned into learning experiences.Thank you for reading some recommendations; and there are probably 100 more things that could be done.  This event took a toll on myself the rest of my shift.  Some things you just can't un-see; but for myself it makes me better and care even more for our pilots in the sky and their passengers.
Report_1_Synopsis: TRACON Controller reported being distracted by attempting to put on a mask and did not issue important traffic to an air carrier on final. Tower Controller reported issuing traffic to an arrival about an unknown aircraft that was pointed out to the TRACON; but the TRACON Controller never advised the Tower Controller.

Report_1_Narrative: We were cleared to FL 230. Passing through 17;500 feet; #1 engine rolled back to approximately 30%N1.  The N1 and EGT had flashing red and yellow arcs and the lower section had a red flashing box around both engine indications. Our initial analysis was engine failure.  We requested to level at FL 180; communicated to ATC our situation and requested vectors to return to ZZZ.  Upon further analysis of the engine condition; the Captain (Pilot Flying) stated the engine was still running but noted the indications were not normal. We also saw the EEC in ALTN mode.  Captain continued to fly and directed me into the QRH for the EEC ALT MODE checklist since the engine was running and not surging; stalling; or any indications dictating complete failure or the need to shutdown.  We completed the QRH for the EEC ALT MODE according to our situation and indications.  We discussed and agreed to also reference and ran the QRH [for] One Engine Inoperative Landing.  I continued communications with ATC; while the Captain communicated with F/A's and made a PA to passengers. I computed [landing] data and set up the FMC. Captain flew the approach and landing; taxiing clear of the runway to a safe location.  Autobrakes were used and no manual braking activated until slowed (approximately 50 knots) and prior to the exit of the runway.  Based on our weight and configuration [calculations] prior to landing required the use of autobrakes and brake cooling calculations.  I calculated the [landing data] for Non-Normal One engine Inop with 15 Flaps landing.   Brake Cooling calculations returned a 58 minute cooling period; which we accomplished at the turnout abeam runway.  Emergency Rescue Crews communicated to us no visible smoke from brakes and heat signature negative. After the 58 minute cool down; we were given clearance to taxi and proceeded to our gate.
Report_2_Narrative: When we arrived at the gate; Maintenance was working on the #1 engine. The previous crew that had the aircraft had returned to the gate. When they started the number one engine they got the Engine Control light. Maintenance cleaned the cannon plugs did an engine run and returned the aircraft to service. Our engine start and initial climb were all normal. We were on radar vectors for our route and climbing through 17;500 feet or so when the #1 N1 Gauge flashed yellow twice. We both saw it; then the #1 engine rolled back to 31% on the N1 but the engine didn't quit. We leveled at FL 180 and requested vectors back to ZZZ. We ran the EEC ALT Mode Checklist and the Engine Failure or Shutdown Checklist from the QRH. Landed Flaps 15; autobrakes 3. We ran the brake cooling calculation prior to landing. We had a 58 minutes of break cooling.
Report_1_Synopsis: B737 flight crew reported returning to departure airport after experiencing #1 engine anomalies that reduced thrust to idle.

Report_1_Narrative: I was in the pit when I loaded an electric scooter. I asked leads loading prior to closing out the flight if this electric scooter was scanned they had said yes. Operations checked the Departure Staging Guide (DSTG) and noticed that the scooter did not show up on the DSTG as a dangerous goods item. We realized that the wrong tag was used to tag the electric scooter.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Ramp personnel reported Dangerous Goods cargo not listed on aircraft cargo Departure Staging Guide (DSTG). Error corrected prior to departure.

Report_1_Narrative: Flying a steeper than usual glide path to a runway with displaced threshold. During transition to visual I inadvertently descended below the glide slope to achieve a normal sight picture. Received a Ground Proximity Warning and Glide Slope. Too much focus outside the aircraft. We were over the touchdown zone and a normal landing was completed. Attention inside and outside the airplane during transition to landing flare.
Report_2_Narrative: We were in the flare over the runway and received the 'Glideslope' EGPWS advisory immediately prior to touchdown. Aural Glideslope advisory while we were in the landing hover/flare. The First Officer hand flew the Visual Approach and maintained the Glideslope until we were approaching the threshold and he shifted his attention to the external environment. The Glideslope and PAPI (Precision Approach Path Indicator) for this runway may have been the cause when he transitioned to flying by outside reference and attempting to achieve a sight picture closer to our typical 3.00 degree glide path. We were over the touchdown zone and completed a very normal and uneventful landing.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight crew reported the First Officer hand flying a steeper than usual Visual Approach with a terrain warning in the flare.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Training / Qualification; Situational Awareness; Communication Breakdown; Human-Machine Interface
Report_1_Narrative: Assigned to descend via. Inside ZZZZZ assigned 300 knots. Captain used the speed window to adjust speed. Approaching ZZZZZ1; realized he was crossing low. He attempted to correct but still crossed low by what I estimate to be 500-800 feet low. I looked and realized he did not use Speed Intervention but instead had used LVL Change. ATC did not query us about the error nor was there traffic in the area.Captain new to aircraft and seat with limited recency of experience confused speed/descent modes. FO (PM) limited recency of experience involved with approach programming and communications did not notice the error.For our part better announcement and verification of MCP changes. Better monitoring during busy descent.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier First Officer reported an altitude deviation and cited the Captain being new to the aircraft and both pilots' lack of flying contributed to the event.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Situational Awareness; Training / Qualification; Communication Breakdown
Report_1_Narrative: We were level 5;000 feet 250 knots approaching ZZZ VOR on the ZZZZZ2 Star. Approach gave a heading 280 and slow to 180 and asked if we had the field in sight.  We were heading 330 and I was thinking a turn to 350 was coming so 280 heading caught me a little off guard. I (FO) was pilot flying. The sun was just above the horizon as I looked west and across the cockpit for the field.  Simultaneously I was looking cross-cockpit and programing the speed and heading change into the FMC. I could make out the field so I said to the Captain (PM); 'I can see the field; you can call it in sight.'  I noticed another aircraft on TCAS at our altitude on TCAS and then saw them visually less than ten miles away; also headed west toward ZZZ [Airport]; I noted the  paint scheme and relayed to the PM all that information and that they were probably headed to the north side of the airport.  In my head I was thinking that our airplane was not slowing down as fast as I would like when the PM said 'where is that airplane; I think we need to turn.' I pushed the localizer button on the FMC but the airplane did not turn so I turned the autopilot off and manually turned to intercept final for [Runway] XXR. As I did; we received at TCAS TA then a few seconds later a TCAS RA to climb.  The ADI showed a red boxed area from level flight down (I was descending) so I just leveled off until we heard 'clear of conflict.'   Then Approach gave us a 180 heading; paused; and then said 'you guys can't do that;' and switched us to Tower.  I was able to correct the high energy level of the airplane using gear; flaps; and speed brakes and continued the approach and landed uneventfully.Fast close to the airfield; sun in eyes; failure on my part to use automation.Something from ATC that I was going to turn towards the runway instead of downwind in the [Runway] XXR pattern or an advisory where we were in the sequence.  My recency of experience led to not arming the localizer; while I did brief that at the start of the first leg I could have reemphasized it during the approach brief.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier First Officer reported a track heading deviation and an altitude deviation during approach resulting in an RA event and cited lack of flying contributed to the event.

Report_1_Narrative: While on climb out shortly after the 10;000 foot checklist; I noticed our oil pressure was in the amber range. The Captain checked the left engine oil quantity on the MFD and it indicated 2 quarts. I started the Low Oil Pressure checklist which lead to the Precautionary Engine Shutdown checklist. We secured the engine; [advised ATC] and headed back ZZZ. I called Flight Attendant and told her what the situation was; made a PA; and we continued to land safely in ZZZ. I cannot answer this as I am not a mechanic and do not know why the engine lost oil. I feel like we took all appropriate actions in a timely manner. If this happens in the future; I would maybe try to slow down a bit and delay the flaps 22 extension to short final as we were heavy and airplane wouldn't hold altitude after we extended the gear down/flaps 22. We retracted the flaps back up to 9 to be able to hold altitude which worked well; and then re extended the flaps to 22 on short final. I think overall; we did what we were trained to do and the Captain even made a smooth landing. After landing; we taxied in and parked with no issues.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier First Officer reported an engine shutdown due to oil pressure loss.

Report_1_Narrative: Arriving in gusty crosswind conditions. VMC. I was hand flying the ILS. At runway threshold; I inadvertently descended below the glide slope during transition to outside and received a glide slope warning. As we were in the flare over the runway landing was the safest option. [Identified by] GPWS warning; glide slope. Began transition to outside too early preoccupation with winds. Failed to continue cross checking indications. I heard the annunciation in the landing flare and completed a normal landing. The flight director indications guide the airplane to the touchdown zone use this information in combination with outside.
Report_1_Synopsis: EMB-145 First Officer reported receiving a glide slope warning on an ILS approach; citing weather distractions as contributing.

Report_1_Narrative: Intended to land flaps 30 in windy conditions with add speed of 14 knots.  Visual approach on Visual Approach Slope indicator and slightly below ILS glide slope. We received a Ground Proximity Warning alert for 'too low terrain'. Rechecked landing gear was down and landed. We realized on very short final that flaps were actually set to 25 instead of 30. We did not select flaps to 30 since we were so low. With the extra speed we had added for the gusty winds; I felt we were safer to leave them set at 25 and land.
Report_2_Narrative: While on final approach  we experienced a Ground Proximity Warning 'Too Low Terrain' aural warnings. Knowing that we were on glide slope and Precision Approach Path Indicator and the runway was in sight in VFR conditions; we decided to continue the landing. We ensured that the landing gear was down and that we were free of terrain; however; on short final the Captain noticed we were at flaps 25 instead of 30. It was decided to safely complete the landing since we were stable on speed and path. We already had built in a 14 knot wind additive for the windy conditions. The entire approach was stable including at the 500 foot 'Stable' call out point. I take responsibility for misreading the flap gauge; and will certainly give it more focus in the future. One potential factor; not an excuse; is there was the distraction of balloons going by our aircraft around the time of the landing checklist. I reported the balloons to Tampa Tower.
Report_1_Synopsis: B737 flight crew conducting a Visual Approach reported the flaps were set incorrectly resulting in a Ground Proximity Alert on short final.

Report_1_Narrative: The taxiway centerline markings on ORD Taxiway K; K3 and A9 are worn off.  The line is almost gone in a number of locations.  At night using a 737 taxi light; it's very hard to see where you are going.  This area is away from the large bright lights of the terminal; and is a mass of darkness with a lot of blue lights.  It's even worse on a night when it is raining.
Report_1_Synopsis: B737 First Officer reported the centerline markings on several taxiways at ORD Airport are worn and difficult to see at night.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Training / Qualification; Communication Breakdown; Other / Unknown
Report_1_Narrative: On the ZZZZZ X arrival into ZZZ; we were given a descent to FL230.  As PF; I re-cruised for FL230.  Prior to ZZZZZ1 we were told to descend via the arrival.  I dialed in 6;000 feet for the Runway XXL approach.  Initially the descent point was visible and looked normal.  After flying several more minutes it became clear that we were past the descent point.  It was about this time that the descent point disappeared from the ND.  We started an immediate Open Descent with full speed brakes.  We were unable to get relief from the altitude/airspeed requirement at ZZZZZ2 (250/110) due to radio congestion.  We were given a frequency change and got relief from ZZZ Approach who gave us a descent to 6;000 feet which we accomplished.  The rest of the approach and landing was uneventful.  When the PF re-cruised he inadvertently typed in '320' instead of '230'.  There was not an immediate erroneous depiction on the ND.  Everything looked normal; however we continued past the descent point.  Just as we realized there was something wrong; the ND descent point disappeared.  The PF has been on reserve and has flown very little in the last two months.  The next two flights went well with no problems.The two pilots were on the first leg of the trip.  It was the first time they'd flow together.  They were working well together and both were attempting to follow policies/procedures.  This was a dumb mistake by one pilot that was not caught by the other.  By re-cruising; the goal was to have the ND provide usable descent point information.  I listed this as a 'Moderate' risk rating because we easily received relief from ATC.  If they had not assisted us; the risk would have been higher.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Captain reported an altitude deviation and explained the PF had been on reserve and flown little in the last two months which may have contributed to the event.

Report_1_Narrative: Advised by Dispatcher (name) that ZZZ had undeclared DG on the aircraft. Advised crew of position and contents. position XX; can [container number]. [Hazmat container] Can was loaded by ZZZ1 ramp and trucked to ZZZ. DG included 4 items.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Dispatch reported a communication breakdown between two different airport ramp personnel which resulted in undeclared Hazmat cargo being loaded on aircraft. Dispatcher notified flight crew.

Report_1_Narrative: After a local solo flight of 30 minutes and a full stop landing; I taxied back to the active runway with the intent of doing more traffic pattern work. I applied full power at the start of the takeoff and confirmed correct engine indications. Shortly after liftoff; 5 to 10 feet above the ground; I perceived what I judged was a loss in engine power and decided to perform a cautionary landing on the remaining runway. Upon landing; directional control of the aircraft was lost and contributed to a ground loop to the left of approximately 270 degrees. The aircraft departed the active runway and came to a stop in the transient parking area to the southeast side of the runway. I secured the fuel; ignition; and electrical systems and exited the aircraft. Minor damage was sustained during the ground loop to the right wheel/hubcap; and the right rear portion of the wingtip. A close inspection revealed no other damage and the propellor did not strike the ground. No immediate visual evidence of a malfunction was evident. The aircraft was secured in place and the FAA and NTSB were notified jointly via phone in the presence of the airport manager; who also took a report for airport records. A bystander notified local fire department authorities; who were dispatched; but they also observed no major damage; fluid; gas; or oil leakage that would cause a hazard to persons or property. No injuries were sustained by myself.
Report_1_Synopsis: Light sport aircraft pilot reported the engine lost power on departure so they immediately landed. Upon landing the pilot lost control of the aircraft resulting in a ground loop and runway excursion.

Report_1_Narrative: Was flying with a friend around the area.  We departed and executed a 45 departure. After reaching 3 miles northwest of the airport (directly over coast) I turned southbound. I made a call on CTAF that Aircraft X was 3 miles northwest at 1;000 feet following the shore southbound. About 20 seconds after making that call I was looking out the left window and noticed an aircraft whiz from underneath and behind me and begin a turn inland. It is hard to judge the distance but he was way too close for comfort. Correcting an incident like this will only happen in 3 ways.1.Pilots use more time looking outside (I am sure he would've seen how close he was to me if he was paying attention).2.Radio usage especially in busy Class E surface like that of Astoria.3.Require the use of ADS-B in all controlled airspace. I had my ADSB on. This aircraft was not on ADSB and was not making calls. Further; he proceeded to preform touch and goes at Astoria without making a single call.
Report_1_Synopsis: Pilot reported a NMAC with another aircraft which was not communicating on  CTAF.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Training / Qualification; Situational Awareness; Communication Breakdown
Report_1_Narrative: I was pilot monitoring. We were given a clearance to maintain 250 knots until advised. Upon reaching 10;000 feet we accelerated to 290 knots (our normal profile). I advised the Captain that we were given a 250 knot clearance...we discussed and I probed the Controller and confirmed we were given a 250 knot speed restriction until 14;000 feet. We began to slow down. I believe the cause of this is the fact that we have not been flying a lot because of COVID. I had been furloughed and brought back to the line and retrained. I believe if I had been flying more often than I would have been able to catch this lapse earlier or could have reminded the Captain once we reached 10;000 feet.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported a failure to notify the Captain that the aircraft's speed was exceeding the clearance limit during climbout. First Officer cited lack of flying as a contributing factor.

Report_1_Narrative: Departed FNL airport to stay in the pattern during uncontrolled operations of Class Echo Airspace XA:00. Operations for Tower begin at XB:00.Reported Visibility ASOS was 1SM. Actual visibility on ground and in air was 10+ due to having a clear view of the entire mountain range; which is a given for visibility. One landing in the pattern was performed; 10+ miles visibility and clear of clouds. The Tower opened and reported that the ATIS was reporting 3/4 SM VIS; however multiple aircraft in the pattern gave a PIREP of 10+ visibility. Tower refused our PIREP; asked if we wanted to request SVFR; however if the reported visibility was under 1 SM they could not grant this. We still asked for SVFR since visibility was clear and clear of clouds. Upon asking Tower for SVFR; he said no; asked if we had visual with the runway; which of course we did; and cleared us to land number 2 behind another aircraft ahead of us in the pattern. We landed and terminated the flight. I have previously flown VFR into FNL Airport when the fires were lowering visibility. The METAR and ATIS were reporting 1/4 mile visibility making it IFR; however having full visibility in the aircraft; I called Tower before entering their airspace and asked if the reported visibility was correct. They said no; the RVR is not reliable; visibility was greater than 6SM and to proceed inbound for VFR landing.
Report_1_Synopsis: Pilot reported FNL airport ASOS visibility is often inaccurate and unreliable.

Report_1_Narrative: Returning to 7B3 (Hampton Airfield) late at night; turned on the runway lights; and landed in-between them. However; the lights border the grass runway rather than the asphalt runway that I meant to land on. As a result; I landed on the grass runway; when I expected to land on asphalt. This was potentially dangerous; if the grass runway was blocked with snow (it was not; fortunately). The grass runway was not operational at the time (NOTAM to that effect).No adverse effect happened; but it was not ideal.It's not clear that in order to land on the asphalt; I'd have to land OUTSIDE the two sets of runway lights which border the turf runway. Adding a third row of runway lights (on the other side of the asphalt runway) would make it much clearer for a night landing.
Report_1_Synopsis: GA pilot reported a loss of situational awareness resulting in landing on adjacent grass runway at 7B3 airport.

Report_1_Narrative: On the above mentioned date and time; I was the designated Pilot Flying. Descending through the Los Angeles area on vectors I was instructed to descend from 4;000 feet to 2;600 feet. I was overflying the city of Los Angeles on vectors to HHR. Autopilot was engaged; 2;600 feet was set in the altitude pre-selector and I began my descent. Another pilot reported to ATC that they flew past a drone off their right wing around 4;000 feet on approach into LAX. That would put the drone in our proximity off our right wing as well. Both the Pilot Monitoring (PM) and I were looking for that drone. I had mentioned to the PM that I have never been this low over the city of Los Angeles and we need to pay close attention to our surroundings. Through the distraction of trying to identify the drone; I descended through 2;600 feet to 2;400 feet before being advised of my altitude by ATC. I immediately disconnected the autopilot and corrected to the assigned altitude of 2;600 feet. No further issues occurred and no near misses were experienced to my knowledge. I was not informed by ATC of any possible pilot deviation nor given a contact number to call. Corrective action was taken to resolve the altitude discrepancy; and I have discussed with my crew and maintenance facility the possible reason why altitude was not captured by the autopilot. As Pilot in Command; I fully take responsibility for the actions on this day; both negative and corrective; and have discussed our safety procedures with my crew. I am filling out this report as I feel aviation is founded on safety and I strive to improve on every aspect of my piloting safety; skills and knowledge. Thank you for your time and consideration.
Report_1_Synopsis: GA pilot reported overhearing a report of a UAS sighting in the area. The pilot focused on locating the UAS in relation to their aircraft and overshot their assigned altitude.

Report_1_Narrative: Lost power at approximately 1;000 feet toward end of climbout to remain in pattern for touch and go's was probably 1/4 to 1/2 mile beyond end of runway; turned back to runway and informed Tower I had lost power and needed to land. I checked for any remedial problems and saw none; but noticed my prop was not turning. I proceeded to land back on runway and coast to a stop on the taxiway. I was able to hand push the plane to the fuel pumps and added fuel and the plane then restarted. the puzzle being the plane only took approximately 26 gallons when the tank holds 36; though only 32 usable; so I think there is some chance I might have had a vacuum created in the fuel tank. I do run un-vented fuel caps per a notice regarding the Aeronca sedans because with vented caps there had been some incidents of planes running out of power attributed to the wing at higher pitch up creating a vacuum at the tank. The Aeronca Sedan has a belly vent that faces forward to pressurize the fuel tanks; or I could just have not realized how low the fuel was and it lost power because of the pitch up for climb then couldn't restart because the prop stopped turning i.e. I didn't pitch down aggressively enough.
Report_1_Synopsis: Aeronca pilot reported the engine lost power during initial climb. The pilot was unable to restart the engine and returned to the runway to a successful landing. Post flight; the pilot conjectured that the engine failure could be due to inadequate fuel or a vacuum in the tanks.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Workload; Training / Qualification; Time Pressure; Situational Awareness
Report_1_Narrative: I was practicing air taxiing and quick stops with a 31-hour student pilot on a taxiway. During the recovery phase of the quick stop; the student did not raise enough collective to arrest the descent. I took controls at around 30 feet AGL and increased the collective to our 5-minute limit; but we continued to descend and impacted the ground hard enough to spread the skids. A piece of non-structural sheet metal detached from the underside of the helicopter and landed beside the taxiway. I reported what happened to the tower and they sent someone to retrieve the sheet metal. I flew the helicopter back to the flight school's ramp and did not observe any damage other than the spread skids. I should have taken the controls earlier and not allowed the descent rate to develop to an unrecoverable state. I was trying to talk the student through the correct control inputs when I should have just abandoned the maneuver and recovered.
Report_1_Synopsis: Helicopter Flight Instructor reported their student was practicing 'quick stops' but did not recover the descent in a timely manner. The Instructor reported they took control too late and this resulted in a hard landing causing minor damage to the helicopter.

Report_1_Narrative: GPS system went into Dead Reckoning mode; but we did not notice right away.  After about 5 minutes; it found the aircraft position again and updated; showing the aircraft track about a mile further west than it had displayed before.  We were traveling north just outside of the ZZZ Class Bravo.  We do not believe we penetrated the edge of the airspace at any time; but once the GPS came back online and updated; we were substantially closer than we had been believed based on the previous; ambiguous; nav data.
Report_1_Synopsis: PA-31 Single Pilot Captain reported a navigation error due to temporary loss of GPS data.

Report_1_Narrative: On date; our aircraft took necessary evasive action to avoid a Near midair collision while on an IFR Flight Plan in Night-time Visual Meteorological Conditions. Our aircraft was descending to an assigned altitude 7;000 feet while established on an assigned heading of 220 degrees. While descending through approximately 7;700 feet; at approximately 17.5 DME from BAPPA Intersection (Initial Fix for RNAV approach Runway 19 at GEU) approximately 229 degrees bearing to the fix; the onboard TCAS System issued a 'Traffic-Traffic Advisory'. About one second later the approach Controller issued a 'traffic alert' in conjunction with an 'immediate left turn' heading assignment of 170 degrees. After hearing the tone in the Controller's voice; I immediately complied with the Controller's (initial) request. As I glanced over to the TCAS portion of the screen; the conflicting traffic and our aircraft appeared to be converging; almost touching our aircraft's position on the screen. Scaled down to lowest distance ring/range; I estimate the distance between aircraft was less than a mile and the traffic was at about our twelve to one o'clock position. The traffic's altitude indicated 700 feet below our current altitude while we were descending before I looked away from the screen. I believe the traffic continued on a converging trajectory relative to our position prompting the Controller to re-issue the traffic alert combined with the immediate left turn heading assignment. I am not sure if the Controller did not receive our first acknowledgement of their Traffic Alert or if it was the fact the Controller saw our targets practically merge on their scope; but the tone in the Controller's re-issuance of the clearance convinced me the conflicting traffic had closed the distance between our aircraft and I was more focused on flying away from the traffic than verifying our distance by staring at the screen. My copilot confirmed the altitude separation was as little as 400 feet on screen and the traffic's position along with our position had merged on screen. At first glance; our distance to the conflicting aircraft appeared so close; I didn't have enough time to try to gauge the aircraft's performance or our convergence trajectory on screen. At that moment I felt there was not enough distance between us to wait for a Resolution Advisory from our TCAS System either. I discontinued the descent and level-off assignment of 7;000 and initiated an immediate power and pitch up maneuver. As a result; I climbed about 1;000 feet about our then current altitude of approximately 7;700 to an altitude of approximated 8;700 and the speed of our aircraft increased by about 30 knots from approximately 250 knots to approximately 280 knots indicated airspeed. When I was clear of conflict; I resumed the descent to 7;000 feet; resumed normal speed and complied with the Controller's new clearance. I am convinced the Controller's immediate left turn heading assignment alone was not sufficient to avoid the conflict. While performing the evasive maneuver; I heard the Controller correcting another aircraft on frequency advising them of a possible pilot deviation by that aircraft; however I don't recall if the term 'Pilot Deviation' was actually used and am not sure if that aircraft the Controller corrected was the same aircraft that caused our Traffic Alert/ Traffic Advisory. The Controller seemed extremely busy at this time; so we opted not to query the Controller on frequency regarding our near-miss. The area in which this occurred lies just north of DVT airport near a practice area; an area notorious for intensive pilot training. The brightly lit city lights on a clear night sky while descending may have masked the exterior lights of the conflicting aircraft just ahead and below us; as we never caught a visual of the aircraft.
Report_1_Synopsis: Pilot reported taking evasive action to avoid a mid-air collision during descent north of DVT airport. Pilot stated there was not enough distance from the aircraft to wait for an RA from TCAS. Reportedly; the area is near a practice area known for intensive pilot training activity.

Report_1_Narrative: Upon second lap around the pattern on ZZZ; I heard Aircraft Y calling 5 miles away with intend to join pattern behind downwind traffic in sight. That radio call came right came in between my Student Pilot call from crosswind to downwind. And there was another aircraft that was just passing the numbers. I made a second left downwind RWY XX call in case my Student Pilot's position call wasn't heard.I was passing mid-runway point and couldn't see the airplane that was joining pattern. Aircraft Y reported 45 degree entry ; left downwind [Runway] XX behind downwind traffic. After I passed the abeam point; I instructed Student Pilot to not turn base nor descend until ahead traffic passed our wing; in which we had momentarily lost sight as they were doing a very wide pattern. At that moment; Aircraft Y and I were about to collide. Aircraft Y was positioned/ entering traffic on left base instead of downwind; behind us; as they called previously. I took controls from Student Pilot executing an evasive maneuver; steep left turn from base to final; while trying to not collide with aircraft on final that had just passed us. Aircraft Y made a turn to their right. No one was hurt nor lost aircraft control.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Instructor reported an NMAC event during traffic pattern training due to inaccurate communication and pattern entry by the conflict aircraft.

Report_1_Narrative: Another aircraft was cleared through ZZZ airspace en route to ZZZ1 and was approved to do so via ZZZ Tower; which indicated that it did not have a visual on that aircraft. ZZZ does not have radar.I was cleared for takeoff on ZZZ Runway XX around the same time. Tower gave a frequency change to the other aircraft approximately one minute later and advised them of the aircraft taking off (me). The other aircraft responded that they were looking for traffic. Tower gave me a frequency change one to two minutes after that and advised me of the other aircraft.I was unable to spot the aircraft; but saw them on my traffic system and used the visual display and audio traffic alerts to avoid the other aircraft. I kept searching for the plane; climbing away from their flight path during this time; but even so; the traffic system indicated that we came within 100 vertical feet of each other.I believe that ZZZ Tower should have visually identified the transiting aircraft prior to clearing me for takeoff; or required me to identify the other aircraft prior to clearing me for takeoff. Both aircraft were in ZZZ airspace at the time of the event; and yet I am fairly certain that the controller did not have a visual on either of us (but certainly not on the other aircraft).If in this situation in the future; I will delay my takeoff until I have identified any aircraft that could become a hazard during my takeoff and climb-out. In addition; I will execute a turn away from the other aircraft; even when in controlled airspace.
Report_1_Synopsis: P-28 Pilot reported an NMAC event during takeoff departure. Additionally; pilot reported concerns regarding ATC's handling of airport departure and transiting traffic.

Report_1_Narrative: During an aerial survey flight at approximately 16;500 feet the flight crew observed a drone pass 1 to 2 feet over the left wing tip of the aircraft. The drone was estimated 3 to 5 feet in diameter. It appeared to be a white color. It happened too quickly to describe the shape and dimensions with any degree of accuracy. Same goes for the direction of the craft. There would have been absolutely no chance of taking evasive action given how fast the event occurred. Same company has observed a drone at 15;500 [feet.] with a similar size and a near miss within 20 feet in the past.
Report_1_Synopsis: A Pilot conducting an Aerial Survey mission reported a near miss with a unmanned aerial vehicle.

Report_1_Narrative: I was pilot in command of a tail wheel airplane. The purpose of the flight was to maintain tail wheel proficiency. I was seated in the forward pilot station with a passenger seated in the aft pilot station. We departed to proceed to ZZZ with the intention of performing upper airwork maneuvers enroute to a landing at ZZZ to exchange pilot stations. Winds at takeoff were reported SW at 6 knots.On our arrival at ZZZ the automated weather was reporting winds as SW 8G16. The main Runway XX/XY [at] ZZZ is closed for resurfacing and the taxiway 'A' is marked as the temporary runway. The midfield windsock indicated the winds were generally SW 8G16 with some intermittent change to W and continuing intermittent gusts. On final approach to Runway XX the apparent winds were significantly more westerly. The aircraft touched down on the right main gear first. I used forward elevator to keep the horizontal stabilizer and rudder in an airflow that kept them aerodynamically effective. As the left main gear touched down I applied additional right aileron to arrest sideway drift and left pedal to maintain runway longitudinal alignment.  As the tail wheel was about to touchdown the rudder became ineffective for maintaining runway alignment I applied left braking action but was unable to maintain runway heading and the nose of the aircraft yawed right and the aircraft exited the runway. As the aircraft weathervaned further nose right it slid sideways a short distance and the left wing tip contacted the ground. The aircraft was partially on the runway. Both tires were inflated and there was no apparent damage to the left wing. I elected to apply power and maneuver the aircraft clear of the runway and taxi into the ramp area of ZZZ to secure and inspect the aircraft.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Instructor reported a ground loop on landing in gusty wind conditions.

Report_1_Narrative: I filed IFR flight plan. The flight was uneventful. I was cleared by ZZZ Center to descend to 10;000 feet MSL. I confirmed that clearance. I descended and was level for a minute or so when the Controller said to climb back up to 11;000 feet which was the altitude to which Controller cleared me. That was incorrect and would have been the wrong altitude for that direction of flight. The Controller admitted on the radio [to] working six frequencies at once. There was no traffic conflict. I think it is unfortunate that the Controller was so busy and the transmissions revealed Controller was very new on the job but the Supervisor should have helped out. Controller cleared me to 10;000 feet about a minute after Controller told me to climb up to 11;000 feet. Controller was clearly confused.
Report_1_Synopsis: Corporate Captain reported the Controller was working 6 frequencies at once and issued an incorrect altitude clearance.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Workload; Training / Qualification; Situational Awareness; Distraction; Confusion
Report_1_Narrative: Aircraft X was descended to 3;000 feet by the trainee with control from the adjacent TRACON sector. We didn't talk to him soon enough to offer a 30 degree intercept for the RNAV Approach.  We vectored him back around after requesting control from the other TRACON again. We were discussing assigning 2;000 feet to Aircraft Y landing at a different airport. The trainee turned Aircraft X heading 340; which I questioned and suggested heading 270. When the trainee issued the amended heading; she also descended Aircraft X to 2;000 feet. I did not catch it as during the same time; the trainee had released Aircraft Y off one airport and Aircraft Z off another airport; who were in conflict; in addition to an air carrier departure requesting practice approaches. I took over the frequency; and noticed Aircraft X already at 2;000 feet but he was not quite established on the approach and therefore; assigned an altitude below the Minimum Vectoring Altitude. When doing something out of the ordinary  the controller trying to help could also put the aircraft on a better heading to intercept especially when we never approved the aircraft descending to 3;000 feet. Offer Aircraft X a different RNAV approach or offer to run the approach for the lows. The Low Altitude Alert never alarmed.
Report_1_Synopsis: TRACON Controller conducting on the job training reported they did not hear the trainee descend an aircraft to an altitude below the Minimum Vectoring Altitude because they were distracted by the trainee releasing aircraft off airports that were on conflicting routes.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Situational Awareness; Other / Unknown; Distraction; Communication Breakdown
Person_2_Human_Factors: Workload; Troubleshooting; Situational Awareness; Communication Breakdown
Report_1_Narrative: Sat in ZZZ for hours for a delayed flight coming from ZZZ1. During the swap; the outgoing Captain informed me that the Crew that brought the aircraft into ZZZ1 said that upon landing the right thrust reverser malfunctioned. The delay was due to Contract Maintenance MEL'ing the right thrust reverser. During pre-flight I checked the logbook; Release; and stickers as well as looked up the MEL on my EFB. During this time the 'A' Flight Attendant informed me that a passenger was refusing to wear their mask and creating a scene and that the CSR had been called. Eventually the passenger was removed and an updated report was sent to the aircraft. During the distraction I neglected to click on the hyperlink in the MEL in the Maintenance portion labeled MEL SP#XX Thrust Reverser System. If I had I would have noticed on that a Circuit Breaker for the #2 Engine should have been pulled and collared. Upon landing in ZZZ2 I informed the outgoing Captain of the MEL. During my commute home I received a text from said Captain that he found the wrong CB had been collared and that he had written it up and ZZZ2 Maintenance was fixing the issue. Upon reviewing the SP#XX I can only assume that the CB for the #1 Engine had been pulled instead.
Report_2_Narrative: Inbound Captain advised that they had received the aircraft late in ZZZ due to Thrust Reverser MEL applied in ZZZ1 on previous flight and then further delayed on their flight due to a Passenger refusing to comply with mask requirements.In reviewing the logbook I found that the MEL sticker in the front of the logbook was not completed. The MEL number was not entered; the Special procedures performed were not entered and the circuit breakers pulled and collared were not entered.   When I reviewed the logbook entry; the special procedures were references SP-XX.  I also observed C/B's  #2 Engine TR Sync Lock and #2 Engine TR INTLK pulled and collared.I then reviewed the MEL and SP-XX and discovered the following errors.1. SP XX calls for the #2 Engine TR Sync Lock c/b and the #2 Engine TR Control c/b to be pulled and collared.  the Control C/B was NOT collared as prescribed in SP XXnd the INTLK c/b WAS collared contrary to SP XX2. There was no MEL sticker placed on the Inoperative TR lever.3. There was no MEL sticker placed above the respected N1 gauge.I contacted Maintenance Control to confirm my understanding of the MEL regarding the incorrect Circuit Breakers and they confirmed the wrong circuit breaker had been pulled.  Notified ZZZ2 Maintenance and entered the discrepancy in the logbook. ZZZ2 Maintenance arrived and corrected the circuit breaker configuration and signed off the discrepancy I had entered. Missing information on the logbook sticker was also corrected.I have long felt that our MEL is VERY inadequate when it comes to circuit breaker identification.  In this particular instance the nomenclature is correct and was just applied incorrectly by the Mechanic; but if the C/B locations were included  it would have been much more apparent to the Mechanic as well as flight crew that the two C/B would not be immediately adjacent to each other.  I have brought this to the attention of Flight Ops previously with regards to other MEL's and have been advised that changes are slated for a future revision that has been delayed due to aircraft out of service returns; COVID and other issues. I also feel it should be reinforced to flight crews that MEL compliance is not solely the responsibility of the Maintenance department and that we should always verify (to the limits of our abilities) those aspects of MEL compliance which we have ready access to on each airplane we accept regardless of previous crews acceptance of the aircraft.
Report_1_Synopsis: Two air carrier captains reported delays due to incorrect MEL procedures performed by maintenance and a passenger not complying with face mask policy.

Report_1_Narrative: About XX minutes after we reached our cruise altitude; my FO (First Officer) and I observed the level on our #2 Oil Qty gauge go from 11 to Y then Z; then blank rather quickly.  It had been normal up until then; we just caught the decrease at 11. After checking the QRC and QRH for Low Oil Qty to no avail; we noticed our #2 Oil Pressure dropping. It stabilized at 29 psi but fluctuated from XX to XY with 29 being the median amber band.  This continued for the remainder of the flight until TOD (Top of Descent).  I referenced the Engine Low Oil Pressure Checklist in the QRH on Page X.XX.  It states that if the oil pressure is at or below the redline: Go to the Engine Failure or Shutdown checklist on Page X.XY. The oil pressure never reached the redline; so the checklist stops there.  All other engine parameters were normal with no vibration.  My FO (First Officer) continued to fly and talk with ATC while I set up a phone patch with our Dispatcher as I decided that there was too much information to use ACARS.  I told them what was going on and that we were continuing on to ZZZ but we were also prepared to divert if need be later on.  They were in agreement as there was no need or requirement at this time to shut the engine down or divert.  I talked with the Flight Attendants and we had a good discussion about the situation.  I told them that our aircraft was operating just fine and that it seems that we have an indication issue and that I was not going to make a PA.  I also asked them if they could discretely look at the aft portion of the right hand engine to see if they saw any oil.  My FO (First Officer) and Flight Attendants did a great job along with our Dispatcher and Maintenance Control.  Later in the flight; our Dispatcher gave us single engine landing data for ZZZ.  Descending into ZZZ when the thrust levers were slowly retarded to idle; the oil pressure and qty actually increased.  By the time we were on final approach; the said indications were normal.
Report_1_Synopsis: B737 MAX 8 Captain reported shortly after arriving at cruise altitude the number 2 Engine oil quantity indication rapidly decreased and extinguished. During approach all indications returned to normal.

Report_1_Narrative: 7 mins after pushback at ZZZ; waiting on the ramp; engines shut down. APU on save fuel for our 20 mins ATC hold. Passenger advised FA they forgot to takeout the spare lithium battery from there valet bag. FA advised CA; Captain called dispatch and advised agreeing we are unable to take flight until the battery is removed from the cargo compartment. We pulled back into the gate found passenger's battery had her remove it. Operation continued as normal after removal.The cause of the event was that Passenger did not advise gate of battery after being asked if there are any lithium batteries in the bag (according to ZZZ manager). Reporter recommends start the [special] tag process prior to boarding and make another announcement making sure there is no batteries in there [special] tag bag. Rethink/possible rewording of battery announcement for more/better clarification.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Captain reported an uneventful flight after a ground gate return at departure to remove spare lithium battery from passenger bag in cargo compartment.

Report_1_Narrative: We conducted the ZZZZZ4 arrival and joined the ILS XX approach from ZZZZZ [Intersection] as briefed. When the Captain contacted the Tower; the Controller cleared us to land XX Right. The Captain read back the clearance. I said; 'Can you confirm Controller wants us to land on the right? We're on the ILS XX Left.' The Captain confirmed with the Controller cleared to land on the right. The Controller responded 'Affirmative. XX Right; Cleared to land.' At the time; we were well above 1;000 feet in visual conditions with the runway in sight and; so I had no objection. I clicked off the autopilot and side-stepped to XX Right and we landed. No issues arose with ATC or any other traffic. The next day; the Captain reached out to me and we spoke over the phone. Captain learned that we had actually been cleared for the ILS XX Right approach and Captain intended to file a report. A couple of days later I was finally able to confirm that this was correct. We aren't able to determine if it was being read back correctly or incorrectly; but there was never a clarification type of response from ZZZ Approach. It's also important to bring up that the Captain was wearing a face mask throughout the flight operations which did contribute to difficulties in communication with myself and with ATC at various times during the trip. This likely was a contributing factor to our deviation. Another contributing factor was the violation of sterile cockpit below 18;000 feet by the Captain and myself. Personally; I was distracted by our conversation as well as the fact that Captain was wearing a mask during the flight.Complacency is also a factor as the ZZZZZ4 Arrival usually results in the ILS or visual to XX Left.I think our company needs to take a harder stance on mask-wearing during flight operations in the flight deck.  I recommend that the company forbids the use of masks by pilots during flight operations to ensure that communications are clear and effective. In this case; it can be assumed that the Captain was repeating the clearance saying 'XX Left' but the Controller did not hear it clearly and assumed Captain was saying XX Right. Therefore; Captain was never corrected and we continued with what we had expected in our heads. There were multiple points throughout our trip that ATC did not understand the Captain and asked who was calling or needed clarification on what Captain was saying because it was difficult to understand with the mask. I thought on several occasions throughout our trip that it was the Captain's choice to wear it but if we have an emergency situation that I really hope Captain would take it off so that effective communication could be established and maintained. An emergency situation did not occur; but clearly an issue did arise with our approach to our destination.
Report_2_Narrative: ZZZ had a broken layer at 1;700 feet and we were expecting to do an approach. Descending into ZZZ on the ZZZZZ4 arrival we had set up for the ILS [Runway] XXL. We were assigned to join the ILS [Runway] XXR at ZZZZZ [Intersection] and then later cleared for the ILS XXR approach. We did not fly the ILS XXR. We flew the XXL approach and when we were on with Tower; we told them we were inbound on the ILS XXL. Tower cleared us to land XXR. By the time we contacted Tower we were out of the clouds and could see the runway. We verified two times that we were cleared to land XXR and not XXL. And Tower confirmed that we were to land XXR. Since we had visual on the runway; we side stepped and landed on XXR. We were probably at 1;500-1;600 feet AFE when we side stepped. We were confused as to why they had changed runways on us; but we knew that XXR was longer than XXL and that the landing speeds were the same and we were familiar with the airport. As we side stepped; I programmed in the ILS XXR so that we had a backup source even though we visually had the airport in sight. Later in the evening it still didn't sit right with me that we had a runway change that late; especially since we had been on an IFR approach. I realized we had in fact been assigned ILS XXR all the way back on with Approach. They never corrected me. So; I either read it back correctly but we were really hearing what we wanted to hear (ILS XXL) or they never corrected me and we all missed it. The approach was stable all the way through for XXL and the sidestep was done in a safe manner.I attribute not being sterile in the descent as a factor even though we were assigned to join ILS XXR at ZZZZZ prior to FL180. I would say complacency and expectancy were the primary factors. XXL wasn't closed and we were set that we would be doing the ILS XXL. It was also the last leg on the last day of our trip and we had had a long day. I had been up since 8 or 9am and we had flown 4 legs. This flight landed around XApm.I can say that I once again am reminded how serious our jobs are and that miss hearing a simple 'L' vs 'R' can be life changing. I can only say that I am thankful that this took place during a low traffic period and that we were able to maintain a safe condition. I'm honestly not too sure how to avoid this situation. I believe that writing down my clearances would assist in allowing me to verify and that maybe I need to make sure to turn my headset up so that I won't miss ATC.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier flight crew reported a track heading deviation during approach due to communication issues with ATC.  The First Officer cited the Captain wearing a face mask on the flight deck may have contributed to the communication problems with ATC and between them.
