Report_1_Narrative: The Captain refused to brief me along with other crew members because I asked to maintain the appropriate amount of social distance.Captain told me to go to the back if I didn't want to come closer. Not receiving a crew briefing jeopardizes the entire crew along with the passengers.[Suggest] for the Captain when time permits; to brief the crew or brief us individually.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Attendant reported the Captain did not give a crew briefing after the Flight Attendant asked for social distancing.

Report_1_Narrative: After completing a fuel stop at PEO; I taxied from the fuel pump near the FBO to Runway 28 for departure. Prior to taxiing I completed my pre-taxi checks and self announced my taxi on CTAF. The wind was 220@17G23 and I wanted to complete my run up into the wind. Runway 28/10 doesn't have a parallel taxiway to the East requiring a back taxi for approximately the half the runway length. The runway; departure and arrival corridor appeared clear and I announced taking the runway for back taxi with no other traffic heard. I completed a short run up; scanned the runway and announced on CTAF I was taking off Runway 28. I applied power; checked instruments and accelerated down the runway. Shortly I noted something in the distance down the runway; a second later noticed engines rise above the crest of the the runway and I immediately aborted takeoff. I was close to rotation speed; pulled power back and aggressively braked. Once at a safe speed I announced I was aborting and vacating the runway. I was close the the north/south taxi and uneventfully exited the runway at that point. At that time I saw a Falcon jet exit runway 10/28 via the next taxiway about 800 feet down the runway heading to the fuel pumps. I turned my aircraft around announced my back taxi and departure. Concerned that I had an equipment issue or was on the wrong frequency I asked for a radio check while I was departing downwind and received a good check. Due to a significant crown/slope in the runway it is not possible to see the opposite ends of the Runway 28/10. The other aircraft operator should follow the best practices identified in AC 90-66b par 10.1 self-announce their intentions and monitor the frequency for other traffic as well. Additionally; the aircraft was taxiing from the west hangars to the fuel pumps and if there's sufficient wingtip clearance they should use the parallel taxiway instead of the runway as an increased measure of safety.
Report_1_Synopsis: M30C pilot reported while on takeoff roll; traffic was observed landing opposite direction not on CTAF. Resulted in taking evasive action.

Report_1_Narrative: I was wrapping up a long training flight with my instructor and we were practicing approaches and landings before wraping up for the day. On the third landing approach there was a Cessna 150 ahead of us in the pattern.  I extended the downwind to make room and turned base and final much further out than typical. One of the things we had been practicing is making sure to be low enough on the approach to not overshoot since it is such a short runway.  On this approach I was quite low and setup a little low on final when I realized that while I had seen the C150 land I wasn't certain it had cleared the runway. I thought it might still be on there and asked my instructor if we should go around. He said no and to go ahead and land since we didn't see the other aircraft on the runway anymore and we would be landing very short. The previous loop around the pattern I initiated a go around because it didn't feel right but was assured that we were setup just right for landing and should've landed.  I think that I was reluctant to do another go around 'for no reason' if I didn't need to according to the instructor.Shortly after landing and rolling out several feet and up the incline in the runway we saw the other airplane at the far end. At just about the same time we heard frantic calls for the other airplane to get off the runway as soon as possible.  I was setup for a short field landing and exited the runway after a very short landing roll about 1;700 feet from where the other aircraft had exited the runway.  We were shaken from the realization that we had shared the runway and scared the other training aircraft.Contributing factors:1. Fatigue- This was one of the first training sessions after a 4 month break and my instructor and I were exhausted.2. Human Factors - I deferred to my instructors experience and decided against the go around.  We have since discussed this issue and agreed that if either of us feel a go around is a good idea we will go around.3. Airport -  The runway X landing zone is at a significantly lower elevation than the XX end of the runway. because of the geography is difficult to see aircraft at the other end.
Report_1_Synopsis: Pilot reported a Critical Ground conflict during landing rollout with opposite direction non-reporting traffic.

Report_1_Narrative: My aircraft does not have ADSB. If I depart Merrill to the north and do not receive the Part 93 deviation from ATC; then because of the combination of Part 93 and the ADSB requirement over Anchorage Class C; I am required to fly over Cook Inlet below 600 ft. MSL; which puts the aircraft in a position out of gliding distance to land. Recent local memory has multiple examples of this situation ending in a fatality. There is a large number of general aviation aircraft operating in the Anchorage area that are ADSB negative and that fatal outcome is likely to occur again in the future due to the airspace rule combinations currently in place.
Report_1_Synopsis: General Aviation pilot who operates in the Anchorage Alaska terminal area reports complying with local Special Federal Air Regulations places aircraft in a position that they are unable to safely reach an airport to land in the case of an engine out landing.

Report_1_Narrative: While navigating to a fix ATC inquired as to where we were navigating. I responded direct to the fix ZZZ1. Our FMS showed us 2 miles south. ATC came back and said we were in fact 12 miles from ZZZ1  so at that point I knew our GPS wasn't working. I asked for vectors to the airport and they were provided. Upon an uneventful landing our GPS still showed us 34 miles from the airport when we were sitting on the ramp.
Report_1_Synopsis: A Pilot reported receiving false information from their GPS.

Report_1_Narrative: I was the Pilot Monitoring (PM) on the flight to ZZZ. Descending on the ZZZZZ FIVE arrival heading to the ZZZZZ1 fix. Approximately 20 miles from the ZZZZZ1 fix ATC called and revised the fixes after ZZZZZ1 but told us to comply with all the restrictions. The ZZZZZ1 fix includes a crossing restriction of 27000 feet. I read back the new clearance and confirm it with the Captain/PF. Done; then I went heads down to re-program the FMS including changing the landing runway.As I transfer my eyes back to the PFD to continue with the PM duties; I noticed the altitude at approximately 25;000 feet. I pointed the deviation to the Captain who stopped the descent.  No traffic conflict was issued by ATC and we continued with the arrival using the depicted profile. While I have the primary duty of PM there are additional duties such as the checklist; FMS Programing; radio calls etc.; that can distract us at important times. Compounding the situation was long days with five legs and 10 plus hours of duty. On top of that; due to the COVID crisis; we are operating with reduced staff and salary freeze creating additional stress and fatigue. I think prioritizing the duties is important and an art. Yet sometimes we reach limits and we don't recognize it.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air taxi First Officer reported an altitude deviation during arrival and cited short staffing; fatigue and stress due to the COVID-19 pandemic as contributing factors.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Situational Awareness; Distraction; Communication Breakdown; Confusion
Report_1_Narrative: Aircraft X was IFR inbound to ZZZ requesting the LOC RWY XX; however; the tower still on their COVID hours closes early. When the tower closed they put the localizer on RWY YY so the LOC RWY XX was unavailable. Due to winds Aircraft X was unable RWY YY. They requested the RNAV Y RWY XX. I had traffic for Aircraft X as they were approaching ZZZZZ with the crossing altitude of 051 and the traffic at 047 I gave a restriction for traffic. This confused the pilot so I went back and cancelled the approach clearance and told the pilot to expect clearance at ZZZZZ1; but this was a mistake; what I meant to say was ZZZZZ. The pilot did not question me but did seem confused. Rightfully so. When Aircraft X was clear of the traffic they reported that they were direct ZZZZZ. I then cleared Aircraft X to cross ZZZZZ at 5;100 cleared straight in RNAV Y Rwy XX approach. Aircraft X appeared to over shoot ZZZZZ before turning to ZZZZZ2. I questioned the pilot that the next fix past ZZZZZ was ZZZZZ2; is that where they show their self going. The pilot stated they just passed ZZZZZ2 and I can't quite understand what they said after that. But at the time I thought they said going to ZZZZZ3 the next fix on the approach. While this was going on I had a couple other aircraft waiting and another facility call me for point outs. When my attention took me back to Aircraft X their path appeared off and had began a go around and the moment they called me I issued the low altitude alert and an immediate climb. They attempted the approach and landed safely on the second attempt. My initial reaction to this approach was that something was off; which is when I questioned the pilot. I gave them the benefit of the doubt and hoped that they had corrected the overshoot at ZZZZZ and was properly on the RNAV Y RWY XX at ZZZ. However; I should have just gone with my gut and broke the aircraft off the approach when I noticed the error and vectored back around for a second attempt. Hindsight when you look back is always better. We try to not delay aircraft and hope that they are truthful when we question them about approaches. However; safety is our number one priority and concern and I did feel like there was something not right and looking back I wish I would have just broken the aircraft off the approach and re-sequenced. It is always easier to watch a replay to see how we can improve; but that is important so we do not repeat our mistakes.
Report_1_Synopsis: TRACON Controller reported having an aircraft that wanted one approach; but the tower was closed and the approaches were set up for the opposite direction.  Controller reported possibly confusing pilot with clearances.

Report_1_Narrative: Captain advised we had a maintenance issue to have checked out before boarding our return flight to ZZZ. I believe pilots saw something had leaked under the engine; observed by FO walk around. Mechanic looked for AC left engine fuel leak suspected by pilots; after a period of time (I do not recall) mechanic could not find leak; he signed off on logbook. Pax began boarding; entry door was closed; on push back; FA's were doing safety demo when FA 4 was called over by passenger sitting in right window seat a few rows aft of the wing. Passenger stated something was dripping from wing. Demo was almost complete; FA 4 continued with demo then looked out to see pax concern. Upon seeing fluid dripping from several places along the underside of the wing; she went to get another FA to see the issue. FA 4 took FA 3 to see the dripping. FA 4 and 3 went to the forward entry area to inform FA 1; I was working FA 4 and standing next to FA 1 so I was also informed at this time. FA 1 called Captain (CA) to advise. Several minutes later we were notified by CA that we were going back to gate and need to disarm doors. Same mechanic (only one I saw) returned. Passengers remained onboard while he checked the issue further. It is my understanding he reported he still found no leak. Sometime later CA advised crew and passengers via PA that we would be starting engines at the gate to further troubleshoot the problem; he advised passengers to remain seated. I was told this test was done at the Captain's request; not the instruction of this mechanic. Engine test was completed; seat belt sign turned off; more time passed and it was decided to deplane passengers. While crew waited on the AC for info from the company as to our schedule and whether this plane was going to be able to be repaired; our FO showed CA a video of the fuel leak while the engine test was running. I saw this video; fuel was pouring from the engine like a running garden hose. CA stated he had no confidence in this mechanics ability to perform his job as he appeared that he had no idea how to handle it. While I was discussing this with CA he told me he asked the mechanic earlier to call Company Maintenance base for instruction. The mechanic told CA yes he did call Company. CA told me he was angry with this mechanic because he himself called Company and was told mechanic did not contact them.  Aircraft was taken out of service hours later.
Report_2_Narrative: Upon arrival at Gate 1 in ZZZ; ground personnel connected to headset after engine shutdown to report a fluid leaking from number 1 (left) engine. He smelled his fingers; reported that it smelled like fuel; and asked me to investigate the fluid. The First Officer and I both investigated; and felt; to the best of our knowledge; that the fluid smelled like fuel. At that point; there was a puddle under the #1 engine; 3 feet in diameter; and fuel was dripping at a rate of 2-3 drips per second. As we stood there discussing; the dripping reduced to 1 drip every 4-5 seconds. The FO and I agreed that we were unfamiliar with any allowable drips on the 737 MAX LEAP engines; and I proceeded to the cockpit to make an entry in the aircraft logbook; dispatch a code in ACARS; and call the Maintenance Control to coordinate for a maintenance technician. The technician arrived and we conferred on the above information; and he proceeded to investigate and coordinate with the maintenance team in Company (my assumptions; although I did hear his telephone conversation at one point). After his investigation; he returned to the cockpit to inform me that he had opened the engine cowl; performed his checks; and found all valves ready for service. He signed off the write up and dispatched the aircraft for service. We boarded the passengers and pushed from the gate at XA:40. Push back was normal; engine start on engine #2 was normal. After push back was complete; we started engine #1. After engine start; and after the push crew had disconnected and given me a salute; ground personnel came back; pointing to the #1 engine. At the same time; the Cabin Crew called to alert me to a passenger that was reporting fluid leaking from the RIGHT side of the aircraft; and a Flight Attendant confirmed that we were leaking fluid. The report that fluid was leaking from the right was incongruous; and caused the FO and I a couple minutes to confer and investigate what that could be. We later found out the leak was in fact from the LEFT side; and was from the #1 engine. I did note in my investigation; that the #1 main tank fuel quantity differed from the #2 main tank fuel quantity by nearly 400 lbs; a discrepancy that didn't exist before pushback as I had noted the fuel during the Before Start checklist. By this time; the same ground coordinator who had reported the previous leak connected to headset and reported that we were again leaking fuel from the #1 engine. His report was that fuel was gushing out from under the engine cowl. The FO and I coordinated and elected to taxi back to the gate to expedite arrival and engine shutdown. The ground crew quickly assembled and we returned to the gate at approximately XA:48; and shut down both engines. I made another logbook entry and called Maintenance Control to inform them that we had returned to the gate and required the maintenance technician to perform more checks before we could depart. The maintenance technician returned; and we performed an engine run at the gate on the #1 engine; which resulted in identifying a large fuel leak; with the technician recording video. At this point the aircraft was taken out of service; and I began coordinating with station personnel and Crew Scheduling for subsequent actions.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Attendant reported to Flight Crew that a passenger noticed liquid streaming from wing and Captain elected to return to the gate. The liquid was later determined to be fuel and the aircraft was taken out of service.

Report_1_Narrative: My Captain and I were in the descent phase of our flight initially level at 4;000 feet MSL while on frequency with DFW TRACON.My Captain and I both heard the Controller give us a descent clearance to 2;400 feet MSL; we both accepted the clearance and my Captain read back/acknowledged the clearance to ATC.The clearance to descend to 2;400 feet did not seem unusual or out of place as we were approximately 20 NM from the RBD airport; upon leveling our aircraft at 2;400 feet my Captain and I were discussing visually seeing radio towers at our 11o'clock and approximately 10 SM in ahead and to the left of our flight path and we were expecting to be vectored around the obstacles.A few seconds after we had discussed the mentioned radio towers DFW TRACON challenged our altitude of 2;400 feet insisting we were supposed to be at 4;000 feet MSL upon hearing that radio call; and confirming with ATC we expeditiously initiated a climb back to 4;000 feet.At no point in the flight did I feel like we were in danger or in an un-safe proximity to the obstacle radio towers or in the vicinity any other aircraft as we were in VMC conditions; with good visibility.In my perspective; the Controller seemed to be over worked at the time of the occurrence and did not verify with my Captain after his read back to descend to 2;400 feet; indicating we had read back a correct clearance.After completing our flight; getting ready to taxi into parking on the ground at RBD; we were informed there was a similar sounding aircraft call sign on frequency and that the descent clearance to 2;400 feet was for the similar sounding call sign and not for us.We were also informed that we were 'stepped on' during our radio transmission; unknown to us during our read back to DFW TRACON to descend to 2;400 feet. It seems to me DFW TRACON should have confirmed who was supposed to descend to 2;400 feet when they did not receive a clear read back.
Report_2_Narrative: While descending for landing at the Dallas executive airport; we were given a delayed descent with a crossing restriction which required an expedited descent. We hustled down and made the assigned crossing altitude restriction.  Shortly following that; we were assigned a new frequency and cleared to descend to 4;000 feet.  We initiated a normal descent and almost at the same time we were leveling; we were cleared to descend to 2;400.I acknowledged the clearance to descend on the radio and we initiated a normal descent to 2;400 feet.  As we were descending; I pointed out the radio towers at our 11 O'clock position to my co-pilot.  My thoughts were that the controller would give us a slight vector to the right; otherwise I would request a turn.Very shortly after that; the Controller challenged our altitude.  I replied that we were cleared to descent and that I had acknowledged the descent. The Controller stated that they needed us back at 4;000.  We immediately complied.The Controller appeared to be very busy.  I tried to keep all communication correct and prompt.  In speaking with the ATC person he stated that there was another aircraft with the same registration ending - same letter and that the Controller referred to that aircraft with an abbreviated call sign.In my opinion; if the Controller does not get a clear read back from an aircraft; especially if there are similar call signs on frequency -- then the Controller should state 'That clearance was for N--- only' I have heard that many times.'Contributing to this was the fact that there were several aircraft that the Controller was working and may have been challenged doing so.I never felt in danger at any time as we saw the radio towers and am not aware of any conflict with any other aircraft in our proximity.
Report_1_Synopsis: Corporate flight crew reported a similar call sign communication issue with TRACON resulted in an altitude deviation and CFTT event during approach to RBD airport.

Report_1_Narrative: We were 3rd in line for takeoff at ZZZ and it was particularly busy. There was a lot of rotary traffic present in the right pattern as I believe there was a helicopter event present. We had been having breakfast at the cafe and witnessed 4-5 Cessna 172's doing power off approach so they were in the left pattern. When we were holding short of [Runway] XX @ [Taxiway] A we could hear the Controller on tower was busy and we waited for around 10 minutes. In that time; myself and the PIC who was left seat agreed that it was standard traffic pattern; I checked the sectional to confirm. We made a comment that perhaps rotary traffic was using the right pattern for separation. We got called by Tower and the Controller thanked us for our patience and said Runway XX clear for takeoff. We proceeded to takeoff and climbed in the upwind to around 650 feet before making a turn to the left. Whilst we were in the crosswind segment; still climbing we noticed a plane that appeared to be 200-300 feet below us in right downwind for Runway XY off to our left; on its way to pass underneath us. It was probably 600 feet away when we first noticed it and it passed underneath our nose. We were both puzzled as to what they were doing. Once we were clear of them; we made another left turn into left downwind for XX the Controller came on the radio and said to us that we had come very close to 'my' ILS traffic for ZZZ1 and that they had it written down that we had requested right traffic; which was incorrect. Our inactions were verifying left or right traffic; assuming left traffic was standard especially due to all the rotary traffic using the right downwind for XX. The Controller was particularly busy and perhaps as we were heading to ZZZ1 they figured it was more direct to make right traffic. We climbed to 200 feet of TPA [Traffic Pattern Altitude] on the upwind so to make sure we were as close to TPA before being in Downwind at the wrong altitude.
Report_2_Narrative: We were cleared for takeoff for Runway XX.  Prior to takeoff; I was monitoring entry of all aircraft entering the traffic pattern.  Helicopters were on right downwind Runway XX; while fix-winged were entering left downwind Runway XX.  I never communicated which way I was going to turn crosswind since I was following the other aircraft that have been in the pattern throughout the morning.  After departure; I climbed to about 700 feet and started to monitor other traffic in the area prior to making my crosswind turn.  I saw a small aircraft to the left of me that was descending about 200-300 feet below.  I then started to make a left crosswind turn from XX0 degrees to approximately YY0 degrees.  I flew over the traffic and continued heading south for ZZZ2.  ZZZ Tower Controller then addressed me on the radio that they had me down for a right downwind turn.  I never once communicated I was making a right downwind turn nor heard the Controller mention; 'make right crosswind upon departure'.  If I wasn't supposed to make a left crosswind because of other traffic on an ILS for ZZZ1; why didn't the Controller mention that to me prior to departure?  I would have gladly complied and made a right crosswind turn and continued my course to ZZZ2.
Report_1_Synopsis: GA pilots reported an NMAC occurred when they departed the traffic pattern using standard left traffic procedures; although the Tower Controller expected them to use right traffic.

Report_1_Narrative: After takeoff; during climb phase; clearance was given from ZZZ Approach [Control] to climb restrict to 12.000 feet direct ZZZZZ intersection. When crossing 10;500 feet; ZZZ Approach instructed to call ZZZ Center on frequency XYZ.AB. I did try to call ZZZ [Center] on XYZ.AB several times; but no contact received. I could listen ZZZ Center very weak on XYZ.AB; and could listen the other aircraft communicating. I tried to ask another aircraft for a relay between me and ZZZ Center; but no answer. No answer from ZZZ [Center] also. I tried to contact back ZZZ Approach and ask for a different frequency; but had no answer from ZZZ Approach also. I started looking on my charts and started calling ZZZ Center on other frequencies; but no answer again. I tried to contact XYX.ZB; but no answer also. This was when I realized that I was facing a communication fail. At this moment; I selected 7600 (communication fail code) on my transponder (squawk). Decided to continue the flight following my flight plan clearance received; towards my destination. Over ZZZ1 tried to call ZZZ [Approach] but no answer. During all time I tried to use different radio equipment on board and also keep trying contact with ZZZ Center; ZZZ1 Approach; ZZZ Tower; another aircraft that sometimes I could listen very weak; but no answer.When approaching ZZZZZ1 intersection; on XYX.ZB I started listening ZZZ Center transmitting blind for me a telephone number for me to call. I also could listen if I received the message to press ident; I did. After that; ZZZ transmitted to me; blind again; to turn left heading 270 and descend to 6;000 feet; and asking me to press ident if I received. I pressed ident; and followed the instruction given. ZZZ [Controller] replied that they see my ident; and weather information for ZZZ [Airport] was given to me; together with a VFR approach and landing clearance on ZZZ3 Runway XX; and ident was requested again. I understood and pressed ident again. ZZZ Center said to me to try contact with ZZZ1 Approach on XCY.DZ I tried; but no answer was received again; and I kept monitoring both frequencies; the reception was very weak and noisy. After few moments I could listen a last transmission saying me the weather and clear to land on Runway XX; after landing try to call ground.I did land on Runway XX; and after landing; vacated the Runway via Taxiway 1; stopped and tried to call Ground. Again; no contact. Decided to turn left on Taxiway 2 and look for a place to park. I couldn't see any signal from Tower or follow me car at that time. When I was closer to the Tower; I could listen to Ground calling me; and I replied back. He said he was receiving me too weak. Instruction was given to continue Taxiway 2; hold short Runway XY. Next instruction; cross Runway XY turn left on [Taxiway] 3 and hold short Runway XX. At the holding; communication was lost again. Parking brakes applied. I took my phone; called ZZZ [Center] and asked ZZZ1 Tower telephone number. I tried to call Tower but phone didn't complete the call. After few minutes; I decided to make a 180 turning back; to not cross the runway. I did it and followed Taxiway 2 back; when I received a transmission on the ground frequency saying to turn left on Taxiway 4 and park. This was what I did. After stopping the aircraft; I didn't move from inside until police and the airport ground personnel came to me and said me that I can leave the aircraft. Before leaving the flight deck; I took my phone and called the ZZZ Tower again and after speaking with [the Controller]; situation explained; he asked me to call ZZZ center on phone number given. I did call ZZZ; asked to call with the supervisor. I explained all the situation and the same I am writing here on this report.After all done; I was asked to taxi the aircraft to another apron. I asked to park the aircraft at the hangar; closer to the FBO; where an aircraft technician could help me to troubleshoot and fix the airplane. A follow me car was provided to me and the taxi was done following the follow me car; and aircraft parked in front of the hangar.
Report_1_Synopsis: Albatross pilot reported that the aircraft's communication system malfunctioned in flight causing weak transmissions and eventually a loss of communications.

Report_1_Narrative: At Gate XX in ZZZ; I was notified of a Passenger with a lithium-ion powered heart monitor. She told the Flight Attendant that her spare battery was in her checked luggage. I asked the Gate Agent if this was okay. The Agent was not sure but was going to check. I then called Dispatch to check on the battery. Dispatch connected me with someone else in Operations who said it was okay to continue. After talking it over with Operations and Dispatch and having been given the okay to continue; we were on are way to ZZZ1. After landing; I received an email saying that the battery needed to be in her carry-on bag; not in the checked bag.
Report_2_Narrative: The cabin was notified of a Passenger with a lithium-ion battery powered heart monitor; of which she had her spare battery in her checked luggage. After consulting Dispatch and others at Operations; the Captain was told that this was okay with our policies and procedures. Once we landed in ZZZ1; we were told this was against our policies and procedures.
Report_1_Synopsis: B737 flight crew reported being notified at their destination that a spare lithium-ion battery in checked baggage should have been stowed with passenger's carry-on bag.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Distraction; Other / Unknown; Situational Awareness; Time Pressure; Communication Breakdown
Person_2_Human_Factors: Time Pressure; Situational Awareness; Other / Unknown; Distraction; Communication Breakdown
Report_1_Narrative: During single-engine taxi out; the A FA called the cockpit; informing us of passengers' non-compliance with the facemask policy.  The decision was made to return to the gate. As we taxied back toward the Ramp; I coordinated with the Captain; advising that I felt it was appropriate to perform an After Landing flow prior to returning to the gate. Captain agreed; and I accomplished the flow.  While holding for a gate; and on the apron with the parking brake set; the A FA called back to the cockpit; advising that the passengers were now willing to comply and that the three FAs were comfortable with continuing the flight.At this point we re-accomplished a Before Taxi flow (as appropriate for our single engine taxi configuration); then ran a Before Taxi Checklist.  We then coordinated with ATC to proceed with a taxi clearance for departure. The Number 1 engine was started and the rest of the taxi and takeoff proceeded uneventfully.  Once airborne; I noticed that we had departed with the autobrake selector in the OFF position. As I thought about the sequence of events leading to that I thought of two things:  placing that switch to RTO takes place in the Captain's Before Start flow.  I also recalled that when I performed the After Start flow (following the Passenger incident); I placed the Window Heat switches to ON; another item that is normally accomplished in the Captain's Before Start flow.Clearly; in our unique situation; a Before Taxi flow; followed by a Before Taxi Checklist was insufficient to reposition all switches to their appropriate positions prior to taxi and takeoff. Of note; neither of us felt rushed; and we both felt that we used good CRM to methodically think through our situation before continuing; yet in the end; something was missing. I've referenced the manuals; looking for a procedure that would have trapped our errors; but am still left wondering.  Since we started the original taxi single engine and never shutdown that engine; the procedure in Flight Ops Manual never entered our minds; yet that guidance probably would've caught the error.Non-standard Ops lead to inadvertent takeoff with auto brakes selected off.
Report_2_Narrative: On taxi out; the A FA called to tell me that there was a family being non-compliant regarding the face mask policy. I made the decision to taxi back to the gate. I asked the FO to complete the After Landing Checklist. While we were waiting for a gate; the FA called to tell us; 'Never mind; the issue is resolved.' At that point; we completed the Before Taxi Checklist and taxied to the runway. After takeoff; the FO pointed out that RTO switch was not re-selected to 'armed.' Our unique situation made it impossible for autobrake re-selection to occur.In this situation; our normal checklist does not catch the error. I should have triple checked everything because our routine taxi out was interrupted.RTO reengage missed during a taxi back to the gate and subsequent cancellation of that.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported missing re-setting the auto-brake system before takeoff and cited dealing with a passenger not complying with face mask policy as a contributing factor.

Report_1_Narrative: When reviewing weight and balance takeoff data; the 'Flap Retraction Altitude/Min Cleanup Altitude Engine Out listed for Runway 35R was different from the that listed on Jeppesen 10-7 chart. The aircraft data showed 7;400 ft. as the cleanup altitude while the Jeppesen chart showed 7;187 ft. We checked the Takeoff/Landing Reference section and it also showed 7;400 ft. We remembered reading somewhere that [performance] data supersedes other data if there is a conflict. I checked the [performance data] link on the COS page and under Normal Operations Section; it states 'In the event an Electronic Flight Plan(EFP) instruction differs between sources; use EFP output from ACARS.' It is apparent that the Jeppesen 10-7 chart is then incorrect as the other two sources state the minimum is 7;400 ft. We set 7;400 ft. as the cleanup altitude because of the statement about using ACARS output if different data exists and because it is the most conservative/higher altitude but this needs to be corrected to prevent confusion for Crews in the future. Thanks. Incorrect engine out minimum safe altitude on Jeppesen Chart.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier First Officer reported the Engine Out Min Safe Cleanup Altitude on the flight plan is different vs the Jeppsen special page.

Report_1_Narrative: We landed [Runway] 26R; and taxied FD NE to hold short [Runway] 26L. A small airplane; a single-engine Piper; was also holding short of [Runway]  26L at NE. As we approached the hold short line at a taxi speed of 2-3 kt; the First Officer asked me if I could see the small airplane ahead of us. We were less than 50 feet away; and I was just starting to see it; but it almost completely blended into the taxiway and surrounding lights. We were configured per Company SOP regarding ground movement; including taxi light on. We were not advised by the Tower Controller of any ground traffic ahead of us. I attached some images that were taken when we were stopped approximately 50 feet away from the small airplane ahead of us.
Report_1_Synopsis: B737 Captain reported taxiing to within 50 feet of a small aircraft while approaching a runway hold line during taxi to parking.

Report_1_Narrative: At XA:36; a baggage tug runner with 2 carts crossing the ramp from the X concourse on the interline baggage route (between 1 and 2 on the X and 3 and 4 on the Y concourse) did not yield to aircraft traffic Westbound on the XX line. The Ramp Tower controller alerted the flight crew of the tug and carts; at which time the crew advised they had the tug in sight. The tug; which is supposed to give way to all traffic while using the interline baggage route; did not yield to the aircraft; which had to come to an abrupt stop; less than 25 feet from the cart. The City and County of ZZZ was notified; and Airport Operations was dispatched in an attempt to track down the tug runner; but they were unable to identify the cart and driver. The Ramp Station Operations Supervisor was also notified. The station's camera system was down to start the morning; and did not come back up until XA:37; 1 minute after the incident occurred.
Report_1_Synopsis: Dispatcher reported an aircraft came to an abrupt stop after a baggage tug with two bag carts failed to yield at a zipper road crossing a taxiway.

Report_1_Narrative: It was determined that pilot's FAA Medical was updated on 202011 with special Issuance / Expiration date and it was defaulted to the 6-month expiration date in Pilot Records.Due to the high volumes of FAA Medical coming in for the past few months and FAA Medical extensions; this one fell through the cracks.Because of the pandemic last year; pilots were granted FAA medical extensions on their 'Expiration Time'; and that may have caused the confusion and to slip by.We are very careful when processing FAA Medicals including other work that we process; and fully intend to process our work as accurately as possible.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Administration Office employee reported a pilot's FAA Medical Certificate was erroneously marked as expired during the COVID-19 extension period.

Report_1_Narrative: DFW has an odd system of ground-frequency assignment for the east side of the airport; that has long concerned pilots for the very reason this incident highlighted. Outbounds from the remote; E Terminal spots of XX to YY are often assigned the discrete Ground frequency of 121.80; even though all other east-side operations for the apt are issued 121.65. However; those of us assigned 121.80 are never switched to the 'main' frequency of .65 that everyone else is operating on.On this day; as we taxied out we were assigned 121.80; but the First Officer; to his credit; decided to take the initiative to also pull up 121.65 on the other radio; so we could hear what was being said to and by the other aircraft operating in the same area and taxiways and the same controller. Northbound on Taxiway K approaching Taxiway Z there was a B737 waiting to pull out. Ground issued instructions to them over 121.65 to pull out ahead of us; and then transmitted to us on the same frequency to give way. The only reason we were aware of these transmissions was because we were monitoring both frequencies. We gave way to the B737 without incident and everyone went on their way none the wiser; except us. Had we not been monitoring 121.65 but just on our assigned frequency of 121.80; there's every reason to believe both aircraft would have gotten much closer together before the ground controller might have discovered his error; and ultimately; it was not his error but the assignment of two; discrete frequencies to different aircraft taxiing on the same taxiway.
Report_1_Synopsis: An Air Carrier pilot reported the crew would not have heard a taxi instruction to give way to another aircraft if they had not been monitoring a different  frequency than the one they were assigned.

Report_1_Narrative: While on the visual approach into HOU on the ILS 4. The FO (First Officer) was Pilot Flying and while he was flying the approach I noticed what I thought were two birds just to the right of the aircraft at around 9 o'clock but outside the course. I made the FO aware of this and continued to keep scanning for more birds in the area since the first one I saw was well clear of our course. However at 2;300 ft. and 0.5NM past ELREN on the ILS 4 the two objects were actually drones that past off our right hand side that were the size of two big birds. I noticed the two were indeed drones because I saw the propellers on two of them and they had a shiny black finish on them. I also checked the TCAS to see if they were there; but it didn't show them on the screen. I relayed this information to HOU tower and told them what altitude and where they were. Upon landing and taxing off the runway and contacting ground; I was given a phone number to call the tower to give them more information on the description of the drones; and where I spotted them on the approach.My suggestion is to always keep scanning the area for any hazards while flying even if the TCAS system doesn't show anything in the area.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier flight crew noticed drone while on final approach to landing.

Report_1_Narrative: Pushback was delayed due to catering (and vehicles impeding the catering truck from approaching the aircraft).  Following push clearance; the tug began the push but we came to a stop after approx. 15 sec. I thought perhaps something crossed behind us and we would resume the push.  But; after a few more seconds; the tug driver said that a catering truck wasn't moving.  That seemed odd; and the Captain and I wondered why a catering truck wouldn't clear a moving aircraft.  That's when the Captain looked through his side window; over his shoulder and told me; 'THAT'S why the truck isn't moving - it's sitting under our wingtip!' We hadn't felt anything and the tug driver was asked if we were touching.  He said that he couldn't tell.  A crowd gathered.  I informed ramp of our situation and our intent to remain in position to investigate. A maintenance rep came on interphone and let us know it was difficult to determine how close the wingtip was to the roof of the truck.  It was judged safe to set brakes. After some time; it was decided to let air out of the truck's tires.  Personnel climbed atop the truck and after getting a closer look; the truck was moved.  No visible contact/damage was noted but the possibility was mentioned that the winds were moving the aircraft slightly and the wingtip may have bounced off the roof and that may have not been enough to show damage but that an inspection would be the best course of action.  We were cleared to be pulled forward to the gate and the aircraft was taken out of service and the crew and passengers deplaned to the aircraft at the adjoining gate.  The remainder of the flight was uneventful.Since we were being pushed straight back; we did not see the events leading up to the potential contact.  It would seem that a combination of catering truck driver and wing walker inattention may have contributed.[Suggest] Company communications to [the catering company] and maintenance re-iterating the need to be vigilant.
Report_2_Narrative: About 60 feet into a routine pushback; the aircraft stopped.  The Tow Driver told us a 'catering truck driver is refusing to move.'  I asked if I should set the Parking Brake.  The Tow Driver said 'No.'  I looked out the left window and saw a catering truck with no driver in the cab.  I called Ramp Control on the radio to report the situation.     I looked out the window again to see a Maintenance Technician on the catering truck's over-the-cab loading platform.  He was leaning on the railing to look toward the aft-right side of the truck.  I opened the aircraft L2 Window to get a better view.  I saw the Left Wing apparently resting on the middle; top-right of the back portion of the catering truck.  I saw numerous Ground Crew and Maintenance personnel walking around the catering truck gesturing at the apparent contact point.     A Maintenance Supervisor saw me looking out the window and got on the Ground Interphone to tell me what was going on.  She said they thought there was actually no contact with the catering truck but couldn't be sure until they employed an operable hydraulic work lift - the first one they tried was inoperative.  I asked how big/small the gap was.  She thought the wing was about an inch from touching the truck; but the wind was causing the aircraft to gently rock; possibly bouncing the wing off the top of the truck.     After many minutes; a plan emerged to deflate the tires of the catering truck and tow it out of the way; preventing any possible further contact with the wing as the wind blew.  After the catering truck was clear; the Maintenance Supervisor got back on the Ground Interphone to tell us the aircraft was being taken out of service as a precaution and a replacement Ground Crew would tow us back to the gate for deplaning.  We were not to set the parking brake until safely at the gate.  Company Operations and Maintenance coordinated a different aircraft for us to continue the flight.     The tow was uneventful.  Once parked; we ran the Shutdown Checklist.  Maintenance Technicians boarded and asked us to not shut down the aircraft.  They also invited the First Officer and me to go outside and get on the work lift to inspect the wing.  To my eye; there was absolutely no indication of any kind that the wing had contacted the catering truck; however; I know that painted panels of modern materials can deform; return to shape; and not show outward signs of damage.  Not that it was my decision; but I concurred with Maintenance in taking the aircraft out of service.     Passengers and crew boarded the new aircraft and departed uneventfully.Cause Unknown.  I would only be speculating on events that occurred out of my view.I can only speculate how this event occurred; so I cannot provide prevention suggestions.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Crew reported a gate return due to possible aircraft damage from a possible collision with a catering truck during push back.

Report_1_Narrative: BWI Approach Control was vectoring us for a visual to RWY 10 and keeping us at 3;000 ft due to traffic below us at 2;000 ft.  Approach turned us in on a short approach between COLUM and JEANS fix to Runway 10 and cleared us to 2;000 ft.  On right base we were asked if field was in sight and we acknowledged it was and we were cleared for a visual to RWY 10 and contact tower.  Crossing altitude at JEANS is 1;500 ft so pilot flying selected 1;500 to catch the glide path.  At 1;800 ft tower said they were getting a low altitude alert and cleared to land.  Pilot flying disconnected the autopilot and leveled which was just about on glide path 6.4 miles from runway. We were never below the 1;500 ft min altitude inside of COLUM and joined the glide slope normally and landed.  The approach was stable at all times.Possible short approach clearance by ATC.Better vectors by ATC or requesting extended downwind.  Possibly alert was issued due to leaving us high and us having to increase rate of descent.
Report_2_Narrative: On arrival to BWI; the Approach Controller kept us at 3;000 ft due to a Cessna at 2;000 ft. As we were turned toward the final approach segment between COLUM and JEANS on the approach; the controller gave us 2;000 ft and asked if we had the field at 1;230 and 8 miles.  We confirmed the airport in sight and we were cleared for the visual approach and told to contact Tower. Crossing alt at JEANS is 1;500 ft. We started to descend to 1;500 as we were rolling into the final at 1;800 ft in the descent the tower called a low alt alert.  We leveled the aircraft at 1;800 ft and 6.4 miles from the runway. GS was captured and normal landing accomplished no other coms about low alt alert.We were cleared for a visual approach and were descending to the Altitude at the Marker. Apparently our rate of descent may have triggered the low alt alert.  The approach controller could have extended us further out in order to give more time to descend at a slower rate since they had held us up high so long.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Flight Crew reported Low Altitude Alert from ATC on approach.

Report_1_Narrative: Aircraft X migrated from [program] to [program 1] records tracking.Prior to migration; [Logbook Deferral Sheet] 70XXXXXX was issued for replacement of the RH MLG FWD Trunion pin at next gear replacement and [Logbook Deferral Sheet] 70XXXXXY was issued for inspection of the pin each 24 month interval as required per [Repair Document] 32-XX-XX-X. At system migration [Logbook Deferral Sheet] 70XXXXXX was converted to [Logbook Deferral Sheet] 02XXXXX and [Logbook Deferral Sheet] 70XXXXXY was deleted. Therefore; the previous accomplishment history doesn't appear to be available since the [Logbook Deferral Sheet] is no longer accessible in [program]. [Maintenance Operations Manual] 03.XX.X states in part; 'Review all [documentation] for correctness of deferral reference; repetitive and/or terminating action.' During system migration the repetitive action requirements are not being transferred to the surviving [Logbook Deferral Sheet].I just happened to catch this one (and will update with a [Repair Document] revised inspection interval) but it is a systemic issue and virtually every migrated item that previously had a separate [Logbook Deferral Sheet] for an interim inspection will have a high potential of missing a required inspection because the previous tracking items are being deleted without the data being transferred and Maintenance Control not have access to the precious item history. As a side note; when Maintenance Control does a Spec Table update we are required to enter ZZZ (line) for the function to work. This results in the entry appearing as if it was made by a ZZZ line station person instead of coming from Maintenance Control. This is inaccurate.
Report_1_Synopsis: Maintenance Controller reported problems with migration of maintenance tracking data during migration to a new program; resulting in missing information.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Training / Qualification; Communication Breakdown; Situational Awareness
Report_1_Narrative: After startup with a student; we performed a brake check; both sides; with a positive exchange of controls and no issues. After receiving our taxi clearance for an intersection departure; I observed my student taxiing faster than usual; and off centerline. I told him to slow down and bring the aircraft back to centerline; and he informed me there was a problem with the right brake. I took control; was unable to slow the aircraft; and with the runway hold short line approaching notified ground of my inability to stop. I swung to the right; and used brake to perform a 180 degree turn at speed; but wasn't able to turn tight enough to avoid crossing. I notified tower of my crossing; and cleared the runway environment. I got a clearance to taxi back to parking; where we ended the attempted flight; and shut the aircraft down until maintenance could diagnose and resolve the issue.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Instructor reported a runway incursion due to brake failure and loss of control of the aircraft.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Confusion; Situational Awareness; Communication Breakdown; Time Pressure
Report_1_Narrative: We were returning to ZZZ from ZZZ1 late on the afternoon. The enroute environment was apparently busier than the recent 'new normal' for that time of year as we had been limited in our climb clearances to between one- and three-thousand feet per climb clearance since our departure 25 minutes earlier.  Our most recent climb clearance was to FL400 (on our way to our filed FL410). Subsequently; ATC called traffic (I don't recall the model or the horizontal distance away) at '1;000 feet ABOVE YOUR ASSIGNED ALTITUDE' (emphasis mine). I would have replied 'Looking' or some similar acknowledgment. I did look and then subsequently noticed my FO (who was PF and in the left seat) had shallowed our climb to 100 FPM or so out of FL390 -- significantly less than the 5 or 600 FPM I would have expected. We were also very light; so a climb rate that shallow would have soon required a power reduction. At about the same time we got a TA and the Controller asked us to confirm we were level (or leveling?) at FL390.  I don't recall the exact exchange; but I would have replied something to the effect that we were climbing to FL400; he would have said something to the effect of maintain FL390.  At that point I fully processed what was happening; gave silent kudos to my FO for correctly interpreting the bad direction this was going; and directed him to 'push.'  As what we had was a TA; not an RA; the autopilot was left engaged; but he did direct the nose down and I dialed 390 into the ASEL.  The Controller asked us to confirm we were at FL390. I interpreted that as him wanting that confirmation on tape and I gave it to him; although we were; in fact; changing our vertical direction from up to down at FL393 at that point.We are a very structured flight department. In order for an airplane to be directed to an altitude during enroute climb or descent; the Controller has to assign that altitude; the PNF has to read it back and dial it into the ASEL; the PF has to verbally and independently repeat that altitude for both of us to hear; and has to acknowledge that he sees that same altitude displayed in front of him. Owing to that routine sequence and cadence of events; we are both 100% certain that we were assigned FL400.That said; I can allow as how I have possibly been wrong at least once in my flying career. My FO was hired on just as COVID came on the scene last year.  With the reduced amount of flying we've been doing since; he is still considered 'new' to the operation and as such not fully comfortable with our procedures. By that; I mean that I sometimes sense a hesitation for him to be as assertive as he should be and as assertive as he would be by now had this been a normal year. That notwithstanding; I would expect any pilot in our organization to question; in no uncertain terms; anything they were uncertain about; especially an ATC clearance. Likewise; no one in our organization; from Director of Flight Ops down; would hesitate to ascertain verification of any such uncertainty; no matter who questioned it. That's the way we move airplanes without bending them. I'm still 100% certain we were cleared to FL400.In retrospect; and we observed this at the time; the primary thing that would have alerted us to this unfolding conflict would have been for the Controller to have called the traffic as '...opposite direction at FL400.' That would have raised the hackles on the back of my neck and elicited from me a request to confirm our assigned altitude. There is no error-trapping possible when traffic is called as '1;000 feet above your assigned altitude.'Additionally; and this is not a negative; just observation and fact: we're flying the oldest; and by far the most reliable; airplane in our fleet of four; however; owing to her age; we're looking at a pair of >XX-year-old TCAS displays on dedicated three-inch round screens. There are no course overlays; no distance rings and; especially on the longer ranges (20 and 40 mile); no way to preciselyassess the relative position; direction or closure rate of traffic approaching; especially when doing so nearly head on. Technology is good. Newer technology can sometimes be better.On a positive note; we did visually acquire the traffic while far enough apart that had evasive action been necessary (it wasn't); we would have had plenty of time to take it. We did debrief this incident immediately after its occurrence; replayed the events out loud and decided the error was ultimately ATC's; that we had done everything we could to mitigate the repercussions to the controller and that we were not at fault.
Report_1_Synopsis: Corporate Captain reported an altitude deviation that caused an airborne conflict (TA) and cites Controller/Pilot communication and the First Officer's (PF) lack of flying as contributing factors.

Report_1_Narrative: We were cruising at FL320 around late afternoon when transmission with ZZZ Center became difficult as we were handed off to the next frequency. ZZZ Center's transmissions were muffled and unreadable at times. Multiple aircraft; including my own; had to ask Center to repeat instruction due to the muffled voice and weak transmission. My belief is that the Center Controller was wearing a mask and that mask was causing the majority of communication difficulty.If true; the use of masks by Center controllers is creating a serious communication and safety issue between pilots and Air Traffic Control. Everything about the national air space system is designed so pilot to ATC communication is to be understood without interference or confusion. The use of masks by ZZZ ATC has the potential to create confusion and ultimately a sacrifice of safety.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Captain reported difficulty understanding Center controllers and believes the problem maybe the controllers are wearing face masks.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Communication Breakdown; Situational Awareness; Physiological - Other; Distraction; Troubleshooting
Report_1_Narrative: I fly X type missions; for which I'm wearing a mask; which I knew harms the sealing of my active noise reduction headset (and as a result reduces the sound quality; bringing in some ambient noise). It was not until yesterday that I realized how disruptive this is.I was flying on the last leg of my IFR flight plan; from ZZZ to ZZZZZ (from there to my destination - ZZZ1). ATC called me and said something about heading 290 with ZZZZZ in it; I assumed they're telling me I need to fly 290 to ZZZZZ (and from there proceed as usual). That's what I did; ATC got (rightfully) upset and told me that I was asked to fly 290; which I then did and later cleared for a visual approach to Runway XX at ZZZ1.Listening to the recording on liveatc.net; I could clearly hear the ATC telling me to depart ZZZZZ at heading 290. That 'depart' is the one piece of the puzzle I didn't hear during the flight.On my way back - no passengers; no mask - all of a sudden ATC sounded much clearer. It made obvious to me this has to change; and I need to find a mask that does not interfere with my headset.
Report_1_Synopsis: Single pilot reported unable to understand the Controller's instruction clearly due to the pilot's face mask interfering with the over ear headset.

Report_1_Narrative: We were approaching ZZZZZ intersection from the west which is a transition onto the ZZZZZ 3 arrival and had received multiple descent clearances out of our cruising altitude of FL350. Eventually we were cleared to cross ZZZZZ at FL230. Flying the ZZZZZ 3 'as published' we would normally cross ZZZZZ1 at FL230 per the STAR and the FMS altitude crossings were set for this. ZZZZZ is 14 miles prior to ZZZZZ1 so crossing ZZZZZ at FL230 requires a change in the FMS and a steeper descent. We acknowledged the clearance and a few minutes later while performing a challenge and response descent checklist and when flying overhead ZZZZZ I realized that we were still on the original profile descent to cross ZZZZZ1 at FL230 and we were crossing ZZZZZ above our assigned altitude of FL230.I attribute this error to our reduced amount of flying in the past 12 months due to the COVID lock down and to distraction by the descent checklist.
Report_1_Synopsis: Corporate Captain reported an altitude deviation during approach and cited lack of flying as a contributing factor.

Report_1_Narrative: Took off from San Pedro Sula and noticed there wasn't a SID or obstacle departure procedure taking off from Runway 22 into terrain either side of centerline and ahead.  There is a SID for runway 4 which is what we took off on.  Shouldn't there be some kind of procedure for this runway?  I filed a report and got a response back asking me to also fill out this report.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Captain reported this airport needs a SID or DP for this runway.

Report_1_Narrative: We were advised that someone had tested positive for COVID.  It had been a long period of time since they were in the building.  It was during the mid shift; so they didn't have contact with anyone.  The TRACON was shutdown and relocated to ZZZ1 Tower at XA:0L on a weekday.  This is a busy day of the week and time for us.  The functionality of working from the Tower is limited.  It also requires all radar sectors to be combined.  The volume and complexity was far too great at this time of day.  Even with trying to limit operations the radar scope was too cluttered.  There were many uncontrolled VFR's.  The data blocks overlapped and the Mode-C was unreadable.  Traffic workload was high.  We asked ZZZ2 Traffic Management Unit (TMU) for 20 Miles In Trail (MIT); but that was not adhered to. Communications were also difficult.  We asked all surrounding facilities to use a single frequency but that was not always followed.  VFR's calling for service were using published frequencies.There was no reason to rush this cleaning.  Everyone in the facility had already been exposed for hours; if not days.  Waiting until XF:00L would have ensured traffic volume and complexity was light enough to work from a reduced area such as ZZZ1 Tower.  The rush for cleaning was not worth the safety risk to the flying public.
Report_1_Synopsis: TRACON Controller reported the facility went to ATC Zero after someone tested positive for COVID-19. Controller stated they were moved to the Local Tower and worked from there.  Reporter advised the move could have been delayed to a non-busy time due to everyone already being exposed.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Workload; Troubleshooting; Training / Qualification; Time Pressure; Situational Awareness; Distraction
Report_1_Narrative: I was working Sector X (AOA [At Or Above] FL360) and another sector was being saturated (Y/Z/A combined. Training was being done at this sector); so they split off A to me. There was a lot of traffic and weather in the area. Apparently; restrictions were put in place that aircraft entering ZZZ1 [Center] from us and landing at ZZZ [Airport] needed to be AOB FL260. I was working an Ultra High Sector. When I was given the briefing by the trainee; the trainer ran over to my scope and said that Aircraft X needed to be AOB [At Or Below] FL260. The aircraft was at FL430 and maybe 40 miles from the boundary; on top of same direction and opposite direction traffic. Aside from that there were numerous conflicting aircraft issues already fixing to happen. My EDST [En-route Decision Support Tool] had a bunch of red alerts of which should have been fixed prior to the aircraft entering our area. Again; this was on the sector I was gaining; NOT the one I was already working. I was bit overwhelmed taking the sector just due to the amount of work that needed to be corrected due to the neglect of the training team.I descended Aircraft X to FL390; knowing I would have to move or quickly descend the aircraft through two others converging at FL390 and another directly below at FL380.I assigned the altitude and realized the speed gain was great enough that I could get Aircraft X down to FL360 (base of my stratum) and miss Aircraft Y; heading the same direction at FL380. To ensure I had room and miss opposite direction traffic at FL390; I turned Aircraft X. My turn was a bit too aggressive and in doing so; the wind caused the aircraft to lose a bunch of speed; resulting in the CA going off. I turned Aircraft Y to the left to keep separation; but it was already lost. From my observation; I showed a loss of separation to where they were separated by 4.9 miles and 900 feet vs the 1000/5 I need. I didn't stare too long as I had to go on to other separation tasks that were not completed prior to receiving the additional airspace/traffic.First; splitting sectors at the last minute has become all too common an occurrence with this COVID schedule and working 'more with less.' The whole environment is unsafe and the things we do are dangerous; resulting in issues like the one I had.Secondly; I won't be taking sectors from a person who doesn't have it all figured out; no matter what the Supervisor says.I take pride in what I do and having separation errors is unacceptable. I had the pilot helping me out the best he could and I second guessed myself that the aircraft would descend through the altitudes fast enough in a straight line Aircraft X started to outrun Aircraft Y as he descended. My turn was too aggressive; and I never played it into my head how much the wind would impact the turn. I think just trying to take action to descend the aircraft to meet a restriction overruled my common sense to think how my actions would play out. Solely my fault; but it could have and should have been avoided had other things been done in a timely manner prior to my taking the airspace. It seems to be a trend to do everything last minute; which is what creates such mistakes. Had I worked that aircraft and known of the restriction; Aircraft X would have descended below all my traffic 100 miles prior. Maybe not to FL260 so as to penalize the aircraft; but at least below those who were deviating and being rerouted around the weather.
Report_1_Synopsis: Center Controller reported having a loss of separation after assuming a busy sector from a training team.

Report_1_Narrative: I was being relieved from the CIC position and opened the X Sector which was combined with the Y and Z Sectors due to volume.  At the time of the incident; Henderson Tower requested a release on Aircraft Y on the SCAMR SID with the RASLR transition.  They advised they could provide visual separation with the inbound IFR which I approved.  At the same time I had a flight overflying HND enroute to VGT and another inbound to HND. Upon departure; I pointed out Aircraft Y to the Y Sector observing Aircraft X on the NIITZ Departure so I could maneuver around inbound and overflight traffic.  I observed Aircraft Y above my existing traffic and what appeared to be safely behind Aircraft X as they were approximately 8 miles and 50 KIAS slower than Aircraft X.  I shipped Aircraft Y to ZLA just prior to them reaching 12;000 MSL.  From replays I observed; the loss appeared to have occurred approximately 15-20 miles down line.We are now approximately 30 days into new Metroplex airspace and this procedure is designed to 'blend in' LAS SIDS.  This particular one causes aircraft to unnecessarily fly into each other.  ZLA also has control of these aircraft by LOA at 15;000 MSL.  A simple turn to the RASLR Fix could have avoided this.  I also mentioned the inefficiencies of the new design to our Metroplex team prior to implementation. .
Report_1_Synopsis: L30 TRACON Controller reported a loss of separation and cited SID design as a contributing factor.

Report_1_Narrative: Aircraft X was inbound to EKO. I issued a descent clearance to 14;000 feet and asked the pilot if he had the weather at EKO and to expect a visual approach. The pilot said he was unable to obtain the weather; so I issued him the current METAR. I also informed the pilot of the airport's location. Moments later; I observed the pilot descending. I immediately issued a low altitude alert since he was in a 13400 ft. MIA (Minimum IFR Altitude) and was descending below. The pilot immediately canceled IFR.
Report_1_Synopsis: ZLC Center Controller reported an aircraft descended below the assigned altitude and flew below the Minimum IFR Altitude.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Troubleshooting; Workload; Confusion; Distraction; Human-Machine Interface; Situational Awareness; Time Pressure
Report_1_Narrative: I just took over the position X. I was briefed that we would be switching from east operations; to west operations because of a wind shift. About 3 weeks ago; we moved scopes and positions around to accommodate increased social distancing. Due to this; there are new macros and procedures that supervisors must adhere to. As our last aircraft landed on the east runways; the Supervisor started to put in new macros. My tags did not acquire; and I had to manually coordinate with the Feeder to let him know when I had radar on traffic. When I was starting to get busy and it was clear the macros being entered were not working; my scope changed from a west operations final pref set to an east operations final monitor preference set. I had to slide over to the adjacent position and work my final off of that scope because mine was completely unusable.This is an absolute safety concern that I have heard has happened before. I recommend they move the scopes back to the normal working configuration because this is clearly not working and is a huge safety hazard and it should concern everyone.
Report_1_Synopsis: TRACON Controller reported having to make a configuration change but the data tags did not change to the correct airport configuration; making the reporter move quickly to a close by position and sharing the scope.

Report_1_Narrative: Aircraft X checked on approximately a 6 mile final on the Visual Approach and I cleared him to land.  At approximately a 4-mile final Aircraft Y asks for an 'S turn to the North' to which I state 'Approved'.  About 30 seconds later; Aircraft X asks for another s-turn to the south to which I also state 'approved as requested' and inform him that there is no traffic in his vicinity and also issued the wind. Aircraft X is now on a 1.5 mile final and well east of the airport and asks 'Tower; Aircraft X we are still plenty high; can we do a left tun and a left 360 around?' I state 'Unable' due to traffic in trail and ask Aircraft X if he needs to go around. Aircraft X replies 'affirmative'.At this point Aircraft Y is approximately 2 miles well east of the airport and it appeared that they were turning toward the airport. Not wanting Aircraft Y to overshoot finals; I issue 'Aircraft Y; fly heading 195; climb and maintain 2;000'.  When Aircraft Y becomes established on the heading; I issue 'fly heading 210 and maintain 3;000'. I did this without coordinating with Approach first because things were rapidly developing as Aircraft Y was indicating 190 knots and they appeared to be headed toward terrain east of the airport.  I realize that this was a vector below the Minimum Vectoring Altitude (MVA). The MVA east of the airport is 2;400 feet but at this point; I wanted to get Aircraft Y away from terrain as quickly as possible without issuing any vague or confusing instructions to the pilot. I did coordinate with Approach with the 210 heading when I got the chance and it was approved.As I stated in my above narrative; I realize that the vector that I issued was below the MVA but from my perspective from the Tower; I needed to get Aircraft Y away from terrain as quickly as possible. This was a unique situation where I had to utilize my best judgment with the circumstances that were presented. I realize that I was breaking the rule of vectoring an aircraft below the MVA but what was the alternative at this point? Let Aircraft Y head toward terrain and possible result in a catastrophe? It was the best of the two bad choices that were presented to me at that point and I had to quickly make a judgment call.
Report_1_Synopsis: SNA Tower Controller reported they issued vectors to an Air Carrier that was below the Minimum Vectoring Altitude due to making S turns during their descent on a Visual Approach.

Report_1_Narrative: WSMR (White Sands Missile Range) was GPS jamming. Aircraft X was significantly off course prior to taking position. Leaving controller put Aircraft X on a vector to miss restricted airspace. Aircraft X asked to go back on course direct to DNA; assuming he could navigate direct by his request; I gave him direct his destination again. I move on in my traffic scan and come back to Aircraft X making a 90 degree left hand turn. I had cleared Aircraft X to descend previously because he was no longer in conflict with WSMR after being vectored out; but with his 90 degree left hand turn he went back into WSMR descending and I didn't catch it in time. After realizing it I told Aircraft X to stop his descent but it was too late as he was passing through FL216. I called WSMR and asked them to 'stop buzzer'; the answered with 'O.K.'. Facility Manager on Duty later informed me we can't ask them to 'stop buzzer' and to just keep putting aircraft on headings. Give controllers the ability to have WSMR stop GPS jamming during high traffic periods and move their jamming operations to mid shifts.
Report_1_Synopsis: ZAB Enroute Controller reported a flight crews navigational capability was affected by White Sands Missile Range GPS jamming.

Report_1_Narrative: Very light 757; 16.7 on the fuel; almost empty payload; operating from ZZZ to ZZZ1; daytime VMC. High winds in effect. Vref was 111; Vapp is 126. I was PF (Pilot Flying); and decided to fly faster on final since we were in a light 757; and my limited experience with this situation led to this. Missed approach procedures were reviewed multiple times as other jets had to go around several times. Runway was dry; over XX;000 feet long; plenty of distance. I decided to fly a new Vapp of 135; as the jet was having problems controlling the airspeed since the winds were about 060/22G30. Our divert was ZZZ1; and we knew that several aircraft attempting to land had to execute missed approaches. All this into account; I decided to fly around 135 KIAS; as this felt like a more stable approach. The airspeed wouldn't stabilize safely below this number; as it was all over the place and I had to fight with the autothrottles to maintain within 15 kts of the initial Vapp of 126--it just wouldn't stabilize at a speed below 135. My reasoning is that since I was light; in a 757; long runway; daytime VMC; and super gusty winds; I had plenty of room to stop safely without encountering hot brakes or running out of concrete. We landed uneventfully; although long; as I touched down past the touchdown zone--this was the only cost of flying faster; and I felt it was worth it; all things considered. We landed and were able to taxi clear on taxiway; no problem.  If I was in a 767 or a heavier 757; I wouldn't have even thought of this; and we would have flown the Vapp given; for better or worse.  Were we technically unstable? Yes; I believe we were. Were we safer; in my eyes; flying a more stable approach with the winds we had? Yes; I also believe this to be the case. We never had a windshear warning; and we never felt unsafe; but looking back; I was in the wrong; even though I felt more stable; which led to a safer approach. However; the AOM procedures don't allow for this; so I was technically in the wrong; even though the airplane flew better and safer; in my opinion. Next time; I will fly the Vapp given; and if we have to divert; then so be it.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier pilot reported continuing the approach and landing with strong winds and an unstabilized approach.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Situational Awareness; Communication Breakdown; Training / Qualification
Report_1_Narrative: While on visual approach to Runway XX and configuring; we had configured normally through gear down. The Captain called 'flaps 30' and I reached for the handle while looking at the speed. The trend indicator was well below 185 and I was too focused on the trend rather than the actual speed. I was too quick to move the flap handle. We were actually about 187 knots. We got the flap overspeed warning for about one to two seconds as our speed continued to dissipate. It was my first flight from furlough and recurrent training. I was allowing myself to rush; even though there was no need to rush at the time. I made an error of referencing the trend before the actual speed.  I also need to refresh my habit of not touching the flap handle until I have stated 'speed checks.'
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier First Officer reported a flap overspeed during visual approach.  It was the First Officer's first flight after being out due to furloughs.

Report_1_Narrative: Since COVID; these particular international schedules have been in a lot of flux. Most sequences; up until now; have been 'rockets' where we only get to rest a relatively short amount of time during the day after an all-night flight; and then fly back all night. I have written about this before; and this is to reiterate: these sequences are sub-optimal in terms of safety due to the limited rest. The threat on these sequences is NOT a virus; it's the cumulative fatigue after being up for two straight nights. There is no reason not to make ALL these flights have a longer sleep opportunity with a 30 plus hour layover.  Three times in the last 2 months we lined up for the wrong runway in ZZZ after the double all-nighter. Fortunately; someone caught the error before it was critical; but it is reflective of the fact that the three of us are sleep-deprived. In this aircraft category; you have an older pilot group to begin with. Give us the opportunity to get enough rest.Upon arrival in ZZZ; I was extremely tired; and felt my ability to monitor was degraded.Schedule all these international trips as longer layovers. It's a safety issue; pure and simple.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier First Officer reported fatigue related concerns with the scheduling of particular international flights since the COVID-19 pandemic began.

Report_1_Narrative: On SID's; when assigned climb via clearances; and when the top altitude is higher than the flies altitude; it is expected to climb to the restriction; top of SID. This particular SID says in the top altitude box; FL230 is the top. Upon further reading; it should say FL230 or filed altitude; whichever is lower; as the SID says in the textual description. Perhaps this is an issue with Jeppesen charts.  Once past the 10;000 foot hold down at MUGBE; the Captain set FL230 as the expected clearance. Just before passing FL200; Captain queried ATC to confirm FL230; but received a response approaching FL220. A clearance was given to descend FL200; and we complied. It was then that we reviewed the textual part of the chart and noticed our error. The expectation that other SID's do not include this exception is biggest cause. Also; not detailed re-reading lengthy textual descriptions on SID's every single use; contributes. ATC clearances can include 'climb via; except maintain...'. This clearance would easily eliminate this oversight and airports like DEN; should have knowledge of the departures to aid in this. Also; Jeppesen charts should include these little nuances in the top altitude box on the SID; since this isn't true of all SID's.
Report_1_Synopsis: Airline Captain reported exceeding clearance altitude.

Report_1_Narrative: Arriving from ZZZ; myself and the Captain were preparing for an ILS to Runway 12 based on available weather at hand. Once handed off to Approach Control; we were instructed to expect the RNP 30. Given our close proximity to the airport; I scrambled quickly to load the FMS and review the changes. I failed to notice the available IAFs available and was instead hastily looking for one of the IFs in the FMS. Given our plan to conduct a visual approach and use the RNP for guidance; I elected to select 'no approach VIAs' and to add the additional fixes requested by ATC. As we progressed on the approach; we got multiple GPWS alerts while in VMC; including 'pull up.' The Captain discontinued the approach and elected for a go-around followed by the published hold to troubleshoot. We later completed an ILS to Runway 12; circle 30 without event. Thoroughly review approach plate and recognize the appropriate approach VIA option. If needing additional time; request delay vectors.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported receiving multiple GPWS alerts on approach to BZN airport.

Report_1_Narrative: On approach to landing at ORD Runway 9C at approximately 200 feet we received a GPWS (Ground Proximity Warning System) alert 'TOO LOW; TERRAIN.' The alert repeated itself several times until touchdown. It was day VMC; some light rain falling. We were on glide slope and in a safe position to land so we continued the approach and considered the alert erroneous. It's possible that since the runway is fairly new at ORD; that the GPWS database had not been updated. Perhaps a message to pilots operating into ORD should be made aware of possible erroneous GPWS alert associated with Runway 9C.
