Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported receiving a Ground Proximity Warning on short final to ORD Runway 9C even though they were stable and established on the glideslope.

Report_1_Narrative: Normal departure and flight enroute to ZZZ with thunderstorm approaching ZZZ airport on arrival from the west. Radar vectors for ILS XXL for approach; multiple speed adjustments from ATC on approach and no reports of wind gusts on initial arrival from ATC with winds 180/6 from ATIS. Storm had moved over field when on approach. On short final there was an RVR (Runway Visual Range) update from recall of greater than 5;000 RVR and moderate to heavy rain but no winds passed from recall. VMC around 1;100 feet and could see right and center runway but then went into torrential rain downpour around 400-500 feet on short final where Captain made an EFIS lights call and then I shortly after picked up runway lights and landing environment just prior to minimums and was a little high but was adjusting in close. Around 30-40 feet we had an instantaneous airspeed loss of around 10kts and at that time I had decided to go-around but with the airspeed loss and instantaneous loss of lift we touched down as go-around decision was made. We had a semi-hard landing and bounced and go-around selected all simultaneously. We were slow to put the speed brake back in after touching down but did eventually secure it and maintained attitude as we executed go around. Go-around procedures were completed airborne. Vectored back around by ATC for uneventful approach; landing and taxi in. The Captain and I both did a walk around of the aircraft post flight to ensure integrity of aircraft and check tail skid as a precaution but didn't notice the skid was ground down as we later were informed from the Director of Operations and Maintenance. We debriefed the event. Windshear/airspeed loss at low altitude while simultaneously executing go-around and didn't maintain proper go-around pitch once touching down as indicated from tail skid damage. Quicker reaction from crew with go-around with instantaneous airspeed loss and loss of lift and maintain proper attitude of aircraft on touchdown when executing go-around. Follow rules to live by; do not make large control inputs when in flare/go-around close to ground.
Report_1_Synopsis: B767 flight crew reported windshear on landing resulting in tailstrike.

Report_1_Narrative: While on approach to ZZZ we were cleared to descend to 3;000 feet at which time we had the runway in sight. Upon reaching 3;000 feet the controller gave us a low altitude alert and wanted to verify we were level at 3;600.  The PNF (Pilot Not Flying) responded that we were level at 3;000 and had the airport in sight. The controller advised he had only cleared us to descend to 3;600 not 3;000. We then called the airport in sight and he cleared us for the visual approach and we initiated a successful landing. After landing the Tower Manager contacted the flight crew via telephone at the FBO and advised there was a possible pilot deviation.
Report_2_Narrative: We were in contact with ZZZ Approach. We were to expect radar vectors for the ILS XX. During the descent there were thunderstorms in the area. The approach controller instructed to descend to 3;000. As we leveled at 3;000 the controller ask to confirm our altitude. I informed the controller we were level at 3;000. He informed us we should have been at 3;600. We informed him we thought he had said 3;000. By this time we were clear of clouds and has the airport in sight. We climbed to 3;600 and received radar vectors as we were cleared for the approach.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Crew flying F-900 aircraft reported altitude deviation on approach.

Report_1_Narrative: Climbing through 16;000 feet to FL 200 we experienced a high whistle sound from the front of the airplane. I felt pressure on my ears; nose; and head and had the air pushed out of my lungs. We identified a cabin depressurization and I reached for my O2 mask. I took a long inhale from the oxygen and then proceeded with additional memory items. The Captain began an priority descent. I reached for the Pax oxygen switch with my right hand and the PA button with my left hand. I communicated with the Captain that I was going off comms to tell Pax to put on oxygen masks. The Captain stated 'Wait. They are going to be fine here in 2-3 seconds and I don't want to replace the masks.' This occurred around 13;500 feet. So I did not complete memory items per the Captain's instruction. I contacted ATC and advised we were on an priority descent because of depressurization. We received a new assigned altitude of 10;000 feet. The Cabin started to repressurize around 11;000. ATC asked if we wished to declare priority handling and the Captain declined. We were able to continue to ZZZ without incident.There were several deviations from our normal operating procedures that concern me. First the disregard from memory items on the checklist. Second; the captain did not have his O2 mask plugged in. He believed he could plug it in fast enough if needed and that he doesn't plug it in because he forgets to unplug it after a flight. This caused a delay in performing a memory item. The Captain was able to plug his oxygen mask in but never donned it during controlled handling decent. Also; we did not formally ask for priority handling with ATC. We could not diagnose the problem for the rapid depressurization so we were unaware of what triggered it. I suggested declaring priority handling to cover our bases if anything else occurred. This flight had already been abnormal with the priority descent. The Captain disagreed saying the problem is over. Lastly; I do not believe the cockpit acceptance was completed for this flight. It is typical that the FO (First Officer) does the walk around and security check while the Captain is completing the acceptance. While doing the walk around it is very apparent that the shaker pusher test is being tested from outside the airplane. You can hear the shaking on the horizontal stabilizer. I did not hear it that morning. Also upon startup; the Captain found a popped circuit breaker on his side for De-Ice. I'm not sure when the circuit breaker popped but no de-icing equipment was on so I assume it was before startup. This is another missed item on the acceptance checklist. Now; these deviations did not cause the priority handling to occur but they could have added on to make the event worse.
Report_1_Synopsis: SA-227 AC Metro First Officer reported deviations from SOP during a Cabin Pressurization Event.

Report_1_Narrative: We were at FL350 in cruise between ZZZ and ZZZ1. ATC had given us left and right deviations and ZZZ1 when able. The radar was not painting much at the time but we were trying to deviate around what we saw on the radar. At the time everything was obscured and we were in the clouds. We did pop out just a little before the front and could make our way around a couple of the darker areas but it was not possible to get around all of it. As we crossed the front we started to get some shear in the winds that caused the airspeed to start to go up and down quite a bit. The autopilot then kicked off so my FO (First Officer) took manual control and the airspeed and altitude varied a lot as he flew the aircraft. The turbulence only got to a moderate level at most of the time but the downdrafts and updrafts made it difficult to keep any specific altitude or airspeed. Soon we hit a downdraft that was much worse than the rest and we were unable to maintain altitude even in climb power. I took control of the aircraft and told him to tell ATC we were descending because we were unable to maintain altitude at the time. We ended up descending about 1;000 feet and were able to level off at FL340 once we were through it. At the time I was just worried about keeping airspeed and not stalling the aircraft. Once we were clear ATC cleared us down to FL330 and we continued on to ZZZ2. At the time of the initial shear we were talking and did not detect the variations in airspeed that were the telling signs of the shear coming. At the time I did not declare an emergency but looking back at it I would now because we were unable to maintain altitude at the time.
Report_2_Narrative: While enroute we were navigating around some weather that was obscured. We were communicating with ATC about the best route to take around the weather. We were not painting much if any precipitation at all angles on the radar. We were on left and right deviations and ZZZ when able. Just after passing the ZZZ1 VOR at FL350. We started to experience some light turbulence which continued to worsen. I turned on continuous ignition and continued to maneuver around the weather the best we could. The VSI (Vertical Speed Indicator) started a small trend of 120 FPM down. Our altitude quickly started to dip 300-400 feet as we encountered an unexpected large downdraft that kicked the autopilot off. The VSI showed 2;000 FPM descent. I continued to hand fly the aircraft but we were unable to maintain airspeed and altitude and began a descent down to FL340. We advised ATC that we were unable to maintain altitude because of the downdraft and that we would be leveling at FL340. ATC then gave us a descent to FL330. We continued down to FL 330 and leveled there. We exited the obscured weather and continued to ZZZ2. Limited visual and pictorial view of the weather as we deviated around it. Access to current weather information through the iPad such as tops reports.
Report_1_Synopsis: CRJ-900 flight crew reported windshear in cruise resulting in a momentary loss of aircraft control and excursion from assigned altitude.

Report_1_Narrative: On vectors 6 SM northwest of TRI airport at 4500; ATC was vectoring us around weather for the approach. We were level; given a left turn from 270 to 090. On about a 180 heading; we got the GPWS 'caution terrain' followed by 'terrain terrain woop woop pull up' one time. I leveled the wings and executed the terrain escape maneuver. We climbed up to 5;300 feet from 4;500 feet. As soon as I started the escape maneuver; the indications went away. We notified ATC and flew the approach without disruption. This seemed like an erroneous activation as we were above what ATC said was the MVA. But; it was night; so not 100% sure.Either a false warning or a terrain clearance issue. It seemed that we were too high to get this in a level turn. ATC indicated we were 100 feet above their MVA. Responded and leveled the wings and executed the escape maneuver. Suggest to fly at or above MSA rather than the minimum vectoring altitude.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported receiving a GPWS alert while being vectored for the approach.

Report_1_Narrative: I completed a thorough walk around and told the Captain there was a lot of ice on the aircraft and we were going to need to deice. I also recommended we take off with full Anti-ice on and the Captain agreed after a minute. We did a full deice type 1 and 4 everything went as planned. I ran the cold weather cold soaked check list to prepare for deicing. Once Deicing was completed I received all the pertinent information from iceman and wrote it down on a TOLD card. I then completed the deicing check list and we called ground for taxi. I made sure all the deice check list was completed and we taxied out for departure. Myself and the Captain talked about leaving the flaps and slats up or down while taxiing and due to having such a long hold over time we chose to lower flaps to proper flap setting for takeoff knowing that our hold over time would be reduced by 50%. As we pulled onto the runway and did our final configuration check we had a no take off and the Captain adjusted the FMS info for takeoff and the neck check was good to go. We were cleared for takeoff and I did all my flows and the before takeoff check list. Power was set and we began to roll and immediately the Captain was going left and right on the runway due to the winds being so strong and at this point I put my feet on the pedals getting ready to help the Captain. We reached V1 and I called out V1 then rotate. As soon as we rotated next thing I know is we are going left of the runway due to the winds being so strong at this point I don't remember if I called out positive rate and this allowing the Captain to call gear up. The next thing I remember is calling out acceleration and the Captain calling out flight level change and auto pilot on. At this point we are getting bumped all around due to the severe weather.  The Captain then says flaps and I raise them watching the airspeed as we are bumped around.  I call out speed since we are getting close to the speed warning and the Captain does not have time to get the nose up higher to stop this warning from happening then we notice all of a sudden we have a packs off message and the Captain says the packs are off and I state they are on.  He resets them but to no avail.  They continue to show off.  At this time the Captain says the gear is down and raises it while we are being thrown all around. I ask ATC if we can level off at 11;000 and they clear us to level off at 11;000.  We are still getting pounded and unable to maintain 11;000.  I reach for the QRH as the Captain calls for the QRH between 11;000 and 13;000 the packs off warning message goes away and due to already being at 13;000; ATC asks if we would like to continue to climb and I state yes after looking over at the Captain and he nodded his head to say yes. I then ask about the weather and they state the weather will calm down above 20;000. We are then cleared to climb to 23;000 and I say to the Captain when we are above 20;000 I'm sorry I don't recall if I called out positive rate allowing the Captain to call for gear up and the Captain responds that he did call for gear up and he always does. But I don't recall any call out for gear up. I would really like to hear the recording just to see what all was said while we were being battered around. Everything ended up normal from this point on.  Once we landed our flight attendant stated the passengers were not happy with the take off and were screaming.Unfortunately; there is not much we could have done on this take off that we did not already do. We had already talked to ground to see if other aircraft had taken off and they said everything was fine with the first 3 departures. We checked the winds with ACARS including gusts and ACARS showed the take off to all be within tolerances. Report_1_Narrative: We were approaching BZN; planning RNAV RNP 30 Approach. When we checked in with Big Sky Approach they assigned us the RNAV A Approach and cleared us direct SURPE. I typed it in manually and we proceeded direct. In my search in the FMS for that approach; it was not in the database. We had it in the Jeppessen FD Pro; but not in the database. Prior to reaching SURPE we became VFR; called the field and completed a visual approach. Having it in the Jeppessen charts and not in the database in the FMS is not cool. Leads one down a path to red. ATIS is not digital so our awareness of what approach is being used was late; late; late in the flight.  Brought us into the red. Into the red at an incredibly critical phase of flight is also not cool. Set up a liaison to make the airports like this aware of our fleet capabilities. Example: we have charts in the Jeppessen; but not in the FMS database so don't assign said approach.
Report_2_Narrative: We were inbound to BZN VOR expecting vectors to the final portion of RNAV (RNP) Runway 30.  We were planning to request direct JAPER intersection for the balance of the approach.   The airport was reporting VFR conditions but we were still IMC in the descent.  We were handed off to Big Sky Approach about 20 DME from the airport.  Without given a chance to request JAPER we were directed to proceed to SURPE intersection on the RNAV (GPS)-A. That's when our situational awareness went red.   We accepted the approach as it was listed in our FD Pro.  I manually put SURPE in the legs page and descended to 10;000 feet as directed.  The First Officer tried to pull up the RNAV (GPS) - A in the FMC but it was not there.  Luckily we broke out into VMC approaching SURPE and completed a visual approach.I can think of three. First; the controllers need to be aware of which approaches they can and cannot assign.  Secondly; if an approach is published in FD Pro but not available in the FMC that discrepancy should be clearly spelled out. Finally; I made an assumption that if a procedure is in the FD Pro it would also be in the FMC.Big Sky needs to know which of their approaches are not in our FMC's.  This would help them immensely to plan for our arrivals.  We also need to complete an internal audit of all airports we serve to either remove or annotate in the  pages which FD Pro approaches are not found in the FMC.  I will now compare each approach in FD Pro to the FMC when arriving at a unfamiliar airport as I never want to be trapped in this situation again.
Report_1_Synopsis: An air carrier First Officer reported they were assigned an approach to BZN that was not in their FMS Database.

Report_1_Narrative: In Governor's Harbor [airport]; there is an over 8;000 foot strip. There is no taxiway; no tower; and a major hill in the middle of the runway where neither side can see the opposite end. When operating there; each pilot must trust that the others are making calls both to taxi out but also for landing. Aircraft there also repeatedly take off with a tail wind so it is difficult to know which side is being used at any time. In our case; we were departing off of Runway 15 and we made three radio calls; one to back taxi; one to position for takeoff; and one for takeoff. While cresting the hill on the takeoff roll we discovered that a multi engine piston aircraft was pointed right at us. We were past V1 and we continued to rotate and takeoff as the other aircraft did a 180 and attempted to head back to the ramp at the end of the runway. I do not know if they were taking off with a tailwind or taxing to 15 but they made no radio call and obviously were not listening to UNICOM. The FBO also made a call to the aircraft telling them that the runway was active and they needed to clear. Our crew followed every procedure to make this a safe takeoff; unfortunately we cannot prevent others from disregarding the rules of safe operations.This was a pretty close call; especially if the aircraft was trying to takeoff with a tailwind. If we had been 20 seconds later it could have been catastrophic. The fact that it is uncontrolled; has no taxiway; and you cannot see either side from either end makes this a very dangerous airport to operate in especially when the locals do not follow proper communication procedures. We as our crew did absolutely nothing wrong; we had no reason to believe that an aircraft would be reckless enough to not communicate and taxi without concern for themselves or anyone else; we made proper radio calls and did everything we could.
Report_1_Synopsis: Pilot reported a near miss during takeoff roll with another aircraft that was possibly departing from the opposite end of the runway at MYEM.

Report_1_Narrative: During boarding there were 2 JS riders; plus nonrevs with seats; plus working crew in the aft galley which I attempted to work around to complete duties. There was some impediment. During MX (Maintenance) delay a NONREV from Cabin C came to aft galley and argued with me about why it was not OK for her to charge her cell phone with the vacuum outlet in the galley. I advised her of the safety policy regarding that. After demo I was in aft galley when I smelled strong oil and oil exhaust smell that extended a few rows into the cabin past Row 31; including lav. It seemed to dissipate after several minutes with forward movement of plane which is common so did not report then. During cruise a pax (passenger) from Row 33 came aft to complain of nausea and headache asking for water and pain med and denied having symptoms prior to flight and complained of fumes bothering him. I smelled oil in the aft galley area intermittently throughout flight; and was experiencing some mild symptoms myself but still did not write report on paper prior to calling CA (Captain) to keep him informed. All 3 MC crew were in galley when pax complained. FA (Flight Attendant) 4 provided water and med to pax. FA3 and FA4 both went forward for pilot breaks and cabin surveillance AFTER I called the FD about this issue so I assumed FA1 would be informed by someone else including the CA; but he was not. My mistake which I apologized to him for. During cruise we were experiencing turbulence in the aft so I waited several minutes before calling the FD to notify we were experiencing turbulence in the aft and to request SB (seat belt) sign on if they felt it was appropriate. During cruise I went forward to provide CDW about aft lav to FA1 but he was in the lav for an extended period of time and I had MC duties to attend to so I slipped the form under the FD door and called the FD to tell them same. At gate arrival a stronger smell of oil entered the aft galley area and cabin and lav so I called the FD; for a 4th time; with out calling FA1 first; to confirm AFT doors showed unarmed; asking to vent aft galley and report the very strong fumes of oil. He asked me to fill out the info on paper and to see him to debrief together and asked who all was involved. I tried to do an ALLCALL from the aft but was unsuccessful in reaching the entire crew with one call so tried to do individual calls. I was only able to reach FA3 and FA1 who began to yell at me about my poor CRM and said he only found out when the FD door opened and the CA said something about it. Both the CA and FA1 said I did not follow CRM procedures and said only the FA1 is to call the FD on cabin issues. I was unaware that was the case even for safety situations; including turbulence in the aft; that I was primarily aware of and apologized. FA1 accused me of intentionally creating conflict and of having a pattern of same. Each of the last 3 times I have flown with him he asks me what I want to be when I grow- up in front of passengers; another time we flew together he yelled at me for making a PA about the seatbelt sign prior to XA:00 as FA2 because he thought the IFM said XB:00 not XC:00 and people were sleeping; and only the FA1 makes announcements. I suppose this factored into why I was directly calling the FD and not using the loud interphone to call FA1 as well. And why I did not opt to make the turbulence without seat belt sign on announcement instead. I can't speak to why no one else told him about fumes and pax complaint. There was an opportunity during the crew briefing to establish cabin to FD flow that I think was missed. With multiple employee pre-boards and a full flight we were all highly tasked during the pre-boarding and boarding processes I have experienced both FD wanting only to speak with FA1 and stating such and also being invited to call with any safety concerns regardless of position in cabin. In my main concern and focus for safety of flight I unintentionally possibly violated CRM flowon this flight.

Report_1_Narrative: While executing a recovery from a power on stall during a training flight; I made visual contact with a high wing Cessna 172 or 182 approximately 100 feet to our left and at the same altitude. I immediately maneuvered to the right and initiated a climb in order to provide more spacing with the other aircraft. I do not believe the other aircraft ever had me in sight because it continued on the same heading and altitude after the event occurred.During the entire flight; I was communicating with ZZZ Approach Control with radar contact and a squawk code. Prior to initiating the power on stall maneuver; my student and I made 2 clearing turns to the right and left; with no traffic noted above; below; or at the same altitude. I believe the other aircraft involved was directly or nearly directly below us during the turns; which caused us not to see it. After the stall recovery; I noticed the aircraft climbing up to; and leveling off at our same altitude within approximately 100 feet traveling south to north.I attempted to make contact with the approach controller; but was only able to get a response after 3 attempts and approximately 5 minutes. I initially told the controller that it was within 300 feet; but after consideration; I believe that distance was significantly less. I was not given a traffic alert or altitude restriction during this particular phase of flight.

Report_1_Narrative: I was conducting a training flight and was headed to N40. Approximately 4 miles south of the airport; I made a radio call on UNICOM announcing I was 4 miles south at 2;000 feet descending to pattern with intentions to join the left downwind Runway 25 using a standard 45 degree entry. As I continued to approach the airport; I was scanning in front; to the left; and to the right of me while listening to the radio for relevant traffic. When I was about to make my entry to join a left downwind; I made a radio call announcing that I was joining the downwind leg of Runway 25. Prior to turning; I made a quick scan to the left; center; and right. I did not see any traffic. As I started my turn; I scanned left again and saw a Piper on downwind approximately 200 feet horizontally to the left of my aircraft and 60 feet vertically beneath me. Simultaneously; I heard the Piper make a radio call announcing they were breaking off the downwind and saw the Piper turn away from my aircraft. I judged that the situation was under control so I continued my turn to join downwind and made a radio call to the Piper stating that I had him in sight and apologized for cutting him off in the pattern. The rest of the flight was uneventful. Contributing factors include: 1; Either a lack of an initial radio call from the Piper; or myself missing the radio call from the Piper. 2; I had made a radio call that I was making a 45 degree entry to join the left downwind; but mispositioned my aircraft and made a turn closer to 90 degrees instead. This positioning error may have led the Piper to scan the wrong area. 3; Too fast a scan to detect an aircraft against the backdrop of the ground 4; Busy UNICOM frequency with a lot of radio calls from multiple airports. Regarding human performance considerations; I made a poor judgment to continue to approach the airport directly from the south rather than change course to put the aircraft into a better position for a 45 degree entry to downwind. Additionally; as I was not aware of any radio calls for an aircraft in the pattern at N40; I should have conducted a more thorough scan to look for unexpected aircraft. While I was scanning in all directions; I moved from one sector to another relatively quickly which likely caused me to miss the Piper and reinforce my perception that there were no other aircraft in the pattern. To prevent a recurrence of the situation; I will start thinking about my initial approach direction to an airport further out than I currently do. This should help ensure proper positioning for entry into the pattern and help other traffic locate me. I will also improve my scan and spend more time on each sector. This should greatly improve my ability to spot any unexpected aircraft.
Report_1_Synopsis: Pilot reported an NMAC event while entering traffic pattern.

Report_1_Narrative: I missed a small silver quad copter UAS by approximately 100 feet.  My altitude at this point was about 2;000 AGL. The area where this occurred is just outside the Leesburg Maneuvering Area of the DC SFRA and therefore is quite busy with traffic going to and from JYO. I strongly support any efforts to compel all UAS operators to equip with ADS-B Out so that other aircraft can have situational awareness.

Report_1_Narrative: After we pushed off gate XX; our pushback crew stopped the aircraft at a slight angle toward gate XY; while we were facing the service road between the ramp and the gate XX Safety Zone. The nose of the aircraft was approximately 30 feet from the service road.  I cleared my left side; my FO (First Officer) cleared the right side; and we began our right turn to taxi to Runway XXR. Since we were very close to the service road; our nose and left wing needed to cross the service road during the right turn.  As I was looking into my turn to the right; I noticed motion from the left side of the aircraft using my peripheral vision.  When I turned my head to the left; I saw a fast moving (Company) tug towing baggage carts approaching from my left traveling east to west on the service road. The vehicle did not stop and continued on the road traveling between my left wing and nose. As the driver was passing by; it appeared that he did not see us. I immediately applied the brakes to prevent the tug from colliding with our aircraft. We came to a stop just short of the road as the vehicle passed by. The driver swerved left off the service road and pulled alongside another (Company) vehicle and began talking to the driver of the other vehicle.  I set the parking brake; called (Company) Operations on the radio to report the near-miss incident with tug. The tug remained stopped momentarily while the two drivers spoke to each other.  The second driver seemed to be telling the offending driver that he was blocking our aircraft and needed to move away.  Tug did a looping turn and departed the area.  If we had not stopped; we would have had a collision with the fast moving tug and baggage carts.

Report_1_Narrative: Filed to climb via DOTSS except maintain 5;000 feet.  Tower cleared us for takeoff on a 210 heading up to 5;000 feet. I switched over to departure and checked on passing 1;500 feet with heading and assigned altitude of 5;000 feet. Departure cleared us direct PEVEE and climb 17;000 feet. I believed he just told me direct ENNEY and 17;000 feet; which I read back. We put it in the box and executed it. Then verified 17;000 feet in altitude window. The Captain said he was surprised we are heading back to ENNEY. I immediately called departure to clarify fix. They had a controller swap during that short time. The new controller advised us to fly 180 heading to PEVEE.Change the name of fix. Depending on how I read and pronounce and hear ENNEY and PEVEE sound the same if you don't hear the P with PEVEE. Which was the case with us. I also read back ENNEY; which the Controller didn't catch me saying incorrectly.
Report_2_Narrative: We were cleared on the DOTSS2.CNERY. We were cleared for takeoff on Runway 24L at LAX and assigned heading 210 after departure. We had VNAV selected and deselected LNAV once we received the revised clearance. After takeoff we contacted SoCal and were given a clearance to a fix on the departure. We believed the clearance was to ENNEY intersection. I began the turn to ENNEY and questioned the turn because it didn't make sense to turn that far right to join the departure. The F/O then asked for clarification on the clearance. There appeared to have been a Controller change while we were turning.  The new Controller then cleared us to turn to a 180 heading. The Controller clarified the clearance and cleared us direct PEVEE. The remainder of the flight was normal.  The SoCal frequency had some static on the frequency which made it a little hard to hear the clearance. There was also some confusion on which fix we were cleared to  due the the frequency static and due to misunderstanding of the annunciation of the ENNEY fix.In hind sight I don't think we clearly heard the fix we were cleared to. We started to ENNEY and the large turn is what made me question the clearance but I don't think we heard the clearance well enough and should have questioned the clearance earlier. The F/O read back ENNEY but I think it might have fell through the cracks due to the Controller change at the same time.

Report_1_Narrative: On pushback from gate.  After tow-bar removal and headset disconnect; we were starting engines.  I observed the marshaller standing in front of our aircraft giving the all clear signal with arms at 45 degrees; waiting for me to flash the taxi light.  However; the tug was still directly in front of our aircraft!  We could barely see the tug if we leaned forward in our seats; it was that close to our aircraft. I tried to point and gesture at the tug in my window; trying to let the ramper know that the tug was not clear of our aircraft.  The ramper did not figure it out; and gave me a salute; and walked to the tug.  I never flashed my taxi light at him.  If we had taxied forward with the position of the tug; our aircraft would have struck the tug for sure. Before we taxied; I called Ramp Control on the radio; and informed them of this unsafe practice by our push crew. Non-SOP procedures.  Unsafe practice.  Poor training.  Frequent occurrence.

Person_1_Function: Flight Attendant In Charge; Flight Attendant (On Duty)
Report_1_Narrative: During cruise; 3 hours in the flight; I heard a loud noise that sounded like a stall/chug. I was near L1 door. I asked the A FA (Flight Attendant); he heard it but he didn't. Later on; I went to the back of the plane. Aft galley & told the C FA what I felt and she told me she felt something 'unusual' on the floor of the aft galley; probably about the same time I was in the fwd galley. We decided to call the pilots (called them twice) but they didn't pick up. We would try again a few minutes later; figured they were busy with the sound but just then; they called for a lavatory break. We ended up forgetting to notify them. During decent; wheels down; the C FA & I felt the aft of the aircraft chug a few times and make the strange popping sounds. We both looked at each other and decided to talk about it upon landing. When we landed; we both agreed it was 'abnormal' so we called the pilots when we were disarmed and at the gate. After calling the pilots and explaining to them; the Captain told us to go to the flight deck and close the flight deck door. He ended up explaining to us that they did feel the abnormal chugs and thought it was a bird strike and didn't know until we were on the ground that the engine had failed (showed us on the monitor a red icon on the engine) but didn't really explain other wise. Myself and the rest of the crew didn't feel that great about the debrief. The A & C were able to go but the D and I had to continue on to ZZZ. That night; going to bed; I realized how serious the situation was and made me feel uneasy. On date; after landing in ZZZ1; a different Captain was talking about the incident because earlier in the day; there was an emergency landing by another airline and the [type aircraft]. Anyhow; when he realized I was on the ETOPS flight; he mentioned that we were lucky to be alive. He did an amazing job explaining that our situation was a 'compressor failure' and many things can cause that but the biggest concern was that after leaving ZZZ2 ; the engine was sending pings to maintenance notifying of the engine overheating...the pilots decided to continue on to ZZZ3. Knowing that bit of information; and then to experience the compressor failure and no good CRM; I am frustrated; annoyed and somewhat uneasy flying to ZZZ2 now after hearing unfamiliar sounds about three hours into flight (the C FA heard these sounds as well); I called the pilots at about 3 hours into flight but didn't get a hold of them. I then forgot until the next set of sounds were heard at gear down. Upon parking at the gate; I called the pilots and I was instructed to talk to them with the door shut when I go to the front. After all guests were off the plane; I explained to the pilots again what sounds we heard and the Captain told me (then the rest of the crew) that the sounds heard were those in line of what is heard of a 'bird strike'. He then mention something to the fact that the engine went off line (he said this because I pointed out that the engine symbol on the instrument panel had a red square on it) about two times and we all were then confused and he said we shouldn't worry about it.  Better CRM and think about the whole ready; safe; go action plan. There should have been a way better debrief by the pilots. After an event like this; I shouldn't be the one pushing for answers when I felt uneasy.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Attendant reported misgivings over Crew Coordination and Communication over compressor stalls during this and other flights; including ETOPS.

Report_2_Narrative: During boarding a passenger came on with a one wheel pint (similar to hoverboard). We were not sure if this was prohibited. The passenger said they had called ahead and was told since the non removable lithium battery was less than 160 [Wh] it was allowed as a carry on. They also had already flown from ZZZ1 to ZZZ with it. They also told me their brother had flown earlier this year with one; no problem. In our flight attendant manual section 6.500 page 7 it does seem to be allowable if stowed overhead; which we did. After take off and upon further review of the manual we discovered in section 6.500 page 4 self-balancing devices (e.g. hoverboards) are prohibited.  We continued on to ZZZ1 landing safely without incident. It would be nice to have this clarified. The customer suggested a certificate of approval.  Clarification and certificates of approval for questionable devices.

Report_1_Narrative: Aircraft X was ready to depart ZZZ. Mechanic called maintenance for a Class 2 Air Bleed message on ECAM; the CA (Captain) just wrote up. I issued MEL 36 XXX left wing loop B fault without checking history. I thought the aircraft was on a thru flight since it was way late in the afternoon. After the aircraft departed; a ZZZ Crew Chief called maintenance and informed maintenance that the aircraft was in ZZZ all night with a Drop Dead MEL 36XXX C/N XXXXXX L/PXXXXXXX. This aircraft did not make one flight without new fault. NO NEW MEL should have been issued.I did not look at history. I thought the aircraft was on a Thru FLT. Maintenance did not say anything about history; which is was just sign-off. I was in a hurry to dispatch the aircraft. I did not take a Class 2 maintenance message as a serious fault. Wing Loops do fault very often.Always review history and do not get in a hurry. Ask the Mechanic to also review the log book.
Report_1_Synopsis: A321 Mechanic reported overlooking requirements for a MEL and allowing the aircraft to fly in an unairworthy condition.

Report_1_Narrative: I departed ZZZ for ZZZ1. My flight plan showed that I should arrive at ZZZ1 with 1;453 pounds of fuel. From the start of my taxi to take off on [Runway] XR was twelve minutes. After a couple of vectors and a brief level off at 10;000 feet; we were cleared to climb to FL370 and given direct ZZZZZ intersection. However; the flight plan called for FL390 for our initial altitude. At ZZZZZ; I was three minutes behind the flight plan and 248 pounds behind on fuel. I was later cleared to climb to FL390 about 1:10 into the flight. I reached FL390. At this time my fuel was falling further behind. When I crossed ZZZZZ1; my fuel gauge showed that I was nearly 600 pounds behind the flight plan. Shortly after; I requested and received permission to climb to FL410. At my next waypoint; ZZZZZ2; the flight plan calculated 4;098 lbs. Thirty-six minutes from ZZZZZ2; the fuel gauge was showing 4;100 lbs. The Point of Safe Return was 2:12 into the flight. A little less than two hours into the flight my co-pilot and I decided to return to ZZZ. I requested a turn from HF Radio. I informed the radio operator that if I did not get an amended clearance as soon as possible that I would have to notify ATC. The operator was unable to receive the amended ATC clearance as quickly as I had hoped. Therefore; I notified ATC and instructed my co-pilot to make a left turn towards R464. Shortly after we completed the turn; we received a new clearance to proceed via to ZZZ2. I canceled the emergency once we were heading toward the ZZZZZ3 intersection. (We chose to return to ZZZ2 because it was nine minutes closer than ZZZ.) The accuracy of the fuel gauge came into question on our return leg to ZZZ2. The fuel numbers on the flight plan began to agree with the quantity on the gauge once we were below 4;000 lbs. The actual fuel flow numbers were close to flight plan fuel flow numbers. When we landed at ZZZ2; we indicated 1;500 lbs. Total flight time was 4:44.
Report_1_Synopsis: During a ferry flight; the Captain elected to divert due to unreliable fuel quantity indications.

Report_1_Narrative: I was taxiing from the parking area to the active runway via the Taxiway at 39N [Princeton Airport]. Active was Runway 28. I noticed a car parked on the grass along the runway behind the PAPI lights. As I taxied down I noticed a person runway along the runway with orange cones on the runway. As I taxied down I noticed a white sports like 'race car' approaching me on the taxiway. They veered into the grass as I taxied down and I have to veer steer my aircraft to the right of the taxiway to avoid them passing underneath my wing. As I approached the run up area I noticed two cars; various tripods with equipment and one of the cars was behind the threshold in grass of the active runway with two people outside the car. I stopped at the runway hold short lines; and had to shut down as they weren't moving. I got out of plane and had to explain to them that they have cars; equipment and cones on an active runway. The person said he worked there and had permission from his boss to be there. I had to state repeatedly that I cannot take the runway safely with people; cars; and equipment on the active runway; which they didn't seem to understand. I reviewed showed them the runway hold short lines and reviewed that anything on the runway side of these lines has to be moved. I asked what they would do about an approaching aircraft; he indicated he had a radio- but this airport doesn't technically require radio use to land there. I reviewed what they are doing is dangerous. After they cleared their cars; equipment; cones; and people I was able to start back up and obtain my departure clearance and depart uneventfully. The field was NOT NOTAM'ed closed for race car activity in my briefings. Monitoring CTAF during my previous landing; parking; then later restarting and taxiing did not indicate any of this activity.I should have notified NY Approach Controllers after establishing contact with them but I didn't. The Controller was very busy but it was my mistake not to notify them in hindsight.
Report_1_Synopsis: Pilot reported airport was being used for car racing without NOTAMs being posted.

Report_1_Narrative: I was descending to land in a targeted landing field east of high-value homes when a drone operator sent his equipment into my balloon. The drone tore through a low panel of fabric; fell into the pilot compartment; hit me on the head; and flopped around on the floor like a fish in a boat. It distracted me and so I overburned and aborted my approach to landing. I then landed at an alternate landing site; [Name] High School - where 2 other balloons had landed.
Report_1_Synopsis: Hot Air Balloon operator on approach had a mid air collision with a drone. The drone caused damage to the balloon and struck the pilot in the head. Balloon was landed shortly after.

Report_1_Narrative: I was seated on the jumpseat on flight deck and the First Officer demanded I wear a face mask after pushback per policy; while they both (Pilot Crew Members) did not; which is inconsistent with Safety and general communication requirements requested of a Jumpseat Crew Member. Here is why:To ride on the jumpseat we must be a current licensed pilot; with current medical license and fit to perform duties.1. We are consistently asked to be a second set of eyes. Because I wear glasses where I wear my face mask my glasses fog up. I'm unable to see instruments and other traffic.2.The face masks impedes verbal communication with the other Crew Members if needing to intervene because the Crew is wearing headsets; jet noise and unable to effectively hear or read lips. This is well documented in studies.3.  The time to useful consciousness is limited. Having glasses and face mask impedes putting on O2 mask on in the event of a Rapid Decompression. The flight deck door is locked; we have NO rubber jungle that falls and I'm solely responsible for my own Safety to get my mask on. This is an impediment to Safety as a Jumpseater. I am not treated the same as the operating Crew Members; even though I'm asked to be a Safety Observer.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier jumpseat pilot reported the First Officer on this flight insisted the jumpseater wear a face mask throughout the flight. Reporter described safety related concerns with having to wear the face mask including fogging of glasses; communication problems; and issues associated with putting on the O2 mask in case of a rapid decompression.

Report_1_Narrative: GPS and radio signals very intermittent when approaching and flying through this area.  We could hear ATC when we received ACARS requesting frequency 133.45 but obviously missed them handing us off to next sector.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported while flying through an area of poor GPS and radio signals they missed an ATC frequency change.

Report_1_Narrative: We were conducting a visual approach on Runway 16L which it was backed up with RNAV X RWY 16L. We were on MYBAD RNAV approach and we decided to call the field in sight in VMC conditions and we were cleared for the visual approach. We sequence the flight plan and verified runway; once we intercepted NAV we disconnected the autopilot and started our descent to cross SEKAW at 7;800 ft. During final configuration we descended below the profile momentarily and we got the EGPWS [Enhanced Ground Proximity Warning Systems] 'Caution terrain' and immediately we corrected the profile and continue with the approach.
Report_1_Synopsis: Pilot reports EGPWS [Enhanced Ground Proximity Warning Systems] alert on approach.

Person_2_Human_Factors: Situational Awareness; Time Pressure; Workload; Distraction
Report_1_Narrative: Out of an abundance of caution and to the best of my memory I can recall that shortly after the initial climb and in a clean configuration the Captain alerted me that he had some difficulty with the electric trim on his control yoke. I observed that it was indeed intermittent. After I completed the Climb Checklist we tried some trouble-shooting with both autopilots and my trim switch. With no caution lights; I referred to the QRH to help diagnose the issue with the proper checklist. During this time the Captain was contacting Dispatch and Maintenance for assistance while I talked to ATC. At some point in this process we were able to notice that my autopilot would engage and I became the Pilot Flying. We stopped the climb and slowed the aircraft. The Captain proceeded with the Stabilizer Trim Inoperative Checklist which calls to cutout both stab trim cutout switches and manually trim the aircraft. As I flew manually we elected to advise ATC and return to ZZZ. The Captain informed the Company; ATC; flight attendants and passengers and offered his assistance to me. I vaguely recall that during the descent a Speed Trim Fail light illuminated as a result from the cutout switches being selected to cutout. There was some discussion that we may or may not be over the max landing weight upon arrival and therefore an AML entry was entered after landing along with a Speed Trim Fail; Stabilizer Trim Failure; and inoperative autopilots entries. I performed a safe Flaps 15 landing [and] all passengers and crew deplaned safely with no injuries. I can attest that the training I have received was very beneficial to the successful outcome from this event. I believe as a crew we worked the problem out very well with the strategy and am thankful for the Captain's knowledge; professional conduct; and reassurance to everyone for a safe outcome. The mechanic did state that perhaps the event may have been caused by a software issue.
Report_2_Narrative: During climbout and after cleanup; I noticed that the electric stabilizer trim was intermittent. Then it became unresponsive. At this point the Speed Trim system appeared to actuate for about half a second and never actuated again. We attempted to engage the A autopilot. It wouldn't engage. The B autopilot did engage and I passed control of the aircraft to the FO (First Officer). We conducted the 'Stabilizer Trim Inoperative' checklist. Within about 5 minutes of engaging the B; it disengaged itself and the FO hand flew the aircraft for the remainder of the flight. We advised ATC and returned to ZZZ. We selected Runway XX and requested a 15 mile final to get fully configured and trimmed as well as possible. The FO was able to manually trim the aircraft without difficulty. During the descent; at about 12;000-15;000 feet; the 'Speed Trim Fail' light illuminated. We conducted a Flaps 15 landing and taxied back to the gate. I made an AML entry for the Stab Trim; Speed Trim Fail light and for possible overweight landing.I think the focus of the MAX simulator session was helpful in dealing with this situation.
Report_1_Synopsis: B737 MAX 8 flight crew reported a stabilizer trim issue that resulted in the autopilot disengaging during climbout. The flight crew elected to return to the departure airport.

Report_1_Narrative: VNAV (vertical navigation) would not arm before takeoff. Because I was flying the Max for the first time I considered this may be something different or weird about the new airplane. After writing this up on the ground the mechanics did a reboot of the airplane and these problems seemed to go away but now we experienced the failure of the Captain's FMC multiple times.  Upon arrival at the airplane that morning I found the FMC switch in the 'R' position instead of the normal 'BOTH.' During preflight; with the FMC programmed; I engaged LNAV (lateral navigation) and VNAV with the Master on my (First Officer) side. A few minutes later I noticed VNAV disengaged. I reengaged it. A few minutes later I noticed it disengaged again. This time I told the Captain and he said he noticed it as well. This was my first flight in the Max so I chalked it up as a Max-ism. I thought it would 'fix itself' airborne. The Captain and I discussed it and decided to just proceed and attempt to engage it airborne after multiple attempts on the ground to keep it engaged. This was the only discrepancy I noticed on the ground. Once airborne we did attempt to engage VNAV but it would disengage within a couple seconds. I climbed out in LVL CHG (level change mode) all the way to FLXXX when ALT HLD (altitude hold) engaged. After a few minutes at cruise the Captain decided we should try switching everything to his side so we switched to CMD A and engaged VNAV. After this we had no further issues with VNAV. We agreed I would continue to be pilot flying utilizing the A autopilot and the master on his side.  During cruise shortly after engaging VNAV as previously discussed I began noticing weird things on my ND (navigation display) and PFD. On the PFD on my speed tape the minimum and maximum maneuvering amber bars would simultaneously shoot out.  The minimum would jump up about 8 knots while the maximum would simultaneously shoot down about 2 knots and then immediately retract. Also the ND would ratchet instead of making smooth movements. This was especially noticeable in turns. Lastly we noticed ANP (actual navigation performance) going as high as 1.3. By the end of the flight I would say it was back in the normal range; less than 0.1. I flew the STAR in LNAV/VNAV to the bottom and performed a visual [approach] with no other issues. We wrote this up on the ground doing our best to explain this to Maintenance. The Captain and I decided if we set up the box and selected the master on my side and engaged VNAV and it stayed engaged we would be satisfied and then switch everything to his side. After boarding was complete and we were just about to shut the door both FMC's blanked with a MAP and VTK (vertical track) on Captain's PFD. We called Maintenance back out for another 'reset'. We then closed the door and pushed back. As I began to start the engine we had the same failure again on the FMC. Captain called Maintenance and they told us to return to gate.  By this point the Captain and I agreed we would not be taking this airplane. With its previous history that we learned about in previous log pages; along with the multiple issues we experienced; combined with the complicated process involving an MEL for both FMCs and an early wake up we agreed it would not be the safest course of action. Hindsight is 20/20 and looking back armed with the information I have now I would have never left the gate in ZZZ.
Report_2_Narrative: During my preflight I noticed the FO (First Officer) engaging VNAV and it disengaging a few minutes later. He tried a couple of times and it would not stay engaged.  He told me he found the FMC switch in the Both on R and switched it back to normal. We discussed waiting for final numbers and trying again.  It continued not to engage after final numbers and I decided to push back and start and try again on taxi.  A couple times during taxi we tried to engage it and would only last seconds. We discussed departing old school bug up N1 flaps 1 and try again airborne knowing the jet can fly without VNAV.  We both were comfortable with that decision. It was his leg and the F/D (flight director) was on his side.  There were no other discrepancies. As we rolled out on the runway and were cleared for take off I engage VNAV and it stayed on until 500 feet and disconnected. I am guessing it held on with TOGA (takeoff/go-around). We tried engaging VNAV a couple times in climb and after level off at FLXXX with no success.  We were on autopilot CMD B (command B). At that point I selected CMD A and then engaged VNAV and it stayed on. We decided to leave it on CMD A.  The remainder of the flight VNAV remained engaged. It was the FO's first time in the Max and my second leg so he remained the pilot flying using CMD A. About the same time we were switching sides we noticed on his speed tape the minimum and maximum amber bars would jump up from the bottom about 5 knots and down from the top about 2-3 knots. Also the ND (navigation display) would glitch from left to right 5-7 degrees. Both of those continued the entire flight; the ND would glitch more in a turn. All 3 airspeeds were matched the entire flight and Captain's side had no issues of glitching and we received no cautions about airspeed.  A little while later we received a scratch pad message that I don't remember exact wording but was about FMC position when I looked at all latitude and longitudes FMC; IRSL (left inertial reference system); IRSR; GPSL (GPS left); GPSR were normal within a couple of decimal points looking normal to me. I then noticed the ANP was 1.3 and bouncing between 1.2 and 1.3.  I monitored that and it started to decrease back to normal around .03; .02 but it took 20 to 30 minutes and would move between .02 and .11.  Towards the end of the flight it seemed to be more steady around .03; .02. No other scratch pad messages and the flight had no other issues. We landed [and] I wrote up the problems and we both talked to the 3 maintenance technicians to relay as much info as we could. I know that they powered down the aircraft and did operation tests that all passed and signed off the aircraft. We boarded the passengers for [our next] flight.  We discussed that we would check both sides for VNAV engagement; also monitor all speed tapes and ND's for any glitching before takeoff.  As we were about to close the door both FMC's blanked out and Map flag; VTK flag; and no runway flag on my side only appeared. No FMC prompt on either FMC screens only ACARS; ACMS (aircraft condition monitoring system); SAT (satellite).  I called Maintenance and they came out and talked about that they had Captain's FMC history. I asked about it and we looked it up in the previous logbook; first I had heard about that. I was thinking new airplane I did not realize that there was an entire logbook already used below the current logbook.  They then switched the FMC switch to both on R and the flags on my side went away and FMC prompts returned. I told them I cannot takeoff like that.  They called Maintenance Control I believe and they did a circuit breaker reset which fixed the flags and returned the FMC prompts and the FMC switch back to normal. We closed the door and started the pushback. As the FO was about to start engine 2 the same flags returned on my side and no FMC prompts on both sides. Maintenance Control told us to return to the gate because he could not MEL it. We returned to the gate and Maintenance again did the circuit breaker reset that only lasted a few minutes before the flags returned. They decided to MEL the FMC with my approval. The FO and I did not want to continue with this aircraft because of our history with it and that it had only been powered down and 2 circuit breaker resets.  We now would be manually setting bugs and thrust for the entire flight in an aircraft we both had very little time in and had an early morning show to start the day and it was now late afternoon.
Report_1_Synopsis: B737 MAX 9 flight crew reported multiple autoflight anomalies that ultimately resulted in their refusal to accept the aircraft.

Report_1_Narrative: As we arrived in ZZZ; the First Officer and myself had planned on the ILS to RWY (Runway) XX as the winds had favored that runway. The winds had shifted and favored RWY XY as we were handed off to approach control. As I was the flying pilot; the FO (First Officer) hastily entered the RNP to Runway XY. This was also our first time into ZZZ. As the aircraft captured Final App... it looked as if we were on profile... and we were also visual. I soon realized that the altitude constraints had not been loaded due to the fact that the approach via had not been entered. I arrested the descent; however; we did get the 'pull up warning ....a go around was performed followed by the published hold. We then performed the ILS to RWY XX; circle to [Runway] XY to a normal landing."
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Flight Crew reported GPWS Alert on approach.

Person_1_Human_Factors: Time Pressure; Situational Awareness; Confusion; Communication Breakdown; Other / Unknown
Report_1_Narrative: I was thanking passengers as they disembarked onto the jet-bridge in ZZZ; and I was trying to call rows to deplane on the PA. The cleaning crew were at the front door (1Left) trying to get on the plane while the passengers were leaving; and the pilots were also trying to gather their bags and leave. This made the situation very chaotic. I was not aware of it being a 'quick-turn'; as I am always happy to try and help out with the quick-turn cleaning.The cleaners slipped on a few at a time; in between passengers leaving. I saw the two aft crewmembers with their luggage; and moving forward through the cabin; towards me. The cleaners were already onboard; cleaning throughout the plane. I said; 'last but not least!' to the final passenger; thanked her and gathered my belongings. I looked back and only saw the cleaners; and my crew who were almost to me. I didn't see any more passengers and thought we were done. I double-checked my doors and the forward lavatory and stepped off the plane. When the aft crew stepped off; there was a male passenger with them who had been mixed in with the cleaners. He did not have his boarding pass with him. He said he wouldn't leave without it; and that his seat was XX6. He wanted to go look for it himself; but crew went to look. His boarding card was found under his seat.A contributing factor is having so many people onboard/in jetbridge and the cleaning crew coming onboard (sometimes in just sweatshirts; hoodies; jackets; hats; masks; etc.) and mixing in with disembarking passengers; and vice versa.  Flights are more full now; and anyone can be mistaken for a cleaner.Other factors: double-checking the passengers haven't lowered or removed their masks; as they often do now; as they are coming down the aisle towards me and the boarding door. The passengers are trying to look down the aisle and gauge how far we've gotten with the row announcements to deplane. Also; 2-3 pilots using the lavatory; gathering bags and leaving; while passengers are disembarking causes more confusion. All of this; and the extra amount of ground-staff/cleaners onboard and in the jet-bridge in civilian clothing; causes more confusion; multitasking/load at the boarding/deplaning door.I assumed the last passenger I saw; and said goodbye to; was our final passenger onboard.I would not have stepped off the plane had I known there was still one passenger onboard.I will also alert corporate security to this incident; and the added potential for this confusion during disembarkation.
Report_1_Synopsis: Flight Attendant reported the aircraft cleaners were slipping onboard to clean the aircraft before the passengers were completely off. One last passenger; resembling a cleaner; remained intermixed with crew and cleaners during the crew's exit.

Report_1_Narrative: Was flying to ZZZ from ZZZ1 for aerial sightseeing trip in newly built (72 hrs) RV-10. Have always wanted to fly over the Canyon. Approximately 75% of the way there; conditions began to slowly deteriorate. Reported ceilings at destination were fine; and from nearest weather reporting airport (ZZZ2). But no weather reported in between on my route. Clouds kept getting lower and terrain kept rising. About 40 miles from ZZZ; I should have turned back to ZZZ2 and landed. But; I was under the clouds and could see the ground just fine. Conditions kept getting worse; then better; then worse then better. I pressed on. At one point; I found myself getting too close to ground (about 1;000 ft AGL) when the clouds 'engulfed me'. I was now in IMC. I should have turned around; but decided that I could see some sunlight peeking through and decided to climb up to get on top of clouds and out of possible rising terrain. At 10;300 [ft.] I still was in IMC conditions. Decided then to get an air-born clearance for IFR into ZZZ. I contacted ZZZ3 Center; and proceeded to get clearance for RNAV [Runway] XX into ZZZ. I was being vectored for entry into approach when auto pilot suddenly disengaged; I lost airspeed indication and my AOA stall warning buzzer was going off! When I informed controller of the situation that just erupted; he [provided assistance] to help get me down. It was VERY unsettling! It took a good 4 minutes to realize that these things were happening due to a frozen pitot tube! I live in [the] south and NEVER have to worry about freezing temps. In the current situation; I didn't' realize outside temps had fallen to 27 degrees. When I finally realized what happened; I turned on pitot heat; and airspeed indication was restored within 10 seconds. I was then vectored for a visual approach and landed safely at ZZZ.What led to situation? Bad decision making. I should have turned around before getting into full bore IMC. I think my instrument rating gave me TOO MUCH confidence. Entering IMC unexpectedly; put me behind the airplane and my situational awareness deteriorated to near zero! I also found myself overwhelmed when alarms went off and auto pilot kicked off and in trying to figure out why; I failed to 'aviate' the airplane. At one point I realized I was in a steep left turn (about 45 degrees) which could have led to more problems. Once I saw this; I did correct; but it could have ended in a loss of control quickly!Another lesson is to WATCH the temps! A frozen pitot might not have become my only problem. I realize now I was also at risk for ice on wings. Another dangerous situation. Many lessons learned; but main one is to not push limits in unfamiliar terrain. I should have turned around and avoided the layering of consequences that followed from that one bad decision.
Report_1_Synopsis: Pilot reported loss of situational awareness and entering an unusual attitude after inadvertently entering unforecast IMC conditions and icing.

Report_1_Narrative: While training on final radar Aircraft X was being vectored for sequence to the runway.  The aircraft was descended below the normal downwind altitude to avoid traffic in an adjacent sector airspace.  Due to traffic volume and complexity; the aircraft was vectored into a 6;000 foot Minimum Vectoring Altitude (MVA).  Upon realization of the error; he was immediately climbed and turned away from the higher MVA area.
Report_1_Synopsis: A11 TRACON Controller conducting on the job training reported the trainee vectored an aircraft for sequencing below the Minimum Vectoring Altitude.

Report_1_Narrative: I wanted to share an experience on the new RNAV Visual Approach Runway 17L in MCO. There are two fixes that initiate this approach; CELOT and FELUK. On paper they look different; but in the heat of the moment over the radio they sound similar. During a recent approach we requested this procedure. Approaching from the northwest we were given direct FELUK; cross it at or above 3;000 ft. and cleared for the RNAV visual. Expectation bias led me to hear CELOT (the closer of the two fixes and the logical transition from our position) and I initially loaded that into the FMC; but fortunately the First Officer had heard FELUK and after a quick clarification with ATC we loaded and flew that transition. Definitely weird since we passed CELOT to fly to FELUK; which also required what I would call an inefficient turn to final. Not sure why the Controller did this. Perhaps for separation; or perhaps in the heat of the moment he thought that was the closest and most logical fix for us. I'd like to see one of the fixes renamed so they sound distinctly different; perhaps change one of the names such that both are not two syllables in length. Perhaps also add an alert that vectoring to the opposite side (further away) fix is possible.
Report_1_Synopsis: Pilot reports similar sounding names of two fixes.

Report_1_Narrative: We were flying the VALLY2 SID out of MIA.  The SID note states; 'SPEED RESTRICTION...Turbojet aircraft accelerate to 250 knots; if unable; advise ATC.' I was the PF (Pilot Flying) and at 10;000 feet; I asked the Captain for Economy Climb.  We accelerated to ECON CLB.  Shortly after reaching this speed; ATC instructed us to fly 250 knots and stated something like...Aircraft X; maintain 250 knots; Center will give you a higher speed; you've already accelerated.  (Not verbatim; I cannot remember the exact phraseology). It gave us the impression that we missed a published speed restriction.  After rereading the SID note; we are both confident that this is not a speed restriction.  We are also confident that we did not miss an ATC assigned speed restriction. If however our interpretation of this SID note is incorrect; it is not written as it should be. The Jeppesen Chart Legends publication has a section written about speed restrictions.  It clearly states that 'speed restrictions vary widely within individual procedures.' If we unintentionally violated a speed restriction in this case; perhaps this 'wide variation' in depicted speed restrictions needs to be better address from a human factors perspective; since the VALLY2 SID does not clearly depict a 250 knot speed restriction with terminology such as 'maintain 250 until advised by ATC' or 'do not exceed 250 knots etc.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported confusion with the '250 Knot' wording on the SID.

Report_1_Narrative: When checking in with MCO final Approach Control we were given speed reduction 190 to mkr (Marker Radio Beacon); Drones reported near ORL Executive; all traffic now arriving Runway 17L and R. Cleared visual Runway 17L maintain GS on approach slow to 170. Caution traffic on right to Runway 17R; contact Tower on freq. We received our landing clearance for Runway 17L. Second birds on path siting. We were on ref and GS. About 1;100 ft. I realized we weren't fully configured. Called for gear/F3 then F Full/Landing checklist. Landing checklist completed by 800 ft. We were still at ref and on GS fully stable; we landed normally and taxied off at Taxiway F. We received no alerts during approach.I believe we were distracted more than usual as well as feeling a little tired that afternoon. I will most assuredly use this experience as a learning example of avoiding potential complacency by carefully applying our procedures to prevent any re occurrence going forward.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported failing to properly configure for the approach due to distraction and fatigue.

Report_1_Narrative: Student Pilot flying. On the 45 to enter downwind on [Runway] 16; at approximately 1;100 ft. MSL (TPA 1;000 ft.); a turn in the opposite direction caused potential collision with traffic on crosswind turning to downwind.  Situation was realized simultaneously by Tower and myself (CFI) at which point I took [control of] the airplane; as I saw other planes in the base for [Runway] 16. 'Traffic to follow' was mis-identified. To avoid collision the turn was continued to the left; away from downwind; at which point Tower instructions to climb to 1;500 ft. MSL and proceed east to a known reporting point were followed.  Situation was stabilized; instructions from the Tower to re-enter the pattern for 16 were followed and successfully completed.What contributed to this situation:1) Student and CFI not adequately briefing the approach based on ATIS.  2) Not correctly identifying 'traffic to follow'.    3) Student Pilot did not realize she could ask for clarification or question my thinking.  4) I did not have the correct runway (16) approach visualized; I was distracted with coaching the Student Pilot.How to avoid in the future: Slow down the process to adequately brief the approach and ask for questions to understand that my student and I are thinking the same procedure with the given information.  Properly identifying the 'traffic to follow' and verifying with Tower.
Report_1_Synopsis: C172 Instructor Pilot reported an airborne conflict occurred in the traffic pattern when a 'follow traffic' clearance resulted in mis-identifying the aircraft to follow.

Report_1_Narrative: I was holding short of [the] runway. I thought that the Tower had instructed me to taxi to [the parallel runway] for take off. I began to move the aircraft. At the same time I looked to the left and observed another aircraft on a half mile final. I applied brakes and at the same time the Tower radioed 'stop; stop'. By that time the nose of the aircraft had passed the limit line and I had committed a runway incursion. Since I was in a tail dragger I was able to lock my right wheel; spin around; and return to the correct side of the limit line. The landing aircraft did a go-around.There were two primary factors that caused the runway incursion. First; I should have waited for a response from the Tower before moving the aircraft. That would have given the Tower time to tell me to remain where I was. Secondly; I should have visually cleared the final approach area before movement. I would have seen the aircraft and not gone past the limit line. Another factor was that; since I was in an open cockpit aircraft there was wind noise from the prop wash as well as engine noise that resulted in me mishearing the instructions from the Tower.In the future I plan to 1. before moving the aircraft; give the Tower time to correct any misinterpretation of instructions; 2. check for traffic before moving the aircraft; and 3. allowing a few more feet distance from the limit line as an added safety margin to prevent movement past the limit line.
Report_1_Synopsis: Pilot of an open cockpit biplane reported a misunderstood communication from the Tower resulted in a runway incursion and a go-around from the aircraft on approach.

Report_1_Narrative: The HOU ATIS states Runway 17/35 is closed; along with Taxiway G2 and G3.  The Jepp 10-9 Page does not identify any of these surfaces. Ground Control gave us a clearance to taxi on H and hold short of Runway 35.  So; does the runway exist or not?  The Jepp 10-9 should reflect the proper surfaces that ATC is using in their communications. I think this can create confusion.  Fix the Jepp or have ATC stop issuing instructions including surfaces that no longer exist.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Captain reported confusion regarding information on the Jeppesen 10-9 vs. instructions given by ATIS and Ground Control.

Report_1_Narrative: On a visual approach to Runway 16L to the RNO airport we received a EGPWS Pull Up Warning. The warning came as I was telling the First Officer who was the Pilot Flying that he looked low. The First Officer disengaged the autopilot and began an aggressive climb.  We rejoined the glidepath and landed. I believe I had expectation bias that he would recognize that we were getting low. The truth is we were momentarily in the red and thanks to the aircraft warning we made a recovery.
Report_2_Narrative: During descent into RNO landing [Runway] 16L on downwind; the Controller cleared us for the visual to after another aircraft that was on final.  Slightly past abeam that aircraft and at 9;000 ft. MSL; I squared the turn to base and began a descent and then angled the turn to final and select LNAV.  We intercepted final and as we rolled out still descending and I noticed; as did the PM; that we were low.  As I was arresting the descent and rolling out; an EGPWS took place. We initiated an escape maneuver with an aggressive climb and corrected and climbed up onto the approach path.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported receiving an EGPWS terrain warning on a visual approach to RNO.

Report_1_Narrative: The information for GRR discusses the clearance from light poles east of Gates B7 and B8; as well as north of the B Concourse.  To have the stated clearance from the light poles; you need to be on the yellow taxi line.  The problem is that the yellow taxi line has been removed from the ramp.  The line needs to be repainted so we can navigate to Gate 2; in all lighting/weather conditions; without the threat of hitting light poles. Repaint the taxi line to ensure taxi safety around the B Concourse. No taxi lines on ramp.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Captain reported taxi lines need repainting on this ramp for safe operation during all lighting conditions.

Report_1_Narrative: We were going to load Aircraft X to ZZZ while loading the mail there was a box that had a Dangerous Goods (DG) sticker on it but there was no paperwork for it. At this time it was decided to be held off and sent back to air freight. The [package] was then rebooked for Aircraft Y to ZZZ and we were told it was ok to load cause we have an agreement with the [US] Post Office. We then notified the Supervisor on Duty in which notified the Manger about the concern they made a phone call and emailed the Regional Freight Manger and was told it was ok to board. We had then notified the pilot which the contacted the DG hotline and was told to hold off aircraft because without paperwork he would not have any ability to react in case of an incident so refused boarding of mail [package]. Also we are unaware of any other DG's being shipped cause of mail items being shipped in sacks.
Report_1_Synopsis: Air Carrier Ground Personnel reported Dangerous Goods package scheduled to be shipped was refused due to no required Hazmat documents provided.

Report_1_Narrative: During the descent at approx 12;000 feet our ACM (additional crew member/jump seater) noticed 2 bright white sparks which came from over the galley area; quickly followed by acrid smell and smoke in the courier area ceiling area.  He came up to the flight deck to report this about the same time the smell and smoke were noticed in the flight deck.  The CA (Captain) left his seat briefly and upon seeing the smoke in the ceiling area; came back up and notified ATC.  I noted to the CA and ACM that they should immediately pull all the galley circuit breakers; that we didn't need that equipment and likely the cause of the problem.  The ACM did this immediately.  As the PF (pilot flying); I continued to fly expeditiously to the airport while the CA (Pilot Monitoring) accomplished the smoke/fire/fumes checklist.  My O2 mask was pulled but not donned.  Shortly after the galley CB's were pulled the smoke and fumes began to dissipate.  The CA notified ATC that the situation was improving but we still requested priority handling.  We were already on final and visual with [runway] XXR and cleared to land.  Landing was uneventful and we exited the runway; taxiing to our ramp followed by fire and rescue equipment.  After shutdown; the CA went to disarm and open doors for personnel with he found that the cabin doors would not open electrically.  That was when he noticed the ground service bus CB was popped.  Maintenance was contacted via interphone and notified that we could not open doors electrically.  Rather than blow the door open pneumatically we chose to wait for Maintenance to get the door open.  (There was no evidence at this point that smoke/fire was a threat).  Maintenance personnel were able to mechanically open the door.  Fire personnel came up and we described the above situation.    Quick action by our ACM and expeditious handling by ATC and all crew members brought this to a successful conclusion.
Report_2_Narrative: During descend into ZZZ1 ACM [Additional Crew Member] onboard brought to our attention that sparks and smoke was coming from behind galley area. Smoke and fumes were confirmed and ATC was notified. We requested priority handling to airport. CB's to galley were pulled. Smoke and fumes subsided. No delay occurred in our handling from ATC.  After block in the ground service CB was noted popped. Communication was established with MX and Manuel operation of entry door utilized due to door on that buss.
Report_1_Synopsis: MD-11 flight crew reported 'sparks and smoke' behind the galley area during descent. The smoke and fumes dissipated after the appropriate CB's were pulled.

Report_1_Narrative: During cruise one of the flights attendants called me up and said they could smell something like burning paper around Row 33. No smoke was observed. As the flight attendants searched for the source of the smell; we started the smoke; fumes checklist in the QRH. The smell dissipated after 5 minutes and before any configuration changes were made in the flight deck. I decided to continue on since there were [no] indications of smoke anymore. There were no complaints or reports of any injuries to passengers or crew members. A smoke fumes report was filled and an AML entry of the event followed by a company report.No smoke was seen; only the odor of smoke smelt. The FA (Flight Attendant) said it was like burning paper. Before I completed our smoke checklist; the smell had completely dissipated.
Report_1_Synopsis: A321 Captain reported a Flight Attendant notified them of burning fumes in the cabin which dissipated within five minutes. Flight continued to destination for an uneventful landing. Maintenance action was requested.
